## Volume front matter

### Series title page

**Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal Library**, complete, uniform, convenient, economical, of all the holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reissue of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have survived from the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, carefully collated with one another and with several manuscript codices, and corrected with the greatest diligence; continually illustrated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by the discovery of all works completed after the extensive editions owed to the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume and each author of any importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with headings distinguishing the upper margin of every page and indicating the subject treated below; expanded by works both doubtful and apocryphal, and also by works possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any topic may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which the reader may readily discover which Fathers have commented on the individual textual passages of each book of Scripture and in what places in their works.

A most accurate edition, and one easily preferable to all others when the following are taken into account: the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the reprinted works, the highly convenient format of the volumes and its consistent similarity throughout the entire work, the low price, and especially the fact that this collection—single, methodical, and chronological—brings together, for the first time in our library, six hundred fragments and minor works previously scattered here and there, collected from works relating to every age, place, language, and form.

**First series**, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and writers of the Latin Church from Tertullian to Gregory the Great. Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of complete series in the several branches of ecclesiastical scholarship.

# In the year of the Lord 492. Pope Gelasius I

*(From the collection of the Councils of Mansi.)*

## [Col. 0009] Prologue

*(From the *Book of the Pontiffs*.)*

[Col. 0009A] **[Note:]** On the second day of March, in the year 492 of our Redeemer, after an interregnum of five days, Gelasius, an African by nationality, was substituted for Felix III. Several letters issued by him are found below under the consuls of this same year. Accordingly, Marcellinus should be corrected, since he places Gelasius’s accession after the year 493.

At the beginning of his pontificate, Gelasius communicated with the emperor Anastasius, who professed the orthodox faith, by means of peaceful letters, which he had previously refused to Euphemius of Constantinople until Euphemius had erased the name of Acacius from the diptychs.

In Gelasius’s time that great patriarch among monks, the glory of the Western Church, Benedict, a native of Nursia, withdrew from Rome—where he had devoted himself to letters—into solitude and laid the first foundations of the higher monastic life.

**Severus Binius.**

Gelasius, an African by nationality, the son of Valerius, [Col. 0009B] **[Note:]** The Vatican indexes attest the same thing. **Severus Binius.** held the see for four years, eight months, and eighteen days. He lived during the reign of [Col. 0009B]

**[Note:]** Theodoric, king of the Goths, after defeating Odoacer, king of the Heruli, three or four times and finally killing him in violation of the pledged faith in the year 493, ruled for thirty-three years over the Ostrogoths and Italians, who were maintained with royal title and insignia. He then sent an embassy and sought and obtained peace from Anastasius and all the kings. He married the daughter of Clovis and gave one of his daughters by a concubine in marriage to Alaric, king of the Visigoths, and the other to the king of the Burgundians.

Cassiodorus in his *Chronicle*, as well as in the first letter, relates these matters. Although Theodoric was an Arian, he nevertheless held the Catholics in esteem and rendered good service not only to Catholic bishops but also to the apostolic see itself. Theodoret, Nicephorus, Zonaras, Cedrenus, and others write that he beheaded a certain Catholic who, out of regard for him, was passing over to the Arians, saying: “If you have not kept sincere faith with God, how will you provide a sound conscience for me, who am a human being?”

He honored Epiphanius of Pavia and Caesarius of Arles and presented them with the most generous gifts. What his attitude was toward Symmachus and the apostolic see will become clear below in the notes on the fourth Roman council under Symmachus.

**Severus Binius.**

[Col. 0009C] **[Note:]** Anastasius, the author of the *Book of the Pontiffs*, is mistaken. For it is established on the authority of Marcellinus, Cassiodorus in his *Chronicle*, Evagrius, Cedrenus, and other writers that the emperor Zeno, during the consulship of Olybrius, in the year of the Lord 491—which was the ninth year of Pope Felix—was seized by epilepsy, so that he appeared to be dead and was buried alive. Thus he received, deservedly and by God’s just vengeance, the reward of his simulated piety and religion.

Pope Hormisdas arranged and ordered that Zeno’s name, although he had already been dead for many years, be erased from the list of Catholic emperors by the emperor Justin. This was not done to condemn a dead man, but to declare that a heretic who had died without repentance was alien and unworthy of that communion with the Catholics by which the Catholic Church, according to certain prescribed rites, customarily communes with the dead.

Baronius, under the year of the Lord 491, no. 2 and following.

**Severus Binius.**

Zeno Augustus.

[Col. 0010A] **[Note:]** Just as in Leo’s time, so also then, Manichaeans were hiding in the City. To avoid discovery, they pretended to hold the orthodox faith and communicated together with the Catholics, but superstitiously abstained from receiving the chalice, because, following Cerinthus and other heresiarchs, they held wine to be a creature of the devil.

Leo’s words in Sermon Four *On the Time of Lent* are these: “Although, to conceal their unbelief, they dare to attend our mysteries, they so restrain themselves in the communion of the sacraments that they sometimes hide more safely: with unworthy mouths they receive Christ’s body, but they avoid drinking the blood of our redemption. We wish your holiness to know this so that such persons may be exposed to you by these signs, and those whose sacrilegious simulation has been detected, marked, and denounced may by priestly authority be expelled from the fellowship of the saints.”

Therefore, so that the Manichaeans secretly hiding in the City and pretending to profess the orthodox faith might be distinguished from the Catholics by some certain and most manifest sign and evident mark, the pontiff, as the needs of time and place required, issued a decree establishing that the sacred Eucharist should for the time being be distributed only under both kinds, of bread and wine.

The words of the canon found in distinction 2, *On Consecration*, are these: “We have learned, however, that certain people, after receiving only a portion of the holy body, abstain from the chalice of the sacred blood. Since they are evidently constrained by some superstition of which I know not what kind, let them either receive the complete sacraments or be kept away from the complete sacraments; for the division of one and the same mystery cannot occur without grave sacrilege.”

From this it is clear how ineptly the heretical innovators of our own time infer that communion must necessarily be received under both kinds, since from this passage rather the opposite is gathered: namely, that at this time it was permitted for the faithful to receive Eucharistic communion under one kind only, while the practice was prohibited for a limited period in order to distinguish and expel the Manichaeans from the City.

See Baronius under the year 496, no. 19 and following; also what we said above in the notes on the Roman council under Leo, and what we shall say below in the notes on the Council of Constantinople.

**Severus Binius.**

[Col. 0010A] During his pontificate, Manichaeans were discovered in the city of Rome. He ordered them to be deported into exile, and he also burned their books before the doors of the Basilica of Saint Mary.

[Col. 0010C] **[Note:]** More extensively concerning these matters below, in the notes on the second Roman council under Gelasius.

Under the proceedings of a synod, with tears and after a written petition of satisfaction, he recalled the bishop Misenus after he had been purged, and restored him to his Church. Misenus had sinned in the matter of Acacius and Peter.

[Col. 0011A] He was a lover [Col. 0011D] **[Note:]** The Lucian codex 490 reads: “a lover of the poor, and he enlarged the clergy,” and so forth. of the clergy and the poor, and he increased the clergy. He delivered the city of Rome from the danger of famine. He issued a decree concerning the whole Church.

[Col. 0011B] **[Note:]** What the author adds concerning Acacius and Peter, as though they had been condemned by Gelasius while still living, is far from the truth. We have already said above, in the notes on the life and sixth letter of Felix, that they had previously been condemned and had died. The same is true in the notes on the Roman council under Felix II. It could be said that many events took place at Constantinople on account of these men, who had already been condemned and were dead.

**Severus Binius.**

During his pontificate, a report again came from Greece that many evils and murders were being committed by Peter and Acacius of Constantinople.

At the same time, John, the Catholic bishop of Alexandria, fled and came to Rome, to the apostolic see. Blessed Gelasius received him with honor and also granted him the second seat.

At that time he held a synod and sent its decisions throughout the East, and again [Col. 0011D] **[Note:]** The same codex reads: “and again he sent and condemned.” condemned Acacius and Peter forever, unless, [Col. 0011D] **[Note:]** The same codex reads: “repentant.” by submitting a written petition of satisfaction, they should seek repentance [Col. 0011D] **[Note:]** In the same codex, the words “according to the humanity of the first see of the Church” are absent. according to the humanity of the first see of the Church.

He dedicated a basilica of Saint Euphemia the martyr in the city of Tibur, twenty miles from Rome.

[Col. 0011B] He also dedicated other basilicas of Saints Nicander, Eleutherius, and Andrew, [Col. 0012A] on the Via Labicana, on an estate at Villa Pertusa.

He also built a basilica of Saint Mary on the Via Laurentina, on the estate of Crispinus, twenty miles from Rome.

[Col. 0011B] **[Note:]** Gennadius, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 14, attests that this was a large and distinguished volume, in these words: “Gelasius, bishop of the city of Rome, wrote a large and distinguished volume against Eutyches and Nestorius, as well as treatises on various Scriptures and sacraments in polished language,” and so forth.

From this it is evident that the work *On the Two Natures*, against Eutyches and Nestorius, found in the *Library of the Holy Fathers* and beginning, “It was also necessary…,” cannot be attributed to Gelasius, the Roman pontiff, since it is only a small work, concluded within the compass of a single book.

This common judgment of the more learned men of our age is first confirmed by the fact that the author of the work just mentioned commends the writings of Eusebius of Caesarea at great length, whereas Gelasius the pontiff listed Eusebius among the apocryphal authors in the proceedings of the Roman council below.

Second, the work produces many testimonies from the Greek Fathers but few or none from the Latin Fathers and therefore appears to have been written by a Greek rather than a Latin author. For although it cites fifteen Greek Fathers, it adduces only two Latins, Ambrose and Damasus, while omitting Cyprian, Hilary, Jerome, Augustine, Innocent, Leo, Prosper, and others of the same kind—writers whom Pope Gelasius, who knew them extremely well, would never have omitted.

It cannot be attributed to Gennadius, because he states that he wrote those six books not against Eutyches but against Nestorius.

It could be maintained, as many recent writers say, that the author of this work was Gelasius, bishop of Caesarea, whom Saint Jerome mentions in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 130, and from whom Theodoret also cited several passages in his dialogues.

The most illustrious Cardinal Baronius, after a lengthy investigation of the matter, concludes with exceptional diligence, more decisively than all others, that the author of this work *On the Two Natures against Eutyches* and of the acts of the Council of Nicaea, which appear above in volume II, was one and the same person.

He reaches this conclusion because in both places the author admits that he composed both works in order to defend the orthodox faith against the Eutychian heretics, who were growing powerful during the reign of the emperor Basiliscus, around the year of the Lord 476. He also reaches it because in both works the author praises Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, at great length, adorns him with titles appropriate to some great orthodox man, and completely clears him of suspicion of Arian heresy—as becomes immediately apparent to anyone examining the prefaces of both works.

Photius, in his *Bibliotheca*, likewise admits that the acts of the Council of Nicaea, contained in three volumes, were written by Gelasius, in the words prefixed above to volume II of the Councils in the history of that council.

We therefore gladly conclude, with Cardinal Baronius, that Gelasius of Cyzicus was the author of this work, concerning whom there had long been much doubt.

Nevertheless, whoever may finally have been the author of this work, in its doctrine concerning the transubstantiation of bread and wine in the sacrament of the Eucharist it does not differ from other Catholic writers.

For when it says, “The substance or nature of the bread and wine does not cease,” this must be understood of the nature and essence of the accidents. It is common for *substance* to be taken, in ordinary usage, for nature and essence. Bellarmine explains the passage in this way in book II, chapter 27, *On the Sacrament of the Eucharist*; Baronius, under the year of Christ 436, no. 10 and following.

Before the victory, then, of the triumphant Lutheran heretics, who boast on the basis of this passage that the orthodox doctrine of the transubstantiation of bread and wine in the sacrament of the Eucharist has been overthrown.

The remaining matters which they maliciously allege against Pope Gelasius we have partly refuted above in the words “During his pontificate Manichaeans were discovered” (col. 9, note e), and shall partly dissolve below in Gelasius’s work *On the Bond of Anathema*.

For Gelasius’s writings, see Possevinus, *Sacred Apparatus*, under “Gelasius.”

There exists an apology of Gelasius against the senator Andromachus and the other Romans who had decided that the Lupercalia should be celebrated according to the ancient custom. We have thought it appropriate to present it to the reader below, taken from Baronius’s *Annals.

**Severus Binius.**

He wrote five books against Nestorius and Eutyches, [Col. 0012D] **[Note:]** In the same codex the words “which are contained today …” are absent. which are today preserved in the library and archive of the Church.

He also composed hymns in the manner of Blessed Ambrose the bishop. Likewise, two books against Arius.

He also composed prefaces and prayers for the sacraments in careful language, and letters concerning the faith in polished language. [Col. 0012D] **[Note:]** The same codex reads: “many letters in polished language. Under his …”

During his episcopate the clergy grew greatly.

He held two ordinations [Col. 0012D] **[Note:]** In the same codex, the words “in the city of Rome” are absent. in the city of Rome, in the months of February and December: thirty-two priests, two deacons, and sixty-seven bishops in various places.

He was buried in the Basilica of Blessed Peter the Apostle, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of December.

After his death, the episcopate remained vacant for seven days.

# [Col. 0013] Letters and Decrees of Pope Gelasius I

*(C, G, S)*

[Col. 0013C] **[Note:]** This is Gelasius’s second letter, a reply to the letter by which Euphemius, bishop of Constantinople, unsuccessfully attempted to force the granting to him of Catholic communion.

Euphemius did indeed profess the orthodox faith; but because he had not yet erased from the diptychs the name of his predecessor Acacius, condemned by the Roman Church—as Pope Felix had instructed him—he was unworthy of communion with the Catholic Church.

When Euphemius received Gelasius as Felix’s successor, he wrote, according to ancient custom, a letter confessing his faith in order to obtain letters of communion. Gelasius, however, returned to him only a letter of communion—which is no longer extant—in which he warned Euphemius that he was seeking Catholic communion in vain until he had removed the name of Acacius from the sacred registers and completely erased it.

On this occasion, when Euphemius sent the pontiff, through another embassy, another letter on the same subject as the previous ones, the pontiff, adhering to his former judgment and letter, sent this second letter to Euphemius in the first year of his pontificate.

For within the same two-month period Euphemius could have sent one letter from Constantinople to Rome and in turn received the pontiff’s reply.

**Severus Binius.**

## First letter of Pope Gelasius I to Euphemius

[Col. 0013A]

He writes that no one can be admitted to communion with the apostolic see who has not condemned the name of Acacius. He therefore urges Euphemius to anathematize Acacius just as he has anathematized Eutyches and the other heretics.

To his most beloved [Col. 0014C] **[Note:]** That orthodox Christians were sometimes called “brothers” even when excluded from communion can be demonstrated by this and many other examples. Through the bond of human nature and the Christian name—though not through the unity of orthodox faith or Catholic communion—such a designation is sometimes found in use among the Fathers.

Baronius, year 492, no. 10.

**Severus Binius.**

brother [Col. 0013D] **[Note:]** Elsewhere: “to Euphemius, bishop of Constantinople,” concerning whom see Marcellinus Comes in his *Chronicle*, Liberatus, chapter 18, Evagrius, book 3, chapter 23, and Nicephorus, book 16, chapter 19.

Euphemianus, Gelasius.

Your Belovedness asserts that what we greatly desire—its confirmation by the complete and sincere restoration of faith and Catholic communion—cannot be sufficiently established by hearing alone unless, through a letter, you have seen the meaningful expression of what divine providence accomplishes concerning us, so that I might thus offer a greeting in the second place.

[Col. 0014D] **[Note:]** That is, “making more certain the one who had previously made an appeal by letter.”

We do not believe that either your Belovedness or anyone else could have hoped for this in such a way as to suppose that we, or anyone superior to us, ought to have deserved a reply after reporting what had been done; for it would have been judged excessively arrogant if he had formed such an opinion of the first see.

But if—as we are more inclined to suppose—you meant to indicate by letter that the apostolic see, with newly appointed priests leading the way, ought to have written to associates to whom the care of presiding had been entrusted by Christ’s gift, then this was once an old ecclesiastical rule among our fathers, by whom one Catholic and apostolic communion was maintained free from all pollution by transgressors.

Now, however, since you prefer to display an alien fellowship rather than return to the pure and undefiled companionship of blessed Peter, “How shall we sing the Lord’s song in a foreign land?” (Psalm 136).

How shall we extend to people of alien communion the ancient covenants of apostolic governance?

How will you announce your ordination to us, when, even by your own testimony, [Col. 0014D] **[Note:]** A manuscript scholium in the Beauvais codex reads: “He calls Acacius and Peter condemned heretics.”

**Hardouin.** you place condemned heretics before it?

[Col. 0014A] **[Note:]** “You say that Acacius and Peter are called condemned heretics. Why, etc.” If it is not permitted to speak thus, let us at least converse through the present letter.

For we call those who share in the Lord’s table one thing, and those who disagree with us in fellowship with him another. The Lord himself spoke in one manner to those separated from his preaching and in another manner disclosed the mysteries of the heavenly kingdom to his disciples.

The apostles, accordingly, did not speak to those separated from their fellowship in the same way as they spoke to those who were at home in the faith and their companions.

But your Belovedness says that you have held such affection for me that you were not content merely to write but wished to hear me speak.

You have read the sentence: “Faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of God” (Romans 10)—that word, namely, which promised, in the confession of blessed Peter, that the gates of hell would never prevail (Matthew 16).

And so you reasonably judged that, because God is faithful in his words, he would not have established any promise without fulfilling the true pledge of his promise.

Finally, your Belovedness says that, by the grace of divine providence—as that providence has shown—you do not abandon love for the holy Churches, since it has placed me on the pontifical seat, not, as you say, in need of instruction, but attending to everything necessary for the unity of the ecclesiastical body.

I am indeed the least of all human beings, sufficiently unworthy of the office of so great a see, except that heavenly grace always accomplishes great things through the lowly.

For what should I think of myself, when the teacher of the nations himself bears witness to this concerning himself, confessing that he was the last and unworthy to be called an apostle (1 Corinthians 15)?

Nevertheless, to return to your Belovedness’s words: if you have truly understood that these things have been divinely bestowed upon me—and indeed whatever good things there are are gifts of God—then follow the exhortations of one who does not need to be taught and who, according to the heavenly ordering that surveys all things, attends to everything that pertains to the unity of the Churches and firmly resists, as you say, the devil, the disturber of true peace and unity.

If, then, you make these declarations about me, you must either follow what, as you say, has been established by Christ, or openly declare—God forbid—that you oppose Christ’s ordinances, or else it is recognized that you make these assertions about me in order to gain indulgence [al. “an opening”] for your licentiousness.

But you add that I am capable, by condescending to you and by excellent ordering, of restoring harmony.

Therefore, since you frequently use this word, let me examine what it means.

The excellent ordering of the Catholic and apostolic Church is to condescend by advancing toward better things, not to decline by descending toward inferior things.

When you say that we ought to condescend to you, you meanwhile show that you are either descending or have already descended.

From where, I ask, and to what place is this descent?

Certainly, having been lowered from some higher place to lower things, you see, acknowledge, and do not deny that you have fallen from Catholic and apostolic communion into heretical and condemned communion. And you are pleased not only to lie in the lowest places, but also wish to drive down those who remain in the higher seat.

You invite us to condescend with you from the heights to the depths; we ask you to ascend with us from the depths to the heights.

Now, therefore, before that exalted justice which judges the human race, let it decide which of us ought to obey the other.

[Col. 0015D] **[Note:]** Perhaps more correctly: “But you say.”

**Hardouin.**

Or do you say—to omit the other matters for the moment—that the Lord himself descended from heaven?

He certainly descended, but in order to free humanity from error, not to mingle himself with its error.

Did he not himself warn that those standing on the housetop should not descend, nor take anything from the house that seemed destined to be removed (Matthew 24)?

Does not the Apostle, on behalf of all, cry out—he who labored more than all others—when the preservation of truth was at issue: “To whom we did not yield in submission even for an hour, so that the truth of the Gospel might remain with you” (1 Corinthians 1)?

Do you see the heavenly Teacher refusing to condescend to those who are harmful?

Finally, let us suppose that someone has fallen and that another wishes to bend down slightly in order to lift him with the greatest kindness.

In that case, for the one lying down to be raised, the compassionate person must bend over—not so that he may be hurled into the pit together with him.

Accordingly, in the letter which you sent through the deacon Syncletius, concerning those whom Acacius baptized and ordained, we offer without difficulty the true remedy prepared by the tradition of our forefathers and especially suited to religious concern.

How much farther do you want us to descend?

Why are you silent?

Why are you ashamed to express in words what you carry in your heart?

Your very shame ought perhaps to have warned you, as sometimes happens.

Or is it perhaps that you want us to agree to admit the names of condemned heretics and of those who communicate with them or with their successors?

This is not condescending in order to provide help; it is plainly plunging into hell.

Spare, I beg you, both us and yourselves.

But if you have so little concern for yourselves, grant us pardon.

We can and ought to grieve and weep; but we neither can nor ought to be led into these precipices. By the favor of our God, we wish to retain the sincere and pure faith and communion of the tradition handed down by our fathers, distinguished from every contagion of transgressors, even at the risk of death. We choose—if God wills—to endure whatever may come rather than fall into the causes of eternal condemnation.

Grant pardon, I say, if, while you willingly incur these things for the love or fear of some human being, we reject them for the love of God and fear of Gehenna.

Do not suppose that by concealing causes and persons you can insinuate yourselves into the friendship of anyone. You are not so subtle that you cannot be understood, nor will you find us, by the favor of our God, unwary.

Have you not often indicated in letters sent here that, together with the other heretics, you reject Eutyches?

If this is true, either reject equally those who have communicated with the successors of Eutyches, or admit those who communicate with the successors of the other heretics as well.

“But Acacius,” you say, “is not recorded anywhere to have said anything against the faith, as Eutyches and his successor did.”

As though it were not worse both to have known the truth and nevertheless to have communicated with the enemies of the truth.

For if, when someone rightly believing concerning the Catholic faith communicates with those heretics among whom you have placed Eutyches, or with their successors, it is not lawful to name them among the altars of the Catholics, then by communicating with the successors of that Eutyches is he not likewise held liable to the same fate?

Concerning such people the following is appropriately said: “Let them descend alive into hell” (Psalm 55). For while they are thought to live by that life in which the righteous person lives (Romans 1), and to live truly and Catholicly, they suddenly turn either toward the precipice of depravity or toward the hell of heretical communion.

Behold the sort of people whom you say should be placed before Christ, although he does not even command that our souls be placed before him.

Indeed, you still ask when Acacius was condemned, as though, even if no one had condemned him previously, he ought not to have been excluded from participation in the orthodox and apostolic communion of which he had been a transgressor and deserter.

So too anyone who was previously a Catholic, if he communicates with any heresy, is rightly judged to be removed from our fellowship; and if he dies in such a condition, he must in no way be counted among the names of Catholics.

Yet we are astonished that you make these statements while professing both to accept the Council of Chalcedon as upholding the Catholic faith and to suppose that those who follow the persons whom it condemned, and those who communicate with them, were not condemned both particularly and universally.

Show, then, what council in the case of any heresy does not condemn, together with the errors, their successors, those who communicate with them, and all their accomplices.

Accordingly, your Acacius, who became a participant in detestable communion with the Eutychian heretics, was without doubt condemned by that same council which, in the form of a synodal judgment, overthrew Eutyches and Dioscorus, together with their successors and those who communicated with them.

[Col. 0017A] Thus it also cast out their followers, Timothy and Peter, by a similar definition. Therefore, if you truly and certainly follow what was defined at the Council of Chalcedon for the sake of the catholic faith and communion according to apostolic law, as is contained in your repeated profession, either reject the successors of those condemned by that council, and those who communicate with them; or, if you admit these men, recognize that you not only falsely claim to retain what was enacted at that council for the sake of the catholic and apostolic faith and communion, but are additionally attempting to undermine it, and are falling back into the Eutychian heresy without recantation; and you are rightly judged by Catholics to be persons to be avoided. For, so that we might always escape such a plague, not only the bishops of the apostolic see but also the catholic pontiffs of the eastern regions have judged that what is read as having been salutarily decreed against it by that assembly of holy Fathers [Col. 0017B] must in no way be mutilated.

Do you say that Peter was purged, with whom Acacius communicated? Teach us by true assertions; show and prove this: by what methods, by what rules was he cleansed from the Eutychian profession or communion? When the matter has nevertheless been shown and established by an evident demonstration of the facts, then you will plainly and openly be able to understand either that you must yield to the truth or that you are to engage in open combat against it.

Nor should you flatter yourselves because you profess to hold the catholic faith, because you have removed the name of Eutyches, or because you seem to preach things such as orthodox antiquity preached. For that evangelical saying cries out to us: “Either [Col. 0017C] make the tree good and its fruit good, or make the tree bad and its fruit bad; for the tree is known by its fruits” (Matt. XII). That is: if in speech, in faith, and in catholic and apostolic profession you faithfully and truthfully glory, receive also the communion of this faith. But if you are pleased with the communion of heretics—namely, of those who have been condemned—or of those who communicate with them or with their successors, why do you stand still? Why do you look around? Defend openly and manifestly, once all obstacles have been removed, the doctrine of those men as well.

For what does it accomplish? Rather, it is a great burden to promise in words what is denied by deeds, so that you may recognize not only how deadly the Eutychian heresy itself is to the Christian sacrament, but also how many and how serious matters this heresy contains in its own definition. Behold to what precipices you provoke us to descend [Col. 0017D], and toward what dangers to eternal life you wish to incline us. Is saving a sick person by this descent, or is it rather perishing together with the invalid?

Will this be the excellent arrangement of that restoration of concord which you mention—or rather, that the catholic and apostolic communion, once the contagions of the faithless have been rejected, may enjoy an unimpaired faith and sincere communion, striving, after the filth of heretics has been driven away, to establish an undefiled confession of its faith, and that there may be unity of orthodox profession and communion mutually agreeing with itself?

As the letters of Your Affection exhort, I too earnestly ask that this be guarded in my time: a faith which, for so many years, has been preserved unblemished and untouched by those glorious Fathers [Col. 0018A]. For this is, as you yourself say, what our God foresaw and established beforehand as destined to be beneficial in every respect and to be governed according to his truth and rule, fitting it suitably by his dispensation to each successive age.

This is the will of God, which you bring into mention, and which I too, according to the measure that the Lord deigns to grant me, desire wholly to fulfill, so that I may not be found guilty of diminishing this heavenly talent. Rather, in this talent, as he himself also admonishes us, I ask to attain increase through the grace of Christ and to suffer absolutely no loss.

This is why, in your earlier letters, as your own page also indicated, I took up sorrow for the sake of your salvation [Col. 0018B], when I learned what was harmful to you and found what was contrary to true peace. For the Apostle grieves over the error of those who go astray (II Cor. VII), and receives joy from those same people when they have been corrected by his preaching.

But if Your Charity, as you said, is constrained by the necessity of certain persons—which, with your permission, I say a priest ought never either to do or to say when truth must be proclaimed—let him pardon us, timid as we are, if, constrained by the terrible and great necessity of divine judgment, we are compelled, as befits whatever sort of ministers of Christ we may be, to lay down our souls to save them for the truth, rather than wish to gain them only to lose them by diminishing the truth—not to say, repudiate them against the faith at anyone’s pleasure. [Note: [Col. 0017] Perhaps rather “souls.” HARDUIN.]

These are for me, as Your Affection commends, the enduring friendships in the bowels of Christ of a sure faith, with whoever may be willing [Col. 0018C]. Here we do not so much desire to be placed above others, as you declare, but to have, together with all the faithful, a holy fellowship pleasing to God.

This is for me the solid, unshaken, and perpetual peace which Your Affection commands; this is the one salutary bond, as you yourself also desire, by which the whole Church can be united. May divine protection perfect those to whom this has been entrusted, as you also pray.

This is that charity which is God (I John IV), which you seek “from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith” (I Tim. I). How, then, can there be a pure heart if it has been polluted by participation with heretics? How a good conscience if it has been mixed with the confusion of evil men? How an unfeigned faith if it has been mixed with the faithless?

[Col. 0018D] If your prudence carefully considers this, as we pray that it may, it will see that the apostolic see does not avoid peace, but avoids the footsteps [al. contagions] of heretics and condemned persons. Considering this reasonably, you believe [Note: [Col. 0017] Perhaps “to stir up”; in Bellov., “to oppose.” HARDUIN.] that the Constantinopolitan people should be admonished, and that they should not be allowed to be removed under the name of the faithless.

Who, I ask you, could hear this in the Church of God, when surely the flock ought to follow the shepherd who calls it back to saving pastures, not follow a shepherd who goes astray through byways? Tell me, I beg you: will the flock render an account for you, or you for the flock? Certainly, if this pleases you, our cause is all the more just, since we have willingly listened to those who do not allow the Roman people to depart from that faith which they received through the praiseworthy tradition of their ancestors [Col. 0019A], if you do not wish to offend the Constantinopolitan people because they refuse to withdraw from heretical communion.

But you say that we ought to send those capable of calming that people. How will it listen to me, whom it appears to regard with suspicion, if it despises its own bishops when they admonish it? Was it not commanded even to the apostles, in certain regions, not to use the preaching of the word—namely, in places where they would not be heard?

We shall come, brother Euphemius, without doubt we shall come to that fearful tribunal of Christ—leaving aside what vengeance must be feared from this [Note: [Col. 0019D] The Codex of the Veronese chapter also has this here.]—with those standing around, from whom the faith itself is [Note: [Col. 0019D] The same codex reads “was defended.”]. There it will not be a matter of denials, delays, or [Note: [Col. 0019D] The same codex reads “deceptions.”] evasions; [Col. 0019B] rather, it must be demonstrated with the greatest clarity whether the glorious confession of blessed Peter took anything away from the salvation of any of those whom he received to govern, or whether obstinate destruction, refusing to listen to it, became rebellious even at its own peril [Note: [Col. 0020D] The same codex reads “became.”].

There it will certainly be made clear whether I am, as you think, harsh, severe, excessively hard, and difficult for you—when, with reason, I labor for your salvation, when I cry out: “Even if the antidote seems harsh, accept it, I beg you; drink it; live; I do not want you to die”—or whether you are the ones who, having been forbidden what is harmful, consider physicians deserving of execration, indeed who wish the physicians to fall ill with you rather than that you receive [Note: [Col. 0020D] Al. “salvation.” HARDUIN.] health.

And in another hand: May the Lord keep you safe and sound.

[Note: [Col. 0019D] This letter is circular and encyclical, written to all the bishops of Macedonia in the first year of Gelasius’s pontificate, on the occasion that the bishop of Thessalonica, metropolitan of the whole province of Macedonia—as is established below from Letter 9 to Dardanus and the Illyrian bishops—had disgracefully adhered to the Acacians, although previously, whenever schisms arose between the Easterners and the Roman pontiff, he had been accustomed to adhere firmly to the apostolic see and to undertake its protection. Therefore, in order to keep the other bishops of his province within the duty of catholic and apostolic communion, he sent this circular letter to the bishops of that province. SEV. BINIUS.]

## LETTER II. TO LAURENTIUS, BISHOP OF LIGNIDUS

[Col. 0019C]

On assuming the pontificate, he prescribes, according to the custom of the Roman Church, the formula of faith which all must profess.

In the length of your letter, Your Affection filled us with great joy in that passage where you said that, when the letter of our predecessor concerning the offenses of Acacius had been read in the Church of Thessalonica and likewise elsewhere, everyone had pronounced anathema against him, and no one had joined himself to the communion of the transgressor.

Therefore, because you admonish us with fraternal affection that we ought to administer, as it were, a medicine of faith to the bishops throughout Illyricum and elsewhere—although this was very fully done by our predecessor of blessed memory—and because it is the custom of the Roman Church for a newly constituted priest to send the form of his faith to the holy Churches [Col. 0019D], I have taken care to renew this same formula in an exceedingly brief summary, so that the reader may recognize, without weariness because of its brevity, according to what faith one must live, in accordance with the decrees of the Fathers, in this letter of ours.

[Col. 0020A] We therefore confess our Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, begotten before all ages, without beginning, from the Father according to his divinity; but in the last days, the same one was incarnate from the most holy Virgin Mary and became a perfect man, consisting of a rational soul and the assumption of a body, *homoousios*—of the same substance—with the Father according to his divinity, and *homoousios* with us according to his humanity.

For an ineffable union of two perfect natures took place. Therefore we confess one Christ, the same only-begotten Son of God and of man, from the Father, and the firstborn from the dead. We know that, according to his divinity, he is coeternal with his Father, according to which he is the maker of all things; and after the consent of the most holy Virgin, when she said to the angel, “Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word” (Luke I), he graciously built for himself from her an ineffable temple and united it to himself.

He did not bring down from heaven a body coeternal with him and derived from his own substance, but received and united to himself a body from the mass of our substance—that is, from the Virgin. God the Word did not turn into flesh, nor did he appear as a phantom; rather, inconvertibly and immutably he preserved his own essence while assuming and uniting to himself the firstfruits of our nature.

For God the Word, who is the Beginning, in his great goodness deigned to unite these firstfruits of our nature to himself. He appeared as one and the same person, not mixed, but in the substance of each nature, according to what is written: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John II).

Christ Jesus is destroyed according to the pure substance which he assumed, and, once destroyed, he raises up his own temple—he himself according to the divine substance, according to which he is also the maker of all things. Never after the resurrection did he depart from the temple proper to the union of our nature, nor can he depart from it because of his ineffable goodness. Rather, the same Lord Jesus Christ is both passible and impassible: passible according to his humanity, impassible according to his divinity.

Therefore God the Word raised up his own temple, and in himself effected the resurrection and renewal of our nature. Our Lord Jesus Christ our God, after he had risen from the dead, showed this to his disciples, saying: “Touch me and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see me have” (Luke XXIV). He did not say, “as you say that I am,” [Col. 0020D] but “as you see me have,” so that, considering both the one who possesses and that which is possessed, you may regard not a mixture, not a conversion, not a change, but a union that has taken place.

For this reason he also displayed the marks of the nails and the piercing of the lance, and ate with his disciples, so that in every respect he might teach that the resurrection of our nature had been renewed in himself [Col. 0021A]. And although, according to the blessed substance of his divinity, he is inconvertible, immutable, impassible, immortal, needing nothing, and perfecting all sufferings, he allowed these sufferings to be inflicted upon his own temple, which he raised by his own power; and through the perfection of his temple he effected the renewal of our nature.

But those who say that Christ was a subtle or insubstantial man, or that God was passible, or that he was changed into flesh, or that he did not have a body united with him [Note: [Col. 0021D] The Roman edition more correctly has *co-unitum*, “united with him.”], or that he brought it down from heaven, or that he was a phantom, or who say that he was mortal, or that God the Word needed to be raised by the Father, or that he assumed a body without a soul, or a man without sensation, or that the two substances of Christ were confused through mixture and became one substance, and who do not confess [Col. 0021B] that our Lord Jesus Christ has two natures without confusion but one person—inasmuch as there is one Christ, one and the same Son—the catholic and apostolic Church anathematizes them.

These, therefore, dearest brother, are the things which you asked us to send as an antidote. Do not refuse any of them as though they were bitter, nor regard any as harmlessly sweet; for we had also arranged to send certain men from our assembly, if circumstances at that time had permitted it. We believe that this can be done at the proper time, when, with the Lord’s help, we trust that the correction of those regions will have been reported to us through a fully authorized legation.

We also hope in the mercy of our God that the most merciful and Christian emperor will join his unanimity and assistance to this preaching of ours, so that, in accordance with the faith with which he is endowed, he may restrain in those regions people who [Col. 0021C], following their petty questions and “according to the elements of the world,” as the chosen vessel foretold, utter empty and vain things, unwilling to be held within salutary disciplines.

But you, as the same apostle says, “have not so learned Christ” (Col. II), if indeed you have heard him and have been taught in him, as truth is in Jesus. Certainly, only the person who, as has already often been said, observes the institutions of the orthodox Fathers will be able to grasp this.

May God keep you safe and sound, dearest brother.

## RESPONSE OF THE BISHOPS OF DARDANIA TO GELASIUS THE POPE (C)

They give thanks that he has warned them whom they must avoid, and write that they desire to be visited by the apostolic see.

[Col. 0021D] To the holy apostolic [al. “apostle”] and most blessed father of fathers, Gelasius, pope of the city of Rome, the humble bishops of Dardania.

We received, with the devotion that was appropriate, the most salutary commands of Your Apostolate, delivered by Trypho, a religious man and our son; and we return the greatest thanks to almighty God and to Your Blessedness, holy apostolic lord and most blessed father of fathers, because you have deigned to visit us with pastoral admonition and evangelical teaching [Col. 0022A].

For it is our desire and prayer to obey your commands in all things, and, as we received from our fathers, to preserve inviolate the commands of the apostolic see—conferred upon it because of your life and merits—and to guard the orthodox faith, whose preachers you are, with faithful and blameless devotion, insofar as the understanding of our rusticity permits.

Even before your command we avoided, as certain pestilential contagions, the communion of Eutyches, or of Peter and Acacius, and of all their followers and associates; and now, especially after the admonition of the apostolic see, we must abstain from that pollution. If any others have followed or should follow the sect of that same Eutyches, or of Peter and Acacius, or consider that they ought to mingle themselves with their accomplices and associates [Col. 0022B], they must by every means be avoided by us, who desire to serve the apostolic see blamelessly according to the divine commands and the statutes of the Fathers.

And if some, perhaps with an evil intention—which we neither suppose nor desire—should believe that they must be separated from the apostolic see, we profess that we are strangers to their association. For, as has been said, observing the commands of the Fathers in all things and following the inviolable institutions of the sacred canons, we strive to obey your apostolic and unique see with a common faith and devotion.

And since Your Blessedness, because of the goodness innate in you, has granted us the opportunity to provide material for a petition, we entrusted certain matters to the religious man Trypho, our son, bearer of your commands [Col. 0022C]. We earnestly beseech Your Apostolate to deign graciously to receive his petition, insofar as we judge it just and reasonable, for the sake of our supplication—and may our supplication obtain the result it deserves—and to order one person from your angelic see to be sent to us together with the aforesaid religious man, so that in his presence those matters may be arranged which the orthodox faith and the sincerity of your command require.

And the subscription:

John, bishop of the most holy Church of Scopia, the metropolitan city, consenting to this response given by us, have subscribed with my own hand to everything contained above.

Bonosus, bishop: I have subscribed as above.

Samuel, bishop: I have subscribed as above.

[Col. 0022D] Verianus, bishop, through Valentinus the archdeacon: I have subscribed as above.

Faustinus, bishop: I have subscribed as above.

Ursinus, bishop: I have subscribed as above.

[Note: [Col. 0021D] In two letters Pope Gelasius admonished the bishops of Dardania to avoid the communion of the Eutychians diligently. He sent the first—which has been lost—through Trypho; to it the preceding letter from the bishops [Col. 0022D] of Dardania was written in response. He sent this second letter, on the same subject, through Ursicinus, as they themselves had requested. It is clear from the words of the letter at the end that it was encyclical and circular. Since at the beginning of the Eutychian heresy, which was exposed in the year 448, this passage counts forty-five years, it appears to have been written in the first year of Gelasius’s pontificate. SEV. BINIUS.]

## LETTER III. TO THE BISHOPS OF DARDANIA

[Col. 0023A] He announces that he has been elected pope; he transmits a statement of the catholic faith, exhorts them not to communicate with the Eutychianists, and urges them to watch over their pastoral office.

To all the most beloved brothers, the bishops established throughout Dardania, Gelasius, bishop.

As soon as it is permitted to draw breath after the storm of continuous wars, whose character has incessantly afflicted those provinces, or rather these times, we have thought it appropriate to address all the priests of the Lord throughout Dardania with the affection of fraternal concern.

First, because, having attained the governance of the apostolic see, and being delayed by public turmoil, as has been said, we have been unable to indicate in our customary letters the sacred ministry entrusted to us, so that your fraternity might rejoice with us in the gift of the Lord’s communion. [Note: [Col. 0023D] The Roman edition has “we were unable.”]

[Col. 0023B] Next, we wished mutual conversation to disclose how we were able to fare with one another after such great worldly hardships and afflictions. Finally, if there were matters concerning the churches that ought to be reported—matters which, because of the snares of the perpetual enemy, must constantly be considered with pastoral vigilance—we wished to reveal them through alternating communications.

Moved, therefore, by these considerations, we arranged for the present letter to be sent through our brother and fellow bishop Ursicinus, preceded by the grace of our greeting. We pray that, with great courage and with the Lord’s help, by enduring the devastation of passing things, we may be the more attentive, lest—God forbid—we suffer the loss of eternal life.

Therefore, the usefulness of catholic truth requires that Your Affection pay attention for a little while. Among the Greeks, among whom it is beyond doubt that many heresies abound, an inquiry concerning the incarnation of our Lord and Savior arose nearly forty-five years ago [Col. 0023C], when Eutyches, once a presbyter of Constantinople, rushed into blasphemies through which he said that we ought to believe in only one nature—or rather, the sole nature or substance of divinity—in the Lord Jesus Christ, the reality of the flesh he assumed being entirely abolished.

This wicked invention, joined as it was to the Marcionites and Manichaeans, would unquestionably dissolve the whole mystery of our salvation, if, as the venerable authority of Scripture says and the teaching of our ancestors bears witness, the Redeemer of the world were not born from the Virgin Mary wholly God and wholly man.

It is certain that he appeared visibly to this world; it is established that he suffered and rose from the dead. It is plainly evident that he remained with his disciples for forty days and ascended into heaven [Col. 0023D], and that he will come to judgment in the manner foretold, with the angel bearing witness: the Son of Man, whom blessed Stephen the martyr saw standing at the right hand of the power of God, will appear manifest, and those who pierced him, his persecutors, will see him.

This plainly cannot be established without the material of human flesh, whose assumption was glorified by divinity, not entirely consumed. Hence blessed John the Apostle also says: “Whoever denies that Christ came in the flesh is the antichrist” (John II). [Col. 0024A] And the glorious Apostle Paul openly declared what sort of Lord Jesus Christ we ought to believe in today, saying: “In him dwells all the fullness of divinity bodily” (Col. II).

In this brief passage he overturned by heavenly preaching both the Arian plague and the Eutychian heresy of which we have spoken: he is also man, since all the fullness of divinity is said to dwell in him; and by expressing “bodily,” it is shown that our body persists in truth.

Moreover, it is certain that the Greeks have frequently been convicted concerning these matters by the apostolic see, both through Saint Leo of blessed memory and through his successors, as is unmistakably shown by their documents, which we possess.

Now, although they do not dare to profess that very plague, they obstinately and with pernicious fury defend those who communicated with such people [Col. 0024B] and who, according to the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon, were rightly condemned by the apostolic see and died obstinate in that condemnation. They also strive to impose their commemoration upon the catholic Church.

If this were accepted—which God forbid!—the contagion of the depravity with which they joined themselves through communion would consequently also be incurred. Likewise—may the Lord avert it!—if the name of Arius or of any heretic is admitted into ecclesiastical commemoration, the fellowship of detestable error is assumed along with it.

Therefore, because they confess the error but think that catholic communion ought to be relaxed for them on the condition that they may lawfully commemorate in the church the names of those who have transgressed—and because they strive not so much to correct themselves as to infect catholic sincerity [Col. 0024C] with the contagion of the faithless—we have not ceased to admonish Your Affection with fraternal charity.

If anyone spreading such things should happen to arrive in your regions, let him be excluded by every means, and may your unimpaired and wholly unshaken communion with the see of blessed Peter the Apostle, as it was handed down by our fathers, endure.

Certainly, if anyone believes that your ears should be approached by such deception, hasten to report it to us as quickly as possible with pastoral concern, so that all the catholic priests may cooperate in a common effort and catholic deliberation for the household of the one Lord; so that whatever accords with orthodox definition may be preserved undefiled, and so that it may be understood, through reasonable deliberation, how assistance ought to be given to those who are in error.

[Col. 0024D] Your Affection should also prudently bring this to all the neighboring provinces and to the neighboring pontiffs, so that the bishops of the Churches, having received instruction in the whole truth, may be able to avoid the deadly falsehood.

And the subscription: May God keep you safe and sound, dearest brothers.

## LETTER III bis. OF THE BLESSED POPE GELASIUS TO NATALIS, THE ABBOT

To his most beloved son Natalis, the abbot, Gelasius, bishop.

Although, in accordance with the divinely established governance of blessed Peter the Apostle, by which the vicars of his see are debtors to all the churches [Col. 0025A], we sent a suitable letter to my brothers and fellow bishops established throughout Dardania, following the path of the ancient faith and communion, so that they might be able to avoid the contagions of the faithless and maintain unimpaired fellowship with us, we have nevertheless not failed to address Your Affection as well.

We saw, from the letters which your Charity sent to my brother and fellow bishop Serenus, how praiseworthy was your concern for avoiding all harmful things and for retaining whatever pertains to Christian advantage. [Note: [Col. 0025D] In the edition: “we have not ceased.”] [Note: [Col. 0025D] In the edition: “from the letters, certainly.”] [Note: [Col. 0025D] Absent from the edition: “therefore.”]

Your Affection has consequently judged that it must labor together with him for the Gospel of God, steadfastly enduring even whatever is adverse, with a view to eternal salvation [Note: [Col. 0025D] The edition correctly has: “on account of eternal salvation, etc.”], so that—God forbid—you may suffer no loss of the heavenly kingdom. To that kingdom, unless you have contended lawfully, you cannot attain.

[Col. 0025B] For, with the Lord’s help, we must strive and remain vigilant all the more because, now that the end of the world itself is near, the enemy of the human race does not cease to press upon us with greater violence.

We indicate that nothing has been omitted [Note: [Col. 0025C] Maffeius reads: “Whatever either … or according to the rules of the Fathers.” Since it is awkward for the second *aut* (“or”) to be redundant, the first also seems superfluous.] which could provide a medicine consonant with the rules of the Fathers for correcting the matters that the enemy has sown in the Churches of the East.

But what are we to do? They refuse to hear the voice of truth with hardened ears, and so great a force of raging disease has settled upon them that they prefer the healthy to become mortally ill with them rather than receive health themselves.

Now they deny everything that we establish by their own documents and their own subscriptions; now, when they have been convicted by the clear light of the facts, they openly and manifestly confess their error, yet declare that they do not wish to return to the path of pure confession and communion [Col. 0025C] [Note: [Col. 0025D] The edition has “testifying,” and below “awaiting.”]; rather, they await our becoming entangled with their transgressors.

Therefore, by the generosity of Christ’s grace, we must act with great zeal. Since the matter concerns either losing or preserving eternal life, let us indeed [Col. 0026A] make every effort, if, with the Lord at work, we can save some of them. Otherwise, as the Apostle says, “Keep yourself pure” (I Tim. V, 22).

Let us strive to avoid the destruction of those who wish to perish; and let us do the one thing we ought to do: pray to the divine mercy for them, so that they may recover from the snares of the devil, by whom they are held captive for his will [Note: [Col. 0025C] The preposition *ab* is absent in Maffeius.]. Thus, drawing breath again from their deadly obstinacy, recognizing that they themselves have fallen through human weakness into this plague, and laying aside the morbid languor of useless shame, may they return with free hearts to recover the eternal remedies.

Having therefore learned these things, which, as we have said, were sent to the bishops of your regions, you too, with the Lord protecting you, ought to be suitably instructed and confidently to preach the same things to each of the adjoining provinces [Note: [Col. 0026D] Absent from the edition: “adjoining.”].

[Col. 0026B] For there is nothing that we ought to fear, since it is certain that the heavenly Bishop does not abandon those whom he has equipped to wield the weapons of his truth. Nor do we see anything that ought in any way to be preferred to him, since he wished us to despise even our own souls for their salvation.

As for how the integrity of religion is progressing there, or what perhaps is being asserted, may Your Affection not fail to make this known to us frequently, so that, with Christ granting it, we may provide necessary assistance through appropriate replies.

The pope’s subscription: May God keep you safe and sound, most beloved son.

## LETTER IV, OR [Note: [Col. 0025C] After Theodoric, king of the Goths, had defeated and killed Odoacer, king of the Heruli, and had gained possession of all Italy together with Ravenna, he was worn out by prolonged warfare. He therefore sent these two envoys, Faustus, master of offices, and Irenaeus, to the emperor Anastasius, who was residing at Constantinople, in order to ask and obtain that peace be granted to him and to establish more securely the kingdom of Italy which he had acquired.

On this occasion Pope Gelasius, in the second year of his pontificate, entrusted to one of the envoys, Faustus, master of offices, the matter that was being disputed with Euphemius of Constantinople, who was still in schism, so that, by obeying the most equitable commands of the Roman Church, he might deserve to obtain the communion that he had hitherto sought in vain.

The conduct of this affair was entrusted to Faustus for the following reason: Patriarch Euphemius, admonished by two letters from Gelasius, had not only failed to erase the name of Acacius from the sacred registers, but had also undertaken to defend him and had uttered the things that heretics and schismatics customarily spew forth against the apostolic see. Finally, in order to arouse hatred against the Roman pontiff in the emperor Anastasius, he had spread among the people that the emperor Anastasius himself was not received either by the bishop of the city of Rome or by the Roman senate, and had thus stirred the emperor against the City and its bishop.

Therefore, lest the Roman Church be brought into danger on this account and, caught between the two heretical rulers Anastasius and Theodoric, be pressed by even harsher straits, it entrusted so burdensome an affair to Faustus, master of offices, a most pious man. While he was at Constantinople, he was to dispel the accusations, undo the attempts, and, acting as an intermediary of peace, come as a reconciler of the Eastern Church with the Western.

Faustus set out and diligently carried out the task he had undertaken; but he did not conclude it according to his judgment or as he had hoped, because Euphemius opposed him and stirred up still greater fuel for quarrels. Euphemius also informed Gelasius of everything that had been transacted with him by sending a letter.

After receiving it, Gelasius sent him this reply as a defense by which he might refute the calumnies of his adversaries. Hence it is not improperly called a *Commonitorium*, since the pontiff himself admonishes him in it how he may effectively repel the insolence of the calumniators.

These matters are taken from Baronius, year 493, no. 3 and following. SEV. BINIUS.]

## MEMORANDUM TO FAUSTUS, MASTER OF OFFICES, SERVING AS ENVOY AT CONSTANTINOPLE

[Note: [Col. 0026D] Some say that it ought to be read “Festus,” and that this envoy was not sent to Constantinople by King Theodoric under Pope Gelasius, but under Anastasius, Gelasius’s successor. HARDUIN.]

[Col. 0026C] Acacius was rightly condemned by the apostolic see and, having died in excommunication, cannot be absolved; nor may anyone communicate with him.

I too perceived that the Greeks would remain in their obstinacy [variant: “I commanded”], and no one can regard as unforeseen what has been foreknown [variant: “foreknown beforehand”]. [Note: The Verona codex, which is a thousand years older than the chapter and with which this *Commonitorium* of Gelasius was compared, reads here, “not so much.”] Therefore they are no longer striving, for religious reasons, to oppose the public arrangements, but rather are attempting, under cover of the royal embassy, to overthrow the Catholic faith, and by such a pretext [variant: “exchange”] are endeavoring to achieve what they hope for.

What, then, does the emperor mean by saying that he was condemned by us in matters of religion, when in this regard my predecessor not only did not even mention his name, but, when he first assumed the exercise of royal power, wrote that he rejoiced in his advancement to imperial authority? And I, although I had never received any writing from him, took care—as you know—to greet him with letters of honor.

My predecessors, the priests who openly confessed that they had communicated with transgressors, removed them from apostolic communion. If they choose to associate with the condemned [variant: “thus”], that cannot be charged against us; if he wishes to withdraw from them, then he cannot possibly have been condemned by us, but rather has been admitted to the grace of sincere communion.

It belongs to the Roman senate, remembering the faith which it recalls having received from its parents, to avoid the contagion of external communion, lest—God forbid—it be made an outsider from communion with this apostolic see.

They propose that pardon be granted them [variant: “add that it ought to be granted”]. Let it be read, from the beginning of the Christian religion—or let an example certainly be produced—in the Church of God, whether from any pontiffs, from the apostles themselves, or finally from the Savior himself, of pardon being granted to anyone except those who corrected themselves. Yet under this heaven it has never been heard, nor is it read or said, that what comes forth from their mouths is: “Grant us pardon, while nevertheless we remain in error.”

Let those who strive to oppose us with canons likewise show [Note: The Verona codex reads, “it is too little.”] by which canons, which rules, which reading, or which document—whether among our forebears, or from the apostles themselves, who were unquestionably superior in authority, or from the Lord himself, the Savior, who is believed to judge the living and the dead—ever established or commanded that this was done or ought to be done. We read that Christ raised the dead; we do not read that he absolved those who were dead in error. And he who alone certainly possessed the power to do this expressly commanded the blessed apostle Peter: “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven” (Matthew 16). He says, “on earth”; for nowhere in this binding did he say that the dead were to be absolved [variant: “that the dead should be absolved”]. Therefore we fear even to conceive what has never been done, knowing that it cannot be wholly excused in the divine judgment.

But if, as they now claim, they are going to separate themselves from the Roman Church, they are shown to have done so long ago.

[Note: The Verona codex has “Euphimius,” and so throughout.] I am astonished that Euphemius does not himself perceive his ignorance when he says that Acacius could not have been condemned by one man. Does he not understand that Acacius was condemned according to the form of the Council of Chalcedon? Or does he not know—or pretend not to know—that in that council the authors of this error are clearly shown to have been condemned by the numerous judgment of priests? The manifest course of events shows that this has both been done and is being done in every heresy from the beginning of the Christian religion. It also shows that my predecessor was the executor of an ancient decree, not the author of a new constitution.

This is permitted not only to the apostolic bishop, but to any pontiff: according to the rule of the heresy itself, already condemned, to separate anyone and everyone from Catholic communion, wherever they may be. Acacius was not an inventor of a new or private error, so that new decrees should be issued against him [variant: “should proceed against him”], but joined himself by his communion to another’s crime. It was therefore necessary that he should fall under the just sentence which the author of the error had incurred, together with his successors, by synodal agreement.

**[Note: Pope Nicholas quotes this passage from the *Commonitorium* in Letter 5 to the Emperor Michael. HARDUIN.]**

They oppose us with canons, while not knowing what they are saying. They expose themselves as violating those very canons because they refuse to obey the first see when it gives sound and righteous counsel. The canons themselves decreed that appeals from the whole Church should be brought before the judgment of this see. Yet they have nowhere at all decreed that an appeal should be made from it; and consequently they have not commanded that it should be judged by the whole Church, that it should itself submit to anyone’s judgment, or that its judgment should ever be judged. They established that its sentence ought not to be annulled, since they instead commanded that its decrees be followed.

In this very case Timothy of Alexandria, Peter of Antioch, Peter, Paul, John, and the others—not merely one, but several who bore the name of priesthood—were deposed solely by the authority of the apostolic see. Acacius himself is also taught to be a witness to this matter, since he was the executor of that command. Just as it is manifest that the apostolic see acted according to the synodal form, so it is absolutely certain that no one could have resisted it.

Thus Acacius, having fallen back into association with the condemned, was condemned—he who had executed their condemnation before he himself became a transgressor.

They have dared to mention canons to us, although they are shown always to have acted against them through unlawful ambitions. [Note: The Verona codex reads, “unlawful ambitions of holding [office].”] By what synod, or according to the form of which synod, did they expel John of Alexandria from the church for which he had been ordained? He could be accused neither beforehand, without evident grounds, nor afterward, when he appealed, even in a competent court. And if they say, “The emperor did this,” by which canons, by which rules, was this commanded? Why did Acacius consent to so wicked an act, when divine authority says: “Not only those who do wicked things are guilty, but also those who consent to their perpetrators” (Romans 2)?

By which canons or rules was Calendion excluded, or the first Catholic priests of the various cities? By what tradition of our forefathers do they summon the apostolic see to judgment?

Should the bishops of the second and third sees, and the other priests fully conscious of their own innocence, have been expelled, while the one who was an enemy of religion should not have been expelled? Let them see, then, whether they have other canons by which to carry out their absurdities.

As for those canons which are called sacred, ecclesiastical, and legitimate, they cannot summon the apostolic see to judgment. And should the bishop of Constantinople—a city which, according to the canons, has received no standing among the sees—not have been removed from communion when he fell back into fellowship with the treacherous?

Were those who are said to have lied to the human emperor, and those alleged to have injured the emperor, to be expelled, while Acacius, who offended against God, the highest and true Emperor, and who sought to mix sincere communion in the divine sacrament with the treacherous, should not have been excluded according to the synod by which that treachery was condemned? Whether they wish it or not, the ancient constitutions of the canons will be confirmed by his judgment [variant: “will be strengthened by the ancient canonical constitution”].

But these religious and perfect men are plainly attempting to wrest from the apostolic see the power granted to it according to the canons, and are striving to usurp it for themselves against the canons. O teachers and guardians of the canons!

We are not permitted to enter into combat with men of alien communion, since divine Scripture proclaims: “Avoid a heretical person after the first and second admonition, knowing that such a person is perverted and condemned by his own judgment” (Titus 3). Let them recognize that a heretic is condemned not only by another, but by himself as well [variant: “is condemned beforehand”].

But it is exceedingly shameless that they pretend Acacius asked for pardon and that we proved difficult. Your brother, my son, the illustrious man Andromachus, is witness to the contrary. We instructed him abundantly to urge Acacius, once he had laid aside his obstinacy, to come to his senses and return to the fellowship of the apostolic see. He testifies under oath that he made great efforts with Acacius, but could not turn him toward what was right, as the outcome of events proves.

Let them certainly produce the judgment: when did he send word, when did he ask for pardon, and when did he promise us that he would demonstrate his correction? Unless perhaps he possessed the disposition which we see in his successors: that if he asked for pardon, he wished it to be granted in such a way that he would nevertheless persist in error. In that case he would not so much appear to be received by us as to draw us over into his own depravity.

What guilt do they assert that they will confess before the contest? If it is guilt, then it must certainly be corrected. If they do not think it should be corrected, then they falsely claim to confess guilt—unless, more unhappily, they both acknowledge the guilt and do not consider it in need of correction.

I also found it laughable that he says, “If it should be necessary to ask for pardon,” imagining, clearly, that he would then necessarily need to ask pardon for his sin if we granted him permission not to cease sinning—or even, God forbid, if we consented to sin along with him. I do not know among what prodigies of the world such a statement could be admitted.

A past fault may be forgiven, certainly with correction following. But if an enduring perversity is contrived [variant: “is represented”] for the future, then the remission does not show the kindness of the one who forgives, but the consent [note variant: “announcement”] of the one who assents [variant: “flatters”].

It is no wonder that they dare to blaspheme the see of the blessed apostle Peter, who either harbor such monstrosities in their hearts or pour them forth from their mouths, and who in addition declare us proud because the first see does not refuse to offer them whatever there is of mercy [variants: “does not cease,” or “does not stop”]; yet they confidently suppose that they can subject that see to themselves by their very insolent spirit. But it is no wonder that the mentally captive do these things. Thus the insane are accustomed to regard physicians as enemies, and either to attack or strike them [variant: “even those who treat them”].

**[Note: Pope Nicholas cites this passage, as well as others from this same letter, in his letter to the Emperor Michael. HARDUIN.]**

Nevertheless, I ask them where the judgment they claim can be conducted: among themselves, so that they may be at once the enemies, the witnesses, and the judges? Human affairs ought not to be entrusted to such a judgment, much less the integrity of divine law.

If, insofar as religion is concerned, the supreme judgment over the whole Church is owed, according to the canons, only to the apostolic see; and if, insofar as secular power is concerned, that power ought to acknowledge divine matters from the pontiffs—and especially from the vicar of blessed Peter—not itself judge or adjudicate them; then no one, however powerful in the world—provided that he is nevertheless a Christian—dares to claim this for himself, unless perhaps he is persecuting religion.

What, though, would they say if they were not defeated in every respect by their own writings? Let them therefore keep their absurdities to themselves, unless they come to their senses, remembering instead that Christ’s declaration was not empty: he asserted that the gates of hell would never prevail against the confession of the blessed apostle Peter (Matthew 16).

Therefore we do not fear that the apostolic sentence will be annulled, since it is supported by the voice of Christ, the tradition of our forefathers, and the authority of the canons [**[Note: Supply “of the Nicene canons.” HARDUIN.]**], so that it may itself always judge the whole Church.

Let them think more carefully, if they possess any religious understanding, lest, refusing in any way to lay aside their perversity, they be condemned before God and men by the perpetual constitution of the apostolic see.

It is said that this was determined so that nothing further should be said about the matter, as though even now I had undertaken to address them personally in my own name, as you know. Nor should an engagement be entered into with these uncorrected men, just as combat with adherents of other heresies must likewise be refused.

As for you, we continually ask the Divinity in our prayers that you may return here safe and sound as quickly as possible.

# LETTER V. TO HONORIUS, BISHOP OF DALMATIA

**[Column 0030D]**

He warns him not to permit the Pelagian heresy, detested by so many pontiffs, to revive.

**To his most beloved brother Honorius, Gelasius.**

Although, amid the various difficulties of the times and our continual duties, we can scarcely draw breath, nevertheless, for the governance of the apostolic see, we attend without interruption to the care of the entire Lord’s flock, which was entrusted to blessed Peter by the voice of our Savior himself: “And when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers” (Luke 22). And again: “Peter, do you love me? Feed my sheep” (John 21).

We can neither conceal nor ought we to disregard whatever form of concern touches our solicitude, since we feel and say with the blessed apostle Paul: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I am not inflamed?” (2 Corinthians 11).

Thus a sudden, grievous, dreadful, and scarcely credible report has overwhelmed us, confounding, wounding, and afflicting our mind. For it has been announced to us that in the regions of Dalmatia certain people have sown the tares of the Pelagian plague anew, and that their blasphemy has gained such strength there that they deceive the simple by insinuating a deadly madness.
