That error is all the more dangerous in its ability to steal upon people because it is more cunning in deceiving them through the appearance of plausibility. Yet, by the Lord’s favor, the pure truth of the Catholic faith is present, drawn from the concordant judgments of all the Fathers. It exposes the subtle poison of destructive depravity and brings to the human race, for its salvation, medicine compounded from the Scriptures.

Therefore let hearts not yet endowed with an abundance of discernment not be disturbed in any way, until both the hidden wound is brought to light and the unique remedy shines forth. For however skillfully the spirit of perdition may arm itself with deception, it is both exposed and slain by the holy sword of the sovereign Spirit.

Accordingly, through your love, we exhort all the priests of the Lord there with fraternal affection: since, with the Lord instructing you, you are fighting against novel errors, you must not receive anew the perversity long ago condemned throughout the world, nor even suppose that it ought rashly to be received. Let it not dare to provoke us again, after our forefathers have suitably extinguished this heresy, so that it may openly and visibly engage us again with newly recovered strength.

Is it indeed permissible for us to dissolve what the venerable Fathers condemned, and to revive the impious doctrines which they cut away? Why, then, do we take such great precautions lest the ruin of any heresy once cast down strive to come again before the tribunal? If we endeavor to restore what our forefathers in ancient times recognized, examined, and refuted, are we not ourselves—God forbid, and the Catholic Church will never endure it—setting an example for all the adversaries of truth to rise against us?

Where is what is written: “You shall not move the boundaries of your fathers” (Deuteronomy 32); and: “Ask your fathers, and they will tell you; your elders, and they will declare it to you”? Why, then, do we reach beyond what our forefathers defined, or why is it not enough for us?

If, in our ignorance, we desire to learn something, namely, how the orthodox Fathers and elders commanded each matter either to be avoided or adapted to Catholic truth, why are these not accepted as having been decreed by them? Are we wiser than they, or shall we be able to stand with firm stability if we overturn what they established?

Or perhaps you do not know that the heresy of which we speak was long ago overthrown by the apostolic see through Innocent of blessed memory, and afterward through Zosimus, Boniface, Celestine, Sixtus, and Leo, by continuous and unceasing judgments? Nor do you know that it was condemned not only by the laws of the Catholic Church, but also by the Roman emperors, in such terms that its adherents were not permitted to have anywhere on earth a place in which to live?

All this is made known both by the acts of the Church composed in each region concerning their perversity and by the sanctions of public authority.

Behold: Catholic ears are willing to hear their doctrine, to receive their questions, to discuss their snares, and patiently to admit their blasphemies. If only they would strive to learn the books and responses of our forefathers against them! There it would be seen in every respect that there is absolutely nothing which has not been debated by these men and crushed by those Fathers with magnificent truth.

Thus all the faithful would be instructed to refute every one of their wickednesses, and nothing more would be sought. But if perhaps certain propositions drawn from their teachings should disturb unlearned minds, the doctrines of the venerable Fathers both expose all their madness and show by what remedies it may be cured. Thus, by God’s favor, when these matters have been foreseen, everything they have woven together from their system will appear both dangerous to those who pursue it and foolish to those who recognize it.

Accordingly, even if someone thinks that resistance is necessary, he does not thereby become a contradictor of the judgments of the ancients; rather, he openly and plainly declares himself an enemy of human salvation and Catholic doctrine. For this reason the vigilant care of shepherds ought all the more attentively to keep the wolves’ savagery away from the sacred flocks.

Should any harm befall the holy sheep, may it not—God forbid—condemn the negligence of the bishops, just as the expulsion of harmful beasts from the regenerated flocks has perpetually increased the rewards of their guardians.

Certainly, if—as we hope all the more—these reports have been conveyed falsely, we desire to learn this as quickly as possible, so that, while we tremble at the affliction of Christ’s members, we may rejoice all the more in their stability.

Given on the fifth day before the Kalends of August, under the consulship of Faustus [variant: “Albinus”], a man of clarissimus rank (in the year of Christ 493).

**[Note: This consular date is erroneous and spurious. No consulship of Faustus is found during the pontificate of Gelasius. It should therefore read, “under the consulship of Albinus, a man of clarissimus rank.” Or else it would have to be said that Gelasius did not begin his pontificate in the year 492, but in 490, on March 2. SEVERUS BINIUS.]**

# LETTER VI. TO THE SAME HONORIUS, BISHOP OF DALMATIA

He writes that Honorius ought not to have been surprised that Gelasius warned him to remain vigilant lest the Pelagian heresy should proliferate again.

**To his most beloved brother Honorius, Gelasius.**

We are surprised that your Love was surprised that the care of the apostolic see—which, following the custom of our forefathers, is owed to all the Churches throughout the world—was concerned also for the faith of your region.

When it was reported to that see that certain people throughout Dalmatia were striving to corrupt Catholic integrity and to introduce again the poison of the Pelagian plague, already condemned by divine and human laws, we did not think that the matter should be postponed in any way. We wished, by investigating it more carefully, either to heal it promptly if it had indeed crept in, or, if the reports proved false, to relieve our anxiety, judging that it was better for us to appear impatient in investigating such things than, through silence, to allow the danger to grow.

For we ought neither to suppress a matter of this kind in silence nor to foster it by delay. Since the teacher of the nations says, “Do not be sluggish in diligence” (Romans 12), and again, “He who presides, with diligence,” they would unquestionably convict us if we did not immediately investigate the matter, even if it had been reported without basis.

Nor does it matter by whom the report reached our ears. Once it had penetrated our conscience, no matter how the matter was reported, our pastoral watch ought not to have been negligent in investigating it truthfully, so that either we might at once confront wolves lying in wait, or, if no beasts were present, the protection of the sheep might continue in security.

The Apostle testifies that he learned of the dissensions among the Corinthians from those of Chloe (1 Corinthians 14), and he did not delay writing immediately, so that either the pious physician might come to the aid of quarrels at their birth, or he might soon rejoice upon learning of their safety. We likewise remember that we indicated this in the letter written on the matter, so that we might either resist the madness as it crept in or, if none of these things had occurred at all, rejoice in the integrity of Catholic truth.

Therefore your Love ought not merely to be disturbed by our vigilance. Rather, having received the greeting of this present conversation, join your own diligence with ours, so that, if such things have been attempted, they may immediately be corrected, or, by more attentive precaution, they may be unable to enter through any stealthy incursion.

But if those whom your Charity has sent wish to be more fully instructed, the following headings, together with their responses, will make the matter known. And since, as they stated beforehand, they have so far professed agreement with these matters that they affirmed they had held them from the beginning, but wished them to be more clearly explained before they were called into question, we have endeavored, insofar as was possible amid the duties that scarcely allow us to draw breath, by the Lord’s favor and following the footsteps of our fathers, not to remain silent about such matters.

Whoever follows this rule of sober judgment with a faithful heart ought rightly to be counted among the orthodox. Whoever thinks it should be rejected should understand that he is exiled from the apostolic teachings. Certainly, if there is anything capable of disturbing the mind, let your Fraternity confidently seek our advice, so that, with the Lord’s grace supplying assistance, fraternal discussion may dispel every uncertainty of obscurity.

**[Note: This circular letter was sent to all the bishops located in Picenum. In it he greatly laments that the Pelagian heresy had begun to grow strong in that same province. It was sent through Romulus, cardinal deacon of the Holy Roman Church. In it he enumerates and refutes three Pelagian propositions. The first is that an elderly, disreputable, and uneducated itinerant preacher denied that infants are afflicted with original sin and made subject to it. The second is that children cannot be condemned without baptism. The third was that a human being, with free will aided by nature itself, could be made blessed, and he said that free will possessed such great power that, if one wished, one could even consort with young women without God’s help, touch them, and nevertheless remain undefiled. Therefore, when he had proposed the lascivious pleasures of the flesh, in the manner of heretics, as a means of accepting the aforementioned heresies, and had spread the net of the flesh which they customarily use to capture the beasts of the earth, it was necessary to exercise this paternal admonition and pastoral vigilance, notwithstanding fear of the emperor Anastasius, the Eutychian, and of the Arian king Theodoric, who was ruling in Italy. SEVERUS BINIUS.]**

# LETTER VII. TO ALL THE BISHOPS THROUGHOUT PICENUM

**[Column 0033D]**

He refutes the three principal doctrines of the Pelagian heresy. First, that infants are born without original sin. Second, that they are not condemned on account of original sin alone. Third, that grace is not necessary for salvation and is bestowed according to human merits.

**Bishop Gelasius sends greetings in the Lord to all the bishops throughout Picenum.**
We had hitherto especially lamented that the provinces nearest the City were being devastated by barbarian incursions and ravaged by the savage storms of war. But from what we have discovered amid the burning dangers of these recent calamities, the devil has inflicted a more destructive stain upon the minds of Christians than the ferocity of the enemy has inflicted upon their bodies. This evil principally concerns the priests of those regions, who, having undertaken their ministry with such sluggishness and such dissimulation of their office, neglect the governance of the souls entrusted to them, so that they even allow those souls to be torn apart with impunity by the smallest beasts, as it were, before their own eyes. Indeed, by fostering creeping wickedness and yielding to the faithful’s corrupters, they not only fail utterly to restrain them but even provide them with the very nourishment of their destruction by their example.

What, then, would such bishops do if—God forbid—some new plague, previously unknown, should break out, or if men of sharper intellect, more crafty judgment, or skillful in some secular learning should bring forth sacrilegious blasphemies? They do not recall or refute the worn-out inventions of an error so ancient, which have been convicted both by the greatest teachers of the Churches and in our own age; nor do they reject what has been uttered by ignorant and foolish men.

We give thanks to almighty God, because through such persons he tests the hearts of his own people—men who do not even know what poison they are uttering. For what would the leaders of the peoples do against more cunning enemies, when they willingly submit themselves to the unlearned? Even if the guardians of the Lord’s flock were possessed of such utter incompetence that they could neither understand nor restrain so base and dull a person, they ought rather, with pastoral care, to have sought from us information about matters that needed to be known than rashly to submit their will to absurd persuasions.

A pitiable old man named Seneca was brought before us [Note: A bishop, since he is said later to have deprived a presbyter of communion. HARDUINUS.]. He is not merely estranged from all learning but wholly alien even to ordinary understanding. In the filth of the Pelagian abyss, like one of the frogs whom we read of in the Apocalypse (chapter XVI), he has shamelessly plunged and horribly wallowed; and he can find no way at all to emerge from it. For, abandoning the purity of Catholic truth, the more he tries to raise himself by the slippery path of falsehood, the more he is enclosed and overwhelmed by its muddy pits. He is one of those of whom the apostle Peter says:

> “But these men, like irrational animals, creatures of instinct, born for capture and destruction, blaspheming in matters of which they are ignorant, will perish in their own corruption, receiving the reward of unrighteousness” (II Peter II).

Indeed, his mind is so stupid and dull that, concerning the poisons he has wickedly swallowed and vomited forth, he is wholly incapable either of grasping any explanation or of giving one. Hardened by diabolical blindness and already handed over to himself, he has been condemned by the deadly obstinacy of his heart. Nothing remains for him except that our God—who said that what appears impossible to human beings is easy with him (Matthew XIX)—may pierce such a mind with powerful remorse, so that, according to the blessed apostle Paul, he may recover from the devil’s snares in which he is held captive (II Timothy II), under the sentence of divine judgment.

We disclosed to him many matters concerning Pelagian opinions that had never even occurred to him in dreams, making more evident what we had shown to have been convicted long ago. We also demonstrated that the very doctrines which he seemed to be bringing forward had long ago been produced by the Pelagian heretics and suitably demolished by Catholic preachers. We proved that Pelagius, Coelestius, Julian, and many other men of oratorical eloquence had been convicted in this assertion and struck down both by ecclesiastical decrees and by imperial commands [Note: Those of Honorius, Theodosius, and Constantius.]. Accordingly, we affirmed that this man could not sustain positions in which men so great and so numerous had been overthrown—men whose arguments he is unable even to understand, much less to present with comparable eloquence.

But, as has been said, a diabolical mind possessed by inspiration, having entered into the depths of evil, no longer consents to remedies (Proverbs XVIII). Therefore, from the countless kinds of blasphemy which the authors of the Pelagian heresy added, we have judged that three, which this pitiable old man has especially adopted, should not be left unmentioned, so that once they have been laid open they may be displayed more clearly and, with God destroying them, more easily seen to have been overthrown.

“They say that infants are created in their mothers’ wombs by divine workmanship. For that reason they do not think it just that God’s handiwork should be born bound to any sin without any actions of its own; and they make God unjust if infants are made guilty before they are born.”

They put forward this as the sharpest argument of their doctrine, not noticing that the first parents of the human race were created not from any parents at all but from harmless material of clay; that they were powerfully fashioned by divine skill, pure and undefiled, and made rational; and that, by their own will, they followed the deceiver, the devil, and were infected with depraved desires through the transgression.

In them, human nature sinned, and human nature became corrupt: plainly receptive of an evil it had previously not known. Having departed from what was good and right, it is evident, by the very course of subsequent events, that it fell back into an inclination toward evil and perversity. Thus constituted as the ancestors of our substance, they made themselves subject to suffering and corruption, violating the gifts of the divine creation to such an extent that they were punished by the vengeance of death. It is beyond doubt that on the very day on which they became mortal they became dead.

Accordingly, whatever these parents brought forth from their offspring is indeed God’s work according to the institution of nature, but it is not without the contagion of that evil which they drew upon themselves through their transgression. Certainly, this very contagion of evil is not God’s work. Thus the defect is not from God’s creation which nature gathered by a voluntary movement; rather, even from a nature corrupted in itself God carries out his institution according to his own creation. But creation brings forth a defect which it did not receive from the Creator’s institution, but which it itself assumed through the fall of its transgression.

For if those first human beings, born—as has been said—from no parents and formed without any contagion, were able through the course of illicit presumption to corrupt themselves and attach the work of diabolical fraud to God’s work, what wonder is it if those same corrupted beings brought forth corrupted offspring? Even though God created the human substance free in its creation, does not slavery, externally imposed under human laws, nevertheless naturally render it bound and liable? People are born subject to obligations by origin and are born bound by a condition of servitude; in being born they become obligated before they have been conceived. If this happens with matters situated outside nature, how much less surprising is it that it should happen with those in whom human substance itself is known to have been corrupted?

Accordingly, just as human substance made itself guilty through its own will, polluted by evil actions, after its sincere institution, so it produced offspring and descendants of its own nature, stained by the guilty will of its actions; for it begot offspring of the kind to which it had reduced itself through the excess of its transgression. Therefore it brings forth not only what God instituted well but also what it itself wickedly and inconsistently added.

That an inward disposition of desire can alter nature is confirmed by the authority of divine Scripture. Thus, when Jacob was feeding the flock (Genesis XXX), that flock of sheep, placed before rods marked with various colors, conceived while drinking, enticed by an emotional attraction; and it conceived what it did not possess by nature, transferring into its offspring, through what had been impressed upon its senses, what it had not received in creation.

What then took place figuratively signified what would occur in the ecclesiastical flocks; and God, foreseeing the Pelagians’ accusations and the disputes they would stir up among the faithful, prepared an understanding of the matter. Divine testimonies, the ecclesiastical sacraments themselves, and the tradition of Catholic teachers handed down from the Lord and Savior himself teach that the beginnings of human generation have been discolored.

Hence the prophet cries:

> “Who can boast that he has a pure heart, or that he is clean from sins? Not even an infant whose life upon earth is but one day” (Job XIV).

Hence Scripture likewise says:

> “Who can make clean what was conceived from unclean seed? Is it not you, who alone are?”  

And elsewhere:

> “For the seed was accursed” (Wisdom XII).

The prophet David also bears witness:

> “In iniquities I was conceived, and in sins my mother brought me forth” (Psalm L).

And if he says this, who can assert that he was begotten otherwise?

The blessed apostle Paul likewise asserts:

> “We too were once by nature children of wrath, like the rest” (Ephesians II).

Of this wrath the Gospel says:

> “Whoever believes and is baptized will have eternal life; but whoever does not believe has already been judged, and the wrath of God remains upon him” (John III).

This is the wrath of which it was said:

> “You shall surely die” (Genesis II).

The Lord Jesus Christ himself declares in a heavenly voice:

> “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (John VI).

Here we see that no one is excepted. Nor has anyone dared to say that an infant can be brought to eternal life without this saving sacrament. Without that life, it is beyond doubt that the infant will remain in perpetual death.

Why, then, is an infant enclosed within this fate if he has no sin at all? God would rather appear unjust—God forbid—if punishment were inflicted where there was no guilt. Therefore, since the infant is not held bound by any guilt arising from personal actions, nothing remains except that he has been polluted by a defective birth; and if he is not cleansed by participation in the Christian mystery, he cannot attain everlasting life.

This is why infants are exorcised and catechized. Since, in God’s work, they were well instituted in their Creator, but the work of diabolical wickedness was added, they are rescued from the power of darkness (Colossians I), as the Apostle teaches, and transferred into the portion of the Son of God and into legitimate purification.

Unless the first generation, which God instituted as good, had fallen into guilt through transgression and had become rejected, a second generation would not have been substituted. Hence the blessed apostle Paul says:

> “Just as through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death, and so death passed to all human beings, in whom all sinned”;  

and shortly afterward:

> “Therefore, just as through one transgression condemnation came upon all human beings, so through one act of righteousness justification unto life came upon all human beings” (Romans V).

Just as he says that all are condemned—namely, all who have been begotten from Adam their father—so he asserts that all are justified unto life only if they have been reborn in the mystery of Christ.

The deadly doctrine of the Pelagian heresy has been convicted by countless such testimonies both by our forefathers and now by their abundant instruction, and it can still be refuted. These things ought not to disturb simple minds; for them it is enough to believe, according to the ecclesiastical rule, what they do not understand. If anyone wishes to know more, it is appropriate to ask.

As for infants, the assertion that without holy baptism they cannot be condemned for original sin alone is a wholly impious and profane proposition. Although no Christian is unaware that infants newly born from their mothers’ wombs are baptized for the remission of sins—and the Catholic Church certainly celebrates this not deceptively but truthfully, lest she appear to lie in the heavenly sacraments—nevertheless, since they have no personal sins, it is clear that only their original sins are entirely remitted [al. “to them”].

Thus, even when only those sins are remitted, they obtain eternal life through baptism. It follows that, when those sins alone are not remitted, they cannot attain eternal life. Hence the Lord, as we said above, says—and this obviously applies only to the baptized:

> “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (John VI).

But to be without everlasting life means nothing other than to be placed in eternal death. Although the kingdom of heaven is the same as eternal life, nevertheless, so that God’s providence might cut off all the Pelagians’ wickedness, it was not only said:

> “Unless one is reborn of water and the Holy Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (John III);

it was also said in the same way:

> “Unless he eats the flesh of the Son of Man and drinks his blood, he will not have life in himself.”

No one doubts that this was said of eternal life, since many who do not eat this sacrament appear to possess the present life.

[Col. 0038B]

They therefore have nothing to say: that unreborn infants are unable to enter the kingdom of heaven alone, but are not punished by eternal damnation, since without baptism they can neither eat nor drink the body and blood of Christ. Without these they could not have life in themselves; and without life they can be nothing other than dead.

[Note: Perhaps “Let them not be called.” HARDUIN.]

Let them therefore say that they are placed in eternal death if they do not consider them condemned. Let them remove from their midst this unknown third place which they invent for deceiving infants. And since we read only of the right side and the left, let them not leave them without baptism in the region on the left, but let them allow the baptized, through sacred regeneration, to be transferred to the saving right hand.

In the third chapter they continue to spread the Pelagians’ delusions, now known and convicted throughout the world. They say that human beings can be made blessed through free will—which they corrupted, defiled, and lost—with the support of the goodness of nature. Yet human beings could not have been expelled from the blessedness of paradise, where their substance had been established as good, except by losing their own good. Thus they became mortal because they had passed through transgression from good to evil and had transferred themselves from participation in God to diabolical crimes.

Therefore, they were rightly made subject to their deceiver, whom they had willingly obeyed; they were excluded from the love of their own happiness and condemned by a heavenly voice to thorns, thistles, and manifold miseries. Such punishment, plainly the result of a just judgment, could never have been inflicted upon one who persevered in the good; and it would not have been imposed unless it had been shown to be fitting for evil.

Behold: without divine assistance—which, while placed in that blessedness, he is never read to have sought—not only was natural goodness unable to help human beings, not only did it fail to make them blessed; but when they trusted in that alone and did not return to its giver, they both lost blessedness and took the beginning of every evil.

As for their attaining blessedness through free will, by the wicked use of which they fell back into perpetual slavery, it is written:

> “Whoever commits sin is the slave of sin” (John II, 34).

For by whatever a person is overcome, to that he is also assigned as a slave.

Is this not that natural presumption which descended into the rights of detestable captivity, as Holy Scripture recalls?

> “A heavy yoke is upon the sons of Adam from the day they leave their mother’s womb until the day of burial in the mother of all” (Ecclesiasticus XL).

The human race was redeemed from this only by our Lord Jesus Christ, through the exchange of his passion, and he rescued us by changing our birth. He alone came to seek and save what had been lost (Matthew XVIII), so that the freedom which had been cast down through reckless pride might be restored and repaired through grace. In corresponding fashion, just as the will of the human being, by following the devil, had merited everlasting captivity, so, by following the author of restored freedom, it might return to the reward it had lost.

Hence the Lord himself says:

> “When the Son has set you free, then you will truly be free.”

And the blessed apostle Paul explains:

> “When you were slaves of sin, you were free from righteousness”—that is, alienated from righteousness—“but when you were freed from sin, you became slaves of righteousness” (Romans VI).

And again the same Apostle says:

> “The freedom with which Christ has set you free” (Galatians V).

Does not the chosen vessel himself affirm and say:

> “It is God who works in you both to will and to accomplish according to his good pleasure” (Philippians II)?

This was said so that God would not be thought to work both willing and accomplishing in an evil will.

But the Pelagians’ distinctive and long-worn poison is the belief that God’s grace can be bestowed according to human merits. May this be far from Christian minds, since the Apostle testifies:

> “Grace is given freely; otherwise, if grace comes from works, it is no longer grace” (Romans XI),

because a payment is rendered not freely, whereas grace receives its name from being freely bestowed.

What Christian would dare to say that he possesses anything good without grace, when the teacher of the nations cries out, briefly gathering all gifts into himself:

> “By the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace toward me was not in vain” (I Corinthians XV)?

He showed that the gift of grace had not been preceded by himself but that he had followed after it; and he demonstrated that he was a co-worker with grace by following it:

> “But I labored more than all of them” (ibid.).

And again, fearing that he might appear to presume upon himself, he added:

> “Not I, but the grace of God with me.”

He did not say, “I and the grace of God with me,” but placed grace before himself and then added what followed.

What, indeed, can be possessed without grace, when faith itself comes through grace, as the same Apostle teaches?

> “I received mercy so that I might be faithful” (I Timothy I).

And divine mercy is nothing other than grace.

Let us also hear how he instructs the Church:

> “By grace you have been saved through faith” (Ephesians II).

He thereby explained that the beginning of salvation and faith came from grace, as he immediately adds:

> “And this is not from yourselves; it is the gift of God, not from works, so that no one may boast” (ibid.).

The same Apostle elsewhere makes a general and absolute declaration:

> “What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (I Corinthians IV).

Who could be sufficient to enumerate each testimony? They clearly show that the choice of natural freedom does not earn grace, but rather receives grace, so that it may be mercifully released from the slavery it had deserved through sin.

Prepared by eternal providence before the foundation of the world through the redemption of this mystery, whether before the Law had been given or under the observance of the Law, the ancient condition of all holy men and women was cleansed by figurative signs and sacrifices. Through the Spirit of grace, the remedies of eternal salvation were granted to all the righteous, who worshiped this mystery from afar. Its fullness, manifested to the nations in Christ, purifies and renews the world and truly makes human beings participants in everlasting blessedness.

Therefore we severely reproach our brothers and fellow bishops, especially those governing the Church throughout the provinces of Picenum. They not only failed to restrain the perverse conversation of a most foolish old man and a contemptible person but even nourished it by their consent.

Who could hear of it? Who could tolerate that bishops allowed some unworthy corpse of a man to deprive of communion a presbyter who was unwilling to comply with him? How was such a person either received by anyone or patiently heard? Moreover, he issued laws, gladly accepted [Note: Perhaps “laws received.” HARDUIN.], by which servants of God were to mingle with consecrated girls in a most disgraceful association. For if spiritual minds, even when such companionships are absent, are harassed by imagined enticements, how much more are they stirred by the sight of the other sex, even when unwillingly and illicitly [Note: Perhaps “even if illicitly.” HARDUIN.]?

A still greater crime was added: in the sight and presence of priests he attempted to tear apart blessed Jerome and Augustine, the lights of ecclesiastical teachers, like a dying fly, as it is written, destroying the oil of sweetness (Ecclesiasticus X).

But why should we wonder that the leaders of the Churches neglect these things, when—as we have heard from many—it is evident that they do everything contrary to the canons and indiscriminately confuse all things contrary to apostolic discipline (I Corinthians XIV)? They ordain without observing the rules; and they permit not only monks but also ministers of the Church to depart with women for foreign places and return again, and to be advanced by other bishops into clerical service.

Since not one of these things ought to be tolerated, who could endure so many and such crimes being committed? By rightly providing a spectacle to pagans, Jews, and heretics, they seem to be working toward the destruction of religion itself—God forbid. The Apostle’s sentence can rightly be applied to those who do such things:

> “For the name of God is blasphemed among the nations because of you” (Romans II).

Let it therefore be enough that these offenses have occurred thus far, and let divine matters now be attended to more carefully so that God may be appeased in human affairs.

Let the advocate of the aforesaid plague be found nowhere at all; let him find no access to a church or participation anywhere in Catholic communion if, by his impious profession, he prefers to follow the fellowship of heretics. Those with whom he is shown previously to have mingled in harmful conversation are likewise to be removed from ecclesiastical service and punished with devoted vengeance unless they repent and withdraw from his society, so that an example may be provided to the rest for avoiding such conduct. Let him approach no one, and let him no longer be permitted anywhere to speak the blasphemy once condemned.

With the dwellings of men and women kept separate, as a holy commitment requires, let vigilant devotion be practiced.

Contrary to the canonical enactments, no one is to be admitted [al. “promoted”] to ecclesiastical office (Nicaea IX, 10). The rulers of each province must understand that they will not obtain pardon for past errors if thereafter they neglect to avoid what has been exposed. No opportunity for excuse will remain if, after these present commands—which we have decided to send through the deacon Romulus, whose diligence on behalf of the Catholic faith and religion we most gratefully approve—any bishop is found to be either contemptuous or negligent in all these matters.

For just as it belongs to the administration of the apostolic see to provide every Church appropriately with the care it owes, so it is necessary that it not conceal the power divinely entrusted to it against the obstinate and negligent.

Given on the Kalends of November, in the consulship of Albinus, a man of illustrious rank (A.D. 493).

[Note: When the envoys of King Theodoric returned from Constantinople toward the end of the year 493 and reported to Pope Gelasius what they had received from the emperor Anastasius, Gelasius himself composed this apologetic letter to the same Anastasius. It is cited in the capitularies of the Frankish kingdom, book V, chapter 167. By this letter he could not persuade Anastasius, once the obstacle had been removed, to restore unity and peace to the Churches. Euphemius opposed him, asserting that the apostolic see was exercising vengeance because it had been despised by Acacius rather than defending justice. It is inferred that the letter was written in the third year of Gelasius’s pontificate, which was A.D. 494, because at that time Anastasius had not yet openly declared himself a heretic Eutychian and standard-bearer of the Acephali sect; it is known that in the following year he fully vomited forth the poison concealed in his breast. SEV. BINIUS.]

## LETTER VIII. TO THE EMPEROR ANASTASIUS

After first explaining why he had not written to the emperor, he urges him to obey the apostolic see and, with the name of Acacius condemned, to take care that peace be restored to the Churches.

[Note: In another copy: “Gelasius, bishop, to the most glorious emperor Anastasius.”]

Gelasius, bishop, to Anastasius Augustus.

The servants of Your Piety, my sons Faustus, master, and Irenaeus, illustrious men, together with their companions, while carrying out a public embassy and having returned to the City, said [or: are said] to have sought Your Clemency, asking why I had not sent you written greetings [Col. 0041C]. It was not according to my usual practice, I confess; but when those recently sent from the regions of the East to see me had spread throughout the entire City that permission to do so had been denied them by your instructions, I thought I ought to refrain from writing, lest I should prove burdensome rather than dutiful. You see, therefore, that this did not result from any dissimulation on my part, but from the prudence appropriate to the circumstances, lest I impose annoyance upon minds that rejected me.

But when I learned from the aforesaid informants of Your Serenity’s benevolence, namely, that you had graciously desired a conversation with my humility, I truly realized [the very ancient manuscript of the Chapter of Verona, with which this letter was collated, reads “reputandum,” “to be reckoned”] that I would rightly be blamed if I remained silent; for, glorious son, as one born a Roman [the same manuscript reads “and as”], I love, honor, and welcome [the same manuscript reads “I esteem”] you as a Roman ruler [or: I love, honor, and welcome you as one born at Rome] [Col. 0041D]. And as a Christian, I desire, together with one who has zeal for God, to have [an object is absent] according to knowledge of the truth [Col. 0041D; Hardouin suggests: “to have peace”]. And as the representative of the apostolic see, however unworthy, whatever I discover to be lacking in the fullness of the Catholic faith, I strive, according to my ability, to supply through appropriate recommendations [variant: “that wherever [something is] fully …”].

For since the administration of the divine word has been entrusted to me, woe is me if I do not preach the gospel (1 Cor. 9)! If blessed Paul the Apostle, the chosen vessel, feared and cried out this, I, a very insignificant man, must fear it much more if I were to withhold the ministry of preaching inspired by God and transmitted with paternal devotion [Col. 0042D; the same manuscript reads: “inspired … transmitted”]. I beg Your Piety not to judge the duty imposed by divine reason as arrogance. May it be far from a Roman ruler to regard truth disclosed to his understanding as an insult.

There are, indeed, two powers, Emperor Augustus, by which this world is chiefly governed: the sacred authority of bishops [or: consecrated authority] and royal power. [This sentence is cited in book V of the Capitularies, chapter 167, and by Hincmar, Opuscule 9, no. 39; Hardouin.] Among these, the burden of the priests is all the more serious because they will render an account before the divine judgment even for the kings themselves [Col. 0042B] [the same manuscript reads: “for human beings themselves”].

For you know, most merciful son, that although you preside over the human race by the dignity of your office, nevertheless you devoutly bow your neck to those who preside over divine affairs, and you seek from them the means of your salvation [or: await them]. In receiving the heavenly sacraments and in arranging them—as is proper—you recognize that you ought to be subject to them, by the order of religion, rather than preside over them.

You know, therefore, in these matters that you depend upon their judgment, not that they are to be reduced to your will. For if, insofar as concerns the order of public discipline, the religious leaders themselves, recognizing that the empire has been conferred upon you by heavenly appointment, obey your laws lest they appear to oppose your judgment even in worldly matters, with what disposition, I ask, ought you to obey those who have been appointed to administer the venerable mysteries?

Accordingly, just as a grave danger rests upon bishops if they remain silent about what is appropriate for the worship of God, so—God forbid—a considerable peril rests upon those who, although they ought to obey, despise obedience.

And if the hearts of the faithful ought rightly to submit to all priests who handle divine matters correctly, how much more ought assent to be given to the bishop of that see whom the supreme Divinity desired to place above all priests, and whom the enduring devotion of the universal Church has subsequently honored?

Here Your Piety clearly perceives that no human counsel whatsoever can raise anyone against the privilege or confession of him whom Christ’s voice placed above all, whom the venerable Church has always confessed and devoutly holds as her primate. What has been established by divine judgment may be attacked by human presumption [Col. 0042D–0043A], but it cannot be overcome by anyone’s power.

Would that audacity were not as destructive to those who resist in this way as the decree established by the very Author of sacred religion cannot be shaken by any force: “For the foundation of God stands” (2 Tim. 2).

When religion has been assailed by some, has it ever been overcome by however great an innovation [the Verona manuscript reads “quantumque”; Quesnellus reads “quacunque”], or has it not rather remained unconquered precisely when it was thought capable of collapsing? Let certain persons, therefore, cease—I beg you—from rashly pursuing in your times, under the pretext of ecclesiastical disturbance, what is not permitted [Col. 0043D; the same manuscript reads: “what is not lawful], lest they both fail utterly to obtain what they wickedly seek and fail to keep their proper measure before God and human beings.

Therefore, in the sight of God, purely and sincerely, I beseech, implore, and exhort Your Piety not to receive my petition with indignation. I ask, I say, that in this life you hear me as I plead, rather than—God forbid—find me accusing you at the divine judgment.

Nor is it unknown to me, Emperor Augustus, what Your Piety’s aspiration was during your private life. You always desired to become a sharer in the eternal promise. Therefore, I beg you, do not become angry with me if I love you so greatly that I wish you to possess perpetually the kingdom you have obtained temporarily, and that you who rule the world may reign with Christ.

Certainly, Emperor, under your laws you allow nothing to perish, and you permit no injury to be inflicted upon the Roman name [or: you allow nothing to perish for the Roman name]. Is it really true, excellent ruler, that you, who desire not only Christ’s present benefits but also those to come, would permit anyone in your times to inflict loss upon religion, truth, the sincerity of Catholic communion [Col. 0043C], and faith?

With what confidence, I ask you, will you seek there the rewards of one whose losses you do not prevent here? Do not regard as burdensome, I beg you, what is said for the sake of your eternal salvation. You have read the words: “The wounds of a friend are better than the kisses of an enemy” (Prov. 27).

I beg Your Piety to receive in your understanding what is said by me with the same affection with which it is spoken. Let no one deceive Your Piety.

Is it true what Scripture figuratively testifies through the prophet: “My dove is one, my perfect one is one” (Song 6)? There is one Christian faith, which is Catholic. But that faith is truly Catholic which is separated by a sincere, pure, and undefiled communion from all the faithless, from their successors, and from their associates [or: divided from them].

Otherwise the distinction commanded by God will not exist, but only a pitiable confusion. Nor will any reason remain, if we decide to admit this in the case of any contagion, why we should not open a way and a door to all heresies. “Whoever offends in one point is guilty of all” (Jas. 2); and, “Whoever despises small things will gradually fall” (Eccles. 19).

This is what the apostolic see takes the greatest care to guard: since the glorious confession of the Apostle is the root of the world, it must not be stained by any fissure of depravity or by any contagion whatsoever. For if—may God avert it; we trust that it cannot happen—something of this kind were to occur [Col. 0044A], where would we find the courage to resist any error, or from where would we demand correction for those who err? [The same manuscript reads: “or from whom would we demand correction?”]

Accordingly, if Your Piety denies that the people of one city can be reconciled in peace [the word “peace” is absent from the same manuscript], what are we to do concerning the whole community of the world if—God forbid—it should be deceived through our transgression?

If the whole world was corrected after rejecting the profane tradition of its ancestors, how can the people of one city not be corrected if trustworthy preaching [or: preaching of the faith] follows?

Therefore, glorious Emperor, I do not want the peace of the Churches [variant: “I do not neglect”], which, even if it could come about at the cost of my blood, I embrace [or: shall embrace]. But I beg you: let us weigh what that peace itself ought to be, not casually, but with a truly Christian mind.

For how can there be true peace when undefiled charity is absent? The Apostle clearly teaches us how charity ought to be, saying: “Charity is from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith” (1 Tim. 1) [the same manuscript reads: “charity is preached to us by the Apostle”].

How will it be from a pure heart if it is infected by an external contagion? How from a good conscience if it has been mixed with perverse and evil things? How will it be from an unfeigned faith if it remains joined to the faithless?

Although these things have often been said by us already, they must nevertheless be repeated without ceasing and not kept silent as long as the name of peace is being put forward. Thus our task is not—as is maliciously alleged—to make peace, but to teach what kind of peace we desire: the kind that alone can be peace, and beyond which no peace exists [the same manuscript reads: “and that there is no peace apart from it”].

If the Eutychian doctrine, against which the vigilant caution of the apostolic see keeps watch, is believed capable of standing in the truth without injury to the Catholic faith, let it be brought forward, asserted, and defended with however much strength, so that it may be shown not only how hostile it is to the Christian faith in itself, but also how many deadly heresies it contains in its own pollution.

But if—as we trust more strongly—it is judged by Catholic minds to be excluded, I ask you why you do not likewise decree that the contagions of those who are shown to have been polluted by it must be rejected, since the Apostle says that not only those who do what ought not to be done are considered guilty, but also those who consent to those who do it (Rom. 1)?

Accordingly, just as, once a participant in perversity has been accepted, perversity itself cannot fail to be approved as well, so perversity cannot be rejected if its complicit follower is admitted.

Under your laws, certainly, those who are conscious of crimes and those who receive robbers are bound by the same judicial penalty; nor is someone considered free from the crime who, although he did not commit it himself, nevertheless accepted the friendship and alliance of the one who committed it.

Accordingly, when the Council of Chalcedon, convened for the truth and communion of the Catholic and apostolic faith, condemned Eutyches, the author of detestable madness, it was not satisfied unless it also struck down his associate Dioscorus and the others along with him.

In this same manner, as it has always either happened or is clearly established to happen in every heresy, his successors Timothy, Peter, and the other Peter of Antioch were subsequently struck down, not individually through another council held separately for each one, but in accordance with the rule established once by the synod [the same manuscript reads: “consequently struck down by the rule of the council that had been held”].

How, then, is it not evident that all who have followed the same pattern are likewise bound, and that those who became their communicants and accomplices, indeed all of them, are rightly separated from Catholic and apostolic communion?

For this reason we also rightly say that Acacius must be removed from our fellowship. He preferred to pass over into the lot of faithlessness rather than stand firm in the sincerity of Catholic and apostolic communion, although for nearly three years he is shown to have been suitably instructed by letters from the apostolic see not to come to this point [Col. 0045D; the years 478, 479, and 480 are given; Liberatus, chapter 18, reckons the period differently. Hardouin]. The beginning of this three-year period should be referred to the fifteenth year of Simplicius, when Acacius committed the offense, as is evident above in the notes on Simplicius’s letters 15 and 17. [Severus Binius.]

Once he had become alien to communion, he could immediately be cut off from Catholic and apostolic fellowship [the year 484 is given], lest, if we delayed even slightly because of him, we too should appear to have undergone the contagions of the faithless.

But, having been struck by such a punishment, did he truly come to his senses, promise correction, and amend his error? Or had that treatment intended to restrain him more gently, when he did not even feel harsh blows? Since he died [or: remained] in his faithlessness and condemnation, his name cannot be entered in the ecclesiastical recitation any more than the contagion of external communion ought to be admitted.

Therefore, either let it be shown that he was innocent of the heretical participation into whose communion he mixed himself, or he cannot fail to be rejected together with them.

But if the bishops of the East murmur that the apostolic see did not write this letter to them [the Verona manuscript reads “Qui si”; the printed text contains an apparent typographical “0”], as though either they themselves had informed the apostolic see by their letters that Peter had been lawfully received, or they had not already likewise become accomplices in this irregular reception, then, just as they truly cannot prove that he had been cleansed of heretical depravity, so they will in no way be able to excuse themselves as associates of heretics.

If perhaps they assert that all of them reported the reception of Peter by Acacius to the apostolic see with a united voice [the same manuscript reads: “by unanimous will”], then by that same man they all understand themselves to have received a reply with one voice.

The authority of the apostolic see [variant: “the primatial authority of the apostolic see”], however—that it has been placed before the whole Church throughout all Christian ages—is confirmed both by the sequence of the ancestral canons and by manifold tradition.

But whether anyone may usurp anything against the decrees of the Council of Nicaea can be demonstrated from the fellowship of a single communion, not disclosed to the minds of an external association [the same manuscript reads: “or whether”].

If anyone among them has confidence, let him come forward and both refute and instruct the apostolic see concerning both sides.

Let the name that causes the Churches’ separation from Catholic communion be removed from their midst, so that sincere peace and the unity of faith and communion may be restored. Then let it be properly and lawfully investigated which of us has risen up, or is trying to rise up, against venerable antiquity.

There it will become clear who, with a modest purpose, guards the form and tradition of the ancestors, and who, insolently leaping beyond these bounds, thinks that by robbery he can make himself an equal.

But if the person of the people of Constantinople is brought forward, and it is said that the name of the scandal—that is, Acacius—cannot be removed, I remain silent, because the people of Constantinople, after the heretic Macedonius had once been expelled and Nestorius had recently been ejected, chose to remain Catholic rather than be held by affection for condemned bishops of earlier times.

I remain silent about the fact that those who had been baptized by those same condemned bishops, while remaining in the Catholic faith, were not disturbed by any agitation.

I remain silent about the fact that even now Your Piety’s authority has restrained popular uprisings over childish matters [Col. 0046B]. For this reason the multitude of the city of Constantinople must obey you all the more necessarily for the salvation of their souls, if you, as rulers, restore it to Catholic and apostolic communion.

For, Emperor Augustus, if someone should attempt anything against the public laws—God forbid—you could not tolerate it by any means. Do you not think that it concerns your conscience to bring the people subject to you back to a pure and sincere devotion to the Divinity?

Finally, if the disposition of the people of one city is not thought likely to be offended lest divine matters be corrected as circumstances require, how much more must we neither harm nor be able to harm the devout faith of the entire Catholic name, lest divine things be offended?

And yet those same people ask to be healed by our will. Let them therefore permit themselves to be treated with suitable remedies; otherwise—God forbid—as we pass over into their destruction, we may perish with them, but we cannot save them.

At this point I leave to your conscience, under divine judgment, which course is preferable: whether, as we desire, we may all return together to certain life, or whether, as they request, we may move openly toward death.

And still they persist in calling the apostolic see, which offers them medicinal remedies, proud and arrogant. This is often characteristic of the sick: they accuse physicians who recall them to health through suitable discipline rather than consenting to abandon or reject their own harmful desires.

If we are proud because we administer appropriate remedies for souls, what should those who resist be called? [The same manuscript reads: “who administer remedies for souls.”]

If we are proud because we say that the institutions of our fathers must be obeyed, by what name should those who oppose them be called?

If we are haughty because we desire the worship of God to be preserved in a pure and undefiled manner, let those who think even against the Divinity say what they should be called.

In the same way, the others who are in error judge us because we do not consent to their madness. But the spirit of pride truly resides and struggles on which side truth itself indicates [or: judges].

## Letter IX. To the Bishops of Lucania

Several ecclesiastical regulations are explained.

[In the very ancient Luccan manuscript no. 490, this title is given as follows: “Gelasius, bishop, to all bishops established in each province.” Mansi.]

To the most beloved brothers, all the bishops established throughout Lucania, Bruttium, and Sicily: Gelasius.

## Titles of the Decrees of Pope Gelasius

I. Concerning ecclesiastical institutions, to be adjusted according to the circumstances of the times.

II. That where no pressing necessity exists, the decrees of the Fathers are to be preserved inviolate; or, when clerics are lacking, that they be chosen from among the monks.

III. That if any laymen are chosen for the clerical order, the matters stated concerning monks are to be investigated in them with much greater care.

IV. That new basilicas be dedicated by bishops at the command of the pope.

V. That no fees [read: prices] be demanded for baptizing and confirming the faithful. Whoever perpetrates this shall be subject to the peril of his rank.

VI. That priests observe the proper measure, neither make chrism nor perform confirmation; that, in the presence of any bishop, they presume neither to pray nor to sit unless ordered by him; and that they neither appoint an acolyte nor a subdeacon.

VII. Likewise, that deacons preserve their proper measure according to the decrees of the Fathers.

VIII. That deacons may not sit in the presbytery, nor, when priests are present, usurp the privilege of distributing the sacred Body.

IX. That the apostolic see guards the ancestral canons with pious and devoted care.

X. That, apart from the season of Easter and Pentecost, no one presume to baptize, except those whom extreme illness has compelled.

XI. That the ordinations of priests and deacons may be celebrated at appointed times.

XII. That virgins be consecrated on the prescribed days.

XIII. That widows not be veiled.

XIV. That no bishop or head of a church or monastery defend, under the religious name, a slave or a person bound by hereditary status against the will of his masters; whoever attempts this shall incur the peril of his rank and communion.

XV. That clerics pursue no dishonorable business or shameful profit.

XVI. That no one ignorant of letters, or mutilated in any part of the body, be advanced to the clergy.

XVII. Concerning those who mutilate themselves.

XVIII. That criminals cannot be promoted to the clergy; and that those already in the clergy, if found guilty of any offenses, be barred from their offices.

XIX. That those entangled in demonic or other afflictions may not handle the sacred ministries.

XX. That those who join themselves to sacred virgins and enter into incestuous unions cannot communicate unless perhaps they have performed public penance.

XXI. That widows, as stated above, not be veiled. And if, after professing continence, they violate it by changing their purpose, they themselves must render an account for it [or: to the Lord].

XXII. That second marriages are not denied to laypeople, although such persons are by no means permitted to enter the clergy.

XXIII. That if anyone receives a deserter from his own church and advances him to some dignity, they shall certainly be subject to the sentence imposed by the canons.

XXIV. That if monks or laymen are chosen for the clergy, when no necessity compels it, the ancient institutions must be observed in them. If they are proved to have purchased a sacred dignity for a price, they are to be deposed from office, for the crime of Simon Magus implicates both the giver and the receiver.

XXV. Concerning newly established sacred places. Although this was stated above, the following is now added: no basilica is to be dedicated under the name of the dead.

XXVI. That it is unlawful for women to serve at sacred altars or to presume to undertake anything assigned to the offices of men.

XXVII. That in every church over which a bishop presides, four portions are to be made both from revenues and from the offerings of the faithful: one for the bishop, another for the clergy, a third for the poor, and a fourth to be applied to the fabric of the church.

XXVIII. That if a bishop, priest, or deacon is truthfully accused by any cleric of having acted against these regulations, he may without hesitation be struck down; and the bishop shall also incur the peril of his honor if he has kept silent about all these matters that the Church ought to know.

## Chapter I

[This chapter is also cited by Pope Nicholas in Letter 8 to Emperor Michael; Hardouin.] We are constrained by the necessary dispensation [the Luccan manuscript reads “arrangement”; variants: “discussion” or “arrangement”] of affairs and bound by the moderation of the apostolic see to weigh the decrees of the ancestral canons and measure them against the instructions of bishops and our predecessors, so that, after careful consideration, we may temper, as far as possible, whatever the necessity of present times demands should be relaxed for the restoration of the Churches.

In this way we will neither appear wholly to depart from the form of the ancient rules nor fail to provide for the restoration of the offices of the clerical service, which the attacks of war and famine have so consumed throughout various parts of Italy that, as we have learned from the frequent reports of our brother and fellow bishop John, priest of the Church of Ravenna, in many churches the service of ministers has completely failed [or: the ministry has completely failed]. Unless the intervals formerly fixed for ecclesiastical promotions are relaxed for a short time—without which they cannot administer—the Churches remain entirely deprived of sacred orders; and in very many places, because of the lack of suitable assistance, the saving aid of redeeming souls is absent [Col. 0049A]. We would also be involved in great guilt if, under the pressure of so grave a danger, we did not in some measure provide a remedy [the same manuscript reads “consulamus,” “we may provide”]. [The same manuscript also reads “had consumed” and “nothing” at the preceding textual points.]

## Chapter II

[This chapter is cited by Pope Nicholas in Letter 2 to Emperor Michael, although some readings there differ from these; Hardouin.]

Let the ancient regulations therefore remain in force out of reverence for them, and let them be regularly observed wherever no distress of circumstances or times presses upon us. But for churches that are either entirely deprived of ministers or so stripped of adequate service that they cannot supply divine gifts to the congregations belonging to them, we grant permission to arrange the periods both for examining and for advancing clerical service [the same manuscript reads: “for instituting”].

If someone trained in a religious way of life and in monastic disciplines should enter the clerical office, his life in past times must first be investigated: whether he is shown to be infected by no serious crime; whether perhaps he has not had a second wife, and is not shown to have taken as his lot a woman abandoned [or: rejected] by her husband; whether perhaps he has not performed public penance; whether he does not appear to be impaired in any part of his body; whether he is not subject to slave or hereditary status; whether he is already shown to have been freed from the bonds of municipal office [or: even from them]; whether he has learned letters, without which he could scarcely fulfill even the ministry of doorkeeper.

If he is supported by all the qualifications mentioned above, let him immediately become a lector, notary, or certainly a defender; after three months, let him become an acolyte, especially if age also supports his candidacy; in the sixth month let him receive the name of subdeacon; and if he proves to possess modest conduct and honorable purpose, in the ninth month let him become a deacon; and after the completion of a year, a priest. Nevertheless, it must be shown that the devotion voluntarily undertaken through his holy purpose has supplied what the intervals of years would otherwise have contributed.

## Chapter III

But if a layman is to be added to the ecclesiastical offices, his person ought to be examined in each of the matters set forth above with that much greater care in proportion to the difference known to exist between worldly and religious life. For the appropriate ministries of the Church must be restored, not imposed upon unsuitable merits; and the more that the institutions of those who are fit for sacred service must be sought, the more time must be taken away from the period in which these things would ordinarily have been attained [or: the more must be taken from the time in which these things would ordinarily have been attained].

His integrity of character must be shown to possess what a longer habit has not conferred, lest, under the pretext of supplying the clerical shortage, we be judged to have introduced vices into divine worship rather than to have provided for the advantages of a legitimate order [the Lucan manuscript omits “be judged”]. For their promotions we nevertheless substitute six months beyond the limits of the year, since, as has been said, it is appropriate that there be a distinction between a person devoted to divine worship and one coming from lay conduct.

We have nevertheless believed this concession should be granted to the extent that the ministries of those Churches in which, because of the devastation of war, none or only a few have remained may be renewed. Once these have been restored, by God’s favor, the ancient form of the ancestral canons is to be preserved in the appointment of the ecclesiastical ranks.

No one should in any way prevail against them on the grounds that provision is being made as a remedy for an accidental deficiency, not that a new law is being proposed against the decrees of the ancestors. Other Churches, which have not been laid waste by a similar disaster, must refrain from using this as an occasion and retain the former rule when making ordinations.

The more we have been reminded by this opportunity, therefore, the more earnestly we commend observance of the venerable canons, warning the consciences of each rank not to attempt to break out into unlawful excesses.

Let no bishop suppose that it is lawful for him to attach to divine ministries bigamists, those who have taken wives abandoned by others, penitents [or: those after penance], persons without letters, those impaired [or: mutilated] in body, persons bound by servile status, those entangled in the obligations of municipal office or public affairs, or persons examined indiscriminately without waiting for the appropriate period. Nor should they strive, according to their own inclination, to invade rights belonging to others without a just disposition and command from the apostolic see.

## Chapter IV

Bishops must not dare to dedicate newly established basilicas without the customary request and commands [below, chapter 25: “by command of the apostolic see”], nor should they seek to claim for themselves clerics belonging to another’s authority.

## Chapter V

Priests must set no fees for baptizing and confirming the faithful, nor seek to harass those being reborn by imposing any exactions, since we are commanded to give freely what we have received freely (Matt. 10).

Therefore, they must make no attempt to demand anything at all from the persons mentioned above, lest, deterred either by poverty or turned back by indignation, they disdain to approach the means of their redemption. They must be certain that those who are found to have committed what is forbidden, or who have not corrected their offenses spontaneously, will incur the peril of their own rank.

## Chapter VI

We likewise forbid priests to extend themselves beyond their own measure or boldly to assume what belongs to the episcopal dignity: they must not seize for themselves the power to make chrism or to perform episcopal confirmation.

In the presence of any bishop, unless perhaps ordered to do so, they must not presume to undertake for themselves either prayer or the performance of a sacred action, nor, in his presence, unless ordered, presume either to sit or to handle the venerable mysteries [the Lucan manuscript reads: “venerable things”].

Let them remember that they are in no way permitted, without the chief bishop, to possess the right to make a subdeacon or an acolyte. Nor should they doubt that if they should undertake on their own initiative anything specially belonging to the episcopal ministry, they will immediately be deprived of the dignity of the priesthood and of sacred communion.

We judge that this must occur if such a transgression [or: presumption] is established upon the report of their bishop; nor will their own bishop be free from the guilt of connivance and from punishment if he has neglected to punish one acting immoderately.

## Chapter VII

We likewise establish that deacons are to preserve their proper measure, and we do not permit them to attempt anything beyond what the ancestral canons assigned to them (Nicaea, canon 18). They must apply nothing at all to their ministry that antiquity decreed properly to belong to the first orders.

They must not dare to baptize without a bishop or priest, unless extreme necessity should compel them when those offices are located at a considerable distance. Christian laypeople are also commonly permitted to do this.

## Chapter VIII

Deacons may not sit in the presbytery while divine rites are being celebrated or any ecclesiastical business is being conducted [or: celebrated]. They have no right to exercise the privilege of distributing the sacred Body in the presence of a bishop or priest, unless those persons are absent.

Since we too strive with the greatest care to preserve the decrees of the venerable sanctions, we believe that even those matters which might perhaps appear capable of being relaxed for the sake of some useful advantage must not be relaxed at the cost of those decrees.

## Chapter IX

Since we desire that nothing be rashly permitted to us against the reverence due to salutary rules, and since the apostolic see, superior to all these matters, strives, with the Lord’s favor, to preserve with pious and devoted purpose what has been established by the ancestral canons, it is most unworthy for any bishop or member of the subordinate orders to reject this observance, which he sees the see of blessed Peter both follow and teach.

It is most fitting that the whole body of the Church should agree with itself in this observance, which it sees flourishing where the Lord placed the primacy of the whole Church, as Scripture says: “Set your love in order within me” (Song 2). And again: “Let all things be done in order” (1 Cor. 14).

Again the psalmist proclaims: “Surround Zion and embrace her; tell it in her towers. Set your hearts upon her strength and distribute her steps, so that you may recount them to another generation, for this is God, our God forever; and he himself will rule us throughout the ages” (Ps. 47).

Without doubt, this one who is spoken of in the height of ecclesiastical dignities, and in whose strength hearts must be set through good works, with the ranks distributed, is to be proclaimed our God and ruler to all Christian peoples. Here no one should think that anything has been diminished for him, since nothing is lost from the perfection of each rank, and, by appropriately retaining what has been bestowed through heavenly dispensation, God is made known to us together and granted to us as ruler [Col. 0051D].

For even if something is granted concerning the length of time, it is compensated by the energetic excellence joined to character. If what had to be cultivated through extended age is already contained in the purpose of one’s life, provided that those things whose presence would rightly prove a person unworthy of clerical insignia do not quietly creep in through neglect [or: slip in].

Even if some things may sometimes be tolerated which, when the integrity of the others is secure, cannot harm by themselves, those things must nevertheless be guarded against with the greatest care which cannot be admitted without manifest disfigurement.

And if even those matters which are sometimes believed capable of being tolerated without harm are excused either by consideration of circumstances and times [the same manuscript omits “and times”] or by the need for accelerated provision, how much less may those things be weakened which no necessity at all, nor any ecclesiastical usefulness whatsoever, compels us to weaken?

## Chapter X

No one should imagine that he has unrestricted freedom to baptize at any time whatsoever, apart from the holy sacrament of the Easter festival and Pentecost, except solely in the event of the onset of the gravest illness. In such a case, it must be feared that, as the danger of the disease increases, the sick person may perhaps depart, overtaken by death without saving remedy.

## Chapter XI

The ordinations of priests and deacons must not be performed except at appointed seasons and days: namely, during the fast of the fourth month, the seventh, and the tenth, as well as at the beginning of Lent and on the middle day of Lent; they must know that these are to be celebrated during the fast of Saturday toward evening [the manuscript reads: “they must not dare”].

Nor, for the sake of any advantage [the word “reason” is absent from the Justinian manuscript and from the editions of 1525 and 1609], should either a priest or a deacon be preferred [or: be advanced before] those who were ordained before them.

### Chapter XII

Moreover, let them not impose the sacred veil upon virgins devoted to God except either on the day of the Epiphany [read: “of the Epiphanies”], or during the paschal festival in white garments, or on the anniversaries of the apostles; unless perhaps—as was said concerning baptism—it is not to be refused to those afflicted by serious illness who implore it, lest they depart from this world without receiving that gift.

[Note: In Codex Lucensis 490, the words “or during the paschal festival in white garments” are absent.]

[Note: Burchard, Book VIII, chapter 15, inserts “and unless they are under twenty-five years of age.” I read it thus in my manuscript codex; I do not know whether it appears in the printed editions. Mansi.]

### Chapter XIII

Let no bishop presume to veil widows, since neither divine authority delegates this power nor the canonical rule prescribes it. It must therefore not be usurped at all; rather, ecclesiastical protections are to be extended [perhaps read: “conferred” or “brought”] to them in such a way that nothing unlawful is committed.

[Note: This is also cited by Charlemagne in the Capitularies of Aachen of the year 789, chapter 59. Hardouin.]

### Chapter XIV

The presumption that gives rise to a general complaint must also be avoided: nearly everyone complains that slaves and persons bound by hereditary status, fleeing the rights and possessions [variant: “possession”] of their masters, are indiscriminately admitted—under the pretext of a religious way of life—either to monasteries or to ecclesiastical service, with bishops also conniving [variant: restraining them]. This evil must be removed by every means, lest, through the institution of the Christian name, another’s property appear to be invaded or the public order to be overthrown.

This is especially so since it is not fitting that the dignity of clerical ministry itself be stained by this obligation, and that it be forced to quarrel over the status and condition of those serving in the ranks, or, God forbid, appear liable to such a charge. Once such persons have been prohibited by an appropriately careful injunction, let every bishop, presbyter, or deacon, and likewise those known to preside over monasteries, understand that they will incur the danger of their own honor and communion if, when holding such persons among them, they judge that they should not be restored to their patrons or thereafter assigned either to ecclesiastical service or to religious communities—unless perhaps they have first been released from their obligation with the masters’ consent, under the testimony of Scripture, or have been granted by a lawful settlement—and if anyone brings a truthful complaint against us concerning this matter.

For, according to the blessed Apostle, great care must be taken lest the faith and discipline of the Lord be blasphemed (1 Timothy 6).

### Chapter XV

It consequently seemed to us that we must not pass over what a report recently sent to us from the regions of Picenum announced: namely, that very many clerics are pursuing dishonorable commercial dealings and shameful profits. They observe without any sense of shame the Gospel reading in which the Lord himself is said to have driven the merchants from the Temple after scourging them with whips (Matthew 21; John 2); nor do they recall the Apostle’s words: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular business” (2 Timothy 2).

They also disregard with deaf ears the Psalmist David singing: “Because he did not know commerce, I shall enter into the powers of the Lord” (Psalm 70).

Therefore, let them know that henceforth they must abstain from such dishonorable gains and cease from every kind of commercial enterprise or desire for it; otherwise, whatever their rank, they must immediately be compelled to withdraw from clerical offices.

For the house of God both is and must be called a house of prayer (Luke 19), lest it rather be a workshop of commerce and a den of robbers (Isaiah 56).

[Note: Codex Lucensis 490 reads “to depart.”]

### Chapter XVI

We have also learned that illiterate persons, as well as those impaired in some part of the body, are being admitted to ecclesiastical service without any consideration. This is accepted neither by ancient tradition nor by the old rule of the apostolic see, since one who lacks literacy cannot be suitable for sacred offices, and the legal precepts have decreed that nothing defective is to be offered to God (Leviticus 21; Deuteronomy 17).

Accordingly, henceforth such practices must be avoided by every means, and no such person is to be received into the clergy. If any such persons have previously been admitted, whether through their own presumption or through the negligence of those presiding, let them remain in the positions to which they have been appointed, but let them never receive any promotion; let them consider it sufficient that this very allowance has been granted to them out of excessive compassion.

[Note: In the same codex, the words “such practices must be avoided” are absent.]

[Note: The same codex reads “let them seize.”]

### Chapter XVII

Concerning those who mutilate themselves, the fathers’ canons have clearly laid down what must be followed; it is enough to have set forth their wording. For they say that those who perpetrate such acts, as soon as they have been recognized, must be excluded from clerical office.

We must observe this in every respect, since no one is authorized to judge anything beyond what that memorable rule has decreed.

### Chapter XVIII

We have also discovered that persons entangled in certain horrifying crimes, with every distinction disregarded, are not only without the repentance required for their atrocious deeds, but, with no correction whatsoever having followed, are striving for divine ministry and honor.

Some who have already been established in the very orders themselves, though guilty of grave crimes, are not rejected, even though the Apostle cries out: “Do not lay hands on anyone hastily, nor share in the sins of others” (1 Timothy 5). The venerable decrees of the fathers also declare (Nicaea 910) that such persons, even if they have somehow slipped in, must be rejected when discovered—both those detected who sinned before their admission and those who have forgotten their sacred profession and betrayed their holy purpose, who must unquestionably be removed.

### Chapter XIX
