We have found that unlawful practices have broken out to such an extent that persons entangled in demonic and similar afflictions [variant: “a demon and other afflictions”] are being entrusted with the handling of the sacred ministries [variant: mysteries].

[Note: The same codex reads “of a demon.”]

If some personal necessity should befall those engaged in this work, who would trust in his own [supplied: “and”] the faithful’s salvation, when he saw the ministers themselves afflicted by so great a calamity requiring human treatment? Therefore they must necessarily be removed, lest scandal be generated for any of the weak, for whom Christ died (Romans 14; 1 Corinthians 8).

Finally, if divine law does not at all permit a person wounded or weakened in body to touch holy things (Leviticus 21), how much less is it fitting that those stricken—what is worse—in mind [variant: struck in mind] should be dispensers of the heavenly gift?

### Chapter XX

We have learned that certain men rashly associate themselves with consecrated virgins and, after a purpose dedicated to God, enter into incestuous and sacrilegious unions.

It is right that such men be immediately driven from sacred communion and not be received at all except through public and approved penance; nevertheless, if they have repented, the viaticum must not be denied to them when they depart from this world.

[Note: Codex Lucensis 490 reads “or at least to such men.”]

[Note: The same codex reads “not to be denied.”]

### Chapter XXI

Concerning widows who are not to be veiled under any blessing, we have already spoken above at sufficient length [perhaps read: “we have discussed this at greater length”]. If, by their own will, they trample underfoot with changeable minds the chastity of their former marriage, which they had professed, it will be their concern, and a matter of danger to them, by what satisfaction they ought to appease God, since, according to the Apostle, “they have nullified their first faith” (1 Timothy 5).

For just as, if they were perhaps unable to remain continent, they were in no way forbidden to marry, according to the Apostle (1 Corinthians 7), so, after deliberation with themselves, they ought to preserve the pledge of chastity promised to God.

We, however, must impose no snare upon such women; we should merely set before them the exhortations of eternal reward and the punishments of divine judgment, so that our conscience may be clear and their intention may render an account to God on their behalf.

Care must be taken, as the blessed Apostle testifies concerning their conduct and actions (1 Timothy 5)—which we refrain from explaining more fully [variant: more clearly; thus in Lucensis]—lest the unstable sex appear not so much deterred as admonished.

[Note: The same codex reads “conduct,” which follows.]

[Note: In the same codex, the words from “just as” through this point are absent.]

### Chapter XXII

Just as secular persons are permitted to enter a second marriage, so no one is permitted, after such a marriage, to enter the clerical college. For one thing is the permission generally granted to human weakness, and another ought to be the life dedicated to the service of divine things.

[Note: The same codex reads “of those to be dedicated.”]

### Chapter XXIII

Whoever, abandoning his own church without any existing cause, thinks he should transfer to another, and is rashly received and promoted there, will not escape the provisions of the revered canons—whether he himself, or the one who received him, or the one who promoted him—which they established for observance concerning such presumptuous persons (Nicaea 15 and 16).

[Note: The words in brackets indicate the destination: “to which he went.”]

### Chapter XXIV

Concerning monks and laymen, the first part of this injunction treated the matter at greater length (see above, chapters 2 and 3): namely, what or how much has been granted to them according to the necessity of circumstances and times, and how, when no necessity [perhaps read: “necessity of the case”] is shown to exist, the ancient institution alone must be observed.

Those who are established to have purchased sacred dignity for a price, being proved guilty, must be kept away; those who perpetrate such a crime must understand that they will not do so without danger. For the condemnation of Simon, attested by the sacred reading (Acts 8), involves equally the giver and the recipient.

[Note: The same codex reads “this part of the injunction.”]

[Note: The same codex reads “the one selling.”]

### Chapter XXV

Concerning the consecration of holy places, although the matter was briefly included above (chapter 4), it has also been made known to us that certain persons presume to consecrate churches or oratories that have been built without a command of the apostolic see.

We have been moved by an even more detestable report: they are said boldly to institute sacred processions [variant: professions] in buildings erected in the name of whatever deceased persons [variant: “of whatever persons”—and, as is said, not even necessarily of the faithful]. Since these practices are so bitter and so harsh, if the spirit of Christianity in those regions is truly firm and established, let these matters be investigated more strictly, and let those by whom they were carried out be disclosed.

For just as, while the names remain hidden in this atrocity, there is no one against whom the due sentence can be pronounced, so, when the offender has been exposed by clear evidence, he [perhaps read: “it”] will in no way escape the punishment demanded by the enormity of so great a crime [perhaps read: “will in no way avoid it”].

[Note: The same codex adds: “so that, if these things are truly so, our hearing can scarcely endure them,” and so forth.]

### Chapter XXVI

We have nevertheless heard with indignation that such contempt for divine things has arisen that women are said to minister at the sacred altars [variant: are asserted to do so], and that everything assigned exclusively to the service of men is being performed by a sex to which it does not belong.

Seeing that [variant: “unless”] the guilt and crime of all the offenses that we have individually touched upon concern those priests who either commit these acts or, by failing to make public those who commit them, show that they favor wicked excesses—if indeed they should still be called priests who strive so to overthrow the religious office entrusted to them that, inclining toward every perverse and profane practice, they follow deadly precipices without regard for Christian rule.

Since it is written, “Whoever despises small things will gradually fall” (Ecclesiasticus 19:1), what are we to think of such men who, overwhelmed by immense and manifold masses of wickedness, have brought about a vast ruin through assaults of many kinds—one that appears not only to crush them themselves, but also, unless they are healed, to inflict deadly harm upon all the churches?

Those who have dared to practice these things, and also those who have hitherto kept silent despite knowing them, must not doubt that they lie under the loss of their own honor unless they hasten with all possible speed to have these deadly wounds cured by appropriate treatment.

For by what manner do they uphold the rights of bishops who conceal the duties imposed upon them as episcopal watchmen to such an extent that they instead carry out actions contrary to the house of God over which they preside? Let them consider how much they could accomplish before the Lord if they sought only what was fitting, and therefore also how much they deserve when they pursue the opposite with detestable zeal.

It is as though this were more truly the rule by which churches ought to be governed: that whatever is hostile to ecclesiastical rules should be perpetrated, although each bishop, if he knew the canons, ought to have maintained an unimpaired observance of them. And if perhaps he did not know them, he ought confidently to have consulted one who knew [variant: one who was ignorant].

Thus no excuse at all comes to the aid of those who err: for he who did not know [“and not knowing” must unquestionably be read here, as in the Justinian codex and the edition of the Canons] proposed to preserve what he knew, yet, though not ignorant, took no care to learn what he ought to do.

### Chapter XXVII

As was reasonably decreed long ago, four portions are to be made from both the revenues and the offerings of the faithful, insofar as the resources of each church permit: one for the bishop, another for the clergy, a third for the poor, and a fourth to be applied to the buildings.

With regard to these portions, just as it is the priest’s responsibility to pay the full amount assigned to the ministers of the church, so let the clergy [variant: the cleric] know that they must not insolently demand anything beyond the sum assigned to them.

The portion allotted to ecclesiastical buildings, which has genuinely been set aside for this work, must be shown by the visible restoration of the holy places. For it is sacrilegious if, when sacred buildings are left neglected, a bishop converts the funds designated for them to his own profit.

Likewise, although he may appear able to show that he has administered the portion assigned to the poor according to divine accounting, it must nevertheless, in accordance with what is written—“that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5)—also be publicly attested and not left unspoken in the proclamations of a good reputation.

### Chapter XXVIII

Therefore [variant: “lest”] no cleric should expect to be free from this offense if, when he sees a bishop, presbyter, or deacon transgressing in the matters we have set forth as salutary obligations, he does not immediately take care to report it to our ears, provided that suitable proofs are presented, so that punishment may fall upon the transgressor and the rest may be forbidden to offend.

Each bishop, however [variant: “Thus”], will in every respect be a destroyer of his own rank and honor if he thinks these matters should be suppressed from any cleric or from the hearing of the entire Church.

Issued on the fifth day before the Ides of March [March 11], in the consulship of the illustrious men Asterius and Praesidius (A.D. 494).

And in another hand: “May God preserve you unharmed, dearest brothers.”

## Letter X. To the Bishops of Sicily

The property of the Church is to be distributed by bishops among the clergy and the poor; dioceses and church property possessed by bishops for thirty years are not to be taken from them.

Gelasius, bishop of the Roman Church, to his dearest brothers, united in the love of Christ and joined together in unanimity, the bishops established in Sicily.

The authority of our predecessors established that bishops should have the power to administer the property of the Church, but in such a way that they must distribute stipends to widows, orphans, and the poor, as well as to the clergy. We also decree that what has hitherto been established should be given to them.

Let the bishops claim the remainder for themselves, so that, as we said earlier, they may be able to act as benefactors to travelers and captives.

We have also judged it appropriate to add that, if—which God forbid—certain bishops claim by right for themselves the property of the Church, as well as dioceses which they possess, the law of thirty years has settled this matter. For the authority of our sons, the princes, has likewise been issued in such a way that no one is permitted to appeal after thirty years concerning what the passage of the laws has excluded [variant: what legal protection, rule, or rather safeguard has excluded].

Issued on the Ides of May [May 15], in the consulship of the illustrious men Asterius and Praesidius (A.D. 494).

[Note: In my manuscript, Burchard’s codex, Book VIII, chapter 46, this decree is cited as chapter 9 of a letter of Gelasius to the Sicilian bishops: “We do not permit widows to enter marriage who have remained in a religious purpose through long observance. Likewise, we prohibit virgins from marrying if they have spent many years of their lives in monasteries.”]

## Letter XI. To the Bishops of Dardania and Illyricum

He commends their religious devotion; he declares that the bishop of Thessalonica, who refused to condemn the names of the heretics, was deprived of communion with the apostolic see, and that Acacius, who died under excommunication, cannot be absolved.

Gelasius, bishop, to all the bishops established throughout Dardania [in certain codices: “and Dacia”] or throughout Illyricum.

Having heard of your orthodox steadfastness in Christ, and that you cling so firmly to the traditions of the ancient faith and sincere communion that the neighboring contagions of transgressors have in no way infected a mind devoted to Christian truth, we have glorified the Lord and taken the greatest pleasure in addressing your charity by letter through our religious sons, the deacons Cyprian and Macarius.

For, on account of the primacy of the apostolic see, whose divinely assigned solicitude is owed to all the churches, we live if you stand firm in the Lord, and we triumph with great joy. Since we know that throughout the world the Lord Sabaoth has left the seed of a pure confession—a seed that, falling not upon rocky ground, did not wither in the heat of temptation; that did not fall beside the road, exposed to idle enemies; that did not rush among thorns to be choked; but that, scattered upon the good soil of your devout allegiance by a heavenly action [variant: sowing], produced fruit thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and a hundredfold—thereby mystically signifying the yield of the Lord’s grain—

therefore, with exultant hearts, we urge you more confidently to preserve your breasts wisely undefiled from the assault of the Eutychian plague. For “the one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew 10); “the Lord is near; do not be anxious about anything” (Philippians 4). For what is in us is greater than he who is in this world, and the kingdom of the Lord is certainly within us, as Scripture also attests (Luke 17).

To guard yourselves from harmful association with those who are in error, do not, under any pretext, receive into your fellowship anyone who communicates with such men. For just as, in every heresy, Catholic integrity must avoid the condemned author of the depravity, his successors and accomplices, and those mixed with such followers in polluted communion, so Eutyches, Dioscorus, Timothy Aelurus, and Peter of Alexandria, together with his associate Acacius, and also Peter of Antioch, along with all their participants, must be entirely rejected.

Nor may anyone who promises to abandon his depravity be allowed, by any means, to enter the immaculate sheepfolds of sacrilege if he nevertheless consents to recite the names of the condemned, or if he is not separated in communion from those who recite them, so that the Church of our God, which does not endure spot or wrinkle (Ephesians 5), may remain inviolate.

Therefore let the dreadful traffic of the serpent’s head be absent from the faithful of Christ, and let deadly poisons be driven far from the heavenly pastures, so that the life-giving nourishment of that bread which came down from heaven (John 6), when the faithful partake of it, may lead them to eternal life.

That we may be able to safeguard these matters through mutual exhortation, let your charity take care not to cease from more frequently revealing to us the desired health of your brotherly love and the earnestness of our common faith. Thus, by encouraging one another through alternating instructions, we may obtain the reward of the Lord’s legitimate priests.

Your charity should also vigilantly endeavor to make these same things known throughout the neighboring provinces, so that those who stand firm in the sincerity of Catholic communion may be strengthened by appropriate exhortations, and those who have perhaps deviated from this right path may be restored to the integrity of Christian doctrine by salutary admonitions.

Let your fraternity know that the bishop of the Church of Thessalonica, although repeatedly urged by our exhortations, never wished to avoid the contagions of external communion, nor did he condemn before us the name of Acacius or of the other similar impious men, and those who communicate with them, by an appropriate profession.

It is therefore clear that he did not receive communion with the apostolic see, since we neither can nor ought to extend the fellowship of the Church of the blessed apostle Peter except to those of pure judgment and free from every wicked association.

For this reason greater caution must be exercised concerning the aforesaid man, lest he slip into Catholic minds through reconciliation with the apostolic see. Just as he cannot prevail by deceitful arts to deceive and circumvent it, so neither can he secure our authority [the wording is corrupt], which, having been directed to the bishops of Dalmatia, we believe should also be directed to you, so that you may know that everywhere we hold a consistent judgment in Catholic truth, according to the form of the ancient tradition.

If you learn of any new disturbances arising, you ought to disclose them to us with fraternal concern, so that thereafter, with the Lord’s help, we may provide remedies corresponding to the rules of the Fathers.

Let no one persuade you at all that Acacius’s crime of transgression was relaxed, since, after falling back into the fellowship of depravity and rightly deserving exclusion from apostolic communion, he died persisting in this same condemnation.

The absolution which, while alive, he neither sought nor deserved, he cannot obtain now that he is dead, since Christ’s voice entrusted this very authority to the apostles: “Whatever you bind on earth, and whatever you loose on earth” (Matthew 16).

As for one who has already been placed under divine judgment, it is not lawful for us to decide anything concerning him beyond the condition in which his final day found him. Therefore, unless you reject his name and that of the other associates of this error, you must not share at all with any of them in the purity of the Lord’s table, which our predecessors always carefully kept separate from heretical pollution.

Nor should anyone attempt to deceive you by saying that the dispute concerns not religion but morals, or that the apostolic see is not dealing with the cause of Catholic communion and faith but is grieving over an insult because Acacius appears to have despised it. Those who are in error do not cease spreading such claims and others like them in order to deceive even the simple.

For you see, as has already been said above, that if the names of transgressors are believed to be recited in the church—which God forbid—the contagion of their transgression is introduced at the same time.

The apostolic see, however, is so far from grieving over an insult that it defends the faith and sincere communion that today it receives with whole-hearted affection all who appear to have burst forth in contempt of it, provided that they return to the integrity of the faith and to Catholic communion, according to the path of the paternal rules.

Issued on the third day before the Nones of August [August 3], in the consulship of the illustrious men Asterius and Praesidius (A.D. 494).

## Letter XII. To Aeonius, Bishop of Arles

[Note: The most illustrious Cardinal Baronius considered this inscription erroneous, as though the letter had been written not to Aeonius but to Caesarius. But in the revisions of the tenth volume he acknowledged that the letter which he had previously cited as written by Felix III to Caesarius had been issued by Felix IV. I therefore thought that this inscription of the letter should be retained—the one which in the earlier edition he judged should be removed. I hope that this revision of ours will please the writer of the Annals when he has been informed of it. Sev. Binius.]

Concerning the beginnings of his episcopate.

He urges that mutual charity be maintained together with the Catholic faith.

To his dearest brother Aeonius, Gelasius.

Amid various difficulties, we rejoice that we have found an opportunity, by which we might disclose that through divine grace we have assumed the governance of the apostolic see, join in conversation with your fraternity after a long interval, send you a greeting, and, concerned by mutual charity, inquire after the prosperity of your affection.

For just as the principal governance of the blessed apostle Peter, entrusted by Christ the Lord with the care of the whole flock throughout the world, ought to embrace all the churches and their rulers with a corresponding devotion, so, amid the various storms of the world, it anxiously seeks out and joyfully recognizes them whenever opportunity smiles, provided they remain steadfast in the faith and tradition of the Fathers.

Therefore, dearest brother, as our religious sons Euphronius the presbyter and Restitutus, a religious man, were returning home after traveling to the regions of Italy to provide resources for the holy congregation, we could not remain silent. With every desire, we judged that your charity should be reminded, so that, as your charity makes it known, the brothers and our fellow bishops established throughout Gaul might know that the inward bonds of mutual grace flourish among us, and might reciprocally convey well-being to all who desired it through whomever your charity wished.

Thus it would be evident that we cannot be separated, however much the world may diminish, but that the Catholic profession remains everywhere and always united.

May the Lord preserve you unharmed, dearest brother.

Issued on the tenth day before the Kalends of September [August 23], in the consulship of the illustrious men Asterius and Praesidius (A.D. 494).

## Prefatory Notice to the Following Letter

The form of this letter of Gelasius to the Dardanians circulates in two versions: one shorter, and another expanded and more diffusely amplified here and there. Ancient manuscript codices of exceptional antiquity and age support both versions.

The oldest, including the Veronese codex and the ancient canonical codex published by Quesnell, prefer the shorter version. The most ancient collection of Avellana, preserved in the Vatican Library, presents the fuller version; indeed, Facundus of Hermiana cited testimony from it in Book V, chapter 4.

This gave rise to disagreement among the scholars, for some judge the expanded version to be interpolated and defend the authenticity of the shorter letter alone. The Ballerini consider both versions authentic in their Dissertation on the Antiquity of Canonical Collections, Part 2, chapter 11, section 3. They reason that Gelasius first wrote the shorter version and then published an expanded version after revising it; they demonstrate that this was not the only example of such a practice among the ancients.

See them in their Preface to Letter 12 of Saint Leo, numbers 10 and 14.

The Venetian editor of Labbe printed the fuller version in his collection, carefully marking in the notes the passages lacking in the shorter letter. Since readers may nevertheless find it less easy to form a clear conception of the shorter letter’s form, I thought I would do something worthwhile by appending here the complete shorter version to the fuller letter as represented in the Venetian edition, which I have transferred here. I copied it from the Codex of Ecclesiastical Canons published by Quesnell, chapter 50, according to the recension of the Ballerini.

[Note: That this letter is circular, and that he intended it to be delivered to all orthodox, heretical, and schismatic bishops, is clear from the words at its end: “Your charity will also do well to make what we write known alike to Catholics and to those who hold contrary opinions,” and so forth.

The occasion for writing the letter was provided by Euphemius, the schismatic bishop of Constantinople, who, embellishing the unjust and impious cause of the deceased Acacius with false texts, attempted to tear the Eastern bishops away from union with the apostolic see.

Therefore, in order to aid the Eastern Church, which was in the greatest danger, he sent this very long and eloquent letter to the bishops of Dardania, demonstrating that Acacius had rightly been condemned by the judgment of the apostolic see.]

[Note: On this letter consult the distinguished Maffei in the preface to the Acacian Supplement (Patrologia, vol. LVIII, col. 937). It was collated with a very ancient codex of the chapter of Verona, believed to be a thousand years old, by Francesco Blanchini, canon of that chapter and keeper of its library. In that codex the letter’s argument is: “Here begins the account showing that Acacius was rightly condemned by the apostolic see”; its title is: “Gelasius to his dearest brothers, all the bishops established throughout Dardania.”]

## Letter XIII. To the Bishops of Dardania

He demonstrates that Acacius was rightly condemned by the judgment of the apostolic see alone.

[Note: Alternatively: “Gelasius to his dearest brothers, all the bishops established throughout Dardania.”]

Gelasius, bishop of the city of Rome, to the Dardanians.

[Note: Euphemius, in defense of Acacius, said that Acacius had not been condemned by synodal judgment and therefore that his name ought not to be erased from the sacred registers. If he means a universal and ecumenical council, this is true; if he means a provincial synod, it is entirely false, as is clear from what we noted above in the notes on the letters and Roman councils held under Felix III.

Acacius could neither have been nor ought to have been condemned by a universal and ecumenical council. Nearly all the Eastern bishops had been polluted by communion with Acacius, and therefore a universal council could not be held. Since it was sufficient that he had been condemned by the judgment of the Roman pontiff alone, there was no need for a universal and ecumenical council.

S. E. Binius.]

We were greatly astonished that your affection desires to know, as though it were a new and apparently difficult question, and as though it were still something unheard of, that the communicants of the Eutychian plague, having nothing to answer in defense of the obstinacy that leads to their perdition, and having already been repeatedly refuted, mutter in wretched [Alternative: “mere”] contention [Note: The same codex has “mutter”]—not because there is any importance in what they chatter, [Note: [Col. 0062D] The Veronese codex has “and as though.”] [Note: The same codex has, “and they do not find.”] but because they simply find nothing to say.

We are more astonished that those instructed in Catholic doctrine still hesitate about this than that those who have fallen away from the truth and departed from the ancient tradition of the Church, and who put forward profane novelties of speech and the absurdities of fleeting perversity, continue to put forward [Note: The same codex has “put forward”] such claims, as your affection has reported them boasting: namely, that Acacius should not be thought rightly condemned because he does not appear to have been deposed by a special synod. They add to the madness of their vanity, childishly asserting in particular that the bishop of the imperial city [i.e. Constantinople] should have this privilege.

Therefore, rejecting the foolishness of empty complaints, you ought to go back to the blessed apostles themselves and prudently consider that our Catholic and learned Fathers, the bishops, whenever any heresy arose, decreed at a properly convened gathering—whatever they had established for the truth, for Catholic and apostolic communion, according to the course of Scripture and the teaching of the elders—should thereafter remain unshaken and firm. [Note: The alternative has “namely, Catholic and learned pontiffs.”] [Note: The same codex has “for the faith, for the truth.”] They did not permit what had once been established in the same matter to be reconsidered through any new presumption, [Note: The same codex has “nor in this same matter.”] wisely foreseeing [Note: The same codex has “clearly seeing”] that, if anyone were permitted to repeat salutary decrees, no ecclesiastical ordinance against any individual error would remain stable at all, and every complete definition would continually be disturbed by renewed outbreaks of the same madness [Alternative: “the residue of madness”].

For if, even within the boundaries fixed for synodal rules once established, crushed plagues do not cease to raise themselves up again through renewed struggles against the foundation of truth and to strike simple hearts, what would happen if the faithless were thereafter permitted to convene a council? For however manifest that truth may be [Note: The same codex has “whatever”; Alternative: “of that truth”], falsehood never lacks something pernicious to bring forth [Note: The same codex omits “and”;] and, although deficient in reason or authority, refuses to yield through sheer contentiousness [Note: The same codex has “intention”].

Our predecessors, seeing this by divine inspiration, necessarily took precautions: whatever a synod convened against any heresy had promulgated for the faith, communion, and Catholic and apostolic truth, they would not allow thereafter to be mutilated by new reconsiderations, lest an opportunity be given to the wicked to assail what had been established as a remedy. [Note: The same codex has: “so that they would not allow what a synod had enacted against each heresy …”] Instead, after the author of each madness and the error itself had likewise been condemned, they judged it sufficient that whoever at any time became a communicant of that error should be bound by the original sentence of its condemnation, since anyone could plainly be recognized either by his profession or by his communion.

And, to leave aside earlier examples, which an attentive investigator can easily examine, a synod condemned Sabellius. It was not necessary afterward to hold separate synods to condemn his followers individually; rather, according to the force of the ancient decree, the universal Church judged all who had become participants either in that depravity or in its communion to be rejected.

Likewise, because of the blasphemies of Arius, the formula of Catholic faith and communion issued by the Council of Nicaea condemned all Arians, or anyone who had fallen into that plague, whether by agreement [Note: The same codex has “understanding”] or by communion, without reconsideration [Note: The same codex has “concludes”].

Thus, when a synod once held condemned Eunomius, Macedonius, and Nestorius, it did not allow them to proceed thereafter to new councils. The Church, by the synodal boundary handed down to it, rejected all who in any manner fell back into these associations [Note: The same codex has “into these blasphemies”]. Nor is it ever apparent that the Church rightly yielded, under whatever necessity, by rashly violating through new initiatives what had been salutarily established. [Alternative: “But we are not unaware that many …”] [Note: The alternative reading is “newly.”]

For this reason, even during the period of the Arian persecution, when many Catholic priests, restored to peace and breathing again after their exiles, set in order the churches that had been disturbed together with their Catholic brothers [Alternative: “after gathering brothers with them in the several provinces, they set the churches in order”] in such a way that they did not alter anything that the Council of Nicaea had defined concerning the Catholic and apostolic faith and communion. [Note: “Apostolic” is absent from the same codex.] Nor did they strike down anyone who had fallen by a new condemnation; rather, according to the force of that decree, they judged them condemned unless they came to their senses [Alternative: “they were judged condemned”]. [Note: The same codex adds: “unless he repented; and it would follow that, unless he corrected himself, he would undoubtedly be subject to condemnation; and concerning these matters …”]

From these considerations, weighed consistently with the paternal tradition, as has been said, we are confident that no one who is truly a Christian is now ignorant that, of every synodal decree approved by the assent of the universal Church, no see ought to carry it out more than the first see. For that see both confirms every synod by its authority and guards it through continual moderation, by virtue of its primacy, which the blessed apostle Peter received from the Lord’s voice, while the Church likewise followed it, and has always held and continues to hold it.

When the Apostolic See learned from certain indications that Acacius had deviated from Catholic communion [Note: The same codex has “from the truth”], it did not immediately believe this, since it knew him to have often acted as the executor of its necessary arrangements against heretics. For nearly three years it did not cease to warn him by letters, as the many letters sent to him on various occasions testify [Note: The same codex has “familiarly”].

[Note: The material enclosed in parentheses is absent for nearly two pages in the Veronese codex. In its place the following appears: “At first, as though he intended to maintain the silence he had assumed, he proposed to answer nothing; but eventually, in letters that he sent, he declared that he had entered into communion, without the knowledge of the Apostolic See, with Peter of Alexandria, whom he himself, as executor of the authority sought from the Apostolic See, had also condemned. The See of blessed Peter, which knew that it had condemned Peter of Alexandria but had not released him, did not receive Acacius; and therefore, lest through Acacius it should be brought into Peter’s fellowship, it also removed Acacius from its communion and made him alien from its society as a transgressor in many ways. If an examination is sought here …” We have substituted the parentheses—as more clearly marked—for the sign used by the editor.]

When he proposed for a long time to give no answer, as though silence were his due [Alternative: “as though he were under an obligation of silence”], an episcopal embassy was also sent to him, together with a letter warning him to remember his earlier actions and to look back to what he had first labored for in defense of the Catholic faith. It admonished him, using both encouragement and threats, not to cut himself off from the body of Catholic unity. At the same time, since John, the bishop of the second see, was pressing him with serious accusations, Acacius was urged to submit to the hearing of the first see, either by coming himself or by sending a representative.

Although a synod did not need to be repeated, it was nevertheless fitting that the bishop of any city should not evade the judgment of the first see. The bishop of the second see had come to that judgment and could not be heard except by the first see—especially since, through prejudiced decisions, he had been excluded by the Greeks from every synod [Note: “Especially perhaps,” according to Hardouin]. Even among them he could neither present nor ought to have presented his case, because a bishop superior to lower bishops could either be examined only by the first see, as has been said, or, if reason required it, be handed over to all the Eastern bishops, who together with Acacius had fallen back into communion with Peter; for a Catholic bishop of the second see could in no way be judged by men of an external communion.

Acacius, however, not only refused to satisfy these demands; he also caused the embassy of the Apostolic See—deceived by flatteries, bribes, and perjuries, through which he promised the emperor that the apostolic bishop’s entire case would be preserved—to return polluted by Peter’s communion. He so despised the authority of the Apostolic See that he not only refused to yield to its authority but even tried through his envoys to draw it into partnership with an external communion. Consequently, the Apostolic See was compelled to deprive those very priests whom it had sent both of their honor and of communion, lest it appear infected by such contagion. It thus sufficiently demonstrated that it did not hate Acacius’s person in particular, but rejected alliances with the lost—alliances that it would rightly abhor even in its own bishops.

Acacius himself also indicated in his letters that he had most readily fallen, without consulting the Apostolic See, into communion with Peter of Alexandria, whom he himself, as executor of the authority sought from the Apostolic See, had also condemned; and he reported in his own words both John’s accusation and Peter’s praises. If he truly trusted his case, he ought either to have come or to have sent a representative, so that he might refute John in person concerning the falsehoods he alleged and reasonably defend the praises of Peter that he had set out. Since he did neither, he clearly showed that he could neither convict John nor confidently demonstrate that Peter had been lawfully received. He showed only that his purpose was to attack Catholics and praise heretics, and he proved himself rather a participant in those whom he praised than a companion of the Catholics whom he sought to disgrace. He pronounced judgment upon himself: polluted by communion with a condemned man, he became a participant in that man’s condemnation.

Thus the Apostolic See omitted nothing required by due diligence; and Acacius appeared condemned by his own judgment, according to the form of the Council of Chalcedon, by which the error with which he had communicated was overthrown, just as it is written concerning a heretical man. The Apostolic See rightly removed Acacius from its communion, since it remembers that it condemned Peter of Alexandria but did not release him, and since it had to prevent the fellowship of Peter—through Acacius’s former communion with him—from being likewise infected, given that Acacius had communicated with Peter.

Why, then, was there any need for a new investigation to determine whether Acacius had communicated with error or treachery? He had already confessed it in his own letters and, as it is written, “By your mouth you will be justified, and by your mouth you will be condemned” (Matthew 12). He was held guilty and justly subject to punishment by the bonds of his own words.

Why did he himself, in a new case not preceded by any synod, refuse to confront John—whom he attacked in his letters, whatever sort of bishop of the second see he may have been—before the judgment of the first see of the blessed apostle Peter? Why did he disdain to come or send someone to present his case? Did he consider it beneath him for a bishop of any city to come to the judgment of the first see, when he saw the bishop of the second see come to it? This is shown by what Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, is reported to have done by sending embassies on his own behalf.

Here, too, his complainants have no voice. Here, I say, he was summoned to a lawful examination, where he could have defended his position with just arguments, if he had wished. If Acacius refused the examination of the Apostolic See in the investigation of the affair of John, the Catholic bishop, how could the Apostolic See have followed Acacius’s judgment concerning Acacius’s reception of Peter, the heretic whom Acacius had purported to release by his own authority? Was the Apostolic See supposed to await the judgment of the Church of Heraclea, that is, of the bishop of Constantinople, or of any others who were to assemble with him or on his account?

When the bishop of Constantinople declined the hearing of that same Apostolic, first see, he had no right to reject its cognizance, even if he had been supported by metropolitan right and had held a place among the sees. According to the canons, he was summoned before it, when the bishop of the second see appealed, for the hearing of our case [Note: The passage is obscure or corrupt, according to Hardouin].

By this very fact he sufficiently showed that he confessed himself guilty: he refused to appear at the lawful judgment of the apostolate. The matter could not be postponed any longer, lest, as has been said, while his former communion continued and he had already joined himself to an external communion, the Apostolic See too should be polluted through him by the contagion of the faithless. It was fitting that one who was plainly despairing of his own case, whether as a traitor or as a despiser of competent judgment, should be excluded from Catholic and apostolic integrity and communion.

If an examination is sought here, there was no longer any need for judgment, since he had both confessed it in his own letters and, when summoned to a lawful judgment, had been afraid to attend. [Note: The Veronese codex has: “After he himself confessed it in his letters, if the weight of authority is sought …”] If the weight of authority is sought, the substance of the Council of Chalcedon, agreeing with the Apostolic See, and the execution of its definition are found in the fact that he became a communicant of the error condemned there. He appeared, moreover, to be a participant in the condemnation there previously laid down [Note: The same codex has “to exist as a participant in condemnation”], because the very error once condemned together with its author carries with it, in anyone who becomes a participant through wicked communion, both its curse and its penalty.

By this same standard, Timothy Aelurus and Peter of Alexandria himself—who seemed in some manner to have held the second see—are shown to have been condemned, not by a repeated synod but solely by the authority of the Apostolic See, at Acacius’s own request or through his own execution of the sentence. [Note: In Justellus’s codex: “They are proved to have been condemned. But if it should perhaps be said that it ought to have been established whether Acacius communicated with error or treachery, we briefly offer this answer: either let them themselves prove … Peter to have been lawfully and truly purged,” and so forth. Labbeus.]

Now let them prove that Peter had been lawfully purged and properly separated from every contagion of heretics when Acacius communicated with him, if they think that Acacius, as Peter’s communicant, can in any way be excused. Or, if—as is more true—they cannot prove that Peter had been cleansed [Note: The same codex has “not proved him cleansed”]—which is why Acacius did not dare either to come or to send a representative to the judgment of the Apostolic See [Note: The material enclosed in parentheses is absent from the Veronese codex]—it follows that he was in communion with one who had not been cleansed [Alternative: “in his uncleanness”], and that the one who communicated with him was infected.

[Note: Pope Nicholas cites this passage in his letter to the bishops of Gaul from Gelasius’s letter to the bishops established throughout Dardania: “Nor do we altogether keep silent.” Hincmar of Laon cites it from the letter to the emperor Anastasius: “Nor let us altogether be silent.” Hardouin.]

Nor do we keep silent about what the whole Church throughout the world knows: that the See of the blessed apostle Peter has the right to release those bound by the sentences of any bishops whatsoever, since it has the authority to judge concerning the whole Church; nor is anyone permitted to judge its judgment. For if the canons have wished appeals from every part of the world to be made to it, no one is permitted to appeal from it.

Since it is therefore sufficiently clear that Acacius, without any pontifical authority, was condemned by the sentence of the Apostolic See, without any knowledge on its part that he could be released, let them say by what synod he presumed to do what he was not permitted to accomplish even without the Apostolic See [Note: The Veronese codex has “by what synod, certainly”]. Of what see was he bishop? Of what metropolitan city was he bishop? Was he not the bishop of the Church of Heraclea? If he was certainly permitted, without a synod and without seeking any consultation with the Apostolic See, to break the sentence of the Apostolic See, was it truly not permitted to the first see, which properly carried out the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon, to cast down such a traitor by its own authority?

Nor do we pass over the fact that the Apostolic See, as has been said, frequently had the authority, according to the custom of the elders, both to absolve those whom a synod had unjustly condemned and to condemn, without any prior synod, those whom it was necessary to condemn. [Note: Labbeus cites this passage in Hincmar of Laon, volume II, page 373, from Gelasius’s letter to the emperor Anastasius; the ending differs somewhat. Hardouin.]

The synod of the East had condemned Athanasius of blessed memory, but the Apostolic See, which had not agreed with the Greeks’ condemnation, received and absolved him. Likewise, a synod of Catholic bishops had condemned John of Constantinople, of blessed memory, but the Apostolic See alone, because it had not agreed, absolved him. Similarly, Flavian, a bishop of blessed memory, had been condemned by an assembly of bishops [Alternative: “of the Greeks”]; in the same manner, because the Apostolic See alone had not agreed, it absolved him. It also condemned by its own authority Dioscorus, the bishop of the second see, who had been received there [Alternative: “who had not been received there”], and, by refusing consent, it removed the impious synod. [Note: The Veronese codex has: “By itself it removed it, and by the truth”—Labbeus: “By itself and by the authority of the Apostolic See it removed the council convened at Chalcedon.”] It alone decreed, for the sake of truth, that the Council of Chalcedon should be held.

[Note: The material enclosed in parentheses is absent for nearly two pages in the Veronese codex. In its place is the following: “Since, therefore, in that matter it alone had the right to absolve those whom synodal decrees had struck down, so it is also known to have condemned, without a synod, many metropolitans in this same matter. If anyone criticizes these actions of the Apostolic See or of the holy synod—wrongly printed ‘second synod’—then, quite apart from the fact that he is refuted by the proof of ancient events, he will meanwhile admit all the more that Acacius had no right to do so. Let him say, therefore …” We have substituted the parentheses here, as above. Editor.]

At that council, when countless bishops who had fallen in the Ephesian robbery sought pardon, the Apostolic See alone granted it; and those who persisted in their treachery it nevertheless overthrew by its own authority. The assembly gathered there to restore the truth followed it. For just as what the first see had not approved could not stand, so what it judged to be condemned the whole Church accepted.

Here it is also consequently demonstrated that a badly conducted synod—that is, one conducted against the holy Scriptures, against the teaching of the Fathers, and against ecclesiastical rules—which the whole Church rightly rejected and which especially the Apostolic See did not approve, could and ought to be changed by a properly conducted synod—that is, one conducted according to Scripture, according to the tradition of the Fathers, and according to ecclesiastical rules, promulgated for the Catholic faith and communion, accepted by the whole Church, and especially approved by the Apostolic See. A properly conducted synod, however, according to the manner described above, must in no way be changed by a new synod.

Therefore, if they admit that Eutyches was a heretic, they will likewise admit that the synod held at Ephesus, by which he was received, was badly conducted. They will then, whether they wish it or not, agree with the properly conducted Council of Chalcedon, by which Eutyches and those who shared his views were rejected, and they will recognize that a properly conducted synod could not lawfully be reopened through new disputes.

If they should perhaps say that the Ephesian synod also could not be changed on the same principle, let them once again consider more clearly the points brought forward above: namely, that a synod not rightly conducted against the faith, against the truth, and against Catholic and truly Christian communion must in every respect be excluded by a lawful synod conducted for the faith, truth, and Catholic and truly Christian communion; and that an unjust synod must be removed by a just synod.

A good and truly Christian synod, once held for the faith, truth, and Catholic communion, can neither be overturned nor ought to be overturned by the repetition of a new synod. Rather, according to the properly conducted synod and its rightly established decree, if anyone deviates from its path, he must consequently and sufficiently be punished by its definition and rightly be subjected to its decrees. There is no need to introduce new synods for each individual who deviates and is rightly subject to punishment. For whoever, in any manner or under any title, becomes involved in the same error, following the path of that synod which condemned its author together with the error, and polluting himself through its contagion, properly becomes a participant in that condemnation and is bound to its penalty, since he chose to enter into the fellowship of the one whose alliance he preferred.

I therefore ask them what they think about Eutyches: was he a heretic, or do they assert that he was not? If they contend that he was not, why do they deal in evasions, circumlocutions, and tricks by which to conceal themselves? Let them openly declare themselves Eutychians, so that, convicted in his sacrilegious madness, they may be overwhelmed by the weight of truth. Let them plainly recognize not only how hostile this Eutychian plague itself is to Christian doctrine, but also how many other and very serious heresies it contains within its depravity, so that they may understand in what pits they are wallowing and into what abyss and chasm they are plunging.

But if they deny that Eutyches was a heretic, it is made entirely clear that, by suppressing this very error, they contend concerning all who communicate with the Eutychian plague in order that, through the treacherous and crafty snares of such men—God forbid—we may be induced to embrace the madness of Eutyches. Even if they do not deny it, they are convicted of doing this, whether knowingly or unknowingly.

If, however, they do not dare to deny that Eutyches was a heretic, it remains for them to agree that what occurred at Ephesus, when Eutyches was restored and the blessed Flavian and all the priests who were present there were compelled by military terror to consent to so great a crime, was not a synod to be called a synod but rather a conspiracy of the lost. They must therefore admit that the action of that conspiracy was wicked, perverse, and a robbery, and that it ought by every means to have been abolished. They must consequently declare that the just, good, and truly Christian Council of Chalcedon proceeded rightly when, after Eutyches had been expelled together with his supporter Dioscorus, it condemned their heresy and error.

They do not doubt, then, that this synod is good, true, just, and Christian, since through it that harmful assembly was removed. Let them therefore perceive, and at last concede, that whoever deviated from the faith, communion, and truth of that just, true, and Christian synod, or entered into communion with those who deviated from it, is sufficiently and properly held bound according to its definitions, since the bad synod ought to have been removed by the good one.

A good synod, however, has no reason to be reconsidered by another synod, lest the reconsideration itself weaken the firmness of its decrees. Therefore, all who are held by affection for the Ephesian assembly, why do they still put forward only the name of Acacius, rather than openly profess themselves followers of Eutyches, who had been received there? If they shrink from doing so and claim to abominate Eutyches, then they must likewise agree that the Ephesian conspiracy, in which he was wrongly received, was rightly brought to an end, and that the Council of Chalcedon, by which he was rejected, was rightly established. In this way they will recognize that the synod established for the Catholic faith, according to the pattern of the ancients, could not, as has been said, be subjected to examination through new questions. Rather, according to its once lawfully and justly promulgated tenor, those who follow the right path must be rightly approved, while those who think contrary to it must be rejected.

The Apostolic See, preserving the ancient tradition as was fitting, did not deem it necessary to repeat the synod; rather, in expelling its betrayer, it chose to execute that same synod.

[Note: “If anyone criticizes these actions of the Apostolic See or of the holy synod—wrongly printed ‘second synod’—then, quite apart from the fact that he is refuted by the proof of ancient events, he will meanwhile admit all the more that Acacius had no right to attempt such things.” Labbeus.]

Therefore, if anyone still criticizes these actions of the Apostolic See on the basis of the Council of Chalcedon, apart from the fact that he can be refuted both by what we established above and by many other arguments, he will nevertheless admit that Acacius had all the less right to attempt them.

Let him therefore say by what synod he decided to exclude John, the bishop of the second see—whatever sort of bishop he may have been, yet certainly a Catholic bishop ordained by Catholics and in no way accused concerning the Catholic faith and communion—and allowed Peter, a manifest heretic who had also been condemned by his own execution of the sentence, to be substituted for him [Note: The material enclosed in parentheses is absent from the Veronese codex]. For even if John had been manifestly guilty, it would at least have been appropriate to place a Catholic priest after him, just as the emperor himself is read to have promised in his sacred letters that this should be done in Alexandria after Timothy of blessed memory, the Catholic bishop.

By what synod did the same Acacius cause Calendion, the bishop of the third see [Alternative: “the holy Calendion”], to be expelled [Note: The same codex has “and Acacius”]? Yet he allowed that same Peter, so manifestly a heretic that he openly claimed it necessary to communicate with him [Alternative: “nor did he claim that it was necessary to communicate with him”], to be substituted by his own arrangement [Note: The same codex has “for the same one”]. Finally, by what synod did he, throughout the entire East, after orthodox bishops innocent of any crime had been expelled, place in their positions various wicked men entangled in crimes?

By what synod did that impious plunderer invade so many privileges belonging to others? Books would not suffice if we attempted to record one by one the tragedies that he inflicted throughout the churches of the entire East [Note: The same codex has “to describe them”]. Do they think they can confront us with that argument of his by which he tried to cast his crimes upon the imperial person [Alternative: “seemed to cast”]?

Why, then, when he wished, did he resist Basiliscus, who was certainly a tyrant and a fiercely hostile heretic [Alternative: “Why did he also resist …”]? Why did he not submit his will to the emperor Zeno himself, because Zeno openly refused to communicate with Peter of Antioch? Behold, he could resist others also, if he wished [Note: The same codex has “if he did not wish it.” Alternative: “but he did not wish to. Does not the Apostle say that not only those who do such things, but also those who consent to those who do them, are likewise entangled in guilt? But …”].

But, to omit what must be explained at greater length, whatever the emperor Zeno himself professes in his letters—that he conducted everything according to Acacius’s counsel—Acacius himself likewise testifies in his letters that this did not escape him. He both wrote that Zeno had conducted everything rightly and did not conceal that these same actions had been carried out on his advice.

As though Acacius had become a traitor only through communion with Peter of Alexandria, and not through all those whom he either caused to be placed, like a tyrant, over various churches after Catholic bishops had been expelled, or with whom, once so placed, he shared a perverse communion—men who, precisely for this reason, ought according to the canons to have been expelled from ecclesiastical communion, because they allowed themselves to be installed as successors while the living priests still remained.

What Christian does not see that, once Catholic bishops had been expelled from their own sees, only heretics could have been introduced in their place? Yet Acacius was either the author of the substitution of all these men or joined himself in communion to those who had been substituted—men who plainly did not differ at all from the communion of heretics.

Why, then, when Acacius saw these things happening, did he not, as he had already done under Basiliscus, refer the matter to the Apostolic See? If he could not act alone, why did he not join his counsels and deliberations with that see, so that they might present to the emperor what was appropriate for religion? For if Basiliscus, as has been said, a tyrant and heretic, was greatly shaken by the letters of the Apostolic See and recalled from many excesses, how much more could a legitimate emperor, who wished to appear Catholic, have been moderated by the measured advice of all the bishops in conjunction with the Apostolic See—especially since he was a particular supporter and admirer of Acacius, and since his letters had praised both Acacius himself and Pope Simplicius of blessed memory? He could have been shown that Acacius had steadfastly resisted heretics [Alternative: “that they had steadfastly resisted heretics”].

Why did Acacius remain silent for so long amid these events, unless he did not wish in any way to impede what he desired to be accomplished on behalf of the heretics [Note: “To be fulfilled,” according to the same codex]?

Let us suppose, nevertheless, that no synod had preceded this one, for which the Apostolic See would rightly have acted as executor. With whom was a synod concerning Acacius to be held? Was it to be held with those who were already bound as Acacius’s participants, who had clearly become companions of the external communion by violently excluding Catholic priests throughout the East and sending them into various exiles, transferring themselves to that fellowship before consulting the decrees of the Apostolic See?

With whom, then, was the synod to be held? Catholic bishops had already been expelled everywhere; only the companions of the faithless remained. With them it was no longer permissible to hold an assembly [Alternative adds: “as the Psalm says, ‘I have not sat …’”]. [Note: The material enclosed in parentheses is absent from the Veronese codex.]

For it was wholly contrary to ecclesiastical custom to hold any council with those who maintained a polluted communion mixed with the faithless. The prophet also says: “I have not sat in the council of vanity, and I will not enter in with those who do iniquity; I have hated the assembly of the wicked, and I will not sit with the impious.” [Note: The material enclosed in parentheses is absent from the Veronese codex. In its place appear the words already printed above in Labbeus’s edition: “Nor is it ecclesiastical custom …” After these follow: “Therefore rightly …”]

Rightly, therefore, such treachery was rejected according to the form of the Council of Chalcedon, rather than being brought before a council which was neither necessary after the first synod nor permissible with such men [Note: The same codex has “to be held”]. [Note: The following material is absent from the Veronese codex.]

For if they had wished to understand what was being done concerning the Catholic faith, they could not have been ignorant of it. They had seen Catholic bishops expelled throughout the entire East without any synodal examination or council, especially when they understood that these were new cases; and the others could have learned what precautions to take from the character of those men.

It therefore remains clear that they belonged to the party to which they surrendered themselves after so many demonstrations. Consequently, the Apostolic See and the other Catholics ought no longer to consult them but rather to mark them out.

[Note: The pontiff ridicules what our innovators of the present day, together with Euphemius, foolishly repeat when they weigh the prerogatives of patriarchal sees on the basis of the dignity of the imperial city, rather than attributing these privileges to the apostolic tradition. Severus Binius.]

We also laughed at their wish to assign a prerogative to Acacius because he was bishop of the imperial city. Was an emperor not present for many periods at Ravenna, Milan, Sirmium [Note: The same codex adds “Sirmium”], or Trier? Did the bishops of those cities ever usurp anything for their dignities beyond the measure anciently assigned to them?

Did Acacius, in order to exclude from Alexandria John—a mere man, certainly, but a Catholic ordained by Catholics—and to receive Peter, already exposed [Alternative: “already deposed”] and condemned as a heretic, dare to undertake this without consulting the Apostolic See, even after holding at least some synod there? Is he shown to have done this in any synod, when he boldly expelled Calendion from Antioch, and again admitted the heretic Peter, whom he himself had also condemned, without the knowledge of the Apostolic See?

If the question concerns the dignity of cities, the dignity of the bishops of the second and third sees is greater than that of the city which is not only not counted among the sees but is not even reckoned among metropolitan rights. For as to the fact that [Note: “The same.”]

[Source ends here.]
manuscript: “which you call the imperial city.” There is one power belonging to secular kingship, and another belonging to the distribution of ecclesiastical dignities. For just as even a small city does not diminish the precedence of the present kingdom, so the presence of an emperor does not alter the measure of religious administration. Let that city be illustrious through the power of the present empire; religion then stands firm under the same [variant: eadem/eodem], then free, then advanced, if, with him present, it retains its proper measure without any disturbance.

[Note: The passages enclosed in parentheses are absent from the Veronese manuscript. Col. 0072D]

(Lastly, if they flatter themselves because of the emperor’s presence and therefore think that the standing of the bishop of Constantinople could be made superior, let them hear the emperor Marcian, the ruler of that same city. When he came forward as an intercessor for the advancement of the city itself and of its bishop, he could obtain nothing contrary to the rules; and he praised Pope Leo of holy memory with the highest commendations because Leo had in no way tolerated the violation of the canons. Let them hear Anatolius, bishop of that same see, confessing that the Constantinopolitan clergy, rather than he himself, had attempted such things, and declaring that everything lay in the power of the apostolic prelate. Let them hear the blessed Pope Leo, bishop of the apostolic see, by whose authority the Council of Chalcedon was confirmed: whatever, beyond what had been delegated to him to do there for the faith and for catholic and apostolic communion, was being attempted on the occasion of that assembly by a novel action contrary to the Nicene canons, he cleared away by an appropriate refutation. Likewise, under Pope Simplicius of holy memory, he had the legate of the apostolic see, Probus, bishop of the city of Canusium, teach—when the emperor Leo was then requesting it and was present—that such things could in no way be attempted; and he gave them absolutely no consent. Therefore, let them not look to the rank of any city, but suitably observe the measure of ecclesiastical administration confirmed by the tradition of the fathers.) [Col. 0072B–C]

It may perhaps be said concerning the bishops of Alexandria and Antioch that, for definite reasons, the emperor ordered what was done rather than Acacius. But it would have been fitting for a Christian priest to advise the Christian emperor—especially one who enjoyed the emperor’s intimacy and favor—that, while the emperor allowed the Church’s rules to be observed, the vindication of the injury and insult done to the same priest would remain secure. For a new case had arisen in the case of each bishop, and consequently a new investigation was required; and, as had always been the established practice (and as both divine and human laws judged), judgments concerning priests ought to proceed from a council of priests. Otherwise it would appear that whatever bishops—even if they had gone astray through human error but had in no way transgressed against religion—were being struck down by secular power. Was this not still something that ought reasonably to have been suggested to the emperor? If he had been exalted by the honor of the imperial city, if he had thereby been made greater than that imperial city, ought he not to have been all the more steadfast in making such recommendations? But if, in matters that had to be undertaken for religion, he proved contemptible and despised—either sluggish or lacking the confidence to speak—how had he been made greater through the imperial city?

[Note: These words are likewise absent from the same manuscript.]

(Was it so that, through these actions, he might exercise the tyranny of his own betrayal rather than legitimately prosecute the causes of religion?) The prophet Nathan (2 Kings 12) openly and publicly declared before King David both the error that had been committed and that David himself had committed it; then, after David’s confession and correction, he absolved him.

[Note: The following passages, enclosed in parentheses, are missing from the Veronese manuscript.]

(Blessed Ambrose of Milan, priest of the Church, publicly and openly suspended communion with the emperor Theodosius the Great and brought the imperial power back to penance. Pope Leo of blessed memory, as one reads, freely rebuked the emperor Theodosius the Younger for exceeding the limits at the Ephesian Robber Council. Pope Hilary of holy memory also publicly and in a clear voice confronted the emperor Anthemius before the blessed apostle Peter, when Philotheus the Macedonian, relying on the emperor’s friendship, wished to introduce into the City new conventicles of various sects, so that this should not happen; indeed, the emperor promised under oath that he would not do these things. Likewise, Pope Simplicius of holy memory, and after him Pope Felix of holy memory, are known to have repeatedly rebuked not only the tyrant Basiliscus but also the emperor Zeno for those same transgressions, with the freedom of their authority. He could have been moved, had not the influence of the bishop of Constantinople intervened: having entered into external communion, he necessarily continued to foster the condition into which he had fallen, preferring to persist in the obstinacy of his betrayal rather than return, once healed, to what was salutary—as the outcome itself proved. Behold, recently, when Eugenius, a great and outstanding priest and bishop of Carthage, together with many catholic priests, steadfastly resisted Honoric, king of the Vandal nation, while he raged against them, enduring every extreme hardship—and even today they do not cease resisting their persecutors. We too, when the barbarian heretic Odoacer then held the kingdom of Italy and ordered certain things that ought not to be done, plainly did not obey him in any way, by God’s assistance.)

But this good man Acacius, an eminent [variant: excellent] priest, showed to what extent he could have offered counsel, and revealed that he had chosen not to do so—or rather, he made clear that he had favored these actions. For the emperor did not conceal that he had done everything on Acacius’s advice, and Acacius himself exalted the emperor with great praises while he was doing these things.

[Col. 0074A] He thus exposed himself as having been a participant in these actions.

[Note: The Veronese manuscript reads “betray himself” instead.]

But let us grant that Acacius had removed Calendion’s name; let John be alleged to have lied to the emperor. Since these were nevertheless new cases, should there not have been a new ecclesiastical investigation? Or should those who were said to have sinned against a human emperor have been deposed without any synod intervening, while Acacius, who had sinned against God, the supreme and true Emperor, and had sought to mingle sincere communion in the divine sacrament with the treacherous, should not have been expelled [variant: excluded] according to the synod by which this treachery had been condemned?

[Note: The same manuscript reads: “What of the catholic priests driven from innumerable cities throughout the East, and heretics installed in their place?”]

What of the innumerable catholic priests driven from their own sees throughout the East, with unequivocal heretics admitted in their place? These were certainly new cases, and consequently a new synod was owed to them.

[Col. 0074B] Why did it not then occur to anyone that, in such cases, at least some kind of synod ought to be requested from the emperor, so that bishops everywhere might appear to be excluded by some pretext or other, or by a specious judgment, under the authority of ecclesiastical tradition—not only priests of whatever cities, but metropolitan bishops without exception? Since Acacius did not resist any of these things by offering whatever counsel he could, he consented to them by communicating with all those who had been substituted for the catholic priests. But the Apostle says that not only those who do such things, but also those who consent to those who do them, are unquestionably counted guilty (Romans 1).

Was it lawful for secular power, with Acacius’s consent, to complete such actions without any synod—even though the novelty of the events themselves demanded one—and without consulting the apostolic see; while it was not lawful for the apostolic see, in accordance with the tenor of the Council of Chalcedon, in an old case, and on the basis of a condemnation fixed by an old decree in accordance with the definition [variant: by a just definition], to expel from its communion Acacius, who was communicating with the enemies of the Council of Chalcedon?

[Col. 0074C] But they say: “Acacius could not oppose the emperor.” Why, then, did he oppose Basiliscus when he wished to do so? Why did he himself not give his assent to Zeno, so that he would not appear to communicate with Peter of Antioch, although he did so secretly? Behold, the emperor did not press one who resisted [variant: did not resist]; behold, he did not inflict force on one unwilling; behold, he permitted one fleeing the manifest contagions to escape. Finally, why, during all the time when these things were being done—or when he knew they were about to be done—did he not hasten to refer the matter to the apostolic see, from which he knew that responsibility for those regions had been delegated to him? [Variant: “why did he not take care to refer it?”]

[Col. 0074D] Instead, he first became a praiser of the deeds themselves, before either warning that such things ought not to be attempted or resisting their attempted execution. Just as he had acted under Basiliscus, why did he consent to communicate with those others who, after the catholic priests had been expelled, had unquestionably been substituted as heretics in the individual cities? Finally, he failed in his own duties and disdained to do what was fitting for a catholic priest [variant: did not take care to do it]. Therefore, was the apostolic see able to overlook—or ought it to have overlooked—what belonged to the same matter?

[Note: The same manuscript reads “to it.”]

Thus, by whatever means, it rejected the accomplice of the heretics and removed from its communion the partner of external communion. There was no need for a new synod, since the form prescribed by the old decree was sufficient for this.

[Note: The same manuscript reads “this form.”]

Nor was there any need to announce to the bishops of the East that these things had to be known [variant: done]. It is evident that they were not unaware of what was being done in the matter of the faith through the expulsion of the catholic priests; and, by communicating with the heretics who had been substituted, there is no doubt that they had consented by such an action.

[Note: The same manuscript reads: “having also become partners in external communion, and therefore they could neither…”]

Having also become partners in external communion [variant: “and therefore, since they had already become partners with them, they could neither…”], they could neither have nor ought to have had the enactments of the apostolic see discussed with them.

Behold, they recognized, in the profession of those who had remained steadfast, what was owed to the faith and to catholic communion. Behold, they recognized how Acacius, by withdrawing from such people—or rather, by acting against such people—had deviated from the catholic faith and communion, and how they too had likewise subjected themselves to error together with him.

[Col. 0075B] Behold, they recognized for what just reasons Acacius had been removed by the authority of the apostolic see, on behalf of the catholic and apostolic faith and communion—to which those who had persevered in it conformed, while those who opposed the persevering were taught by it to be alien. [The following passage is absent from the Veronese manuscript:] (He did not take care either to come or to send someone when summoned especially to that see’s judgment, so that it might absolve him, as he trusted, from all these matters.) And likewise, all who had been his accomplices were removed from that communion, and rightly separated from the communion in which they had shared with him—the communion from which he himself is known first to have separated, together with his associates, by disagreeing with the catholic bishops. He rightly received the sentence of condemnation, which was to be proclaimed against the other associates together with their associates; for he alone, on behalf of all his associates, confessed in letters sent to the apostolic see that he had fallen back into communion with the treachery.

If the Eastern bishops had communicated with Acacius before he referred the matter here [variant: before it was referred here], they were unquestionably shown to be involved in the same guilt.

[Note: The same manuscript reads “were proved.”]

Through him they rightly received the sentence of transgression, as having shared with him in the deed of external communion. They ought no longer to have been consulted as people belonging to our communion, but rejected as standing in the opposing fellowship.

But if they had not communicated with him before Acacius referred the matter here [variant: before it was referred here], they ought both to have censured the one who was communicating and themselves to have referred the matter concerning him here instead. They ought to have approved his being struck down by the authority of the apostolic see and to have maintained their concord more closely with that apostolic see and with those great catholic bishops.

But because they had departed from the fellowship of those bishops and had chosen to communicate with their successors, they did not agree with the apostolic see. [Col. 0076A] For they had fallen back into the lot of the transgressor Acacius, and they plainly perceived that they too were consequently bound by his sentence.

[Variant: “and for this reason…”]

For this reason they did not want him to appear to have been condemned: they recognized that they themselves had been condemned in the same transgression, in which they persist even today.

But just as people bound by the same condition cannot judge their accomplice not to have been rightly condemned, nor can they competently absolve the guilty [variant: the guilty person], so, once that transgressor had been rightly condemned, they too lie prostrate under a similar condemnation and can in no way be absolved from it unless they repent. For just as, through the one who wrote, the transgression of all who had fallen into the same act of treachery was made public [variant: “the transgression was made public”], so, since the transgression was punished in the one person who had written on behalf of all—or who, by writing, had betrayed the will of all—the transgression of all his accomplices was likewise punished together with him, or in him.

[Note: The same manuscript continues: “of all his accomplices. We judge that these matters are more than sufficient to instruct your affection, although, if the Lord grants us the opportunity, we shall endeavor to explain them more fully, so that each of the faithful may recognize that the apostolic see has decided nothing rashly, God forbid.”]

This sentence, however, directed against Acacius, although it is shown to have been issued only in the name of the apostolic bishop—whose legitimate authority it certainly was—especially since it seemed that it ought to be sent secretly, lest, with guards posted everywhere, a salutary measure, obstructed by various difficulties, should be unable to achieve its necessary effect, was nevertheless reasonably recognized as having been pronounced against Acacius by a gathering of many catholic priests in Italy. For, since the orthodox had everywhere been deposed and only heretics and their associates had been left in the East, either no catholic bishops at all remained or they possessed no freedom.

[Col. 0076C] This assembly of bishops was not acting against Chalcedon, nor did it recognize itself as a new synod against the old and first synod; rather, according to the tenor of the old decree, it became a participant in the execution of the apostolic judgment.

[Note: The same manuscript reads “it agreed.”]

Thus it becomes entirely clear that the catholic Church and the apostolic see, since this could no longer be done elsewhere, omitted nothing wherever and with whomever they could act that pertained to the matter of fraternal care on behalf of undefiled and sincere communion.

[Note: The same manuscript reads “on behalf of the undefiled faith.”]

[Note: The Veronese manuscript ends this letter here; it adds the following: “Here ends the explanation demonstrating that Acacius was condemned by the apostolic see, and that no one can become a participant in his communion without danger to his soul.”]

Those who now appear to preside over the Eastern Churches know all these things.
