For this reason they refuse to restore Christian unity through legitimate healing: they refuse now to lay aside the opportunity that this dissension provides for their ambitions; without the authority of the apostolic see, they confuse everywhere the rights of all the Churches, choosing to persist in error rather than lose the power of their presumptions, loving the license of their usurpations more than they keep in their hearts regard for divine judgment.

[Col. 0077A] In this matter, whether they wish it or not, they must receive what they deserve—both for neglecting the sincerity of the catholic faith and communion and for manifestly violating the canons of the fathers—unless, while time still permits, they endeavor with corrected minds to avoid these dangers of eternal condemnation, so that they may not remain among those against whom an irrevocable sentence has been issued.

But those who withdraw from such people are not held by the same sentence. Just as it has been fixed never to be annulled for those who persist in error, so it will not apply to those who prove themselves free from the perversity that is to be punished.

We judge, however, that these matters are more than sufficient to instruct your affection, although, if the Lord grants us the opportunity, we shall endeavor to explain the same things more fully, so that every one of the faithful may recognize that the apostolic see has decided nothing rashly, God forbid,

[Col. 0077B] and that perverse wickedness may be shown to have no just objection to raise.

Your affection will do well to make what we write known equally to catholics and to those who think otherwise, so that both necessary firmness may be supplied to the sound and appropriate medicine to those who are unsound.

Given on the Kalends of February, in the consulship of Victor, a man of illustrious rank.

[Note: It should be written “Viatore”; he held the consulship in the year of Christ 495.]

# SHORTER FORM OF THE SAME LETTER

To our most beloved brothers, all the bishops established throughout Dardania, Gelasius.

We have been greatly astonished that your affection desires to know, as though it were a new and seemingly difficult question, and as though it were still something unheard of, what the communicants of the Eutychian plague—having no answer to give for their obstinacy in perdition, and having already been convicted on frequent occasions—mutter amid continual contention. Not because what they babble has any importance, nor because they have found anything at all to say. We are even more amazed that those instructed in Catholic convictions still hesitate than that those who have fallen away from the truth and deviated from the ancient tradition of the Church should produce profane verbal novelties and absurdities of their fleeting perversity.

Your affection reports that they boast that Acacius should not be considered lawfully condemned because he does not appear to have been deposed by a special synod; and, moreover, that they childishly add to the madness of their vanity: “the bishop of the preeminent royal city.”

Therefore, rejecting the foolishness of empty complaints, you ought to proceed from the blessed apostles themselves and prudently consider that our fathers—namely, Catholic and learned bishops—whenever any heresy arose, decreed once and for all, after assembling according to the course of Scripture and the preaching of their predecessors, whatever had been done for the faith, for the truth, and for Catholic and apostolic communion. Thereafter they wished it to remain unshaken and firm, and they did not permit what had been established in the same matter to be reconsidered under any recent presumption.

They wisely took precautions, because if anyone were permitted to repeat salutary decrees, no established ordinance of the Church would remain stable against each successive error, and every complete definition would continually be disturbed by recurring outbreaks of the same madness. For if, even after the boundaries of synodal rules once established have been fixed, defeated plagues do not cease to raise themselves against the foundation of truth by renewing their struggles and to strike simple hearts, what would happen if the faithless were repeatedly permitted to convene a council? Whenever the truth is manifest, pernicious falsehood never lacks something to bring forward; and although it may be deficient in reason or authority, it nevertheless does not yield in intention.

Our predecessors, seeing this by divine inspiration, necessarily took precautions so that what a synod convened against each heresy had proclaimed for the faith, communion, and Catholic and apostolic truth would not afterward be mutilated by new reconsiderations. They did not wish to provide the wicked with an opportunity to assault what had been established as a remedy. Rather, once the author of each insanity and the error itself had been condemned, they judged it sufficient that whoever at any time became a participant in that error should be bound by its principal sentence of condemnation, since anyone could plainly be recognized either by his profession or by his communion.

To pass over earlier matters, which a diligent investigator can easily discover: the synod condemned Sabellius, and it was not necessary afterward to condemn his followers by holding separate synods for each individual. In accordance with the force of the ancient decree, the universal Church judged all who had become participants either in that perversity or in its communion to be rejected. Thus, on account of Arius’s blasphemies, the form of Catholic faith and communion promulgated by the Council of Nicaea comprehends without reconsideration all Arians, and anyone who has fallen into that plague either in belief or in communion. Likewise, when a synod had once condemned Eunomius, Macedonius, and Nestorius, it did not permit them to come to new councils thereafter. Instead, the Church rejected all who in any manner fell back into these blasphemies, according to the synodal boundary handed down to it. It is clearly never right, under whatever necessity, to tamper anew with what had been salutarily established.

Nor are we unaware that, during the storm of the Arian persecution, many bishops, breathing again after returning from exile, restored the churches that had been disturbed by assembling with their brothers in particular provinces. Yet they did not do this in order to alter anything that the Council of Nicaea had defined concerning the faith and Catholic communion, nor to strike down by a new condemnation anyone who had fallen away. Rather, according to the force of that decree, they judged him condemned unless he repented; and it followed that, unless he corrected himself, he would undoubtedly remain subject to condemnation.

Having considered these matters appropriately, as has been said, in accordance with the tradition of our fathers, we are confident that no one who is truly a Christian is now ignorant that the constitution of every synod approved by the assent of the universal Church ought to be carried out by no see more than by the first. That see both confirms every synod by its authority and safeguards it through continuous moderation—on account, of course, of the primacy which blessed Peter the apostle received at the Lord’s command, and which the Church, following him, has always held and continues to hold.

When this see had learned through reliable indications that Acacius had deviated from the truth, it did not believe the matter for a long time—especially since it knew him to have often acted as the executor of its necessary arrangements against heretics. For nearly three years it did not cease warning him by letters, as the familiar letters sent on various occasions testify. At first he apparently resolved to remain silent, as though he had surrendered; but finally, after letters had been sent, he confessed that he had entered into communion with Peter of Alexandria, whom he himself, as executor of the apostolic see, had condemned without the knowledge of that see.

The see of blessed Peter, which knew that it had condemned Peter of Alexandria but had not released him, did not receive Acacius. Therefore, lest Acacius should bring it also into Peter’s fellowship, it removed Acacius himself from its communion and in many ways made him a transgressor alien from its society.

If an investigation is sought here, judgment was no longer necessary once he himself had confessed in his letters. If the weight of authority is in question, the execution of that definition is found in the tenor of the Council of Chalcedon: whoever became a participant in the error condemned there would nevertheless become a participant in the condemnation already established. For the very error that was once condemned together with its author carries both its execration and its punishment into anyone who becomes a participant in its wicked communion.

According to this principle, Timothy and Peter of Alexandria himself—both of whom plainly appeared to occupy the second see—are shown to have been condemned, not by a repeated synod, but solely by the authority of the apostolic see, at the request or through the action of Acacius himself.

If it should perhaps be said that it ought to have been established whether Acacius had communicated in the error or treachery, we briefly offer this answer: either let them show that Peter had truly and lawfully been purified and properly separated from every contagion of heretics when Acacius entered into communion with him—if they think Acacius can in any way be excused as Peter’s communicant—or, if, as is more truthful, they cannot prove that Peter was fittingly and lawfully cleansed, it remains that Acacius was infected in Peter’s pollution, and that he who entered into communion with him was infected as well.

Nor do we remain silent about what the whole Church throughout the world knows: that the see of the blessed apostle Peter has the right to loose those bound by the sentences of any bishops. It has the authority to judge concerning the whole Church, while no one is permitted to judge its judgment. Indeed, the canons have wished appeals from every part of the world to be made to that see, but no one is permitted to appeal from it.

It is therefore sufficiently clear that Acacius, a bishop, had no right to dissolve the sentence of the apostolic see without any knowledge of that see. By what synod, then, did he presume to do what even without the apostolic see he had no right to accomplish? Whose bishop was he? Whose metropolitan bishop? Was he not bishop of the jurisdiction of the Church of Heraclea? If it was permitted to him to break the sentence of the apostolic see without consulting it, was it truly not permitted to the first see, when carrying out the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon as was fitting, to remove such a transgressor by its own authority?

Nor do we pass over the fact that the apostolic see, frequently, as has been said, according to the custom of our predecessors, has had the power even without a preceding synod to release those whom an unjust synod had condemned, and to condemn, when no synod existed, those whom it ought to condemn. A synod of the East had condemned Athanasius of holy memory; nevertheless, the apostolic see, which had not consented to the condemnation of the Greeks, received and absolved him. Likewise, a synod had condemned John of Constantinople of holy memory, even though the bishops who condemned him were certainly Catholic; the apostolic see, because it had not consented, absolved him in the same manner, by itself alone.

Similarly, the apostolic see absolved the holy bishop Flavian, condemned by the assembly of the Greeks, because it alone had not consented. Rather, after receiving him there, it condemned Dioscorus, bishop of the second see, by its own authority; by refusing consent it alone rejected the impious synod; and for the sake of the truth it alone decreed that the Council of Chalcedon should be held.

Therefore, just as in that case it alone possessed the right to absolve those whom synodal decrees had struck down, so it is known to have condemned many metropolitans in this same matter even without a synod.

If anyone criticizes these actions of the apostolic see, whether as undertaken according to a synod or otherwise, he will be refuted by the ancient proof of events; but meanwhile he will have to admit much more that Acacius had no such right. Let him say, then, by what synod he undertook to exclude a bishop of the second see—whoever he may have been, but certainly a Catholic and ordained by Catholics, and in no way accused concerning the Catholic faith and communion—and permitted Peter, a manifest heretic condemned also through his own action, to be substituted for a Catholic bishop.

By what synod did he cause the holy bishop Calendion of the third see to be expelled, and nevertheless permit that same Peter, so manifestly a heretic that he openly pretended not even to communicate with him, to be substituted in his place by his own arrangement? By what synod throughout the entire East did he, after orthodox bishops untainted by any crime had been expelled, install by his own provision every sort of wicked person entangled in crimes?

By what synod did that impious people invade so many privileges belonging to others? Books would not suffice if we attempted to describe individually the tragedies he inflicted upon the churches throughout the entire East.

Do they think they can bring against us that argument of his by which he seems to have boasted of his crimes to the imperial person? Why, then, when he wished, did he oppose the tyrant Basiliscus, who was certainly also violently hostile as a heretic? Why did he not submit his will to the emperor Zeno himself, because Zeno refused to communicate openly with Peter of Antioch? Behold, he was able to resist others if he wished.

Does the Apostle not say: “Not only those who do these things, but also those who consent to those who do them, are likewise ensnared in guilt”?

But, to omit matters that should be explained at greater length, what of the fact that the emperor Zeno himself declares in his letters that he had done everything on the advice of Acacius? Acacius himself also testifies in his letters that Zeno was not deceived by him: he both wrote that the emperor had done everything correctly and did not conceal that these same actions had been carried out on his advice.

It was not as though Acacius had become a transgressor only through communion with Peter of Alexandria, and not also through all those whom he either caused to be placed over various churches, like a tyrant, after Catholic bishops had been expelled, or with whom, after they had been so installed, he entered into perverse communion—even though, according to the canons, they had been required to be expelled from ecclesiastical communion precisely because they had allowed themselves to be placed as successors while living priests were still in office.

What Christian does not understand that, once Catholic bishops had been driven from their own sees, only heretics could have been introduced? Yet Acacius was either the author of the substitution of all these men or joined in communion with those who had been substituted—men who certainly did not differ from him in communion.

Why, then, when he saw these things being done, did he not—as he had already done under Basiliscus—refer the matter to the apostolic see? If he could not act alone, why did he not join with others so that, through the same counsels and deliberations before the emperor, what was appropriate to religion might be brought forward? For if Basiliscus, the tyrant and heretic, was decisively shaken by the writings of the apostolic see and recalled from many excesses, how much more could a legitimate emperor, who wished to appear Catholic, have been restrained by the apostolic see through the measured representations of all the bishops—especially since Acacius himself was his particular supporter and favorite, and since the emperor had greatly praised both Acacius himself and the holy Pope Simplicius in his letters for having resisted the heretic with the greatest steadfastness?

Why did Acacius remain silent for so long amid these events, unless he did not wish in any way to obstruct what he desired to have accomplished?

Let us suppose, nevertheless, that no synod had preceded this one, of which the apostolic see could rightly have been the executor. With whom was a synod concerning Acacius to be held? With those who were already held as Acacius’s participants, while Catholic priests throughout the entire East had been violently expelled and scattered into various exiles, and who plainly belonged to the fellowship of external communion, having transferred themselves to that association before consulting the decisions of the apostolic see?

With whom, then, was a synod to be held? Catholic bishops had already been driven out everywhere, and only associates of the faithless remained—men with whom it was no longer lawful to hold an assembly, as the Psalm says: “I have not sat in the council of vanity, and with those who act unjustly I will not enter.”

Nor is it the custom of the Church to mingle a council with those who possess a polluted communion mixed with the faithless. Therefore this sort of treachery was rightly rejected according to the form of the Council of Chalcedon, rather than being brought before a council which, after the first synod, was neither necessary nor lawful to hold with such men.

For if they wished to understand what was being done concerning the Catholic faith, they could not have been ignorant when they saw Catholic bishops driven throughout the entire East without any synodal examination or council—especially when they recognized that these were new cases. The others, moreover, could have discerned what they ought to beware of from the character of those events.

It remains, therefore, that it is clear they belonged to the party to which, after so many proofs, they gave themselves. With good reason they were no longer to be consulted by the apostolic see and the other Catholics, but rather marked out.

We laughed at their wish to compare a prerogative with Acacius because he was bishop of the royal city. Was there not an emperor for many years at Milan, Ravenna, Sirmium, and Trier? Did the bishops of those cities ever usurp anything for their own dignities beyond the measure anciently assigned to them?

Did Acacius, in order to exclude John—a mere human being, certainly, but nevertheless Catholic and ordained by Catholics—from Alexandria, and to receive Peter, already exposed and condemned as a heretic, without consulting the apostolic see, undertake this audaciously after holding at least some synod there? Is it shown that he did this through any synod when he expelled Calendion from Antioch and again admitted the heretic Peter whom he himself had condemned, without the knowledge of the apostolic see?

If the dignity of cities is at issue, the dignity of the bishops of the second and third sees is greater than that of this city, which is not only not numbered among the sees at all but is not even reckoned among metropolitan jurisdictions.

As for what you say—“the royal city”—the power of secular kingship is one thing, and the distribution of ecclesiastical dignities another. Just as a city, however small, does not diminish the prerogative of the present kingdom, so imperial presence does not alter the measure of religious administration. Let that city be illustrious through the power of the present emperor; religion under him will then stand firm, free, and advanced if, in his presence, it preserves its own measure without any disturbance.

Someone may perhaps say that, concerning Peter of Alexandria and Peter of Antioch, the emperor, rather than Acacius, had ordered what was done for particular reasons. But it was fitting for a Christian prince to be advised by a bishop—especially one who enjoyed his familiarity and favor—that vengeance for the injury and insult done to him would remain secure, provided that the Christian prince allowed the rules of the Church to be observed. For a new case had arisen concerning both bishops, and consequently a new investigation ought to have been sought.

And if, as would always have been the proper outcome, judgments concerning bishops had arisen from a priestly council, they would not have appeared to be bishops of any sort judged by a secular authority; and, even if human error had been involved, they would not nevertheless have been struck down by any power exceeding the bounds of religion.

Were these things not also to be suggested to the emperor on sound grounds? If Acacius had been exalted by the honor of the royal city and thereby made more exalted than that royal city itself, he ought all the more to have been steadfast in making such recommendations.

But if, in matters that had to be undertaken for religion, he proved contemptible and despised, whether sluggish or lacking the confidence to speak, in what respect did he become greater through the royal city?

The prophet Nathan openly and publicly, before King David, both declared the error that had been committed and did not conceal that David himself had committed it; then, once David had corrected himself by confession, Nathan accordingly absolved him.

But this good man and excellent bishop showed to such an extent that he both could have offered advice and had chosen not to offer it—in fact, he revealed that he had favored the actions—that the emperor did not conceal that he had done everything on Acacius’s advice, while Acacius himself exalted the emperor with great praises for carrying out these deeds and exposed himself as having participated in their execution.

But suppose that Calendion had removed the emperor’s name, or that John was alleged to have lied to the emperor. Since these were new cases, should there not nevertheless have been a new ecclesiastical investigation?

Were those said to have sinned against a human emperor to be deposed without any intervening synod, while Acacius, who was sinning against God, the supreme and true Emperor, and striving to mix the pure communion of the divine sacrament with the faithless, should not have been excluded according to the synod by which this faithlessness had been condemned?

What of the Catholic priests expelled from countless cities throughout the East and the heretics substituted in their place? These were certainly new cases, and consequently a new synod was owed to them.

Why did it not then occur to them to allow the emperor at least some sort of synod to be held in such cases, so that by whatever judgment, even if merely colorable, of the ecclesiastical tradition, bishops might appear to have been expelled everywhere—not only the priests of whatever cities, but metropolitan bishops without exception?

Since Acacius did not resist all these things by whatever recommendation he could offer, he consented by entering into communion with all those who had been substituted as heretics in place of Catholic priests.

The Apostle says: “Not only those who do these things, but also those who consent to those who do them, are unquestionably reckoned guilty.”

Was secular power, and was Acacius, consenting to such actions, permitted to accomplish these things without any synod, although the novelty of the events themselves demanded one, and without consulting the apostolic see? Was it not permitted to the apostolic see, according to the tenor of the Council of Chalcedon, to expel from its communion Acacius, who entered into communion with the enemies of the Council of Chalcedon—men rightly condemned in an old case and by an old decree?

“But Acacius,” they say, “could not oppose the emperors.” Why, then, did he oppose Basiliscus when he wished to do so? Why did he not give his consent to Zeno himself, so that he would not appear to communicate openly with Peter of Antioch, although he did this secretly?

Behold: the emperor did not resist him when he objected; behold: he did not impose force on him when he refused; behold: he allowed him, when he withdrew, to avoid manifest contagions. Finally, why, when he had been carrying out these things for so long—or knew that they were being carried out—did he not refer them to the apostolic see, from which he knew that the care of those regions had been entrusted to him?

Instead, he first became a praiser of the actions already undertaken, before either warning that such things ought to be attempted or resisting their attempt, just as he had already done under Basiliscus.

Why did he consent to communicate with the others who, after Catholic bishops had been expelled, had unquestionably been substituted as heretics in the individual cities?

Finally, if he failed in his own duties and did not take care to do what belonged to a Catholic bishop, was the apostolic see therefore permitted or able to neglect what belonged to it?

In whatever manner, the apostolic see rejected the accomplice of the heretics and removed from its communion the partner of external communion. No new synod was necessary, since the form of the old decree prescribed this sufficiently. Nor was it necessary to notify the bishops of the East that these things had to be done, since it is clear that they had not been unaware of what was being done through the expulsion of the Catholics in a matter of faith, and that by communicating with the substituted heretics they had consented to the deed itself.

There is no doubt about the effect of external communion. Therefore, the decisions of the apostolic see could neither be discussed nor ought to have been discussed with them any longer. Behold, they recognized in the profession of those who persevered steadfastly what was owed to the Catholic faith and communion.

Behold, they recognized how Acacius had deviated from the faith and Catholic communion by withdrawing from those who had persevered steadfastly, or rather by undertaking measures opposed to theirs, and how he had likewise subjected himself to the same error.

Behold, they recognized that, for just reasons, Acacius had been removed by the authority of the apostolic see from the faith and Catholic and apostolic communion—communion to which those who had persevered in it conformed, while those who opposed them were taught to be alien from it. Likewise, all who became his accomplices were removed; and he was rightly separated from that communion with them from which he himself, together with his associates, is known to have first separated by differing from the Catholic bishops.

He rightly received the sentence of condemnation, which was to be proclaimed against his other associates, because he alone, on behalf of all his associates, confessed in letters sent to the apostolic see that he had fallen back into communion with the faithlessness.

If the Eastern bishops had entered into communion with him before he referred the matter here, they are plainly proved beyond doubt to have been involved in equal guilt, and through him they rightly received the sentence of transgression, as participants with him in external communion.

They ought no longer to have been consulted as though they were men of our communion, but rejected as placed in the opposing fellowship.

If, however, they had not communicated before Acacius referred the matter here, they ought to have marked the communicant themselves, to have referred the matter concerning him here instead, and to have approved him as rightly struck down by the force of the apostolic see. They ought also to have maintained concord more with that apostolic see and with those many Catholic bishops.

But because they had defected from the society of those bishops and chosen to communicate with their successors, they did not agree with the apostolic see. They had fallen into the lot of the transgressor Acacius and plainly perceived that they were consequently bound by his sentence.

For this reason they did not wish him to appear condemned: they recognized that they themselves had been condemned in the same transgression, in which they still persist to this day.

But just as men bound by the same condition cannot judge their accomplice not to have been lawfully condemned, nor can the guilty suitably absolve the guilty, so, when that transgressor has been justly condemned, these men too lie prostrate under an equal condemnation. They can be completely absolved from it only if they repent.

For just as the transgression of all who had fallen into the same act of faithlessness was published through the one man who wrote on behalf of them all, so the transgression of all was punished in that one and the same man who had written on behalf of everyone—or who, by writing, had exposed the will of them all.

We judge that these matters are more than sufficient for the instruction of your affection, although, if the Lord grants the opportunity, we intend to explain the same things more fully, so that each of the faithful may recognize that the apostolic see has judged nothing rashly, God forbid.

Although this sentence sent against Acacius is proved to have been lawfully issued in the name only of the apostolic bishop, whose authority it certainly was—especially since it appeared that it should be sent privately, lest the salutary arrangement, impeded by difficulties through guards posted everywhere, should be unable to achieve its necessary effect—nevertheless, because the orthodox had everywhere been expelled and only the heretics and their associates remained in the East, and because Catholic bishops either no longer existed at all or possessed no freedom, an assembly of many Catholic priests in Italy reasonably recognized that a sentence had been issued against Acacius.

This assembly of bishops did not meet against the Council of Chalcedon, nor as a new synod against the old and first synod. Rather, according to the tenor of the old decree, it became a participant in the execution carried out by the apostolic see.

Thus it is sufficiently evident that the Catholic Church and the apostolic see, since it was no longer possible to act elsewhere, omitted nothing wherever and with whomever they could act that pertained to fraternal concern for undefiled faith and sincere communion.

# LETTER XIV, OR A TREATISE OF POPE GELASIUS

[Col. 0085C]

In it he also gives examples from letters of Pope Simplicius and Felix, showing that they formerly recognized, or appeared to have judged, the impiety of Timothy Aelurus and Peter of Alexandria. He then continues in his own words, explaining what ought to be answered to the Greeks.

## From a Letter of Pope Simplicius to Acacius (Letter 17)

He says:

“What greatly astonishes me is that, in the same letters of yours, you consider Peter—who is proved to have long been an associate and leader of the heretics, a fact which we remember is not hidden from your conscience, and whose refutations we trust you know—to be suitable for advancement to the governance of the aforesaid Church, even though there can be no doubt that he still remains outside Catholic communion and that we have repeatedly written concerning his expulsion from that city.

“You promise that he agrees with the definitions of the true faith, although, as I said above, he is as much a stranger to their fellowship as he is separated from their communion.

“If he now strives to return to it, he cannot enter except through a satisfaction appropriate to Christian rules. Accordingly, he must not ascend to the summit of priestly dignity, but must instead be fitted to the remedy that is to be provided after repentance. He should seek reconciliation and assistance for his soul, not pursue the rank of supreme honor, although he is proved to have been perverse for a long time.

“Otherwise, under the appearance of returning, he may seek not the remedy of sincere salvation but the opportunity to spread his perversity. By doing this, we would not so much withdraw him from error as inflict destruction upon the faithful; and in this way, violating the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon, we would open the way for ravenous wolves to storm the Church through a savage union.

“Finally, he is said to be requested as bishop by those very people from whose participation in Catholic communion he was formerly separated. It therefore becomes sufficiently clear that they do not want the true faith, but seek power for their wicked doctrine in their own bishop. Nor can faithful peace be generated between them and those who think truly from a source from which the deadly condemnation of heretical minds and the pitiable captivity of Catholics are growing.”

## From a Letter of Pope Felix to the Emperor Zeno (Letter 2)

“You clearly see what must undoubtedly follow: the usurper of the Church of Alexandria, who has long been raging through disastrous impunity, must nevertheless be condemned by your injunctions, by which he is rightly proved to have been expelled long ago.

“Is he not the very man who, for thirty years, has been a deserter from the Catholic Church, a follower and teacher of its enemies, and always swift and ready to shed blood? Are we still to accept this dissimulation through some sort of connivance? In his case no subtle investigation is necessary, because his crimes are open.”

A careful reader will find many similar passages in their various letters if he searches for them. I now pass over the writings and admonitions of Pope Simplicius, which many regard as worthless and judge contemptible.

Let us consider more attentively what Acacius judged concerning this same Peter when Peter perhaps still held sound opinions, and what sentence he pronounced concerning him to the apostolic see.

## Acacius to the holy Lord and most blessed Father Simplicius, archbishop

You continually exhort us, in accordance with the Apostle, to bear the concern of all the churches (1 Cor. XI), although we are willingly vigilant and anticipate your wishes. But you display your divine zeal in the customary manner by seeking more certain information about the condition of the Church of Alexandria, so that, in accordance with the canons of our fathers, you may undertake the labor and shed your most pious sweat for these matters, as has always been approved.

But Christ our God, who works all things together for the good of those who love him (Rom. VIII), presiding over our thoughts and recognizing that we have one and the same mind in these matters for his glory, has brought every victory to completion. He has made us partners with the most tranquil emperor, and has withdrawn from human life Timothy, the predecessor [Aelurus is added in another copy], who breathed storms and, as appeared, disturbed ecclesiastical tranquility, saying to him: “Be silent and be still” (Matt. VIII; Mark IV).

He also scattered Peter (Mongus), who had similarly risen from Alexandria like a storm, and, with the Holy Spirit blowing, put him to perpetual flight—him who was one of those formerly and previously condemned.

For, as has been found in our archives, and as you will be able to learn from your own repositories if you deign to inquire, what later followed concerning him was reported in due course from the bishop of Alexandria to Rome and from Rome in return.

Peter, being a son of night and appearing alien to the shining works of day, found darkness suitable for carrying out robbery and as a fitting accomplice. In the middle of the night, while the corpse of the man who had overturned the canons of the fathers was still lying unburied, he slipped into the see—as he himself supposed—with only one person present, and that person one who persisted as his associate in madness.

For this reason he was subjected to greater punishments, and what he hoped for was not accomplished. He himself, judging himself at least in some small measure, disappeared completely and nowhere appeared again.

But Timothy (Salophaciolus, or Albus), guardian of the canons of the fathers, who, following the example of David’s gentleness, submits himself and remains patient to the end, restored by Christ to his own authority, rejoices in the honor of his own see. Receiving the voices of his spiritual children, he awaits the grace of healing, with honor multiplied in him by Christ, the chief of priests.

Behold the strongest testimony of Acacius: what he thought of Timothy and what he thought of Peter. For truly, as it is written in the Gospel concerning that pontiff Caiaphas, what happened to Caiaphas happened to Acacius. It is said of Caiaphas that, since he was high priest that year, he spoke concerning the Lord’s passion: “It is better that one man should die for the people, lest the whole nation perish” (John 11). And blessed John the Evangelist adds this, saying: “He did not say this on his own, but, since he was high priest that year, he prophesied.”

So too this man, when he had been placed in the dignity of the highest priesthood, whether unwillingly or against his will—for his fickleness and inconstancy make us hesitate—delivered a most truthful judgment concerning the enemies of God. Had he wished [Col. 0087C] to uphold it, he would not himself have recalled into the Church the storm that he had rightly driven from the Church; and he would not again have permitted Peter, of whom he had said, “Be silent and hold your peace” (Matthew 8; Mark 4), to speak in the Church.

He had likewise declared that this storm had been dispersed by the Holy Spirit; he had asserted that Peter was a son of night and had described him as estranged from the work of light and as loving the darkness suitable for the deeds of robbers. By deceitful arts he had assumed for himself the false name of priesthood from one who, as Acacius himself says, had overturned the ancestral canons.

This Peter—concerning whom Timothy of blessed memory, the catholic, as he himself said, guardian of the ancestral canons and formerly pontiff of the Church of Alexandria, reported much worse things to the apostolic see than those contained above [Col. 0087D]—specifically asserted and affirmed that Peter had been an enemy of the faith and an enemy of the Council of Chalcedon throughout all his unfortunate efforts.

What, then, are we to do? Do we not believe so many priests of such great sees, all of whom with one voice and one accord declared Peter to be the public and deadly beast menacing human salvation, into whose communion Acacius had unhappily joined himself by a pernicious association, at the persuasion of a demonic spirit, rebuilding once more what he had rightly destroyed? There is no need to say more on this point, since the matter is sufficiently clear and evident to those who fear God, dread the day of judgment, and love the unity of the Church.

For this is the sole principle that divides unity and scatters concord: so long as the names of transgressors are not removed from the Church, they do not permit the bond of peace to be restored in any way. If the names of the followers of, or communicants with, Eutyches may be listed in the Church—as Peter was his follower and Acacius his communicant—why should the followers of, and communicants with, Arius or the other heretics not be permitted the same treatment? Or is Eutyches thought to have been less impious and treacherous than Arius? No sane person would dare say this.

If, then, their impiety is equal, let their detestation also be equal, lest, once such permission has been admitted, everything thereafter be permitted to everyone, and—God forbid—such indiscriminate confusion and mixture of matters arise that, according to the prophet, there is no certain distinction between the clean and the unclean (Ezekiel 22:26).

[Col. 0088A] It is not for our humility to pronounce judgment on the dissension of the whole world; yet it is our concern to be solicitous about our own salvation, since each person will render an account for himself before the tribunal of that judge and eternal king (2 Corinthians 5). There we shall also give an account of our deeds, even of an idle word and the smallest farthing (Matthew 5 and 12).

Therefore we desire, whatever and however great the dangers the enemy may bring upon us, to endure them in the present age, provided only that we do not incur the causes of eternal death.

Yet it is said of Peter—although it is said without proof, especially of a man of remarkable insight [it seems that *pervicacissimo*, “most stubborn,” should be read]—that, after doing penance, he was received into the Church, although for thirty years he had been a notorious opponent of the truth.

[Col. 0088C] Could he, then, never have done penance during those thirty years, except at the time when he was burning with love for the episcopate and the fervor of ambition? What a thing resembling a monster! He was able to obtain his priestly position before he could even appear penitent, however briefly, for so enormous a crime.

“But Acacius first absolved him by his own authority,” it is said, “and thus received him.” Would that the most wretched of all men had not bound himself, and very many others with him, in the fetters of eternal death! Inflated with an exceedingly proud spirit, he attempted to raise the throne of humility higher than was fitting; by his presumptions he sought an entrance from every direction; and, by right and wrong alike, he trampled upon and passed over the inviolable statutes of the saints.

Together with the very author of the pride whom he imitated, he was cast into the deepest ruin, and left this legacy to the Church: something for the peacemakers to mourn and for the faithful and humble to weep over.

[Col. 0088D] For if he had observed moderation in exercising his authority, the Church today would not be sighing because Peter, a heretic who had not been absolved according to any canonical procedure, was audaciously and rashly received into his fellowship; nor would the children of peace suffer such great losses in charity, which is the perfection of all virtues and without which, according to the Apostle, everything we do is vain (1 Corinthians 5); nor would they consume one another by biting one another.

However Peter is said to have been received, it nevertheless appears that he was a heretic, since he is defended as having done penance for his perversity. There can be no doubt or uncertainty that he was wicked and faithless, and that he had been expelled from the Church by ecclesiastical law.

But let us concede for a little while that he did penance—which is in no way true. It must therefore be considered how—that is, whether he who had been cut off and uprooted with proper procedure and canonical severity was rightly and consistently received as a penitent.

[Col. 0089A] Yet it will never be taught, never be shown, never be proved in any way that his purification was legitimate, since it was not carried out according to the appropriate rules. No one either could or should have expelled or recalled the bishop of the second see without the consent of the first see.

Unless, perhaps, now that the order of things has been confused and disrupted, neither the first, nor the second, nor the third see ought to be observed or received according to the ancient statutes of our forefathers; and, once the head has been removed, as we see, all the members should fight among themselves in varied conflict, so that what is written concerning the people of Israel might come to pass: “In those days there was no leader in Israel; each person did what seemed right in his own eyes” (Judges 21).

[Col. 0089B] For by what reason or consistency should deference be shown to other sees if the ancient and venerable reverence due to the first see of the most blessed Peter is not maintained? Through that see the dignity of all priests has always been strengthened and confirmed, and by the invincible and unique judgment of the three hundred and eighteen Fathers its most ancient honor was judged [alternatively: vindicated].

This is fitting, since they remembered the Lord’s declaration: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. And I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and whatever you bind or loose on earth will be bound or loosed in heaven” (Matthew 16).

And again to that same man: “Behold, I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail; and you, when you have turned back, strengthen your brothers” (Luke 22); and: “If you love me, feed my sheep” (John 21).

[Col. 0089C] Why, then, is the Lord’s speech so frequently directed to Peter? Were the other holy and blessed apostles not girded with equal virtue? Who would dare affirm this? Rather, it was so that, once the head had been established, the opportunity for schism might be removed (Saint Jerome, chapter 14, book 1 *Against Jovinianus*), and so that the one structure of Christ’s body might be displayed, converging upon one head in the most glorious fellowship of love; so that there might be one Church which would be faithfully believed in, and one household of one Lord and one Redeemer, in which we would be nourished from one bread and one cup (1 Corinthians 10).

[Col. 0089D] For this reason, as I have said, our forefathers—those revered teachers of the Churches and those most illustrious lights of the Christian people, whom the merits of their virtues raised to the most glorious palms of confession and the shining crowns of martyrdom—filled with the love of Christ, would send to that see in which Peter, the prince of the apostles, had sat the first-fruits of their priesthood, seeking from it the most weighty supports of firm stability for their own solidity.

[Col. 0090A] Thus, through this example, it might be evident to everyone that the Church of Christ is truly one in every respect and indissoluble: formed by the bond of concord and the marvelous fabric of charity, it would be shown throughout the world to be the one and undivided tunic of Christ, which even the soldiers who crucified the Lord themselves had not dared to divide (John 19).

If now, because of Peter’s faithlessness, Acacius’s tyrannical pride, and his impious presumption, this tunic is violated and torn apart, consider and wisely weigh into what grave danger our conscience is being led, while such great observance of our forefathers is dissolved.

For who would not do whatever he pleased if once a corrupted order became customary? But if even thinking this is sacrilegious, why should this pattern of our forefathers not be maintained with the most diligent observance, since within this observance there is a clear and profound mystery of ineffable and unquestionable unity?

Or are there two Churches and two shepherds? God forbid. For there is one who made both one (Ephesians 2), removing in his body the dividing wall of hostility.

[Col. 0090B] Why, then, is a hostile hedge again woven through the names of Peter and Acacius—the hedge that Christ’s cross, death, and blood once destroyed, broke apart, and overturned? Therefore, let the name of Peter and Acacius not divide those whom the precious blood of so great a mediator united.

Finally, it is just that you, who willingly and properly wish to have others subject to you, should yourselves yield according to the ancient custom to your superiors, so that you may confidently command those beneath you.

There were certainly twelve apostles, endowed with equal merits and equal dignity. Although all shone equally with spiritual light, Christ nevertheless willed one of them to be their leader; and, by a marvelous dispensation, he sent him to Rome, the mistress of the nations, so that in the chief and foremost city he might send the first and chief man, Peter.

[Col. 0090C] There, just as he shone forth exalted by the power of his teaching, so he rests in an eternal dwelling, adorned by the glorious shedding of his blood. He grants protection to the see that he himself blessed, so that, according to the Lord’s promise, it may never be conquered by the gates of hell (Matthew 16), and so that it may be the safest harbor for all who are tossed about.

Whoever rests in that harbor will rejoice in a blessed and eternal station; whoever despises it will see for himself what kinds of excuses he may offer on the day of judgment.

For I believe, hope, and trust in Christ that neither tribulation, nor distress, nor the sword, nor persecution, nor life, nor death will ever be able to separate me from his love (Romans 8). Let persecution press upon us, let the laws rage: for Christ’s soldier it is more glorious to die than to be conquered; it is better to be deprived of present benefits than to be deprived of future ones.

## LETTER XV. OF POPE GELASIUS TO THE EASTERN BISHOPS

[Col. 0090D]

That no new synod was necessary for the condemnation of Acacius and the others, and that Acacius could not absolve Peter of Alexandria without the authority of the apostolic see. Then, concerning the catholic bishops expelled from their sees without an examination.

To all the most beloved brothers, the Eastern bishops: Gelasius.

[Note: In a very old manuscript of the Verona chapter, with which this letter of Gelasius was collated by Francesco Blanchini, its heading reads: “Here begins the matter of rendering an account to the bishops of the East.”]

What, then, were these prudent men, probing the inner matters of the whole religion with subtle minds, doing in the regions of the East? If they learned that such a person had been installed in the Church of Antioch [Note: He means Peter Gnapheus, or the Fuller.], why did they consent by communicating with such men? Why did they not immediately protest? Why did they not withdraw from such contagion, when they so clearly perceived that Calendion had been expelled (in the year 483) in order that access might be opened to heretics? Why did they discuss nothing here concerning the matter, the Christian faith, or the examination of persons? [Note: The Verona manuscript has: “nothing concerning the matter, nothing concerning the synod, nothing concerning the Christian faith.”]

But if they voluntarily submitted themselves to the communion of those men, they were certainly separated from the apostolic see; and, with such men and among such men, even if it had been necessary for one to be held, no synod could possibly have come about.

If they should say that they did not know what sort of bishop had succeeded Calendion at Antioch [Note: The same manuscript reads “at Antioch after Calendion”; throughout that manuscript, Calendion is written with a *K*.], what is surprising if men situated in the East, who were unable to know what had happened in their own region, were ignorant of what had been done at the apostolic see? Yet, after it came to their knowledge what sort of priest had been installed at Antioch, why did they not immediately reject his company? Why do they put forward the excuse of ignorance as a pretext, when even today they pursue both the manifest contagions of the faithless and those whom we have repeatedly reproached? From this it is sufficiently clear that, even then, they would not have rejected them had they known; for even now they do not refuse those whose condition has been made public.

Let them turn their argument and excuse in whatever direction they please: they are so strangled by the snares of manifest truth that they can be trapped by their own words and deeds, and nothing remains for them to advance except the sheer ruin of their obstinate faithlessness.

What has been said about the venerable Calendion [Col. 0091C] also applies, with sound reasoning, to the person of John of Alexandria. Indeed, if the matter is investigated more fully, such great tragedy and such great errors are found there that, if those who perpetrated them were themselves the judges, they would not refrain from condemning themselves once they had been plainly refuted.

For it is openly and unmistakably shown there that nothing else was sought than a pretext by which, once any sort of Catholic bishop had been expelled, access might be opened to the heretic Peter. At that time no one examined the matter; no one demanded a synod. Everything seemed licit to be done indiscriminately by anyone. No distinction among the facts was required; no examination was demanded by the Church. Rather, as it occurred to each person, the Catholic bishop was expelled from his own city—not only a metropolitan, but even a bishop of the third [Col. 0091D] and second ranks of sees [Note: Calendion of Antioch and John Talaia of Alexandria. LABBEUS.]. In these matters no investigation was sought, and no councils to be held were proclaimed.

Heretics were substituted, and no one protested [Note: The same manuscript reads “were substituted.”]. Like mute cattle being led into captivity, they followed the faithlessness with submissive wills. It is not surprising if they now attempt to defend those whose unexamined [alternative: schismatic] advantage they followed with blind minds [Note: The same manuscript reads “baseness.”]. But we are astonished that they are not ashamed to plead, in condemning these men, that no synod was held, when they know that so many and such great pontiffs were expelled without any synod.

If they complain that these men were rejected without a council, let them recognize that they are being accused of not having sought one for this matter as well as for the rejection of others. But if councils were not necessary for the rejection of the others, let them recognize that they were not necessary for these men either. Was there no need for one when Catholics were being deposed, yet a council had to be assembled with great urgency for the condemnation of those who had betrayed the faith? What, then, remains except for them to say that the heretics were not heretics? Let those who openly declare themselves followers of an external [alternative: heretical] communion not complain about a synod. [Note: The same manuscript reads: “Why, then?”]

Why should a synod have seemed necessary to them, when they acknowledge that they were proceeding against the Council of Chalcedon, by which the Eutychian error, together with its authors, was condemned by the universal voice of the Church? [Note: The same manuscript reads: “together with its authors, by the general Church.”]

There is no doubt that, as in every heresy—and this must be repeated continually, since no Christian doubts that it is firm—so all accomplices, followers, and communicants of an error once condemned are judged to share the same lot. It follows, therefore, that just as Timothy and Peter, as followers of such men, were condemned according to the terms of that synod without any new gathering of bishops, so Acacius, who communicated with Peter, having become a participant in the crime, likewise became a sharer in the punishment.

Why, then, do they cloak these matters in evasions and fog, attempting rather lethally to conceal their shamelessness and deranged mind with empty tales [Note: The same manuscript reads “to conceal”] than to heal them medicinally by exposing them? We have nothing in common with men of an external communion [Col. 0092C]. A person is certainly summoned to judgment so that either he may admit the charges brought against him or be convicted by them.

After the confession had been extracted in the tenor of the letters, why should Acacius have been summoned to judgment, when he had confessed that he had joined himself in communion to Peter, whom he had condemned after seeking the apostolic see’s instruction? Once he had become a member of an external communion, he could no longer be believed either on his own behalf, or on theirs, or in Peter’s defense; for he had previously mixed himself with him in an impious association and had thereby made himself, without doubt, a participant in his cause. [Note: The same manuscript reads: “With what examination having first been made.”]

Only after that examination had been conducted and, if it were the case, a legitimate purification had been received, could he have been joined to him according to the rules. But since he had joined himself in communion with that same man before he had been legitimately examined and purified, he had mingled himself with one who was still accused, and therefore did not possess the confidence to speak on his behalf. For since Acacius was supported by no privilege enabling him to pass judgment on the second see—that is, Alexandria—he could not lawfully condemn anyone. [Note: The same manuscript reads: “he was able by right to condemn.”]

In the same way, unless he had received the authority of the first see—that is, Rome—he had neither the right to examine Peter nor any power at all to receive him. Once this has been established according to the rules, and since Peter was in no way absolved by us—for we know that we condemned him, [Col. 0093A] but we do not know that we examined or absolved him—it remains for us to demonstrate that this same Peter, whom Acacius claims to have received into communion after he had been purified, never ceased from the contagion of heretical communion.

Not only at the time when Acacius communicated with him [Note: The same manuscript reads: “when he communicated with him, and thus communicated.”], but even after Acacius, having betrayed the faith, entered into communion with him, Peter of Alexandria continued always within the fellowship of the heretics. Thus Acacius, through this Peter, contracted the contagion of faithless communion, and through that same Peter was joined by the same plague to those heretics with whom Peter communicated.

Acacius presumed to receive Peter without observing the proper order. He neither received him after examination, nor is he known to have received him purified. Therefore, apart from the knowledge of the apostolic see, he sought to usurp for himself an illegitimate reception of Peter, so that he might falsely claim [alternative: measure] his examination and purification according to his own will and receive him without examination and wholly without purification. [Col. 0093B]

If he truly wished to receive him as examined and purified, he should rather have observed the order in his examination and reception [Note: The same manuscript reads: “but so that he might seem…”], lest he appear to purify him in appearance rather than be able truthfully and lawfully to purify him [Note: The same manuscript reads “to purify.”].

Therefore, just as previously Acacius did not condemn Peter until he had both reported the matter and requested from the apostolic authority that he be condemned, so in receiving him he ought to have observed the proper procedure: before joining himself to him in communion, he should have asked the apostolic see to examine him and have him legitimately purified. For Acacius himself possessed neither the episcopal authority to examine or receive him, nor could he accomplish this except through the authority and consent of that see, without whose authority he himself had not been able to condemn Peter, and by whose principal diligence Peter could be examined, purified, and suitably admitted to communion. [Col. 0093C]

Since it is established that persons of this kind have always either been examined or purified by the authority of the apostolic see, or have been absolved by other bishops who possessed the appropriate authority, yet in such a way that their absolution depended upon the consent of the apostolic see, where both were lacking, there was neither a legitimate examination nor a firm purification, and consequently the reception was improper.

If you judged Peter to be Catholic without my communion, and, disregarding me, received him by your own right, why should you complain if I expelled him from my communion—which you chose to despise—as though without your knowledge or consultation?

Do you wish to obey? You are mine. Do you not wish to obey? You are not mine. For whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters (Matthew 12).

I ask you: do you think Peter was a heretic, or a Catholic, or was he later corrected from heresy? If he was a heretic, you ought in no way to have communicated with him; and by communicating with him, it is clear that you became a participant in the heretic’s guilt and were consequently bound by the condemnation that followed him according to the terms of the synod [Col. 0094A].

If he was a Catholic, you are openly a defender of the entire doctrine that you declare to be Catholic. Nevertheless, if you define him as having been a heretic but claim that he was later corrected, and declare that you communicated with him after he had been purified, you are still judged by his error. Meanwhile, in whose person you thought I should be disregarded, you cannot complain that in this same person I disregarded you.

Moreover, since without me you had no right either to absolve or properly to receive a person of this kind, it is clear that he was neither legally purified nor regularly received [Note: The same manuscript reads “purified.”]. As he was not regularly received [Note: The same manuscript reads “received.”], so it is not established that he was legally purified; and for that reason he was not purified by right, because he was not legally received.

Since my sentence against him remained in force, and you did not possess episcopal authority without me to revoke my sentence [Note: Another version reads: “without my episcopal authority, since you had no right to revoke my sentence.” LABBEUS.], by what power is he said to have been examined, or by what authority received? [Col. 0094B]

Behold, in these matters your case wavers and collapses [Note: Another version reads “authority”; and: “if these things alone were so, the whole matter would be utterly overthrown.”]. And if this alone were so, the whole matter would be utterly overthrown. But there is still another point, which adds to the accumulation of your conviction. [Note: The Verona manuscript reads “but it is brought forward.”]

For what if it should be shown that not only before you entered into his communion, and not merely when you entered into his communion, but even afterward he continued nevertheless in the communion of heretics? Would it not follow either that a heretical communion reached you through him, or that through your association with him you passed into a heretical communion?

Show, then, that Peter of Alexandria ever ceased from communion with Peter of Antioch, and that the two did not remain in an undivided partnership until the day on which Peter of Antioch lived in this world. Will you also say that Peter of Antioch was corrected, with whom Acacius boasted that he had not communicated to the end? [Note: The same manuscript reads “why, until…”]

But what did it accomplish that he refused to communicate with that man personally, when he thought that, through Peter of Alexandria, he communicated with him without incurring any blame? [Note: The same manuscript reads “what did it accomplish?”]

What are we to make of so many and such great cities from which Catholic pontiffs were expelled? If Catholics were substituted for them, why were Catholics rejected? But it is plainly evident that when Catholics were rejected, non-Catholics were substituted. It remains, then, that heretics of whatever kind succeeded Catholics.

Why did you rashly communicate with them? Why did you not act so that this new state of affairs, and so great a tragedy concerning the succession of bishops, might be examined by a synod? Or does Acacius grieve over one man because he was not refuted in a special synod, although he himself exposed his own crime in his letters and, having voluntarily confessed, should no longer have been heard, while he does not grieve over so many Catholic pontiffs being excluded without any examination?

If they had known those whose communion they had avoided to be Catholics, they would certainly have preferred to communicate with them rather than be driven away by harsh persecution while refusing communion with them. Behold, by this very fact so many Catholic priests show what they understood the apostolic see to have judged and steadfastly approved as something to be retained: while preserving Catholic communion, they chose as their companions those who communicated with the apostolic see; whereas they refused, even to the point of persecution, to be companions of those with whom the apostolic see had decreed that they should by no means communicate [Note: The same manuscript reads “with whom the apostolic see by no means communicated.”] [Col. 0095A].

It is claimed that what the apostolic see had decreed was not known to the bishops of the East. How, then, did so many and such great pontiffs, sharing the same judgment as the apostolic see and approving that it had established what was appropriate to sacred religion and true—not only judging it necessary for themselves to follow, but also to exercise courageously even to the point of persecution [alternative: to execrate]—come to exist?

Behold, you had men who could have conveyed to you knowledge of the apostolic constitution and supplied examples of steadfastness in retaining it. If the apostolic see had sent messengers, it could scarcely have sent two or three. Behold, so many pontiffs, following the decrees of the apostolic see, convey knowledge to you and provide examples of preserving the truth.

How could you close your eyes to so many men established there, yet listen to two or three? By this very fact you undoubtedly knew that those men pleased the apostolic see, since you saw that they displeased you. Either follow those through whom you understood the will of the apostolic see, or there is no reason for you to put forward ignorance as an excuse, since, misusing such great and such clear indications, and with so many testimonies proclaiming the decrees of the apostolic see, you preferred to reject them rather than accept them.

Did all the bishops we have mentioned lie to the emperor? [Note: On this pretext John of Alexandria was expelled in the year 481. LABBEUS.] Did they all remove the emperor’s name from the diptychs? [Note: On this pretext Calendion was expelled from Antioch in the year 483. LABBEUS.] When they were expelled, and heretics were created as successors to living Catholic pontiffs—not merely in lesser cities, but even as metropolitan bishops—while those pontiffs remained steadfast in Catholic communion, why did you not sympathize with such great numbers of your brothers? Why did you not approach the emperor? Why did you not lament in continuous cries the cause of the Church and the pitiable degradation of the priesthood, declaring that the Church alone had ever judged bishops; that human laws had no right to pass sentence concerning such matters without the bishops whom the Church had principally established; that Christian rulers were accustomed to obey the decrees of the Church and not to place their own power first; that a ruler was accustomed to submit his head to bishops, not to judge their heads?

By what councils of the Church, by what synod, were they expelled? What, finally, had they done, so that, without any examination of the facts, so many prelates of the Churches could be expelled according to human whim and the will of secular power? Men unheard, unexamined, and [Note: The same manuscript reads “unconvicted.”] unconvicted ought not to be struck down.

This was especially so when a new case and a new state of affairs had appeared: these rulers of peoples were being deprived of their sacred dignities by sudden attacks, according to the will of worldly power [Col. 0096A]. They were not to be held or convicted on the basis of any old cause, any prior association of guilt, or participation in an error already condemned, as though they were bound by a previous judgment. Therefore, since no prior causes had restrained them [Note: The same manuscript reads “recent causes.”], the circumstances that occasioned their expulsion ought to have been demonstrated, and the matter ought, as always, to have been established by ecclesiastical laws.

At the very least, on account of your office you should have thought it necessary to relieve their misery, fearing that what you saw being violently inflicted upon others contrary to every custom might be inflicted upon you. If they were stained by some crime, it ought to have been established by an ecclesiastical examination. [Note: “I say nothing…”]

Let me say nothing about the customary referral to the apostolic see, lest we seem to be concerned with our own privileges. It is enough to show what you ought to have done according to the rules and the canons of the Fathers. This was especially so because even the public laws themselves [Note: Codex Theodosianus, concerning bishops, chapter 41 and the appendix, chapter 15; likewise Book XVI, title 2, chapter 23. LABBEUS.], obeying the ecclesiastical rules, decreed that such persons could be judged only by bishops.

But if they had been accused of any heresy, all the more ought those men to have investigated the matter who could examine it according to the rule of religion and possessed the ancient episcopal authority for judging, which has existed since the Christian religion began. Either they were Catholics or heretics—those men upon whom such arbitrary mockeries were inflicted and against whom such detestable acts of brigandage raged.

If they were heretics, they ought by every means to have been exposed, examined, and legitimately convicted, either refuted by their own confessions or disproved by the testimony of others. I say nothing of the fact that, according to the custom handed down by our fathers, the matter ought to have been referred to us; I merely remind you of what ought to have been done according to ecclesiastical law. [Col. 0096C]

But if they were proved to be Catholics, then you, who not only did not desist from their expulsion [Note: The Verona manuscript reads “did not cease.”] but also chose to communicate with those who were substituted for them, are unquestionably heretics [Note: The same manuscript reads “with heretics.”]. When Catholics had been expelled and had withdrawn [Note: The same manuscript reads “with those succeeding the expelled Catholics.”], you could not have been unaware that the cause of the faith and of Catholic communion had been made manifest throughout the world through so many bishops. Rather, knowingly and willingly, without any examination of the facts, without any synodal investigation, and without any reverence for the apostolic see, you assented to heretics, gladly accepting and patiently allowing Catholic bishops to be thrust down in an unprecedented and pitiable manner.

If you thought that these men were departing from the sound faith and Catholic communion, you ought to have referred the matter to the apostolic see according to the decrees of our forefathers and as had always been done—as Acacius is shown to have done concerning Peter of Alexandria (Mongus), Peter of Antioch (Gnapheus, “the Fuller”), John of Apamea, and Paul [Col. 0096D].

But since you knew that they shared the judgment of the apostolic see, and since, through so many and such great bishops, it is established that the Eastern bishops could not possibly have been unaware of what the apostolic see had judged by its own definition [Note: The same manuscript reads “and through them”], you have shown yourselves hostile to Catholic and apostolic communion and have defected from it. You were not joined to those bishops by sharing their suffering; rather, you were bound in fellowship with their persecutors.

Here no synod ever came to your mind, even though, as has been said, these were persons bound by no ancient law. Here it did not enter your thoughts that, by a priestly council, the Churches of the entire East—not merely one city or one bishop—ought to be cared for. But because you had withdrawn toward the opposing side with your whole purpose and all your affection [alternative: fallen back], you deliberately avoided councils that were all the more necessary, lest through them a judgment be issued that, once the facts had been plainly demonstrated and you had been legitimately refuted, would prevent you from entering into fellowship with heretics.

Why, then, do you put forward ignorance as an excuse, when throughout the whole East you saw so many pontiffs not only recognizing the Catholic faith and sincere communion corresponding to the apostolic see, but also defending them with the utmost steadfastness to the very end? If you would not listen to us concerning what we judged about the faith and Catholic and apostolic communion, you ought to have looked to those men and either followed them, if you believed them to be Catholics, or accused them before the apostolic see, if you believed that they had erred.

What does it benefit them that they held that judgment according to their own purpose, or that they recognized what the apostolic see defined? [Note: The same manuscript reads “or by recognizing…”] You ought, therefore, either to have followed your colleagues and brothers who were close at hand and before your eyes, if you regarded them as Catholics, or to have attacked them if you believed them to be in error. You ought not to have given your consent to those by whom they were harassed indiscriminately, until the truth had been made clear from every side [Col. 0097C] and the ecclesiastical form of judgment had proceeded regularly concerning them.

But if, by following the rule of the apostolic see, you perceived that those men were maintaining this steadfastness, then through them you could not have been uncertain what our definition contained; and by assenting to their persecutors, you withdrew from fellowship with the apostolic see, even though you were not ignorant of its judgment [alternative: you drew yourselves back].

And still you say that you did not know what the apostolic see had judged, although you learned everything from those priests endowed with Catholic faith and communion—not through words or letters, but through their actual presence—and seem by your own judgment to have separated yourselves from that same communion.

You also say that the matter ought to have been dealt with in the case of one man, although you did not seek a synod when so many Catholic pontiffs were being condemned. [Note: The same manuscript reads: “And still you say that a synod…”]

Whom, then, do you wish us to trust concerning the report of such cases: Catholics or heretics? Those separated from every heretical contagion, or those polluted by communion with heretics?

Who does not see that those men are Catholics and wholly alien to every heretical plague—those who were driven from their own cities and sent into exile—and that those who dared to become their successors while the Catholics were still alive are not Catholics at all, but either manifest Eutychians or communicants of the followers of Eutyches?

This plague still persists among them today. For those who had succeeded the Catholics were mixed indiscriminately in communion both with Peter of Alexandria and with Peter of Antioch, and to this day they are mixed with the successors of both Peters. Add also those who, although they did not succeed Catholics, joined themselves to the communion of such men while the Catholic pontiffs were still regarded as bishops.

This is that mixture; this is that confusion through which, throughout the entire East, there is no distinction between Catholic and heretical communion. Indeed, whoever attempts to make a distinction is rather regarded as a heretic, struck by persecution, and punished with exile and affliction [Col. 0098A].

It remains, therefore, that in this cesspool of all things, just as anyone who has separated himself from it is proved to belong to sincere communion and therefore to be Catholic, so whoever is found to be a participant in that detestable association is as far removed from Catholic and apostolic communion as he is from sincere communion.

No one should offer as a pretext that he perhaps did not communicate, or does not appear to communicate, with some particularly notorious heretic. For what does it accomplish if he does not communicate with that man, yet joins himself in communion to those who do not differ from that man’s communion? [Note: The same manuscript reads “is joined.”] But if he has communicated with none of them, or does not communicate with them at all, he will be a man of sincere, Catholic, and apostolic communion and faith. Otherwise he can in no way avoid the insincere contagion of that indiscriminate mixture.

In this way the good man Acacius is also exposed as having communicated, through others and without ambiguity, with Peter of Antioch, with whom he publicly boasted that he did not communicate. For Acacius did not withdraw himself from communion with all those who communicated with Peter of Antioch. What, then, did it accomplish that he wished to appear not to communicate openly with the man to whom, through his accomplices, he was bound by a residual [alternative: sign-marked] communion?

Acacius communicated with Peter of Alexandria. But as long as Peter of Antioch lived—and it is shown that he died after the pact between Acacius and Peter of Alexandria had been made—Peter of Alexandria never ceased communicating with Peter of Antioch. This is contained in the report of Catholic priests and of the others who remain in the Catholic faith [Note: The same manuscript reads “of the others remaining in the Catholic faith.”], and it cannot be hidden from the conscience of the entire East.

And to say nothing of the fact that Acacius communicated through the emperor Zeno himself—who, having introduced Peter of Antioch and approved his priesthood, was undoubtedly joined to him in communion—we can demonstrate that Acacius likewise communicated with many bishops of different cities who communicated with Peter of Antioch, and through them consequently communicated with Peter of Antioch himself.

But among the Greeks this mixture is considered easy and blameless. Among them there is no distinction between truth and falsehood; and while they wish to be joined in common fellowship with all the reprobate, they are shown to possess no integrity at all.

This, then, is that Peter of Antioch whom Acacius did not even ask the apostolic see to receive back into Catholic communion through repentance. Consequently, they complain to us that Acacius was condemned, although, after making this profession and receiving communion through the infected channels of Peter of Antioch [Note: The same manuscript reads “what do they complain about?” and “through the winding paths”], he is shown to have condemned himself.

Yet Acacius is not the only one held guilty here. All the Eastern pontiffs who fell into these contagions in the same manner are rightly bound by a similar condemnation [Note: The same manuscript reads “are held bound”], and they can in no way free themselves from it except by abstaining from such things while they remain alive.

Nor ought we, in cases of this kind, to believe anyone except those who know that, by divine favor, they are wholly separated from the bonds of this faithlessness, or those who have withdrawn from fellowship with the faithless.
