For what confidence can we place in the testimony of men situated in the contagion of the faithless as evidence of sincere communion, when they have been polluted in that sincere communion? [Note: The same manuscript reads “in insincere communion.”] Nor can we rely upon the testimony of those who do not hesitate [alternative: strive] to attack the truth with falsehoods.

It remains that we ought to believe only those who are free from every contagion.

# Ten Fragments of Letters of Pope Gelasius

(From the Collection of Canons of Cardinal Deusdedit)

## Gelasius to Bishop Coelestinus

(Book I, chapter 141)

In the church of the blessed martyr Eleutherius, which is known to have been built in the parish of the city of the Histonienses, you shall honor Julian the deacon with the dignity of the priesthood, provided there is nothing in him contrary to the established canons. You should understand that you have appointed him in the capacity of a visitor, not with the authority of the cardinal bishop.

## The Same to Bishop Sabinus

(Same work)

The people of the city of Grumentum request that a fourth deacon, a defender, be consecrated for themselves. Therefore, if there is nothing that can be held against his person, you shall honor him by advancement to the diaconate. Nevertheless, let Your Dilection know that you are carrying this out at our appointment in the office of a visitor, not with the authority of your own priesthood.

## Gelasius to Bishops Quingesius and Constantinus, among other matters

(Book IV, chapter 56)

Felix and Peter, clerics of the Church of Nola, obstinately and in rebellion against the established order, thought they should hasten to the court of my son the king. They claimed that force had been applied to them while the duties of their clerical office were being suppressed. By the authority they had obtained, and after purchasing barbarians for themselves against the requirements of civil order, they inflicted serious insults and losses upon their aforesaid bishop.

Therefore it was necessary for our aforesaid brother Serenus, bishop, to hasten to the same lord, my son. After exposing the fraud, the most excellent man, my son King Theodoric, in accordance with the blessed character of his times, sent the contumacious clerics back to our judgment [Col. 0100A].

## Gelasius to Bishop Victor

(Book III, chapter 95)

Some time ago you suspended the procession at the basilica of Saint Agatha, which is known to have been established long ago on the Caclanus estate, after consulting us. You asserted that the owner of the property was receiving everything that was contributed there and applying it to his own uses, and that no ministers of God could come there for the procession, since they received no provisions there.

But recently our distinguished man Peter reasonably informed us that he had arranged the matter which had become a source of blame in such a way that everything contributed to the aforesaid church by the offerings of various people should belong to the bishop, or to whoever might be assigned the basilica by him, so that the church’s buildings might be maintained from this income [Col. 0100B]. Therefore, brother, after receiving this profession of sound administration, it is fitting that you arrange the procession of the aforesaid church.

## Gelasius to Bishops Respectus and Leoninus

(Book III, chapter 99)

John, archdeacon of the city of Falerio, has complained to us in an earnest petition that the church was overthrown by the man who is regarded as its bishop, so that, after being expelled from the administration of his position, he opened a free path for himself to plunder the church’s property.

For after disposing of its furnishings and ornaments according to his own will, he claimed for his personal uses even the ancestral estate which his predecessor had left for the support of the clergy [Col. 0100C]. He also thought that the aforesaid archdeacon and many others who were protesting together should be excluded from their orders.

Therefore, dearest brothers, weighing the cause of the Church with the utmost care in view of the divine majesty, and after investigating the whole truth, mark down in a report to our ears what you have discovered, so that, once your diligent inquiry has been considered, we may determine what ought to be done.

## Gelasius to Bishops Justus and Stephanus

(Book III, chapter 97)

Our brother and fellow bishop Proficuus, priest of Salpina, has informed us by a petition that the distinguished man Brumarius, after slaughtering a church slave with the gravest violence when no grounds existed for doing so, then also subjected the aforesaid bishop to the most serious insults in order to increase the obstinacy of his violence.

Therefore, dearest brothers, if, after being admonished by you, he comes before your judgment and inquiry, investigate the truth concerning the source from which such a spirit of arrogance or outbreak of violence arose, and what it was that caused the bishop to be abused with such insolence; then report your findings to our ears.

But if he should perhaps contemptuously reject your summons in the same presumptuous manner, let the aforesaid bishop know that authority has been granted to him to seek redress before the provincial judge by presenting the atrocious injuries [Col. 0101A].

## Gelasius to Majoricus, Serenus, and John, Bishops

(Book III, chapter 98)

Those who, trampling human laws with uncivil presumption and casting aside reverence for religion, either attempt to trample ecclesiastical privileges or rush anywhere into the harm of the poor, and who, even when admonished and convicted of such wickedness, refuse to suppress it and to make good the damage inflicted upon sacred property, are rightly to be deprived of participation in the divine gift, so that they may not lack the experience of what they held in contempt through sacrilegious acts.

Therefore, let Dionysius and his associates, who—as the text of your report shows—not only attempted to disturb the rights of the Church of Vibo but also rejected the repayment of what they had wickedly undertaken, be barred from access to sacred communion until they learn to offer with devoted minds what belongs to the honor of God. [Col. 0101B]

Nor should anything that can be done against them under the public laws be neglected. Those who have despised both forms of authority should be restrained by both, so that, restrained in this way, they may provide both for themselves and for others the example that necessary discipline requires.

As for the presbyter Coelestinus, presbyter of our brother and fellow bishop Serenus, who, rising up against the episcopal judgment and against the commands of the apostolic see, dared to administer sacred communion to the aforesaid men: since he could not have been unaware of the sentence of his own priest, let him be expelled immediately from ecclesiastical office. Thus no minister of the Church may attempt to act against episcopal regulations.

## Gelasius to John, Bishop of Pisa

(Book III, chapter 99)

[Col. 0101C]

Ecclesiastical ministries that the devotion of the faithful has assigned to each basilica must not be carried off and transferred to another church by anyone. Therefore, if the petition of the bearer of this legal claim is supported by the truth, return without delay the chalice that your predecessor took to the church to which it belonged.

## Gelasius to Bishop Natalis

(From Anselm, Book VI, chapter 39)

Because certain persons are not ashamed, through illicit ambitions, to disturb the rights of churches and, with reckless presumption, to invade the privileges which antiquity decreed for metropolitan or provincial bishops, they consequently desire to maintain a breach with apostolic communion, so that, divided from its authority, they may exercise their own usurpations as though with impunity [Col. 0101D]. They do not consider that before the eternal Judge they will have to render an account—with everlasting damnation—not only for the injury done to catholic integrity but also for their prejudice against the traditions of the fathers.

If they persist in this obstinacy, we have thought it necessary to instruct your Charity that we have likewise urgently commissioned the metropolitans of your province, or of any adjoining province that preserves catholic unity, so that when bishops die in that region their own metropolitan should ordain their successors [Col. 0102A]; and that, if that metropolitan himself should pass away by human death, only the bishops of his province should diligently ordain his successor according to the ancient form. Thus no one may attempt, contrary to right, to usurp for himself what venerable antiquity has decreed.

## Gelasius to the Clergy, Ordinands, and People of Brundisium

*(From Anselm, Book VI, chapter 46.)*

Since we had granted you the bishop whom you requested, my brother and now my fellow bishop Julian, it was necessary, immediately sending him back to his church, to send you our letter as well. Through it you would learn that he had been instructed never to presume to perform illicit ordinations: he was not to permit a bigamist, a man who had not taken a virgin as his wife, an illiterate or one under legal accusation, a man disabled in any part of his body, or one branded in any manner, to approach the sacred orders [Col. 0102B]. He must also take precautions regarding foreigners, unknown persons, and those who seek such orders; for persons of this kind are prohibited from venerable offices. Nor should he dare, on any pretext, to transfer to another anything belonging to the church—whether from its ministries, its adornments, or anything else whose attachment to the church is established.

He is to divide the revenues and the offerings of the faithful into four parts: one he himself is to retain; another he is to distribute to the clergy in proportion to their diligence in their offices; a third is to be assigned to the fabric of the churches, for an account of which he will have to answer before the divine tribunal. Those to be admitted to the sacred orders he is likewise to promote according to this observance: he is to know that presbyters and deacons are to be ordained on the Saturday evening of the fast of the fourth, seventh, and tenth months [Col. 0102C]. He must not presume to administer the venerable sacrament of baptism except at the feast of Easter and Pentecost, apart from those suffering from illness.

[Note: In the very old manuscript of Freising this treatise is found, and there likewise it begins with these words: “Lest perhaps they say what they are accustomed to say.” It bears the following title: “The Tome on the Bond of Anathema of Pope Pelasius” (thus written).]

# The Tome of Gelasius on the Bond of Anathema

### The Acts of the Council of Chalcedon: Only Those Things Approved by the Apostolic See Are Valid; What Was Decreed Against Acacius Was Just; and Peter of Alexandria Could Be Absolved Only by the Apostolic See

[Note: The beginning of the tome is abrupt; indeed, it is credible that its beginning is missing.]

Lest perhaps they say what they are accustomed to say: that if the Council of Chalcedon is admitted, everything which appears to have been produced there must be accepted as valid. For either it ought to be admitted in its entirety, or, if it is rejectable in part, it cannot be sound in its entirety.

Let them therefore recognize that, according to the holy Scriptures and the tradition of our ancestors, according to the canons and rules of the Church, it was made for the common faith [Note: The Veronese manuscript of the chapter, with which this treatise was collated by Francesco Bianchini, reads here: “for the faith of communion,” etc.] and for catholic and apostolic truth—the very truth for which the Apostolic See commissioned this council to be held and confirmed what was done there—and that it is to be accepted without hesitation by the whole Church [Col. 0102D].

But regarding the other matters which were brought forward there through incompetent presumption, or rather subjected to dispute, matters which the Apostolic See in no way commissioned to be undertaken, it is manifest that they were immediately opposed by the representatives of the Apostolic See [Note: The same manuscript reads: “which presently by the vicars …”]. The Apostolic See did not approve them even when the emperor Marcian requested it [Col. 0103A].

The bishop of the Church of Constantinople at that time, Anatolius, also declared that he had not presumed to do these things and did not deny that the matter lay within the power of the bishop of the Apostolic See. For this reason, as has been said, the Apostolic See did not accept them: whatever is proved contrary to the privileges of the universal Church, it supports in no way [Note: The same manuscript reads: “subsists.”].

Why, then? In the sacred books—which we certainly venerate and follow—there are said to be both the profanities of certain people and accounts of wicked deeds. Are we therefore to venerate or follow all these things merely because they are contained in those holy books?

Saint Peter, first of the apostles, thinking that the grace of the New Testament should be preached in such a way that the ordinances of the old law were not abandoned, is read to have acted in a certain matter by way of pretense among Jews and Gentiles [Col. 0103B]. Are those actions therefore to be followed—actions which his fellow apostle rightly reproved and afterward avoided—or are they to be taken up together with those things which, as the first apostle, he preached for the salvation of others? Is his upright doctrine to be rejected together with the things that happened to him as a human being? Or is that former weakness of ignorance to be accepted along with his perfected doctrine?

Again, are not many things belonging to the truth read in the books of the heretics themselves? Is the truth therefore to be rejected because their books, in which depravity is present, are rejected [Note: The same manuscript reads: “where depravity is concerned”]? Or are their depraved books to be accepted because the truth inserted in them is not denied?

The Apostle says: “Test everything; hold fast to what is good” (1 Thessalonians 5). We know that the Apostle also cited certain things from the books of the pagans (Acts 17) [Col. 0103C]. Are we therefore to accept everything else that was brought forward together with those things? The Apostle himself says (2 Corinthians 15) that many preachers proclaim Christ in different ways. Although Christ preached in any manner whatsoever must be admitted, he nevertheless does not thereby fail to warn us to avoid the manner in which Christ was not rightly preached. He complains of wicked workers (Philippians 1), teaching that some of what they say is to be rejected and other things followed.

These and similar examples instruct us, and divine testimonies confirm, that we must not indiscriminately accept everything said by anyone or written anywhere, but must retain what is good and reject what causes harm.

Death was inflicted upon sinful man; yet, when death was inflicted upon the man Jesus Christ, it made the devil guilty, because where there was no cause of death—namely, sin—punishment was not owed [Col. 0103D].

A sentence is fixed, or has been fixed, forever against error. That sentence once fixed against this error will never be undone. For just as error, insofar as it is error, never ceases to be error, so it will never be released from the sentence fixed against it, because error that is recognized as condemned is proved to remain bound by that sentence so long as it remains error.

Therefore those who are in that error are bound by the sentence against error; and so long as they remain in it, they are in no way absolved, just as the error itself in which they are is not absolved [Note: The same manuscript reads: “in which the errors are.”] [Col. 0104A].

Error itself never earns pardon; rather, pardon belongs to the person who truly abandons it and withdraws from participation in it. Therefore, so long as error is in them, it retains its condemnation and is never released, because error always merits punishment. Those who participate in it are either always participants in its punishment, if they do not cease to persist in it, or, if they withdraw from it, then, to the degree that they have become alien to error and separated from participation in it, they will consequently be alien to its punishment.

For the erring person to whom punishment is fixed, so long as he remains erring, is bound by that same punishment; for no one can be erring without the punishment of error [Note: The same manuscript reads: “when.”]. That same punishment is perpetual and will never be released so long as he persists in being erring.

But if he ceases to be erring, the punishment which was fixed perpetually for the erring person—now that he is not erring, that is, now that he has become other than the person for whom it was fixed—not only cannot remain perpetual but can no longer be punishment at all. For he is no longer the person for whom it was fixed. It was fixed for the erring person, not for one who is no longer erring.

That which was fixed perpetually for the erring person and perpetually binds the erring person can no longer hold one who is not erring. Let it be said that the punishment is perpetual for the erring person; let it be said that for the erring person it will never be released. It remains altogether and truly fixed, and it is certain that what was fixed in it [Note: The same manuscript reads: “in that.”] cannot be released so long as the erring person remains one to whom it is owed.

For one who is not erring, however, the punishment cannot exist, since it is not owed to one who is not erring. That which is owed to the erring person is neither changed nor released. Thus the fixed punishment remains in its own condition; in its own right it cannot be undone at all. But in a condition that is no longer its own—a condition in which it cannot exist—it is now shown to have been emptied of force and to have no right whatsoever where it has no cause for existing [Col. 0104C].

The holy Scriptures are full of this form of justice. It is said: “Let sinners perish from the earth, so that they are no more”—that is, let sinners cease to be sinners. Let them perish in this respect, that they cease to be sinners (Psalm 103).

But if sinners were to perish altogether, as though they no longer existed substantially, according to the prophet’s sentence, whom could our Redeemer have saved, he who came not to call the righteous but sinners (Luke 5)? Or of whom would the Apostle say: “Christ came into this world to save sinners, of whom I am the first” (1 Timothy 1; Romans 5)? And: “When we were sinners, God sent his Son” (Galatians 1), and other statements of this kind?

Here indeed many sinners also perished substantially, remaining in their sins [Col. 0104D]; and the true sentence pronounced against them remained, never having been undone. Yet while that same sentence remained perpetual in such persons, the sentence fixed against them was in a certain manner fulfilled in those who did not remain altogether such—that is, who did not continue forever in their sins.

They too perish; but they perished in a certain manner in respect of being sinners, not by way of punishment but by way of remedy. In a certain manner the fixed sentence also remained in them until, by remaining, it made them no longer sinners or perfected them so that they were no longer sinners [Col. 0105A].

The sentence was fulfilled in them as well. [Note: Here there appears to be a textual error, which the manuscripts and Hardouin do not remedy.]

[The following transmitted clause is defective:] nor, once its tenor had been fulfilled, did that continuing sentence remain for sinners who were perishing, so that they were no longer sinners.

It could no longer remain in those who were not sinners, because it had no right to remain at all in those upon whom it had not been inflicted. Thus the sentence was in no way undone in its own right or course; and while it remained in those upon whom it had been inflicted, it became wholly alien to those who had been separated from its jurisdiction. Nor would it be lawful for it to remain, while preserving its own condition, in those upon whom it had not been inflicted.

The Lord said that those who sin against the Holy Spirit would be forgiven neither in this age nor in the age to come (Matthew 12).

How many, however, do we know to have sinned against the Holy Spirit—various heretics, such as Arians, Eunomians, and Macedonians—who returned to the catholic faith, received forgiveness of their blasphemy in this life, and gained hope of receiving indulgence in the future [Col. 0105B]?

The Lord’s sentence is not thereby untrue, nor should it be thought to have been in any way undone, since, with respect to such persons if they remain what they are, it persists as something never to be released, while it is not inflicted upon those who have ceased to be such.

Likewise there is the statement of blessed John the apostle: “There is sin unto death; I do not say that one should pray for it. And there is sin not unto death; I do say that one should pray for it” (1 John 5). There is sin unto death for those who remain in the same sin; there is sin not unto death for those who withdraw from that sin.

For there is no sin for which the Church either does not pray for forgiveness [Note: The same manuscript reads: “for remission”] or which, by the power divinely granted to it, it cannot absolve those who desist from it or release the penitent. To the Church it is said: “Whatever you forgive on earth will be forgiven also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven” (Matthew 16:18).

In these words, “all” includes everything, whatever its extent and whatever its character. Nevertheless, the true sentence concerning such persons remains—the sentence which declares that it will never be released [Note: The same manuscript reads: “which will never …”]—remaining in force for those who persist in that condition and not extending beyond it to those who subsequently withdraw from it.

This too must reasonably be considered in the sentence against Acacius. Even if it was said to him that he would never be released, it was not added: “even if you repent, even if you withdraw from error, even if you cease to be a transgressor.”

Therefore it is clear that “he will never be released” was said of him as one who is bound, not of one who had become different: just as he was not to be bound if he no longer possessed the cause of bondage, so he would certainly be absolved once he had become different, so that he would no longer seem unable in some manner to be released by necessity of the sentence pronounced [Col. 0105D].

For one who has become different and is free from bondage would thereby become absolved, and the sentence fixed against such persons would in no way be made unreleaseable [Note: The same manuscript reads: “releasable.”]

Did he not send, ask, seek, and then get rejected [Col. 0106A]? Thus he himself made the sentence unreleaseable in his own case, because he chose to remain such a person as could truly not be absolved. He did not wish to become such a person that, while the sentence remained in force against those who were such, it would not remain unreleaseable against one who had become different—because the sentence would have no authority to remain against one who had become different.

For this reason, warned by the example and danger, those who are bound by the same condition ought to hasten not to remain such persons as have had fixed against them a sentence that cannot be released, but to begin to be such persons for whom a sentence fixed as unreleaseable can become releasable.

For when someone has become not such as the person against whom an unreleaseable sentence was fixed—when, I repeat, he has become not such—the sentence can be releasable. But just as, in Acacius’s case, because he was unwilling to become not such, the absolute sentence remained against one who persisted in being such to the end, so a sentence cannot be releasable for one unwilling to become not such [Col. 0106B].

Did Acacius not have before him the example of so many bishops whom he could have followed—bishops who had fallen into the Ephesian robber-council and in one way or another had relapsed into agreement with wickedness? Yet they too could have incurred perpetual condemnation, although it was not stated, unless they repented and ceased to be such as those men had become and as deserved perpetual condemnation. By withdrawing from the cause of perpetual condemnation, they could have deserved that condemnation to be released from them [Note: The same manuscript reads: “they deserved.”] [Col. 0106D]. Those who persisted made the condemnation unreleaseable against themselves.

It makes no difference, then, whether one says “he will never be released” or does not say it. Ecclesiastical judgment binds the guilty and transgressors. Although it was not said of him that he would never be released, if he remains in error he persists in every respect as one who cannot be released, and he can be absolved only after becoming different; therefore the omission of the phrase cannot help him.

Nor, for the same clear reason, can the phrase “he will never be released” prejudice anyone, since such a person will indeed never be released if he persists as the person who was bound, or if he remains such a person as is never to be released because he is bound.

But since it was not added, “even if he repents and corrects himself,” it is plainly evident and open that one who has become different from the person of whom it was not said that he would never be released—one who has become such as is not said never to be released, namely, corrected and amended—may consequently be corrected and released [Col. 0106C].

It should be noted that those who blaspheme against the Holy Spirit in whatever manner, if they repent and correct themselves, receive forgiveness both in this age and in the age to come. The Lord’s sentence cannot thereby be shaken, for it was declared to remain with those who persist in such a condition, not with those who have become different.

So long as they remain in this condition, they are such persons as have had fixed against them the sentence that they will not be forgiven. But when they withdraw from it, they become different from those of whom it was foretold that they would not be forgiven. Therefore, once they have become different, they can both in this age and in the age to come not be forgiven [the transmitted double negation is retained] [Col. 0106D].

Otherwise—God forbid—the Church would seem to receive such persons into reconciliation in vain. But since it cannot do so in vain, this must be preached in every way, consistently with the Lord’s sentence, insofar as it concerns us: that it is entirely possible [Note: The same manuscript reads: “not possible.”] [Col. 0107A].

Acacius was therefore said to be such a person as is bound and will never be released. He remained such to the end; he did not cease to be such. Thus today he is such as he was said to be [Note: The same manuscript reads: “and is said to be.”].

He can no longer become not such. Therefore, by remaining such, he is never to be released. If he had ceased to be such and had remained not such [the transmitted wording is apparently corrupt], he could be absolved, since “never to be released” would not apply to one who was not such as had been declared never to be released; and, by becoming not such, he would depart from never being released and thus attain release.

The Apostolic See did not consent to this; the emperor did not impose it; Anatolius did not usurp it. Everything, as has been said, lay within the power of the Apostolic See.

What the Apostolic See confirmed in the synod obtained authority; what it rejected could possess no validity. It alone rescinded what the synodal assembly had thought to usurp contrary to order—not as the promulgator of a repeated sentence, but as the executor, together with the Apostolic See, of an ancient one.

What has been said of one and the same man—whether he persists as the person who rightly received the sentence, or has become different—is also read as having been fixed in every city, and as having been set forth alike for the people and nation together, which is a portion of the whole world [Col. 0107B].

For the world is the same world which has been declared destined to perish, and the word of God cannot fail; yet in that same world, when it withdraws from wicked intentions, the former declaration is no longer applied [Col. 0107C].

Thus Tyre and Berytos [Note: The manuscript reads “Beryton.”], and Gaza (Jeremiah 47), and Egypt (Jeremiah 44) were declared destined to perish, yet afterward we know through the Gospel that they were saved (Luke 10).

They therefore perished in two ways: either by remaining in the condition in which they had received such a sentence, or by departing from the condition in which they had been such and beginning to be what they had not been. The sentence had been fixed against them, but consequently did not apply to those who were no longer such, since it had not been fixed against persons of that kind.

The same is true of the Jewish people. God, through the prophet Isaiah, pronounced against them in the form of a definitive sentence: “Close their eyes and shut their ears, so that, seeing, they may not see, and hearing, they may not hear, lest at any time they should understand; and harden the heart of this people, lest they should ever be converted and I should heal them” (Isaiah 6) [Col. 0108A].

Here correction and amendment are also shown to have been forbidden, and all hope of repentance is entirely cut off. Yet we know that from this people the apostles [Note: The manuscript reads: “the apostles and the primitive Church”] and the primitive Church arose [Note: The manuscript adds: “and so many”], and that thousands of people were saved by baptism on a single day (Acts 2).

Behold: in those who persisted, the sentence once promulgated remained in force; they were not admitted at all to the correction that brings healing, but were judged to perish in their wickedness. Yet, while the divine sentence remained, they were not converted and healed through their own amendment, understanding, movement, strength, or ability; rather, they were healed by the grace of God so that they might be converted [Col. 0108B].

“He says, ‘lest they should be converted and I should heal them,’” lest they should be converted by their own will or by their own works—which they certainly trusted in—and, pursuing their own righteousness, fail to submit to the righteousness of God, trusting in their own powers rather than subjecting themselves to divine mercy and illumination.

Therefore the effect of proud presumption is restrained in them, lest they should be converted by their own intentions and efforts, as they had imagined, and lest saving grace should be given to them as though it came through merits arising from their own capacity. In that case grace would no longer be grace, if it were not freely given to the undeserving, but were repaid as a reward to those who had earned it.

Therefore they are not themselves to be converted, “and I will heal them”; rather, healed by grace, they are to recognize how they may be converted to the humility of Christ.

Thus in both groups—both those who remain in the condition in which they received such a sentence and those who were afterward saved—the Lord’s sentence remained fixed. Yet, while that sentence remained, healing was introduced into them in a wondrous manner, so that the sentence appeared not to have changed; rather, while it continued, healing came not through their confidence in themselves but through the gift of God [Col. 0108C].

But if they are afraid to attempt these matters and recognize that such things do not belong to the measure of their authority—for they have been permitted to judge only human affairs, not to preside over divine ones—how do they presume to judge those through whom divine things are administered?

[Note: Gelasius here indicates that Christ our Redeemer, king and priest according to the order of Melchizedek, wished the political authority which he found on earth to be preserved and circumscribed within definite limits, so that it would not interfere in sacred matters. He distinguishes the ecclesiastical order from political authority in such a way that he nevertheless subjects political authority to ecclesiastical jurisdiction in matters pertaining to God. This is clear from his letter to the emperor Anastasius, in which he says: “For you know, most merciful son, that although by your dignity you preside over the human race, nevertheless, as one devoted to the leaders of divine matters, you humbly submit your neck.” A little farther on, concerning the Roman pontiff himself, he adds: “And if it is right for the hearts of the faithful to submit to all priests generally who rightly administer divine things, how much more should consent be given to the bishop of that See, whom the highest divinity has wished to preside over all priests and whom the subsequent devotion of the universal Church has celebrated?” Let the innovators of our own time therefore see how they can maintain that Gelasius the pontiff—who wrote about the fourfold division of the Church’s goods and at the same time defended the possessions of that Church—was a disturber of these matters. We do not deny that he forbade priests the activities about which the Apostle says in 2 Timothy 2: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular affairs.” What those affairs are has been explained elsewhere in various canons. — Severinus Binius.]

These arrangements existed before Christ’s coming, so that certain men, still engaged in carnal actions, were at once figuratively kings and priests. Sacred history records that Saint Melchizedek was such a person (Genesis 14) [Col. 0109A].

The devil also imitated this arrangement among his own followers, since he has always attempted, in a tyrannical spirit, to claim for himself whatever belongs to divine worship, so that pagan emperors were called both emperors and supreme priests.

But when the true king and priest came, neither did the emperor any longer assume for himself the name of priest, nor did the priest claim royal majesty. Although his members—that is, those of the true king and priest—are said, through participation in his nature, magnificently to have received both dignities in their sacred nobility, so that royal and priestly stock might subsist together [Note: The same manuscript reads: “because”], Christ nevertheless, mindful of human weakness, tempering by a magnificent dispensation what was suitable for the salvation of his own [Note: The same manuscript reads: “he tempered”], distinguished the offices of both powers by separating their proper actions and dignities.

He wished his people to be saved by healing humility, not once again destroyed by human pride. Thus Christian emperors would need priests for eternal life, while priests would use imperial arrangements for the course of temporal affairs, so that spiritual action might remain distinct from carnal incursions; and therefore one who serves God should not entangle himself in secular affairs (2 Timothy 2). Conversely, one involved in secular affairs should not appear to preside over divine matters, so that the modesty of both orders would be maintained, lest anyone, supported by both, become arrogant, and each profession might be appropriately fitted to the specific character of its actions [Col. 0109B].

When all these points have been properly gathered, it is shown with sufficient clarity that a pontiff can neither be bound nor released entirely by secular power.

This makes it still clearer that Peter of Alexandria could in no way have been completely absolved merely by an imperial sentence. If the assent of the bishops was also joined to it, we ask whether that assent preceded or followed [Col. 0109C].

If it followed, the conclusion nevertheless returns to this: an absolution commanded and principally initiated by secular power could not have validity, and the assent of the bishops that followed would have been an act of flattery rather than a lawful decree [Note: The same manuscript reads: “if it followed, and by an imperial sentence, from which nevertheless …”].

If it preceded, let it be shown by whom and where it was carried out; whether it was celebrated according to the rule of the Church; whether it proceeded from the tradition of the fathers; whether it was issued according to the custom of the ancestors; and whether it was produced after a competent examination.

It must unquestionably be asked whether it was celebrated by a synodal assembly—for, since the case was new, this was certainly required in the reception of one who had been condemned and the expulsion of one who was catholic [Note: The same manuscript reads: “newly”]; whether it was referred, according to the rules of the Church, to the First See, whose sentence held Peter bound; whether the same authority which bound him absolved him; and whether the authority that had bound him could have released him without acting, or even knowing that it was doing so [Note: The same manuscript reads: “with that which had not bound him releasing him.”] [Col. 0109D].

If these things were not done, by what custom or rite is Peter of Alexandria claimed to have been absolved, when he was neither lawfully freed by the bishops according to ecclesiastical laws nor able to be wholly absolved by secular power outside the course of the Church?

Perhaps it will be said: “The emperor did not absolve him; he merely asked the bishops to absolve him.”

All the more, then, the bishops should have instructed the emperor who made the request that, if he wished him to be lawfully absolved, a lawful absolution according to ecclesiastical order should result, and that all the matters stated above should be observed according to the Church’s procedure—especially since the matter concerned the bishop of a second-ranking see, who could be absolved by right not by any inferior authority but by the First See.

An inferior cannot absolve a superior; only the superior can appropriately absolve the inferior.

Accordingly, the bishops of an inferior rank, who knew that they could in no way release one superior to themselves without the First See—especially one whom they knew to be bound by its sentence—did not truly strip him of his bonds by their transgressive absolution; rather, they bound themselves more deeply by their transgression [Col. 0110B].

Thus Peter’s absolution is invalid on both grounds. They could not absolve the guilty by a transgressive absolution; and, after catholic bishops had been expelled everywhere and heretics or men contaminated by communion with heretics had been installed in their place—men likewise polluted by the insincerity of their sacred religion—they could no more absolve their associate than they themselves had been absolved.

How, then, could men who were both transgressors against ecclesiastical rule and polluters of the integrity of holy communion through fellowship with the impious pass judgment on one who was guilty and so like themselves?

As for the catholic bishops throughout the entire East, whoever persisted was expelled; or else the man who remained had consented to error and had not withdrawn from the contagion of those who erred.

[Col. 0110C] What judgment, then, could they render concerning anyone’s error, when they are shown to have nowhere remained free from error? With the confessions of heretics and catholics mixed together, they had disturbed all the sees of true and sincere religion [Note: The same manuscript reads: “to have disturbed all”] and had confused catholic and apostolic purity [Note: The same manuscript reads: “to have confused all.”] [Col. 0110D].

Behold the men who were able to absolve the guilty—men who were proved to have become guilty above all others. Behold the men with whom a synod concerning the absolution of the guilty had to be convened.

If the catholic faith and communion were being maintained, why were catholic bishops expelled? If catholic bishops were expelled, how were not merely the heretics being preserved?

[Note: In the very old manuscript of Freising, at the end of this work, it reads: “Here ends the Tome of Saint Gelasius the pope against those who say that Acacius was unjustly condemned.”]

# Pope Gelasius I Against the Senator Andromachus and the Other Romans Who Resolved That the Lupercalia Should Be Celebrated According to the Ancient Custom

[Col. 0110D] He condemns the superstitious celebration of the Lupercalia and proves that Rome’s misfortunes arose not from the discontinuation of the Lupercalia but from its crimes.

Some sit in their houses, knowing neither what they are saying nor about what they are making assertions, striving to judge others while they do not judge themselves; they wish to accuse before they know, and to teach before they learn. Without examining the facts, investigating the causes, or seeking the rationale of events, they thoughtlessly pour out and hastily vomit whatever comes to their lips. They do not pass judgment by putting forward an assertion of truth, but attack what they do not know out of a zeal for malicious speech. They have advanced so far that they even strive to tear apart things rightly done with malicious intent. If they were wise, they would not rush to a judgment at all, but, after investigating the facts, would bring forward what ought to be said.

Yet because they accuse us of being sluggish judges in restraining the vices of the Church, they consequently acknowledge from us not only that bodily adultery is a sin—which ought both to be examined and legally punished—but also that there is a kind of fornication far worse than that of fornicators and adulterers, a kind which, in any Christian—for every Christian is a member of the Church—ought rightly to be punished. For the crime of sacrilege is all the greater as the fornication of the soul is worse than that of the body; through fornication of the soul one departs from union with God himself and passes over to unclean spirits by a kind of spiritual adultery.

But how can one who wishes to appear and profess and call himself a Christian not fall into this category, when he does not shrink, refuse, or fear to proclaim openly and publicly that diseases arise because demons are not worshiped and offerings are not made to the god Februarius? I see where he may have discovered these ravings. How is one not a traitor who falls into such profane blasphemies? How is one not judged sacrilegious who, having renounced the providence and power of the one God whom he confessed, is led away to monstrous superstitions and empty fictions? According to the Apostle, it is far worse—and rightly deserving of condemnation—to abandon the truth once confessed than never to have believed in it at all. For although the fictions he puts forward are ridiculous, his very disposition and will are nevertheless criminal, and his profession and proclamation are rightly subject to condemnation. Therefore, whoever wishes a sentence of condemnation to be pronounced without delay against another should recognize that, in judging another, he condemns himself.

Should a bishop punish those who commit bodily adultery, but not punish those who commit sacrilege—that is, spiritual fornication and adultery? Did not the Lord himself, when the adulterous woman had been brought before him, say to her accusers, “Let the one among you who is without sin be the first to throw a stone at her” (John VIII)? He did not say, “If any one of you is not likewise an adulterer,” but, “If any one of you is without sin.” Therefore, whoever is bound by any sin whatsoever should not dare to throw a stone at one guilty of another sin.

When they had then departed according to their consciences, the Savior of the world added: “Woman, where are your accusers? Has no one condemned you? Neither will I condemn you; go, and from now on sin no more” (ibid.). You hold, and you are held; you press, and you are pressed; you bind, and you are bound. You demand an episcopal investigation and call for punishment. Remember that every accusation must be brought against the accuser as well.

Do not even human laws say that a guilty person cannot make another guilty? You see the speck in your brother’s eye, but you do not see the beam in your own (Matthew VII). You accuse adulterers, yet commit adultery yourself; you attack bodily adulterers, though you are a spiritual adulterer. Certainly you demand an investigation: you are a careful, mature, religious man; you do not want anyone to sin in the Church, and you desire that the sinner be examined and then handed over to punishment. Whatever you promise against another, you will be compelled to bring forward against yourself. This is necessary so that the bishop’s negligence may not be accused and the Church defiled.

Therefore a bishop’s care and severity must not be lacking in any wrongdoing, and the Church’s reputation must be cleared of them all. But perhaps you will say that you are a layman and that he is a minister of the Church. You are right, and I do not deny it: he must be examined with all the greater care the closer he is to the Church, and he is all the more guilty because, having been placed in that ministry, he ought least of all to have done such things. See, the process of judgment is not lacking. Listen, and if he is convicted, he will consequently be handed over to punishment.

Now, what do you say about yourself? Are you not in the sacred congregation merely because you are not in the sacred ministry? Or do you not know that you too are a member of the supreme bishop? Or are you unaware that the whole Church is called the assembly of priests? Finally, if the one who approaches the ministry of the Church and sins is guilty, are you not also guilty, when, after confessing the truth, you return to the corrupt, perverse, profane, and diabolical fictions to which you professed that you had renounced?

Therefore, after openly and publicly pouring forth blasphemies, you too must by every means be kept from the sacred Body. You cannot partake of the Lord’s table and the table of demons; you cannot drink the Lord’s cup and the cup of demons. You cannot be the temple of God and the temple of the devil. Light and darkness cannot coexist in you.

I shall see whether you press and compel punishment for another’s wrongdoing. Nevertheless, you cannot escape the weight of your own crime. The more you refuse to allow a crime in another to pass unpunished, the more you show what, according to the nature of the case, we ought to do against you.

Nevertheless, in the very blasphemies for which you are rightly punishable, recognize your ignorance plainly, and, as that man says, recognize that you have the will to lie but not the art of fabrication. You understand yourself to have such an evil disposition and such a perverse intention of apostasy that the material for that vanity is wholly lacking; you cannot establish what you conceive in your heart and bring forth with your mouth.

Tell me: since the Roman histories frequently record, on Livy’s authority, that immense thousands of people very often perished in pestilence arising in this city, and that matters were repeatedly brought to such a point that scarcely any means remained by which an army could be enrolled in those warlike times, was your god Februarius then not being worshiped, or did this worship not help at all during the time when the Lupercalia were being celebrated? You will not say that these rites had not yet begun at that time, since they are said to have been brought into Italy by Evander before Romulus.

As for why the Lupercalia were instituted, insofar as the fictions of that superstition itself are concerned, Livy speaks in the second decade. He does not mention that they were instituted to prevent diseases, but, as he thinks, to remedy the barrenness of women that had then occurred [perhaps: “to demand relief from”]. Therefore, if this rite had any power even for that purpose, when it was interrupted, not disease—against which the Lupercalia were not devised—would have occurred; rather, women, for whose fertility these rites were said to have been invented, ought not to have given birth.

What will you say about pestilence, barrenness, and the continuous violence of wars? Did these too occur because the Lupercalia had been abolished? But if the Lupercalia were not provided either to prevent or to cure these things, why do you throw yourselves into such empty agitation? What did the offense of the Lupercalia do to Tuscany, to Emilia, and to the other provinces in which scarcely anyone remains to be consumed by military necessity—provinces that were laid waste long before the Lupercalia were abolished?

When the emperor Anthemius came to Rome, the Lupercalia were certainly still being performed, and yet such a pestilence crept in that it could scarcely be endured. Were the Lupercalia being performed throughout Campania, so that, once abolished, they might produce disease and pestilence there? But you will say that everything pertains to Rome as to its head, and that what was not done here harmed the various provinces belonging to it.

Why, then, before these provinces belonged to Rome, did they flourish by their own resources despite the absence of the Lupercalia? Has the removal of the Lupercalia produced the continuing barrenness of the lands, or have our merits—that is, our sins—done so? Of these it was said long ago that whatever the Roman character deserved to lose would come upon it. Certainly the barrenness of women should have followed, since the Lupercalia are said to have been instituted to remove it—not the barrenness of the lands, which the Lupercalia were not instituted to remove.

What of Africa, where there is barrenness? What of Gaul? Did these things result from the Lupercalia, or from our morals—our thefts, murders, adulteries, injustices, iniquities, ambitions, desires, perjuries, false testimonies, oppression of the wretched, attacks upon good causes and defense of bad ones, and, finally, unheard-of perversity in everything? Above all, what of minds falsely devoted to God, sacrileges, and magical arts, which are dreadful even to pagans?

Behold the things that bring about every adversity and hostility toward us—not the Lupercalia, which have been abolished for your safety. But what do you yourselves say, you who defend the Lupercalia and propose that they be performed? You yourselves cheapen them; you yourselves make their worship and celebration common and contemptible. If the abolition of the Lupercalia has brought adversity upon us, the fault is yours, since you treat with the utmost negligence what you think is uniquely beneficial to you and do not celebrate it with a cult and devotion far different from those with which your ancestors celebrated it in their profanity.

Among them, the nobles themselves ran, and matrons were beaten in public with their bodies uncovered. You, therefore, were the first to commit an offense against the Lupercalia. It would have been better not to perform them than to celebrate them with insult. But you have brought down the worship you deem venerable and salutary to yourselves to lowly and ordinary persons, to the abject and the lowest.

If you truly profess that this rite—or rather, this object of execration—is salutary for you, then celebrate it yourselves according to the custom of your ancestors; run about naked with your cloak, so that you may duly enact the mockery of your own salvation. If these things are great, divine, and salutary, if the integrity of your lives depends upon them, why are you ashamed to celebrate them yourselves? If you are ashamed and it is disgraceful, how can what you yourselves admit to be disgraceful be salutary, divine, and beneficial?

No one professes a religion that he is utterly ashamed and unwilling to practice himself. Your very shame should teach you that this is a public crime, not salvation, and not worship of Divinity—no wise person is ashamed of that—but instruments of depravity, which your mind, bearing witness against itself, is ashamed to carry out even while professing that they ought to be performed.

Certainly your Castors, from whose worship you refused to desist, did not provide you with favorable seas, so that ships might come here with grain during the winter and the city might not suffer from want. Or is this benefit, which God has ordained, destined to come in the days that follow in summer, rather than being the result of the Castors’ empty persuasion?

Tell us, you who are neither Christians nor pagans, faithless everywhere and faithful nowhere, corrupt everywhere and upright nowhere—you who cannot hold both positions, since the two are mutually opposed. Tell us, I say, patrons of the Lupercalia, truly mockers of Divinity, defenders of shameful songs, worthy teachers of madness, and, since you do not have sound minds without reason, worthy adherents of a religion celebrated with the voices of obscenities and crimes: see for yourselves what salvation is in store for you when such a religion proposes such a stain and destruction for morals.

Nor can you say that by performing these things, and by publicizing everyone’s crimes, you deter people from committing such deeds and restrain them through shame, so that no one will sing of them in a public voice. For, as that man says, these mockeries seem not so much to deter minds as to admonish them; and, as he said, “They derive anger and courage from crime.” People become all the more shameless when the crime has been made public and shame exposed: nothing remains of which they need be ashamed, nor do they fear that anything will be publicized. Rather, they now boldly reveal themselves. Whoever the person may be, once his character has been sung aloud—not through restraint but through a kind of joy and public celebration—he is confident that he excels even in religion, so that there may be occasions for celebrating the solemnities of names, which are honored only by singing of crimes.

Tell us, then, you who possess the will to profanation but cannot defend its causes, who are determined to protect a falsehood that you cannot defend: what will you say about drought, hail, whirlwind, storms, and various disasters, which arise according to the quality of our morals? Did all these things also occur because the Lupercalia were abolished, or are they inflicted as deserved retributions for the punishment of evil morals?

It is not surprising that people do not wish these things to be thought to occur by divine judgment, but by the assault of empty superstition. In order to cover their crimes and misdeeds, they claim that heaven and the stars lend authority to them, that a fatal error and an obligation to sin are imposed, and that their crimes do not proceed from the perversity of their own hearts but depend upon heaven as their author.

State, then, what evils your Lupercalia were instituted to remove, or what good things to obtain. Let us see what good things occurred while the Lupercalia were being performed and what evils followed when the Lupercalia were thought to have been abolished.

Stand firm and tell us for what destruction of yours you say these prodigies were devised—you who are worthy to celebrate some monster composed of a mixture of beast and man, whether it was truly or falsely produced. If you claim that they were devised to remove pestilence, then, leaving aside earlier times, it is indisputable that before they were abolished in my own time, severe pestilence existed both in the city and in the countryside among human beings and animals.

If you claim that they were devised for barrenness, why do these things occur in Africa or Gaul, where the Lupercalia never existed and where there is no evidence that they were abolished? Why does the East now overflow and abound in an abundance of every good, though it never celebrated and does not celebrate the Lupercalia?

Or do you say that they cause harm where they had been celebrated for many centuries and were suddenly abolished? Let us see whether, during the times when you say they were performed and completed correctly, with their full devotion—as you think—there was never famine and never pestilence. But if these disasters repeatedly reached the utmost extremity of danger, it is clear that the Lupercalia did nothing to remove them, even at the time when, as has been said, they were performed in the proper order, as you suppose. The same argument applies to each of the various needs for which you claim they were provided. If it is established that these calamities did not cease even then, the presumption that this remedy was effective is shown to be empty.

Nevertheless, why do you not even now test whether they have any power when properly celebrated? Run about yourselves in these mockeries according to the custom of your ancestors, so that by celebrating more devoutly this divine and salutary rite, as you claim it to be, you may look after your salvation more and more.

Was Rome not captured by the Gauls while these rites were being celebrated, and did it not repeatedly reach the utmost extremities? Did it not fall into civil wars under this celebration? Were the Lupercalia absent when Alaric overthrew the city? And recently, when it was destroyed by the civil fury of Anthemius and Ricimer, where were the Lupercalia? Why did they provide no benefit in these circumstances?

Certainly the rite is divine. If it is salutary for you, why do you not perform it yourselves, as your ancestors did? Why do you diminish the causes of your salvation? Why do you discolor them? Why do you weaken them and reduce them to what is lowly? Why do you blame us when you yourselves trample upon your remedies?

It is better not to attempt a rite than to perform it insultingly. Certainly your ancestors, if they had celebrated some sacred rite improperly, as they thought, considered that it ought to be renewed. Why do you not restore, with a proper renewal, what you have reduced to an improper worship by having it carried out by every unworthy person, so that you may pursue the causes of your salvation more fully and perfectly? Why are you ashamed to perform it if it is salutary? If it is divine, how can it be disgraceful to have performed it?

But you say that even an image of the rite itself ought not to be removed. If it is beneficial and salutary, why is it only an image among you and not the reality itself? Or, if it was certainly of no benefit even then, when it was carried out according to the complete rite, as is said, why do you seek an image of something whose reality itself you see was of no benefit?

[Col. 0116A] But you say that a rite practiced for so many centuries ought not to be excluded. Nevertheless, the superstition of paganism was also carried on for many ages. Let sacrifices be offered in the temples of demons, and let profane vanity be celebrated in the Capitol. Why do you defend one portion while passing over the greater things? If very many kinds of vanities practiced for many centuries are acknowledged to have been abolished, why should one portion, however long it was practiced, not be removed?

If you appeal to the passage of time, charge your ancestors with this: by not making use of the prescription of time, they showed that what is superfluous can and ought to be removed, since many greater things were abolished. But you also say that these rites existed in Christian times. Yet those other rites too continued to be celebrated for some time during Christian times. Because they were not abolished under the first bishops of the Christian religion, should they therefore not have been removed under their successors?

There are many harmful things that individual bishops have removed or discarded at different times. Medicine does not treat all illnesses in the body at once; it treats what it sees threatening most dangerously, lest either the body’s resources prove insufficient for the treatment or, given mortal conditions, it be unable to avert everything simultaneously.

Consider the nature of the thing about which you are acting. If it is good, divine, and salutary, then it rightly ought never to have been removed. If it is neither salutary nor divine, you have greater reason to complain that what is clearly superstitious and empty, and manifestly incompatible with the Christian profession, is being removed too slowly.

Finally, as far as I am concerned, let no baptized person and no Christian celebrate this rite; let only pagans, whose rite it is, perform it. It is fitting for me to declare that these things unquestionably exist as harmful and deadly to Christians. Why do you accuse me if I declare that what you yourselves profess to be hostile must be removed from those who share the Christian profession?

I shall certainly clear my conscience. Let those who have neglected to obey just admonitions look to themselves. I do not doubt that my predecessors may also have done this and attempted to have these things removed before the imperial authorities. Since it is not evident that they were heard, and since these evils still persist today, those empires have therefore failed; and therefore the Roman name, even without the removal of the Lupercalia, has reached every extremity.

For this reason I now urge that these rites be removed. Since I know that they have accomplished nothing, I declare that, as contrary to true religion, they have instead proved harmful.

Finally, if you think that my predecessors’ persons should be invoked against me, each of us will have to give an account of his own administration, just as you see done in public offices. I do not dare accuse my predecessors of negligence, since I rather believe that they perhaps attempted to remove this depravity, and that certain circumstances and opposing wills existed which impeded their intentions—as you can judge even now, when you are unwilling to desist from these insane efforts.

## Pope Gelasius I Against the Pelagian Heresy

[Note: [Col. 0115] We present this treatise of Gelasius, carefully collated with the edition of Mansi, though it is in many places involved and extremely obscure, as the reader himself will readily perceive. Editor.]

He demonstrates that a human being does not live without sin, and explains the Apostle’s saying, “The unbelieving husband is sanctified through the believing wife” (I Corinthians VII), etc.; he also expounds the mystery of the resurrection.

There is abundant material concerning the Pelagians’ opinions and sacrilegious blasphemies, which were condemned by a just investigation under both divine and human laws by our ancestors. Their pernicious perversity is manifold, and all the more harmful because it is subtler under the appearance of plausibility. From a wicked and destructive fiction concerning the originator of the human race himself, they wove a fabric of lies about the consequences of things, which had not been properly conceived.

For whoever has deviated from the sound path at the beginning proceeds wandering everywhere; and the more strongly he thinks he is running, the more he goes astray. In refuting such matters, therefore, an extended discussion ought properly to be employed. It is indeed the practice of perfect medicine first either to understand or to expose the origin of diseases, and, once these have been revealed, to prepare a suitable remedy. If the Lord grants life and ability, we shall endeavor on another occasion to explain all these matters insofar as, strengthened by heavenly dew, we are able.

For now, however, we have judged it sufficient to explain this point, which is said to trouble certain people in the meantime, so that, once it has been properly examined, they may understand, with the Lord our God granting it, what they ought already to have guarded against in other matters.

Some therefore think that in this life a person can attain such perfection that he is not at all assailed by any impulses of human frailty and is not harassed by bodily allurements. But whoever thinks that he can attain this by his own strength and by the determination of his own will deceives himself, and the truth is not in him.

For if even the first human beings, while they were confident in their own happiness and receiving such great grace from God in vain—since they did not pray, something which they are nowhere reported to have done; nor did they give thanks for what they had received; nor did they humbly implore that these gifts might remain undefiled—could not remain unharmed, how much less can people, after the fall of transgression into which they lethally fell through an evil confidence in themselves, by not seeking the Creator at all, stand by their own strength, whether sick or well, without divine help. Without that help, they could not even remain whole.

But if someone asserts that this can be granted in this life to any saints not through the capacity of human ability but through divine grace, he does well—since all things are possible through God’s gift—to hold such an opinion confidently and to hope faithfully.

Whether, however, any such people have existed, who reached this perfection in the present life, is nowhere clearly established. Therefore it is not fitting for us either readily to affirm or to oppose it. It is more prudent to recognize from the words of the prophets and holy apostles themselves how far the progress of this life ought to be measured. Clearly, as far as the discipline of a holy life is concerned, no one was or is superior to them.

Even if, through a more abundant gift of God, they were assailed either by exceedingly few or by very slight sufferings of the human condition, and through richer grace easily overcame the defects of mortality, they nevertheless do not testify that they were so completely free of them that it is proper to the spotless Lamb alone to have had absolutely no sin—lest, if any other saint were believed to have been free from fault, that distinction should no longer seem to belong to him alone.

Let us therefore be content with the profession of the saints, and let us hear what they themselves pronounce about themselves, rather than follow either what we might rashly think or what we might toss about according to our own opinions without certain authority.

Why, then, after the mystery of the restoration of humanity, when almighty God could also have granted human beings immunity from every vice, did he prefer that his faithful should be saved and await the stability of perfect blessedness, so that what we desire in hope we may be able to attain in reality? Why did he judge it better now to perfect virtue in weakness than to remove weakness and allow the human condition to be disturbed by no affliction of frailty at all?

[Col. 0118B] As the Lord provides, this will be discussed through the testimonies of Scripture. Nothing should be rashly asserted concerning these matters contrary to the tenor of Scripture, by which we are instructed.

It is established that Christ and the Church were prefigured in the very first human being, as the blessed Apostle Paul teaches us when he was speaking about the covenant of holy marriage: “This is a great mystery,” he says; “but I speak of Christ and the Church” (Ephesians V).

Thus, from that time onward, each of the saints who came forth was reckoned within the figure of this mystery; and all the saints, from Abel onward, enacted this mystery through their sacrifices and actions. In Christ and in the Church, in which the remission of sins was universally preordained, all the faithful lived in holiness before God, and until the time of the law given through Moses they were cleansed by appointed sacrifices through the power of this mystery.

Therefore, if all needed to be continually purified by mystical offerings, there is no doubt that they were assailed by the vices of the human condition. Through those remedies of the future sacrament it was necessary that they be continually absolved from them.

Moreover, the venerable reading testifies that, in the time of the law, there was no saint who did not offer a victim for sin. The priests themselves even acted before God as advocates for the people who were then faithful in such a way that they too sacrificed victims for their own sins; and everywhere the prophets proclaim that they sought forgiveness for their sins.

Hence holy Job says: “No one is clean from defilement, not even an infant whose life upon the earth is but one day” (Job XV). And elsewhere: “The stars are not clean in your sight.”

The prophet David is also known to have delivered a definite statement concerning the universality of the saints, saying: “Do not enter into judgment with your servant, for no living person will be justified in your sight” (Psalm CXLII). Here it is plainly evident that he distinguished no human being at all. The same man speaks more clearly and explicitly of this very matter: “I said: I will declare my injustice against myself to the Lord; and you forgave the wickedness of my sinful heart. For this every holy person will pray to you at the proper time” (Psalm XXXI).

He was not merely holy under the law, but was destined to be holy in the future grace of God through a more eminent calling. Therefore, when he says “at the proper time,” he adds this not without knowledge of future things; and the most wise Solomon likewise says in his prayer: “There is no human being who has not sinned.” And again he himself says: “Who will boast that he has a pure heart, or that he is clean from sin?” (Ecclesiastes VII).

But lest the saints of those times be thought perhaps exempt from this inability to suffer because they made use of wives granted by God—although the blessed Elijah too is remembered as having been subject to suffering, as what follows will show—and since the holy prophet Daniel is reported to have prayed not only for the sins of the people but also for his own, as he himself says, “When I prayed and confessed my sins and the sins of my people to the Lord my God” (Daniel XIX), let us finally come to the blessed apostles.

Let the blessed James speak, who, although all the apostles were certainly righteous, is read to have obtained particularly and specifically the distinction of a righteous man: “Blessed is the man who endures temptation, because, when he has been tested, he will receive the crown of life, which God promised to those who love him” (James I).

And shortly afterward: “Each person is tempted when he is drawn away and enticed by his own desire. Then desire, when it has conceived, gives birth to sin; and sin, when it has been completed, produces death.” Again the same man says: “For we all offend in many things.” He then follows this by adding: “Elijah was a human being subject to suffering like us” (James III).

Let the blessed Apostle Peter speak: “Beloved, I urge you, as resident foreigners and sojourners, to abstain from bodily desires, which wage war against the soul” (I Peter II). And again: “Do not be astonished at the fiery ordeal that comes upon you for your testing, as though something strange were happening to you” (I Peter IV).

Later he says: “Be sober and watchful, because your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, prowls about seeking someone to devour. Resist him in faith” (I Peter V), knowing that the same sufferings occur throughout your brotherhood in the world. In speaking of that brotherhood, they themselves often proclaim themselves brothers of all the faithful, and are not shown to have set themselves apart from them.

Let the blessed Apostle and Evangelist John speak—that man who reclined upon the breast of the Savior: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. But if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and cleanse us from all iniquity” (I John I).

Again: “If we say that we have not sinned, we make him a liar, and his Word is not in us” (I John II). The same man says: “I write these things to you so that you may not sin. But if anyone sins, we have a righteous advocate with the Father, and he himself is the propitiation for our sins, not for ours only but also for the sins of the whole world” (ibid.).

Again he himself says: “Everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the ambition of the age, which is not from the Father but from the world. And the world passes away, and its desire; but whoever does the will of the Lord remains forever” (II Corinthians XII).

Let the least of the apostles come, but the Vessel of God’s election; let Paul come, teacher of the nations, preacher uniquely devoted to divine grace, and abundant expositor of the heavenly mystery; he who, not knowing whether he was in the body or outside the body, was lifted up to the third heaven and heard unspeakable words.

He overflowed with such great grace that, although he was last of all, he labored more than all. Let him not only make known to the faithful what he thought concerning this matter, but also freely proclaim, as a teacher of truth, what he declares about himself.

Since it would be too long to review everything that pertains to this issue, let a few passages be set forth from among many, by which it may be demonstrated sufficiently that we ought to become weak with Paul so that Christ may dwell in us, rather than appear strong with anyone who thinks differently from Paul and, God forbid, seem not to need Christ’s remedies.

He says: “For I know that good does not dwell in me—that is, in my flesh. For the desire to do good lies close at hand, but I do not find the means of accomplishing it. For I do not do the good that I desire; it is not I who perform it, but sin that dwells in me” (Romans VII).

Again: “For I delight in the law of God according to the inner person; but I see another law in my members warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin, which is in my members. Wretched man that I am, who will free me from this body of death? The grace of God, through Jesus Christ our Lord” (ibid.).

Why, then, does he call himself a wretched man? Why does he rejoice at being freed through Christ’s grace from the body of death, if he was assailed by no impulses of human misery and harassed by none of the attacks from which he might be freed?

Again the same man says: “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh; for these oppose one another, so that you do not do the things you desire. For the spirit does not accomplish what it desires, lest it become proud of perfection” (Galatians V). And again: “The flesh does not accomplish what it desires,” so that he may thus remind us of the human condition.

Yet lest the faithful proposition be altogether undermined, and lest perhaps— as some are accustomed, in accordance with their empty opinions, to suppose— the blessed Apostle Paul should be thought to pronounce these words under the persona of someone else, rather than confessing them concerning himself (although nothing of the sort can in fact be demonstrated there), nevertheless, when he says, “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord,” let us prove that the persona both of the Gentile and of the Jew has been excluded. Let us hear him elsewhere, however, as though pointing to himself with his own hand and expressly indicating his own person: “I myself serve the law of sin with my mind” (Rom. VII); and again concerning himself: “I chastise my body and bring it into servitude, lest, after preaching to others, I myself should be found reprobate” (II Cor. IX).

Who, then, would fail to perceive [Col. 0120D] what significance there could have been in his restraining his members by chastising them, lest he become reprobate, if he were not assailed by impulses of this kind—since, by neglecting them rather than subduing them through chastisement of his body, he could have become reprobate? Therefore, since these statements are shown to have been professed by the Apostle concerning himself—and even if he had revealed none of these things, nevertheless all would undoubtedly both preach the Lord’s Prayer as necessary and utter it with a truthful heart, in which they are taught to ask daily that their debts be forgiven, to pray that they not be led into temptation, and humbly to implore deliverance from evil—for this reason the blessed Apostle John also is understood to have issued the statement already mentioned, saying: “If we say that we have no sin, we make him a liar” (I John I), namely Christ, who had given this form of prayer to his disciples, in which they would either obtain the remission of their daily debt and implore that they not fall into temptation, or ask to be delivered from evil. Otherwise there would be absolutely nothing that could either weigh down a debt requiring forgiveness, or bring upon them the temptation of sin, or constitute any evil at all from which they might be delivered.

Some, however, are disturbed by the stealthy illusion of those who sleep, as though the concupiscence of those who are awake were not considered more serious. For although bodily immodesty must frequently be restrained either by the discipline of fasting or by the moderation of the food consumed, lest material be supplied for deceiving the human senses through the imagination of phantasmal pleasure, or although this must be implored from divine mercy through fervent prayers, so that minds lulled to sleep may be kept free from seductive visions, nevertheless, whether such things occur to those who act incontinently or to those who live continently, certainly, if there is guilt, that of those who are unaware is less than that of those who openly and manifestly desire the appetite for carnal activity.

Finally, although whoever is afflicted by no such snares, if that is possible, or by only very rare ones, enjoys no small gift of God, nowhere do we read that dreams’ phantasms are charged as guilt. But we plainly know from the Lord’s own voice that this statement was uttered: “Whoever looks upon a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. V). There, consequently, it is beyond doubt that guilt is present. Therefore it must be expiated both by continual supplication and by almsgiving and other good works. For it is not without a mystery that it was said that all things can be cleansed through almsgiving, when the Lord, speaking figuratively about inward and outward purifications, says: “Nevertheless, give alms, and behold, all things are clean for you” (Luke II). The same applies to the statement that “charity covers a multitude of sins” (II Pet. IV), namely, that whatever is drawn in through the insincerity of body and mind may be erased by the work of rational piety.

Concerning the blessed Apostles, however, as we have already said above, we ought to know only what they themselves disclosed in their own words concerning their manner of life.
