Whatever they left unspoken, no permission to investigate remains to us. But let us now examine more diligently why, even after the restoration of the human race and the renewal of nature that takes place through the sacrament of baptism, these vices were not only not removed, but also do not cease to assail those established in the purpose of great continence—whether less or more, according as each person has advanced through the dispensation of divine grace. Why were they left behind as adversaries against which the religious mind must fight?

And although we have already been saved through faith and have received the hope of redemption, nevertheless, as the Apostle says, “the redemption of our body” is still awaited. Although, having been reborn through the heavenly mysteries, we already possess the implanted pledge of adoption, the adoption itself is still awaited for completion thereafter. Thus, when these same vices against which we wage continual combat in the present age have failed, we shall be liberated from this necessity and shall obtain, through the desired affections for those very realities, what we have received by faith and awaited in the hope set before us. In this way, wholly stripped of this plague of assaults, we shall live always in tranquil sanctification. This is promised as destined to be completed in that future blessedness, when, as the Apostle says, “this corruptible shall have put on incorruption, and this mortal shall have put on immortality” (I Cor. XV), and the animal body shall have assumed spiritual dignity.

Therefore, there is no doubt that pride is above every sin, since it is written: “Pride is the beginning of every sin” (Ecclus. X). So great is this evil that individual wrongful acts are judged worthy of condemnation precisely because they are wrong, while pride alone is taught to be dangerous even in good deeds. It is pride that not only prevents the rational creature placed on earth from remaining what it is, but also cast down the angelic nature [Col. 0122B].

For when almighty God, who made all things very good, had established and fashioned everything according to its proper modes and fitting orders, granting each thing the capacity to remain or advance according to its own measure, an impulse crept into the rational creature. Because the creature had been constituted in a manner more excellent, this impulse caused it to place greater confidence in its own dignity than, as its condition required, in the giver of that dignity. Thus, by desiring the stability of its own summit in a way other than the fitting and proper order demanded, it caused the creature, through its desire for a more excellent height of merit, to break beyond the natural order. This excess brought guilt upon the one who exceeded the limit, and likewise offended the justice of the Creator, against whose order the attempt was directed. And when the course by which alone it could advance toward perpetual participation in the highest good was abandoned, defect necessarily entered—as was fitting for the uses of a rational creature—which could not attain stable participation in that good.

That angels were created for progress toward the earning of eternal stability is shown by the fact that, if they had been made so that they needed to do nothing further, no part of them could have possessed any defect. Nor should one say that there was a different nature among them, lest the angel who fell by his own will be excused, if it should seem that this was not imposed upon him by his own insolence but by the necessity of the condition implanted in him.

How, then, did the blessed and sublime angels deserve to advance and be raised toward God’s perpetuity? Grateful for what they had received, they fulfilled the duty of pious devotion, preferring not themselves but rather the author himself. Those, however, who are reprobate, consequently became ungrateful for what they had received. Concealing the service they owed, they attempted to prefer themselves to the one who had created the substance of such great dignity. Ensnared by delight in their own creation, they abandoned the honor of the Creator; and, lifted up in proportion to their arrogance, they failed through irreverence to follow the rectitude of eternity. Thus they were simultaneously withdrawn from his indignation and from participation in him; and, departing from what is eternal, they were reduced to that which is always failing. By the favor of our God, we trust to pursue this matter more fully elsewhere.

For the present, insofar as suffices for the matter at hand, this is that cause, this is that evil, by which the angel, even without bodily vice, was moved by a certain spiritual fornication and fell away from the divine grace and participation by which he was illumined [Col. 0123A]. Becoming degenerate in this way and excluded from the heavenly seat because of this disfigurement, he, inflamed by envy, overthrew the image of God in the second-order creature.

He attacked the human being living in security with the same impulses by which he himself, wickedly trusting in himself, had fallen from the heights to the depths. Hence it was that the happiness of paradise could not remain established for the first human beings; hence the integrity of the original condition. For, trusting in itself as though it did not need the one who had created it, it neither gave thanks for what it had received—which is nowhere recorded as having been done—nor asked for help in preserving what it had taken possession of. Even when the tempter’s approach assailed it, it did not devoutly hasten to him or seek his counsel. Entrusting itself amid prosperity to its own will, it readily exposed itself, without the Creator’s protection, to the snares of the deceiver. Consequently, drawn into transgression of what had been forbidden, it encountered the condition of the death that had been decreed and was deservedly subjected to fitting punishment.

For it had neither been devout in preserving the good things it possessed nor guarded against the evil previously foretold. Through its ambition for greater power—presuming, that is, that it would be God—it fell into the pits of the enemy’s persuasion. Though, had it remained grateful to its maker in the order proper to it, it could have attained perpetual communion with the supreme Divinity, having been cleansed by abundant promise and fittingly without any debt owed to the service of the supreme Godhead, it could not attain Divinity.

Thus, without the affection for that principal and highest reason—which remains undefiled in always retaining good things and rejecting their opposites, and in whose likeness the rational creature had been made, so that by imitating it according to its capacity through fitting actions, by preserving reverence for it, and by following its grace, it might remain truly its likeness and image—the creature could have obtained a worthy participation in divine reason as its parent and author, and through this, as a participant in eternity, could likewise have remained eternal. But, trusting in its created dignity, it supposed that it was subject to itself in the very state in which it had been made, and did not venerate its maker with submissive devotion. It therefore departed from participation in him and did not remain established in itself, apart from him in whom it possessed its being.

And so, exceeding the order of legitimate rationality, it was led into the chasm of irrationality by a semblance of reasoning through which it believed that it could become God [Col. 0123D]. By the deprivation of him who is eternal life, it fell back into that condition which could not retain perpetual life without the fountain of life.

Although, therefore, this creature deserved punishment for these transgressions, God, the just judge, corrected it with the equity of a prescribed law in such a way that he justly abandoned it to itself—the creature that had disdained to follow the divine path amid prosperity. Yet because it had also been deceived by the assault of a superior creature, namely the one who raged because he thought that earthly substance could advance from the place from which he himself, a spiritual being, had fallen, and who desired, as it were, to obtain consolation from the ruin of another creature, he compassionately provided for it through an ineffable dispensation of mercy.

The deceived creature seemed to imply not only that it itself should be blamed for another’s transgression, but also to refer its own fall to the Creator’s workmanship, as though his other work could scarcely have remained sound. Yet God showed by this reasoning that both creatures had been rightly made: the degenerate angels are reproved by the blessedness of the holy angels. The latter attained, by the same means—namely, through the duty of due piety, by praising their Creator with fitting proclamation, through the increase of his favor and the progress of appropriate reverence, through participation in the good parent, and through the stability of eternal glory—the advancement and perpetual stability they deserved.

So too the former could have reached a similar blessedness if they had striven in the same manner. But, sluggish in praising their maker and failing to follow fitting reverence, they withdrew from the desire for participation in him and could not receive from him the growth and perfection of their own dignity. Detained by the splendor of their creation, they presumed that they needed nothing further and could suffice for themselves. Confident that they could obtain by themselves whatever they might have attained through the grace of the Creator alone—something they could not possess in the mutable condition of their creation—they are refuted by the human being himself through clear indications.

Humanity was made so rightly that the one who, through divine grace, can rise after a fall is shown to have been able to remain whole to a far greater degree had he followed that same grace with a devoted mind. The greater the power of this grace, the more clearly it is recognized from the fact that the creature could neither stand unharmed without it nor return to that same safety after falling.

God is therefore the good craftsman, who always possesses the eternal and supreme being that belongs to what is good and therefore never harbors any further desire to increase, since nothing exists above that which is eternally good and always supreme. Nor can he be diminished by any inclination from the very fact that he is the supreme and eternal good. Hence he is also said to have been established “in the form of God” not by robbery: he possessed this by nature. The spirit, however, which possessed neither eternity nor supreme status at all, preferred to seize by robbery what it could have attained through the Creator’s perpetual grace, from whom it had received the substance of angelic splendor. The blessed angels, remaining in divine grace, attained the stability of eternal blessedness; but the wicked spirit could not obtain even what it appeared improperly to seize, and, exceeding the course of its condition, could not even remain in what it had been made [Col. 0124D].

Therefore, when the good Creator wished to establish that he had created a good work, had it remained in the same condition of its creation, he mercifully took upon himself both the nature and the cause of his inferior creature’s offense. The spiritual substance, which had proceeded from itself and from another, had become a deceiver and, persisting in its wickedness, was wholly unworthy to attain what it sought. Accordingly, he compassionately assumed the nature of the earthly condition and of the substance deceived through fraud. Thus, to explain briefly, he purposed to restore what had fallen through a fitting dispensation: in himself this same nature, which through the disobedience of death might return to life—he alone knowing no sin [perhaps: “knowing sin”]—assumed the substance [Col. 0125A] that he had powerfully and benevolently undertaken to restore after sin, so that he might charge to himself the undeserved death which, being without sin, he certainly did not owe, on behalf of those who through sin had become debtors to death.

At the same time, he would justly deprive the devil, the deceiver of humanity, of the human being who had consented to him and whom he held subject to himself by divine sentence—one who now owed him nothing. When he had killed the one over whom he had no authority without sin, he was deservedly subjected to him in turn; and he who boasted that he was lord and god of human substance as his captive was himself in turn subjected both to a just man and to the true God.

For it belonged to immeasurable equity that the devil should be conquered not by a sudden exercise of divine power, but by the justice of the very human being whom he boasted he had overthrown. Yet the exalted Restorer was not content that Christ alone should celebrate this triumph over the enemy of the human race in the nature he had assumed. What benefit would be bestowed upon our entire creature if Christ alone were victorious over the devil? Therefore, with immeasurable mercy, he graciously granted his faithful a share in it. He granted it through his grace and the faith bestowed, so that thousands of human beings, through the ineffable economy of the mystery, might obtain participation in him; and, made like their Savior in the renewed nature, they too might become victors over their deceiver, the order of things having been transformed.

Thus, against the proud spirit that persists, provision was made through healing for those being saved, so that they might advance by fitting means toward the integrity of their condition and toward heavenly dignity. The impulse of deadly exaltation—which had cast down not only human nature but also, as has been said, the angelic nature itself—was medicinally turned aside by the necessary humanity, so that integrity might be restored. For after the fall humanity had to be deprived of the evil through which, while whole, it had been unable to remain steadfast.

It was also necessary that the rational human creature should recover, through the grace of God, what it had lost by its own will; and that what was healed without merit should be granted to it so that it might also pursue this through merit. Therefore that unique Savior preferred to perfect strength in weakness rather than once again to make human substance, without weakness, secure in itself or negligent of its author.

Hence the blessed Paul, who disclosed the ruin of the human condition and its restoration more fully than the others, cries out concerning himself as well: “Lest the greatness of the revelations should exalt me, there was given to me a thorn in my flesh, an angel of Satan, to buffet me. For this I besought the Lord three times, that it might depart from me; and he said to me: ‘My grace is sufficient for you, for strength is made perfect in weakness.’ Therefore I will gladly glory in my weaknesses, that the strength of Christ may dwell in me” (II Cor. XII).

And again he himself says: “The creature was subjected to vanity” (Rom. VIII)—still to vanity, insofar as it remains entangled in worldly senses and weighed down by a corruptible condition. It is that creature of which he likewise says elsewhere: “If anyone is therefore a new creature, the old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new” (II Cor. V); and of which he says elsewhere: “For we are his workmanship, created in Christ for good works” (Eph. II). Again, concerning the same creature: “For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision has any power nor uncircumcision, but a new creature” (Gal. VI).

This is the creature in which we have been restored in Christ, not the creature in which we were made at the beginning. Concerning it the blessed Apostle James also says: “Of his own will he begot us by the word of truth, that we might be a kind of firstfruits of his creature” (James I). It is not that creature which was created in Adam, but the creature that, by the will of the Father of lights—from whom every good gift and every perfect gift comes—was begotten through the word of truth, taking its beginning in Christ.

This was done so that human substance might not trust in any of its own goods; rather, whatever rectitude it recognized to be in itself, it might understand to have descended from above, from the unchangeable and immeasurable light that is without the shadow of alteration. Through that light, the mutable creature darkened by the shadow of change might perceive that the gift of true light had been bestowed upon it.

This, then, is that creature which, living spiritually, unwillingly bears the impulses of mortal affliction. It fights against them without ceasing and would prefer not to have enemies to conquer rather than to struggle continually with a hostile foe. Therefore it is unwillingly subjected to vain desires, insofar as they are without doubt destined to perish. Hence the Apostle says: “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh, so that you do not do the things you wish” (Gal. V). But, he says, it is “because of him who subjected it in hope” (Rom. VIII), so that no one in this life, in other words, might again grow arrogant through complete happiness. And lest it perhaps collapse again through despair, he subjected it to these hardships to be endured while nevertheless consoling it by the hope that had been raised up.

This, then, is unquestionably the creature of which he says that “the creature itself also will be delivered from the slavery of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God” (Rom. VIII). He made clear which creature he intended to be understood by saying “into the freedom of the children of God”: it is the creature that now serves in this world insofar as it is assailed by human vices, but that will then come to the freedom of the children of God in perfect security, when “this corruptible shall have put on incorruption, and this mortal shall have put on immortality.” Then the saying that is written will be fulfilled: “Death is swallowed up in victory. Where, O death, is your victory? Where, O death, is your sting? The sting of death is sin, and the strength of sin is the law. But thanks be to God, who has given us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ” (I Cor. XV).

Therefore the blessed Apostle, wishing to show more clearly both which creature he was discussing and what slavery and what freedom belonged to it, as the one through whom Christ was speaking, repeats the point and says: “For we know that every creature groans and is in labor” (Rom. VIII). This can only be the rational creature—and that rational creature which, having already been reborn, knows what it is groaning over and what it is in labor to bring forth; which mourns its weakness and awaits the promise of perpetual tranquility.

We must observe more carefully how far the excellent teacher carries the argument: “Not only that,” he says—that is, not only the creature of the Christian people—“but we ourselves also, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit.” These are, in particular, the Apostles, the leaders and fathers of the Church, who received the gifts of the Holy Spirit at the beginning so that they might administer spiritual growth to the churches [Col. 0127A]. Without controversy, he included himself among them as well, although endowed with greater grace. Hence he says, “having the firstfruits of the Spirit,” as though they were the chief recipients of God’s grace; nevertheless, he established himself, along with the whole Church, in one and the same general condition.

“But we ourselves also,” he says, “having the firstfruits of the Spirit, groan within ourselves.” He revealed whose that groaning was which he had mentioned above, and clearly explained what they were groaning over: “awaiting adoption.” Yet they have already received the pledge of adoption through the sacrament of regeneration. What, then, is this adoption that is still awaited after the beginnings of adoption? And what is this redemption of our body whose coming is proclaimed?

Have you therefore not received what you say you are awaiting? “I have received it,” he replies, “but I have been renewed and initiated into the heavenly mysteries while still surviving and remaining in this mortality. Since these mysteries are working in me what properly belongs to them, may I attain their fullness and perfection; and may the victory of those who fight here be completed there, where it will be said: ‘Death is swallowed up in victory. Where, O death, is your sting?’”

“Now we have been saved in hope; but hope that is seen is not hope. For who hopes for what he sees? But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience” (I Cor. XV; Rom. VIII). He has disclosed with sufficiently clear light what is the condition of the faithful in this life: what they hold in faith, what they endure in hope, and what they desire with their whole love.

All this unquestionably happens for the reason that a certain teacher of the Church, Augustine, wisely explained, saying: “For the material of struggles has been preserved for the great benefit of the faithful, so that holiness may not become proud while weakness is being assailed. Thus, warned at least by its own fragility after the fall, our condition may not trust in itself but continually return to the mercy of him by whose restoration it may be renewed. It could not remain in the undefiled happiness of paradise because it did not seek his grace; let it learn, through such assistance, that it fell from there and that through the same assistance it is instructed to return to everlasting joys after its afflictions. It could have endured in safety all the more through this aid, since it is not merely brought back to the design of its creation but also prepared for a heavenly dwelling.”

This argument should in no way be considered contrary to what the blessed Apostle and Evangelist John discussed in his Epistle: “For whoever is born of God does not sin” (I John IV)—as though from this it should be believed that those who have been regenerated do not sin. For if that great man had uttered this in the sense that some wrongly judge, then universally whoever had been reborn would no longer be able to sin.

Moreover, anyone who claims that John defined this is proved to hold an opinion contrary to the same Apostle. For he also says elsewhere: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (I John I). And again: “If we say that we have not sinned, we make him a liar, and his word is not in us.” Surely it was this very great and eminent Apostle who said this. If anyone dares to consider himself superior to him in merits, let him see to it and beware lest he fall into the abyss of deadly presumption [Col. 0128A].

Certainly, the very man who said these things had been born of God; nevertheless, he taught and proclaimed: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves,” and the other statements contained above. But let that divinely filled man himself explain how one who is born of God cannot sin: “If we say,” he says, “that we have not sinned, we make him a liar. But if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all iniquity” (ibid.).

He made clear how one who is born of God cannot sin: after each of the faithful has been born of God, just as he ought not to declare that he has no sin, so whatever sin he has contracted by committing an act cannot remain in him once it has been removed through confident forgiveness. As he himself adds immediately afterward: “I write these things to you so that you may not sin. But if anyone sins, we have a righteous advocate with the Father; and he is the propitiation for our sins—not for ours only, but also for the sins of the whole world” (I John II).

The prudent reader will be able to find and establish this point more clearly through abundant testimonies throughout the entire body of Scripture.

Thus the antidote of our salvation has been suitably prepared, so that, laying aside all arrogance, “whoever glories may glory not in himself but in the Lord” (II Cor. X). Those who love truth should also carefully consider what we have observed to disturb certain people in the Apostle’s statement, when he was speaking to married believers: namely, that an unbelieving husband or wife is sanctified through the faithful partner of either sex.

First, what was said concerning the marital covenant appropriately presents itself: “The two shall be one flesh” (I Cor. VII). From this it may consequently be understood that, since the body of any faithful spouse is the temple of God, cleansed through regeneration and sanctified by the purification of the mystery, in a certain manner, through the unity of marital flesh, the sanctification of the unbelieving spouse also reaches the body. This association is vastly different from that union in which both spouses are devoted to idols and polluted by the habitation of unclean spirits.

In the former kind of marriage, through the law and covenant of marriage, divine blessing reaches the other spouse—even if perhaps that spouse is unaware and unwilling—through the flesh united to the faithful partner. In the latter, however, the principal fornication by which the soul is alienated from God, together with the contagion of the evil spirit, stains both spouses with detestable pollution and makes them outsiders to the faith that purifies hearts for the supreme Divinity [Col. 0128D].

Next, as I judge, it is not unreasonable to add this consideration: through the prayer of a faithful spouse, some measure of mercy is also granted to the unbelieving spouse, or at least mercy that pertains to temporal salvation. Through this mercy the unbeliever acquires no small share in divine compassion and is, in a certain manner, declared to have become a participant in divine favor.

For if the foods described as unclean by the sacred law are testified by the Apostle to be sanctified through the word of God—hence also the statement, “What God has cleansed, do not call common” (Acts XI)—it will not be absurd or inappropriate that, through the prayer of the faithful spouse, which is certainly offered because of marital affection, the unbelieving spouse should also obtain some degree of sanctification, receiving the divine mercy for which the faithful spouse’s supplication pleads.

This is altogether different, as has been said, from that marriage in which both spouses are excluded from the purity of the true Divinity, deliberately removed from it, and, invoking unclean spirits on both sides, are filled with equal uncleanness.

For if, by comparison with lesser or greater sins, the person justified is said to be justified in relation to one entangled in greater vices—just as it is said to Jerusalem, which at that time was seething with the enormity of crimes and transgressions, “You have justified your sister Sodom” (Ezek. XVI)—how much more may justification or sanctification, though not full and perfect, nevertheless appropriately be understood in a certain manner where not only does the faithful spouse sin less, but the sinful spouse also seeks the remedy of the supreme Divinity, than where both spouses sin?

That this sanctification reaches the unbelieving spouse in a certain manner through the faithful spouse is attested by the Apostle’s own words. For he does not affirm that the unbelieving spouse has already received legitimate sanctification, but that the unbeliever acquires something of sanctification through the faithful spouse.

Finally, he added the condition by which the unbelieving spouse is to be judged: “But if the unbeliever departs, let him depart” (I Cor. VII). He does not thereby indicate that the unbeliever is to be received as though already faithful because, through the things just mentioned, something from the faithful spouse—whether the companionship or the prayer of divine sanctification and grace—has reached the unbeliever. Rather, unless the unbeliever also becomes faithful, he is without doubt to be judged as an unbeliever [Col. 0129C].

There is also another manner in which sanctification may be imparted to an unbelieving spouse through a spouse who has already become faithful: if the faithful spouse suggests conversion to God and belief in the supreme Divinity, impresses upon the unbeliever God’s majesty and power, and, through marital affection, more easily instructs and inclines the unbeliever toward faith. The faithful spouse may explain what hope awaits those who believe in the one God, whether during the course of this life or, after its passage, what rest will be theirs.

When, through the confidence of marriage, the faithful spouse frequently presses these truths upon the unbeliever’s heart in holy words and with continual speech, the effect of divine sanctification is offered both to the unbeliever’s mind and to the body, as the blessed Apostle Peter says: “Likewise, let wives be subject to their husbands, so that, even if some do not believe the word, they may be won without a word through the conduct of their wives, observing your chaste conduct in fear” (I Pet. III).

If the unbeliever receives this through the intimacy of marriage and does not receive the grace of God administered through marital affection in vain and reject it, the unbelieving spouse is sanctified through the faithful spouse, being drawn from unbelief into participation in sanctification by these means.

Otherwise, if the unbeliever does not receive through marital affection the grace offered to him, and, forgetful both of divine favor and of singular human affection, judges it to be rejected as vain, and therefore attempts to renounce the spouse’s affection as well and to withdraw from the law of that pious union, the unbeliever is rightly permitted to depart. For such a person is not worthy of that marriage by which he has judged himself unworthy.

The faithful spouse should patiently bear having been deprived of that marriage in which the other spouse fornicates away from God, while the faithful spouse, by cleaving to God, preserves primary chastity toward God. Thus the faithful spouse is rid both of the adulterer and of the one who refuses truly to become one flesh with a spouse who has already become faithful. The faithful spouse should not suppose that the union which the other has despised in defiance of God’s law of marriage was legitimate, but should rather willingly accept that the one whose soul was separated from God has also been separated bodily from the faithful spouse.

In accordance with this same principle, what is subsequently asserted concerning the children of such people must also be understood. The Apostle says that, unless this sanctification took place between spouses of this kind, their children would be unclean; but now they are holy. They are holy in a certain manner, by comparison with those born from two parents alike devoted and contaminated by diabolical uncleanness.

# HERE BEGIN

For these children, insofar as they have arisen from the holy flesh of a believing parent, from the temple of God, and from one who bears the one God in his heart, have drawn something of divine blessing. In that blessing, sanctity is certainly contained; touched by its gracious favor, they are not undeservedly called holy. Through this sanctification some are even taken up, so that they may attain to it as is fitting: through the believing parent they already receive its beginnings and recognize the fragrance of holy adoption. Through the prayers of the Christian parent—by which divine mercy is undoubtedly implored for them—sanctification is already bestowed. Often, moreover, through the zeal of the believing parent, the little ones are either brought to venerable places or, while they are unaware, are granted full sanctification in the baptismal font through rebirth. Or, when they have already become capable of reason, the exhortation and instruction of the devout parent are impressed upon them.

It is clear that all these are instruments of sanctification, by which they either come—perhaps [the text may read *aut*]—to its firmness [F.: “they come”; and below, *dispoliant*], or, if they despise these things, strip themselves of sanctification and plainly empty out the grace of God that is conveyed to them through the affection of their parents. Thus, cut off from the holy and from the teachings of holiness, they are reduced to the profane company of the unholy.

Concerning these, nevertheless, let the same be said as was commanded concerning their unbelieving parents: “If the unbeliever wishes to depart, let him depart” (1 Cor. 7). Are these forms of holiness or sanctification perhaps being intimated with regard to children born from two profane parents? Behold what difference there is between offspring born from this marriage and from that one; behold how these are sanctified as members of the household and kindred, and therefore are not undeservedly born holy; how divine mercy is consequently implored for them by that parent’s prayers; and how they are imbued with holy instruction and initiated into the devotion of sacred religion. If they attain firmness in it, they obtain through the sacrament the fullness of that sanctification whose beginnings they had already received through the believing parent even before the sacrament. Through those beginnings they were appropriately called holy, since they were being prepared by holy instruction.

But because it has been said that the unbelieving spouse is sanctified through the believing spouse, was this said so that the unbeliever no longer needs the sanctification of personal faith, and not rather because, through that familiarity with the believing spouse, he has been brought close and made near to the sanctification that must be received? For if he were said to be already sanctified, so that he had no need at all of sanctification, Scripture would not subsequently say of the same person: “If the unbeliever wishes to depart, let him depart.” Thus their children too are called holy because, through the affection of the holy parent, they are close to receiving holiness—not because they themselves already have no need of personal sanctification, which, as no Christian doubts, is neither received nor possessed without the mystery of sacred rebirth.

Their unbelieving parent likewise is called sanctified through the believing spouse in such a way that, if he does not personally receive the legitimate effect of the sanctification conveyed to him through the believing spouse, he is still called an unbeliever. Therefore, just as the one whom he called sanctified through the believing spouse he later calls an unbeliever, because he himself or she herself did not personally believe, so also the children who, through the believing parent, were sanctified in the same manner as the spouse and were called holy are consequently unbelievers unless they themselves also personally believe.

It is sufficiently clear that this sanctification was called that of the spouse in a certain sense, even though that spouse is later asserted to be an unbeliever. The same, therefore, must be understood concerning the children.

Can the offspring of profane parents—which exists under the domination of unclean spirits and is enslaved to diabolical transgressions and contaminations—be covered by any portion of this kind of holiness, or receive through such disciplines, prayers, and exhortations any share, knowledge, hearing, or instruction in holiness? In this respect it is always unclean, just as its parents are, so long as it remains in the same perversity.

Often, however, through anticipation—which occurs very frequently in the text of Holy Scripture—what is going to happen is already said to exist. Thus we read in the Gospel: “Because Jesus was about to die for the nation, and not for the nation only, but also to gather into one the children of God who were scattered” (John 11). He already calls them children of God, although they were still to be summoned throughout the world by the widespread calling of grace, renewed through sacred mysteries, and adopted as children of God.

Likewise, when it is said, “Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed” (John 20), those who at that time were still going to become blessed are already called blessed, since they were to be blessed when they believed what they had not seen. Similarly, things that are to be done are often reported as already done, as in: “They pierced my hands and my feet” (Luke 24).

Again, something is expressed as though it were being professed and defined, although it was not to be done because some circumstance intervened. Thus the blessed Apostle professes, out of devotion to the preaching entrusted to him, that he will go to Spain, although, by a definite dispensation of the Godhead, this did not come to pass.

Alternatively, something is called what it has ceased to be or will cease to be. Thus Judas is called an apostle, although by his transgression he lost what he had been called; likewise he is called a disciple, although he was not a disciple of Christ but rather of the devil, as it was said of him: “One of you is a devil” (John 6), because he was the devil’s agent. Nevertheless, he was called a disciple even when he was not a true one and was going to cease to be called this.

There is also the manner in which something is often stated generally and absolutely, although it is clear that it does not apply generally to everyone. Thus it is said to Abraham: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 22). All nations will indeed be blessed, and there will be no nation under heaven to which the Gospel will not be preached, and then the end will come; but the nations themselves will not all be blessed in their entirety, because faith does not belong to all.

Likewise: “Let every tongue confess to God” (Phil. 2). To this expression is connected the sense in which the whole is often named from a part, just as on that occasion the man Judah undoubtedly named the whole nation.

So those faithful people may also be called holy, because many, or very many, of them will be made holy through the heavenly mysteries with which they are imbued by the things already mentioned. They are rightly already said to be what they will become; or, because through that portion by which they were participants in holiness through the religious parent they were called holy as though they were already holy in their entirety; or because many such children would become heirs of complete sanctification.

These, too, therefore, are called from what they were going to become. And although perhaps very many of them were going to become this, they are generally all called holy from the portion of the holy.

## On the Nature of the Resurrection

Let us hear the Apostle preaching about the quality of the resurrection and about what form will exist after the resurrection. He says: “But someone will say, ‘How are the dead raised? And with what kind of body will they come?’” (1 Cor. 15). Rebuking the unbelief of the human mind—which rightly deserves to be called foolish when it judges anything impossible for God—the distinguished teacher suitably introduces a magnificent likeness and comparison drawn from visible things and from ordinary human experience, saying: “Foolish one” (that is, you who think these things impossible for God or doubt that they can be done), “what you sow is not made alive unless it first dies” (ibid.).

He aptly applied this comparison to the resurrection of the body that will follow death. Then he added what follows: “And what you sow, you do not sow the body that is to be, but a bare grain, perhaps of wheat or of some other kind. But God gives it a body as he has willed” (ibid.).

He took care to apply a comparison concerning the quality and form that will exist after the resurrection: “as he has willed,” he says. What more do you seek? As God wills, so he will give each person a body raised by ineffable power. But perhaps you think that this more strongly signifies that each person’s own body will not be restored in its proper identity, since it is asserted that it will be restored as God wills.

Therefore, if you seek to know what kind of body God will restore to each person, precisely in the manner he wills, carefully attend to the fuller meaning of the Apostle as he treats this subject, and consider it as though the Apostle were then answering you in these words.

Do you desire to know why God will give the resurrected body as he wills? Understand wisely: “to each of the seeds its own body” (ibid.). The man of God certainly does not add this without cause, unless it was to remove the future doubts of human beings about such matters.

Listen, I say, to what he wisely added, and recognize from the likeness the reality to which it is compared: “to each,” he says, “of the seeds its own body.” If there is an own body in the likeness, then in the reality whose likeness it is, it is certain that an own body will also be restored. For without dispute he compared these seeds with human beings, whose death and resurrection he was discussing. Therefore, matching each thing with its counterpart, he wonderfully explained, insofar as it concerns bodies to be made alive after death, by the comparison with the grain that is not made alive before it dies.

Next, he disclosed by that same comparison what kind of body each person would be considered to have after the resurrection: whether in the condition he had possessed in dying or in a much better one. He then explained the comparison: “And you who sow, you sow a bare grain, perhaps of wheat or of some other kind; and God gives it a body as he wills” (1 Cor. 15).

In this form he clearly expressed that God gives the body in a condition more excellent than that in which it had died, as is said in what follows: “It is sown in corruption, it rises in incorruption; it is sown in dishonor, it rises in glory; it is sown in weakness, it rises in power; it is sown an animal body, it rises a spiritual body” (ibid.).

Behold how what is sown is not the same as the body that will exist after the death of the human being. Behold how “as he wills” is understood: God reforms the body of those who will rise after death according to the ineffable will of his mercy. What had been sown in corruption he restores with incorruptible nobility; what had been laid to rest in the dishonor of earthly condition he raises in heavenly glory; what had been dissolved through the weakness of mortality he restores, clothed in the beauty of immortality; finally, what had died as an animal body he restores and reforms as a spiritual body. All these things concern a condition of improvement and exaltation.

The remaining part of the comparison, however, is affirmed to pertain specifically to the restoration of each person’s bodily identity, where it is subsequently said: “And to each of the seeds its own body.” Here it sufficiently appears that, in whatever glory belongs to those who rise, the identity of the body will remain. Nor is it without purpose that the blessed Apostle, when speaking only of the human race—which alone is to be raised, since no other substance is to be adorned with this gift—and therefore when one species of seed would have been sufficient as a comparison for the one human race, so that he might teach both that it is not made alive before it dies and that a more honorable body rises than was sown, nevertheless took care to assert that the bodies of the two sexes would be renewed.

A single species of seed, considered as a likeness, did not contain what would correspond to this distinction. Therefore, lest anyone think that by this he signified only one species of the bodies that would be raised, with the distinctions of their identities removed, he carefully and appropriately brought different kinds of seeds into his comparison. Thus the diversity of seeds could indicate the identity of bodies, which one species could not distinguish. It also supplied the comparison with the full capacity by which he could most appropriately say, to designate the particularity of bodies: “and to each of the seeds its own body” (1 Cor. 15). What one species of any grain could not express with regard to the distinct sexes—since one could not regard that grain as having sex—was supplied, as has often been said, by the diversity of seeds, which furnished understanding concerning the identity of bodies.

There are therefore three elements in this comparison: proposition, argument, and definition. As far as understanding the bodily resurrection is concerned, an appropriate and sufficient comparison has been drawn from the grain that is not made alive before it dies.

As for the point that the body which is to be is not what is sown, but that God gives it a body as he wills (ibid.), the reason is necessarily disclosed within the same passage, when it is asserted that the corruptible body which was sown will be returned incorruptible, and so forth—everything that is shown to adhere to this meaning.

As for the identity of bodies, which is to be taught, it is declared most fully. The blessed Apostle was not content with the comparison of a single seed, by which he could not demonstrate the identity of bodies, since, as stated above, one species of seed did not contain this distinction. He therefore endeavored, through the diversity of seeds, to show that each of those who rise—who are, of course, compared with seeds—will have his or her own body restored.

Human beings will therefore rise, made alive after death; they have been compared with seeds that first die and afterward are made alive. They do not rise as what they are when they die, that is, as what is sown; rather, God gives them a body as he wills (ibid.): from corruptible, incorruptible; from mortal, immortal; from non-spiritual, spiritual. What had been disfigured by the condition of death is restored in the integrity of immortality and beauty, and they will undoubtedly receive their own body, just as each seed receives its own body.

Because this could not be compared with the different sexes in a single seed, the comparison was made through the diversity of seeds, so that the identity of bodies might be signified through the diversity of seeds.

If, then, each resurrected person will receive his or her own body, it unquestionably follows that each person’s own body will be restored, because, as has been said, each seed is assigned and restored its own body. And if each seed receives its own body—and through these seeds the whole human race in both sexes is signified—it follows that the whole human race, which is signified by these seeds in both sexes, will resume its own body.

It is lawful for us to measure this by sober consideration from the Apostle’s words; beyond them we must beware of rushing forward through rash curiosity. For this reason we are also admonished: “Do not seek what is above you, and do not scrutinize what is too difficult for you” (Ecclus. 3); and: “Do not be wise in high things, but consent to the lowly” (Rom. 12).

Finally, attending to what has also been confirmed by apostolic preaching—that “what eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart, God has prepared for those who fear him” (1 Cor. 2)—whoever is not satisfied with the Apostle’s sense or comparison as explained above is nevertheless compelled, whether he wishes it or not, to this conclusion: if he dares to compose for himself by any means whatsoever those things which eye has not seen, ear has not heard, and which have not entered the human heart, as though some members of the human body had been created blameworthy, beautiful, or reprehensible, he must remember that God made all things “very good” (Gen. 1).

Each kind was endowed with an appropriate beauty in its own order, except that the excess of primordial desire discolored those things that we have called dishonorable. They had been instituted in such a way that, obedient to the command of the human mind, they would perform their functions solely at the direction of the rational soul for the purpose of producing offspring. Apart from this purpose, they would bring no rebellion against the command of the mind, which would precede the will insolently—or even when the will desired it.

But after the soul did not remain subject to its highest principles, it was punished within itself by the corresponding law of a rebellious nature for its pride. Consequently, the obedient functions subject even to the soul’s dominion also resisted, and the disobedient appetite of the human mind—which had contradicted the command through the presumption of what was forbidden—was revealed in that part of the body in which, without doubt, the flawed propagation of a degenerate, discolored, and proud root was to be carried forward.

If these parts, had they not here been defiled by this deviation, could have remained in an earthly body with a beauty entirely honorable and moderate for the propagation of the human race, how much more must we believe that in a spiritual body they can exist with ineffably greater beauty—especially since in that perpetual glory they will no longer perform any genital function?

Nevertheless, they will not be lacking for the form of their own kind and appearance, so that what is raised may be judged to be not some form other than the human form, to which resurrection has been promised. Nor will anything be absent that remains visible in the resurrection of the flesh, so that some other species may appear to have been raised rather than the features that mark the integrity of human flesh.

Whoever perhaps does not wish to weigh these matters with measured reason must, whether willing or unwilling, as has been said, either return to the earlier point—that what eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor entered into the human heart (1 Cor. 2), should not be investigated—or, if he attempts to break beyond these limits, let him himself see the precipice of his rashness.

That the human limbs of bodily substance were created honorable is also shown by this consideration: when the first parents were naked in paradise, they had no shame. Hence, after sin and the entry of the poison of desire, they were ashamed at the disordered disturbance of their bodies.

It therefore sufficiently appears that, if they could be seen without shame while placed in whatever happiness of paradise and nevertheless established in an earthly body, much more can they exist in that spiritual body and in that exalted blessedness which will bear the likeness of angels, and in the resurrection of the flesh the human being will be restored whole.

And lest the Creator appear to have created something deformed, if some good were removed from the resurrected body, his work would rather be confirmed even by this: its condition would remain in those parts also in the beauty of glory. Unless perhaps such people should even there still suppose that bodily motions will arise, where—as the Lord himself says—“they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are as the angels” (Mark 12).

If everyone were to be raised in one bodily form and one sex, there would have been no reason at all for this to be said. Rather, since marrying more properly belongs to the female sex, the statement indicates that marriage will not be absent there but will entirely cease.

Since it is nevertheless written that each person will receive the bodies he or she has borne, whether good or evil (2 Cor. 5), how will this happen unless each sex either undergoes judgment in the identity of its own body or receives the reward of blessed resurrection?

Those are mistaken who think that the Apostle’s testimony supports them in claiming that all human beings will be raised in male form, where he says: “Until we all meet in one perfect man” (Eph. 4).

What, then, will they do when the same Apostle again says: “I have betrothed you to one man, to present a pure virgin to Christ” (2 Cor. 11)? This will undoubtedly be contrary to their opinion unless, having properly examined the mystery, they understand with a modest mind how the two statements agree.

We shall explain, insofar as we understand it with the Lord revealing, what is meant by the Church’s being described in both sexes. From the beginning, Holy Scripture testifies that Christ and the Church are represented in human flesh under the likeness of marriage.

Therefore, when the Church is reckoned under the female sex, the weakness of the human condition is indeed shown, and this is appropriately expressed in the Church as Christ’s spouse. But under the name of virginity or continence, her purpose or integrity of faith is intimated, concerning which the blessed Apostle himself also speaks.

When it is said, “Until we all meet in one perfect man,” this is neither different nor divine [F.: “divided”]. Whatever is contained in the body of the Church—which is one flesh with Christ according to the law of sacred marriage—is also, in every respect, his flesh, so that what is said may be understood in both sexes: there, “a pure virgin”; here, “a perfect man.” Thus they live in the Catholic Church with undefiled faith and in holy purpose of continence.

Although the weakness of the human condition may still be present, nevertheless, through the one flesh of the Church and Christ—that is, of spouse and husband—the Church receives in him also a masculine firmness and perfect strength. Through the virginal chastity of the Church’s faith, by which she becomes one flesh with him, she also becomes the perfected members of the man.

Here too the words of the blessed Apostle Paul must be considered: “We were all baptized into one body in Christ” (1 Cor. 12). Insofar as the unity of the sacrament is concerned, we are one body in Christ. Insofar as the distinction of the sexes is concerned, he says elsewhere: “Whether male or female, we are all one in Christ” (Gal. 3).

For Christ is perfect together with his whole body, which is his fullness. Therefore, because through one and the same mystery one body is received, although the sexes are different, Christ is perfect through the fullness of that body.

Since Christ, as the man, is both head and strength and perfection of the Church as his spouse, the whole Church is rightly said to meet in this one perfect man, whose one flesh she is.

# TWO DECREES

*(Taken from the letter to the bishops of Dardania.)*

## FIRST

### Things possessed peacefully for thirty years cannot be reclaimed.

After five hundred years, I hear that some wish to overturn the arrangements of Christ, although the law of human beings cannot be broken after thirty years.

## SECOND

### One must not abstain after death from the alms of those with whom we did not cease to share during life.

Let no one persuade you at all that Acacius was released from the guilt of his transgression. For after he fell back into the fellowship of wickedness, he deservedly was excluded from apostolic communion by law; and he died while persisting in that same condemnation. The absolution that, while alive, he neither sought nor deserved, he cannot obtain now that he is dead.

For by the voice of Christ it was entrusted to the Apostles themselves: “Whatever you bind on earth …” (Matt. 18), and so forth.

As for one who has been placed before the divine judgment, it is not lawful for us to decree anything else concerning him except that in which his final day found him. Therefore, unless you reject him by name, along with the other companions of this error, you must not participate with any of them at all in the purity of the Lord’s table, which our predecessors always carefully kept separated from heretical pollution.

[Note: In the *Book of the Daily Office of the Roman Pontiff* it is entitled “The Synodical Letter Received by the Bishop.” It is also fourth among the letters of Gregory II. It is cited also in Gratian, from Gelasius, 26, XII, question 2, “To the clergy, order, and people of Brundisium.” Hardouin. It is also attributed to Gelasius in the very ancient Lucca manuscript. Mansi.]

# CONSTITUTIONS OF POPE GELASIUS, WHICH BISHOPS RECEIVE AT THEIR ORDINATION

*(In which the ordinations of Africans are prohibited among other things, according to the *Daily Office of the Pontiffs* and other trustworthy manuscript codices.)*

To the clergy, order, and people residing in that city, our most beloved sons in the Lord: greetings.

[Note: In Lucca codex 490, “greetings in the Lord” is lacking.]

We have brought no delay to your worthy requests. We have ordained for you that brother and our fellow bishop as priest.

[Note: The same codex adds “your.”]

We have instructed him never to presume illicit ordinations; not to permit to approach the sacred orders a bigamist, or one who has not taken a virgin as wife; nor an illiterate man, one physically impaired in any part of his body, a penitent, one subject to the curia or to any other condition, or one under legal censure. If he should happen to find anyone of this sort, he must not dare to promote him.

He must in no way receive Africans who put themselves forward indiscriminately for ecclesiastical orders, because some of them have been proven to be Manichaeans and some to have been rebaptized repeatedly.

He must strive not to diminish the ministries and adornment of the Church, or anything whatsoever belonging to its patrimony, but to increase them.

As for the revenues of the Church and the offerings of the faithful, he must divide them into four portions. One he shall retain for himself; a second he shall distribute to the clergy according to their diligent performance of their offices; a third he shall know to be given to the poor and to strangers; and a fourth he shall reserve for ecclesiastical buildings. For these things he will have to render an account before the divine judgment.

He must know that the ordinations of presbyters and deacons are to be celebrated only during the fasts of the fourth, seventh, and tenth months, and also at the beginning and middle of Lent, on the evening of Saturday.

[Note: The same codex reads “of mid-Lent.”]

He must remember that the sacrament of holy baptism is to be administered only at the feast of Easter and at Pentecost, except for those who are pressed by the danger of death, lest they perish eternally; such persons ought to be aided by these remedies.

You ought therefore to obey with devoted hearts this precept of our see, so that the body of the Church may become irreproachable and peaceful, through Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns with God the almighty Father and the Holy Spirit throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

And his subscription:

May God keep you safe, most beloved sons.

# LETTER XV

### It recounts what assistance he received from Rusticus, bishop of Lyon, and how much persecution he suffers from Acacius.

*(From the papers of the Reverend Father Hieronymus Vignerius.)*

Gelasius to his most beloved brother Rusticus.

Amid the storms of evils that are pressing upon us and the afflictions of various trials by which we are almost overwhelmed, your charity, most loving brother, has furnished us great consolation.

For what more consoling thing could happen than to see dearest brothers suffering with one another and bearing a share of the burden—brothers to whom no small portion of blessing has been granted? Blessed be God, who has so moved your heart toward us that you not only feel inwardly what we suffer, but also show it by extending the mercy of holy generosity, demonstrating what charity you possess in a compassionate heart, and adding to the words of sweetest consolation the chief forms of assistance among friends.

Yet we will not weary your love by writing how hard-pressed we have been. Our brother and fellow bishop Aeonius (of Arles) knows how useful both the assistance he sent and that which you sent to us have been.

Moreover, our brother Epiphanius (of Pavia), who is being sent to your region to relieve and redeem the captives of his people, will inform your fraternity how great a persecution we endure on account of the most impious Acacius.

But we do not fail. Amid so many pressures, our spirit neither gives way, nor does our zeal slacken, nor does fear overthrow us. Although we are perplexed and distressed, we trust in him who with the temptation will also provide a way through; and although he allows us to be humbled for a time, he will not allow us to be crushed.

Take care, dearest brother, that the affection of you and your people toward us—or rather, toward the apostolic see—does not cease. For those who will be established upon the rock will be exalted with the rock.

Assist our brother Epiphanius, and let him perceive that you love me. When he has returned to his own people, let your love write concerning both what has appeared to him and what has appeared to our brothers and fellow bishops established throughout Gaul regarding the case of the most impious Acacius.

May God keep you safe, dearest brother.

Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of February, in the consulship of Asterius and Praesidius, illustrious men (A.D. 494).

[Col. 0139]

# FIRST APPENDIX: VARIOUS FRAGMENTS

*(C, S)*

## POPE GELASIUS

*(From Baluzius’s *Miscellany*.)*

What division of the ancient churches could prejudice a new building, since it determined not future matters but those then present?

Now, with regard to this basilica that is to be dedicated, it must be investigated with the greatest care who—that is, the bishop of which city—baptized the inhabitants of that territory before the constructed basilica was founded, or to whose confirmation they assembled in annual devotion.

For the matter ought not to be defined by any boundaries or places. Rather, the diocese should be determined by what is stated above, so that it may be clear by whom those dwelling there were cleansed through the bath of regeneration.

Therefore, most beloved brothers, once all ambiguities and every circumlocution have been removed, it is fitting for you in every way to investigate this, so that the one whom you know ought to be permitted in the manner we have prescribed may be summoned especially to the consecration.

The same matters must also be sought and ordered in every other church that, after the constitution recorded in the acts of the holy memory of Pope Leo was recently reread in synod, is found to have been consecrated in these places that were distinguished by subreption from the bishop of [*virunnis*—the passage is corrupt].

[Note: The place is corrupt.]

Nevertheless, the document mentioned above must be preserved in every constitution. For whatever is shown to have been requested through suppressed petitions must rightly be annulled out of regard for so great a prelate.

## GELASIUS IN THE DECREES, TO DULCIUS THE DEFENDER

Your Experience, having received this present admonition, should not fail, at our exhortation, to speak to our sons, the magnificent men Aemilianus, master of the soldiers, Constantinus, the judge, and Ampelius.

Behold, just as the desire of your Magnificence requested, without any delay or expense—and in such a way that we did not even permit the customary payments to be made to ecclesiastical offices—we have ordained Anastasius the deacon priest for the city of Lucera.

Therefore let your Magnificence now willingly provide for the needs of that bishop and of the Church of Lucera in all necessary matters, and, with Christian devotion, grant the support appropriate to his vigilance.

## GELASIUS TO BISHOP STEPHANUS

Antistia, who sent a petition concerning the chastity she desired, ought to have remained in the chastity she had requested, since she should not easily have rejected what she had previously thought ought easily to be sought.

After having considered and matured the decision concerning her youth and the matters she ought to have weighed in her petition, she should not afterward seek support or opportunities for breaking the choice of the widowhood that had been declared.

But because, in her desire to incur blame, she rashly indulged the inconstancy of her mind and instead sought a husband for her incontinence—something forbidden by no laws—you should know that she is to be restored to the customary procession and is to enjoy access to the church and the sacred communion of the ministries.

[Note: Widows did not make a formal profession of chastity. If, having assumed chastity bound to God by the religion of a private vow, they violated it by entering marriage, they rendered an account only to God. See Gelasius’s letter to the bishops of Lucania, chapter 21. Mansi.]

## POPE GELASIUS TO THE BISHOPS MAXIMUS AND EUSEBIUS

*(From Baluzius’s *Miscellany*.)*

Although it is contained in the ancient regulations that the parishes assigned to each church by the original arrangement cannot be removed by any means—lest, through the worst custom and the growing boldness of a bad example, universal confusion arise everywhere—we nevertheless ordered in our decrees sent not long ago that everything that had been invaded in this manner should be restored.

But because the boldness of those who encroach thinks that it can create a law for itself if it adds obstinate retention to its crime, we wish the matters that we decreed between our brother and fellow bishop Constantinus, priest of the Church of Camisium, and the persons sent by the bishop of Ancona, to be fulfilled through you.

We have also written out the rule that is to be followed in the other matters under consideration.

Therefore, we do not permit the status of parishes—which has endured with the firmness of perpetual age—to be changed by any presumption. Neither the negligence of a bishop, nor a temporary addition perhaps generated through carelessness, nor consent produced by sloth, nor a command obtained through stealthy petition can tear apart a diocese once established, from which the devoted people have always been accustomed to come for regeneration and confirmation.

## THE SAME TO JUSTINUS THE ARCHDEACON AND FAUSTUS

Concerning the division of the property of the Church into four portions.

[Col. 0140C] We have deemed it advisable for you and for your reputation that, in place of your bishop, someone appointed by him should be installed among you, who would administer everything in his name as well, so that you may bring all the estates under your own administration and may not suppose that any particular piece of church land should be assigned to any cleric as his share, lest it be diminished through carelessness and negligence. Rather, you are to deliver to the bishop the entire sum of the revenues collected from all the rural and urban estates. From this collection, however, an account is to be made of what is evidently needed for ordinary business or for the expenses of unforeseen necessities, so that it may be set aside; and in every way four portions are to be made from the offerings of the faithful or from this revenue, so that the bishop may take one for himself, distribute another among the clergy according to his judgment and choice, and arrange for a third to be given to the poor with everyone’s knowledge. As for the fourth portion, which belongs to the building works, we decree that it is to be paid out according to the bishop’s direction and through your disbursement. If anything should remain from the annual expenditure, let it be deposited in chests [Col. 0140D] under the care of a suitable guardian chosen by both parties, so that, if a larger building project should arise, there may be funds available from what diligent care over a period of time has been able to preserve; or else let a property be purchased whose returns will serve the common interests.

## THE SAYINGS OF POPE GELASIUS BEGIN

*(From the manuscript codex of Lucca, ninth century.)*

Catechumens, in Latin called “the instructed” or “the hearers,” are those who, having been instructed in the faith of Christ, hear Christ’s commandments, believe rightly, have also been signed by the priest, and have been cleansed by exorcism [Col. 0141A] and repent, but have not yet been washed in holy baptism. “Penitents” are those called by this name in the canon who publicly perform penance for crimes and for more serious offenses.

It must be understood that, according to the canon’s prescription, the faithful—that is, those already baptized—are not permitted during the time of prayer and canonical praise to stand in the church at Mass with the “hearers,” that is, the catechumens, or to pray and sing psalms together with them. Nor are clerics or other laypeople permitted to pray or sing psalms together with the penitents while mixed in with them.

[Here there was] formerly a separate place assigned to them, either outside the church or at the beginning of the church entrance, where the catechumens, that is, the instructed or hearers, stood to pray and hear the divine office, and [there was also a place] within the church. Above these there was likewise a separate appointed place where the penitents stood, so that all entering the church might know that they were repenting of criminal offenses and might pray for them; and that they, humbled by this, might more readily receive forgiveness for their sins. Above these, in another part of the church, stood the other lay faithful, though separated from the clergy.

[Col. 0141B; 0142A]

When it is said in certain chapters of the canon that anyone guilty of any criminal—that is, more serious—offense is to be expelled from the church, this must not be understood to mean that he is altogether prohibited from every assembly and from hearing the divine praise and the Lord’s commandments. That would be exceedingly absurd and contrary to the command of divine mercy: that a sick person should be excluded from God’s divine medicine, although God became incarnate and suffered for the salvation of sinners, and that someone cast out from every assembly and consolation of the faithful should be handed over to the devil.

Rather, the foregoing is to be understood reasonably: he is to be excluded from communion, that is, from association with the other faithful who stand inside the church during the time of prayer and praise of God, and for the prescribed number of years he is to stand outside the church among the hearers, that is, the catechumens, praying and listening to the praises of God. When all this has been completed, according to the judgment appropriate to the offense committed, he is to enter the church into communion, that is, into fellowship in prayer with the penitents. After spending among them another period of years according to the judgment appropriate to his offense, he is then to return more fully to communion, that is, to the fellowship of the other faithful and to the reception of the sacred body and [Col. 0142B] blood of Christ.

[Col. 0141]

## SECOND APPENDIX. CANONS ASCRIBED TO GELASIUS (C, S)

### NOTICE

Among the ancient pontiffs scarcely any one appears—if Gregory the Great and perhaps also Leo are excepted—under whose name so many decrees are read ascribed by the old collectors. I have undertaken here to present all or nearly all of them in something like a single view, not because I consider all of them to be genuine offspring of Gelasius, but with precisely the same intention as the other collectors of councils before me, who judged that even those less genuine, but regarded by others as genuine, ought to be included.

For collecting these materials I made particular use of the codices of Burchard, Ivo, and Gratian. I have sometimes added brief notes of my own [Col. 0141C], especially where they readily concern variants taken from manuscript codices. I could also have appended judgments on each individual text, but since the reasons for my judgments would have had to be supplied, the matter would have drawn out at excessive length.

Those who wish may consult the excellent work of Carlo Sebastiano Berardi, priest of Uneli, director of jurisprudential studies at the royal Academy of Turin, entitled *Gratian’s Genuine Canons Distinguished from the Apocryphal*, Turin, 1752, divided into four volumes.

## GELASIUS TO BISHOPS MAJORICUS AND JOHN

### The Lord’s body must not be received without the chalice

We have learned that certain people in the same region, having received only a portion of the sacred body, abstain from the blood of the sacred chalice. They are evidently bound by I know not what superstition. Either let them receive the sacraments in their entirety, or let them be kept from the complete sacraments, because the division of one and the same mystery cannot occur without grave sacrilege.

## GELASIUS TO BISHOPS MAJORICUS AND JOHN

[Col. 0141D]

### Concerning those who killed their two bishops, so that they might be without a bishop thereafter

The repeated slaughter of Latin bishops confused us with the horror of such an atrocious crime, so that for a long time the decision of our deliberation remained suspended, since we hesitated to place any bishop over people who had furnished examples of parricide. Therefore, now turning away from what was, as it were, a sacrilegious practice and custom, we deemed it necessary to provide for religion to the extent that the affairs of the parish should be governed by priests appointed from outside. For the inhabitants who remained there had learned to kill their shepherds with the sword, and this city was found to have committed an unheard-of crime—something that has happened nowhere at all in any provinces, even those afflicted by continuous and varied incursions of war—by overthrowing the ministers who supplied it with the Christian faith, without any persecution being involved.

It must therefore be arranged that this deadly destruction be healed by suspending its own bishops, and that at least the material for such great madness be removed. In this way either the madness will desist from such a cessation because it will have no one against whom to rage, or it will not provide other imitators with a dreadful contagion. Let it therefore lack episcopal assistance, supplied to it from elsewhere, since it stained with cruelly shed blood the dignity bestowed within its own bosom; for it must be punished by this retribution in either case, whether it commits this sacrilege at the instigation of those within or driven by frenzies from outside.

Therefore let your Affection, placed in this situation, provide the ministry of visitation to the church; and, either by meeting together or in turn, as the circumstances and the case require, let it present the divine ministries [variant: mysteries] to the ungrateful people, lest, while avoiding the weeds, we appear to pass by the Lord’s wheat.

## GELASIUS TO BISHOP JOHN

We have been stirred by the impious audacity of Asellus, who held the office of archdeacon. Although, when the bishop had been mortally wounded by a cruel accident, he ought above all others to have guarded the church and prevented anything from being removed from the episcopal residence, he nevertheless allowed the bishop himself to be killed amid the present tumult, although he ought to have been kept alive for confession. It must be investigated whether he did these things of his own will or was driven on by someone’s impulse; and first, since he is said to have been the bishop’s steward, the ecclesiastical property is to be sought from him.

Who, moreover, would not clearly understand that the bishop was removed more quickly for this principal reason: so that he would neither expose his accomplices nor leave the church’s resources unknown and thus more easily subject to plunder? For a document of the bishop’s is also said to have been found cut into pieces. And this good Asellus, worthy of his rank—something never attempted before—compelled the decree against himself to be carried out by the church’s ministers before a report concerning the death had been sent to the Apostolic See according to ancient procedure.

What Christian could doubt how intolerable an evil this is? When, even in the ordinary course of events, upon the death of a bishop his passing is customarily reported first of all, a suitable visitation is appointed, and arrangements are then made for the appointment of a successor, this man alone appeared, after the religious leader had been killed, to think immediately about his own advancement rather than to take care that what had happened should be reported.

Although what is being done outside remains hidden, nevertheless the abruptness of his attempted seizure of power does not free his conscience from suspicion—he was also seeking the place of the deceased bishop [variant: perhaps, “while seeking it”]. Meanwhile, so that no one may ever dare to usurp what no one before this man had dared to usurp, let him be removed by our authority from the office he held, until we reconsider more fully what we judge should permanently be ordained concerning such a matter. If he is proved to have taken away any ecclesiastical property, he must in every way be compelled to restore it.

## GELASIUS TO BISHOP ELPIDIUS

The sacred religion that observes Catholic discipline claims such reverence for itself that no one dares approach it unless with a pure conscience. For how will the heavenly Spirit, invoked for the consecration of the divine mystery, come if the priest—the very person who begs for the Spirit’s presence—is condemned as being full of criminal deeds?

## GELASIUS TO BISHOP HELPIDIUS OF VOLATERRA

### They must not travel to the imperial court without the authority of the Roman pontiff

With what audacity and recklessness do you write that you are preparing to travel to Ravenna, when the canons plainly prescribe that no pontiff at all should proceed to the imperial court without first seeing and consulting us? Recently this was done, as is shown, by the bishops of Pistoia, Lucca, and Fiesole, men advanced either in age or in episcopal dignity. You, who appear to have held the priesthood for only a few days—how do you suppose that you may do what is not permitted? Unless, perhaps, you are eager to lose the office that you show yourself unworthy to hold by these excesses.

## GELASIUS TO BISHOPS MAXIMUS AND EUSEBIUS

Although it is contained in ancient rules that parishes assigned to each church by the original arrangement cannot be removed by any means—lest, through the worst custom, as the recklessness of a bad example increases, universal confusion arise everywhere—we nevertheless ordered in decrees issued not long ago that everything which had been seized in this way should be restored [Col. 0143C]. But because those who invade such rights think that persistence in retaining what they have seized can generate a law in their favor, we wish the measures that we decreed between our brother and fellow bishop Constantius, priest of the Church of Camiscana, and those sent by the bishop of Ancona, to be carried out through you.

We then prescribed the rule that is to be followed in other investigations. Therefore we do not permit the condition of parishes, which has endured with the stability of perpetual age, to be altered by any presumption.
