Neither the negligence of a bishop, nor a temporary encroachment that may perhaps arise through carelessness, nor consent produced by indolence, nor an order obtained through furtive petitioning can tear apart a diocese once established, from which the devoted people have always assembled for regeneration and confirmation. [In Gratian there is an addition, but the words may belong to Gratian himself rather than to Gelasius:] For it is known to have been ordained formerly that territory does not make a diocese.

## GELASIUS TO BISHOP EPIPHANIUS

We have sent an order to the other bishops that those who are said to have violated churches are to be judged unworthy of entering them [Col. 0143D].

## GELASIUS TO BISHOPS VICTOR, CONSTANTINE, MARTYRIUS, FELICISSIMUS, SORANUS, AND TIMOTHY

Our brother and fellow bishop Epiphanius informed us in his report that Benenatus and Maurus, citizens of the municipality of Beneventum, had risen in a very bitter and punishable defiance against religion. They had not allowed their own curial official, who had fled to the protection of the church, to be safe or secure there from injury. They had dared, in their reckless minds, to commit what not even magistrates or princes have ever been permitted to perpetrate: taking advantage of the priest’s absence, they forcibly dragged away a man who had taken refuge in the sanctuary, although he resisted and protested.

As far as their report has revealed to us, Epiphanius rightly judged them unworthy of sacred communion. If it is indeed established that so great a crime was committed, our authority likewise agrees with this judgment. For a person ought not lawfully to be admitted to petition for mercy in a place where he did not hesitate to commit sacrilege.

Let no one within the thresholds devoted to such great reverence suppose that, at his own will, he may claim both humility and violence. Therefore, dearest brothers, if the complaint makes the aforesaid men manifestly guilty, prohibit them, by the authority of our command, from all the churches of your parishes. Thus not only will those who are proved to have risen against the holy places rightly receive punishment proportionate to their deed, but others too will be deterred from such presumption by fear of this retribution.

*Berardus discusses the authenticity of this letter on both sides and leaves the matter undecided; I myself find nothing genuinely suspicious.*

## GELASIUS TO BISHOP JUSTUS

Let your Affection diligently seek the truth of all the matters in question, so that, if a definite decision was long ago issued concerning the boundaries about which the dispute is reported to have arisen, it may be preserved inviolate. Otherwise, if nothing was ever established as settled, let whichever party disagrees with the limitation of time provide an oath [Note: [Col. 0143D] Read *diffidit*. Gratian has *confidit*.], while nevertheless allowing the party who is said to have possessed the property up to now to offer an oath [Note: [Col. 0143D] The manuscript and Gratian read: “so that.”].

## GELASIUS TO BISHOPS MARTYRIUS AND JUSTUS

### Concerning slaves ordained without the consent of their masters

It is established by ancient rules and by a recent synodal explanation [Note: [Col. 0144D] *Epistle to the bishops of Lucania*, chapter 14.] that persons subject to slavery are not to be girded with the belt of the heavenly militia. But I do not know whether you are being carried away by ignorance or by intention, so that, for this reason, scarcely any bishop appears to be free of the offense. For the frequent complaint of many people resounds around us so loudly that absolutely nothing seems to have been established on this point.

The agents of the illustrious man, our son Amandianus [Col. 0144C], complain grievously that men subject to his legal authority—some still clerics, others already ordained deacons—have been ordained. This is contrary not only to the recent decision, which is known to have been completed with the assent of the most beneficial provision of so many bishops, declaring that such persons must not be received, but also to the rule that, if any such persons were previously received into the service of the divine militia through ignorance, they should be expelled altogether and, stripped of their religious privilege, compelled by proper warning to return to their masters’ possessions.

Therefore, dearest brothers, restore without delay, following the course prescribed by the laws, those whom the agents of the aforesaid man show to be retained in clerical office, after they have been examined and proved to be subject to another’s authority. If any of them is found already to be a presbyter, let him remain in that rank, with the sole loss of his peculium. A deacon, however, must either provide a substitute or, if he has none, be returned. Let those holding the remaining offices know that no one can be rescued from the status of subjection if he is convicted of it, so that, while the order of things is preserved, neither the rights of masters nor the privileges of the Church are disturbed on this account.

## GELASIUS TO BISHOPS RUFINUS AND JUSTUS

[Note: [Col. 0144D] In the manuscript codex of Laborans, a different reading occurs in place of *Rufino*.]

[Col. 0144D]

The distinguished and leading citizens of the city of Varulana [perhaps Verulana] petitioned us at length, as appears in the following document, to which they also affixed their own subscription. They stated that they had been subjected to severe insults by the deacon Agnellus, to the point that, as they themselves say, they claim to have been driven toward perjury. Therefore, dearest brothers, relying on the truth of the petition, have the aforesaid deacon promptly brought before your judgment, with Laurentius, defender of the Roman Church, present. After the truth has been examined, if the integrity of the petitioners is established, let the deacon either prove the charge he has brought or let him understand that punishment must be exacted for his insolence. Thus, for such grave excesses and the aforesaid wicked presumption [Col. 0145A], let him be excluded and let deserved punishment follow him, and let the man who entangled himself in vulgar insults be barred from access to sacred communion.

## GELASIUS TO CRESCONIUS, ILLUSTRIOUS MAN

We wish you in every way to guard the following rule: let no bishop in Sicily presume to receive from the parishes belonging to him, under the name of the *cathedraticum*, more than two solidi, nor compel the priest or clergy of his parishes to prepare banquets for him beyond their means.

Ivo cites both provisions in part 3, chapters 135 and 136, and Gratian took them from Ivo in *Decretum* 16, question 3. The first, beginning “Your Affection,” is chapter “Illud te modis,” 10, question 3. Gratian attributes the final fragment not to Gelasius but to Pelagius. Since it is easy to judge that Gratian took it from Ivo, and since Ivo reads “Gelasius,” Gratian must also have written Gelasius. Yet this canon is at odds with the discipline in force in the time of either Gelasius or Pelagius.

## GELASIUS TO JUSTINUS, ARCHDEACON, AND FAUSTUS, DEFENDER

[Col. 0145B]

### That a bishop may not alienate Church property by any device, and that privileges must be preserved intact in every respect

We have decided to entrust to your care the administration and patrimony of the church of Volaterra, which we have so far found neglected or, after the condemnation of Eucharistus, who had corrupted it, scattered. We believe that you are vigilant for the church’s interests; therefore restore the estates to their ancient cultivation. Recall any slaves who have been sold or given away, and also reclaim any possessions that you see being held under any legal title by the bishops Ennatius and Oppilio or by anyone else. For an estate cannot be alienated by a bishop by any device contrary to the decrees of the synod. Let them nevertheless be reclaimed, and let the purchasers have recourse to the person who presumed to dispose of any church property by an unlawful sale.

You are to deliver the annual revenues to the bishop, whose privileges must in every respect be preserved intact, so that by his administration the customary portions may be distributed. The bishop is to distribute the fourth portion belonging to them according to his own arrangement, as he recognizes the place and merit of each person [Col. 0145C]. The same is to be done with the offerings of the faithful, so that the bishop may distribute a fourth portion to the clergy according to his judgment of their suitability. The portion for the building works is likewise to be paid from your disbursement, with the bishop’s knowledge and direction, so that you allow nothing at all to arise to the detriment of any interest.

If you see your bishop committing anything to the detriment of your church, or anything prohibited by the commands we have issued, immediately report it to our ears, so that we may determine what ought to be done. It has seemed right not only to us but also to our predecessors that tithes should be owed only to those parishes where holy baptisms are administered.

## GELASIUS TO BISHOPS HERCULENTIUS, STEPHANUS, AND JUSTUS

### On the same matter

A frequent and persistent complaint resounds around us concerning those bishops who, disregarding both the ancient rules and our recently issued decrees, do not reject persons subject to property ownership and bound to servitude when they come to receive the belt of clerical office.

Recently, the agents of the illustrious woman Placidia complained in a petition that Sabinus, of the city of Marcelliana or Casilinum, had, taking advantage of the absence of Antiochus’s lawful patroness and mistress, promoted Antiochus, her slave, all the way to the honor of the priesthood; and that he had also adorned Antiochus’s brother Leontius with the privilege of clerical office.

Therefore, dearest brothers, we assign to you by our authority the examination of the dispute between the aforesaid agents and those who are alleged to be of servile status. After the entire truth has been investigated, if he cannot by a proper defense clear away the stain charged against him [Col. 0146A], return the cleric Leontius—whom the rank prescribed by the laws does not protect—to the servile status required by the judgment [Note: [Col. 0145D] Gratian reads “of his condition.”].

As for Antiochus, since, because of the priesthood, he can no longer be recalled, if he wishes to place him in his own church in the position of honor he now holds, let him retain him not as though restored to him, but as someone received for the celebration of the ministries.

## GELASIUS TO PHILIPPUS AND CASSIODORUS

The case of Caelestinus is as follows, and I do not think you are unaware of it. He was convicted of complicity in the murder of a parent and of a bishop, as the record of the proceedings shows, and by the judgment of everyone he was in no way considered worthy of the office of the altar. For such a detestable crime communion was forbidden him for one year, so that he might, through suitable repentance, repair the breach caused by so great an offense.

Even if this had been ordered by us, he himself, reflecting more deeply, ought to have returned to the sacrament of the divine body with a more purified mind. We nevertheless think that this period has either been completed or is now nearly over [Col. 0146B]. Afterward, there is no doubt that the opportunity for communion is to be opened to him, so that the synodal sentence may be ended and, for his greater benefit, he may be cleansed through greater satisfaction.

## GELASIUS TO SECUNDINUS OF VISINIUM

[Note: [Col. 0146D] Perhaps “of Vulsinii.”]

### On the correction of one accused of magical practice

We consider it wholly improper that atrocious insults should be inflicted by the words of the Church’s ministers, since laypeople generally avoid such conduct. Tempus Bonum, an honorable woman, learned from Master Paul, a deacon, and alleges that she was not merely assailed by accusations, but was also implicated in the guilt of the condemned art of magic.

Therefore, brother, we have appointed you investigator concerning the aforesaid persons. If this insolence convicts the deacon, after the woman has been proved to have been indecently assaulted, either compel him to substantiate what he has alleged or restrain him with suitable correction.

## GELASIUS TO BISHOP QUINIGESIUS

[Col. 0146C]

### That converts from Judaism are to be honored

The distinguished Telesinus, although he appears to belong to the Jewish faith, is striving to show himself to us as such that we ought rightly to call him our own. He has made a special request on behalf of his relative Antonius [Antio], asking that we commend him to your Affection. Therefore, in consideration of our will and commands, it is fitting that you treat this brother in such a way that he is not only in no respect oppressed, but also rejoices that, wherever he has need, he has been assisted by your Affection.

## POPE GELASIUS TO BISHOP QUINIGESIUS

### Property involved in litigation is not to be transferred to anyone before the outcome of the inquiry

Since property involved in litigation cannot at all be transferred to any person until, by the outcome of a lawful inquiry and judicial debate, it can be determined to whom it ought rather to belong, no one is to be allowed to exact revenues from that property. The property is to remain in the same condition in which, as has been stated, it was previously established. Whoever thinks that anything may belong to him should bring the matter before a legal examination, with all prejudicial claims removed from it.

## GELASIUS TO BISHOPS SIRACUSIUS, CONSTANTIUS, AND LAURENTIUS

### How carefully the matter of Jewish slaves must be examined

Judas, a slave of Jewish profession, whose owner, he says, acquired him a few years ago, reported that he had now fled to the church of Venafrum, as the attached petition shows. He says that, although a Christian from infancy, he had recently had the mark of circumcision imposed on him by the aforesaid master.

Therefore, let your concern diligently and faithfully examine the truth of the matter between the two parties [Col. 0147A], so that neither religion may appear to have been violated nor the slave, by means of this false accusation, attempt to evade the lawful rights of his master.

## GELASIUS TO BISHOPS MAJORICUS, SERANUS, AND JOHN

### No one is to associate with excommunicated persons contrary to ecclesiastical satisfaction

Caelestinus, a priest of our brother and fellow bishop Seranus, presumed to administer sacred communion to the aforesaid persons contrary to episcopal judgment and to the commands of the Apostolic See. Since he could not have been unaware of the sentence of his own priest, let him at once be removed from ecclesiastical office, so that none of the Church’s ministers may attempt to act contrary to pontifical statutes.

## POPE GELASIUS TO FAUSTUS, MASTER OF THE SOLDIERS

We read that Christ raised the dead; we do not read that he absolved the dead from error. And the one who alone possessed the power to do this entrusted it principally to the blessed apostle Peter:

“Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven” (Matthew 16).

He says, “on earth,” for in this binding he never said that a dead person was to be absolved.

## GELASIUS TO BISHOP JOHN OF VIVANUM

[Note: [Col. 0147D] Gratian reads “of Vienne.”]

### An example of punishment for those who falsely pretend to have just causes

The wife and daughter of Felix came to Rome, as was appropriate. We had ordered this man, who had first gone to the basilica of the barbarians and boasted that he had good causes, to depart under the following condition: if he faithfully and reasonably stated his case, we would allow nothing harsh or severe to be done against him; but if he were proved to have acted against the faith and the interests of the Lord, he would have only himself to blame and would be subjected to an appropriate sentence.

When our son, the distinguished man Orthasius, arrived [Col. 0147C], Felix was so convicted on every single point that he could not open his mouth and confessed in his own words that the charges made against him were true. Therefore he is being held in custody.

## GELASIUS TO BISHOP HONORIUS

### That persons under ecclesiastical jurisdiction must not make a testamentary document for themselves

We also wish your sincerity not to be unaware that it has been reported to us that a tenant named Amplatus, who is known not only to be a slave of the Church but also to have been so entangled in accounts for many years that, even if he were freeborn, he would in every way be held liable until he had settled all the accounts, rashly attempted to draw up a testamentary document. The whole of his peculium is unquestionably bound by law to the rights of the Church.

Therefore, let your Fraternity, acting in our place, oppose such presumption and by no furtive maneuver allow it to take place. If anything human should happen to him—he is reported to be advanced in years—let your unanimity immediately, without delay, place his property under the faithful inventory of his sons alone, to whom the patrimony is shown to have been entrusted [Col. 0147D], until he is compelled to make good the Church’s shares for all the periods during which he is known to have administered this patrimony [Col. 0148A].

## GELASIUS TO BISHOP HONORIUS

Remembering divine retribution, do not doubt that it belongs to episcopal conscience to refuse no pious concern for the needs of the poor.

## GELASIUS TO BISHOPS CRESCONIUS, JOHN, AND MESSALA

[Note: [Col. 0147D] The codex of Deusdedit reads this way, whereas the printed edition has “Messaliae.”]

### Predecessors’ statutes must be preserved

Just as successors ought to preserve the statutes of their predecessors as lawful and just, so too they must correct their misdeeds.

## GELASIUS TO BISHOP JOHN OF SORA

It is certain, and established by our commands, that no one should presume to arrange a public procession in a church or oratory of our see that is not recorded as having been dedicated with permission. This is to prevent founders from making illicit advances through furtive evasions contrary to the statutes of the rules.

But since the distinguished woman Magetia reported to us in a petition that she had buried the bodies of her family members on her own estates, dearest brother, out of consideration for humaneness, ensure that the earlier statutes are not defiled by funerals. In the places identified in the petition, know that only the services appropriate to burial are to be provided, so that divine offices may be celebrated solely in the name of the deceased, while public attendance and processions are discontinued.

[Note: [Col. 0147D] The continuation is absent from the printed edition but was found by the Ballerini in Vatican Codex 3833.]

Given on the Ides of April.

## POPE GELASIUS TO BISHOP SENECIO

### In a church that someone builds, he must claim no special right for himself

The devotion of a pious mind is to be embraced, by which Julius U.H. [Note: [Col. 0148D] The Ballerini restore this from the codex of Deusdedit; the codex read “Julius nobis” in the matter of Juliana.] is said to have founded, on the Juviana estate belonging to him, a church, which he wishes to have consecrated under the name and in honor of Saint Vitus the Confessor.

Therefore, dearest brother, if you do not doubt that it belongs to your diocese, it is fitting that this church be dedicated according to custom, after a solemn gift has first been presented. The aforementioned man testifies that he has assigned this gift to the ministers of the church [Col. 0148C]. He should know without any doubt that, apart from the right of procession owed to every Christian, he will have no proprietary right there.

[Note: [Col. 0148D] These words are absent from the printed editions and were supplied by the Ballerini from the manuscript codex.]

Given on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August.

### On the same matter

Frigentius reported to us in a petition that, on his own property, called Sextilianum, he had founded for his protection a basilica of Saint Michael the Archangel and Saint Martin the Confessor. Therefore, dearest brother, if it belongs to your parish, confer the blessing of the aforementioned basilica with solemn reverence. The founder, however, is to claim nothing for himself from this basilica except the right of procession, which is owed in common to all Christians.

### Bishops are to be consecrated by their metropolitan, and the metropolitan himself by the bishops of the same province

[Note: [Col. 0147D] Anselm of Lucca, in his collection, book 6, chapter 39, cites this passage in exactly the same words from Gelasius’s letter to Bishop Natalis, but near the end varies it as follows: “We have deemed it necessary to instruct your Charity that we have jointly entrusted a most important duty to the metropolitans of your province or of any neighboring province that preserves Catholic unity: when bishops die, their own metropolitan must ordain their successors in the same region; and if that metropolitan himself passes away by human death, only the bishops of the province should take care, according to the ancient form, to ordain him, so that no one may attempt, contrary to right, to usurp what venerable antiquity decreed.” Mansi.]

Because some people are not ashamed to disturb the rights of churches through unlawful ambitions and, by reckless presumption, to invade the privileges that antiquity decreed for metropolitans or provincial bishops—and because they also desire to maintain a rupture with apostolic communion, so that, divided from its authority, they may exercise their own usurpations with impunity, without considering that, if they persist in this obstinacy, they will have to render to the eternal Judge an account both of the injury done to Catholic integrity and of their contempt for the traditions of the fathers—we have deemed it necessary to instruct your Charity.

Accordingly, all of you together, brothers, who are established either throughout Dardania or in any neighboring province, and who remember that you are subject to your metropolitans and appointed by them, are unanimously to establish bishops, as ancient custom requires. Conversely, if a metropolitan should happen to die in the human condition, you are in every way to decree that he be consecrated by the bishops of the same province, according to the form handed down.

Do not allow anyone to claim for himself more than ancient arrangement has granted to you. Thus, even amid the storms of opposing wills, do not cease to preserve the ancient rules, just as it is certain that our fathers steadfastly did so in times of various persecutions.

## GELASIUS TO BISHOP ANASTASIUS

It is fitting that a pontiff who has been entreated should come to the aid of those deprived of the assistance of their own defense, and of those who, because of the weakness of their age, cannot be present through their own actions; for divinity itself has commanded that protection be provided even to orphans.

Therefore, through our delegation, you are to provide assistance to Maximus and Januarius of clerical office, who assert that they have been deprived of the support of parents or relatives. Thus protected against the wrongdoing of their adversaries by the support of your execution of this order, they will not suffer harmful schemes.

## GELASIUS TO BISHOP FORTUNATUS

### The Church must protect those whom it has taken under its defense

We judge it wholly irreligious and detestable if anyone fails to raise and educate, with complete fidelity and the full holiness of his heart, even outsiders whom he has received under his protection. Since the deacon Olympius is said to be the uncle of your beloved Felix and Olympius, and since he accepted the children to be raised under his guardianship, we judge it to be worse than robbery that he left them deprived of their parents’ small properties, as they claim, retaining some things and selling others contrary to the laws and legal rights.

## GELASIUS TO JUSTINUS, ARCHDEACON, AND FAUSTINUS, DEFENDER

### Nothing belonging to the Church is to be alienated
We have judged it necessary to safeguard your interests and your reputation, so that someone may be appointed in place of your bishop, from among yourselves, who may arrange everything in his name as well. Thus you may restore all the estates to your own administration, and you should not think that any tract of church land ought to be assigned to any cleric according to his share, lest it be diminished through carelessness and negligence. Rather, you shall deliver to the bishop the entire sum of the revenues collected from all the rural and urban estates. From this collection, however, an account must be made of whatever is seen to be needed for legal cases or for the expenses of unforeseen necessities, so that it may be set aside; and four portions shall in every way be made either from the offerings of the faithful or from this revenue [Col. 0149D]: one portion the bishop shall take for himself; another he shall distribute to the clergy according to his judgment and choice; the third he shall cause to be distributed to the poor with a clear conscience; but the fourth, which belongs to the buildings, we decree must be paid out according to the bishop’s arrangement, through your disbursement. If anything should remain after the annual expenditure, it shall be entrusted [Col. 0150A] to a suitable guardian chosen by both parties, to be placed in the treasury, so that, if a major building project should arise, there may be assistance from what diligent care over a long period has been able to preserve; or, alternatively, property may be purchased that will serve the common interests.

## GELASIUS TO THE CLERGY, THE ORDER, AND THE PEOPLE OF BRUNDUSIUM

### Two portions of revenues and offerings are to be entrusted to the clergy

Once your request for Bishop Julian, now my brother and fellow bishop, had been granted, it was necessary—since he was immediately being sent back to his own church—to send our letter to you as well. Through it you would learn that he had been instructed never to presume to perform illicit ordinations, and as follows. He shall divide the revenues and the offerings of the faithful into four parts: one he shall retain for himself; another he shall distribute to the clergy in proportion to their diligence in their offices; a third to the buildings; and a fourth he shall faithfully distribute to the poor and to travelers. For these matters he will have to render an account at the divine judgment.

## GELASIUS TO THE EASTERN BISHOPS CONCERNING THE CONDEMNATION OF DIOSCORUS

[Col. 0150B]

### Absolution must not be sought when a sentence has been unjustly imposed

[Note: [Col. 0149D] These words occur in a treatise of Felix III concerning Acacius, properly condemned, given here from Maffei. MANSI.]

When a sentence has been imposed on someone, let him abandon his error, and the sentence is void; but if it is unjust, he ought to care about it no more than a person can be burdened by an unjust sentence before God and his Church. Therefore, he should not desire to be absolved when he plainly sees that he is in no way bound.

## GELASIUS TO [Note: [Col. 0149D] Perhaps “Leontius.”] GERONTIUS AND PETER, BISHOPS

### Bishops ought to assist those who implore their protection

Although we ought not, insofar as we are able, to deny ourselves to anyone who places hope in us, we nevertheless consider the cases of widows and orphans more deserving and more urgently to be pursued, since divine testimony makes clear that they are to be protected by us or by everyone.

## GELASIUS TO LEONTIUS AND PETER, BISHOPS

[Col. 0150C]

Whoever hopes that remedies may be granted for his affairs through the intercession of our name may fittingly expect us to grant them with ready willingness.

## GELASIUS TO THE CLERGY, THE ORDER, AND THE PEOPLE OF [Note: [Col. 0150D] Alternatively, “of Brundusium.”] BRENDESIUM

[Note: [Col. 0149D] Gratian divided this entire letter into two, also assigning different titles. Beginning with the words “Once your request had been granted” and ending with “he will have to render an account at the divine judgment,” he prefixed the title “to the clergy, order, and people of Brundusium,” as in 12, question 2, canon 26. Beginning with the words “The venerable sacrament of baptism” and continuing to the end, he begins a new canon, with the title “Pope Gelasius to the clergy and people of Tarentum,” in De consecratione, distinction 4, canon 17. In fact, these words are found in the *Liber Diurnus* of the Roman pontiffs, and it is a formula of letters that were delivered to newly ordained bishops. That this formula was taken from the writings of Gelasius is sufficiently indicated by an ancient manuscript codex of Lucca, in which this very formula is read under Gelasius’s name. That codex was written at the end of the eighth century. MANSI.]

Once your request for Bishop Julian, now my brother and fellow bishop, had been granted, it was necessary—since he was immediately being sent back to his own Church—to send our letter to you as well, so that you might learn that he had been instructed never to presume to perform illicit ordinations. He must not permit a bigamist, or one who has not taken a virgin as his wife, or an illiterate person, or one under legal accusation, or anyone disabled or marked in any part of his body, to approach the sacred orders under any circumstances. He must also take care concerning foreigners, unknown persons, and those who seek office, since persons of this kind are prohibited from venerable ministries. Finally, he must not dare, by any means, to transfer to another anything from the ministries or ornaments, or from any other property that is known to belong to the Church [Col. 0150D]. He shall divide the revenues and offerings of the faithful into four parts: one he shall retain for himself; another he shall distribute to the clergy in proportion to their diligence in their offices; a third to the buildings; and a fourth he shall faithfully distribute to the poor and to travelers. For these portions he will have to render an account at the divine judgment. He shall also advance those who are to be admitted to sacred orders according to this rule: he shall know that priests [Col. 0151A] and deacons are to be ordained on the Saturday evening of the fasts of the fourth, seventh, and tenth months. He must not administer the venerable sacrament of baptism except at the festivals of Easter and Pentecost, with the exception of those suffering from illness.

## GELASIUS TO BISHOP COELESTINUS

### Clerics of a church should be promoted to its ministry

[Note: [Col. 0151D] This canon clearly corresponds to a fragment published by Holstenius from the collection of Cardinal Deusdedit and printed here. MANSI.]

The priests, deacons, and all the clerics of the city of Stomensis (Histoniensis) presented us with a petition, stating that the priest who had been appointed in the church of the blessed martyr and bishop Eleutherius—which is known to have been built in the parish of the aforementioned city—had died, and that Julian, a deacon of that church, ought to be ordained as quickly as possible in his place, because of the importance of that location. Therefore, dearest brother, if there is nothing in his life or conduct contrary to the provisions of the canons, you shall honor the aforementioned man with the dignity of the priesthood, knowing that you have created him a priest under the title of visitor, not a cardinal priest. Likewise, if his conduct permits it, you shall substitute the deacon Felicissimus in the ministry of that church, so that this highly frequented place of processions may not lack either a priest or a minister for the consecration of the mysteries.

## GELASIUS THE POPE TO HEZEKIAH, THE COUNT

### A cleric is not to be heard by a secular judge

Christians ought always to regard as welcome whatever is requested from their dignity to be provided, since it is not fitting to deny a benefit to those who serve God. Silvester and Faustinianus, therefore, who acknowledge that they have been clerics from infancy, complain that they are being violently oppressed by Theodora. They say that, although they are freeborn and, by God’s authority, released from the bonds of their former condition, they are once again being assigned to the lot of the worst slavery; and that, by royal authority and contrary to the public laws, while bound by the clerical belt, they were summoned by the archdeacon of the city of Grumentum, although it is clear that one who attacks a heavenly soldier ought to pursue only the forum belonging to that soldier [Col. 0151C]. Therefore, beloved son, after extending the greeting due to you, I commend the aforementioned clerics to you, so that, if their adversaries disdain to come to the judgment of the delegates, they may be protected by the shelter of your high office. Let neither secret influence nor excessive and violent necessity contrary to the laws be imposed upon them, since the person who flees judgment plainly shows that he distrusts justice.

## GELASIUS TO CRISPINUS AND SABINUS, BISHOPS

### A cleric is to be summoned only to the judgment of bishops

[Note: [Col. 0151D] Berardus judges that both these canons are falsely attributed to Gelasius, and not without reason, since the jurisdiction of archdeacons belonged to a later discipline. MANSI.]

Silvester and Faustinianus, clerics of the Church of Grumentum, complained to us in a tearful petition that the freedom granted to them by the benevolence of their master was being attacked by the oppression of his heirs. Although they had served in the clerical office almost from infancy, and although their manumitter was still alive, they were nevertheless being prevented from performing service in the divine mysteries. If the truth supports their petition, then those who act contrary to the deed of their father and patron are, as unworthy persons, to be deprived of the inheritance by law; nor may those who take the inheritance act against their patron’s judgment.

Therefore, dearest brothers, since they also complain that they have been oppressed by the archdeacon of the said Church, who promised that, in their absence, they would submit to the judgment of the governor, yet, trampling upon every legal consideration and summoning them contrary to the divine and public laws, thought that their proper forum had been removed to your judgment—whoever he is who attacks a cleric, let him come, so that [Col. 0152A] the rights of the Church, which the ancient rulers have confirmed by repeated enactments, may not be denied to clerics who are being prosecuted.

## GELASIUS THE POPE [Note: [Col. 0151D] Alternatively, “to Sabinus.”] TO BISHOP FABIANUS

### No number is to be imposed on those to be baptized, nor is the cathedraticum to be demanded beyond the ancient custom

Nor is it rightly believed that a fixed number may be imposed upon those to be baptized, since those who ask, or who hasten toward regeneration, are not to be rejected at another person’s will. Therefore, dearest brother, you shall remove this kind of superfluous regulation by every means, so that each person may be baptized either in the church nearest to him or in the one he chooses according to his own inclination. You shall also know that the cathedraticum is to be demanded from the priest of that place only to the extent that it is established as belonging to the ancient custom; and, concerning what is contributed by the devotion of the donors on the day of dedication, you shall observe the custom prescribed generally for all churches.

## GELASIUS THE POPE TO PHILIPPUS AND [Note: [Col. 0152D] Perhaps “Gerontius.”] GERUNTINUS, BISHOPS

[Col. 0152B]

### At the election of a bishop, the parish priest ought to be present

[Note: [Col. 0151D] Berardus considers this letter suspicious; indeed, astonishingly, he suspects Anselm of Lucca, from whom Gratian alone received it, of being its author or forger. Why, one may ask? Because this letter deals with the election of bishops, whose freedom it was in Anselm’s interest to assert—unless perhaps what is decreed here was contrary to the discipline of Gelasius’s age. MANSI.]

The people of Diotria, in a petition submitted to us, lamented that they had long been scattered without the governance of their own rector. And, as is asserted, the man who is said to have been approved by you has been elected by a few and is now regarded as chosen by a small group, although it belongs to you [alternatively, “to us”] to compel everyone by continual admonition to agree together upon the one whom they judge worthy of the priesthood and free from any reproach. Therefore, dearest brothers, you ought to summon frequently the priests, deacons, and entire multitude from all the parishes of the aforesaid place, so that they may seek—not according to whatever each person happens to desire, but with minds in agreement and at your urging—a person whom they may choose by attending solely to the will of the Divinity, and whom no opposition can recall from the established prescriptions.

## GELASIUS TO BISHOP BONIFACIUS

### Servants fleeing their masters to a church ought to seek intercession, not hiding places

Servants who fear their masters, if they have fled to the precincts of a church, ought to seek intercession, not hiding places, lest this very presumption of delay increase their boldness in resisting. For our son, the distinguished man Peter, complains that his servant has been staying for a long time in the church of Saint Clement, and that, although he had assigned persons to provide him with security by oath, the servant had refused for any reason to leave. Therefore, you shall immediately send with him the beloved servants of the aforementioned man, together with whichever person he chooses; after they have given him assurances of his safety, you shall in every way make him return at once to his master. Or, if he should persist in this obstinacy, he is to be returned against his will after the promised security has been given.

## GELASIUS TO RUFINUS AND APRILIS, BISHOPS

Who would say that the laws of rulers, the regulations of the Fathers, or recent admonitions ought to be disregarded, except one who thinks that the offense committed may pass unpunished? [Col. 0152D] The agents of our daughter, the illustrious and magnificent woman Maxima, complained to us in a petition that Silvester and Candidus, her *originarii*—tenant-bound persons attached by birth to an estate—had been ordained deacons by the bishop of Luceria, contrary to the aforementioned constitutions and despite a prior objection. Therefore, dearest brothers, know that the excess of so great a transgression must be investigated with the greatest care; and if the complaint is confirmed by the truth, those who were not lawfully created [alternatively, “consecrated”] because an objection had been raised beforehand shall immediately be excluded from the sacred offices.

## THE SAME TO THE SAME

### The laws of rulers and the regulations of the Fathers may not be disregarded

Who, then, would say that the laws of rulers, the regulations of the Fathers, or paternal admonitions ought to be disregarded, except one who thinks that the offense committed may pass unpunished?

## GELASIUS TO KING THEODORIC

### The laws of the Roman rulers must be observed by everyone

It is certain that Your Magnificence wishes the laws of the Roman rulers—which you have commanded to be observed in human affairs—to be observed all the more in matters concerning reverence for the blessed apostle Peter, for the increase of your own happiness.

## GELASIUS THE POPE TO BISHOP PALLADIUS

[Col. 0153B]

### A dignity received in a time of soundness is not lost when weakness subsequently follows

Just as the provisions of the canons, by which ecclesiastical discipline is governed, do not allow persons physically disabled to attain the priesthood, so, if someone has already been established in it [Note: [Col. 0153D] Ivo adds “in office.”] and is then wounded, he cannot lose what he received at the time of his soundness. For the priest Stephanus lamented in a petition submitted to us that, although the dignity of the priesthood had been conferred upon him many years earlier, and he had truly received it with a body judged to be unimpaired [Note: [Col. 0153D] Ivo reads “received.”], recently, because of the devastation of the province—which the ferocity of the barbarians, pursuing various factions, and the uncertainty of men’s minds had inflicted upon Tuscany—he tried to escape the swords threatening him by flight. As he leapt over sharp stakes that happened to lie in his path, he reported that he had driven them into the lower parts of his body, which, even with treatment applied, could scarcely have been healed within two years [alternatively, “bound up”]. Therefore, dearest brother, restore to the aforementioned man his place and dignity [Col. 0153C], so that he may perform the sacred mysteries as he was accustomed to do. For it is not fitting that he be deprived of the order he had previously received, in which he is shown to have afterward fallen into bodily infirmity through an accidental occurrence.

## GELASIUS TO RUSTICUS AND FORTUNATUS, BISHOPS

### One who is repeatedly thrown to the ground is to be suspended from governing a church

Recently the clerics of the Church of Foropopulus [Note: [Col. 0153D] The Lucca codex has “Foropopiliensis.”], together with Bishop Sabinus and Pelagius and the laymen [Note: [Col. 0153D] In my oldest Lucca codex it reads “Sabinus and Pelagius, laymen,” which is the more suitable reading], disclosed in a personal petition that their bishop was afflicted by a serious condition, saying that he had repeatedly been thrown down by its attacks. Lest this appear to cause scandal among the faithful and disturb the Church of God everywhere through this offense—especially since they affirmed that he himself had wished to come here—we sent a letter to Your Affection so that you might make a suitable visitation to the Church whose rector is held bound by such a condition.

But since the same bishop has now come here [Col. 0153D] and is spreading false claims about everything said concerning him, under the contemplation of divine judgment, and with regard for your conscience and reputation, investigate the matter most diligently and in good faith. Determine whether he has ever been proved to have suddenly collapsed [Note: [Col. 0153D] The Lucca codex has “fallen down”] in a house, in a procession, or in any other place, uttered confused cries, and cast foam from his mouth. Let the matter be investigated with the greatest possible scrutiny. Whether the event cannot be confirmed by the testimony of anyone [Note: [Col. 0154D] The Lucca codex lacks the word “event”], or whether it is said never to have occurred [Col. 0154A], this must not be thought sufficient; there must be certain and evident proof, since a matter of such importance must not be handled carelessly. Let Your Affection, brother Rusticus, act according to your customary practice and in a manner suitable for a great bishop: order him to remain with you for thirty days and compel him, as a necessary test, to eat meat without distinction [Note: [Col. 0154D] “Anellinis” is added in the margin of my codex, that is, lamb meat].

## GELASIUS TO BISHOP VICTOR

### When senior orders are declined, promotion may be made from the lower orders

Your Affection consulted us about the promotion of your clerics, reporting that the deacons refuse to advance to the rank of priesthood, which you mention that your church needs. Therefore, since ecclesiastical governance and gravity do not permit unwilling persons to be made into unwilling persons, that ordination can be accomplished if you strive to promote to the priesthood those among your acolytes or subdeacons who are more mature in age and whose life is commendable. Thus those who have refused to advance in their own orders may be relegated behind their inferiors in the lower orders; and they may receive the advantages of the priesthood more abundantly than those of the diaconate, so that, constrained at least by this consideration, they may strive to desire both the honor they had shunned and the income.

## GELASIUS THE POPE

### The testator’s disposition must be observed

Consideration of ecclesiastical usefulness requires that the testator’s disposition be observed.

## GELASIUS

### What priests have given, succeeding pontiffs must not presume to take away

We have judged that the following must be established: whatever benefactions preceding priests have given to clerics or to those serving them, whether from church property for use or from their own property as ownership, succeeding pontiffs must in no way presume to take away. If, however, some fault has occurred, then, according to the character of the persons involved or the rule of the preceding canons, the penalty is to be imposed upon the person, not upon the property [Col. 0154C].

## GELASIUS THE POPE

### One who has no intention of deceiving does not lie

The blessed apostle Paul must not be thought—God forbid—to have deceived anyone, or to have contradicted himself, merely because, after promising that he would go to Spain, he was prevented by divine providence, being occupied with more important matters, from fulfilling what he had promised. To the extent that his will was involved, he declared what he truly wished to accomplish. But insofar as the hidden purposes of divine counsel were concerned—which, although full of the Spirit of God, he could not as a human being recognize in their entirety—he left the matter aside because he was forestalled by the supreme disposition.

Nor, because the blessed apostle Peter replied to the Lord himself out of reverence for the divine: “You shall never wash my feet,” is he to be thought—God forbid—to have deceived Him or to have failed to remain steadfast in his judgment. For he immediately yielded to the same divine will, and, compelled by the circumstances of human salvation, willingly allowed what he had said he would do to be done [Col. 0154D].

[Note: [Col. 0154D] Ballerini published this and the following letters from the Vatican collection of Cardinal Deusdedit, book II, chapter 100.]

## GELASIUS TO AGILULPHUS

I ask you to deem worthy of defending the rule of the blessed apostle Peter established among the Dalmatians, and to order that whatever my brother and fellow bishop Honorius [Note: [Col. 0153] This Honorius was bishop of Salona, to whom two other letters of Gelasius were published. BALLER.] may have proposed to you for its benefit, or whatever the tenants may have thought ought to be reported, be provided as fully as possible.

## GELASIUS TO JANUARIUS

[Col. 0155A]

I confidently enjoin upon you the affairs through which you greatly desire the benefits of the blessed apostle Peter to be continued. Let Your Nobility therefore ensure that assistance and protection are granted to the affairs of the poor, and let it protect their tenants with pious favor, so that it may receive in return a corresponding recompense from the one whose merits and honor it devoutly serves through this contribution.

## GELASIUS TO FIRMINA, AN ILLUSTRIOUS WOMAN

It certainly belongs to the increase of your reward if the estates that have been unjustly seized either by barbarians or by Romans are restored through your arrangements to support the needy. So great a multitude of people from various provinces devastated by the calamity of war has flocked to Rome that, God as our witness, we can scarcely provide enough for them. You therefore see how much good work you acquire if the estates that each person contributed to the blessed apostle Peter for the sake of his own soul are restored, having been freed through your protection after God’s [Col. 0155B]. I ask you to receive with a grateful mind the blessings—the *eulogiae*—that I have sent out of affection.

## GELASIUS TO THE AGENTS OF URBICIUS

It is established that you have paid into the Church’s accounts, from the payment due from the estate Claculas, which you hold under a leasehold title, thirty gold solidi from its produce, for the year of the consulship of Asterius and Praesidius, men of consular rank, in the third indiction, as recorded on the fifth day before the Kalends of August [Note: [Col. 0155B] That is, under Flavius Viator, who was consul in the year 495. Another payment of the same day and in the same words is appended by the same Gelasius, given to Vincomalus; only the name of the estate is lacking. BALL.], with Flavius, a man of consular rank, as consul.

## GELASIUS TO QUEEN HERELEUVA

[Note: [Col. 0156B] An anonymous writer published by Valesius in his account of the deeds of King Theodoric mentions this queen as the mother of that same Theodoric. She was called Ereliva in Gothic; she was indeed Catholic, and at baptism was called Eusebia. BALL.]

Since he was to petition our lord son, the most excellent king, with my letters on behalf of the sustenance of the poor, I hastened to send Peter, the Church’s defender. When he arrived, I did not cease to greet Your Highness also, earnestly asking you to deem it worthy, for the increase of your health and prosperity [Col. 0156A], to assist the causes of the needy. Given on the fifth day before the Kalends of March.

[Note: [Col. 0155] From a manuscript codex of the University of Turin, folio 4, page 7.]

## GELASIUS TO PETER, BISHOP OF POTENTIA

According to what the letter of your bearer reported, we have learned that you have in hand an unusual case. He reported that a certain deacon had committed incest, a matter widely known in the surrounding area through many indications. But because no one can prove that sexual offense canonically, the aforementioned deacon refuses to submit to any judgment on the matter. To this I, entangled in many unavoidable concerns, respond as reasonably as I can and with the greatest brevity.

No judgments among human beings would be necessary if all truths were open to everyone. It follows, therefore, that the judge must seek proof according to the order of judicial procedure, since otherwise the truth of the offense cannot be known. But when the offense is not in doubt, we order that neither a synod should be convened for this reason nor a trial conducted. Rather, only a measured sentence should be determined in council, one that does not appear to exceed the gravity of the offense [Col. 0156B].

As it was said to the ancients, “an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth”; and a balanced measure was commanded in the Law so that, in accordance with the gravity of the offense, the punishment of the penalty might be weighed. If some people who are perhaps less capable of understanding these matters waver because they find written in our laws, “No one is to be judged concerning hidden things, nor is he to judge them,” let such persons consider the matter with alert minds. For what is denied concerning hidden things is, by an implicit understanding, granted concerning manifest things.

It is consequently clear that this statement concerns hidden matters themselves when they cause no scandal to the Church. But if scandal should arise because of a crime, it must in no way be passed over, because the Church must be pacified by satisfaction, and the guilt must remain publicly punished in such a way that others may also have fear. For that is satisfaction by which a person who was believed guilty by those who accused him is shown to be innocent.

[Col. 0157]

# THIRD APPENDIX: ACCOUNT OF THE COUNCILS HELD UNDER GELASIUS (C, G)

[Note: [Col. 0157B] In order to preserve the Catholic faith unimpaired, remove disputes, and restore peace in the Church, the pontiff, together with the council, labored above all to ensure that the communion of the apostolic and Catholic Church, untouched by any stain, however slight, should remain wholly intact and undefiled, secure and preserved in every respect. In carrying this out, he showed particularly diligent care. He not only wished to vindicate the Church, as had always been done, as free from all heresies and from association with heretics, but also, in order to make it secure from the contagion of corrupt writings, he applied every effort and selected the ecclesiastical books that had hitherto been published and were customarily read. He distinguished and separated, like the mouth of the Lord, what was clean from what was unclean, and separated what was precious from what was vile. To complete this work, he established a decree to be observed perpetually by the Catholic Church. After listing the canonical books of the Old and New Testaments, he added provisions concerning the primacy of the Roman Church and the rights of the other patriarchal Churches, in order to restrain and break the presumption and audacity of the bishops of Constantinople, by which Acacius first, and afterward his successors, had raised themselves with excessive arrogance against the Roman Church. SEV. BINIUS.]

## FIRST ROMAN COUNCIL

[Col. 0157A]

At which the sacred and authentic books were distinguished from the apocryphal by seventy bishops, under Gelasius, in the year of the Lord 494, during the consulship of Asterius and Praesidius.

### I

[Note: [Col. 0157C] Nearly all the books of the Old Testament enumerated here and included in the canon of sacred books were likewise listed above in the final canon of the Council of Laodicea, in canon 47 of the Third Council of Carthage, and in the third letter of Innocent I to Exuperius. We have shown at length above, in the notes to the same canon, that the eighty-fourth Apostolic Canon—since it omits sacred books and includes apocrypha among the sacred books—is spurious and illegitimate. The most reverend and illustrious Cardinal Bellarmine, throughout book I of *On the Word of God in Writing*, has most learnedly and fully vindicated the sacred books of the Old and New Testaments from the slanders of all heretics. The illustrious Cardinal Baronius likewise, in various places in volume I of the *Annals*, has defended the letters of Saint Paul and the other canonical letters, together with the Apocalypse of Saint John the Apostle, from the fury and madness of heretics. To avoid prolixity, I refer the kindly reader there. Concerning the apocryphal books and their authors, Baronius made observations worthy of attention in various places in the *Annals*, and after him Antonius Possevinus did so in the *Sacred Apparatus*. SEV. BINIUS.]

The order [Note: [Col. 0157C] It is in the collection of Isidore, of which there are two very ancient copies in the library of the Jesuit College at Paris. In the Dacherian manuscript codex of the Dionysian collection, as he thinks, this decree is attributed to Damasus. Baronius, at the year 69, from a Roman council under Damasus, of which the Cresconian collection contains material, gives part of this decree. In the Jurensis manuscript it is attributed to Pope Hormisdas, according to Father Labbe. In ours it is headed: “A list of the sacred Scriptures, or canonical books, with the description or annotation of Pope Gelasius.” This decree is described by Vincent of Beauvais in the prologue, chapters 13 and 14. Much earlier, without mentioning Gelasius’s name, Aldhelm cited it in *On the Praise of Virginity*, chapter 11; later, however, with Gelasius named, it was cited by Hincmar of Rheims, Lupus of Ferrières, Pope Nicholas, and in the Chronicle of Centula in Dacherius, vol. IV of the *Spicilegium*. See also the Capitular of Atto, vol. VIII. HARDUIN.] of the books of the Old Testament which [Note: [Col. 0158C] This decree occurs in distinction 15, canon 3. Its text differs so greatly from the original that it cannot be determined with sufficient certainty which is Gelasius’s true and uncorrupted text; nor is it greatly surprising if some points present difficulties. See the notes of the correctors of Gratian’s Decree, etc. SEV. BINIUS.] the holy and Catholic Roman Church receives and venerates, arranged by the blessed Pope Gelasius I together with seventy bishops.

One book of Genesis. One book of Exodus. One book of Leviticus. One book of Numbers. One book of Deuteronomy. One book of Joshua [*Jesu Nave*]. One book of Judges. One book of Ruth. Four books of Kings [*Regnorum*]. [Col. 0157B] Two books of Chronicles [*Paralipomenon*]. One book of 150 Psalms. Three books of Solomon: Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and the Song of Songs. Also one book of Wisdom [Note: [Col. 0158C] Jerome affirms that this book is not found among the Hebrews, but only among the Greeks. He also indicates that Jesus son of Sirach composed it, just as he did the following book. LABBEUS.]. One book of Ecclesiasticus.

Also, the order of the prophets [Note: [Col. 0158D] Sixteen prophetic books. LABBEUS.]: [Col. 0158A] one book of Isaiah; one book of Jeremiah; *Cinoth*, that is, “of his lamentations”; one book of Ezekiel; one book of Daniel; one book of Hosea; one book of Amos; one book of Micah; one book of Joel; one book of Obadiah; one book of Jonah; one book of Nahum; one book of Habakkuk; one book of Zephaniah; one book of Haggai; one book of Zechariah; one book of Malachi.

Also, the order of the histories: one book of Job, omitted by others; one book of Tobit; [Col. 0158B] one book of Ezra [Note: [Col. 0158D] Alternatively, two books. LABBEUS.]; one book of Esther [*Hester*]; one book of Judith; one book of Maccabees [alternatively, two books].

Also, the order of the writings of the new and eternal Testament [which the holy Catholic Roman Church receives and venerates].

Four books of the Gospels: [Col. 0159A] one according to Matthew; one according to Mark; one according to Luke; one according to John. One book of the Acts of the Apostles. Fourteen letters of the apostle Paul: one letter to the Romans; two letters to the Corinthians; one letter to the Galatians; two letters to the Thessalonians; one letter to the Ephesians; one letter to the Philippians; one letter to the Colossians; two letters to Timothy; one letter to Titus; one letter to Philemon; one letter to the Hebrews. Also, one book of the Apocalypse of John. Also, seven canonical letters: one letter of the apostle James; [Col. 0159B] two letters of the apostle Peter; three letters of the apostle John; one letter of the apostle Jude the Zealot.

### II

[Note: [Col. 0159D] In Justellus’s codex this title reads as follows: “Decree of Pope Gelasius concerning books to be received and not to be received, written by him together with seventy most learned bishops.” LABBEUS.]

The decree of Pope Gelasius, issued with seventy bishops, concerning the apocryphal writings.

After all these prophetic, evangelical, and apostolic writings, upon which the Catholic Church has been founded by the grace of God, we think it should also be stated that, although all the Catholic Churches throughout the world are one bridal chamber of Christ [Note: [Col. 0159D] These words also occur in the eighth letter of Pope Nicholas to the emperor Michael, and in the ancient preface to the Council of Nicaea, which we published in volume II; Aeneas of Paris also quotes it in volume VII of the *Spicilegium*, pages 95 and 97. HARDUIN.], nevertheless the holy Roman Catholic and apostolic Church [Note: [Col. 0159D] These words also occur in the previously cited eighth letter of Pope Nicholas. [Col. 0160D] HARDUIN.] has been placed before the other Churches not by synodal enactments, but has obtained primacy through the evangelical word of our Lord and Savior: “You are Peter,” He says, “and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it; and I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven. And whatever you bind on earth [Col. 0159C] shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven” (Matthew 16).

To this Church was also given [alternatively, “added”] [Note: [Col. 0160D] Pope Nicholas, in the passage cited. HARDUIN.] the fellowship of the most blessed apostle Paul, the vessel of election. Contrary to the babbling of heretics, he did not die at a different time, but at one time and on the same day as Peter; struggling in a glorious death in the city of Rome under the emperor Nero, he was crowned, and together they consecrated the aforementioned holy Roman Church to Christ the Lord. By their presence and venerable triumph they placed it before all the other cities throughout the world [alternatively, “and before all others”].

Therefore, the first see of the apostle Peter is the Roman Church, having neither spot nor wrinkle nor anything of this kind (Ephesians 5) [Note: [Col. 0160D] Pope Nicholas, in the passage cited. HARDUIN.].

The second see is at Alexandria, consecrated in the name of blessed Peter by his disciple and evangelist Mark. Sent by the apostle Peter himself to Egypt, Mark preached the word of truth and brought his glorious martyrdom to completion.

The third see, at Antioch, is held in honor in the name of the same most blessed apostle Peter, because he lived there before he came to Rome, and there the first name of the new people, Christians, arose.

### III

[Note: [Col. 0160D] They are listed in another order in the manuscript. LABBEUS.]

And although no one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ [Col. 0160A] Jesus (1 Corinthians 3), nevertheless, for our edification, the same holy Roman Church, after the books of the Old and New Testaments that we have regularly received [alternatively, “listed above”], does not prohibit the reception of these writings also [alternatively, “other writings”], namely:

The holy Council of Nicaea of the three hundred and eighteen Fathers, held under the mediation of the most powerful Emperor Constantine Augustus, at which Arius the heretic was condemned.

The holy Council of Constantinople, held under the mediation of Theodosius the elder Augustus, at which Macedonius the heretic received the condemnation he deserved.

The holy Council of Ephesus, at which Nestorius was condemned with the agreement of the most blessed Pope Coelestine, through the mediation of Cyril, bishop of the see of Alexandria, and Bishop Arcadius, sent from Italy.

The holy Council of Chalcedon, held under the mediation of Emperor Marcian and Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, at which the Nestorian and Eutychian heresies were condemned together with Dioscorus and his accomplices.

[Col. 0160B] But if there are any councils instituted by the holy Fathers up to the present, after the authority of these, we both decree and command that they be observed and received.

## IV.

Likewise, the works of Blessed Cyprian, martyr and bishop of Carthage, are to be received in their entirety. Likewise, the works of Blessed Gregory, bishop of Nazianzus. Likewise, the works of Blessed Basil, bishop of Cappadocia. Likewise, the works of Blessed Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria. [Note: [Col. 0160D] In the manuscript of Labbe they are listed in another order.] Likewise, the works of Blessed Cyril, bishop of Alexandria. Likewise, the works of Blessed John, bishop of Constantinople. Likewise, the works of Blessed Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria. Likewise, the works of Blessed Hilary, bishop of Poitiers [alternative: Proterius, bishop of Alexandria]. Likewise, the works of Blessed Ambrose, bishop of Milan. Likewise, the works of Blessed Augustine, bishop of Hippo [alternative: Hippo Regius]. [Col. 0160C] Likewise, the works of Blessed Jerome, presbyter. Likewise, the works of the most religious man, Blessed Prosper. Likewise, the letter of Blessed Pope Leo sent to Flavian, bishop of Constantinople; if anyone disputes its text down to a single iota and does not reverently receive it in every respect, let him be anathema. Likewise, we decree that the works and treatises of all the orthodox Fathers who in no respect departed from communion with the holy Roman Church, nor separated themselves from its faith or preaching, but by the grace of God remained participants in that communion [alternative: communication] until the last day of their lives, are to be read. Likewise, the decretal letters which the most blessed popes, at various times, issued from the city of Rome in response to the consultation of various Fathers [Note: [Col. 0160D] Hincmar, volume II, p. 543, reads “consolation”; p. 545, “consolation or consultation.” Hardouin.], are to be received with reverence.

Likewise, the acts of the holy martyrs, who shine forth through manifold torments and the wondrous triumphs of their confessions [Col. 0160D] [alternative: “are illumined”]. [Note: [Col. 0160D] Alternatively: “Who among Catholics would doubt this,” or “What Catholic doubts that they endured greater things,” and so forth. Labbe.] What Catholic would doubt that this was so, and that they endured greater sufferings in their struggles, and bore everything not by their own strength but by the grace and aid of God? But for this reason, according to ancient custom [alternative adds: “and with singular caution”], they are not read in the holy Roman Church with particular caution: the names of those who wrote them are entirely unknown, and they are thought to have been written by unbelievers [Col. 0161A] or ignorant people with superfluous material, or with material less suitable than the order of events required [alternative: “they are read as having been inserted”]. Such are the passions of a certain Quiricus [alternative: Cyricus] and Julitta, and of George and others of this kind, which are said to have been composed by heretics. Therefore, as has been said, they are not read in the holy Roman Church, lest even a slight opportunity for mockery should arise. Nevertheless, together with the aforesaid Church, we venerate with complete devotion all the martyrs and their glorious struggles, who are known more to God than to human beings.

Likewise, we receive with all honor the Lives of the Fathers—of Paul, Antony, Hilarion, and all the hermits—which the most blessed man Jerome wrote. [Note: [Col. 0161C] See Baronius under the year 315, no. 10, and under the year 324, no. 31. Hardouin.]

Likewise, we have learned that the Acts of Blessed Sylvester, prelate of the Apostolic See, although the name of their author is unknown, are read by many Catholics in the city of Rome, and that many Churches imitate them on account of their ancient use. [Note: [Col. 0161C] See Papebroch on 3 May and 4 May. Hardouin.]

Likewise, the writings concerning the discovery of the Lord’s cross, and other writings concerning the discovery of the head of John the Baptist, are certain new accounts [alternative: “indeed, accounts”], and some Catholics read them. But when these have come into the hands of Catholics, the judgment of the blessed apostle Paul must precede them: “Test everything; hold fast what is good” (II Thess. V). Likewise, Rufinus, a religious man, published many books of ecclesiastical works and also interpreted some Scriptures. But since Blessed [alternative: “the venerable”] Jerome censured him in certain matters concerning freedom of choice, we hold those opinions which we know the aforesaid Blessed Jerome to have held; and this not only concerning Rufinus, but also concerning all those whom that frequently mentioned man rebuked out of zeal for God and devotion to the faith.

Likewise, we receive for reading certain works of Origen which the most blessed man Jerome does not reject. All the rest, however, we declare must be rejected together with their author.

Likewise, the chronicles of Eusebius of Caesarea and the books of his Ecclesiastical History: although in the first book of his narrative he was lukewarm, and afterward wrote one book in praise and defense of the schismatic Origen, nevertheless, on account of his exceptional knowledge of matters relevant to instruction, we do not declare them altogether to be rejected.

Likewise, we praise Orosius, a most learned man, because he composed a history that was exceedingly necessary for us against the calumnies of the pagans and assembled it with remarkable brevity.

Likewise, we rank highly, with distinguished praise, the venerable Sedulius’s Paschal Work [Note: [Col. 0161C] The work of Sedulius did not appear until after the consulship of Asterius. Isidore cites it in his book On Ecclesiastical Writers, chapter 7. Hardouin.], which he composed in heroic verse.

Likewise, we do not disdain the laborious work of Juvencus, but admire it.

The Catholic and apostolic Roman Church in no way receives the remaining works that were written or proclaimed by heretics or schismatics. [Note: [Col. 0161D] Alternatively: “What, then, are the works that are not received.” Labbe.] Of these, we believe that a few which have come to mind, and which Catholics ought to avoid, should be set down below.

## V.

The book called The Shepherd is apocryphal. All the books produced by Leucius [alternative: Lucius], a disciple of the devil, are apocryphal. [Note: [Col. 0161D] At Atto of Vercelli one reads “Seleucius.” At the end of Innocent’s letter to Exuperius, “Leucius.” This appears to be Λεύκιος Χαρίνος [Leucius Charinus] in Photius, codex 114. Hardouin.] The book called The Foundation is apocryphal. The book called The Treasure is apocryphal. [Note: [Col. 0162C] “Treasures” [Θησαυροί] in Photius, codex 85. Hardouin.]

[Note: [Col. 0162D] This word is absent from the Justel manuscript at this point; but near the end it says “A cento concerning Christ.” Labbe.] [Note: [Col. 0162D] See Isidore, On Ecclesiastical Writers, chapter 5. Hardouin.]

The Revelation called that of the apostle Paul is apocryphal. [Note: [Col. 0162D] Absent from our manuscript and from Justel’s. Labbe.] The Revelation called that of the apostle Thomas is apocryphal. The Revelation called that of Saint Stephen is apocryphal.

The book called The Passing, that is, The Assumption of Saint Mary, is apocryphal. [Note: [Col. 0162D] By Melitus or Melito of Smyrna. Hardouin.] The book called The Penitence of Adam is apocryphal. The book called Ogia, bearing the name of a giant, which heretics pretend fought with the dragon after the Flood, is apocryphal. The book called The Testament of Job is apocryphal. The book called The Penitence of Origen is apocryphal. The book called The Penitence of Saint Cyprian is apocryphal. The book called The Penitence of Jamnes and Mambres is apocryphal.

The book called The Lots of the Holy Apostles is apocryphal. [Note: [Col. 0163C] They were published in the old code of the canons of the Roman Church, issued from the library of D. Le Pelletier, administrator of the kingdom, in 1687, p. 370. Hardouin.] The book called The Praise [alternative: “The Game”] of the Apostles is apocryphal.
