The works of Montanus, Priscilla, and Maximilla are apocryphal. All the works of Faustus the Manichaean are apocryphal. The works of Commodianus are apocryphal. The works of the other Clement of Alexandria are apocryphal. The works of Tatius [alternative: Tharsus or Tascius] Cyprian are apocryphal. The works of Arnobius are apocryphal. The works of Tychonius are apocryphal. The works of Cassian [alternative: Cassio] the presbyter of Gaul are apocryphal. The works of Victorinus of Poitiers [alternative: Petabion] are apocryphal.

[Col. 0164A] The works of Faustus of Riez in Gaul are apocryphal. The works of the blind Frumentius are apocryphal. The letter of Jesus to Abagarus [alternative: Abgar] the king is apocryphal. The letter of Abagarus [alternative: Abgar] to Jesus is apocryphal. The Passion of Quiricus [alternative: Cyricus] and Julitta is apocryphal. The Passion of George is apocryphal. The writing called Solomon’s Contradiction [alternative: “Interdiction”] is apocryphal. All phylacteries, which they falsely claim were written by angels, but were rather composed by the art [alternative: “under the names”] of demons, are apocryphal.

All these and all similar works, which Simon Magus, Nicolaus, Cerinthus, Marcion, Basilides, Ebion, Paul of Samosata as well, Photinus, and Bonosus, and those who fell away through a similar error, taught or composed; and likewise Montanus with his most obscene followers, Apollinaris, Valentinus or Manichaeus, [Note: [Col. 0163C] With the comma removed, it is better to read “Faustus Africanus,” as a reference to a disciple of Faustus of Riez in Gaul, and others; so also the manuscripts of Justel and our manuscript. Labbe.] Faustus, Africanus, Sabellius, Arius, Macedonius, Eunomius, Novatus, Sabbatius, [Col. 0164B] Callistus, Donatus, Eustathius, Jovinianus, Pelagius, Julian of Eclanum, [Note: [Col. 0164C] Absent from the Justel manuscript; in ours it is written “Calipsus.” Labbe.] Caelestinus [alternative: Caelestius], Maximinus [alternative: Maximianus], Priscillian of Spain, Nestorius of Constantinople, Maximus [Note: [Col. 0164C] Alternatively: “Cynicus”; this must certainly be read from the manuscripts. Labbe.] Unicus, Lampetius [alternative: Lapicius], Dioscorus, Eutyches, Peter, and another Peter—one of whom stained Alexandria and the other Antioch—Acacius of Constantinople with his associates [alternative: “companions”;] and likewise all the heresiarchs, their disciples, or schismatics, taught or composed works whose names are not at all retained; we confess that these works were not merely rejected but also expelled from the whole Roman Catholic and apostolic Church, and that, together with their authors and the followers of their authors, they are eternally condemned under the unbreakable bond of anathema. [Note: [Col. 0164C] In our manuscript: “Here ends the decretal issued by Pope Hormisdas of the city of Rome.” Hardouin.]

# ROMAN COUNCIL, OR DECREE

Concerning books to be received and not received, held by Pope Gelasius with the bishops around the year 496.

## ADMONITION

(From the supplement of Jean-Dominique Mansi.)

[Col. 0163]

That celebrated decree concerning books to be approved and rejected, issued in a certain Roman council, long and greatly exercised the learned. The chief dispute concerns its author. All collectors of councils attributed it to Pope Gelasius, a view supported by Burchard of Worms, Gratian, and most manuscript codices. Yet in the oldest codex of the collection of Dionysius Exiguus, which Dacherius communicated to Baluzius, this same decree bears the name of Pope Damasus. Finally, in a very old codex from Urgell, Baluzius found the name of Pope Hormisdas prefixed.

Chiffletius encountered this decree in a Jurensian codex nine hundred years old; and, judging it to be the most accurately corrected of all those that had appeared up to that time, he undertook to transcribe and publish it in his notes to the works of Vigilius of Thapsus. In that codex it is ascribed to Pope Hormisdas, and consequently the authority of the opinion that Hormisdas was the author of the decree received great reinforcement.

Once matters stood thus, it happened that, not many years ago, the distinguished Fontaninus came upon a nine-hundred-year-old Vatican codex which presents this same decree. Since it omits much that is found in the printed editions, he judged that its authenticity could above all be vindicated by this argument. It is characteristic of such compositions that the shortest versions are considered genuine; for over time they are repeatedly enlarged by new additions, so as to be adapted to the discipline of successive periods.

Fontaninus therefore published the decree as it is read in that Vatican codex in his Commentary on the Antiquities of Horta, and he judged that the question of the work’s author could be settled by this authority alone, since it bears the title “Gelasian.” I believe that all those skilled in sound criticism will agree with this most distinguished man, both concerning the author of the work and concerning the judgment he gave about its authenticity, especially in those passages which the Vatican version omits or wholly alters. For if the matter concerns what it shares with the other versions, it certainly yields in many respects to Chiffletius’s Jurensian text, in which the reading is preferable, as will be clear to anyone who compares them.

It would therefore remain desirable for some third codex of equal antiquity to be produced, one in which both the Vatican omissions and the approved Chiffletian readings would appear. If chance should ever bring this about, I do not doubt that learned men would welcome it with open arms.

But good fortune has intervened! As I was examining an ancient Lucensian codex nine hundred years old, this finally came to me. Here, reader, is from it the decree concerning books to be approved and rejected, in which all the passages omitted from the Vatican version have been restored. In the remaining passages it follows the Chiffletian reading rather than the Vatican one. It bears the name of Gelasius and is at last the text one could have wished for.

Nor does it surpass the other editions published thus far only in that respect; it is also made more commendable by the fact that it is adorned with a preface nowhere found in the printed editions. I regret, however, that the copyist’s carelessness has corrupted it and that it cannot easily be repaired. So far as one may judge from the similarity of style, it is entirely Gelasian.

This is my judgment concerning this new edition of the Gelasian decree: [Col. 0165] to commend it to learned readers, I present three versions of the same decree—the Vatican, the Jurensian or Chiffletian, and the Lucensian.

After writing this, I came upon a Gelasian decree published from a very old Florentine codex by P. Joseph Blanchinus, a most distinguished priest of the Roman Oratory of Saint Philip Neri, in the prolegomena to volume IV of the Roman edition of Anastasius the Librarian. That learned man judged that this codex represented the genuine decree of Gelasius. I would certainly not deny that its reading is better than the Vatican version.

But when this very learned man says that the catalogue of the sacred books, which is absent from Fontaninus’s Vatican manuscript but is read in his Florentine one, was removed from the Vatican either through the copyist’s negligence or through someone’s fraud, this is futile and empty. The catalogue is likewise absent from my Lucensian manuscript; and no one will persuade himself that the Lucensian was copied from that Vatican manuscript, or that both derived from some third source, since they often differ.

If one omits this catalogue of sacred books, the Florentine manuscript agrees almost entirely with ours, apart from a few exceptions which I carefully noted at the edge of the page. [Note: [Col. 0165] We have placed these Florentine variants, together with the others, at the bottom of our columns, preceded by the name of the Florentine codex. Editor.]

The Florentine manuscript of Blanchinus is mutilated at the end: after “Faustus of Riez,” and so forth, the rest is missing, although those passages are found in all the other manuscript codices.

This is what I had written in my previous edition. Now, however, something has been added to adorn this new edition: namely, variants from a very old Frisingian codex, approximately one thousand years old, which the learned P. Frobenius Forster, prior and librarian of Saint Emmeram at Regensburg, supplied to me with his customary courtesy.

In that codex this decree of Damasus’s council is followed by the following words, immediately after the council has ended: “Likewise it was said: Now we must deal with the divine Scriptures: what the universal Catholic Church receives and what it ought to avoid. Here begins the order of the Old Testament,” and so forth. Immediately afterward the complete decree concerning books to be read follows.

[Note: [Col. 0165] The following manuscript versions—the Lucensian, Fontaninus’s Vatican, and Chiffletius’s Jurensian—are printed in parallel in Migne.]

## LUCENSIAN

Here begins the decretal issued from the city of Rome concerning books to be received or not received.

A synod held under Pope Gelasius of the city of Rome, with seventy bishops.

### THE PROLOGUE BEGINS

For examining or understanding the Scriptures published by many authors in the New or Old Testament, it is appropriate for us to preserve that apostolic saying: “Do not despise prophecies,” he says; “but test everything,” so that, by the fuller working of God, we may believe that those writings were composed which spoke with complete certainty about the Lord’s coming, his birth, passion, and resurrection—for through them we believe that we have been saved. There we understand the saying in which he declared: “Hold fast what is good.” We have learned that the Scriptures which ought to be rejected or refused by Catholics are those which the most learned man Jerome also rejected and condemned. It is enough for us to say this, so that we may abstain from every appearance of evil.

[Col. 0167] After [Note: [Col. 0168] The Florentine codex adds: “all these.”] the prophetic [an ancient hand adds: “and evangelical”] and apostolic Scriptures [Note: [Col. 0168] The same codex adds: “which we have set forth above.”], on which the Catholic Church has been founded by the grace of God, we have also thought it necessary to make known the following. Although all the Catholic Churches spread throughout the world constitute one bridal chamber of Christ, nevertheless the holy Roman Church was not placed above the other Churches by synodal decrees; rather, it obtained primacy through the evangelical word of our Lord [Note: [Col. 0168] The same codex adds: “and Savior”]: “You are Peter,” he says, “and on this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. And I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven; and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven.”

[An ancient hand supplies: “To whom”] There was also added the fellowship of Blessed [an ancient hand supplies: “the most blessed apostle Paul, the vessel of election,”] who, contrary to what the heretics chatter [Note: [Col. 0168] The same codex reads “heretics”], was not crowned at a different time but, struggling in glorious death at one and the same time and on the same day with Peter in the city of Rome under Caesar Nero, was crowned together with him. Together they consecrated the aforesaid holy Roman Church to Christ the Lord, and by their presence [Col. 0169] and venerable triumph they placed it before all the cities [Note: [Col. 0168] The same codex reads “all cities”] throughout the whole world [Note: [Col. 0169] The same codex reads “they carried it forward”].

Therefore the first see of the apostle Peter is the Roman Church, having neither spot nor wrinkle nor anything of that kind.

The second see is at Alexandria, consecrated in the name of Blessed Peter by Mark, his disciple and evangelist. Sent by the apostle Peter into Egypt, Mark preached the word of truth and consecrated a glorious martyrdom [an ancient hand corrects this to: “completed”].

The third see, at Antioch, is held in honor because of that same most blessed apostle Peter, since he lived there before he came to Rome; and there the first name of the new people, Christians, arose [Note: [Col. 0169] The same codex reads: “and there”].

And although no one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, [Note: [Col. 0169] In the same codex, “which is” is absent.] which is Christ Jesus, nevertheless, for the building up of the Church, that same Roman Church does not forbid the reception, after those Scriptures of the Old and New Testament which we regularly receive, of these Scriptures also. [Note: [Col. 0169] The same codex does not contain “that is.”]

That is, the holy Council of Nicaea, consisting of three hundred and eighteen bishops [Note: [Col. 0170] The same codex reads “Fathers”;] [an ancient hand adds: “Fathers”], held under the mediation of Maximus Constantine Augustus.

The holy Council of Ephesus, [an ancient hand: “Ephesian”] in which Nestorius was condemned, with the agreement [Note: [Col. 0170] In the same codex “with” is absent.] of Blessed Pope Celestine, through Cyril, bishop of the Alexandrian see, and Arcadius, a bishop sent from Italy.

The holy Council of Chalcedon, under the mediation of Augustus Marcian and Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, in which the Nestorian and Eutychian heresies were condemned together with Dioscorus and his associates [Note: [Col. 0170] The same codex reads: “were condemned.”].

[Note: [Col. 0170] The Florentine codex has “likewise,” and so forth.] The works of Blessed Caecilius Cyprian, martyr and bishop of Carthage.

[Col. 0171] The works of Blessed Gregory of Nazianzus, bishop.

The works of Blessed Basil, bishop of Cappadocia.

The works of Blessed Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria.

The works of Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria.

The works of Blessed Cyril, bishop of Alexandria.

The works of Blessed Hilary, bishop of Poitiers [Note: [Col. 0171] The same codex reads “of Poitiers.”].

[Note: [Col. 0171] In the Florentine manuscript this appears here after Saint Athanasius.] The works of Blessed John, bishop of Constantinople.

The works of Blessed Ambrose, bishop of Milan.

The works of Blessed Augustine [Note: [Col. 0171] The same codex reads “bishop of Hippo Regius of the region.”], bishop of Hippo Regius.

The works of Blessed Jerome, presbyter.

The works of Blessed Prosper, a most religious man.

[Note: [Col. 0171] The same codex reads “letters.”] The works [alternative: “the letter”] of Pope Leo sent to Flavian, bishop of Constantinople; if anyone disputes its text down to a single iota and does not receive it reverently in every respect, let him be anathema.

We decree that the works and treatises [Note: [Col. 0171] The same codex reads “and treatises”] of all the orthodox Fathers who in no respect departed from communion with the holy Roman Church, nor separated themselves from its faith or preaching, but remained participants in its communion [the manuscript reads “communication”], by the grace of God, until the last day of their earthly life, are to be read.

Likewise, the decretal letters which the most blessed popes issued from the city of Rome at various times for the consolation of various Fathers are to be received with reverence. [Note: [Col. 0172] The same codex reads: “are to be received.”]

Likewise, the acts of the holy martyrs, who shine forth through manifold torments and the wondrous triumphs of their confessions. Who among Catholics would doubt this [Note: [Col. 0172] In the Florentine codex, “this” is absent.]—that they endured greater sufferings in their struggles and bore everything not by their own strength but by the grace and aid of God?

But for this reason, according to ancient custom, they are not read in the holy Roman Church with particular caution: the names of those who wrote them are entirely unknown, and they are thought to have been written by unbelievers [Note: [Col. 0172] The same codex reads “and”] or ignorant people with superfluous material, or with material less suitable than the order of events required. Such are the passions of a certain Quiricus and Julitta, and of George and others of this kind, which are said to have been composed by heretics. Therefore, as has been said, lest even a slight opportunity for mockery should arise, they are not read in the Roman Church [Note: [Col. 0172] The same codex adds “holy”].

Nevertheless, together with the aforesaid Church, we venerate with complete devotion all the martyrs and their glorious struggles, who are known more to God than to human beings.

Likewise, we receive with all honor the Lives of the Fathers—of Paul, Antony, Hilarion, and all the hermits—which the most blessed man Jerome wrote. [Note: [Col. 0173] In the same codex “with all” is absent.]

Likewise, the Acts of Blessed Sylvester, prelate of the Apostolic See, although the name of their author is unknown, are nevertheless known to be read by many Catholics in the city of Rome, and many Churches imitate them on account of their ancient use.

Likewise, a writing concerning the discovery of the Lord’s holy cross, and another writing concerning the discovery of the head of John the Baptist, are certain new accounts [Note: [Col. 0173] The same codex reads: “they are accounts,” and so forth.], and some Catholics read them. But when these writings have come into the hands of Catholics, the saying of the blessed apostle [an ancient hand: “the preceding”] is to precede them: “Test everything; hold fast what is good.”

Likewise, Rufinus, a most religious man [Note: [Col. 0173] The same codex reads “a religious man,”], who published many books of ecclesiastical works [Note: [Col. 0173] In the same codex “who” is absent.] and also interpreted some Scriptures. But since the most blessed Jerome censured him in certain matters concerning freedom of choice, we shall hold those opinions which we know the aforesaid Jerome to have held; and this not only concerning Rufinus, but also concerning all those whom that frequently mentioned man rebuked out of zeal for God and devotion to the faith.

Likewise, we receive for reading certain works of Origen which the most blessed man Jerome does not reject; all the rest, however, we declare must be rejected together with their author. [Note: [Col. 0174] In the same codex “all” is absent.]

Likewise, the Chronicle of Eusebius of Caesarea [Note: [Col. 0174] In the same codex “bishop” is absent.] and the books of his Ecclesiastical History: although in the first book of his narrative he was lukewarm, and afterward wrote one book in praise and defense of the schismatic Origen, nevertheless, on account of his exceptional knowledge of matters relevant to investigation [an ancient hand: “instruction”], we do not declare them altogether to be rejected. [Note: [Col. 0174] The same codex reads “instruction.”]

We praise Orosius, a most learned man, because he composed a history that was exceedingly necessary for us against the calumnies of the pagans and assembled it with remarkable brevity. [Note: [Col. 0174] The same codex reads “who.”]

We present with distinguished praise the Paschal Work of the venerable bishop Sedulius [Note: [Col. 0174] In the same codex “bishop” is absent.], which he composed in heroic verse. [Note: [Col. 0174] The same codex reads: “we rank highly.”]

Likewise, we do not disdain the laborious work of Juvencus, but admire it. [Col. 0175] The remaining works, however, which were written or proclaimed by heretics or schismatics, the Catholic and apostolic Roman Church does not receive at all [Note: [Col. 0175] The same codex reads: “the Catholic and apostolic Roman Church does not receive at all.”; an ancient hand adds the same words]. Of these, we believe that a few which have come to mind, and which Catholics ought to avoid, should be set down below.

Likewise, a catalogue of apocryphal books [an ancient hand: “books”] which are not received. [Note: [Col. 0175] In the same codex “which are not received” is absent.]

We confess that the Council of Ariminum, convened by Constantius, son of Constantine [Note: [Col. 0175] In the same codex “Augustus” is absent.] Augustus, through the prefect Taurus, is condemned from that time, now, and forever.

The Itinerary in the name of the apostle Peter, which is called the books of Saint Clement [an ancient hand: “ten books”]—ten [Note: [Col. 0175] The same codex reads “nine”]—is apocryphal.

The Acts in the name of the apostle Andrew are apocryphal.

The Acts in the name of the apostle Thomas are apocryphal.

Ten books are apocryphal. (But this has been deleted by an ancient hand.)

These and similar works, which Simon Magus, Nicolaus, Cerinthus, Marcion, Basilides, Ebion, and also Paul of Samosata, Photinus, and Bonosus [an ancient hand adds *and*] and those who fell away through a similar error; likewise Montanus with his most obscene followers, Apollinaris, Valentinus or Manichaeus, Faustus, Africanus, Sabellius, Arius, Macedonius, Eunomius, Novatus, Sabacius, Caelestus, Donatus, Eustacius, Jovianus, Pelagius, Julian of Celum, Caelestius, Maximinus [an ancient hand: Maximianus], Priscillianus from Spain, Nestorius of Constantinople, Maximus the Cynic, Lampetius, Dioscorus, Eutyches, Peter, and another Peter—one of whom stained Alexandria and the other Antioch—Acacius of Constantinople with his associates, as well as all heretics, disciples of heretics, or schismatics who taught or wrote, although their names are scarcely remembered: we confess that these works were not merely rejected but expelled from the entire Roman and apostolic Church, and that, together with their authors and the followers of their authors, they are to be condemned eternally under the unbreakable bond of anathema.

# VATICANUM FONTANINI

[Col. 0165]

Here begins the decretal of Saint Gelasius, pope of the city of Rome.

## I.

[Col. 0167]

After the prophetic, evangelical, and apostolic Scriptures, upon which the Catholic Church has been founded through the grace of God, we have also thought it necessary to make known the following: although all the Catholic Churches spread throughout the world are one bridal chamber of Christ, nevertheless the holy Roman Church has been given primacy over the other Churches not by synodal decrees, but by the evangelical voice of our Lord and Savior, which says: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I shall build my Church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it; and I shall give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven; and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven; and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven.”

To this Church was also granted the fellowship of the blessed apostle Paul, the vessel of election. He was crowned—not at a different time, as the heretics babble, but at one time and on one and the same day—by suffering a glorious death with Peter in the city of Rome under the emperor Nero. Together they consecrated the aforesaid holy Roman Church to Christ the Lord, and carried it before all the other cities throughout the world by their presence and venerable triumph.

[Col. 0169] Thus the Roman Church is the first see of the apostle Peter, possessing neither stain nor wrinkle nor anything of that kind.

The second see is at Alexandria, consecrated in the name of the blessed Peter by Mark, his disciple and evangelist. Sent by the apostle Peter into Egypt, Mark preached the word of truth and completed a glorious martyrdom.

The third see, at Antioch, is likewise held in honor as that of the most blessed apostle Peter, because he lived there before he came to Rome, and there the first name of the new people, Christians, arose.

## II.

Although no one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, namely Christ Jesus, nevertheless the same holy Roman Church does not prohibit the following Scriptures from being received for its holy edification, after those books of the Old and New Testament that we regularly accept:

The holy Council of Nicaea, of the 318 Fathers, held under the authority of Maximus Constantine Augustus.

The holy Council of Ephesus, at which Nestorius was condemned, with the agreement of Pope Celestine, under the authority of Cyril, bishop of the Alexandrian see, and Arcadius, sent from Italy.

The holy Council of Chalcedon, held under the authority of Augustus Marcian and Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, at which the Nestorian, Antiochene, and Eutychian heresies were condemned together with Dioscorus and his accomplices.

## III.

Here begin the works to be received.

Likewise, the works of the blessed martyr Caecilius Cyprian, bishop of Carthage.

[Col. 0171] Likewise, the works of the blessed Gregory of Nazianzus, bishop.

Likewise, the works of the blessed Basil, bishop of Cappadocia.

Likewise, the works of the blessed Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria.

Likewise, the works of the blessed John, bishop of Constantinople.

Likewise, the works of the blessed Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria.

Likewise, the works of the blessed Hilary, bishop of Poitiers.

Likewise, the works of the blessed Ambrose, bishop of Milan.

Likewise, the works of the blessed Augustine, bishop of Hippo Regius.

Likewise, the works of the blessed Jerome, presbyter.

Likewise, those of Prosper, a most religious man.

Likewise, the letter of the blessed Pope Leo to Flavian, bishop of Constantinople, which was sent to him. Whoever disputes its text even to a single iota, and does not receive it reverently in every respect, let him be anathema.

Likewise, we decree that the works and treatises of all orthodox Fathers who in no respect deviated from fellowship with the holy Roman Church, nor separated themselves from its faith or preaching, but through the grace of God remained participants in its communion until the end of their lives, are to be read.

Likewise, the decretal letters which the most blessed popes, at various times, sent from the city of Rome for the consolation of various Fathers are to be received with reverence.

Likewise, the acts of the holy martyrs, who shine through the many torments of their sufferings and the wondrous triumphs of their confessions. What Catholic would doubt that they endured greater sufferings in their contests, and that they endured them not by their own strength but by the grace and aid of God? They are not read in the holy Roman Church with particular caution because the names of those who wrote them are entirely unknown, and because they are thought to contain material supplied by unbelievers and ignorant persons that is excessive or less suitable to the order of events. Such are the passions of a certain Quiricus and Julita, and of George, and of others of this kind, which are said to have been composed by heretics. Therefore, as has been said, lest even a slight opportunity for mockery should arise, they are not read in the holy Roman Church. Nevertheless, together with the aforesaid Church, we venerate with complete devotion all the martyrs and their glorious contests, who are known more to God than to human beings.

[Col. 0173] Likewise, we receive with all honor the *Lives of the Fathers*, of Paul, Antony, and Hilarion, and of all the hermits, which the most blessed Jerome nevertheless composed.

Likewise, we know that the *Acts of the blessed Silvester*, prelate of the Apostolic See, are read by many Catholics in the city of Rome, although the name of the person who wrote them is unknown; and many Churches imitate this on account of ancient custom.

Likewise, the writing concerning the discovery of the Lord’s cross, and another writing concerning the discovery of the head of John the Baptist, are indeed recent accounts, and some Catholics read them. But when these come into the hands of Catholics, the sentence of the blessed apostle Paul should take precedence: “Test everything; hold fast to what is good.”

Likewise, Rufinus, a deeply religious man, published many books of ecclesiastical work and also interpreted certain Scriptures. But since the most blessed Jerome censured him in certain matters concerning freedom of choice, we hold those opinions which we recognize the aforesaid blessed Jerome to have held—not only concerning Rufinus but also concerning all those whom that frequently mentioned holy man reproved out of zeal for God and devotion to the faith.

Likewise, we receive for reading certain works of Origen which the most blessed Jerome does not reject; but we declare that all the rest are to be rejected together with their author.

The *Chronicle of Eusebius of Caesarea* and his books of *Ecclesiastical History*, although he was lukewarm in the first book of his narrative and afterward wrote one book in praise and defense of Origen the schismatic, we nevertheless do not declare entirely rejectable, because of the knowledge of particular matters that are useful for instruction.

Likewise, we praise Orosius, a most learned man, who composed for us a very necessary history against the calumnies of the pagans and wove it together with remarkable brevity.

Likewise, we highly commend the venerable *Paschal Work* of Sedulius, which he composed in learned verses.

Nor do we despise the laborious work of Juvencus; rather, we admire it. The other works composed or preached by heretics or schismatics the Catholic and apostolic Roman Church in no way receives. Of these, we have thought that a few which came to mind, and which Catholics ought to avoid, should be set out below.

## IV.

[Col. 0179] The works of Victorinus of Pettau, apocryphal.

The works of Frumentius the Blind, apocryphal.

These and similar works, which Simon Magus, Nicolaus, Cerinthus, Marcion, Basilides, Ebion, and also Paul of Samosata, Photinus and Bonosus, and those who fell away through a similar error; likewise Montanus with his most obscene followers, Apollinaris, Valentinian or Manichaeus, Faustus, Africanus, Sabellius, Arius, Macedonius, Eunomius, Novatus, Sabacius, Caelestus, Donatus, Eustacius, Jovianus, Pelagius, Julian of Elane, Caelestius, Maximianus, Priscillianus from Spain, Nestorius of Constantinople, Maximus the Cynic, Lampetius, Dioscorus, Eutyches, Peter, and another Peter—one of whom stained Alexandria and the other Antioch—Acacius of Constantinople with his associates, as well as all heresies and the disciples of heretics who taught or wrote, although their names are scarcely remembered: we confess that these works were not merely rejected but expelled from the entire Roman, Catholic, and apostolic Church, and that, together with their authors and the followers of their authors, they are to be condemned eternally under the unbreakable bond of anathema.

The decretal ends.

# JURENSE CHIFFLETII

[Col. 0166]

Here begins the decretal issued in the city of Rome by Pope Hormisdas.

Concerning the divine Scriptures that the universal Catholic Church receives, and what it ought thereafter to avoid.

## 1.

The order of the Old Testament which the holy and Catholic Roman Church receives and honors is as follows:

The book of Genesis, 1. — The book of Exodus, 1. — The book of Leviticus, 1. — The book of Numbers, 1. — The book of Deuteronomy, 1. — The book of Joshua son of Nun, 1. — The book of Judges, 1. — The book of Ruth, 1. — The books of Kingdoms, 4. — The books of Chronicles, 2. — The book of the 150 Psalms, 1. — The books of Solomon, 3: Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and the Song of Songs. — Likewise, the book of Wisdom, 1. — The book of Ecclesiasticus, 1. — Likewise, the order of the prophets: the book of Isaiah, 1. — [Col. 0166] The book of Jeremiah, 1, together with *Cinoth*, that is, with his Lamentations [variant in the Freising codex: “One book of Jeremiah together with *Cinoth*, that is, with his Lamentations”]. — The book of Ezekiel, 1. — The book of Daniel, 1. — The book of Hosea, 1. — The book of Amos, 1. — [Col. 0168] The book of Micah, 1. — The book of Joel, 1. — The book of Obadiah, 1. — The book of Jonah, 1. — The book of Nahum, 1. — The book of Habakkuk, 1. — The book of Zephaniah, 1. — The book of Haggai, 1. — The book of Zechariah, 1. — The book of Malachi, 1. — Likewise, the order of the histories: the book of Job, 1. — The book of Tobit, 1. — The books of Ezra, 2. — The book of Esther, 1. — The book of Judith, 1. — The books of the Maccabees, 2.

Likewise, the order of the Scriptures of the New and Eternal Testament [the addition reads: “which the holy and Catholic Church receives”]: four books of the Gospels: the Gospel according to Matthew, 1. — The Gospel according to Mark, 1. — The Gospel according to Luke, 1. — The Gospel according to John, 1. — Likewise, the book of the Acts of the Apostles, 1. — The letters of the apostle Paul, fourteen in number: the letter to the Romans, 1. — The letters to the Corinthians, 2. — The letter to the Ephesians, 1. — The letters to the Thessalonians, 2. — The letter to the Galatians, 1. — The letter to the Philippians, 1. — The letter to the Colossians, 1. — The letters to Timothy, 2. — The letter to Titus, 1. — The letter to Philemon, 1. — The letter to the Hebrews, 1. — Likewise, the book of the Apocalypse of John, 1. — Likewise, seven canonical letters: two letters of the apostle Peter. — [Col. 0167] One letter of the apostle John; two letters of another John, the presbyter [so too in the most ancient Dionysian codex of Saint Emmeram]. — One letter of the apostle James. — Three letters of the apostle John. — One letter of Jude the Zealot, the apostle.

## II.

[Note: [Col. 0167] The canon of the New Testament ends here. The following was also stated: “After all these prophetic…”]

After all the prophetic, evangelical, and apostolic Scriptures which we have set out above, upon which the Catholic Church has been founded through the grace of God, we have also thought it necessary to make known the following: although all the Catholic Churches spread throughout the world are one bridal chamber of Christ, nevertheless the holy Roman Church has been given primacy over the other Churches not by synodal decrees, but by the evangelical voice of our Lord and Savior, which says: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I shall build my Church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it; and I shall give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven; and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven; and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven.”

The fellowship of the most blessed apostle Paul, the vessel of election, was also added. He was crowned—not at a different time, as the heretics babble, but at one time and on one and the same day—by suffering a glorious death with Peter in the city of Rome under the emperor Nero. Together they consecrated the aforesaid holy Roman Church to Christ the Lord and placed it before all the other cities throughout the world by their presence and venerable triumph.

[Col. 0170] Thus the Roman Church is the first see of the apostle Peter, possessing neither stain nor wrinkle nor anything of this kind.

The second see, at Alexandria, was consecrated in the name of the blessed Peter by Mark, his disciple and evangelist. Sent by the apostle Peter into Egypt, Mark preached the word of truth and completed a glorious martyrdom.

The third see, at Antioch, is likewise held in honor as that of the most blessed apostle Peter, because he lived there before he came to Rome, and there the first name of the new people, Christians, arose.

## III.

Although no one could lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, namely Christ Jesus, nevertheless the same Roman Church, for our edification, does not prohibit the following Scriptures from being received after those of the Old and New Testament which we have enumerated above in due order:

The holy Council of Nicaea, according to the 318 Fathers, held under the authority of Augustus Constantine the Great, at which Arius the heretic was condemned.

The holy Council of Constantinople, held under the authority of the elder Augustus Theodosius, at which Macedonius the heretic received his deserved condemnation.

The holy Council of Ephesus, at which Nestorius was condemned, with the agreement of the most blessed Pope Celestine, under the authority of Cyril, bishop of the Alexandrian see, and Bishop Arcadius, sent from Italy.

The holy Council of Chalcedon, held under the authority of Augustus Marcian and Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, at which the Nestorian and Eutychian heresies were condemned together with Dioscorus and his accomplices. [Note: [Col. 0170] The following words are absent up to section IV.] We have also decreed that any councils established by the holy Fathers up to the present are to be preserved and received after the authority of these four.

## IV.

What now follows concerns the works of the holy Fathers received in the Catholic Church.

The works of the blessed martyr Caecilius Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, are to be received in every respect.

[Col. 0172] Likewise, the works of the blessed Gregory of Nazianzus, bishop.

Likewise, the works of the blessed Basil, bishop of Cappadocia.

Likewise, the works of the blessed Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria.

Likewise, the works of the blessed John, bishop of Constantinople.

Likewise, the works of the blessed Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria.

Likewise, the works of the blessed Cyril, bishop of Alexandria.

Likewise, the works of the blessed Hilary, bishop of Poitiers.

Likewise, the works of the blessed Ambrose, bishop of Milan.

Likewise, the works of the blessed Augustine, bishop of Hippo Regius.

Likewise, the works of the blessed Jerome, presbyter.

Likewise, the works of the blessed Prosper, a most religious man.

Likewise, the letter of the blessed Pope Leo to Flavian, bishop of Constantinople, which was sent to him. Whoever disputes its text even to a single iota, and does not receive it reverently in every respect, let him be anathema.

Likewise, we decree that the works and treatises of all orthodox Fathers who in no respect deviated from fellowship with the holy Roman Church, nor separated themselves from its faith or preaching, but through the grace of God remained participants in its communion until the last day of their lives, are to be read.

Likewise, the decretal letters which the most blessed popes, at various times, sent from the city of Rome for consultation with various Fathers are to be received with reverence.

Likewise, the acts of the holy martyrs, which shine through the many torments of their sufferings and the wondrous triumphs of their confessions. What Catholic would doubt that they endured even greater sufferings in their contests, and that they endured everything not by their own strength but by the grace and aid of God? For this reason, according to ancient custom, they are not read in the holy Roman Church with particular caution, because the names of those who wrote them are entirely unknown, and because they are thought to contain material supplied by unbelievers and ignorant persons that is excessive or less suitable to the order of events. Such are the passions of a certain Quiricus and Julita, and of George, and of others of this kind, which are said to have been composed by heretics. Therefore, as has been said, lest even a slight opportunity for mockery should arise, they are not read in the holy Roman Church. Nevertheless, together with the aforesaid Roman Church, [Col. 0174] we venerate with complete devotion all the martyrs and their glorious contests, who are known more to God than to human beings.

Likewise, we receive with all honor the *Lives of the Fathers*, of Paul, Antony, and Hilarion, and of all the hermits, which the most blessed Jerome nevertheless composed.

Likewise, we know that the *Acts of the most blessed Silvester*, prelate of the Apostolic See, are read by many Catholics in the city of Rome, although the name of the person who wrote them is unknown; and many Churches imitate this on account of ancient custom.

Likewise, the writing concerning the discovery of the Lord’s cross and another writing concerning the discovery of the head of the blessed John the Baptist are indeed recent accounts, and some Catholics read them. But when these come into the hands of Catholics, the sentence of the blessed apostle Paul should take precedence: “Test everything, and hold fast to what is good.”

Likewise, Rufinus, a deeply religious man, published many books of ecclesiastical work and also interpreted certain Scriptures. But since the venerable Jerome censured him in certain matters concerning freedom of choice, we hold those opinions which we recognize the aforesaid blessed Jerome to have held—not only concerning Rufinus but also concerning all those whom that frequently mentioned holy man reproved out of zeal for God and devotion to the faith.

Likewise, we receive for reading certain works of Origen which the most blessed Jerome does not reject; but we declare that all the rest are to be rejected together with their author.

Likewise, the *Chronicle of Eusebius of Caesarea* and his books of *Ecclesiastical History*, although he was lukewarm in the first book of his narrative and afterward wrote one book in praise and defense of Origen the schismatic, we nevertheless do not declare entirely rejectable, because of the knowledge of particular matters that are useful for instruction.

Likewise, we praise Orosius, a most learned man, who composed for us a very necessary history against the calumnies of the pagans and wove it together with remarkable brevity.

Likewise, we highly commend the venerable *Paschal Work* of Sedulius, which he composed in heroic verses.

Nor do we despise the laborious work of Juvencus; rather, we admire it. The other works composed or preached by heretics or schismatics the Catholic and apostolic Roman Church in no way receives. Of these, we have thought that a few which came to mind, and which Catholics ought to avoid, should be set out below.

## V.
