# OBSERVATION OF P. ANTONIUS PAGI

*(On the year of Christ 494, no. 2 and following)*

[Col. 0179]

The decree concerning the divine Scriptures and the works of the holy Fathers that are received in the Catholic Church presses hard upon the heterodox, who reject tradition and mutilate the number of the canonical books at will and for the advantage of their sects. For the books of Job, Tobit, Judith, and the Maccabees, the Letter to the Hebrews, the Apocalypse of John, the two letters of Peter, the three of the apostle John, and the one of Jude are mentioned in it.

Pearson, in his *Vindiciae Ignatianae*, devoted a lengthy discussion to its author and the time at which it was composed, and on page 53 says that he believes this decree was promulgated after the Fifth Synod, celebrated in the year 553. Catholics likewise do not agree among themselves concerning the author of this sanction or the year in which it was issued, since manuscript codices attribute it to three different pontiffs.

The oldest codex of the collection of Dionysius Exiguus, which Baluzius testifies was communicated to him by Dacher, attributes this decree to Pope Damasus. Baronius, in the year 69, no. 4, reports that the collection of Cresconius contains a Roman council under Damasus in which the apocryphal books are discussed; Baronius believes its decrees were repeated by Gelasius in the decree of the seventy-two bishops, concerning which he speaks with the collectors of the Councils under the year 494.

But the oldest codex read by Pearson and brought to England by Lanfranc from the monastery of Bec bears this title: “The decrees of Pope Gelasius concerning books to be received and not to be received, written by him together with seventy most learned bishops.”

Nicholas I, Roman pontiff, in Letter 42 to the bishops of Gaul, delivered around the year 865; Lupus, abbot of Ferrières, at the end of his letter to Charles the Bald and at the end of his question concerning the Blood of Christ; Gratian, in distinction 15, chapter *Sancta Romana*; Burchard, bishop of Worms; various manuscript codices; and all printed editions identify Gelasius as the author of this decree.

Finally, Baluzius and Chifflet, in the Jurense codex, testify that it is attributed to Pope Hormisdas in the most ancient codex of Vergelli. Hence Chifflet, at the end of his notes on Vigilius of Thapsus, thought that this decree was first sanctioned by Gelasius in a Roman council in that year—but in such a way that it did not appear as a papal decree, but rather as a canon of the entire council; and that afterward it was issued by Hormisdas in the form of a papal decretal, divided for the sake of arrangement into five titles and perhaps restored in certain places.

I shall demonstrate that Gelasius was the author of this famous decree and that it was attributed to Hormisdas only through error; and, unless I am greatly mistaken, I shall settle the dispute.

When the catalogue of condemned volumes is drawn up in it, the books of Cassian and Faustus of Riez are included among them, with the following sentence prefixed: “The other works composed or preached by heretics or schismatics the Catholic and apostolic Roman Church in no way receives. Of these, we believe that a few which came to mind, and which Catholics ought to avoid, should be set out.”

And when the Fathers of the Roman synod had condemned many books of heretics and other uncertain authors, they placed among them the works of Cassian and Faustus under this heading: “The works of Cassian, presbyter of Gaul, apocryphal; the works of Faustus of Riez in Gaul, apocryphal.”

In the following century, when controversies concerning divine grace arose from the works of Faustus in particular, some defended Faustus and others attacked him with the greatest vehemence, not only in the West but also in the East—especially the Scythian monks, who, emerging from Asia, stirred Europe and Africa against him, as we shall explain under the year 520.

In this state of affairs, Possessor, an African bishop sent into exile by Trasamund, king of Africa, consulted Pope Hormisdas while he was staying in Constantinople. There the books of Faustus were defended by many as Catholic, but condemned by Maxentius and the Scythian monks as heretical. Possessor himself asked Hormisdas what opinion ought to be held concerning those books, and sent his deacon Justin to him for this purpose.

His *Report* to Hormisdas is extant in the preceding volume of the Councils, and is said to have been received “on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August, in the consulship of Rusticus, a man of consular rank”—that is, in the year 520.

These are Possessor’s words in it:

“I believe that your Blessedness is not unaware how many plots the Church in the city of Constantinople is suffering, and how, following the pattern of an old disease, a wound that is believed to have been covered by a scar is again seeking to break out into suppuration. Therefore, when the minds of certain brethren were stirred to scandal concerning the book of a certain Faustus, a Gaul by nationality and bishop of the city of Riez, who appears to have argued eloquently about various matters, and more frequently about the grace of God, while others, as human opinions tend to do, resisted in the opposite direction, they believed that I should consult you concerning this uncertainty.”

Possessor later adds:

“I ask that those who consult you may learn, through an authoritative apostolic reply, what should be thought concerning the statements of the aforesaid author—especially since the sons of the master of soldiers, Vitalian and Justinian, also particularly desire to be informed on this matter by a rescript of your Blessedness.”

Hormisdas received Possessor’s letter on 18 July 520 and replied to him on 13 August with Letter 70, in which, among other things, he says:

> “As for those concerning whose consultation with you about the statements of a certain Gallic bishop Faustus you have informed us by letter, let them have this answer: neither is he to be received, nor can anyone whom the examination of the Catholic faith or ecclesiastical discipline does not receive among the authority of the Fathers generate ambiguity or bring prejudice upon the religious. The institutions established by the Fathers, which the faithful ought to follow, are fixed. Whether interpretation, preaching, or a word composed for the edification of the people agrees with right faith and sound doctrine, it is admitted; if it disagrees, it is abolished.”

Cardinal Baronius, under the year 520, no. 21, and Cardinal Norisius, in *Cenotaphium Pisanum*, p. 445, rightly observed that here Hormisdas was speaking of the decree of Gelasius. Yet what the same pontiff adds shortly afterward clearly implies that Gelasius himself, the author of that decree, rather than Hormisdas, was its author:

> “The venerable judgment of the Fathers did not imprudently define for faithful posterity what the Catholic doctrines were; under the instruction of the Holy Spirit, it also established which books of ancient times were to be received as authoritative, lest a reader, indulging his own opinion, should assert not what suited the edification of the Church, but what his own pleasure had conceived.”

Therefore the decree concerning books to be received and not to be received was issued not by Hormisdas, but by one of his successors at some Roman synod—not indeed by Anastasius or Symmachus, who followed Gelasius and preceded Hormisdas, since no one has ever asserted this and no manuscript bears the name of either of them, but by Gelasius, to whom countless manuscripts attribute it.

Nor can it be said that the writing was composed by Damasus, whose name appears through a scribal error in the Cresconian collection, since most of the authors of the little works mentioned in it lived and wrote after Damasus. Nor did Hormisdas alter anything, as Chiffletius believed; for in his cited letter to Possessor, Hormisdas refers him back to what had already been fixed by the Fathers and wished to establish nothing new concerning Faustus, about whom he had been consulted.

It therefore appears that Hormisdas sent the decree of Pope Gelasius both to Possessor and to his legates who were then staying at Constantinople, and instructed them that it should be religiously observed by everyone. In this way he satisfied Possessor’s request. It happened, however, that the decree was then copied into various exemplars and disseminated more widely throughout Europe, Africa, and the East, especially by Faustus’s opponents; and because it had been sent by Pope Hormisdas and was everywhere circulated in his name, it was imprudently attributed to him by some people as time passed. This is undoubtedly the origin of that false superscription.

Baronius and the compilers of the councils write that the decree of Gelasius was issued under the consulship of Asterius and Praesidius, that is, in this year. But manuscript codices refute them—those in which that chronological note is absent. I read it in the Royal Library, written in a very ancient script but without the consular note, and another in the Library of Saint Victor in Paris, from which it is likewise absent. Nor do I doubt that it is missing from the other manuscripts, since the Roman council of seventy bishops at which it was issued was not held before the year 496.

For in the aforementioned decree these words concerning Sedulius are read:

> “Likewise, we place before others in venerable honor the work of the venerable man Sedulius, *Paschale*, which he composed in heroic verse and distinguished with praise.”

At the end of the *Bucolics* in the very ancient Medicean manuscript of Virgil, the following is found:

> “Turcius Rufus Apronianus Asterius, a man of clarissimus rank and illustrious, former count of the domestic protectors, former count of the private largesses, former prefect of the City, patrician, and ordinary consul, read and punctuated the codex of his brother Macarius, a man of clarissimus rank—not trusting in my own judgment, but in the decision of him to whose will I am wholly devoted—at Rome, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May, [the text] of Publius Vergilius Maro:
>
> “Correcting, I punctuated it—the welcome gift of a friend;
>
> “Taking up the task, I applied myself diligently. The book of the *Bucolics* ends.”

The eminent Cardinal Norisius, already cited, who produced this clausula, observes that in an ancient Vatican codex, no. 1165, after Sedulius’s *Paschal Poem*, the following is read:

> “Sedulius left this work scattered among loose sheets; having been collected, brought together, and published with every elegance, it was issued by Turcius Rufius Asterius, a man of clarissimus rank, former ordinary consul, and patrician.”

Cuspinianus also saw a codex similar to this one. In connection with the consulship of Asterius and Praesidius, he says that Sedulius’s poem was written “by Turcius Rufus Asterius, a man of clarissimus rank, former ordinary consul, and patrician.”

The same annotation was also present in the codex used by Aldus Manutius the Elder, since he remarks that the work was published not by Sedulius but by “Turcius Rufus Asterius, a man of clarissimus rank, formerly ordinary consul, and patrician.”

It is indeed true that Sirmondus, in his notes on Letter 24 of Ennodius’s Book, writes that the following appears in the Reims manuscript of Sedulius’s *Paschal Poem*:

> “Sedulius left this work scattered among loose sheets; collected and adorned with every elegance, it was published by Turcius Rufus, a man of clarissimus rank, ordinary consul, and patrician.”

But from the manuscripts cited above it is clear that, instead of *formerly ordinary consul*, the copyist mistakenly wrote *ordinary consul*; and since Asterius could not be called formerly consul before the following year, he neither collected nor published Sedulius’s poems before that year. Consequently, neither was the Roman synod held before that year in whose decree Sedulius is mentioned, as Usserius correctly shows in Book III, chapter 16, of *On the Origins of the British Church*; Pearson in *Vindiciae of the Letters of Saint Ignatius*, p. 46; and the aforementioned Cardinal Norisius, who provides further material concerning Sedulius and his work.

Since another Roman synod was held in March, the one under discussion belongs to the year 496. It was the Second Roman Synod under Gelasius—not the First, as it has hitherto been incorrectly called by the compilers of the councils and, following their example, by others.

[Note: [Col. 0183C] When Vitalis and Misenus, legates of the Apostolic See, had, at the prompting of Emperor Zeno, communicated with Acacius and had heard without objection the name of Peter Mongus, usurper of the Church of Alexandria, publicly recited in the diptychs, they were therefore excommunicated by the just judgment of Pope Felix in the synodal assembly of the Fathers. At last, after an interval of eleven years, and after Vitalis had died under excommunication, Misenus, aided by God's grace, came to his senses. Deeply detesting his offense, he asked to be received for penance and into the unity of the Church. Accordingly, when a council had been convened for this purpose, after the examination of the case he was, amid the great applause of all, placed upon the shoulders of the shepherds and in turn brought back to Christ's sheepfold, from which he had strayed for almost [Col. 0183D] eleven years. This synodal judgment was held [Col. 0184C] in the basilica of Saint Peter in the year of Christ 495, on the third day before the Ides of May, under the consulship of the most distinguished Flavius Viator; it was the fourth year of Gelasius and the fifth regnal year of Emperor Anastasius. The acts of this council were translated by Dionysius Exiguus. The acts obtained from the Vatican Library and still printed in volume I of the Papal Letters are somewhat corrupt and lack authority. Those published by the most illustrious Cardinal Baronius, under the year 495, from the Verdun manuscript through Fronto Ducaeus, professor of the Society of Jesus, are more complete and more accurately corrected. Collated with the Roman exemplar and almost wholly restored to their original clarity, we present them below after our notes, kind reader. — Severin Binius.]

[Note: [Col. 0183D] Baronius published these with variant readings from the Verdun manuscript, communicated to him by Fr. Fronto Ducaeus. — Harduin.]

[Note: Since the synod in which the matter of the apocryphal books was treated was held only in the year 496, as we said above on the authority of Pagius, it follows that this council, in which Misenus was absolved, must be called the First under Gelasius, and that other one the Second.]

## SECOND ROMAN COUNCIL

In which Misenus was absolved by Gelasius and fifty-five bishops, in the year of the Lord 495, on the third day before the Ides of May.

[Col. 0183]

[Col. 0183A] When the venerable Pope Gelasius was presiding in synod together with Boniface, Maximinus, Epiphanius, Basil, Vitalis, Clarus, Irenaeus, Decius, Asellus, Euplus, Valentinus, Martinianus, Bassus, Benignus, Primitivus, Palladius, Vindemius, Constantius, Martyrius, Candidus, Laurentius, Deodatus, Mercurius, Stephanus, Dulcitius, Fortunatus, Paschasius, Sanctulus, Innocentius, Chrysogonus, Colonicus, Molensis, Maximianus, Valentinus, Constantius, Gaudentius, Felix, Vitalianus, Peter, Serenus, Aucupius, Timothy, Stephanus, Laurentius, and Probus, bishops; and Castinus, Laurentius, Canusius, Eugenius, Januarius, Martianus, Gordianus, Peter, Urbicus, Paulinus, Valens, Peter, Asterius, Smaragdus, Boniface, Maxentius, Epiphanius, Justinus, Felix, Redemptus, Projectitius, Callistus, [Col. 0183B] John, Valentinus, Sebastianus, Martinus, Epiphanius, Andreas, Servus Dei, Apellio, Peter, Servandus, Agapitus, Abundantius, Marcellinus, Litorius, Laurentius, Agatho, Sebastianus, Valentinus, Anastasius, Genesius, Dionysius, Epiphanius, Acontius, Paulinus, Agapitus, Adeodatus, Benedictus, Dominicus, Redemptus, Severus, Julianus, Stephanus, Crescentianus, Septiminus, Cyprianus, and Epiphanius, presbyters, were also sitting; and the illustrious man Amandianus and the respectable man Diogenianus were present; with deacons likewise standing by, Gelasius, bishop of the Catholic Church of the city of Rome, said:

“Your affection remembers that at the previous gathering a petition submitted by Misenus was read in your presence. If it pleases your affection, let this same petition be reviewed again, so that it may be included in our acts. And since he also professes to have another petition at hand, let us be able to learn what it contains as well.”

And he added:

“Let Misenus’s petition be read again.”

The deacon Anastasius read:

“Submitted by your servant Misenus on the eighth day before the Ides of March, under the consulship of Viator, a man of clarissimus rank.

“As far as concerns the abruptness of my misery, I determine that my error, contracted in whatever manner, ought not to be spared; for I ought not to be free from punishment precisely because I deserved to be brought before a criminal proceeding, whatever its nature might be.”

[Note: The manuscript had: “to be brought by whatever means into a penal case.” It is read in the same way shortly afterward in this very council. — Fronto Ducaeus.]

“As far as concerns remedial assistance, however, there are two things that constrain me to come and implore it suppliantly: first, lest in despair I should be judged more deserving of being handed over to perpetual torments, after the example of the traitorous Judas; and second, because that ineffable clemency is so great that, through apostolic authority, it can absolve every offense.

“This, venerable pope, is the one plea that, miserable as I am, I pour forth in my case: spare one prostrate, extend your hand to one lying fallen. I do not rely on any excuses of ignorance; I offer no traps of evasion; nor do I seek to transfer the danger of my calamity onto anyone else, because I ought not to accuse others when I am asking to be mercifully absolved. Although I bring forward nothing for my defense, I nevertheless do not doubt that all these matters are to be handled by your judgment.

“I ask only that, obeying the heavenly Majesty, which declares through the prophet, ‘I do not desire the death of the one who dies, until he turns back and lives’ [Ezekiel 33], you should rather weigh with kindly consideration all that was done in my case; and, regarding me as consumed by old age, illness, and continual wasting away,

[Note: Through continuous illness and wasting. — Fronto Ducaeus.]

“do not refuse me the viaticum, lest I be snatched away without ecclesiastical communion. Do not, by looking at the example of another’s fall, refuse to consider my fear: that man could not obtain help even when you wished to confer it upon him. Show me graciously that I, who was entangled in this calamity more through inexperience,

[Note: He shows with indignation that this was so. — Fronto Ducaeus.]

“have nevertheless been worthy of reaching, while still alive, the grace of the Church’s reception.”

[Note: “This very fact,” he says, “shows that I was undeservedly overwhelmed by calamity: unlike Vitalis, I was not taken from this life before I could be restored to Catholic communion.” Hence Gelasius adds shortly afterward: “The danger of one who has been taken away urges us not to delay the means of healing for the one who survives, who is divinely shown to be destined for reception.” — Fronto Ducaeus.]

When this had been read, Bishop Gelasius said:

“The acts shall retain the petition.”

And he added:

“Let Misenus himself now enter, and let the petition he submitted be read in his presence.”

When Misenus had entered, he prostrated himself on the ground, submitted another petition, and asked that it be received. When it had been received, Bishop Gelasius said:

“Let both petitions that he has submitted be read, with him also present.”

Again the deacon Anastasius read:

“Submitted by your servant Misenus, on the eighth day before the Ides of March, under the consulship of Flavius Viator, a man of clarissimus rank.

“As far as concerns the abruptness of my misery [another reading: ‘appearance’], I determine that my error, contracted in whatever manner, ought not to be spared; for I ought not to be free from punishment, since I deserved to be brought by whatever means into a penal case.

“As far as concerns remedial assistance, there are two things that constrain me to come and implore it suppliantly: lest in despair I should be judged more deserving of being handed over to perpetual torments, after the example of the traitorous Judas; and the other matters contained above.”

Then another petition was read:

“Submitted by your servant Misenus on the third day before the Ides of March [another reading: the fourth day], under the consulship of Flavius Viator, a man of clarissimus rank.

“When I first submitted my petition, I implored nothing else in supplication than that the mercy of the Apostolic See should not be denied me forever. Since, through the immense kindness of God by which that See is governed, I now perceive its hope shining upon me, I increasingly and more fully declare, under the gaze of the divine presence, that my consent has been and is free and cleansed from the contagions of the impious, into which I had fallen unhappily rather than deliberately, having been deceived.

“With all my heart and mouth I profess that I reject every heresy and everything hostile to the Catholic and apostolic faith and to sincere communion; and especially that I reject, condemn, and perpetually anathematize the Eutychian heresy, with its author Eutyches, and its follower Dioscorus, together with their successors and communicants, Timothy the Cat, Peter of Alexandria, Acacius of Constantinople, Peter of Antioch, and all their accomplices and communicants. I execrate all these and those like them with horror, and I profess that I will never in any way have fellowship with such men, but will remain wholly separate from all of them.

“Although I never accepted their depravity by deliberate choice, nevertheless, because under the pressure of calamity I seem to have fallen into it through insufficient caution, I condemn, detest, and abhor it before God, before blessed Peter the Apostle and his vicar, and before the whole Church, by my profession—as I have said [another reading: confession]—and by my voice. I affirm that I will always remain in the Catholic and apostolic faith and communion alone.

“I have subscribed this petition with my own hand on the third day before the Ides of March, under the consulship of Viator, a man of clarissimus rank. I have judged that this should be offered by my own hands to Your Beatitude in the gathering of the venerable [another reading adds: ‘bishops’].”

And in another hand:

“I, Misenus, have subscribed this petition of mine, submitted by me, on the day and under the consulship written above.”

Bishop Gelasius said:

“Let what has been read be transcribed.”

And he added:

“We desire to learn what your fraternity thinks should be determined, with your counsel also taking part.”

All the bishops and presbyters rose, asking and saying:

“Hear us, O Christ!”—said twenty times.

“What God has given you the power to do, grant!”—said twelve times.

“Do what the Lord Peter does!”—said ten times.

“We ask you to forgive!”—said nine times.

When they had sat down again, Bishop Gelasius said:

“The Apostolic See, which, by the delegation of the Lord Christ, retains primacy over the whole Church, in accordance with the general administration and care that it always exercises with vigilance, whether on behalf of the Catholic faith or on behalf of the paternal canons and the rules of the ancients,

[Note: “It always exercises with vigilance.” — Fronto Ducaeus.]

“had formerly sent Misenus and Vitalis to the East, supported by the authority of its legation, against the followers of the Eutychian pest or against those who had polluted themselves by communion with such men, under my predecessor, the bishop of holy memory. When it became clear from the synodal acts and examination of the matter that, having declined the apostolic commands, they had in some way fallen back into fellowship with those against whom they had been sent, the See rightly and justly removed them both from communion and from honor.

“Nevertheless, remembering the mercy of heavenly kindness, it reserved a place for mercy according to its own moderation. Although it imposed a condition upon the punishment, it did not allow the hope of pardon to be cut off. It so tempered its sentence that it preferred the pardon of these men to arise together with the salvation of those by whose participation they had been deceived; and that they should offer to those whom they had strengthened in depravity by their agreement both the salutary fear of correction and the opportunity to imitate amendment.

“Finally, the words of the punishment itself were so balanced that they would recognize themselves as struck together with those men,

[Note: “They should recognize themselves as struck together with those men and should not despair of being saved on account of their condition.” — Fronto Ducaeus.]

“and from the condition of those men would not despair of being saved. In this way the path of return has not been entirely closed to these men; and for the others, if they preferred it, correction was offered through these men, together with an opportunity by which they might compensate for their former lapses with a better effort, if they would turn the favor that they had readily shown to traitors toward the reformation of Catholic priests.

“For it was declared that these men would remain suspended until, by God’s agency and through the efforts of Catholic rulers or of the Christian people,

[Note: “Until the Church of Alexandria had begun to rejoice in receiving a Catholic priest, so that this should be believed.” — Fronto Ducaeus.]

“the Church of Alexandria had received a Catholic priest. It was to be believed, of course, that the Greeks could in no way refuse what they saw had been condemned by the Apostolic See, and that they could easily be moved by the punishment of these men to learn what they should avoid and what they should consequently seek,

[Note: “And should be thought to wish, by coming to their senses.” — Fronto Ducaeus.]

“and should be thought to wish, by coming to their senses, to agree with the upright rather than to err continually with the impious.

“For a long time it was awaited that, moved by these considerations, they would lay aside their detestable contagions and agree with the Apostolic See, as had been hoped concerning their will;

[Note: “Striving to support the Catholics.” — Fronto Ducaeus.]

“and that, striving to support the Catholic priests, they would rather lend their efforts to recall them, so that they themselves might return to orthodox

[Note: “They would return to the truth.” — Fronto Ducaeus.]

“unity, and might provide the effect of the prescribed reception for those who had become participants in their error. Nor was any opportunity neglected by which, suitably admonished and sufficiently instructed, they might learn together what dangers were to be avoided and might recognize that the door of apostolic communion stood open to them if they sought it with sincere hearts.

“But since matters have reached the point where, even when they had no contrary answer to report, they nevertheless delayed to give their assent to medicinal exhortations, we ought indeed to feel toward their difficulties a certain paternal affection of pious sorrow, beseeching the omnipotence of our God, who alone can turn even wandering wills into the way of truth, graciously to infuse into them, through the wondrous operation of his mercy, the spirit of repentance and the efficacy of correction.

“Until these things come to pass through divine appeasement, as we trust in his power, let us meanwhile in no way allow this man, who supplicates and earnestly seeks what is desired, to perish. Let those whom the Orientals were not terrified by his deposition into ceasing to persist in error at least be stirred by his healing to return to salvation, especially since the tenor of the statements themselves accompanies the clemency of the Apostolic See’s disposition, and the decree that was issued must not be judged to contradict itself.

“For it was determined—as has already been stated above—that those concerning whom we are speaking must be suspended until, with God’s agency and with the aforementioned persons making the effort, the Church of Alexandria should receive a Catholic priest. This was not proposed abruptly and without exception; rather, it was formulated on the condition that the sentence should not appear to have been imposed indifferently, whether those men made the effort or did not make the effort. Therefore, since the condition was balanced according to a certain stipulation, when that stipulation no longer exists, it releases the obligation imposed by that condition.

“For what was pronounced must be done with the effort of the aforementioned persons plainly cannot be done when that effort does not follow. But since it is expressly said that it must be done with their effort, it is sufficiently clear that it cannot be accomplished without it. Therefore, although those whose effort is shown to be lacking are to be pitied for their obstinacy, nevertheless, just as the thing presumed capable of being accomplished with their effort cannot be accomplished without it, so, when the causes through which this condition would reach its fulfillment have ceased, the condition cannot remain indissolubly binding.

“Consequently, when the circumstances by which the sentence could maintain the measure assigned to it until its conclusion are absent, the sentence will grant counsel to these men and liberty to those who had been held under constraint. The Apostolic See, indeed—as must often be repeated—had judged that the Orientals could in no way fail to reject what the Apostolic See had rejected, and that they could prefer no person to their own salvation and apostolic communion. It had judged better concerning their minds.

“But what must again not be left unsaid is that the lamentable disaster should not accuse the Apostolic See, which had thought well of the Orientals without foreseeing this, as though it were mistaken; rather, it should be attributed to their own obstinacy, because they did not follow the path of their own restoration that had been offered to them. Nevertheless, they ought not on account of their obstinacy to impede the opportunity of others who desire healing.

“For statements about the consent of the Greeks were then made confidently because they seemed both able to prefer the fellowship of blessed Peter to any persons and, having formerly been Catholics, were thought likely to agree easily with the truth. For that reason it was judged that the affection of any individual could not be preferred to the desires of apostolic communion. Since, however, they have not yet received the wills through which this process was to run, what was presumed capable of being accomplished through them is seen to have been released; for when those through whom something was to be accomplished are absent, no effect can result.

[Another reading: “If those through whom they might accomplish it are absent.”]

“Indeed, when those very people through whom it was judged that the matter should be accomplished resist its accomplishment, if—God forbid—they persist in this obstinacy, the condition of that matter is dissolved, although it had confidently been judged capable of fulfillment through their efforts.

“But if, as we rather hope, they have been converted to better things, let not the man who meanwhile seeks mercy be intercepted by age or illness, by which he is frequently hindered, while counsel is being sought concerning them, lest, once he has died, no remedy can be substituted for him. For it was said that the matter could stand whether those men made the effort or perhaps even opposed it, although it had been promulgated with the greater expectation of their effort.

“Thus, just as peace fixed

[Another reading: “previously fixed.”]

“with those men does not last when they make no effort, so in this respect blessed Paul the Apostle must not be thought to have deceived anyone—God forbid—or to have contradicted himself. He had promised that he would go to Spain, but, occupied by greater matters according to the divine disposition, he could not fulfill what he had promised. As far as his own will was concerned, he declared what he truly wished to accomplish; but as far as the secrets of the divine counsel were concerned, which, as a human being, he could not recognize in all respects, even though filled with the Spirit, he was forestalled by the heavenly disposition.

“Nor, because blessed Peter the Apostle, out of reverence for the divine Lord, replied to the Lord himself, ‘You shall never wash my feet’ [John 13], should he be thought to have deceived anyone—God forbid—or to have failed to stand by his own judgment, because he soon yielded to that same divine will. What he had said he would not do,

[Note: “What he had said he would not do.” — Fronto Ducaeus.]

“he willingly undertook to do, compelled by considerations of human salvation.

“Therefore, since that path by which their reconciliation had been established has not been opened,

[Note: Since that path has not been opened; perhaps read ‘has not favored.’ — Fronto Ducaeus.]

“let us nevertheless pursue another path by which aid may be given to those whom it has been determined should be helped—especially since, in the case of Misenus, whatever excess or whatever punishment of betrayal may suffice has been dealt with to such an extent

[Note: “So that only the supreme consideration of the human condition…” — Fronto Ducaeus.]

“that the punishment may be relaxed in view of the supreme consideration of the human condition, and the penalty should be remitted when it has no further possibility of increasing.

“For since almighty and merciful God has not wished, through ecclesiastical compassion, to deny a remedy to any soul that seeks it, there is no doubt that this very thing proceeds from God’s agency and divine compunction: that his reception should be considered at the time when necessity compels that it not be postponed.

“Moreover, our Savior delegated to blessed Peter the Apostle above all others:

> ‘Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven’ [Matthew 16].

“Just as nothing is established as excepted in these words, so through the office of apostolic administration everything can generally be bound and, consequently, everything can be absolved.

“This is especially so because an example of apostolic mercy ought thereby to be offered to all: so that, when the condemned repent, all who withdraw from error and return to the sincere unity

[Another reading: “purity.”]

“of apostolic communion may not doubt that they are to be stripped of the bonds of that condemnation which all traitors had justly incurred.

“For we who strive to restore those who are far away to complete faith must not refuse those who return as suppliants in the present, where we must carefully guard against falling—God forbid—by denying relief to a conscience,

[Note: “To the final material of sin.” — Fronto Ducaeus.]

“into the final extremity of sin

[Another reading: “for the one asking.”]

“and against allowing the severity of truth’s censure, persisting without end even toward suppliants, to become guilt.

“Therefore, insofar as human possibility permits, let us, with the Lord’s warning before us, provide remedies to one who desires them,

[Note: This entire passage, through the words “the affairs of the dead,” is cited by Pope Vigilius in his *Constitutum* of the year 553. — Harduinus.]

“leaving to divine judgment everything that lies beyond the measure of our ability. They will not be able to charge us with why we remit the offense of betrayal to the living, something that, by God’s gift, is possible for the Church; while they ask us also to grant pardon to the dead, something clearly impossible for us. For since it has been said, ‘Whatever you bind on earth,’ he reserved those who are no longer upon the earth for judgment not human but his own. The Church does not dare claim for itself what it sees was not granted even to the blessed Apostles, because the case of the living is different from that of the dead.

“Vitalis has undergone the lot of divine judgment; even though we earnestly wished to help him, assistance could not be given to him. Let the experience of one suddenly taken away at least benefit this man while the opportunity afforded by a living person permits remedies to be obtained.

“And since we know that it is written, ‘One will be taken and one will be left’ [Luke 17], the danger of the one who has been taken away urges us not to delay the means of healing for the survivor, who is thereby shown to be divinely destined for reception, since he survives the man

[Note: “Who did not deserve to reach this point.” — Fronto Ducaeus.]

“who did not deserve to reach this point.

“A certain examination of heavenly judgment shines forth concerning both of them, and it is shown more clearly in these two cases where there was a cause without pardon and where there was a case that ought not to be without pardon.

[Note: “Perhaps read: ‘where pardon ought not to be lacking’; and therefore that he himself also…” — Fronto Ducaeus.]

“Consequently, what Acacius himself might also have obtained, had he competently sought it while he survived—for concerning him it was stated that his case would be insoluble, without the words ‘even if he should perhaps correct himself’—it is much more the duty of apostolic compassion not to deny to this man, who has been infected by Acacius’s communion and is tearfully imploring it, the same mercy.”

Thus, after Misenus had formally professed that he detested all heresies, especially the Eutychian heresy with Eutyches, Dioscorus, [Col. 0190C] Timothy the Cat, Peter of Alexandria, Acacius of Constantinople, Peter of Antioch, and all their successors, followers, and communicants, and that he perpetually struck them with anathema, he received the grace of apostolic communion and the dignity of priesthood, which he had received through Catholic tradition.

All the bishops and presbyters rose in the synod and acclaimed:

“Hear us, O Christ! Life to Gelasius!”—said fifteen times.

“Lord Peter, preserve him!”—said twelve times.

“Whose see and years…”—said seven times.

[Note: “We see you as Christ’s vicar!”—said eleven times. “We see you as the Apostle Peter!”—said six times. “Whose see…” — Fronto Ducaeus.]

“We see you as Christ’s vicar”—said six times.

“Whose see and years…”—said seven times thirty.

Sixtus, notary of the holy Roman Church, by order of my lord, the most blessed Pope Gelasius, issued this from the archives on the third day before the Ides of May, under the consulship of Flavius Viator, a man of clarissimus rank

[Col. 0183D]

(Christ’s year 495).

## In the Year of the Lord 494. Saint Avitus, Bishop of Vienne.

*(From the Library of Galland.)*

[Col. 0191]

## Prologue

[Col. 0191A] As the fifth century was drawing to a close and the sixth was beginning, Alcimus Ecdicius Avitus flourished no less in piety than in learning. He was the son of Hesychius—or Isicius—first a most distinguished senator and then bishop of Vienne, and he succeeded to that see around the year of Christ 490, toward the end of the reign of Zeno, as the Bollandists infer from his Acts

[Note: Bollandists, *Acts of the Saints*, vol. I, February, p. 661, no. 1.]

“to whom the writers of the literary history of Gaul add their testimony”

[Note: *Literary History of France*, vol. III, p. 116.]

“In the episcopate he produced remarkable examples of virtue, of which, in accordance with the purpose of our work, it will be sufficient to relate one or two here.

“Thus the holy bishop labored intensely to persuade Gundobad, king of the Burgundians, to renounce the Arian heresy, as Gregory of Tours relates,

[Note: Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, Book II, chapter 34.]

“also reporting certain excerpts from the public debate held at Lyons between the Catholic bishops and the Arians, apparently in the year 501 according to Pagius,

[Note: Pagius, under the year 501, §§ 3, 4.]

“or, as others judge, in the year 499.

[Note: *Debate of the Bishops*, below.]

“This debate first came to light only in the preceding century.”

[Note: *Literary History of France*, at the place cited, p. 117.]

“But it is preferable to hear Agobard on this matter.”

[Note: Agobard, *Book Against the Law of Gundobad*, chapter 13, works, vol. I, p. 120, Baluz’s edition.]

> “Avitus,” he says, “Catholic in faith, most eloquent in speech, keenest in intellect, a most gracious interpreter of Sacred Scripture, highly learned also in secular literature, and very skilled in verse, frequently arguing about the faith with Gundobad, conducting dialogues with him when present, and responding to him by letters when absent, left behind many distinguished works of his genius and virtue. When Gundobad was lost in his own perfidy, Avitus converted his successor, his son King Sigismund, to the Catholic faith. At his conversion he delivered before the people a homily filled with the sweetness of thought and the most pleasing arrangement of words.”

“From this,” to use the words of Hadrianus Valesius,

[Note: Hadrianus Valesius, *History of the Franks*, Book VII, under the year 516, vol. I, pp. 330–331.]

> “it was very easily obtained from the Burgundians that they should imitate the example of their king and, renouncing their error, follow the Catholic religion in which their ancestors had lived.”

For in the year 517, as the same Valesius immediately observes, which was the second year of Sigismund’s reign, a council was held at Epaon, where the bishops of Burgundy assembled. Avitus subscribed its decrees first, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of October, under the consulship of Agapetus, a man of clarissimus rank.

Concerning this council Pagius has more to say.

[Note: Pagius, under the year 509, §§ 6, 7.]

### III

In addition to the Arian heresy, which the blessed prelate attacked with the utmost vigor, he also refuted the heresies of the Eutychians, Nestorians, Photinians, and Bonosians.[^c0021-1] He also wrote against Faustus of Riez,[^c0021-2] who, as Baronius says, pretended to condemn Pelagius while in fact reinforcing Pelagian perfidy itself.[^c0021-3] This is attested especially by Gregory of Tours,[^c0021-4] Agobard of Lyon,[^c0021-5] and Ado of Vienne,[^c0021-6] all bishops. Moreover, in a letter addressed to Faustus and Symmachus, senators of Rome, he vigorously supported Pope Symmachus against the schismatics.[^c0021-7]

We deliberately pass over his other outstanding deeds, for it would be lengthy to go through them individually. Therefore, with the fullest justification, distinguished men renowned for learning and virtue celebrated with great praise our most holy and learned bishop of the province of Vienne. Among them was Ennodius, bishop of Ticinum:

> “Avitus, bishop of Vienne, was the foremost among the Gauls; in him learning enclosed itself, as though in the guest-chamber of a radiant house.”[^c0021-8]

Gregory of Tours writes:

> “At that time the blessed Avitus was a man of great eloquence. … Admirable letters of his still exist among us; just as they then overthrew heresy, so now they build up the Church of God.”[^c0021-9]

Isidore of Seville calls him “most learned in knowledge of secular literature.”[^c0021-10] Agobard likewise writes of him:

> “Almost the whole Church of Christ knows how outstanding a teacher and eloquent speaker Alcimus Avitus, bishop of the Church of Vienne, proved to be.”[^c0021-11]

Finally, Ado says that he was “pre-eminent in eloquence and holiness, writing in a most lucid and sufficiently polished style and with the clearest faith.”[^c0021-12]

[^c0021-1]: Avitus, Letters 2 and 3.  
[^c0021-2]: Avitus, Letter 4.  
[^c0021-3]: Baronius, under the year 516, §31.  
[^c0021-4]: Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, Book II, chapter 34.  
[^c0021-5]: Agobard of Lyon, *Against Felix*, chapter 41, in the cited edition of the works, volume I, page 55.  
[^c0021-6]: Ado of Vienne, *Chronicle*, under the year 492 and before the year 519.  
[^c0021-7]: Avitus, Letter 31.  
[^c0021-8]: Ennodius, *Life of Blessed Epiphanius*, in the works of Sirmond, volume I, page 1686.  
[^c0021-9]: Gregory of Tours, in the cited passage.  
[^c0021-10]: Isidore of Seville, *On Illustrious Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 23.  
[^c0021-11]: Agobard, *On Jewish Superstitions*, in the cited edition of the works, volume I, page 70.  
[^c0021-12]: Ado, *Chronicle*, under the year 492 and before the year 519.

### III

There is no single opinion among learned men as to the year in which the holy prelate departed this life. Yet, so far as possible, the difficulty of this question must be resolved by examining the matter more closely.

Ado therefore reports that Avitus was still alive after the death of Sigismund, king of the Burgundians; the same bishop of Vienne, he says, “grieved most bitterly when Sigismund was captured and killed by the Franks.”[^c0021-13] An anonymous author of the life of that same Saint Avitus, preserved by the Bollandists, copied Ado’s account.[^c0021-14] Since he was therefore writing after Ado’s time—at least in the tenth century, or perhaps later—he is consequently found to possess little authority.

But Ado himself also seems not to deserve credence when he relates that Avitus survived King Sigismund. For the Avitus who lamented Sigismund’s removal from the world was not Avitus, bishop of Vienne, but Avitus, abbot of the monastery of Micy, “a great priest at that time,” as Gregory of Tours writes.[^c0021-15] Cointius examines and explains Gregory’s words at greater length.[^c0021-16]

But in what year, finally, did Sigismund die? If we follow Marius of Avenches in his *Chronicle*, whom Aimoin also follows, it occurred during the consulship of Maximus, in the first indiction—that is, in the year of Christ 523. Gregory of Tours and other Frankish historians, however, report that Sigismund was killed in the following year, 524, during the consulship of Justin II and Opilio, in the second indiction. Hadrian Valesius pursues this matter in fuller detail.[^c0021-17]

On these premises, most recent writers, deceived by Ado, judged that Avitus closed his final day after Sigismund’s death. Some place it in the year 523;[^c0021-18] others after that year;[^c0021-19] and still others in the year 525.[^c0021-20]

But since it is certain that the Avitus who survived the extinction of Sigismund was a different man from the bishop of Vienne, our Avitus must already have been summoned to heaven when that Burgundian king perished, as the learned scholar observes.[^c0021-21] His death must therefore have occurred during the period extending between the councils of Epaon and the Second Council of Lyon.

For, as we saw above, Avitus was the first to subscribe to the Council of Epaon, convened in the year 517. Yet he is acknowledged not to have attended the Second Council of Lyon, held shortly afterward under King Sigismund. His name does not occur among the subscriptions of that council, as may be seen in the collection of councils.[^c0021-22] There, however, the council is incorrectly entitled the First Council of Lyon, as we understand from Avitus himself, who writes:

> “When the holy bishop Chartenius was returning from the city of Lyon, where, after we had departed from the council, he had remained to attend to certain private affairs,” and so forth.[^c0021-23]

I therefore judge that the blessed prelate ascended to heaven at the beginning of the year 518—that is, on the fifth day before the Nones of February, the day on which his name is recorded in the Church’s calendar. I accept this view all the more readily because the anonymous author of the life of Saint Avitus, first published by Labbe[^c0021-24] and afterward by the Bollandists,[^c0021-25] left it written that Avitus died while Anastasius was still emperor; Anastasius is said to have died on the seventh day before the Ides of July in that same year, 518.

### IV

Now, finally, to speak of Avitus’s literary remains, Sirmond is chiefly to be heard. He published at Paris, in the year 1643, everything he had been able to discover, whether newly edited or restored and revised. Thus the distinguished scholar writes:

> “It was to be feared that the letters of Avitus, which we had owed you, reader, for so many years, might now have lost their value with you through the delay, unless I could see that this delay had produced some benefit for us. For while we were searching for a more accurately corrected copy of them, if one might anywhere come to light, we came upon a volume of the deacon Florus at the Carthusian monastery. Through its assistance we learned not merely the titles and names of seventeen of Avitus’s little works, most of them previously unknown, but also obtained many notable fragments that would lend distinction to the edition.

> “The usefulness and elegance of the letters enabled us to endure more cheerfully the tedium that had to be swallowed in correcting a corrupt manuscript; and we would even have embraced the division into five books which it promised, if it had supplied it complete. But the confusion was so great that for the present it seemed preferable, leaving aside the distinction of books, to present all the letters to you continuously in a single text. I do not doubt that you will approve this decision. It will then remain for you to bear more indulgently the faults of the corrupt readings that still survive.

> “In the fragments, at any rate, none of the labor was ours. We followed Florus’s sound and carefully corrected copy. As for the poems, those who compare this edition with the Gagneian edition will understand what has been done. Its author, otherwise a learned and eloquent man, besides the other changes he made everywhere on his own authority, inserted nearly five hundred of his own verses in place of Avitus’s. Our concern, however, was to measure everything exactly against the fidelity of the ancient copies, so that, rejecting the spurious and restoring the genuine, we might present to you an Avitus pure and authentic, while overlooking certain blemishes characteristic of that age.

> “If, in this matter, your own judgment, reader, should also give its support, we shall have reason to rejoice that we have not labored in vain, even in this respect, for a bishop of the Church who was most holy and not easily placed second to anyone among Christian poets.”

Thus far Sirmond.

### V

Nor should we omit a description of the materials with which the most learned Baunius enlarged Sirmond’s edition. They are as follows:[^c0021-26]

> “To the works of Saint Avitus, bishop of Vienne, edited by Sirmond, certain writings by the same author have now been added. First, four letters which the distinguished Stephanus Baluzius published from an old book belonging to Petrus Marnaesius, senator of Grenoble.[^c0021-27] Next, several fragments of a work *On the Divinity of the Holy Spirit*, which the same Baluzius published from an ancient manuscript of the monastery of Saint Gall.[^c0021-28]

> “In addition, there is the *Conference with King Gundobad against the Arians*, held at Lyon when nearly all the bishops of the Church of Lyon had assembled there, as Hieronymus Vignierius had noted; Dacher published this work of Avitus from Vignierius’s papers.[^c0021-29] Dacher warns, however, that there is no compelling reason to assign it—as the learned man seems to have done—to that Council of Lyon at which Avitus testifies that he was present together with a certain Bishop Chartenius.[^c0021-30]

> “First, Agobard writes that Avitus often disputed about the faith with Gundobad, sometimes in person through dialogues and sometimes, when absent, through letters; this is sufficiently clear from Avitus’s surviving letters themselves.[^c0021-31] Furthermore, those letters also show that it was customary, as Sirmond notes,[^c0021-32] for bishops of neighboring sees to invite fellow bishops to the solemn celebrations of their cities. In particular, the solemnity of Saint Justus at Lyon was extremely celebrated; Sidonius also mentions it.[^c0021-33]”

Such is Baunius’s account.

### VI

Having set these matters forth, we append the sermon of Blessed Avitus delivered on the Tuesday of the Rogation Days. The distinguished Martenius published it from a manuscript of the Grande Chartreuse,[^c0021-34] prefacing it with the following notice:

> “We found the sermon of Saint Avitus, archbishop of Vienne, pronounced on the Tuesday of the Rogation Days, in an old manuscript of the Grande Chartreuse. The Reverend Father Dom Innocent Bouchart, a monk of that house and an especially good friend to us, transcribed it for us with his customary kindness.

> “Two points in particular may be observed in it. First, the Rogations—or solemn supplications—which are celebrated in the Church before the Ascension were instituted in his time, or, as he himself says, in our age; and they were instituted by Saint Mamertus, who governed the Church of Vienne in the year 472. Avitus teaches this elsewhere; he succeeded Hesychius in the same see. Sidonius Apollinaris, bishop of Clermont, also says so.[^c0021-35] To these may be added Gregory of Tours, who describes both the reason for this institution and its manner in the following words:[^c0021-36]

> “ ‘At this time there was a very great earthquake in the city of Vienne. Many churches and many houses were shaken and overturned. Many wild animals—wolves and savage bears—roamed about and entered through the city gate, devouring very many people; they did this throughout the entire year. When the solemnity of holy Easter arrived, Saint Mamertus, who was bishop in that city, was celebrating the solemn rites of the vigil, and the royal palace that stood in that city was also set on fire by a divine blaze. As these things were taking place, and the Ascension of the Lord was approaching, the holy man of God imposed a three-day fast upon the people, with lamentation and contrition,’ and so forth.

> “The second point is that in the Church of Vienne, on the Tuesday of the Rogations, the prophecy of Amos was read during the divine offices; Avitus undertakes to explain this passage in the present sermon.

> “In the ancient Gallican lectionary, however, which our Mabillon brought into public circulation from a manuscript of Luxeuil, the prophecy of Amos was not read on the Tuesday. At the third hour the First Epistle of Saint Peter was read, at the sixth hour the First Epistle of John, and at the ninth hour the Book of Judith. This should not seem surprising, since the manner of celebrating the divine office was not the same in all the Gallican churches. Nor was the same order everywhere observed in reading passages of Sacred Scripture, since everything was done at the bishops’ discretion.

> “Moreover, it will not be superfluous here to note what Herbert, archbishop of Tours, records:[^c0021-37] namely, that in Normandy ‘on the days of the Rogations, when clergy and people extended the procession by proceeding a considerable distance, it was customary, when the clergy paused from time to time, for the women to take their turn, singing melodiously.’”

Thus far Martenius.

[^c0021-34]: Martenius, *Thesaurus of Anecdotes*, volume V, pages 49 and following.  
[^c0021-35]: Sidonius, Book I, Letter 7, and Book VII, Letter 14.  
[^c0021-36]: Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, Book II, chapter 34.  
[^c0021-37]: Herbert, Book I of the *Miracles*, chapter 21.

### VII

We therefore present this Sirmondian edition of the works of Saint Avitus, enlarged with these little works and, in addition, illuminated by our efforts with several observations separated from Sirmond’s notes in certain more obscure places. At the end of Poem 6 we have also added three verses which Labbe brought to light after transcribing them from manuscript 26 of the Naudé Library,[^c0021-38] because they were lacking in all the published copies.[^c0021-39]

[^c0021-38]: Avitus, *Poems*, Book VI, below (column 381, top, note a).  
[^c0021-39]: Labbe, *New Library of Manuscripts*, page 226, Paris edition, 1653.

## Testimonies of the Ancients Concerning Saint Avitus

### I. Ennodius, Bishop of Ticinum

From the *Life of Blessed Epiphanius, Bishop*:

> “The outstanding Avitus, bishop of Vienne, foremost among the Gauls, was also endowed with learning, which had enclosed itself in him as in the guest-chamber of a radiant house.”

### II. Gregory of Tours

From Book II, chapter 34 of the *History of the Franks*:

> “At that time the blessed Avitus, bishop of Vienne, was a man of great eloquence. When a heresy arose in the city of Constantinople, teaching that our Lord Jesus Christ possessed no divinity, King Gundobad asked Avitus to write against it, and he did so. Admirable letters of his still exist among us; just as they then overthrew heresy, so now they build up the Church of God. He also wrote one book of homilies, and six books composed in verse on the beginning of the world and on various other acts of creation. He wrote nine books of letters, among which the letters mentioned above are included.”

### III. Fortunatus, Bishop of Poitiers

From Book I of *The Life of Saint Martin*:

> “What the ancient genealogist explained in sacred sequence, Alcimus the distinguished bishop arranged in excellent verse.”

### IV. Isidore of Seville

From chapter 23 of *On Illustrious Ecclesiastical Writers*:

> “Avitus, a bishop most learned in knowledge of secular literature, published five little books composed in heroic meter. The first is on the Origin of the World, the second on Original Sin, the third on the Judgment of God, the fourth on the Flood of the World, and the fifth on the Crossing of the Red Sea. He also wrote one book to his sister Fuscina on the Praise of Virginity, composed in most beautiful verse and fitted together with an elegant epigram.”

### V. Agobard, Bishop of Lyon

From *Against the Law of Gundobad*:

> “During the reign of Gundobad, king of the Burgundians, there was in the city of Vienne a bishop named Avitus, Catholic in faith, most eloquent in speech, keen in intellect, a most pleasing expositor of the Sacred Scriptures, and highly accomplished in verse, as his works also testify. He frequently disputed about the faith with Gundobad himself, sometimes conducting dialogues with him in person and sometimes responding to him in letters when absent. He left many distinguished works of his intellect and virtue. When Gundobad himself was lost in his perfidy, Avitus converted his successor, King Sigismund, to the Catholic faith. At Sigismund’s conversion he recited before the people a homily filled with the greatest sweetness of thought and the most pleasing arrangement of words.”

From the same author, *Against the Dogma of Felix*:

> “The blessed Avitus was the most powerful conqueror of the Photinian heretics.”

Also, from *On Jewish Superstitions*:

> “Almost the whole Church of Christ knows how outstanding a teacher, orthodox scholar, and eloquent speaker Alcimus Avitus, bishop of the Church of Vienne, proved to be.”

### VI. Florus, Deacon of the Church of Lyon

> “Sentences from the Epistle of the blessed Apostle Paul to the Romans, explained by the holy and illustrious doctor of the Church, Avitus, bishop of Vienne, and arranged in order from his little works.”

### VII. Ado, Bishop of Vienne

From the sixth age of his *Chronicle*:

> “Avitus, bishop of Vienne, distinguished in eloquence and holiness, and his brother Apollinaris, bishop of Valence, renowned for miracles—two lights and illustrious sons of Isicius, first a senator and afterward bishop of Vienne.
>
> “This blessed Avitus fought with great labor against the Arian heresy, which at that time had occupied not only Africa but also much of Gaul and Italy. His splendid works bear witness to this. For he wrote a dialogue attacking that heresy, addressed to Gundobad, king of the Burgundians and son of Gundoveus, with a most faithful, learned, and immortal intellect. He also wrote two other little books against Nestorius and Eutyches, the authors of error, in a brilliant and sufficiently polished style.
>
> “There were also many other outstanding works of his, highly approved in the Church of Christ. He instructed King Sigismund in the faith and devotion; afterward, through Avitus’s influence, Sigismund built the monastery of the holy martyrs of Agaunum, Maurice and his companions. When Sigismund was later captured and killed by the Franks, Avitus grieved bitterly. Whoever wishes to know fully how great he was in the Church of Christ should, after considering his innumerable labors in divine matters, read his epitaph.”

## Epitaph of Blessed Avitus, Bishop of Vienne

> Whoever you are, as you behold the mournful honor of the tomb,  
> as you see all Avitus enclosed beneath the turf, you will lament him,  
> yet cast anxious cares from your sorrowing heart.  
> For the man whom full faith, whom the glory of a lofty mind,  
> whom piety, generous hand, and enduring fame preserve—  
> he has nothing in common with death. Rather, look upon  
> the deeds of the holy man: how, flowering first with such great natural gifts,  
> he despised the offices handed down through ancient lineage,  
> while granting mature wisdom to his tender years,  
> and by the virtue of his vow banishing the permitted things of the world.  
> Without delay he assumed the insignia worthy of a bishop,  
> so that he might increase the happy beginnings of his customary labor.  
> Yet he was not puffed up by the height of the highest honor;  
> he did not esteem himself above others, but rather  
> though great, he subjected himself; though highest, he preserved humility.  
> Sparing of his own resources, he fed others; fasting himself,  
> he terrified through love and mingled indulgence with severity.  
> He helped those who delayed through persuasion, consoled the sorrowful,  
> dissolved quarrels, and joined those who fought together in an alliance.  
> He subdued doctrines that defiled the truthful law with discordant teachings,  
> by exhortation, intellect, admonitions, and merits.  
> Alone upon the citadel, in every kind of speech,  
> no orator was his equal, no poet his equal:  
> the books scattered through countless volumes proclaim this.  
> He lived, he lives, and through all ages he will live.

A manuscript cited by Duchesne reads the following instead of these two verses:

> “He reaches the summit of sweetness; grandeur does not obstruct severity.”

[^c0021-40]: Duchesne, volume I, page 514, reads *prompta* (“ready”) for *larga* (“generous”) in “generous hand.”  
[^c0021-41]: The same source reads *diremit* (“settled”) for *dissolvit* (“dissolved”) in “dissolved quarrels.”  
[^c0021-42]: The same source reads *fingunt* (“fabricate”) for *inficiunt* (“defile”) in “doctrines that defiled the truthful law.”

## Alcimus Ecdicius Avitus: Letters

### Letter One

Avitus, Bishop of Vienne, to the Lord King Gundobad.[^c0021-43]

[^c0021-43]: Gundobad was king of the Burgundians in Gaul, well known from the history of the Franks. Clovis defeated him in war and imposed tribute upon him, according to Marius’s *Chronicle*, during the consulships of Patricius and Hypatius—that is, in the year of Christ 500. Gundobad’s sons, Sigismund and Godomar, succeeded their father as kings, but the sons of Clovis deprived them of life and kingdom. Avitus’s letters, however, do not extend to the period of Godomar.

The truth, sought and learned through various concerns, has so thoroughly instructed your mind—by Christ’s favor—that nothing at all remains unknown to you concerning the definition of Catholic doctrine. Therefore, when your Highness’s piety deigns to inquire about these matters, you are no longer descending from the summit of complete instruction as one who does not know, but engaging in discussion as one who does know. Indeed, the Gospel saying that you touched upon in your letter contains no ambiguity concerning the faith; rather, it seeks an examination, at the highest level of exposition, of the Jewish objections.

Thus the Gospel reading which you mentioned in the letter says:

> “But you say, if a man says to his father or mother, ‘Corban’—that is, in the Hebrew language, a gift specifically offered as a devout oblation—‘whatever benefit you might have received from me,’ that is, [said] to his father or mother, ‘you no longer permit him to do anything for his father or mother’” (Mark 7:11).

I think you begin your discussion with this passage because you expressly mentioned it in your letter, asking what the words “you no longer permit” mean and from where they were derived. They mean nothing other than “you do not dismiss” or “you do not release him.”

From this proper meaning of the expression, the word *missa* is said to be used in churches, palaces, and courts when the people are dismissed from an assembly. For you will find this kind of noun even in secular authors, unless reading, neglected amid your occupations, has escaped your memory.[^c0021-44]

Thus, “you do not dismiss him”—that is, “you do not release him to do anything for his father or mother,” whom he has been commanded to honor in their old age, not merely with words but through deeds and services.

> “And you do many similar things,”

the passage says, “placing your tradition before the commandments of God.”

But these words were spoken only to the scribes and Pharisees, who, flattering themselves on the eminence of the Law, demanded rewards as though they were the due price of their teaching. I find that they have no place in a discussion concerned with the faith.

*Racha*, however, is a Hebrew word; in Latin it means “empty” or “vacant.” The Greek speaker renders it more appropriately for us in a single word: **κενός** (*kenos*, “empty”).[^c0021-45] We are forbidden to address this insult to a brother—that is, to one placed under the one God as Father and in the one Church as mother, within the one faith. By this reproach of emptiness, one who is not empty of salvation is unjustly assailed.

But leaving these matters for an exercise more suited to discussion than to clarifying the faith, let us return instead to what you wrote had been alleged by your priests.

When you were examining whether the Holy Spirit, who in the hidden rite of baptism asserts the unity of the undivided name, should be believed to be Creator or creature—since, if he is Creator, he cannot be separated from the Godhead, and if he is a creature, he cannot be united to God—the opposing party, lacking an answer, raised a question under the slippery cover of another issue: whether our spirit should be judged created or eternal.

[Editorial note: Against Gundobad’s priests, Avitus proves clearly and fully that the divine Spirit is Creator, not creature, and that our spirit is created, not eternal. Why their cause should be helped by saying *insufflavit* (“breathed into”) instead of *inspiravit* (“inspired/breathed”) in Genesis is not entirely clear; Greek manuscripts read ἐνεφύσησεν (*enephysēsen*, “breathed into”), as do Tertullian, Cyprian, Ambrose, and Augustine, not to enumerate others. Wisdom 15 joins both expressions: τὸν ἐμπνεύσαντα αὐτῷ ψυχὴν, καὶ ἐμφυσήσαντα πνεῦμα ζωτικόν, “he who inspired a soul into him and breathed into him a vital spirit.”]

They introduced as an example a passage of Sacred Scripture which says:

> “God breathed the spirit into the soul of life” (Wisdom 15:11).

First, consider what those who lie about a testimony will do in their exposition, or how they will fill their inventions with the swelling of deceit when they alter the words of divine authority. For what they said—“God breathed the spirit into the soul of life”—was fabricated by their artful fraud.

If your piety decides that this passage should be brought forward for examination, you will find it written as follows:

> “And God made man from the clay of the earth, and breathed into his face the breath of life; and man became a living soul” (Genesis 2:7).

Now weigh how great the difference is in the wording. They said, “He breathed into the soul,” whereas it is written, “He breathed into the face.” An incorporeal being may inspire; no one can breathe into something unless he is corporeal. God is not read to have breathed a spirit into an already living soul, adding it to the soul; rather, as the ancient books have it, he infused the breath of life into matter that was not yet living, so that it might be raised into a living soul.

Therefore, if the human soul was made by this inspiration, and if the human soul is nothing other than spirit, it follows that spirit does not lack a beginning.

This is what they understood had immediately to be opposed to them when you reproved them—unless, through their carnal fiction about breathing, they falsely claimed that the spirit itself had been placed in the soul rather than in the body. For when they pursue their deadly intention—not to recognize what is written, but to make people think that what they proclaim is written—what, we may ask, do they do to the ignorant, since they do not fear the authority of your instruction?

Let us examine, if you graciously permit it, what absurdity is being proposed: if the Spirit of God is not a creature, then, they say, the spirit in man cannot be called a creature either, since God is said to have breathed it into man.

It has often been definitively established that there are only two things: the Creator and the creature. The Spirit of God must be understood as the Maker, while the spirit of man must be understood as something made. Therefore the spirit that lives in us is understood to exist through God’s power, not through God’s nature.

For if the substance of the Holy Spirit is believed to be mingled with us in order to give us life, may God and your hearing be gracious toward such a blasphemy, for it can scarcely be repeated without sin even when it is being refuted. If the human spirit sins after being carnally overcome, then the Holy Spirit must be said to sin in it. Or else, when we pray for the spirits of the dead, we would be asking that remission be granted to the Holy Spirit.

Was it not enough, I ask, that one be called the Holy Spirit and another the Paraclete, unless this multitude is added as the final refuge of necessity, so that, being enslaved also to the contagion of sins, there should be counted as many divine spirits as there are human beings?

And the priestly authority has supposedly decreed wisely that the spirit of divinity is infused into everyone in one and the same manner. Does the Holy Spirit perhaps reveal himself equally to a Jew, heretic, or pagan and to a Catholic? Or is he perhaps forced unwillingly into the limbs of criminals at the command of the Father or the Son?

But what shall we do with the fact that “the Spirit blows where he wills”? If he sanctifies unworthy bodies without exercising his own will, he refutes the prophet who says that the Spirit “does not dwell in a body subject to sins” (Wisdom 1:4).

Therefore, the human spirit begins through creation, whereas the divine Spirit is granted through benevolence. Those upon whom hands are laid in the Acts of the Apostles so that they may receive the Holy Spirit were not without the spirit of their own life (Acts 8:17; 19:6).

But if they also want the Holy Spirit himself to become a creature because he enters the minds of created believers, then, according to the conclusion stated above—when they say peremptorily, without actually asserting anything, “If the Spirit of God is not a creature, then the spirit in man cannot be called a creature”—what will they now say about the divinity of the Father or the Son? They will be unable to invent that it was created, yet, frightened by the reading of Scripture, they will not deny that it dwells in the bodies of the saints, since the Apostle declares to believers:

> “For the temple of God is holy, and that temple you are” (1 Corinthians 3:17).

But although there are incomparably more matters that could be brought before your glorious presence, at the conclusion of this speech—in which you not only grant but command freedom—I entreat God and you, relying upon your divine promise, not to allow those who contradict the Holy Spirit to continue to be called your priests; not to permit those who refuse to learn to teach in your presence; and lest those who refuse to understand what you believe persist in blaspheming what they hear, thereby delaying your perfection to some extent.[^c0021-46]

Through his letter, the holy Apostle Paul cries out to you:

> “What peace can there be between the faithful and the unfaithful? What fellowship can light have with darkness? Therefore,” he says, “go out from among them and separate yourselves” (2 Corinthians 6:12, 17);

that is, do not let the proximity of the left-hand side stain those whom the truth of the right hand has won, by making them share any longer in the sins of others.

[^c0021-44]: This passage first refutes the fruitless labor of those who have dared to claim that *missa* is an exotic word, that is, a Hebrew word, rather than Latin—which it is, as Avitus’s words clearly show. It then teaches something which, so far as I know, no one had previously brought to light: that the word *missa* was customary not only in churches but also in palaces and courts, when the people were dismissed from an assembly. From this dismissal, or sending away, of the people, which took place after the business had been completed, the word was transferred to designate the proceedings themselves. Thus morning and evening *missae* came to be the names of the liturgies, or solemn offices, celebrated in the morning or evening hours. This should seem all the less surprising because, conversely, the terms *synaxis* and *collecta*, which properly signify an assembly and gathering for divine offices, were also commonly used for the divine offices themselves, both morning and evening.  
[^c0021-45]: Hilary, *On Matthew*, chapter 4: “Raca is an insult expressing emptiness; and whoever, by an insult of emptiness, charges one who is full of the Holy Spirit with being empty becomes liable to the council of the saints and pays the penalty for insulting the Holy Spirit through the judgment of the holy judges.”  
[^c0021-46]: This letter, the following letter, and others on the same subject, which are mentioned in the *Excerpts of Florus*, are praised by Gregory in the same passage. He writes: “When a heresy arose in the city of Constantinople—the heresy taught by Eutyches and that taught by Sabellius, namely, that our Lord Jesus Christ possessed no divinity—King Gundobad asked Avitus to write against them. Letters of his still exist among us; just as they then overthrew heresy, so now they build up the Church of God.”

### Letter Two

Avitus, Bishop of Vienne, to the Lord King Gundobad.

A single yet manifold gift has been granted to our age by the will of God: amid the royal ordinances of your most glorious rule, you take particular care to safeguard the truth of the Catholic party. From the piety of this devotion arose your recent command, issued after the authority of your gracious instruction had been conveyed, that against the renewed fury of the Eutychian doctrine—springing up like fuel for a fire rising again from extinguished embers—rivers of examples should be drawn from the sacred fountain of the heavenly Scriptures.

O matter most worthy that so great a prelate should give the command, if only one worthy to receive it were chosen; if the power of eloquence answered the author of the theme; if our tongue could speak for the multiplication of the peoples’ salvation as adequately as your benevolence suffices to command it. You love the emperor’s fatherland and person, bound as you are to him, not merely—as is customary with other kings—for the advantage of worldly peace; rather, because before you he fears being anticipated by error, you wish all the friendship that exists between you to benefit him in this respect: that he may not sin. You raise him up with praise and commend him as faithful and devoted to God. Concerning this especially, who could be worthy to speak fully enough when seeking the favor of your triumphal plenitude?

Nevertheless, I beseech God with all my strength that the very man of whom we speak, the Caesar of the Greeks, may be persuaded—if he is faithful to you and therefore honorable to us—by our prince to urge upon his people what he himself should urge; and that, when he has made himself receptive to you in holding the truth, he may rejoice that he has been made an ally of your preaching in overthrowing the contagions of his own region.

[Note: Liberatus testifies in the *Breviarium* that Eutyches presided over the most celebrated monastery at Constantinople, but neither he nor the others disclose the monastery’s name. In the year of Christ 447, he began to establish the heresy named after him; he was first condemned at the Constantinopolitan synod of Flavian, and thereafter at the ecumenical Council of Chalcedon.]

Eutyches, then, that baleful instigator of the ruin just mentioned, was indeed a presbyter of the Constantinopolitan Church, but he was placed in charge of a large multitude of monks; the bishops of the East call persons holding this office *archimandrites*. Burning eagerly with a passion for introducing some novelty, in order to attain the highest priesthood through the support of public reputation, he is said to have introduced that doctrine which we shudder to see among his followers more by whispers than by writings. For there was in the man no conspicuous learning by which he might have supported, with any semblance of truth, the meaning of his conceived hostility.

Having first infected the minds of the monks with this poison—while, under the wicked guise of a pilot, he instructed them and exposed them to shipwreck—he became, as we said above, the leader of a numerous band of heretics. After the council of many bishops had judged the matter, and after presbyters of the city of Rome had likewise been sent for this purpose, he was examined, exposed, and condemned. But since no schism has ever been abolished together with its author in such a way as to drive out completely the ruinous effects of his teaching, the evil that had been cut off by the bishops’ worthy precaution soon rose again, preserving within the contagion the seeds that had long since been received, like weeds springing from infected soil.

Here now, hear the proposition of the heresy against which we speak. They deny that the Son of God, existing with the Father before the ages—and whom the true faith confesses to have descended from heaven for our salvation in order to assume a body—could have been confined within a woman’s womb. Yet the Son of God, being God indeed, had said through the prophet: “I fill heaven and earth” (Jer. XXIII, 24).
