He could not have come to the place where he was not unless, through the assumption of flesh, he consented to become what he was not.

Fearing this conclusion, that Eutyches of whom we speak, when he was being earnestly pressed by his hearers in the synod mentioned above to declare and subscribe that the virgin Mary was *Theotokos* (Θεοτόκος), that is, “she who gave birth to God,” turned by deceit to the perversity of his ingenuity and confessed her to be *Christotokos* (Χριστοτόκος), “she who seemed to have brought forth Christ alone,” so that the person who preserves the divine nature might be believed to be separate from the one who endured the injury of suffering.

[Note: He attributes to Eutyches what properly belonged to Nestorius. Nestorius’ error was that holy Mary should not be called *Theotokos* (Θεοτόκος), but *Christotokos* (Χριστοτόκος). Thus the whole epistle, although it contains points directed against Eutyches, is chiefly engaged against Nestorius, who posited two persons in Christ, one divine and the other human, and said that Mary had not given birth to God but to a man who was afterward endowed with divinity at baptism. Avitus, by contrast, teaches that in Christ there is one person of two substances, and that he was equally the Son of God and man: the one whom the Father begot without a mother, whom his mother conceived without a father; finally, that God in Christ is God by nature, not by grace.]

[Note: Nestorius admitted only one of these alternatives, Eutyches neither, while the Catholic Church admits both. As has been said, Nestorius denied that Mary was the Mother of God but confessed her to be the Mother of Christ, though in a heretical sense, asserting that Christ had emerged from Mary as a mere man. Since Eutyches taught that Christ had flesh from heaven and that it had not been supplied by Mary, he had no reason to call her the mother of God or of Christ. Orthodox faith, however, embraces both in such a way that it tacitly professes both in each. Since it does not divide God from man in Christ, it excludes neither man from the Mother of God nor God from the Mother of Christ; for, because of the singular unity of the person, the Word is flesh in the flesh and man is God in God, as Vincent of Lérins says.]

Fleeing the left-hand side, which must be restrained from its precipitous twofold danger, while not venturing upon the right and thus fearing either side alike, I choose the safer middle path: in it, we say, the Redeemer’s two substances can be distinguished but not divided.

Nor do we insist that the inviolable Godhead should be believed to have suffered bodily pains, since every pain of every body naturally precedes the death that follows. Therefore, just as our own flesh, after death, will become incapable of suffering through the gift of resurrection, so God, who cannot experience death, compassionated the body he had assumed and to which he remained united, without the bitterness of suffering. He was neither absent from the glorious struggle of our salvation nor did he suffer pain.

Against the meaning of this distinction, the hostile heresy rises up and refuses to let Christ bend beneath true torments, although even in the Godhead itself, in which bodily affliction cannot be found, an affection of compassion is sometimes found. Thus we read of the Israelites: “They cried out to God, who was grieved by their miseries” (Jud. X, 15–16); and the Apostle commands us not to “grieve the Holy Spirit of God” (Eph. IV, 30). Any similar statement recorded in the sacred books expresses goodness of mercy rather than necessity of nature.

Meanwhile, leaving aside for what follows the assertion of the two, the unity in Christ of a twofold substance will be established for me. For where are there such great heavenly mysteries of truth in the Scriptures, which strive for nothing else than to persuade us of the incarnation of the Word together with the divinity of man?

“In the beginning,” he says, “was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John I, 1). Behold, we have recognized what existed without beginning; now let us strive to see what began and followed. “And the Word,” he says, “became flesh.” What was God in the beginning with God has neither beginning nor end; what is clothed with flesh has no end, but is established from a beginning.

Let that Emmanuel now attend our discourse, foretold by the ancient prophetic oracle, who, so that God might be with us, was thus announced by Isaiah: “A child is born and a Son of God is given to us” (Isa. IX, 6). The corporeal nature is divided from the mystery of the Godhead in vain if the prophet truly confirms that the Son of God came forth in a child. “And he shall be called,” he says, “Wonderful, Counselor, Mighty God, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace.”

As far as the proper meaning of the name is concerned, it is enough for the child to be called Emmanuel. But when he says that he shall be called Wonderful, Counselor, Mighty God, and the rest that follows, what explanation, I ask, can there be for so many names, unless we recognize that the truthful prophet, expressing in one and the same person what belongs both to divinity and humanity, has enumerated the benefits of the Mediator that would follow from his works rather than his names?

Yet I shall compel the heretic to answer: who can be understood as being called “Mighty God, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace”? If he is the Son of God remaining before the ages, why will he still be called in the future by names that he has always possessed? If he is the son of man who will be born, the fullness of time preserves the mystery of the union of what is different.

When the Apostle consequently repeats this, saying, “But when the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman” (Gal. IV, 4):

[Note: The Vulgate reads *factum*, “made,” corresponding to the Greek *γενόμενον*, “having become.” Nevertheless, various readings are reported in both Greek and Latin manuscripts. As Avitus does, Irenaeus (*On Heresies* III, 18) and Cyprian (*To Quirinus* II) also read *natum*, “born.” Augustine likewise reads it so. — The notes marked by numbers are Gallandi’s; the others belong to Sirmond, whose edition Gallandi reproduces. Editor.]

What the mother bore, the Father sent: that is, what was bodily in birth was divine in coming. God did not wish the one whom he appointed to remain hidden; let the world receive the signs of the Lord’s advent. The one whom the Father begot without a mother and whom his mother conceived without a father will be equally the Son of God and the son of man.

Yet concerning this mystery, let us consult the archangel Gabriel, the chief of ministers, to whom the ineffable secrets of manifest majesty are shown not merely to be understood but to be contemplated, since he stands in the presence of everlasting splendor as the minister of tireless obedience. He was the first to bring heaven’s embassy to earth; he endowed the virgin, made fruitful by the word, with the promise of a divine offspring; through the greeting of one woman, he filled the whole world with salvation.

“The Holy Spirit,” he says, “will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore also the holy one who will be born from you shall be called the Son of God” (Luke I, 35). Since no reasoning permits us to believe that a mere man was conceived from the Holy Spirit, while the Psalmist asserts that every human being is conceived in iniquity and born in sin (Ps. L, 6), the angel shows that, through the power of the Holy Spirit infused into the woman’s members, the one born from such a ministry was to be called holy.

The Apostle now understands and defines this in a connected sequence: that for our redemption God was in Christ. But perhaps a crafty opponent will wish to misuse this testimony of the Apostle’s words, agreeing that God is in Christ, but by grace and not by nature, just as he is in the hearts of the saints, whose minds, freed from sin, are illumined by the indwelling of the Godhead.

Let us now see whether this interpretation stands when the statement is completed. “God,” he says, “was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (II Cor. V, 19). Let this opposing teacher choose who, at almost the very beginnings of the world, reconciled to himself the world offended against its most gracious Creator by the sin of its first parent.

If God alone did so, what need was there for him to excuse to himself what he was sufficient to forgive? But if man alone did so, by what effect could a mortal reconcile to himself what the Godhead did not release? Therefore one is God and man, who himself commends the world to himself: the Son who, for the life of the world, pleads with the Father on behalf of himself, the son of a mother.

Hence the Apostle did not say, “reconciling the world to God,” but “to himself,” lest you should suppose that, for the redemption of the human race, only a man had prayed. Unless, having been assumed, he passed into the nature of the Godhead, he would not only have failed by any intercession to dissolve the liability of the human race, but would himself have borne the burden of the common debt through his ancestral bond.

The same Apostle therefore says that this remedy was arranged through angels “in the hand of a Mediator” (Gal. III, 19). Showing the reason for which he would present himself as mediator, assumed from below and bent down from above, he says: “Now a mediator is not of one; but God is one” (ibid., 20).

Since this is so, just as mediation is improperly named unless it acts between two, so the one whom we call mediator, if he received only whichever one of the two substances you please, would have nothing with which to occupy the middle ground. He concludes the matter in one statement, and in one incapable of being obscured by any deceit, saying: “For he is our peace, who made both one” (Eph. II, 14).

He himself is the peace of the lowly and the exalted; made one from both, he made one from the two. Certainly, as we stated above, the example seems to require either an exposition of the testimony or an argument.

What is clearer than that statement of the Apostle in which, adapting himself to different kinds of people, he reports that he became all things to all, eager to acquire the souls of all as a heavenly investor doubling his talents? “To those who were without the law,” he says, “I became as though I were without the law—not being without the law of God, but being within the law of Christ” (I Cor. IX, 21).

Is anyone so deeply sunk that he thinks this needs explanation, if he is within the law of Christ while without the divine law? The Father, surely, is the one giver of the law; and he, one and the same, as the Psalm signifies (LXXXIII, 8), embracing past and future, will give the blessing at baptism, he who had given the law in the commandment.

The unity of such great disparity—divine fullness and human condition, the humility of a servant and the majesty of the Lord, the power of the Creator and the servitude of the creature—forced together into one person seems offensive to minds weighed down by carnality and dulled by the conjectures of human custom.

Yet the reasoning behind this solidity is not far removed from the solidity of the wise, which appears to hold the chief place among heirs: the one who formed man from clay alone could restore the human condition from its ruin. Hence the most blessed Paul says: “The first man was from the earth, earthly; the second man was from heaven, heavenly” (I Cor. XV, 47).

He certainly called him a true man, but earthly with the contagion of pollution, heavenly with participation in divinity. Now I ask: when the Apostle says that man descended from heaven, who would dare deny that God returned from the earth?

If what the chosen vessel asserted is still insufficient, let us consult the one who filled the mind of that most precious chosen vessel. “No one,” he says, “has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John III, 13).

If God himself, who is the truth, so agrees with his incarnation that before every age his foreknowledge united what he had determined to assume in nature at the end of the ages, consider whether the one who ascended after the triumph of the resurrection is God, since he is said to have been the Son with the Father before the beginning of the flesh; or consider how great the solidity of past events has become, when such unity is proclaimed in future events.

[Alternative reading: “how great is the solidity.”]

But lest we hesitate concerning this immutability, the Apostle further adds a testimony from the Psalm: “Therefore he says: ‘Ascending on high, he led captivity captive; he gave gifts to men.’ But that he ascended,” he says, “what is it except that he also descended into the lower regions of the earth?” (Eph. IV, 8).

It is little to say that God came to earth unless he confirms that, because of the unity of the person he had assumed, he descended into the underworld.

[Alternative reading: “descended into hell.”]

[Note: Agobard will bring forward this passage against the doctrine of Felix toward the end. The blessed Avitus, too, a most powerful opponent of the Photinian heretics, wrote as follows: “Certainly, when the Jews were raging around him,” and so forth.]

Certainly, while the Jews were raging and hurling weapons of blasphemy against our Lord, what do we believe he answered except: “Amen, I say to you, before Abraham was, I am” (John VIII, 58)? He said this because, through the harmony of begetter and begotten, he descended through the line of his maternal ancestors from the seed of Abraham, while by an eternity without years he preceded Abraham.

Abraham, greatest of the patriarchs, when he saw that day in which God remains without end, nevertheless desired to see the day in which man was united to God. “He saw,” it says, “and rejoiced” (ibid., 56): for just as he beheld the one in whom innate majesty existed, so he had conceived in desire the one in whom assumed humility was illumined.

“Then they took up stones to throw at him” (ibid., 59). Why, then, are we surprised that the Eutychians rage against the Catholic faith, when we see that our Head endured from those to whom he had come their faithlessness, which he will repay with indignation at the end? The Jew rages there with the same sense of insult with which the heretic is embittered here.

There the stones hurled at the Lord of heaven were indeed an act of parricide; but you may suppose that these men, in their own time, are likewise hurling stones against the manifest truth with hardened minds. The fury of both conspires so that God and man may not be believed to be one.

Let me ask that what we have become may be advanced toward something better; let the material joined to clay be raised to the honor of heavenly things. Why do you strive so fiercely against yourself, O man, lest you be believed capable of passing into God? Heavenly majesty calls you to participation in itself; why do you reject the one who offers himself? Why do you despise the one who presents himself to you?

I honor the truth in order to attain likeness; I love the teaching in order to pursue imitation. If Christ is our Head, the members will receive from the summit, in their exaltation, some share—however small—of that exalted state.

Let others who destroy the faith seek from the body of both Testaments a likeness of examples with which to defend their position. For this task the library of both Testaments is so well equipped that, if we wished to confirm what we say with supporting testimony, all the oracles of the canonical books would seem to have to be gathered into one work.

From their multitude, however, selected and extracted passages are rightly set forth in order to avoid excessive length. For just as statements brought forth merely from ourselves, unsupported by any aid from the heavenly Scriptures, are of little effect, so the person who disdains to receive a few words casts the matter away not through strength but through bulk. Fearing to be overcome, unwilling to be instructed, and desiring a volume rather than proofs in order to abandon knowledge of the truth, he thinks that the causes of things consist in their size, not in their evidence.

Our Lord and Redeemer, therefore, making the advent of his glory especially clear to his disciples amid all his instructions, says:

“When the Son of Man comes in his majesty, and all the angels with him, then all the nations will be gathered before him; and he will separate them from one another, and he will place the righteous like sheep at his right hand, but the wicked like goats at his left. Then the King will say to those at his right hand: ‘Come, blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world’; and to those who are at the left, that they should depart from him into the eternal fire, which God the Father prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. XXV, 31, 34, 41).

What, I ask, is there here for human pride to despise as contemptible in Christ? What is so worthy of fear, so conspicuous in honor, so worthy of reverence and terror? Let the heretic determine whether he attributes this to the glory of the Father or to that of the Son.

For the matter at hand, it is enough for me to hear: “When the Son of Man comes in his majesty.” In the present age: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble in heart” (Matt. XI, 29). In the future, know beforehand that he will come in his glory with his holy angels, exalted and terrible in splendor.

Let the one who divides the united Mediator now say, with the body bowed beneath insults, whence comes all this majesty, if there is no divinity at all—leaving aside the fact that the Father assigns kingdoms and nations according to the merits of each.

It may seem more dreadful that a man should determine appropriate recompenses in judgment than that God the Father should be understood to have prepared the instruments of judgment for the Son of Man. “For the Son of Man will come in the majesty of his Father with his holy angels, and then he will repay each according to his works” (Matt. XVI, 27).

He did not say, “He will come with the angels of his Father,” but “with his own,” because whatever the Father has is also his. Since, therefore, the son of a mother receives in exaltation what the Son of the Father, when despised, possessed in humility, what heretic could ever be so rebellious as to refuse to submit to God the one whom he sees the immortal substance of the angels obeying, while he himself, mortal, died a mortal death?

In a certain passage of the Gospel, Abraham—the one whom we mentioned above—said, when a man was praying to him in vain and too late for relief from the burning fire, that if someone had not wished to receive Moses or the prophets, he would certainly not listen even to one coming back from the dead (Luke XVI, 31).

Who, however, is the preacher raised from the dead except Christ Jesus, in whose twofold substance, of which we speak, the unity of the two Testaments is gathered from their diversity? The things preached in the prophets are related in the Gospels, and the unity arises from the strength of the Testament—not from diversity, but from time.

What is newly occurring today is new; what was long awaited is Old. Since, then, an opportunity for speaking of Abraham has arisen—and he is read as the founder of both Testaments, introducing the Old [alternative reading: “the Former”] by instituting circumcision, and the New by pleasing God through faith; in the former the father of the Jews alone, but in the latter the father of many nations—let us examine whether, in harmony with the Gospels’ account of Christ’s generation, he recognizes himself as the father of nations, or understands the eternity of that very offspring whom he was to beget.

Does he recognize himself as younger than his grandson? Does he himself consent to the Redeemer’s statement that he existed before Abraham? Does he, without parental pride, reverently render service to the Creator who arose from bodily seed?

Let the following oath, inserted briefly into our present discussion, enter as a witness: it demands the fidelity of an oath while revealing its mysteries. Abraham adjures the steward of his household, not without the mystery of the grace that was to follow:

“Place your hand under my thigh, and swear to me by the Lord, the God of heaven, that you will not take a wife for my son from the daughters of Canaan” (Gen. XXIV, 2).

Tell me, I ask, what reverence for an oath is thought to lie in the thigh? If this were done merely for a personal reason, the one being adjured could more easily touch his head. Or what is the reason for the thigh, with mention made of God and the Lord in the oath, unless the oath was sworn by that God and Lord of heaven whom the ages seemed destined to bring forth from it?

He surely knows to what ancestry he himself does not so much preside as serve. He knows what he must adore in his own body; he understands which members he should venerate with a special honor contrary to human custom.

After these preceding indications and the miracles that follow, although we might produce very many testimonies from the Gospels and the Apostles, I fear that in the end, since the Eutychians are moved neither by the deeds of the patriarchs nor by the sayings of the prophets, if they have not listened to Moses and the prophets, they will not believe even the one who returned from the dead.

## LETTER III. AVITUS, BISHOP OF VIENNE, TO LORD KING GUNDOBAD

[Col. 0210B]

I now think it worthwhile to touch, in this brief page, upon the matter of no small importance: the occasion on which, at the present time, the poisonous growth of a sudden division broke forth in exuberance. Thus, after [Note: In his early years he seemed to hold sound views and to contend for the Council of Chalcedon against the Eutychians. Afterward, having changed his policy, how serious disturbances he stirred up in the Church, whether secretly or openly adhering to the same party against that council and its defenders, is shown by the letters of the popes—both of Simplicius, who tried to recall him to a better mind, and of Felix, by whom at length he was condemned and struck with anathema for his obstinacy. Nevertheless, with the favor of the emperor Zeno, he retained the episcopate until his death. After Acacius died, Felix ordered his name erased from the diptychs; various disputes among the bishops arose again over this matter, and only with difficulty was it finally secured, under Hormisdas, that his name should be expunged at Constantinople.] the death of Acacius, once priest of Constantinople, the persuasion concerning the evil that we have undertaken to combat began to sprout, having been propagated by Eutyches. Acacius himself, as Your Highness may have learned, was more a timid admirer than an open defender of it: he praised what he had found in Eutyches, but did not then dare to proclaim it to the devoted and still uncorrupted people.

For the concealment of this feigned fiction [Col. 0210C], to win favor with the emperor of his age, he perished not merely unpunished but also without investigation. From this, popular and—what was more grievous—priestly interests were divided over whether communion should be granted to the dead man. And as each person had conceived rightly or wrongly concerning the nature of the faith, so also did he judge concerning the memory of the preacher who had passed away.

Meanwhile the disagreement, not through open disclosure but through suddenness, and less by formal separation than by mutual hostility, was prolonged. Accordingly, in the preceding year, an arrangement was made with the king of the East [Note: This took place under the emperor Anastasius in the year of Christ 512, as what follows will show.] that he should confer with the bishop of his city as though in gentle conversation and friendly reflection.

There exists there [Note: The Church of Constantinople was the first of all to begin using the Trisagion hymn in the age of Theodosius the Younger, but without the words “ὁ σταυρωθεὶς δι᾽ ἡμᾶς, ἐλέησον ἡμᾶς” (“you who were crucified for us, have mercy on us”), which were then unknown. The author of the later addition at Antioch was Bishop Peter Gnapheus, who, in order to introduce the Theopaschite heresy with which he was infected, added this clause to the Trisagion; thus suffering appeared to be ascribed to the triune God to whom the preceding words referred. To remedy this evil, Calendio, Gnapheus’s successor after the latter had been driven into exile, prefixed to the clause “Χριστὲ βασιλεῦ” (“Christ the King”), and by these two words cut off the occasion for error—unless Gnapheus, having returned from exile and been restored to his see, removed them and reinstated the former corruption. Theophanes says in his Chronicle concerning Calendio: “He added to the Trisagion ‘Christ the King: [you] who were crucified for us.’ But Peter, having returned, again removed ‘Christ the King.’” This occurred at Antioch. At Constantinople, however, the emperor Anastasius, together with Patriarch Timothy, attempted to introduce the same addition of Gnapheus into the Trisagion; after various tumults, killings, and fires, he could achieve nothing, because the orthodox people objected, as the Chronicle of Count Marcellinus teaches under the consuls Paulus and Muschianus—that is, in the year of Christ 512, the twenty-second year of Anastasius. Theophanes assigns the same events to that year in his Chronicle, where he also mentions Timothy’s memorandum, by which he commanded all the churches to do this very thing: “When Timothy too, by a written memorandum, commanded all the churches to say the Trisagion in the litanies with the addition.” Anastasius has the same account in his Ecclesiastical History. We had to set all this forth beforehand so that from it we may recognize that Avitus, who tells a different story, was subsequently misled.] a custom [Col. 0211A] in the churches of the eminent cities: a supplication accompanied by divine praise is celebrated at the beginning of the Mass. The united crowd raises such a cry with such devotion and eagerness that they rightly believe the whole efficacy of the sacrifice that follows will be made acceptable by the service of this devotion offered beforehand.

I thought it appropriate to set down here the innermost part of that supplication, although it is very well known to Your Piety:

> Holy God, holy mighty one, holy immortal one, have mercy on us;  
> O you who were crucified for us, have mercy on us.

Thus, just as it had been whispered to the emperor, and as he himself conveyed the suggestion to the bishop, nothing would become a cause for complaint, nor would any mention of the schism be made, if the bishop, entreated by the emperor, either ordered or permitted the words that stirred the minds of a few in the prayer itself to be removed [Col. 0211B].

Some people were displeased that at the conclusion of the proclamation it was cried out:

> O you who were crucified for us, have mercy on us,

which you understand to mean in Latin:

> You who were crucified for us, have mercy on us.

The negligent bishop was persuaded—one insufficiently instructed for what befits the patriarch of so great a city and, consequently, of the whole East. He therefore conceived and arranged to make a rash decision concerning the abolition of this solemn proclamation, chiefly because a practice that had been handed down neither in the canonical Scriptures nor instituted in the times of the apostles seemed easily capable of being changed, even against the wishes of the people.

But when the hymn customarily sung in the Church was first curtailed by removing its final portion, and this satisfied the hearers less, it became clear that everything attributed to the conception of the Eutychian heretics was being preached by the bishop [Col. 0211C]. [Note: As we have seen, the orthodox were not offended by removing this final portion of the Trisagion, but by adding it; nor could the Eutychians have favored its removal, since Gnapheus himself added it for the purpose of establishing the Eutychian heresy. Nor did the orthodox object to its addition to the hymn because they denied that one ought to supplicate the Crucified, but because the Theopaschite Eutychians thereby asserted that God had been crucified.]

For what faithful person would not rightly be disturbed on hearing that one must not at all supplicate the one crucified for us to have mercy? In short, as the storm of seditions increased, while the people pressed the matter and the emperor did not resist, the aged bishop—and, what is more grievous, an innocent man—was driven from his see [Col. 0212A], just as we read in a certain passage of Scripture:

> If a man sins against a man, the priest will pray for him; but if a priest sins against God, who will entreat for him?  
> (1 Kings 3:25)

Above all other sins, the one who contradicts apostolic teaching and strays from the rule of truth sins more particularly against God. Nothing is more serious than for a blind man, presuming to lead, to begin as a preacher of the faith and become its destroyer.

Consider now the madness of the whole heresy in the rejection of a single phrase. In this matter, little indeed may seem to have been taken away from the ears; but together with that word the whole meaning of Catholic truth is excluded. [Note: No one who thought rightly ever denied that one should supplicate Christ crucified for us; but they did not approve of subjecting this supplication to the Trisagion. Discussing this matter in chapter 228 of the Photian Excerpts, Ephraemius, patriarch of Antioch, in his letter to Zenobius the scholasticus, excuses his Eastern brethren by saying that the Constantinopolitans and Westerners, because they refer the Trisagion to the Trinity, therefore do not tolerate the addition of “who were crucified for us,” lest suffering seem to be attributed to the Trinity. The Easterners, however, since they refer the Trisagion to Christ, are free from blame when they add, “who were crucified for us.” Although he writes this about the Easterners falsely, as is apparent—for from the letter of Damascenus *On the Trisagion* it is clear that all the ancients always understood this hymn of the triune God, never of the Son alone, and for that reason called it *Triadic*—and although it is certain that when Gnapheus added this addition he had not the Son in mind but God, whom he was endeavoring, with the Theopaschites, to assert had been crucified, nevertheless, as I say, it does not seem necessary to deny that in Gnapheus’s addition, once his wicked purpose is removed, there would be nothing objectionable. The words would then be addressed to the Son after the praise of the Trinity: “You who were crucified for us, have mercy on us.” It is also clear that Bishop Calendio thought this, when he prefixed “Christ the King” to Gnapheus’s addition. Damascenus recognizes that it is not foreign to the Church’s practice, since after the doxology of the Trinity—“Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit”—there is often added: “to him who was crucified by his will and who rose from the dead,” words that properly concern the Son.]

For they do not wish us to supplicate the one who was crucified, lest the person of the man seem to have been able to accomplish as little as the substance of the divine majesty could suffer nothing. [Note: He next treats two arguments against two heresies. The first, at this point, is that Christ was both God and man, against the madness of Nestorius, who said that he had been merely a man—*ψιλὸν ἄνθρωπον*, “a man only.”]

But what else is this than returning hatred for love and repaying benefits with insults? The dignity of heavenly things was inserted into a human body. God indeed is not subject to torture, but the divinity is present in the suffering. At the time of the cross, the world shuddered at the outrage done to God, darkened by daytime shadows; the earth, which trembled, testified that the Jews had sinned against heaven.

The truth, shining forth by necessity, needs no conjecture; nor does it await our assertion, since it is sufficient in its own authority. Let us hear the Apostle proclaiming from these events:

> For if they had known it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory.  
> (1 Corinthians 2:8)

But that prophet who, because of his foreknowledge of future things, is called the Angel, had said this even earlier:

> Will a man fasten his God to the cross, since you fasten me to the cross?  
> (Malachi 3:8)

I ask: who could block so clear a statement by the obstacle of disputation? If the Lord of glory hung upon or was fastened to the cross, let the adversary say why we should not ask the man in heaven.

For at that time he had still kept heavenly power hidden within the secrecy of the body; he still owed death from the womb; he was still practicing, for our instruction, the exercises of humility even in the work of glory.

When a certain Canaanite woman—of Israelite faith, indeed, but of a foreign race—with manly courage, praiseworthy petition, and victorious persistence, supplicated Christ for her daughter, saying, “Have mercy on me, Son of David” (Matthew 15:22), this understanding, by its inward wisdom, overcame the sex of the flesh; it perceives what is above the human in the man.

The Eutychian teachers do not consent to supplicate the one who was crucified for us. In the Crucified, this woman prayed both to the divinity that could not die and to the humanity that could be raised up. “Son of David” resounds of the flesh; “have mercy on me” declares God. The Lord of heaven was invoked in respect of his power; the author of man was called upon in respect of his lineage.

By now, as I think, a long time after the death of David, from whose seed Christ shone forth upon the earth through Mary, the line of the royal family was traced through the succession of generations. I now ask: with these successions of ancestors and descendants, with the whole inheritance derived in an unbroken course from the father just mentioned to the virgin birth, let the line of a phantom be traced—does it descend through the line, or does it not?

There can be no doubt, moreover, that true flesh proceeded from the lineage, whereas a phantom could possess no lineage. Nevertheless, let us test whether Christ rejected the words of the aforementioned Canaanite woman in her prayer, or perhaps reproved the foolishness of the one who supplicated him. He said:

> Woman, great is your faith; let it be done for you as you wish.

If that is faith—and it is certainly great, if it is genuine—it will not be wrong. He had given another answer to his mother when, invited with his disciples’ company to the festive wedding, he was asked to perform a miracle because the wine had failed, and said:

> What have I to do with you, woman? My hour has not yet come.  
> (John 2:4)

It was as though he were saying:

> Why do you believe me to be only what you have borne? If you think that only that which belongs to the flesh is established in me, I cannot accomplish what you demand. These sublime things that you ask of me I brought from the Father; I did not receive them from my mother. To the body formed in you, in accordance with the appointed weakness of its condition, you assign works of power. You rightly think that I can do what you ask if you understand yourself to be the mother not only of my body but also of your Creator. But if you wish to have given birth to me as merely a man, my hour has not yet come.

No one should be considered so foolish as to want to apply the statement “My hour has not yet come” to fixed decrees of fate, as though by pagan error. For understanding the mystery of that hour requires discrimination rather than a decree. Since even the condition of our mortality is not chosen by us, but every necessity of our state is governed by the will of the eternal ruler, how much more did Christ, who had power to lay down his life and to take it up again (John 10:18), refuse to entangle himself in any prescription of fate?

But when the hour of undergoing the cross should come, the heavenly things begotten by the Father and the bodily things poured forth by the womb would appear.

Therefore, since the Lord himself, moved to perform a miracle by divine action, did not repel his mother but instructed her in her ignorance, let us see what he discussed with greater care with his apostles on this subject.

In one passage of the Gospel he asked them what opinion the varying populace held concerning his person. When they suggested, on the basis of the diversity of popular opinion, that people thought him to be either one of the ancient prophets, or Moses, or certainly Elijah, he said:

> But who do you say that I am?  
> (Matthew 16:15)

Then the leader of his fellow disciples, taking up the beginning of the response, said:

> You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.

What Peter confesses here could plainly have been sufficient, even if Christ had not confirmed it with so manifest a reply. He said:

> Blessed are you, Simon son of Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven.  
> (ibid.)

Blessed are you, I say, because, in order to see God, you judged not only the flesh but also the blood; nor did the features of the body assumed by me offer you my glory to be revealed. You did not turn away the sight of your noble mind from what was brought forth in the flesh.

But my Father, who is in heaven, revealed to you the Son who is joined to it on earth: whose glory is now covered by poverty, whose honor is now concealed by insults.

For the body of our mediator hung upon the height of the saving wood, lifted up in triumphal eminence, and the power of the saving stake demanded from the innermost recesses of each heart its judgment concerning him. One man mocked the insult:

> Behold the man who destroyed the temple of God, in order to raise it up in three days.

Another offered him a drink of vinegar corrupted by animal gall in a sponge’s cup (Matthew 26:40). Yet he, preserving amid human sufferings the mercy of the Creator, grieving that those for whom he had come were still wandering during the very time of their redemption, cried out:

> Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.  
> (Luke 23:40)

What does “they do not know what they are doing” mean, except that they believed they had brought only a man to judgment? He does not know what he is doing who does not perceive majesty in the tortured body.

And if those who believed they were killing only the son of his mother did not know what they were doing, why does Eutyches still pretend not to know that, if they had known then, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory, as both Christ and the Apostle testify?

Therefore, since this Lord wishes forgiveness for those who were ignorant, it is clear that such forgiveness cannot be granted to the consciences of those who know.

Or should we perhaps wonder that Christ deigns to expound the mystery of his passion so clearly? I dare say that here we have still more to wonder at.

As you read, the death of the Lord was accompanied by the crucifixion of the thieves hanging beside him; yet the cruelty of judicial authority, not the merit of servile guilt, had made them equal to the innocent man. The horror of neighboring pollution could not stain the incorruptible brightness of the holy offspring, just as the sun, even if it sends a ray into filth, does not experience the contagion as an injury to itself.

One of these thieves, exchanging a life of long crime for the brief conclusion of a short gain, became a physician from a murderer, a martyr from a thief; bound in his limbs, absolved from his crimes; fixed by a nail, free in his affections, he said:

> Lord, remember me when you come into your kingdom.

O blessedness of a happy testimony! O unspeakable strength of faith! Signs had not conquered this man so that he might perceive divinity in the human being; rather, from the evidence of weakness he gathered the love of power. He desired to invoke one who was likewise bound, while Eutyches still despises praying to one who has been exalted.

The thief trembled at the dying man; Eutyches scorns the reigning one. The thief did not fear death from the one who would judge, while he asked life from the dead.

Compassionating his redeemer in the mortification of his squalid old life, he joined his own cross to the Lord’s. He worshiped the one who was free from guilt while sharing his punishment. Once eager to seize, he changed his desire into a prayer for plunder. Armed with beam-like nails, he used force against the kingdom of heaven.

He understood the poor man to be rich in Christ; he found near at hand what he could take from the naked man; he received the fullness of pardon and seized a share in innocence. On the wood he saw God; in heaven he obtained the man.

[Note: This is the second head of the discussion: that Christ truly possessed a body consubstantial with ours, contrary to what Eutyches thought, for he attributed to Christ a fictitious body resembling a phantom. Hence these letters of Avitus, which refute this madness, once bore the title *Against the Phantom*. Thus, as the monk Leontius observes, the impiety of the Nestorians and that of the Eutychians is equal but opposed: “For the one group says that the divinity, and the other that the humanity, is present in the Savior merely in appearance”—*Οἱ μὲν γὰρ τὴν θεότητα, οἱ δέ τὴν ἀνθρωπότητα δοκήσει λέγουσιν εἶναι ἐν Σωτῆρι*. Therefore the abbot Nonnus aptly called both groups *Enantiodoxites*—*Ἐναντιοδοκίτας*. Theodoret also calls those who introduced this kind of phantom *Docetists*—*Δοκῖται*—in book 5 of his *Heretical Fables*. There, treating the same passage concerning Christ’s body, he proves by the same arguments as Avitus that Christ allowed his body to suffer and die, to hunger and to grow weary: “so that the Docetists might have no occasion to strengthen their false heresy”—*Ἵνα μηδεμίαν λάβωσιν ἀφορμὴν οἱ Δοκῖται κρατύναι τοῦ ψεύδους τὴν αἵρεσιν*.]

Now, since the completed passion demonstrates a true man, tortured by sufferings, reckoned among thieves, exhausted by punishment, and buried in a tomb, the truth of the body assumed contradicts the advocates of a phantom in all these respects.

When the manifest testimony of the evidence clearly convicts them of the unity of both substances in Christ, they disturb the whole sequence of the Lord’s passion, which is repeated in what follows, by constructing an imaginary and dishonorable conception of his dignity. They assert that some fictitious body, like a mist, existed and seemed to have been exposed on behalf of our redeemer to insults, punishments, and sufferings; and that, through the semblance of an unreal man, true flesh—which could not have undergone the sufferings that majesty could not endure—did not exist: the flesh that the people revile, the judge tortures, blows strike, insults mock, thorns pierce, a reed smites, a nail fixes, and blood is drawn forth.

Moreover, since we place everything that belongs to our hope in the single mystery of our redemption, and since our rising again is nothing other than the Lord’s having endured death, it is false that he saves us through his incarnation if it is also thrown into doubt that he assumed in the flesh what had to be endured for us.

Come rather, holy Isaiah, prophet indeed of your own age but evangelist of our time; come quickly to defend the salvation of Christians against Eutyches’ lies. Do not hesitate to say—or rather to swear—concerning Christ:

> Truly he himself bore our infirmities, and he himself carried our pains.  
> (Isaiah 53:4)

And:

> By his bruise we were healed.

This healing was not assumed through a secure capacity to cure, but through the truth of his voluntary suffering for us.

If he truly bore our pains, then we too are secure that a fictitious phantom did not endure real pains. And if we were healed by his bruise, the deceitful lie begrudges me a healing conferred in vain.

The conclusion follows correctly from every definition: if the bruise could have been fictitious, the feigned bruise could not at the same time have been real.

But even in this prophetic statement the distinct property of the two substances is evident. He says:

> Truly he himself bore our infirmities, and he himself carried our pains.

These are two things which neither God alone nor man alone could have done in their entirety: one belongs to God, the other man could accomplish. By saying, “He himself bore the infirmities; he himself carried the pains,” the prophet plainly expressed one person consisting of divinity and body.

The infirmities that Adam’s wounded offspring drew from the wound of its corrupted origin were healed by the one who alone had previously created it sound. But he carried our pains who could not undergo the battles of suffering except through torture and labor.

Thus God bore what we had as an evil in our nature; Christ endured what we suffer as an evil in the body.

Hence we must consider how much more deeply the Eutychians are plunged than the Bonosiacs into the abyss. [Note: Bonosus was, as we conjecture, bishop of the see of Naissus in Dacia. Abandoning the Catholic faith, he passed over to the heresy of those who followed the poison of Photinus and denied that Christ was God, preaching him as man only. His disciples are also called Bonosiacs by the Second Council of Arles and the Third Council of Orléans; Gregory the Great, in book 9, letter 61, calls them Bonosians in his letter to Quirinus and the other bishops of Ireland.]

The former deprive Christ only of the honor of divinity; the latter deprive him even of the truth of his body. Photinus mocks us for worshiping the person of a man; this man makes us worship a cloud.

Or do these heretics perhaps begin the origin of this very illusion with the swaddling clothes of Christ’s sacred birth? Will it therefore be false that he lay in cloths, that he appeared to the Magi, that he cried in the cradle?

I say nothing of his later progress through successive ages, in which he embraced both the divine and human nature: weariness received refreshment, compassion poured forth tears, light slept, bread hungered, and the fountain thirsted.

I say nothing of the weeping that he shed over the dead Lazarus (John 11:35), before he showed by the effect of raising him that he had first exhibited the human emotion of his condition.

But if doubt is cast upon the one who accomplished such things, then it is necessary that what he did begin to become doubtful. Thus the paralytic falsely thinks himself healed, the lame man falsely believes himself raised up; the ray of the sun that the man blind from birth sees after the darkness of his natural prison must be deceptive—or Lazarus himself was deceived by this phantom, believing that, although he slept among the dead, he had already risen.

If they accept all these things as true but contradict only the insults of the passion, let them answer where the Son of the Virgin was at that time, when, offering in his place a shadow deceiving through a thin cloud, he whom we believe was offered for us would deceive both his persecutors and the faithful by the empty appearance of himself.

By this illusion he would also make the Father a liar, of whom the Apostle says that he did not spare his own Son but delivered him up for us (Romans 8:32). Whom did he deliver up, if he was not real? How did he deliver him up, if he deceived us? How did he not spare him, if he prevented him from suffering?

Or, in what death did our Lord’s life end, since he could not fail to owe a little death to the mortality of his mother, in order to fulfill the lawful condition of undergoing death, while he would not see corruption because his resurrection was at hand?

The law of both natures was signified by that gall, which, after tasting it, he refused to drink: he refused to drink, on account of his divinity, the death that all owe through Adam our father, but he had to taste it according to the dispensation.

But when what the Apostle said had occurred—“Christ, having risen, dies no more, and death shall no longer have dominion over him” (Romans 6:9)—let the heretic now dare, if he has any power, either to confess Christ without God or God without man.

The holy Thomas had been absent (John 20:24 and following), when the Savior, returning from the dead, restored by his visible presence the hopes of the disciples waiting for him, and when life, recovering from death, in a manner repaired the wavering faith of his followers.

The disciples therefore reported that they had seen the Lord. Thomas refused to believe and promised that he would in no way offer faith unless he received it through sight.

After some interval of time, Jesus came again, but now to all of them together. Having first offered the greeting of peace, he reproved the lingering Apostle’s slowness with the gentlest rebuke. At the Lord’s command, lest what the eye judged should still be insufficient, faith examined the matter by touch.

> Put your finger here into my side, and do not be doubtful but believing.  
> (John 20:27)

For you will now persist in unbelief without excuse, when by touching you have been made an eyewitness.

Thomas searched with his finger the marks of the passion. The healing wound remained as it had been inflicted, and the opening of the pierced side preserved, as a blessed sign, the passage of the life-giving wound.

Then at last, returning to himself and enlightened by the holy body, he said:

> My God and my Lord.

What, I ask, did the holy Apostle understand of heavenly things in the flesh? What did he perceive as divine by the touch of a curious hand upon the wound? Nothing other than that he had long before learned that Christ could not be without God, and that these very wounds which he touched had indeed prevailed over man but had yielded to the victor.

Nevertheless, they could neither inflict death except upon a man nor be conquered by God except through the one who raised him up.

Thus, when they are overwhelmed by the great wonder of the miracles and hear that our Lord, in the condition of his restored body, visible to the eyes and tangible to the fingers, entered the place where the Apostles were accustomed to be, through closed doors, they resort to the familiar fiction of asserting a phantom. They complain that human eyes were deceived by the tricks of an empty mist and by the fraud of illusory shadows.

They perceive something divine in the greatness of the event, a power of subtlety by which a body entered a secret inner chamber through doors barred shut, without an entrance. Rather than be compelled to acknowledge a miracle, they invent uncertainty.

Consider to what an outrage against divinity this leads: the teacher of truth, who forbids us even verbal lies, would himself be believed capable of lying by his deeds.

It would unquestionably be a kind of lie if he wished his followers to believe that he was what he was not, and if Christ were thought to have done what a Christian is not permitted to do.

He was instructed by sight for the recognition of the mystery of the dispensation—enough for the sound—and convicted by touch, which is added for the blind.

But weakness voluntarily sought has no remedy. Whatever medicine is applied to inflamed eyes, the man who delights in walking about blinded cannot be cured.

Or what use of the eyes remains in such obstinacy, when a man refuses to accept as true what sight affirms? It is no less possible for God to pass through closed things than for heavenly realities to be exposed to human beings.

Yet after his resurrection he often testified to his disciples:

> Touch and see, because a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me have.  
> (Luke 24:39)

What is so closed in Eutyches? What is so open against phantoms? It is as though he were saying that a bodily mass and the appearance of bones and flesh cannot be admitted into what is to come.

He did not wish to be called a spirit, either alone or as any ordinary man—that is, without a body—but wanted you to recognize him at the judgment as the one whom you see to have returned from the tomb.

Therefore, after the struggles of the passion, as the triumphant one, he had nothing that any earthly necessity of a restored body demanded. Hunger did not ask food of him, thirst drink, labor rest, or activity sleep.

All these things were brought to an end not only in our head, who is Christ, through that brief death of a short time, but they will also remain powerful in us until death, and will then be ended through the resurrection.

Yet, as I had begun to say, although those limbs of the Lord were no longer held subject to any necessity, he appeared with the apostles in order to remove from their hearts the suspicion of a phantom. He ordered food to be set before them and deigned to eat with them after blessing it.

What they were doing still for the redemption of the body, the good teacher did for the testimony of the truth.

Unless perhaps the preacher of the phantom should say that the mist, which deceptively assumed the appearance of limbs, ate what was set before it, and that the food, a pledge of the holy meal, entered the Lord’s body without the burden of corruption but weighed down the empty belly with the weight of an uncertain eating.

Certainly, if the deceptive image snatched up that food, it must be corporeal [the reading is uncertain]; but if it ate, it is not airy.

I know, however, that no one other than Christ testifies among the final memorials of that food:

> For all things that are written about me in the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms must be fulfilled.  
> (ibid., 44)

And we seek a few examples when he says that all Scripture is fulfilled in its entirety in him.

And after these things, he says, while he blessed his own, he was carried up into heaven (ibid., 51).

Withdraw far away, Eutyches, with the tricks that you have conceived in your mind. Let the one who rejoices in being blessed or redeemed by a phantom be the only one deprived of this blessing.

Meanwhile, the Son of Man was being carried into heaven—formerly there by foreknowledge, now there by nature. He did not need the assistance of angelic hands, although he is said to have been carried; rather, the Son of the Father carried the son of his mother. What he was as God went; what he was as man was carried.

The heavenly gate stood open to him on his return, and the glory of his original homeland invited his God, returning with the addition of his body.

When he had been received there, two angels stood by and spoke to the Apostles:

> Men of Galilee, this Jesus who has been received from you  
> (Acts 1:10),

that is, the one whom the Father has received into his seat, or whom you have received in faith, will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven.

Therefore, in these words those for whom what occurred seems to have been a phantom have something to hope for, if he will come in the same way as they saw him going into heaven.

There the Catholics will see the one whom they embrace; the adversaries, the one whom they pierced. There, when they behold the same marks of the nails, let Eutyches cease to think that those fires were feigned; after the smoke of his phantom, he will burn eternally in a log of belated repentance.

To mark his former doctrine, or to correct his followers for a little while, as we hope, it is enough to have said these few things, so that from the resemblance of the testimonies we have set forth they may themselves necessarily seek more numerous ones.

But if they persist in the wickedness of their former doctrine and preserve the obstinacy of their unbelief, or if they add some new contrivance—for it is a distinctive habit of those who go astray always to wish, in their perverse obstinacy, to say whatever may lead them to ruin—may God grant that, at your command and through my service, the perversity that is still inflamed by its growth may be driven back by the one and ever-consistent teaching of the heavenly Scriptures.

## LETTER IV. AVITUS, BISHOP OF VIENNE, TO THE LORD KING GUNDOBAD.

Your inquiry is full of religion and piety. But since, in putting forward the question, you prefaced it with the names of the one consulting and the one responding, I think I should suggest that there was in Africa a certain Faustus, a Manichaean bishop [Note: Against him there exist books by Saint Augustine, and he is frequently mentioned in other works of the same author. Moreover, neither Paulinus’s letter to Faustus nor Faustus’s response to his questions, which are now read among the works of Faustus of Riez, permits doubt that this is the Faustus meant here. Avitus teaches that he was British by birth; as we have noted in the notes to Facundus’s letter to the scholasticus Mutianus, this must be understood not of the islanders but of the Armorican Britons. The Paulinus who writes to Faustus cannot be taken as Paulinus, bishop of Nola, and therefore seems to be understood as Paulinus, author of the *Eucharisticus*, who likewise was Bordeaux-born and, after leaving his homeland and settling in Marseilles, could have enjoyed the companionship of Faustus of Riez.], author of certain treatises—truly execrable ones, and in some respects also written in the most shameful language.

As far as appearances were concerned, he professed an almost exceedingly abstinent life; and, magnifying not the hidden cross but public vanity through the boastfulness of an inflated self-display, he imposed upon his hearers, as far as he could, a poisonous discourse, as though he were an unshakable guardian of the virtues. And because you have read that, in response to a certain Paulinus of Bordeaux who was consulting him, a reply was given by a bishop of the aforesaid name—for at that time a certain Paulinus, whether or not he was the one you mention, God knows, but nevertheless a man of Bordeaux, wrote not a little in a Catholic style and with irreproachable faith—I have therefore prefaced the mention of the aforesaid heretic, lest the unfortunate work of that Manichaean Faustus, or another whom Your Glory also knew, British by birth and resident at Riez, should be accused merely by the title of his name; and so that the person might also be found who either could consult concerning questions of doubtful meaning, or could be deemed worthy of a reply to be preserved for posterity. Yet whichever of them placed his words in your hands, they moved you—holy, solicitous, and royal as you are. [Note: Faustus had also called it “momentary”; Paulinus, “sudden.” “I approach as an inquirer,” he says. “I am entangled in carnal sins; I practice everything that a criminal can practice; when I have completed the day of the human condition, I have obtained sudden repentance. I wish to know whether it excludes sin in part or completely.” Faustus replied that this repentance was useless. Avitus shows that this was falsely said; before Avitus, Gennadius of Marseilles had taught the same in this province of Gaul, in *Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, chapter 48: “We unhesitatingly believe that sins are abolished by repentance, even if one repents of what he has committed in the final breath of life and sins are disclosed through public lamentation; for God’s purpose, by which he decreed to save what had perished, stands immovable. And therefore, because his will does not change, whether through amendment of life, if time is granted, or through humble confession, if life is immediately ended, forgiveness of sins is confidently expected from him who does not desire the death of the sinner, but rather that he should turn from destruction through repentance and, saved by the Lord’s mercy, live. If anyone thinks otherwise concerning God’s most just mercy, he is not a Christian but a Novatian.”]

To define the repentance which you specifically called “momentary”—that is, received in sickness, as though at the moment of death—as benefiting nothing or no one is a definition opposed to the truth and exceedingly harsh. For in the presence of divine mercy, even the humility of one who confesses ought not to be said to lack its fruit. Since we read that, once the quality of one’s former life has been set aside—for it often happens both that the righteous sin and that sinners recover their senses—a person is judged according to the way in which he is found at the time of his death, we must confidently believe that even the will to amend is pleasing, provided that it is genuine.

But everything is weighed before heavenly clemency according to the quality of faith. Hence, among those laborers whom you read in the Gospel were hired (Matthew 20:9), even those who came later receive, because of the fervor of their devotion, a wage made equal to that of the first. Likewise, the exceedingly brief repentance of the Ninevites, obtaining the whole measure of indulgence through three days of fervor, blunted the sword hanging over the necks of the sinful city—a sword which, already destined for the blow, had been brandished by the hand of the prophet Jonah on the appointed day (Jonah 3:10)—with the barrier of a corresponding satisfaction.

Let those whose sought-after pride makes them swollen, rather than an unblemished conscience makes them secure, contradict examples of this kind. Yet here I confess something over which I often grieve, since you deem me worthy to speak freely. We are sometimes distressed by the laxity of our people, because it is a grave danger to treat so precious a matter as something trivial. For when they appear to seek repentance with prayers and tears, we call it impious to deny it. But if it should sometimes happen that whoever has received repentance, upon recovering bodily health, either neglects it or becomes, as the Apostle says, “a dog returning to its vomit” (2 Peter 2:22), then the person who was more leniently burdened by the frailty of sin will be more severely crushed by the abuse of the remedy; and that saying addressed to Ananias in the Acts of the Apostles will be applied: “While it remained, did it not remain yours, and it depended on your power to promise it?” (Acts 5:4).

As the prophet says, “It is better not to vow than to vow and not fulfill” (Ecclesiastes 5:4). Hence ordinary speech has acquired the usage that, until each of us fulfills his vow, he is called liable for his vow. Therefore, I admit that repentance ought not to be given to those placed in peril without fear. If, however, without capital offenses, [Note: He sets marriage against repentance, because those who professed repentance abstained from marriage. Hence the councils forbid repentance to married persons except by mutual consent: the Second Council of Arles, canon 22, and the Third Council of Orléans, canon 24.] the final day should find them engaged in marital intercourse—as they presume upon something lawful—we neither regard them as deserving condemnation nor exclude them from the sacrifice of commemoration.

But, on the other hand, if they nullify their professed contrition by being drawn back into the world, they must be suspended from communion as though they were already apostates—that is, fallen from the firmness of standing—since it is better to remain within even the smallest measure of salvation through moderate humility than to destroy salvation altogether by violating what is supreme; and it is found safer to live honorably in marriage than, under the guise of a false chastity, to defile lawful things with unlawful acts.

Foreseeing this, the Apostle (1 Timothy 5:12), while declaring that widows who have made their first faith void will incur a greater condemnation, [Note: The conjunction *et*, required by the context, is absent from the printed edition of Sirmond.] also permits persons bound in the peace of a legitimate and irreproachable marriage-bed to devote themselves to prayer for a time and then return again to the same relationship, lest Satan, as he says (1 Corinthians 7:5), through their lack of self-control, tempt those who are faithless to their promise, though he had not conquered them as married persons in the flesh.

In the second question also, I by no means approve the denial that faith alone can benefit a person. I do not declare myself to be on the side of those who, as the Lord says (Matthew 23:4), lay a heavy burden upon the shoulders of the disciples, while they themselves refuse even to move it with one finger. For this reason, such a rigid judgment concerning faith could have been assumed by an outsider, or ought to have been moderated by one of our own.

If you graciously permit this, I shall make the matter clear briefly by reasoning and examples. That faith is the foundation of all spiritual goods is shown by the Christian beginnings first formed through it. For if a baptized child—or even one transferred from any heresy—or perhaps someone advanced in age, is snatched away by a swift death after baptism, even the boastful advocate of works will not deny that the person was saved by faith alone.

Apart from this, let us consider how little any good actions have benefited the philosophers of the world: men who despised the world and loved wisdom, who professed chastity and rejected wealth, and who practiced whatever we Catholics proclaim today. Because faith was lacking, their works profited them nothing. Thus the structure of vanity, built upon wavering heights, was unable to stand by itself, because it had risen without a foundation.

What if I now retraced the faith of various persons in the heavenly Scriptures, a faith which praiseworthy belief has always brought to the fulfillment of desire? Abraham, because he believed God alone, “it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Romans 4:5). Rahab the prostitute cleansed a past stained by prostitution by awaiting the people of Israel through faith (Joshua 2:3). Likewise that Canaanite woman in the Gospel (Matthew 15:27), although repulsed with an insult, nevertheless drew from him, through the perseverance of her petition, the children’s bread for her little dogs. Another woman faithfully stopped the flow of obscene bodily discharge by her healing touch (Matthew 9:20). [Note: Or, “extinguished”?]

Yet the devotion of good works is also commended as something to be joined to faith, and neglecting it is not proper to one who is faithful. But when the Apostle says, “Whatever is not from faith is sin” (Romans 14:23), you see that even the action we believe to be righteous can be changed into sin unless it is supported by faith.

That Pharisee in the Gospel experienced this (Luke 18:10–14). He proudly and arrogantly boasted that he gave thanks because he was not like other people—robbers, unjust men, adulterers—that he regularly gave alms and fasted twice a week. Meanwhile the Publican, bowed down in appearance but upright through faith, surpassing the merits of good works by humility alone, entered his house justified, though he had not left it justified.

Why should I recall more? Receive one further example patiently. That thief (Luke 23:40–43), whose body, accustomed to crimes, had been hung beside the cross of the Lord’s purity upon a slave’s gibbet as punishment for his offenses, perceived majesty in the body of the dying Christ. Condemned to punishment for his earlier cruelty, but added to paradise for his subsequent confession, he was led through an unjust life so that from a just death he might seize martyrdom.

These, then, are virtues arising from faith. Let anyone show, if he can, virtue without faith. In the Gospel (Matthew 13:31; Luke 13:19), the Lord compares the smallness of faith to a mustard seed and promises that it will accomplish whatever it wishes. Thus it comes about that, although works can exist without faith, faith cannot exist without works, because “with the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Romans 10:10).

According to the understanding of the Holy Spirit, which follows the promises, the beginning of a good work in its integrity is to have believed. Provided, however, that, as the Apostle says (Romans 8:16), “the Spirit himself bears witness to our spirit”—not the spirit which is a creature in us, as you have heard asserted above, but the Creator infused within us, who is the author and witness of our spirit, not its nature.

This is what I have suggested concerning the letter of Faustus the bishop, whoever he may have been, and I believe it accords with the truth. May the fullness of faith be granted to me and to those whose salvation I desire; may their works suffice them, if they have been given life by faith.

## EPISTOLA V. AVITUS VIENNENSIS EPISCOPUS DOMNO GONDOBADO REGI

[Note: A consolatory letter on the death of a daughter who, betrothed to the king and soon destined to become queen, died in her father’s house before the wedding. He does not state either her name or that of her fiancé.]

If, having experienced the grace of your ancient piety, I rightly interpret the artifice of your holy condescension, I think that, at your command, your lords and fellow-servant priests have come to console me. Yet, as I speak under divine witness, I have not presumed, out of the reverence owed in my service, to offer anything to so exalted a lord. For it detracts from your virtue if anyone should suggest, in writing or speech, some consolation concerning the misfortune that has occurred. Nor will the rejection of grief yield to a royal mind—or rather, to a philosophical one.

It is true that your love has provoked the tears of everyone. But if your safety is granted to the surrounding world, it is a small loss that the father of all has lost one pledge. The mourning is temporary when one so innocent has died—one whose death no one expected. Let each person judge according to what he feels: nothing can ever occur in your time that I would not always consider beneficial.

Therefore, I presume nothing here to be accidental, nothing harsh. Rather, a hidden dispensation ordered this anguish; it did not inflict it. [Note: He says that the funerals were mourned whose author he himself had been. Of three brothers, Gundobad removed two at the beginning of his reign: Chilperic, the father of our Clotilde, and Godomar. After sharing the kingdom with the third, Godegisil, he ruled together with him for several years. Finally, offended by an injury, he killed him as well and thereafter alone possessed the undivided kingdom for sixteen years, up to the consulship of Peter, under which Marius’s *Chronicle* records Gundobad’s death—that is, in the year of Christ 516.]

Once you wept, with ineffable piety, at the funerals of your brothers; the public grief of everyone followed your tears, and, through the hidden gaze of the Divinity, instruments of sorrow were being prepared for joy. The prosperity of the kingdom reduced the number of royal persons, and only that was preserved for the world which sufficed for the empire. There was stored up whatever was favorable to Catholic truth. At that time we did not know that only that was being broken which thereafter would not know how to bend.

And what shall we say about the fate of your brother? He whom your nature enclosed and caused to be called “the little one” served your interests without any malice: he served you while you were unaware of the danger threatening the people, while the disturbance of the region was arranging the future peace. Believe one who has experienced it: whatever harmed here benefited here; whatever we then wept for, we now love.

For those unable to foresee these things, it may indeed seem harsh that a maiden near the bridal chambers was snatched away as weariness pressed upon her. Yet she was sought as a queen and died undefiled. Indeed, I should say that she would have left a greater cause for mourning if she had closed her final day after recent vows. For then perhaps she might have been found where envious hatred, after tying the knot of jealousy, would have fixed the tooth of insult against me.

But now, what mind could be so barbarous as not to pity a virginity and happiness received into her father’s and royal embrace? She neither changed her dwelling nor experienced exile: there she could not long be a mistress, nor was she briefly a stranger. Therefore, since everyone awaits your joy as though it were the serenity of heaven, restore yourself to the rejoicing of the peoples; for the commonwealth never falls into the ruin of orphanhood so long as Mother Church, sustained by you, does not experience bereavement.

## EPISTOLA VI. AVITUS VIENNENSIS EPISCOPUS VICTORIO EPISCOPO

[Note: To the bishop of Grenoble. I believe this is the man who attended and signed, together with Avitus himself, the Council of Epaon, and who in the commonly circulated editions of the councils is called Victurius, but in the Lyon manuscript Victorius, as here.]

[Note: On not accepting the oratories of heretics. Anyone who compares this letter with canon 33 of the Council of Epaon, *On the Basilicas of Heretics*, will easily notice that the canon was composed and expressed not only according to the mind of Avitus, who presided over the council, but also in his very words. It reads as follows: “We disdain to apply to sacred uses the basilicas of heretics, which we hate with such execration that we do not think their pollution can be cleansed.” A few years earlier, the judgment of the First Council of Orléans had been different: it approved the reception of the Goths’ basilicas and their consecration according to the same order by which ours are ordinarily renewed. That this was long ago customary and practiced everywhere among the nations is shown by Greek as well as Latin histories, which testify to it in many places.]

### On not accepting the oratories of heretics

You asked—or rather, most pious brother, you commanded me—to indicate in a letter to Your Blessedness whether the oratories or basilicas of heretics could be adapted for the uses of our religion when their founders, correcting their error, have transferred themselves to the Catholic law. It is certainly a worthy matter about which you inquire, if you had found someone competent to answer. Nevertheless, because you have commanded it, I shall disclose below what I think follows, with this qualification: I leave no room for blaming others, provided that what they believe should be established is confirmed either by clear reasoning or by authority drawn from the canonical books.

The question you asked about private oratories or small basilicas is difficult to decide, just as it is concerning their churches. For this is what must be commended to Catholic kings: whatever has been established concerning their subjects. Therefore, first, I ask that the bishops of our ruler, through whom God has granted us agreement in the true religion, be consulted: whether we can say that buildings established by his father for heretics ought to be assigned to the Catholic side.

If we either give such advice or he agrees to it, the heretics will not unjustly complain that persecution has been stirred up against them, since Catholic gentleness ought rather to endure the accusations of heretics and pagans than to make them. For what is so harsh as for those who are perishing through open perversity to flatter themselves with the claim of confession or martyrdom?

And because, after us and after our king, God may grant the most fortunate longevity—for nothing concerning the course of time ought to be believed immutable—it may perhaps happen that some heretic will reign, and whatever persecution he stirs up against churches and persons will be said to have been done not from zeal for his sect but as repayment in turn. It will also be reckoned as a sin against us, burdening us even after death, whatever our descendants may have suffered.

Perhaps divine mercy may further grant that the offspring of the ruler of whom we speak may follow his Catholic ancestor through the fullness of the faith he has received. But what if someone among the neighboring kings of a different law should now wish similarly to avenge in his own territory what he grieved to have been inflicted upon his priests here?

Suppose someone mocking me over this should burst out in these words: “I shall use the glory of my time; let the age that follows look to its own condition.” But let the person who considers such matters grant me briefly the reason I ask: if heretics ought to be received by us in truth, let them be received. “Salvation is most clear,” because, as it is written, “I believed, and therefore I spoke” (Psalm 95:1). Faith precedes speech, confession follows belief, and through the laying on of the priestly hand the perversity is removed and the fullness of faith is restored.

But as for an insensible object which is polluted when first renewed, I confess that I do not know by what subsequent sanctification it can be cleansed. Certainly, if an altar polluted by heretics can be consecrated, then the bread placed upon it can also be transferred to our sacrifices. The heretical founder himself did this at the beginning. He passes over into the divine promise; rejoicing in freedom, he departs from Egypt. Migrating happily to the right faith, he left behind a stain rather than drawing one in: when something illegitimate is added to an impurity that cannot be cleansed, pollution weighs more heavily upon what is touched than it receives a remedy from the one touching it.

Thus in the prophet Haggai we read: “Thus says the Lord of hosts: Ask the priests about the law, saying: If a man carries sanctified flesh in the fold of his garment and touches with its edge bread, or anything else, will it become sanctified?” The priests answered, “No.” And Haggai said: “If one who is polluted by any of these things touches it, will it become defiled?”—that is, the bread which had previously been holy. And the priests said, “It will be defiled” (Haggai 2:12).

Therefore it must be inferred that, if that bread can be consecrated upon these altars, then a consecrated bread touching it would become defiled. The prophet Malachi likewise says: “If you offer the blind for sacrifice, is that not evil? And if you offer the lame, is that not evil?” (Malachi 1:8). And shortly afterward: “Cursed is the deceitful man who has in his flock a male and, when making a vow, sacrifices to the Lord what is weak” (ibid., 14).

What is more sincere than this judgment? What more manifest than such authority? The building which you desire to presume upon renewing repeatedly: if it is sound, what is being blessed? If it is diseased, why is it being offered? However much you may desire to turn gifts offered by evil persons toward good, the lame will not be able to follow you into sanctity.

The Apostle says that he has betrothed a chaste virgin to present her to Christ (2 Corinthians 11:2), that is, the Church. But the Church which belonged to heretics, even if it is permitted to marry a better husband, was not a virgin. Why, then, should a priest desire what is unlawful, when he is altogether forbidden contact with a rejected and widowed woman? After an incestuous bond, a late union is still a union.
