“Whoever is joined to a prostitute,” he says, “becomes one body with her. Shall I then take the members of Christ and make them members of a prostitute?” (1 Corinthians 6:15). See whether a prostitute can be restored by being joined to Christ’s members, when Christ’s members—that is, Christians—are turned by pollution into members united to her body.

The Apostle also says elsewhere (Ephesians 5:27) that he wants the Church to be such that it has no stain or wrinkle or anything of the kind. Can this in any way be said of buildings belonging to heretics? Blessing bestowed upon objects devoid of sense and polluted neither cleanses the stain nor removes the wrinkle.

Indeed, if we examine the matter more carefully, whatever is a symbol is without stain when it is made rough by novelty. But what has been doubled through repetition is covered by a wrinkle. Holy sincerity, stripping off the old Adam, can in no way be compared with such a thing as the new man offered to God. The authority of the New Testament commends this novelty to us through the voice of the Gospels (Matthew 19:30).

Hence the Lord himself commanded that a colt be spread beneath him, one upon which no one had previously sat (Mark 11:2). Untouched by all secular use, it would happily be made subject not by whips imposed upon it but by holy beginnings, gentle under its first burden.

And so that the mystery of the Lord’s death might likewise not lack the honor of novelty, we read that our redeeming Lord’s flesh rested in a new tomb cut in rock (Matthew 27:60). Who, then, would try to persuade me that after the errors of the dead a tomb can be cleansed? Even if the moisture of decay has dried up, the flesh has already been consumed, and white burial mounds have been raised, uncleanness remains in memory, even if it is thought absent from sight.

You expelled the dead thing of an alien doctrine and cast its dead strength from its tomb, like bones deprived of honor. But I think that the members of the sacred body ought not to be placed amid foulness.

And perhaps you will say that heretics, if power is given them, might profane our altars. That is true, and I do not refute it. When they can, the invaders of other people’s houses rage with filthy claws. But to employ force, invade places, and change altars does not belong to the dove. Therefore, what the heretic thinks is permitted to him must be avoided with particular care. It is fitting to shun by example what the enemy embraces.

Nor is it surprising that they dare to repeat dedications when they multiply baptisms. As to this matter, I have briefly indicated not what I decree but what I desire. I would not have the places of heretical worship invaded; I would prefer that they be abandoned like prisons. It must always be desired that they not pass into use after being altered, but that, left unfrequented, they grow inert.

For the salutary correction of the peoples, let eternal widowhood remain as an offering. Let our people never receive what its own adherents reject in the zeal of conversion.

Concerning the ministries of heretics—objects regarded by them as sacred but by us as execrable, namely, plates and cups—you commanded me to write in the same way what I think. A powerful example of observance is found in the Pentateuch [“Heptateuch”] (Numbers 16), concerning the censers of sinners: those who presumed to offer unlawful fire were consumed in a temporal conflagration that marked eternal Gehenna.

The vessels we mentioned lay mixed with ashes and embers, for the judgment of the dead and the terror of the living. Accustomed to the fragrances of incense, they had contracted the abominable uncleanness of perverse use through their stench. Then the lawgiving leader was instructed by divine speech, when he consulted, to pour these into furnaces, spread them out into sheets, and attach them to the sacred altar.

You see, therefore, that we are taught there as well that the execrable use of metals cannot be transferred to good use unless it has passed through fire. To such an extent does fire confer upon metals, for Catholic use, what faith confers upon rational beings. Hence the Prophet prays in the Psalm: “Burn my kidneys and my heart” (Psalm 25:3).

Let anyone, according to the discernment of his own mind, reproach what I feel. I confess that I take no pleasure at all in those objects used in ministry which came as captives to the churches of our law from the regions of Upper Gaul; and since they bear nothing voluntary, nothing innocent, if they are taken from those who grieve, they cannot benefit those who offer them.

Why should a victor say to me, “What I present to your altars, whatever the manner in which I obtained it, I present because it is commanded: ‘Honor the Lord from your just labors’” (Proverbs 3:9)? It is not enough that they come from labors, unless they come from your own; nor is it enough that they be your own, unless they are just. I should never call gifts “offered” which, before they were offered, had been taken away.

But I always rejoice that such gifts are placed upon the holy altars: gifts of the kind that can be offered religiously, not merely because they are one’s own, since what belongs to them appears to belong to them wherever the Catholic faith is present. Why, when he brings forth the choicest things from his treasures, does he not take every care that, in matters belonging to the sacred ministry, preciousness should not please more than newness?

Pray for what remains: that for a long time, after God has entrusted him with the riches of his vows, he may possess them not in hidden heaps but in public gifts, and, rejoicing with the people subject to him, may always have something to donate for sacred uses.

## EPISTOLA VII. AVITUS VIENNENSIS EPISCOPUS PAPAE CONSTANTINOPOLITANO

[Note: To John, patriarch of Cappadocia, who, after restoring the Council of Chalcedon to the diptychs and erasing the name of Acacius from them, ended through restored peace and concord the long division that had separated the Eastern churches from the Roman Church. There survives a letter of John himself to Pope Hormisdas, dating the event by its subscription: given in the month of March, on the twenty-eighth day, in the twelfth indiction, during the consulship of the lord Justin, emperor Augustus, and Eutharic, vir clarissimus, in the year 557 of the era—that is, in the year of Christ 519. Cedrenus, in the first year of Justin, says:

“Bishops having come from Rome, sent by Hormisdas, bishop of Rome, through the zeal of Vitalian, while John the Cappadocian, bishop of Constantinople, was still alive, he entered the holy fourth council at Chalcedon into the diptychs together with the other three councils.”

When the bishops sent by Hormisdas, bishop of Rome, came from Rome through the efforts of Vitalian, while John the Cappadocian, bishop of Constantinople, was still alive, he entered the Fourth Holy Council of Chalcedon into the diptychs alongside the other three councils. It is therefore clear which ruler he understands here, which Roman bishop, and finally which Constantinopolitan pope.]

### To the bishop, the pope of Constantinople

While my lord, your son, the patrician Sigismund, sought the most glorious ruler in the office of an embassy, he also opened for us, through a twofold holy opportunity, the way to bring our service to you. For while we longed for you with a rightful desire as our chief priest, the illustrious man Laurence added honor for you to our minds, informing us in his letters that every cloud which, through uncertain darkness, had obscured the peace of the Eastern peoples had been wiped away by the serenity of restored peace; and that you possessed with the Roman bishop a concord such as it is fitting to assign to the world as belonging to twin princes of the apostles.

For who, if he can be called Catholic, would not rejoice at the peace of churches so great and so distinguished, which the world awaits as though they were the sign of religion set in heaven, twin stars? Who would not rightly delight in the return of the sick and the stability of the healthy, when, with the other sheep saved within the folds, that one which had wandered through the fault of erring judgment is recalled amid the rejoicing of the heavenly sheepfolds?

Therefore, as fathers, guard the ecclesiastical discipline entrusted to you, even over us. Your concord requires as much instruction as example. What love shall we commend to the peoples if we do not know it in our rulers? What can appear sound in the body if what is at the head is tottering and maimed?

Therefore give a pious proclamation to those returning, lest anyone perish through obstinacy. Take care lest, if Rome should break away from the unity of your mind, so savage a beast ravage the watch-signals. Remember us, for if the sun should set upon your disagreement, the loss belongs to the East. Confirm for our knowledge, through the most faithful man, the very prosperous news which I mentioned above by a written reply, so that the Western Church, awaiting in your words the gift of a heavenly oracle which it rejoices to have received through a fellow disciple, may rejoice that it is multiplied for it through the teacher.

## EPISTOLA VIII. AVITUS VIENNENSIS EPISCOPUS EUSTORGIO EPISCOPO

[Note: To the bishop of Milan, as is shown by the letter of King Theoderic, which is the ninth of Book I of the *Variae* of Cassiodorus, and by Book II, letter 29, to Count Adela, in these words: “Moved by the petition of the most blessed man Eustorgius, bishop of the holy Milanese Church, we admonish you by our present address to strive to provide protection, while preserving civil authority, for the estates or honors of that Church situated within Sicily.” We have also interpreted an epigram of Ennodius, number 149, concerning the baptismal font of Saint Stephen and the water that comes through the columns:

> Here, beneath the roof, rain falls without cloud in serene showers,  
> and the pure face of heaven supplies the waters.  
> Rivers flow forth over the sacred marble,  
> and behold, the stone again gives birth to dew.  
> For the dry pergola pours forth liquid springs,  
> and again the heavenly water comes to what has been born.  
> Holy water flows forth through the ethereal recesses,  
> drawn by the ministry of the prophet Eustorgius.

That is, by the ministry of the bishop. There are Greeks by birth who, on the basis of the name, make Eustorgius a Greek. But the claim they add—that he was a disciple of John of Damascus—is absurd, since the dates do not agree.]

At the arrival of the present bearers, behold, for the second time already, gifts of your words have come from you, words to be desired and revered. They would, however, become more auspicious through a second success if they came in greater abundance.

Indeed, a twofold reason for congratulation was added in your letter. First, you show that your gracious favor toward me remains safe, displaying toward me the hereditary affection that existed in the heart of your predecessors. Second, you commanded me to serve in a matter in which, while you are concerned with protecting or [Note: These words seem to refer to the remains of captives whom Gundobad had taken from Italy into Gaul during the Ligurian war. Epiphanius of Pavia and Victor of Turin were sent by King Theoderic to redeem them and undertook the embassy, which Ennodius describes in the *Life of Epiphanius*.] restoring liberty, you judged me not unworthy of such a ministry.

Your Blessedness’s holy and spiritual command has therefore been fulfilled. You increased the reward through your prayer: through your intervention, the price you sent was made more precious. Through reverence for you, barbaric harshness was conquered by humility, cruelty by intercession, and greed by the offering.

We infer how you tame the harder hearts there through your preaching, since, though absent, you shatter rocks through the strength of your intervention. Through your work, the distress of our regions is visited; and the abundance of the flowing fountain issuing from the treasury of generosity, when it has watered Italy, sprinkles Gaul as well.

Therefore, after rendering the service of an honorable greeting, I commend myself to your intercession and favor with a prayer poured forth in vows: although I desire letters from you in every matter, I desire them especially concerning my own affairs, in which it may be fitting for you to act mercifully, so that through obedience the fruit of your works may also reach me.

# LETTER IX. AVITUS, BISHOP OF VIENNE

[Note: To the bishop of Arles, concerning whom, in addition to what we have noted elsewhere regarding Ennodius, the noteworthy eulogy of the monk Florianus in his letter to Nicetius of Trier may be added. “And also,” he says, “the companion of your crown, the blessedly remembered lord Caesarius, bishop of Arles, who lived piously among barbarians, peacefully amid wars, father of orphans, shepherd of the needy, who lost nothing through the outpouring of so great a fortune, demonstrating by word and deed the rule of Catholic discipline.” Messianus the presbyter also recounts his eagerness and confidence in God in feeding captives, and the ships full of grain sent to him at an opportune moment, when bread was lacking, by Gundobadus and Sigismund, kings of the Burgundians.]

## TO BISHOP CAESARIUS

[Col. 0229C] Although the very person of the venerable bearer naturally commends himself to hearts of brotherly charity, nevertheless the holy bishop Maximianus [Note: It is unclear of which see he was bishop. There was indeed at this time Maximianus, bishop of Perugia, whose name is read in the Roman synods of Pope Symmachus. But whether the matters here reported about the bishop Maximianus, his homeland, and his eye trouble can apply to him is uncertain.] particularly requested that this page of my service be sent to you through him; and it is clear that I ought rather to be commended by him to you than he by me.

And since he deigned to command me to disclose his needs in my words, I have undertaken to say nothing about the hardship of his journey. For however long, whether through the passage of time or the vastness of the road, a priest may leave the dwelling-place of his native land, he cannot be called a pilgrim or stranger wherever the Catholic Church can be found. Nor should the overthrow of his own region be exaggerated to you as something unknown, since your piety, which everywhere seeks openings for mercy, cannot be unaware where misery exists.

His principal [Col. 0230A] reason for coming, however, insofar as he deigns to assert it, is to seek out wherever possible a more skilled physician who may assist the weakness of his bodily eyes by some art of healing. Yet the vision of a devout mind, occupied rather with contemplating spiritual things and not excessively terrified by the blindness of the outward person, requires this care, as I have learned, with such moderation that he strives rather to satisfy his loved ones in this matter. At the same time, it should not seem that the capacity for his priestly office has been culpably diminished through neglect of health.

As I think, the hope of recovering his sight also derives from an example: namely, that our Tobit (Tobit 11:13–15), though his earthly eyes were clouded, nevertheless seeing what was invisible to the world, attentive to eternal light and already almost forgetful of being mortal, was restored by a hidden medicine in the angel, through an eye-wash of gall, to the sweetness of health. [Col. 0230B]

Therefore receive your brother with the reverence due to him, in your customary sincerity; and if anything is owed to the holy man as consolation, bestow it. Our common desire will be fulfilled if healing also comes to an illness of whatever kind. But if that should not happen, at least may the eye of his priestly conscience, subject to no blindness, recognize the incorruptible face of reciprocal piety.

# LETTER X. AVITUS, BISHOP OF VIENNE

[Note: To Magnus, bishop of Milan, successor to Eustorgius, who was mentioned immediately before, and predecessor of Datius. For when some, in listing the bishops of Milan, place Datius before Magnus, their order is reversed; this very letter disproves it.]

## TO BISHOP MAGNUS

Although I have earned none of the writings of your apostolate that might have prompted me to presume upon this very service, nevertheless, when you have not ordered me to address you, your reputation compels me to offer this page of dutiful service. [Col. 0230C] Indeed, if we do not deserve your sight, we are drawn toward your hearts by report, even while absence restrains us.

This is reinforced by the fact that you touch the hardships of the unhappy Gauls with such consolation of counsel and generosity that, under the appearance of that mercy which I have learned about, those who hasten to Italy to recognize the needs of their own people, after a long exile, when by Christ their guide they have been granted the sight of your person, rightly believe that they are entering their own homeland.

What remains of our region I commend to you: namely, the presbyter who bears this present service. Although he has undertaken the hardship of labor in order to ransom the daughter of one of his relatives, he has nevertheless been sent by a certain noble provincial, with my recommendation, so that he may seek out and recall, with the assistance of your intercession, the son of the aforesaid noble provincial, Avulus by name, who was taken as a hostage by Count Betanco about four years ago. [Col. 0231A] [Note: Theoderic, king of Italy. Besides this man, the province had other noble provincial sons in the same age, whom he calls Avuli or Avoli: for example, Avulus, bishop of Segesterica, and Avolus of Aquae Sextiae. The former subscribed the Fourth Synod of Orléans; the latter the Fifth.]

I ask that, through a gracious rescript of your blessedness, you may teach both those rejoicing there that their status as free persons can be restored and those longing here that a common avenue of writing is open to them.

[Col. 0231]

# LETTER XI. APOLLINARIS, BISHOP

[Note: Bishop of the see of Valence, Avitus’s elder brother. Agobard, writing to Emperor Louis concerning Jewish superstitions, says of him: “Saint Apollinaris, bishop of the Church of Valence—how great he was and is, not only the deeds written about him but also his frequent miracles, continuing to this day, testify in exalted fashion.” The subject of both letters is the same. It concerns a dream of Apollinaris, which came to him on the night when, in his absence at Vienne, the anniversary of his deceased sister was being celebrated.]

## TO AVITUS, BISHOP OF VIENNE, HIS BROTHER

Although tardy repentance has already paid a sufficient penalty, nevertheless I was not worthy to be present, even by a substitute’s service, on the feast-day that we ought to honor before all others. I neither showed the devotion I should have shown nor took care to offer satisfaction. To this, as I truly believe, I was admonished by you, blessed and most reverend lord, through a visitation of the spirit.

For on that holy night something—I do not know what—had clung to my hands, which a most radiant dove, sitting beside me but red in an unusual colour, desired. When I awoke, I recognized indeed the daily horror of my hands, but nevertheless remembered that I had been undeservedly cleansed. While I sorrowfully and anxiously turned this perplexity over in my mind, suddenly, as though struck by a spur, I immediately remembered the interest that had been left unpaid. Holy piety can judge what confusion and bitterness then pressed upon me.

Yet I was somewhat consoled by this hope: that the one who had deigned to admonish me might forgive me, so that, in pity toward me, I would not be deprived of every opportunity for service to the saint. My one petition, mingled with the duties owed in commemorating her, asks that she also breathe this portion of her indulgence into the perceptions of your judgment, which is already more than just toward me.

# LETTER XII. AVITUS, BISHOP OF VIENNE, TO APOLLINARIS, BISHOP

It is plainly evident how great the grace of God is in your merit—or how great a heap of virtues must be inferred—when even the error itself is so holy. For while a righteous accuser of himself tries to convict himself of what he could not have committed, the humility of the confessor increases his merit, not the truth of the confession his guilt.

You have exceeded custom, I confess; but you rightly deign always to remember this day by an increase of piety. A sweet solicitude has come from you, but forgetfulness has preceded it in a way that cannot be compared. The result, no doubt, appears deficient while observance remains intact; yet you have shown how spiritually you delight in exercising yourselves, since you grieved so much over having let it pass.

The holy revelation of your offense is truly secure in its dignity; and in the sleeper a punishment was found corresponding to the sin that had existed in the waking man. I speak the truth in Christ; I do not lie: when I read, with eyes giving birth to tears, the dream that you saw, the whole memory of the prior obligation came upon my mind. Through your visitation, I understood that we had been reminded to render the honor due.

But what I have thought about the revelation itself I shall state plainly. Thus, then, you say:

“For on that holy night on which the burial of our common sister was being celebrated, something—I do not know what—had clung to my hands, which a most radiant dove, sitting beside me but red in an unusual colour, desired.”

But when your piety, sitting beside you and not flying far away, settled through swift recollection, you rightly felt that this dove signified the debt which you, most holy and most dutiful toward your relatives—you, I say—owed. It was most radiant, since you shine with simplicity; it was reddened in an unusual color, since, being uniquely innocent, you blush as though pierced by your own goads.

You have therefore increased, as was said above, the customary interest; yet what you thought was lacking did not fail to belong to custom. For on the very night which Christ roused you and did not permit you to forget, an offering from the abundance of the preceding year still shone forth from you. Thus, from a certain irrigation of heavenly blessing, what you give each year is sufficient for many. I ask God that your piety may someday render this also to me.

# LETTER XIII. AVITUS, BISHOP OF VIENNE

[Note: Contumeliosus was bishop of Riez in the Second Province, as the subscriptions of the Fourth Synod of Arles, the Synod of Carpentras, and the Second Synod of Vaison show. That he was an educated man is indicated by the fact that Avitus chose him among the critics and judges of his books. His uncommendable morals, however, were established both by the judgment of Caesarius and his synod and by that of the Apostolic See, whose sentence removed Contumeliosus from the episcopate for his disgraceful conduct and confined him in a monastery, as can be seen in the first volume of the councils of Gaul.]

## TO BISHOP CONTUMELIOSUS

[Col. 0232C] As the days of whatever vow I have draw near, with you interceding for me before God, so too the desire and shame of my heart contend. For I ask a blessing upon an unfinished work. There would be at least some excuse if the greatness of the work concealed and covered the fault of my negligence. But now what could be more misshapen than something at once small and unpolished?

There is therefore one thing that consoles my trembling heart with bold encouragement: namely, that, if God deigns to hear us, everything must be turned for the better by your arrival. For there is nothing you could not either set right by praying or excuse by pleading your case. Only, just as we are certain of the intention of your proven piety, so may we rejoice in the advance notice of the visitation we await.

[Col. 0232D]

# LETTER XIV. VICTURIUS, BISHOP

[Note: Victurius of Grenoble. I do not doubt that he is the Victorius mentioned in Letter 6, and he is likewise called this in Letter 16 and elsewhere. Here he replies to Avitus of Vienne, the bishop of his province and apparently his suffragan, concerning what should be decided about a man who had married the sister of his deceased wife. This man was a citizen of Grenoble, named Vincomalus, as appears from Letter 14 and Letter 16. At the same time and in the same Burgundian kingdom, there was a similar incestuous case involving Stephanus, an official appointed over the royal treasury by King Sigismund, who had likewise married the sister of his deceased wife. This matter is treated in the First Council of Lyon and in the Life of Saint Apollinaris, bishop of Valence.]

## TO AVITUS, BISHOP

To separate the darnel from the wheat in the Lord’s threshing-floor, the winnowing-fans of your ordination must be sought. For the one who appointed you to hold the primacy of the chief place wished us to carry out in action what you command, and wished you to command what must be done.

For, as has now been reported, one of our citizens married the sister of his deceased wife many years ago. I heard this accusation now in the presence of many. The accuser of so great a crime did not describe the character of the atrocious deed by secret whispering, but brought the charge before the very man who had committed it. With the same boldness with which he had presumed the illicit act, the wretched man almost did not deny it when you were dispensing judgment.

Therefore prescribe under what condition he must abstain: whether both should mourn alike, whether separation should be imposed, or what form of penance should be required. For, as I think, it is no less wrong to take one’s wife’s sister in marriage than to take one’s brother’s wife. Yet, as I have suggested, determine what seems right, since, apart from your ruling, I scarcely know what ought to be pronounced in such a case. I withdraw him from communion—or permit him to remain—only if I am strengthened by your authority.

# LETTER XV. AVITUS, BISHOP OF VIENNE, TO BISHOP VICTURIUS

It is a mark of proven and supreme piety that you consider my counsel also worth consulting concerning matters belonging to your pontificate. You show that you do this, as you said, not from a spirit of uncertainty but from affection.

Therefore, in opposition to the fault you reported in your letter, I think you are rightly moved. For what layman would not perceive that a marriage arising from a relationship of affinity cannot take place without a serious stain? Accordingly, although a most justified grief arising from the necessity of strictness weighs upon your solicitude, it is nevertheless salutarily intensified in temporal matters for the sake of the one whom we desire to save in eternal matters.

[Note: The Greeks and Latins formerly followed a similar discipline in restraining incestuous unions. Concerning men married to two sisters, Saint Basil explains the Greek custom, which had the force of law, in Letter 197 to Diodorus:

“Ἐάν τις πάθει ἀκαθαρσίας ποτὲ κρατηθεὶς ἐκπέσῃ πρὸς δυοῖν ἀδελφοῖν ἄθεσμον κοινωνίαν, μήτε γάμον ἡγεῖσθαι τοῦτο, μηθ` ὅλως εἰς ἐκκλησιαστικὸν πλήρωμα παραδέχεσθαι, πρότερον ἢ διαλύσαι ἀπ` ἀλλήλων.”

“If anyone, overcome at some time by an impulse of impurity, falls into an unlawful union with two sisters, this is to be considered neither a marriage nor is such a person to be admitted at all into the ecclesiastical assembly until they have been separated from one another.”

Among the Latins, the custom was as follows; since many sources agree, the canon is Canon 30 of the Council of Epaon: “For incestuous unions we reserve absolutely no forgiveness unless they have healed the adultery by separation.” Among incestuous persons it counts the case: “If anyone has taken his wife’s sister.”

Avitus therefore distinguishes four elements in this matter: excommunication, separation, public penance, and reconciliation. Thus the mark of excommunication is to be placed upon them until they separate; once separated, they are to perform penance so that they may receive the grace of reconciliation.]

Therefore a man married to two sisters must not be struck with irrevocable anathema, but, after the prescribed observances have been set out, must meanwhile be separated from the Church. And since you report that he entered into the illicit union with his second wife many years ago, let the crime of incest, which has carried on its revelry with impunity for so long, suffice.

Here you should have no hesitation on account of fear of divorce; separation is rightly judged legitimate wherever a criminal union has existed. Therefore, if it seems good, impose upon both of them, while they persist in such unhappy obstinacy, the mark of excommunication, until by a public profession of penance they abandon the criminal relationship. Then, with your compassion, let them receive the grace of reconciliation as an example of fear and correction.

I have offered to your sincerity what I believed reasonable, since you considered it important enough to command me. [Note: It is within the power and discretion of the bishop, toward penitents, after observing their contrition, to act more humanely and indulgently and to moderate the order of severity, so that he may receive them into communion sooner. See Canon 2 of the Synod of Ancyra and Canon 10 of the Second Council of Arles. On the other hand, the Fourth Council of Carthage, Canon 75, decrees that more negligent penitents are to be reconciled more slowly.]

It belongs to your authority, after observing the contrition of those who have erred, to moderate the order of severity. Nevertheless, if they are truly contrite, I think they will comply with the conditions written above.

# LETTER XVI. AVITUS, BISHOP OF VIENNE, TO BISHOP VICTORIUS

[Col. 0234B] You satisfy both prudence and affection when, by asking me something, you deign to burden me no less than you honor me. Yet you rightly knew that you could judge me, if not by my expertise, at least by my friendship: never has my reply suggested anything to you except what I desire to be preserved by the Church of Vienne.

As you reported, Vincomalus has followed our son the deacon. May God grant that you overcome evil with good. I saw a man exceedingly coarse, whose wretchedness makes it clear that scarcely anyone can pity him. Young in virtue, old in faith, he is cold with age and hot with adultery. What more need be said? In this corrupt passage, the sense is materially uncertain; it is to be hoped that he may be permitted to separate by a willing divorce rather than perish.

For when he was reproved for the crime of incest, more by exhortation than by harshness, he accused our severity solely by pleading delay, alleging that we had condemned only belatedly his thirty-year partnership in an illicit union. Here, I confess, I yielded to the shameless man: namely, by postponing the sentence out of affection for him, we had preferred to leave the correction of the man to his own contrition and will; and consequently it was just that, after so many years, he should now restrain even criminal behavior, since, with the advance of old age, he ought already to have curbed what was lawful.

At this, as I believed he felt it, he groaned—not contrite, but confused—and began to promise for a little while that the woman of his unworthy cohabitation would immediately be prevented from approaching or appearing before him. I replied by advising him to make these promises to you and, repentant of his deed, to ask to be released by the same means through which he had been bound.

Nevertheless, since you commanded me to disclose whatever seemed right to me, [Note: Here he moderates his earlier sentence and decides more leniently. Above he required two things, separation and public penance; now he is content with separation alone, and concerning penance he suggests that the man be urged to undertake it but not compelled to receive it.] let the separation of the persons suffice for your censure. Let the unhappy marriage be severed by a more innocent divorce; let the end of the evil suffice as the fruit of strictness.

Nor should his promise be considered trustworthy, since his life has proved untrustworthy. Let the amendment be believed only through the very guarantors by whose intervention the earlier fault will be relaxed. As for what concerns penance, let him meanwhile be urged to perform it, but not compelled to accept it. His crimes are enough for the unhappy man; and, when he rejects it, let no burden be imposed upon one who, with so unstable a mind, ought scarcely to have undertaken it even if he had asked for it.

Let treachery cease in its weakness; let an increase of rebellion not be added to the accumulation of carnality. If you command, I shall offer a brief conclusion. Once shaken free of the crime, let him be received into pardon; let him undergo penance when he has lost the opportunity to sin; let him make his profession when he has lost the will.

# LETTER XVII. AVITUS, BISHOP OF VIENNE

[Note: Viventiolus later became bishop of Lyon, as Letter 52 will show. At this time, having come to Lyon from the Jura wilderness and visited Apollinaris, Avitus’s brother and the newly appointed bishop, who was ill there, he also sought to console Avitus himself through a messenger sent for that purpose. Avitus thanks him for this, as well as for the chair he sent; in return for the chair, he prays for him to receive a cathedra—that is, a bishopric—which he later obtained at Lyon.]

## TO THE PRESBYTER VIVENTIOLUS

What you have done is full of piety in two ways: by going to Lyon and by sending someone here, you took care to inquire there after one sick brother and to visit another who was anxious here. Nor will it be thought that your purpose was interrupted when you turned this spiritual service toward a religious brother to whom you owed more in affection and honour, even though the sick man had not asked for it. For the novelty of a priestly brotherhood would have required encouragement even if anxiety had not required consolation.

Therefore cease entirely from excusing the labor you undertook with a just fatigue, lest you appear to have erred by the uncertainty of attempting or determining this matter.

As for how I should properly thank you for the gift you sent, I feel that I must seek it more through prayers than through letters. You also draw human desires toward the place of your dwelling with a certain elegance when you say that such things can be brought forth from the wilderness. Without doubt, through the care, instruction, and teaching of your person, even if it were found to be a wilderness, it would become paradise.

Therefore, in return for the chair you sent, praying that you may receive a cathedra in exchange, I ask you to cherish with spiritual consolation and priestly instruction the school of our beloved common Eugendus, which is wavering and, as far as its condition is concerned, deprived of a bishop. [Note: This is now the monastery of Saint Claudius in the Jura mountains. We supplied the name Eugendus, which was absent from our manuscript, from the Thuane manuscripts. This letter also teaches us when he died. Avitus therefore advises Viventiolus to take up the school, vacant and deprived of its rector, so that, approved as a presbyter in the second rank, he may be advanced to greater governance—that is, to the first rank of bishops.]

Nor should this hold you back from extending your charity [alternative reading: withdraw you from it]: namely, that, as I think, their request for your care in the matter of ordination is made more from simplicity than from an intention to abuse it, and less worthily than it should be. We desire, with God’s favor, that you be advanced to greater helm and, rising to double the five talents by adding to the two, be proved faithful in the second rank and carry this great secret of conscience to the peoples, so that where fraternal dissension might have made a wilderness in others, fatherly affection may strive to preserve a monastery in you.

[Note: It cannot be determined how much is missing at this point. I conjecture that the title of the letter was to Pope Symmachus. By “the bishop of the city of Aelia,” I understand Elias, who then governed that see. Thus, when Avitus wrote to him to obtain a gift of the Holy Cross, he also sought Symmachus’s intercession, through which he might obtain what he desired. But Avitus’s letter to Elias is missing.]

# LETTER XVIII. * * * * *

Therefore, even if we suppose that a relic of the sacred Cross is with you, we nevertheless believe that this particular generosity should be requested from the holy bishop of the city of Aelia. He truly preserves the genuine and inviolate purity of this sacrament through the administration of the place, and is powerful enough to grant us the desired gift in such a way as to free us from every uncertainty of hesitation.

For this reason I earnestly ask, through this page of service, that your apostolate grant its bearer a letter to the priest of the aforesaid church, so that a double assurance may come to us: either the authority of your see, consulted by the foremost churches of the world, or the humanity of that man, entreated by us, may present it.

[Col. 0236]

# LETTER XIX. DOMNUS GUNDOBADUS, KING, TO AVITUS, BISHOP OF VIENNE

[Note: Avitus, as Agobard testifies and the example makes clear, was accustomed frequently to discuss the faith with King Gundobadus, not only in person but also to reply to him by letters when he was absent.]

I have decided to consult your holiness concerning a prophetic passage, a copy of which I have appended below. Therefore deign to declare in your letter whether these times have already come or are still future:

“From Zion the law will go forth, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem; and he will judge among many peoples and rebuke mighty nations far away; and they will beat their swords into plowshares and their spears into pruning-hooks; and nation will no longer lift up the sword against nation, nor will they any longer stand to wage war” (Isaiah 2:3–4).

And:

“Each man will rest under his own vine and under his own fig tree, and there will be no one to make them afraid” (3 Kings 3:21).

# LETTER XX. AVITUS, BISHOP OF VIENNE

[Note: Avitus, as Agobard testifies and the example makes clear, was accustomed frequently to discuss the faith with King Gundobadus, not only in person but also to reply to him by letters when he was absent.]

## TO KING LORD GUNDOBADUS

Although you ought to consult priests more learned in prophetic interpretation—among whom I do not dare to count myself—I nevertheless desire to satisfy your command by obedience, even if I cannot answer through learning. Thus what you command me to explain is lengthy even in its text, not to mention its exposition, and requires more leisure for discussion than the concise speed of an epistolary reply allows.

Therefore I shall answer as briefly as I can. The passage from the prophet Isaiah that you appended at the end of your letter has already long since been fulfilled—that is, at the time of the Lord’s incarnation.

For when it says, “From Zion the law will go forth, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Isaiah 2:3), consider more carefully whether any authority for promulgating a law remains to be awaited. [Note: He takes “the Word of the Lord” to mean God the Word. This interpretation is foreign to Isaiah’s meaning in this passage and is refuted by our Theodoret:

“Here he calls it the word not God the Word, but the teaching of the Word of God. For God the Word did not go forth from Zion, but in Zion he taught the truth.”

Greek: “Λόγον γὰρ ἐνταῦθα οὐ Λόγον Θεὸν καλεῖ, ἀλλὰ τὴν τοῦ Θεοῦ Λόγου διδασκαλίαν. Οὐ γὰρ ὁ Θεὸς Λόγος ἐκ Σιὼν ἐξελήλυθεν, ἀλλ᾽ ἐν τῷ Σιὼν τὴν ἀλήθειαν ἐξεπαίδευσεν.”]

Certainly, after the Word of God became flesh so that, through the birth of a body, he might dwell among us, if another word is still to be expected from Jerusalem, the one Word mentioned above is not unique. Accordingly, in the passage you cited, the speech of the Father—Christ—and the Christian law were unquestionably proclaimed.

For since there are two laws, namely the Jewish law, which came first, and ours, which follows, and since the former was already called ancient even in the time of the prophets, you see that Isaiah announces only this latter law, which arose through the calling of the nations and the instruction of Christ the teacher.

The passage continues: “And he will judge among the nations and rebuke many peoples.” These are the peoples whom our Lord established by judging and converted by rebuking, gathering them from every nation of the earth into one Church.

As for the words, “They will beat their swords into plowshares and their spears into pruning-hooks,” although this may be understood to some extent of the Lord’s bodily age, during which unshaken peace flourished throughout the world, it applies more clearly to Christian believers. Among the greater number of these, the use of weapons has ceased and is absent—the weapons with which the malice of the first birth had armed them for the destruction of humanity—and a second birth has converted them to the uses of salvation and life-giving cultivation.

For when the Gospel proclaims concerning the end of the world, “Nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom” (Mark 13:8), and when from the very signs of evil we gather that the end of the world is now almost at hand, unless what I said above is understood figuratively of Catholics, I do not know why, after the end of the world, the blunted edges of weapons would be changed into mattocks and plowshares.

But the passage that you ordered to be added at the bottom of the reading—“Each man will rest under his vine and under his fig tree” (3 Kings 4:23)—I suggest neither belongs to the same reading nor pertains to the matter about which you consulted me. Yet in ancient times it was frequently granted to the Jewish people, according to the changing distinction of their merit, either as correction for sin or, again, withdrawn as punishment for succeeding faults.

# LETTER XXI. AVITUS, BISHOP OF VIENNE

[Note: This is one of those dialogues and conferences which, from Agobard’s words, we learn Avitus frequently held with King Gundobadus. These took place sometimes with the king himself and sometimes, as here, with him present together with his Arian bishops. The reason why this discussion was initiated is not stated. He is content to mention a little about the outcome of the dispute, promising to set forth the whole sequence of the altercation in person when he comes to Sigismund.]

## TO LORD SIGISMUND

[Col. 0238A]

You blame me for not reporting to you what took place in the royal conference. I had reserved it for your arrival at the proper festival, because the length and complexity of the debate truly do not permit everything to be reported to you in due order through the service of a letter.

For, insofar as I think I perceived the mind of my lord, your father, a fierce contest burns in his eagerness, under the contrived appearance of leisure. What we thought had been laid aside in the abandonment of hostility and moderated by silence, seeking sudden opportunity rather than repose, did not cease because of the shortness of the truce but lay hidden. So much so that even the weapons of controversy, which had almost already failed in our region, are sought from outside, nor does the heat of his meditation wait until the return of his envoys.

When I returned from the journey of which you know, expecting nothing meanwhile concerning such propositions, his keen intelligence set to plowing through the exceedingly tangled knots of the questions’ falsehoods over a long interval, and the matter was stirred up. A forceful treatment burns through an extended disputation; yet it remained calm, introducing nothing turbulent from the arrogance of domination. He took care, with prudent foresight of the necessities and of the matter, that whatever the outcome of the contest, he would not allow the defeated party to suffer disgrace.

What more need be said? Without boasting I tell you freely: concerning the proposals, as it seems to me, something was put forward that could have pleased you had you heard it. Yet I fear that it satisfied the judgment of the hearer more than it pleased his enthusiasm.

But when, by God’s favor, I have been granted your presence, I shall explain to you personally the whole sequence of the altercation. For now, gather the course of the speech from its conclusion, and from what he commanded me as I was departing, judge whether he had been moved toward a reply. He ordered me to write down and send to him whatever testimony from our Scriptures I had brought forward in response to his questions—or any other passage that might have occurred—and to arrange it according to each point to which I had adapted it during the conference.

When he declared that most of this was unknown to him, he added simply that I should send such written material to his priests—or rather, to speak more accurately, to those whom he called his deceivers, his followers. From this your piety can infer that, although he was an intent opponent, yet as a wise judge he did not regard the arguments as weak or without force: they had the power to weary the position of his own people, even if he did not wish it corrected.

I, however, though I knew that one must often refuse to yield to powers, and even to kings, for the sake of truth, long wavered in uncertainty over whether I should obey. I knew—and certainly feared the man’s disposition—that I would never satisfy him by these means, and that I must guard against him no less than against an enemy, while the opposing line encircles private hatreds with a public siege.

But by the height of eminence in which God has granted you strength, by your zeal for religion, and by the privilege of your authority, drive away the discord fortified with walls; scatter the fury in the camps, as across the fields of Emath, more than civil wars.

For since we have long been wearied by the double burden both of the complaints of those who cry out and of the stubbornness of those who do not listen, it is just—if you deign to do so—that your severity should either counsel those who must be corrected there or sympathize here with those who are ashamed.

# LETTER XXII. AVITUS, BISHOP OF VIENNE

[Note: This should, I think, be joined with Letter 44, written to the same Apollinaris, son of Sidonius, although in that letter he is called “illustrious,” whereas here he is called “most illustrious.” At this time the people of Auvergne were subject to the Visigoths and to their king Alaric, son of Euric, to whom they had been surrendered by the emperor Nepos under treaty. Thus the lords whom they obeyed here were the Visigoths. Gregory of Tours testifies that, at the battle of Vouillé, where Alaric was killed by Clovis, Apollinaris fought together with his people of Auvergne.]

## TO THE MOST ILLUSTRIOUS APOLLINARIS

[Col. 0239B] Your piety has done something that causes concern, both by extending your concern about us and by believing that we are concerned about you. For when news of your departure reached us, we weighed it with the utmost fear and trembling, because various messengers were saying that you had all been summoned together at the command of the lords whom you serve.

The consciousness of my sins therefore made it seem to me that the fewer of you remained, the more there was to fear for those who remained. But thanks be to God, who has recalled your people to joy and you to your homeland through a prosperous return.

May Christ henceforth preserve this freedom for our common desires, so that it may be possible for us both to console ourselves in your absence and to reach your presence.

# LETTER XXIII. AVITUS, BISHOP OF VIENNE

[Note: To Elias, called the bishop of the city of Aelia in Letter 18. Avitus thanks him for the gift he had sought in his earlier letter: namely, a fragment of the sacred Cross, to be valued, as he says, not for its size but for the price of salvation. Paulinus of Nola likewise wrote in Letter 15, when he sent Severus and Bassula a small fragment of that same Cross, which he had received at Jerusalem through Melania: “Receive,” he says, “a great gift in a small thing, and in the almost atom-sized fragment of a little shaft, take a defense for the present and a pledge of eternal salvation.”]

## TO THE POPE OF JERUSALEM

[Col. 0239C]

Your apostolate exercises the primacy granted by the Divinity, and, because it holds the foremost place in the universal Church, strives to demonstrate this not by privileges alone but by merits. Your see adorns our law, and your person adorns your see. Therefore, bound to your graciousness by a debt of generosity, I discharge through the one by whom these gifts reached us [Col. 0240A] the vows of my gratitude—gifts to be valued not by the price of their quantity but by the rewards of salvation.

For you have enriched the poverty of the world’s farthest regions with the treasures of sanctification, and, sharing with us the light of the radiant East, have touched the darkness of the setting sun. The brilliance of your gift wiped from our provinces the rust of sluggish religion; by the irrigation of an ever-flowing good it rewarded our faith with contemplation, when, after your piety had opened the inner chambers of the heavenly treasures, we observed whatever Catholics are commanded to believe.

Pray for what remains: that you may have sent such things to those who are worthy. Commend us to the mysteries that you have judged fit to entrust to us. By these things may our devotion be built up, and our kingdom defended; so that, having received from you the saving pledge, you may render fit for the heavenly dwelling those whom you did not consider unworthy of the earthly Jerusalem. [Col. 0240B]

## LETTER XXIV. AVITUS, BISHOP OF VIENNE, TO STEPHANUS, BISHOP

[Note: To the bishop of Lyon, who, as the ancient records show, succeeded Bishop Rusticius and was himself succeeded by Viventiolus. Lupicinus, whom more recent writers usually place after Stephanus, is situated in those same records before Rusticius, after Patientius. As I have noted elsewhere, a letter of Ennodius to this Stephanus survives in Book III, Letter 17. Ruricius of Limoges also writes to him, if I am not mistaken, in Book II, Letter 51, although the title omits the word “bishop.”]

However attentive the servants of the Lord’s cultivation may be, amid their constant zeal for planting there always arise things that ought to be cut down. Thus, through the unceasing efforts of your vigilance, the profit of acquiring salvation increases most opportunely for these works.

But [Note: In these times the Visigoths and Burgundians encouraged the Arian heresy in Gaul, both peoples having been infected by that stain. Hence Avitus had frequent contests with the Arians concerning the faith, and published books against the Arians. The name of the Donatists, however, remained almost entirely within the boundaries of Africa, where it had arisen, and scarcely ever spread to other peoples, except Rome, where they were called the Montenses.]

amid the tares of Arian offspring, spread through a numerous—and, what is worse, widespread—corruption, I cannot determine from what source there has appeared the face of the enemy’s seed, not indeed new but sufficiently rare, or what wind has carried transmarine contagions to the shining world. But with God governing you, this stain, supported by no assistance, is little to be feared. A storm does not gain strength from multitude, nor does a light breeze complete a shipwreck.

Therefore, bury the name of the Donatists immediately with a life-giving blessing, so that it cannot live long in a foreign place. At the very birth of its fuel, let the fire of this wandering spark grow cold. And lest even the smoke of its reputation stain the nose of innocent Gaul, [Note: Hands were laid upon those converted from heresy, so that they might receive the Holy Spirit, whom they could not have received from heretics. The First Council of Arles, canon 8: “If someone comes to the Church from heresy, and they ascertain that he has been baptized in the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, hands alone shall be laid upon him, so that he may receive the Holy Spirit.” Leo the Great, to Rusticus of Narbonne, inquiry 18, concerning those baptized as infants by heretics: “They are not to be rebaptized, but through the laying on of hands, after the power of the Holy Spirit has been invoked—whom they could not have received from heretics—they are to be joined to the Catholics.” The same, to Nicetas of Aquileia, chapter 7: “Those who received baptism from heretics are to be confirmed solely by the invocation of the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands, so that they may obtain from Catholic priests what no one receives from heretics; for, as Augustine says in Book III of *On Baptism against the Donatists*, chapter 16, the Holy Spirit is said to be given only in the Catholic Church through the laying on of hands.” This passage therefore concerns that laying on of hands by which the Holy Spirit is given, lest anyone suppose that it should perhaps be interpreted of another kind.]

apply the laying on of hands to the person concerning whom you have written, [Col. 0241A] while henceforth forbidding mention of the name itself, if she is converted from the heart; [Note: As though he were saying that she should also have been anointed, unless she had already been anointed. For, in receiving heretics, in addition to the laying on of hands, a sealing with chrism was also customary. Notable examples of this practice occur in Gregory of Tours: Lantilde, the sister of King Clovis, who was converted from the Arian heresy and anointed with chrism, Book II of the *History of the Franks*, chapter 31; Brunichilde and Gosvinta, sisters, Book IV, chapters 27 and 28; King Hermenichild of the Goths in Spain, Book V, chapter 39; and finally Chararic, king of the Suebi in Galicia, concerning whom the same Gregory says in Book I, chapter 6 of *The Miracles of Saint Martin*: “The king, having confessed the unity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, was anointed with chrism together with his entire household.” Chrismation was otherwise administered to converts when they had not been chrismated in heresy.]

which, if she truly was involved in the profession of the schism mentioned above, was evidently sealed with chrism together with the ministry of baptism. This much is plainly observed by them in that region.

In that region, then, may God first grant that all who belong to this error be corrected; and thereafter, since they are as far removed from us in sect as in homeland, may those who do not wish to be saved be unable to pass over to our side and be acknowledged.

[Note: He seems to say that she should also have been chrismated, unless she had already been chrismated. For, in receiving heretics, besides the laying on of hands, the sealing with chrism was also customary. See the examples cited above.]

[Note: According to the ancient custom, he joins the sealing with chrism to baptism and separates it from the laying on of hands, by which the Holy Spirit is given. This matter was discussed at length elsewhere, when we explained the canon of Orange. That Avitus says the Donatists were accustomed to chrismate along with baptism is clear from Optatus and Augustine. Among them, as in the Catholic Church, three rites were celebrated: baptism, chrismation, and the laying on of hands. When they returned to the Church, the first two were not repeated but remained untouched, contrary to their own practice, since they condemned the baptism and chrism of Catholics and repeated both. Optatus, Book VII: “What was anointed by you, we preserve just as we received it.” And elsewhere: “You led people astray, rebaptized them, and anointed them again.” Only the third rite—that is, the laying on of hands—was repeated, for the reason stated above: heretics cannot give the Holy Spirit. Saint Augustine, *On the Baptism of the Donatists*, Book III: “The laying on of hands, however, may be repeated, unlike baptism.” For what else is it than prayer over a person? For through prayer and the laying on of hands, those baptized by the leaders of the Church received the Holy Spirit according to apostolic custom.]

## LETTER XXV. AVITUS, BISHOP OF VIENNE, TO APOLLINARIS, BISHOP

[Note: To his brother, the bishop of the city of Valence, as was stated in the note to Letter 11. This letter should be compared with Sidonius, Letter 15 of Book IV, to Elaphius. Sidonius, likewise invited to the dedication of a new church, promises with equal elegance that he will attend and predicts the multitude of guests flocking from every direction.]

You command, and it is the fulfillment of my desire, that I attend the dedication—both its new rites and its customary observances—with the zeal appropriate to a double celebration. But I fear that what you have held for so long may now hold us back. [Col. 0241B] Nevertheless, pray that the outcome may correspond to our equal desire.

Unless perhaps you count as more fully expended that which still burns in your spirits while the pantry remains cold. Therefore, although you say that you invited only a few, although you rejoice that, after dismissing the courtly assembly, you have been relieved: if I am given any opportunity to set out, you will invite even those who arrive unwillingly.

God will provide food for the multitude of your guests. There the food of the poor will be increased, while the jar of oil and the vessel of flour remain undiminished. There, even if there are only five loaves, it will be enough to have provided two fish. After these experiences of miracles, I faithfully promise this: since Christ will certainly not be absent from the gathering of his poor, the more thousands of peoples you collect, the more baskets you will carry away.

As for our son, who, as you write, graciously seeks mutual reconciliation, be his surety yourselves: if he wishes to act with a peaceful intention, I do so also with friendship; if he asks that discord be removed, I wish concord to be [Col. 0242A] confirmed. Yet, as a man of my order, who ought neither to deceive nor to be deceived, he should not begin by trusting a Catholic senator solely in order to be found off guard.

## LETTER XXVI. AVITUS, BISHOP OF VIENNE, TO A CERTAIN PERSON

[Note: Apparently to a bishop whose name he spares, reproving him for excessive openness because he had revealed our secrets to the uninitiated—that is, to heretics. Concerning a bishop converted from heresy, he replies that, if nothing else obstructs, such a man may be admitted in our Church to any grade of the priesthood. By a similar example, we read that Symphosius and Dictinius, heretical bishops who condemned the Priscillianist heresy, were received with their rank retained at the First Council of Toledo. Concerning heretical clerics who come to the Catholic faith, the First Council of Orléans, canon 10, made this general provision: “If they are faithfully converted and profess the Catholic faith in its entirety, they shall assume office if their bishop judges them worthy of it.”]

I received your letters after a long interval. In them you show that you know I must preserve charity, however sorrowful I may be, and yet you ought not therefore to believe me negligent. For God is truly my witness that, from the greatness of your affection, my grief and sighing are greater still.

I cannot, without causing you great pain, suggest how seriously your holiness, forgive me, has been overtaken by excessive openness. You armed your adversaries with your own weapons; you betrayed our secrets to the uninitiated; you sang the Lord’s song [Col. 0242B] in a foreign land (Ps. 136:4). You brought forth, like the vessels of the Lord (Dan. 5:3), for the spectacle of a banquet, things that invite mockery; you exposed them, like Noah stripped naked (Gen. 9:22), to laughter that will never be free of disgrace.

If they retain or follow these things, a dangerous quality has crept in against the truth. Certainly, if what you thought ought to be made public was precious to you, the fault of King Hezekiah ought at least to have frightened you (2 Kings 20:13), for the prophet rebuked him when he sinned through the odor of vainglory (Isa. 39:5–6).

But since you say that this trepidation has been wiped away from the mind of one who is converting, it is right that we should speak with rejoicing: “This is the change of the right hand of the Most High” (Ps. 77:11). For the savage beasts contradict you pointlessly, however threateningly, when God protects you—beasts who are weak, and, what is more remarkable, lack teeth and feed upon frenzies; for, while they lament that the disciples of their destruction are perishing, they begin to destroy their teachers as well.

Such gains are profitably sought before God and human beings. Nothing coercive is involved in receiving one who seeks it: the blessing given confirms the devotion of the willing. It is not robbery but grace; what Christ deigns to receive cannot be called something we have seized.

As for the rest, since you believe that I should advise you concerning the status of the convert, I determine, by divine inspiration, that a person may rise to any rank of the priesthood, provided that there is nothing in the condition of marriage or in any rule or moral circumstance that prohibits clerical office.

Why should he not feed Christ’s flock who has wisely recognized that the sheep he had been feeding were not sheep? Since he is neither a thief nor a robber, why should he not rightly become a shepherd, having chosen to enter through the doors to the altars? Why should he not stand upright in our priesthood who, out of love of humility, wished to be cast down from his former position? Let a true priest arise from a layman who is content to become a layman from a deceitful priest. Let him hold his own people in our Church who despised another’s in his former one.

The fullness of heavenly grace will grant increase to such great blessings, so that the one who has obtained this may begin to rejoice over what he lamented, while the other, becoming more fruitful day by day, may understand that he has surpassed those whom he left behind.

## LETTER XXVII. DICTATED BY BISHOP AVITUS UNDER THE NAME OF LORD SIGISMUND, KING, TO SYMMACHUS, POPE OF THE CITY

[Note: Through the deacon Julianus, King Sigismund asks Pope Symmachus for sacred relics; he had already received others from him some time earlier. Pope Symmachus died during the consulship of Senator, in the year of Christ 514. Gundobad, Sigismund’s father, died two years later, under the consulship of Peter. Yet Sigismund is called “king” in the inscription of the letter. It is therefore clear that he had obtained the title of king while his father was still alive. Fredegar, in the Epitome, chapter 34: “Gundobad’s son Sigismund was elevated to kingship near the city of Geneva, at the village of Quadruvium, by order of his father”; the Chronicle of Marius likewise confirms this in the following words: “During the consulships of Florentius and Anthemius”—that is, in the year between the deaths of Symmachus and Gundobad—“the monastery of Agaunum was built by King Sigismund.” Yet during those consulships Hormisdas, Symmachus’s successor, was already bishop of Rome. Sigismund therefore was not first called king in that year, since the inscription of this letter indicates that he already bore the name in the time of Symmachus.]

Since I do not presume to refuse the sacred pledges of relics by which, through me, you enriched your Gaul with spiritual recompense when petitioners requested them, I too must ask for the protection of the saints from the irrigating spring of your apostolate.

Although there is still among us, from your gift, something that ought to be celebrated through devotion to the Catholic religion, it is nevertheless fitting that this too should be understood as an act of proper devotion: through the services of written correspondence directed to you, we seek those conversations by which your pontificate has instructed me when present through admonitions, and won me when absent through intercessions.

Nor does the present page encompass every service that the opportunity has found; rather, by sending to you the venerable man Julianus as a deacon and bearer of letters, we hasten to represent ourselves in spirit before the prelate of the universal Church.

The memory of benefits increases desire. Nor can those things ever be erased from my thoughts which your pontifical kindness and royal courtesy bestowed upon us in your Italy: after familiarity, which is to be preferred to every advantage of generosity, loosened the way for my return there, while here it bound affection more tightly.

May a more attentive prayer be offered for what remains on your behalf. For as the number of sheep increases, so does the shepherd’s watchfulness. By constant remembrance, present us at the sacred thresholds of the apostles; and, for as long as I live, obtain for your special preacher, where you secured his beginning, the advancement he needs.

Write to us as often as possibility or freedom allows, so that your teaching and safety may flourish for us. And, as we have hoped above, grant us the protection of venerable relics that we may seek. Through their veneration, may we deserve always to have blessed Peter in his power and you in his gift. [Col. 0244B]

## LETTER XXVIII. AVITUS, BISHOP OF VIENNE, TO LORD GUNDOBAD, KING

[Note: The deacon Florus calls this the *Book on the Divinity of Christ* whenever he cites this letter in connection with Paul’s words to the Romans, Galatians, and Hebrews. In it, responding to a question from Gundobad, Avitus demonstrates that Christ the Lord possessed eternal divinity before he became human, against the heresy of those who maintained that he began from Mary. Augustine, concerning this heresy, says in Heresy 44: “The Paulianists, from Paul of Samosata, say that Christ did not always exist, but assert that his beginning was when he was born from Mary; nor do they consider him anything more than a human being. This heresy once belonged to a certain Artemon; but after it had died out, it was revived by Paul and later confirmed by Photinus, so that they are now more commonly called Photinians than Paulianists.” That Photinians, or Paulianists, troubled Gaul in this period is indicated by the Second Council of Arles, chapter 16, and by Sidonius, Letter 12 of Book IV, to Patientius, bishop of Lyon. Hence the blessed Avitus is also called by Agobard a most powerful opponent of the Photinian heretics.]

As the holy Bishop Chartenius was returning from the city of Lyon, where he had remained to settle certain private affairs while we were departing from the council, he reported that you had proposed to him a question—indeed, more to all of us than to him. If it had been presented in the presence of those who were there, the Holy Spirit supplying the answer, we could easily have offered your inquiry whatever pertained to the matter.

But since we must not defraud so holy a concern of a response through any delay, and since, by Christ’s favor, I know that my judgment agrees with that of my brothers in the faith, I presume to answer your questions through the service of this page. [Col. 0244C]

You therefore command me to show you the reasoning—or rather the authority—by which it may be demonstrated that God possessed substance in divinity before he assumed human nature through the Incarnation; and thereby that most pernicious heresy may be defeated which, asserting that our Lord began from Mary, also blasphemes God the Father in its repudiation of the Son.

For, as far as they are concerned, something must have been added to the imperfection of God if, remaining without a son for so many past ages, he began to have a son only near the end of the world’s decline, when Mary began to have offspring and he began to have fatherhood. Constrained by the necessity of their own assertion, they deny that the one whom they call “son” is God.

They perceive that sound ears cannot endure the belief that, only a few years ago, God began from a human being. But to what end did our redemption arise, if God did not become the price of his own creature? A human being alone could not redeem humanity; nor did one who is God in the heights require redemption.

You therefore command us to teach by authority the things we gather by reason. Let the small number of examples suffice for your keenness: they are taken from many and are enough for one who wishes to know. For minds that resist and persist in unbelief, nothing will help if some things do not satisfy them; nor will everything help.

Isaiah, the most emphatic of the prophets, looking forward to Christ’s birth as the Spirit revealed it, says: “A child is born to us, a son is given to us; and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counselor, Mighty God, Father of the coming age, Prince of Peace” (Isa. 9:6).

Consider, I ask, the force of the words: “A child is given to us, a son is given to us.” A child was born, and a son was given: the son of a human being was born for us; the Son of God was given, and he shall be called Mighty God. As though he were saying: God and human being—God who created life, mighty because he would conquer death.

The prophet Jeremiah, showing his divinity under the words of his scribe and disciple, says: “This is our God; no other shall be reckoned beside him. He found the whole way of discipline; he gave it to Jacob his servant and to Israel his beloved. After this he appeared on earth and lived among human beings” (Baruch 3:36).

If perhaps these things drawn from the ancient writings seem obscure to someone, let him read the Apostle Paul, who, when mentioning the Lord’s ancestors according to the flesh, says: “Their fathers are theirs, and from them is Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed forever” (Rom. 9:5).

The Apostle Thomas also, when he had touched with his finger the imprints of the nails in the body of the risen Mediator and the gaping sign of his pierced side, gathering proofs of power amid indications of weakness, cried out: “My Lord and my God!” (John 20:28).

Behold the testimonies by which the heretics themselves, whether they wish it or not—neighbors of the Jews in their destruction—are defeated concerning the divinity of the Son. By their words, you may believe that the Jews in the Gospel of John questioned the Lord, saying: “You are not yet fifty years old, and have you seen Abraham?” (John 8:57). But he replied: “Amen, I say to you: before Abraham, I am” (ibid., 58).

Is there anything here, I ask, that anyone could obscure even by wishing to do so? What remains now except that the one recognized as older than Abraham should be called younger than the world? And even this, however contentious it may be, can be overcome by the Lord himself, who, amid the insults of his Passion, proclaimed: “Father, glorify me with the glory which I had with you before the world existed” (John 17:4).

But perhaps it should also be added that we prove by the authority of some example that he was named Son. In the psalm he says: “The Lord said to me: You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Ps. 2:7).

Here “today” signifies eternity, which is equally without end or beginning. Tomorrow does not give it a future, nor does yesterday take away its past. Among us, therefore, these things change through the alternation of darkness; but with God, for whom there is no night, it is always today.

Yet if the heretics wish to understand this otherwise, that does not concern us. For since we are dealing only with the name “Son of God,” let them understand “today” as they wish; they will have to concede that the Father begot the Son before the mother gave birth to him.

Certainly even Solomon, to whom singular wisdom gives the greatest authority in the ancient Scriptures, names the Son most plainly and clearly in Proverbs, saying: “Who gathered the waters as though in a garment? Who established all the boundaries of the earth? What is his name, and what is the name of his son, if you know?” (Prov. 30:4).

Let these things from the past suffice. The Apostle says: “When the fullness of time came, God sent his Son” (Gal. 4:4). Indeed, the one who is sent existed before he was sent. If he had not existed before Mary, adoption, not nature, would have made him, like the rest, a son of God.

Nor would he himself have said in the Gospels: “God so loved the world that he gave his only Son” (John 3:16). He was therefore not chosen by that ineffable fatherhood but begotten by it. He is truly God and truly human, properly so in each nature: in divinity he remained from the Father; in the body he began from his mother.

Since you commanded it, I have therefore sent these indications of our answer and a few seeds of testimony to clarify the truth. Your keenness, or eloquence, may nourish them into a harvest of salvation, with Christ providing the irrigation.

But if there is anyone among those against whom we are arguing whom you judge, by your decision, to have answered everything through these arguments—however vigilant they may be as Catholic interpreters and however faithful—God will nevertheless grant that I too may suggest to you both a greater number of examples and an argument that satisfies, having presumed to undertake this writing at your summons.

## LETTER XXIX. AVITUS, BISHOP OF VIENNE, TO LORD SIGISMUND

[Note: The occasion of both letters was the same, namely the apostolic festival—the feast of blessed Peter—which was celebrated annually at Geneva. Blessed Peter was the protector and patron of the church of Geneva; and, I think, Sigismund had established his residence at Geneva after dividing the kingdom with his father. Ennodius also writes this concerning Godegisil, Gundobad’s brother, when they were reigning together, in the *Life of Epiphanius*. Thus, when heretics also came indiscriminately to Geneva, the matters contained in the preceding letter had their occasion: in that letter, unless I am mistaken, he speaks of two heresies, Arian and Photinian.]

I acknowledge that throughout my entire life I am a debtor to the service I owe you; but especially at the present festival, which occupies your concern no less with the examination of heretical efforts than with the celebration of the rites belonging to our side.

For, when adversaries are gathered through a kind of annual contagion, you must labor attentively to ensure that, through the deception of foreign cunning, what has already been cut down in God’s name by your victorious and praiseworthy courage does not sprout again, however much, with Christ’s favor, it may resist you who are present. [Other reading: “withdraw.”]

This is why the congestion at Geneva weighs upon me with such concern: following the custom of its first origin, the poison of serpents has sounded in manly hearts through the hiss of feminine speech. Thus, if I deserve it, I desire to know as soon as possible whether, in conversation with the lord your merciful father, mention was made of that arrangement which admitted, while Catholics and Arians were contending, the pest of the good, raised from infernal hiding places; or whether the deception of that belief—or rather simulation—still persists, a deception not impressed upon minds but written upon sheets, which a written promise gradually recalls to the ancient cruelty of its doctrine.

[Note: Not only senators but also patricians, both had been ordinary consuls: Faustus in the year of Christ 483, and Symmachus two years later, each without a colleague. To them, therefore, as the foremost dignitaries in the city, Avitus writes in his own name and that of all the Gallic bishops concerning the Roman synod and the judgment established there against Pope Symmachus by the authority of King Theoderic, rebuking the bishops of Italy because inferiors had accepted judgment over a superior.]

Certainly, if it is still mingled with the Arian association, as it began to be, our triumph under your rule shines all the more gloriously; for, when the two heresies have been brought together into one, and you both acquire and convict them, the number of schismatics and of schisms decreases.

Therefore graciously regard this service of my inquisitiveness, and, on the feast of your special patron, the apostle, double the gifts of prosperity and of your address that we await.

## LETTER XXX. AVITUS, BISHOP OF VIENNE, TO LORD SIGISMUND

Recently, when I sent the services always owed to your highness according to the custom of the apostolic festival, you said in a speech as distinguished for courtesy as for eloquence that you had therefore given your reply more slowly, so that the humility conscious of its own status—which rightly restrains itself from the boldness of writing—might suffer the punishment of dryness for all the longer period in proportion as it thirsted more intensely for the splendid spring of your conversation.

You judged, as you graciously wrote, that it was a kind of vengeance for the bearer sent by me to arrive late and remain longer with you. O repayment of the gentlest vengeance! O sentence of cruelty to be desired! Who, after all, could bear so intolerable a punishment calmly—that he should be enclosed in the paradise of your presence and see you through an even more blessed delay?

I fear, plainly, that you will often command me to write if you intend to avenge tardiness in this manner. Or, if I had been certain that I was to be punished by such a chastisement, I would undoubtedly have presented writings that I had composed much more rarely.

Would that, while placed with you, I might have been denied the speed of returning, and might have been granted to hear for a longer time, along the very course of their passage, the words that I read only after a long interval.

Certainly God will see what I deserve in your judgment, whether for the boldness of my service or for my trepidation. Yet I would be liable to my bearers of letters if, through the length of their stay with you, I were accused of having deprived them of the twofold correction of their fault. [Col. 0248A]

## LETTER XXXI. AVITUS, BISHOP OF VIENNE, TO FAUSTUS AND SYMMACHUS, SENATORS OF THE CITY

[Note: Not only senators but also patricians, both had been ordinary consuls: Faustus in the year of Christ 483, and Symmachus two years later, each without a colleague. To them, therefore, as the foremost dignitaries in the city, Avitus writes in his own name and that of all the Gallic bishops concerning the Roman synod and the judgment established there against Pope Symmachus by the authority of King Theoderic, rebuking the bishops of Italy because inferiors had accepted judgment over a superior.]

The first state of affairs to be desired would have been that we ourselves might visit the City, venerable to the world, in order to discharge divine and human duties.
