But since the course of time has long since made this impossible, may we at least approach that degree of security which must be acknowledged: that your Excellencies might learn, through the report of the assembled priests of Gaul, what ought to be requested in a common cause.

But since the province, confined by the boundaries fixed among kingdoms, does not permit even this desire to be fulfilled, I humbly ask at once that this page, dictated by one person, not arouse any irritation in your most celebrated order. For all my Gallic brothers have burdened me with this task—not less through commands than through letters—and I alone have undertaken to report whatever we all seek from you.

While we were anxious and fearful concerning the cause of the Roman Church, sensing that our position was wavering because its summit had been attacked—for one accusation had struck us all together, without jealousy arising from our number, if it had overwhelmed the position of the prince—there arrived from Italy, in copies, for our anxious consideration, a priestly form of decree which the bishops of Italy assembled at Rome had issued concerning Pope Symmachus.

[Note: This decree survives from the synod held under the consulship of Rufius Magnus Faustus Avienus, in the year of Christ 502. They say: “We decree that Pope Symmachus, prelate of the apostolic see, insofar as human judgment is concerned—for it has been entirely committed to divine judgment—shall be immune and free; and that, without any objection concerning the accusations brought against him, he shall administer the divine mysteries to the Christian people in all his churches belonging to the right of his see.” There is therefore no doubt that Avitus means this synod, which in the Narbonne codex and other more ancient copies is correctly entitled “the fourth and palm-bearing synod.” Later writers falsely give the name “palm-bearing” to another synod held under the consulship of the younger Avienus, although that synod contains neither mention of this decree nor the absolution of Symmachus, which is known to have been issued in the palm-bearing synod.]

Although the assent of such a numerous and venerable council makes this decree worthy of observance, we nevertheless understand that the holy Pope Symmachus, if he had first been accused before the world, ought rather to have accepted the support of his fellow priests than to have submitted to their judgment.

For just as the Judge of heaven commands us not to be subject to earthly powers, while foretelling that we shall stand before kings and rulers in every accusation, so it is not easily understood by what reason or law a superior may be judged by inferiors.

When the Apostle, in a celebrated command, cries out that an accusation ought not even to be received against a presbyter (1 Tim. 5:19), what should we judge to be permitted against the foremost person of the universal Church?

The venerable synod itself, foreseeing this through a praiseworthy decree, preserved for divine examination the case which, with respect for it be it said, it had almost rashly undertaken to investigate; yet it briefly indicated that neither to itself nor to the most glorious King Theoderic had anything concerning the accusations made against the pope been established. [Col. 0248D]

Having learned these things, I appeal as a Roman senator and as a Christian bishop: may prosperity according to your desires advance in your times through the gift of heavenly divinity; may the dignity in which you flourish preserve throughout the whole world the appearance of the Roman name as the world declines; may, in your sight, the condition of the Church be no less than that of the republic; may what God has granted you the power to accomplish benefit us as well; and may you love the see of Peter in your Church no less than the summit of the world in your city.

If, by the profound deliberation of your counsel, you see the matter clearly, it is not only the case being conducted at Rome that must be considered. Something perhaps can also be corrected among the other priests concerning the matter that occasioned this. But if the pope of the City is called into question, it will now seem that the episcopate, not merely a bishop, is tottering.

You know well amid what storms of heresies, as though winds were blowing around us, we guide the vessel of the faith. If you fear such dangers with us, it is fitting that you protect your helmsman by sharing the labor. Otherwise, what vengeance is there if, while the sailors rage against the master, he is yielded to this danger—not without peril to them?

The one who presides over the Lord’s sheepfold will render an account of how he administered the care of the lambs entrusted to him. But it is not the flock’s role to terrify its own shepherd; that belongs to the judge.

Therefore restore to us the principal concord, if it has not yet been restored. We instructed your client, the venerable presbyter Symmachus, to undertake this exhausting labor for this reason: that, through the oracle of your letters, he might bring us the outcome of our petition in the message of restored peace.

## LETTER XXXII. AVITUS, BISHOP OF VIENNE, TO LIBERIUS, PREFECT

[Note: First prefect of Italy, then of Gaul, a man distinguished by many merits, and later a patrician. Cassiodorus, Book XI of the *Variae*, Letter 1: “Let Liberius, the patrician and prefect also of Gaul, be regarded—a military man, most welcome in fellowship, renowned for his merits, striking in appearance but more beautiful through his wounds, having obtained the rewards of his labors, so that he might not lose the prefecture he had administered well and that doubled honor might adorn an exceptional man.” Ennodius, to the same Liberius, Book IX, Letter 23: “Gaul agrees with me in this affirmation: since Christ the living God has so ordained, after the cycles of many years you brought civilization to those whom you organized, who had never before been allowed to taste the flavor of Roman freedom, may you be brought back to your Italy at our request and at theirs, since they hold fast to you.”]

[Col. 0249C]

After the many labors of Gaul had been visited by the most fortunate arrival of your authority, I had not previously experienced any fulfillment of my desire in your affections. Hence, although I believe that the benefits which you have long been distributing among the provincials may also profit us, yet to me, still thirsting for your letters, it is as though you have only now arrived for the first time. Indeed, I feared that, by voluntarily offering myself for epistolary services, I might obstruct those occupations by which I believed myself, over so long a period, to have been kept from the reading I desired. But since, although late, at your urging, and with me replying to your lofty letters, the order of alternating exchange has been preserved in literary communication, you who have made me respond without embarrassment should, as I desire, make me your debtor by frequent correspondence. Nor, if you approve, are there lacking reasons for giving orders: there is an abundance of things which you may impose upon those eager to obey. For civility is greater than authority, and graciousness is not lesser in dignity.

Indeed, this very matter, whose reward has supplied you with material for writing to me, has shown in what works amid the tribunals you strive most earnestly to flourish. Therefore, what was suggested to us by your distinguished man, your deputy, on behalf of the liberation of certain captives, I have gladly fulfilled at your high command, though I did not accept the payment which the bearers brought.

[Note: He soon names Gemellus, whom Theoderic, after gaining possession of Italy, appointed deputy of the prefects. Thus he writes to him in Cassiodorus, Book II, Letter 16: “For this reason, at the present time our authority sends you as deputy of the prefects into Gaul, which, with God’s help, has been subjected to us.” Moreover, just as Avitus here frees captives at Liberius’s request, so Ennodius, Book IX, Letter 39, asks Liberius on behalf of his kinswoman Camilla that her little estates in Gaul be relieved from the burdens of the treasury.]

For if those very persons owe anything, by their origin, to the aforesaid magnificent man, my son Gemellus, he can distribute what he had offered me for the redemption of freeborn persons. But if you recognize these men as born free, it is enough that the payment has served its purpose.

## LETTER XXXIII. AVITUS, BISHOP OF VIENNE, TO THE ILLUSTRIOUS MAN APOLLINARIS

[Note: That this was the son of Sidonius may be inferred from the name Archadius at the end, whom Apollinaris seems to indicate as his son. That Archadius was the son of Apollinaris, the son of Sidonius, is shown in our Sidonian notes, Book III, Letter 13.]

[Col. 0250B]

I know that our Domnolus, on returning to my most devoted lords, having found me before him burning with anxiety over your pious concern, would bring back a report different from what he wished; and by the haste of his return he increased rather than diminished the burden. For, when he arrived at Lugdunum, a severe pain in my eyes had suddenly rendered me incapable of seeing the light. Thus, since he himself was not effective in obtaining a reply, nor I fit to return one, I entrusted to the bearer’s ears, rather than to writing, the whole expression of gratitude which might have been owed either through the cost of gifts or through the goodwill of those who gave them. I was in no way doubtful, however, that, in the eagerness for holy affection, the series of instructions would be regarded as slight beside the desire for letters.

But as soon as, with the darkness of my chamber-prison beginning to thin, I had some opportunity to arrange my duties, I did not delay paying my debt. I sent the present bearer, laden with more greetings than can be expressed in words; and, so far as concerns lengthy instructions, I reckon that I have given him a very brief page. For behold, God is my witness how great a light our aforesaid dearest friend poured into that very nocturnal dwelling of my darkened retreat, when, by announcing the return of our sweetest pledge—something of which I had previously been unaware—he assured me that, through Christ’s favor, I would find my household restored, and that the person whom I had sent would be found again.

Therefore, do not now suppose that anything concerning yourselves has been only half accomplished: through your companionship, by God’s favor, even my eyes, satisfied by this present page, grow stronger. Then, in perfect sincerity, you will receive me with the joy of daylight, if your sweetness, forgiving me for having replied only now, compels me, weak and anxious though I am, to devote myself nevertheless to the desired frequency of letters in God’s name, with Archadius now dictating and my hands occupied only with the subscriptions.

## LETTER XXXIV. AVITUS, BISHOP OF VIENNE, TO THE ILLUSTRIOUS MAN AURELIANUS

[Note: In this case the conjecture is more difficult, since in this period there were several distinguished men named Aurelianus. Consider whether the reference may be to the patrician Aurelianus, whose servant Gregory of Tours says was freed from a demon at the basilica of Saint Victor in Massilia, *Miracles*, Book I, chapter 77. Certainly, unless the dates conflict, his rank presents no obstacle, since all patricians were illustrious.]

It is plainly a sign of however slight a prosperity that we are visited by the speech of friends, shining for a while with the color of temporary peace. Yet that flood-tide which you have compared with the storms of time continues, while we travel across the world’s sea, amid the waves of continual disturbance. For the very fact that we breathe amid the adversities of the times ought to be regarded more as an interval between dangers than as an end to them. The reason why, amid the inconveniences of calamities, a certain light seems to play upon us—not so much to heal them as to mark their limits—is that, after minds have been relaxed by deceptive security, a collapsing anxiety may afflict them with renewed fear more severely.

Therefore, excellent man, cease to believe that fervent evils are the end of evils. When the face of the storm, produced by a different movement, alternates with a small measure of serenity, do not delight in the changing results, but make use of them. Let neither prosperity lift you up nor adversity break you in such a way that, in your minds, the cause of your friends changes as the times change. Always remember the charity you have undertaken, if it is permitted me to write; if not, then at least love it, for that cannot be forbidden. And after the whirlpools which you have described in your letters, hope more earnestly for a harbor in that age in which established tranquility will not be able to fear shipwreck.

## LETTER XXXV. AVITUS, BISHOP OF VIENNE, TO THE DEACON ELPIDIUS

[Note: He was the physician of King Theoderic. A letter of his to Elpidius himself, also bearing the title of deacon, is preserved in Cassiodorus’s *Variae*, Book XIV, as are several letters in Ennodius. Alluding to him, Ennodius likewise writes in Book IX, Letter 30: “I know that God has bestowed upon you the grace of the unconquered prince, so that ecclesiastical humility might not perish.” That Elpidius was especially dear to Theoderic is attested by the deacon Cyprian in *The Life of Saint Caesarius*, Book I: “Elpidius, deacon and physician, was, through his diligent services, among the foremost familiar and intimate associates of the royal power.” There Cyprian relates that Elpidius was freed, through the work of Saint Caesarius, from the demonic attack by which he was tormented at home.]

Through certain clerics of another law I received, as a divine gift, the news of your well-being. Nor did the quality of the bearers diminish the favor of the one who was diligent, just as the food sent from heaven to our Elijah (5 Kings 17:6) was not made worthless by the dreadful beaks of its winged carriers. Yet the sweetness of your letters, which I received with sufficient eagerness, was sprinkled with a certain bitterness by your denial that the letter I previously returned to you had reached you.

[Note: It is unclear who this “chief of the house of Tullius” was, or what house of Tullius gave him his name, unless perhaps the reference is to the house of King Servius Tullius, which P. Victor places in the fifth region of the City; many will not readily be persuaded of this. Avitus will write Letter 43 to Celer, whose son’s health he here commends to the physician Elpidius.]

For I was delighted to learn from the chief of the house of Tullius—who, having been sent by his father on an embassy, had found your beloved, my lord Sigismund, in the city of Vienne—that you had received my letters. Through him I again discharged the duties of my most overflowing affection and cultivated, by the devoted labor of a page, the feeling for you which I had conceived in my heart. The chief whom I mentioned above cannot be unaware by what mishap that letter failed to be brought into your hands. I was distressed by it, and yet glad that it had distressed you, that, at so suitable an opportunity, the exchange of a single service had perished from the desires of two people.

Nevertheless, since each side is secure in the purpose of the affection established between us, accidents must sometimes be forgiven—accidents by which our conversations, rather than our wishes, are frustrated. Harm may come to concern, but not to love. Nor should you think that, whether opportunities are denied or discovered, there is any time of negligence in which, amid all other activities, the desire to receive news of your well-being grows cold in me. I therefore judge that to be most precious in the minds of friends in which it is established that chance has no power: what neither the length of a journey can disperse nor the abuse of forgetfulness frustrate.

For the present, however, I repay the word of affection, if you have deigned to regard silence as a loss. At the same time, if you will permit me, I commend to you more particularly the young son of the illustrious Celer: after God, you will enable his father to begin hoping for the life of his only child. For he is so constrained by the grievous illness of this dear child that, uncertain what to hope for, he is compelled, as a father, to lament the life of one whose death he is forced to regard as imminent, as though already bereaved.

Therefore join your aid to the assisting Divinity, according to what we infer from your exceptional skill. For you to promise is already, in part, to have acted. May Christ grant that, by rejoicing and praising you more fervently in this care under your instruction, both Italy may owe you the reputation of a physician and Gaul the boy’s health.

## LETTER XXXVI. AVITUS, BISHOP OF VIENNE, TO THE ILLUSTRIOUS MAN SENARIUS

[Note: He was a *comes* of King Theoderic’s patrimony and a patrician, concerning whom we have already said much in connection with Ennodius. We must now add his epitaph, composed in verses that are not without merit and reported by Pierre Pithou in Book IV of the *Poematia*.

### EPITAPH OF SENARIUS, ILLUSTRIOUS MAN, COUNT OF THE PATRIMONY AND PATRICIAN

I am that Senarius, once a traveler through the boundless world,  
now enclosed in a tomb in body, though not in name,  
always exalted by love for the unconquered prince.  
In whose realm I was the voice of kings, the tongue of salvation,  
the ambassador of treaty, the road to peace, the enemy of disputes.  
The East knows this, and the farthest Iberian sky;  
the frozen North knows it, and Africa scorched by the sun.  
My embassies, twenty-five in all,  
marked journeys throughout the world and were never impeded by hardship.  
Swift was my course, for in a single sleepless year  
I saw the shores of the Ocean twice and the Pontic coasts twice,  
following Europe and Asia, the world’s two thresholds.  
To these merits I added a train of honors.  
As a distinguished courtier, I governed the patrimonies,  
and my belts shone with the attire of a patrician.  
Piety cherished me, holy faith cherished me, honesty cherished me.  
Let the ages sing my titles, for by my character I hold the stars.]

Having frequently experienced the favor of your magnificence, and knowing that you receive it graciously, I have sent you, through this devoted page, the duty of a greeting. And because you know that the synodal laws require that, when any doubt arises in matters concerning the state of the Church, we, the members who follow, should turn to the chief priest of the Roman Church, as to our head, I have, with the agreement of the bishops of the province of Vienne, sent to holy Hormisdas—or whoever he now is who occupies that office—the service of due reverence, together with my concern. I wish to hear from the authority of that aforesaid see what he has learned concerning the outcome of the embassy which he himself sent to the East.

Therefore, since, as I have said, I am consulted by my provincials, I do not presume to give an answer without first consulting him. Your assistance is consequently needed, so that this may be completed in proper order by both sides: either an inquiry may reach its destination from us, or a reply from the one explaining the matter may return to us. The state of the Church does not concern only its priests; this concern is shared by all the faithful. Whoever and wherever we appear to govern the Church, we conduct your business in the catholic religion. When someone is either sick or healed concerning the rule of faith, you ought to rejoice or grieve with us.

Therefore you should not believe that anything about the matter on which I am consulting is hidden from you. If I were acting only for myself, your knowledge would be sufficient for my inquiry; we can hear no more truth from the pope than from you. But the usefulness of the Churches requires that the teacher should disclose what you know. For my part, as your particular friend, if you will deign to grant it, I shall await from you a reply with particular eagerness. Through it, as I have said, the truth will become known to me only to the extent that the bishop of the Roman city will rejoice to have answered those who seek him by virtue of his privileged authority.

[Note: Avitus’s letter to Hormisdas, and Hormisdas’s reply to Avitus, were published by us at the end as Letters 87 and 88. The interpretation of this letter and the following one should be sought there.]

## LETTER XXXVII. AVITUS, BISHOP OF VIENNE, TO BISHOP PETRUS

[Note: In my opinion, Petrus of Ravenna. The preceding letter concerns the same matter. Envoys having been sent to Hormisdas so that he might become better informed about the state of the Eastern Church, Avitus asks the bishop of Ravenna, through whose city they would have to travel, to instruct the Gallic ignorance. In the Roman synod, the following distinguished subscription of this Peter is found: “I, Peter, bishop of the Church of Ravenna, have subscribed to this decree of ours, in which we have committed the whole matter to God’s judgment.” We also conjecture that Theoderic’s Letter 27 in Book III of the *Variae*, addressed to Peter the bishop in the consulship of Felix—that is, in the year of Christ 511—belongs to this same man. If this is true, those who report that Peter of Ravenna died before that time are mistaken.]

Even if there were no other reason for seeking an encounter with your Blessedness through the service of a letter expressing my devotion, it would be right for everyone to honor you, since by your holy reputation you make your desire known to all. For it is fitting that you should be sought no less than the Roman see, because you shine not less through charity than that see does through power.

After offering the greeting which such reverence requires, I confess to your apostolate—though with embarrassment—the ignorance of Gaul. Nor do I think it better for someone to pretend that he knows than to learn if he does not know. We do not know what is being done between the Roman and Constantinopolitan Churches through any definite authority; rather, we gather it from rumors and the variety of messengers’ reports. Therefore, lest we perhaps be thought as negligent as we are rustic, the whole province now consults, through clerics from Vienne, both the holy pope and your Blessedness.

[Note: The presbyter Alexius and the deacon Venantius. This is how they are called in Avitus’s letters to Hormisdas and in Hormisdas’s letters to Avitus.]

You should therefore make clear, through the illuminating light of a salutary reply, what has been decided with you concerning the state of the faith in relation to the East. Since it is fitting that teachers should voluntarily extend instruction even to those placed far away, care must be taken for the soundness of the body, so that the members may always know the prosperity of their head.

Therefore, if permission is granted for your servants, my sons, whom I have sent for this very purpose, to proceed as far as Rome, Gaul will have abundant instruction through two princes of the Church. But if those whom we sent should perhaps return from your see, the faithful reply of your apostolate will be for us the fullness of all instruction that may reach everyone.

## LETTER XXXVIII. AVITUS, BISHOP OF VIENNE, TO EUFRASIUS

[Note: Although the title of bishop is not added, I would say that he was bishop of the Arverni. Two letters of Ruricius were also addressed to him, and in one of them the name of his rank is likewise omitted. He subscribed through a representative at the Synod of Agde in 506 and was himself present at the First Council of Orléans in 511. Avitus therefore asks him to submit for review and excuse his book, which had come into his hands, to Apollinaris, the son of Sidonius.]

I have already sent letters through my boys, by which I wished to let you know how greatly your recommendation had benefited my brother Imeterius. Yet, not doubting that at the beginning of his pontificate he will attend, as is fitting, to the duties owed to his elder brother, I have gladly added this letter through him also. I rejoice that the long-sought plunder of my little work has come into my hands.

And since, as he had informed me, he is bringing the little book itself back to you, I hope that, if you will deign to do so, you may present and excuse this little work—whatever it is, neither carelessly published nor corrected in every respect—to our exalted and most pious brother Apollinaris. It would have been impious for me not first to offer it to him by right of charity, if it had not again been absurd for me to offer to the son of my lord Sidonius, amid the delights of his father’s eloquence, something that would nauseate him in my time and impose upon him the annoyance of presumption.

Therefore, if the volume is more temperately introduced through you, I shall be able to learn from any writing of his magnificence whether the aforesaid brother judges that it ought to be read even by infants. But if, as I rather think, after the rivers of his father’s fountains he has rejected the poverty of a vein flowing with the thinnest dew, without embarrassment to me or impiety toward himself, it will be enough for me to understand the severity of his criticism from this alone: if he remains silent—

## LETTER XXXIX. AVITUS, BISHOP OF VIENNE, TO THE LORD KING GUNDOBAD

[Note: He explains why he sent back to Lugdunum for examination a slave who had come from Lugdunum to Vienne and denied a deposit, and he clears himself of the charge that the man claimed Avitus had warned him not to return it.]

That I sent under guard from the basilica of Vienne to the basilica of Lugdunum a slave whom it was thought necessary to examine was plainly an act of fear and obedience. For just as I did not presume to hand him over here without an accusation, so there I took care that he should be kept alive for the interrogations which the hearing required.

Since, however, the rule is everywhere one and the same impossibility or possibility remains for us in the observance of a common ministry, I considered not the property of the Lugdunum and Vienne basilicas, but reverence for both Churches. Therefore the bishop who was present could more easily plead for an intercession to be suggested nearby, since it could affect both of us.

[Note: This was customary among bishops, who habitually interceded earnestly both for slaves before their masters and for any accused persons—wretched or oppressed—before judges or princes. Ennodius, in his *Life of Bishop Epiphanius*, while he was still a deacon, writes: “Even then he was rehearsing the contests of intercession. For wherever a bishop was sent by command to secure relief for the wretched, he demanded the benefit with such skill in supplication that many people perceived that he had helped them in their cases, although the bishop himself had not come in person.” The histories of the holy bishops are full of examples. Particularly illustrious is Saint Augustine’s intercession, in Letters 159 and 160, before the judge Marcellinus and the proconsul Apringius on behalf of the Donatist circumcellions, who had confessed atrocious crimes, so that they might be punished without the penalty of death. He also writes at great length to Macedonius in Letter 54 concerning the justice and religious character of such intercessions.]

For in all holy places, just as the same charity belongs to our ministry, so equal authority belongs to your command. To say nothing of the fact that the slave himself, having departed from an interview with his lord, ought not to have sought Vienne in order to provoke your anger against me, since, while remaining there, he could have kept himself within the Church of Lugdunum.

Concerning the case in which, before the examination of your highness, he is accused as a crafty denier of a deposit, my conscience is such as is displayed to God and to you in all my actions and conduct. Moreover, the simplicity of the petitioner itself bears witness with me that, as your pious lordship says, I did not avoid by my conduct confessing what I had wished, for his consolation, to acknowledge, had he been thought mindful of Christ.

Some of your slaves, our fellow citizens, have learned this from the present testimony. But when people under pressure are shaken outside their proper order, their response is said to be somewhat unstable. Whether that applies to me, may God suggest to you and truth declare. For the man who, chastised by me, perhaps grows angry in the same spirit of falsehood by which he lies against an innocent person about denying the deposit cannot deny what he received, even though, with God and you favorable to me, his contrivance has contributed little to his defense: he says that I warned him not to return it.

This confession of his, even if you judge that it ought to weigh against me, cannot raise him up. I nevertheless await your pious command. Whatever my little church has—or rather, whatever all our churches have—is yours, from the substance which you have either preserved for us until now or bestowed upon us.

[Note: A free and ingenuous declaration. The property of the Church is credited to princes, either because they themselves donated it or because, under the law of Constantine the Great, they granted permission for it to be donated. “Let each person,” he says, “have the freedom, when he departs, to leave to the most holy and venerable catholic council whatever property he has chosen.” *Codex Theodosianus*, concerning bishops, and so forth. Since princes ought to defend the property of all their subjects, they owe particular protection to ecclesiastical property. In this respect the piety of the ancient Frankish kings especially shone forth; in their Capitularies they professed that they held the Church’s goods and slaves in the same position as the treasury’s goods and slaves.]

Whatever you command with God’s inspiration, I shall strive to obey insofar as I have the strength. Moreover, before the gaze of the divine Majesty, nothing can avail against an offence which I have always feared as yours and eternal. I humbly ask only this: let that unhappy man, for whose accusation the fact that he excuses himself is sufficient, not make me a partner in his faithlessness before the minds of your justice, even if he should see himself punished because of your anger.

## LETTER XL. AVITUS, BISHOP OF VIENNE, TO THE LORD SIGISMUND

[Note: Sent when Sigismund was preparing for some military expedition; it is uncertain where and against whom. The fact that Avitus indicates that Sigismund had already embraced the catholic faith when he wrote this makes it seem that his promise, near the end of the letter, to speak of the matter of a more precious triumph alludes to a homily which Avitus delivered to the people at the conversion of King Sigismund. Agobard says that it was full of the sweetness of its ideas and most delightful in the composition of its words.]

[Col. 0256B]

I returned from the festival to which I had gone with the utmost haste. But because you had already set out under Christ as your leader, your return—one which, as we believe, was to be a source of joy—nevertheless leaves me excessively stunned by your departure. For I did not deserve, at the very return of the prosperity that was to follow, to fall at the knees of my lord, caress his hands with kisses, and adore the seat of our faith in that holy breast.

Nor do I dare say that this was withheld from me because of sin, lest I prove ungrateful for the divine grace which has given me such foreknowledge of your presence. For although it is generally just and proper for everyone to seek what we owe in honor of your glory, I rejoice that I have received this special privilege: although inability prevents me from offering you in person the service I owe for the accomplishment of my wishes, may your piety judge it to have been rendered to you.

But I alone am struck by grief whenever I do not deserve to be present for my consolation; whenever the heat of tribulations, kindled within me, is enclosed in me alone, shut out from the cooling of your speech; whenever the hand of that physician does not soothe the inward pains which it has experienced. He, striving in piety and persisting in strength to protect his servant amid such circumstances, deigns to add labor when it would have been enough if he had wished merely to offer favor.

But I presume upon the divine Majesty that he will cling more tenaciously to your feelings because the love of catholic law has poured him into our hearts. Under the holy protection afforded by this occasion, it will be impossible for you to reject as a servant one whom you have received and have learned does not love a master.

For the rest, having set out happily, go safely and return victorious. Insert your faith into your weapons; admonish by promising divine provision; demand heaven’s aid through prayers; arm your javelins with vows. May God grant that I may magnify the trophies of the wars which he himself grants you, through whatever service of speech I may offer under the subject of that more precious triumph which I have been pursuing for some time.

## LETTER XLI. AVITUS, BISHOP OF VIENNE, TO KING CHLODOVECH

[Note: There are also two letters of the Italian King Theoderic to this Frank at Cassiodorus, *Variae*, Book II, 61, and Book III, 4; but both call him Luduinus. The earlier letter corresponds to ours if the date is considered: it was written after the victory over the Alamanni, which became for Clodovech the occasion of the Christian faith and baptism, whose splendor Avitus describes here with great elegance. He further teaches what we had previously not known: that the baptism was celebrated on the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord, not on the vigil of Easter, as Hincmar of Rheims had falsely persuaded himself and the writers of our history.]

[Note: In this letter Avitus vividly describes Clodovech’s baptism but makes no mention of the vial sent down from heaven and filled with sacred chrism, with which Clodovech is said to have been anointed by Saint Remigius. Nor have we found any mention of this remarkable matter in Gregory of Tours, Fredegar, or the other ancient historians of the Franks. Some recent critics use this negative evidence to weaken belief in the truth of the prodigy. The distinguished Monsieur, the Abbot de Vertot, responds to them in a dissertation entitled *On the Holy Ampulla Preserved at Rheims for the Coronation of Our Kings*. This dissertation appears in the *Mémoires de l’Académie des Inscriptions*, volume II, page 619, quarto. Joannes Jacobus Chiffletius had earlier published an investigation of the Rheims Ampulla. Hadrianus Valesius also discusses the matter in volume I of the *Rerum Francicarum*, Book VI, pages 260 and following.]

The followers of whatever schisms, by their varied opinions, diverse in number and empty of truth, seemed to veil the sharpness of your subtle judgment beneath the shadow of the Christian name. But while we entrust our present condition to eternity, while we reserve for future examination what each person thinks right, a ray of truth has nevertheless shone out amid present events.

Divine providence has found for our age a certain arbiter. In choosing yourself, you judge all. Your faith is our victory. In this same matter, many people, when they are admonished to believe for the sake of seeking salvation, whether by the exhortation of priests or by the urging of any companions, are accustomed to oppose the custom of their race and the rite observed by their fathers. Thus, by harmfully preferring embarrassment to salvation, while they show useless reverence toward their parents by guarding unbelief, they confess that in some sense they do not know what they should choose.

Let harmful shame, therefore, withdraw from this excuse after such a deed’s miracle. Content with the nobility alone of your ancient lineage, you wished everything that can adorn the height of nobility to arise from your ancestry through you. You have the authors of good things; you wished to be the author of better things. You answer for your ancestors by reigning in this world; you instruct your descendants by reigning in heaven.

[Note: Anastasius was indeed a Christian emperor, but not sufficiently orthodox. At Rome and in Italy, King Theoderic; in Gaul, Alaric, king of the Visigoths; and Gundobad, king of the Burgundians, were thoroughly Arian, as were the Suebi and others in Spain. In Germany and Britain the people were still pagan. Therefore those who assert that, after Clodovech—the first of all kings to belong to the catholic Church—the Frankish kings deserve the first place among Christian princes are not unjust.]

Let Greece indeed rejoice that it possesses a prince of our law; but let it no longer be thought to deserve alone to be illumined by the gift of so great a privilege, since the rest of the world, too, has its own splendor. For in the western regions also the light of a new radiance shines forth in a king who is not new. The birth of our Redeemer appropriately began this radiance, so that you might accordingly be reborn from the water unto salvation on the very day on which the world received the Lord of heaven, born for its redemption.

Therefore, let the day of the Lord’s birth also be yours: on it you were born to Christ, Christ to the world; on it you consecrated your soul to God, your life to the present age, and your fame to posterity.

What can now be said about the very glorious solemnity of your regeneration? Although I was not bodily present at its rites, I was not absent from it in the fellowship of joy. For divine kindness also added this to our regions as a cause for celebration: before your baptism, tidings of your most exalted humility reached us. Thus, after this expectation, your sacred night found us already secure.

For we discussed and considered among ourselves what it would be like when the assembled company of bishops, with the hand of a holy man and the ambition of service, should bathe royal limbs in life-giving waters; when the head feared by nations should bend before the servants of God; when—

[Note: Historians report that the Frankish kings wore their hair uncut. Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, Book VI, chapter 24, says of Gundovald: “When he was born in Gaul and carefully raised, as is the custom of these kings, with locks of hair hanging down his back,” and so forth. In Book VIII, chapter 10, concerning Clodovech, he introduces someone who relates the following about a slain man: “Although I did not know who he was, I recognized Clodovech by his long hair.” Agathias Scholasticus gives similar information in Book I of *On the Reign and Deeds of the Emperor Justinian*, page 14 of the Paris edition. On this matter see the *Mémoires de l’Académie des Inscriptions*, volume VIII, pages 487–488, quarto edition.]

—when hair grown beneath the helmet would be covered by the saving helmet of sacred anointing; when, with the covering of the armor removed, immaculate limbs would gleam with a similar whiteness.

If you believe anything, most flourishing of kings, this softness of garments will make the rigor of arms more powerful for you hereafter; and whatever prosperity has granted until now, holiness will add from this point onward.

I should like to attach some exhortation to your praises, if anything lay beyond either your knowledge or your practice. Shall we preach to one who is perfect the faith which, before perfection, you saw without a preacher? Or perhaps humility, which you have long since shown toward us by your devotion, although now for the first time you owe it by profession? Or mercy, which the captive people, recently released by you, announces to the world through joy and to God through tears?

There is therefore one thing which we would wish to see increased: since through you God will make your entire nation his own, extend seeds of faith from the good treasury of your heart also to the farther nations which remain established in natural ignorance and have not been corrupted by any shoots of evil doctrines. Do not be ashamed or reluctant, even through embassies sent for practical affairs, to uphold God’s cause, since he has raised yours so high.

Thus let foreign peoples also—who, because of religion, are destined first to serve your rule, while they still seem to exercise authority over others—distinguish the nation from the prince. Let no homeland claim for itself, as though it possessed a special seat, all those whom you raise through the ranks of honor. It is clear that you are wherever all things enjoy the common radiance of one sun. Those nearby rejoice more in the light, but those farther away are not without its brilliance.

Therefore radiate perpetual light: a diadem to those present, majesty to those absent. All celebrate the successes of the happy triumphs which that region achieves through you. Its happiness touches us also: whenever you fight there, we win.

Amid these things, however, care for those deserving pity preserves in you an affection for the catholic religion. And at the summit which contains the government of all things, holiness shines no less than power. It was certainly because of this that you ordered, by a royal decree, that the son of your servant, the illustrious Laurentius, be sent to you.

[Note: He is mentioned again in the next two letters. When Anastasius wished him to return to his father, he employed Clodovech as an intercessor, asking him to reclaim the man from Gundobad, with whom, as I think, he was being held captive as a hostage for his father.]

I report that I obtained this from my lord, who is indeed king of his own people but your soldier. For there is nothing in which he cannot serve. He commends the man sent; I rejoice with the one dispatched; I envy you, who will see him. It must count less toward his benefit that he be restored to his own parent than that he be presented to the father of all.

# LETTER XLII. DICTATED BY BISHOP AVITUS

[Note: [Col. 0259D] Likewise in Letter 84, under the name of Lord King C. S., that is, Count Sigismund. That it was dictated in the name of King Sigismund, and that Sigismund speaks in it, is clear from the fact that he calls Gundobad his father, from whom, as stated, Anastasius’s order concerning the son of Laurentius had been fulfilled. Therefore, if he called him “count” here, as in Letter 7 he called the patrician Sigismund, it should be understood that, among the other honors with which the Romans adorned foreign kings, the office of count was customarily bestowed as well.]

## UNDER THE NAME OF LORD C. S.

[Note: [Col. 0259D] The son of Patriciolus and grandson of Aspar, who, according to Victor of Tonnona, openly displayed himself as an enemy of Anastasius because of his zeal for defending the orthodox faith and the Council of Chalcedon; and when Anastasius was raging over the Trisagion, the emperor was acclaimed in his place. Theophanes, in his Chronicle, says: “When the crowd shouted against Anastasius and demanded another emperor, while they hailed Vitalian as emperor”—although Marcellinus Comes later attributes this to Areobindus, not to Vitalian. After Anastasius finally died, Vitalian was recalled from Constantinople by Justin and appointed master of the soldiers and consul together with Rusticus. In the seventh month of his consulship he was stabbed to death in the palace, in the thirteenth indiction, as Marcellinus himself records—that is, in the year of Christ 520.]

## TO VITALIAN, SENATOR

In keeping with the worthy integrity of your judgment, you ought to regard as Romans all whom you raise by the privileges of honor. Therefore, relying on this confidence, it is not fitting that those should be considered wholly absent whom, although their homeland separates them, military service represents. Hence, in the only way now available to me, while showing the devotion of my heart through the usefulness of my service, I set forth whenever opportunity permits what I constantly desire. Assert to our most merciful common ruler what we wish. More attentively point out the obedient service which we now render in action and have always held in our desire. Suggest and likewise commend that, through my intercession, the imperial order has been fulfilled by your admirer, my lord and father.

The son of your client, the illustrious Laurentius, restored through my efforts, is added to the province. Earlier we had sent a servant back to his father; behold, through his son we add a service. From this one person sent to you, observe how matters are handled with the others. It remains for your aforesaid soldier, whose offspring is offered to your favor there and preserved for his homeland here, commended to you through my efforts, himself to commend what he has already obtained concerning that offspring or what he confidently hopes concerning the prosperity of this one who returns with us.

# LETTER XLIII. AVITUS, BISHOP OF VIENNE

[Note: [Col. 0260D] With the same inflection by which in Letter 35 he called the son of Celer “Celeris,” whereas the Greeks also say Κέλερος, “Celer.” This man was master of offices, known for the Persian expedition, in which, as Procopius writes in Book II, he commanded among the other leaders: “Celer, commander of the palace regiments.” The Romans have customarily called this office “master.” He was also known for the disturbance that arose when Anastasius sent him to pacify the populace enraged over the Trisagion, as Marcellinus Comes relates in his Chronicle, during the consulship of Paulus and Muschianus. The Fasti also attest that Celer held the consulship with Venantius, the son of Liberius; and that he belonged to the orthodox party is testified both by the letter of Hormisdas to Celer, Letter 34, and by another letter of Celer himself to Hormisdas concerning the settlement of peace between the Churches.]

## TO CELER, SENATOR

It is clear that it belongs no less to my desire than to my duty that the services which the world, devoted to your renowned greatness, rightly offers should be cultivated more particularly by me, who have long seemed indebted to your favor—especially since divine favor has now provided an appropriate opportunity in which I may deserve to serve the authority of your exalted position with complete devotion.

Therefore I commend to your magnificence, with the honor of the aforesaid most generous protection, the son of your admirer, the illustrious Laurentius, whom the revered command ordered to be sent to his own world. Increase through the zeal of defense what you desired through the affection of your heart. In the province he seeks his father; in you let him find fatherhood. Protect him together with the offspring he has received. Although through his honor he is sufficiently indebted to you, he will nevertheless begin to owe you more through his child: what he will obtain through you—the consolation of his own affection—he will repay by demonstrating affection toward you.

For the rest, as regards your faithful dependents, we always desire the command we await and long for the opportunity to obey. By God’s favor, grant that we may learn of the prosperity of Rome under our most glorious prince, at whose summit you shine from the worthy citadel of honor, both through the serenity of his august speech and through a rescript expressing your dignity.

# LETTER XLIV. AVITUS, BISHOP OF VIENNE

[Note: [Col. 0261D] I think Avitus dictated not only the preceding letter to Vitalian in Sigismund’s name, but also the following one to Celer. He alludes to these letters as they are about to depart for Greece and offend Greek ears, and he congratulates him on the son of Laurentius having been restored to his father.]

## TO LORD SIGISMUND

If I were able to speak as you deem worthy, then Latin speech would inopportunely offend Greek ears. But since, in our language, what is less polished will be more readily understood, in the letters which you ordered to be delivered through my fellow servant, faults may safely be dictated as well.

Certainly, let them discover through whatever interpreter they choose what we wish to say; for my part, in our customary address, I have learned—with the experience of the most devout lord himself interpreting, if it may be said—that your graciousness is greater still. For the rest, may Christ repay you for the perseverance of the favor which you preserve for your special servants. This is also shown in the young man whom you are sending: although you considered not the advantage of either party, but the reward in both, you have in a sense nourished a son for yourselves and in a sense restored him nourished to his father.

# LETTER XLV. AVITUS, BISHOP OF VIENNE

[Note: [Col. 0261D] To the son of Sidonius, if we have correctly conjectured this in relation to Letter 22, after he had returned unharmed in the king Alaric’s favor, to whom he had been reported.]

## TO APOLLINARIS, ILLUSTRIOUS MAN

It is a long time—whether you believe my words or hold worthy opinions concerning our mutual affection—since, desiring to receive some letter from you, I nevertheless wished rather to offer an expression of my own duty, which I owe to your person first through affection, then through relationship, and finally through respect.

We ought not always to entrust what must be conveyed to passing opportunities, since, although the opportunity of messengers ought indeed to be something we pray for because of their frequency, that concern must nevertheless take precedence which presents itself through its own desire, without the intervention of another’s necessity.

Knowing that I was bound to this service, I had long been silently grieving that a just repayment was being obstructed by the unjust barrier of a hindering obstacle. For news had reached us—not merely our knowledge but our sorrow—of the arranged smoke of a fire which had attempted in vain to stir your holy and guileless innocence, as though a stormy conspiracy, blowing upon it with lying winds from exhausted ashes.

For this reason we feared burdening your anxiety with a votive offering and sending an increase of grief instead of consolation. While we therefore hung suspended in confused expectation beneath this cloud of uncertainty, God unexpectedly brought your letter to me, full of your former serenity and proved piety.

There I recognized, to my considerable delight, your hand; the pious, paternal eloquence of your discourse; and, above all, your hereditary kindness. You wrote that, by Christ’s favor, you had already returned, that everything was safe, and that around you the regard of Lord King Alaric remained unharmed and unchanged.

Although I judge that, after any wavering, the favor shown to such persons is not restored without increase, just as it does not end without danger. They wish, as it were, to make amends to injured innocence, and then choose to believe when they see; their conscience is satisfied if their own knowledge also comes forward as witness.

Yet when I received the news of your security—or rather of ours—behold, with God as my witness, I burst into tears mingled with joy as I recalled the past. For, as your poet says, “the image of my dear father came to mind” (*Aeneid* II), when I reflected on how, even to our own persons, however unequal in calling, the common lot of our parents had been brought by the spiteful parity of their sufferings.

That which was their consolation is also granted to us in God’s name: although our family has been assailed by the entire effort of rivals and by the tooth of envy barking all around, whenever it seemed to be attacked, it was subjected to accusation, not to crime.

For if you learned from your father, Archadius, that a man engaged in the world’s service is endangered less amid arms than amid slanders, then I too accept from my Sidonius, whom I do not dare to call my father, as much as a cleric can be made to endure. Accordingly, may the Divinity grant that, just as it is no novelty for such things to be brought against us, no novelty may make us deservedly accused.

[Note: [Col. 0261D] Soon afterward, “our family seemed to be attacked.” So great was the connection between Avitus’s family and that of Sidonius that he makes them one family and transfers and exchanges their names in turn. Why, then, does Avitus call Sidonius his father? It is clear: Sidonius was Apollinaris’s father. But who was Archadius, whom he presents as Apollinaris’s father, and what slanders did he suffer? This must be investigated. Concerning Sidonius, the matter is evident from his life and letters.]

But let speech sharpened by bitterness now cease during a time of joy; rather, let the boldness of idle folly provide something at which you may laugh. Some months ago I saw a letter addressed to a certain mutual friend of your magnificence. After the salutation, and in the declining portion of the letter’s rhetorical treatment, you wrote that you had been pleased by the little books which, amid the serious and more necessary business of writing, I nevertheless composed playfully from the deeds of sacred history.

[Note: [Col. 0262D] He rejoices that Apollinaris approved the books of his poems, concerning which in Letter 33 he had anxiously awaited his judgment. And not without reason: the son was not unworthy of his father Sidonius. Ruricius writes to him in Book II, Letter 25: “You prove yourselves to be his sons not only through the nobility of your lineage, but also through the flower of eloquence and every kind of virtue.” And afterward: “If divine mercy had wished him to survive until this time, just as he was then already rejoicing in your imitation, so now he would rejoice in your perfection, seeing that hope had reached its fulfillment, and would not begrudge himself an equal whom he had wished to be better.”]

Here, before your sincerity, I call God as witness that I speak neither falsely nor flatteringly: I was so delighted by your judgment, as though I had confessed before the ears of my lord, your father, what I had composed, and had been rewarded by the approval of whatever excellence under a discerning critic.

First, I rejoiced that you disclosed your opinion of this work more freely than another would have done. Then I recognized that you desired no less than you believed some good to come from the effort of a brotherly work; certainly, since you found its merits of expression not equal to what you wished, you supplied by good will what you could not fulfill by judgment.

The friend who, as I think, had caused the little book to reach you snatched it from me not from the copyist’s hand but still from the notary’s, so uncorrected and raw that you could scarcely tell whether you should be angry more with the author’s faults or the scribe’s. Therefore I quickly sent the work itself, transferred onto parchment but not yet polished with as much correction as I had wished, so that I would not delay my desire.

If it truly pleases you—not only as one who loves but also as one who judges—then, since among outsiders there may perhaps be someone whom the boldness of the undertaking will provoke to envy, it is entirely sufficient for me that you feel what I desire you to feel. For just as the distinction of the work of our common Sollius reaches my glory no less than yours, so, with Christ’s favor, as you flourish ever more in military activity, whatever Archadius may produce, even without me, in the smallest matters something worthy of reading would not shame him.

# LETTER XLVI. AVITUS, BISHOP OF VIENNE

[Note: [Col. 0263D] To the same son of Sidonius, concerning the same matter, namely the favorable outcome of the danger he had faced before King Alaric. He further advises him, now that he has experienced the deceit and ambushes of his enemies, to beware of them more carefully in the future.]

## TO APOLLINARIS, ILLUSTRIOUS MAN

It has rightly become a common but truthful saying that those who are united by mutual affection perceive the movements of one another’s hearts. For it is evident that our concern for one another is so single and shared that, if you measure well, I would have answered the letter brought by my son, its bearer, before it arrived.

In the page of service which I had sent through my people on this matter, I breathed out the joy conceived at your prosperity more through affection than through words, and I touched upon the distress of our family and of our common parents, mingling tears with rejoicing.

For the rest, may divine mercy—which has established hope of restoring our lineage in the honor of your person and, through you alone as father, has granted that we too should be fathers of our posterity yet to come—grant that, as you continually trample underfoot the conspiracy of enemies and the envy of the treacherous through prosperous success, the first step of your victory may be to restore integrity to your conscience; the second, to prove it when it is examined in court; and the third, to spare your accusers after the judgment.

May the defeated enemy, even because indulgence has been granted him, be tormented in spirit; and, through our twofold benefit—his punishment—may he grieve, when you lament, that you cannot be deceived, but can show mercy. Thus, restored to your power only so that he might not perish, while angrily resenting the pardon freely offered, he may in a sense be forced to envy his own life.

For the rest, ever most devout lord and brother, concern of my heart and glory of your family, bear for a little while the foolishness of a trembling brotherly admonition. Beware carefully of evil men and of the hissing wiles of biting tongues, which contrive flatteries and poisons; after experience, do not trust them too readily.

Let prudence make you no less cautious than innocence makes you secure. Since the way of investigating and harming the good has been closed to them, you ought to labor all the more gladly to defeat their efforts, because, while reserving vengeance for divine judgment, you have always resolved to forgive those whom you defeat.

Although, as I have already admitted above, the man whom you have challenged in your glory should not go away entirely unpunished.

# LETTER XLVII. AVITUS, BISHOP OF VIENNE

[Note: [Col. 0263D] To a senator, not in Italy or Greece, like most of the preceding recipients, but in Gaul and at the court of the king of the Burgundians, a noble orator whom, because of the defense of the Catholic faith which he undertook before Gundobad, Avitus predicts will become a bishop. If this prophecy was not empty, I think this Heraclius was that bishop of Tricastina whose name we find recorded in several councils, such as those of Carpentras, Orange, Vaison II, and finally the Fourth Council of Orléans. Letter 86 was also written to the same man, and his reply is appended to it.]

## TO HERACLIUS, ILLUSTRIOUS MAN

While unceasing concern for the faith and safety of my friends occupies me, I recently learned, among the first matters of importance, about your prosperity—something which I ought not to conceal from a Catholic friend. Yet I can magnify in you the reward acquired in this way less through words than through joy.

For unless the restraints of senatorial maturity and most temperate modesty held you back from proclaiming your own praise, the tongue which wondrously defeats your opponents might perhaps worthily praise the outcome of your glorious struggle among your own people.

I hear, then, that you held a discussion with the king. Since, as I understand, they were not guiding themselves by gentle measures, you passed to battle. By divine will, he was confounded—the man long known to heaven and now also apparent to human beings as an assertor of religion.

Your mouth, accustomed to the pomp of secular eloquence and to the overflowing streams of Roman profundity, eagerly seized the subject sent down from above for worthy debate. The eloquence which, when it was involved in other matters, defended either the delights of describing the world or the praises of royal triumphs, felt no shame, when the better cause demanded it, in serving the establishment of truth.

Thus, just as on other occasions by praising the king you rendered to Caesar what belonged to Caesar, so here, in rendering to God what belongs to God, you did not spare Caesar. Therefore royal power has in you something to admire, even if it does not follow your example; it now feels itself more evidently adorned by the speeches in which you have repeatedly proclaimed it.

For you also showed, by resisting when the matter required it, that you do not know the lure of flattery. Let the wisdom of rulers, then, mark those who see that such men can easily alter human loyalties because they prefer earthly things to divine ones.

For the rest, it is readily apparent that the guardian of the primary cause will preserve what remains as well.

These things have been said while we are dealing with secular affairs. But when we come to the cause of priests—whose school you do not yet enlarge, whose injury you endure, and whom you first educate by example so that they may later be adorned by your companionship—which of them, who, I ask, does not know that you have come to the contest of this spiritual arena not inexperienced or ignorant of the law, but after the long gymnasium of salutary meditation?

Therefore let it be new to others that you begin the necessity of this battle from the perfection of virtue. But I, in whose heart you hold the citadel of charity, have long recognized without hesitation that, in your zeal for contemplating Catholic principles and defending them through speech, what you lack is not desire but time.

Accordingly, having offered the service of my greeting, and indicating that I too have been refreshed by the nourishment with which, though your body fasted, you satisfied your mind—whence these few words of my fullness belch forth—I ask God for what remains: that he who has already imposed upon you the office of preacher may add the honor, and that what is exercised in action may also be displayed in outward form; that the chair may receive not one teachable but one taught, not one learning but a teacher.

In that chair, as a conspicuous victor bound with the garlands of victorious glory, amid the harmonious voices of cheering joy, however greatly you rise against the shield, even your experienced enemy will be compelled, unwillingly, to support you. He will never find anything to dispute concerning the quality of your merit, but will always have reason to fear the inequality of the battle.

# LETTER XLVIII. REPLY OF HERACLIUS, ILLUSTRIOUS MAN

Would that it might happen to me repeatedly to be enlarged by the richness of your conversation and strengthened by your learning. For a twofold fruit of glory follows such an outcome: faith, withered by the chill, grows warm through the speech of fervent exhortation, and an intellect fasting through natural poverty becomes rich through the aid of a distinguished cultivator.

Therefore, if you deem me worthy, I presume to offer you the greatest thanks, together with the service of a greeting, because my reply delivered before the prince—and carried to you by report, as you have indicated—earned an appropriate judgment not from my own mouth but from your affection.

Although the most excellent prince is ardent in discovery and fluent in speech, and so searches human minds that he always gives the gentlest hearing to assemblies, I shall set forth the course of my labor while cutting short the sea of prolixity.

I call it labor because an inexperienced sailor scarcely withstands storms rushing upon him with unexpected blasts. When, then, by God’s favor, weariness finally ceased and public tranquility returned, I found a contest prepared, as though the camps had long been changed. For a more aggressive conflict always attacks sluggish and unwarlike persons.

First, from the opposite side, speech gave a preliminary signal of the struggle itself. Then, as though poured out from a sudden ambush, came an overseas torrent. Finally I encountered a blank sheet, rubbed over with age, which mocked itself with errors wound around it in such a way that, while the respondent’s freedom remained intact, the perversity of the proposition had no means of escape and, from its own documents, supplied weapons against itself.

What more need be said? The page which had begun to be read preferred to withdraw into silence, so that everyone might learn with good reason how divided, how facile, and how contemptible is the persuasion which, despite devising numerous arguments, could not disturb one who lacked divine instruction.

I repeat these things so that, whatever there is in the cause of God that is pleasing, I may undoubtedly recognize as attributable to you. Indeed, it is publicly evident that the file of your conversation once shaped me in this way, and that the entire cultivation of your preaching enriched me in common, so that the seat to which heavenly judgment assigned you seems to have contributed much to the administrator of the office, but to have deserved no less through the person who administers it.

Apply yourself, therefore, to prayer, lord of my heart, and implore God’s help—both for yourself and, as you have been accustomed to do, for everyone—as a devout and persistent guardian, so that the wall of faith may not be shaken by any assault. You must also take care to protect your sons and pupils by continual public correction and, with the strongest weapons of doctrine, compel them, as we read, to conquer together with you.

# LETTER XLIX. AVITUS, BISHOP OF VIENNE

[Note: [Col. 0265D] This name is clearly Celtic, and perhaps Burgundian here. Names of this kind among the counts who subscribed to the laws of the Burgundians include Aunemundus, Andemundus, Fredegundus, and Godemundus. Letters 71 and 72 are also addressed to the same Ansemundus.]

## TO ANSEMUNDUS, ILLUSTRIOUS MAN

I am greatly astonished that the person for whom you deign to intercede, while I was staying at Lyons, alone denied to me the crime which everyone was proclaiming, and afterward came to the point of repenting so as to beg you for pardon. If he asks simply, it is clear that the man also confesses the sequence of his guilt.

Therefore, although in every case, out of regard for the favor you show me, I have no freedom to do anything other than what you command, I nevertheless cannot, because this is your wish, grant remission without first emphasizing what grieves me.

For your piety knows—and has often heard read in church—that in the very crime of adultery divine Scripture expresses how many degrees there are. At the first fall into fornication, he sinned who, inflamed by lust, desired a woman lacking a husband. At the second, and worse, level stands the man who, by theft—damnable beyond all else—violated the chastity of an unblemished marriage bed.

And since the human mind can imagine nothing more serious than this injury, consider how the chastity of heavenly justice is disturbed if someone has even looked wantonly upon a bride devoted to Christ and endowed by blessing in the bridal chamber of the holy altar, to say nothing more.

[Note: [Col. 0265D] The judgments of the Gallican bishops concerning those who take consecrated virgins as wives are explicit, to say nothing of others. At the First Council of Tours, canon 6: “Those who have joined themselves to consecrated virgins through an abominable union, or who have abandoned the religious profession they had made, are both to be excluded from communion; for if anyone violates the temple of God, God will destroy him, until, repenting, they return to the aid of penance.” At the Third Council of Paris, canon 5: “Let no one obtain a marriage with consecrated virgins, whether through abduction or through any kind of claim. If anyone acts against these prohibitions, refuses to obey his priest, and persists, let him in the present be held outside the Catholic Church’s communion and be struck with perpetual anathema. Finally, at the Second Council of Tours, canon 20, it was similarly decreed: ‘Let no one presume to abduct, claim, or join in marriage to himself a virgin consecrated to God who has exchanged her garment in honor of Christ. If they disdain to obey their pastor and to separate themselves from the forbidden marriage, let them be condemned to perpetual excommunication.’ Thus far the ecclesiastical laws. Under civil law also among us, a man who had joined a consecrated virgin to himself in marriage was condemned to death, according to the constitution of King Chlothar II, which is appended among the councils of Gaul to the Fifth Council of Paris.]

Yet I hear it said that the young man himself did not violate a virgin, since the carnality of many others had already abused her through their shameful vows. Therefore, since he is plainly guilty of the crime, unless his satisfaction and your intercession free him, it is impossible to say how wretched it is that, in seeking reconciliation, he confesses the crimes of others.

Here I accuse the priestly negligence of our time. We do not investigate such matters; the magnitude of crimes presents itself to us without examination. Who would seek a companion in evil? Who would involve himself in the stains of others? And would that his own obscenity had at least restrained itself enough to remain hidden.

Then let him choose between two possibilities. If he first sinned carnally with a girl, he still awaits what the Apostle foretells: “If anyone violates the temple of God, God will destroy him” (1 Corinthians 3:17). But if he aggravated with an addition the corruption he had not begun, what more shameful, what more horrifying thing can be imagined than that even this did not keep him from a prostitute, on account of the one reason for which God alone permits a husband to separate from his wife?

[Note: [Col. 0267D] From this it is clear that in those times it was still believed in Gaul that, on account of fornication, a husband might separate from his wife and, with Christ’s permission, marry another. This is also evident from canon 2 of the Council of Vannes: “We decree that those who, having abandoned their wives—as it is said in the Gospel—except for the cause of fornication, have taken others without proof of adultery are to be barred from communion.”]

Nor, if you consider the matter, am I moved only by this aspect. Religious parents mourn the crime committed and, as though lamenting a lost child, proclaim their bereavement in their wailing. What shall I say of the mother’s grief, whom the shameful life of the aforesaid husband has long since widowed by a death worse than any other?

Although he had been accustomed to be moved by intercourse, she had nevertheless patiently endured these things: a son without filial devotion, a husband without offspring, a father without an heir. Moreover, through his efforts he had nurtured a noble evil born, however it might have arisen, from adulterers of noble birth. Yet in the birth of the desired portent there was not an increase of lineage but evidence of disgrace.

And indeed, without prejudice to the defense which God has granted me through you, I fear the guilt of the aforesaid man more than his repentance. But I ask that he not be angry with one who says these things. I am a watchman; I hold the trumpet; I am not permitted to be silent.

Would that the sinner had acted from a human disposition, which is accustomed to fall through weakness and return through satisfaction. But to burn with anger, swell with pride, and reek with lust is bestial.

Therefore, even if he again spews different flames against me, summons me, perhaps, to a hearing before the Roman Church, and, if he still pleases, says that I also have children, I will not appease his threats with flattery, nor fear the weariness of journeys. I am more greatly wearied by civil crimes in my own homeland, and I will not deny having many children, though I now grieve to have brought forth one of them.

[Note: [Col. 0267D] Leo the Great shows that this was also customary in the provinces of Gaul, in his letter to the bishops of the province of Vienne: “Let your fraternity recognize with us that, because of its reverence, the Apostolic See has been consulted by countless reports from the priests of your province as well, and that judgments have been either reconsidered or confirmed through appeals in various cases, as ancient custom required.”]

This little speech was indeed extorted from me by error. But you, to whom the privilege of supreme power grants greater authority to chastise, rebuke the man forcefully. Tell him of my reconciliation with him, since you command it, and declare that I will take care that this evil not be renewed either by commands or by messages, so that, if he cannot be persuaded to repent and reform voluntarily, at least by restraining him through custody, the opportunity for wrongdoing may be removed from him, even if the healthfulness of repentance cannot be persuaded upon him.

# LETTER L. AVITUS, BISHOP OF VIENNE

[Note: [Col. 0268D] Besides this man, two other Messiani are known in Gaul in these times. One was Avitus the emperor’s patrician, whom Ricimer killed when he stripped Avitus of the imperial power at Piacenza. The other was the notary of Saint Caesarius, later a presbyter, who together with the deacon Stephen composed the second book of his life. Between the two stands our Messianus, older than both: proconsul of Africa after the consulship of Bauto, concerning whom Saint Augustine writes in Book I, chapter 23, *Against the Letters of Petilianus*.]

## TO MESSIANUS, ILLUSTRIOUS MAN

The greatest increase to our desire is supplied by the desired abundance of joy if our eager wishes learn that the magnificent condition of your piety is flourishing and strong in prosperity. For whatever the diffusion of heavenly blessings has bestowed upon your eminence increases, as a certain source of happiness, the progress of our own affairs.

We measure the growth of our success by the happy increase of whatever support your actions provide without end. Therefore, offering an honorable greeting, I ask that, if—as we desire—all things are proceeding favorably for you, your greatness may make this known most fully through the expression of the letter now arriving.

# LETTER LI. AVITUS, BISHOP OF VIENNE

[Note: [Col. 0268D] He refutes the ignorance of an incompetent man who had criticized Avitus’s accent in the homily which he delivered at Lyons during the dedication of the basilica. This homily has perished. Sidonius likewise praises the preaching of Bishop Faustus of Riez at the festivals of the dedication of the same church at Lyons, in Book II, Letter 3; those sermons too have likewise perished.]

## TO VIVENTIOLUS, RHETORICIAN

I have heard that, in the homily which I seem recently to have delivered to the people of Lyons at the dedication of the basilica, you say that I committed a barbarism, publicly chastising, of course, what I did wrong in a public speech. I admit that this could have happened, especially to me, for whom, if there was any study of literature in my greener years, age now carries everything away (Virgil, *Eclogue* 6).

Yet I had wanted to hear this very thing from you face to face, even though my ability to know such matters is already diminishing. But since I discovered that you had spoken while absent, I have taken care to answer while absent as well.

They say, then, that you blamed me because I pronounced *potitur* with a long middle syllable, evidently not following Virgil in this word, who used the syllable as short when he said *vi potitur* (*Aeneid* III). But this is excusable by the necessities of poetry, since we often find Virgil presuming to do this in his work, so that, when necessary, he may settle the matter by accepting a barbarism in obedience to the law of meter, and in certain places may invert the natural quantity of syllables without following the rules of art. Examples include “*Non erimus regno indecores*” (“We shall not be unworthy of the kingdom,” *Aeneid* VII), “*Fervere Leucatem*” (“Leucas boiling,” *Aeneid* VIII), and “*Namque ut supremam falsa inter gaudia noctem / Egerimus*” (“For when we have passed the final night amid false joys,” *Aeneid* IX).

No educated person will deny that naturally long penultimate syllables ought to be used by an orator. Virgil, exercising the license of poets, shortened the middle syllable in accordance with what we have said above and used *potitur*. Let us set poetic freedom aside for a little while and treat the verb according to the rule of the art.

The common verb, in the present tense and singular number, has *potior* in the first person; in the second person, the middle syllable of *potiris* is long. It remains that in the third person, namely *potitur*, it must likewise be long. Just as we say *sortior, sortiris, sortitur*, so in the perfect past tense, in the first, second, and third persons, we say *potitus sum, potitus es, potitus est*. Likewise, in the imperative mood, present tense, second person, *potire*, just as *sortire*.

Similarly, in the optative mood, present and imperfect past tenses, throughout all three persons, the syllable is equally long: *utinam potirer, potireris, potiretur* (“would that I might possess, you might possess, he might possess”).

But if in the third person, *potitur*, you make the syllable short, you will be forced to do the same in the second person and say *potiris*. Yet the integrity of Latin excludes this entirely from every example and usage.

Behold the verb for which I had been criticized by you. I have dared to draw my argument from it. Now, offering an honorable greeting and entreating you earnestly, I ask that, since by right of friendship I expressed in a freer written page what seemed to me correct, you likewise respond in turn. Setting aside, as stated above, the example of Virgil’s authority—whom for this reason alone we ought not to imitate in the use of barbarisms—even though Virgil himself used *potitus* or *potiti* with a long syllable, as in “*auroque potiti*” (“and having gained possession of the gold,” *Aeneid* VI), provide me in a written reply with the rule I ought to follow.

Or, if you prefer to instruct your questioner briefly by the testimony of some authority, I hope that you will investigate and disclose more carefully what is found among the ancient orators whom you rightly teach to your students. Without any argument of art, whether rhetorical or otherwise, one will find a father and a common son—men whose talents I would rather you had imbued in the present age as the first teacher than as the sole one—content with this one fault alone.

Yet, since even at their beginnings they drink from that rich fountain of learning from which you flow, let them drink not only letters, but also this: that it befits a friend to attract by study rather than detract, and to make an orator speak rather than speak against him.

[Note: The following several letters belong to the class by which bishops formerly used to greet one another on the most solemn days of the Nativity of the Lord and of the Resurrection, and to announce how successfully they had celebrated the feast.
