Several of this kind are scattered throughout the letters of Theodoret recently published, representing this custom and its rationale—namely, the mutual cultivation of goodwill and charity. Thus, in Letter 4: “We have customarily used festive letters”; in Letter 5: “We discharge the duty of friendship, as the law of the feast requires”; and in Letter 26: “For this is enjoined both by the law of the feast and by the law of love.” Finally, this was the sole subject of one of those letters, as can be seen from Letter 56, which, because it is shorter, we append here in full.

**FESTIVE LETTER.**

“Although the things of sorrow are still at their height, and sorrow presses grievously upon the mind, I nevertheless judged it right to fulfill the law of the feast. Accordingly, I now both write, and greet your Reverence, and discharge the debt of love.”

From this it is clear that *festive* or *festival* letters were so called because they were written on feast days. In the same way, among the Alexandrians the Paschal letters of Theophilus, Cyril, and the other patriarchs were also called *festive letters*, since through them they announced the date of Easter to the other churches. [Col. 0270C] Those letters, however, were called Paschal because they all concerned the date of Easter; these could also partly be called Nativity letters, since they were sent on both festivals, as Avitus’ Letters 54 and 56 were sent at the Nativity of Christ, and Theodore­t’s Letters 38, 63, and 64 at the Resurrection.]

## LETTER LII. AVITUS, BISHOP OF VIENNE

[Note: To the bishop of Lyon, whom Avitus, while still a presbyter, predicted would become bishop in Letter 17. That he presided over the see of Lyon is shown by the councils to which he subscribed, the Council of Epaon and the Council of Lyon under Sigismund. From Agobard’s book *On Jewish Superstitions* we learn how eminent a man he was in learning: “Viventiolus,” he says, “bishop of the Church of Lyon—what kind of learning he possessed is attested not only by his own writings but also by those of others concerning him.”]

### To Viventiolus, Bishop

The holy festival, which through your intercession we celebrated with such success, was increased by the marks of affection contained in the letters you sent; and for that reason it made us happier in many ways, because unity embraces the one Church, everywhere one, in a common joy. May Christ grant that, just as in the present year you have fulfilled our desires by favorable signs, so also in the time to come you may continually bestow upon the Church of Vienne the visitation for which she always longs.

## LETTER LIII. AVITUS, BISHOP OF VIENNE

[Note: His subscription at the Council of Epaon shows that he was bishop of Vaison. The reason for believing him different from Gemellus, whom we saw in Letter 32 as deputy of the prefects in the same province, is that at the synod which followed a few years later he was already a veteran bishop and held the leading place among his colleagues. For the same reason he is placed here before Apollinaris, Victorius, Claudius, and Gregory, who subscribed in that same order at that synod. We know Apollinaris as bishop of Valence from Letter 11, and Victorius as bishop of Grenoble from Letter 16. Claudius and Gregory, both men of illustrious name and reputation, governed respectively the Church of Besançon and the Church of Langres.]

### To Gemellus, Bishop

The letters of Your Beatitude, which the passage of time had made desirable, were rendered more welcome by the approaching festival, which we celebrated successfully in God’s name; and we rejoice that it was likewise observed suitably by you. Pray always that, through the intercession of the saints, what the Divinity knows to accord with rule and peace may come to pass for the Catholic Church, with brotherly charity preserved in every respect.

## LETTER LIV. AVITUS, BISHOP OF VIENNE, TO BISHOP APOLLINARIS

[Col. 0270C]

After the sacred offices of the Lord’s Nativity, at which I attended in great distress and truly more than exhausted, I await your message, which after God is my first and singular concern. If I should be deemed worthy to receive it, whatever harshness I have deserved, as I trust, will be tempered, and whatever harshness you have deserved will be wiped away.

## LETTER LV. AVITUS, BISHOP OF VIENNE, TO BISHOP VICTORIUS

The auspicious beginnings of the festival, by God’s favor, have been made still more auspicious because you obtained its benefits through your intercession and visited it through your affection. For while you continue to show the customary care of a father, and announce concerning your safety what accords with our prayers, you offer us what we rejoice in and demand from us what we owe. May Christ grant abundant continuation to this very piety and kindness of yours, through which, by the gift of your renewed instruction, your elders may be strengthened by the benefit of your solicitude, and those who come after may be taught by the example of your charity.

## LETTER LVI. AVITUS, BISHOP OF VIENNE, TO BISHOP CLAUDIUS

[Col. 0271B]

According to your custom, you increase our desires by the votive signs of your pious devotion; and, having received your visitation, the feasts of the Lord’s Nativity are doubled for us by the increase of your prosperity. For this favor, which Your Beatitude multiplies toward us by your continual kindness, may the propitious Divinity prolong your presence through the succession of many years.

## LETTER LVII. AVITUS, BISHOP OF VIENNE, TO BISHOP GREGORY

The delicacies you sent are indeed abundant and most remarkable in quantity, timing, and distinction; yet they do not equal your affection, piety, and solicitude. By these things it is proved that what we lacked was not so much your kindness as your presence. The festival was completed in the prosperity of your intercessions; but in proportion as bodily feasting was added to it, spiritual banquets were lacking according to custom. If God grants me such provision in the future, may he deem me worthy then to offer them with you, just as I now send them through you.

## LETTER LVIII. AVITUS, BISHOP OF VIENNE

[Note: Invited to the festival of the Church of Lyon, he excuses himself because he cannot be absent from Vienne on account of the arrival of the rulers; the following letter has the same subject. The solemnity of Saint Justus was celebrated with great distinction at Lyon. Concerning it Sidonius also writes, Book V, Letter 17: “We had assembled at the tomb of Saint Justus; the procession had taken place before dawn, it was the anniversary solemnity, and there was such a great crowd that the largest basilica could not contain it. This belongs to another class of letters, however, by which bishops customarily invited the bishops of neighboring sees to the celebrations of their cities. A notable example of this custom is found in Basil the Great, Letter 291, where, for the annual festival of the Caesarean martyrs, he summons not only neighboring bishops but those of the entire diocese of Pontus:

‘Since Eupsychius, Damas, and their company are among the most distinguished martyrs, whose memorial is celebrated yearly by our city and throughout the entire surrounding district, the Church reminds you—her own particular glory—and through our voice entreats you to restore the ancient custom of visiting us.’

“Accordingly, since Eupsychius, Damas, and their companions are the most illustrious among the martyrs, whose anniversary memory is celebrated in our city and throughout the entire surrounding region, the Church reminds you of her distinctive glory and exhorts you through our voice [Col. 0272C] to resume your ancient custom of visiting us.”]

### To Viventiolus, Bishop

Had our common vows not frequently been obstructed by circumstances, I would ordinarily have wished to obey the customary command of charity through my usual service. For since it would have been a matter of double advantage to meet both the festival and you, you see that the failure to fulfill this obligation concerns only my own loss. For the arrival of the authorities is expected here at every moment, so that unless I take care to be present when they come, my simple absence will be reckoned not merely negligence but even defiance by those who are accustomed to criticize in us matters still less serious. Therefore, having recognized the common necessity, kindly forgive my inability, and pray that we may satisfy our desires, if not continually, at least from time to time.

## LETTER LIX. VIVENTIOLUS TO BISHOP AVITUS (C)

May your decision be tempered, in imitation of the divine goodness, toward the petitions of those who serve you, so that on the solemnity of Saint Justus the visitation of your apostolate may bless its own little people.

## LETTER LX. AVITUS, BISHOP OF VIENNE, TO BISHOP VIVENTIOLUS

For the firmness of the divine promise, let what you formerly granted be “Yes, yes,” and what you later repeated be “No, no”; for if the nature of present circumstances is properly considered, the agreement made between you ought now to be fulfilled in a particular way, even if it should not then have been inserted.

## LETTER LXI. AVITUS, BISHOP OF VIENNE

[Note: At this time two bishops of this name subscribed to the Council of Epaon, one of Octodurum and the other of Gap. It does not seem doubtful that the letter should be attributed to one of them; which one, however, is uncertain.]

### To Constantius, Bishop

I received a letter from Your Holiness at Easter, but it was not a Paschal letter, since it conveyed nothing of charity or solicitude. Rather, you ordered me to send our brother and fellow priest Candidianus, whom I had commended as my particular charge, not only to the hearing of the clergy but also [Col. 0272C] to that of laymen, although it is established that his deacon had been consigned to servile custody by them on a civil charge.

[Note: This is contrary to the freedom of the clergy and to their most ancient privilege, which was renewed by Caesar Valentinian after the destruction of the tyranny of John, in the final law of the Theodosian Code, *On Bishops*, and so forth: “We reserve clerics, whom the unfortunate usurper had ordered indiscriminately to be brought before secular judges, for episcopal judgment. For it is not right that ministers of the divine office should be subjected to the judgment of temporal authorities.”]

Therefore, if you think that everything concerning your clergy must be believed on the testimony of laymen, write back. It will follow that, while we consult secular knowledge about everything that comes to public rumor, we expose the freedom of the clergy. Nevertheless, I venture, as though prompted and admonished by your affection, to say this: let no one, not even laymen—much less clerics—be deprived of holy communion for trivial causes and matters that concern not God but the world.

[Note: The canons repeatedly insist on this, and it was later expressly decreed among the Gallicans by the Fifth Council of Orléans: “Let no priest suspend anyone of orthodox faith from communion for minor and insignificant causes, except for those offenses for which the ancient Fathers ordered offenders to be excluded from the Church.” Accordingly, just as Avitus here censures Constantius on this point, Leo the Great censures Hilary of Arles in Letter 89, because he easily denied communion.]

For a person who does not know the dignity of communion itself is the one who, setting aside all resentment, does not suspend it with great grief and restore it with the greatest haste.

[Note: A contest worthy of the brothers’ affection. Apollinaris, taking revenge on the lack of brotherly duty—or, as Avitus himself calls it, the lack of devotion—of his brother Avitus, because he had not come to the festival of the Church of Valence, had sent gifts in place of punishment. Avitus, praising this form of fraternal punishment, repays him with equal zeal.]

## LETTER LXII. APOLLINARIS, BISHOP, TO BISHOP AVITUS

As I considered and examined by what punishment I should strike your lack of duty, I judged nothing more fitting than, having waived the injury, to pursue nothing less earnestly. Therefore, do not fear anything in the future, since you see that the present offense has immediately been expiated.

## LETTER LXIII. AVITUS, BISHOP OF VIENNE, TO BISHOP APOLLINARIS

[Col. 0273B]

Necessity prevented me from attending the festival; humanity arranged for the festival to attend me. You write, therefore, that I have paid for my lack of devotion with sea-borne supplies. Clearly this is a fitting kind of punishment, which makes me struggle . . . with an appetite for the table. I should have wished to be presented to you in sufficient measure, if you did not punish absentees in such a fashion. Would that your severity did not end with punishment of the stubborn. I fear nothing more than what you command me to fear nothing in the future. Grant indulgence to the one who asks for it; forgive the one toward whom you have chosen to be miserly.

But as for me, having experienced the character of your strictness, I plainly desire your offense more than your pardon. For the rest, may our God grant through your prayers that, although this year I was absent from the festival’s offices rather than its delicacies, in the time to come you may present me through your prayers with an affection unlike that of the present; and, when I return, may you consider yourselves to have been absent with similar severity.

I have sent eight marsh-fish because I hear that you were somewhat moved by two pairs of soles, which you may grind with your teeth—though I have not returned evil wholly for evil.

## LETTER LXIV. AVITUS, BISHOP OF VIENNE, TO BISHOP VIVENTIOLUS

You preserve the custom of sweetness—or, more truly, you increase it. You restored our concern for you by announcing favorable news; you visited the festival by wishing to learn what you desired to know about us. Yet amid these many feasts of the spirit you also adorned the table with bodily delicacies, having fed the Church with spiritual nourishment. Therefore, unequal to giving thanks, I turn to prayers, asking divine mercy that the charity whose progress you zealously uphold may benefit you as a reward, me as a joy, and all others as an example.

## LETTER LXV. AVITUS, BISHOP OF VIENNE

[Note: To the bishop of Geneva, whose name appears among the bishops present at the Council of Epaon. After receiving from him *eulogiae*, or gifts, namely lavish delicacies, Avitus wittily jokes about Maximus’ servant, the bearer of them.]

### To Maximus, Bishop

As far as my infernal condition and my end are concerned, I retain some slight bodily strength; yet I am anxious because I know nothing about your lordly son, nor have I received any account of his conversation, since I was not in a position to learn anything.

[Note: These are the monasteries about which Sidonius writes in Book VII, Letter 17: “I hasten to reform the wavering rule of the abandoned brothers according to the statutes of Lérins or Grigny.” The community of the monks of Grigny was formerly numerous near Vienne, under the care and discipline of the bishop of Vienne. Avitus therefore indicates that he was occupied with visiting them at this time.]

For I had been occupied with the monasteries of Grigny and had already been absent from the city dwelling for some time. Indeed, the delicacies you sent with your customary kindness found me on the road and still at a considerable distance from the city. And your servant Leonianus transmitted them, groaning greatly and taking very little, with an eager but empty stomach.

You might have thought that your *eulogiae* were being carried by the beaks of tenacious ravens, like the food brought to Elijah by their claws (1 Kings 17:5). So hungry was he that, rather than undergo the insults I would more justly have directed at you, he sent what he desired to devour but could not. I should now like to know what benefit you gain by being so attentive to the appetite of this particular servant, when the desirable opportunity for absence carries me away lest he snatch from my mouth or hands the food given to me by God and by you.

As for the fresh wines, since you press them upon him, I yield my share and give him many of his.

[Note: He calls “fresh” the drinks of fresh or newly refreshed wine, that is, wine brought back to full strength, which Leonianus consumed with a heated throat. Thus in Letter 77: “I insist with the greatest importunity that I presume upon three fresh wines more than the others.” The following therefore means that he should use larger cups instead of small vessels, as though he were saying: instead of little cups, let him drink from larger bowls. Here *capis* is used by a new inflection in place of *capidibus*. *Capides* and *capulae* in Varro are kinds of drinking vessels with which they used to empty oil jars. The following also belongs to the same point: “Let him wear down the phials with his lips, which he should surround with the density of labels in place of circles.” The use of *pitacia* is explained by the words of Petronius Arbiter in the satiric work: “Immediately glass amphorae, carefully sealed with gypsum, were brought in; on their necks labels had been attached with this inscription: ‘Falernian, Opimian, one hundred years old.’ On wine vessels, therefore, labels attached to them indicated the wine’s region, age, price, and quality.”]

Let him use the capacity of bowls instead of little cups; let him wear down the phials with his lips, surrounding them with a dense arrangement of labels in place of circles. For I too shall take care that what I know he wants—when I have extracted something similar from your blessing—be placed, if no method is devised in the cups, among the fish, so as to multiply the fresh wines for his heated appetite.

## LETTER LXVI. AVITUS, BISHOP OF VIENNE, TO BISHOP VICTORIUS

The event you reported in your letter had reached me previously through a slight rumor, before your message. When I learned of its bitterness through the holy Archdeacon, I lamented the grief caused by your disturbance no less than you did, if you deign to believe it.

For it is a sufficiently grave precedent that priestly ordination should now be said to be governed by the people, when the reason that election by the congregations is preserved in the consecration of bishops is only that, through the regularity of the institution, the elect may be permitted, as though by a certain mandate, to read what seems appropriate. You should not regard as something new what the wickedness of the clergy, supported by the resources of secular insolence, can contrive for our affliction.

I think that, by ecclesiastical discipline, the consent of your sons ought to be sought, on account of those whose customary misconduct has led them to care little for excommunications. I have also examined the letter you sent to the priest who was presuming illicitly; it was no less pious than regular, and in it you reserved more patience than the person deserved.

Therefore, although the devil has been permitted to act in such a horrible rebellion, correct the injury done to God and to yourself without any disturbance of spirit. And take care, by applying suitable severity, that no similar audacity seize anything in the future.

## LETTER LXVII. AVITUS, BISHOP OF VIENNE

[Note: Both letters were written after Easter, though not in the same year. The first was written when Sigismund had celebrated that festival at Chalon; the second when he had celebrated it at Lyon while attending his father Gundobad.]

### To the Lord Sigismund

[Col. 0275B]

While others feast upon your holy and serene presence, I sustain the barrenness of my desire, being more impoverished by the inadequacy of my service than by reason. Accordingly, after the festival—always beloved by everyone, but now especially significant for the people of Chalon—I sent letters expressing the concern of your servant.

If they attempted to touch even the smallest portion of your praises, they would not sufficiently honor even this: that I am permitted to offer them in my humility, or that Your Kindness is pleased to receive them. Therefore, inferring that by God’s favor you are multiply joyful amid such great happiness, I ask that you make the Paschal days happy for us by your return. For while, in your absence, a certain austerity of Lent continues for us, it is customary for all Catholics to see a Christian prince, a most pious lord to his particular servant, even during the solemnity.

## LETTER LXVIII. AVITUS, BISHOP OF VIENNE, TO THE LORD SIGISMUND

By God’s favor we celebrated the Paschal festival with you—indeed, with you not in place but in spirit—we poor people of Vienne. But if you ask how we celebrated it, it was because anyone who was nearby and could more easily have been present grieved more deeply at being absent. Yet when we lament these things, do not say that we differ from your will.

For a long time, as we devoutly believe, affection for that place has held you there; it is not contempt for this place that excludes you from it. You love one Church equally in both your cities; but, as is expedient for a dutiful father, you remain attached to the one until he consents to follow you to the other.

Therefore, as commanded, we first render to God what is owed for the solemnity, and then what is owed to Caesar. Since you are concerned for our joy and safety, give back to our devotion what you require from your lords, although you are yourselves Caesars.

## LETTER LXIX. DICTATED BY AVITUS, BISHOP OF VIENNE, UNDER THE NAME OF SIGISMUND

### To the Emperor

[Note: To Anastasius. Avitus wrote this in Sigismund’s name when Sigismund was sending envoys with a letter to the emperor on official business. When he writes that he is adorned with military rank, companionship in the court, and participation in the Roman name, I think he means military rank and the patriciate, as discussed above. Letter 83 likewise alludes to this: “Consider now how much they must owe whom you elevate with honors, whom you join to the titles of your dignities as companions of all your triumphs and successes.”]

If the obstacle of time and distance prevents the devotion with which we serve you in spirit from being presented to you bodily, we nevertheless attempt to express what we hold in our prayers through our duties. For we believe that we are admitted into the presence of your sacred glory as often as we offer the debt of our solicitude through the devoted service of a written page.

Although your prosperity cannot be hidden from the world, and visibly illuminates your own sphere with rays of splendor, it is nevertheless sweet if those whom you raise up by military rank and the favor of your particular benevolence, whom you enrich at the ends of the earth by their companionship in your powerful court and by their venerable participation in the Roman name, recognize personally the joys of your everlasting rule, which fame celebrates publicly for all.

The remoteness of your subjects adorns the greatness of your empire, and the extent of your commonwealth is affirmed by the fact that we are possessed at a greater distance. Therefore, graciously receive the bearer with his service. Although for all who seek it, it is sufficient for attaining the summit of honor to deserve to behold you, nevertheless graciously receive also those whom we have presumed to commend.

Judging that the persons of these dear and familiar men may also benefit us through this exchange of passage, with the advantage of desire springing forward, we meet them in those whom we send. Above all, we entreat this: since Your Highness’s kindness cannot forget its own benefits, may we, in return for the thanksgiving we offer, deserve as soon as possible a reply from your most serene lips.

## LETTER LXX. AVITUS, BISHOP OF VIENNE

[Note: It could be inferred from Letter 67 that Sigismund frequently visited Chalon. The same is now confirmed by the annual solemnity of Saint Vincent the Martyr, whom the people of Chalon hold in special worship and honor as their patron. The Council of Chalon, convened during the reign of Clovis II, was also celebrated in the church of Saint Vincent, as the preface of the synod shows.]

### To the Lord Sigismund

The presence of your lordly father, Your Glory, detained for two days by business, caused me to delay somewhat in sending the bearer through whom I might discharge the customary annual service concerning the solemnity of Saint Vincent, and, amid the affairs in which your labor watches over our safety, offer the devotion merited by a mind that is always dutiful.

It is enough for the consolation of my desire if the health of all of us rests, after God, upon your prosperity. Nevertheless, it cannot be accepted without some uneasiness that, when traveling from Sapaudia, you seem to pass by the province through carefully chosen routes.

[Note: Not because the direct route for those traveling to the province of Sapaudia runs through Vienne, but because the detour is not great; he complains that Vienne appears to have been passed by deliberately.]

## LETTER LXXI. AVITUS, BISHOP OF VIENNE

[Note: To Ansemundus, a leading man of the royal court of the Burgundians, to whom Letter 49 was also addressed. Both letters were written after the days of the Lord’s Nativity. Since the king had not been present at Vienne for the solemnity, Avitus wishes to know whether he had attended it at Lyon. After learning this from the earlier letter, he added the later one.]

### To the Illustrious Man Ansemundus

[Col. 0277A]

Your servant’s account of our lord is as extensive as my feelings: the unevenness has not yet been completely wiped away, and it keeps us attentive and anxious, so that, in view of the kindness of that man which we are accustomed to desire especially at festivals, we consider your convenience sufficient for all the joy of the solemnities.

Therefore, after honoring the Nativity of the Lord, while preserving my customary service of solicitude, I desire with the full ambition of my wishes to know whether the common distinction that the little Church of Vienne did not deserve on this occasion at least doubled the joy of the people of Lyon.

For if you write back that, with Christ’s favor, you were able to proceed to the church or fulfill your customary devotion, we shall declare that, made participants in the joy of our neighbors, we will feast through hearing the news, if we learn that those to whom your presence was granted have been refreshed by seeing you.

## LETTER LXXII. AVITUS, BISHOP OF VIENNE, TO THE ILLUSTRIOUS MAN ANSEMUNDUS

When, by remaining away, you suspend the hopes of your personal servants, you prevent us from fully receiving or announcing the things for which we pray. Since, therefore, you have solemnly celebrated the feasts of the Lord’s Nativity as far as was possible without you, we eagerly await the opportunity to learn, through your worthy greeting, the prosperity of our most pious lord, which we had justly desired to see.

You have refreshed that people with joy; enrich this one by your reply. May your affection, through me, illumine this people until my own visit presents its service to you.

## LETTER LXXIII. AVITUS, BISHOP OF VIENNE, TO THE ILLUSTRIOUS MAN VALERIANUS

Your kindness preserves its customary solicitude by visiting us alike with your favor and your letters. You added to the solemnity which, by God’s providence, we joyfully observed, and you supplied what was expected in the completion of our votive worship.

For me, who rejoice over the joy insofar as I learn of it, it is no less sweet that after a long period of absence you have returned safely than that you have passed the Paschal feasts in exultation.

## LETTER LXXIV. AVITUS, BISHOP OF VIENNE, TO THE ILLUSTRIOUS MAN CAERTIUS

In sending a servant of my letters to our common lord, I also discharge the services that I always owe to Your Excellency, to whom I am bound. I urge you—or rather, since you have become so hardened, I implore you—to wear down your stomachs, nauseated by the many delicacies of Saxony, at last with the more sparing fasts of your medical regimen.

If you are so ignorant of how to repay the exchange of desire that your absence still does not seem sufficient to you, compelled by injury I wish this, and avenge myself with the staff of this imprecation: let the roles of presence be changed, and let what Vienne has in abundance be found at Chalon.

Thus, if we do not have here what should be desired, let us send there what you may wish to avoid. And since what I say is already on the road, if you are still delaying in that place, receive it; if you are already preparing to return, pass it by.

## LETTER LXXV. AVITUS, BISHOP OF VIENNE, TO THE ILLUSTRIOUS MAN HELLADIUS

[Col. 0278B]

Since a perpetual cause of charity always supplies an occasion for rendering service to Your Greatness, and since I rightly owe a special observance of devotion to your earnest kindness, the circumstances of the festival have nevertheless now imposed upon me a welcome necessity: that I should present myself to your affection at least through the service of a letter, though I should have wished to do so in person.

Accordingly, with the reverence that is your due, I ask how you celebrated the feasts according to your desire. I pray for the inexhaustible generosity of our Redeemer, that by his protection he may advance you to a hundred years of age and, for the adornment of us all, raise you up, rewarded with every good thing, as he has done until now.

## LETTER LXXVI. AVITUS, BISHOP OF VIENNE, TO THE ILLUSTRIOUS MAN RICO

[Col. 0278C]

After the festival in which your vows and merits shone forth through the presence and safety of our lord, I have rightly offered you, through these letters, the service of my particular affection, in addition to the letters of service sent to him. Through them I announce that, amid the many reports of affairs, we passed Easter successfully, judging that the fullness of the divine gift would come to me if I should also deserve the kindness of your conversation together with a similar acknowledgment of prosperity.

## LETTER LXXVII. DICTATED BY AVITUS, BISHOP OF VIENNE, UNDER THE NAME OF LEONIANUS, ARCHDEACON

[Note: Different from this man are Sapaudus, bishop of Arles, son of the patrician Placidus and not much younger in age, and Sapaudus the abbot, who subscribed to the Fifth Council of Orléans on behalf of Albinus, bishop of Angers. Leonianus, now an archdeacon, appears to be the same man as Leonianus, the servant of Bishop Maximus, whose appetite Avitus mocked in Letter 65. The letter composed in his name agrees with that man’s character and habits.

“Very different and unlike him, however—although, as is said, neither separated from him by much age nor by residence—is Leonianus the abbot. We recently observed his tomb at Vienne in the suburban church of Saint Peter, with an epitaph, crude indeed but by no means unworthy of the grace of a holy man, in these words:

### Epitaph of Saint Leonianus

Here lived a man distinguished for holiness, abbot in this city of Vienne. Born in Savaria of Pannonia, captured by barbarians, he came into the territory of Gaul. First enclosed at Augustodunum, then at Vienne in the cloister of a private cell, he served Christ in this manner for more than forty years, with such strictness that he scarcely appeared within to anyone arriving from any direction and remained almost unknown to all, although through the word of his teaching he was widely known to many for salvation.

Thus, beside his cell, he ruled a great number of monks; and the monks enclosed within the city in the monastery precinct he nourished and disciplinarily guarded, in a marvelous arrangement, to the number of sixty.”]

### To the Illustrious Man Sapaudus

Although you have described in brilliant language the splendor of the principal banquet, shining with sea-borne and land-based delicacies, you have nevertheless made your customary affection unmistakably clear. For you recite such things confidently after disposing of the material given to you, not in verses but with your teeth: when, at a single meal—one that scarcely two pack animals could have carried on their backs—one belly contained everything; when, neglecting the duty of the meal, you ‘combed’ with scallops a stomach clogged by excess.

Although it is clear that you have exaggerated this for the purpose of mocking me, I nevertheless firmly maintain that no one like us—whether he is hungry or eating—can rightly be called blessed. To speak, then, of the first dish you described: you thought it a small kind of punishment that a peacock, enclosed in an edible covering, shut out and swallowed your appetite gaping within, and that, trembling, with your throat inflamed, you hung for a little while at the discretion of the skilled carver.

[Note: Either it was like the warbler enclosed in a peacock’s egg in Petronius, or he means a peacock made into *isicium* (forcemeat), like Apicius’ minced chicken, chopped into small pieces and made into forcemeat. Apicius, Book VIII, chapter 7, *On a Stuffed Piglet*: “A garden piglet is boned through the throat in the manner of a bag; into it are put a minced chicken, cut into pieces, thrushes, warblers, forcemeat from its own flesh, and so forth.”]

[Note: The person who was the master of cutting up food was called the *scissor* by Seneca, the *scissor* by Petronius, and the *chironomus* by Juvenal, from the gesticulation he used while cutting the food. Petronius also writes of this: “Immediately the carver came forward and, gesticulating to the music, tore the food apart so that you would have thought Darius was fighting while an organ-player sang.” Although, therefore, he cut the dishes with an educated hand, very quickly and with a flying knife, as Juvenal puts it, he seemed slow to Leonianus’ eager throat.]

And so it happened that you spent the first part of the meal hungry and complaining, the middle part eating and snatching, and the last part full and weeping—drinking your food and chewing your cups. I would not say that my absence benefited you. Yet whatever remained over for you satisfied all of us to the extent that it exceeded your needs.

For when you, amid such great banquet bliss, had feasted most abundantly and been filled only very slowly, you could scarcely prove yourself happy, what, I presume, would you judge of poor me? I am not permitted to share the abundance of the royal table, and I am not filled by ecclesiastical frugality. Under the name of honor I am committed to custody; as though summoned to the front and prevented from going to a better place, I am forced to lie down so that I cannot escape.

I am filled with vegetables and puffed up with turnips; I abound in legumes, but in those produced by the earth, not the sea. Amid all this I do not even remember what oysters of blessed memory once tasted like.

If a little wine, scarcely filling a very small vessel halfway, is supplied, this measure or rule is carefully observed. I say nothing further about food: in receiving fresh wines the punishment is greater. When I ask for must, I either suffer starvation or am accused of having stolen something. With the greatest importunity I insist that I presume upon three fresh wines more than the others.

Even the bowls that I break by pretending that accidents occurred grow fewer through daily replacement. Therefore, cease insulting one who labors so greatly under these conditions. For since it is the daily fate of both of us to bear whatever lot each has drawn, I shall be able to forget my familiar misery if our lord orders me to be present at his feast in such a way that you happen to be absent.

## LETTER LXXVIII. AVITUS, BISHOP OF VIENNE

[Note: To his brother, the bishop of Valence, to whom several other letters are addressed.]

### To Bishop Apollinaris.

I trust completely, and do not doubt, that common joy has been announced by the divine gift of your common presence. For, as I suspect has already reached you, even those who were said to be laying waste the frontier have returned. For this reason, owing to my anxiety, I have sent these lines, so that you may inform me of whatever you later learn concerning any increase of security—or whether free access to the city has already drawn you away from your accustomed practice, or rather from your love of the siege.

Moreover, I ask that you order those little *magdalia* which you promised to be sent along with a brief set of instructions.

[Note: *Magdalia* is a familiar term in the shops of apothecaries. Even today they call smooth cylinders *magdaleones*, into which compounded plasters are formed. Scribonius Largus, describing the plaster of the surgeon Tryphon, writes of a greenish preparation: “When it ceases boiling, it is kneaded by hand and, having been reduced into larger round pieces—which they call *magdalides* (μαγδαλίδας)—it is put away.” He therefore asks that, together with the little *magdalia* he promises, he be sent a memorandum specifying how each is to be used.]

Thus far in a familiar vein. What remains I shall now, since I am inclined to it, report somewhat more cheerfully.

[Note: A signet ring, or seal, whose shape and material, together with all its ornaments, Avitus describes with great elegance, specifying how he wants it made.]

As for the signet which your piety has deigned not so much to promise as to offer, I want it made in the following fashion. Within a very thin iron ring, as though enclosed by dolphins meeting one another, let the form of a double seal be set with two little hinges. As one side or the other is turned, whether concealed or exposed, let it alternate before the eyes of those who look upon it, displaying either the face of a flourishing little stone or the pale face of amber.

Nor do I mean such amber as recently—as I myself have learned—lay dull amid the pure and undefiled brightness of that hand, in which I should believe there was a mixture of gold not yet refined in the furnace, rather than gold that had been properly prepared.

[Note: As Pliny teaches, all gold contains silver in varying proportions. Wherever one-fifth is silver, it is called *electrum*. When it is found naturally in metal, it is called native electrum. It is also produced artificially by adding silver to gold; but if the proper proportion is exceeded, the mixture is corrupted. Such is the alloy Avitus rejects for his seal.]

Or at least let it have that kind of color which, evenly and moderately, draws redness from gold, whiteness from silver, preciousness from both, and brilliance from the other elements, while an artfully balanced and delightful degree of greenness commends it.

[Note: Alaric, defeated by Clovis—for then the Visigothic kingdom in Gaul collapsed. Avitus wishes the adulterated coinage to have foreshadowed that ruin. Even now old Gothic coins of electrum may be seen, so pale that one would think they contain less gold than silver. They nevertheless bear the impressed image of their kings. Procopius seems either not to have known this or to have deliberately passed over it as illegitimate, when, in Book III of the Gothic War, he writes that only the Frankish kings were permitted this, while it was forbidden to the other barbarian kings. Speaking of the Franks and their king Theodebert, who controlled part of the province, he says: “They made a gold coin from the mines in Gaul, impressing upon this stater not, as is customary, the image of the Roman emperor, but their own image. Yet the king of the Persians commonly has a silver coin struck if he wishes, but to place his own image upon a gold stater is permitted neither to him nor to any other king whatsoever among the barbarians.” We possess a gold coin of King Theodebert, whom Procopius mentions: small in weight but of sound quality, bearing his image and name: “Our Lord Theodebert, King of the Goths” (*D. N. THEODEBERTUS C.*).]

If you ask what should be engraved upon the seal:

[Note: What Avitus orders to be done on his seal is precisely what King Charles the Bald later prescribed for his denarii in the Edict of Pistres of 864, chapter 11: “On the denarii of our new coinage, let our name appear in a circle on one side, and in the middle of our name let there be our monogram”—that is, let the intertwined and confused letters of the monogram be read through the name written around it. In this way, on ancient royal charters, one sees the king’s name added alongside the monogram. Yet, surprisingly, the royal order was not obeyed on the moneyers’ denarii. For there are denarii both of Charles himself and of his son Louis in which, around the monogram, not the name but the royal dignity is expressed: on Charles’s, “By the grace of God, king”; on Louis’s, “By the mercy of God, king.”]

Let the sign of my monogram be read as the indication of the name written around it. The center of the ring, on the side nearest the closed palm, shall be held by the tails of the dolphins whose heads I described above. A little stone, sought expressly for this purpose, oblong and shaped with pointed ends, should be set between them.

There you have merely a kind of model for carrying out the design. Yet I do not constrain the breadth of your elegance to the pattern I have mentioned, as though it were not free to add whatever seems appropriate. Your overflowing ingenuity may go beyond the limits of the commission prescribed.

At the end of the letter, however, my muddy task—without which the matter cannot be completed—demands a thickly worded request: send at once a potter skilled in the work, who may show us according to what measurements the much-perforated dining room of the furnace should be constructed, and within what space a pit, enclosed by the filth of excavated earth and by the feet of animals, may be made so that the bond of baked mud can be kneaded.

## LETTER LXXIX. AVITUS, BISHOP OF VIENNE

[Note: To the same man, giving thanks for gifts which he had sent for the adornment of the church of Vienne, since Avitus himself could not attend his celebration.]

TO BISHOP APOLLINARIS.

Bound and burdened alike by your gracious solicitude, by the greatness of your gift, and by the habitual kindness through which it was bestowed, what gratitude—or rather, what diligent service—could I offer in return? Unless perhaps, being utterly unequal to the task, I am sustained in this very matter by the same grace of yours that overwhelms us.

May almighty God grant that you remain an ornament to the Church and a consolation and refreshment to us, so that, since you truly live not only for yourselves, you may increase your merits through the consolations you provide to others.

My sins brought about a certain necessity, because of which, on the day of our little celebration, we were deprived of the bodily presence of your piety. Yet you restored and represented to us the exchange of your presence: your appearance in light, your face in speech, and your touch in action.

I hope in the mercy of our God that our little church will venerate the gift of your offering not only during my lifetime, but also in the time to come. Just as I, while I live, desire to preserve it as a testimony to your inexhaustible generosity, so may God grant me that your authority may especially commend it to the man whom, when God commands, your election shall appoint after me.

## LETTER LXXX. AVITUS, BISHOP OF VIENNE

[Note: It is acknowledged that Quintianus was at this time bishop of Clermont. Therefore the heading of the letter seems false. Since it was written to the bishops of the province of Vienne, summoning them to the Council of Epaon, what place could there be for the bishop of Clermont, who was not only outside the province of Vienne but also outside the dominion of the Burgundians? For just as the Council of Agde belonged only to those subject to the rule of the Visigoths, and the First Council of Orléans only to those under Frankish power, so only those enclosed within the borders of the Burgundians assembled at Epaon. It is therefore evident that a letter to Quintianus is missing here, of which only the heading remains; whereas the heading of the present letter, which we have said was written to the bishops of the province, is missing.]

TO BISHOP QUINTIANUS.

[Col. 0282B]

It is long since, whether through forgetfulness or preoccupation, we have neglected a matter of great necessity, established by the Fathers not without divine inspiration. Yet the bonds of necessity must sometimes be broken, so that the commands of the Teacher may at last be fulfilled.

[Note: The Council of Nicaea had decreed this in canon 5: “It has seemed good that, in each province, councils should be held twice a year.” In keeping with this, the Council of Riez, canon 8, states: “It has decreed that, according to ancient custom, if the times are peaceful, assemblies should be held twice a year.” And the First Council of Orange, canon 29: “Those who disregard the decrees of the Fathers, by which it has been ordained that we assemble twice a year—a requirement difficult for us because of the circumstances of the times.” I think that, because of this difficulty, it was subsequently agreed that synods should be celebrated once each year. This was established among us at the First Council of Agde and repeated later in many others.]

The assemblies which the care of the elders decreed should be held by priests twice each year—if you weigh the matter carefully, may we at least hold them once every two years! For I know that letters have sometimes been brought to me from the venerable pope of the City, angry with us for this negligence.

Therefore, through me the Church of Vienne implores you, if you are willing; the renewed health of an interrupted custom asks that what has until now lain torpid through infrequency be awakened. It is just, as I think, that when the earlier decrees have been considered in the opportunity afforded by our common presence, we should together communicate the old matters to our own people and to ourselves, as the order of discussion may determine, or, if necessary, add matters of our own.

For this reason we ask you all together, brothers, to deign to be present on the eighth day before the Ides of September [Note: for the Council of Epaon. It is often called Epaon, elsewhere Epauna. It is certain that this council is meant; but the location, and its present name, have until now remained uncertain, and many have proposed various conjectures. The author who wrote the life of Saint Firmatus says that, after leaving Tours, he reached a place called Eona on the Rhône and settled there. If we accept that Eona is a variation of Epona—which is certainly not absurd—one who has found the tomb of Saint Firmatus may not be far from the place of the council.] in the parish of Epaon [Col. 0283A]. This place was chosen as sufficiently convenient for the assembly after everyone’s exertions had been considered; and the season, as far as possible free from the pressure of rural labor, permits everyone freer travel, although the more important cause of the Church ought to require that all earthly occupations be interrupted.

We therefore ask, beg, appeal, and solemnly implore that no obstacle of any excuse keep anyone from so holy an arrangement, and that no bond of temporary necessity hinder anyone from such a tie of charity.

But if, God forbid, such severity of bodily illness should assail anyone [Note: The Gallican canons recognize no excuse preventing bishops from attending a synod except bodily illness. Thus, at this very Council of Epaon, canon 1 decreed that, unless there were an evident cause of illness, no one should make an excuse. The Second Council of Orléans, canon 1, likewise says: “Let no bishop, unless detained by a definite cause of illness, refuse to come to the council under any pretext whatsoever.” Accordingly, they usually exclude other excuses, such as the division of royal property, in the Third Council of Orléans, canon 1: “Let them know that this excuse has been removed from them, if they think to excuse their absence by the division of the inheritance.” The Second Council of Tours excludes all others: “Except in the case of the most certain illness, no one should be separated from the council under any pretext, whether because of the king’s command or because of an impediment connected with royal administration, or under the pretext of public usefulness or private business.”], so that spiritual desire is overcome by bodily weakness, let him arrange for two priests of eminent and approved character, strengthened by written instructions, to represent him to the brothers.

Let him choose men whom the council of bishops may rightly allow to participate no less because of their knowledge than because of their reverence; men with whom the chief pontiffs will take pleasure in conversing, and whom, when their skill has been judged sufficient, authority may select to establish and sign definitions on behalf of their bishop.

[Note: Those who could not come to the council because of illness sent representatives in their place. The Second Council of Arles, canon 18, says: “If anyone, having been summoned, is absent because of illness, let him send a person in his place.” And the Council of Carpentras, in its letter to Bishop Agraecius: “Although you ought to be present at the synod either in person or through a representative.” Although the present passage therefore requires two, and it is known that two representatives signed for one bishop at the Fifth Council of Arles, the earlier evidence shows that one was generally sufficient. Nor was it necessary to send all the priests, since the subscriptions of the councils make clear that sometimes abbots and priests, and sometimes archdeacons or deacons, were accustomed to be delegated.]

Yet let this be demanded only by the greatest necessity. Otherwise, the greatness of brotherly affection and pastoral diligence is not proved except by the greatness of the labor.

For your holiness can infer, after this long silence caused by our abuse of the matter, how the things that must be considered with God’s help should be defined, and how all the ministers of the churches of our province ought to follow what has been defined.

## LETTER LXXXI. AVITUS, BISHOP OF VIENNE, TO THE LORD SIGISMUND

[Col. 0283C]

I know that, amid the cares and occupations in which, with heavenly assistance, you keep faithful watch for the safety of your country, it is presumptuous to intrude the service of a letter. Yet since your exalted piety has not so forgotten a particular servant that, in the very preparations for the campaign you had undertaken, you doubled my longing for you through a holy exchange of words, who could fail to understand how patiently you will endure my foolishness, which your clemency itself has provoked?

Accordingly, I presume to ask anxiously how you are in health, with God’s help, and how the hope of our common wish smiles upon your undertaking. But I ask not merely this; rather, by the grace which you received from God and extend to me, I beg that, although we rightly feel secure about the firmness of your pledged faith, you may, through the greater gift of your care, provide for our trembling and our sluggishness. Do not consider more that the whole people, devoted to you, prays for you than that it waits in fear.

Yet, although we are sinners, frightened by conscience, we confidently believe that even if, with Christ protecting you, our fear should move you to laughter, it will at least move the divine ears to grant us the joy of your prosperity.

## LETTER LXXXII. AVITUS, BISHOP OF VIENNE, TO THE LORD SIGISMUND

Anyone who is less secure about your prosperity seems to distrust the divine promise. But if you weigh my heart with solid generosity, you will easily understand that my cowardice, arising from excessive fear, deserves pardon.

For all who sincerely claim the name of Catholics ought now to beseech God in sleepless prayer that he may faithfully join what is near to you and happily subject what is hostile, while you return to us bearing our wishes inviolate and whole.

Thus, amid the manifold necessities of affairs, with Christ fighting for you, may both the outcome you desire and the victory you deserve be granted to you.

Therefore, if the time of anxiety has diminished the favor of my memory in your wavering heart, your special servant, not daring to send greetings but awaiting your safety from the Lord, has dispatched this service of the present page with a sufficiently anxious and attentive mind, concerned first for your health and then for that of the army.

Although, in God’s name, we learn good news through all kinds of travelers, you can nevertheless imagine how much sweeter it will be for me if, just as the recognition of a holy affection feeds me through every report, your reply should make me glad—if, in place of your presence, I may obtain your words before my eyes, and in place of your hand, deserve to kiss your signature.

## LETTER LXXXIII. DICTATED BY AVITUS, BISHOP, IN THE NAME OF THE LORD KING SIGISMUND

[Note: Anastasius, as the following letter makes clear. Since this letter is said to have been written at the beginning of Sigismund’s reign, after the death of his father Gundobad, it confirms that Avitus did not preserve chronological order in arranging his letters. He complains about the king of Italy, who prevented the embassy he was sending to the emperor from proceeding.]

TO THE EMPEROR.

It is known to all that your Highness measures not the obstacles of time but the wishes of your subjects. In the security and joy of this confidence, we who are absent in body present ourselves in spirit to our most glorious prince.

Although this service has been performed by your servant, my lineage, out of devotion, my obligation to gratitude has been created no more by ancestral duty than by the benefits bestowed upon me. My people are indeed yours, but I take greater pleasure in serving you than in ruling them.

This has been handed down from my ancestors: the Roman devotion that has always animated my family toward you and your predecessors, so that we considered that glory greater which you extended to us through military titles than any distinction we might receive from our own ancestry. All my forebears have always sought more eagerly what they might receive from princes than what they had brought from their fathers.

Although we seem to govern our people, we believe that we are appointed as nothing other than your soldiers. Your prosperity shares its joys with us. Whatever you care for there on behalf of all belongs also to us. Through us you administer the regions of distant lands; our homeland is your world.

The light of the East touches its Gaul, and the ray believed to rise in those regions shines here. We do not grasp the splendor of your presence by looking upon you, but through longing we possess the light of your serenity, which you spread everywhere.

No barrier confines the dominion granted you by God, and the extension of your fortunate scepters is not limited by the boundaries of any provinces. Let this be said without dishonor to the Divinity. It does not diminish your majesty that not everyone can hasten to you; it is sufficient for the reverence owed you that all adore you from their own seats.

You reign over the eastern world by virtue and over the West by prosperity. You are loved everywhere, even where it is not granted to everyone to behold you.

But since this may rightly be said of the whole world, now consider how much those owe you whom you raise to high office, whom you attach to yourself as companions in all your triumphs, successes, and dignities, so that the honors of your virtue may be ours, and whatever the source of honors has achieved may contribute to the adornment of those whom it honors.

Therefore, illustrious prince, I offer the service of letters and the vows of gratitude; I await the utterance of your august speech; I seek to know whether there is anything you deign to command.

For even if your eternity does not believe that it needs our service, whoever has deserved to serve one blessed serves his own cause.

Let the distance of the eastern nations therefore offer its submission. Let it ask that our ruler be made their prince. Let the Parthian commander rejoice, for the sake of peace, to pass into the Roman Empire. Let the Indian himself, after experiencing a gentle countenance, recognize through a Greek interpreter the laws by which he is commanded to serve, his shrill voice having been silenced.

If there is any heat by which the southern axis is scorched, cool it with moderation, and through reverence tame whatever nature had previously left untamed before you.

Let whoever does not desire to receive the scepters of unconquered religion pressing upon him do so. Through you, let religion be extended no less by power: among peoples that serve, it both establishes the truths of heaven and the objects of veneration and offers freedom; through its mediation, as you rely upon the summit of eternal salvation, it befits us to serve you for a long time, not only by human order but also by divine love.

## LETTER LXXXIV. DICTATED BY AVITUS, BISHOP, IN THE NAME OF THE LORD KING

[Note: The count Sigismund.]

C. S. TO THE EMPEROR ANASTASIUS.

[Col. 0286B]

Nothing shows more clearly whether your serenity, in the judgment of your pious majesty, either makes light of the obstacles of time or takes account of the hearts of your servants than the fact that, in extending sacred letters over great distances, you fulfill the wishes of those who long for you and do not await the services of petitioners.

Everyone’s mind desires to meet you; what few are able to do is not so glorious as the fact that everyone wishes to see you.

As the address of your august speech now anticipates the service owed to you in this letter, let no pious judge attribute anything to lack of devotion or to delay. If an intervening obstacle had not suspended access to our efforts, that word venerable to the world would surely even now have sent responses rather than prophecies.

Yet the delay did me less harm than jealous rivalry begrudged me. You did not find me in possession of my office, but you made me happy by addressing me with your gracious words. It makes no difference whether august speech receives us or awaits us: it is enough for us that we are not despised by your most exalted favor, just as it is enough for you that we are granted your favor.

Therefore, after the death of my father, most devoted and faithful to you, one of your nobles, to whom, in addition to a succession of the happiest fortunes in unbroken prosperity, it was granted by divine favor to know the commonwealth joyful and flourishing while you ruled the world, and to leave you, lords of the nations, with a peaceful end of his life: in order to report these things to you and commend to you also the beginnings of my service—which, while my father yet survived, you fostered and will increase more and more after him by the accumulation of your sacred favor, as I ought and might fittingly have wished—I was presenting to the ears of your venerable court one of my advisers, who is thought, as far as Gallic ignorance is concerned, to surpass the rest in learning, with particular confidence, because—

[Note: Theoderic, who sought this peace through ambassadors from Anastasius, as Cassiodorus writes in *Variae* 1: “It is fitting, most merciful emperor, that we seek peace, since we are known to have no causes for anger.” And afterward: “Let the sincerity of peace, which is known to have been disturbed by emerging causes, remain thereafter restored to its former firmness when conflicts have been wiped away.” Alluding to this peace, the Roman Senate addressed Anastasius in a letter incorporated into the letter of Hormisdas: “Therefore, most pious emperor, the Senate has added this, that you who were so kindly disposed toward reconciling the two commonwealths may likewise be recognized as pious in restoring unity within the Church.” Following the example of this peace, Totila also sought peace from Justinian, in Procopius, Book III of the *Gothic War*: “We ask you to receive and grant us the benefits of peace, of which we possess the finest memorials and examples, Anastasius and Theoderic.” Theoderic ultimately prided himself on this peace and commended it to his heir, urging him to maintain peace with the Eastern emperor. Jordanes, *On the Gothic History*: “He appointed Athalaric, the son of his daughter Amalasuntha, king, and charged them—as though issuing a testamentary command—that they should always keep the Eastern emperor appeased and favorable.”]

—the ruler of Italy publicly rejoiced in your peace and, by spreading the report, portrayed the favor of the East as restored to him.

The journey undertaken for the dispatch of these reports was therefore blocked and forbidden. Let the sequence of truth itself determine what this means before your august joy. Yet it seems a small indication of friendship when one who claims to honor you does not wish you to be honored by others, since all who receive you with worthy reverence ought to wish that the same be done by everyone.

Someone shows little personal devotion if, having condemned the freedom to meet you, he strives to make others likewise disloyal. Yet the holiness of a heavenly character cannot judge guilty one whom even the will alone has made innocent.

You therefore plainly see that he himself bears witness to what I desired, since he took such pains to prevent me from being able to do it.

And so, since by your divine and your own gift both sacred letters and favorable opportunities arise, how different are the things you provide! Those to whom you bring new things pray for an increase of your kingdom; those to whom you preserve what is customary desire its protection.

Thus, with the pious moderation of your governance, he sought remedies of two kinds, and neither side suffered rejection. Among these matters, however, I owe a more particular debt: the outcome of this petition has been granted to my humble regard.

You have shown freely how much favor you bestow upon a special servant. For this advantage alone you wished the reward deposited in your treasuries to consist not in a price but in a recompense, since you gave it to the poor.

And with what elegance worthy of praise did you choose to return what had been offered by your servants rather than spurn it, and, in order to make the gift more welcome, choose to burden the service?

Although whatever reaches your hands is devoted to the poor, and therefore perhaps the man who envies generosity tries to dissuade you from accepting, nevertheless provide the means of divine recompense, so that you may distribute to the needy who are destitute and grant to debtors when they petition.

Run, therefore, most pious lord, along the twofold path of your united work. If you believe, nothing sufficient will ever be lacking to such a heart. Since the one who grants ability has given you the means by which it may be bestowed, and has infused into your will the power to refuse nothing, you possess from him the capacity to give.

## LETTER LXXXV. AVITUS, BISHOP OF VIENNE, TO THE ILLUSTRIOUS HERACLIUS

Unless, shaken in spirit, I groaned over the misfortune of a friend, I would surely enlarge upon the matter: you lie on your couch, fearing the deceptive gout, while your physician, vigorously practicing his customary art, makes you more concerned with climbing mountains than with poetry, more dependent upon feet than upon verses.

In grief I dictated this letter hastily, having evidently been summoned to the burial of our former common son Protendius—if even this may provide the father with some consolation.

As for you, if you care that our loss has been complete, keep us safe, while I am away, from the feared attacks bounded by the Rhône. And keep our Ceratius, who has something of me and something of you: from me he claims to be a man of letters, from you a warrior. From his mother’s wisdom he takes the fact that he gladly flees barbarians; from his father’s courage, that he does not turn his back on letters.

## LETTER LXXXVI. REPLY OF THE ILLUSTRIOUS HERACLIUS

You indicated only the cause of such grief that it would close the response required by a letter, and the harsh message that inflicted the wound compelled me to serve you more with tears than with writing. Yet, fearing the fault of silence, I have stolen a few words from my sighs, as best I could.

The circumstances therefore show to whom the charge of fear should more properly be assigned, and whose foresight, entrusted with defenses, proves him the more timid.

Accordingly, scorning the city’s shelters, I displayed the firmness of my heart on open ground amid the neighboring danger, and long ago reached the level spaces of exposed places, so that by the freedom of my dwelling I might show this deed to be an act of courageous daring.

But when you learned the rumor, you hurried to the city’s enclosures as though an enemy were approaching. The man whom the countryside continually held during days of peace is not now brought out even from the hiding places of the dead.

Indeed, just as the city then demanded your presence, so now the abandoned estate seeks you, shut within the walls.

## LETTER LXXXVII. TO THE LORD, MOST EXCELLENT IN HOLY MERITS, MOST GLORIOUS IN CHRIST, AND MOST WORTHY OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE,

[Note: This letter was not found in the manuscript of Avitus which we used. It had formerly been incorporated into the letters of Hormisdas; we have therefore transferred it here, together with Hormisdas’s reply. Hormisdas also refers to it in his letter 11 to Anastasius, writing: “The anxious hearts of all hang in suspense: an embassy sent to us from the furthest parts of Gaul asked whether our concern had advanced anything toward restoring unity, if a form of reply had followed.”]

POPE HORMISDAS, FROM AVITUS.

[Col. 0288C]

Since you see that the discipline of religion and the complete rules of the Catholic faith require that the flock entrusted to you throughout all the members of the universal Church be instructed by the unremitting care of your exhortation, you visited the province of Vienne last year, if you deign to remember, by letters addressed to my humility. Those letters reached me through the clergy of the Church of Arles, in accordance with the opportunity that had arisen, and indeed with the fullest pastoral concern.

In them, just as you summon us to share your joy through the conversion of provinces—that is, of Dardania, Illyricum, and Scythia—so you instruct us, with the most cautious admonition, about what may overtake us through ignorance.

The condemnation of Eutyches and Nestorius, whom the authority of your holy see, through its most blessed predecessors, crushed long ago, was already brought to our knowledge through the apostolic care exercised toward us.

But what now greatly leaves us suspended and anxious is that, while you had ordered us to await with every expectation the outcome of the embassy sent a second time to Constantinople, you have indicated neither what your holy son and my brother Ennodius reported nor whether the embassy that followed has returned; and you have suspended your promise through such prolonged silence that now the silence of the preacher makes us no less astonished than previously the delay of the embassy made us suspicious.

[Note: Ennodius was sent twice to Constantinople by Hormisdas, but only one embassy had taken place when Avitus wrote this. Therefore Hormisdas replied to him: “Our embassy, which we sent once, not twice as you write—if it had met with the desired outcome, we would immediately have shared with you the things you desired.” The first embassy of Ennodius took place during the consulship of Florentius, in the year of Christ 515. When the treachery and dissimulation of the emperor Anastasius rendered it fruitless, a second was added on the third day before the Nones of April, during the consulship of Agapitus, in the year of Christ 517. In that same year Hormisdas replied to Avitus’s letter in February. Therefore a false report had reached Vienne that the second embassy, which was then still being prepared, had already departed for the East.]

For this sole reason I have sent the servants who are your sons and my brothers, the priest Alexius and the deacon Venantius, in the name of the whole province of Vienne, which has been entrusted to the Church belonging to me by all your predecessors and by the apostolic see.

Through them I shall learn, from the oracle of your most blessed reply, whether the fervor of the aforementioned schisms—which had broken out within the city of Constantinople through the pernicious vice of obstinacy, and to which, what is more grievous, you say that the Churches of Alexandria and Antioch are also bound—has been extinguished by a worthy correction under your instruction, with Christ’s favor;

or whether the returning embassy displayed in clear documents something that could be read plainly; or whether perhaps it reported only through a messenger, leaving some sort of suspicion concerning you.

For we fear that, while the pontifical judgment does not announce good news, it may have encountered adversity.

We have also learned through the reliable reports of various people that Greece boasts of the reconciliation or concord of the Roman Church. This is something to be welcomed if it is said truthfully, but feared lest it be deceitfully feigned.

We therefore all beg, through my service, that you instruct me what I ought to reply to your sons and my brothers, that is, to the Gallic bishops. And because I confidently promise this—not merely concerning Vienne but concerning the devotion of all Gaul—I ask that you inform us all of your judgment concerning the state of the faith.

Pray that the disguised profession of the lost may not deceive us, just as discovered truth may not separate us from the unity which you govern.

Received on the third day before the Kalends of February, during the consulship of Agapitus, through Alexius the priest and Venantius the deacon.

## LETTER LXXXVIII. HORMISDAS TO AVITUS, BISHOP, OR TO ALL THE BISHOPS OF THE PROVINCE OF VIENNE UNDER YOUR DIOCESE

(C)

Whoever wishes especially to be instructed by one who is well informed about matters pertaining to Catholic discipline, what zeal . . .

[This letter will be given where Hormisdas’s letters appear.]

## HOMILY OF ALCIMUS AVITUS ON THE ROGATIONS

### HOW THE CUSTOM OF THE ROGATIONS ORIGINATED

[Note: Gregory of Tours, *History*, Book II, chapter 34, speaks of this homily: “Avitus reports in a certain homily which he wrote on the Rogations that these very Rogations, which we celebrate before the triumph of the Lord’s Ascension, were instituted by Mamertus, bishop of the city of Vienne, who was also presiding there at that time, when that city was terrified by many prodigies,” and so forth. That Avitus delivered many homilies on this subject is confirmed by the *Excerpts* of the deacon Florus, in which passages are cited from sermons delivered on the first, second, and third days of the Rogations. I believe there were still more of them, but that Florus did not mention either the present homily or the others because they contained no reference to the Epistles of Paul. The passages in our present edition that differ from Gagneius’s first edition of all are based on an old exemplar from which they were taken.]

[Col. 0289C]

Indeed, along the path of life, not only through Gaul but almost throughout the whole world, the irrigating stream of the observance of the Rogations runs, and by the abundant flow of its annual act of penitence cleanses the earth infected with vices. Yet for us there is a more particular reason for both the institution of this service and its joy, because what now flows from here for the benefit of all first sprang from our own fountain; and perhaps the beginning of the institution first undertaken may now contribute something to the adornment of its privilege.

But when an ineffable necessity subdued the stern hearts of the Viennese to such humility, our church, recognizing the cause of its distress, did not suppose that it needed the observance to be instituted especially more than all others, but that it alone among all needed it; it sought the remedy more earnestly than precedence.

[Col. 0289D]

I know that many among us recall the causes of the terrors of that time. Frequent fires, continual earthquakes, and nocturnal sounds [Col. 0290C] seemed to threaten some portentous funeral pyre for the whole world. Amid crowds of people, the appearance of wild beasts was seen within the city—God knows whether they were deceiving the eyes or had been brought forth by prodigies. Whatever the truth of those two possibilities, the event was understood as equally monstrous: either that the savage hearts of enormous beasts could truly be tamed in this way, or that phantoms of a false vision could be so horribly fashioned before the eyes of terrified spectators.

Amid these events there were differing judgments among the common people and various opinions among the several classes. Some concealed what they felt and assigned to accident what they were unwilling to assign to lamentation; others, with a healthier spirit, interpreted the abominable novelties according to the appropriate significance of the evils. For who would not fear Sodomitic rains amid frequent fires? Who would not believe, when the elements trembled, that either falling roofs or ruptured earth threatened? Who, seeing—or certainly thinking that he saw—[Col. 0291A] naturally timid deer entering through the narrow gates and penetrating as far as the open marketplace, would not fear an impending sentence of desolation?

Why say more? These matters were discussed amid public fears and private rumors until the night of the approaching solemn vigil, on which the annual custom required the feast of the Lord’s Resurrection to be celebrated. Everyone was awaiting that night with a common expectation as the help of their labors, the end of their evils, and the security of those who feared.

That venerable night therefore arrived, opening a solemn occasion of prayerful hope for public deliverance. But suddenly a much more violent uproar thundered there, as though a blow from a heavier scourge had struck—so that, once the successive stages had already been traversed, nothing but chaos seemed likely to follow. For the public building which an immense height had raised above the lofty summit [Col. 0291B] of the city began to burn with dreadful flames at dusk.

The joy of the solemnity was therefore interrupted by the announcement of danger, and the church was emptied of a people filled with fear. Everyone feared a similar fate for his possessions or his own house, because of that towering center of the fire. Yet the unconquered bishop remained before the festive altars, and, kindling the heat of his faith with a stream of tears, restrained the power that had been permitted to the flames, so that the fire withdrew.

When despair had been laid aside, the people returned to the church, and, the light of the flames extinguished, the beauty of the lamps shone forth. Nor was there any further delay in taking up the medicine of repentance. My predecessor, and my spiritual father from baptism, the priest Mamertus, to whom, many years before, my father in the flesh had succeeded in the priesthood as God had willed, [Note: [Col. 0291D] This was Isicius, or Hesychius. Ado of Vienne says in his Chronicle: “Avitus, bishop of Vienne, outstanding in eloquence and holiness, whose brother Apollinaris, bishop of Valence, was distinguished by miracles, were the two most illustrious sons, two lights, of Isicius—first a senator, afterwards bishop of Vienne.” Avitus too, his son and successor in the episcopate, professed himself a Roman senator in Letter 31. Later another Isicius held the same see of Vienne; he subscribed at the Fifth Council of Orléans and the Third Council of Paris.] conceived the Rogations in his holy mind throughout that night of the Paschal vigil mentioned above; and there, in silence before God, he determined what the world now proclaims in psalms and prayers.

When the Paschal solemnity had passed, a private consultation first considered not whether this should be done, but how and when it ought to be done. Some thought that the senate of Vienne, whose council at that time flourished with numerous distinguished men, could not be brought to accept it, since it scarcely consented to bend even to lawful demands. But the pious and watchful shepherd, generous in the salt of wisdom, first softened the minds of the sheep by prayer before softening their ears by exhortation.

He therefore disclosed the plan, prescribed the order, and explained its salutary purpose; [Col. 0291D] and for a man of such religious and practical intelligence it was not enough merely to set forth the proposed institution to those who obeyed, unless at its beginning he also established the bond of custom.

With God inspiring the hearts of the penitent, all heard it, confirmed it, and magnified it. The present three-day period was chosen, placed between the celebration of the holy Ascension and the Lord’s Day, as though the solemnities bordering it enclosed it within a fitting boundary of opportunity.

But the bishop, testing the fervor of the beginning and especially fearing that, because of the people’s slowness to follow, the observance itself might immediately lose esteem in its novelty if only a few were led out, ordered the prayer of the first procession to take place at the basilica that was then nearer to the city walls. The people went with public enthusiasm, in great numbers, and with the deepest compunction, so that the short and narrow procession truly seemed to be made long by the tears and labors of the people.

When the holy priest had gathered from the success of the lesser undertaking indications of greater things, it was established on the following day that we should labor at what we now undertake on the first day—that is, tomorrow, if the Lord permits.

[Note: [Col. 0291D] The Church of Arverni was the first of all, or among the first, according to Sidonius, book VII, letter 1, to bear witness to Mamertus himself as the author of the Rogations. Soon all Gaul both ordered and observed them; then they were instituted in the kingdom of the Franks, which had already occupied the Gothic kingdom, by decree of the First Council of Orléans, canon 27: “It has pleased all the churches to celebrate the Rogations, that is, the Litanies, before the Lord’s Ascension.” Then they were instituted in the kingdom of the Burgundians, which contained almost the rest of Gaul, as is clear from canon 6 of the Second Council of Lyon: “It has also pleased all the brethren that in the first week of the ninth month—that is, before the Sunday which first dawns in that month—the Litanies should thereafter be celebrated by all churches or parishes, just as the holy Fathers decreed that they should be performed before the Lord’s Ascension.”]
