In the time that followed, certain churches of Gaul adopted this practice, which was so persuasive an example, though they did not all celebrate it on the same days on which it had been instituted among us. Nor did it matter greatly which three-day period was chosen, provided that the services of psalmody were fulfilled annually by the labor of tears. Nevertheless, as love for the Rogations increased, together with the concord of the priests, concern for universal observance yielded to a single period, namely, these present days.

The reason for prefacing this account is that, whether we have told it to those who remember it or perhaps to those who do not know it, all may nevertheless take heed that the Church which gave others the model of this institution must be shown to be indebted in many ways to the display of zeal; and she ought to be first in the duty of compunction, since in a matter so necessary for everyone she became the mother of others by her example.

Therefore, as the most laborious festival of our Rogations now approaches, if God permits, we do not announce it as though to people who do not know it, but commend it as to those who are awaiting it. For although the custom of observing this profession is maintained only with labor, the harshness of the medicine is nevertheless pleasing, since the hope of salvation has often been proved to be found in it.

“If we say,” says the Apostle, “that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves” (1 John 1:8). And if we must constantly confess that we sin, we need the duty of confession and the humility of repentance. Especially when the compunction of an assembled people can be directed toward the encouragement of good works in such a way that the rebellious person would be more appropriately ashamed if, opposing the whole multitude in the isolation of his own mind, he did not mourn his sins or vices together with the weeping people.

[Col. 0293A]

The united striving for good works is therefore necessary. One person receives from another either an example of humility or consolation in confession. A solitary battle is more dangerous, since only a few are able to test their strength against an adversary. But when the agreement of a multitude fights against the common enemy, another’s courage also draws along the timid soldier. When the strong are fighting, weakness lies hidden; and by a certain support of unity, the weak gain praise by being counted in the army of the brave. Finally, when victory comes, it is acquired by all; and although the right hand of a few has fought, the glory of all has triumphed.

I say this about common weakness: if it does not withdraw itself from those who pray, even when it has accomplished less by itself, it will nevertheless not be deprived of the fruit in its entirety. In that glorious and especially remarkable history of the Ninevites, when the sword of the aroused Divinity was unsheathed against them, even childhood was compelled to fight alongside the strength of the elders. The hunger of the animals increased the human reward and favor of the fast. Indeed, irrational creatures themselves, which could not fear having given offense, in a certain way asked for pardon. And because human beings had sinned by living like animals, they in turn compelled the animals to fast as though they were human beings.

For this reason, distinguishing these matters, the Lord says in the Gospel: “Ask and you will receive; seek and you will find; knock and it will be opened to you” (Matthew 7:7). To ask belongs to one who knows; to seek, to one who is devoted. One who knows asks; one who does not know seeks. When you ask, you wish to receive what you understand; when you seek, you are still trying to discover what you should ask for. Therefore, let those who are already stronger ask by praying; let the weak seek by laboring.

But knocking is common to all. No one knocks at a blocked entrance with words: this belongs to the hands and is an act of the body. Let knowledge therefore ask, love seek, and action knock, especially in the present observance.

For this is a festival whose entire joy is sobriety alone, whose feasts are tears, whose nourishment is hunger; whose beginning arises from necessity, whose perseverance is in love, whose activity is in rest, and whose rest is in labor. For throughout this observance there is confession for sin and petition for pardon.

Moreover, the Gospel reading appointed for today has explained the usefulness of supplication, when the company of the disciples, trembling amid the roar of the storm, awakened+ the Lord sleeping in the boat (Matthew 8:24). For what else could it mean that, amid so great a conflict of winds and waves resisting one another, our Lord lay in profound and fearless rest, except that amid the dangers we suffer we should flee to him because of our fear?

This storm continually batters us; the thunder of the world cries out against us with terrible force; the world’s upheaval, with flashes that glitter for an instant, does not illuminate but merely dazzles. The Church is the ship that carries us through various dangers, as through marine whirlpools. It strikes our ears with slander and the shrillness of blasphemies, as though the joints of its sides had been loosened; but what wearies us cannot penetrate the stern built upon the solidity of truth.

And because our Lord promised the Church, “Behold, I am with you all days, until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28:20), he is indeed in the ship in which we are, but he can no longer fear what we fear. After his resurrection and ascension he rests wholly amid our dangers. It is another’s fear that needs him, so that he who lay secure may awaken.

Let him therefore be called upon with voices of supplication; and, if he does not yet hear when danger grows heavier, let him be struck with hands of generosity, and let it be said to him: “Arise; why do you sleep, O Lord? Forgetful of our poverty and tribulation” (Psalm 43:23–24). Once awakened, he will say: “Why are you afraid, you of little faith?” (Matthew 8:26). Let him restore salvation and rebuke weakness.

And if faith is small because we fear worldly things, it is nevertheless some faith if we turn back to the Lord. We would not fear before him if he himself were feared. But the slightest consciousness of uprightness is the greatest cause for trembling, especially in our life, in which the continuation of crimes becomes a multitude of dangers.

Therefore, if we have not said to Christ, “Keep watch with us,” let us at least say, “Awaken for our sake.” We did not ask him not to depart; let us obtain that he return, and let him not abandon the course of our frail voyage until he commands the wind and sea to be silent, restrains the fury of the raging world with a swift end, and brings about, at the judgment’s recompense, the great tranquility that cannot exist in this world.

“For if you were of the world” (John 15:19), the world would love what belonged to it. But once the world has been overcome, let us reach the rest above, where, because the possibility of perishing will be absent, no cause of danger will arise; where the Lord will always be with us, and, if he grants it, we shall always be with him; and he who here sometimes sleeps while we are negligent will there remain eternally awake, without end, for those who enjoy him.

[Col. 0293C]

## Fragments of Certain Minor Works of Saint Avitus

### Notice

[Col. 0293D]

Besides the foregoing homily and another delivered on the conversion of King Sigismund, which Agobard mentions, the oldest papers of the Thuane Library preserve the titles of eight other homilies, together with the first words of each, as follows.

### Titles and Beginnings of Eight Homilies

I. Delivered at the dedication of the upper basilica: “I had resolved, by the patience of today’s silence…”

II. Delivered in the basilica of Saint Mary: “I had determined, dearly beloved, and, as I think…”

[Col. 0294D]

III. On the restoration of the baptistery in his city of Vienne: “…The disturbances of the times by which…”

IV. Delivered at the dedication of the basilica of Geneva: “We know and marvel from the Gospel reading that the rich man…”

V. Delivered at the dedication of …: “It pertains to the place…”

VI. Delivered in the basilica of Saint Peter, which the holy bishop of Tarentaise founded: “…It is fitting that the capacity of strength should diminish as the material for rejoicing increases.”

VII. Delivered in the basilica of the saints of Agaunum, at the renovation of that monastery or on the passion of the martyrs: “The proclamation of the blessed army, in whose assembly…”

VIII. A homily delivered on the conversion of Lord Sigisricus, on the day after his sister had been received from the Arian heresy: [Col. 0295A] “Very often, by divine providence, what belongs to our beloved prince…”

## Fragments of Those Same Homilies

*(From the same papers.)*

### I

Thus once Peter, the head of the apostles (Matthew 13:29), that is, the prince of princes, although he feared the sea stirred by the winds, nevertheless grasped the path across the shifting waters and completed it in victory; and, as though he had struggled through the masses of hostile whirlwinds, he crushed the breath of adverse temptation by faith before it reached its destination. There serenity followed the journey he had completed.

Here too, in habitation no less than in likeness, the security that had not gone before follows the house of Peter, founded upon faith.

[Col. 0295B]

Let the same apostle now renew a dwelling worthy of his name. Let him open this place with the same keys with which he opens the kingdom. Let him now loose whatever bonds of sin are shown to him.

And a little earlier:

The solidity sought at the beginning of buildings here also occupies the summit. Our heights are made safer by the firmest foundation of other buildings.

### II

What praise should I give to his Moses of old (Exodus 15:23), who sweetened waters harsh from antiquity by means of a piece of wood? What praise to Elisha (2 Kings 4:41), equal in power, who seasoned a pot filled with the bitterness of wild food by pouring in a meal that served as medicine? Who does not know that these deeds were examples of wonderful power?

But no less has been granted today to your priest, whom an equal diversity of fortunate outcome will approve as equal to those equals. For it requires almost less power to convert creatures by prayer than to invite the Creator into a building after driving away the enemy.

Here, moreover, the turbulent jealousy of the neighboring Arians fulfills the role of the pagans. And if perhaps no pagan now remains who wishes many gods to be worshiped, the heretic groans when he sees one being invoked. For the divider of the Trinity loves the plurality of gods; and, with a kindred affection for separation, having broken through unity, he accepts the making of many gods by those who agree with him, under whose favor he himself may count three in a seemingly excusable way.

Why should the one who names Christ but is empty of Christ lament that a place formerly closed to deities has been made subject to powers? No one is excluded from sharing in salvation. Let them share equally with the saved what until now we were unwilling to have in common with the lost. We condemn the barriers of profane worship; we open the temples to worshipers who are about to be converted.

Let anyone who formerly loved what was divided now seek what is whole; let anyone who once worshiped stones here recognize Christ as the rock. The altar perishes through sacrilege; an altar comes through sacrifices. The name is one; the cause is different. The bronze serpent heals by the very thing by which the fiery serpent had bitten.

### III

There should be rejoicing with universal exultation that, while the scepters of Catholic power flourish, places of prayer, temples of martyrs, and sacred shrines adorn the towns, no less with buildings than with patrons; indeed, rather, cities become illustrious from being towns through the splendor of their protectors.

And if we also touch upon the joy of the particular feast in a running proclamation, the present building is certainly pleasing to the place; it stands above the river and, like the terror of an impending reverence, restrains the rugged tumult of the neighboring torrent. The river, confined within venerable banks, is checked, and lays beneath the suspended path of the intervening bridge a route toward the sacred heights desired on either side.

The building, sufficient for expansion, has become narrow for the assembly; and although by the joy of its dwelling it draws both earthly and heavenly things to itself, while scarcely sufficing for its people, it is sufficient because of its construction. Shining with the varied ingenuity of its craftsmen, it drove away night and brought in light. After the long, gloomy darkness had been expelled by human skill, daylight was enclosed in a happier kind of prison of brightness and held in blessed custody.

Thus once the prison of Peter (Acts 12:7) shone when a ray illuminated his precious bonds: the iron fitted for punishments shone more brightly than precious metals, the bolts gave way through an open passage, and the chains fell with a ringing clatter.

### IV

Rejoice, therefore, unconquered merchant, entrusted with this stewardship; bring forth from your treasure new things and old (Matthew 13:52), instructor of the unlearned, restorer of what is falling; let there be one solemnity amid manifold consecration.

By the instruments of tears you raised up what the enemy had cast down. The form of the temples that had been lost has returned; let holiness also return. You did not, like the servant in the Gospel (Luke 19:13), bury the mina entrusted to you in earthly soil, with the napkin condemning you. Nor were you content merely to return what had long ago been committed to you, bringing back that and offering this; rather, so that you might present the first fruits more abundantly, you first took care to discharge what you owed.

[Col. 0296C]

Therefore, dearly beloved, pray for what remains: that if adversity steals anything sacred, it may return in such a way that God, taking vengeance, restores it. Let the grain of wheat once thought mature grow into many fruits. Like the wealth of our Job (Job 42:10), let what was lost amid the battles of temptation be restored, with patience doubling the reward of victory.

And, to conclude everything briefly, let him who acts as well as he who endures recognize from present and past successes how salutary our tears will be in eternity, since we see that they do not perish even in temporal things for the faithful.

### V

In the glory of the present age it is little if we are said merely to have been permitted to build these things. What is greater is that, if we wished to remain idle, we are driven toward such endeavors. For the scepters of our age know where the strength of their time lies; and, as we confidently believe, this city is more securely fortified by these basilicas than by fortifications.

It is surrounded on every side by the protection of the sacred buildings’ rich approach, and one does not reach the thresholds of even open gates except under safer conditions, guarded by holy doorkeepers. Here, plainly, the use of weapons ceases by heavenly command. To prevent hostile effort from prevailing here, it is enough to have provided these guardians. Thus he, distinguished by the strength of his merits, either leads native inhabitants to the entrances or, by presenting himself, repels ambushes.

Let him raise these towers around himself, like Jerusalem “which is built as a city” (Psalm 121:3 and following), so that whenever we go into the house of the Lord, these towers of the saints’ worship and this abundance of peoples may fall to the lot of those who rejoice in the towers. Thus let there be peace for him in strength and strength in peace: strength for rulers, peace for those ruled; the former for those presiding, the latter for those serving. Yet when our princes desire either of these, and deserve both, may the peace of devoted submission cherish them and strength increase them.

Now my speech is freer to you, O present ruler, if anywhere there is one: father of Catholic peoples, light of religion, bulwark of the region, strength of examples, pledge of the churches, glory of the age, exalted in civil rank, formidable in fellowship, reverence … which you receive when you are worshiped by the people.

You are distinguished on the tribunal as one above all, and at the altar as one among all; surrounded by groups of subjects, you are recognized not by the splendor of a diadem but by the light of your mind. It is now time for you to recognize the gifts you have placed in our hands.

We obey you when you command that they remain secret when they are given; but by conferring such things you proclaim gifts that no one but a ruler could possess. What you have done in these buildings is most glorious; yet your joys reserve themselves for something loftier.

Today your offering has produced a common joy here, but what our expectation has conceived is still greater. Here contemplation of what follows is offered beforehand through conjecture from present things. It is rightly reckoned that there is so much in us as you will be greater in the highest realm. Certainly, just as there we shall weigh the account of works, here we weigh that of gifts. You are not alone in seeing in the present what delights, but you alone will be able to bring forth in the future what surpasses it.

### VI

[Col. 0297C]

[Note: [Col. 0297D] Ruinart discusses this fragment in the *Acts of the Sincere Martyrs*, p. 238 of the Verona edition. In his notice preceding the passion of the holy martyrs Maurice and his companions, he writes in section 2: “A fragment of this kind was copied from ancient papers written on bark in the library of Thuane by Jacques Sirmond, a man most devoted to the study of sacred antiquity. Those who examined these papers, now preserved in the Royal Library, highly skilled men, affirm that they were written while Avitus was still alive, or at least shortly after his death.”]

The proclamation of the blessed army, in whose assembly no one perished, although no one escaped, unfolded the sequence of the passion as it had been read according to customary obligation. The sequence of the passion as read unfolded, as a duty of custom, how the unjust death of the holy martyrs was judged by the justice of the lot: by it, after the gentle battle-line had twice been scattered, a hundredfold fruit increased from those decimated; and, with hatred aiding a favourable outcome, individuals were chosen until the chosen were gathered together.

### VII

Its entrance is not closed at night, because it has no night. Its doors are always ready, open to the just and inaccessible to the impious; it is not bolts but merits that alternate as its barriers. Its foundation is Christ, its machinery faith, its wall a crown, its gate a pearl, its street gold, its lamp the Lamb, and its chorus the Church.

Amid divine praises, with every necessity of work excluded, the sincerity of activity alone will be repose.

There are many things, most devout bishop, in which we must say that we have owed you thanks until now: in the tribunal you are younger than some, but at the altar prior to all. I say, there are many things in your works. Enriched by gifts, poor in words, we have received much and repaid little.

You have adorned your churches with a heap of treasures and a multitude of peoples. At great expense you have built altars that you have enriched with gifts. We have never indeed matched words to merit; but when we reached the present solemnity of psalmody, I think it is little to say that today you have surpassed even your works by our words.

And after other matters:

Let our Gaul flourish. Let the world desire what this place has introduced. Let eternity begin today for the burning, and dignity for the region. Let death renew rather than end the activity of those who praise God in the present age and will likewise praise him in the future.

May you recognize in heaven the custom of rewards that you will carry from this earth; and may such honor follow your perseverance that what is work for you in your exercise may be rendered to you in reward as the repayment of your merit.

## Other Fragments

*(Gregory of Tours, book II of the History of the Franks.)*

When Gundobad learned that the assertions of the heretics were worthless, he confessed, through Saint Avitus, bishop of Vienne, that Christ the Son of God and the Holy Spirit are equal to the Father, and secretly requested to be anointed. The priest said to him: “If you truly believe what the Lord himself taught us, carry it out.”

He replied: “Whoever confesses me before human beings, I too will confess him before my Father who is in heaven.” Thus, when he taught his own holy and beloved blessed apostles about the temptations of future persecution, he also declared: “Beware of people. For they will hand you over to councils, and in their synagogues they will scourge you, and you will stand before kings and governors because of me, as a testimony to them and to the nations.”

But although you are a king and fear being seized by no one, you fear the uprising of the people, lest you confess the Creator of all publicly. Abandon this foolishness, and proclaim with your mouth among the people what you say you believe in your heart. For the blessed Apostle also says: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation.” Thus the prophet says: “I will confess to you, O Lord, in the great church; among a weighty people I will praise you.” And again: “I will confess to you among the peoples, O Lord; I will sing a psalm to your name among the nations.”

Fearing the people, O king, you do not understand that it is better for the people to follow your faith than for you to favor the people’s weakness. You are the head of the people, not the people your head. If you set out for war, you go before the enemy ranks, and they follow wherever you go. It is therefore better that, with you leading, they recognize the truth than that, while you perish, they remain in error.

For God is not mocked. He does not love one who, for the sake of an earthly kingdom, does not confess him in this world.

Confounded by this reasoning, Gundobad persisted in this madness until the end of his life and refused publicly to confess the equality of the Trinity.

*(Agobard, in his book On Paintings and Images.)*

Such being the case, there is a measure of divine, angelic, and even human glory, as Alcimus Avitus, bishop of Vienne, says in his dialogue with King Gundobad:

“Yet when you exclude the Father and the Son from equality with heavenly glory, just as you exclude an angelic creature, you charge me with a kind of unlawful envy of the honour bestowed upon the heavenly powers, saying: ‘Then we ought also to render glory to angels and archangels and to whatever exists in the heights.’

“Although this does not belong to the matter at hand, I do not altogether reject it even for the present, as though we feared to render glory to a sublime and excellent creature. There is indeed a measure of divine glory, a measure of angelic glory, and also a measure of human glory. We find it in many places of Scripture and can ascribe it without the fault of flattery both to the merits of the saints and to the insignia of kings.

“For what is the first glory among human beings? This is the glory of all his saints. And in the Gospel the Lord says that ‘not even Solomon in all his glory was clothed like the flower of the lily in its natural beauty’ (Matthew 6:29).”

*(Agobard, likewise, in his book Against the Law of Gundobad.)*

If it pleases your kindness, hear what that venerable and holy man, Avitus, replied to the aforesaid Gundobad concerning the conflicts mentioned above.

When a discussion about these matters arose between them and blessed Avitus criticized such contests, Gundobad replied: “Why is it that among kingdoms and nations, and even among individual persons, matters requiring settlement are so often entrusted to divine judgment through battles, and victory goes especially to the side to which justice belongs?”

To this blessed Avitus replied: “If, I say, kingdoms and nations sought divine judgment, they would first fear what is written: ‘Scatter the nations that desire wars’ (Psalm 67:31). And they would love what is likewise said: ‘Vengeance is mine; I will repay, says the Lord’ (Romans 12:19).

“Or does heavenly justice not judge the movement of causes without weapons and swords, when often, as we see, either the party holding justly or the party seeking what is just struggles in battle, while either superior strength or secret deception prevails on the unjust side?”

*(Agobard, likewise, in his book On Paintings.)*

As Alcimus Avitus, bishop of Vienne, says in his dialogue with King Gundobad: “There is indeed a measure of divine glory, a measure of angelic glory, and also a measure of human glory.”

## To the Reader

Other numerous and distinguished fragments from various works of Avitus were supplied to us from the library of the Grande Chartreuse: [Col. 0299D] a codex of Florus, deacon of the Church of Lyon, in which he undertook to explain the Epistles of blessed Paul from the writings of several ancient Fathers. After the passages of Cyprian, Hilary, Fulgentius, and others, which he sets out individually in order, he finally arranges excerpts from Avitus’s works—only those that treat some passage of Paul—in the following manner.

[Note: [Col. 0299D] We owe great thanks to this codex, through whose benefit so many remains of Avitus’s books have reached us. This work of Master Florus—for that is how he is called—is an exposition of the Epistles of Saint Paul compiled from ten Fathers: Cyprian, Hilary, Ambrose, Pacian, Jerome, the deacon Ephrem, Paulinus, Pope Leo, Fulgentius, and Avitus.

“After this book, the same codex of the Grande Chartreuse contains book II of Florus, On the Mass and Certain Other Ecclesiastical Institutions. In another volume of the same library, Florus’s preface, together with Agobard’s letter, is prefixed to the works of Irenaeus. Florus also wrote the book Against John Scotus, published in the name of the Church of Lyon, and a sermon on predestination, which Hincmar quotes in full in the preface to his later work against Gottschalk.

“Finally, not to pursue the remaining evidence concerning Florus, there are verses by Walafrid Strabo to that same bishop Agobard of Lyon, and among Agobard’s minor works a letter to Bishop Bartholomew inscribed with the names of Agobard himself and Florus. For Florus was a deacon of the Church of Lyon and, as appears, a close associate of Agobard.”]

### Passages from the Epistle of Blessed Paul the Apostle to the Romans, Explained by Saint Avitus, Most Distinguished Doctor of the Church and Bishop of Vienne, and Arranged from His Minor Works

I. “Who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh.”

II. “That he might be the father of circumcision and the father of believers through the foreskin.”

III. “Therefore, just as through one man condemnation came upon all people, so also through one man justification came upon all people.”

IV. “For we do not know what we ought to pray for.”

[Col. 0300B]

V. “Who did not spare even his own Son.”

VI. “Also concerning the same subject.”

VII. “I myself wished to be anathema from Christ for the sake of my brothers.”

VIII. “Whose fathers are, and from whom Christ is according to the flesh,” and so forth.

IX. “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God!”

X. “Everything that is not from faith is sin.”

XI. “So that through the patience and consolation of the Scriptures we may have hope.”

### I

*(From the books Against the Phantom.)*

For this reason Scripture mentions David so often at the beginning of the Lord’s generation: once the truth concerning the author has become clear, there can be no doubt concerning the offspring. For, to say nothing of the fact that in the Gospels two blind men cried out with one voice of harmonious faith, “Have mercy on me, Lord, Son of David” (Matthew 15:22), knowing that a man rightly believed to have been born from the patriarch could nevertheless fruitfully be entreated as God, who has mercy, for the healing of their eyes—who explains this more clearly than Saint Paul?

“Set apart for the Gospel,” he says, “of God, which he had promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures, concerning his Son, who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh” (Romans 1:1–3).

He asserted two natures in a full description: one in which, according to divinity, he is the maker of all things, and another in which he was made from the seed of David according to the flesh. In neither substance can any suspicion of a phantom be found. For just as the divinity that descended from heaven was invisible in itself, so the truth of Christ’s flesh, descending from David’s stock, could possess nothing deceptive. This flesh is traced not only through his ancestors as far as David, but through David himself as far as Adam, with the names of his parents explicitly set out.

And therefore the Apostle says that he is from the seed of David according to the flesh: when he explains that he is consubstantial with his mother, from whom he certainly also took death—for phantoms can neither be born nor die, but their beginning is to deceive and their end to vanish.

### II

*(From the books Against the Phantom.)*
Abraham, author of both Testaments, etc., as in Letter 2, col. 000, through “father of many nations.”

## III.

*(From the books Against the Arians.)*

I declare that Abraham, Moses, and the prophets are not only saved but also supremely blessed, and I establish that they were saved only through Christ, since the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “Your father Abraham rejoiced that he might see my day; he saw it and was glad” (John 8:56). Concerning Moses: “If you believed Moses, you would certainly believe me also, for he wrote about me” (ibid. 5:46). Likewise concerning the prophets: “How many prophets desired to see what you see and to hear what you hear!” (Matt. 13:17). And elsewhere in the Gospel the Lord himself, summarily encompassing all the things I have mentioned individually, says: “That all things might be fulfilled which are written about me in the Law, and in the Prophets, and in the Psalms” (Luke 24:42).

Now you must determine whether those men believed in Christ whom it is so manifestly established wrote about Christ. For the Apostle Paul too, explaining that those who were saved before Christ’s coming were redeemed in Christ, settles the whole matter as follows: “Just as all die in Adam, so all will be made alive in Christ” (1 Cor. 15:22). Therefore, just as no one perishes except through the old Adam, so no one is acquired except through the new Adam.

## IV.

*(From the books Against the Arians.)*

Because “we do not know what we should pray for as we ought” (Rom. 8:26), we must hold firmly and steadfastly that whatever the Almighty has not done remains to be understood as something he does not will.

## V.

*(From the sermon on the sixth day of Easter.)*

After the flashing of the luminous cloud, the sweet yet awe-inspiring voice of the eternal Father thunders over the Son: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him” (Luke 17:5). Indeed, as the Apostle says, we are all sons of God (Gal. 3:26), and in prayer we presume to cry out, “Our Father, who art in heaven.” But he is a son in a different sense of whom it is proclaimed: “This is my beloved Son.” In his case, in order that the Father might have a son, no will preceded his generation; we, however, by which we are made sons, receive birth in the font. And therefore every human being can be a son of God, and can also cease to be one. Hence the evangelist John says that he “gave them power to become sons of God, to those who believe in his name” (John 1:12), so that a person may either remain a son by living well or reject his sonship through carnal conduct.

But Christ, whom the grace of God the Father did not make his Son, but nature, can in no way fail to be what he was begotten as; so completely is this the case that the substance proceeding from God was not prejudiced even by that substance which was born from a human being.

## VI.

*(From the books Against the Phantasm.)*

“If all these things are accepted as true,” etc., as in Letter 3 (col. 216, c), through “how did he not spare him, if he prevented him through grief?”

## VII.

*(From the sermon on the Nativity of the Chalice.)*

In considering any matters whatsoever, one must take into account not what was done but what was intended; and, in the case of that detestable person who benefited the good unwillingly, greater thanks should be rendered to God, who most readily and piously makes good use of evil. For although our Joseph was made a ruler by exile alone, piety does not therefore praise the seller. The holy Apostle Paul (Rom. 9:3), content simply to wish to be accursed from Christ for his brothers, is crowned, beyond his own labors, even for the sake of the brothers whom he had won. Judas, on the contrary, because he pursued Christ not out of love for his brothers, became accursed from Christ.

## VIII.

*(From the book On the Divinity of Christ.)*

Isaiah, the most resounding of the prophets, etc., as in Letter 28 (col. 245, b), through “which I had with you before the world was made.”

## IX.

*(From the books Against the Arians.)*

“O the depth,” he says, “of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments, and how unsearchable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor? Or who has first given to him, so that he should be repaid? For from him, and through him, and in him are all things; to him be glory forever and ever” (Rom. 11:33–35).

Therefore it is not the depth of the wisdom and knowledge of the Father alone, but of God, in whom you acknowledge the person of the Son also; no one was his counselor, and no investigator has recognized his mind—how much less one who directs an insult of diminution against him who is supreme and receives no increase? For the Apostle himself, because of bodily weakness, sighs before the unsearchable depth of God.

But who first gives to God, so that he may be repaid, except the one who gives a beginning to the Creator, so that he too may appear to have recovered the beginning of himself from God’s substance as though from a substance already begun? Here one alone is named; one God alone is expounded.

Certainly, if it is otherwise—if “from him, and through him, and in him are all things” belong, as you wish, to three—tell me now to whom belongs the phrase, “to him be glory forever and ever.” If to three, why is it not “to them”? If to him, to which one of the three? Certainly, let it be as you wish: the substance of the majesty is divided into three parts. Why did he not say, “from one, through another, in a third,” unless it is because the one named “himself” exists as one in the three?

The Apostle says elsewhere of this one: “He himself is before all things, and all things are in him” (Col. 1:17). Furthermore, if, as you have said, all things subsist in the Holy Spirit, and he himself is before all things—so that he does not begin to exist only after many things—he will not be a creature. And if he is not a creature, he will owe no service. It remains, therefore, that he is God, if he is not a servant; and he who cannot be inferred to serve by the logic of servitude must be believed to rule in truth.

## X.

*(From the letter Against Faustus.)*

That faith is the foundation of all spiritual goods, etc., as in Letter 4 (col. 221, c), through “the witness of our spirit, not nature.”

## XI.

*(From the books Against the Arians.)*

I openly profess, in a free response, that when God inspires the minds of his own people, the brightness of truth shines forth far and wide. For that apostolic statement, which you often repeat, is sufficient to recognize in the Redeemer: “If you confess the Lord Jesus, and that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved” (Rom. 10:9). Yet this must be understood in such a way that his divinity, together with the Father, restored life to the crucified man.

As he himself testifies through the evangelist John: “I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again” (John 10:18). It is by no means sufficient for salvation to believe only correctly concerning Christ as man, unless you also join to this, in catholic understanding, the belief concerning his divinity. For the Photinians too assert that Christ died and was raised again.

And since the judgment of both your law and ours detests their most wicked blasphemy in this matter, if you say that only the assumed man died and was raised again by the Father’s power alone, I ask what you are accusing in the profession of the aforesaid plague, when our Lord himself, as it is written, raises by his own command the temple destroyed by his adversaries?

It is evident what temple is meant, since the restoration of the temple within two days, returning it to its former state, plainly explains the resurrection of the Lord’s flesh, which his divinity had inhabited in place of a temple. Therefore the same Son of God, who is God and could not die, raised the dead man and restored to the divinity, in the unity of his person, the temple destroyed by hostile hands, with the flesh that he had assumed made whole again.

## XII.

*(From the sermon on the second day of the Rogation observances.)*

The blessed Paul says that through the patience and consolation of the Scriptures we ought to have firm hope (Rom. 15:4)—all Christians, indeed, but especially those who in this world are granted either to suffer persecution for God, to be afflicted for love of the truth, or to be pierced with sorrow because of their pilgrimage through this life.

# FIRST EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS

I. “God chose the ignoble and contemptible things of the world,” etc.  
II. “For if they had known it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory.”  
III. Also on the same subject.  
IV. “For the Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God.”  
V. “So also no one has known the things of God except the Spirit of God.” [Col. 0304A]  
VI. “Do you not know that you are the temple of God, and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?”  
VII. “For Christ our Passover has been sacrificed” (1 Cor. 5:7).  
VIII. “Although I was not without God’s law, but was under Christ’s law.”  
IX. “But the head of Christ is God.”  
X. “For there must also be heresies,” etc.  
XI. Also on the same subject.  
XII. “God, who works all things in all.”  
XIII. “But all these things one and the same Spirit works, distributing to each as he wills.”  
XIV. “When he has handed over the kingdom to God and the Father.”  
XV. “But when all things have been subjected to him,” etc.  
XVI. “The first man was from the earth, earthly; the second man was from heaven, heavenly.”  
XVII. Also on the same subject.

## I.

*(From the sermon at the ordination of a bishop.)*

Birth has no bearing on the testimony of authority; nor did Peter, that gatekeeper of heaven, whom the nets he had abandoned made a fisher of men (Matt. 4:15), please by the origin of his birth, but by the end of his merits. Likewise Matthew (9:9), when he was taken from the tax office, began his profit there where he was commanded to bring his business to an end.

Why should I speak of individuals? Such was the calling of them all. In their persons (1 Cor. 1:28) God, choosing the ignoble and contemptible things of the world, set the poor in spirit above the rich in possessions, proving that the truly wealthy man is the one who reaches true and complete nobility not by taking up bundles of goods, but by laying down bundles of crimes.

## II.

*(From the books Against the Phantasm.)*

“For they do not wish us to pray to him who was crucified,” etc., as in Letter 3 (col. 212, a), through “let us not pray in heaven.” And shortly afterward (col. 215, c): “Come rather, holy prophet Isaiah,” etc., through “Christ endured the evil that we suffer in the body.”

## III.

*(From the books Against the Arians.)*

The Lord of majesty is said to have been crucified, although, if one considers the property of the two substances, the divine loftiness was removed from all the insults of the cross, and only the humility of the assumed body experienced the passion. For after God, reconciling the world to himself in Christ (2 Cor. 5:19), had been united to the creature he assumed, man is often signified through God and God through man, as in the statement: “When the Son of Man comes in his majesty” (Matt. 25:31), although no one doubts that majesty belongs more properly to God than to man. The Psalmist also explains this of God, saying: “And you will see him in his majesty.”

And the prophet Malachi, called “the Angel” because of the clarity of his sayings, speaks of the Lord’s crucifixion: “If a man,” he says, “fastens his God, because you fasten me” (Mal. 3:8). Yet no one will deny that it was not God but man who was fastened to the cross.

## IV.

*(From the sermon on the Creed.)*

[Col. 0305A]

Hear what the Truth says: “No one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son” (Matt. 11:27). And if no one attains this knowledge in the present age, from where does the Arian derive a measure in dividing the substance itself? If the Father alone knows the Son, and the Son alone knows the Father, from where does the blind guide understand one to be greater or lesser?

Or perhaps he responds: if the Divinity alone reserves for itself the secret of this knowledge, how have you recognized the Son as equal to the Father? But I reply: the Son speaks of fatherhood; the creature testifies to omnipotence. Concerning the innermost matter of the substance, however—if no one knows the Son except the Father, nor the Father except the Son—where knowledge is equal through reciprocal counsel, there is unquestionably one nature in the perfection of the substance. For the one who is known neither less nor more is neither greater nor lesser.

What shall we now say about the Holy Spirit, whom the corresponding section of the Creed commands us to believe in the Trinity? If this knowledge compares the Father and the Son with one another, the Holy Spirit cannot be alien to it, since it is written of him that “the Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God” (1 Cor. 2:10). Therefore the Father and the Son know not only one another but also their Spirit; and nothing at all is hidden from him because nothing is known in truth without him.

Accordingly, knowledge corresponds to the cooperation of the Trinity. For after that mystery of divine generation, if we consider the human reality in Christ—the reality we celebrate, that the Virgin gave birth—the Father sent, the Son came, and the Holy Spirit infused. Therefore the brightness of equality is not concealed even in the humility of diminution.

## V.

*(From the books Against the Arians.)*

[Col. 0305C]

“God has revealed to us through his Spirit. For the Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God. For who among human beings knows the things that are in a human being except the human spirit that is in him? So also no one knows the things that are in God except the Spirit of God” (ibid. 10–11).

I earnestly ask you, as judges enlightened by God, to examine this passage and determine from the very depth of his knowledge whether the Holy Spirit is equal to the Father or the Son. “No one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son.” But because neither the Father nor the Son knows anything without the Spirit, therefore no one knows the things that are in God except the Spirit of God—because the Spirit too cannot know anything without the Father or the Son.

What does “no one knows except the Father; no one except the Son; no one except the Holy Spirit” mean, unless it means that in the Trinity we can find nothing apart from unity? We read elsewhere: “Whoever does not have the Son does not have the Father” (1 John 2:23). And again elsewhere: “If anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he is not his” (Rom. 8:9). How can what cannot be possessed in its entirety together be divided?

## VI.

*(From the sermon on Pentecost.)*

[Col. 0306A]

“Do you not know that you are the temple of God, and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?” (1 Cor. 3:16). Behold, then, the Spirit is also God, if he dwells in a temple, since no one except God inhabits a temple. Hence he says: “Your members are the temple of the Holy Spirit within you, whom you have from God” (1 Cor. 6:19).

Therefore, if you have God from God, and you are the temple of God, and your body is the temple of the Holy Spirit, wherever the Spirit has not been received, God is not received. Accordingly, when we say such things, let those to whom we are trying to persuade the Holy Spirit not be angry with us. For unless he is believed to be God, I do not know what can be said about the present festival, or what honor a heretic renders at his coming—since, as far as it lies within him, he lowers him even by the name of servitude.

For “if the Son makes you free, then you will truly be free” (John 8:36); and yet, “where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (2 Cor. 3:17).

## VII.

*(From the sermon on the Nativity of the Chalice.)*

The impiety of the rebellious Jews is punished by this superstitious rite: they eat a corruptible animal, that is, a lamb, with veneration, while they disdain, with the most perilous hunger, the food of the true and spotless Lamb. Thus they seem to themselves to perform the sacrament of the Paschal feast, whose beginning the whole Church takes up today, whose mystery it understands, and whose reward it desires. The word of the Lord clearly indicates this to his disciples, saying: “You know that after two days the Passover will take place” (Matt. 26:2).

“To take place” means something different from “to exist” or “to be celebrated.” Let the Jew, therefore, count for me as many years as he wishes from the departure of Israel until now. Nevertheless, the first Passover will still take place after two days, when, fulfilling the figures of the past, as the Apostle says, “Christ our Passover has been sacrificed” (1 Cor. 5:7).

## VIII.

*(From the books Against the Phantasm.)*

“What is clearer than that saying of the Apostle?” etc., as in Letter 2 (col. 206, c), through “who had given the law as a commandment.”

## IX.

*(From the sermon on Jonah.)*

[Col. 0306D]

“The sea covered my head,” he says (Jonah 2:6). He did not say this pointlessly of the head alone, since the sea had undoubtedly covered him on every side; rather, the insult of the world concealed the Lord of heaven. “The head of a man is Christ, and the head of Christ is God” (1 Cor. 11:3). My humility veiled my glory; and God, who was present in Christ as the head, reconciling the world to himself (2 Cor. 5:19), could not be perceived by those who had fastened the man to the gibbet.

## X.

*(From the third sermon of the Rogation observances.)*

[Col. 0307A]

The activity of the present age, with the outcomes of causes deferred and the whole disorder of actions confused, is not the time of judgment but its cause. Now make the distinction between good and evil evident in present circumstances: what remains for examination? Grant that no one here may do evil: what more will eternity possess? Grant that no one here depart from the faith: how can there properly be heresies? (1 Cor. 11:19).

For we cannot conceal the fact that what the Truth proclaims must be. Heresy must indeed exist—not because Christ is diminished by its inventions, but because the Christian is increased through its snares.

Thus also are the other evils, apart from fornication, which alone sins against one’s own body: if you do not clothe the naked; if you punish the innocent; if you rob your neighbor; if, when he is ready even to surrender his cloak, you take his tunic; if you strike the evil right hand even when the left is offered; if you force a burdened man along for a thousand paces, and one intending to serve for two further [paces]. Why should I pursue the kinds of violence at greater length? In every exercise of the stronger person’s power, arrogance gains a temporal reward for commanding, but innocence gains an eternal reward for suffering.

## XI.

*(From the books Against the Arians.)*

[Col. 0307B]

The Apostle says that there must be heresies (ibid.). But it must be, not that heretics should be what they are, but that Catholics should endure what they are not. Thus the Lord said concerning his betrayer Judas that it would have been good for that man not to have been born (Matt. 26:24). He said this to him because his birth was evil for the one who betrayed him, but good for us, to whom salvation came through the betrayal.

## XII.

*(From the books Against the Arians.)*

When the angels appeared on earth, they cried out: “Glory to God in the highest” (Luke 2:14). If the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are in the highest, we rightly say, “Glory to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit.” Nor can we give glory and honor to the Father without the Son, since he himself commands in the Gospel: “That all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father” (John 5:23). And the Apostle says that no one honors the Lord Jesus except in the Holy Spirit (1 Cor. 12:3).

## XIII.

*(From the letters Against the Arians.)*

[Col. 0307D]

Concerning the divinity of the Holy Spirit, whom we read to have been neither made, nor begotten, nor created, the Apostle says: “God, who works all things in all” (ibid. 6). And in the same passage: “But all these things one and the same Spirit works, distributing to each as he wills” (ibid. 11). And Peter says in the Acts of the Apostles: “Why has it agreed among you to lie to the Holy Spirit?” (Acts 5:3–4). And afterward: “You have not lied to human beings, but to God.”

Likewise elsewhere: “Do you not know that you are the temple of God, and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?” (1 Cor. 3:16). And elsewhere: “If anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he is not his” (Rom. 8:9).

## XIV.

*(From the sermon on the ascension of Elijah.)*

“And although the gifts are many, one and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing to each as he wills” (1 Cor. 12:11). He is not lesser in the fewer gifts, nor greater in the greater ones. Through him, even if one person receives less than another, let him understand that it is the gift that can be diminished, not the giver.

## XV.

*(From the books Against the Arians.)*

Because I had cited from the Gospel, “All authority has been given to me in heaven and on earth” (Matt. 28:18), in order to show that the authority he said had been given to him had always been preserved in the nature of his divinity, I recalled that apostolic statement concerning the Son: “When he has handed over the kingdom to God the Father” (1 Cor. 15:24).

Certainly the Father could never have been without a kingdom; nor is the Father, who gave authority to the Son, thereby greater, since the Son too is said to hand over the kingdom to the Father. For wherever someone confers something by a benefit, the giver is rightly judged greater than the recipient. But in the divinity, from which what is ineffably given to the Son is not grace but nature, the equality of giver and recipient remains.

## XVI.

*(From the books Against the Arians.)*

[Col. 0308B]

“But when all things have been subjected to him, then the Son himself will also be subjected to him who subjected all things to him, so that God may be all in all” (ibid. 28). The Apostle took this from the example of Psalm 8. For it is written: “You made him a little lower than the angels; you subjected all things beneath his feet” (Ps. 8:6).

Therefore he subjects all things beneath the feet of the one whom he made a little lower than the angels. Nor is it surprising that he is said to be less than the Father in that created nature in which even angelic blessedness was greater than he.

## XVII.

*(From the books Against the Phantasm.)*

“He alone [the condition of man],” etc., as in Letter 2 (col. 207, a), through “to descend into the lower regions in the flesh he had assumed.”

## XVIII.

*(From the books Against the Arians.)*

[Col. 0308C]

The Apostle Paul, writing to the Galatians and designating the inseparability of the person, says that the very one who was born of a woman was the one whom God sent as his Son. Likewise elsewhere he says: “The first man was from the earth, earthly; the second from heaven, heavenly” (1 Cor. 15:47). Yet the one and the same mediator is God from heaven and man from earth. Born from the Virgin’s womb, he is rightly called heavenly even before he ascended into heaven, because, joined to the loftiness of the heavenly substance, he became Lord of heaven.

# SECOND EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS

I. “The children of Israel could not look steadily at the face of Moses because of the glory of his countenance.” [Col. 0308D]  
II. Also on the same subject.  
III. “For while we are in the body, we are pilgrims away from the Lord,” etc.  
IV. “Indeed, God is in Christ, reconciling the world to himself.”  
V. “He heard secret words which it is not permitted for a human being to speak.”

## I.

*(From the sermon on the Nativity of the Chalice.)*

Let us consider the grace of our Redeemer, compared with that of Moses and greatly surpassing it. To compare new things briefly with old: Moses came to this people with veiled face; Christ came with divinity concealed. Moses was exalted with horns; Christ was gentle in humility. Moses’ face was radiant with beams and beauty; Christ’s was to be defiled with spittle and blows. Moses’ fellow servant was not worthy to see his human face; a leper looked upon Christ’s divine face.

## II.

*(From the sermon on the sixth day of Easter.)*

[Col. 0309A]

Since the flesh, not yet purified in the furnaces of death, burdens the mind that thinks of many things and obstructs the sight that sees only a few, nevertheless the dignity of future things shines through in certain deeds, and the splendor of immortal secrets sends a faint ray even into mortal eyes through rare revelation. But this is granted only to those whom flesh alone, and not carnality, holds captive, and whom the world’s companionship does not defile because they are pure in heart.

Thus a heavenly conversation was once granted to the law-bearing seer; and he was given a certain vision of divine glory until something horned appeared on his shining forehead—not as though harshness had produced it, but brightness.

## III.

*(From the sermon on the Creed.)*

[Col. 0309C]

We read in one passage that “while we are in the body, we are pilgrims away from the Lord” (1 Cor. 5:6). Whatever is handed down to us concerning heavenly mysteries, however firmly it may stand in undeniable truth, we must believe, because we cannot see it. For in this age, our knowing consists only in believing.

“Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8). He did not say, “they see,” but “they shall see.” Therefore whoever possesses faith in the present will receive contemplation in the future.

## IV.

*(From the books Against the Phantasm.)*

“The Apostle understands and defines,” etc., as in Letter 2 (col. 206, a), through “he might endure it by a parental written bond.”

## V.

*(From the sermon on the sixth day of Easter.)*

There sounded in the ears of the Apostle Paul that which it is not permitted for a human being to speak (2 Cor. 12:4), and which he was permitted to say if we deserved to hear. For “if you have not been faithful in what is least, who will entrust to you what is greater?” (Luke 16:12).

# TO THE GALATIANS

I. “A mediator, however, is not of one; but God is one.”  
II. “God sent his Son, made from a woman.”  
III. Also on the same subject.  
IV. “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

## I.

*(From the books Against the Phantasm.)*

[Col. 0309D]

“The Apostle says that this remedy was arranged,” etc., as in Letter 2 (col. 206, b), through “he made one from both.”

## II.

*(From the books Against the Phantasm.)*

“Let Emmanuel now be present to our discourse,” etc., as in Letter 2 (col. 205, a), through “here he will be both the Son of God and the Son of Man.”

## III.

*(From the book On the Birth of Christ.)*

The Apostle says, “But when it came” (Gal. 4:4), etc., as in Letter 28 (col. 246, b), through “to have begun in the body is from the mother.”

## IV.

*(From the third sermon of the Rogation observances.)*

For just as the law of the Jews, so the glory of the nations, is grace. And therefore the Apostle Paul says to one side: “Your glorying is not good” (2 Cor. 5:6), but to the other: “Far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal. 4:14).

# TO THE EPHESIANS

I. “In whom you were sealed for the day of your redemption.”  
II. “One Lord, one faith, one baptism.”  
III. “The one who descended is also the one who ascended above all the heavens.”  
IV. “For we are members of his body, of his flesh and of his bones.” [Col. 0310B]  
V. “And the two shall be one flesh,” etc.

## I.

*(From the books Against the Arians.)*

There is one name of the Trinity. For there is no other name, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles, by which it is necessary for us to be saved (Acts 4:12). If, with the Son set aside, this name is believed to belong to the Father alone, the Savior must be said not to save. And again, if, with the Father excluded, we are acquired by the name of the Redeemer alone, the Father has ceased to participate in this redemption, although it is written of him that he sent redemption to his people (Ps. 110:9). The Apostle also says concerning the Holy Spirit: “In whom you were sealed for the day of your redemption” (Eph. 4:30).

## II.

*(From the books Against the Arians.)*

[Col. 0310C]

Whenever something plural resounds within the divinity, one must understand not a duality but a Trinity, as is related in the destruction of the city of Sodom. “The Lord appeared,” it says, “to Abraham sitting at the door of his tent, in the very heat of the day. And when he had raised his eyes, three men appeared to him. When he saw them, he ran to meet them and worshiped toward the ground, and said: ‘Lord, if I have found favor in your eyes, do not pass by your servant’” (Gen. 18:1, 3).

Certainly, none of the three was distinguished by a more elaborate appearance or a more exalted form. Yet Abraham, understanding the sacrament of the undivided Trinity, addresses three with one name, because there is a threefold person in unity and one substance in the Trinity. Of this the Apostle also says: “One Lord, one faith, one baptism” (Eph. 4:5).

Who would dare to confuse this unity with plurality against the chosen vessel? For he knew that the Holy Spirit rules together with the Father and the Son, to whom he consecrated our bodies as a kind of dwelling, saying: “Do you not know that you are the temple of God, and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?” (1 Cor. 3:16). By what testimony could the Holy Spirit ever more clearly be proved to be God than by the fact that we are his dwelling and that God dwells in us?

But Paul had long owed this kind of belief to the divine calling. For if it is written in the Acts of the Apostles: “As they were serving and fasting, the Holy Spirit said, ‘Set apart for me Paul and Barnabas for the work to which I have called them’” (Acts 13:2), this calling was, as I think, not made at the command of a superior but spontaneously. He commands them to be set apart for himself; he says that they are to be taken up for himself. Without ambiguity, he is God who inspires, chooses, and sends the apostles.

And yet the same holy Paul, although he teaches in several passages distinctly that the Father, the Son, or the Holy Spirit is Lord, completes the summit of faith with the definition I mentioned above: “One Lord, one faith, one baptism” (Eph. 4:5). Therefore we cannot speak of two gods, just as we cannot speak of two faiths or two baptisms.

The Gentiles desire to name gods; the Jew believes that he is frequently cleansed from sins by washing; truth forbids faith to be called in the plural, as though there were many faiths, and Latin usage does not permit it. There is one Lord—we do not divide him; one faith—we do not split it; one baptism—we do not repeat it.

While preserving his honor even in the reception of the Bonosians and others, if they answer that they were baptized in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, we receive them because they have confessed correctly; what they had believed wrongly we heal by blessing; and whatever had been lacking in the preceding invocation is supplied by their confirmed belief.

## III.

*(From the books Against the Arians.)*

[Col. 0311B]

The Psalm says: “His going forth is from the highest part of heaven, and his return is to its highest point” (Ps. 19:6). No one returns except to the place from which he came. Therefore, when Christ ascended, the Son of Man returned to heaven, although he had previously been in heaven.

The holy Paul likewise explains this, saying: “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive; he gave gifts to human beings” (Eph. 4:8–9). And shortly afterward: “The one who descended is the one who also ascended above all the heavens, in order to fill all things.”

Although throughout his discourse he proclaims that God came, he concludes by saying that man returned. Yet here he says that the one who descended is the one who ascended, because in Christ God and man are one—not another and another, not two from different sources, but the same mediator from both. His substance is twofold, but his form is one.

## IV.

*(From the sermon on the passion of the Lord.)*

[Col. 0311D]

The Apostle, adapting the Lord’s death to Adam’s sleep (Eph. 5:31–32), says that at the very beginning of the world the building of the woman from the rib of the sleeping man signified the structure of the Church that was to be born.

For when the man formed from the earth lacked a wife, if we recall the account, and although inexperienced, his untutored mind nevertheless desired the companionship of a helpmate, Adam was bound in his senses and released into sleep. When the sacrament of this likeness had been enacted, so heavy a weight of new sleep fell upon him that, by that motionless and insensible rest, it rightly appears to have signified death.

From the man lying in this condition one of his ribs is removed; and when the woman has been formed from it, the man who is restored to life receives, in exchange for the loss of a member, the gain of a wife.

Behold, today also the new Adam, destined to heal ancient sins, receives the rest of the sleep imposed by the cross. Now we must see what it means that the Church is said to have been formed from his side alone, when the whole man himself dies for the salvation of the Church.

The evangelist John relates how, when the Lord was crucified with two robbers—on the sixth day of the week, toward evening—lest the solemnity of the festival day find the bodies of the hanged still hanging, the robbers’ legs were broken to hasten their death. When they learned that the Lord had already died, they refrained from applying the same punishment to him, because, even when truth is oppressed by the conspiracy of enemies, it is not broken—especially since it had been foretold concerning the sacrifice of the Lamb: “You shall not break any of its bones” (Exod. 12:46).

Yet in the case of the Lord, what was not necessary for his death was completed for the sake of the sacrament. One of the soldiers took up a missile and, to use the very wording of the text, “opened his side” (John 19:34). Therefore he did not break it, pierce it through, or finally cut his throat; rather, the text says, he opened it, so that we might understand the opening in the wound to be not merely a trace of injury but the entrance to life and salvation.

For we read that the ark (Gen. 6:6), whose enclosure safely protected Noah while he alone swam unharmed through the swelling waves of the world and the raging death in which all others perished, had a door in its side, through which he entered into safety and returned to the light.

Therefore I recognize even today in the Lord, who rises through the cross into his rest (Ps. 132:8), the ark—that is, his flesh—of his sanctification. I recognize, I say, our entrance in the side of this ark.

Let us first see what proceeds from it; afterward let us consider how the Christian entered there. When the Lord’s side was opened, there issued forth abundant streams of water or blood. What is more astonishing than this event? What clearer sign? What mystery more complete?

It is certain that Christ suffered; it is certain that he died. Yet the truth of his death preserves its dignity in him. What condition of a human body has ever produced a flow of water or blood? Granted—although even this is scarcely allowed by ordinary experience—that dead flesh may retain its blood; but where was the little spring of living water concealed in a dying body?

From where does this double stream proceed, destined to fertilize the parched world: pure liquid and precious blood? From where does the wave of the holy river burst forth, alone sufficient to extinguish the fires of Gehenna?

Behold, you see the wife of our Adam being built from his side. Behold, the bride is prepared for the one who will live even while he dies. Behold, the command is given to the sleeper that he should gladden the one who will awaken.

The whole Church consists of two kinds of people. One is saved by a faithful death, the other by an exalted passion; one has fallen for Christ, the other has lived for Christ. Let us therefore receive water from the Lord’s side, and let the martyrs receive blood. Let the precious purple of blood clothe them; let the snowy water of baptism sprinkle us.

## V.

*(From the books Against the Arians.)*

[Col. 0313A]

When the Lord was asked in the Gospel what he had determined concerning the permanence of the marriage bond, he said: “They are no longer two, but one flesh. Therefore what God has joined, let no human being separate” (Matt. 19:6).

Behold what the Apostle says about marriage: “This is a great sacrament; but I speak of Christ and the Church” (Eph. 5:32). The height of the mystery is born from the humility of the example. If bodily union is said to make one from two, why should one substance not consolidate the whole Trinity? Or, when we say that on earth what God has joined in harmony must not be separated, with what danger should we wish to separate in heaven what God has joined by nature?

Let us set aside for the moment the statement that the multitude of believers had one soul and one heart (Acts 4:32): their individual hearts were made one heart by unanimity, just as equality solidifies and unites the distinct persons in the Trinity.

# TO THE PHILIPPIANS

I. “Though he was in the form of God, he emptied himself.”  
II. “He became obedient unto death.”  
III. “Therefore God exalted him and bestowed on him the name that is above every name.”  
IV. “So that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow.”  
V. “And every tongue should confess that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father.”  
VI. Again, on the same subject.

## I

*(From the books Against the Phantom.)*

“Though he was in the form of God, he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, and humbled himself unto death, even death on a cross” (Philippians II, 8–9). He is true God who deigned to bow down; he is true man who was able to die. Therefore, he says, God the Father also exalted him and bestowed on him the name that is above every name. Between him who gives and him who receives honor, the whole name is threefold. The lowest is man, the middle is angel, the highest is God. He bestowed the name that is above every name not on the one whom he begot, but on the one whom he sent, who became obedient unto death.

Or what is new in believing that he possessed the form of a servant, when he did not disdain even to bear the insults of the accursed? As the Apostle declares, God “made him who knew no sin to be a curse for us” (II Corinthians VI, 21). For, he says, it is written: “Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree” (Galatians III, 13). Therefore he was exalted, so that at the name of Jesus every knee might bow—that is, not only the knee of man but also that of the angel—to him who, according to the same Apostle’s statement, “for your sake became poor, though he was rich” (II Corinthians VIII, 8–9): rich from eternity, poor from the womb; rich in heaven, poor in swaddling clothes.

## II

*(From the books Against the Arians.)*

The equality of the Son of God is not diminished by the fact that the Son of Man obeyed. For how could he not obey the Father who was subject to his mother? The evangelist says of his parents: “And he came to Nazareth, and was subject to them” (Luke II, 51). Thus, as the Apostle says, he became “obedient unto death” (Philippians II, 8), just as the Lord himself said: “My soul is sorrowful unto death” (Matthew XXVI, 38).

## III

*(From the books Against the Arians.)*

[Col. 0314A]

Or is the Father alone to be called Lord? In the Gospel Christ says to his disciples: “You call me Teacher and Lord, and you speak rightly; for so I am” (John XIII, 13). And the Apostle says (Philippians II, 8–9) that after Christ’s death—“even death on a cross”—the Father exalted him and gave him the name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee might bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth—that is, might worship him; for elsewhere the Lord himself says: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve” (Matthew IV, 10).

## IV

*(From a sermon on Pentecost.)*

That cross on which Life hung and death perished, as the evangelist John narrates in the account of the Passion (John XIX, 20), because it could not contain a multitude, was a page written in three languages: so that the whole world might believe without hesitation what had been written in Hebrew letters and also in Latin and Greek, as though it were confirmed by the mouth of three witnesses. Henceforth, “every tongue should confess that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father” (Philippians II, 11), that is, in one glory with the Father. However much the intention of some may persist in denying this, and even if it is not the speech of all, certainly every tongue proclaims it.

## V

*(From the books Against the Arians.)*

I have said that we declare the Son equal with the Father in glory and honor, because we read: “That every tongue should confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” [Col. 0314C] (the same passage). If he had said only “in God’s glory,” one might perhaps suppose that he was in God’s glory, certainly in a lesser glory. But when he says “in the glory of the Father,” what is unequal? What is inferior? What is divided? For he is not in angelic or human glory, but in the glory of God the Father.

Otherwise, unless this glory is believed to be equal, contrary to the Lord’s own command (John V, 23), “not all will honor the Son just as they honor the Father.” For no one can honor a greater as a lesser. But whoever does not honor the Son as he honors the Father, whatever glory he has taken away, he has counted as an insult.

## VI

*(From a sermon at the dedication of the church of the archangel Michael.)*

May this be that place, as sweet as it is terrible, in which Jacob (Genesis XXVIII, 11), seeing the Lord resting upon a ladder and seeing angels ascending and descending upon it, understood the house of Divinity. There, with his head resting on a stone prepared for the mysteries, he applied oil as a sign of future things; or when the flowing water of fragrant alabaster, through the service of a justified sinner, poured over the hanging hair of the Mediator who was destined to suffer: so that what was suitably necessary for the living stones in the spiritual structure might flow from the irrigating spring of the cornerstone, and so that the children of Abraham, raised from stones through the laver, might escape the dryness of natural contagion and, with grace making them fruitful, grow rich through the gift of fragrant chrism.

Jacob, asleep, saw this in the spirit; awakened, he enacted it in a sign. When the prayer of the consecrating minister cries out to us from there, the dream of the sleeper keeps watch over us here. The ladder he saw signifies the steps of human supplication, by which each person, according to his strength, is sent upward to the divine ears in the form of prayers. Angels ascend it when they raise our vows to heaven; they descend when they transmit from heaven what has been obtained. They attend our prayers, not by the breath of their wings, but by the spirit of their gifts: for them, to have willed is to have flown.

Among these, Michael claims for himself the foremost place as their prince. Daniel (X, 13), that exalted man of desires, powerful in visions, solver of riddles and interpreter of figures, during the fervour of a three-week fast, would scarcely have obtained a visible sight unless he had received a helper. Therefore our Michael too, summoned by the sincerity of our vow, the joyfulness of the place, and the devotion of the people, stands near: bestowing great things, obtaining the greatest things, and drawing here the presence of Divinity by which he is always illumined.

Since we have recognized in many places of Scripture that, borne by angels, whatever is piously requested or rightly done reaches God, let us pursue blessedness through acceptable works and salutary vows, since in the archangel we have provided a bearer.

# TO THE COLOSSIANS

I. “He is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead.”

## I

*(From a sermon on Easter Day.)*

At today’s festival Christ is shown to be not the only-begotten but, as the Apostle says, “the firstborn from the dead” [Col. 0315C] (Colossians I, 18). Yet I see that some may be troubled here about why Christ is called the firstborn from the dead, since, as the sacred course of heavenly readings has often taught us, certain dead persons were restored to life—even through the intercession of saints—and, when nature’s bonds were loosened, received a second light of life.

The Lord himself had also performed this wondrously and triumphantly (Matthew IX, 24; Luke VII, 12; John XI, 43), when, after first forbidding two spirits from the underworld and bodies from the tomb, he finally raised Lazarus by a third command on the fourth day. He drew back the funeral rites—not from the throat, but, in a manner of speaking, from the belly of death—bound by burial, released from corruption, stinking with time, yet living by the command.

But whoever rose temporarily in such a way that afterward they would die again, we cannot call them the first fruits of the dead—that is, the firstborn from the dead—a title spoken of Christ alone. For these, returning from death with the bonds of death, are not under a remedy but still under the written bond; they are not free from their condition, but released as occasion required.

But Christ, rising again, as the Apostle says, “dies no more; death no longer has dominion over him” (Romans VI, 9). Therefore, up to the present, he alone has risen in such a way that he will not die; and this he will afterward grant to his own, when he raises them from the dead to live forever. Accordingly, that will be a second joy, when the faithful rise. But the first joy of rising belongs by right to the firstborn from the dead.

# TO THE FIRST LETTER TO THE THESSALONIANS

[Col. 0316A]

I. “For the Lord himself will descend with a command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the trumpet of God,” etc.  
II. “We shall be caught up in the clouds to meet Christ in the air.”  
III. Again, on the same subject.

## I

*(From a sermon on the Ascension of the Lord.)*

The chosen vessel and teacher of the nations, in whom an angelic utterance still lived within mortal man, when he described the resurrection of the dead not with dead words, and declared that our Lord would appear “with a command”—that is, with authority—and “with the voice of an archangel,” as though he were displaying the terror of a herald, then went on to say: “Afterward we who are alive shall be caught up in the clouds to meet Christ in the air” (I Thessalonians IV, 15).

Then what is now difficult will be possible. What is now the truth of divinity in Christ will then be likeness in us. Then, with the air also subdued beneath our feet, we shall set the limbs of purified bodies upon the light elements—provided that, when this same King of ours comes, a fearful conscience does not hold us back by postponement, but that faithful confidence hastens to meet the dignity of heavenly glory and receive it.

## II

*(From a sermon on the first day of the Rogation Days.)*

“Prepare to meet your God, O Israel” (Amos IV, 12). The Apostle Paul, when describing the coming of the Redeemer (I Thessalonians IV, 15), does indeed say how we shall be caught up into the clouds to meet Christ in the air. Yet I think that this meeting refers to something else.

For we who are alive also meet God, as it were, if we embrace the command that is offered; and because he is ready to forgive, let correction meet him in repentance. Moreover, whoever, for the love of eternal life, not only abstains from what is unlawful but also restrains himself from what is lawful, must be judged to have come forward voluntarily to meet him.

For, to give one example, although adultery is generally forbidden, simple marriage is permitted by law; yet the radiance of virginity is incomparably preferred to it. Therefore “he who gives his virgin in marriage does well, and he who does not give her does better” (I Corinthians VII, 36). We must understand every observance in this way. Whoever does wrong flees; whoever does good waits; whoever does better comes forward to meet him.

## III

*(From the books Against the Arians.)*

[Col. 0316D]

It must be understood that when the Son says, “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven” (John III, 13), he speaks of the power of divinity alone ascending from where it had come, not in the manner in which the same Lord either granted or promised ascent to the saints.

Among these, Enoch (Hebrews XI, 5) was transferred from earth on account of his merit, and Elijah (IV Kings II, 11) was carried up into heaven in a chariot. I say nothing of the man who, whether in the body or outside the body, I do not know—God knows—heard in the third heavens words that it was not lawful for men to utter (II Corinthians XII, 2 and following), because he saw mysteries that mortals were not permitted to behold.

But perhaps it seems insufficient to repeat personal examples of the ascent of the faithful.
