The Apostle clearly knew the rewards of the future when he promised those to whom he was writing (Philippians III, 20) that the citizenship of those who live rightly was already in heaven, where their dwelling would also be preserved after the resurrection of the body. Our Lord likewise intimates this to his disciples in the Gospel of John, saying: “I go to prepare a place for you. And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again and take you to myself, so that where I am, you also may be” (John XIV, 2).

According to this promise, the saints will be in heaven. Will they enter the height of the heavenly kingdom without ascent? And how does the saying stand: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven” (John III, 13)?

But because unchangeable Truth cannot be deceived about itself when it testifies, nor deceive us when it promises, although those who will be glorified will be there with him, he alone ascends who does not need to be lifted by another’s aid. When he wished, the steps of the air were solidly placed beneath him. As he returned to the place from which he had come, the air, struck by his heavenly power and made substantial by his earthly body, served as a path and supported the footprint of him who hung above it.

Apart from this one, therefore, to whom, as I have often said, this power was supplied through a double generation, many will be in heaven, but no one will ascend. For, so that the divine promise may be fulfilled for the faithful, height will be granted not to those who ascend but to those who are taken up. The Apostle foresaw this (I Thessalonians IV, 15) when he foretold that we would be joined to the Lord, would always be with him, and would be caught up through the cloud into the air.

It is easy to understand that one who is carried by another’s will does not walk by the proper freedom of his own will when he is seized and carried away. Yet do not suppose that those who are seized are always unwilling. Grace frequently reveals that it has seized its own. For, as the Gospel bears witness (John VI, 46), the Father draws those who come to the Son, and the kingdom of heaven is seized by force (Matthew XI, 12). This seizure makes the holy person possess what he desires, and so provokes even more the generosity of the God from whom it is violently seized.

# TO THE FIRST LETTER TO TIMOTHY

I. “One mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus.”  
II. “If anyone desires the office of bishop, he desires a good work,” etc.  
III. “For when they have grown wanton in Christ, they wish to marry,” etc. [Col. 0317D]  
IV. “We brought nothing into this world,” etc.

## I

*(From the books Against the Arians.)*

In Christ, God and man are not two different beings but one and the same; not two from different sources, but one mediator from both. He has a twofold substance but one person.

If anyone presumes to divide this unity by making two, the first thing he openly professes against the Apostle’s judgment is what the Apostle says: “There is one mediator between God and human beings, Christ Jesus” (I Timothy II, 5). Next, he must choose which of the two natures—the divine or the human—he wishes to have assumed the mysteries of this mediation.

If he is God alone, there is no other before whom he may intercede; if he is man alone, there is no one able to reconcile. Join the two, so that there may be “God in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (II Corinthians V, 19). He is the one before whom the matter is to be conducted, and he is the one who conducts it: thus the same one was sent and the same one returned; the same one was judged and the same one will judge.

## II

*(From a sermon on the ordination of a bishop.)*

It remains now that he always remember this reading, which has been read especially for him today, while the Apostle calls out, the people acclaim, and judgment resounds: “If anyone desires the office of bishop, he desires a good work” (I Timothy III, 1).

Many customarily moderate the fire of their own ambition with this apostolic saying, as though it were a cooling breeze, because the desire for a good work is permitted. But such desire would immediately cease if what follows were examined. “He must,” it says, “be blameless” (ibid., 2).

Here let growing ambition and spirited desires for honors contend with themselves; here let the security of desire granted to them consider their own merits after scrutinizing them: whether the unstained integrity of the divine image is guarded from every blemish of forbidden blame; whether the impulse of the mind has ever exceeded the boundary of moderation; whether anyone has withheld his surplus from those in need; whether the insolence of speech has ever broken through the dignity of more salutary silence; whether the boundary of the setting sun has ever released the burning anger of the fervent day (Ephesians IV, 26); whether words, sounding one way while the heart thinks another, have ever fashioned something different from one’s vows; and, finally, whether worthy care for observance is present—leaving aside oaths, whether perjuries are feared.

This is not because all of us can be free from all these faults, but because it is dangerous for each person not to recall his own merits and to seek what is owed only to the blameless.

What, then, should be said of those who, purchasing the preciousness of grace with the cheapness of money, are brought by the loss of modesty even to the loss of money? Hired lies serve in their acclamations; mercenary shouting inflames their itching ears with praises that scratch them; and, remembering not Simon Magus (Acts VIII, 18), who wished to purchase the administration of the divine gift for money, they are assigned, together with their money, not to the priesthood but to destruction.

Therefore let me freely denounce these things in the face of ambition, whether sought or imposed: one who has pleased himself even to the point of his own election can in no way please God.

Rather, let us speak of the labor of innocent bishops. For the office of the bishop who is about to administer is not a light matter. A twofold burden awaits him: his speech makes him a teacher of the people, and his conduct makes him a disciple of Christ. He will govern the people no less by compassion than by severity. He must be concerned for his own losses and must not share in the crimes of others. He burdens another while testifying against himself; he suffers loss when another perishes.

When he hears that he must be free from the desire for shameful gain, he must regulate himself so as to be desirous of gain, but not shameful gain: that is, he must strive to polish the talents entrusted to him through constant preaching and to double them through the acquired and multiplied salvation of his flock.

He is commanded to be adorned; this must not be understood bodily. The bishop whom the ornaments rightly entrusted to him supply is adorned not by pomp but by grace.

Thus the priestly office, following that narrow and afflicted path of the Gospel and drawing the people behind it through its narrow passages, fleeing the left and not presuming upon the right, must fear the slippery danger on both sides. Weighing the balance of apostolic speech with an equal measure of judgment: if he wishes to be strict, let him not be violent; if humane, not drunken; if sober, not greedy; if submissive, not degraded; if a servant, not arrogant; if merciful, not lax; if terrifying, not bloodthirsty; if ruling his household well, let him order everything, neglect nothing, acquire much, and distribute very much.

Therefore, on the basis of the tested and upright judgment with which he has administered his household, much money is entrusted to him upon that evangelical money-changer’s table; you will be the profit that must be returned multiplied.

## III

*(From a letter against Faustus.)*

“I confess to those placed in necessity,” etc., as in Letter 4 (col. 221, a), through “had not overcome the married in the flesh.”

## IV

*(From a sermon on the second day of the Rogation Days.)*

Come now; as far as it can be done, let us see what belongs to us and what belongs to others. The Apostle Paul says: “We brought nothing into this world, and we can take nothing out of it” (I Timothy VI, 7). And what can be called ours that we did not bring in and will not take away?

“I came naked from my mother’s womb,” says Job, “and naked I shall return to the earth” (Job I, 21). It is clear how unreliable the use of riches is, since they accompany us neither at our beginning nor at our end.

Why do you greedily multiply gold and silver? Why do you call something yours to which you came naked? The world’s property is what you call yours; what you regard as private is common. The road of travel along which we walk can briefly be called ours while we are walking upon it; but once we have passed beyond, it belongs to those who follow.

How can a fleeting and earthly possession be ours if it does not feed the needy, though it can feed the violent? How can that be ours in which we are neither innocent in acquiring, nor just in retaining, nor secure in possessing, nor safe in preserving?

And just as we know with certainty that we came naked into the earth, so let us know with equal certainty that we can take nothing earthly away from it. The Apostle recalls that he brought nothing in and will take nothing away. Job confesses that he was born naked and will die naked. Solomon proclaims that the same death and a similar departure await all. However much each person wishes to be distinguished by ambition, beginning and end unite him with everyone else.

For when he said, “There is one entrance for all into life, and an equal departure into death” (Wisdom VII, 6), he taught not an equality of merits but an equal condition. Since, as I think, it is apparent that what belongs to the faithful is not unreliable, nor what belongs to the saved perishable, let us briefly distinguish what is ours.

Behold, as I said above, when we come into this world we bring in no earthly possession; nevertheless, we present a soul endowed with free choice and capable of reason, able to choose the good if God inspires it. As the quality of our will is confirmed over the course of time, it is God’s will that we do good, but what we have done is ours.

Perhaps someone will say that even this very good action can be lost by a human being when the devil lies in wait. It is true that a person can lose his own good when an adversary steals it. But from this it must be inferred all the more that it is ours, because it is not taken away by force.

For we do not lose our reward in the same way that we lose our property. What is outside us a carnal enemy can seize and carry away; but what is within us a spiritual enemy can steal only by lying in wait. Therefore, “if the master of the house had known at what hour the thief would come, he would surely have watched and would not have allowed his house to be broken into” (Luke XII, 39).

That, then, is our house which, if we keep watch, cannot be destroyed; but what can be occupied while we are keeping watch is altogether someone else’s.

# TO THE SECOND LETTER TO TIMOTHY

I. “In a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and earthenware.”

## I

*(From a sermon on the third day of the Rogation Days.)*

“How,” it says (Isaiah LXVI, 20), “shall the children of Israel bring an offering in a clean vessel into the house of the Lord?” We read in the Apostle that in a great house there are found not only vessels of silver or gold but also vessels of wood and earthenware (II Timothy II, 20). All these, in the very diversity of their ranks, can be useful, even if they are not equal in dignity.

Every distinction requires its own brightness. An offering can be presented to the divine house in little earthen vessels, provided that cleanliness is not lacking—if the vessel formed from the same clay, because through sin it had fallen into dishonor, returns to honor through repentance.

“For we have this treasure in earthen vessels” (II Corinthians IV, 7). Let these little vessels, as I said, contain the remorse of penitents. Let the wooden vessels display the lawful simplicity of married people; let those of gold glow red with the blood of the martyr; let those of silver shine with the radiance of virginity.

The capacity of vessels such as these is the fact that we have been fashioned as rational beings. Let each person now carefully consider what he may offer from his own resources: the preciousness of the vessels is determined by the quality of the gifts.

I believe that Elisha (IV Kings IV) once poured the liquid of living oil into such vessels. When it flowed abundantly, it did not run out as they were filled.

# TO THE HEBREWS

I. “You are my Son; today I have begotten you.”  
II. “You made him a little lower than the angels.”  
III. “For where there is a testament, the death of the testator must intervene.”  
IV. “By faith Abraham offered Isaac when he was being tested.”  
V. “They were stoned; they were sawn in two.”

## I

*(From the book On the Divinity of Christ.)*

“You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Psalm II, 7). “Today” here means eternity, etc., as in Letter 28 (col. 246, a), through “the name of his Son, if you know it.”

## II

*(From the books Against the Arians.)*

[Col. 0321A]

“You made him a little lower than the angels” (Psalm VIII, 6). The Apostle explains this saying as referring to Christ, although no one doubts that in the nature of his divinity he is greater than the angels.

Concerning him the Apostle says in writing to Titus: “Denying ungodliness and worldly desires, let us live prudently, justly, and devoutly in this present age, awaiting the blessed hope and the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ, who gave himself for us” (Titus II, 12).

Of him Scripture says elsewhere: “He who is, who was, and who is to come, the Almighty” (Revelation XI, 17). If he is Almighty, how is he lesser? Indeed, after his resurrection, according to Matthew, the Almighty himself says: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matthew XVIII, 28).

If anyone considers the recipient lesser than the giver, let him also read that the Apostle says of Christ: “When he has handed over the kingdom to God and the Father” (II Corinthians XV, 24). Yet the Father cannot be without the kingdom that the Son is said to hand over to him, just as the Son cannot be without all the authority that he says was given to him in heaven and on earth.

Concerning him Saint Paul says to the Colossians, warning us not to believe according to human tradition, according to the elements of this world, and not according to Christ: “For in him the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Colossians II, 9).

## III

*(From a sermon on the Nativity of the Chalice.)*

[Col. 0321C]

Our Redeemer, about to fulfill the mystery of the flesh he had assumed, as an eternal and most loving father, opened to the children he had created and redeemed the hope of the adoption he had granted, and assigned us a heavenly substance before the day of his death. He made a testament by which he appointed us heirs of what he bestowed—not according to human comparison, but without human necessity—not about to lose what he assigned to his children, but rather to have more children together with the inheritance he had written.

We call this the New Testament. In it, after all others have been disinherited, the Christian people alone is appointed heir. This inheritance is not divided according to earthly custom, nor is it weakened by being distributed among many through corruptible apportionment. It has received all and invites all; nothing is removed from the portion of those who hold it in order to assign it to others being born.

Let the will of children eager to be reborn grow and multiply as much as it wishes: the inheritance preserves itself undefiled for everyone.

But this New Testament is enacted with the Old Testament completing its proper order, and it is celebrated through the mysteries of complete validity. Our ineffable Redeemer himself, having summoned highly suitable witnesses—his disciples—wrote it when he was handed over, sealed it when he suffered, and opened it when he was raised.

And because everything was properly accomplished, the Apostle Paul rightly says: “No one annuls or alters a testament confirmed by a human being” (Galatians III, 15). Let us now faithfully recognize the substance of the inheritance we have received. It is what he consecrated when the apostles were dining: the order of the eternal offering.

Thus we see that he diminished nothing for us from the fullness of his substance, since he left us everything that he assumed for our sake. Others give their possessions to their heirs; he gives himself—that is, the flesh or blood of his body.

## IV

*(From a sermon on Easter Day.)*

Therefore, carry to all people what you receive. What I placed upon the table, I have transmitted to the world; the chalice that you rejoice to have tasted belongs to everyone.

Of the New and Eternal Testament he appointed a few witnesses but many heirs. Yet no condition of lot admits an outsider. Heavenly knowledge receives certain individuals; the people is indeed adopted, but it is one.

## V

*(From a sermon on King Hezekiah.)*

That great father of the patriarchs long ago (Genesis XXII), commanded to offer his son for sacrifice, courageously undertook the task, judging that a human being could not resist majesty and that a command of parricide could not accord with devotion.

Yet, although he did not know the outcome of the mystery, he placed his son upon the altar as though he were about to slaughter him, holding firmly to this one conviction: if God had been pleased to maintain an irrevocable judgment concerning this victim, what obedience had done would be not murder but sacrifice.

## VI

*(From a sermon on the second day of the Rogation Days.)*

These prophets instruct us more deeply, and they console our weakness, as it were, through the words of their own endurance. Their patience is attested by the many virtues they displayed amid weakness.

To mention only a very few of them, by way of example, because of the one who grieves that the just man is devoured by the impious: Jeremiah is proved by the more glorious freedom he possessed in captivity, with the liberty of his speech not fettered by the bonds of his body.

Isaiah is proved by this: on account of his proclamation of the truth, when the savage fury of his fellow citizens stretched him upon the sharp pains of a saw with spreading, blunt teeth, it tortured him mortally as far as punishment was concerned, but killed him with life as far as glory was concerned.

And when the victor had died while the defeated man survived in grief, the latter found that the mind could not be torn apart by lacerated flesh. Though he counted the many parts of the limbs that had been separated, he could find more than one faith nowhere.

[Col. 0321] *(From an old manuscript.)* From various sayings of Catholic Fathers. Florus of Lyon collected these into one volume.

# FIVE BOOKS OF POEMS ON THE EVENTS OF THE MOSAIC HISTORY

[Col. 0323]

## OF ALCIMUS ECDICIUS AVITUS

[Note: [Col. 0323B] Concerning these books Avitus himself wrote to Apollinaris, the son of Sidonius, in Letter 45: “I have seen,” he says, “the letter of Your Magnificence, in which you wrote that you were pleased with the little books [Col. 0323C] that I composed in poetic form concerning the events of sacred history.” This title is common to all the books, for each has its own particular title. In place of the more broadly encompassing “sacred history,” we have substituted the name “Mosaic,” which Avitus himself, I think, would not disapprove.

The first editions of this work—the earliest of all being that of Strasbourg in 1507, followed by those issued at Cologne and Paris in the second and third years thereafter—agree with the manuscripts and differ very little among themselves, except insofar as different copies ordinarily vary.

But the Lyon edition of John Gagneius, which followed these in 1536, is very different. As we stated above, it was corrupted in countless places and interpolated by nearly five hundred verses through an unheard-of crime—indeed an incredible one, unless its very perpetrator had disclosed it. It was afterward commonly received into the other editions and infected them so thoroughly that learned men were necessarily deceived and quite often read and used Gagneius’s verses in place of Avitus’s.

Therefore, so that Avitus may henceforth be free of this contagion, we have attempted to restore him to his origin and genuine purity, relying on several old copies with which we carefully compared these books, rejecting no variant readings except useless ones or those refuted by the agreement of other manuscripts.]

# FIVE BOOKS OF POEMS ON THE EVENTS OF THE MOSAIC HISTORY

*(C, G)*

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0323A]

[Note: [Col. 0323C] Sirmond had previously published this letter in a less corrected form among his notes on Ennodius’s little work *On the Life of Blessed Epiphanius, Bishop of Ticinum*. [Col. 0324C]]

To the holy, most devoted, and most blessed lord in Christ, Apollinaris, bishop, Alcimus Ecdicius Avitus, his brother.

Recently, after a few of my homilies had been brought together into a single body, I entered upon the risks of publication at the urging of my friends. But now that you urge me toward greater things, I put on the buskin of bolder audacity with brow hardened.

For you command that if anything has been written in accordance with the law of meter on any subject whatsoever, it should be dedicated under the form of a little work to your name. I do indeed recall having said several things in verse, so many that, if they were arranged, the multitude of epigrams could be compressed into a volume of no small size.

While I was planning to do this while preserving the order of subjects or periods, nearly everything was scattered amid the necessity of that notorious upheaval. Since it would have been difficult to seek out these pieces individually, or impossible to find them, I cast them from my mind, because either arranging what had been preserved or restoring what had been scattered seemed burdensome to me.

Later, however, I found certain little books in the possession of a friend. Although their proper names and titles correspond, they also touch upon other subjects when the opportunity provided by the material presents itself. Since you command it, these works, though obscure in relation to my own, will at least be illumined by your name.

However sharp and learned a person may be, if he preserves a style suited to a religious purpose according to the rule of faith no less than that of style, he can scarcely be fitted for poetry. For the licence to lie, granted equally to painters and poets, must be kept far from the orderly sequence of events.

In composing a secular work in verse, a person is called more skilled the more elegantly—or, to speak truthfully, the more foolishly—he has woven falsehoods. I say nothing now of those words or names which we are not permitted to use frequently even in the works of others, much less to write in our own: expressions, signifying one thing by another, that are highly useful for poets’ concision.

Therefore, according to the judgment of secular people, who will attribute to ignorance or laziness the fact that we do not use the licence of poets, we have undertaken a task more arduous than fruitful and have distinguished divine judgment far from human estimation.

For in affirming any matter, or explaining it as far as ability permits, if one must err in any respect, it is healthier, as a cleric says, for display rather than rule to go unfulfilled, and safer to limp with the foot of art than with the track of truth. Freedom of expression is not excused by the commission of sin.

For if human beings will be required to give an account for every idle word they have spoken (Matthew XII, 36), it is readily understood that one does greater harm when he presumes to treat something that has been considered, meditated upon, and set before the laws of life according to the law of speech.

# BOOK ONE: ON THE BEGINNING OF THE WORLD

[Col. 0323]

[Col. 0323C]

Whatever brings about varied sufferings among humankind,

whereby mortal time plucks its brief life,

or whatever corrupts morals through a tainted origin,

morals oppressed by the alien deeds of ancient parents—

although guilt is added on our own part—

[Col. 0324C]

yet I shall ascribe to you, first father, the sin committed since honor was long ago lost: through the seed of death

you destroy the life-giving shoots of your succeeding offspring.

Although Christ paid in himself all that the posterity, struck in its stock, had incurred:

[Col. 0325A]

yet through the fault of the author, who established the debts of death

and sent diseases and funerals to his own descendants,

the scar of sin lives on in mortal flesh.

Now the almighty Father, balancing the weight of his word,

had separated on every side the dry land from the waters he had gathered,

confining the sea within shores and rivers within banks.

Already, with beautiful light, he was displaying their proper forms;

while dark day was setting, grace painted the world,

marked out by many different colors.

Then, after the heavenly lights had received their appointed turns,

the lights of sun and moon shone forth in alternating courses.

Indeed, the starry brightness at night

tempers the frightening darkness with the light of the constellations,

quickly bringing forth all things in sweet generation.

The earth, clothed in sudden grass, became beautiful.

[Col. 0325B]

They received the command to be created as a kind without seed,
And that he willed the seed also to exist. Thus, nourished by the word, the forests put forth foliage; the tree, with tender roots, endured and in a short time spread enormous branches.

At once many animals rise in diverse forms and wild creatures run throughout the empty world. Birds, lifting themselves high, pursue their suspended paths with swift movement and balance the weight of their bodies in the clear air upon their rapid wings.

Then, enclosed beneath the vast abyss, the fish breathe in the waters and draw breath beneath the sea. What denies us life, the watery element grants them. Nor are the great whales less alive in the deep; they receive broad dwellings worthy of their hidden retreats. And whatever monsters the rare sea now and then reveals,

[Col. 0325C] skill fashions by gathering them into shapeless forms.

Whatever the ignorant human mind falsely considers foul is beautiful according to its own form, with nature as judge.

Therefore, when all things shone forth, complete in their appointed substance, and the world stood perfected in its own adornment, the almighty Father brought his face, joyful in eternal light, from the lofty heavens toward the earth. He illuminated whatever he saw: the work itself pleased its watching Maker, and the Creator praised the world he had fashioned, arranged in beautiful order.

Then at last Wisdom spoke in this manner:

“Behold, the world’s structure shines splendid in its ornament. Yet what good is it for the world, filled with every perfection, to remain without a cultivator? But lest long idleness distress the newborn earth, let man now be formed, one whom the image of the highest God may touch, and who, endowed with lofty honor, may inwardly clothe himself with a beautiful likeness in his mind.

“It pleases me to set upright man above those who bow down, so that he may rule the world subject to an everlasting covenant, tame the wild creatures, impose law and names upon all things, mark the stars, and know the paths of heaven and the constellations. Let him learn to distinguish the seasons by observing their signs; let him subdue the savage sea and, with enduring intelligence, possess whatever he sees. Let the snarling beast serve him, and let the beasts of burden, their fury laid aside, learn to submit to his command; let the frightened oxen hasten to be bound in their accustomed yokes when ordered.

“And that the nature of man may appear all the more exalted, let him receive a face raised directly toward heaven. Let him seek his own Maker, to whom, with faithful mind, he may devote a life of service through long ages.”

She spoke; and, deigning to touch the fragile earth, he tempered the moist mud, sprinkled with dust, and, rich in wisdom, fashioned a new body.

Just as now an artisan skilled in his craft bends pliable wax into whatever forms he wishes, fills out faces with his hand, shapes bodies from plaster, or composes a likeness from sluggish mass, so the almighty Father immediately handled the living earth and contemplated its inward parts in the slow-moving clay.

From it he marked the citadel of the head upon the lofty crown, adapting the sevenfold face to the senses of reason, so that it might possess smell, hearing, sight, and taste.

[Col. 0326B] Touch alone would be spread throughout the whole body, judging and perceiving, and scattering its proper strength through the limbs.

Thus the flexible tongue is pressed tightly against the hollow palate, so that, struck within its chamber like the vibrating plectrum of a lyre, it may make articulated speech resound through the air.

Next, from the extended body he spreads the chest and, beyond the strong arms, the branching hands. The belly follows, placed between the two sides, to shelter the vital organs beneath a soft covering. The divided thigh receives the legs, so that the alternating stride may move more suitably upon doubled knees.

At the upper part, which the one Creator fashions, the neck begins to descend from the back of the head, and adds great sinews to the joints. The rigid spine, with its frequent interlocking knots,

[Col. 0326C] spreads the double framework of the ribs in ordered succession.

The inner part is formed for the new purposes of life. It prepares a natural covering for the heart and vital organs, while a mass of gathered entrails hangs concealed within.

To these is added the lung, which must be nourished by thin air. Drawing in the breaths of air it has taken in, it receives and returns them, and in turn the inhaled breath is repeatedly driven out.

The right side holds the source of the liver, to be nourished by blood; from it the veins pour a stream through the enclosed organs. The ordering assigns the left side to the spleen, whence, they say, hair and nails grow again after being cut and do not suffer pain; from it the things that live yet lack sensation in the body recover their growth.

When the image of the completed new creation lay finished, and the fashioned clay had attained its full form,

[Col. 0326D] the mud was turned into flesh, and the hardened bones drew marrow from the soft inner organs.

Blood was inserted into the veins, and with living color stained the face with red. Then pallor was driven from the whole body, and purple painted the snow-white features.

When the whole man had grown accustomed to living through his completed limbs, and his warmed organs awaited only the soul, the Creator brought it forth from a pure source and sent it to govern his upright limbs.

He breathed a gentle, perpetual breath from his mouth and breathed it into the man. The man immediately drew it in when he received it and learned to draw in the air of repeated breaths.

When wise understanding had filled the newborn sense and shone with the pure light of reason,

[Col. 0327A] he rose and planted his feet firmly upright.

Then the Creator addressed him, as he gazed in wonder at the world’s various forms and the shapes of heaven:

“These things, which you see as most beautiful among worldly creations, new growths stretched throughout the world as its adornment, possess alone; be the first to rule them all by enjoying them.

“Let everything serve me for you; this is the highest order, that everything has been subjected to you so that you may obey your dutiful Father.

“Let no images be worshiped, nor false divinities; not anything that flashes lofty and new in heaven, nor anything formed that lives upon the earth or in the waters, nor anything that nature, perhaps pressing upon it, prevents from being seen.

“Remember that these things exist for your use, not for worship. Bow down and adore the Maker, who surpasses all his works.”

[Col. 0327B] Meanwhile, the evening of the sixth day brought back the beginnings of night, driving away the light in its alternating course. While all breathing creatures sought sweet rest, Adam, his body relaxed, was released into sleep.

The almighty Father cast a deep sleep through his heart and weighed down his senses with immense heaviness, so that no force could rouse his sleeping mind—not if some sudden crash struck his unsuspecting ears, nor if the sky then thundered upon its moving axis, nor even if a hand pressed upon his limbs.

Then from all the bones of his ribs he withdrew one from his left side and restored the flesh. A woman’s form, raised in beautiful grace, emerged at once into a new face.

God, joining her to her husband by an eternal law,

[Col. 0327C] balanced the loss of the limb with the fruit of marriage.

The sign of this sleep was followed by that death which Christ willingly underwent when he took on a body. When he hung exalted upon the wood, bound there while the world paid the penalty for its sins, the executioner drove a spear into his extended side.

Immediately water sprang forth from the wound, by which he already promised the peoples a living washing, and a stream of blood flowed out, signifying martyrdom.

Then, while he lay resting through the twofold night, the Church rose from the limb of his side and was married.

At the beginning, the ruler, arranging the figure of so great a mystery, joined marriages by his word:

“Live in harmonious devotion and fill the world. Let a long-lasting offspring grow from blessed seed.

[Col. 0327D] Let there be no number of years and no limit to life. I have given you offspring without end; throughout all time you will behold them, as the first ancestor appointed for your race.

“Your great-grandchild, scattering descendants through the ages, will count living ancestors, and children born after many years will bring the pledges of their offspring to the faces of their parents.

“Then the law of marriage, venerable throughout every age, will be preserved inviolate in its proper order for all. Let the woman taken from the man’s side remain faithful to her marriage; let no one separate what God joins and unites. Let the husband, bound by rightful love, leave father and mother.

“Let concern for parents not break these bonds; rather, the life of both shall be held in one flesh.”

[Col. 0328A] Thus, joining their vows in an eternal covenant, he proclaimed the festive marriage song, and an angelic hymn answered the chaste union with joined melody.

Paradise was their bridal chamber, and the world was given as a dowry; the stars rejoiced with joyful flames.

There is a place at the eastern axis of the world, reserved in nature’s secrets, where the newborn dawn, rising from the sun’s birth, strikes the neighboring Indians.

Here a people lies beneath the burning axis of heaven, whom the blazing whiteness of the shining sky darkens. Pure light always reaches them, and, living close to heaven, their black bodies preserve their native night.

Yet upon their dark limbs shining eyes gleam with captive radiance, and, because of their bright gaze, the horror of their black faces grows more certain.

[Col. 0328B] Their unkempt hair stands stiff; it is bound with hair drawn backward, so that the bare forehead is free of flowing locks.

But whatever is brought to us for our uses, great nature has given entirely to them from the earth’s abundance. Whatever fragrant and beautiful things are carried here comes from there.

A branch the same color as ebony rises from a pitch-black trunk; and the beast that offers ivory to the world lays down its shapeless but beautiful teeth.

Therefore, where the world’s head begins beyond the Indians, where they say the boundaries of the earth join heaven, a grove remains inaccessible to all mortals, enclosed by an everlasting boundary. After the author of the first crime fell, driven out, and the guilty were rightly torn away from their blessed dwelling, this holy court now receives heavenly ministers.

[Col. 0328C] Here winter never succeeds the alternating seasons, nor do the suns return after the cold, when the lofty circle restores the warm year or when fields grow white with frost as the ice thickens.

Here the mercy of heaven preserves perpetual spring. The stormy south wind is absent, and beneath the ever-clear sky the clouds continually scatter, yielding to unbroken calm.

The nature of the place does not demand rains that it does not possess; its plants, content with their own condition, are nourished by dew.

Every soil is perpetually green, and the face of the warm earth shines gently. Grasses always stand upon the hills, and foliage upon the trees. When they spread themselves in abundant blossom, they strengthen their growth with swift nourishment.

Whatever is now born for us throughout the year there gives fruit each month when it ripens.

[Col. 0328D] Lilies gleam, never fading beneath the sun, and no touch harms the violets; grace continually suffuses their faces while preserving their rosy color.

Thus, since there is no winter and no scorching summer, autumn occupies the year with fruits, and spring with flowers.

Here cinnamon grows, which rumor falsely claims is given to the Sabaeans—the living bird gathers it, and, when its life reaches its natural end, it perishes in its nest, burned up, and rises again through the death it has sought, succeeding itself.

Nor is it content to be born only once in its own order. The long age of its worn-out body is renewed, and frequent beginnings lift away its enflamed old age.

There a branch sweating balsam continually pours forth fragrant liquid from its rich trunk.

[Col. 0329A] Then, if perhaps a light breeze stirs the air, and the rich forest is moved by slight gusts and a gentle rustling, it trembles with leaves and health-giving blossom, which, scattered widely, distributes sweet fragrances.

Here a spring rises, gleaming in a transparent stream. Such grace does not shine in silver, nor do crystals draw such light from their polished coldness.

Green pebbles sparkle along the banks, and the stones that the world’s pride admires as gems lie there. The fields display various colors and paint the plains with a natural diadem.

The river drawn gently from the spring’s source immediately divides into four broad streams. They are called the Euphrates and the Tigris, which with a fixed boundary establish the long frontier of the bow-bearing Parthians.

[Col. 0329B] The third is the Gêon, which the Latins call the Nile, more famous in its unknown source than all know. Its gentle waters flow through Egypt, enriching its land at the appointed season.

For whenever its swollen channel breaks through the banks and floods the fields with black sands, the abundance of water is assessed; while the sky is empty, the spreading river supplies an earthly rain.

Then Memphis lies hidden beneath the broad flood, and its owner sails above fields that have disappeared.

Every boundary vanishes; the fluctuating surface levels everything, and the concealed annual boundary suspends its disputes.

The joyful shepherd sees familiar grasses sinking beneath the water; in place of the green acre of pasture, fish swimming through foreign waters take their place.

[Col. 0329C] But after the water, fertilizing the growths with abundant drink, has married the thirsty earth’s inner parts, the Nile withdraws and gathers back its scattered waters.

The lake disappears and becomes a river; the barrier of the banks returns to its former channel, enclosing the waves, until, dividing at the end and scattering through remote paths, it runs out into the open sea in seven streams.

But why is it said, Nile, that your source alone is hidden from the world? For though you are unknown from your source, you were not alone, but the fourth, flowing forth from that one

[Col. 0330A] who looks down from his lofty course upon all rivers and, as father of the sea itself, rises above all the waters that mountains, plains, and clouds pour forth.

The fourth will be the Physon, which India possesses as the Ganges. Whenever it swells from its fragrant source, it flows past the falling riches scattered through the beautiful grove and carries them away, leading them into exile in its stream.

For just as both banks of our rivers are generous, and it is customary for them to carry smooth papyrus, reeds, and light seaweed, so the great Ganges, drawing along its rich refuse, gives this also to the world by casting it from its channel.

Meanwhile the first parents, whom the supreme Author had joined, were placed in the seat of paradise.

Then the ruler set before them rewards under this law:

[Col. 0330B] “O supreme work of the Maker, whom my hand alone created, when I commanded all other things to arise at a word: do you see how beautiful this grove, rich in abundance, serves you throughout its many resources?

“All these things will be given for your food without end; let nourishment be sought here. Take the permitted fruits and pluck the apples.

“Here let life rest secure, enjoying itself in the sweet occupation of its work and its delights through long ages.

“Yet in the middle of the grove you see a tree bearing, in its fruit, the knowledge of right and wrong. Restrict your touch from approaching it.

“Let no reckless desire to learn oppress you concerning what your teacher forbids. It is better for the blessed not to know what harms them to seek. I call to witness the world we have made: if anyone presumes to take forbidden fruit from the tree,

[Col. 0330C] the bold offender will hang under the threat of death.

“I speak of no great matter; guarding what is right is easy. The guardian will possess life; the reckless one will have an end.”

The young pair received his command and gladly obeyed, promising to preserve the law for all time.

Thus, while they were ignorant of evil and conscious of no deception, no fear touched their unwary minds.

But the Father, leaving them instructed in the sacred dwelling, joyfully rose into the star-bearing court of heaven.

## BOOK TWO: ON ORIGINAL SIN

[Col. 0329]

[Col. 0329C] Meanwhile, secure liberty, unaware of coming disaster, made use of good things and enjoyed the blessed abundance of the place. From here the willing earth extended rich food to them; moreover, the constant fruit of the fertile shrub was taken from the tender turf.

[Col. 0329D] But if branches, bent beneath their fruitful weight, lowered mellow apples from a lofty tree, the empty branch immediately began to swell into blossom and to promise fruit in its new buds.

If they were delighted to gather exceedingly sweet sleep, they reclined in soft meadows and upon painted grass.

Since the sacred grove offered their will every delight and presented itself spacious with fresh riches, they nevertheless took meals and sought food—not because hunger compelled them, nor because a belly tired from nourishment urged them, needy, to fill their organs.

[Col. 0330C] And if it had not pleased them to know the food that was permitted, hunger would not have sought any unknown nourishment, nor would any foods have supported their life as it stood firm.

They saw their naked bodies, and were not ashamed to behold each other’s limbs; the unformed sense of honor felt nothing foul.

It was not human nature but the cause of sin that made them ashamed. For whatever limbs the good Creator had formed, later bodily use compelled them to become shameful.

Then the mind preserved its untouched vision, such as the glory of angelic life is said to possess while inhabiting the starry heavens, and such as Christ promises to restore to the redeemed after the time of death:

[Col. 0331A] for them there will be no concern with marriage, nor will carnal union mingle the warm sexes in a shameful covenant.

Sighing, luxury, fear, anger, pleasure, deceit, pain, fraud, sorrow, discord, and envy will cease. No one will be needy, no one desirous; under a single peace, Christ’s glory will suffice for all the saints.

These sacred beginnings continued the minds of the first-created parents in such blessings until, in their first contest, deceitful guilt overcame them through the hostile enemy.

This one had once been an angel; but after he was inflamed by his own crime, he burned with swollen ambitions. Thinking that he had made himself and was himself his own Creator, he conceived furious anger in his heart.

Denying his Maker, he said: “I will attain the divine name and establish an eternal seat above the heavens. I will be like the Most High and not inferior to the highest powers.”

[Col. 0331B] As he boasted such things, exalted power hurled him from heaven and, once expelled, stripped him of his ancient honor.

He who had once shone first in the order of creation now awaits the first punishments under the coming Judge.

Since a harsher sentence punishes such a being, should you be surprised that he fell? Crime is aggravated by the dignity of its author; guilt is less in the ignorant offender, and the evil committed by the greater is considered more severe.

Yet because his living intelligence reaches into hidden things, sees the future, and reveals the secrets of events, the angelic nature retains its burning strength.

A monstrous thing, dreadful to tell and remarkable in its signs: whatever terrible deed is committed throughout the world, he teaches it, directs the hands and weapons of crimes,

[Col. 0331C] and fights unseen through public wickedness.

Now he takes the face of a man, now that of a savage beast, continually changing his deceptive forms. Sometimes, suddenly pretending to be a flying bird, he assumes its appearance; then again he fabricates respectable shapes. He even appears as a virgin in a beautiful body and draws the eyes into burning obscenities.

Often immense silver flashes before the greedy, and he kindles the mind with love of deceptive gold, while his touch, deluded by an empty phantom, flees.

No fixed trust or beauty of form belongs to him. Whatever outward appearance is suitable for capturing and harming each person, convenient for deceit and adapted to concealed fraud, he assumes with a feigned face.

Still greater power was permitted to the savage one: to overcome the holy. The nature once bestowed upon the created being, which the Maker had established as upright, still possessed strength, but afterward the subverter transferred it to perverse uses.

When he saw the new human beings leading a happy life in a peaceful dwelling, serving the Lord under an accepted law, and enjoying with tranquil delight the things subject to them, a sudden spark of jealousy stirred his heat.

His envy grew hot and flared into savage fires. Perhaps he was then near the place where he had fallen from on high, slipped down, and dragged his bound host along the slopes.

Remembering this and pressing his recent fall into his heart, he grieved all the more that another possessed what he himself had lost.

[Col. 0332A] Then, mingling shame with bile, he unfolded his complaint in his breast and released his sighs in these words:

“Alas! That this creature should suddenly arise for our harm, and that a hated race should have grown out of our ruin!

“Power once held me high; now behold, rejected, I am driven out, and clay succeeds to angelic honor. Earth possesses heaven; dust, raised by a lowly structure, reigns, and power transferred to them perishes for us.

“Yet it has not perished altogether. A great part retains its proper strength and shines with the highest power of harming.

“There is no reason to delay. I shall now engage in a gentle contest, while their first innocence, experienced in no deceptions, lies open to weapons.

“It is better that they alone be captured by fraud before they send fruitful offspring into the eternal ages.

“Nothing immortal must be allowed to emerge from earth. Let the source of the race perish; the overthrow of the head will be the seed of death. Let the beginning of life bring the danger of death; let all be struck in one. A root cut down will not make its top live.

“These are the consolations left to me in my fall. If I cannot climb the closed heavens again, let these too be closed to them. My fall will seem lighter if a new substance is destroyed by a similar fall, if the companion of my ruin undergoes punishment in common with me, and if those whom I foresee share our fires.

“But lest the means of deceiving them seem difficult, this is the path that must be shown—the path down which I once ran willingly when I fell headlong. The pride that drove me from my kingdom will drive man from the threshold of paradise.”

So he spoke, and sighs closed the voice of the grieving one.

Perhaps there was among all living creatures a being superior in cunning: the serpent, skilled in an ingenious mind.

He chose to take the form of this transgressor among all creatures, surrounding an airy body with a covering, and, transformed suddenly into a snake, stretching himself into it.

He became a dragon with a long neck, painted his shining throat with spots, roughened the coils of his rounded back, and armed his body with rigid scales along the spine.

As in early spring, when summer sends ahead the first months’ pleasant warmth after sluggish winter, escaping the old year through renewed movement and casting off its dry covering from its shining body, the serpent comes forth, leaving the earth’s hidden places, and displays a terrifying beauty in its dreadful form.

His eyes flash ominously; then, with keen light, his sight learns more joyfully to become accustomed to the desired sun.

Now he pretends to be gentle, as though his throat were playing with frequent song, and he scatters his forked tongue from his jaws.

After he had put on the serpent’s form through persuasive deceit and, deceptive, advanced wholly as a snake, he flew toward the light. For the young pair happened to be plucking bright-red apples from a green branch.

Then, fearing that he might not be able to overthrow the heart of the man with firm resolve by injecting poison, he stretched himself upward along the coils of the erect tree, equalizing his length with its lofty branches,

[Col. 0333A] and lightly nipped the woman’s easy hearing with a gentle voice:

“O happy and most beautiful virgin, glory of the world, whom radiant beauty adorns with rosy modesty; future mother of your race, the greatest world awaits you as its mother.

“You are the first and certain delight and comfort of your husband, without whom he would not live. As he is greater, so by your right he is subject to your love; as your sweetest spouse, he will return offspring to you under the marriage covenant.

“A dwelling worthy of you has been given at the summit of paradise. The world’s substance, subject and serving, trembles before you. Whatever heaven and earth create, whatever the deep sea produces, is assigned for your uses.

“Nature denies you nothing; behold, power over all things is granted. I do not envy you; I wonder instead. Yet I should like to know who commands that a free person restrain a sweet touch upon a single tree,

[Col. 0333B] who imposes such a dreadful order, begrudges such gifts, and mingles deprivation with abundant blessings.”

These things his hissing tongue fashioned into a falsely flattering voice.

“What stupor, woman, has closed your mind in darkness, that you speak with a serpent? Are you not ashamed to entrust speech to a brute, so that a beast dares to use your language, and you tolerate the monster and even return an answer?”

When the seductive Eva therefore received the death-bringing poison in her ears and consented to the wicked disaster, she spoke to the serpent with these empty words:

“O serpent, powerful in gentle speech, sweetest of speakers, God has not, as you think, commanded us to fast, nor does he forbid our bodies to be nourished by abundant food.

“Behold the food that the whole world offers, which our most generous Father has permitted us to use. He has loosened all the reins of life.

“This alone is the tree in the middle of the grove that you see forbidden as food; only its fruit may not be touched. The abundance of nourishment allows everything else.

“For if harmful freedom should violate the law, the Creator, swearing in a terrible voice, foretold that we should immediately pay the penalty with a certain death.

“Now tell me willingly, most learned serpent, what he calls death, since the matter is unknown to the uneducated.”

Then the crafty dragon, now willingly teaching death, explained destruction and spoke to her captured ears:

[Col. 0333D] “Woman, you fear a name empty of terror. The sentence of swift death will not come upon you.

“But the envious Father did not assign you an equal lot, nor did he allow you to know what supreme power he reserves for himself.

“What good is it to be enclosed within an adorned world and to have minds confined in a miserable prison of blindness? Nature creates bodily senses and open eyes alike for brutes; the sun serves all alike, and a beast’s sight does not differ from a human one.

“Rather, take my counsel and raise your mind; lift your senses upright toward the heavens.

“For this fruit, whose forbidden touch you fear, will give you knowledge of whatever secrets your Father keeps.

“Only do not restrain your suspended hands; do not allow pleasure, held captive by the law, to be curbed for long.

“For when you have tasted the divine flavor with your mouth, your eyes, purified in an instant, will soon make you equal to the gods, so that you may know the holy as harmful,

[Col. 0334A] distinguish the unjust from the just and the false from the true.”

The woman, credulous and submissive in face, marveled at him as he promised such gifts in a deceptive whisper.

More and more she began to hesitate and bend her judgment, adding a mind uncertain about death.

When he sensed that she was conquered and near disaster, he again invoked the name and citadel of the gods. He plucked one apple from the deadly tree, covered the beautiful fruit with a sweet fragrance, enhanced its appearance, and offered it to the wavering woman.

The foolish woman, badly deceived, did not reject the miserable gift. She took the deadly apple in her hands and drew it back.

At times she brought it of her own accord to her open nostrils and lips, and, unaware, played with the death that awaited her.

How often, pricked by fear, she drew it back from her mouth,

[Col. 0334B] and her bold right hand, wavering beneath the burden of the daring evil, yielded; trembling, she shrank from completing the crime!

Yet she desired to become like the gods, and the poison crept in, doing harm through ambition. Opposing impulses seized her mind: love on one side, fear on the other. Pride struck against the law, and at times the law itself came to her aid. The wavering current of her divided heart seethed amid harsh battles.

Yet the serpent, the instigator, did not cease to deceive. He displayed the food to the doubtful woman, complained of her delay, and rejoiced in the downward fall of one already hanging over ruin.

At last, when the more serious sentence settled upon the conquered woman—to attempt eternal hunger through the food of crime and to feed the serpent with the food she herself would eat—she yielded to the ambush and, devouring it, bit the apple.

Sweet poison entered; dreadful death was seized by the food.

[Col. 0334C] The crafty serpent kept his joy within himself and concealed the savage triumph of his cruel victory.

Unaware of what had happened and returning from another direction, Adam, happy in the open meadow, sought his wife’s embrace and chaste kisses.

The woman met him. Courage for the first time was breathing savage passions into her womanly heart.

She began to speak, carrying the half-eaten apple and preserving the fatal fruit for her unfortunate husband:

“Take this food, my sweet husband, from the life-giving tree. Perhaps it will make you like the supreme Thunderer and equal to the gods. I bring it to you not in ignorance of its gift but now as one who knows.

“The first taste reached my inward parts, dissolving the covenant through a bold danger. Believe willingly: it is a crime for a manly mind to have doubted what I, a woman, was able to do. Perhaps you feared to go first.

“At least follow me, and raise your fallen courage. Why do you avert your eyes? Why do you delay the favorable fulfillment of your vows? Why do you steal for so long the time appointed for your coming honor?”

With these words she offered the fare of death that would prove victorious, while the soul perished and crimes fed death.

The unhappy man received the words of the evil whisperer and cast his senses, bent backward, down to their final ruin.

No trembling anxiety of fear shook him, nor did he hesitate over the taste as the woman had first done. Rather, he followed swiftly and steadily seized the bridal poison from his wavering wife’s mouth.

He extended the hostile food into his open throat. Scarcely had his greedy appetite tasted the apple with a single juicy bite

[Col. 0335A] and scarcely had the food given its full flavor when, behold, sudden radiance surrounded their faces and, with a mournful light, sprinkled their eyes with new sight.

Nature had not made them blind, nor had the perfection of their form produced a face deprived of the use of light.

Now you will be more blind, since what so great a Creator wished you to know is no longer enough for you to recognize.

The power of seeing was made for your life; you also see death by your own will.

Then they lamented that their eyes had been opened. Rebellious guilt shone forth, and their bodies became aware of shameful movements.

Then for the first time shame surveyed their naked limbs—whether shame, as I hesitate to say, had been extinguished or born.

The mind, now conscious of its own guilt, blushed, and the law implanted in the flesh ruled its members.

[Col. 0335B] For from this source posterity derived, through a corrupted seed, the desire to learn the future by illicit arts, to thrust sluggish senses into sacred secrets, and to investigate things issued from heaven or submerged in the dark abyss, breaking through the guarded laws of nature.

They began to ask under which star each person had been born, what prosperous course the remaining time of life would take, and how unequal outcomes might be discerned from similar signs.

They also began to mark twins born at the same time, whom an undifferentiated birth had brought forth into the light, according to differing movements and varied destinies.

They assigned certain indigenous gods to the stars, an age younger than the ancient stars preferring them, and arranged empty names throughout the immense sky for those long buried in infernal night.

[Col. 0335C] Who could adequately describe magical fraud, which attempts hidden powers in a silent heart and desires to be joined to divine virtues?

Once, under a proud king, the lawgiving prophet, while displaying new marvels at the command of a sign, stirred the magicians through envy to attempt such things and pile up their own ruin in burning jealousy.

If they had possessed genuine power, let them remove the marvels, not hasten to add them. But, rivaling the signs though unequal in power, what it could not remove, their more justified anger doubled.

Hence the Marsians, celebrated for their song, can accomplish what they do when, by silent art, they bring forth fierce serpents and often command them to fight one another even when absent.

Then, whenever an enchanter senses a heavy serpent in battle and recognizes the closed ears of an asp or hard snake, he shakes inwardly the weapons of a secret spell.

At once, when the word struggles against the exhausted poisons, the snake is handled safely by hand, disarmed; only its bite, not its venom, is feared.

Sometimes the enchanter dies if the crafty serpent, deaf, despises the mutterings of its adjurer.

Because they derive this from their mother and are skilled in the origin of the serpent’s deceit and tongue, they exchange their mutual commerce of speech through an outward appearance.

No less does the opposing concern for safety torment them, as they grieve for those whose appointed span of life has been foreseen, while they think that they mingle conversation with shades drawn from infernal dwellings and report familiar things.

[Col. 0336A] But the spirit of error, which rages in them, prepares answers to their inquiries in empty forms.

And, lest each detail be stated at length, whoever attempts to learn what is forbidden, though deceived in the present, will be condemned by everlasting judgment.

Nor was Eva now the only investigator of evils. I shall speak of another woman who, afflicted by such a plague and joined to a husband, did not overcome her own Adam.

The ardor of sin had inflamed certain cities, allowing crimes with loosened reins. Incest was their law, and lust possessed every right; pleasure, having marked out its seat of rule, held the native peoples beneath the dominion of the flesh.

And because their commonwealth had long commanded obedience to an eager populace, they believed it wicked to abstain from crimes and shameful not to sin—those whom a single offense had joined together.

Offended by such people, the judge and arbiter of the world raged and prepared flames and an end for the place. He summoned a certain man unlike all the rest, hidden under a roof, who at that time happened to be a stranger in his own city; and, standing among the many, addressed Lot alone:

[Col. 0336B] “The towns, long filled with wanton frenzy, sprinkle heaven with stains and weary our ears, though they are closed against the cries of their crimes.

“Destruction hangs over them. The earth, kindled by guilt, will burn with fire; a rain of lightning will extinguish the crimes that tears did not extinguish.

“The land itself will dissolve into everlasting ashes. Preserving living embers even after the conflagration, it will imitate soil and, lightly touched by a heel, flee away pale at the slightest contact.

“Now leave your home; abandon the lands destined to perish, and let the guilty fields sink with their deserving inhabitants.

“Do not let impending death join you to them, whom life did not join. Let your wife provide you comfort; depart content with her alone as your companion.

“Hasten your flight, take the straight path, and let no one look back upon the cities that are about to be overturned.

“Let those who are to be saved remain ignorant of the evil. Whoever is to suffer punishment may look upon it, and let those who have earned death carry the spectacle of their own death with them. Let terror be absent from those being saved.”

Thus spoke the Father. But they hurried to leave the land, cut short their delays, and abandoned the cruel fields.

The sky had begun to be covered with thick darkness and to pour down strange murmurs unknown before.

Nor was it like thunder, when the stirred heavens frequently display harmless lightning to frightened lands.

Rather, final evil was sending dreadful signs through the regions of the air with threatening shrieks.

They hastened forward together as instructed, holding to the commands, and went with faces turned toward the dwelling granted to the upright.

But the crafty serpent, who sought the heights and had overthrown Eva, accustomed to touching a woman’s mind, here too feared to test the man’s spirit. He breathed into the wife’s desires the wish to know the ruins and to grasp the disasters that had been escaped by seeing them.

“O foolish mind, for whom it is not enough to have yielded once to deceit! You have already lost a share of the good because you learned evil. If the examples of those before you do not frighten you, you will become an example yourself; and after you, may the dreadful desire to know the secret perish, at least for our fear.

“What was illicit to know and forbidden to behold—you will only look back upon, without being able to describe what you see.”

When the woman therefore heard the greater tumult from the neighboring city, she turned her face backward.

At first glance she scarcely lingered, her movements restrained, ceasing to look just as she had begun. Then, with her blood frozen, a marble-like numbness spread through her limbs; her cheeks stiffened, and a new pallor stained her face.

She did not close her eyes, nor did she collapse beneath the weight with which falling corpses strike the earth.

Rather, she stood as a dreadful mass shining through with an awful brilliance, and her deceived form preserved its appearance.

[Col. 0337B] It would not have been easy to know whether she had become glass, stone, or metal succeeding the human form, if salt had not been marked upon her mouth.

From then on, the woman, overcome by tasteless guilt, …

What is more salty, without understanding, than that which pricks the senses  
and can season those who see with the salts of an example?

Yet this is the great point here: he is not swayed,  
nor does he follow his companion; strong Adam is not overcome.

[Col. 0338A] I believe, indeed, that it would have been better had the wife not encountered her husband  
to tell him what had happened. For if she had reported what she had learned,  
perhaps she would also have persuaded him, on seeing it, to despise the command,  
just as the first woman herself did by tasting it:

After she had thus deceived herself and her companion,  
and had struck the offspring not yet born with the wound;

then the victorious serpent, rejoicing from the contest itself,  
shaking a purple crest upon his scaly crown,  
no longer concealing the triumph he had won by cunning,  
insults the vanquished more fiercely and begins in these words:

“Behold, the glory of the promised praise remains divine.

Whatever it was possible for me to know, believe now to be yours.  
I have shown you everything and led your understanding through hidden things;  
and whatever evil ingenious nature refused to grant,  
I taught, and gave you the means to join the left hand with the right.

[Col. 0338B] From this point I have devoted you both to myself by an everlasting lot.

Nor does God, although he formed you earlier,  
now possess any greater right over you. Let him keep what he himself created;  
what I taught belongs with me: the greater share remains mine.  
You owe much to the Creator, but more to your teacher.”

He spoke, and, leaving them trembling amid the darkness,  
vanished through the clouds, leaving behind the body he had feigned.

# BOOK THREE. ON THE JUDGMENT OF GOD

[Col. 0337]

[Col. 0337B] It was the hour when the sun had crossed the middle of the sky,  
sloping downward and leaving the heights of the lofty center,  
already sending forth light breezes before the approaching night.

But a greater surge of anxieties rolls over them,  
[Col. 0337C] and burning griefs occupy their guilty hearts.

And when shame had turned their eyes away from the awareness that had seized them,  
and had driven their sight back and forth from one body to the other,  
they could no longer safely endure looking upon the light  
or beholding flesh marked with the fixed stigma of sin.

They seek clothing, so that both may cover their limbs with soft leaves  
and their naked disgrace may show through the garment.

Near them stood a fig tree with shadowy branches,  
spreading its leafy crown. Adam immediately took from its stripped bark a damp sheet of bark,  
sewed it together, and consoled his shame with green clothing.

The woman, too, clothed herself in a similar, tearful fashion;  
those whom deceptive madness had nourished with the wretched fruit,  
whom the savage tree had made naked,  
she covered more heavily upon the slender tree.

[Col. 0337D] Yet a time will come when the crimes of the tree  
will be healed through a tree, and the final Adam will cleanse them,  
making that very material a medicine of life  
through which death gained power: death will be destroyed by death.

A bronze serpent will hang from a lofty stake,  
and, while it presents the likeness of something poisonous,  
will cleanse every poison and destroy the ancient dragon by its own image.

Meanwhile the father was catching, through the tender greenery of the grove,  
breezes dripping from the clear air.

At once, with astonished ears, they both sensed the Lord’s presence.  
They dreaded the day, now sorrowful to them,  
as a witness exposed in their crime.

For if by chance the earth had opened vast caverns before them,  
or the abyss had suddenly displayed a cleft,  
[Col. 0338B] they would not have hesitated to descend in a headlong leap;  
and if the sentence of death had already been available,  
the shame-driven desire for consolation would have sought even that remedy.

Whether by flames or waters they might perish,  
or an avenging hand might strike their breasts with a cruel wound.

Thus the wretched desire death, still unknown in its peril,  
as soon as they have first deserved it. Beginnings mark the end  
and foretell that similar griefs will come  
when the world’s old age has consumed its final era;

when a sudden flash strikes everything from heaven,  
while the trumpet sounds—the herald that once before  
terrifies the shaken world at the Judge’s arrival.

Then, when the shepherd separates the innocent lambs  
and places the unlike goats in a different part,  
with chaos dividing them in the midst—a whirlpool  
that fills itself with sulfurous waves and rolls watery fires—  
with a lake of flames standing still, in which, it is said,  
the Sodomite cloud, drawing in a burning storm,  
once poured out lightning drop by drop as punishment for crimes,

[Col. 0338D] when black night rained fires  
and falling deaths dripped everywhere through the heated air.

Such streams, sent from the fiery spring of Gehenna,  
flowed sadly into alien ages.

But those whom the Judge, at that dreadful hour, decrees  
will live after death amid punishment and everlasting heat,  
a sentence heavier than the desired death will withdraw from death.

Although it would have been better, with their bodies scattered in pieces,  
to snatch perpetual sleep beneath harsh death,  
nevertheless the urn will vomit them forth unwillingly—  
those whose only desire is once more to be able to die,  
while consciousness itself is a prison of suffering.

Yet the flame of the burning furnace will receive them  
in such a way that it will never finish consuming its own food.

Meanwhile the first human beings, young in age,  
[Col. 0339A] rush through the wilderness in a vain effort,  
thinking their deeds safely hidden and wishing they had lain concealed  
in blind darkness.

What does it avail you, unhappy man, to turn your eyes away from the Judge?  
The Judge sees you. Why do you yourself refuse to see,  
when you are plainly seen?

The kindly sun does not become dim  
because lowered eyes fear the heavy light,  
nor can feeble sight endure the bright orb.

Then God first rebukes him in a terrible voice  
and, knowing where the wretched man is, asks Adam.

He draws forth a trembling voice from his fearful breast  
and barely gives this short reply:

“Your terror, O Most High, sitting deep within our minds,  
forced us to seek a hiding place.

For since our bodies were naked, with uncovered limbs,  
I was ashamed, I confess, and fled from heaven into hiding.”

And he said: “Who struck your heart with submissive shame?  
And from where came this new awareness? For until now  
neither wool nor woven clothing had covered you with a garment.

Your unformed nature, content with its own beauty,  
pleased itself before its own judge. But after, the covenant broken,  
your taste touched the forbidden growth,  
your natural covering no longer sufficed by itself.

What was previously naked is now exposed after being stripped bare,  
because an obscene impulse has accused your shameful bodies.”

When he saw himself convicted in the clear light,  
and just examination had exposed all his guilt,  
he does not ask forgiveness for his crime in a humble prayer;  
he does not beg with vows or tears, nor, weeping as an avenger,  
does a submissive confession anticipate the deserved punishment.

Though he has now become wretched, he is not yet pitiable.

He rises in spirit, and pride, kindled by timid complaints,  
[Col. 0339C] pours itself out in reckless words:

“Alas, for the woman joined to me for my destruction!  
You gave her to me as a companion under the first law.  
She overcame me through her evil counsels, herself overcome,  
and persuaded me to take the fruit already known to her.

She is the source of evil; the crime arose from her.  
I myself was credulous, but you taught me to believe,  
when you granted marriage and bound us with sweet ties.

Would that the happy life which once flourished alone  
had remained unmarried, and had never experienced  
the bond of such a wife, subject to a wicked companion!”

Thus, moved by this hard-hearted speech,  
the Creator addresses Eve in lofty words:

“Why, slipping away, did you drag your wretched husband  
down the slope into misery?

And not content with your own deception, deceitful woman,  
did you cast the man’s understanding down from its lofty citadel?”

She, ashamed and suffused with sorrowful blushes upon her cheeks,  
declares the dragon, who deceived her, to be the author of the crime:  
he persuaded her to touch the fruit with a forbidden bite.

After this, the final sentence proclaims the law  
and, in his first words, marks the serpent as guilty:

“You serpent, whose deceit caused the woman to sin  
and made the man your companion in error—  
guilty on account of them both, you will hang for what each of them did.

Nor will your head remain upright upon a lofty neck;  
you will crawl forward, bent low, across the ground.

And, so that your winding coils may run in frightened motion,  
you will not have steps but a sliding movement; you will follow yourself  
in your own bends, and your spirals will form living bonds.

[Col. 0340A] Then, because of the food you persuaded the wretched to take,  
you will seize the earth and consume empty nourishment.

Driven from the upper world at fixed months,  
you will be shut within the earth and deprived of the common sun.

Among all the creatures that now fill the world,  
you will be the author of death and become a grievous terror to all.

Especially against the unhappy woman and her future offspring  
let enmities be renewed in a running hatred,  
so that seed may gnaw at seed with desires to harm.

You will always pursue her heel as she stands in fear;  
she will crush your head and, at the end, overcome you as victor.”

After this the Judge, moved, turned to the terrified Eve:

“But you, woman, who first violated the law,  
accept the diminished span of life that remains throughout the age.

You will endure the rule of the marriage bed and fear the man  
whom I gave you as your companion; subject to commands, you will obey.

And, with bowed head, accustom yourself to male desires.

Soon, when your womb senses that it has conceived a fetus,  
you will testify to the burden of your belly with groans,  
and your anxious entrails will carry the growing load enclosed within you,

until, the time having passed and your aversion fulfilled,  
the natural evil hangs upon its avenging birth,  
and the offspring brings forth life as the punishment of its parent.

Why should I speak of the mother’s later and different trials?  
For when, exhausted by severe labor,  
you have brought forth the desired child in such a birth,  
you will sometimes lament your empty pains, deprived of it.”

Meanwhile trembling Adam, for some time already,  
endures what the terrible sentence will finally reserve for him.

To him the Father says:

“Now listen with attentive ears, and you also,  
learn what you deserve, you whom a weak woman has overcome.

The earth, previously unblemished beneath a beautiful growth,  
no longer wholly trustworthy or simple in pure seed,  
will display its corrupted back throughout the world.

And, rebelling against you as an example of your own rebellion,  
the earth will learn to resist with thorns and thistles.

Or, if it yields to the breaking plough  
and is subdued by the ploughshare’s fixed, biting tooth,  
its rich fields will deceive you with a false crop.

For instead of wheat you will grieve  
that darnel rises as the fruit,  
and that counterfeit grain and empty oats appear.

Thus the fields will scarcely produce bread wrested from them,  
which poverty, relying upon unceasing sweat, must consume,  
and food will avenge itself as the enticement of punitive nourishment.

Fodder will make your life equal to that of the beasts,  
[Col. 0340D] as you seek both the juices of herbs and pasture;  
your belly, pressed down, will be burdened with dung of the same kind.

Your troubled age will long revolve through such things,  
until the appointed ages set an end for you  
and your limbs, compacted from clay, are dissolved by time.

Formed from mud, you will again be reduced to the soil.

Yet before your own death, you will see the death of your child precede you  
and behold your punishments in your offspring,  
so that the image of death may appear all the more dreadful.

You will understand what it means to have sinned,  
what it means for something to become dead,  
and what it means to die.

And lest anything perhaps be lacking among the evils  
that the corrupted world brings forth for its chastisement,  
a fiercer anger will be mingled with immense grief.

For when the first ages bring forth children for you,  
[Col. 0341A] devouring envy will contend within the world’s narrow bounds.

The empty world will no longer suffice as it stretches outward,  
and the whole earth will be compressed between two brothers.

One brother will rise against the other’s death  
and stain the new earth with kindred blood.

Afterward, posterity, destined to endure varied sufferings,  
will pay the debt of mortality through many disasters,  
until the appointed end dissolves the ancient world,  
everything living falls, and the end refutes all that has arisen.”

He had heard, and the terrified earth gave a shudder.

When these things had been accomplished, the Father clothed them both  
in skins of goats and expelled them from the holy seat of paradise.

Then they fell together upon the earth, entered the empty world,  
and traversed everything in rapid movement.

Although it was various in its growth, adorned with grass,  
[Col. 0341B] displaying green fields, springs, and rivers,  
the appearance of the world nevertheless seemed foul to them.

After your paradise, as they looked upon all this,  
the whole sight filled them with horror;  
and, as is human custom, what has ceased to be is loved more.

The earth grows narrow, and the world, groaning, is confined;
