the boundary of the lands cannot be seen, and yet it presses near.

The day itself grows squalid. Beneath the sun they complain  
that the light has been withdrawn; the stars, suspended in the distant sky,  
groan, and the axis, previously scarcely perceived, is now touched.

Then, amid cares mingled with the gall of grief,  
they felt new emotions. Weeping, striking their breasts,  
burst forth into streams not yet known to them,  
and unbidden moisture flowed down their attentive cheeks.

No differently does the living spirit, deceived by its mortal burden,  
when the end of its allotted life has come,  
mourn its sins after death.

Then it recalls to mind whatever wrong it has done;  
then it repents of every slip of error,  
which it condemns in itself before the Judge.

And if it were granted the opportunity of former life,  
it would willingly undertake whatever labors the commands imposed.

For holy Luke tells of a certain rich man,  
whom a life dissolved in excessive luxury sustained.

He himself, shod in gemmed buskins and shining with gold,  
changed silk garments twice dyed in purple.

Then, once the seasons had encouraged a reveling table,  
courses ran in abundance, everything that the whole world provides.

When a harvest gathered from distant lands had been brought in,  
old Falernian wine boiled in cooling crystal.

They even mixed moist cinnamon with incense,  
and the fumigated house exhaled the fragrance of rich amomum.

[Col. 0341D] Whatever the sea, the earth, and the rivers produce,  
the pallid servant, exhausted by the succession of tables,  
carried from every direction to the banquet, together with a burden of gold.

At that time a poor man happened to lie before the rich man’s door,  
his limbs relaxed in a body bound by affliction,  
and, like a suppliant, sought help rather than gifts.

He awaited only whatever leftovers abundance had thrown out;  
his fasting belly begged for these.

But the rich man did not lend an ear to his cries,  
and no compassion regarded the sick beggar.

No one gave him even what had fallen from the full tables as excess  
for the poor man’s nourishment. On top of that, the sick man’s face was despised,  
and his rotting wounds were viewed with horror.

Yet when dogs gently licked his ulcers with their tongues,  
and the fierceness of animals offered a healing kindness to the exhausted man,  
the human mind alone, always hard, does not know how to be moved.

While these things, under wholly different destinies, were taking place,  
approaching death struck both alike—  
the rich man caught unprepared, who had never believed this would happen.

The poor man came afterward, though only after a long delay,  
to the death he desired, and, victorious, left behind  
his diseases and limbs.

The man who had recently flourished in a lofty palace  
was carried amid a funeral crowded with mourners to the tomb;  
his body was buried in a gilded sepulcher,  
and precious linen covered the raised marble.

But soon his spirit, cast down into hidden Avernus,  
fell amid savage fires into everlasting punishment.

From within these fires he saw the poor man’s countenance, transformed and rejoicing  
in the bosom of righteous Abraham—not far away, so he supposed  
(the outcome, however, shows it to have been far away).

It no longer resembled the man whom, while he was still received in the light,  
perhaps only on the fourth day someone had scarcely been generous enough to bury,  
lest the corpse, quickly decaying by nature, spread the dreadful contagion  
of its stench through the populous city;  
covered in a thin wrapping of torn rags, he had been laid on the bare earth  
while people held their nostrils shut.

Then, raised aloft by angelic hands,  
the poor man was now rich and now healthy.

But opposite him, the proud man,  
who had melted away amid abundant riches while holding on to his amassed wealth,  
begged for drops with his dry throat amid the flames.

“O Father, who gathers chosen souls into a blessed dwelling  
and distributes just rewards according to merits,  
I do not deserve these things. But at least I beg one favor:

[Col. 0342C] let Lazarus be sent, and let him bring here upon his finger  
some liquid from there, raised to my burning lips.

Let it, if it does not extinguish all of them,  
at least for a time mitigate such great heat,  
until my weary limbs briefly breathe again in rest.”

As he made this request with a shriek mingled with tears,  
the great-hearted patriarch at last addressed him:

“Cease now to pour out late words in vain  
and to mingle empty prayers.

You did not speak such words earlier,  
when, while you feasted, he himself—unknown, needy, sick, fasting, empty—  
lay at your doors.

Your table could not contain the provisions piled upon it,  
yet the poor man’s cry did not reach your ears.

Therefore, at last, when the balance of truth has been weighed,  
each has received the lot of his former life,  
and their positions have been exchanged.

You have already had enough of overflowing in abundant goods;  
let the man who grieved at the beginning of his sufferings rejoice at their end.  
There is no further limit.

Moreover, the boundary that encircles us with a dreadful passage  
and separates the regions with a broad intervening chasm  
does not allow the separated parts to mingle in alliance,  
and denies access—so always for you, as for those here.”

He, groaning, begs again in repeated words:

“If confessing what was done is of no use after death,  
and your fixed sentence is not changed by my words,  
grant me this, which no law forbids.

I left behind five brothers when I departed from the light.  
I ask that someone be sent to them, to correct the living,  
before they fall into such torments, released from the flesh.

For although they persist in hard-hearted rebellion,  
if someone should return from the dead,  
they would believe one who had experienced it  
and fear entering into punishment.”

But he obtains no effect from his request.

We, however, while life remains and while we are alive in the light,  
are terrified by the message of Adam, long ago dead.

While there is still a place for weeping, while petitions that are not unjust are made,  
and while the door is not struck with bolts shut,

we all know what that first man lamented,  
who, expelled from his ancient dwelling, did not know how to return.

For by that very event he suffered a kind of death,  
so that he might not restore what had been lost by any prayers or tears.

From then onward, life gradually began to slip backward,  
and power was loosened for evils.

Then grievous diseases and various sufferings arose,  
[Col. 0343B] and the earth, sufficiently corrupted by a dreadful fertility,  
poured forth certain shoots with deadly sap.

Then fierce wild beasts began to rage.  
The conscious courage that had once feared them first aroused itself for battle,  
and claw, tooth, hoof, and horn were restored to weapons.

Even the elements themselves then broke their laws,  
and all things strove to violate their faith with mortals.

The sea swelled with winds, and waves rolled;  
the stirred ocean rose into a new surge.

Then for the first time, with the heavens covered by foul darkness,  
clouds pierced the fearful with hail-bearing storms,  
to punish the thankless labors of humankind,  
and the hostile sky begrudged the earth its growth.

Indeed, the earth itself, hostile to itself, refused what it had received as seed,  
turning the bright promise of the seed into deception.

[Col. 0343C] The two first ancestors experienced these things then for the first time.

But how many losses of human affairs their descendants would suffer  
no one could enumerate—not even one with a hundred tongues  
or a voice of iron; nor could the poet sent from Mantua  
or the Maeonian poet sing them in varied speech.

Who could recount such upheavals? Who, finally, could unfold in speech  
all the waves that the ages roll onward?

Weapons roar; the world is shaken by repeated terror;  
irrigating blood is poured out, and more blood is thirsted for.

Why should I speak of lofty cities, once filled with splendid assemblies,  
being given over to deserts?

Of peoples scattered by ruin as it lays them waste,  
and of the lacerated world emptied of its parts?

Of masters being subjected to slavery,  
and servants in turn being preferred to their masters,  
and of men perishing by the lot of war?

What has become of the lot of the race, which once produced men  
of illustrious blood?

[Col. 0343D] But if wars perhaps rest for a brief time,  
laws armed with disputes rage into battles;  
the law, uncertain, fights in the forum,  
where quarrels between brothers strike no less fiercely with words  
than battles with weapons.

But who records vows when the deeds of criminals cry out?  
Who laments frauds and thefts while robbery rejoices?  
Or who mourns lesser crimes? Even the greatest cannot be fully grasped.

Yet lesser crimes become significant when joined to the greatest;  
for, judged in itself, no crime is small before the Judge.

Nor is it necessary to traverse every cause in song.

I will speak in this brief account: after the earlier losses,  
nothing evil remains which the world, full of crimes and labors alike,  
either does not commit or endure,  
having danger in its circumstances and guilt in its action.

[Col. 0344A] But you, powerful Christ, to whom it is always easy to spare,  
you, the potter, can repair the fallen mass  
and reshape vessels long broken and dissolved.

You find the drachma that has long lain hidden in much dust,  
with lamps lit by the power of the word.

Leaving the sheepfolds, wandering in disgraceful error,  
the shepherd deigns to seek the sheep with swift steps;  
you lift it up, and, rejoicing that it may be returned to its own fold,  
the burden that was once a care becomes a joy.

So, after that younger son had scattered his amassed wealth  
and his prodigal life had changed when his resources were consumed,  
he pursued the shameful banquets of pigs,  
and desired to fill his belly with cheap pods,

until savage hunger, after prolonged danger,  
forced him at last to return to his offended father.

When he confessed his guilt, his crime was released,  
and finally the gentle father willingly raised up the prostrate son  
and soothed his trembling shame with a kind voice.

The first robe gives the returning son a second adornment,  
and the joyful assembly celebrates a solemn feast,  
because a child, as it were, returned from death to his own,  
rises again, and new light returns to the bereaved father.

But you, supreme Creator of humankind and of all things,  
although you will everything to remain directed toward faithful salvation,  
do not suffer any loss through our death.

Nor can any of your riches suffer harm through the destruction of anyone;  
you know neither decrease nor increase,  
and your glory remains established in a kingdom full and complete.

But restore to your servants what Adam lost;  
[Col. 0344C] let what the first origin of the corrupted stock took away  
be restored by a better life in a second birth.

The old form, surrounded by a torn garment,  
has become too foul. Let it lay aside the rent clothing with its crime;  
Father, extend the first robes to the returning child.

You once pitied a man found half-dead,  
thrown by the road, whom savage robbers had stripped  
of all his clothing and covered with wounds from their blows.

But you, holy one, while traveling the road in assumed flesh,  
find him cast down and do not pass him by.  
Indeed, you carry the sick man beneath a roof  
upon the beast of your own flesh.

We were once given as prey to raging fury.

But if grace, bringing oil, now passes over the wounds with healing care,  
and wisdom supplies wine,  
let the foreign care of the Samaritan commend him to the inn;  
then the strong disease will be driven away from the medicated body.

Receive those who do not wish to increase the causes of dying,  
those whose pious hearts pour out groans confessed to you.

As once, while you shared the time of flesh,  
the thief hanging beside you upon the monstrous stake  
was held by punishment, not by guilt like yours:

though bound in his limbs, he was not bound in heart;  
and although he could not stretch out palms fastened with nails,  
he extended his liberated mind through his words.

And so, while guilty of crimes, he paid the deserved penalty  
and seized martyrdom from death.

His greatest care, with an astute end, was not to lose such punishments;  
he forestalled them by climbing toward the entrance,  
and, destined to be raised to heaven,  
he reached the lofty shortcuts by a sublime leap.

[Col. 0345A] Thus extend to us your lofty right hand, illustrious Father.

Let perpetual life seek us also for salvation,  
and, profaned by the deception of the robber,  
[Col. 0346A] come to our aid in pity, as you came to the crucified robber.

Those whom the enemy’s livid anger drove from paradise,  
let your stronger grace restore to the ancient dwelling.

# BOOK FOUR. ON THE FLOOD OF THE WORLD

[Col. 0345]

[Col. 0345A] I shall now recount the Flood,  
when the world, once infected by harmonious vices,  
and legitimate wickedness was expiated by a loosened death.

But not the flood of which lying myth reports  
that Deucalion scattered stones throughout the world  
to make them live, from which a hard race of men descended,  
suited to every labor and displaying a stony origin  
through an unyielding mind.

I shall follow the true account of those waves,  
[Col. 0345B] through which, while created things had scarcely come into being,  
a swift end overtook the world still in its infancy.

The mortal race had raised its spirit to great heights  
through cruel enterprises.

It believed that whatever each person desired was permitted,  
and private will had become powerful in place of law.

There was so little justice that it was thought there was no difference  
between right and wrong; nowhere was right guarded.

There was no judge, no witness, and finally no ruler,  
no arbiter of morals or one who might advise what was honorable.

Each person was master of himself in the power to do harm.  
Not by merits but by mass and strength the powerful man prevailed;  
whoever was stronger was better in his own estimation  
and pleased himself as his own judge.

Thus the mind, inclined toward bestial impulses,  
held human life according to the custom of beasts.

It was drunk with blood; the entrails of the slain  
everywhere supplied torn food to savage jaws.

Moreover, the four-footed creature that was killed by its own death,  
or the fiercer creature that had been captured after overcoming it,  
became food—something no faith and no law forbade.

But when pleasure, permitted in the manner of animals,  
and lust openly spread after the reins had been broken,  
and the marketplace of luxury and the commerce of an obscene world  
were boiling, it is not lawful to speak of these things in a chaste song.

By such and so many deeds the wicked race of humans  
had put on woodland minds, having broken the covenant of nature;  
reason was driven out, and at the same time they raged.

The image of the heavenly Lord lay abandoned  
and had cast down every adornment of the mind through shameful action.

Just as, when a fertile field of a beautiful plain,  
made available by a forest cut down and cleared of timber,  
is cultivated, it obeys proper labor,  
is subjected to the harrow, responds with crops,  
and preserves the grace of the countryside with an ordered appearance;

but if the farmer happens to withdraw his arms,  
loosen his hands, and rest from the weary plough,  
the earth first grows sluggish beneath its hardened turf.

Soon, with rough branches and dense, harsh vine-shoots,  
it unlearns to produce cultivated fruits,  
spreads various thickets, and threatens to become a forest.

If no late cutter cleans it again with his sickle,  
the grove is no longer woven from bushes  
but from a dense trunk, spreading sterile foliage into the air.

At last, when shade enclosed by running branches  
and then darkness, welcome because it drives away the sun,  
invite wild animals to trust the secure thickets,

[Col. 0346A] so the life of the human race, no longer proceeding in a straight order,  
after losing the law entrusted to it in the beginning,  
gradually slipped into depravity.

Advancing along a worse path,  
it became more firmly established through the repeated practice of nurtured crime.

And yet the growing boldness of the succeeding generation  
overcame the originator of vice and master of guilt,  
more learned in errors and more skilled in every fall.

[Col. 0346B] As a river, first spreading from a small urn,  
sends forth a clear spring in a gentle stream,  
which anyone can cross with an easy leap at its shallowest course;

then, drawn onward from its watered source,  
it gains sudden strength, drives back its banks,  
and extends its growing waters across the plains.

It occupies space and threatens the dying field;  
then, passing through neighboring valleys,  
it swallows the rivers around it  
and begins to end the external waters by its own increase.

Mixed together under one name,  
with its current spread across the swept-up lands,  
it carries along beams, cattle stalls, and wild beasts’ lairs.

Fiercer as it advances and possessing a long fury,  
it finally ceases only when it has borne its waters into the sea.

Amid these movements, and resembling a whirlpool,  
the human race moved on in its vices.

Yet time itself, extended over too long a period,  
had dissolved their mad minds.

When a stubborn life repeatedly completed nine times a hundred years,  
there was no terror of death during such a long delay.

If late fortune carried someone away,  
he was thought as though he had never been born  
and would never be relieved by death.

Thus no hope of the future existed for anyone,  
and the world, destined to perish, had founded all its love  
upon itself, in blind sensations.

Moreover, at that time the sinful earth  
nourished savage, monstrous giants.

Yet it is not permitted to say from what seed they were born.

They claimed a common origin from one mother,  
but the mysteries prevent them from declaring  
what their race was or who their fathers were.

[Col. 0346D] If you seek their appearance, they had more of a human face  
than the form of a human body;  
thus a line corresponding to human limbs showed a man,  
while their discordant mass revealed a monster.

For this reason, afterward, Greece increased the unspeakable disgrace  
with invented tales, and described bodies with monstrous limbs:

from the waist upward they had the form of men,  
while enormous dragons supplied the lower parts of their bodies  
as a mixed substitute for legs.

Dark half-men, whose limbs bore open jaws,  
carried them, and their reversed heads furnished their gait.

They were also accustomed, with terror commanded by thunder,  
to send insults against heaven with blasphemous feet,  
and their biting feet roared with the movement of poison.

Like them, the lying story of the Phlegraean war  
imagined that they hurled rocks through the air,  
because their broad hands scattered mountains in a whirlwind as weapons  
and shook heaven with the fields they cast.

[Col. 0347A] These are the things which Greek poets of old sang in false verse  
about the terror of the giants.

Yet every rebel who wished to contend  
attempted to do so in audacious battle.  
When he could not clash with weapons,  
he conceived battles in savage prayers.

It is not lawful to believe that they placed mountains upon mountains.  
Yet I shall suppose that they attempted this too,  
those who thought that baked bricks, joined with slow-setting bitumen,  
could be raised aloft by their proud hands  
and that lofty masses could rise to the stars.

While the mortal race raged and, in vain labor,  
carried its useless masonry upward beyond the clouds,  
the structure pursued the retreating sky,

until discord subjected their tongues  
and varied speech confused everything.

Then the bond was scattered; the law of speech was torn apart,  
and disturbed pride broke the agreement of crimes.

Each person gathered to his own people through words  
that he alone could understand,  
and every nation pursued new languages.

Thus the interrupted heights of the mass perished,  
and the tower, lacking its intended result, stopped in the air.

These things occurred before the Flood.

For how many giant citadels the earth produced in ancient times,  
and how much contempt it poured upon the challenged stars,  
the fact that God wiped them away sufficiently condemns our silence.

The Creator of earth and humankind had long watched, patiently,  
as the peoples of the lands raged madly,  
waiting to see whether a better concern might admonish someone  
who would leave the fellowship of the empty world and come to his senses.

But after the conspiratorial world began to travel the road of destruction,  
and, having conquered every mind,  
obtained the insignia of sin,  
and no one could recall his step or turn his foot back,  
the Creator shuddered and repented when he saw  
the whole world he had made.

Then, moved from on high, he is said to have uttered such threats  
and released his anger in these words:

“O race drawn toward no good, restrained by no laws,  
subject only to the ancient dragon,  
a savage race of humans, more corrupt as the ages advance!

It was not enough for Eve to fall;  
the inventor of death is surpassed in every kind of falling.

It is not enough that the ancient serpent overcame  
the inexperienced Adam.

Not content to defile life through its first parent,  
the race strives to deserve death by its own strength.

Waiting so long has done no good;  
moreover, crimes have stolen the entire time granted for mercy.

Patience has now suppressed anger for too long.  
The time of vengeance is already here.

A fiery blaze will not drive thunderbolts from heaven,  
nor will the earth, yielding beneath an immense upheaval,  
be opened by a vast chasm.

The world will be wiped away by a filthy flood of vices.

Let the world’s appearance return to the ancient chaos,  
and let the waters’ masses return to their own abodes.

Let the dry land withdraw before the waters,  
and let the flood again cover the buried, formless shape of the earth.

[Col. 0348A] Let this disaster be the end for the living and for flesh.”

Thus the eternal Father, arranging the deaths of all things,  
brandished the Flood over every land with his hand.

Meanwhile, throughout the full world, one just man lived alone  
and alone preserved an upright mind.

No one except him brought vows to God with gifts and prayers,  
him whom the supreme Creator knew to be worthy of praise  
and whom he planned to preserve, set apart for life.

He belonged to a holy lineage. He descended nobly  
from a great-grandfather whom ancient faith and conscious virtue  
carried into heaven without death.

Thus, as he sought the heights,  
a great-grandson equal to him in mighty achievement succeeded him.

There is no greater distinction in being saved  
than to leave earthly dwellings with the use of the body  
and enter the dwellings above.

Finally, just as once Enoch had ascended,  
after a long interval Elijah followed in a chariot.

He is written to have climbed through the fiery quadriga  
while the suspended orbit passed through the light breezes,  
or while its hoof pressed the clouds beneath its weight.

Though carrying the holy man within it, the surrounding fire did not burn him,  
and, preserving its movement, the flame did not know heat.

It is enough, therefore, that these men were able to deserve heaven  
while still subject to the law of their limbs.

Yet I admire no less that, because of the merit of one holy man, Noah’s age  
was able, amid the destruction of the world,  
to carry salvation for his sons and daughters-in-law.

There is in heaven an angelic choir, superior to every number,  
which endlessly proclaims and celebrates God with perpetual praise.

It is accustomed to bear out its attendant service  
and obey the commands above.

[Col. 0348C] Whatever these angels now receive—the upright requests  
conceived by worthy hearts in sacred prayer,  
and whatever a generous hand scatters among the needy—  
they accept and carry above the stars in holy flight.

They also protect the just while fragile life wearies them  
and preserve them amid the dangers of the world.

Yet one among them is especially pre-eminent,  
the minister through whom the greatest affairs of God are accomplished  
and who prepares mysteries for the highest purposes.

At God’s command, he foretold that the Lord of heaven  
would come in an assumed body into the untouched womb of a virgin,  
and filled the sacred bridal entrails with the word.

He also, as the messenger preceding the Baptist’s birth,  
while he brought long-despaired-of offspring to the father,  
frightened the man amid the sacred rites  
and immediately restrained speech in his ungrateful mouth,

until he should restore to fertility, through the birth foretold,  
the old woman who, tested through many years of sterility,  
gave birth to a child as a doubting, exhausted mother.

This skillful and highest archangel,  
moving through the clear air of the upper atmosphere,  
surrounded by light breezes,  
and moving wings that flashed upon his fiery body,  
went to earth with movements seen by no one.

At that time Noah, groaning over the crimes of all,  
lay prostrate on his knees and, with submissive lament,  
begged forgiveness for the world and its earthly inhabitants,  
though the world did not wish it.

Suddenly, when the doors were closed, the winged being entered,  
conspicuous, a messenger shining with a bright face.

The hero, terrified by so great a sight, shuddered;  
the mortal eye could scarcely bear the heavenly figure,  
and he turned the eyes of his frightened face away.

First approaching to soothe the fearful man with saving words,  
the angel bore the commands of heaven:

“Peace to you, righteous man; peace to you.  
Sent from above, I pray for peace for you,  
so that, once fear has been driven away, you may receive my words.

The supreme Creator of earth and sea commands these things.

An unexpected sentence of death indeed threatens all;  
but you alone deserve to pass through it  
and are able to foresee it.

For pleasure, trampled beneath you long ago,  
has separated you from the whole world in uprightness.

But since life alone can drive away savage death for you,  
and can enable you to escape such great disasters,  
I shall tell you briefly and in order how you should begin.

The end of the world will come,  
with the waters released everywhere,  
and the world will be ravaged by the opened abyss.

Now then, let a most powerful structure grow  
from gathered timbers,  
one that, rising, may float above all the waves.

Drawn out to a length of three hundred cubits,  
it will be enclosed by fifty in breadth, and by twice twenty [the measure is unclear in the supplied text].

Its height will consist of thirty [cubits].”

Through the middle, extending three times its length, raised floors shall support the upper chambers with suspended houses,

so that the inhabitant, preserving the fellowship of his own kind, may arrange the scattered sleeping quarters in separate cells.

Then, lest the fissures in the joints admit hostile rain, remember to smear the seams of the sides and pour in sluggish bitumen.

When you have completed the structure thus treated, enter it at once, and abandon the world as it falls—

[Col. 0349C] the world which frequent guilt has shut out; let life begin to enclose those whom it has excluded, and let deaths rage around you as you survive.

Moreover, command your companion of the same side to enter beneath the roof, and your sons to enter with their wives.

You shall be the second founder of the destroyed race, so that through you, after the first, the earth may again be filled with inhabitants.

But since, after the world had been perfected by divine powers, after the work was completed, after the laws and the sacred Sabbaths, it is no longer fitting that anything should be formed:

lest, when everything created has wholly ceased, all breathing creatures perish—of cattle, swift-flying birds, wild beasts of the forests, and those called beasts of burden,

or those that crawl, gliding through silent movements—take two of each and store them with you, destined to live within the enclosure.

Yet let them retain their proper bonds of sex, so that from them the race may again take up its origin and refill the earth.

[Col. 0349D] Do not fear that the animals might retain savage impulses or venture upon anger with sudden jaws.

There shall be peace among all those things which nature produces in discord through its various modes; and whatever you enclose there shall obey your commands in faithful concord.

Only beware always of the serpent’s deceptions.

Even if, with lowered head, he should fashion a bland expression with his three-forked tongue, concealing beneath his sweet hissing an immortal hatred, never trust him—

Adam, who has experienced him too fully, warns that he must be avoided.

For whoever once wished to do harm as an enemy will always be suspect, and must be utterly shunned, lest a prudent person join treaties with one who has already lied.

[Col. 0350A] Remember, after that example, to obey the commands.

Having spoken these words, he cleaves the empty air with his light wings, fleeing mortal sight; carried back to heaven, he leaves the trembling hero with the message.

Yet he himself, raising his hands and speaking thus, said:

“Whoever you are—whether sent or whether by your own will you have come from the high heaven to promise us such salvation and establish a peaceful compact by covenant—be our helper, let your promises strengthen your words, and bring your aid into our efforts, so that a feeble hand may be able to produce so vast a structure.”

After these brief words he restores hope of life to his heart, and swiftly undertakes the commands of the sacred task.

Who could contain such thoughts? What speech, finally, could explain the quantity of timber that was brought?

[Col. 0350B] The hills were stripped bare, the forests deprived of their strength; every mountain, as it stood, pleased the servant by its materials.

When Pelion sent immense oaks from its summit, it also displayed a great wood cut down with mighty strength; and a winged fir was taken from Pindus.

Atlas himself felt new axes resounding with their blows and gave up ancient pines for the shipyards.

Then the unconquerable work arose: the house of the lofty roof was raised, woven together from extended beams.

Meanwhile, the judgment of the various crowd was divided.

For many mocked the man who was preparing such immense barriers against the waters, since an enclosed mass could not be moved or given over to the rivers—rivers which perhaps even the Euphrates and Nile could scarcely contain within their banks.

“What are you thinking, incredulous mind of the human race? Do you think a mortal hand unable to join a distant house to the sea? The sea itself will run forward to meet it, and, standing there, will touch the shore reached by the structure.”

[Col. 0350C] But the novelty of the thing compelled others to marvel and fear the lofty mass compacted of timber, though they were ignorant of the disaster and its hidden cause.

Even then, concern had divided everyone, just as it now stirs the world.

Some say that their hearts had been pierced by faithful devotion to the work and that they knew the final crisis was imminent—the crisis in which every body would perish and the ages would consume the flesh that had long reveled.

Then that person will escape evil who, prepared, builds a strong ark of exceedingly hard covering, saved from the waters through the life-giving wood of the cross; then he will see with what profit he despised ease.

[Col. 0350D] Not far away, observing this man intent upon his work, would not some idle person, weary of labor and profitless, think him insane because he alone was burning with empty concern and refused to make use of things destined to perish?

Thus every miser, feasting, laughs at the frugal man; thus the generous man is mocked by the miser; thus the adulterer laughs at the chaste; thus the predator rejoices while entrapping the simpleton whom he has deceived.

Thus the rich man regrets having been wise when he gathers gold, considering the man who scatters his coins and, with his resources spent among the poor, miserable.

[Col. 0351A] Then, when the Judge saw that the day was suddenly approaching for the world, he said:

“Thus the end is immediately at hand, as once in the time of the righteous Noah, when the Flood encountered the world’s varied deeds and consumed flesh with its waters, while the author of salvation escaped the dangers abroad within the enclosure he had prepared.

“These things have been loudly proclaimed through evangelical figures.”

Meanwhile the provident builder completed the ark.

Then the birds hastened to it at the command; then every beast, abandoning its accustomed roaming beneath the forest canopy, came stripped of its wildness and offered itself to be taken, gladly submitting to confinement after relinquishing its freedom.

Such is the force of the decrees of the future: a hidden terror burns in the minds even of brutes and agitates their awaiting lives with fear.

But human beings, whom the lot of certain disaster presses, do not fear even when death is near; it is sufficiently clear everywhere that fear often precedes the vital indication.

[Col. 0351B] The sentence had already been pronounced against the secure and joyful people of Gomorrah, and they saw themselves near the flames.

By contrast, among the people of Nineveh, fear prevailed as a salutary terror for the sake of peace. For he had come there by command—he who had been much tossed about both on land and on the deep, who, as a prophet while the world still stood, feared to proclaim the dangers of so great a flood to the people.

A beast had swallowed him, passing through with its powerful jaws, and had enclosed him, immersed in the sea, within its belly.

Although the ravenous monster had been given power to swallow the man and fill its capacious throat, it was not permitted to bite him; its teeth accomplished nothing.

It swallowed its eager prey, deceiving the devouring creature, and the food attacked lived, starving, within its belly.

[Col. 0351C] While the sun spent three days of light and one night upon the prophet, until a new shore should behold the prison emptied, the beast vomited out the food it had confined.

When the prophet had been released from the monster and had regained the sky, touching the earth, he was then stirred to address the great city with a terrible voice:

“For what crime are you burning in flames?” he said. “Punishments will restrain everything. Now the end has come; it is slow to say this, but it has come.”

He had said no more when the whole people conspired in lamentation: weeping rushed forth from every side, breasts were beaten, and sighs struck the heavens.

They cast away their soft garments and put on Cilician goat-hair coverings; they poured ashes into their food and tears into their cups.

The ruler himself, worthy at such a time to carry before the ranks of the weeping the standards of salvation, and fearing an unprecedented doom, overcame the danger:

he cast away his scepter, abandoned his lofty tribunal, unfastened his purple robes, scorning the gold, despised silk, and took up rough coverings.

But the pious Ruler, observing such things from above, recalled his drawn-out anger with movements now stilled, and, holding back the lightning bolt he had hurled, extinguished it.

Thus, at the proper time, the righteous builder of the ark will rejoice that he alone feared the dangers while the world was secure, bearing an end for all and salvation for himself, seeing the differing lot assigned according to merit.

Therefore, when he had gathered the wild animals, male and female, and enclosed them, he then selected the animals that were permitted to be eaten, or were called clean.

[Col. 0352A] From these he placed only seven living animals within the enclosure, so that, with three pairs preserved as seed, the seventh might at some time be offered in sacrifice.

By then the life-giving prison had enclosed everything.

Then it received the righteous man, all his household, his sons and daughters-in-law, awaiting them and preserving their lives.

For nature had not yet given servants that name, nor had social order learned to distinguish masters from servants.

The middle one of Noah’s sons was the first to experience the stain of the servile name: with laughter he approached his unfortunate father when he saw him exposed, and, himself the more shameful product of an origin, mocked his father’s nakedness—now yet more wicked because the innocent man had been uncovered.

When holy Noah became aware of this, he gave his son as a servant to his brothers. From that came the condition that was discovered, for we are all born from one seed.

It is clear that guilt caused the origin of servitude, and that a free person who sins becomes a servant through his crime; but if a servant is again bound by an honorable relationship, making descendants for himself, he is now noble.

Meanwhile, the messenger who earlier had been sent from above and had carried heavenly words to the righteous man, as soon as he saw that the ark was closed and everything prepared for the day’s waiting, hastened to descend again from heaven.

He secured the loosened doors on their hinges, enclosed the men, drew the strong doors shut, and immediately lifted himself back to the upper axis.

He had passed beyond six hundred years of age, and the moon had added two full monthly courses; the seventeenth day, which had dawned after that upon the world,

[Col. 0352C] was now about to give everything over to death.

At once the sky was covered, and the sun’s darkened lights, overcome by excessive darkness, were driven away.

Terror had scarcely begun to touch the senseless minds of human beings when an unfamiliar cloud soon poured forth from the sky and first descended like a powerful rain.

The dry lands everywhere were moistened alike; one appearance covered the whole sky with cloud.

Then Egypt herself shuddered at the new waters; the Garamantes grew cold beneath the inundation, and damp chills touched the Massylian Syrtes, which had long been hot.

It was not the appearance of rain, nor drops, that dripped for long; rather, rivers poured down when the sky broke open.

So too, when the Tanais is fed by white snows, rushing down from Mount Riphaeus, it strikes against the river and at once casts forward what it carries along its long course.

The earth was shaken by such a struggle of waters, and the air became like a lake compressed by waves.

Yet the waters above did not pour forth only from there: the earth too rose into anger.

All the soil burst open; the fields gave out frequent channels; springs leapt forth and unknown rivers flowed.

The cloud, its weight changed, was turned upward; falling from the heavens here, while rising everywhere from the earth there, the water soon met itself.

The elements conspired together in joined fury for destruction; every limit of the riverbanks was exceeded, and the water, bursting its barriers, raged and ran about with loosened reins.

But when all things strove to occupy the expanse of the spreading earth and fill the capacious world, perhaps the sentence of death could have been delayed and drawn out by a longer postponement, so that the final fate, surrendering space more slowly, might seize all flesh later.

The ocean, the summit of the elements, boiling upon a single shore by which it surrounds both lands and seas, might have gone forth, breaking its covenant, and flooded the fields.

It would have scattered the eternal laws, abandoned its own seat, sought foreign kingdoms, and disturbed the covenants of nature.

When the illustrious rivers first sensed the sea’s dreadful fury—those great rivers whose fame is celebrated for their course—and were briefly astonished by the new movements, they seemed, one might think, to have understood the need for flight.

Turning backward, they spread the sea across the lands, lifted in their swirling mass.

Yet Ocean followed, hung over the retreating streams, and drove the rivers onward with salty masses.

[Col. 0353B] Then, amid such great noise, fear became greater for the suffering mortals.

They climbed towers and the lofty roofs of houses, and it pleased them to delay their imminent death even for a brief time.

While many tried to climb, the rising water dragged them away; it pursued some who sought the mountains, and caught their futile flight with death.

Others, tossing their limbs in prolonged swimming, exhausted their breath and died; others, overwhelmed by the weight of the cloud and mixed with the river waters across the seas, drank death from whatever mountain they reached.

Others perished when their houses were driven down in ruin; masters and houses alike entered the waves together.

A crash assembled from every sound went up to heaven, and the herds of four-footed animals falling amid human death increased the confused tumult with mingled voices.

Amid these seething funerals of the wretched world, the greatly burdened ark was struck by raging movements; its joints trembled, and the creaking seam labored.

Yet the hostile force did not penetrate the blocked structure, although it battered it and wearied the solid wood with waves striking against it.

In the same way the true Church endures frequent storms and is now likewise harassed by savage waves.

On one side the pagan world drives its swollen rages without restraint; on another, Judaism rages and is dashed against it with rabid mouth; from elsewhere the frenzied Charybdis of heresies provokes madness.

The swollen wisdom of Greek philosophers rejoices in setting its waves against one another.

With insults they inflate empty winds of lies, but they strike the closed ark with futile barking and do no harm.

By then the rising water had covered the middle of the ark and, lifting the hollow mass, had set it moving everywhere.

And it was safer that the weight should be carried by an easy swim; wherever the waves called it, the moving burden now followed.

Let us yield to the world while we are being led: let everything that resists, if it does not know how to bend, fear being broken by its own weight.

But if we yield, let it not feel the current within, nor let an impenetrable mind draw in any sin.

Meanwhile the fountain of life, entrusted to the enclosure of all, sails on and preserves, above all else, the world’s deposit amid the raging sea, to bring it forth from its faithful covering when the peace owed to the earth demands its return.

Thus the waves continued; the whole earth was submerged.

[Col. 0354A] The waters rose above the hills and conquered the heights.

Then pine-bearing Othrys disappeared beneath the covering sea; the summit of Parnassus no longer displayed its lofty rock; the stones of cypress-bearing Lycaeus themselves lay hidden; the Alps, their ridges submerged, were leveled by the waves.

With everything excluded, at last the whole world was nothing but axis and water.

For once all had been subdued by death, sea-monsters ruled in the forest-filled abyss.

Already the waters were striking against the neighboring sky; and rain had been pouring for forty nights.

It had completed the work of death, and Death no longer had anything left to remove; the sea pressed down upon the floating corpses.

At last the rains were restrained, the sky shone again, and its face was restored to the heavens.

The sun itself returned, but found no lands to which it could give back its light; it shone only upon the waters.

A sorrowful brightness looked upon the seas, and whatever brief rays it sent down, touching the waves, it brought near and fiercely pressed upon the waters to consume them.

No less were the earth’s open fissures closed, and the abyss, constrained by its own barriers, swallowed back the streams that it had earlier vomited from its deadly mouth.

Yet the water did not retreat as briefly as it had come.

Many months dried up what a few days had poured forth.

The ark, already carried along by the waters, was now pressing against the high mountains of Armenia, and had not yet settled upon the exposed fields below.

When the old man sensed that it had become stable and no longer moved, and believed that the wood, floating over the windy waters, no longer drifted, he thought that the world had grown bright after the waters had been withdrawn.

Then he opened the upper window in the lofty front,

[Col. 0354C] so that, by sending out a bird, he might investigate the waters as they receded.

Flying, it beat the air with a long flapping of its wings and shook the empty breezes with their movements.

After it had long skimmed the waters with its weary wings, and no place offered the rest it desired, it returned to its accustomed enclosure when it saw the open expanse of sea.

The old man then gathered it inside with his hands, observing that no lands were yet exposed amid the waters.

Meanwhile, the sea, moving with its great mass, was returning to its ancient chaos, leaving the things of the world behind.

At last the summits of the heights began first to emerge, after which the low mountains grew more numerous.

But when the sea had enclosed the ancient shores, and holy Ocean, gathered back into its familiar boundaries, content with its customary course, had swallowed the flowing rivers,

[Col. 0354D] and their channels had everywhere enclosed the torrents, the dry lands shone freely after the waters had withdrawn.

Then, after an interval of time, the old man sent out the raven, wishing to know whether the world was empty.

When the bird sought the shining air with outstretched wings, looking down upon the lands packed with abundant corpses, it settled upon the flesh and soon forgot to return, leaving its peaceful master in the common dwelling.

Thus you do not know how to keep faith with your teacher, Jew; thus, once released, you love the flesh; thus no gratitude is ever returned to the Lord who preserves life.

Thus, with wandering mind, you depart unrestrained; thus you have broken the covenants of the Law and first violated the pact, faithless one.

[Col. 0355A] When the old man had determined, after a period of time, that the sluggish raven could by now have returned sufficiently to the enclosure, unaware of the delay and the reason for its lingering—lest perhaps the water, entangled with its weary wings, had consumed it, and the returning flood had joined it to all the dying—

he immediately sent out the white dove from its dwelling.

Mindful of the command, it sought the lands in swift flight; seeing a branch of green olive, bearer of peace, it plucked it and brought it back in its gentle beak to the enclosure.

By such a sign the simple messenger confirmed the covenant, and thus the pious man learned that the world was pure.

The complete circle of time had measured out a full year, during which the fortunate enclosure held all breathing creatures.

Then the father opened the barriers, whose bolts had been removed, and began to restore the unfamiliar sun to those enclosed, so that the seeds might return to the exhausted world.

But before the righteous man ordered them to scatter and wander, he summoned his sons and daughters-in-law and took one from each of the seven clean animals that he had earlier arranged to enclose.

He arranged them upon an altar constructed of turf and sacrificed them, kindling sacred fires upon that first altar.

While many bodies were consumed by great flames and a numerous victim raised thick smoke, a sweet odor touched the joyful heaven beyond the sky, and the first offering of the purified world was received.

Then, mingled with the sacred fire, this voice thundered:

“Thus far the world has dragged along the contagions of defilement. Let it be enough that wickedness has reigned. Let the earth, cleansed by washing, shine forever, and let the elements retain the features restored to them.

“Let the worldly mass, disturbed by no further evils, no longer collapse.

“You also, whom life saved in the time of death and whom it preserved untouched, defending you from every disaster, live out a secure age while keeping the laws that have been preserved.

“And you, the head of the race, scatter offspring from fertile seed, so that they may fill the world far and wide, restore the number that was destroyed, and rule the earth.

“Moreover, the animals shall again produce fertile offspring, yet this will serve in its proper order as before.

“Nor from this time onward will a flood reign upon the earth, one that might crush all flesh.

“There will be one such event only; it will be shown by one sign.

“Sin will not see a similar death repeated; and if there is crime, another terror will not be absent.”

Thus the Father, swearing that baptism was one, consecrated it, so that the guilty, once the world had been washed by cleansing waters, might not hope for a second washing.

When scarcely three divisions of the sky had passed and the ray was moving headlong toward the setting, he was commanded to touch a distant cloud beneath the eastern axis and brought forth a sign shaken from the rain-soaked air.

An arc flashed forth, which Greek poets call the Thaumantian Iris and Roman poets call Iris.

When suspended moisture has felt the slanting sun, it sends forth colors with changing brilliance.

You could not count them: thus the circles, mingled with light, deceive uncertain sight with various appearances.

Green sapphire, spotted, blue, and white, it draws purple from the cloud, sparkling from the sun, brightness from the sky, and blackness from the earth.

Yet although these things are composed of separate elements, you might think them so diverse that you see them in harmony.

God gave this form to the bow as a sign for trembling mortals, promising serenity in the cloud and that the sky would no longer owe dangers to the earth.

Now whoever wishes to preserve true salvation will look upon that sign which signs signify.

For Christ, the giver of life, prefigured such things and, in a twofold substance, gave the Savior.

In the radiant flesh taken from a virgin upon earth there is a natural brightness from the father’s stock.

And a certain mediator in the lofty heaven, varied in manifold gift but bright in all things, displays the living arc of the sacred pledge.

[Col. 0356C] Whoever you are, washed in baptism, and go forth to heaven freed from piercing sins, behold this in your heart.

“For this is the form of the Law that will save you,” says the Apostle, “when the ancient time of Noah described eight souls enclosed in wood.”

He compares the gift; cherish it while preserving it.

Bear it through vows and prayers; desire it with tears, lest sins return to you, lest what has been submerged rise again, lest the dead stand up, lest what has been conquered rebel, lest dangers prevail after the crime has been washed away, and lest you fear the flame because water is no longer available.

# BOOK FIVE. ON THE PASSAGE OF THE RED SEA

[Col. 0355]

[Col. 0355D] Thus far, while my song has told that waters were spread upon the earth, the order of the poem now opens the earth amid the waves.

There the flood previously sought those whom it would destroy; now, inflamed with full fury, thousands of a doomed people will of their own accord run toward the flood.

If language cannot receive the praises of so great a deed in a manner worthy of it, the will directed toward divine praise is sufficient, and the servant’s gratitude is shown by the gift.

If anyone cannot repay thanks in words, it is no small virtue at least to believe in the deeds and signs that passed through the chosen men of former times.

[Col. 0356D] Among these, one far surpasses the others: the deed accomplished in the Red Sea, which the most celebrated sequence of the Scriptures recounts.

Within its sacred weight there was a greater pledge of the underlying causes; and, beautiful in its telling, it surpasses in beauty the form of the salvation announced beforehand.

That which is great enough in histories, and greater still in figures, brought forth life conceived from a pregnant covering.

The oppressed people endured harsh labors in a foreign dwelling while subject to the Pelusian nation.

The weight of dense mud, the measured numbers of bricks, and the daily quota of work tormented them, afflicted by the cruel fraud of the tyrant.

He hated the people and, gnashing his teeth, grieved that the crowd was growing and that his servants were increasing.

For he had ordered that every male child who saw the light should immediately be killed by every midwife instructed to do so, and that their skill should suppress the newborn sex.

Yet the mothers turned away from such commands and refused to destroy their forbidden offspring, while God persisted in spreading abroad his holy people.

The more the blind mind pursued its cruel wishes, the more the beginnings of the tender race increased.

Meanwhile the Father had seen from his heavenly seat and had looked upon the afflicted hand with a peaceful face.

Already the sacred fire had given innocent flames from the bush, and the green shrub had remained amid the red heat.

By this sign, the devout person would understand that the thorns of our mind grow hot and shine with a holy fire that does not consume them.

At once the chosen prophets carried the commands.

First Moses brought such words to the king:

“The people, wearied by the long burden of servitude, have shoulders oppressed by baskets, necks rubbed raw, and palms hardened by unceasing labor.

“The time to release them has come. At last let them go, so that they may pay their vows to the heavenly Lord and fulfill the rites given under their ancestral rule.”

He, raging, replied:

“What is the reason for such great tumult? What new god demands the people through a command that has been sent?

“Surely these empty concerns reach the heavens, as though the Lord wished now to take away ancient servants from their masters and send commands to rebellious men swollen with pride.

“Who would this god be, to whom I must obey? Or what is formidable to a king exalted by his sceptres?

“But your leisure deceives your minds too much. If an allowed rest did not support the released people, no time would be wasted on empty words.

“And if a greater burden restricts them by chastisement, their forbidden attempt will cease.

“But you who, under a standard-bearing leader, prepare such demands and overturn the people with empty speech, avoid my presence and beware my face.

“For I call wealthy Pharaoh to witness—and you, Nile, most powerful in your course, and Anubis of the divine voice, when he rages and barks—that this will not go unpunished if they bring these words again before our tribunal.”

The lawgiving hero happened to be carrying a staff in his hand.

[Col. 0357D] While he used that staff to steady his step with his right hand, he hurled it forward with a powerful stroke.

Then, wondrous to tell, the wood, set in motion, began to crawl—not as lifeless branches send forth shoots from a vine, moving only the life that enables fruit to grow, but crawling with a bending movement and, through the use of its changed body, possessing sense and spirit.

The staff began to move along and soon, formed into a serpent, returned the shape.

The tyrant, terrified, stood fixed, and the black ruler then grew pale in his everlasting face.

But lest the attendants see him yield in confusion before such a sign, his face wavering, he pretended to believe that the deed had been performed by supreme command.

Unwilling that it should be divine, he wanted it to be thought a human act.

Then he ordered all the magicians and those skilled in incantations, who tested the unlawful art of Egypt through dreadful deceits, to bring long staffs and, by funeral murmuring, compelled the minister to produce what had been displayed.

At once they all hastened together at the command, and each armed his own staff with the familiar poison.

The cast staffs produced empty appearances, and serpents, as they seemed to be, terrified deceived eyes with an illusory form.

But the magicians’ pride did not last long.

Everything they thought they had made was consumed, for the horned viper, still biting, first swallowed the dragons they had fashioned by art.

When Moses had ended the displays of power and, holding the victor by the tail, raised it from the ground, the serpent withdrew into the wood, and its appearance receded; the wandering coils stiffened in the hardened body.

What more need be said? It became again the staff it had been before, with which the priest later displayed many signs as time passed.

Then the dreadful rage of Pharaoh, aware of what had happened, raged and began to resist the divine power in everything.

Though he recognized what had happened, he himself refused to confess it and immediately ordered the prophets to depart.

They struck the divine ears with their tears, asking that the rage of the wicked people might at last be restrained.

The heavenly warnings had made it even more savage, and it was threatening arms even against heaven itself.

Then the Father, receiving the groans and tears of those who prayed, consoled their bitterness with gentle encouragement:

“Do not surrender your hearts to such empty fear, my people, whom I chose from the whole body of the world and devoted to myself alone by a particular lot.

“Now you will see with what aid I pursue your beginnings and pursue your savage enemies.

“I shall lead forth a lofty hand through every portent; nor will the king of Pharos wish to yield after only a few signs, so that miracles may overcome his hard mind only after a longer time.

“After this, he will even be compelled to release you and make you depart; what he now refuses, he will voluntarily impose upon you.”

“After your courageous battles you will go to great dwellings, where a land waiting with abundant fertility calls you, and you will establish shining cities among conquered peoples.

“For now, trust only in the gifts promised, and let cheerful courage bear the labors that great deeds will demand, preserving itself for prosperity.”

When they heard these words, a better hope received them.

They raised their spirits, stretched their hands toward the stars, conceived faith in their prayers, and returned thanks.

[Col. 0358D] The following light had first sent forth uncertain beginnings and, with night driven away, carried the day as dawn advanced upon it.

Then blood stained the rivers, and the fields were suddenly wet with gore.

But this portent did not occur merely in the lesser waters: the king of rivers himself grew red, and the Nile no longer displayed the distinctive brightness it had received from its source.

Moreover, lest the former mud touch it, blood struggled to flow into an external channel.

It was not fleshly blood, nor was it poured from a body, nor was it a slaughter of many victims whose wounds could supply the loss of the waters with their own blood.

The foreign inhabitants, their nostrils blocked and their swimming overcome, perished together in the thick current.

[Col. 0359A] The fish increased the gore with their own corpses.

And I might perhaps think that, as an indication of the future disaster and death, the ruin had already come before them in the sign of blood, if this itself had not been a punishment.

For clearly the whole extent of Egypt, as far as broad Canopus lies open, would soon have failed, thirsty amid its fertile waters, if the Almighty had not scattered swift healing over the fields and restored the shining rivers to their valleys.

But when the removal of the plague brought back relief, the tyrant was raised up again by delayed death.

Scorning the scourge he had barely escaped, he persisted in subjecting the innocent people to blows.

But why should my pen burn to pass through all the proud man’s treachery, counting the perjuries of the stricken kingdom?

Yet lies force forth a varied monstrosity, and the water scarcely cleansed of its nearby blood covered the cities with the foul songs of frogs.

The cells, inner chambers, and tables were filled.

The royal purple endured innumerable leaps, and, pressing upon human beings, growled as they succumbed to frogs.

Soon, when the heaps had been subdued by flame and thunder and piled together, a sounding cloud of flies went forth into the air, corrupting the atmosphere with its breath.

There were the creatures they call gnats, and such flights as their dangling little bodies commit to the light winds, making lanes through the air with buzzing wings.

They poured forth together and filled the troubled walls.

Although they fixed wounds with their immersed beaks, horror caused more distress than pain.

But even that was removed by the driving wind; as the annoyance was loosened, it ceased little by little.

[Col. 0359C] As soon as fear ceased, the anger was felt no longer than the wound remained hot.

But when that plague was removed, others followed, more grievous.

Every beast of burden was consumed, and a single night carried off all the herds.

Nor did the destructive portents weary the guilty only in this way: the anger turned upon the flesh and aroused painful torments.

Swollen wounds settled deeply upon the limbs, and a sacred fire lay upon the stricken joints.

This illness too is believed to have arisen by chance, but the disease of the mind presses upon the body’s dangers.

That day passed.

Then, when daylight followed, the sky was shaken by thunder, and the gathered clouds flashed with terrible brilliance.

Lightning struck everything, driving bolts.

At one time, with the sky disturbed, the elements threatened the earth with every kind of death.

[Col. 0359D] Enormous hail was inserted among the fires in the body of the storm—not as it usually comes to the earth from a rain-bearing cloud, but so that, wherever it fell, it might crush and cause ruin by its weight alone.

Thus the cold of hail was joined to the burning flames in the air, and nature, preserving destruction, assigned both together.

This rain first spread slaughter through scattered deaths.

Afterward the grub rose to consume the remaining fruit, and the locust, trusting in its springing leg, followed.

But pride, schooled by these evils and already hardened by repeated danger, regarded this as sufficiently mild.

A swifter anger followed to exact a heavier vengeance.

At the beginning of a new morning the rising sun had spread blind shadows, and, joyful, shone with a bright forehead beneath a clear mane,

[Col. 0360A] when a black cloud, rising, stretched across the middle of the sky and closed off the newborn day by driving away its light.

Dense night gathered into a mass; the air perished, buried beneath it.

Hands felt their way through the thick darkness, and the breath, driven back, was tormented and labored.

If anyone tried to revive sleeping fires by blowing, or wished to draw out flames, the compressed lights died, nor could their restricted movements vibrate beneath the weight.

Wherever the dark horror found anyone, it held him fast.

No one saw anyone, nor was anyone seen by anyone.

You might think that the foul multitudes of living things had entered infernal dwellings, or that, perhaps, having torn away the barrier of the earth, they had migrated upward from the homeland of the filthy abyss and, after banishing the light from the world, subjected it to their laws.

This darkness destroyed three days.

The earth, deserving of punishment, bore these losses for its perjury; for the rest, the shining world remained, and the accustomed cycles distinguished the seasons.

Meanwhile Moses continued his tears, fasts, and vows, and persisted in prayers, frequently and watchfully, supported by the comfort of his elder brother.

The Creator instructed them together in sacred matters and taught them the mystery by which the solemn victim should reveal the rite.

“Do you see how Egypt, sweating beneath so many disasters, crushed and struck on every side, groans under its guilt, yet remains rebellious, persisting with an unmoved neck?

“These things do not long precede ruin.

“Whatever swells with pride is sick; no sound cause supports the arrogant, and the swollen mind reveals that death is joined to it.

“One grief still remains, destined to avenge everything and, after the nine plagues, strike the guilty with a tenth slaughter.

“For now, learn the perpetual customs of the sacrifices, and hold fast to them by an enduring law in their proper rites.

“Among all the months through which the year’s orbit revolves, let this one be first and chief, the month which the Gentiles call by the name of war; you must call it only the first.

“When the moon has added twice seven nights, then, late in the evening, you shall begin the sacrifices.

“Take a gentle lamb of perfect age, free from blemish, whose fleece is pure upon its body.

“You shall slaughter this animal at the festival.

“Its blood from its shining body shall mark both doorposts.

“This shall provide the sign by which salvation is carefully preserved.

“When the destroyer carries out a silent slaughter without a wound, he will see that the threshold has been moistened with sacred blood.

“This separation alone, if he wishes to pass by, protects your houses from the deaths scattered around them.

“So may your sign, Christ, set above all things upon our foreheads, save us.

“So may the sacred blood—the blood of the lamb announced long ago, which is then poured out—be believed, when infused upon our mouths, to have purified the doorposts of your people amid the burning funerals of the passing world, and to distinguish your people from every disaster.

“While the sword of death passes through those who are not marked, recognize your figure among the people destined to be saved.

“Wherever the holy lamb is sacrificed, and the offering has extended the holy body as food, let the sacred rite celebrate the promises of the life to follow.

“Let unleavened bread, with the wicked double leaven torn from the heart, season pure and sincere minds.”

[Col. 0361A] The ruler had finished commanding the men concerning the laws and covenants of the Passover festival.

Immediately they all took them up together; they joyfully completed the feast, and the solemn meal was arranged in a new rite, whose established form would pass down to distant descendants.

It was night, and everything was enjoying the middle of its rest; the shadow had just divided the balanced hours.

Behold, through the dreadful silence, an angel came in silent motion, sent with a drawn sword to rage.

The sentence of sudden death did not fall indiscriminately, but every disaster came according to its assigned lot, and in the darkness it could be seen from far away whom the order of the appointed death would strike.

The eldest perished; only those were chosen for death whom the first light had brought forth.

[Col. 0361B] Servants perished with their masters, and the children of the powerful fell mingled with the common people.

So did the lowly fall, as did the one whom purple had held while he was dying upon a lofty couch.

Some lay upon the bare earth; others were covered with silk.

Bodies were laid out for death upon unequal beds.

Death, impartial, feared no one and spared none of the distinctions by which the living alone are honored.

It was moved by no pity toward the poor man’s weeping,
That he may spare the wealthy, he is corrupted by no gold.

The healthy departs before the sick, the younger before the long-lived: in this alone no one should put confidence.

Yet this is the one distinction between them: those who complete their allotted time live on through their merits.

Death is never permitted to take these away utterly; and even if, by right of its power, it can carry off one created in an earthly frame,

[Col. 0361C] born from mortal seed and returned to the earth, death is believed to have no claim upon the deeds of the righteous.

Therefore, when the palace suddenly sees its offspring struck down in confusion, mothers run weeping to the funerals; they beat their breasts with their fists, tear out their hair with their nails, and hasten to lacerate their blackened cheeks.

Nor did they mourn their lords for long: soon each person’s own grief seized everyone. One cry resounds in the air, though it is composed of many weepers; no house is free from death. Then, amid much light, the funeral of all the people is attended throughout the city.

A just judgment compels the grieving to mourn. And while each person keeps watch over his own sorrow, grief delays the funerals, and the unburied multitude lies waiting for a time, deferred by the lot of the grave;

[Col. 0361D] and unless at last they are either laid in the bare earth, stripped now of every honour, or burned with fire, a hand scarcely assembled could hardly enclose so many in an urn.

Then the mournful crowd surrounds the king amid agitated murmuring, drawing complaints from the ground in their voices:

“Alas! How excessively hostile to our affairs is the power of the Hebrew people, against whom every evil wages war so often with an avenging hand; against whom, finally, the whole world fights, while prosperous events follow beneath an angry heaven.

“Scarcely do certain hidden designs of God—and a greater power—rage against this scepter and avenge the people themselves through the city’s destruction. The elements, as they perish, save only their conquerors and redeem them by their own falling.

“Look: Egypt lies prostrate, no longer capable of restoration.

[Col. 0362A] “Would that the divine hand were still inflicting punishments upon the living and bringing ruin across the fields, and had not emptied Canopus, deceived by so great a slaughter, through sudden death!

“At last, spare the land and drive away the causes of ruin, while the devastation is lighter; while anyone is still held by the light; while someone remains to press upon the backs of the departing and drive them to the boundary; and, if any should perhaps wish to linger in their hearts, let no one move him to calamity by driving away the expelled guest.

“May our grief at the death of our children move you—and perhaps your own grief move you; or may a few survivors remain as pledges, preserved to wipe away such great sorrows and repair the losses of the mutilated nation.”

At these words the people shed tears; the proud ruler himself was broken by weeping and confessed that he had been defeated.

While these matters were being dealt with in the troubled palace,

[Col. 0362B] the Hebrews, at the urging of the prophets and in obedience to heavenly instructions, devise all the best things that sacred rites require for feasts, and seek the many vessels demanded by solemn worship.

They ask also for ornaments, clothing, necklaces, and jewels, saying that these too must be returned. Nor is the host slow to lend them; unknowingly he enriches the trembling people with an emulous hand.

“What mouths worthy of your praises can now be opened, supreme Father, who use such a savage enemy in this way?

“He nods against his will and, unwillingly, grants gifts which they may carry away with them. Nor is it enough merely to release the oppressed: those departing are enriched by wealth, and restored liberty takes possession of new treasures.

“Amid the raging furies in the hostile palace, the fugitive plunders his master and deceives him as he watches; he empties the presence of its wealth, lest you think that those driven out departed so much as joyful emigrants rather than expelled exiles. Thus the greedy carry away Pharaoh’s riches, whom you might then believe to have assessed the long labor of servitude as wages paid.”

Sometimes what is contrary benefits the righteous, and what the evil man intended for the left returns transformed; when God turns it toward the right, the force of hatred destroys only the guilty, leading them into the wounds they had planned and compelling them to fall into the snares prepared for their brother.

Meanwhile, the ministers who had gone out from the trembling king compel them to conceal their flight and force them onward willingly; they hurry them eagerly and press upon those hastening, thinking that the ruins should be driven away together with the people already driven out.

The foreigner had now completed nearly a hundred years in your kingdoms, Egypt, from the time when the ancient patriarch Jacob once brought there

[Col. 0362D] twelve sons with their offspring and dear descendants, and through the fertile father their thousands grew.

At last the people proceed and soon, in united formation, leave the dread land, bereft amid darkness and mourning. For the neighboring day had not yet brought forth its rising:

“This night shall be sacred to God for those returning to the yearly rites; this shall be the solemn night of the people freed from the enemy.”

At the head of the column the lawgiver shone conspicuously, advancing before the ranks with his brother beside him.

Behind them the cohorts of war arrange their weapons and lead strong companies in ordered formation. They carry arms upon their shoulders; swords hang at each left side; helmets gleam upon their pressed-down heads, and the iron light competes with the whiteness of the moon.

[Col. 0363A] Some lean upon spears and turn their shields in their left hands, rehearsing battle with rapid rotations.

Others rejoice in quivers and fit their swift arrows for deaths to be sent against the enemy,

or, if they should happen to follow a man fleeing with his back turned, so that the feathered shafts may pass lightly through the winds.

The common people proceed last through the frightened ranks, not inferior in number to the stars painted across the sky, or to the rippling waves stirred by the sea’s movement, or to the sands that the surf turns upon the shore, or to the drops with which the damp clouds drip.

The satraps of Pharos marvel and see that they had not thought such a thing possible; they are pleased to have driven out so many enemies.

But you will not be saved by the hard iron of this battle line. However many infantry troops may surround you,

[Col. 0363B] one commander will fight on behalf of all the thousands.

But the people, with their steps regulated by a slow pace, made their way along the route they had taken, advancing only as far ahead of their leaders as either sluggish old age or infancy, crawling in its early years, could endure, lest premature exertion distress their fragile age and sex. Thus the heavenly command arranges everything and assists the rejoicing people.

When the thousands had settled within marked camps, and the armed foot soldiers had surrounded the unarmed crowd, at the first evening a column resembling a standing pillar, set upright, shone with flame in the clear sky.

Yet it did not gleam like the dreadful fire that flashes across the familiar axis when signs revealed to the earth threaten disasters from heaven—when they foretell a year darkened by diseases, wars, or calamities;

[Col. 0363C] rather, shining with rays and bright with joyful light, it displayed a brilliant fire to the astonished camps.

The darkness fled, and the neighboring stars withdrew. At first the men stood dumbfounded; the novelty terrified everyone and struck them with fear. Then, gradually, the use of the light commended the heavenly radiance to their affection.

The greater part of the night had already passed, and the approaching day was drawing near according to its allotted course. The column was seen moving across the sky before everyone’s eyes, and it took the road while the people watched.

At once the holy fathers perceived that it was to be followed and that it was the leader of leaders. Soon, rejoicing in so great a guide, they broke their delay and vied with one another to leave the camp.

Then, as each tribe, having first received its appointed labor, began the journey in order, the rest of the people followed.

[Col. 0363D] Meanwhile the returning light opened the bright heavens; the fiery column grew pale at the sight of the sun. The whole fire that had shone was turned into a cloud, but the shape of the extended form remained stretched across the upper air.

The third hour had wiped away the nocturnal moisture, and the sun, climbing upward, had overcome the shadows of morning. Behold a new marvel: beneath a serene sky, a cold cloud was commanded to oppose itself to the burning rays and prepared a dense covering from the thinnest substance.

Thus, when the earth beneath it burns with eastern heat, the multitude does not feel its natural warmth; you would think that evening winds were sprinkling it with a gentle breath or that mild breezes were spreading cool moisture.

Nor did this cloud take on a form steeped in oppressive heat, nor was it so dreadful in its congealed appearance

[Col. 0364A] as when clouds bring forth powerful storms that terrify the strong. Rather, its appearance was like that of a rainbow when it sees the sun through moisture: such was the beauty of the column extended above them.

By night it was fire and carried a light kindled within it; when the sun scorched, it gave forth cool moisture like dew.

As it led these alternating changes in accordance with time, nature changed its turns; its unlike substance made its use harmonious with its particular gifts. If it remained, the men remained; if it moved, they followed.

If it was also seen to hang in place for many days, the ranks stationed beneath it remained delayed at the fixed camp.

This act of providence continued for forty years, while you, Judaea, traversed the vast retreats of the wilderness; while the road strengthened the fetters on your feet; while, for so long a time, unfrayed clothing preserved its original weight, and ancient garments were made enduring by a new softness.

Thus it would have been long-lived, because age did not harm it.

While the shining manna carried sacred food to the people and earthly beings saw the harvest of heaven,

through it a lofty figure had foretold that a pure body, without seed, would be brought forth from the womb,

so that salvation, needing nourishment, might receive food from its heavenly seat, as God poured it upon the holy altars.

By this sign the supreme priest, striking the rock, brought forth streams of water for the thirsty people.

For you see Christ standing as the enduring rock: struck by the blow, he supplied abundant waters and offered drink to his own from his sacred wound.

Meanwhile the joyful Hebrews, with the column leading them,

[Col. 0364C] traveled across the lands, while it moved through the heavens before their eyes.

Behold, once again anger settled in the minds of the people of Pharos, and the savage populace arms itself without restraint with these words, directing its final fury against those near to death:
