“O error, mocking minds that are excessively foolish, and deceptions carried out through a sufficiently clouded fraud!

“Are you not ashamed that a slave people should thus be carried away with impunity, without any battle, because so great a resident has abandoned empty lands without a leader?

“The fields lie vacant; the towns cease from their unfinished walls. No customary work rises up, nor does the cultivator exercise his strong hoes in the hardened soil.

“The turbulent tax collector is silent, and the feverish revenues no longer return amid their accustomed tumult.

“Rather, let an army rush forward with weapons seized, and bring back the defenseless band and the fugitives.

“And if the hand should be so inflamed by the audacity of slaves that they wish to contend with weapons, let the entire force perish at once, mingled with the common people. Let mothers, intermixed amid the blazing weapons, die with pierced breasts; let arrows transfix the children clinging to their mothers’ breasts.

“Let each person, seeing his own offspring fall before his eyes, wish to hasten death by offering his throat.

“Let the final lot make our people taste the grief of bereavement; let them lose everything while alive, and then perish. Let the unburied corpses lying beneath the dense slaughter of the field be committed to the sorrowful sky.

“Then, when his sword has satisfied all these furies, let the victorious hand recall the fleeing treasures.”

[Col. 0365A] With such breaths they stirred and sharpened their anger, while God mocked them—he alone who looks down upon every effort that, rigid with empty fear, devises vanity, and who, having rendered the leaders’ plan void, scatters it in action.

Therefore they call for war; the eager youth seize their weapons. Foaming horses are led forth, and the powerful riders hang gleaming bits upon their decorated steeds.

The warlike display shines; with a gilded pole they draw the axles set beneath the chariots. Then the rest of the people clothe themselves in steel or surround themselves with yellow bronze.

Some delight in the vast covering of their cuirasses, which a dense, clinging circle weaves together for them; the chain-linked fabric rattles across their bodies.

But on others, a thin iron mesh, meeting their eyes as it rises in linked rows along the descending edges, formed, by its varied workmanship, a frightening covering of compacted metal.

And yet, amid all the weapons of the armed men, their appearance was more terrifying still: for who could look upon those raging men whose joyful faces could scarcely be seen?

Their faces were enclosed in helmets, and iron clothing surrounded the angry darkness with the gleam of arms.

The assembled force advances; the king himself drives the snorting horses in his chariot. Yet, surrounded on every side by weapons, he lies hidden; the spear shafts make a dense forest.

The earth is shaken by the wheels striking it and by the weight; the packed youth narrow the broad ground and close the roads. Whatever strength Egypt could possess, imminent death leads it all.

Meanwhile, at the place where Magdalus presses upon the sea,

[Col. 0365C] the Hebrew people had joined their camp to the reddening deep, believing in their secure minds that they had escaped the enemy.

While they rest and prepare to sleep beneath the fixed rampart, they see clouds of dust rising toward heaven.

At first the ranks remain hesitant; soon the savage columns become visible. Yet the neighboring evening, beneath the setting sun, does not permit the hostile forces to join battle.

The tyrant, enclosed within his ramparts, postponed the fighting until daylight. Chance might not yet have restrained his burning anger, nor could his fury have preserved the treaties of the night; he might even have wished to precede the dawn with standards already in motion, had not the fiery column, standing back by chance, separated the two peoples with its intervening barrier.

The king himself, nevertheless, gazed upon the wondrous light. Thus he feared the fire, because he burned with fervor in his mind.

Little by little, however, his dying did not help him: they proceed toward the single place that will close them all when the sea opens its ruin.

The enclosed people tremble in the confined place and, terrified, await the coming day as their end. They have prepared neither weapons nor any countermeasure of war, but, raising their voices, they appeal to the prophets:

“O thrice and four times blessed are those whom Egypt took away by death, for whom the broad earth prepared an urn in their final lot!

“They are worthy not to feel such great sufferings, nor to see the slaughter of their offspring or their captured children.

“We have been given as food to birds; our bodies, buried in no tomb, will be scattered across the deserted wilderness.”

The men uttered these words; the entire populace responded to the mourning, and the crowd leaped about in kindled tumult.

[Col. 0366A] Then the holy leaders began to recall the promises, console their fear, and wipe away their tears with words:

“We ask you: lay aside your ungrateful fears and, having experienced so much, do not suppose that those things should be despaired of which heavenly gifts promise through such great signs.

“Can it ever slip from your faithless hearts that Egypt, struck down by so many evils and that land collapsing amid the scourges it experienced, allowed you and all that belonged to you to live safely under an afflicted kingdom and an enemy?

“What need is there to speak of what has happened? Surely you see how the protecting column, serving as mediator, takes care that we need fear no deception from the opposing side.

“Rather, raise your minds upright in firm hope.

“For the final day has been fixed for the people tomorrow—the people that now, clanking with war, trusts in its weapons.

“This time the battle will not be borne in the usual way, nor will you meet weapons with weapons, nor will triumph come to you through your own sweat. Heaven’s anger will fight; the battles will be carried out for you by a peaceful command.”

With such exhortations the prophets raised the men’s cast-down hearts and calmed their fear with sacred speech.

But a mighty wind, with burning breath, scorched the sea, consuming the whole depth throughout the night, while the Father, against nature, hurled lightning upon the waves; the wave, struck in the gulf, burned beneath the blast.

The dreadful morning had now arrived. Scarcely had the dawn, striving to display its first blushes, scattered them through the world when all at once they burst from the dark camps, and the youth roared as it moved on every side.

When the terror of the sounding trumpet reached the ears of the frightened people and struck their breasts,

[Col. 0366C] they seize and follow the road by which the nearest shores of the sea are troubled, marked by the red liquid.

When the people reached the highest shores of the sea, the reverence owed to their leader immediately caused the waves to withdraw, and it opened a path for which the enemy had closed the land.

The machine that the watery scene had built, hanging above them, held back the restrained waters suspended in the lofty air.

The chosen people of God enters the middle, fleeing and overcoming those who follow. It plants its footsteps upon the earth in the region of the sea; the rocks of the deep are trodden, and the wheel-track runs across the bare mud.

The scorching sun inserts its gaze through the cleft waters and touches the unknown land with new light. Its ray struggled to descend through so great a space, and the exhausted radiance scarcely reached the depths.

At first the tyrant of Pharos believed that those shut out, repelled by the waves and turned to flight, were retreating.

He orders the ranks to hurry their delay with these words:

“Look! Again the fleeing cohort abandons the suspended battle and withdraws, trusting in the aid of its feet.

“Press them with your weapons, and persist only in closing upon them; the sea will deal with the rest.”

He had scarcely finished speaking when they leap forward and rush in their course to reach the shore.

When they arrived, they saw the vast depths, now dry, offering an unaccustomed road, and, with the retreating expanse laid open, it was as though the waters had fled in fear before the pious people who trod upon them.

They too descend safely by the dry path, secure from the sea and from its own power; they do not sufficiently fear either their weapons or the sea itself, which patiently endures its bonds.

The column halted briefly, its movements restrained, and the bridles drawn tight held the suspended horses back.

Then someone, to whom perhaps a changed warmth was at that moment giving even a slight spark of feeling to his heart, spoke as follows:

“What god turns the world from its ancient axis by a new law, changes its cycles, and throws created things into confusion?

“For if nature is preserved in the things that have been created, what is the cause of this monstrous road? What, finally, remains, if the sea is crossed on foot, except that fields be plowed by ships, that heaven descend from its axis, that the underworld be raised into the upper regions, that the hot zone of heaven grow cold, and that a scorpion set the blasted Bear ablaze?

“Unless a confused order of things has overturned all this, no one shall descend upon the savage sea under my leadership. Let the path by which it directs the enemy be suspect to me.

“For if the divine power, weighing equal battles, wishes it, it had enclosed the fleeing army behind a barrier.

“Let them now go away, and let their own prodigies follow the wandering people.

“Nor am I sufficiently embracing the fact that the sea, lying around the dry ground, rises high and conceals dangers beneath its bare bed.”

This speech, burning with sedition, provokes an uproar; a hidden sentence of death presses upon those who are already advancing.

The renowned people had conquered the watery valley with their feet and, leaving behind the convex waves of the empty gulf, were climbing from the abyss up to the higher lands of the shore.

The commander of the black army is brought forward, and anger seizes Pharaoh, called by his own name Cenchres.

Together they seize the opened hollows of the sea and invade the path. What would mad fury not dare?

[Col. 0367C] On one side part of the cavalry drives the column; on the other, it orders the swift chariots to race across the plain with rapidly applied goads.

When the snorting cavalry came into the middle of the sea and its burning anger reproached the delays of so broad a gulf, one side trembled as the world narrowed around them.

Then a voice sent from heaven through the lofty, shining cloud of the column thundered. The interpreter of the heavenly word, addressing Moses by his sacred name, said:

“The time has come when my commands are to be tested. Egypt’s end is now at hand; now the sentence will punish and overthrow the mind that has been chastised so many times by its final disaster. Let the sword succeed the scourges.

“You, for your part, strike the divided wave now with your staff, and let the waters, once withdrawn, resume their own appearance.”

He fixed his knee upon the edges of the dried shore and, ordered at once to be present upon the shore from which the waves were absent, struck it, trusting in the mysteries of the remarkable wood.

Immediately a sudden crash begins to crackle; water thunders all around as it rushes down, and the wave first closes there where the final destiny of the king of Pharos had pointed out the way.

After the path has been closed and the waves repel those who are trying to leave, they regret having entered the gulf and attempt too late to retreat. The cohorts turn their backs in panic and throw away their weapons; the sea presses upon those fleeing,

[Col. 0368A] and, following them, confronts them. The wall of the descending water perishes on every side, its reins released.

He, always savage, now gentle in the very presence of death, says:

“This victory does not yield to human warfare; we are being conquered and overturned by heaven as our enemy.

“Let each attendant escape if he can, and, defeated, get away; do not now hurl weapons against God in futile efforts.”

If only human pride would wish to change its stricken minds before death! What does it finally profit to have put an end to evils then, when the limit presses upon one, when the span of the present life is cut short by time?

“Confess while you are sound, Scripture, and strong,” he says, “if anyone vows to abandon sin only when he cannot sin, he himself is abandoned by his indulgence.”

Thus the phalanx, already lifted high above the waves, is raised up amid the waters that will soon drown it. Raised by a mountain of water, it is weighed down by the burden of its weapons, and the dying bodies, clothed in iron, are carried back to the tenacious bottom.

When one part, its limbs first stripped of weapons, entangled its swimming body in the wretched embrace of another, deceived by the hope of aid it perished; and those clinging together alike fell beneath the eternal burden and died bound together.

Others, while for a long time they fling their exhausted arms, run into swords and cling to swimming javelins; the sea is mingled with blood of the same color.

Moreover, the conspicuous prince of the palace of Memphis, leading white horses with a black driver, a spectator of his own disaster and the last survivor of his people to enter, is shipwrecked in the waves through his chariot.

Battles cease, for the sea is fighting, and Israel, at rest, wins by sight alone as it completes the combat.

Then the valley, filled, perishes, and, as the wave returns, the surface of the flattened gulf is drawn away.

At that point dreadful corpses are cast along the entire shore, and the sea displayed its triumph over the fields.

The renowned leader describes this glorious deed in a solemn song, which is sung throughout the world, when, cleansed by sacred streams, guilt is erased,

and the water of the bath that gives birth sends forth a new offspring, after the ancient transgressions that Eve produced.

From this he took up the subject after introducing it in song, while the slender page repeats its sorrowful falls.

If anything sorrowful was said in poor verse, let the memorable water of the sacred triumph wipe it away; let joys resound through it, and through it let every crime be removed.

[Col. 0368D] Through the bath the new person lives while the old age perishes; through it good things rise up and harmful deeds are put to death; through it the true Israel is dipped in sacred waters; through it the rejoicing crowd resounds in harmony with the trophy; through it the gifts of the preceding figure are fulfilled, gifts which the pious prophet unfolded through five books.

We, following the trumpet with a reed and keeping the measure, now set this harbor at the shore of a slender skiff.

# PREFACE TO THE FOLLOWING BOOK

[Col. 0367]

[Col. 0367D] To the holy, most blessed, and most devout brother Apollinaris, bishop: Avitus, his brother.

After the completion of the little books which my plan did not publish as it had wished—for your pious eagerness, and that of certain companions, forestalled it, affectionate indeed but ill-advised—you now compel me, in addition, to give you more particularly those verses which I composed for our venerable sister Fuscina, concerning the consolatory praise of chastity.

At the time when, after announcing the end of the poem, I would more properly have called them an epigram, you first named them a book, asserting that this title suited their length. Therefore consider me, in this matter also, serving your judgment—or rather your affection—since it is surely unjust that I should obey you in greater matters and contradict you in small ones.

But let your devotion remember that, because you call this work a little book, it should be given for reading only to those whom either the bond of kinship or the purpose of religion truly joins to us, since it discusses, in a somewhat intimate manner, either the religion of our common parents or the virgins of our family.

For from the nature of the subject you can measure that what was composed in secret meditation concerning the affection of a sister vowed to holiness, I scarcely confess even to you, overcome by repeated commands, when or how I would wish it to come into the hands of outsiders.

Indeed, I shall henceforth withdraw my foot from composing verses and joining metrical feet, unless the reasoning of an obvious cause should force upon me the necessity of some epigram; and I promise that it will be so short that you yourself will scarcely dare to give it another name.

For it is fitting that our former profession, and now also our age, should devote effort and time to a more serious style, if anything is to be written, and should not linger over what sings for a few who understand by preserving the measure of syllables, but over what serves many readers through a measured exposition of the faith.

# BOOK SIX. THE CONSOLATORY PRAISE OF CHASTITY, TO FUSCINA, A SISTER CONSECRATED TO GOD AS A VIRGIN

[Col. 0369]

[Col. 0369B] Receive and embrace, virgin most worthy of Christ, these gifts which your brother Alcimus sends you; and, in the light reed, regard the weight of the subject, and let the slender song commend a strong love.

For whenever you have completed in due order the sacred course, singing alternate psalms in sweet melody—psalms which the lyre living in your heart fits to chaste harmonies through sonorous virtue and inward sound—

then, if you wish, you may play with a polished verse and release your mind, wearied by meditation.

Here no deceitful barbitos will be dipped in water, from which Pegasus is imagined, outstripping the light breezes in his movements, to hang suspended and neigh in assumed flight, while the heavy hoof of the horse is carried by a swift wing.

Nor will songs here be led by the Pierian game, which popular report falsely claims for itself as nine sisters.

But true music gives you a brother’s plectrum, and the pipe that resounds with Christ will be closed to Phoebus.

When your mother Audentia gave birth to a fourth child and, fertile in childbirth, presented you to the highest family, she immediately promised to lead a frugal life.

From then on, the devoted care of your parents determined by equal vows to preserve a chaste marriage bed.

And because you were to be the beginning of so holy a covenant, you too were offered to Christ, who immediately received your nursing limbs, dedicated to him, in the cradle.

Thus once, when the earth first shone with a new rising and its seeds produced beautiful crops, Abel, righteous through faith, had recognized that a living young creature was being led to the holy altars and bleated harmlessly to God; and the whole flock pleased him, offered by one head.

Therefore, when the life-giving water of the bath had nourished you and heavenly grace had already produced its pledge,

they did not place jeweled necklaces upon your neck, nor did a garment glittering with woven gold enclose you in its drawn-out threads worth talents.

Nor did the purple of Sidon, twice dyed in murex, clothe you, nor the purple gleaming with ruddy dye, nor the soft fleeces that the Seres send, gentle to the touch.

Nor did they fasten gold through pierced ears, so that hanging pearls might adorn the wounds and precious evils—yet stones—weigh them down.

The holy Isaiah describes these things more fully and recounts the various ornaments that beautify the limbs, limbs that soon will provide food for worms.

Perhaps, while life remains, no one can run through in words all the savage dangers of diseases which we are taught all must fear before death;

For every part is liable to death in its entirety, while every body is dissolved by its own end, and one death forestalls all the other calamities.

And why does anyone desire to adorn a face that will perish, while the inner person is foul and defiles itself with sin?

But when you had completed two five-year periods, a white robe soon veiled you in pure adornment,

[Col. 0370C] dignifying the face and appearance of a virgin; and your mind, already mature above all in its flowers, conceived all modesty.

No differently did the rejoicing barren woman, after the losses of youth, when made fertile and carrying a new child, happily weave a small garment for her nursling, so that Samuel might already learn as a boy to be a priest.

Thus the joyful household, adapting you to the holy altars, taught you to grow worthy of the accustomed temple, writing you into the bridal chamber and the covenant of the great king.

Christ wishes to join to himself an elect beauty, which powerful grace enriches with varied adornment.

When your mother, breathing again, anticipated these joys and saw the great gift bestowed upon you in your small years, while virtue was entrusted to your age,

and, about to give birth to you again more nobly than from the womb of the body, she carried her hopes and fears between them—although already free through your vow—yet, joyful and anxious, she bore astonished cares; then she conveyed the reason in her tears and gave these instructions:

“Although you are fourth by birth, you are first by sacred gift, my sweet daughter, whom I have borne twice—in the flesh and in heaven through faith—and whom, still unformed in my womb, I dedicated to Christ.

“Until now this belonged to us, but as time has passed it is now fitting that it should be yours. For what you are to preserve, which had its beginning from me, has come to you; you will begin to be capable of everything when the will is present.

“Your footsteps are ardent: by following them, climb heaven along the path.

Nor are examples lacking at home. Look how many crowns our flourishing family has already sent to heaven for virgins—crowns which our mother Severiana, raising them with sacred instruction, wishes to join also to you.

“Aspida, now rejoicing and once veiled with a consecrated head, not much older than you, undertook your duties and joined twelve years to the holy altars.

“Although the final lot carried her away from here by swift death, nothing is sudden for those always prepared to depart.

“Now look upon the pillar shining with a twin virginity, an outstanding ornament, whose rightful relation you call Fuscina, the daughter of Fuscina. Do not neglect her,

[Note: [Col. 0371D] Euphrosine.]

who, powerful in devotion—if her name is pronounced in Greek—signifies a mind of good cheer, taking its meaning from the name assumed.”

[Col. 0371B] Although their accomplished years may yield to your summit and their life may tower above all others in its lofty citadel, nevertheless, if you follow these noble mothers with your heart, they will rejoice to be surpassed as you advance and will freely give you the highest palm, while your vows surpass your teacher.

Saying this, she moved your tender feelings with sacred exhortation, kindling you to love virginity.

Thus the fertile mother in womb, more fertile in deed, powerful like the Maccabean mother and blessed through the death of her children, rejoicing to be bereaved and overcoming old age through strength of spirit, teaches her offspring by exhortation not to yield to the world and inflames the devout to courageous deeds.

What need is there now to rehearse your achievements—achievements stronger than your tender age, since you carried a mature spirit before your years and gave your answer before your age?

This small page has taken up your praise.

[Col. 0371C] The victorious outcome will come when the appointed time is fulfilled; praise is better sung when, with triumph already proclaimed, the rewards of your completed deeds are returned.

Now it is fitting to warn you, astonished, in a cautious voice; to share and consider your anxious cares with you; and to aid your efforts with words of encouragement,

while fickle fortune struggles through repeated dangers, while life runs along a slippery path beneath fragile feet, while the serpent, trampled by your steps, seeks your footprints, climbing toward the right side where your foot may crush it.

The present ages lead everything toward its end, and no secure rest is granted in perishable flesh.

For good people often change; virtue is overwhelmed and perishes, and the rewards of past praise, once gained, depart.

And often a mind that had recently been cold, suddenly kindled by heat, is accustomed to abandon the world and restrain its sins with a sudden rein.

Thus the fates change their alternating rotation, so that the impious may hope for pardon, while the righteous, advancing through fear, adds a summit to great virtues.

For if devotion to holy labor should by chance relax, and sluggish leisure dissolve its accustomed cares, the glory of a life that brings harm slips headlong.

Merit cannot stand if it does not acquire strength as it proceeds; it loses what it has when it turns back. One must strive with great strength to keep one’s footsteps on the sufficiently narrow path.

For the one who now runs playfully along the broad road, loosened by spaciousness, will be bound by a stricter prison under a cruel fate.

[Col. 0372A] You, however, pardon the love of the one exhorting you, who warns you as you run, although he himself scarcely follows. The slow man recommends shortcuts to the swift.

For in the instruction that we sing in poor verse, you come already better taught: younger by birth, you dedicated yourself to the law of life, prior in religion.

And, though following in years, you surpass in the lot of merits.

If we attain this, it may perhaps be considered ours; but what we pursue is nevertheless yours. The conversion of your brothers, which must be owed to your devout example, looks to you as its author, and offers its first fruits to you from sacred harvest.

But holy faith commands that, shared with a kindred heart, the brotherly burden should be lightened.

You are a sister who bears a pious burden from the breast; you have submitted your faithful neck to bear the yoke not of flesh but of the law, and not to enter the bonds of a husband: to hate worldly paths and traverse pure ones; to reject marriage beds and seek Christ as bridegroom; thus to despise the marriage torch, because you burn with pious love; to make hearts sluggish toward pleasure and fervent toward labor; to know no husband, yet to produce such offspring as sorrowful misfortune can never take from you.

You will not lament, bereaved, the pledges of a fertile life, nor fear, as a widow, to outlive an eternal spouse, being yourself free from harm.

Nor will the sentence touch you by which Eve, mother of offspring and death, is addressed: giving birth to a slaughtered child while living in guilt,

[Col. 0372C] she is subjected to a husband and destined to endure the lordship of the marriage bed, serving while she tolerates obscene unions in the marriage chamber.

Thus, captive to the marriage bed, although she bears an empty name and is called a partner through the vain image of a spouse, she alone is pressed beneath the yoke, compelled to endure an unequal lot.

And when ten long months have brought their vexations, and the belly, heavy with its completed fetus, is stretched,

the seeds that had belonged to the father inflict upon the mother these burdens and harsh pains in her swelling womb.

For when her innards are loosened through laborious childbirth, one woman alone pays the price for what two have cultivated, hanging in so great a danger of the flesh, while hope perhaps touches the suffering mother: whether the son brought into the light will live.

Yet it often happens that, groaning, she gives birth to one who is dead.

Often, too, the mother’s limbs, dying together, give a double grave to offspring that were born only to die.

How much lighter is it when the parent alone perishes and, once the burden has been discharged, gives up her life with the child?

What if the pledge, nourished and raised for a long time, is suddenly snatched away by death—the only thing toward which hope repeatedly looks—and all that they promised themselves as joy through their conceived wishes perishes?

More grievous than all these things is this: if envious death should seize a tender child, generated under a harsh destiny, before he has received the heavenly bath, leaving him deprived of it.

And when the son ceases to be his mother’s, he will belong to perdition; then parents do not want the offspring they have brought forth, limbs born only for the flames.

Who could recount the dangers of so great a fate, into which the glory of beloved flesh is dragged?

But your lot can be distinguished far and wide by the freedom that accompanies the law by which you are bound, so that the impious chains of a deceiving world do not hold you fast.

You follow Mary, to whom the high gift granted the double joy of the virgin’s and mother’s crown,

when she conceived God in the flesh, and the Creator of heaven entered the enclosed womb, unlocking its mysteries.

Born from a mother whom he himself had formed, he chose a pure womb from which he would proceed—he alone who could determine the origin of his flesh,

[Col. 0373B] and who knew the day far in advance and saw the time when he was to be born: will preceded limbs.

God the Word himself, clothed in flesh and having taken up residence in the womb, who commands with the Father, serves in a mother’s body; and the Lord who had ordained the ages accepts the role of a servant.

He knows neither times through the father nor seeds through the mother.

That woman indeed was fruitful who was worthy to bear her Maker, her everlasting Lord, in chaste pregnancy and to bring him forth; but neither will you lack glory for so great a deed, if, believing in your heart, you conceive Christ and bring forth for heaven the holy offspring of your works.

“If anyone,” he says, “fulfills our law in due order, that person will always be my brother, mother, and sister.” Do you see how the heavenly image is without sex, which the inner human being, allotted it, retains in the mind?

[Col. 0373C] The Redeemer, rising from death, provided the example, when in this way he placed feminine honor before men. Christ, hanging guiltless upon the lofty cross, tasted the death he had assumed for our crime. And while still fixed there by the holy nails, he breathed out from his mouth the soul that was soon to return alive to his limbs.

The crowds left such a spectacle. The signs that threatened a grieving heaven could not be endured. For the sun, covered over and turning its face away from the world, had withdrawn the unjust hours into nocturnal mourning and itself granted access to foreign darkness, when the order of time was greatly altered. It was night in the heavens, while the underworld saw the light. The earth trembled, and with a mighty effort the walls, their battlements shaken, nodded at the highest point of their crowns.

[Col. 0373D] The rocks felt themselves descend, commanded from their ancient places, and struck against one another with new sounds. Amid these disturbances, while everyone else was fleeing, those mothers, though trembling, resolved to remain: so that, living in vigilant care, they might serve the holy tomb and, present in their devotion, pay the honor they had vowed.

They arranged rich ointments spread with fragrant juice, which, by saving what was saved, would preserve the body in the linens. Love was preparing these mournful gifts at its own expense, believing that it was paying the final service. And since, by rising, he had so swiftly forestalled what was thought to require this service of preservation, Christ is pleased by the gift although he had no need of it.

For this, grace immediately responding, grants that human eyes may behold angelic faces.

[Col. 0374A] A shining garment gleamed upon the heavenly body, and a ruddy radiance had spread brilliance everywhere over his face. So that the heavenly word might sound to the worthy mothers, the angel addresses them with holy lips:

“Pass beyond womanly sex into manly minds; do not tremble with new tumult, you strongest hearts. These signs seek adversaries; no cause for fear remains for you, whom the care of devout love strengthens.

“You seek, I know, Jesus, recently buried with solemn funeral in the precious seat of the tomb. But you ought to remember what he had earlier said, with prophetic and faithful mouth, before his death: that he would no longer be kept through two nights, and that this is already the third day that completes his promise. Behold, the tomb is open; he has left it empty, rising after conquering death.”

Thus, by his exalted speech and commanded message, the minister—about to scatter throughout the world the life-giving gifts of triumph—first gave these women joy and lifted them from their grief.

[Col. 0374B] The mothers went on unafraid, already with joyful hearts, keeping hearts made confident by their belief in the salvation they had conceived. As they walked, Christ presents himself among them, commands them to recognize him, and greets them with gentle speech.

“Go,” he says, “and now report these commands of mine to my disciples, so that they may know that their master has risen.”

They clasp his feet and imprint kisses upon them. Then, with eager minds, they return to the disciples, teaching the teachers. What was to be proclaimed throughout the world they first learned through women’s words, and they recognized that it is the soul, rather than sex, that gives life.

[Col. 0374C] Thus virtue and danger are shared by mothers and men; there is no difference of heart. The will to do what is right is present in both, provided grace is maintained—yet life must toil diligently in attention to it.

For what do gifts help a person if, with the mind released into vice, disgraceful idleness squanders the gift bestowed? Effort loves assistance: who could help one who is idle, or join virtue to sluggish sleep?

That heavenly king, preparing to depart from the earth, gave silver to his servants according to each one’s ability: five minas to the first, two allotted to the second, while the third, unequal to great things, received one.

Then, departing, he instructed all the servants in this way:

“Now, if any one of you proves faithful with devoted mind, he will be known by this: by what virtue he possesses and by what skill he is endowed. Double my treasures and refine them through use, lest the dark face of tarnish stain what you receive as shining metal with a pure countenance. If I return, rewards will be added to the deserving.”

He spoke, and at his departure sought the heavenly kingdoms.

[Col. 0374D] Two servants entered eagerly into the contest of their work. One quickly lent out part of the shining heap, distributing much to the poor in generous gifts; whatever he contributed to the needy grew into heaps. The other, explaining the mysteries of the sacred word, rejoiced that interest was accumulating through holy profit, and, eager for righteousness, added to life while preaching.

But the one who had received the pound alone, with the smallest burden, buried it in a trench and placed the submerged moneybags there. He chose to live in degenerate luxury, which flowed away.

At last, when the world’s appointed time was finished, the judge returned. The senseless servant, who had scorned his master’s delay, now despised his return. He ordered everyone to give an account, so that they might return to the one who demanded it the profit produced by their business during so long a time.

The two servants brought forth their silver, doubled in mass, and reported their dealings with joyful faces. That lazy third man brought out the drachma hidden in the earth; having absorbed the contamination of the clinging soil, it had lost its proper appearance within its enclosed darkness.

Then the master rebuked him with terrifying words:

“Did such forgetfulness of me hold you sluggish, lazy servant? Did concern for my return flee from you in this way? The silver that you carried away pure in bright light—behold, you bring it back dark and crushed. Its former appearance has disappeared, and, no longer answering as it often did, its form is hidden from me and the image of my face assigned to you does not appear. But if it had been put to use and had touched the table entrusted to my altar, the coin inscribed with my name would have increased.

“Now therefore, faithful servants, take the whole away, so that the final allotment may add it to the useful servant and take it from the idle one. This wicked man, untrustworthy in small things, will not be worthy of any. Whoever knows the master’s will and despises it is beaten with many blows; the one who errs in ignorance is beaten with few.”

Come, then, with your loins girded for strong battles and with an armed mind. Do not, as a woman, fear the war that the mind wages; for this glory has long been a mark of your sex, as you have often learned by reading.

[Col. 0375C] Nor do I think that you are unfamiliar with the story of Deborah, who once led troops equipped for battle after the sound of the trumpet. A woman, having taken up the standard, went before the ranks; she urged on the astonished men, whom she herself, by leadership, example, and speech, encouraged against the enemy.

But after the spirited commander, leading the eager troops, drove forward their weapons, animated by fury, the barbarian hands fell. All the enemy’s strength was dissolved, and wherever the woman showed herself, the men, scattering, turned their backs and sought hiding places, believing that they had won if they survived.

Then great Sisera himself—whom the form of a gigantic mass joined to his body and whose immense height raised a towering citadel of a head—King Sisera began his flight, casting aside his bundle of weapons and going without companions. He feared that his lofty body would be recognized and that his great bulk would betray him as a fugitive.

But after he thought himself hidden and had taken refuge beneath a roof, he surrendered his soft eyes to perpetual sleep. A woman struck him down as well, and with a hammer drove a nail through his temples into the earth where he lay.

Thus feminine was that triumph in every respect.

But you, virgin of God, whom holy conduct adorns with modesty on one side and faith on the other, wage wars with inward weapons stronger still—wars that rouse the savage enemy against what is right. Let faithful hope be a happy helmet upon your head; let a belt of precious modesty contain your loins; let the breastplate of righteousness bind your garments around you; let the Word always defend you as a sharp sword.

[Col. 0376A] Prudentius once described these resources of virtue and these comforts of battle, as the mind engages in various struggles with the body, and sang of them with learned speech. For there virginity, a warrior strong in full power, comes armed; foul lust attacks it and calls it to battle with fruitless effort.

So may the rival serpent recognize you as a warrior; and when you have been challenged, may you carry away, rejoicing, the highest trophy from the enemy you have trampled.

For whatever the sacred divine books teach in word and meaning, whatever the ancient prophet teaches when he retells the world’s beginnings—whether he weaves histories or perhaps figures—whatever the successive ages of many kings accomplished after Ruth, or whatever the Davidic kingdom wrote after rejected Saul in its song of three times fifty psalms;

[Col. 0376B] whatever peaceful Solomon, amid his broad sceptres, said in lucid proverbs but with obscure meaning; whatever the sixteen prophets after him saw; whatever gentle Job said, though shut in with his wound laid open;

why should I mention Esther and the guiles of chaste Judith, when the satrap is inflamed by the deceit of her adorned countenance, and the woman, deceiving him, approaches the obscene bed and, after cutting off his savage head, checks his gaze?

whatever Tobit, seeing more clearly in his blinded body, and Ezra, the author who beheld hidden things, wrote down.

Whatever grace, succeeding the ancient law, thunders forth, and whatever miracles of the New Testament proclaim—on one side the face of a man, on another that of a lion, and the swift eagle and the strong bull in battle;

[Col. 0376C] whatever the twelve lambs accomplished with pure minds, scattering seed throughout the whole world; whatever pious Paul sets forth in his twice-seven epistles; what Peter and James teach, what Jude teaches, and John himself, who reports the secrets of heaven that he saw;

indeed, the many mysteries worthy of truth which expounders have set forth in their books—you have drunk all these, holding them in your thirsting mind.

Nor is anything sacred that our poets have sung hidden from you. You read, recognize, and preserve what has been composed, and commend foreign verses by your own singing. Why should I repeat everything? Use your learned understanding, and turn what is known to you, or what you have traversed in reading, to the work of virtue with manly zeal.

For unless faithful life is joined to learning, what is recognized but not observed will do greater harm.

[Col. 0376D] After the Lord had grown hungry, while traveling he noticed a fig tree spread with light foliage. It was not yet the season for gathering the foretold fruit from the tree; but as soon as he found it clothed only in leaves and bare of fruit, he utterly condemned the useless ornament of its verdant emptiness. Its root was suddenly struck, blasted by heat, and the trunk dried up, deprived of its covering of branches.

By such a sign we are instructed to understand the law: let no living action be lacking to Christ’s servant who confesses him in word alone, though his name has been confessed.

For if we consider ourselves Christians and holy, this makes the matter even worse if deeds do not follow what has been said.

[Col. 0377A] So virginity, too, devoted to sacred modesty, needs accompanying virtues. Unless, preserving an untouched mind, it joins itself to a chaste body, it succumbs to vices; nor can one rightly call flesh chaste when the adulterous mind corrupts it.

Anger, fury, grief, envy, discord, luxury, a double tongue, a closed hand, and unrestrained pleasure commit adultery with the human heart; then, through the seed of death, they nourish the offspring of death. Behold where every woman is led who, while boasting of the name of virgin, does not know that inwardly she is swelling with a mind pregnant with crimes.

Here is one example from many, by which you may recognize the rest. When the Lord was teaching the people, with vigilant care, to recognize the final time and to await the day when the judge hangs over the world,

[Col. 0377B] he presents ten virgins marked with holy chrism as a lesson, showing them to us at the summit of his instruction. Yet wisdom adorns five of them, while sluggishness has made the understanding of the others foolish.

Rest embraces them all equally, and sleep lowers their eyes as a sign of death. Scarcely had half the period of rest passed—indeed, it was the hour of night when Christ, having taken flesh, had already broken through the barred gates of death by bursting the bolt, broken open your gates, O underworld, and, spurning the tomb, was returning joyfully from the darkness he had conquered into the light—

when a sudden cry resounded and shattered the silence:

“At last the bridegroom is here! Let the bodily sleep of night depart; hurry swiftly, wise maidens.”

Immediately they all sprang up and, leaving their beds, fitted their lamps with the light they had sought. But the five who had greater prudence at heart, although they hurried, were still concerned to add oil to what they had brought in their vessels, and with the rich liquid, armed with fire, to break the squalid night.

[Col. 0377C] But the other group, which had neglected to bring the oil, raised its flame-bearing torches in vain. A tiny fire leapt out from the disturbed light, but, lacking strength, the heat abandoned the failing lamp. The flame ran through the dry papyrus, and the ashes, growing sluggishly amid cloudy volumes of pitch-black smoke, vanished.

When they saw themselves unworthy of such an arrangement and unable to meet the bridegroom as he approached them directly, belated concern moved them to slow labor.

[Col. 0377D] Then they prayed in subdued voices and foolish words, asking that outstretched hands might revive their numbed fires and that abundant wisdom might divide its rich olive oil.

Their sisters answered them in these words:

“Your misfortune is indeed pitiable, but here no one has more oil than is sufficient for himself, because each person’s supply is contained in the capacity of his vessel, and a complete measure preserves its own liquid.

“It is not lawful to divide or squander the oil that has been acquired, lest, once scattered, the fuel be lacking in the hollow lamps, and, while our profit provides you with loss, all our lights together grow numb with exhausted flames.”

Rejected by such words and with a sorrowful refusal, they explored every place where commerce is active and the hands of sellers.

[Col. 0378A] But while they were departing, behold, the bridegroom entered the chamber, brought in those who were ready, and, leaving the wandering sisters outside, shut them out at the door.

You see how the honor of the virginal name perishes unless holy fire is carried into the heavenly bridal chamber.

Blessed is that hand which, provident in generous gifts, nourished the kindled light with pure oil. For as much oil is poured into broad vessels as the merciful person has extended to the one in need who asked.

Therefore the Lord urges you to carry burning lamps in your hands: this is the work, this the glory, of a radiant life.

Let piety, patience, and virtue therefore be available to you—virtue of the mind, that is; for firmness of mind has sometimes brought frail girls in the flesh to heaven.

The fame of Eugenia, once celebrated throughout the whole world,

[Col. 0378B] spread when she gave her life for Christ’s name. Yet before that, a woman had advanced to courageous deeds: surrounded by a choir of saints, she became an abbot, and, fulfilling the role of a father, concealed her mother beneath her robe.

But after she became renowned to all by holy report, and, venerable for merits and years, ruled in youthful age old men respected for their long religious life, the serpent, impatient of righteousness and always devising a thousand arts of injury, sought to violate her reputation and thereby gave her a crown. He stirred up a girl to pretend that Eugenia was inflamed with mad love and burning with masculine desire.

A crowd of old men gathered in confusion because a mind cast down by such a great crime had been able to dissolve so rigid a life, and because the perfection deprived of its supreme ruler, wavering, grieved that it could accomplish nothing against the flesh.

[Col. 0378C] The young man is led into the forum and, still a monk, enters the savage tribunal. The conspiracy of deceit prevails, and the public force, ignorant of the secret, already held the accused, inflamed only by wrongful hatred.

Then, conscious of her own sex and of her chaste heart, the woman is defeated in order to conquer, revealing the deception. Although compelled outwardly to confess the flesh, inwardly she remains a hero. The guardianship of her chaste vow had always been secure. However cunningly the wretched world’s deceit attacks it, however it stretches out snares through tricks and weaves lies, the mind, ignorant of guilt, does not fall into an easy ruin.

Those whom the raging enemy torments by deceitful cunning, patience purifies in holy fire.

[Col. 0378D] Once, the envious hands of brothers had sold a young man, and the land of Memphis held Joseph as a servant. He endured his master, when he was falsely accused of having wished to commit an outrage—a deed from which he had recoiled in grief. He patiently endured the workhouse, bonds, and chains, while the sun, repeating its course, joined two years together.

He had already forgotten the light; already his hair, flowing over a body nourished by wasting, touched his back. But, with God giving it strength, his mind, enclosed by no darkness, foresaw whatever hidden thing would be accomplished after his release.

At last glory was eagerly bestowed upon him, not pardon alone; then, when he was asked to accept willingly the diadem upon his head, he exchanged exile for a kingdom and the servant’s condition for that of a prince.

[Col. 0379A] Thus he received the rewards of a heart preserved.

After him, who could ever honor Susanna with worthy praise? In her tender years she overcame the wicked desires of the elders and their conspiratorial passions.

At first, the matter that separately ensnared them, one by one in their own deliberations, caused each to promise himself alone the hope of sin. But the shameful fire burning in their hearts fused their minds in the furnace of a shared crime.

They met, for it happened one day that, pretending to depart, they returned from different directions. They came together into the grove, and the pleasure burning in each heart was disclosed in turn.

Immediately, deceiving the unsuspecting girl by fraud, they attacked her together. Before the rumor of so great a disgrace could rebel against them, they demanded that she consent; and, if she refused, they planned to turn the crime back upon her.

[Col. 0379B] Having jointly confessed their passion, they revealed the lies they had prepared and spread the snares they wished to weave.

For a long time she struggled inwardly with herself, hesitating and wavering over where the scales of her uncertain mind might incline. The law forbade her to sin, while infamy frightened her. From this side and that she tried through prayers to soften the hard passions and to extinguish the obscene flames with tears.

But after their related lust overcame the old men, bound and removed from all prayers and warnings, the woman, inflamed by splendid modesty, then resolved to die chaste, lest through so great a crime they should encompass her miserable life with carnal relations.

Calling heaven as witness, she rejected empty fame, content with her own judgment. Since her heart was conscious of its integrity, she entrusted it to the faith above and preserved it for future generations.

[Col. 0379C] He, however, preferred that the investigator of the secret should conduct an open examination in the proper place, reveal the hidden crime, and bring forth the frauds that had been laid in snares.

That younger boy was watching the city, shaken by vain lamentations—the boy who would later be companion to the three youths whom Parthian wrath, hotter than flames when royal authority was despised, cast into the billowing fire.

As the gathered heat increased on both sides, fury on one and faith on the other burned equally, until the fire, made gentler by the holy men, served them and enclosed the coals in warm redness. At last, amazed that the fire had ceased, the satrap gave the order, and a multitude of flames surrounded the bystanders.

Daniel’s virtue, next in merit to theirs, restrained the dreadful jaws of the roaring lions. First inflamed by the goads of hunger and fury, and at the same time lowering their bodies with muzzles restrained, they licked their unharmed food amid their fasting.

Yet Daniel received the food brought to him by the prophet, who, hanging from above, was carried through the empty air by an angelic hand holding the bundle in balance, while he trod upon the air beneath with unmoving steps. Daniel received the provisions sent down from above.

Dishes hot from distant lands migrate through the air and preserve their flavors in a foreign place.

[Col. 0380A] Thus this unripe boy happened to see Susanna being dragged to punishment, whom the ignorant crowd had previously condemned unheard; everyone at once strove to witness the death of the innocent as though she were guilty.

Suddenly the boy thrusts himself into the middle of the crowd and, with a tender voice reproving the tumult, asks why no one in so great an assembly judges the case, and declares himself innocent and unwilling to go to an unjust death.

At once the obedient crowd, moved by the boy’s words, restrained its passions. He himself is appointed judge and counselor of the elders, through whom the true path may be revealed.

He asks what the order of the crime was from those separated for questioning. But while each gives a conflicting answer, they confess by differing voices that their crime was joined.

Then fear seizes everyone alike. A cry rises everywhere; the whole people overwhelm the authors of the crime, and God is praised, who never abandons the vows of the good and reveals his help at the proper time.

[Col. 0380B] Yet superior to these is she who, in chaste virginity, presents an untouched body for eternal vows.

For if a girl who marries according to earthly law, preserves her marriage bed, and knows one husband only, is praised merely by the mortal assembly of judges, consider how much is appointed for virgins there, where Christ calls them by their merits, where the judge of the world, seated on high, will divide the human race into its parts.

Lifting the sheep with his right hand, he will despise the goats on the left. Angelic choirs will stand in wonder at the deeds of the good and praise them. The merit of the life they have completed will be manifest to all; no fraud will be able to hide in darkness or withdraw known sins from view.

[Col. 0380C] There, let the life known to you be sought, where the just judge, distributing rewards, enriches it.

This is what was once said briefly by the teacher’s mouth, while Martha’s diligent service was active and her sister held fast, through the power of the word, to a care better than food and worthy of eternal nourishment.

Then Martha, bringing her empty complaints before the Lord, said:

“O teacher, do you not see that I alone am troubled with the preparations, while this sister contributes no assistance?”

Christ replied to her:

“There are many things that hold you bound, but Mary has chosen the better cause of quiet, and the better portion she has chosen cannot be taken away from her.”

So, sister, while the ages burn with their own concerns, do not cease to preserve the portion chosen for you.

Your whole family has deserved you as its first patron. Now we follow you as our standard-bearer, and, while you carry Christ’s banners, the family line willingly follows the emblem.

[Col. 0380D] Although the world may have bestowed ancient honor upon them and may display them as always noble by their origins, the divine insignia borne by them has adorned them more greatly: according to their proper order, they deserved holy sees.

I will not now recount your ancestors and forefathers, whom distinguished life made worthy priests; look upon your father, raised to sacred pontifical office.

And although your father or uncle, great everywhere, may please you by receiving the fasces of the peoples after their public offices, accept those humble men whom the Church, joining them to the company of the fathers as brothers equal in office, has united.

For their sake, do not grow weary of offering continual thanks to Christ or of pouring forth tears, so that none of your brothers may be missing from the number when you receive the rewards worthy of your deeds,

[Col. 0382A] and, having become the mother of your parents, you may joyfully be joined to the victorious crown of virginity.

[Note: [Col. 0381A] In his New Library of Manuscript Books, Paris edition of 1653, p. 226, Labbeus transcribed from the manuscript of the Naudé collection the following three verses, which are missing from all printed editions:

[Col. 0382A] “Alcimus has these poems, woven in slippery verse,

I have written in six volumes, each with two short wings,

Behold, in the swift tenth light of the sun.”]

[Col. 0381A]

GALLAND’S NOTE ON OTHER POEMS OF AVITUS WITH THE SAME SUBJECT, NOT PUBLISHED

Besides these five books, and the sixth book customarily appended for his sister Fuscina, no poem of Avitus has so far come to light; nor is it evident that Gregory of Tours and Isidore formerly knew more poems of Avitus than these. Nevertheless, a letter to his brother Apollinaris shows that he wrote quite a few other verses on various subjects. We are not concerned with those here, but only with the books that continue the Mosaic history, pursuing Exodus and the remaining parts of the Heptateuch, and that are found under the name of Alcimus Avitus in certain libraries.

Although I would not deny that these belong to Avitus, I observed in the three copies I saw that they are everywhere so rough and unpolished and so full of errors that it would be an act of religious scruple to publish a work which, unless I am mistaken, the author himself would prefer to remain burdened in this condition. Anyone who wishes to know the beginnings of the individual books will find them in the following index.

[Note: [Col. 0381C] We did not wish to omit the few pieces of Avitus that follow, which were published by others after Sirmond, so that Avitus might appear here as complete as possible. We also thought it appropriate to append Pope Symmachus’s letter to Avitus, as well as the conference of the bishops before King Gundobad, in which Avitus plays the leading role—or rather, in which he alone among the Catholic bishops delivers a speech.]

ALCIMUS AVITUS: VERSE ON EXODUS

The poem contains 1,327 verses.

Meanwhile, while the times pursue their various courses,

and a new offspring rises from a falling shoot.

ON LEVITICUS

The poem contains 308 verses.

After the final hand had been laid upon the distant paths

in the conspicuous temple, soon the care of sacred things

fell upon the prophets.

ON NUMBERS

The poem contains 689 verses.

Meanwhile the year had turned through its accustomed courses,

running along its tracks when the months had been completed.

ON DEUTERONOMY

The poem contains 287 verses.

Thus far the people, wearied by the sands

of the shapeless wilderness, had advanced their arms

to the river Jordan.

ON THE BOOK OF JESUS SON OF NUN

The poem contains 452 verses.

Amid these things the Lord, deigning to approach Jesus,

promises that he will be endowed with lofty gifts of strength,

having been instructed to cross the ford of pleasant Jordan.

ON THE BOOK OF JUDGES

The poem contains 695 verses.

After Jesus had departed from his conspicuous task

and God had granted his servant rest after the wars,

swollen with pride, Judaea immediately began

to demand a king for itself and asked what the Lord’s decision was.

[Col. 0381C]

APPENDIX TO SIRMOND’S EDITION OF AVITUS: FOUR LETTERS OF SAINT AVITUS OF VIENNE

(First published in 1661 by John Ferrand, priest of the Society of Jesus, from an old manuscript belonging to the distinguished man Peter Marnaesius, senator of Grenoble; then published again in 1678, more accurately edited by the distinguished man Étienne Baluze from the same manuscript, in the first book of his Miscellanea.) (C)

[Note: [Col. 0381] Baluze had previously published this letter in the Appendix of Ancient Acts relating to Agobard, vol. II, p. 156.]

LETTER ONE. TO GUNDOBAD, KING OF THE BURGUNDIANS

[Col. 0381D]

Avitus, bishop, to his lord the king.

The question that Your Piety has proposed for discussion must be referred wholly, through spiritual reflection, to an inner figure. For what a person has contributed in a pious profession, moved by a merciful desire to nourish the poor, is not promised to be restored with a hundredfold return. Indeed, in this very generosity of almsgiving, in which the intention of the giver rather than his wealth is considered, it is not the quantity of the gift that must be weighed, but the zeal.

This is why, according to the evangelical reading, the offering of a poor woman’s two coins was preferred to countless gifts of gold and silver. If it were certainly returned to the donor widow in a hundredfold measure, she would undoubtedly receive less than all the others, since she had brought less than all the others. Therefore, when Saint Peter said, “Behold, we have left everything and followed you” (Matthew 19:27)—although, as the passage shows, he had left nothing other than the nets by which he earned a meager livelihood through the craft of fishing—the answer given to him was:

“Everyone who has left house, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or fields for my name’s sake will receive a hundredfold and will possess eternal life.”

Since in the Holy Scriptures the number one hundred is consecrated to complete perfection, distinguish this: it is not what is given in Christ’s name that is returned a hundredfold, but what is abandoned for Christ’s name. For although almsgiving brings a great and saving reward, it is incomparably greater to abandon everything than to distribute very much.

Therefore let Your Glory decide that this is spoken solely of martyrdom, whose crown is not equaled at all by any merit of human labor. This is the hundredfold fruit that awaits eternal life in the future, but that also, in the present age, compensates the insults inflicted upon martyrs with wondrous honor.

Hence, elsewhere in the Gospel, the Lord’s word testifies that, when the seed falls upon good earth, the growth of the nourished seed produces a hundredfold harvest. Parents, therefore, a wife, children, or brothers are to be left only for Christ’s name—that is, when, in upholding the confession of his name, we must sacrifice not only such relationships but even our souls and bodies.

Concerning this division the same Lord says elsewhere: “I have come to separate sons from parents, and a daughter-in-law from her mother-in-law” (Matthew 10:35)—that is, if persons bound to us by any affection, while we are advancing toward Christ, are unwilling to accompany us, they are to be abandoned.

Apart from this meaning, however, it is shown by examples and reason that these relationships should not always be abandoned as though they were prejudicial to us. Those relatives, too, who hasten toward heavenly crowns through contempt of the world and by trampling death are not to be abandoned. Nor can we advise the faithful to cast away spouses or parents, since the Lord cries out that it is not lawful for a man to dismiss his wife: “What God has joined, let no human being separate” (Matthew 19:6; Mark 10:9).

And the Apostle declares (1 Timothy 5:8) that whoever does not provide for his own, and especially for his relatives, has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever.

Peter followed the Lord, and Peter’s own wife followed Peter. When carnal intercourse ceased, spiritual consolation remained. With his brother Andrew accompanying him, he had abandoned neither brother nor wife, in whose company he clung to Christ’s footsteps.

Therefore we must fear not that such persons harm us, but that they impede us. For since the divine word proposes the heavenly kingdom for every class, order, and dignity of human beings, the preacher is rash if he advises rulers—whose kingdom is administered by divine commands—to abandon everything we have mentioned. Yet even to persons of this rank the contempt of the world may be suggested and the kingdom of heaven promised, as the Apostle, as you remember, declares to the rich (1 Timothy 6:17–19): that they should be rich in good works and store up for themselves a good foundation, so that they may take hold of the true life.

In accordance with this teaching, the use of fields or revenues may also benefit them, provided that desire does not harm them.

There is, however, another kind of holiness in which, if a time of persecution arises, a complete confession may imitate a kind of martyrdom. For if someone, through a better understanding, changes the ancient custom or sect of his parents, and is not held back by the privilege of custom when truth calls him to love salvation, such a person rightly abandons parents, brothers, and sisters.

Thus Abraham, rich and enjoying all heavenly gifts, making proper use of sons, servants, gold, silver, inheritance, and marriage, nevertheless freed himself from his homeland and kin by his resolve to change his religion. When he was already advanced in age, he received the sign of circumcision, by which Christianity was symbolized, and taught that boys already advanced in years could become children through conversion.

Concerning them the prophetic word also says: “A child shall die a hundred years old” (Isaiah 65:20)—that is, he will receive a hundredfold because he has become a child. The blessed multiplicity of the sacred number makes him excellent: just as the newness of life at mature age made him a child, so a preserved renewal will make him advance in longevity toward immortality.

LETTER TWO. OF BLESSED AVITUS, BISHOP, TO THE ILLUSTRIOUS MAN ARIGIUS

Avitus, bishop, to the illustrious man Arigius.

I know indeed with what devoted affection you wished me to go to the common celebrations, yet in such a way that you must have believed me destined merely to rejoice with you, not to contribute anything. For when priests, both highly distinguished in merit and many in number, came to meet you worthily and eagerly, I alone am struck by loss, since I do not deserve to take part in the joys of my singular patron. If my presence had turned out as I desired, then, just as I had hoped to hear from the praise of so great a work whatever worthy speech might be offered, those who had examined all the parts of the sublime structure could fittingly have ascribed to its creator elegance in the quality of its arrangements, lavishness in the expenditure, harmony in the proportion of its dimensions, breadth in its spaces, height in its summits, and solidity in its lowliness; they could have polished with their praises the dignity of the marbles, whose very magnitude makes the name of gems seem envious; they could have praised the day, gathered together and, as it were, enclosed by human industry, revived by the beneficial radiance of gleaming metals; and they could have worthily introduced among all these splendid displays relics before which the world is unworthy.

These matters, then, I had rightly conceded should be magnified by better men. Nevertheless, my own speech would have claimed for itself a particular reward, recalling that time when, amid the fiercest storms of upheaval, you brought the solid strength of the completed work safely into the harbor of its dedication, like unconquered helmsmen, while shipwrecks roared all around. You will recall, as a common necessity requires, that I paid tears instead of rejoicing. With regard to this premature renewal itself, I advise you—after weighing the reasons—not less to heap up thanksgiving than lamentation: for it was not like a bride being joined, however she might be joined, to such a bridegroom as had been promised her, even though the instruments of adornment were greatly desired; rather, the weapons of the plunderers ought to have been feared still more.

Accordingly, after weighing all these matters in counsel, you changed the mode of a brave man’s steadfastness. Laying aside the audacity of secular command in which you flourish [Note: Perhaps “most aptly”], you overcame by fear whatever danger had threatened from the opposing side. Therefore, let everyone who sees the joy placed before him praise the haste of the past. The security snatched from adversity corresponds to your arrangements. What you had chosen to adorn in such a manner ought earlier to have become ours.

But you perceive—even if nothing is said—both what cause prevents me from enjoying the sight of these things now, who my noble patrons are, and what sort of judges they are. For the festival of the Apostles lives among your Viennese people, amid the days of the annual martyrdom, with particular devotion. I have a presence appropriate to the occasion, since the dedication of the little structure of the Passion-day, which you know, seems to have been entrusted to the men. There is nothing toward which your affection could direct my spirit.

In excusing the absence of the little congregation, I would have placed my singularity before my customary practice, except that, as you know, among our own penitents an eager fervor, bordering on vice, had long been creating both disturbance and clamor; for among our people ambition will draw some away, youthful anxiety others, and gluttony many. I feared that, if even a few should be found who, avoiding what belonged to others, might add to their own festival a more zealous devotion of gentleness, some person’s mind, as usually happens in such turmoil, might suppose that on that day the course of our devotion had been omitted because of my absence, precisely when different observances seemed to be instituted.

For this reason we deserve pardon. If you have properly understood the reason, forgive me; recognize the common festival through remembrance of what has passed and the fullness of what is present; celebrate it by your duties as belonging equally to the absent and the present [sic]. I trust in the mercy of our God that, in this place also, whenever He grants me a more suitable access to the word, He will provide me with a more splendid result of the doubled consecration which He has granted you to adorn.

## LETTER III. OF THE BLESSED BISHOP AVITUS TO BISHOP STEPHANUS

Avitus, bishop, to Bishop Stephanus.

After the holy festival—which, though eager and anxious, we nevertheless passed through by your intervention and by divine protection—we continue to serve with the dutiful obedience of a servant and the devotion of assiduous concern, wishing, through recognition of your prosperity, which may God always increase, to find consolation for whatever harshness we have deserved.

## LETTER IV. OF BISHOP AVITUS TO BISHOP GREGORIUS

[Col. 0386B]

Avitus, bishop, to Bishop Gregorius.

I attribute rather to my own sins the fact that bodily frailty prevented you from carrying out the disposition of your most pious will, although your customary graciousness accompanied us with prayer and offering. Therefore, while paying the duties of greeting through this devoted page, I give thanks beyond what I can express in speech: although you did not satisfy our festival, which thirsted for you with complete desire, by your presence, you refreshed it by what you sent.

[Col. 0385B]

[Note: [Col. 0385D] The most illustrious Stephanus Baluzius published these fragments in *Miscellanea*, book I, from an old manuscript codex of the monastery of Saint Gall in Switzerland.]

## FRAGMENTS OF THE BOOK ON THE DIVINITY OF THE HOLY SPIRIT. (C)

[Col. 0385C]

Saint Avitus, in the book on the divinity of the Holy Spirit which he wrote against Gundobad, the Arian king, thus explains the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son.

[Note: [Col. 0386D] See above, the fragments of the works of Alcimus, no. 13.]

Concerning the divinity of the Holy Spirit: we read that He was neither made, nor begotten, nor created; He is God, the God who works all things in all. And in the same place:

“But all these things are worked by one and the same Spirit, distributing to each one as He wills” (1 Corinthians 12:11).

And Peter in the Acts of the Apostles:

“Why has it been agreed among you to lie to the Holy Spirit?” he said (Acts 5:3).

And afterward:

“You have not lied to human beings, but to God” (ibid., 4).

Likewise, elsewhere:

“Do you not know that you are God’s temple, and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?” (1 Corinthians 3:16).

And elsewhere:

“If anyone does not have the Spirit of God, he does not belong to Him” (Romans 8:9).

But we say that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son and the Father.

## THE SAME AVITUS IN THE SAME BOOK

The Lord Himself certainly says:

“The Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father” (John 15:26).

Indeed, by not saying “proceeded,” but “proceeds,” He did not indicate the time of the one proceeding; rather, with past and future removed, He displayed the power of procession in the eternity of an unbounded present. Thus, just as it is proper to the Holy Spirit to proceed from the Father and the Son, the Catholic faith, even if it has not persuaded those who resist, nevertheless does not exceed the rule of its own teaching.

## AVITUS AGAIN

I confess that the Holy Spirit belongs equally to the Father and the Son, and that He is likewise sent by the Father or the Son. The statement of the Apostle, brought forward together with my own, seems also to have approved this. For we read:

“The Paraclete, whom the Father will send in my name” (John 14:26).

And elsewhere:

“Whom I will send to you from the Father” (John 15:26).

Yet, as we discussed in the conversation recently held [Note: [Col. 0386D] This is the discussion that follows], the Divinity is not divided by the distinction of the Persons. For if the Spirit, as you admit, is either sent or proceeds from the Father and the Son, the one who is sent cannot be confused with the one who sends, nor can the one from whom He proceeds be confused with the one proceeding.

[Col. 0387A]

[Note: [Col. 0387D] The most illustrious Lucas Dacherius gathered this from the papers of Hieronymus Vignerius; the printed bibliographic notice also reads “Orat. D. J.” He published it in volume V of the *Spicilegium*.]

## DISPUTATION OF THE BISHOPS, ESPECIALLY AVITUS, BISHOP OF VIENNE, BEFORE KING GUNDEBALDUS AGAINST THE ARIANS. (C,G,S)*

[Col. 0387A]

By the Lord’s providence for His Church, and by His inspiring the heart of our lord Remigius for the salvation of the whole people—he everywhere destroyed the altars of idols and powerfully increased the true faith with a multitude of signs—it came about that, with the king not objecting, several bishops were assembled, if it could be done, so that the Arians, who were dividing the Christian religion, might be able to return to unity.

To make this happen more effectively, and so that it might appear to have occurred not by design but by opportunity, our lord Stephanus wrote to many bishops and invited them to the festival of Saint Justus, which was imminent and at which, because of the frequency of miracles, a very great gathering of people took place. Thus Avitus came from Vienne, Aeonius from Arles, from Valence [lacuna], from Marseille [lacuna]ius, and several others, all of Catholic confession and of praiseworthy life in the Lord.

They all went with our lord Stephanus to greet the king at Sarbiniacum, where he then was. Certain more powerful Arians were there with him; if they had been able, they would have prevented our men from approaching the king. But, with the Lord cooperating, they accomplished nothing.

After the greeting had been given, our lord Avitus—although he was neither senior in rank nor advanced in age, great deference was nevertheless paid to him—said to the king:

“If Your Excellency would arrange peace for the Church, we are prepared to demonstrate so clearly that our faith accords with the Gospel and the Apostles that no one will doubt that the faith which you retain is not according to God and the Church. You have here men of your own who are instructed in every branch of learning. Command them to converse with us and see whether they can answer our arguments, just as we are prepared to answer theirs.”

The king replied:

“If your faith is true, why do your bishops not restrain the king of the Franks, who has declared war against me and joined my enemies to destroy me? For there is no faith where there is desire for what belongs to another and thirst for the blood of peoples. Let him show his faith by his deeds.”

Then our lord Avitus humbly replied, with an angelic face and likewise an angelic speech:

“We do not know, O king, by what counsel or for what reason the king of the Franks does what you say. But Scripture teaches us that, because of the abandonment of God’s law, kingdoms are often overthrown and enemies are raised up on every side against those who set themselves as enemies against God.

“But return, together with your people, to the law of God, and He Himself will give peace within your borders. For if you have peace with Him, you will also have it with the others, and your enemies will not prevail.”

The king said to him:

“Do I not profess the law of God? Yet because I do not want three gods, you say that I do not profess the law of God. In Holy Scripture I have not read that there are several gods, but one.”

Our lord Avitus replied:

“Far be it from us, O king, to worship several gods: ‘Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God is one God’ (Deuteronomy 6:4; Mark 12:29). But that one God is three in Persons while one in essence. The Son and the Holy Spirit are not other gods, but one God, whose first Person is the Father, the second the Son, and the third the Holy Spirit. The Father does not have a substance different from the Son, nor does the Holy Spirit have one different from the Father and the Son.

“That God who formerly spoke through the prophets has spoken most recently in the Son and still speaks daily in the Holy Spirit. Although formerly through the prophets, then through the Son, and now through the Spirit, one and the same God speaks, this is said for the distinction of the Persons, since in reality they are coeternal and consubstantial. This is what we profess, and we are prepared to demonstrate it.”

When he saw that the king was listening peacefully, he prolonged his speech and said:

“O if only your discernment wished to recognize how well founded our faith is, and how much good would thereby come to you and your people! For heavenly glory would not be lacking to you, nor peace and abundance within your towers (Psalm 122:7). But your men, since they are enemies of Christ, kindle wrath from above against your kingdom and people. As we hope, this would not happen if you wished to hear our admonitions and command your priests to converse with us about these matters before Your Sublimity and your people, so that you might know that the Lord Jesus is the eternal Son of the eternal Father, and that the Spirit, coeternal with both, is one God, blessed forever, together before all times and without any beginning.”

After saying this, he fell at the king’s feet, embraced them, and wept bitterly. All the bishops also prostrated themselves with him. The king was greatly moved, and, bending down toward them, raised our lord Avitus and the others. He told them in a friendly manner that he would give them an answer concerning their requests.

This was done the following day. As the king was returning to the city through Sagona, he sent for our lords Stephanus and Avitus, asking them to come to him. When they had arrived, the king said to them:

“You have what you ask for, for my priests are prepared to show you that no one can be coeternal and consubstantial with God. But I do not want this to take place before the whole people, lest the crowds be stirred up. Let it take place only before my senators and others whom I shall choose, just as you may choose from your own people whomever you wish—not in a large number. It will take place here tomorrow.”
