After saying this, the bishops greeted the king and departed, returning to report everything to the other bishops. It was the vigil of the solemnity of Saint Justus. Although they had wished that this might take place on the day after the solemnity, they nevertheless did not wish to postpone such a great good any longer. With one accord they therefore resolved to spend the night at the tomb of Saint Justus, so that through his intercession they might obtain from the Lord the requests of their hearts.

It happened that night that, when the reader began the reading from Moses according to custom, he came upon these words of the Lord:

“But I will harden his heart and multiply my signs and wonders in the land of Egypt, and he will not listen to you” (Exodus 7:3–4).

Then, after the psalms had been sung, when he was reciting from the prophets, he encountered the words of the Lord spoken to Isaiah:

“Go and say to this people: ‘Keep hearing, but do not understand; keep seeing, but do not perceive. Harden the heart of this people, and make their ears heavy, and close their eyes, lest they see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their heart, and turn and I heal them’” (Isaiah 6:9–10).

When more psalms had been sung and he was reading from the Gospel, he came upon the words in which the Savior reproaches the Jews for their unbelief:

“Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the mighty works that have been done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would long ago have repented in sackcloth and ashes” (Matthew 11:21).

Finally, when the reading was taken from the Apostle, these words were pronounced:

“Do you despise the riches of his goodness, patience, and long-suffering? Do you not know that God’s forbearance leads you to repentance? But according to your hardness and unrepentant heart, you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath” (Romans 2:4–5).

When all the bishops had noticed this, they understood that the readings had occurred in this way by the Lord’s will, so that they might know that the king’s heart had been hardened and that God was leaving him in his impenitence in order to display the riches of His justice. They consequently became very sad and spent the night in tears. Nevertheless, they did not cease to assert the truth of our religion against the Arians.

Accordingly, at the time appointed by the king’s command, all the bishops assembled and went together to the royal residence with many priests and deacons and certain Catholics, among whom were Placidus and Lucanus, who were among the king’s leading military officers. The Arians also came with their own people.

When they had sat down before the king, our lord Avitus spoke for the Catholics, and Bonifacius for the Arians. After our lord Avitus had set forth our faith with testimonies from Holy Scripture, speaking like another Cicero, and the Lord inspired grace in everything he said, such consternation fell upon the Arians that Bonifacius, who had offered an especially friendly hearing, was entirely unable to answer our lord Avitus’s arguments. He merely proposed difficult questions by which he seemed to wish to weary the king.

But when Avitus pressed him to answer what had already been said, promising that he would also respond to the matters Bonifacius had proposed, he could not answer even one of the arguments put forward by our lord Avitus, nor could he produce any argument in defense of his own party. Instead, he opened his mouth only for insults, calling the Catholics sorcerers and saying that they worshiped a multitude of gods.

When he was saying only this, and the king saw the confusion of his sect, the king rose from his seat, saying that Bonifacius would answer on the following day. All the bishops therefore departed. Since the day was not yet far advanced, they went together with the other Catholics to the basilica of our lord Justus, confessing the Lord because He is good and praising Him who had given them such a victory over their enemies.

On the following day they again went to the royal residence with those who had been present on the preceding day. As they were entering, they encountered Aredius, who tried to persuade them to turn back. He said that such quarrels irritated the minds of the multitude and that nothing good could come from them.

But our lord Stephanus knew that Aredius favored the Arians in order to gain the king’s favor, although he professed our faith. He replied that there was no reason to fear that quarrels would arise from the investigation of truth and love for the salvation of their brothers; indeed, nothing was more useful for joining minds in holy friendship than to know where the truth lay. For wherever it is, it is lovable and makes its confessors lovable.

He further added that everyone had come here in accordance with the king’s command. Aredius did not dare to resist this answer any further.

They therefore entered. When the king saw them, he rose to meet them. Standing between our lord Stephanus and our lord Avitus, he again said much against the king of the Franks, whom he claimed was inciting his brother against him. But when the aforementioned bishops replied that there was no better way to establish peace than to agree in the faith, and promised their assistance, if he found it acceptable, in bringing about so holy a bond, he said nothing further. Each man took the place he had occupied on the preceding day.

When they had sat down, our lord Avitus so clearly proved that the Catholics did not worship several gods that both Catholics and opponents marveled at his wisdom with astonishment. He did this in answer to the insults which Bonifacius had hurled against our faith.

After Avitus fell silent to make room for Bonifacius’s replies, Bonifacius could say nothing other than what he had said on the preceding day. Adding insult to insult, he shouted with such force that, because of hoarseness, he could no longer speak and seemed almost to be suffocating.

When the king saw this and had waited long enough, he finally rose, displaying indignation against Bonifacius in his face. Then our lord Avitus said to the king:

“If Your Sublimity would command these men to answer our propositions, you could judge which faith ought to be retained.”

The king gave no reply, nor did the other Arians who were with him; they were so stunned by our lord Avitus’s teaching and wisdom.

When Avitus saw their silence, he added:

“If your men cannot answer our arguments, what prevents us all from agreeing together in the same faith?”

When they began to murmur, Avitus, secure in his faith in the Lord, added:

“If our arguments cannot convince them, I do not doubt that God will confirm our faith by a miracle. Let Your Sublimity command that both they and we go to the tomb of Justus, the man of God, and that we ask him about our faith; and let Bonifacius likewise ask about his. The Lord will pronounce through the mouth of His servant in which faith He is pleased.”

The king, astonished, seemed inclined to agree. But the Arians began to shout and say that, in order to manifest their faith, they did not wish to act as Saul had acted, for which reason he had been cursed; nor did they wish to resort to incantations and unlawful practices. It was enough for them to possess Scripture, which was stronger than all sorcery.

As they repeated these statements continually and bellowed rather than shouted, the king—who had already risen—took our lords Stephanus and Avitus by the hands and led them as far as his chamber. When he entered, he embraced them and told them to pray for him.

They certainly recognized his perplexity and the anguish of his heart. But because the Father had not drawn him (John 6:44), he could not come to the Son, so that the saying might be fulfilled:

“It depends not on human willing or running, but on God who shows mercy” (Romans 9:16).

From that day many Arians came to repentance, and after a few days they were baptized. The Lord magnified our faith through the intercession of our lord Justus in the sight of all.

[Col. 0391A]

## LETTER OF POPE SYMMACHUS TO AVITUS, BISHOP OF VIENNE

(We shall publish this letter together with the works of Pope Symmachus.)

[Col. 0391A]

## SERMON OF THE BLESSED AVITUS, ON THE THIRD DAY OF THE WEEK DURING THE ROGATIONS

(From the manuscripts of the Greater Charterhouse.) (C)

[Col. 0391B] We read in the history of the Kings that a certain famous prophet, nourished for many days by a small portion of heavenly food, traveled a very long journey without any assistance from earthly sustenance; so greatly did the power of divine beneficence, overcoming the weakness inherent in the human body, prevail. This comparison, however, is not the reason for the present sermon. Thus, as we too run through the annual journey of our activities amid a diversity of circumstances and fears, a certain bread is taken for us, as it were, extended from heaven through the Rogation observances, to strengthen us in the midst of these things. Its strength and healthfulness not only supplies the want produced by the sterility of the past, but also keeps the danger of famine away from our spirit, which lives not by bread alone but by the living word of God.

If anyone is astonished that the Rogations were instituted in our age, although the multitude of the Churches knew nothing of them so many ages earlier, it is clear that such a person could also disparage the gifts of redemption, which appeared at the end of the ages, when the age of the world was already almost exhausted. Let whoever it may be see what he certainly thinks [Note: Perhaps “is.”]; in his frenzy let him mock the quality of the medicine, or in despair fail to recognize it, though otherwise he has often experienced it. But who is so perfectly healthy that he does not need medicine, that he does not succumb to any sickness of the soul, that he does not either burn with desire, grow pale with greed, become livid with envy, swell with pride, grow hot with anger, or itch to speak evil of others?

If, therefore, anyone is conscious of some weariness arising from these things—one who ought to do penance throughout the whole of time—let him not refuse the three-day observance. The prophecy that has been read also indicates this in full and ordered sequence, if it is repeated according to its several steps. Thus it begins at the outset of the sermon:

“You alone have I known from all the families of the earth” (Amos 3:2).

At once the Jewish people rush headlong into a kind of seizure, not through love but through ambition, so that they may seem to have been chosen above all others for knowledge of divine intimacy. But let the opportunity for interruption cease here, because matters must rather be weighed under the judgment of reason [Note: This passage is plainly corrupt, although its sense is clear. Avitus says that the Jews were mistaken when they interpreted the words of Amos as referring to themselves, since those words must be measured by the judgment of reason rather than by the literal propriety of the expressions. If we follow the letter, they do indeed concern the children of Israel; if we follow the judgment of reason, they are truly and properly spoken of Christians.] than by the literal meaning of the words.

He said, “I have known you,” not “among all,” but “from all the families of the earth.” Who, then, are those who are acquired from all the families of the earth, except those who, gathered together from the whole collection of the nations, become one people from the diverse regions of the world, and from many members become one body under Christ the head?

To recognize and proclaim this calling, blessed Peter, transfixed in amazement of mind, saw a certain linen cloth descending from heaven. Lowered by its swelling folds at the four corners, it contained every kind of living creature, together with birds and reptiles. He was instructed to kill whatever he wished for necessary nourishment. When such a mode of food was prescribed, he recoiled from such an appetite because of his observance of the Law. But immediately the divine word came to him:

“What God has cleansed, you must not call unclean” [Col. 0393A] (Acts 10:15).

And he said:

“In truth I have discovered that God is not a respecter of persons, but in every people and nation whoever fears God and does his will is acceptable to him” (ibid., 34).

You see, then, how those who are known “from all the families of the earth” agree in this unity with the prophets and apostles. This is precisely what the reading now says:

“Will two walk together unless they have agreed?” (Amos 3:3).

The two agree: Christ and Moses, because Moses wrote about Christ. The Law and grace agree, because the former imposed its demands more strictly so that the latter might relax them more generously. Truth and prophecy agree, because the latter gave birth to what the former conceived.

Among the Jews these two do not walk together and therefore do not agree. Between the two Testaments they introduce certain petty distinctions. There is only one road to the one true God. Certainly, if for any other reasons a person can travel by a different road, he cannot travel by an opposing one. Among us, however, these two are joined and agree together.

Yet there is also something in the prophet’s word that can be understood personally, if the duality that must agree is first found within one human being and then within the human race. Our spirit and our body are composed of substances unlike in quality. These two cannot travel the road of this age at all unless, guarded by the law of divine ordering, they agree with one another.

For if the spirit is not subject to the flesh, but the flesh instead yields to the mind so that desire may be restrained, the harmony of reason leads the two together along the road of the Law to the homeland of eternity. But if, while the journey of this age is being traveled, the flesh outruns the soul because the spirit lags behind, and, having been granted the freedom of sin, blocks the road, then the equality of their running—which the Creator has commanded for the human being—is abandoned. With the law of the mind hindered, the flesh begins to perish and to exalt itself above the law of the body. The two no longer proceed together: one lies fallen and the other presses upon it.

And these things—which is more grievous—creep in not so much upon the ignorant as they rule over those who have been struck down. The following passage teaches this:

“The lion has roared; who will not fear? The Lord has spoken; who will not prophesy?” (ibid.).

Sin appears from afar; why do we not flee? Scripture cries out nearby; why do we not believe? Who is the roaring lion except the one of whom the Apostle says:

“Your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, prowls about, seeking whom he may devour” (1 Peter 5:8)?

The lack of self-restraint produces this frenzy, lest the one who announces his roar from afar lie silent in ambush. Yet the person who hears the roar and does not take care brings with him the consciousness of the commandment to the very beginnings of sin; and unless he is terrified by the warning sound that precedes it, he is immediately attacked by the beast’s furious bite.

Nor do we infer this without reason, for the quality of the bite is immediately shown in what follows:

“How, then, if a shepherd rescues from the lion’s mouth two legs of a sheep or the end of an ear?” (Amos 3:12).

Without doubt, that shepherd is the good shepherd who, leaving the ninety-nine sheep, did not disdain to seek the one that had wandered away.

It is worthwhile to observe more carefully that the ninety-nine sheep whom this shepherd left in the mountains, when he was revealed in the flesh, he did not abandon, since he remained in his nativity. They clearly represent the angels who glorify God in the heights of heaven and who, of course, can no longer go astray.

The lion of whom we spoke above, after the ruin of his own fall—by which, desiring a share in divinity, he became even more wretched than humanity because he disdained to be inferior to the Creator—was stripped of the dignity of all archangelic power. Yet he nevertheless attached to the fall of his own overthrow whatever small power he possessed over the heavenly ministers, so that he would not perish alone.

Even so, this much remains to them from the strength of that exalted creature: they already endure the future condemnation while foreseeing it; they have lost the merit of living, and they cannot even possess the remedy of dying.

From that fall, then, as I have said, everyone who remained in the love of his Creator and in the honor of angelic blessedness could no longer be led astray, and therefore could not be placed in peril. Thus, at the beginning, what is to be done with the angels was accomplished; at the end, what is to be done with human beings will be accomplished, so that the course of salvation and perdition, once unfolded and the appointed number completed, may come to its conclusion.

The good shepherd therefore left these sheep of the heavenly height and came to that one lost sheep, in whose figure the human race lay represented. The sheep that had been gnawed by this lion and could not of itself climb up to the ninety-nine, he carried upon his shoulders, because he lifted it up in his own body. And when he returned to the heavenly heights with the human being united to his assumed flesh, he brought back to the angels that same sheep which had wandered from paradise.

Thus it is now clear who the shepherd is who rescues the two legs and the portion of the ear, and who the lion is who devours the remainder: this one is Christ, that one the devil.

Leaving aside, for the moment, any merely physical interpretation, let us see what the smallest part of the body is that Scripture says remained for the devouring lion. For I do not think that the good shepherd would have wished to rescue something so torn apart and almost consumed with such care unless he knew that the remnant itself still possessed some throbbing life.

This sheep, as we have already said, is any sinner whatsoever. If he has wandered from the folds that protect him and, through his own fault, is about to encounter the beast, he has turned away from the shepherd. For while he walks through the deserts—that is, while he thinks upon empty and perishable things—the devil meets him and attacks his thought with the bite of a deadly persuasion.

When he has begun to hold captive human desire under his power, the ravenous destroyer has, in a sense, swallowed its forward part. Yet if the desire is not followed by the execution and determination of sin, the two legs are rescued, that is, the hindmost part which had not yet been eaten.

Although, through desire, he has lost in the lion’s throat certain forward feet of his thought, the mercy of the shepherd has rescued the remaining steps that he did not carry through into action [Note: Avitus appears here to have had in mind the canon of the Council of Neocaesarea: “If anyone has desired a woman and has even had the desire for intercourse with her, but the act does not follow, it is evident that he has been freed by divine grace.” This is how it appears in the ancient version of the canons that was in use in the Latin Churches during Avitus’s time.].

[Col. 0395A] [Note: The passage is corrupt.] Nevertheless, it must be observed that he also rescued the portion of that body which was mixed with the extreme part of the ear [Note: Perhaps “of the extremity.”], which appears to have remained. After saying, “How the shepherd rescues two legs,” he added, “and the end of an ear.” Our ear, therefore, is our obedience. For when we pray and repent, the lion devours the first part of this ear, while the shepherd [Note: Perhaps “preserves.”] saves the last.

The first part of the ear is: “You shall not covet.” This has already been swallowed, because the thought has coveted. The next part is: “Do not follow your desires.” Therefore, if we do not fulfill in action the evil that we have conceived in thought, although the first part of our obedience has been wounded, that part which is last is rescued from the lion’s mouth. How? Certainly, through repentance and correction.

[Note: The passage is corrupt.] The reading itself, as the Lord unfolds it throughout, repeatedly shows what and how many things we have suffered, and yet we do not repent:

“I sent among you want of bread and a dullness of teeth; I struck you with scorching wind” (Amos 4:6).

Want of bread means that we should know that, when one departs from the Lord, there is no means by which one may live.

But from what does dullness of teeth arise? I think it agrees with what Solomon says in a certain passage, when he gives a comparison:

“As an unripe grape is harmful to the teeth.”

An unripe grape is a promise seized prematurely and held onto while the fullness of time is delayed. To want to possess in this world the sweetness and pleasantness promised to us in eternity is exceedingly immature and unripe.

Adam tasted this still harsh and green grape—not wine but poison—within paradise, to the destruction of himself and of us. And because the parents had eaten the unripe grape, the children’s teeth were set on edge. But Ezekiel, foreseeing that the original debt would be voided when Christ paid it, says:

“As I live, says the Lord, this proverb shall no longer be used in Jerusalem: ‘The fathers have eaten an unripe grape, and the children’s teeth are set on edge’” (Ezekiel 18:3).

Adam’s actions no longer harm you, whatever he may have desired proudly, presumed upon illicitly, or sought carelessly. Fear for yourself the dullness of teeth arising from your own eating; restrain the touch of your appetite from useless greed. You desire an unripe grape, but wait for the maturity of the promise.

That pleasure is not owed to you in this age. If you seek what is sweet, await the heavenly sweetness; if you crave what is human, you will suffer what is harsh.

What is the glory of the world except the very thing he calls below “scorching wind”? Even if its gentleness delights people, its terror nevertheless strikes its lovers:

“And because you did not return to me even then, says the Lord, now prepare to meet your God, O Israel” (Amos 4:10).

The Apostle Paul, when he describes the coming of the Redeemer, says how we shall be caught up into the clouds to meet Christ in the air (1 Thessalonians 4:18). Here, however, I think that this meeting refers to something else.

Even in this life we, as it were, meet God if we embrace the commandment that is offered to us. And because he is ready to forgive, let correction meet him in repentance. Whoever, because of love for eternal life, not only refrains from unlawful things but also restrains himself from lawful things must be judged to have met him willingly.

To give one example: although adultery is generally forbidden, simple marriage is permitted by the Law; yet the splendor of virginity is incomparably preferred. Hence, “he who gives his virgin in marriage does well, and he who does not give her does better” (1 Corinthians 7:38).

We ought therefore to understand every form of observance in this way: he who does wrong flees; he who does good waits; he who does better meets him.

Now, after many devout admonitions, which also stand firm according to the literal sense and contribute to our progress, the reading appropriately describes our Rogations at its conclusion, saying:

“In all the squares and streets let there be mourning” (Amos 5:16).

These streets and squares signify our actions, through which we pass through human life in mortality. The streets are lesser offenses; the squares are broader sins, which lead to that broad and spacious way that leads to destruction, and many are those who find it.

By the narrow path one goes to him of whom the prophet foretold that no one heard his voice in the square, since his word certainly did not sound in the freedom of sin. Therefore, because this square is our conduct, let our mourning also be there. The following passage testifies, however, that this mourning should not be confused and disorderly:

“He will call the farmer to mourning, and those who know how to mourn to lamentation” (ibid.).

You see that not everyone knows how to mourn, but only those who know are to be called.

The farmer is the one who, through the mourning of repentance and the feeling of compunction, cleanses the earth—that is, his substance—from thorns; tames it by commandments; waters it with tears; makes it fruitful through humility; enriches it with seed; and multiplies it with fruit.

Indeed, according to the condition of human calamity, there is no one who does not know how to mourn. Human nature is such that even the one who knows nothing else knows this: as the new generation of infants entering this world bursts forth with its first cry of weeping, as though by a kind of prophecy of calamities, it brings forth in its nature the mourning that it does not yet possess in knowledge. Without any assistance from instruction, the very beginning of its troubles produces the lessons of tears.

Since this is so, let us ask, according to the spiritual sense, what difference there is between those who know how to weep and those who do not. Since there are different classes and orders of human beings, each person ought to possess this knowledge of weeping. One cause of tears belongs to a king, another to a subject, another to a sinner, and another to a righteous person.

Secular history reports that a certain Parthian king [Note: Herodotus, Book VII, relates this of Xerxes, king of the Persians, but somewhat differently: “When Xerxes looked upon the entire Hellespont covered with ships, and all the shores and plains of Abydos crowded with men, he boasted that he was blessed; but afterward he shed tears. When his uncle Artabanus observed this, he asked him in these words: ‘How differently, O king, you are acting now from what you said earlier! You called yourself blessed, but now you shed tears.’ He replied: ‘As I reflected upon how brief the whole of human life is, pity for these people came over me, for although they are so numerous, not one of them will survive to the age of one hundred.’] wept after surveying from an elevated place, following a victory [Note: Rather, Xerxes had not yet fought a battle or crossed into Europe.], the immense multitude of his army. When the satraps soon afterward asked him what reason there could be for weeping amid such happiness, he replied: “I mourn this multitude, which, however victorious it may be, must within a few years be entirely brought to an end by the law of nature.”

If we turn to secular wisdom [Note: Some word is missing here, perhaps “let us consider” or something similar.], behold, tears worthy of an earthly king. How much more would they suit a Christian ruler who, after triumphs, thinks about death rather than eminence, and does not swell with pride but mourns!

But what if, in the presence of the cause itself, we know this to be the weeping of a religious ruler [Note: Here he calls him a religious ruler, although shortly before he had called him an earthly king. This should not seem especially surprising, since the emperor Gallienus is called “most reverent and most devoted to God” (ὁσιώτερος καὶ φιλοθεώτερος) by Dionysius of Alexandria in Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History, Book VII, chapter 23.] when that David, great in virtue, endowed with power, and exalted in piety, amid golden garlands and jeweled diadems, sighed with the most intense heat of longing for the crown of the heavenly kingdom, saying:

“When shall I come and appear before the face of my God?” (Psalm 41:3).

Did he not have his tears as bread day and night while they said to him each day, “Where is your God?” His persecutor from outside did not say this to compel him to deny God; rather, his own spirit desired to see him. His spirit, intent upon heavenly things, spoke to itself:

“Where is your God? When shall I come and appear before his face?”

If such tears were fitting for a holy king, what shall we now say of the Holy One of saints, who, before displaying the power of resurrection, devoted the weakness of weeping to a corpse four days dead?

Such tears therefore belong, at the highest level, to the Redeemer. For there he himself wept greatly. There was Adam’s sin; there was the penalty of sin, death; there was Lazarus, that is, the human race; there was the dead man covered by a stone, that is, the hardness of the condition; there were the tearful comforters, that is, disbelief in the resurrection; there was the dead man’s fourth day.

These four things occur among sinners who are summoned at the funeral of their souls: first, thinking evil; second, determining upon it; third, carrying it out; fourth, remaining in the crime.

For this fourth condition, we all return through Lazarus so that we may be raised again. We need not only the sweetness of compassion but also the bitterness of weeping.

After this, because by such instruction he also taught us to mourn, let us distinguish knowledge from ignorance in the matter of tears.

Behold, many come together today in the church. If someone prostrates himself in prayer and begins, with however great a flood of tears, to ask for something belonging to this world—either happiness in worldly conduct, the death of enemies, an increase of riches, a longer life, or the honor of worldly dignities—do not such tears teach us that the person does not know what he should mourn? Surely he has wasted such tears as useless and entirely ignorant whenever he has poured them out in this way.

And this is not so pitiable as if, by weeping, he should ask to be granted those things that many who do not know God appear to obtain through sinning without any prayers.

By contrast, you see another person groaning and crying out:

“Lord, have mercy on me, a sinner.”

He mourns his bad life, seeks a good one, and with the same tears by which he waters his bed washes away his sin. In groans he displays before God the weakness of his flesh, the ardor of his mind, the horror of death, and the love of resurrection.

This person is skilled in mourning; this one is most learned in weeping. Such a tear does not fall to the ground, because it has been entrusted to God, to whom it is said:

“You have placed my tears in your sight” (Psalm 56:8).

Finally, since our Rogations, if they are properly fulfilled, cannot be completed without mourning, I shall distinguish the knowledge of mourning as briefly as I can.

The greatest skill is to shed tears here so that the dullness of teeth mentioned above may be healed, and to preserve tears there where the gnashing of teeth will never end. For to the former it is said:

“Woe to you who laugh now, for you shall mourn and weep.”

But to the latter:

“Blessed are you who weep now, for you shall laugh and rejoice, and no one shall take your joy from you.”

# In the Year of the Lord 496. John the Deacon

(From the Galland Library.)

[Col. 0397C]

## Prologue

[Col. 0397D] I. Mabillon published the letter of John, deacon of the Holy Roman Church, to Senarius, an illustrious man [Note: Mabillon, *Museum Italicum*, vol. I, part 2, pp. 69–76.].

“The writer of the letter,” says the distinguished editor [Note: The same, ibid., pp. 76 ff.], “is the illustrious John the deacon, but who that Senarius was to whom he wrote, we do not know. We recovered this letter from an ancient codex of Queen Christina, which formerly belonged to our monastery at Ferrara. It contains several observations worthy of notice concerning the minister of confirmation; concerning the seven altars customarily erected and consecrated in the Roman Church on Holy Saturday; and concerning the mixing of milk and honey into the chalice on the same day. We have found no mention of either of these latter rites even in the Roman Order—unless the blessing of milk and honey prescribed after the blessing of the lamb on the holy day of Easter is to be referred here.

“As for John, he was, for his age, a very learned man endowed with sound judgment, as is proved by the four books he composed on the life of Saint Gregory the First, the pope. These books provided later writers with an example of how to compose the lives of the saints from their own writings.”

Thus far this very learned man has spoken both about the value of the letter and about its author. The very learned Edmund Martene agreed with Mabillon’s opinion concerning the author of this letter [Note: Martene, *De antiquis Ecclesiae ritibus*, Book I, chapter 1, article 15, §16, vol. I, p. 156, Antwerp edition, 1736.]. Nor did Fabricius [Note: Fabricius, *Bibliotheca Latina mediae et infimae aetatis*, vol. IV, p. 197, Hamburg edition.] and others hold a different view.

II. Yet in our judgment the very learned Muratorius clearly perceived that the author under discussion was much more ancient. We therefore consider it worthwhile to set down his words here. Thus he writes in the excellent dissertation on liturgical matters that he placed before the old Roman Liturgy [Note: Muratorius, *De rebus liturgicis*, dissertation, chapter 3, p. 32.]:

“I cannot agree,” he says, “with the very learned men Mabillon and Martene when they attribute the letter to Senarius to that John the deacon who, in the ninth century after Christ, acquired no slight renown for himself through his *Life of Gregory the Great* and other books. Was there only one John the deacon in the Roman Church? They would have understood that the author of this letter was much more ancient than the other if they had more carefully considered what he writes about confirmation conferred by priests.

“Here are his words [Note: John the Deacon, letter, §8, below, col. 404.]:

‘Nor should this trouble the mind, that necessity sometimes assumes a certain force for itself—something now said to occur in Africa—so that priests may prepare the sacred chrism. This would rightly cause concern if pontifical authority had not granted this permission.’

“In the ninth century after Christ, the Christian religion had been completely cut off in Africa, since the empire and superstition of the Arab people had spread everywhere there. What you read here, therefore, suggests that this John the deacon should be assigned to the end of the fifth century, at which time Huneric, the Arian king of Africa, stirred up a barbarous persecution against the Catholics. This began in the year of Christ 485 and afterward grew more violent. At that time, when the Catholic bishops had been driven into exile, priests were permitted, out of necessity, to confer the chrism.”

III. It is also possible that that John the deacon flourished before those times. Here we may repeat what is found in the Council of Carthage of the year 397 [Note: Council of Carthage III, canon 24.]:

“In the sacraments of the Lord’s body and blood, nothing more is to be offered than what the Lord himself handed down, namely, bread and wine mixed with water. First fruits, however—that is, honey and milk—which are customarily offered on the most solemn day in the mystery of infants, namely baptism, although they are offered upon the altar, nevertheless have their own proper blessing, so that they may be distinguished from the sacrament of the body and blood.”

Since John the deacon did not condemn the mixing of milk and honey with the Lord’s blood, although the Carthaginian Fathers condemned it, the suspicion arises that he flourished in that same fourth century after Christ.

Thus far the learned author has spoken.

IV. Of the two conjectures put forward by this learned man concerning the time in which the author of the letter lived, we accept the former, while the latter seems less convincing to us.

The opinion that our John existed toward the end of the fifth century is chiefly supported by the fact that the letter is found addressed to Senarius, an illustrious man. We know that the Senarius whom Mabillon entirely failed to identify, as he himself admits, and whom Muratorius passed over, became highly distinguished only toward the end of the fifth century.

There is no legitimate room for doubt that the illustrious Senarius to whom John, deacon of the Holy Roman Church, wrote his letter is the same Senarius—also an illustrious man—to whom various letters are known to have been addressed both by Avitus of Vienne [Note: Avitus, letter 36, above, col. 252.] and by Ennodius of Ticinum [Note: Ennodius, Book I, letter 23; Book III, letter 11; and Book V, letter 15.].

For he was a patrician, and was advanced by King Theoderic to the rank of *comes patrimonii* in the year 511, as Cassiodorus teaches [Note: Cassiodorus, Book IV of the *Variae*, letter 3.]. The same senator also provides further information about him elsewhere [Note: The same, ibid., letters 4 and 7.].

The epitaph of this illustrious man, reported by Peter Pithaeus in Book IV of his *Poematia*, presents his splendid praises; Sirmondus also cites it [Note: Sirmondus, on Avitus’s letter 36, above, col. 252, note d.].

[Col. 0399C]

## Letter of John the Deacon to Senarius, an Illustrious Man

Concerning various rites pertaining to baptism and other matters worthy of notice. (C)

[Col. 0399D] I. To Senarius, a deservedly illustrious and always magnificent son: John the deacon.

[Col. 0400D] We received the page of your Sublimity, delivered by our son Renato, a distinguished man. In it you both gave us the pleasant remembrance of your former kindness and, with Catholic concern, did not conceal how great a fervor for divine worship burns within your breast.

For, as your letter says, you wished certain things to be written to you and certain things to be sent to you in transcription. In transcribing, the labor of the copyists has assisted our efforts to some extent; but in the matters that must be written, I confess that you impose a great deal of labor upon me, and, with an embarrassed face, I reply that this exceeds my measure.

First, my ability is not capable of discussing these matters as it should, and not in the way your friend’s esteem believes. The judgment of those who love is often mistaken when affection grants more than the beloved person’s merits display.

In addition, to say nothing of other things, I am weak in body and continually bound to ecclesiastical office. Finally, the matter requires leisure, so that, when reviewing the volumes of our predecessors, our discourse may proceed securely with their assistance concerning what ought to be said about each matter.

What, then, can I do in response to this, except perhaps what your wishes and desires have enabled me to do? I shall therefore attempt briefly to touch upon what you have asked, lest, if I remain altogether silent, I suffer the penalty of unproductive silence.

I trust that I can be helped by your prayers, since you have compelled me to dare these difficult things. Therefore, I ask you to expect from me neither eloquence nor the highest learning, for I have not devoted myself fully to either, and I still prefer to be taught rather than to hear myself called a teacher.

If, then, in this inquiry my discourse—such as it is—is pleasing or expected, let us now consider each of the matters proposed. Meanwhile I announce this to your prudence: the order of the inquiries will not follow the sequence in which your page presents them. Rather, each matter will be brought to completion with a fitting answer as it presents itself.

Thus the words of your inquiry are as follows.

II. “I ask you,” you say, “why, before someone receives baptism, he is a catechumen; what this word or this catechesis means; and by what rule it was anticipated in the Old Testament—or, at any rate, whether it is a new rule and derives its beginning more particularly from the New Testament.

“Likewise, what is the scrutiny, or why are infants scrutinized three times before Easter? What does this strictness or concern of the scrutiny claim for itself? And so forth.”

III. To these questions I respond as follows.

We are confident that we understand your concern: the whole human race, as it were in the very cradle of the world, fell by the transgression of the first human being under the just sentence of death, and cannot be redeemed unless the grace of the Savior is present. Although he was begotten from the Father before the ages, he did not disdain, for our sake, to become in time from his mother alone.

There is therefore no doubt that, before anyone is reborn in Christ, he is held bound under the power of the devil. Unless he is first stripped of those snares, at the very beginnings of faith, by renouncing them through a true profession, he does not approach the grace of the saving bath.

Therefore he must first enter the assembly of the catechumens. *Catechesis* is the Greek word for instruction. Through the ecclesiastical ministry, by the blessing of the one who lays on his hand, the person is instructed so that he may understand who he is and who he is to become. That is, from one condemned he becomes holy; from unjust, he appears just; finally, from a slave he becomes a son. Thus the one who had been lost in the first parent, restored by the benefit of the second, may become possessor of the paternal inheritance.

Having been exsufflated, he is exorcized, so that, once the devil has been driven away, an entrance may be prepared for Christ our God. Rescued from the power of darkness, he is transferred into the kingdom of the glory of God’s love, so that the one who was recently a vessel of Satan may now become a dwelling place of the Savior.

He is exsufflated because the ancient deserter is worthy of such disgrace. He is exorcized—that is, adjured—so that he may depart and withdraw, recognizing the advent of the one whose image, standing upright in the happiness of paradise, he had cast down by his evil persuasion.

The catechumen will now receive blessed salt. By this he is marked, because just as all flesh is preserved when seasoned with salt, so the mind, drenched and dissolved by the waves of the age, is seasoned by the salt of wisdom and by the preaching of the word of God. Thus, after the moisture of corruption has been thoroughly removed, it reaches the firmness of stability and permanence through the sweetness of divine salt.

This is accomplished by the frequent laying on of hands, by reverence for the Trinity, and by the blessing of the Creator invoked three times over his head.

IV. Then, after a certain progress and advancement, the one who had earlier been exsufflated and had renounced the devil’s snares and pomps is now deemed worthy to receive the words of the Creed handed down by the apostles. The one who shortly before was called only a catechumen is now also called a *competens* or an elect.

He has been conceived in the womb of Mother Church and has already begun to live, even though he has not yet completed the time of sacred birth.

At that point the rites that ecclesiastical custom calls scrutinies are performed. We examine their hearts through faith, to see whether, after renouncing the devil, they have fixed the sacred words in their minds; whether they have recognized the future grace of the Redeemer; and whether they confess that they believe in God the almighty Father.

When their response has made clear that these things are so—for it is written, “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Romans 10:10)—their ears are touched with the oil of sanctification, and their nostrils are touched as well.

Their ears are touched because through them faith enters into understanding, as the Apostle says:

“Faith comes through hearing, and hearing through the word of God” (ibid., 17).

Thus, as though protected by a wall of sanctification, their instructed ears should admit nothing harmful, nothing that could draw them back.

V. When their nostrils are touched, they are undoubtedly admonished that, for as long as they draw the breath of this life through their nostrils, they should persevere in the service and commandments of God.

Hence that holy man said:

“The Lord lives, who has removed my judgment, and the Almighty, who has brought my soul into bitterness; for as long as breath remains in me and the spirit of God is in my nostrils, my lips shall not speak iniquity, nor shall my tongue meditate deceit” (Job 27:2–4).

Another meaning is also signified by the anointing of the nostrils. Since that oil is blessed in the name of the Savior, the inner senses are led toward his spiritual fragrance by an ineffable sweetness, so that, delighted, they may sing:

“Your name is poured-out ointment; we shall run after the fragrance of your ointments” (Song of Songs 1:2–3).

By this mystery, the sense of smell, fortified beforehand, should be unable to admit anything voluptuous belonging to the world, or anything capable of weakening the mind.

## VI

Next their breast is anointed with consecration oil, in which lies the seat and dwelling-place of the heart, so that they may understand that with firm conscience and pure heart they must promise to follow Christ’s commandments, having now abandoned the devil. They are also ordered to walk barefoot, so that, having laid aside the garments of death and the flesh, they may recognize that they have entered upon the path of that way in which nothing rough and nothing harmful can be found.

Thus this ecclesiastical concern was established through the succession of ages by prudent arrangement, although the ancient page does not display the traces of these practices. Accordingly, when the elect or catechumen has advanced in faith with these, so to speak, spiritual vehicles, then he must also be consecrated by the baptism of the one font, in which sacrament the baptized person is completed by a threefold immersion.

And rightly so. For whoever approaches baptism in the name of the Trinity must surely signify that Trinity by a threefold immersion and acknowledge himself indebted to the benefits of the One who on the third day rose from the dead for him.

Then, after white garments have been received, his head is anointed with the unction of sacred chrism, so that the baptized person may understand that the mystery of kingship and priesthood has come together in him. For priests and rulers were anointed with chrism-oil: the former to offer sacrifices, the latter to rule peoples.

Indeed, to express more fully the image of priesthood, the head of the one being reborn is arranged with the adornment of linen. For the priests of that time always adorned their heads with a certain mystical veil. All who have been regenerated, however, are clothed in white garments [Col. 0403C] for the ministry of the Church rising again, just as the Lord and Savior himself was transfigured on the mountain before certain disciples and prophets, so that it was said: “His face shone like the sun, but his garments became white like snow” (Matthew 17:2).

By this act he prefigured, as has been said, the splendor of the Church that will rise in the future; concerning it, too, it is written: “Who is this that comes up made white?” (Song of Songs 3:6; 8:5). They therefore use white garments so that, although the infancy of their first birth had been darkened by the cloth of ancient error, the clothing of their second generation may bring forth the garment of glory, and the new person may come to the table of the heavenly Bridegroom clothed in a wedding garment.

## VII

But lest this seem to have been passed over, we state beforehand that all these things are also done for infants, who, because of the beginning of their age, as yet understand nothing. You should therefore know that, when they are presented by their parents or by any others, it is necessary that those who had been condemned by another’s error should be saved by another’s profession.

Accordingly, you add that I should say why only the pontiff is permitted to consecrate the holy chrism, whereas this does not seem to have been granted to a presbyter. And deservedly so: because the bishop holds the rank of the supreme pontiff, while the presbyter is known to retain the place of the second priesthood. Every pontiff is a priest, but not every priest can be called a pontiff.

For in the Old Testament, to say nothing of other matters, they also differed in the form of their garments, so that the priests used four kinds of mystical vestments that appeared to be shared with the pontiff; but the pontiff used four others, with which priests were entirely forbidden to be clothed. It is also added that only the pontiff had access to the Holy of Holies once a year.

Thus in the new people the bishop has deservedly obtained the power to ordain presbyters. Rightly, therefore, the power of blessing and anointing is, in a certain manner, reserved to this apostolic tradition, which clearly holds the beginning of the ecclesiastical orders.

## VIII

This also should not be passed over: the consecration of the presbyterate does not obtain the same words of blessing that the pontifical summit customarily hears.

[Note: [Col. 0403D] It seems that “because” should be read.]

For if nothing special had been reserved for the bishop, the rank would appear undifferentiated, and there would be no need for a different title if the same blessing consecrated both. Nor should it trouble the mind that necessity sometimes assumes a certain power for itself—for example, as is now said to happen in Africa, that presbyters prepare the holy chrism. This would rightly be disturbing if pontifical authority had not granted this permission.

It is therefore clear that even now what is done by pontiffs is, in a certain manner, what the higher order established, so that in such great necessity the chrism may be prepared by presbyters.

## IX

You also wish to know which heretics returning to the Catholic Church it does not baptize. I shall conclude this briefly, according to my limited ability: those who come are to be baptized if it has not been established that they have likewise received the mystery in the name of the Trinity.

For whether someone confesses the Father alone, denying the Son and the Holy Spirit, he must certainly be baptized; or whether, confessing the Son, he denies the Father or the Holy Spirit, he must undoubtedly receive the sacrament of baptism; or if, denying the Holy Spirit, he confesses the Father and the Son, he will likewise, as we have recalled, be cleansed in the mystical font, in accordance with that rule of the Lord who says: “Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19).

But if someone has received the name of the Trinity while in any way making a distinction of inequality—as did those who at that time followed Arius—he cannot be baptized at all, because he has received that rule of the Lord, even though he may appear to be in error.

Such people, therefore, are to be taught rather than baptized, and incorporated into the womb of Mother Church through the blessing that follows from the pontiff, so that, through the love by which God and one’s neighbor are truly loved, they may recognize what they lacked and what has been completed in them.

Regarding the Pelagians, Eutychians, and Nestorians, everything is clear and widely known. When you have read it in the book *On Heresies*, you will be able to consider it more fully.

## X

Acolytes differ from exorcists in this respect: exorcists are denied the power of carrying the sacraments and ministering them to priests; they are occupied only with the laying on of hands, for which reason they are called exorcists. They should hasten to carry out the other duties that are recognized as belonging within the order of acolytes.

Acolytes, however, receive the vessels in which the sacraments are to be carried and hold the office of ministering to priests. Therefore an exorcist may become an acolyte, but the acolyte cannot, by any advancement whatsoever, descend to the office of exorcists.

If they have ministered their office with the greatest diligence, they may advance to the rank of subdeacon. Among us, the order is this: once he has received the most sacred chalice in which the pontiff customarily offers the mystery of the Lord’s blood, he is then called a subdeacon.

If thereafter he remains blameless and unstained by any fault, he may attain the most sacred dignities of the diaconate or presbyterate.

## XI

Regarding the seven altars that it is customary to consecrate in the city of Rome on Holy Saturday, I say this: whether our predecessors decreed that it should be done because of the sevenfold Spirit of grace; or because ecclesiastical service among us is contained in seven regions, from which these very altars are prepared, so that a blessing might be bestowed upon each; or because the number seven itself is mystical and sacred, since the whole world believes in the name of the Trinity and is often described by Scripture as having four parts—and thus the ternary joined to the quaternary produces the septenary, which, as it were, among those sacred and fearsome things represents the image of the whole world—or whether it was established for some other reason, I certainly do not know.

Yet I firmly preserve this conviction: the Church would not preserve what had been handed down by our predecessors unless a certain reason for it had demanded this. Nor can we say that these things appear empty and frivolous merely because we have not received their rationale.

For many things were established in the churches by those who lived immediately before us, and by us as well, insofar as reason persuades us. When we transmit them to posterity for observance, even if a much later age does not know for what reason they were done by us, it will nevertheless not consider them empty if it understands the pious intention toward God of those who preceded it.

In this way, therefore, we too [lacuna] what the reasoning of our predecessors itself has not come down to us; for where the reason has come down to us, both the reason and the practice are maintained, but where the cause is hidden and the practice does not conflict with faith, it is necessary that it be observed and maintained.

## XII

You have also asked why milk and honey are put into the most sacred chalice and offered with the sacrifices on Holy Saturday. The reason is that it is written in the Old Testament and figuratively promised to the new people: “I shall bring you into the promised land, a land flowing with milk and honey” (Leviticus 20:24).

The promised land, therefore, is the land of resurrection and of the happiness that endures forever. It is nothing other than the land of our body, which at the resurrection of the dead will attain the glory of incorruption and peace.

This kind of sacrament is therefore offered to the baptized, so that they may understand that it is not others but they themselves who, becoming partakers of the Lord’s body and blood, will receive the promised land. As they begin its journey, they are nourished like little children with milk and honey, so that they may begin to sing: “How sweet are your words to my throat, O Lord, more than honey and the honeycomb” (Psalm 118:103; 18:11).

Milk and honey are therefore brought to the new people after their bitter sins, so that those who in their first birth were nourished with the milk of corruption and began with tears of bitterness may, in their second generation, receive the sweetness of milk and honey in the womb of the Church, and, nourished by such sacraments, be consecrated to the mysteries of everlasting incorruption.

[Note: [Col. 0405D] Or, “are they drunk?”]

## XIII

You have also been pleased to ask why the Alleluia is sung in the Church until Pentecost. You should know that in the Catholic faith there are certain things by which every Christian throughout the world is bound, such as the authority of the New and Old Testaments.

There are also institutions of the Fathers from which no Catholic is permitted to depart, such as the canons of Nicaea and anything similar. There are, again, practices that each Church retains as its own and preserves as handed down to it by its predecessors. While faith and Catholic peace remain intact, one Church of another region does not observe these—for example, the Roman Church fasts every Saturday, which the Eastern Church does not appear to do; or here seven altars are arranged, whereas no one elsewhere attempts this; and elsewhere, in turn, other practices are performed that are not approved here.

All these things are therefore done in different Churches in different ways, yet all of them form the garment of that queen of whom it is said: “The queen stood at your right hand, clothed in a golden garment, surrounded with variety” (Psalm 44:10).

Let no one therefore be troubled when some things are seen to be done here in the praises of God that are demonstrably done elsewhere in another way. Whether the Alleluia is sung until Pentecost, as is clearly done among us, or is said elsewhere throughout the entire year, the Church sings the praises of God.

Among us, however, something is reserved for Easter reverence, so that with greater joys, and with minds renewed, the heart’s affection may return to the praise of God. For this reason Alleluia, in Latin, means “Praise the Lord.”

Nevertheless, the voice of the peoples also resounds daily in other words as they say: “Praise the Lord from the heavens; praise him in the heights” (Psalm 148:1). And again: “Praise the Lord, all his angels” (ibid., 2). And once more: “Praise the Lord, all nations” (Psalm 116:1).

Whenever, therefore, God is praised in any manner with a faithful heart, the Alleluia is sung.

## XIV

There remains what you thought should be asked: if someone baptized without the anointing with chrism and without the blessing of the pontiff should depart from this life, does this harm him in any way or not?

On this matter I would rather hear a fuller answer from learned men than say anything myself. Nevertheless, subject to a better understanding and the complete judgment of our predecessors, I shall say what seems to me, since in all the matters mentioned above I wish to maintain this principle: I have tried to comply with your wishes, yet we should both preserve whatever better statement—which I do not doubt has been made by our predecessors—may exist concerning all these things.

I shall therefore state briefly what seems to me. Let an analogy be drawn from this first birth in which we were born, so that we may understand that second birth from which we truly live and in which we have been justified.

When an infant has been born and has come to participate in the light of this world, we say that a complete human being has been born. He is of the same substance as the one who generated him—that is, a rational mortal animal—although the one is grown and the other small. These are terms relating to accidents, not to nature.

If aids to the advancement of age should be added, has anything been added to the definition of substance? Certainly not, because the property of nature is neither extended nor diminished … [lacuna]

The rest is missing.

# At the End of the Fifth Century: Saint Faustinus

[Col. 0407A]

## Edmond Martène’s Notice

[Col. 0407B] I have not yet been able with certainty to determine who that Saint Faustinus was. I do find in Gennadius’ book *On Illustrious Men of the Church* a presbyter Faustinus who wrote seven books addressed to Queen Flaccilla against the Arians and Macedonians, published in the *Library of the Fathers*, and another book which he presented, together with the presbyter Marcellinus, to the emperors Valentinian, Theodosius, and Arcadius in defense of his associates.

But this Faustinus was not a saint; indeed, he openly consented to the Luciferian schism. There was also another Faustinus, a bishop, whose homily for the Sunday before Lent is cited by Aeneas of Paris in his book *Against the Greeks*, *Spicilegium*, volume VII, page 86. Our Acherius found this homily complete in a Corbie manuscript and conjectures that this Faustinus was the same as Faustus, bishop of Riez, although only on the basis of conjecture.

Whether he was also the same as Faustinus, the author of the following homily, I dare neither affirm nor deny. Whoever he may finally have been, it is beyond doubt that the homily belongs to a very ancient author.

[Col. 0407B]

## Homily of Saint Faustinus on the Passion of the Lord

*(Published by Martène from the manuscript of Saint Illidius of Clermont.) (C, G, S)*

[Col. 0407C] Although the benefits of our God are great and wonderful, they are nevertheless shown to be neither new nor sudden, but were foretold from the beginning of the world in oracles and prefigured in mysteries.

The utterances of the Old Testament sang of the Lord’s sacred Passion from the very beginnings of the world as it was coming together. Therefore we openly establish from the books and volumes of the Jews themselves that Christ the Lord was proclaimed and announced. He who asserts his case from the documents of his adversaries is undoubtedly supported by powerful privileges.

It is a splendid victory to entangle the opposing party in its own written documents, as in its own snares; to refute it with the words of its own testimonies; and to overcome one’s rival with his own weapons, so that the arguments of your opponent may be shown to serve your own interests.

[Note: [Col. 0407D] Thus Augustine writes excellently on Psalm 40: “We produce the books of the Jews; plainly, the Jews are our enemies. The adversary is convicted from the papers of his enemy.”]

[Note: [Col. 0407D] Again Saint Augustine says in his treatise *Against the Jews*: “Testimonies must be taken from the holy Scriptures, which are held in great authority among them also; and even if they do not wish to be healed by the benefit offered, they can be convicted by the evident truth.”]

[Note: [Col. 0408D] Hence the same holy doctor says on Psalm 56: “The Jews,” he says, “have become our copyists.” And on Psalm 40: “The Jews serve us, having become, as it were, our book-carriers; while we study, they carry the books.” And in Book XII *Against Faustus*, chapter 23: “What else is that people itself even today but a kind of record-office of Christians, carrying the Law and the Prophets as testimony for the Church’s claim?”]

Thus, while in the person of our Lord the mother of all the living, Eve, is produced from the rib of Adam, the first man, the Church, the parent of all the faithful, is shown as needing to be restored from his sacred side and saving wound.

In his type, righteous Abel is killed, and the innocent brother is slaughtered as though by Jewish impiety. This same Lord, in the final age of the world as it grows old, is offered through the figure of the blessed and long-lived father Abraham.

At that time, while the pious parricide rises up for a new sacrifice against the throat of his only son, a ram suddenly appeared before his eyes, as the divine word says: “And Abraham saw a ram caught by its horns among the brambles” (Genesis 22:13).

“Among the brambles,” it says. Let us inquire what this novelty signifies: that is, among the multitude of surrounding sinners. “Caught by its horns,” that is, hanging from the horns of the cross, fastened by the nails, as we read in another passage: “He has horns in his hands” (Habakkuk 3:4).

This is because his venerable hands received the arms of the cross. He was reckoned among the thorns when the author of innocence and justice was mocked with a crown of thorns.

But we must look more deeply into what it means that Isaac is brought by his Father to the altar and that a ram is suddenly substituted for him—not by an altered offering but by a doubled one. Here the two substances of the Redeemer, both worthy of adoration, are displayed: the Only-begotten of God is offered, and the Firstborn of the Virgin is sacrificed.

This also prefigured the marks of the Lord’s Passion: we read that the blessed Elisha, buried in a tomb, revived a corpse thrown by robbers into his grave when it touched the body of the deceased prophet. Who else was prefigured here but our Lord Jesus Christ, who grants resurrection from death and, though buried, brings about life?

In the robber recognize the guilty world; in the prophet’s powers recognize Christ the Lord.

Again and very prominently throughout the Holy Scriptures, the Passion and resurrection of Christ are foreshadowed in the labors and sufferings of the prophet Jonah.

This Jonah, whose role as a type of the Lord we do not think unknown to our faith, is expressly presented as such. For the Lord himself says: “As Jonah was in the belly of the sea monster for three days and three nights, so will the Son of Man be in the heart of the earth” (Matthew 12:40).

This Jonah, I say, is sent at the Lord’s command to preach to the Ninevites the offense of heavenly wrath. But, foreseeing that the sad prophecy would be emptied of its force by the people’s conversion, he fled and sought Tarshish. He entered a ship, but when the sailors were thrown into confusion by a storm that arose, he was given by lot to the waves and swallowed by the mouth of a sea-monster. Yet when the fish vomited him forth unharmed, after depositing him within itself, he was returned to the land on the third day.

See how the Lord also appears wondrously in the Old Testament in the form of a servant. See how, in the ages that had already passed, he judged that he would come in the humility of a servant’s form.

Jonah, about to proclaim the Lord’s anger to the great city of the Ninevites, is to say: “Yet forty days, and Nineveh will be overthrown” (Jonah 3:4). Christ is sent to the city of the world to announce the day of salvation and the appointed time of judgment.

Jonah seeks a ship; Christ seeks the Church. Jonah is tossed by the waves; Christ is tried by the storms of the world.

Unless Jonah is given over to destruction, the danger of the shipwrecked vessel is not calmed. So the Church is not delivered unless it is saved by the death of Christ.

The sailors, though about to cast Jonah away, are nevertheless afraid and say: “Lord, do not place innocent blood upon us” (Jonah 1:14). Does not the sailors’ plea seem to you a confession by Pilate, who handed Christ over and yet washed his hands, saying: “I am innocent of the blood of this righteous man” (Matthew 27:24)?

How fittingly, through the person of a Gentile, the faith of the Gentiles is proclaimed!

[Note: [Col. 0409D] By the person of a Gentile he means Pilate.]

Jonah therefore says in his prayer: “Take my life, then, Lord, for death is better for me than life” (Jonah 4:3).

[Col. 0410A] That is: while alive, I could not save the one nation of the Jews; let me die, and let the whole world be saved by my death.

The sea-monster received Jonah after he had been submerged, but it did not reach the point of devouring him. The wickedness of human beings destroyed him, but the hungry beast guarded him.

With its belly full, it suffers hunger, and it marvels that it has no power over the prey it has swallowed. Who is this one who can be taken into those greedy jaws but cannot be consumed? He is food, but not corruption; he is delivered to the depths of destruction and preserved through the service of death itself.

Who is this one who enters whole into the vastest chambers of danger, and, enclosed beneath an immense and deadly depth, is nourished by vital air; who, released into an alien nature, journeys with life into the exile of life; and, surviving death, announces the salvation of the world that is to come?

[Col. 0410B] I think this is our Lord Jesus Christ, whom savage death, an insatiable beast, seized as its food, while the captive beast trembled before its own prey.

It trembled, I say. For although it knew that he had been crucified, since it did not remember him as guilty, it could not hold him as condemned. Punishment does not establish guilt; the cause does.

It devoured the human being, its customary food, lost at the beginning of the world. But, choked, it recognized the great dignity of that food; and therefore the divine word records: “And the Lord commanded the fish, and it vomited Jonah onto the dry land” (Jonah 2:11).

We must understand this to mean that victorious life returned from the innermost entrails of death, and that destruction, wounded in the deepest recesses of hell, restored life from within.

We therefore see death and resurrection alike prefigured most plainly in the prophet’s sufferings. Therefore, what you see fulfilled in the servant, do not hesitate to believe in the Lord.

Since these things are so, consider, O man, how great is your worth, and weigh what you owe. Consider how great is your worth, so that you may finally cease to regard yourself as worthless, and may disdain to remain subject to shameful vices, measuring your nobility by the dignity of our Creator and Restorer.

He has reasons to be ashamed that he should be overcome in heart and submit to unworthy masters, when eternal glory is promised to him; and thus, by a double privilege, you who were formerly made a participant in the divine image have also become precious through the nobility of this exchange.

See how strong you can be against your enemy. Examine your condition: the Lord has granted you free power to conquer in your members the ruler of this world and to overcome spiritual wickedness. Therefore do not consider it impossible for you to attain transfer into angelic blessedness, since in this world you have conquered angelic powers.

Let life therefore not make you degenerate and despised, when either creation or grace is shown to have brought you forth illustrious. Rather, let Christ’s faithful confidently raise their course toward heavenly things. For those who see themselves redeemed at a heavenly price do not doubt that they have been prepared for heaven.

*Here ends the homily of Saint Faustinus.*

# At the End of the Fifth Century: Julian Pomerius

## Prolegomena

[Col. 0411A]

## Notice from Cave

[Col. 0411A] Julian Pomerius, a Moor by nation, went to Gaul, opened a school of rhetoric in the city of Arles, and was eventually ordained a presbyter. He flourished around the year 498. Gennadius testifies to his excellence in holiness of life and in writings published day after day (*On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 98), at the time when Gennadius closed his *Catalogue*.

He wrote eight books *On the Soul*, whose arguments Gennadius and Isidore enumerate individually (*On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 12); they note that he argued in the second book about the corporeality of the soul. So far as can be conjectured from these arguments—for the work itself no longer survives—these books have been largely excerpted from the eight books *On the Soul* by Nemesius.

He also wrote a treatise *On Contempt for the World and Transitory Things*, addressed to Principius; another *On Vices and Virtues*; and a little book *On Instructing Virgins*. These works have perished.

His only surviving work is *On the Contemplative Life*, or *On the Contemplation of the Future Life*, or *On Actual Conduct*, divided into three books. It is commonly and wrongly attributed to Prosper, is usually counted among his works, and was published separately under his name at Cologne in 1487 and in 1536, in octavo. Dacherius first published the second prologue to this work in *Spicilegium*, volume XIII.

[Col. 0411A]

## Notice Prefixed by Mangeant to the Books *On the Contemplative Life* in His Paris Edition of Saint Prosper of Aquitaine

[Col. 0411B] We place first in the appendix the two books *On the Contemplative Life*, a work both elegant and celebrated with the praise of nearly everyone, and attributed to Saint Prosper from eight hundred years ago down to our own age.

From the middle of the eighth century onward, writers were found who praised this work under the name of our author. Chrodogangus, bishop of Metz, who flourished in that century and was highly commendable for his zeal for regular discipline, to which he wished the canons of his Church to be subject, recognized Prosper as the author of the books *On the Contemplative Life* in his rule for canons.

The same attribution is made by Jonas, bishop of Orléans, who flourished under Popes Eugenius II and Gregory III, while Louis the Pious and Charles the Bald were emperors—that is, in the following century—in his book *On Lay Instruction*. This book was first brought to light by the most learned D. Luke Acherius, a monk of Saint-Germain, of the Order of Saint Benedict and the Congregation of Saint Maur, in volume I of his *Spicilegium of Ancient Writers*.

Then the Council of Aachen, held under Louis the Pious in the year 818 concerning the same institution of canons, seems to favor this opinion, since it uses these treatises as works of Prosper, just as did the sixth Council of Paris, convened under the same emperor thirteen years later.

Moreover, the name of Prosper is found inscribed on this work in manuscript codices of the same period and is included in the earlier printed editions. Thus, finally, all writers of later ages believed this attribution without opposition.

Nevertheless, it is now established among learned men that this work *On the Contemplative Life* is not Prosper’s. Nor did they hesitate to withdraw their confidence from such ancient and seemingly suitable witnesses and to attribute the books about to be presented to another author, namely Julian, surnamed Pomerius, a Moor by nation. He taught rhetoric at Arles with great renown and had as a pupil Caesarius the Great, later bishop of that city, as is testified by the Life of that holy pontiff.

There are not a few proofs supporting this opinion. First, to derive our initial argument from the testimony of the author himself: this author—as Jacob Sirmondus skillfully observed before all others in his notes on the Council of Aachen—composed a eulogy of Hilary of Arles, who died in 449, in Book II, chapter 9, as though he were someone whom he assumes to have died long before his own final day. Prosper, who was Hilary’s contemporary, could certainly not have said this.

You may also add, if you wish, the argument advanced by H. Norisius: Prosper would not have praised so generously one whom he himself, in a letter to Augustine, testifies to have been less inclined toward the teaching of the holy doctor’s grace—even though he acknowledges him as otherwise distinguished in merit, a man of outstanding authority and devoted to spiritual studies.

There are further arguments which, while restoring the work to its true author, necessarily separate it entirely from Prosper’s works.

First, Saint Isidore, in Book 12 of his *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, explicitly attributes those books to Julian Pomerius in these words: “He also published three other books *On the Contemplation of the Future Life, or on Actual Conduct*, and likewise *On Vices and Virtues*.”

That description certainly sets out the division of the entire work and the subject of the whole treatise, as becomes clearer from the preface to the third book.

Second, the already mentioned Sirmondus testifies that he saw a manuscript codex that had once belonged to the viscount of Saint-Salvator and later to the most illustrious and learned archbishop of Toulouse, Charles de Montchal, in which those books are entitled with the name of Julian Pomerius.

According to the same most trustworthy witness, these treatises of ours are again attributed to Saint Pomerius—for that is what he calls him—in the Collection of Canons of the Angers codex.

P. Quesnellus subsequently reports finding another copy in the library of the Abbey of Blessed Mary of La Trappe. This abbey, suddenly transformed from an obscure little monastery into a very numerous and holy ascetic community through the zeal and piety of its most religious abbot, has in our age restored to the Gallican Church its Bernard, and to Bernard his Clairvaux.

To these two eyewitnesses one may add a third witness of no lesser authority: the learned author of the *New Library of Ecclesiastical Authors*, of the most distinguished reputation. In the second part of the third volume he states that he has heard—from persons undoubtedly worthy of credence—that an extremely ancient manuscript is still preserved in the library of the chapter of the distinguished Church of Beauvais, in which the three books *On the Contemplative Life* are marked with the name of Julian Pomerius as their certain author.

Nor should it perhaps be thought that Gennadius was referring to another work of Pomerius in his *Catalogue of Illustrious Men*, or *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, when, after listing the work in which that author, responding in the manner of a dialogue to the questions and requests of Bishop Julian and the presbyter Verus, composed eight books *On the Nature and Quality of the Soul* by dialectical art and language suited to his talent, Gennadius adds:

“I remember that I once read his composition addressed to someone named Principius, and another work entitled *On Vices and Virtues*.”

Nor will it be useless to preface this discussion briefly with something about the reputation and circumstances of Julian Pomerius.

When he wrote these works, this Julian Pomerius had advanced from the disciplines of rhetoric to the ecclesiastical orders. It is not reasonable to believe that Bishop Julian, at whose command he took up his pen, had commissioned him to discuss the offices of clerics before he had attained the rank to which the Church entrusts teaching and the instruction of others.

Gennadius also records that he was ordained a presbyter. Ennodius, bishop of Pavia, praises him most eloquently in Book II, Letter 6, which he addresses to him. Near the end he writes:

“Farewell now, my lord, and exercise yourself more diligently as a supporter of ecclesiastical discipline toward me,” and so forth.

Ruricius of Limoges is also said to have sent him two letters. Ruricius himself asks Aeonius of Arles, in Book II, chapter 8, to order Pomerius to come to him.

Since he calls him an abbot at that time, this indicates that Aeonius had placed him over the government of a monastery after he had attained the priestly order, just as the pontiff himself had likewise appointed Caesarius, already a presbyter, abbot of a monastery.

When it is said that Caesarius was substituted for the deceased abbot in the religious community, we may perhaps infer, without an empty conjecture, that he had been chosen to succeed Julian, once his former teacher, in this office. It follows that Julian should by then be considered advanced in years.

Gennadius himself suggests this in chapter 98 of his *Catalogue*. Composing or expanding it around the year 494, he says: “He is also said to have written other works, and still to be writing … he lives to this day in a manner worthy of God and suitable to his profession and rank.”

It is rightly believed that these final words designate both his monastic life and his priesthood.

Those books, however, are inscribed to Bishop Julian, although it is uncertain of which see he was bishop.

Certainly a pontiff named Julian of Carpentras is observed among those who signed the Council of Epaon in the year 517. Neither the difference in date nor the distance between the regions seems to prevent us from judging that this work might have been dedicated to him.
