But since this name was common in those centuries, there could also have been other Julians to whom Pomerius might have dedicated his writings.

For, if credence is given to the circulating Life of Saint Honoratus, a pontiff of this name held office among the people of Fréjus. Since the author relates that this Julian received Honoratus and Caprasius as guests returning from Italy, the author of the dissertation *On the Origins of the Church of Fréjus* conjectured that he was the same as Quillinus, to whom letters of Leporius’ retraction are extant.

But since compilers commonly join more remote chronological periods together, or tear apart periods that were joined, that author may have found Bishop Julian within this span of time, in any event after Victorinus, who took part in the Council of Agde in 506. A letter from Victorinus to Ruricius of Limoges is extant, as is a letter from Ruricius to Victorinus.

While this Julian was seated at Fréjus, the *Secrets of Lérins* show that he traveled through the regions of the province and formed special connections with provincials.

From this familiarity with those regions, it is easy to suspect that he acquired the opinion which, from the testimony of the aforementioned Isidore, we learn he maintained in the eight books he composed *On the Nature of the Soul*: misled by Tertullian’s errors, he strove even through deceptive arguments to establish that the soul was corporeal.

For at that time Faustus of the monastery of Lérins was celebrated with great renown. After Maximus, then bishop of Riez, he was abbot in the territory of Fréjus. He did not refuse to revive the ashes of an opinion that had almost been buried, and is reported to have defended it vigorously in written books.

Against him, on the other side, stood Claudianus, a presbyter of the Church of Vienne, who chose as arbiter of the dispute Prefectorius Patricius, a most learned man, and the excellent C. Sollius Sidonius; for in the letter prefixed to his books he addresses him by these names.

He appointed as arbiter a man who, although exceedingly friendly to Faustus, seems to have given sufficiently abundant proof that he was even more a friend to truth, when he praised those books with such carefully chosen encomiums in his third letter to Claudianus, Book IV.

Moreover, Pomerius arranged his books *On the Soul* at the request of that same Bishop Julian, to whom he dedicated his books *On the Contemplative Life*—so Gennadius asserts, while also mentioning another presbyter named Verus as a promoter, together with Julian, of the publication of this work. Concerning this [Col. 0415A] Verus, since scarcely anything has so far been noticed, it may not perhaps be an unsuccessful conjecture of the author of the seventh dissertation on the writings and treatises attributed to Saint Prosper that this Verus is the same man whom Salvian commends with such elaborate praise in his seventh letter, addressed to him and to Aper. These praises indeed indicate the man’s very great renown, all the more because Salvian himself appears to have been a greater man and more sparing in his praises. But these considerations would again sufficiently suggest that neither Julian nor Verus should be sought outside the province or its vicinity.

In Verus’s favor there is also the still stronger consideration that, during this period, a bishop of this name is found in the succession of the bishops of Orange [Col. 0416A]. It is scarcely credible that he was different from our Verus—not the one whose name we read subscribed to the letter of the bishops of the province to Leo concerning the restoration of the rights of the bishop of Arles (since it is established that Eutropius, bishop of Orange and Verus’s predecessor, had lived beyond the middle of the fifth century, having received letters from Pope Hilary as well as from Sidonius, already a bishop), but that Verus who succeeded Eutropius at the end of this century, and whose Life was also written, according to Sigebert. For his period agrees very well with the time when Julian and Salvian, by whom he is commended, were active. Let this suffice for insertion immediately before the following book and among the writings of the most learned critics.

[Col. 0415A]

# THE THREE BOOKS OF JULIAN POMERIUS, ON THE CONTEMPLATIVE LIFE (C)

## BOOK ONE

[Col. 0415B]

### PROLOGUE

#### 1

For a long time and with great resistance I opposed your will, my most devoted lord Julian, foremost among bishops—not as one stubbornly hard-hearted, but warned by the awareness of my own inability. For it seemed to me—and perhaps with justice—that you might even have accused my presumption of reckless imprudence if I had readily and without any deliberation undertaken so great a subject, which certainly required painstaking treatment [Note: Two manuscripts, one Regius and one Camberonensis, read “if I had undertaken it.”]. I ought first to weigh the importance of the subject itself, on which I was to speak [Alternative reading: “to test”]; and then, with the Lord’s help, if an examination of my abilities promised that I had the capacity, I ought to approach the task you commanded.

After carefully considering these and similar matters, I judged it necessary to suspend myself for a while from the presumption of writing. But since, just as the difficulty of the work imposed had to be considered [Col. 0415C], so too the authority of the one imposing it had to be considered, I neither wished nor ought to resist altogether. I was certain that your prayer, as the one issuing the command, would assist my strength far more than the magnitude of the subject would burden it.

Moreover, this consideration led my spirit, which distrusted its own powers, to dare undertake your command: for it would no longer be humility to maintain silence persistently, but pride to continue refusing, even though a heavy burden had been placed upon weak shoulders [Note: Thus five manuscripts, together with the Lyon edition of 1539. Two manuscripts and the Douai and Cologne editions read: “although the burden placed upon weak shoulders is heavy.”]. Although my rusticity made me incapable of bearing that burden, I believed that your faith, because you were the one commanding it, would make me capable.

#### 2

This also gave me confidence to attempt something: that the very attempt at great things was great, even if no result followed the discussion [Col. 0416B] [Note: One Colbertinus manuscript reads “of the discussions.”]. For the treatment of necessary questions, even if it does not instruct the mind of one who does not find what he seeks [Note: Four manuscripts, together with the Lyon edition, read: “does not instruct the mind of the one who finds nothing”; but this appears less satisfactory.], at least exercises the intelligence of the seeker. Thus one may either come to know, through seeking and finding nothing, that one does not know what one had perhaps presumed to know; and, consequently reminded of one’s ignorance, seek what one sees to be lacking, hold on to what one finds, and persistently practice what one has held [Note: Thus five manuscripts. One manuscript and the editions read “carefully.”]; or, if one has been able to treat profitably and explain sufficiently what had been proposed to one from the divine Scriptures [Note: One Camberonensis manuscript reads “will be able”], one should not be puffed up by the discovery [Note: The word “of truth” is absent from the Camb. manuscript], but should glory in the Lord, who inwardly enlightened him so that he might recognize what was to be illuminated [Note: Two manuscripts read “to be cleared of clouds”; one reads “unclouded.”].

For knowledge, just as it puffs up without the gift of God, which is love, so, when love is added to it, it builds up (1 Corinthians 8). Therefore, one who wishes to speak about God either says nothing, and no conceit throws him down [Note: The Camb. manuscript reads “no conceit will cast him down”;] or, if he says something and believes that he has received from God what he has said [Note: The editions, together with one manuscript, read “what he says”], he has reason to give thanks to God, but no reason, exalted by the powers of his own intellect, to credit it to himself.

#### 3

But now I shall append the very chapters which you proposed that I should resolve as best I could. You command me, therefore, to explain briefly what the distinctive character of the contemplative life is, and to distinguish as concisely as I can what difference there is between it and the active life. Whether one to whom the care of governing the Church has been entrusted can become a participant in contemplative virtue [Note: One manuscript reads “in the contemplative life.”] Whether those who trample upon the divine commandments should be endured with equanimity, or whether, according to the measure of their sin, they ought to be reproved with ecclesiastical severity.

Whether it is advantageous to possess the Church’s resources for gathering or supporting the brethren [Note: One manuscript reads “for gathering them together”], or whether they should be despised out of love for perfection. What perfection of abstinence ought to be believed in; and whether it should be judged necessary only for the body or also for the soul [Note: Thus two manuscripts, together with the Lyon and Douai editions. In the others only “also” is absent.]. How far likenesses of virtues fall short of true virtues. Through what preceding causes and subsequent developments vices are usually born or increased, and by what remedies, with the Lord’s help, they can be diminished or healed, as by medicines.

By how many ways or degrees each virtue can be fulfilled. And whether that opinion of the philosophers is true which defined four virtues as certain fountains of all virtues, and likewise four vices as certain origins of all evils [Note: One manuscript reads “origins of all evils.”].

These, then, are the ten chapters which you wished me to unravel [Col. 0417B]—not because their resolution would bring you any knowledge, but so that your more careful concern, if I should fulfill the task regularly imposed, might contribute some edification to those interested in such chapters and in others like them [Note: Thus six manuscripts, together with the Lyon edition. Other printed editions, with one manuscript, read: “but so that your greater care might know whether, by a regular …, it could be joined to the explanation of the chapters.” The Camberonensis manuscript reads: “so that your teacherly care …”]. Besides, if you did not know these things, you would never have proposed them for clarification in such an orderly fashion. But you wished matters known to you to be illuminated through discussion so that either, if I explained something contrary to reason [Note: Two manuscripts read “differently from what is correct”], you might have me corrected or amended, or, at least, through your diligence and my discourse, matters discussed in a Catholic manner might be conveyed to the knowledge of others [Note: Five manuscripts read “might be able to be conveyed.”]. Now, then, with the Lord assisting through your prayers, let us discuss what the distinctive character of the contemplative life is [Note: Five manuscripts read “Now, therefore, let us begin.”].

## TABLE OF CONTENTS

[Col. 0417C]

**CHAPTER I.** That the distinctive character of the contemplative life is found where the Lord will be seen with a pure heart [Note: The Camb. manuscript reads “God.”]

**CHAPTER II.** On the nature of the future life.

**CHAPTER III.** That the saints will be separated from wicked people by God’s judgment in the same way that the blessed angels have already been separated from unclean spirits [Note: Two manuscripts read “already before”; two others, “in which they already are.”].

**CHAPTER IV.** On the resurrection, or the life of the saints.

**CHAPTER V.** That even here the blessedness of the contemplative life delights those who despise present things.

**CHAPTER VI.** That the perfection of the contemplative life which can be possessed here cannot be compared with future perfection [Note: Two Regius and Camberonensis manuscripts read this way. The printed editions add “there.”].

**CHAPTER VII.** That the saints cannot see the Lord perfectly until they have attained the blessedness of the future life.

**CHAPTER VIII.** What and how great the perfection of the contemplative life is in this flesh, and how those who despise the world cling to it in order to enjoy it.

**CHAPTER IX.** That the difference between the perfection of this life and that of the future life is as great as the difference between those who do not wish to sin and those who can no longer sin.

**CHAPTER X.** That here the saints saw God in assumed creaturely form [Note: The Camb. manuscript reads “the Lord.”].

**CHAPTER XI.** On the quality of the glorified bodies that will exist at the resurrection.

**CHAPTER XII.** How great the difference is between the contemplative and the active life.

**CHAPTER XIII.** That holy priests can become participants in the contemplative life.

**CHAPTER XIV.** Where the speaker excuses himself for not daring to teach the teachers of the Church.

**CHAPTER XV.** On the negligence of a priest who, by acting contrary to his teaching, cannot fulfill the role of teacher.

**CHAPTER XVI.** What danger awaits those who either wish to abandon the Church entrusted to them or disdain to govern it energetically [Note: Two Regius and Camberonensis manuscripts read “who wish to abandon it.”].

**CHAPTER XVII.** Where he encourages one anxious because he can neither abandon nor govern the Church, by suggesting that he govern it better through his example.

**CHAPTER XVIII.** That it is of little use to show by example what should be done [Note: One Regius manuscript reads “by doing the examples”] unless the priest also demonstrates by teaching what should be believed.

**CHAPTER XIX.** On the virtue of faith: that it consists not only in believing or understanding, but also in doing good.

**CHAPTER XX.** That it does a priest no good, even if he lives well, if by keeping silent he does not correct one who lives badly [Note: The Regius and Camberonensis manuscripts read: “It does priests no good if they live well, if by keeping silent they do not correct those who live badly.”].

**CHAPTER XXI.** A mournful description of a priest living carnally [Note: The Regius manuscripts and the Camberonensis read: “of priests living carnally.”].

**CHAPTER XXII.** That, according to the prophet’s saying, those who perversely despise the priests’ reproofs or admonitions perish through their own fault [Note: Two manuscripts read “of prophecy.”].

**CHAPTER XXIII.** That even priests who are able to teach otherwise ought to teach so simply that everyone understands them when they teach [Note: Thus two manuscripts. The printed editions read “however they can.”].

**CHAPTER XXIV.** What difference there is between teachers who build up the Church by teaching it simply and those who parade their eloquence in brilliant declamations [Note: Two manuscripts read “cast down”; one reads “throw down.”].

**CHAPTER XXV.** What priests who wish to become participants in the contemplative life ought to be like.

# CHAPTER ONE

## The distinctive character of the contemplative life is found where God will be seen with a pure heart

[Col. 0418D]

The contemplative life, in which the intellectual creature, purified from every sin and healed in every respect, will see its Creator, received its name from contemplating—that is, from seeing. If this is so, that life in which God can be seen must itself be understood as contemplative [Note: Thus two manuscripts. Regius and the printed editions read: “that life itself must be understood as contemplative.”].

In the present life, however, which is filled with miseries and errors, there can be no doubt that God cannot be seen as he is [Note: One Regius manuscript reads “for indeed.”]. In the future life, therefore, which for this reason is called contemplative [Note: This word “life” is absent from two Colbert manuscripts], he must be seen, and rightly so. For if seeing God is the highest and most substantial joy, the highest true joy, and is rightly believed to be the reward of the blessed; and if the reward will be given not to those still fighting but to those who have already conquered, after the triumph [Note: One Colbert manuscript reads “a reward which is not yet …”; the Lyon edition reads “also.”], who does not see that all the saints will see God in that eternal life where they will rejoice without end?

There they will rejoice, where they will receive their reward; there they will receive their reward, where they will triumph not only over defeated but also over finished enemies [Col. 0419B]; there they will triumph, where they will have no further adversary [Note: Four manuscripts read “they will no longer fear.”].

### 2

In this life, however, although we fight vigorously and, with the Lord’s help, overthrow the hosts of enemies surrounding us, nevertheless, if we do not wish to be defeated by them, we never cease fighting [Note: Seven manuscripts, two Regius, four Colbert, and Camberonensis read “we do not cease”; the printed editions read “let us not cease.”]. Nor do battles already fought with manly exertion make the victors secure; rather, the renewed struggles of their adversaries trouble them even more.

And so, because, according to the saying of Holy Scripture [Note: The printed editions read “Sacred Scripture”; the manuscripts read “Holy Scripture”], the whole human life is a trial upon the earth (Job 7:1, according to the Septuagint), the trial is ended when the battle also ends; and the battle is ended when, after this life, a victory secure from combat follows. Thus all Christ’s soldiers who, aided by God to the end of the present life, have resisted their enemies without weariness will, once their laborious pilgrimage has been completed, reign happily in their homeland.

Human nature must be restored there and healed from every weakness so completely that no sins remain in it and it is no longer able to sin [Note: One Colbert manuscript reads “no sin of another remains.” The Lyon edition reads “may be able to [sin] no longer.”]. Its entire reward will be this: having once attained possession of the contemplative life, it will gaze insatiably upon the author of its blessedness [Note: One Regius manuscript and the Camberonensis read “it will desire its own [blessedness]”], rejoice in him, obtain from him what it hoped for [Note: Seven manuscripts omit “from him”], and remain forever in that state to which it attained by holy living [Note: Thus six manuscripts. The edition reads “to which it attained by living holily.”].

# CHAPTER TWO

## On the nature of the future life

### 1

What shall I say now about the nature of that future life, which ought rather to be believed than described [Col. 0420A]? Nevertheless, I ought not to remain silent about what I can say [Note: One Colbert manuscript reads “as much as I can”] simply because I cannot say as much about it as I wish. For although we believe God to be ineffable, we ought not therefore to refrain from speaking about him as much as we can.

Indeed, more should be believed about that life than can be written [Note: Five manuscripts read “written down”], because speech cannot convey as much about it as the mind can embrace; and however profound the human mind’s act of comprehension may be, it grasps less than the greatness of the reality itself [Note: One Colbert manuscript reads “than the reality itself possesses.”].

The future life, then, is believed to be blessedly eternal and eternally blessed. There are certain security, secure tranquility, tranquil joy, happy eternity, and eternal happiness; there is perfect love, no fear, eternal day, lively activity, and one spirit in all, secure through contemplation of its God and through remaining with him [Col. 0420B]. There the city itself, which is the blessed assembly of the holy angels [Note: One manuscript reads “of the angels and of all the saints”] and human beings, shines with resplendent merits [Note: Three manuscripts read “gleams”; “eternal salvation” follows], and eternal salvation overflows; truth reigns there. No one deceives and no one is deceived; no blessed person is cast out from there [Note: All the manuscripts read “no blessed person is expelled”], and no wretched person is admitted there.

# CHAPTER THREE

## The saints will be separated from wicked people by God’s judgment in the same way that the blessed angels have already been separated from unclean spirits

### 1

We believe that this too will occur through God’s just judgment. In it the righteous will be separated from the wicked forever, not only according to their merits but also according to their places [Note: One Regius manuscript reads “they are to be distinguished”], so that neither those who have been rewarded will bring their reward to an end, nor those who have been condemned their punishment [Note: Only the Lyon edition reads “nor will it end the reward for those who have been rewarded, nor the punishment for those who have been condemned.”]. For this reason incorruption and immortality will also be given to the bodies of the wretched: so that they themselves will neither bring eternal punishment to an end, nor will immortal punishment consume them, but it will punish them.

The bodies of the righteous, however, will be endowed with blessed incorruption and immortality so that glory may remain in them and they in eternal glory [Note: One Colbert manuscript reads “so that they themselves may remain in eternal glory”; another manuscript has “and they themselves,” with the rest omitted].

### 2

We believe that this judgment, which we say will take place between righteous and unrighteous human beings, has already taken place between holy angels and unclean spirits [Note: One manuscript reads “has taken place.”]. Both had been created without sin and appointed to serve their God happily and faithfully [Note: One manuscript adds “faithfully”]. But some of them, corrupted by their own will, did not wish to remain what they had been made [Note: One Regius manuscript reads “in what they were made.”]. When they had raised themselves in hostile arrogance against their Creator, through the pride of a deadly conceit [Col. 0421A], they were cast down from the heavenly region of the sky (Isaiah 14:13).

The divine sentence condemned them to this punishment: because they did not wish to persevere when they could, they neither wish to be restored nor can be restored [Note: All the manuscripts read this way; the printed editions read “nor would they wish to be restored, nor could they be.”]. For it was a consequence of their transgression that they were struck by the punishment of an irrevocable judgment [Note: Five manuscripts read “of an irrevocable judgment”; one reads “of an incredible judgment”; the printed editions read “irrevocably”; the Camb. manuscript reads “the transgression of them was the irrevocable judgment”].

And it certainly belonged to their most just condemnation that they utterly lost both the will and the ability to return. Conversely, it belonged to the will of the holy angels that, while the wicked were willingly falling, they remained in their own dignity. Through a divine and just judgment it was brought about that the will they had to remain with their God became a willing and blessed necessity of remaining [Note: One Colbert manuscript reads “so that, for those whose will was to remain with their God …”].

Therefore, because they have never sinned and can no longer sin, once they have become participants in that contemplative life [Col. 0421B], they gaze insatiably upon the author of their blessedness [Note: Two Colbert manuscripts read “inexplicably”]. Made eternally blessed by the merit of their steadfastness, they are secure in their permanence. They receive the highest and most substantial joy, which they enjoy without satiety, from the contemplation of God; and they serve their God tirelessly and lovingly—so perfectly blessed that they neither desire to become more blessed nor are able to do so.

# CHAPTER FOUR

## On the resurrection, or the life of the saints

### 1

This is the contemplative life, the blessed life, to which those who attain through the completion of good works will be like the blessed angels and will reign with God forever [Note: One Colbert manuscript reads simply “This is the life”; the others, together with the printed editions, read “This is the blessed contemplative life.”].

What they believed here, they will see there [Note: Six manuscripts read “they believed”; the printed editions read “they had believed”; one manuscript reads “they will have believed.”]. Contemplating the substance of their Creator with pure hearts, they will rejoice with eternal exultation. Possessed by divine and mutual love [Note: The Douai and Cologne editions and three manuscripts read “possessed by divine and mutual love”; the Lyon edition, together with one manuscript, reads “possessed by the love of God and mutual delight”; another manuscript reads “possessed by divine delight and mutual love”; another, “possessed by the possession of divine love and mutual charity”], they will cleave happily to their God and to one another forever.

Having received bodies with incorruption and immortality, they will receive citizenship in their heavenly homeland. Made its citizens forever, they will obtain the promised rewards. There such great joy and such abundant grace of heavenly delights will overflow for them that they will give thanks to their Rewarder for such great gifts and will suffer no weariness from the very enjoyment of the blessings that overflow.

There the minds of individuals will be open to one another just as bodily faces are exposed to bodily eyes. For the purity of human hearts will there be so great and so perfect [Col. 0422A] that they will have reason to give thanks to God their purifier, not reason to blush because they have been stained by some sins. For there will be neither sins nor sinners there, and those who are there will no longer be able to sin.

Nothing secret will remain hidden from those who are perfectly blessed, since—something far more excellent—they will see God himself with pure hearts. For human nature will be so perfected that it will no longer be able to change either for the better [Note: The Camb. manuscript reads “either for the worse”; the others, together with the editions, read “or for the worse.”] or for the worse.

### 2

All the good things which this human substance, exalted to the likeness of its Creator, had naturally received but corrupted through sin [Note: One manuscript reads “by sinning”] will be restored in a better condition: intellect without error, memory without forgetfulness, thought without wandering, love without dissimulation, sensation without injury, soundness without weakness [Col. 0422B], health without pain, life without death, ease without impediment, satiety without weariness, and complete health without disease.

For whatever the bites of wild beasts may have taken away from human bodies here by injuring them [Note: The Camb. manuscript and the Lyon edition read “may have taken away”], whatever unforeseen accidents may have removed, whatever different kinds of illness may have torn away [Note: Thus three manuscripts. Others, together with the editions, read “may have mangled”; the Lyon edition lacks the word “limb”], whatever human cruelty may have amputated, whatever weakness fire or any other thing may have inflicted, and whatever old age itself, burdensome even to the healthy, may have denied—these and similar losses of the body will there be restored by the one resurrection, and incorruptible health will possess bodies restored in all their members.

### 3

Therefore, whoever is there, although they will differ from one another in merit, will nevertheless all be blessed with one perfection. For each person’s rewards will be sufficient, and those who are already perfected by their rewards will be unable to contain anything more [Col. 0422C].

Just as bodily satiety makes everyone equally satisfied, although individuals have not received equal amounts of food but only what their capacity allowed, so all the saints, even if distinguished by some diversity in their degrees, will be perfected in one blessedness [Note: One manuscript reads “nevertheless in one blessedness”; another, “which is also one”], because they will be blessed in one perfection [Note: One manuscript reads “because they have been made blessed in one perfection.”].

Moreover, in that realm of such great blessedness, no one will claim anything for himself on account of greater merit [Note: The Camb. manuscript reads “nor will anyone of greater merit claim anything for himself”; another, “they will claim nothing”], because there will be no arrogance there. Nor will an inferior envy a superior [Note: One Colbert manuscript reads “nor will inferiors envy their superiors”], because envy will not be possible there [Note: Five manuscripts read this way; two others, “he will not be able to be envious”; the editions, “because there no envious person will be possible.”].

Therefore, although there will be a difference among their dwelling places, there will nevertheless be in them all the supreme equality of one perfection, and they will share one happiness of the heavenly kingdom.

# CHAPTER FIVE

## Even here the blessedness of the contemplative life delights those who despise present things

[Col. 0423A]

### 1

He longs to earn this blessedness who renounces all present things through contemplation of the future. Lifted up to the sublimity of divine contemplation, away from domestic occupations—which sometimes obstruct the progress of those who wish to live perfectly—he even rises above the affections of his own flesh [Note: Thus seven manuscripts together with the Lyon edition. Other editions read “who also places them beneath himself”;]. Looking down upon everything beneath him which commonly casts down to earth souls that feel secure in the holiness of their former life [Note: One Regius manuscript reads “he himself already”; another, “he himself also”], he approaches even the heavenly beings.

He is made that much nearer to divine things by how much he rises above all human things through his zeal for perfection [Note: Three manuscripts read “as much nearer to divine things as …”]. He is certain that, if here he willingly prefers the contemplative life to uncertain honors, anxious riches, and fleeting pleasures [Col. 0423B], he will find true honors, secure riches, and eternal pleasures [Note: Two manuscripts read “he will discover them”] when, in that blessed life where it will exist, he reaches the perfection of contemplative virtue, with God as his rewarder.

And indeed, what will be more honorable than that which divine mercy has blessed with equality to the angelic dignity? What will be richer than one whom the ineffably overflowing blessedness of the heavenly kingdom has enriched? Or what even here will be more delightful than divine contemplation, which pours incorruptible sweetness from the future reward into the one who truly longs for it?

For the contemplative life even here delights its lovers through consideration of future blessings. It illuminates those who devote themselves to it with the full attention of their minds, as far as this is possible in the present life, by the gift of spiritual wisdom [Col. 0423C]. By a kindling incentive to attain that very perfection, it inflames them toward that fullness of divine vision, the hope of which they carry while devoting themselves to heavenly pursuits, so that what they now see in an enigma, without discerning it perfectly, they may then behold in that revelation.

# CHAPTER SIX

## The perfection of the contemplative life which can be possessed here cannot be compared with future perfection

### 1

For this reason I have praised the sublimity of the contemplative life in the future, where perfection is to be perfected, not in such a way as to deny that it can be grasped in the present by all who despise the world—provided that they turn to it with complete devotion; that, inflamed by desire for it, they reject present allurements; and that, made far too strong for earthly occupations to ensnare them, they cling to the consideration of divine things and future promises.

But if we consider the saying of the apostle Paul, in which he distinguishes between the knowledge that exists here and that which will exist there, saying, “We know in part and we prophesy in part” (1 Corinthians 13:9) [Col. 0424A], we can neither compare nor ought we compare the divine contemplation that exists in this life with that which will exist in the future.

The same apostle adds: “But when that which is perfect has come”—signifying that future life—“then that which is in part will be done away” (ibid., 10) [Note: One Colbert manuscript reads “that life”; two manuscripts and the Cologne edition read “as if in some way.”]. Thus what we now perceive in part, when we have been brought to that fullness of divine contemplation, we shall then see perfectly [Note: One manuscript reads “we shall perceive.”].

### 2

Nor, because there the knowledge of all things will be seen not in parts but simultaneously and as a whole, should even some measure of knowledge in this fragile body be despaired of [Note: All the manuscripts read this way; the editions read “should it be despaired of.”]. Although the corruptible body weighs down the soul and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind occupied with many thoughts (Wisdom 9:15), nevertheless, as far as it can, let the human mind—which its Creator made in his own image—strive even here to see God intelligibly through faith, so that it may see him more fully when, by the gift of its Creator, it reaches the vision itself.

Observe how divinely the holy Apostle distinguished vision from faith when he said: “We walk by faith, not by sight” (2 Corinthians 5:7) [Note: One manuscript reads “through which he is seen”; the Lyon edition reads “Faith, therefore, by which we walk, and the vision which is seen, must be held.”].

Faith, then, is the means by which one walks, and vision is what is seen. In this life, where by living well through faith we make progress, we walk, as it were, with the steps of good works. But when we arrive at vision in the future, there will no longer be anywhere for us to walk as though making further progress [Note: One manuscript reads “but in the future there will no longer be anything …”; the Lyon edition, together with one Regius manuscript, reads “there will no longer be anything which …”]. Rather, we shall see with insatiable delight the vision itself to which we have arrived by walking spiritually through faith.

# CHAPTER SEVEN

## The saints cannot see God perfectly until they have attained the blessedness of the future life

[Col. 0424C]

### 1

Accordingly, all who wish fully and, with God’s help, are able to do so should be urged toward the contemplative life in such a way that they remember that the perfection of divine contemplation itself is reserved for that blessed life which is to come. There they will see God perfectly as he is, when they themselves too will have been perfected through the attainment of eternal life and the heavenly kingdom [Note: One manuscript reads “and, with the Lord’s help, has been able to attain”; the Lyon edition reads “has been able to attain.”].

Besides, if human frailty could have contemplated God’s substance perfectly here, the holy Evangelist would never have said: “No one has ever seen God.” He did not say, “No one will see him.” Indeed, to show clearly that the vision of God was not denied to holy people but postponed, what he denied in the present he promised for the future, saying: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.” Here too he did not say, “For they see God.”

Therefore, if God, who in this life could neither be seen nor can be seen without the assumption of some element, is to be seen in the future life, then the perfection of divine contemplation must be hoped for there, where there will be the fullness of every good thing.

# CHAPTER EIGHT

## What and how great the perfection of the contemplative life is in this flesh, and how those who despise the world cling to it in order to enjoy it
Therefore, the devotee of the contemplative life should approach his Creator with an enlightened heart; he should serve him attentively by contemplating him and enjoying him tirelessly [Note: [Col. 0425D] Two Colbert manuscripts, “so that he may approach the Creator.” Another manuscript, “and enjoy him insatiably”; another, “insatiably attain him,” or “use and enjoy him”]; he should continually long for him and, out of love for him, flee everything by which he could thereby be turned away [Note: [Col. 0425D] Five manuscripts, “flee”]. He should suspend all his thoughts and his entire hope upon delight in him [alternative reading: love of him]; devote himself to sacred meditation on the divine Scriptures; take pleasure in them, divinely enlightened [Col. 0425B]; and examine himself wholly in them, as in a kind of resplendent mirror [Note: [Col. 0425D] One manuscript, “shining forth”]. He should correct whatever he discovers to be morally wrong in himself, hold fast to what is right [Note: [Col. 0425D] The Cambrai manuscript, “what is right”], put what is misshapen into proper form, cultivate what is beautiful, preserve what is sound, and strengthen what is weak through assiduous reading [Note: [Col. 0425D] Two manuscripts, Regius and Cambrai, “preserve what is beautiful and cultivate what is sound”]. He should read the commandments of his Lord tirelessly, love them insatiably [Note: [Col. 0425D] Three manuscripts, “unfailingly.” One manuscript, “inexhaustibly”], fulfill them effectively, and, sufficiently instructed by them, recognize what he must avoid and what he must pursue. He should devote himself to searching out the mysteries of those same divine Scriptures; read there of Christ who was promised [Note: [Col. 0425D] The printed editions, “the promised Christ”] (John 1:45); see him represented there; understand the destruction of the obstinate people foretold by the prophets; mourn that it has been fulfilled [Note: [Col. 0425D] One Colbert manuscript, “fulfilled”]; rejoice in the salvation of the nations [Note: [Col. 0425D] One Colbert manuscript, “mourn what was prophesied and fulfilled concerning Christ’s death; future promises”]; hold fast to what was foretold and fulfilled in the past; believe the future promises; remain as far removed as possible from the tumult of worldly affairs [Note: [Col. 0425D] One Colbert manuscript, “let him be most remote”; another, “but let him pursue these things fervently”]; and fervently ponder those things by which he may kindle his soul with longing for the future reward [Note: [Col. 0425D] One Colbert manuscript, “frequently”]. He should devote himself to spiritual pursuits by which he may become better and better each day; love holy leisure, in which he may conduct the business of his soul; regard the world as dead to him; and present himself crucified to the seductive allurements of the world [Note: [Col. 0426D] One Colbert manuscript, “the flatteries and enticements”; the Cambrai manuscript, “the flatteries and enticements”]. He should place the vision of his Creator incomparably above the pleasure of present spectacles; continually raise himself, as his progress advances, to the summit of divine contemplation [Note: [Col. 0426D] Thus two manuscripts, together with the Lyon edition. Other codices, “as one who is making progress”]; never turn away, even for a moment, from considering the future promises to look back upon earthly things; direct the gaze of his mind unceasingly toward the place he desires to reach; set the blessedness of the future life before the eyes of his spirit [Col. 0426A] [Note: [Col. 0426D] One manuscript, “of his soul”; another, “of his mind”] and love it; fear and desire nothing temporal, lest either fear of losing a temporal possession or desire to acquire one soften the focus of his mind. Let pleasant things not corrupt him, nor adversity shake him; let favorable opinion not inflate him, nor unfavorable opinion cast him down; let false blame or praise neither increase his joys [Note: [Col. 0426D] One manuscript, “his joy”] nor diminish them. Let him not rejoice in temporal things at all, nor grieve over them. Unconquered amid joyful and sorrowful circumstances alike, let him maintain the same expression of a steadfast spirit [Note: [Col. 0426D] Six manuscripts, “with a steadfast mind”]; let nothing that the world promises or threatens shake the firm stability of his heart [Note: [Col. 0426D] Four manuscripts; the others, together with the printed editions, “of his breast”]; but, always remaining the same and like himself, let him be insensible alike to the losses and the gains of this world [Note: [Col. 0426D] Seven manuscripts, “to the losses and gains together”].

And when, moved by desire for the contemplative life, he has fulfilled these and similar requirements, let him believe with immovable conviction that he is not yet wholly perfect here, but is to be perfected [Col. 0426B] in that blessed life which is to come; and let him stretch himself toward that life, where he may see the substance of God with unveiled face [Note: [Col. 0426D] Thus all the manuscripts; the printed editions, “toward the same”].

## CHAPTER IX. That the difference between the perfection of this life and that of the future is as great as the difference between those who do not wish to sin and those who are no longer able to sin

1. For just as here, in comparison with those who live righteously [Note: [Col. 0426D] One manuscript, “by comparison”; another, “for comparison”], a person is called perfect because the righteous person fulfills the commandments, while the perfect person transcends the commandments, so, when compared with those who will be absolutely perfect in the blessed life, he is not, so to speak, perfectly perfect. Although all his iniquity has been forgiven, it has not yet been healed; rather, his weakness is being healed [Note: [Col. 0426D] Two manuscripts, “will be healed”]. And therefore, although he does not sin, so that he may be truly perfect, he can nevertheless sin [Col. 0426C] because he has not been healed by the removal of all weakness [Note: [Col. 0426D] Two manuscripts, “although he does not sin”]. Consequently, when he has been cleansed from every sin and will no longer be able to sin, there he will be perfectly sound and supremely perfect.

2. Here, however, no matter how greatly someone excels in holiness, no matter how outstandingly he surpasses others in perfection, he can indeed become perfect according to the measure of this life; but he is not so secure in his perfection that he need not be anxious about falling. And certainly, where there is anxiety, there is not complete blessedness. It must in no way be believed perfect if it is not secure; nor will it be secure unless eternal security has consumed all anxiety. Therefore those who are called blessed in this life are blessed in hope of the future blessedness [Note: [Col. 0426D] One Colbert manuscript, “but the saints themselves are not blessed here, but in that life”]; but in reality they will be blessed not here, but in that life [Col. 0427A], because there the blessedness of all the blessed will be perfect: there human nature, perfectly blessed, will see the glory of its Creator and its own glory, and will cleave to him without any defect in its blessedness.

## CHAPTER X. That here the saints saw God in an assumed creature

Nor should it disturb us that we read that God was also seen here by the righteous of ancient times. For he was not seen in this state of our humiliation as he will be seen in that state of glorification. Without a visible form of creation—in which, according to the dispensation of the times, he appeared wherever and to whatever righteous persons he wished—he neither could nor can be seen [Note: [Col. 0427D] Two Regius manuscripts and the Lyon edition read “in a form,” but apparently incorrectly]; but he will be able to be seen when our pilgrimage reaches the heavenly homeland, and blessed immortality clothes our mortal nature [Col. 0427B], and faith itself, by which all the truly faithful here believed in future things, brings them to divine contemplation and to the perception [Note: [Col. 0427D] Thus one Colbert manuscript. All the other manuscripts and the printed editions, “or perception”] of heavenly rewards.

## CHAPTER XI. On the nature of the glorified bodies that will exist in the future resurrection

There will indeed be bodies of different sexes, but without any bodily lust. There will be perfect love among all, and no desire [Augustine, *On the City of God*, Book XXII, chapter 17]. There, too, nothing belonging to visible creation will be hidden from bodily eyes, because the sight of incorruptible bodies will itself be incorruptible; and it will be incomparably more vigorous than it was here, so that nothing visible can be closed off from it. For sluggishness, not integrity, must be removed from bodies endowed with immortality; necessity, not will, must be removed, so that there they may be wherever they wish to be without delay of time [alternative reading: “of times”] or hindrance from weight. Thus the spiritual body, already perfected in equality with angelic blessedness, will follow without any difficulty wherever the spirit wishes to go.

Then the misery of sons, parents, and spouses who are not there will not be able to grieve the blessed [Augustine, *Retractions*, Book I, chapters 13 and 19], because the names of all the bodily relationships that our weakness possessed here are not admitted by the excellence of that blessedness. There, whoever they are, all will be one body, and each will rejoice either in his own happiness or in that of each individual other.

Let what has been said about the contemplative life suffice.

## CHAPTER XII. How great the difference is between the contemplative and active lives

[Col. 0427D]

1. Let us now briefly discuss the difference between the contemplative and active lives themselves. To make this distinction clearly evident, let us compare the two lives with one another by bringing forward their respective virtues. It belongs to the active life to make progress amid human affairs and to restrain the rebellious movements of the body by the command of reason; to the contemplative life, to rise above human things through the desire for perfection [Note: [Col. 0427D] One Colbert manuscript, “in desire”] and to labor unceasingly at increasing virtue [Note: [Col. 0427D] Two manuscripts and the Lyon edition, “to devote oneself more closely”]. The active life has progress; the contemplative life has the summit. The former makes a person holy; the latter, perfect.

It belongs to this life to inflict injuries on no one at all; to the other, to endure injuries inflicted with equanimity. Rather, to speak more precisely, the practitioner of the active life strives to forgive the person who sins against him; the devotee of the contemplative life is more ready to disregard the offenses by which he is assailed and not at all shaken than to forgive them.

The former restrains anger through the virtue of patience; he places the bridle of frugality on immoderate desires [Note: [Col. 0427D] Thus two Regius and two Colbert manuscripts; the others, with the printed editions, “brakes”]; he is touched by carnal desires but does not consent; he is assailed by the curiosity of this world but is not swept away; he is shaken by diabolical attack but is not overcome; and, subject in devoted mind to his God, he is not crushed by various temptations but tested.

The latter conquers with holy virtues all the affections by which mortal life is diversified; free from every desire and disturbance, he enjoys blessed tranquility; made superior to seductions and pleasures by an unencumbered mind, he is lifted up by the ineffable joy of divine contemplation [Note: [Col. 0428D] The Cambrai manuscript, “is made full”; the Regius manuscript, “is made”; another hand, “is affected”].

The former, by receiving the stranger, clothing the naked, governing the subordinate, redeeming the captive, and defending the violently oppressed, continually cleanses himself from all his iniquities and enriches his life with the fruits of good works [Note: [Col. 0428D] One manuscript, “with the fruits of good things”; another, “with the fruits of his good works”]. The latter, distributing his possessions for the use of the poor, strips himself from the world altogether [Note: [Col. 0428D] Two manuscripts, “strips himself from the world once for all”], draws himself heavenward with all his strength, casts the affairs of the world back upon the world, and restores himself in devoted mind to Christ. From him he prays, as a poor man, to receive immortal riches; as a weak man, he asks daily for protection; as a naked man, he longs to be clothed with immortality; as one oppressed by the weakness of the flesh, he begs to be defended from the assaults of invisible enemies; and, as a pilgrim, he desires that the heavenly homeland be granted to him.

2. The active life has an anxious course; the contemplative life, everlasting joy. In the former the kingdom is acquired; in the latter it is received. The former makes people knock at the door of good works as though with hands; the latter calls those who have been perfected into the homeland. In the former the world is despised; in the latter God will be seen.

And, to pass over much that I cannot mention, in this active life those who have become stronger than unclean spirits will, in that contemplative life, which is supremely blessed, be made equal to the holy angels by God’s rewarding them [Col. 0428D] [Note: [Col. 0428D] Three manuscripts, “will become so by the Lord”], and will reign with him forever, happy in that heavenly city.

Therefore, since much has already been said above about the contemplative life, and since the second book contains what is to be said about the active life, let what we have said suffice, so that we may consider the remaining matters, which we shall discuss in the following treatment from the third chapter to the end of this book. Let us now see whether the person entrusted with the care of governing the Church can become a participant in the contemplative life.

## CHAPTER XIII. That holy priests can become participants in the contemplative life

1. Whoever carefully considers what was said above about the contemplative life and, sufficiently instructed, understands when and where its perfection can be attained will not doubt that the leaders of the Churches can and ought to become devotees of the contemplative life. For whether, according to the opinion of some, the contemplative life is nothing other than knowledge of hidden and future things; or freedom from all worldly occupations [Note: [Col. 0429D] The Douai and Cologne editions, “calling”]; or study of the divine Scriptures; or, what is proved to be more perfect than these, the very vision of God [Col. 0429B] [Note: [Col. 0429D] Three manuscripts, “of the Lord,” and likewise somewhat below]; I do not see what obstacle could prevent holy priests from attaining these four things I have mentioned.

The first and the last—namely, knowledge of hidden and future things and the very vision of God—will be incomparably greater in that blessed life than in this one, which is entangled in various errors, since there both the knowledge of all things and the very substance of God will be seen fully and perfectly.

The two middle things, namely freedom from all worldly occupations and study of the divine Scriptures, can also be possessed by bishops here; but only by those who, removing themselves from all entanglements of secular business, do not languish in idleness but devote themselves to the business of their perfection; who, turning away from the folly of secular wisdom, devote themselves tirelessly to the word of God [Col. 0429C]; truly become wise, understand heavenly things, despise earthly things, rebuke those who contradict sound doctrine, instruct those who obey [Note: [Col. 0429D] Two manuscripts, “teach”], and devote themselves to the holy virtues by which they may draw nearer to God each day.

Such men, renowned both for their own progress and for that of all who are instructed through them [Note: [Col. 0429D] The Cologne edition, “among them”; one manuscript somewhat later, “in their advances”], receive here, as it were, a taste of the contemplative life, by which they may be summoned to it more ardently; but there, having been made eternally blessed, they will rejoice in its perfection.

Therefore they are not inflated because here they are honored as the heads of all Catholic believers; rather, they rejoice because there they will be more illustrious members of Christ, who is the head of priests and of all the faithful.

2. But if—God forbid—they become entangled in worldly business, extend the boundaries of their estates without limit through limitless greed [Col. 0430A], and give themselves everywhere to carefully contrived delicacies [Note: [Col. 0429D] One manuscript, “injure themselves”; another, “give themselves”; another, “eat”; another, “enrich themselves”], which weaken both soul [Note: [Col. 0429D] Two Colbert manuscripts, “the soul”] and body; if, deceived by the honors of a flattering crowd, they seek not the glory of Christ but their own, and put greater trust in the tongue of others than in their own conscience; if they place all their joy not in the reward of future things or in holiness of life, but solely in their own dignity [Note: [Col. 0429D] Four manuscripts, two Regius and two Colbert, together with the Lyon edition, which adds “that they are such”; two other manuscripts, “such as themselves, such as ...”; the Douai and Cologne editions, “not yet being such as they are believed to be” [Col. 0430D]], and, because they love being such as they are believed to be, never displease themselves and, pleasing themselves, are not concerned about their correction [Note: [Col. 0430D] Thus all the manuscripts, together with the Lyon edition. The Douai and Cologne editions, “about their salvation and correction”]—who would not understand that, if they persist in such conduct and do not reform before the end of this present life, such men cannot become participants in the contemplative life?

They do not attain it unless they have striven to be what they have been made; they must not strive to appear to be what they are not [Note: [Col. 0430D] Thus all the manuscripts, together with the Lyon, Douai, and Cologne editions, “to appear to be what they are not”], but to be what they are; distinguished not by the praises of others but by their own conduct [Col. 0430B]; conspicuous not merely for their dignity but rather for the nobility of priestly life [Note: [Col. 0430D] Thus four Colbert manuscripts, together with the Lyon, Douai, and Cologne editions, “distinction”]; priests not merely in title but in virtue, capable of the contemplative life and co-heirs of heavenly joys.

## CHAPTER XIV. Where the speaker excuses himself for not daring to teach the teachers of the Church

And lest my speech appear presumptuous to anyone if it shows what all priests ought not to be or ought to be [Note: [Col. 0430D] Two Colbert manuscripts and the Cologne edition, “to anyone.” One Colbert manuscript, “I should show”], I see that I ought not to speak generally, but about one person—and especially about you, who, if I may say so with your permission, rashly assigned to me this office of dangerous speech [Note: [Col. 0430D] One manuscript, “so that I might speak with your permission”].

I ought to address matters not unknown but familiar to you, matters that we customarily discuss among ourselves in mutual conversation [Col. 0430C]. Once these have been briefly explained, I do not think anyone could justly accuse my account [Note: [Col. 0430D] In one Colbert manuscript and two Regius manuscripts these words are absent: “rather than my discussion.” The Lyon edition, together with two Colbert manuscripts, reads, “my account rather than my discussion,” while the later editions have, “could”] of excessive presumption—as though I dared to teach my fathers, from whom I am ready to receive and learn the rule of life.

## CHAPTER XV. On the negligence of a priest who, acting contrary to his teaching, cannot fulfill the role of teacher

Recall, then, how many things, and of what kind, you used to say, while I listened and approved [Note: [Col. 0430D] The Douai and Cologne editions, “which you approved”; two manuscripts, “you used to say”], about the administration of a bishop who, neglecting the care of the people entrusted to him, desires present goods more ardently than future ones; and, forgetting that he must render an account to the Shepherd of all shepherds not only for himself but also for the flock entrusted to him [Col. 0431A] [Note: [Col. 0431D] One Regius manuscript, “will render an account”], does not consider his own losses or those of his people.

He is not saddened by the sins of those who fall, nor gladdened by the good conduct of those who advance; rather, concerned only for himself—and often not even for himself—he is unaware of what good or evil is being done by his people.

He does not preach perseverance to the righteous, repentance to the wicked [Note: [Col. 0431D] One Colbert manuscript, “to the unjust”], contempt for the world to the converted, or future punishments to those who turn away. He cannot say to those who despise his admonition, “Consider the judgment to come” [Note: [Col. 0431D] The Cologne edition, “the sentence to come”], when perhaps he himself does not consider it; to lovers of the world, “Do not love the world,” if the love of the world delights him; to the ambitious, “Put an end to ambition,” if ruinous ambition is rushing him to destruction [Note: [Col. 0431D] Five manuscripts, “Put an end to ambition now”]; to drunkards, “Beware of drunkenness” [Note: [Col. 0431D] The Cambrai manuscript, “of drunkenness”], if he himself stuffs himself with wine to the point of loss of reason.

Sickened by sumptuous banquets [Col. 0431B] [Note: [Col. 0431D] One Colbert manuscript, “weighed down”], he cannot commend abstinence to his people, since he tramples upon it. Addicted to the vice of greed, he cannot dissuade the greedy from loving money. Clinging to enmities, he will not dare to reconcile the minds of those at odds with priestly tranquility. He is ashamed to preach justice to judges, which he himself corrupts by favoring a powerful person. Nor does he defend the oppressed if he either honors or despises persons according to their standing.

Whatever good he fails to do or evil he commits, he will neither command to be done nor forbid, because by the contradiction between his conduct and his teaching he either loses or diminishes the authority necessary for teaching [Note: [Col. 0431D] One Colbert manuscript, “the authority of speaking”].

## CHAPTER XVI. What danger awaits those who wish either to abandon the Church entrusted to them or to neglect governing it energetically

As you recalled these and similar matters [Note: [Col. 0431D] Two Colbert manuscripts, “you accepted the episcopate”], you regretted having accepted the episcopate, which, just as it brings honor to its administrator when properly administered [Note: [Col. 0431D] One manuscript, “if he administers it well”; another, “if it is properly administered”], so condemns the person who despises it.

Finally, when you wished to leave the Church entrusted to you, as though unequal to governing it, and to withdraw into some solitude—not so much out of a desire for quiet as out of despair of your own office [Note: [Col. 0431D] Seven manuscripts omit “not”], no other consideration compelled you to change your decision for the better except that you feared incurring a greater danger [Note: [Col. 0431D] One manuscript, “greater”; three manuscripts, “to bear down more heavily”]. For if it is dangerous not to steer a ship cautiously amid waves, how much more dangerous is it to abandon a ship tossed by swelling waves in a storm?

Just as it is better not to board such a ship, so, once it has been undertaken, it is fitting—casting away fear of the surging sea and embracing hope of reaching the destination—to bring it into port without throwing away any of its cargo [Col. 0431D] [Note: [Col. 0431D] One manuscript, “it is holier”; seven manuscripts, “not to approach”].

When this comparison pleased you, I added: “And therefore the Church, which like a great ship sails across the sea of this world; which in this life is battered by the various waves of temptations; which is tossed in different directions by the persecutions of unclean spirits, like stormy waves; which is dashed against the shoals of scandals; and which is enclosed as though by a bank of burdensome sand [Note: [Col. 0431D] All the manuscripts, “which is enclosed as though by an embankment”]—must not be abandoned but governed.

For just as, when guided by the vigilance of its pilot, it brings safely to port all whom it carries, so, if submerged by waves or broken apart, it will destroy not only all whom it contains but also the pilot himself.”

## CHAPTER XVII. Where the anxious man, distressed that he can neither abandon nor govern the Church, is encouraged by the suggestion that he may govern it better by his example

[Col. 0432B]

As I continued with these and similar remarks [Note: [Col. 0432D] Three manuscripts, “these and similar things”], you were deeply moved and groaned, saying that you had been brought into a predicament which you could neither fulfill by any effort nor abandon without sin.

Then, sympathizing with your devout groans through the affection of heart by which I am bound to you [Note: [Col. 0432D] One manuscript, “to which I am bound by you”], I said, entreating you, that you could accomplish what you could not set forth by teaching [Note: [Col. 0432D] Thus the printed editions. Five manuscripts omit “I said”; another manuscript, “while entreating, I suggested that you could accomplish what you could not accomplish by teaching”; another, “by saying”; another, “you cannot”].

I said that faithful Catholics are usually advanced more by good examples than by eloquent words; that the highest and perfect form of teaching is that which a spiritual way of life displays, not that which empty speech boasts of [Note: [Col. 0432D] Thus the printed editions. Three manuscripts, “which it displayed, not which empty speech boasted”; two manuscripts, “boasted”; one manuscript, “will have boasted”]; that on the day of judgment words, but deeds, will be sought from us [Note: [Col. 0432D] The Lyon edition, together with six manuscripts, “from you”; other editions, “from us”]; and that it is not easy to persuade anyone that what the tongue teaches is possible if life disagrees with the tongue [Note: [Col. 0432D] Four manuscripts, “to persuade”].

But what you confirm by doing—whether you preach it or do not preach it [Col. 0432C]—can be proved possible, and you impress it upon those who wish to imitate you with a certain pleasure in its very possibility [Note: [Col. 0432D] One manuscript, “you make it welcome”]. You took some pleasure in this suggestion of mine and immediately replied, if I am not mistaken, as follows.

## CHAPTER XVIII. That it is of little value to demonstrate what must be done by example unless the priest also teaches and shows what must be believed

And indeed, if all perfection consisted only in conduct and not also in faith, and if on the day of judgment it were asked not what a person had believed but what he had done, who would be so arrogant as to flatter himself about his own righteousness while neglecting the authority of ecclesiastical teaching? [Note: [Col. 0432D] Three Colbert manuscripts, “the usefulness”].

For, according to the Apostle (2 Thessalonians 3:9; 1 Peter 5:3), we must not only provide an example for the faithful, but must also instruct those very faithful people who have been divinely entrusted to us for instruction [Col. 0432D] [Note: [Col. 0432D] Two manuscripts, “to be protected”; one manuscript, “to be observed”; another, “to be instructed”; another, “entrusted by divine ordinance”].

We must teach concerning the Father how he alone is understood to be unbegotten; concerning the Son, how he is begotten from him; concerning the Holy Spirit, how he proceeds from the Father and the Son [Note: [Col. 0433D] One manuscript, “is proceeding, and is neither unbegotten ...”], and can be called neither unbegotten nor begotten; how these three are one; and how this one is not divided but distinguished into three.

We must teach how neither the Father nor the Holy Spirit, but the Son alone, ineffably born from the Father alone, assumed the whole human being without any change in his substance; how he proved himself true God and true man through his powers and sufferings; allowed himself to be grasped; willed to be killed; rose again on the third day; raised into heaven by his own power the human nature assumed from us [Note: [Col. 0433D] Thus three Colbert manuscripts. The printed editions, “into heaven.” One manuscript, “into the heavens”]; and, through the example of his resurrection, gave us who have been regenerated in him the blessed hope of rising again.

We must teach how he made us his members; threatened punishment to those who did not believe in him or departed from him [Col. 0433B]; and promised the heavenly kingdom to those who cling to him.

## CHAPTER XIX. On the power of faith: that it includes not only believing and understanding but also doing good

A priest must know these and other things in order to teach them, and the people must believe them in order to understand what is taught [Note: [Col. 0433D] Three manuscripts, “so that they may understand what is taught”], as the Apostle says: “Unless you believe, you will not understand” (Isaiah 7:9, according to the Septuagint) [Note: [Col. 0433D] One manuscript, “I shall speak concerning the prophet—or perhaps concerning the prophecy—who says ...”].

From this it is understood that faith does not arise from understanding, but understanding from faith. A person does not believe because he understands, but understands because he believes; and whoever understands acts well, as it is written elsewhere: “He refused to understand, so as to act well” (Psalm 35:4). It does not say, “He was unable,” but “He refused to understand,” so that we may recognize that “refusing to understand” means nothing other than refusing to believe [Col. 0433C].

Thus, in order to act well, a person should strive to understand; and in order to understand, he should believe. But because the same Apostle says, “Faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of God” (Romans 10:17) [Note: [Col. 0433D] One Colbert manuscript, “through the word of Christ”; two manuscripts, “through the word”; the others, together with the printed editions, “through the word of God,” according to the Greek text of the Apostle], the teacher of the Church must preach what the one who is to believe should hear, because without preaching there will be no hearing. The same Apostle bears witness and says: “How will they hear without a preacher?” (ibid., 14) [Note: [Col. 0433D] The printed editions, “bearing witness”; one manuscript, “testifying”].

Therefore, if no one hears without a preacher, if no one believes without hearing, if no one understands without faith, and if no one acts well without understanding, the word of faith must be preached [Note: [Col. 0433D] Three manuscripts, “the word of God”] so that the hearer may believe, the believer may understand, and the one who understands may practice good works with perseverance [Note: [Col. 0433D] One manuscript, “so that he may hear and believe”].

For a person who can exercise the freedom of the will is justified neither by works without faith nor by faith alone without works [Col. 0434A] [Note: [Col. 0433D] These words, “the person who can exercise the freedom of the will,” are absent from the Lyon edition. Two manuscripts, “those able to exercise”; another, “of one able to exercise”].

And therefore, if one believes with the heart for righteousness but confesses with the mouth for salvation, whoever has not believed, because he does not have faith [Note: [Col. 0433D] The Cambrai manuscript, “because whoever ...”], can possess neither righteousness of heart nor salvation.

## CHAPTER XX. That it does a priest no good to live well if, by remaining silent, he does not correct those who live badly [Note: [Col. 0434D] One Colbert manuscript, “does not rebuke.” Two Regius manuscripts, “For priests, even if they live well, . . . correct [them].”]

1. But as for what the Apostle says (1 Peter 5:3), that we ought to provide an example for the faithful, what good will it do if the person entrusted with the care either of exhorting the good or of chastising the wicked presents himself, by living well, as an example for the good to imitate, but does not correct the wicked by remaining silent?

For, unless I am mistaken, a priest must live holily for this reason: so that his words may not be rendered empty by deeds that contradict them; so that he may not fail to do what he preaches should be done, or presume to preach what he does not do [Col. 0434B] [Note: [Col. 0434D] Seven manuscripts and the Lyon edition omit “but if he acts otherwise”; they then read “he advances,” not “he does not advance.” One manuscript, “he will advance”].

But if he acts otherwise, he accomplishes nothing among those who know his life. For he has been placed over the Church of God so that, by living well, he may not only instruct others through the example of his conduct, but also, by preaching boldly, place their sins before the eyes of each person [Note: [Col. 0434D] Two Colbert manuscripts, “make himself imitable to each person and place [these sins] before their eyes”]; show what punishment awaits the stubborn and what glory awaits the obedient.

Let him not, by despairing of anyone’s salvation, despise them [Note: [Col. 0434D] One Regius manuscript, “let him not despairing of salvation despise the souls of those unwilling to be corrected, but mourn for them”]; let him mourn for the souls unwilling to be corrected, imitating the Apostle who says: “That I may mourn over many of those who sinned previously and did not repent” (1 Corinthians 12:21); and again: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I am not on fire?” (2 Corinthians 11:29).

2. Knowing, therefore, that if he spares any rich and powerful people or favors those who live badly [Note: [Col. 0434D] Two Regius manuscripts and the Cambrai manuscript, together with the Lyon edition, “if he spares or favors any rich and powerful people who live badly”; one Colbert manuscript, “and spares or favors the powerful”], he will destroy them and perish with them [Col. 0434C] [Note: [Col. 0434D] One manuscript, “destroy them”], he must live holily for the sake of example and teach for the sake of his administrative office [Note: [Col. 0434D] One manuscript, “and teach piously”], certain that his own righteousness will avail him nothing when the soul of one who perishes is required from his hand.

When anyone else perishes, if no obligation to teach rests upon him, he alone will pay the penalty for his own crime [Note: [Col. 0434D] Two Regius manuscripts, “for his own crimes”]. But the person entrusted with the stewardship of the word—even if he lives holily, yet either blushes or fears to rebuke those who live ruinously—perishes together with all those who perish while he remains silent.

And what will it profit him not to be punished for his own sin, when he is to be punished for another’s? I am mistaken, unless the Lord speaks of this through the prophet Ezekiel under a terrifying warning, saying to him: “And you, son of man, I have appointed you as a watchman for the house of Israel” (Ezekiel 33:7).

Nor should we hear this casually, that he calls the priest a watchman: for just as it is the duty of a watchman to look out from a higher place and observe more than everyone else, so the priest ought to be higher than all in the sublimity of his purpose and to possess the grace of a greater knowledge [Note: [Col. 0435D] Thus all the manuscripts; the printed editions, “of his stated purpose”], by which he can instruct those who live under his care.

### 3. Let us now see what the divine word contains. “Hearing a word from my mouth, you shall announce it to them from me” [Note: One Colbertine manuscript has “contains.” Another has “continues.”] (ibid.). This means that the priest should say what he has learned from divine reading, what God has inspired in him, not what he has discovered through human presumption [Note: Two manuscripts have “presumption.”]. “You shall announce it to them from me,” he says. “From me”: you shall speak my words to them, not your own [Note: Two manuscripts have “you shall not speak words from yourself”; another has “you shall speak to them.”]. There is no reason for you to be puffed up by them as though they were your own possessions [Note: Printed editions have “in which among them”; five manuscripts have “which from them.”]. “Announce it to them from me,” he says.

But let us now hear what he is to announce: “If, when I say to the wicked man, ‘Wicked man, you shall surely die,’ you do not speak, so that the wicked man may guard himself from his way, that wicked man shall die in his iniquity, but I shall require his blood from your hand” [Note: Printed editions have “if you do not speak”; the manuscripts have “if you have not spoken.”] (ibid., 8). What could be expressed more clearly [Note: Four manuscripts have “what could be said more plainly?” Printed editions have “what can be said more plainly?”]? What could be said more openly? “If,” he says, “you do not speak to the wicked man so that he may guard himself from his wickedness, and he perishes, I shall require his blood from your hand” [Note: One manuscript has “he indeed perishes, but his blood.”]. This is what he means: “If you do not announce his sins to him, if you do not rebuke him so that he may turn from his wickedness and live, I shall destroy with everlasting flames both you, who did not rebuke him, and him, who sinned while you were silent.” Who, I ask, will have a heart so stony, who so hard-hearted, that this sentence will not terrify him? Who will be so estranged from faith that he will not believe this sentence?

## CHAPTER XXI. A sorrowful description of a priest living according to the flesh

[Col. 0435C]

### 1. Yet we, delighting in present things, while in this life we seek our own comforts and honors—not to be better, but to be richer; not to be holier, but to be more honored—we hasten to preside over others [Note: One manuscript has “we hasten to be superior to the others.”]. We think about our own pleasures, domination, wealth, and the other fleshly allurements, not about the Lord’s flock, which has been entrusted to us to feed and protect [Note: One manuscript lacks the word “fleshly.”]. We want to be called shepherds, yet we do not strive to be shepherds; we avoid the labor of our office and seek its dignity.

We do not drive away the beasts of unclean spirits as they tear the flock apart, and what they leave behind we ourselves consume [Note: One manuscript has “but what…”]. When we see sinners who are rich or powerful [Note: One manuscript adds “we observe”], we not only fail to rebuke them, but even honor them, lest, offended, they fail to send us their customary gifts or withdraw the services we desire. Thus, captivated by their gifts and services—or rather, through these things made dependent upon them—we fear speaking to them about their sin or about the future judgment.

And therefore the divine word harshly crushes our pride, but our hearing admits nothing by which we might improve, because, captivated by the sweetness of the present life, we do not wish to consider what eternal punishment awaits our negligence [Note: One manuscript from the Colbertine collection and the Cambrai manuscript have “and what eternal punishment awaits our negligence.”].

### 2. These words, then, are addressed to shepherds, whose empty title we flatter ourselves with:

“Thus says the Lord: Woe to the shepherds of Israel who fed themselves. Are not flocks fed by shepherds? You ate the milk and clothed yourselves with the wool; you slaughtered what was fat, but you did not feed my flock. You did not strengthen the weak, heal the sick, bind up what was broken [Note: Three Colbertine manuscripts have “what is broken”; the Lyon edition has “what was broken you did not bind up.”], or bring back what had been cast away. You did not seek what had perished, but ruled them harshly and with power. And my sheep were scattered because there was no shepherd, and they became food for every beast of the field” (Ezek. 34:1 ff.).

And a little later:

“Therefore, shepherds, hear the word of the Lord. As I live, says the Lord God [Note: Two manuscripts do not have “because” here], because my flocks became prey and my sheep food for every beast of the field, because there was no shepherd—and because the shepherds did not seek my flock, but the shepherds fed themselves and did not feed my flock [Note: Six manuscripts lack the word “my”]—therefore, shepherds, hear the word of the Lord. Thus says the Lord: Behold, I myself am against the shepherds. I shall require my flock at their hand, and I shall make them cease, so that they will no longer feed my flock [Col. 0436C] and the shepherds will no longer feed themselves” (ibid., 7 ff.).

### 3. Who would not tremble at these words? Who would receive them without unbearable fear of the coming examination, unless he either does not understand or does not believe what is to come? But because God set down everything he wished to be observed so openly and confirmed it with the authority of his name, we more readily—something that is also unspeakable to say—despise it [Note: Four manuscripts lack “because.”], pretending that we do not understand or believe such clear and divine statements [Note: The Cambrai manuscript has “and that we in no way fail to understand such clear things.”].

When we hear, “Thus says the Lord,” who would not believe that what the Lord says will come to pass [Note: Four manuscripts have “who would not believe that it will come to pass?” Printed editions have “who would not believe that it will come to pass?”], unless he does not believe God? When he says, “Woe to the shepherds,” who would not understand that this “woe” is pronounced as a curse [Note: Two manuscripts have “he places”; one has “it is placed”], and that we are signified by the name of shepherds, unless he gives no thought to what is to come [Note: Four manuscripts have “what is to come”]?

We have undertaken, as shepherds, to receive the Lord’s flocks in order to feed them [Note: All manuscripts have this wording; the printed editions have “we, having become shepherds, undertook the Lord’s flock to feed it”].
