Yet we feed ourselves when we do not look after the welfare of the flocks, but attend to whatever nurtures and increases our own pleasures [Note: Four manuscripts have “desires”]. We gladly receive the milk and wool of Christ’s sheep—namely, the daily offerings and the tithes of the faithful [Note: The Cambrai manuscript has “that is, the daily offerings and the tithes”]—and lay aside the care of feeding and restoring the flocks from which, by a perverse ordering, we wish to be fed.

We do not heal by spiritual counsel the person weakened by sins; we do not strengthen or restore by priestly aid the person broken by various tribulations [Note: Five manuscripts have this reading; the printed editions have “and restore”]; we do not call the erring back to the way of salvation [Note: Three manuscripts have “the one who is mistaken”]; we do not seek with pastoral concern the person already lost through despair of forgiveness. We have become powerful only for this purpose: to claim tyrannical domination over our subjects, not to defend the afflicted against the violence of the powerful, who rage against them like wild beasts.

### 4. Hence it is that some, grievously wearied not only by the powerful of this world but, worse, by us, perish; and the Lord terrifies us with the threat that he will require them from our hand, saying: “I shall require my sheep at the hand of the shepherds, and I shall make them cease, so that they will no longer feed them” (Ezek. 34:20) [Note: The Cambrai manuscript has “not so much.”].

What else does this mean than that I shall strip shepherds who feed themselves and not my flock of the eminence of their dignity, and cast them among the reprobate because they were unwilling to preserve their honor?

Terrified by consideration of these and similar things [Note: This is the reading of the Lyon edition and five manuscripts. Other editions, those of Douai and Cologne, have: “The prophet, terrified, says, ‘Fear and trembling came upon me, and the darkness of my sins covered me.’” Two manuscripts among these have “came upon me.”]:

“Fear and trembling came upon me, and darkness covered me, and I said: Who will give me wings like a dove, and I shall fly away and rest?” (Ps. 54:6–7).

This is the whole reason why, remembering my ignorance and the future end, I groaned and wished, laying down the burden of my episcopate, to flee far away, remain in solitude, and there await the Lord, who would save me from my faintheartedness and from the storm of anxieties unbearable to me.

## CHAPTER XXII. That, according to the prophet’s word, those who perversely despise the reproofs or admonitions of priests perish through their own fault

### 1. To this I replied [Note: One Royal manuscript has “with you”]:

“You toss these matters about in spiteful complaints, exaggerating them as an attack upon bishops—or certainly upon the episcopate itself—as though, in the place where you read the things that reasonably move you, there were not also the things that, omitted by you, I shall briefly touch upon in defense of the priestly office [Note: One Royal manuscript has “as though, in the place where you read those things to which you are reasonably moved, there were not also…”; one Colbertine manuscript has “unreasonably,” though less appropriately].

“After those words in which the end of negligent priests is displayed, the prophet speaks in this way about a bishop who attends to his duty: ‘But if, when you announce to the wicked man that he should turn from his ways, he does not turn from his way, that wicked man shall die in his iniquity, but you have delivered your soul’ (Ezek. 33:9).

“Here it is certainly shown clearly enough that, whether their hearers make progress or do not make progress, priests must not be silent toward them. Nor are priests guilty if perhaps the people do not hear their words or, having heard them, despise them [Note: Three manuscripts have “hear them, despise them … withdraw from them”], but only if they cease correcting them. For if the people, whether by the example of the life of their superiors or by the word of instruction, remain obstinate and fail to improve, they themselves become the cause of their own destruction; and they will certainly not be able to involve their teachers—whose examples and words they alike despise—in their own crimes.”

### 2. The same prophet develops this more clearly elsewhere, saying:

“If the watchman sees the sword coming upon the land, and blows the trumpet and announces it to the people, then whoever hears the sound of the trumpet and does not take heed, and the sword comes and takes him away, his blood shall be upon his own head. He heard the sound of the trumpet and did not take heed; his blood shall be upon him. But if he guards himself, he shall save his soul” (Ezek. 33:3 ff.) [Note: Six manuscripts have “when he sees.”].

The divine word sufficiently shows what the one who performs the watchman’s office must do: when he sees the sword coming upon the land—that is, God’s anger upon sinners devoted to earthly deeds [Note: One manuscript has “devoted to earthly actions.”]—he must not be silent at all, but must not cease to announce to them, as long as they remain attached to their iniquities, the destruction of divine indignation that threatens them [Note: One manuscript has “is impending.”]. He must rebuke them clearly and publicly, for this is indicated by the name “trumpet,” so that, correcting themselves from their crimes, they may escape the punishment of future condemnation.

But if earthly people despise the one who rebukes them and announces the future anger that already threatens those who despise it [Note: Five manuscripts lack “already”], their blood will be upon themselves; and the priest who did not keep silent about their sins cannot share in the punishment awaiting them.

## CHAPTER XXIII. That priests, even when they are otherwise capable, should teach so simply that everyone understands them as they teach

Nor will a bishop excuse himself on the ground of inexperience, as though he were unable to teach because he lacks adequate and polished speech. For a priest’s teaching ought to be nothing other than his life, and hearers can make sufficient progress if they hear simply preached to them what they see being done spiritually by their teachers, as the Apostle says: “Though unskilled in speech, yet not in knowledge” (2 Cor. 11:6).

From this it is understood that a teacher of the Church should not boast of displaying refined speech, lest he appear to wish not to build up the Church of God but rather to display how learned he is [Note: Two manuscripts have “not to wish to build up the Church.”]. Let him therefore place all his confidence in preaching not in the splendor of words but in the power of deeds. Let him delight not in the acclamations of the people shouting for him, but in their tears; nor seek to await applause from the people, but groaning.

Let the ecclesiastical teacher labor especially for this: that those who hear him become better through sound discussions, not supporters through empty flattery [Note: One Colbertine manuscript has “empty flattery.”]. Let him first shed the tears that he wishes to see poured out by his hearers, and thus kindle them through the compunction of his own heart.

The bishop’s speech should be so simple and clear—even if less Latin, nevertheless disciplined and serious—that it excludes no one, however unlearned, from understanding it [Note: One Colbertine manuscript has “so that no one, however unlearned, is excluded”], but descends with a certain delight into the hearts of all who hear it [Note: One manuscript has “the breasts,” i.e. hearts].

## CHAPTER XXIV. The difference between teachers who build up the Church by teaching simply and those who flaunt their eloquence in polished declamations

[Col. 0439B]

The way of declaimers is one thing, and that of teachers ought to be another. The former passionately desire, with all the strength of their eloquence, the splendor of elaborated declamation; the latter seek the glory of Christ in sober and customary speech. The former clothe empty matters in costly verbal ornament; the latter adorn true propositions and commend simple words [Note: The Lyon edition alone has “and lend distinction to.”]. The former try to conceal the deformity of their thoughts beneath a kind of ornamented veil of speech; the latter strive to beautify the rusticity of their expressions with precious meanings. The former place all their praise in the favor of the crowd; the latter in the power of God.

The former speak in a way that wins applause, yet by their declaiming provide their hearers with no benefit [Note: Two manuscripts and the Lyon edition have “provide no benefit”]; the latter teach in ordinary speech and form imitators of themselves, because they do not corrupt their reasoning [possibly “their discourse”] through any affectation of artificial composition [Note: Three manuscripts have “through affectation.”].

## CHAPTER XXV. What priests who wish to share in the contemplative life ought to be like

### 1. Therefore, if holy priests—not such as those whom divine threat declares destined for judgment and condemnation, but such as apostolic teaching commends—convert many to God by living holily and preaching; if they act in everything humbly rather than commandingly, and present themselves through the zeal of holy love as equals of those placed under them [Note: Three manuscripts lack “from”]; if they heal the weaknesses of those living according to the flesh, sometimes with the medicines of salutary words, sometimes enduring with the strength of patience those whom they judge incurable; if in their conduct and preaching they seek not their own glory but Christ’s; and if they do not miserably squander their words and deeds in exchange for winning favor [Note: The Cambrai manuscript has “at the price”], but always ascribe to God whatever honor is shown to them as priests who live and teach;

if they are not puffed up by the dutiful greetings of those who approach them, but are burdened by them, and believe that they are not being honored but weighed down by the praises of their flatterers; if they comfort the afflicted, feed the needy, clothe the naked, ransom captives, and receive strangers; if they show the erring the way of salvation and promise those in despair the hope of obtaining forgiveness [Note: One manuscript has simply “to those in despair”]; if they urge on those who are running [Note: One manuscript has “impede them”], kindle those who are lingering, and steadfastly perform whatever belongs to their office—who could be so estranged from faith as to doubt that such men share in the contemplative virtue [Note: Two manuscripts have “the contemplative life”], since through their example and word many become fellow heirs of the heavenly kingdoms?

### 2. These are ministers of the word, God’s fellow workers, the utterance of the Holy Spirit [Note: This is the reading of the manuscripts and the Lyon edition; the Douai and Cologne editions have “hearers of God”]. Through such men God is reconciled to the people, and the people are instructed by God [Note: One Colbertine manuscript has “the people are instructed by the people.”]

These are the successors of the Lord’s apostles. They govern the Churches that the apostles founded through wondrous works, endowed with wondrous apostolic virtues [Note: The Cambrai manuscript has “by judgments”]. They defend the catholic faith either by disputation or, if necessity demands it, by the laceration of their own limbs; for the sake of preserving it with all their strength [Note: Six manuscripts and the Lyon edition have “with all their entrails”], they are even prepared to die after having lost their possessions.

They grow through the virtues of catholic believers, who make progress through them with God as their author. Clinging inseparably to their God, in whom they believe that solid and lasting goods have been stored up for them, they disdain the fleeting joys of this world.

Thus far, over three chapters, we have prolonged our discussion through the length of an extensive exposition [Note: The Cambrai manuscript has “a discussion full of gaps”]. In it, as I think, we have sufficiently shown what the distinctive character of the contemplative life is, what its difference from the active life is, and how priests may become sharers in contemplative virtue [Note: One manuscript lacks “of virtue”; another has “of the contemplative life.”; one manuscript has “may become participants.”].

And so, bringing this book at last to an end, in the second volume, with God aiding our undertaking through your prayers, we shall discuss three other chapters; and in the third book we shall treat the remaining four, which contain the discussion of vices and virtues.

# BOOK TWO

## PREFACE

[Col. 0441A]

### 1. In the preceding book I embraced the subject of the contemplative life [Note: The Cambrai manuscript has “I have embraced it; now, as far as my strength allows.”]. Now, according to the strength that the Lord will deign to grant, I have resolved, as I promised, to discuss the active life.

Therefore, just as I did in the preface to the first volume, here too I briefly explain the necessity of my office [Note: Six manuscripts have “the necessity in which…”]. For if I could have refused without the guilt of disobedience what you commanded, I would never have voluntarily exposed myself to be gnawed by the malicious tooth of detractors [Note: One Colbertine manuscript has “the malicious tooth”]. They are unwilling to notice how reluctantly I undertook to write these things and will perhaps attribute everything that belongs to your command to the fault of vanity.

This will be especially so if, when speaking about matters in which the conduct of nearly all ecclesiastics is described as something to be maintained, I set down something that offends the minds of those living according to the world. And when, in the description of ecclesiastical life, they see their own customs—customs that they prefer to be unknown rather than corrected—made public, they will rage against me, moved by fleshly feeling, as though I were a betrayer of their actions. Although, by God’s gift, they may judge what has been brought forth to have been reasonably said, they will nevertheless insist that it ought not to have been said by me; and thus they will mock either the subject of the discussion or the person discussing it.

But since a sound mind ought incomparably more to desire the fruit of obedience than to avoid the reproach of unjust detraction, I judged that I would be less burdened by the words of my critics than exposed to the danger of obstinate disobedience [Note: One Royal manuscript has “I judged that I would be less burdened in my judgment by the words of those criticizing me.” Another Royal manuscript, with the Lyon edition, has “I believed I was lightly burdened by the words of those criticizing me, in my judgment.” The Douai and Cologne editions, with four Colbertine manuscripts, have “I judged that I was lightly burdened by the words criticizing my writings, in my judgment.” The Cambrai manuscript has “to burden the words of those criticizing, in my judgment.”].

Accordingly, confident that you will obtain from the Lord through your prayers the ability to complete the work which you ordered me to undertake, and that you will excuse my presumption before those who will judge me, I shall complete the work I have undertaken with your prayers assisting me [Note: One manuscript has “while your prayers assist.”].

### 2. But before I deal separately with each of the matters you proposed, I think I should say a few general things about the very subject to be treated in this little book. These will make it evident why I prefaced that I might be resented by those who attend more to who is speaking than to what is said; who examine not the reasoning of statements but the dignity of the speakers by a perverse judgment [Note: One manuscript from the Colbertine collection has “by a perverse examination”]; and who disdain even to hear what they do not wish to do or to have done [Note: One manuscript lacks “for themselves.”].

They are more ready to remain ignorant of some point of teaching, even one they wish to know, than to learn it from an inferior person. Yet truth, from whatever source it shines forth, should be attributed not to human ingenuity but to God. Nor should it be thought to belong to certain persons rather than to everyone. In itself it is so great and of such a character [Note: Five manuscripts have “such and so great”] that it is not great because great men have taught it; rather, it makes great those from whom it can be taught or learned [Note: Six manuscripts have this reading; the printed editions have “from whom it can be spoken.”].

You therefore wished me to explain to you the distinctive character of the active life, so that you could prove that you had always lived and were living according to it with your own people, not so that you might learn from my discussions how you ought to live [Note: The Lyon edition has “how you should live among them.”].

For the religious mode of life is active life. It teaches how superiors should govern and love those living under them, and, being no less concerned for their salvation than for their own, provide with paternal care whatever they know to be beneficial for them. It also teaches how those subject to their superior should serve him as members serve the head, and guard his commands with the greatest love as though they were the command of God, judging that to be holy, salutary, and necessary for themselves which pleases their ruler—not what the arrogance of a corrupt mind dictates to them for their destruction.

Therefore, founded upon the virtue of obedience and patience, they do not scrutinize the decisions of their superiors but carry them out. And when the rigor of discipline requires that they be rebuked severely [Note: Three Colbertine manuscripts have “so that they are rebuked severely”; the printed editions have “with severity”; three manuscripts have “severely and harshly”], they bear the correction they have received with courage. They attribute their punishment not to the moods of those by whom they have been rebuked, but to their own negligences.

The contents of this little book will also explain how priests should treat and govern their fellow citizens, both commoners and nobles, rich and powerful. I would not have dared to write these things, as I have often said, if I had been able to refuse you anything [Note: One manuscript has “if I had been able.”].

But now let us set out the chapters themselves for discussion. You have therefore asked whether those who trample upon the divine commandments should be endured with equanimity, or whether they should be rebuked with ecclesiastical severity according to the measure of their sin.

## TABLE OF CONTENTS

**Chapter I.** That, according to the diversity of sinners, some are to be borne and others chastised.

**Chapter II.** On the praise of holy priests.

**Chapter III.** On apostolic testimonies and their exposition.

**Chapter IV.** An objection: why holy priests, whose duty it is to rebuke those living disastrously, should nevertheless endure religious hypocrites with equanimity.

**Chapter V.** A response showing for what necessary reasons the weakness of certain people should be treated gently.

**Chapter VI.** That those who accuse the sins of others impatiently are the ones who do not consider their own.

**Chapter VII.** How much remedy confession of sins contains, and what punishment deceitful concealment deserves.

**Chapter VIII.** That those who rebuke unjustly and not simply are vain and must be condemned by divine judgment.

**Chapter IX.** That priests should possess nothing as their own and should receive the resources of the Church as common property, since they are destined to render an account to God.

**Chapter X.** With what harm to their souls those who can support themselves from their own means receive from the Church that feeds the poor.

**Chapter XI.** Who are the people who are supported by the resources of the Church even with benefit to their souls.

**Chapter XII.** What clerics should do when their weakness prevents them from despising their own possessions.

**Chapter XIII.** What true joys and true riches are, and what impediment present goods bring to those who love future goods [Note: Three manuscripts have “what impediment they bring.”].

**Chapter XIV.** How the Apostle’s statement is to be understood: “Those who work in the sanctuary eat what comes from the sanctuary.”

**Chapter XV.** On greed, and how it rules those whom it has once invaded.

**Chapter XVI.** That those possess God more perfectly who renounce earthly possessions from the heart.

**Chapter XVII.** That those accomplish nothing who abstain from foods but serve their vices; nor does it benefit those who cast away their possessions if they carry out their own wishes.

**Chapter XVIII.** How many good things the first human being lost by neglecting the good of abstinence.

**Chapter XIX.** On the sin of the first human being and the evils that followed upon his sin when God passed judgment.

**Chapter XX.** That all the good things we lost when corrupted in Adam we shall receive again when restored in Christ [Note: The Cambrai manuscript has “we receive.”].

**Chapter XXI.** How those who desire to imitate Christ ought to live.

**Chapter XXII.** With what temperance those should live who desire to abstain from the pleasure of delicacies, from immoderate consumption of ordinary foods, and from immoderate use of wine [Note: The printed editions have “with what temperance”;].

**Chapter XXIII.** That in those who eat meat it is the lust for meat, not the nature of meat, that pollutes them.

**Chapter XXIV.** How useful it often is to prefer the charity of visitors to fasting or abstinence [Note: The Cambrai manuscript has “to be preferred.”].

## CHAPTER ONE. That, according to the diversity of sinners, some are to be borne and others chastised

### 1. If all were suffering from one and the same sickness of mind, and were afflicted with equal diseases of the soul, differing from one another in nothing, then it would be necessary either to endure them all or to rebuke them all [Note: One Colbertine manuscript has “it would be necessary either to endure everyone or to rebuke them.”]. But now some are to be borne and others chastised because, according to the diversity of sinners, the measure of the precepts also differs [Note: Three Colbertine manuscripts and one Royal manuscript have “according to the diversity of sins”; another Royal manuscript has “of penitents.”].

Certainly, remedies unlike one another must be applied to unlike sins, just as the sins themselves arise from unlike causes [Note: One Colbertine manuscript has “Thus, unlike remedies must be applied to unlike sins.”]. Many are pleased by the habit of sinning; others are invited to sin by the opportunity for some temporal gain; weakness inclines some; ignorance of the good causes others not to know that what they are doing is sinful; and the sweetness of evil prevents those who have been rebuked from ever coming to understand what they do not know [Note: One manuscript has “the evil sweetness.”].

I say nothing of those whom the sins of others, to which they consent, stain. I also pass over those who, desiring to obtain what they love or avoiding what they fear to suffer, either betray the catholic faith or subject the excellence of truth to a lie [Note: Printed editions except the Lyon edition have “and prefer a lie”; one Colbertine manuscript has “or prefer a lie to the truth.”].

But this I do say: Who does not know that people sin in one way through a sudden thought, in another through a settled decision, in another through speech, in another through action, in another through necessity, and in another through desire [Note: One Colbertine manuscript has “through pleasure”]?

### 2. Since, then, people sin in ways so numerous and so far removed from one another [Note: One manuscript has “differing from one another”], who does not understand that those whose diseases are so different cannot all be cured in one way?

Human weakness therefore despises God’s commandments in two ways: either by doing what he forbade or by failing to do what he commanded [Note: One manuscript has “either by doing what he forbids or by not doing what he commands.”]. But just as people despise him in his commandments not only for the reasons I have mentioned but also for others I have not mentioned, when they do not carry out his commands [Note: All manuscripts have “because”; shortly afterward three manuscripts have “they despise the Lord”], so all must be treated—sometimes by teaching, sometimes by exhorting, sometimes by enduring, and sometimes by rebuking [Note: Two Royal manuscripts and the printed editions have “to care for”; four Colbertine manuscripts and the Cambrai manuscript have “to be cared for”]—so that, with Christ’s help, the salvation of no one may be despaired of in this life [Note: One Colbertine manuscript has “no evil person’s salvation should be despaired of in this life”; one Royal manuscript has “the salvation of no one should be despaired of.”].

Now, if it has become sufficiently clear that those who trample upon the divine commandments are not only to be borne but also chastised, I must explain by whom this is to be done, in what manner and order, and for how long those who are being treated are to be cared for, with the assistance of your merits and prayers [Note: The words “with the assistance of your merits and” are absent from all manuscripts].

## CHAPTER TWO. On the praise of holy priests

### 1. And lest my speech lack credence, as though it were merely a human conjecture, and lest its effect be lost because it is insufficiently believed, I shall try to show by divine testimonies that the things I have resolved, with the Lord’s help, to demonstrate are true, after first bringing forward a few things about the praise of true priests, who are the teachers of the Churches.

The care of souls is properly entrusted to them. They bear usefully the burden of the people entrusted to them [Note: Six manuscripts have “bearing manfully”], and they unceasingly pray to God for the sins of all as though they were their own. Like another Aaron, offering the incense of a contrite heart and a humbled spirit, they turn away from the people the anger of future judgment, by which God is appeased [Note: The Cambrai manuscript has “by which God, being appeased, turns away…”; one Royal manuscript has “by which God, being appeased, turns away the anger of wrath and punishment”; another Royal manuscript has “by which he, being appeased, turns away the anger of future punishment.”] (Exod. 30:10; Lev. 16:2; Num. 16:46).

By God’s grace they become interpreters of the divine will, founders of Christ’s Churches after the apostles, leaders of the faithful people, defenders of the truth, enemies of false doctrine, beloved by all good people and terrifying even by their appearance to those conscious of evil, avengers of the oppressed, fathers of those regenerated in the catholic faith, preachers of heavenly things, the foremost ranks [possibly “the foremost rank”] of invisible battles [Note: Three manuscripts, following the reading of ancient codices, have “the foremost fighters,” or “combatants”; one Colbertine manuscript has “the foremost athletes”], examples of good works, examples of virtues, and models of the faithful [Note: Two Colbertine manuscripts have “a model of life.”].

They are the Church’s glory, in whom the Church shines more brightly [Note: The Cambrai manuscript has “leaders of the Church”]. They are the strongest pillars upon which the whole multitude of believers, founded in Christ, rests. They are the gates of the eternal city, through whom all who believe enter to Christ [Note: Six manuscripts, together with the Lyon edition, lack “in Christ”]. They are the doorkeepers to whom the keys of the kingdom of heaven have been given. They are also stewards of the royal household, by whose judgment ranks and offices are distributed in the court of the eternal King.

### 2. These are the men who earned the priesthood not by seeking it but by living spiritually. Raised up not by the support of human favor but by divine gift, they applaud themselves in nothing because of the excellence of their leadership [Note: Two Colbertine manuscripts have “because of the prominence of their position.”]. The honor they have received does not inflate them but puts them to work [Note: Two Royal manuscripts have this reading; others, together with the printed editions, have “inflames them”]. They do not think about their advancement [Note: One Colbertine manuscript has “they do not think about their own advancement”], but about their burden; nor do they glory in the dignity of their office, but rather sweat beneath the burden imposed upon them.

Holy Scripture calls such men watchmen (Ezek. 3:17). They watch over everyone’s conduct and, with the attentive concern of religious curiosity, investigate how each person lives with his household and how he lives in the city with his fellow citizens. Those whom they find good they confirm by honoring; those whom they discover to be vicious they correct by rebuking. If they refuse to be corrected, they bear them with equanimity, expecting an abundant fruit either from their severity, if those rebuked make progress, or from their patience, even if those whom they endure refuse to be corrected.

## CHAPTER THREE. On apostolic testimonies and their exposition
1. But now, as we promised, let us produce the divine testimonies. In the Acts of the Apostles the Apostle Paul says to the priests:

“Behold, I know that you will all see my face no more—you among whom I went about preaching the kingdom of Jesus Christ” [Note: One Colbertine manuscript, “Jesus Christ.”]. “Therefore I testify to you this day that I am innocent of the blood of all. For I have not held back from declaring to you the whole counsel of God. Take heed to yourselves and to the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit has appointed you bishops, to govern the Church of God, which he acquired for himself with his own blood” [Note: Six manuscripts, “acquired for himself.”] (Acts 20:25ff.).

“I preached,” he says, “the kingdom of God as I went about among you, so that I might keep myself apart from the perdition of all who, having heard the word of saving doctrine, make no progress toward salvation” [Note: Two manuscripts, “make progress.”]. He preaches the kingdom of God who does not cease to preach about the future life, which has no end; about divine contemplation, which has no wearisome satiety; about the blessedness of the saints, which suffers no decline; and about attaining likeness to the angels—so that, if those who hear do not wish to be summoned to these ineffable goods, the one who did not keep silent in preaching them may nevertheless stand acquitted [Note: One manuscript, “if they do not wish to be summoned to these ineffable goods”; four manuscripts, after a few intervening words, “did not keep silent about what ought to be preached.”].

2. But what else does what he adds mean—“For I have not held back from declaring to you the whole counsel of God” (ibid., 27)—except that the ecclesiastical teacher should disclose God’s disposition, which the Apostle calls “the counsel of God,” to those whom he teaches? He therefore discloses the counsel of the divine disposition when he teaches that fathers should earn from the Lord, who is the Father of all, the piety they show to their children [Note: Seven manuscripts and the Lyon edition read thus. Others insert: “He discloses the counsel of divine piety when he teaches.”]; that sons should render due honor to their fathers [Note: One Colbertine manuscript, “to their parents”], not deterred by fear of disinheritance but moved by desire for future recompense—for they fulfill the Lord’s command both by fathers’ loving their children and by children’s showing honor to their fathers, since he commanded both to be done [Note: Seven manuscripts, “of God”; one of them shortly afterward reads, “by showing it to their parents.”].

He teaches that husbands should preserve fidelity to the marriage bed for their wives [Note: The editions of Louvain (1565), Douai, and Cologne add here, and again four lines later, “He teaches”; all manuscripts except the Lyon edition omit the word.]; that wives should delight their husbands not through the practice of seductive beauty or the careful arrangement of varied clothing, but through seriousness of character and holiness of conduct [Note: Two manuscripts, “and wives”]; that masters should treat servants mercifully, as their fellow servants in Christ, and that servants should serve their masters so wholeheartedly that they fulfill the will not only of their masters but also of God, who commands this very thing; that citizens should maintain true concord among themselves, friends with friends, and relatives with relatives; that in no transaction one person should deceive another by cunning fraud [Note: Four manuscripts, “so that he may not”], or in a common contract should himself violate the trust he wishes another to keep for him.

3. Through these and similar teachings the priest announces, by preaching, and the people receive God’s counsel by obeying [Note: One manuscript, “The priest announces these and such things.”], without which one does not arrive at the kingdom. In that kingdom alone, those who carry out the divine counsel will, by God’s authority, become participants in heavenly rewards [Note: Two manuscripts, “the sole executors.”]

Then, when the Apostle says, “Take heed to yourselves and to the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit has appointed you bishops to govern the Church of God, which he acquired with his own blood” (Acts 20:28) [Note: Four manuscripts, “which he acquired for himself with his own blood.”], who does not see that priests take heed to themselves when, by living holy lives and confidently preaching the Lord’s will [Note: Seven manuscripts, “God’s will.”], they care for the Church of God, so that it is no longer burdensome for them to sustain the Church’s weak, for whose redemption the Author of life deigned to offer himself to death?

Those also who are taught, so that they may become wise; who are rebuked, so that at least when reproved they may improve; and who are borne with, so that they may at some point blush at their own crimes and offer joy to their teachers, whose patience treats them gently, through the benefit of their correction [Note: All manuscripts read thus. The printed editions instead have, “through the progress of their usefulness”—]—these people, I say, should gladly hear what the divine word commands them through the apostolic mouth [Note: One manuscript, “the Holy Spirit, that is, the divine word”]:

“Obey your leaders and submit to them. For they are keeping watch, as those who will have to render an account for your souls, so that they may do this with joy and not with groaning; for that would be of no advantage to you” (Hebrews 13:17) [Note: In one manuscript, “not beneficial” is corrected in accordance with the Apostle’s text.].

4. Therefore those who hear must obey their teachers and be subject to them with reverence. They do this when, after being disciplined, they willingly accept it and do not contradict those who rebuke them.

But when he says, “For they are keeping watch, as those who will have to render an account for your souls” (ibid.), he clearly demonstrates the priestly care owed to the people. Priests remain watchful both in their conduct and in their preaching, diligently searching out the snares of the ancient enemy, lest the devil, the wolf [Note: One Colbertine manuscript, “the wolf, that is, the devil.”], by crafty fraud, carry off someone as though the shepherd were sleeping, and lead the one seized to the eternal punishments, to the shepherd’s ruin.

Yet because among those who are rebuked some correct themselves in obedience, while others persist in their perversity, he says of the priests: “So that they may do this with joy, and not with groaning” (ibid.). Priests rebuke with joy when those who are reproved make progress; they do so sadly when they groan that their contemptuous hearers are making no progress. Thus he says that it is advantageous for them that priests rebuke them with joy and not with groaning—those who gladden their teachers by their correction and increase their teachers’ joy by the growth of their own progress [Note: One manuscript adds “holy” before “priests.”].

# CHAPTER IV. OBJECTION: Why holy priests, whose duty it is to rebuke those living destructively, bear religious pretenders with equanimity.

[Col. 0447D]

1. I had not yet completed my discussion of holy priests, about whom I was trying to say more, when, behold, one of our own people came in and, curious about what I was dictating [Note: Two Colbertine manuscripts, “more inquisitively”], asked me a question. When I had it read back to him, he said:

“There is no doubt that all bishops ought to be such as your discourse has described, and that there are now among us many who are filled with priestly virtues, such as you have truly proclaimed. But since it is evidently part of their office to rebuke the disorderly by priestly authority, teach the uneducated, and refute those who contradict sound doctrine [Note: One Colbertine manuscript, “why is this correction of theirs not extended to everyone?”], why is it that their care does not extend to all? Why do they not chastise others also with similar authority? I mean those who, as though converted, cast off nothing of their former ways of life—changed not in mind but in clothing, not in conduct but in appearance.”

2. These are people who, content merely to have renounced the world in speech and not in deed, live in a worldly manner. They conceal their vices under an empty profession of a better life; covered by the name of an imaginary religion, they accept a reputation for virtue in place of virtue itself. They preach great things but do not do them; they condemn vices but do not lay them aside; they pretend publicly to dislike what they commit secretly; they strive to seem great, not to become great. They praise those whose praise they desire to obtain through preaching [Note: One manuscript, “while praising those…”]; they fast so that they may sell the pallor of their faces for ruinous praise.

Ready to rebuke others, they do not allow themselves to be rebuked by just anyone, even lightly [Note: The Lyon edition, “gently.”]. To the face they feign patience, while hiding the poison of anger in their hearts, prepared to do harm when they find an opportunity. Neglectful of their own conduct, they become censors of others with insolent freedom.

They shamelessly attach themselves to consecrated virgins and widows, to whom they cling with such affection [Note: Four manuscripts, “they cleave”] that they would more readily depart from the Church—which it is even sacrilegious to say—than from their companionship. Even if they perhaps do not sin with them [Note: Three manuscripts, “do not perish with them”], nevertheless, by providing grounds for evil suspicion, they stain their lives with the blemishes of a sinister reputation.

3. I say nothing of those who, with the surging, stumbling movement of their bodies [Note: Four manuscripts, “with a weary, staggering movement”], walk with their garments flowing down to their ankles and, wavering in the twisting mobility of their steps, reveal in a manner the dissolution of their minds through the undulating movements of their feet.

Who could endure those who, while putting forward an image of affected respectability [Note: These four words—“putting forward an image of affected respectability”—are absent from the Cambrai manuscript], undertake the cases of orphan girls and widows as though to defend them, under a pretence of piety, in order to add their resources to their own? Thus, having become rich from the poor—or richer from the rich—they accumulate their meager wealth by wickedness [Note: Four manuscripts, “to the shame of it!”], so that, once they have become more lavish through an overflowing inheritance, the material for their pleasure and gluttony may never fail [Note: One Colbertine manuscript: “May the material for their pleasure and gluttony never fail them.” Another: “May the material for pleasure and gluttony never fail him.”].

Why, then, do those who have received divine authority to rebuke such people not rebuke them? [Note: One Colbertine manuscript, “and are not afraid … to approve what they do?”] Do they not fear that, when they spare those living so disgracefully, they may appear to approve what they do? What is more, they even admit them to the clerical office and—shame upon it!—as though it were not enough that they fail to rebuke such people while concealing their severity, they actually honor them as well.

# CHAPTER V. RESPONSE: The circumstances requiring the gentle treatment of certain people’s weakness are shown.

1. I replied: “If you recall what was discussed about holy priests, you have received a sufficient answer. As we have already said above, ecclesiastical teachers must possess both severity, so that they may rebuke, and patience, so that they may firmly endure those who refuse to be corrected, fulfilling the Apostle’s command to Timothy [Note: One manuscript and the Lyon and Louvain editions, “he commands”], when he says: ‘Reprove, exhort, rebuke, with all patience and teaching’ (1 Timothy 4:2).

It is as though he were saying: Reprove those of equal rank, exhort your elders, and rebuke those who are younger. But he therefore added, ‘with all patience and teaching,’ because a person disciplined gently shows reverence to the one disciplining him; whereas, offended by the harshness of excessive rebuke, he accepts neither the rebuke nor salvation.

Again, in another place the same Apostle says: ‘You who are stronger ought to bear with the weaknesses of the weak’ (Romans 15:1)” [Note: Six manuscripts, “of the infirm.”]. They therefore bear equanimously, as weak people, those whom they have been unable to correct even after disciplining them.

Accordingly, because it is neither advantageous to rebuke everyone nor to treat everyone gently, holy priests know and discern whom they ought to correct with measured severity and whom they ought to bear with priestly magnanimity. Therefore, in all whom they care for by God’s grace, they look not to their will but to their benefit.

Finally, they pass over some who improperly seek to be honored, knowing that honor would not benefit them—not through anyone’s envy, but by the counsel of deep prudence. Others who wish to remain hidden they honor, so as to open for them a path to greater progress [Note: One manuscript adds, “And those whom they approve…”]. They discipline those whom they judge able to endure rebuke; those unable to bear reproof they handle gently, as sick people—not flattering them for being what they are, but having compassion on their weaknesses, if they cannot be healed in any other way.

2. Moreover, if weak people who cannot be healed by rebuke are deprived of communion with the Church, they may either collapse under an unbearable weight of sadness and avoid the faces of all the saints, through whom they could be restored to God; or, if embittered, they may rush into every shamelessness of sinning and publicly commit whatever evil they had previously done in secret. They may fall into such madness, through despair of recovering salvation, that they turn the serious words of those rebuking them into deadly jokes with shameless wit [Note: One Colbertine manuscript, “severe”; another, “serene”; other manuscripts, “salutary.”] [Note: The Cambrai manuscript, “speaking curses against themselves”; one Colbertine manuscript, “curses against themselves, and so forth”; another Colbertine manuscript and two Regius manuscripts, “a curse against themselves, and so forth”; the Lyon edition likewise has this reading.].

By the very boasting of their disgrace, they may feed the malicious pleasures of those who live wickedly [Note: One manuscript, “Therefore, for this reason…”]. For this reason, then, those who cannot be rebuked because of their weakness must be borne with compassionate gentleness.

Indeed, if, while you blush on behalf of the sinner, you instill in him a salutary shame, and if, through compassionate kindness of heart, you pour into him the embarrassment you assume for his sins, you will easily restrain in him every license to sin and remove from him all the shamelessness that encourages licentious disgrace.

Then shame, the guardian of integrity, will adorn his character, so that he will come to take pleasure in what formerly seemed sordid, when he was in filth [Note: All manuscripts and the Lyon edition read thus; the Louvain, Douai, and Cologne editions instead have, “when he was in filth and was himself sordid”]; and he will find sordid what formerly pleased him, when he himself displeased all good people [Note: The printed editions read, “so that it may seem sordid.”].

He will love and follow holy men, and by following them he will gradually be formed into their likeness through the correction of his former life, so that it will seem to him as disgraceful to descend again into the vices from which he rejoices to have escaped as it was difficult to rise to the heights of virtue.

For just as virtue is burdensome to the vicious, so vicious pleasure is bitter to the friend of virtue [Note: It was formerly read otherwise: “Thus vicious will is bitter to the friend of virtue.” Two Colbertine manuscripts, “vicious will is bitter”; one Regius manuscript, “the will of vices”; another hand in that manuscript, “vicious pleasure”; another Colbertine manuscript, “vicious pleasure is bitter.”].

This is how the one who considers nothing except the salvation of those whom he wishes to benefit treats all sinners gently or rebukes them.

# CHAPTER VI. That those who do not consider their own sins accuse the sins of others impatiently.

As long as a person remains ignorant of or does not lament his own sins, which he ought to know and lament, he examines the sins of others with curiosity [Note: One Colbertine manuscript, “For as long as anyone … as long as he examines others’ sins curiously.”].

But if, turning toward himself, he examines his own conduct, he will not seek something particular to rebuke in others, but something to mourn in himself [Note: One Regius manuscript, “if, turning toward himself, he looks upon himself”; another Regius manuscript has, “But if, turning toward himself, he looks upon himself.”].

Therefore we ought not readily to accuse the vices of our brothers, but to groan over them, so that, bearing one another’s burdens, we may fulfill the law of Christ (Galatians 6:2). He certainly did not accuse our sins but bore them, as the Evangelist says: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1:29).

Therefore, if he who was without any sin bore us sinners with ineffable compassion and does not cease to bear us, desiring not our destruction but our progress, not the death of sinners but their salvation, why should we not, following the example of our Savior and Lord, bear with the weak, since we ourselves are either weak and wish to be borne by God, or, if we are healthy, can still become weak as fragile human beings?

# CHAPTER VII. How much remedy confession of sins contains, and what punishment deceitful concealment deserves.

[Col. 0451A]

1. It must also be added that sins themselves are so hidden—either the sins of others from us or our own sins from others—that often a saint remains concealed among sinners, while a sinner obtains the reputation of a saint. If an innocent person cannot defend himself, an unwary judge’s suspicion condemns him [Note: One manuscript, “careless”;]; and the cleverness of a lively intellect excuses the guilty.

Nevertheless, such things deceive not divine judgment but human judgment. And what wonder is it if, without their confession, we do not know what other people’s minds are like, when we know ourselves today in such a way that we do not know what we shall be tomorrow [Note: One manuscript, “on the following day”]?

But when any of our brothers opens to us, as to physicians, the sins that afflict them—their wounds—we must strive, with God as the agent, to bring them to health as quickly as possible [Note: One manuscript, “as soon as possible”], lest, while treatment is concealed, they progress toward something worse.

As for the crimes of any people, if they become known by whatever means while the criminals themselves refuse to confess them, whatever has not been healed by the gentle medicine of patience must be burned and treated, as it were, with the fire of compassionate rebuke.

2. But if even then the remedy of one who bears with equanimity and rebukes compassionately has not benefited those who, after being borne with for a long time and salutarily reproved, have refused to correct themselves [Note: Six manuscripts, “has made progress”], then, like rotten parts of the body, they must be cut off by the sword of excommunication [Note: Two manuscripts, “rotten”; one, “decaying”; five manuscripts together with the printed editions, “cut off”].

For just as flesh deadened by disease, if it is not cut away, corrupts the health of the remaining flesh through the contagion of its putrefaction, so these people, who disdain correction and persist in their sickness, if they remain in the company of the saints with their morals corrupted, will infect them by the example of their own destruction [Note: One manuscript, “of their perversion.”].

Moreover, those whose sins escape human knowledge, having been confessed neither by themselves nor publicized by others, if they refuse either to confess or to correct them [Note: Three manuscripts, “or to be corrected”], will have God, whom they have as their witness, as their avenger as well.

What does it profit them to avoid human judgment, when, if they persist in their evil, they will go into eternal punishment, with God repaying them? But if they themselves become their own judges and, as avengers of their own iniquity, impose upon themselves here a voluntary punishment of the severest discipline, they will exchange eternal punishments for temporal ones, and with tears flowing from true contrition of heart they will extinguish the fires of the eternal flame.

But those who, established in some ecclesiastical rank, secretly commit some crime deceive themselves through a vain persuasion if they think that they ought for this reason to continue in communion and fulfill their office merely because they deceive people by concealing their crime.

3. Except for sins so small that they cannot be avoided, for the expiation of which we cry out daily to God and say, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matthew 6:12), those crimes must be avoided whose public disclosure causes their perpetrators to be condemned by human judgment.

But those who have committed such crimes and therefore fear to expose them, lest they receive the sentence of just excommunication, participate in communion without cause. Indeed, they intensify the anger of divine indignation against themselves twofold: they pretend innocence to human beings, and, disregarding God’s judgment, they are ashamed to abstain from the altar because of human beings.

Therefore those will more easily placate God who, without being convicted by human judgment, voluntarily acknowledge their crime [Note: The printed editions read “recognize”; six manuscripts, “acknowledge”]; who either disclose it through their own confessions, or, while others do not know what they secretly are, pronounce upon themselves the sentence of voluntary excommunication [Note: Three manuscripts, “because either”; below, four manuscripts, “they are hidden.”]. Separated from the altar at which they ministered, not in spirit but in office, they mourn their life as though it were dead, certain that, once God has been reconciled to them through the fruits of effective repentance, they will receive back not only what they lost [Note: One manuscript, “they will receive, but will also … attain”], but, having become citizens of the heavenly city, will arrive at everlasting joys.

# CHAPTER VIII. That those who rebuke unjustly and not candidly are vain and must be condemned by divine judgment.

Now, concerning those who, moved by a slight suspicion, rebuke people living simply, so that by their disorderly correction they may both confound and cast them down, and thereby seek for themselves the glory of I know not what severity, I have nothing to say. The divine word pronounces so clearly upon them that it needs no interpreter [Note: Two Colbertine manuscripts, “interpretation.”].

For the Holy Spirit says in Ecclesiasticus: “There is a lying rebuke in the anger of an insulting man; and there is a judgment that is not good” (Ecclesiasticus 19:28) [Note: Seven manuscripts, “in the mouth of an insulting man …”; shortly afterward, six manuscripts add, “and there is judgment.”].

The rebuke of an insulting and proud person, which is called lying, is certainly a judgment of pride, not of any humility [Note: Two manuscripts, “it is pride.”], and therefore it is not good [Note: Six manuscripts together with the Lyon edition, “judgment.”].

What could have been said more clearly or openly than for him to call the person who rebukes falsely insulting? For the person who rebukes falsely is insulting, and the person who commits an insult rebukes falsely [Note: In two Regius manuscripts the words “and he rebukes falsely” are absent. One Colbertine manuscript reads, “for he is also insulting who falsely rebukes the one who commits an insult.”].

Again, in Proverbs: “A false witness will not go unpunished, and he who rebukes unjustly will not escape” (Proverbs 19:5). Who is a false witness except one who rebukes someone for crimes that have not been investigated? It says that the one who rebukes unjustly will not remain unpunished because, by accusing an innocent person who has given no cause, he wants him to appear guilty [Note: All manuscripts read this way. The printed editions instead have, “he wants him to be guilty.”].

But when it says of the one who rebukes unjustly, “he will not escape,” what else should be understood except that he will not escape God’s anger—the one who corrects someone not so that he may amend, but so that he may boast insolently? [Note: One manuscript, “But what follows”; another, “I speak of him … unless because of anger.”]

But concerning despisers of God’s commands and the power of rebuke and patience, let what we have said suffice, lest by lingering too long on one chapter we either pass over the remaining matters more briefly than necessary or burden your attention by extending the volume excessively.

Let us therefore see what the contents of the following chapter also teach us [Note: One manuscript, “what the authority of the following chapter teaches us.”]: whether, he says, it is advantageous for the gathering of the brethren and their support that the Church’s resources be possessed, or whether they should be renounced out of love for perfection [Note: Perhaps it should be read, “I say.”].

# CHAPTER IX. That priests ought to possess nothing as their own, but should receive the Church’s resources as common property, since they will render an account to God for them.

[Col. 0453B]

1. It is advantageous that the Church’s resources be possessed and that private possessions be renounced for the love of perfection. For the Church’s resources are not private but common. Therefore, whoever, after relinquishing or selling everything he possessed, becomes a despiser of his own property, when he has been made head of a church becomes the steward of everything the Church possesses [Note: Three manuscripts, “Finally,” together with the Lyon edition.].

Furthermore, the holy Paulinus—as you yourselves know better—sold the great estates that had been his and distributed the proceeds to the poor [Note: The Lyon edition, “because.”]. But when he later became a bishop, he did not despise the Church’s resources; rather, he administered them with the utmost fidelity.

By this action he showed clearly both that private possessions ought to be despised for the sake of perfection and that what belongs in common to the Church can be possessed without impeding perfection [Note: Five manuscripts together with the Lyon edition read, “that the Church’s possessions, which are certainly common, can be possessed.” One Colbertine manuscript reads, “that the Church’s resources, which are common, can be possessed.”].

What of the holy Hilary? Did he not also leave all his possessions to his relatives [Note: Six manuscripts, “all his own possessions”], or sell them and distribute the proceeds to the poor [Note: One manuscript, “to the poor.”]? Yet when, by the merit of his perfection, he became bishop of the Church of Arles, he not only possessed what that Church then had but also enlarged it by receiving numerous inheritances from the faithful.

These men, therefore—so holy and so perfect—proclaim by their evident deeds that what they did can and ought to be done. Certainly, if these men, who were beyond doubt most learned in both secular and divine writings, had known that the Church’s possessions ought to be despised, they would never have retained them after leaving behind all their own [Note: Two Colbertine manuscripts and one Regius manuscript, “they would never have possessed them.” Two others together with the Cambrai manuscript, “they would have them.” Another Regius manuscript, “they ought to have received them”; at the end these manuscripts omit “retain.”].

2. From this it is understood that such great and eminent men—who, wishing to be Christ’s disciples, renounced everything they possessed—possessed the Church’s resources not as owners but as stewards [Note: Two manuscripts, “to become.”].

And because they knew that the Church’s possessions were nothing other than the vows of the faithful, the prices of sins, and the patrimonies of the poor [Note: Four manuscripts, “the patrimony of the poor”; one of them adds, “and the defensible patrimony of all the poor”], they did not claim them for their own use as private property, but distributed them to the poor as entrusted goods.

This is what it means to despise by possessing: to possess not for oneself but for others; not to seek the Church’s resources out of a desire to have them, but to receive them in order to provide assistance through compassion.

What the Church possesses, it possesses in common with all who have nothing; nor ought it to distribute any of it to those who are self-sufficient from their own resources, since giving to those who have is nothing other than wasting.

# CHAPTER X. At what cost to their souls those who are self-sufficient from their own resources receive from the Church, which feeds the poor.

[Col. 0454B]

1. Those who possess their own property and nevertheless wish something to be given to them cannot receive, without committing a grave sin, what a poor person would have lived on [Note: The Cambrai manuscript, “that from which…”].

The Holy Spirit says through the prophet: “They eat the sins of my people” (Hosea 4:8) [Note: Three manuscripts, “the prophet says”; three Colbertine manuscripts, “they will eat.”].

But just as those who possess nothing of their own receive not sins but the food they appear to need, so proprietors receive not food, of which they have an abundance, but the sins of others.

Even the poor themselves, if they can support themselves through their crafts or labor, should not presume to take what the weak or infirm ought to receive. Otherwise the Church, which can provide necessities to all who are deprived of every kind of support, may be burdened if everyone, including those who need nothing, receives, and may then be unable to assist those whom it ought to assist.

2. Those who serve the Church and, believing that what they regard as due ought to be repaid for their labor, either gladly accept or demand what they do not need, are thinking in an excessively carnal way if they suppose that, by serving the Church faithfully, they receive earthly stipends rather than eternal rewards.

Since secular military service possesses no heavenly goods, it offers earthly benefits to those who serve energetically. It is therefore exceedingly shameful if the faithful and laborious devotion of clerics despises eternal rewards for the sake of temporal payment.

But if some minister of the Church has no means of living, the Church should not repay him here with a reward; it should provide what is necessary [Note: The Lyon and Louvain editions read, “not a reward here, but the Church provides what is necessary.” Two manuscripts, “it does not repay him here, but the Church provides what is necessary.” Three manuscripts, “it should not repay him here, but the Church should provide what is necessary.” All printed editions have “provides”], so that in the future he may receive the reward for his labor, which in this life he confidently awaits through hope in the Lord’s promise [Note: Six manuscripts omit “confidently.”].

As for those who, as though self-sufficient, do not indeed demand anything as owed to them but nevertheless live at the Church’s expense [Note: The printed editions read, “those who are able”; five manuscripts, “as though able”], it is not for me to say with what sin they presumptuously receive the food of the poor—people who ought to have aided the Church from their own resources but instead burden it further with their expenses. Perhaps they live in a community for this very reason: so that they may feed no poor people, receive no newcomers [Note: Six manuscripts, “welcome them”], and not diminish their own wealth through daily expenditures [Note: One manuscript, “But if…”].

And if they contribute something from their revenues toward the Church’s expenses, they should not, through empty boasting, place themselves above those who, possessing nothing, are fed and clothed by the Church. For the person who strips himself of the world’s goods is more perfect—or the one who, possessing nothing, does not desire to possess anything—than the person who, from the many things he owns, gives something to the Church and perhaps boasts of what he has given.

3. What I am saying is harsh, and I do not deny it. It is harsh for those unwilling to observe it. But if these practices are put into effect, things that are difficult for those who do not perform them immediately become easy for those who do.

It is not impossibility, then, that makes the things we do not wish to observe difficult for us, but unfamiliarity. Let them become habitual, and frequent practice will trouble no one.

For I ask: what is difficult in what I have said? Is it for a person not to accept from the Church what he does not need, or for him without cause to renounce what he possesses? If he does not wish to leave his own property because he wants the means to live, why does he accept from that for which he will have to render an account? Why does he multiply his own possessions from the sins of others? [Note: All manuscripts and the Lyon edition read thus; other printed editions have, “from the sins.”]

# CHAPTER XI. Who are those who are sustained by the Church’s resources even with benefit to their souls.

Therefore the priest entrusted with the care of administration receives from the people, not only without greed but even with praise for his compassion, what he is to distribute, and faithfully distributes what he has received. He has either left all his possessions to his relatives, distributed them to the poor, or added them to the Church’s resources, and has placed himself among the poor out of love for poverty [Note: The Lyon edition, together with the Cambrai manuscript, has only this: “either leaves them, or adds them to the Church’s resources, and himself…” Two Regius manuscripts and four Colbertine manuscripts read, “either left them, or added them to the Church’s resources, and himself,” and so forth.]. Thus, from the same resources with which he supplies the poor, he himself lives as a voluntary poor person [Note: One manuscript, “and he himself already lives as though…”].

Clerics also whom either choice or birth has made poor receive the necessities of life, with the perfection of virtue, whether they live in their own houses or in a community. For they are led to receive these things not by the desire to possess, but by the necessity of living.

# CHAPTER XII. What clerics whose weakness prevents them from renouncing their possessions ought to do.

[Col. 0455D]

Those, however, who are so weak that they cannot renounce their possessions, if they leave with the steward what they would otherwise have received, so that it may be given to those who possess nothing, possess their own property without sin. For they too in a certain sense renounce their own possessions when, content with what belongs to them, they receive none of what they think is owed to their labor or their rank.

But if they think that they ought therefore to receive a share of what is contributed to the Church, lest they appear to cast it away, and that they themselves cannot renounce their own possessions because it would be disgraceful for them among their peers to be made poor, let them know that it is more disgraceful for proprietors to be fed from the alms of the poor [Note: One Regius manuscript, “lest they receive shares.” The Cambrai manuscript, “that they ought to receive a share of the portions contributed to the Church, lest they appear to reject them.”].

# CHAPTER XIII. What true joys and true riches are, and what hindrance present goods bring to those who love future goods.

1. Alas, how subtly that master of deception deceives us, how great a blindness he draws over the eyes of our mind, [Col. 0456B] lest, eager for rejoicing, we discern from what we ought more rightly to rejoice; or lest, desiring to grow rich, we know which riches we should incomparably prefer to which others. For rejoicing is indeed a good thing; but if the one who rejoices does not rejoice over what he ought, what he rejoices over cannot be good. For the robber rejoices when he has seized what he desired; the drunkard rejoices when he has found an opportunity for the drinking he longed for [Note: One manuscript: “the desired opportunity”;]; the adulterer rejoices when he has attained the pleasure of enjoying the body he desired. Yet although rejoicing is good, rejoicing over these things and things like them is a great evil. These are the things over which the world, destined to perish along with its lovers [Note: One manuscript: “those who will perish”;], wants us to rejoice. These are the things we must repudiate, so that we may rejoice ineffably in a good conscience, holiness of conduct, the acquisition of virtues, God’s gift, and the promise [Col. 0456C] of the future kingdom.

2. To be enriched with riches is also a great good; [Note: Two Colbertine manuscripts: “but to be enriched from the source from which we ought not to be enriched.” Another manuscript: “but to be enriched from the source from which you ought not to be enriched.”] but to be enriched from a source from which one ought not to be enriched is not a resource to be welcomed, but a calamity to be detested. For nothing is more calamitous, nothing more wretched, than one who grows through unjust acquisitions, whom frauds and plunder make wealthy. The riches we should seek are those able both to adorn and to protect us—riches which we cannot acquire unwillingly, nor lose; which arm us against hostile attacks, separate us from the world, commend us to God, enrich and ennoble our souls [Note: Three Colbertine manuscripts: “our minds”;], dwell with us, and dwell within us.

Our riches must be considered to be chastity, which makes us chaste; justice, which makes us just; piety, which makes us pious; humility, which makes us humble; gentleness, which makes us gentle; innocence, which makes us innocent; purity, which makes us pure; prudence, which makes us prudent; temperance, which makes us temperate; and charity, which makes us dear to God and to human beings, powerful in virtue, despisers of the world, and followers of every good thing [Note: Three manuscripts: “unable to master vices, despisers of the world.” Another manuscript: “unable to master vices, despisers of the vicious world.”]. These are not the holy virtues of everyone, but of the saints; not the resources of proud rich people, but the possessions of humble poor people; the patrimony of hearts, the incorruptible riches of character. No one abounds in them unless he renounces those carnal riches from the heart [Note: Printed editions: “unless those who renounce them.” Four manuscripts omit “those.” One Colbertine manuscript: “which are not given to others except those who …”].

Although those riches too are good, since they were created by the good God, nevertheless, because they are shared by good and wicked alike, spiritual people strive to despise them so that they may attain those incomparably better riches which belong exclusively to the good. For the good possessed by the wicked is not of the same kind as that which only the good possess [Note: Two manuscripts: “which the wicked possess.” Another manuscript: “which the good possess.”].

3. When the wicked possess bodily prosperity, it is their reward [Note: One manuscript: “but when …”; another manuscript omits “their.”]; when the just possess it, it is not their reward but a temporary consolation. Likewise, the loss of temporal good becomes an exercise for the just and a punishment for the unjust. The just, seized by desire for heavenly things, does not feel temporal possessions at all, whether he has them or loses them; but the wicked cannot lose without pain what he possesses with delight [Note: Seven manuscripts: “what he possessed.”].

Therefore riches must be fled from with all one’s heart by those who serve as soldiers of God. Those who wish to possess them do not seek them without labor, find them without difficulty, preserve them without care, possess them without anxious pleasure, or lose them without pain. The Apostle says to Christ’s soldiers: “I want you to be without anxiety” (1 Cor. 7:32); and: “The root of all evils is avarice; by desiring it, some have wandered from the faith and pierced themselves with many sorrows” (1 Tim. 6:10). Thus this earthly wealth, for those who love it viciously, is not a source of pleasures but of sorrows [Note: One manuscript: “this earthly wealth, regarded as wealth …”].

Accordingly, it is advantageous that the Church’s resources be possessed [Note: Four manuscripts: “be held”] so that those who do not serve the world—whose fleeting joys they reject—but serve God, whose ineffable goods they desire, may live from them [Note: Four manuscripts: “serve him.”].

## CHAPTER XIV. How the Apostle’s statement is to be understood: “Those who work in the sanctuary eat what comes from the sanctuary.”

The Apostle seems to speak of such people when he says: “Those who work in the sanctuary eat what comes from the sanctuary, and those who serve at the altar share with the altar” (1 Cor. 9:13) [Note: Three manuscripts: “share with what belongs to the altar.” Two manuscripts: “share with the altar.”]. Unless he wanted this understood of those who despise their own possessions, he would never have added immediately afterward: “So also God ordained that those who proclaim the Gospel should live from the Gospel” (ibid., 14). Those who do not want to possess anything as their own live from the Gospel; they neither possess anything nor desire to possess anything, but are possessors of common goods.

What else is it to live from the Gospel than to receive from the place where one labors the necessities of life needed by the one who labors? Yet the Apostle, who preached the Gospel in such a way that he did not live from the Gospel but supplied his necessities with his own hands, speaks confidently about himself [Note: Two Regian manuscripts: “speaks about himself”]: “But I have used none of these things.” He then explains why he said this, adding: “It is better for me to die than that anyone should make my glory void” (ibid., 15) [Note: Thus two Regian manuscripts. Others, with the printed editions, read “deprive [it] of me.”]. He says that his glory would be emptied if he had wanted to receive the expense of bodily life from those to whom he preached [Note: Five manuscripts: “temporal [life].”]; for he did not want to receive the fruit of his labor in the present, but in the future.

Therefore, if the one who possessed nothing did not want to live from the Gospel, where he labored, but lived by his own hands [Note: One Colbertine manuscript: “lest he lose the reward of his glory.” Another: “the glory of his reward.”], so as not to lose the glory of his reward, what are we doing? We are unwilling to abandon what is ours out of love of possessing, not because of the necessity of living; and, in addition, we want to receive—not what we may live from, but what may increase our wealth through damnable accumulation.

## CHAPTER XV. How greed rules those whom it has once invaded.

1. Behold, imperious greed commands us to disregard the divine commandments [Note: Four manuscripts: “For behold, greed commands us …”; one Regian manuscript: “despising the divine commandments”], to consider the destructive profits of earthly possessions, to place all our anxiety and care in them [Note: One manuscript: “and in them …”;], to boast of ourselves through them with diseased vanity, and, elated by the extent of a more expansive patrimony [Col. 0458C], to neglect becoming poor in spirit.

An unheard-of crime! Having despised Christ’s gentle yoke, we voluntarily incline our minds to accept the iron rule of greed. And, having rejected the light burden of our Lord [Note: The Cambrai manuscript reads: “and we despise submitting to our Lord’s light burden—which does not burden those subject to it, but honors them; it does not crush them at all, but lifts them up. Having therefore set aside this light burden …” Four Colbertine manuscripts and one Regian manuscript agree, except that one Colbertine manuscript reads “but exalts.” Another Regian manuscript reads: “and we flee our Lord’s light burden, which does not burden those subject to it, but honors them; it does not crush them at all, but lifts them up; having therefore …” Other manuscripts read: “we proudly reject the light burden”; the rest agrees with the manuscripts cited immediately above.], which does not burden those subject to it but lifts them up, we heap upon our necks a leaden weight [Note: Two manuscripts: “we pile up”], which can be laid down more quickly than it can be carried. For greed itself, which imposes this weight upon us when we willingly submit to it, can be despised more easily than it can be satisfied. Therefore those who willingly surrender themselves to it as it conquers them will no longer have the will to resist it when it rules tyrannically.

This happens by the just judgment of God: those who were unwilling to resist greed when it was entering them are no longer able to resist it after it has entered [Note: Five manuscripts: “because we did not want to resist the greed that was entering.”].

[Col. 0459A] 2. O the pitiable slavery of a mind conquered [Note: One manuscript: “the vice of a conquered mind.”]! O the intolerable [Note: Four manuscripts: “the accursed”; another four: “the rule of the mistress Greed.”] rule of demonic greed! From the enemies it is able to conquer, it makes its own victors; it promises immense things and, deceiving the wretched and pitiable with promises of temporal goods, drives them into shameful acts. It holds us captive, bound by chains of profits that are sweet only as punishment [Note: One manuscript: “it holds us in punishment as captives of sweet profits.”], and keeps us prisoners in its power. It does not drag us unwillingly but, what is worse, leads us willingly wherever it wishes [Note: The Lyon edition: “whomever it wishes.”].

It ravages in us whatever modesty and shame it finds. Those whom it has already assigned to its triumphs it still disarms of every power of virtue, as though suspecting that they might repent [Note: One Regian manuscript: “as though they had been received in order to repent”; the Cambrai manuscript and others: “as though they had already been received for repentance.”], lest at some time we rebel against it, against which we were unwilling to wage war.

It snatches us away and scatters us everywhere, greedy to acquire through every kind of acquisition. [Col. 0459B] It does not permit the mind to be free, nor the body to be stable or at rest, with the mind wandering restlessly [Note: Other manuscripts: “while the mind is vacant.”]. Like corpses thrown out as food for wild birds and beasts, it delivers its captives to unclean spirits—not to be torn apart, but to be devoured by the most ravenous jaws of deadly crimes [Note: Four manuscripts: “it will deliver them.”]. Yet it does not do this so that they may cease to exist, but so that they may live under punishment. Finally, while still alive, they carry their own funerals in their bodies—that is, they are at once living and dead [Note: Three manuscripts: “that is, simultaneously living and dead.” One manuscript: “the same,” perhaps “the same people.” Two manuscripts, with the Lyon edition: “but the same people.”].

Hence, while living in sin, we feel how much the increase of accumulated wealth delights us [Note: Three manuscripts: “entices us”; one manuscript: “makes us boast”; other manuscripts: “delights us more fully.”], through the very pleasure of enjoying carnal things; and, as though dead to the virtues, we do not recognize how great a poverty of virtues we endure.

## CHAPTER XVI. That those possess God more perfectly who renounce earthly possessions from the heart.

[Col. 0459C]

[Note: One Regian manuscript adds here: “precepts . . . .”; and in another hand: “to be possessed.”]

1. It is for these reasons that the Church’s resources ought to be possessed—not for satisfying pleasures and nurturing them, but for gathering brothers together or supporting them. Thus, while one person bears the anxieties of all who live in his community, everyone under his authority may enjoy spiritually and peacefully a fruitful freedom from worldly occupations.

For this reason I inserted the adverb “spiritually,” since one who enjoys idle rest without living spiritually lives like the animals. Therefore, when a person is troubled by no concern for bodily necessity, disturbed by no domestic occupation, harassed by no litigant, and driven by no slanderer, what else should he care for, freed from these and similar annoyances, except how he may advance toward better things; how he may diminish his vices through daily progress [Col. 0460A], increase his virtues, and possess spiritual goods in place of the carnal goods he has despised?
