With divine assistance, let him exercise himself in these things; let him always embrace and love them; and let him prefer them not only to all his other pleasures but even to the torments of his own flesh. Thus, having left himself nothing that he would fear to lose, let him hold fast with such firmness of faith to the things for which he cast away all that he possessed that, if necessary, he may gladly offer his body for them.

2. Therefore, whoever delights in the ambition of possessing should possess God, who possesses all that he created, with an unencumbered mind; and in him he will have whatever he holily desires to have. But since no one possesses God unless he is possessed by God, let that person first become God’s possession, and God will become his possessor and his portion [Note: Seven manuscripts: “and he will become God’s possession.”].

What can be happier than the person for whom his Creator becomes wealth and for whom Divinity itself deigns to be an inheritance [Note: Six manuscripts omit “his.” One manuscript reads: “the Divinity itself, worthy to be [his inheritance], and not to be …”], provided that he honors God through holy works, receives every fruit from him, continually lives in him and from him, and possesses nothing earthly together with him?

For the Creator of all things, to whom nothing he has made can be compared, does not deign to be possessed together with the things he created [Note: The Lyon edition, together with three Colbertine manuscripts and one Regian manuscript, reads “does not deign.” Another Regian manuscript omits the negative particle and reads “disdains.” Other editions read “does not disdain,” but apparently less correctly.].

Finally, what more does the person seek for whom his Creator becomes everything? Or what can be sufficient for one for whom God himself is not sufficient? [Note: Two Colbertine manuscripts: “Who is sufficient for him?” Another: “What is sufficient for one for whom …?” Another reads: “Or what is lacking for him?” but incorrectly.]

He possessed God, and God possessed him—the one who said in the Spirit: “The Lord is my portion; I said that I would keep your law” (Ps. 118:57). And: “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance and of my cup” (Ps. 15:5).

He himself also says: “You shall not give a portion to the sons of Levi among their brothers; I, the Lord, am their portion” (Num. 18:23; Deut. 18:1) [Note: One Colbertine manuscript adds: “to the sons of Levi: ‘You shall not give …’”]. He plainly shows that those who have despised a share in an earthly inheritance deserve to possess God spiritually. Enriched by his gifts, they disdain everything regarded as excellent in this world, and desire to possess him—or to be possessed by him—to enjoy him alone, and to cling to him inseparably.

3. From this it is understood that whoever pursues and loves temporal goods and the perishing joys of the world has not learned what and how great is the abundance of divine sweetness [Note: All manuscripts read this way. The printed editions instead read: “the abundance of heavenly sweetness.”]. For who, when God deigns to be his possession, seeks anything else? Or who, out of love for him [Note: Two Regian manuscripts: “for love of him”], does not despise everything considered great?

Therefore, whoever wishes to possess God must renounce the world, so that God may be his blessed possession. The person who is still delighted by the ambition of earthly possession has not renounced the world. For as long as he does not abandon what is his [Note: The Cambrai manuscript: “has not abandoned his possessions.”], he serves the world, whose goods he retains; and certainly he cannot serve both the world and God.

Thus God wanted his worshipers to renounce everything for which the world is loved, so that, once love of the world had been excluded, divine charity might be increased and perfected in them. For this reason he ordained that tithes and first fruits of crops, firstborn things, sacrifices for sin, and vows that God commanded to be offered [Note: One Regian manuscript: “or vows”] should be distributed to priests and ministers. Thus, while the most devoted people supplied the necessities of life, the priests and ministers might serve their Creator and Shepherd with free minds and advance in his worship without any bodily anxiety [Note: One Colbertine manuscript: “in that worship.”], lest, entangled in earthly occupations, they be unable to attend energetically to the watchfulness appropriate to their office.

[Col. 0461B] 4. Now, because the priests of Christian times bear the care of the Church’s possessions more than they manage them, they serve God even in this [Note: Five manuscripts: “they serve God.”]. For if what is contributed to the Church belongs to God, the person who does not abandon things consecrated to God out of any desire, but with the intention of the most faithful administration, is carrying out God’s work.

Therefore, the possessions that priests receive as offerings from the people must not be regarded as belonging among the things of the world, but as belonging to God [Note: All manuscripts read: “They must not be considered things of the world any longer, but God’s.”]. For if clothing, vessels, and other things that served sacred use [Note: Three manuscripts: “that served ministers in sacred use”; one manuscript: “in ministries”] were called holy and, once consecrated to divine services, could no longer be returned to human uses, how should not those things contributed to the Church be considered sacred? Priests use them not luxuriously, as worldly possessions, but religiously, as things consecrated to God, for necessities [Col. 0461C]—so that the Church’s resources, gathered for this very purpose, may suffice for all who establish themselves together under one authority out of love for perfection and do not claim their own possessions for themselves [Note: Five manuscripts: “so that the Church’s resources gathered for this very purpose may suffice.”].

Whatever progress they make after being freed from all occupations should become the fruit of the one who is occupied for the sake of many. Thus the person who bears the anxieties of all who live under him should advance as his community advances [Note: All manuscripts read this way. The printed editions read “of those who serve.”]. Just as his occupation has become the fruitful freedom from occupation of all his people, so the perfection of all his disciples should be counted the teacher’s glorious honor and glory.

## CHAPTER XVII. That those who abstain from foods but serve vices make no progress, and that renouncing possessions benefits those who do their own will not at all.

[Col. 0461D]

1. You also asked what perfection should be attributed to abstinence [Col. 0462A], and whether it ought to be judged necessary only for the body or also for the soul. If this virtue, called abstinence, sanctifies the whole human being perfectly, it is necessary not only for the body but also for the soul, because every human being consists of body and soul.

But in those who are subject to various vices and forbid themselves some of the things granted for our use [Note: All manuscripts read this way. The printed editions instead read: “which are necessary.”], abstinence must be understood as merely carnal and imperfect [Note: The Cambrai manuscript: “it is indeed abstinence, but …”]. It must instead be judged spiritual and perfect when it makes the person abstaining alien both to the enticements of carnal pleasures and to every sin. In such a person, illnesses of desire do not corrupt the mind, nor do delicacies sought at the command of a ruling appetite weaken the body’s strength.

Therefore, the truly abstinent person is the one who has become free from every vice [Note: Three manuscripts: “having been made free, after cutting away …”] and, having cut away bodily pleasures [Note: The printed editions: “carnal pleasures.”], labors not to glut the desire of his flesh [Note: One manuscript: “inflames …”], but to sustain mortal life by taking what is necessary. For whatever is taken without which one can live is spent not on sustaining life but on nurturing the flesh’s luxury [Note: The Cambrai manuscript: “on stirring up …”].

2. This virtue, then, which is called abstinence not only from delicate foods but also from every evil [Note: Five manuscripts: “this virtue, therefore …”], is necessary for everyone, but it must be regarded as especially familiar and closely joined to those of whom we read in the Acts of the Apostles (4:32) that they had one heart and one soul, fused by the fire of divine charity, and who, living under one authority, made everything common to everyone—provided that life becomes one for them [Note: Four manuscripts: “provided that their life is one”; one manuscript: “just as their substance is one.”], just as their substance is made one [Col. 0462C], and that there is no diversity of spirit among them, since their possessions are held in common. For the holy union of minds to be formed and maintained, the common ownership of possessions has rightly been judged necessary [Note: One Colbertine manuscript: “the unity of common possessions.”].

But what does it benefit them that they cast away their possessions [Note: Two Regian manuscripts: “if they cast away their possessions …”] if they do not abandon their own wills, when renouncing one’s own will is far more excellent than renouncing things? The philosophers of this world were also able to cast away their possessions [Note: The printed editions: “anyone.”], and any heretics can do so now. Yet when those philosophers became lovers of their own will [Note: Thus two Regian manuscripts, one Colbertine manuscript, and other manuscripts. The printed editions instead read: “when they became lovers of their own pleasure.”], they did not live according to God’s will; and these heretics, by their devotion to their own will, contradict the Lord’s will.

Therefore, it is not the act that commends us to God which even God’s enemies perform, but that which only true Christians—and, through this, lovers of God—accomplish [Note: One Regian manuscript: “but that which …”]. These are the people who, having cast away their own wills and possessions [Note: Two Colbertine manuscripts: “pleasures”], submit themselves wholly to their Creator and suspend their own willing from his will. Therefore, whatever the sense of the flesh suggests that they should pursue and do [Note: The printed editions: “suggests”], they despise, captivated by the delight of righteousness.

## CHAPTER XVIII. How many goods the first human being lost by neglecting the good of abstinence.

1. If the first human being had wished to preserve himself in that blessedness of paradise by fasting from the fruit of one forbidden tree [Note: Four manuscripts omit “himself.” One Colbertine manuscript reads: “had wished to preserve that blessedness of paradise, so that he might …”], he would neither have lost that state of such great happiness nor, through the voluntary transgression of the saving commandment, become subject to the necessity of corruption and mortality—thereby corrupting through sin or losing so many benefits of his God, which he had received in the nature of his creation.

For who could sufficiently enumerate how many and how great goods contempt for that abstinence took away from him [Note: One Regian manuscript: “which that abstinence took away from him”]? He had been endowed with the dignity of an intellectual mind and had received the image of his Creator; subject only to his God, he saw all visible things subject to himself; by divine command, the fruitfulness of every tree that was in paradise served him abundantly for the uses of life (Gen. 2:9); the tree of life, as a mystical food, supplied by the gift of his Creator not food by which he would live, but food by which the life of his body would not end.

As long as that food was received, it would preserve the one receiving it in an unchanging state through the figurative meaning of a hidden sacrament: it would not permit him to be corrupted by any sickness, altered and aged by time, or dissolved by death.

Troublesome anxiety did not disturb the tranquil; anxious labor did not tire the one at rest; sleep did not oppress the unwilling; fear of losing life did not torment the one secure in immortality [Note: One Regian manuscript: “fear did not torment him. Secure concerning immortality, he possessed …”]. His body, sound in every respect [Note: All manuscripts: “sound in every part”], had an easy sustenance; his movement was tranquil, his heart pure, and he was ignorant of punitive evil—a dweller in paradise, free from sin, capable of God.

2. Finally, who was happier than one to whom the world was subject, no one hostile, whose mind was free, and whose God was visible? [Note: Thus two Regian manuscripts and the Cambrai manuscript. The printed editions: “Since indeed …”] For unless Adam had been accustomed, before sin, to see God in the assumption of visible creation, how could he, having now become a sinner, hide himself from the face of the Lord whom he had never seen? Adam could therefore see God before he sinned, just as the patriarchs saw him [Note: Three Colbertine manuscripts: “the holy patriarchs.”]. But when he said, “I heard your voice, and I was afraid” (Gen. 3:10), he had already fallen from that holiness of seeing God; he had already made himself unworthy to see God [Note: These words concerning seeing God are absent from one Colbertine manuscript, and quite properly so, according to the editor.].

“I heard your voice,” he said, “and I was afraid, because I was naked, and I hid myself” (ibid.). [Col. 0464A] O how much security those possess who are conscious of doing well! And how greatly the shameful commission of sin humbles the disturbed—as in the case of these people, who hid themselves from the face of the Lord, ashamed of their disgrace [Note: One Regian manuscript: “not ashamed because of their fear”], not of their nakedness! They were not ashamed because they were outwardly naked in clothing, but because they had been inwardly stripped of divine protection [Note: Four Colbertine manuscripts, together with the Lyon edition: “inwardly.” Others, together with the editions of Louvain, Douai, and Cologne: “outwardly.”]. Finally, they had been naked even before sin, and they were not ashamed, because they had done nothing against the will of God for which they should be ashamed.

## CHAPTER XIX. Concerning the sin of the first human being and the evils that followed upon his sin by God’s judgment.

1. But now, if you please, let us examine how those first human beings committed so great a sin—one that both cast them out of paradise into this exile of punitive life [Col. 0464B] and, through them, condemned the whole human race in its origin.

It seems to me that they would not have eaten from the forbidden tree unless they had desired it; they would not have desired it unless they had been tempted; they would not have been tempted unless they had been abandoned; they would not have been abandoned by God unless they had first abandoned God; and they would not have abandoned God unless they had become proud and damnably desired the likeness of God [Note: Thus four Colbertine manuscripts and others. The printed editions read: “miserably desired.”].

They would have attained that likeness without bodily death if, living under their God, they had kept the commandment they had received. Thus, having received the ability not to die in nature, they would have attained the inability to die in glory; and there they would have received the reward of being unable to sin, if here their merit had consisted in refusing to sin.

Therefore, open desire for divinity would not have moved them when they had fallen from their Creator into the creature through their aspiration to divinity [Note: Five manuscripts: “through an affection for divinity.”] unless hidden pride had first corrupted them; nor would the devil, through the serpent, have offered them such a deadly counsel unless he had first detected their desire.

“For if you eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil,” he said, “your eyes will be opened, and you will be like gods, knowing good and evil” (Gen. 3:5).

These are the three things that, as the holy apostle John testifies, are in the world and ought not to be loved by those who love God: “Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world; for everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the ambition of the age, which is not from the Father but from the world” (1 John 2:15–16) [Note: One Colbertine manuscript: “not from the Father, but from the world”; another: “from the Father, but from the world.”]. Unless those people, who had already fallen away from the love of God, had begun to love these things [Note: Three manuscripts: “to desire them”; others: “had desired them.”], they would never have believed the counsel of the serpent who offered evil advice [Note: One Colbertine manuscript: “of the one giving evil advice”; the Cambrai manuscript: “of the evil counselor.”].

[Col. 0464D] 2. Thus the desire of the flesh was fulfilled by them when they tasted the forbidden tree; the desire of the eyes, when they desired their eyes to be opened [Note: One Colbertine manuscript: “when they desired to open their eyes”; the Cambrai manuscript: “to open their eyes”]; and the ambition of the age, when they believed that they could become what God is.

Accordingly, corrupted by the pleasure of the flesh, the curiosity of the eyes, and the ambition of the age, they were cut off from the tree of life, from which the means of warding off death and continuing health had been provided for them [Note: One Colbertine manuscript: “from which a great promise of warding off death depended”]. Their bodies contracted a diseased condition, so that, according to God’s sentence, they are believed to have died on the day when the necessity of dying was imposed upon them as a punishment.

Through that tree which received its name from the knowledge of good and evil (Gen. 2:17), and from which they had been able to abstain but miserably neglected to do so, they came to distinguish through their own punishment the difference between the good they had lost and the evil they had incurred [Note: The Lyon edition: “they discerned.”]. If, after losing so great a good, they had incurred no evil, perhaps they would not have known what good they had lost.

Salvation becomes sweeter when pain torments, and the bitterness of sickness commends the sweetness of lost health. Thus they began to perceive this evil—not by learning but by experience—although they would have been better off not knowing it, so that through their very misery they might perceive how great a blessedness they had lost. In this way, the loss of natural good, which perhaps had not moved them, would at least be followed by the just endurance of punitive evil, which would move them.

We have said these things as a necessary digression [Note: The Cambrai manuscript: “These necessary things have been said.” One Regian manuscript: “The necessary things have been said.” One manuscript: “by us.”] about the first human beings, so that those who do not wish to undergo the punishment of their condemnation may beware of the example of their fall.

## CHAPTER XX. That we receive in Christ, restored, all the good things that we lost when corrupted in Adam.

Although we were born carnally from Adam, we must not imitate Adam but Christ, in whom we have been reborn and live, when, renewed for salvation, we lay aside our former way of life.

What is it to imitate Adam except to be punished with death for carnal desires and passions [Note: Three Colbertine manuscripts and the Cambrai manuscript: “for carnal desires and passions”?]? And what is it to imitate Christ except to be crucified with respect to carnal desires and passions?

For to lay aside the former way of life is nothing other than to live not according to the flesh, which grows old and dies, but according to God, who alone can eternally renew and bless those who persevere in him [Note: Three manuscripts: “and have them”; another: “and make them blessed.”].

Therefore, just as, when we were all in Adam, we fell when he fell [Note: The printed editions: “we died.” All manuscripts: “we fell.”], so now, because we have begun to be in Christ, who deigned to die for us all [Note: Four Colbertine manuscripts: “because we are in …”], we too, having died with him through our sins, may rise spiritually with him.

In Adam we lost every good we could have possessed; in Christ we will receive even greater goods, to be possessed without end, if we hold fast to his footsteps with perseverance. Adam made us subject to every evil through his own fault [Note: Three Colbertine manuscripts read “Adam subjected us to all evils.” The printed editions read “Adam held us under guilt.” Other forms found in the tradition are “made us liable,” “summoned us under,” or “made us subject.”]; Christ’s coming freed us from them by grace.

Adam transmitted to us both his guilt and his punishment. Christ, who could not take on our guilt, since he was conceived and born without sin, abolished both our guilt and our punishment by taking on our punishment [Note: Three manuscripts: “because he took on the guilt”; only the Lyon edition reads “was able to abolish our guilt.”]. To say everything in brief: Adam snatched paradise from us; Christ gave us heaven [Note: Two Colbertine manuscripts: “gave us heaven as well.”].

## CHAPTER XXI. How those who desire to imitate Christ ought to live.

1. Therefore, if we wish to be in him what we ought to be, let us walk spiritually as he walked, as the holy apostle John says (1 John 2:6) [Note: The printed editions read “in him.” All manuscripts read “in God.”].

What is it to walk as he walked except to despise all prosperity that he despised, not fear the adversities he endured, gladly do what he did, teach what he commanded to be done [Note: The printed editions: “what he taught.” The Cambrai manuscript: “teach what he commanded to be done”; one Colbertine manuscript agrees. Two Colbertine manuscripts: “do what he did and do what he commanded.” Another Colbertine manuscript: “teach what he commanded to be done.”], hope for what he promised, and follow where he went before us?

[Note: The words “For what is it to follow except …” are absent from four Colbertine manuscripts, the Cambrai manuscript, and the Lyon edition.]

What, then, is it to follow him except to bestow benefits even on the ungrateful, not repay the malicious according to their deserts, pray for one’s enemies, love the good, show mercy to the perverse, invite those who are turned away [Note: The Lyon edition: “those who are opposed.”], receive those who have turned back with charity [Note: One Regian manuscript: “the perverse who have turned back.”], and endure the deceitful and proud with equanimity?

This also pertains to what the holy apostle Paul says: “If you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God” (Col. 3:1). Those rise with Christ who die to sin as he did, with this distinction maintained: he died to sin not his own but ours; each one of us, however, dies not to everyone’s sin but to his own [Note: One Regian manuscript: “not to the sin of human beings.”].

## 2. What does it mean to die to sin, except to live no longer for deeds deserving condemnation, to desire nothing carnally, and to pursue nothing?

[Note: One manuscript: “What is it to die to sin? To live no longer for deeds deserving condemnation,” etc.]

Thus, just as one who is dead in the flesh now slanders no one, opposes or despises no one, corrupts no one’s chastity by crafty deceit, uses violence against no one, brings charges against or oppresses no one; does not envy the good or insult the afflicted; does not serve the lust of the flesh; is not devoted to drunkenness, kindling within himself an ever-greater thirst for drinking by drinking; does not burn with the torches of hatred; does not pursue dishonest gains; does not flatter the powerful or the rich; is not carried away by restless curiosity; is not distracted by the concerns of household anxiety; does not take pleasure in the dutiful greetings of those who come to him, nor is he wearied by the insults of the proud; pride does not inflate him; airy ambition does not hurl him headlong; empty glory does not shamefully parade him; desire for a glorious reputation does not inflame him; the expansion of another’s activity does not entangle him; love of shamefulness does not invite him into the company of the shameful; the fury of deranged rage does not drive him on; the pursuit of costly pleasures does not slaughter him; the ardor of spirited contention does not exhaust him; audacity does not make him shameless, injustice unjust, harshness savage, inconstancy fickle, insolence stubborn, madness insane, gluttony indulgent, disobedience rebellious, boastfulness vain, treachery faithless, easiness frivolous, cruelty cruel, shameful greediness of eating a devourer, restlessness impatient, instability changeable, spiritual weakness wandering, high spirit angry, perversity suspicious, vanity talkative, and malice injurious—one who is altogether removed from worldly enticements, removed from impurities and enmities, removed from the snares of others, removed from robberies, whether more hidden or open, removed from lies and perjuries, and finally removed from every kind of disgraceful act and crime by which those who live carnally offend God and those dead to sin do not serve it.

[Note: One manuscript of Reg., “turns away from no one.” Another Colbertine manuscript, “opposes no one.”]



[Note: One Regius manuscript, “the perverse.”]

[Note: One Colbertine manuscript, “when he does not burn with the torches of hatred.”]

[Note: One Colbertine manuscript, “or the rich.”]

[Note: Five manuscripts, “the distinction of another’s activity.”]

[Note: One manuscript, “a desire for glory.”]

[Note: Five manuscripts, “distinction.”]

[Note: One Colbertine manuscript, “the pursuit of costly lawsuits.” Another, “the pursuit of extravagant revelers.”]

[Note: All manuscripts, “a shameful glutton.” One of them, “a glutton whom ugly greediness of eating makes so.”]

[Note: One Colbertine manuscript, “severe.”]

[Note: All manuscripts, “a shameful devourer.” One of them, “a devourer whom ugly greediness makes so.”]

[Note: One Colbertine manuscript, “immovable stability.”]

[Note: Three manuscripts, “a mocker.”]

[Note: These words, “from impurities and,” are absent from seven manuscripts and the Lyons edition.]

[Note: Two manuscripts, “or crimes”; another manuscript, “or crimes.”]

[Note: One manuscript, “who live in order to live for God.”]

I say, just as one dead in the flesh can neither do nor suffer these things I have mentioned, so those who live for God and crucify their flesh with its vices and desires do not live at all for these and similar vices.

# CHAPTER XXII  
## What moderation those should practice who wish to abstain from the pleasure of delicacies, from excessive consumption of ordinary foods, and from immoderate use of wine

### 1

They put to death their members that are upon the earth when they discipline their undisciplined body by prolonged fasting; when they restrain their appetite within its necessary limits;

[Note: One manuscript, “when [they restrain it] within what is necessary.”] when they not only hold themselves back from more delicate foods with measured severity, but also, even in ordinary foods, allow their flesh nothing for the sake of desire, but only what is necessary to sustain life. They are certain that no delicacy, if consumed without desire, does harm, whereas cheap foods, if taken eagerly, often impede the progress of abstinence.

[Note: The Cambrai manuscript, “so that, since”; six manuscripts, “so that, just as one dead in the flesh now no longer …”]

[Note: One Regius manuscript, “turns away from no one.”]

This is why holy David restrained his craving for water within himself and poured out the water offered to him by his men, lest he appear to satisfy his desire by drinking it (2 Samuel 23:16; 1 Chronicles 11:16 and following); while the food received by holy Elijah, though not desired by him, did him no harm (1 Kings 17:6).

[Note: One manuscript, “not desired by him.”]

From this it becomes clear that those who truly abstain condemn not the natures of foods but their desires, and put to death their pleasures through the misuse of desired food or drink.

[Note: Five manuscripts, “their wills.”]

[Note: One manuscript, “through its release.”]

Those, however, who wish to abstain not only from the quality but also from the quantity of food strive for nothing other than to indulge themselves to the extent that seems sufficient for restoring the stomach and removing hunger. They do not satisfy their appetites through greed in taking food, but restrain them; and it is not fullness from eating that brings them to an end, but their will. They will abstain both from the desire for costly foods and from excessive consumption of cheap ones.

[Note: The editions add here “their minds”; this word is absent from all the manuscripts.]

[Note: One Colbertine manuscript, “their flesh luxuriating.”]

[Note: Two Colbertine manuscripts, “exercise restraint.”]

They do not wish their flesh to be relaxed by richer foods, nor burdened by the distension of the belly with cheap ones.

[Note: This word, “cheap,” is absent from the editions but is found in all the manuscripts.]

For men who abstain are ordinarily neither luxurious nor greedy.

### 2

What shall I say now about abstaining from or consuming wine, concerning which the holy Apostle established a definite rule when he said: “Do not become drunk with wine, in which there is debauchery” (Ephesians 5:18)? It is as though he were saying: Excessive consumption of wine causes and nourishes debauchery, not its nature; and therefore I forbid you not to use wine, but to become drunk. For moderate use of wine strengthens a weak stomach, whereas drunkenness weakens both mind and body.

[Note: One manuscript, “heals.”]

Finally, he commands his disciple Timothy, who had already weakened himself by the prolonged rigor of abstinence and had damaged his stomach by drinking water, to use a little wine, saying: “Do not continue to drink water, but use a little wine for the sake of your stomach and your frequent illnesses” (1 Timothy 5:23).

[Note: One manuscript, “that he ought to use.”]

Accordingly, those who take wine not for drunkenness but only for the health of the body do nothing contrary to abstinence; nor does their will offer it to them, but weakness permits it.

[Note: One manuscript, “brings it forward.”]

If weakness is absent, one should abstain from wine, lest the consumption of wine, which supports the weak, inflame a healthy body.

For no one would say that using wine and making use of oil is a sin. Yet we ought not provide these things to the flesh when it desires them, lest, once we begin granting it what is permitted, it demand what is not permitted and, having become accustomed to our obedience in small matters, compel us into deeds deserving punishment. Thus the natural order would be disturbed, and the body would not serve the spirit, but the spirit would serve the body as its master.

To this may be added that the fruit of abstinence makes the mind itself cheerful and renders the flesh active—not exhausted to the point of weariness, but subject to the spirit that directs it.

[Note: All manuscripts, “subject to the one who directs it in an orderly manner.”]

The senses also, which accumulated delicacies are said to make dull or weigh down, are relieved by the habit of frugality and, as though by a kind of polishing, are refined by religious discipline.

[Note: Three manuscripts, “a certain polishing.”]

# CHAPTER XXIII  
## That it is desire for meat, not its nature, that defiles those who eat meat

### 1

If, while abstaining from four-footed animals, they feast on fattened pheasants, other expensive birds, or fish, they do not seem to me to cut away the pleasures of their body but to change them. They do not do this for the sake of abstinence, but as though because of some sort of impurity—or, more truly, because of the delicacy of a queasy stomach, they reject ordinary and cheap meats so that they may satisfy their pleasures with other meats, even more delicate and expensive meats.

[Note: One Colbertine manuscript, “pheasants or other expensive birds or fish.” Another, “fattened pheasants, capons, peacocks, and others,” and so forth.]

[Note: Four manuscripts, “the pleasure, but change it.” One of them, “but invite it.”]

[Note: One manuscript, “cleanliness.”]

[Note: Two manuscripts, “because of the delicacy of a queasy stomach.” Three manuscripts, “because of the delicate queasiness of the stomach, they reject those common and cheap meats.” Four manuscripts, “they reject those delicate and cheap meats,” together with the Lyons edition.]

As has already become clear above, we ought not condemn the nature of any meats granted for human use, which God created; rather, we must flee carnal desires, which the devil introduced into the sense of the flesh.

Those, however, who wish to appear more frugal and seek glory for themselves as though from stricter abstinence judge that one must abstain from all animals in such a way that, with foreign fruits, delicate little broths, and all sorts of other foods, they fill the enormous appetite of their bodies.

[Note: One manuscript, “fewer.”]

[Note: Two manuscripts, “and with all sorts of other inanimate things belonging to the body.” One manuscript, “and with all sorts of other small things.” Two Regius manuscripts, “and with all sorts of other things belonging to their mind and body,” and so forth. The Lyons edition reads likewise.]

Yet spiritual abstinence urges the restraint not of the use of certain foods but of desire; and those should be judged to serve frugality more faithfully who forbid themselves not the consumption of certain things but the pleasures of the body.

[Note: Two manuscripts, “should be judged to do so.” Others, together with the editions, “should be judged to do so”; but the reading of the former seems more elegant.]

### 2

Those also who, while denying themselves the consumption of wine, flood themselves with drinks of various kinds do not seem to me to fulfill abstinence at all. Perhaps they hold themselves back from wine for this purpose: to purchase praise from people and to compensate for the consumption of wine forbidden to them with more pleasant drinks that provide pleasure.

[Note: Two Regius manuscripts, “who deny themselves the drinking of wine,” and so forth.]

[Note: These words, “from people,” are supplied from six manuscripts; the same number of manuscripts read, “and for this purpose.”]

[Note: Two Colbertine manuscripts, “and compensate for the wine forbidden to them with the pleasure of sweeter cups.” Another, “and compensate for the drinking of the wine forbidden to them with the pleasure of a sweeter cup.” Another, “and compensate for the consumption of the wine forbidden to them with the pleasure of a sweeter cup.”]

In the use of wine, one must abstain not only from wine but from everything that intoxicates those who consume it, and from other things which, even if they do not cause drunkenness, certainly produce pleasure when consumed, so that one may be perfectly complete in the truth of abstinence—not outwardly splendid in its appearance but inwardly hollow, seemingly pure to human beings but full of the filth of simulated virtue before God.

[Note: Four manuscripts lack the word “perfectly.” One manuscript, “perfectly completed in true abstinence.”]

We must abstain no less from the desire to possess superfluous things than from the pleasure of consuming them. For since we possess everything we have for our uses, to desire ardently to have things that we do not wish to use, or even to increase them through gains acquired here and there, is nothing other than serving not a necessity that must be endured but an insatiable desire.

[Note: The Lyons edition, “those things which we are permitted to use.” Two Colbertine manuscripts, “those things which we use.” Another manuscript, “those things which we are not permitted to use.” The Cambrai manuscript, “those things which we wish to use.”]

Nor can I say, “I possess my goods so that I may have something to distribute daily to the poor,” since no one will have distributed more perfectly than the one who, with the intention of perfection, keeps nothing for himself from his own possessions.

[Note: Five manuscripts, “left for himself.”]

# CHAPTER XXIV  
## How useful it is often to prefer hospitality toward those who arrive to fasting or abstinence

[Col. 0470B]

### 1

Nevertheless, we ought to abstain or fast in such a way that we do not subject ourselves to the necessity of fasting or abstaining, lest we perform a voluntary act no longer willingly but unwillingly.

For if I refresh any visitors who arrive by interrupting my fast, I do not break the fast but fulfill the duty of charity.

[Note: One manuscript, “I do not merely break the fast, but …”]

But if, because of abstinence, I grieve spiritual brothers whom I know to take pleasure in my relaxation, my abstinence should not be called a virtue but a vice. For the very continuation of abstinence and fasting, unless it is interrupted when circumstances require, both inflates me and grieves my brother, whom charity commands me to serve—or at least demonstrates that I possess no fraternal charity.

[Col. 0470C]

For charity alone perfects any Catholic person even without abstinence; and every abstinence either destroys a person without the addition of charity or itself perishes.

[Note: Two manuscripts, “all abstinence.”]

### 2

Since, then, even the Manichaeans or any other heretics can abstain or fast—people who, detesting all meats not for abstinence but because of impurity, wear out their bodies by consuming bread and water—we should not regard it as a great achievement when we abstain from things that they also reject.

[Note: Three manuscripts read this way. The editions, “afflict their bodies.”]

Rather, let us consider it great when faith commends our abstinence and charity completes it. Lacking these virtues, heretics can kill themselves, but by abstaining in this manner they cannot be built up or perfected.

[Note: Four manuscripts, “build up.”]

[Note: Six manuscripts, “because.”]

[Col. 0471A]

As for Catholic Christians themselves, who—whether unable or unwilling to abstain—receive with thanksgiving everything granted for our use, let us not place ourselves above them because of our abstinence. Perhaps they possess greater humility and other virtues, by which they can rightly be preferred to us who abstain.

[Note: One Colbertine manuscript, “by right of abstinence.”]

Therefore, if we wish our abstinence and fasting to benefit us, let us first depart from pride, which either drives out all virtues or diminishes them, and from boastfulness, which is hostile to every virtue; indeed, let us depart altogether from every vice, so that our abstaining from pleasurable foods may benefit us.

[Note: One Colbertine manuscript, “while we abstain, to make our fasts beneficial.” In one manuscript the word “abstinence” occurs without “our”; in two, “fasts” occurs without “our.”]

[Col. 0472A]

For then it will benefit us that we discipline our bodies—or at least the incentives of our bodies—with the severity of stricter abstinence, if, freed from carnal desires, we flourish in holy virtues.

But now let the book come to an end, so that, with God’s gift, we may discuss more broadly and fully in a third volume the virtues and vices of which we have touched upon only a few here.

[Note: Elsewhere, “demands.”]

[Note: One manuscript, “in a subsequent volume.”]

[Note: Five manuscripts, “the Lord.”]

# BOOK THREE

# PREFACE

I completed in the first volume my discussion of the contemplative life, how greatly the active life differs from it, and how, with God’s help, you might become participants in that contemplative virtue.

[Note: One Colbertine manuscript, “participants, with God’s help, in the first [volume],” and so forth.]

[Note: Six manuscripts, “I completed the first volume.”]

In the second book, with God’s gift, I discussed the active life as well: what benefit religious admonition and the virtue of patience possess, as was shown; how the resources of the Church ought to be administered; and what should be said about the measure of spiritual abstinence.

[Note: One Colbertine manuscript reads, “in which the usefulness of religious correction and the virtue of patience were shown.” Others, together with the editions, “was shown.”]

[Note: Four manuscripts, “or about the measure.” Another manuscript, “or about the movement.” The editions, “or about the gift.”]

Now it remains for me to begin a discussion of vices and virtues—not relying on my own ability, of which I am not conscious, but aided by your prayers.

[Note: One Colbertine manuscript, “by your prayers.”]

# TABLE OF CONTENTS

**Chapter I.** How far likenesses of virtues differ from true virtues.

**Chapter II.** That pride is the cause of all evils.

**Chapter III.** That pride, from which all evils proceed, is conquered by the virtue of humility, and that all vices, once driven away, perish if they yield to the virtues.

**Chapter IV.** On desire, which is so mingled with pride that no sin occurs which does not proceed from both.

[Note: Two Regius manuscripts, “which is so mingled.”]

**Chapter V.** With what torment of mind envy afflicts the envious.

**Chapter VI.** Into what and how great evils the desire of the flesh breaks forth if the corrupted mind consents to them.

[Note: The Cambrai manuscript, “if the mind consents to it.”]

**Chapter VII.** That even those whom some necessity prevents from sexual immorality, if they become accustomed to living chastely, may rise to love of chastity.

[Note: The Cambrai manuscript, “from shamelessness.”]

**Chapter VIII.** By what indications pride may be shown, whether it is openly displayed in the depraved or hidden in the pretended.

**Chapter IX.** By what signs the envy of the envious is revealed.

**Chapter X.** In how many evils vanity entangles the vain.

**Chapter XI.** On the usefulness of fear, and how effectively it resists sins.

**Chapter XII.** On the future judgment, the eternity of punishment, and the nature of Gehenna.

**Chapter XIII.** On the praise of charity.

**Chapter XIV.** How what the holy Apostle said about charity may be understood.

**Chapter XV.** How much perfection charity bestows upon those grounded in it.

**Chapter XVI.** On the nature of virtue, and how it shapes those who agree with it.

**Chapter XVII.** By what steps converts ascend to the summit of perfection.

**Chapter XVIII.** What perfection should be attributed to the number four; and that the four virtues called principal, living from faith, justify those to whom they are granted by God.

**Chapter XIX.** On the nature and practice of temperance.

**Chapter XX.** What those should be like whom strength of mind ennobles.

**Chapter XXI.** On justice, and on the faith that proceeds from it.

**Chapter XXII.** On equality, and how the usefulness of human society belongs to it.

**Chapter XXIII.** That there are two kinds of injustice.

**Chapter XXIV.** On generosity, and how the work of beneficence ought to be performed.

**Chapter XXV.** On the differences among forms of love, and how perfect love differs from them.

**Chapter XXVI.** What it means to render to each person what is his.

**Chapter XXVII.** That the active life is completed by three virtues—temperance, fortitude, and justice—and that prudence, the fourth virtue, provides the mind with knowledge of hidden things.

**Chapter XXVIII.** On social virtue, and that those who can contribute nothing to human society do not act rightly.

**Chapter XXIX.** That those who zealously devote themselves to acquiring knowledge drink from the source of prudence and wisdom the understanding of all things.

**Chapter XXX.** That the prudent neither harm others nor permit themselves to be harmed, and that their consummate prudence is found there without any admixture of error, where perfect life will exist without any sin.

**Chapter XXXI.** On the four emotions, and that they should not be counted among the vices if their use proceeds from a good will.

**Chapter XXXII.** That these emotions, without which one does not live rightly in this life, will not exist in the blessedness of the future life, which will possess neither fear nor grief.

**Chapter XXXIII.** How the four virtues called principal either defend us from sin in the present or remain with us eternally without any sin.

**Chapter XXXIV.** Where the speaker excuses himself concerning the entire work.

# CHAPTER I  
## How far likenesses of virtues differ from true virtues

### 1

You asked how far likenesses of virtues differ from true virtues.

[Note: All manuscripts, together with the Lyons and Leuven editions, “You ask.” The Douai and Cologne editions, “You will ask.”]

I will not say that they differ as poison differs from medicine, because medicine sometimes heals the body in such a way that it cannot defend it from the necessity of death, while poison does not take life away from the body as though life ought not to be taken away unless poison had been received, but hastens the body’s death, although the body might perhaps have lived somewhat longer.

Rather, I plainly say that likenesses of virtues differ from true virtues as falsehood differs from truth. For a likeness of virtue, which appears to be virtue although it is not virtue, is nothing other than falsehood; and therefore it should not be called virtue but vice.

[Note: Five manuscripts, “since it is not.” One manuscript, “and it is not.”]

[Note: Two manuscripts, “anything else except.”]

True virtue is truth. Whoever lovingly clings to truth, having been raised from the death of sin, will no longer be able to die—unless he withdraws from it through a corrupted will.

By contrast, the simulation of virtue—which, as I have said, is falsehood opposed to truth—separates the soul from God, its life. The soul will not perish, but will live forever in punishment, which is its death, suffering its penalty.

[Note: The word “in” is absent from five manuscripts. Two Colbertine manuscripts read, “separated from God and not seeing its life, but living in punishment,” and so forth.]

Scripture says: “The mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wisdom 1:11).

Accordingly, just as true virtue, if it is true, justifies the soul that truly clings to it, so simulated virtue condemns it.

[Note: One Colbertine manuscript, “the mind clinging to truth.”]

And what is the justification of the soul except its life—perpetually blessed and blessed perpetually? Likewise, the condemnation of the soul is to be understood as its punishment, which is proved to be death, and death itself is perpetual.

[Note: One Colbertine manuscript, “And what is the justification of the soul except its life?”]



### 2

Therefore the soul is guilty in two ways: if it does not do the good by which it may live spiritually, and if it desires the likeness of good under which it may live wickedly and remain concealed.

The proud person wishes to be believed steadfast; the prodigal, generous; the miser, diligent; the rash person, courageous; the inhuman person, frugal; the glutton, humane; the lazy person, tranquil; the timid person, cautious.

[Note: One Colbertine manuscript, “wishes to appear steadfast.”]

[Note: One Colbertine manuscript, “a lavish squanderer.”]

Shamelessness assigns itself the name of confidence; impudence puts forward the title of freedom; verbosity pretends to be eloquence; and the evil of curiosity lies hidden under the appearance of spiritual study.

[Note: The Cologne edition, together with four Colbertine manuscripts, “Imprudence.”]

[Note: The editions, “displays”; all the manuscripts, “puts forward as a pretext.”]

Although these things can be distinguished by human ingenuity, nevertheless, as it seems to me, without God’s gift neither can virtues be desired or possessed, nor can their likenesses—which are vices imitating virtues—be avoided.

So much so that we should believe that nothing has benefited unbelievers, even if they have performed certain virtues through the body, because they neither believed that they had received these virtues from their God nor wished to refer them to him who is the end of all good things.

[Note: Two Colbertine manuscripts, “who did not believe that they had received them from their God.”]

And what do I mean by saying that these things benefited them nothing? They even harmed them, as the Apostle says: “Everything that is not from faith is sin” (Romans 14:22).

[Note: Six manuscripts, “the holy Apostle.”]

He did not say, “Everything that is not from faith is nothing.” Rather, by saying, “Everything that is not from faith is sin,” he made clear that all good deeds are either virtues when performed from faith—and these certainly justify—or, if they are performed without faith, they are not to be regarded as any kind of good but as vices. These do not help those who perform them but condemn them; they hurl down those who are puffed up and drive them away from the bounds of eternal salvation.

### 3

But why do I emphasize these matters concerning unbelievers, about which no one seems to have any doubt, when the holy Apostle also calls certain believers who, although believing in God, live not according to God but according to human beings, “carnal”? He says: “And I, brothers, when I came to you, could not speak to you as spiritual people but as carnal people. For you were not yet able to bear it; indeed, even now you cannot, for you are still carnal” (1 Corinthians 3:1–2).

[Col. 0474C]

And as though we were asking what he wishes “carnal” to mean, he continued: “For while there is jealousy and contention among you, are you not carnal and walking according to human ways?” (Ibid., 3).

What could be found worse than these two diseases of the soul—jealousy and contention—which torment the carnal, who live according to human ways, even in this life? Contention makes people heretics, while jealousy makes them imitators of the devil, who envied the first human beings their paradise.

Thus, when believers rejoice in justice, piety, mercy, gentleness, humility, innocence, and the other virtues, they either live according to God—and must be believed to possess true virtues, which, having been acquired by those who live spiritually, sanctify them and commend them to God—or they live according to human ways, and their virtues are not true virtues but likenesses of virtues, which benefit those living carnally nothing.

[Note: One manuscript, “and they are virtues that …”]

### 4

Therefore, whoever lives religiously, continently, soberly, and mercifully, if he attributes this to God, by whose gift he is helped to live well, lives spiritually according to God.

But if he attributes everything good that he does to his own powers, as though he were sufficient to do good even without God’s help, he lives carnally according to human ways. Consequently, either he does not live well, or whatever good he does for the sake of human beings will benefit him nothing. For, taking pleasure in human praise, he receives here and now the temporal reward of his deeds, which he performed for temporal purposes.

Thus, the person who lives according to human ways is the one who lives according to himself, because he is a human being and lives according to himself.

[Note: These words were absent from the Cologne edition and two Regius manuscripts; they are found in three Colbertine manuscripts and in the Lyons, Leuven, and Douai editions. One Colbertine manuscript reads, “because he too is a human being, and he lives according to himself who lives according to himself.” Perhaps it should read: “because he too is a human being who lives according to himself.”]

If he is able, he stays with the people he chooses, goes where he wishes, sleeps when and as long as he wishes, speaks what he wishes and where he wishes, eats and drinks when he wishes, what he wishes, and as much as he wishes; he laughs and plays among those he wishes.

[Note: Two Regius manuscripts, four Colbertine manuscripts, and the Cambrai manuscript read, “plays.” The editions read, “rejoices.” The whole passage is read differently in the Colbertine manuscripts. One reads: “If he is able, he stays with those he wishes, goes wherever he wishes; he sleeps when he wishes; he speaks when and as long as he wishes, what he wishes and where he wishes; he eats and drinks when and what he wishes, and as much as he wishes; he laughs and plays among those he wishes.” A second: “If he is able, he is with those he wishes, goes wherever he wishes, sleeps when and as long as he wishes, and wherever he wishes; he eats and drinks when and what he wishes; he laughs and plays among those he wishes.” A third: “If he is able, he is with those he wishes and goes wherever he wishes; he sleeps when and as long as he wishes; he speaks what he wishes and where he wishes; he eats and drinks when and what he wishes; and however much he wishes, he laughs and plays,” and so forth. A fourth: “If he is able, he is with those he wishes; he sleeps when and as long as he wishes; he speaks what he wishes and where he wishes; he eats and drinks when and what he wishes, and as much as he wishes; he laughs and speaks among those he wishes.”]

Finally, whatever is pleasant to the nostrils, whatever is pleasing to the touch, whatever delights the eyes, whatever is agreeable to his other bodily senses, he practices and pursues as he wishes—he who carnally desires everything permitted or forbidden.

But the person who lives according to God does not do what delights him carnally, but what builds him up spiritually. He restrains every desire of the flesh through the delight of spiritual desire; he prefers future things to present things; he subjects the flesh to the spirit; and whatever he desires or does, he wishes it to proceed not from his own will but from the will of his God, whom he longs with all his strength to please.

[Note: Three Colbertine manuscripts, “from the will of God.”]

### 5

Since it has now become sufficiently clear that those who pretend do not appear to possess true virtues, and that those pretend who perform something good not from faith or for God’s sake but solely for human beings—serving almsgiving, fasting, abstinence, and other good works not in order to become good but to present themselves as good to others, not to receive an eternal reward but to acquire popular glory—let us now examine the causes that precede vices and the developments that follow them, by which vices ordinarily arise or increase, and the remedies, with God’s help, by which they may be diminished or healed as though by medicines.

[Note: Two manuscripts, “worldly.”]

[Note: Six manuscripts, “the Lord.”]

[Note: One Colbertine manuscript, “by what remedies they may be diminished or healed.” Another Colbertine manuscript, “by what remedies they may be diminished, and by what medicines they may be healed.”]

# CHAPTER II  
## That pride is the cause of all evils

### 1

This is indeed a very difficult chapter. But if you pray to the one who said, “It is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matthew 10:20), and elsewhere, “Open your mouth wide, and I will fill it” (Psalm 80:11), then, with the Lord enlightening or teaching, what is impossible for me as a human being becomes possible.

Let us therefore consider what causes precede and what vices follow.

[Note: All manuscripts, “this chapter.”]

[Note: Three manuscripts, “what vices follow them”; in one of these the words were corrected by a second hand to “what causes vices.”]

To make this seem more credible, let your wisdom not inquire into it from me, but let divine Scripture, consulted by you, me, and everyone, answer. As though we had already questioned it, Scripture has given an unchanging judgment, saying: “The beginning of every sin is pride” (Sirach 10:15).

[Note: Three Colbertine manuscripts, “let it be heard”; one, “let it be advised.”]

[Note: One manuscript, “let this not come from me.”]

What could be said more plainly, what more convincingly? “The beginning,” it says, “not of some sin but of every sin is pride,” clearly showing that pride itself is the cause of all sins. For pride is not only itself a sin; no sin could have been, is, or will be committed without it.

For every sin is nothing other than contempt for God, by which his commandments are trampled underfoot. No other thing persuades human beings to this contempt for God except pride. In the devil himself, pride became the cause of eternal ruin, through which he became a devil from an angel (Isaiah 14:13; Luke 10:18).

Indeed, knowing that through pride he had fallen from the heavenly places and been thrust into this prison of the dark air, the devil, by serpentine cunning, persuaded the human being whom God had made without any sin to the vice of pride (Genesis 3:14). He was certain that, once pride—the cause of all evils—had been received, the human being would easily commit all sins, which are conceived only in a proud mind.

[Note: One manuscript, “he implanted the vice … of pride.”]

### 2

This is why that first human being, corrupted by the elevation of a proud spirit, subjected all his posterity, which was radically present in him, to the necessity of corruption and mortality. Having thus become corruptible and mortal, he begot corruptible and mortal descendants; and what punishable pride had brought about in him became the punishment of sin in all who were born from him.

Therefore we can no longer resist sin in the way he could, for whom not sinning consisted in nothing other than willing not to sin.

[Note: One Regius manuscript, “we can no longer resist sin as we now wish; just as he could.” Another Regius manuscript, “we can no longer in any way do so,” and so forth.]

[Note: One Colbertine manuscript, “who would not have sinned if he had not wished to.”]

For us, however, the desire to live irreproachably is not sufficient unless divine power helps our very will, which fails through its weak capacity.

For him, even his still-healthy nature could help him not to sin; our corrupted nature now hinders us.

[Note: One Colbertine manuscript, “which now, being corrupted, hinders us.” One Regius manuscript, “drives us onward.” Others, “drove us onward.” In one, a second hand has written, “now, being corrupted, cannot.”]

His will to sin alone made him sin, whereas the necessity arising from sin already committed often compels us.

[Note: Six manuscripts read this way. The editions, “pleasure”; one manuscript, “was making him.”]

[Note: One Regius manuscript, “the necessity of the sin already committed.” Two Colbertine manuscripts, “the already established necessity of sinning.”]

For this reason we cry out to God and say: “Deliver me from my necessities” (Psalm 24:17).

[Note: One manuscript, “deliver me.”]

Accordingly, perhaps divine Scripture says, “The beginning of every sin is pride” (Sirach 10:15), because pride first arose in the devil, and through him the human being was overthrown. Of this the Apostle says: “Through one human being sin entered the world, and through sin death, and so death passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Romans 5:12).

[Note: Two Colbertine manuscripts, “and through it.”]

### 3.

Furthermore, we who sinned when the first man sinned did not sin in a life already separated from his, but in his nature, in which we were one with him [Col. 0477D: four manuscripts, “in which we were that one”; another manuscript, “in which we are that one”; another, “in which we were one in him”]. In that nature we were, and we contracted, as though from the root of pride, a corruption like a disease [Col. 0477D: one manuscript, “the corruption of that corrupted one”; six manuscripts read “corruption”; one, “of the corrupted”; all printed editions, “a corruption conceived”]. We possess in this corruption of ours all the causes of sins. [Col. 0477D: two manuscripts omit “and.”] We do not become corruptible because we sin; rather, because we are corruptible, we commit every sin from this corruption of ours [Col. 0477D: one manuscript reads “we sinned”; the others more correctly, “we sin”].

The first man, however, did not sin because he was corruptible; instead, while incorruptible, he corrupted himself by sinning and transmitted his corruption to us by propagation. Therefore, there our whole mortality and every corruption that arose from sin must be taken away, when we shall be without any sin [Col. 0477C]. Here, however, where our nature has not yet been healed but is still being healed by grace [Col. 0477D: in six manuscripts the words “by grace” are absent here; the Camb. manuscript and four Colbertine manuscripts read: “but our nature, which was weakened by guilt, is being healed by grace” [Col. 0478C]], this vicious concupiscence resists our pious efforts. It is not natural, but was imposed and implanted in our nature as a punishment. It was produced by sin, and, if it conquers, it produces sin.

Although we possess it as long as we live in mortal flesh, we must not assist it by the intention of our will, but overcome it [Col. 0477C: one Regius manuscript reads “but let us overcome it”; the Camb. manuscript, “we assist it, but overcome it”]. For we sin not by merely feeling it within us, but by consenting to it; nor does it conquer us as soon as it assails us, but only if it casts our mind down—may that never happen—from the height of its purpose into consent to sin [Col. 0478A].

## CHAPTER III. How pride, from which all evils proceed, is overcome by the power of humility; and how all vices, once driven away, perish if virtues take their place

### 1.

Therefore, if pride is the beginning of every sin and concupiscence is the punishment of sin, vicious concupiscence cannot be overcome in any other way than by first guarding against pride through the power of humility, since pride is its enemy [Col. 0477C: one Colbertine manuscript reads “pride causes”]. A proud will causes God’s commandments to be despised [Col. 0477C: two manuscripts, “humility”]; humility causes them to be kept. Pride made demons from angels [Col. 0477D: one manuscript, “makes”]; humility makes human beings like the holy angels [Col. 0477D: the Camb. manuscript, “restored”]. Pride makes rebels subject to the devil [Col. 0477D: the Camb. manuscript adds “to God”; the source as printed is internally difficult], whereas humility joins the humble to Christ.

The proud want what they do not do to be proclaimed as their own [Col. 0477D: one manuscript, “from themselves”]; the humble shrink from having whatever good they perform recognized [Col. 0478B]. The former, by alienating their vices from themselves, excuse the perversity of their will, and, attributing their good deeds to their own strength, disgracefully boast of themselves. [Col. 0477D: one Regius manuscript reads, “they excuse their life by alienating from themselves the perversity of their will.”] The latter, if they have committed any sins, accuse themselves by confessing them willingly; and, attributing all their good deeds to the divine gift, continually praise God.

Therefore, if virtue does not dwell in a vicious soul [Col. 0477D: the Camb. manuscript lacks the negative], let pride yield to the authority of humility [Col. 0477D: four manuscripts read “yield”; the printed editions, “give way”], for the mind cannot possess the kingdom of virtues unless it has first shaken off the yoke of vices [Col. 0477D: one Regius manuscript reads “unless the kingdom can be possessed”]. Then vices, faithfully expelled, depart [Col. 0477D: five manuscripts, “faithfully driven from the breast”; two Colbertine manuscripts, “faithfully depart from the breast”], if they yield to virtues [Col. 0477D: one manuscript, “if virtues succeed them”]. Otherwise, once cast out, they either subside for a time [Col. 0477D: one manuscript, “spring up”] or return, unless virtues take the places of the vices that have been driven away.

### 2.

Therefore let piety resist cruelty; let patience, firmly established, restrain anger; let chastity conquer lust; let tranquility remove irritability; let measured silence curb excessive talk; let spiritual delight diminish carnal desires; let the rigor of abstinence blunt the goads of the flesh; let spiritual devotion succeed curiosity [Col. 0477D: one Colbertine manuscript, “let spiritual zeal cut off curiosity”]; let drunkenness yield to sobriety; let savagery submit to gentleness; let maturity rule over frivolity; as love of God and neighbor grows, let all desire for the world be consumed.

Let true frugality exclude extravagance; let the virtue of diligence chastise laziness; let profound humility repress boastfulness; let pure simplicity drive away foolishness; let steadfastness not be hindered by the variety that has been expelled [Col. 0479D: one Regius manuscript reads thus; another omits the entire phrase; other codices have “let affected variety not hinder steadfastness”]; let reformed conduct increase discipline; let religious clemency break cruelty; and let acquired goodness uproot malice completely, so that, by the expulsion of vices, the glorious introduction of virtues may be celebrated.

But we shall consider virtues in the following chapter [Col. 0479D: four manuscripts, “in the following chapter”; the wording here is otherwise], and for now let us continue, as we began, with vices.

## CHAPTER IV. On desire [Col. 0479D: two manuscripts, “which is thus mingled”], which is so mingled with pride that no sin is committed which does not proceed from both

### 1.

If it has now become clear, in some measure, how we should understand what Scripture says—“Pride is the beginning of every sin” (Ecclesiasticus 10:15)—let us also examine what the holy Apostle says: “Desire is the root of all evils” (1 Timothy 6:10). Since the Holy Spirit, who spoke through the prophet, also spoke through the Apostle [Col. 0479B], his speech cannot be inconsistent with itself [Col. 0479D: the Camb. manuscript reads “there cannot be different modes of speech”; the Lyon edition reads “there cannot be a different mode of speech”].

We must carefully consider why the one wished pride to be called the beginning of every sin, while the other wished desire to be called the root of all evils [Col. 0479D: four Colbertine manuscripts, “to name”]. Or perhaps the Apostle Paul, as is his custom, explained the prophetic expression? For whether you say “the beginning of every sin” or “the root of all evils,” you mean one and the same thing [Col. 0479D: the printed editions, “you signify”].

Moreover, desire and pride are so entirely one evil that neither can a proud person be found without desire, nor a desirous person without pride. Indeed, the devil, in whom pride holds the chief place, was desirous of his own power and of the destruction of the human race [Col. 0479D: all manuscripts read “of his own”; the printed editions, “of his own will”]; and the man himself, through his craving for the forbidden tree and his aspiration to divine likeness, displayed the diseased character of his desire [Col. 0479D: six manuscripts, “showed himself afflicted by the disease”; Col. 0479C].

From pride arise heresies, schisms, slanders, envy, excessive talk, boastfulness, quarrels, irritability, ambition, exaltation, presumption, vanity, restlessness, lying, perjury, and other things of this kind. But who could doubt that these also proceed from desire, since all who are corrupted by all the maladies I have named are also considered desirous [Col. 0479D: one Colbertine manuscript reads “are considered corrupted by desire”]?

### 2.

Likewise, since desire makes people gluttonous, intemperate, drunk, greedy, rapacious, fornicators, adulterers, sexual offenders, incestuous, and profligate, how could such people become so without pride, since God’s commandments—by which all the evils I have listed are prohibited—cannot be despised without pride?

Therefore, if we wish to complete the course of our struggle, let us first beware of desire and pride: not two evils, but one, from which all evil acts take their beginning [Col. 0479D: one Regius manuscript reads “the beginning of every evil act”; in the same manuscript, another hand reads “the beginning of all evil acts”]. For without pride, what sins could even be begun, since it is said, “Pride is the beginning of every sin”? Or without desire, which is the root of all evils, what evils could be committed, since without a root all things are either counted as nothing or as dead?

Furthermore, if I cannot commit any sin without consenting to evil pleasure, which is characteristic of desire [Col. 0479D: all manuscripts, “my evil pleasure”], and without despising God’s commandments, which is the evil of pride, how could every sin not proceed from desire, which is called the root of all evils, and from pride, which is called the beginning of every sin?

## CHAPTER V. With what torment of soul envy afflicts the envious

The envious person, who makes another’s good his own punishment by envying it, seems to be provoked to envy by no desire, but to be tormented only by the disease of pride. Yet if you examine carefully and deeply the plague of his soul by which he is hurled headlong [Col. 0480D: one manuscript, “his destruction”; another, “inflamed”], you will find him both desirous of the destruction of the person whose ruin he desires [Col. 0480D: five manuscripts, “desirous”] and held by the evil of pride [Col. 0480D: the Camb. manuscript, “and by the evil of pride”], through which he continually groans that the person he envies is preferred to himself.

Who could easily express in words what kind of evil this is [Col. 0480D: one manuscript omits “what kind it is”—an apparent lacuna in the witness], an evil by which the envious person pursues God’s gift in another with hatred of the person [Col. 0480D: one manuscript, “which the envious person…”], even though the person ought rather to be loved, including on account of the holiness of his merit?

The envious person has as many torturers of just punishment [Col. 0480D: one manuscript, “of just punishment”] as the person made an object of envy has praisers. Excellence of merit makes the other person envied; the punishment of sin makes the envious person what he is. No human being can apply a remedy to him whose wound is hidden.

## CHAPTER VI. Into what and how many evils the concupiscence of the flesh breaks forth if the corrupted mind consents to it

[Col. 0480C]

### 1.

Does a person devoted to the concupiscence of the flesh not seem to have any pride, especially since the passion itself appears to humble him through lust? [Col. 0480D: the Cologne edition, with two manuscripts, reads: “Does one who is devoted to the concupiscence of the flesh perhaps not seem…”] Yet unless he had first become rebellious against God, despising through the presumption of a proud spirit God’s salutary command concerning the preservation of chastity [Col. 0480D: two manuscripts read “he would despise”; one Colbertine manuscript gives the whole passage as: “Yet unless he had first become rebellious against God, whose salutary command concerning the preservation of chastity he would despise through the presumption of a proud spirit…”], no desire for lust would provoke him.

In his soul, contempt and fear of God contend for a long time. Either contempt of God prevails, and the proud soul, having received desire, loses chastity; or fear prevails, and the soul subject to God resists both desire and pride.

For many are disgracefully relaxed into lust by gluttony and an abundance of wine; filthy thoughts inflame others to violate chastity [Col. 0480D: alternatively, “to an injury against chastity”]; opportunities that arise cast some down from their purpose of chastity; and examples of those living recklessly bring others beneath the yoke of impurity.

### 2.

There are others whose lives are inflamed by filthy speech [Col. 0481D: two manuscripts, “and by filthy speech”], or whose shameful conscience is exposed. At first they willingly utter or listen to shameless expressions; then, as the disease gradually increases, they fall away from decency [Col. 0481D: one manuscript, “fall away”]. Their modesty worn away and themselves made contemptible, while they wish to appear elegantly unconventional, they now rave shamelessly everywhere in filthy words [Col. 0481D: the Cologne edition, “they are accustomed to”].

For everyone speaks what he loves, and listens with pleasure to what he turns over continually in his thoughts. Thought is what pollutes the mind, just as a filthy thing does, and, if it is honorable, purifies it. Or, if the appearance of the mind does not arise from thought but the quality of thought from the mind, then filthy thoughts do not make a filthy mind [Col. 0481B]; rather, filthy thoughts arise from a filthy mind [Col. 0481D: the Camb. manuscript, “come forth”].

If this is so, the forms of beautiful bodies, entering through the eyes, do not move an incorrupt mind; and when they move it in a corruptible manner, they do not corrupt a sound mind but reveal that it has already been corrupted by its own will.

### 3.

What power do filthy words, entering through the ears, have if they are not admitted by the mind’s judgment? When they do have power, they do not corrupt the mind itself [Col. 0481D: four Colbertine manuscripts, “they do not corrupt”], but find it already voluntarily corrupted. For obscene expressions lose their force with chaste ears and do not break into the secret recesses of a chaste heart.

What power can a tender touch [Col. 0481D: the Camb. manuscript, “an earthly touch”], which wickedly flatters an already vicious mind [Col. 0481D: one Regius manuscript, “which wickedly flatters a mind already desirous”], have to enter the soul through touch, if the soul preserves uncorrupted the purpose of its profession? [Col. 0481C] Thus the soul first loses the integrity of its own accord through self-corruption, and only then admits the pleasure of touch.

I have already spoken sufficiently, I think, about the pleasure of food and drink that must be avoided, in the second volume, where, as briefly as I could, I commended the perfection of spiritual abstinence.

### 4.

But here too I say briefly that the pleasure of taste does not break into the mind through the mouth of the flesh, nor does filthy speech burst forth from the mind, unless the mind first corrupts itself voluntarily [Col. 0481D: three manuscripts, “the voluntary mind”], before it receives anything by which it may be corrupted or brings anything forth.

But if the soul remains firm under its God through the gift of that same God, it neither yields to any enticing delicacies [Col. 0481D: three manuscripts add “that seduce”; one reads “it will yield” instead of “it yields”], nor utters or receives anything filthy.

I shall now touch briefly on odors, so that I may encompass in words the whole temptation of the five divided senses. Through the passage of the nostrils, the sick mind either seeks these odors or, assisted by God, rejects them. [Col. 0481D: one manuscript, “because if it…”] If it subjects itself to its Creator and lovingly clings to him who is its dignity and salvation, not only is it disfigured by no foulness of vices, but no carnal pleasure makes it effeminate [Col. 0481D: two Regius manuscripts, “of the flesh”].

But if, swollen, it recoils from the love of its Creator and Enlightener and casts itself outward toward external goods, abandoning the solid good within [Col. 0481D: three manuscripts, “but if it recoils from the love…”], whatever sinew it may possess is relaxed; whatever strength it has is weakened and broken. [Col. 0481D: all manuscripts, “then it becomes burdensome to it.”] Then spiritual action becomes burdensome to it, and it becomes restless amid carnal things, so that it shamefully desires everything it perceives through bodily sensation—not things needing corruption, but things already corrupted.

And when the body perceives nothing sensible, the soul itself, by delightfully recalling them, represents images of things sensed. Within itself it hears without a voice whatever of sweet song and obscene joking flowed in through the winding passages of the ears [Col. 0482D: one Colbertine manuscript, “sweet song or obscene jokes”]. There, an unpleasantly sweet odor corruptibly exhales for it [Col. 0482D: the Camb. manuscript, “a sweet odor”], the odor that entered through the open caverns of the nostrils. There, a flavor delights it, one that it admitted to itself through the enticement of pleasurable taste. There, it senses something softly flattering, impressed upon it by external touch [Col. 0482D: one Regius manuscript, “which wickedly flatters a mind already desirous”]. There, it sees with desire various colors and alluring forms that the curiosity of the eyes reported to it.

### 5.

The mind, affected carnally, takes such delight in images of bodies—usually when the bodies themselves are absent [Col. 0482D: three Colbertine manuscripts include “bodies”; in the others this word is absent]—that, fixed by the excessive concentration of filthy thought, it seems not to embrace images of bodies but the bodies themselves.

Hence it is that the bodily discharge that occurs without guilt in those who sleep sometimes occurs through guilt in those who are awake [Col. 0482D: one Colbertine manuscript, “with guilt”]. For one thing occurs in a sleeping person and another is done by one who is awake [Col. 0482D: one manuscript, “one thing occurs in those who sleep, another is done by those who are awake”; another, “one thing occurs in those who sleep, another occurs in those who are awake”]. In the former, the fullness of bodily fluid is naturally expelled; in the latter, desire is shamefully made public.

But this desire elicits such discharge in those who are awake when filthy conversation has stirred their foul appetite. These are the people for whom descriptions of women are useful: “This one is plain, that one witty [Col. 0482D: five manuscripts, “silly”], another ugly, another beautiful; one’s adornment is pleasing, another’s manner; one woman’s liveliness is praised even without beauty, another’s beauty alone.” [Col. 0482D: one manuscript, “Thus the transition is made.”]

From there they pass to character: one is commended by such people for her restrained silence, while another is made to appear shameful by her undisciplined freedom. In conversations of this kind and similar ones, they supply material for their desire.

Yet they do not desire such things merely because they speak or listen willingly [Col. 0482D: six manuscripts read thus; the Lyon and Louvain editions, “Yet they desire these things for this reason: because…”; the Douai and Cologne editions, “Yet they desire these things for this reason, whether they…”; one Colbertine manuscript agrees with them].
