If they had not been corrupted by the disease of desire, they would never speak or listen to such things, because these things do not corrupt them but reveal them as already corrupt.

### 6.

And lest anyone judge that, because I truthfully rebuke these things, I myself ought to be rebuked, let him know that perhaps for this reason the ancients decreed that no adolescents should read the book of Genesis, likewise part of the prophet Ezekiel [Col. 0483D: the printed Lyon edition reads “and likewise part of the prophet Ezekiel”], or the Song of Songs, and other works of that kind, in which the generations, deeds, and names of certain women are written.

Although we believe that these women truly existed according to history, we understand virtues to be represented figuratively by their names. For just as those women pleased not only their husbands through holy conduct but also outsiders, without any loss of their modesty, because of their extraordinary beauty, so holy virtues make their own people admirable to everyone and strike outsiders with a certain admiration of themselves.

Hence even those who live viciously place virtues above vices, because one thing is what they do through disease and another what they are compelled by judgment to approve [Col. 0483D: the printed editions read “to please”; all manuscripts, “to approve”].

But lest those who were still carnal receive these spiritual matters according to the flesh, and think not of the virtues signified by those women but perish by thinking carnally about the women themselves [Col. 0483D: one manuscript, “thinking carnally”], the younger were deliberately forbidden to read those passages. For, received spiritually, they give life; but to those who understand them carnally, the very carnal understanding supplies occasions for carnal desire.

Each of these people frequently has on his lips the names of women whose desires he carries wounded within his heart [Col. 0483D: three Colbertine manuscripts read thus; others, with the printed editions, “or whose shamefulness…”], and the shamefulness he is embarrassed to enact in fact, he retains in his mind, guilty not by human judgment but by divine judgment.

## CHAPTER VII. How even those whom some necessity prevents from impurity [Col. 0483D: the Camb. manuscript, “from shamelessness”] may rise to love of chastity if they become accustomed to living chastely

Such people are kept from acts of impurity either by bodily restraint, by fear of temporal punishment, or by the absence of opportunity [Col. 0483D: the Camb. manuscript, “from shamelessness”]. Yet even if the person who is chaste from necessity is impure in will, if the one of a temperate body gives thanks to God, the author of all natures, for the benefit of his nature; and if the one whom fear keeps in the good of chastity, as well as the one whom lack of opportunity prevents from committing adultery, becomes accustomed to living chastely, they generally advance from necessity into virtue [Col. 0483D: four manuscripts omit “generally”; two Colbertine manuscripts instead read “such people advance from necessity”].

As the pleasure of chastity itself gradually increases, they truly become chaste. They advance so far that, now detesting the filth of impurity not merely in speech but through virtue, they resist the incentives of the flesh not from fear of punishment, which is characteristic of beginners, but by abhorring sin they restrain the restless affections of the flesh, which is the summit of perfected chastity.

This does not mean that the soul ever ceases in this flesh to struggle with vices; rather, the very number of its triumphs nourishes, advances, and, as far as possible in the present life, perfects it—provided that it does not, seized by the pleasure of sensible things, cast itself down into the body, but, strengthened on high by abhorrence of pleasures, rises above the body as victor over bodily things, and clings to its God, who is to be glorified eternally, under whom rejected desires do not overcome it while it lives [Col. 0483D: the printed Louvain and Lyon editions read “while he lives with him”].

## CHAPTER VIII. By what signs pride may be shown, whether it is open in the depraved or hidden in the hypocritical

### 1.

Let us now see by what signs pride may be detected, so that, just as it became clear above that no sin can be committed without it, here its signs may shine forth and show that it must be avoided. I pass over those whom even their appearance and gait reveal to be proud [Col. 0483D: three manuscripts, “reveal”; the others, with the printed editions, “reveals”]: their raised necks, grim faces, fierce eyes [Col. 0483D: one Colbertine manuscript, “savage”], and frightening speech proclaim naked pride.

Possessed by the lust to rule [Col. 0484D: the Regius and Camb. manuscripts, “when the lust to rule dominates”], they violently subject to themselves whomever they can; they confuse human and divine laws; they swell with honors; they plunder everything indiscriminately; they rejoice in their crimes; and, corrupted by the disease of pride, they do not even understand themselves.

I therefore pass over these people, in whom pride reigns so openly that it neither deigns nor is able to conceal itself. I point out only those pitiable people and warn against their examples: those who, already converted and making some progress, are secretly captured by pride [Col. 0484D: two manuscripts, “hidden”]; whom its deceptive domination hurls into the depths of evils [Col. 0484D: one manuscript, “condemnation”] and continually tramples down so that they may never be able to rise from there.

Pride itself makes a place for the devil in the hearts of such people; it familiarly opens an unguarded breast to him when he arrives; it welcomes him as he enters; it establishes for those it has captured the right to live wickedly; it strips all virtue from everyone it once invades [Col. 0484D: seven manuscripts, “it strips them of every good”]; and it destroys whatever remains in them that might resist vices [Col. 0484D: five manuscripts, “might be able to resist”; one, “that might resist its virtue”], lest it perhaps grow strong against pride.

### 2.

Hence those whom the festering corruption of a proud mind has infected [Col. 0484D: two manuscripts, with the Douai and Cologne editions, “the corruption of a proud mind”] do not obey the commands of their elders but judge them [Col. 0484D: one manuscript, “they judge”]. When rebuked for their negligence, they either rebel insolently [Col. 0484D: one manuscript, “violently”] or murmur. They dispute about the higher place; shamelessly they desire to be preferred even to those who are better; they mockingly disparage the simplicity of spiritual brothers [Col. 0484D: one manuscript, “they exaggerate”]; they brazenly flaunt their own opinions; they disdain services offered to them; they stubbornly seek what is denied them; they place birth before character; in their arrogance they look down on those younger than themselves [Col. 0484D: one manuscript, “loftily”]; they do not believe that anyone can be compared with them; they disdain being equated with their elders [Col. 0485D: one manuscript, “having scorned”]; and by the mere swelling of their spirit they set themselves above them.

In obedience they do not preserve reverence, in speech modesty, or in conduct discipline. They have obstinacy in their purpose, hardness in their heart, and boastfulness in conversation. They are deceitful in humility, persistent in hatred, impatient of submission, followers of power, hateful to all good people; lazy in good works, fierce in fellowship [Col. 0485D: the Cologne edition and four manuscripts, “late for fellowship”], harsh in service, quick to speak about what they do not know, ready to undermine others, and inhuman toward everything on which fraternal society depends.

They are rash in daring, loud in speaking, disdainful in listening [Col. 0485D: all manuscripts, “in hearing”; the printed editions, “in seeing”], presumptuous in teaching, and grotesquely unrestrained in laughter [Col. 0485D: two Colbertine manuscripts read thus, and more correctly than “savage,” which appears in other codices]; burdensome to friends, hostile to quiet, ungrateful for benefits [Col. 0485D: the Douai and Cologne editions, with one manuscript, “to benefactors”; others, “for benefits”], inflated by services rendered, and domineering toward their subjects.

### 3.

These are the signs of rampant pride, by which God is offended, withdraws, and abandons proud hearts. Nourished by these evils, the devil rejoices; he is invited to come, enters proud minds to possess them, raises them up in order to dash them down, and cherishes them in order to destroy them. He exults insatiably in the captivity of the lost [Col. 0485D: one Colbertine manuscript, “inexpressibly”], so that he may rightfully possess as captives those whom he has subjected to himself through the power of pride, and exercise through them all the evils I described above.

Therefore, deservedly and by God’s just judgment, such people, secretly condemned [Col. 0485D: six manuscripts, “already condemned”], are abandoned to punishment, because they are not forcibly enslaved but willingly yield to the rule of deceptive pride. They can, if they wish, resist it by the judgment of free will, having been freed and fortified by the gift of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0485D: these words, “if they wish,” are absent from two Regius manuscripts and the Camb. manuscript].

Nevertheless, even such people, if divinely inspired to receive salvation, conceive hope of repentance, and do not despise themselves in despair because of their sins, may be healed by the remedy of fruitful satisfaction. By taking up firmly established humility, they may condemn the pride that had shaken them off from their God after swelling them, and may be released from the bonds of eternal damnation.

How this may be done we have already explained above, when we discussed pride itself—where it came from, how far it advanced, and what it accomplished. For it proceeded from the devil, reached the first man, and in him corrupted the whole human race, as a fruit in its root, through the natural corruption of the one who sinned [Col. 0485D: the Colbertine manuscript reads thus, with others; the printed editions and some manuscripts read “through the corruption of sin”; one Regius manuscript reads “of the one sinning,” with another hand adding “by sins,” perhaps for “of the one sinning”].

## CHAPTER IX. By what signs the envy of envious people is revealed

[Col. 0486A]

### 1.

The order of discussion itself seems to require that we say a little also about envy, which flowed so fully from the fountain of pride that the devil, who perished through pride, immediately destroyed the first man after being inflamed by the gall of envy; for pride proceeded from the devil [Col. 0485D: three manuscripts, “for since”; the Lyon edition, “not because, but”—a faulty reading].

Therefore, since the same devil appeared envious by being proud, not proud by being envious, pride was not the fruit of envy; rather, envy proceeded from pride as from a root.

Since the preceding discussion has already shown how greatly envy afflicts the envious [Col. 0486D: one manuscript, “the preceding discourse has already…”], it does not seem necessary to speak here of the punishment by which the envious destroy themselves by lacerating their own souls [Col. 0486D: one Colbertine manuscript, “of their punishment”; three manuscripts, “of his punishment”]. We need only show, with the Lord’s help, how envious people make the merits of those who live holily into sins by envying them, and how much envy corrupts whatever good is in them [Col. 0486D: the Camb. manuscript, “of good”; two Regius manuscripts, “how much envy corrupts good in them. Whatever…”].

Whatever good they hear being done or said by holy people, they either do not believe at all [Col. 0486D: one manuscript, “they do not believe … they turn”] or turn rightly accomplished deeds into evil by interpreting them maliciously. Every evil that lying rumor has broadcast about those people they immediately believe, as though they themselves had seen it. They fiercely contradict anyone who tries to prove that it is not true.

They invent everything about their rivals; they are weakened by their rivals’ progress; they hide hatred within themselves and nourish it for their own torment; they envy those who advance and favor those who sin. They rejoice at the evils of the good and grieve at their progress [Col. 0486D: the printed editions add “over enmities”; the manuscripts do not]. They burn with gratuitous hatred; they fear that the malice of their hearts will be detected [Col. 0486D: two manuscripts, “of sin”]; they are always anxious to be loved and never secure in it. They are friends of the devil and enemies even of themselves; hateful to everyone; anxious when there is cause for rejoicing and joyful when there is cause for mourning—perverse in both cases [Col. 0486D: the printed editions, “scattered”; one manuscript, “perverse everywhere”].

Among friends they sow discord [Col. 0486D: two manuscripts, “discord”]; and, if they can, they strengthen those who are temporarily at odds in their disagreement [Col. 0486D: one Colbertine manuscript, “they strengthen those who disagree, if they can, more attentively in their dissension”]. They stain the reputation of good people with lies [Col. 0486D: two manuscripts, “opinions”]. In spiritual people they praise carnal things, so as to persuade others that spiritual goods are lacking in those people.

They pretend friendship so that, by whatever means they can, they may deceive those who unwisely entrust themselves to them [the printed editions, “who have entrusted themselves”; the source reading is grammatically uncertain]. By wicked suspicions they pile up occasions for hatred. They gladden the demons whose deeds they imitate. They grieve holy men who know them, appearing as friends in service but enemies in spirit.

They are restrained in speech but shameful in deed [Col. 0486D: one manuscript, “unrestrained”]; lavish with secrets [Col. 0486D: another, “adorned”], tenacious of evils, ready to entertain evil suspicions, but empty of good things [Col. 0486D: four Colbertine manuscripts give the whole passage as: “tenacious of evil suspicions, empty of good things, full of filth…”]. Full of filth and equipped with frauds, they are opposed in heart to virtues, wicked in character, and treacherous toward all who live with them in simplicity [Col. 0487D: one manuscript omits “with them”].

2. These and similar things show all the envious to be enemies of the good, whether by the intention or disposition of their minds. They fall into these evils by persecuting those whom they ought to follow, abhorring those whom they ought to love, and savagely excluding themselves from the fellowship of all good people. Thus the good which they persecute in good people is rightly not found in them.

[Note: Three manuscripts read: “These and other things are.” Three others read: “These things likewise are.”]

[Note: One Colbertine manuscript reads: “enemies of the good by the intention of their own mind.” Another reads: “enemies of the good by a disposition known to themselves.”]

[Note: The Cambrai manuscript reads: “those who ought not to be pursued.”]

[Note: Four manuscripts read: “abhorring those whom they ought to love.”]

[Note: One manuscript reads: “of good men.”]

Consider, I beg you, how severely their own evils punish the envious—those whom even the good things of others punish. Where could such people become good, who are evil in the midst of goodness? Or when will they use evil things well, since they never cease to use good things badly?

The holy martyrs used evil things well: truthful witnesses to our Savior and vigorous combatants in the spiritual armies [Col. 0487B]. Afflicted by tribulations, losses, and various tortures, and thereby tested as well, they exchanged earthly things for heavenly ones; and, advancing through the good use of evils, they reached the joys of everlasting good things.

[Note: The Cambrai manuscript reads: “and, advancing through the good use of evil things, using that good thing—the profit arising from evils—toward joys,” and so forth. One Colbertine manuscript reads: “and, making good use of this, advancing through the profit arising from evils toward joys,” and so forth.]

An envious person likewise uses good things badly, because, separated from all the good things that wretchedly he detests, he is left to be tormented by the punishment of his own mind. Who could come to his aid, when by his envy he presents himself as his own executioner? Or from where will he prepare salvation for himself, when, by using good things badly, he turns the material of salvation into destruction?

[Note: One manuscript reads: “he is left.”]

[Note: The Regius and Cambrai manuscripts read: “will prove.”]

[Note: Seven manuscripts read: “who, by using the material of salvation badly, brings about destruction.” The Lyon edition reads: “who, by using salvation badly, makes it destruction.” Other printed editions read: “who, from the material of salvation, by using good things badly, makes it destruction.”]

Nevertheless, if the envious, like other sinners, rise—divinely inspired—to the hope of recovering salvation, and, recognizing what they are, become displeasing to themselves in the desire to please God, let them not imitate Cain. Blinded after he had been seized by the fury of his ruling envy, Cain wickedly took life from his brother and, by the death of his brother’s body, struck his own soul and condemned it to the punishment of eternal death. Crushed by despair of obtaining pardon, he said to the Lord: “My iniquity is greater than that I should deserve pardon” (Gen. IV, 13). That is, he was saying to God: “I do not ask to be forgiven, because the magnitude of my sins outweighs the magnitude of your forgiveness.” Indeed, nowhere is it read that he either repented of his crime or obtained pardon.

[Note: Four manuscripts read: “to God,” instead of “to the Lord.”]

Therefore, if they recoil from this example, remove themselves from themselves, and restore themselves to their God, not throwing themselves into the depths of evil by despairing of salvation, who could doubt—or rather, who would not firmly believe—that pardon for their former wickedness can be granted them, provided that, once the wound of envy has been healed and they have been corrected, they drive the bitterness from their hearts by the sweetness of brotherly love, simply loving those whom they had hated, so that they may be helped toward the good of brotherly fellowship and peace by the examples of those whose merits had weighed heavily upon them?

[Note: Four manuscripts read: “recoiling from this example.” One reads: “recoiling from abhorring this.” Another reads: “of one who recoils.” Another reads: “abhorring this,” without *ab*.]

[Note: Two Colbertine manuscripts omit the word “simply.”]

[Note: One manuscript reads: “are weighed down.” Another, incorrectly: “were rejoicing.”]

## CHAPTER X  
### How great evils vanity entangles the vain

1. Having thus discussed envy, I shall next explain how serious an evil vanity also entangles the vain in. So that it may more easily be avoided, let us briefly explain what corruption it contains within itself.

[Note: Three Colbertine manuscripts read: “These things likewise.”]

Vanity is a kind of inflated disposition of a languishing mind concerning various pleasures, eager for the possession of honor and yet ignorant of how to possess it; puffed up by the disease of empty excellence; hollow, diseased, turbulent; mistress of shallow minds; flattering to all who are badly founded, smoky toward those who resist, seductive toward those who can be captured, and unconquerable by those whom it has captured; a kind of pretense of virtues, but the soul of vices; a tinder for carnal pleasures; a stain upon morals; an appetite for dignities; sweet to the wretched, bitter to the perfect, dangerous to the uncertain, imperious toward subjects, and weak toward those who are well founded. It easily captivates, delights those whom it has captured, harasses the ambitious, inflates the narrow-minded, and humiliates the inflated. The proud serve it; the exalted lie beneath it; the lost discover it; those destined to fall run toward it; and those who have already fallen imagine themselves standing in it.

[Note: One manuscript reads “the disease of knowledge.”]

[Note: One Regius manuscript reads “inflated.”]

[Note: The Cambrai manuscript reads “a friend of vices”; one Colbertine manuscript reads “love of vices.”]

[Note: The words “weak toward those who are well founded” are absent from one Colbertine manuscript.]

[Note: Two manuscripts, one Cambrai and one Colbertine, read: “make the unwary yield”; three other Colbertine manuscripts read: “easily captivates.”]

2. This is the vanity which, contrary to what is thought, does not utterly drain certain virtues but, once welcomed by vicious people, strengthens their license for vice. It does not penetrate minds full of virtues at all. It therefore tests those who are empty and supported by no virtues; and, having inflated them with the arrogance of ruinous ambition, it plunges them into hidden disgraces through a certain delight in publicly raging, just as a storm tosses an empty ship in various directions upon swollen waves, and, while the grain remains in the threshing floor because of its weight, the wind snatches away the light chaff.

[Note: Two Regius manuscripts read “strangles.” One Colbertine manuscript reads “drains lifeless.”]

[Note: Five manuscripts read “light.”]

If this is so, vanity does not make them vicious but reveals them. Its own wind carries them about and spins them around, once they have been whirled by slippery emotions. They adapt themselves to all its impulses through the zeal of their own will. They shamefully boast of deeds of which they are not conscious. They wickedly desire to be praised by everyone. They disparage holy men by comparison with themselves. Lifted up by the breeze of popular approval, they think that they lack nothing in perfection.

[Note: The Lyon edition reads: “That them.” Two Colbertine manuscripts read: “because them”; the Cambrai manuscript and one Colbertine manuscript read: “them, puffed up by its wind”; another reads: “them, by the wind of its breath”; another reads: “them, its wind having puffed them up.”]

They rejoice at the greetings of those they meet, favor their flatterers, obey their pleasures, and please all the dishonorable. They eagerly teach what they do not know. They want sublime things to be believed about themselves, and they prefer pleasant things to serious ones. In speech they curse what they desire in their hearts. They attach the names of virtues to their vices.

They deceive themselves and, by favoring themselves, deceive themselves.

[Note: One Colbertine manuscript reads: “they despise or deceive themselves.”]

Swift in making honorable promises, they are liars in fulfilling them. Changeable in good, tenacious in evil. Serious in speech, shameful in mind, deceitful everywhere. Joyful in prosperity, fragile in adversity. Inflated by services, anxious at reproaches. Immoderate in joys, compliant toward worldly matters, and always difficult where honorable things are concerned.

[Note: Three manuscripts read “wills.”]

[Note: Two Regius manuscripts read “they attach”; the Cambrai manuscript reads “they place before.”]

3. Vanity oppresses such people, lulled by these and similar things, and does not allow them either to feel their disease or to come to the physician. And what is coming to the physician except for the sick person to recognize his illnesses and not be pleased with himself, but to be ashamed of deeds that had seemed glorious to him?

[Note: Five manuscripts omit “therefore.”]

Those who, inflamed by the desire to acquire a reputation, devote themselves only to those works by which human favor is purchased, and despise the good qualities of character, certainly do not do this. The ardor of human praise so inflames them that they eagerly undertake laborious tasks and difficult works which the people admire and through which fame is spread, while they regard them as impressive without effort.

[Note: One Regius manuscript omits “of conscience.”]

[Note: One Regius manuscript reads “and greater goods.”]

Hence those who desire to please people by such things fast, abstain, keep vigils, attend church, and sing psalms with delight, although none of these things can be done without effort. It is not that God’s people do not also do these things; rather, God’s people are shown to offer them more to God than to human beings, because they strive more fervently to excel in holy conduct.

4. But if someone shines outwardly, where he can be thought great, and is foul within, where God alone sees him, who does not understand that all those continual labors of abstinence, fasting, and vigils—which the love of God makes bearable for us, but which love of human praise and inflamed vanity makes bearable for them—are not ornaments of character but coverings for vices?

[Note: Two manuscripts read “may shine.”]

[Note: The Lyon edition reads “all those abstinences.”]

[Note: Three Colbertine manuscripts and the Lyon edition read: “which vanity makes bearable for us,” omitting the intervening words. Two Regius manuscripts and one Colbertine manuscript read: “which vanity inflamed by the ardor of human praise makes bearable for us.” The Douai, Louvain, and Cologne editions have the reading represented in the text.]

Therefore true fasts, abstinences, vigils, almsgiving, and other things of this kind ought to increase our goodness, not conceal sin; and they are to be offered to God not in place of righteousness but together with righteousness. For those who are prepared to transcend the commandments through love of perfection ought to fulfill them with much greater care.

[Note: Three Colbertine manuscripts omit “true.”]

[Note: Four Colbertine manuscripts read “through love of perfection.” The others read “by the work.”]

Otherwise, if the envious, the proud, the arrogant, and the greedy do not restrain these and similar evils of their hearts, yet wear out their bodies with fasting and the labor of abstinence, even if continued without interruption, those works expended upon vanity do not justify them; rather, they condemn the vices which they neglect to correct.

Thus, although throughout this book, as each vice has been dealt with, I have also supplied remedies by which such vices can be avoided or corrected, nevertheless, for the sake of brevity, a general rule must here be set forth, with the Lord’s illumination, upon which those who rely faithfully may resist all sins.

[Note: Two manuscripts read “by which they can be avoided.” Two others read “which we shall set down.”]

[Note: Two manuscripts read “with God illuminating.”]

[Note: Elsewhere: “quickly.”]

Nothing will preserve us free from every sin as does fear of punishment and love of God.

[Note: One Regius manuscript reads “nor one thing.” Another reads “thus us.”]

But we shall discuss love later, when the Lord—whose gift love itself is—has granted it.

[Note: Two Colbertine manuscripts have: “which the Lord, whose gift love itself is, has granted.” Another Colbertine manuscript reads: “which the Lord, who is love itself, grants.”]

## CHAPTER XI  
### On the usefulness of fear, and how effectively it resists sins

Let us now say a little about fear of punishment. Before the mind sins, let it contemplate the punishment owed to sins; let it set against carnal enticements the tortures and pains that ordinarily follow the sinner. Then no pleasure of sin will delight it, and no bodily pleasure will incline it toward sinning.

[Note: One Colbertine manuscript reads: “Here, about fear.” In one manuscript “of punishment” is absent.]

In the end, we do not yield to our enticements and pleasures because we are unable to resist them, but because we ourselves promise ourselves the security of concealing the crime. While we believe that what we do can be disguised or redeemed, enticed by the presumed hope of impunity, we surrender dominion over ourselves to our pleasure.

[Note: One manuscript reads “let it place it beneath.”]

[Note: One manuscript reads “and nothing delights it.”]

[Note: One Colbertine manuscript reads “the hidden danger of concealing the crime.”]

[Note: One manuscript reads “through presumed hope and chosen impunity, perhaps enticed,” instead of “through the presumed hope of impunity, enticed.”]

[Note: Three manuscripts read “to our will.”]

[Note: One Cambrai manuscript reads “pleasure.”]

[Note: One Colbertine manuscript reads “carnal pleasure.”]

But if, at the time when someone is deliberating whether to sin, he considers with a sound mind what punishment awaits those caught in their crimes and wicked deeds, what torture torments the convicted, what trembling shakes their limbs, what pallor covers their faces, and, finally, how greatly it humiliates them and makes them hateful to everyone, I do not know whether even the reproach of a sordid reputation could permit him to consent to any vice.

For what evil deed could be done from which even those who take pleasure in their own crimes would not blush? This is why those who vainly and shamefully boast of their good qualities conceal the disgraces by which they are stung and humiliated.

[Note: The Lyon edition reads: “whatever there is from which the sinner…”]

Moreover, even without human judgment, the torments of a judging conscience rage against the sinner, and the very thoughts of secret guilt crush the mind that knows itself to be guilty through tormenting remembrance.

[Note: One Regius manuscript reads: “and, with a mind conscious of its guilt, the very thoughts of secret guilt produce torment and remembrance.” One Colbertine manuscript and the Cambrai manuscript read: “and they crush a mind conscious of its guilt through torment and remembrance.” Another reads: “they torment and crush through recollections.”]

## CHAPTER XII  
### On the future judgment, the eternity of punishment, and the nature of Gehenna

1. Come now: when we have arrived at that final judgment, to be judged by the Judge who can neither be deceived by the concealment of crimes nor corrupted by the offering of any gift to obtain impunity; when the secrets of everyone begin to be revealed, and not only deeds and words but even thoughts themselves are displayed—what shall we do beneath the majesty of so great a Judge? What excuse will we be able to offer? By what art of defense shall we clear ourselves? What repentance will come to our aid, when we despised it in this flesh? What good works will defend us, which we did not do in this life?

[Note: One Colbertine manuscript reads “from obtaining impunity.”]

[Note: One manuscript reads “beneath so great a Judge.”]

[Note: One manuscript reads “which we ought to carry in the flesh.”]

[Note: One manuscript omits “good.”]

To which apostles, or to which other saints, shall we flee for refuge, when we have despised both their examples and their words? Perhaps the weakness of the body will excuse some people there? But all the examples of the saints will protest against their excuse. Living in the flesh with the weakness of the flesh, they overcame the weakness of the flesh while in the flesh, and by what they did they certainly showed that it could be done—especially since they too resisted sin not by their own strength but by the help of the merciful Lord. He revealed himself even to those who were not seeking him, so that he might be sought and believed in; and he defends those who believe in him with unconquerable protection, so that they may not be overcome by sin.

[Note: One manuscript reads: “To which apostles, or to which others, shall we flee?”]

[Note: One Colbertine manuscript reads “some bodily weakness will excuse itself there.” One Regius manuscript reads “some weakness will excuse itself.” The Cambrai manuscript reads “some frailty.”]

[Note: The words “living in the flesh with the weakness of the flesh” are absent from four Colbertine and two Regius manuscripts. One Regius manuscript reads “living in the flesh, perhaps overcoming”; another reads only “overcoming.”]

[Note: Two manuscripts read “of God.”]

2. What, then, will they answer if the Lord says to them: “If you were able, why did you not resist sinful desires? If you were not able, why did you not seek my help against sins? Or, once wounded, why did you not apply a remedy to your wound through repentance?”

[Note: One manuscript reads “not applying repentance.”]

Will he not say, when they are silenced by these questions and have no answer to offer: “Bind them hand and foot and cast them into the outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth there; where their worm will not die and their fire will not be extinguished” (Matt. XXII, 13; Isa. LXVI, 24; Mark IX, 44)?

[Note: One manuscript reads “let them give an answer.” The manuscripts present the whole passage in varying forms. The Cambrai manuscript reads: “When they are silenced by these questions and have nothing to offer in their defense, he says: ‘Bind them hand and foot and cast them out,’” and so forth. Two Colbertine manuscripts read: “When they are silenced and have nothing to say in their defense, he will say: ‘Bind their hands,’” and so forth. Another reads: “Bind them,” and so forth. One of the Regius manuscripts likewise reads: “Bind them hand and foot; cast them out,” and so forth.]

[Note: One Regius manuscript reads “their worms will not die.”]

And what is it for those who are silent to be bound hand and foot except to be deprived of action in hell, where no one confesses God?

[Note: One Colbertine manuscript reads “where no one confesses God, to be deprived of the action of good works.” Another reads “where he will confess God.”]

Likewise, what else will it be to be cast into the outer darkness except to be expelled from the Lord, who is the light of minds?

Weeping, gnashing of teeth, and the sharpest pains reveal the sufferings of those who, condemned to the punishment of eternal death, will possess not the faculty of seeing, but that of suffering. Their continual groaning, eternal torture, supreme pain, and punitive sensation torment their souls but do not wrest them away; they punish condemned bodies but do not bring them to an end.

[Note: Three manuscripts read “not the life of living.”]

The unquenchable fire does not extinguish them, because they have been assigned to it, so that, while the life of sensation remains, punishment may remain; and so that it may hold their eternal bodies bound for suffering rather than for living—those whom the immortality of the second death kills amid living flames.

[Note: Three manuscripts read “it will not extinguish.”]

[Note: One Regius manuscript reads “the life of sensation in punishment remains.” One Colbertine manuscript reads “so that the life of remaining and sensing may remain in punishment.”]

[Note: Two manuscripts read “and seeing.”]

[Note: One manuscript reads “voracious.”]

As for what is said—“Their worm will not die and their fire will not be extinguished” (Isa. LXVI, 24)—this refers to the whole punishment of the condemned person: the fire of ineffective repentance burns him, and the immortal worm of a consuming conscience gnaws him.

[Note: The words beginning “But what he says” through “they are preserved” are absent from the manuscripts and from the Lyon edition; in five manuscripts they refer to the whole preceding passage, while in one they begin with “since their worm…” and refer to the whole passage. The Lyon edition reads “are preserved.”]

[Note: One manuscript reads “because.”]

Therefore, all who are said to be killed in Gehenna are not treated in such a way that, consumed by the greatest pains, they eventually cease to exist; rather, they live there in punishment.

3. To hear or read these and similar things willingly, to bring them continually before the eyes of the mind, to believe that they are future, to fear them without any disturbance, to consider what an evil it is to be excluded from the joy of divine contemplation, to be deprived of the most blessed fellowship of all the saints, to become an exile from the heavenly homeland, to die to blessed life, to live for eternal death, to be cast into eternal fire with the devil and his angels, where the second death is exile for the condemned and life is punishment; not to feel in that fire what gives light, but to feel what torments; to endure the terrible crackling of the fire as its flames surge; to have one’s eyes blinded by the bitter darkness of the smoking abyss; to be plunged into the depths of the wavering Gehenna; to be torn apart forever by the most ravenous worms; and not to come to an end—to think about these and many similar things is nothing other than to reject every vice and restrain all carnal allurements.

But now, if it seems good, let us ascend from these terrible evils—which shake the minds of the faithful with a saving terror, draw them away from every vicious pleasure, and which lovers of their pleasures will then learn by the experience of their own condemnation, when, more wretched than every misfortune, they will no longer be able to amend themselves—from these terrifying and sorrowful evils, I say, let us ascend to those sublime realities by which the minds of those making progress rise in hope of earning blessedness, renouncing earthly things and desiring heavenly ones.

[Note: Four manuscripts read “and renouncing.”]

And since those who desire to make progress begin with salutary fear and arrive at love by advancing, we too, judging that what we have discussed about the fear of beginners is sufficient, shall also discuss love, insofar as he who gives it grants it.

## CHAPTER XIII  
### On the praise of love

Love is, as it seems to me, a right will wholly turned away from all earthly and present things, inseparably joined and united to God, kindled by a certain fire of the Holy Spirit, from whom it comes and to whom it is directed; foreign to every pollution, incapable of being corrupted, subject to no vice of changeability, exalted above all things loved carnally, most powerful among all affections, desirous of divine contemplation, and always unconquered in everything.

[Note: One Colbertine manuscript reads “kindled.”]

It is the summit of good actions, the salvation of morals, the fulfillment of the heavenly commandments, the death of crimes, the life of virtues, the strength of those who fight, the palm of those who conquer, the soul of holy minds, the cause of good merits, and the reward of the perfect.

[Note: One manuscript reads “a friend.” Another reads “love.”]

It raises the dead in their sins, heals the sick, restores the lost, inspires hope in the despairing, and dwells in peaceful minds. It is fruitful in the penitent, joyful in those making progress, glorious in those who persevere, victorious in martyrs, and active in absolutely all the faithful.

Faith conceives it; hope hastens toward it; the progress of all serves it; whatever good work exists lives from it; obedience grows beneath it; through it patience conquers; because of it religious devotion despises carnal allurements. Without it no one has pleased God; with it no one could have sinned, nor will anyone be able to sin.

[Note: One manuscript reads “conceived.”]

[Note: One Colbertine manuscript reads “flourishes.”]

This is true, genuine, perfect love, which the holy Apostle calls “the more excellent way” (1 Cor. XII, 31). And truly it is the way which leads those who walk by it to their homeland. For just as no one arrives without a road at the place toward which he is heading, so without love, which has been called the way, people cannot walk but only wander.

## CHAPTER XIV  
### How the words spoken by the holy Apostle about love may be understood

1. Let us now learn, with the Apostle teaching us, what kind and how great this love is—not a way for the feet, but for conduct. “If I speak,” he says, “with the tongues of men and angels, but do not have love, I have become like sounding bronze or a clanging cymbal” (1 Cor. XIII, 1).

[Note: One manuscript reads “with us teaching”; five read “with us saying.”]

By the tongues of men or angels we ought to understand the empty eloquence of certain people, who express everything they wish with precision and eloquence.

[Note: Two manuscripts read “because everything.”]

Yet, however elegantly and abundantly they discourse, if they undertake the office of teaching more from the vanity of pleasing than from the love of helping; if they teach not in order to instruct others but to display themselves as learned; if they seek applause rather than improvement from their hearers; if they transfer all the diligence of their conscience into their wickedly talkative tongue and wish to cultivate eloquence more carefully than life; if, lifted up by the arrogance of vain loquacity, they desire their words to be praised rather than put into practice; and if they are concerned not with the holiness of their works but with the beauty of their elaborated speech—are such people not rightly compared to sounding bronze or a clanging cymbal?

[Note: Three manuscripts read “discuss.”]

[Note: One manuscript omits “of conscience.”]

[Note: One manuscript omits “others.”]

Like sounding bronze or a cymbal, they desire above all to make splendid sounds rather than to perform splendid deeds. They are not ashamed that the way they live contradicts what they preach. In order somehow to obscure the shamefulness of their conduct, they never cease preaching honorable things—not so that their hearers may progress through their preaching, but so that they themselves may appear to care about what they preach.

[Note: One manuscript reads “in some way.”]

[Note: One manuscript reads “the conduct of their shamefulness.”]

2. But let us see what the Apostle adds to these statements. “If I have prophecy,” he says, “and know all mysteries and all knowledge; and if I have all faith, so that I remove mountains, but do not have love, I am nothing” (ibid. 2).

[Note: Three manuscripts read “what the Apostle adds here to these things.” Another reads “what the Apostle adds, joining these things.”]

He does not say this as though some people could not possess certain good things without love, but because those who possess them gain no benefit from them if they fall away from love.

[Note: Five manuscripts—three Colbertine and two Regius—omit the negative particle “not,” reading “as though some people could possess certain good things.” One Colbertine manuscript reads “as though some people could not possess certain good things.”]

Love itself is necessary here so that all good things may benefit those who possess the supreme good of love; and there it will remain even more perfect, when it has led all who persevere in it to the vision of God.

[Note: Seven manuscripts read “love.”]

[Note: One manuscript reads “more perfectly.” Three read “perfection.” Other copies incorrectly read “progress” or “more advanced.”]

As for prophecy, knowledge of all mysteries, knowledge itself, faith, and other such things, which are judged necessary not for the perfection of the faithful but for their weakness: in that perfection of the saints toward which those rooted in love strive to arrive, once they have arrived, these things will no longer be necessary, because incomparably better and more perfect realities will have taken their place.

[Note: Four manuscripts read “of prophecy.”]

[Note: The printed editions add “holy,” a word not found in the manuscripts.]

[Note: “To arrive” is absent from the Colbertine manuscripts and the Lyon edition. One manuscript reads “they aim.”]

Prophecy will not be needed there, since it will have brought them to the fulfillment of what it promised would be future. Nor will knowledge be needed, which is like a lamp illuminating the faithful in the night of this present age, when in the day of that life the living Sun will shine perpetually upon the righteous. Nor will knowledge of mysteries or faith itself be necessary, when Christian perfection has arrived at the realities signified mysteriously and believed by faith.

Love, however, is necessary here: it separates us from the devil, purifies us from sin, and reconciles us to God. But there it will be perfect, when it has joined the perfect to God, from whom it was given.

[Note: Two Colbertine manuscripts read: “from whom it has been given to them.”]

3. Continuing to enlarge upon the praise of divine love, the Apostle adds: “If I distribute all my possessions as food for the poor, and if I hand over my body so that I may burn, but do not have love, it profits me nothing” (1 Cor. XIII, 3).

[Note: Six manuscripts read “so that I may burn”; the printed editions read “so that it may burn,” and below, “if I do not have.”]

And rightly so. For if, at that final examination, it is asked not what we do but why we do it, what benefit will almsgiving or the handing over of the body to death bring to those who do not have love?

[Note: The printed editions read “handing over.” The manuscripts read “the handing over.”]

Love, therefore, must be possessed; love must be pursued. Without it neither almsgiving, nor the killing of the body, nor any of the things mentioned above, nor any other good deeds, bring anyone to salvation.

[Note: Two manuscripts read “any whatsoever.”]

For any good action or suffering, unless it has arisen from faith working through love (Gal. V, 6), cannot benefit us.

[Note: One manuscript reads “a person”; another “people.”]

[Note: Six manuscripts read “unless they have arisen … they will not be able.”]

Therefore, nothing of damnable sin will be able to remain in them, nor will anything good be lacking to those upon whom love has flowed—the cleansing of every pollution and the mother of every good thing.

[Note: Four Colbertine manuscripts omit the particle “and”; three of these, together with two Regius manuscripts, read “and what could be lacking to them?”]

For if love is patient, kind, does not envy, does not act wrongly, is not inflated, is not ambitious, does not seek what is its own, is not provoked, does not think evil, does not rejoice over iniquity but rejoices with the truth; if it bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things (1 Cor. XIII, 4–7); and if it bestows upon those in whom it exists all the good things that it possesses—what could be more perfect in this life than those who abound in such virtues, with love reigning within them?

4. Therefore, when we see certain people firmly founded upon the mass of patience, presenting an unshaken heart to raging evils; affected by an abundance of holy kindness and wishing to share their good with everyone; not being scorched by any flames of burning envy; not acting wrongly, but offering purity straightforwardly to everyone; not being inflated by any arrogance of destructive vanity; not coveting anything belonging to others through the crime of greed; not seeking what is their own, for the sake of the good of fellowship; thinking no evil of anyone, however provoked by injuries; rejoicing not over the iniquity of another or of themselves but over the truth; enduring all the restless people or all disturbances with a firmly established tranquility of mind; believing, with fear, the punishments divinely threatened after this life; hoping, with joy, for the rewards promised; and awaiting with steadfast endurance the revelation of the children of God—when, therefore, we see these and similar good qualities, let us understand that they are not able, through the greatness of their own virtue, to do what they ardently desire and accomplish. Rather, they are able through the gift of that love which is not from us but has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us (Rom. V, 5).

[Note: The Cambrai manuscript reads “firmly founded in patience.” One Colbertine manuscript reads “founded in patience.”]

[Note: One manuscript reads “more affectionately.” The Cambrai manuscript reads “wishing to make their good effective with everyone,” and so forth.]

[Note: Three Colbertine manuscripts read “to whom purity ought to be shown.” One Regius manuscript reads “but to show simplicity with everyone, displaying purity.”]

[Note: One manuscript reads “to be polluted by no burning [flame].” The printed editions and one manuscript read “not to be scorched by any burning [flames].”]

[Note: One manuscript reads “incited”; another “inflicted.”]

[Note: One manuscript reads “and of their own”; others “or of anyone’s adverse deed.”]

[Note: One manuscript reads “having firmly founded all disturbances or the disturbed”; another “firmly enduring all disturbances of mind,” and so forth.]

[Note: Four manuscripts read “without fear.”]

## CHAPTER XV  
### How much perfection love displays in those firmly founded upon it

1. Therefore, if we show love toward God and our neighbor from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith (1 Tim. I, 5), we easily resist sin, abound in every good thing, despise the allurements of the world, and accomplish with delight all the things that are difficult or harsh for human weakness—provided that we love God with the perfect love that comes to us from him, with all our heart, all our soul, and all our strength (Deut. VI, 5; Matt. XXII, 37; Luke X, 27; Mark XII, 30).

For a person sins from that part of himself by which he loves God less. If we love him with all our heart, there will be nothing in us by which we serve the desires of sin.

And what is it to love God except to be occupied with him in mind, to conceive an affection for enjoying his vision, hatred of sin, and disdain for the world; and also to love one’s neighbor (Matt. V, 43), whom he himself judged should be loved in himself; to preserve within that love the proper measure, and not to overturn the established order of love?

[Note: The printed editions, together with some manuscripts, read “to occupy the mind for him.” Three manuscripts read “to be occupied in mind by him.” Other copies read “to join the mind to him.”]

Those overturn the order of love and do not preserve the proper measure of loving who either love the world, which ought to be despised; or love their bodies, which ought to be loved less, too much; or do not love their neighbors as themselves; or perhaps do not love God more than themselves (see Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine*, book I, chapter 27).

[Note: One Colbertine manuscript reads: “to preserve within that love the proper measure, and not overturn the legitimate order of love. Those who overturn the established order of love,” and so forth.]

[Col. 0496D] 2. But concerning the world, which ought not to be loved at all, it is the voice of our God himself, speaking through the holy apostle John: “Do not love the world” (1 John 2:15). Our body, however, because it is part of us, must be loved for this purpose: that we naturally care for its well-being and weakness, and act so that, being duly subject to the spirit, it may attain eternal salvation after receiving immortality and incorruption. It must not, by dissolving into its own pleasures, soften the rigor of the soul as it yields to it, pollute its purity, and corrupt its entire dignity through the disease of pleasure.

[Note: [Col. 0497D] One manuscript: “which orders.”]

[Note: [Col. 0497D] Three manuscripts: “its love.”]

We love our neighbors as ourselves when we love them not for any of our own advantages, not for benefits hoped for or received, not for family connections or blood relationship, but solely because they share our nature. For we do not love them as ourselves when we love them for the reasons just mentioned.

[Col. 0497B] For no one loves his neighbor as himself merely because that person is his brother or sister, father or son, mother or daughter, nephew or niece.

[Note: [Col. 0497D] Six manuscripts: “For this reason each person does not love someone because he is his brother or sister, etc.”]

Whoever loves in this way loves carnally. For we must not consider only those joined to us by degrees of blood relationship to be our neighbors; rather, all human beings who, as I have said, share our nature must be considered our neighbors. If we love our relatives—even though they may be disorderly, disgraceful, and badly behaved—more than any saints whom, because they are unrelated to us by blood, we call outsiders, we love not only carnally but also sin gravely in such love.

3. Accordingly, we love all our neighbors as ourselves when we care for their salvation, as for our own, so that they may attain good conduct and eternal life; when we think of ourselves in their sins and dangers; and when, just as we wish to be helped, so we help them according to our ability—or, if we lack the means, retain the will to help them.

[Note: [Col. 0497D] Three manuscripts: “we would wish.”]

[Note: [Col. 0497D] In one manuscript: “according to our ability.” In another, these words are entirely absent.]

Therefore the whole of love for one’s neighbor is this: that you should wish for your neighbor the good you wish to be conferred upon you; and that you should not wish for your neighbor the evil you do not wish to happen to yourself.

[Note: [Col. 0497D] The words “And the evil that you do not wish to happen to yourself, do not wish for your neighbor either” are absent from three manuscripts.]

Those, however, love God more than themselves who, for his love, do not spare their own temporal well-being. They are ready to hand themselves over to tribulations and dangers, to be stripped of their possessions, to become exiles from their homeland, and to renounce parents, wives, and children. To say everything: they not only do not shrink from death itself, but even gladly welcome it, longing to depart from the life of their body rather than from God, who is the life of their life.

[Note: [Col. 0497D] Two manuscripts: “from God, the life of their life.”]

4. This, then, is the order of love that we must observe, in accordance with what the Holy Spirit says: “He has ordered love within me” (Song of Songs 2:4).

[Note: [Col. 0497D] Six manuscripts: “Orderly within me.”]

Thus, as ordered love requires, we must love God above all; and for his sake, in him, we must love those things that ought to be loved, to the extent that he commands (Lev. 19:19). For he commands that we love our bodies for our own sake, our neighbors as ourselves, and him more than ourselves (Matt. 22).

[Note: [Col. 0497D] Five manuscripts: “he commanded.” The same reading occurs shortly afterward.]

[Note: [Col. 0498D] One manuscript: “our neighbors as ourselves, and him more than ourselves; less well.”]

This must be understood in such a way that we show greater care to those whom familiarity makes closer to us, provided that their reputation does not condemn them and their life commends them; that we regard the progress of all as our own; and that we mourn the sins of others compassionately, as though they were our own.

Thus, in this life, those can be perfect who love God perfectly. And they love God perfectly who desire what God desires and do not desire what he does not desire; who do not consent to any sins by which he is offended; and who continually strive to love and possess the virtues that he graciously grants.

These are the people who truly believe that, in everything good they are able to accomplish, they have been helped by him so that they can accomplish it. Whatever evil they have committed, they attribute to the fault of their own will. Whatever good they have been unable to accomplish, they continually ask him to enable them to accomplish. When they have succeeded, they give him thanks. The good things of his that they have obtained, they wish also to share with others; and, extending the breadth of their love even to their enemies, they desire everyone to become what they themselves are.

Enough has been said about their vices and remedies. Let us now briefly discuss how each virtue may be acquired.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the character of virtue and how it forms those who are in harmony with it

[Col. 0498C]

1. Every holy virtue is a divine reality, wholly incorporeal and utterly pure. Defiled minds do not defile it; rather, it cleanses the defiled. Through participation in it, formless things are formed, the dead are raised, the weak are healed, the crooked are corrected, and the alienated are reconciled.

[Note: [Col. 0498D] Three manuscripts: “the weak are strengthened.”]

[Note: [Col. 0498D] One manuscript: “the sick are healed.”]

[Note: [Col. 0498D] Four manuscripts: “the opposed”; one: “the overthrown.”]

No one possesses this virtue except God and the one to whom God gives it. It dwells in the soul, but sanctifies both soul and body. No one approaches it unwillingly, and no one loses it except one deceived by his own will. No one can bestow it upon himself, though he can take it away; nor can he bestow it upon another or take it away from another.

[Note: [Col. 0498D] One Colbertine manuscript: “nor is he able either to bestow it or to take it away.”]

2. Therefore, when such a great virtue shines upon someone still wasting away amid his pleasures, and awakens in him a wholesome desire to long for it, a conflict between two contrary pleasures immediately arises in his soul. The will, divided by a twofold pleasure, leads the mind this way and that: at one moment reproving what it had chosen, at another choosing what it had reproved. Thus, as it turns now to one side and now to the other amid the variety of its thoughts, it is tormented and torn apart by that lukewarm middle state between virtue and vice.

[Note: [Col. 0498D] Three manuscripts: “and moved him by a wholesome desire to desire it.”]

[Note: [Col. 0499C] Six manuscripts: “divided.” The printed editions shortly afterward do not have “thus.”]

[Note: [Col. 0499C] One Colbertine manuscript: “turning itself mutually.”]

[Note: [Col. 0499D] One manuscript, in another hand: “a trembling [middle state].” Another manuscript: “a lukewarm middle state, as it were, between virtues and vices.”]

For as long as a person has not been firmly established in what he has chosen, and as long as he alternately does not want what he wanted and begins to want what he did not want, the very diversity of his wills tears him apart, as though he were standing at an uncertain crossroads of deliberation.

[Note: [Col. 0499D] One manuscript: “in an uncertain fork of deliberation.”]

[Note: [Col. 0499D] One manuscript: “what he had chosen.”]

[Note: [Col. 0499D] Two manuscripts: “of pleasures”; the Cologne manuscript: “the will.”]

On one side virtue warns him of his salvation and calls him; on the other, vicious habit delays him as he wishes to depart from it, calls him back, and, when he has turned away from it but has not yet fully turned toward virtue, seduces him with reminders of his customary pleasure. It displays all the enticements in which he once indulged ruinously. It introduces shameful desires by which he may be conquered and, when he is already almost disgusted, softly whispers something seductive—I hardly know what—and begs him not to prefer hard things to soft, sorrows to joys, uncertainties to certainties, or the future to present pleasure.

[Note: [Col. 0499D] One Colbertine manuscript: “by which he is conquered.” Another: “by which he was conquered.”]

[Note: [Col. 0499D] Six manuscripts: “to the pleasure of present things, [rather than] future things.”]

It tells him to consider how painful and difficult it is to do without sweet luxuries, to renounce carnal enticements, to be weighed down by the continual labors of abstinence, to be tortured by prolonged fasting and vigils, to seek the reward of uncertain recompense through definite affliction of the flesh, to seize weapons by resisting the devil, skilled as he is at deception, and to avoid his ambushes and frauds through the vigilance of a watchful mind.

[Note: [Col. 0499D] Two manuscripts: “riches.”]

[Note: [Col. 0499D] Three manuscripts, including Colbert: “to seize weapons of resistance”; and shortly afterward, the Cambrai manuscripts: “to grasp.”]

[Col. 0499C] Finally, it tells him how miserable it would be, overcome by the enormity of such harshness and deceived by diabolical fraud, to return to the pleasures he had rejected, enjoy the pleasures he had cast aside, and delight in everything he had despised when he heedlessly undertook his laborious resolve.

[Note: [Col. 0499D] The Lyon edition, together with three manuscripts: “afterward.”]

3. By these and similar arguments vicious habit afflicts the uncertain resolve of holiness.

[Note: [Col. 0499D] One Colbertine manuscript: “the uncertain resolve of holy conduct.”]

Virtue, on the other hand—the virtue called continence—boldly rebukes the one who lingers. It invites him to pure pleasures and chaste delights, which all its lovers enjoy. It offers clothing to the naked in the form of justice. It displays the adornment of its illuminated equipment. To one who distrusts himself, it promises the help of its protection.

[Note: [Col. 0499D] One manuscript: “the one who delays.”]

It urges and challenges him, once he has laid aside his uncertain resolve, to undertake a spiritual purpose; to trust that he will persevere in the labor of the purpose he has undertaken not through his own ability but through the Lord’s mercy; and, relying not on his own strength but on the help of omnipotent grace, to seize victorious weapons against diabolical assaults.

[Note: [Col. 0499D] Two manuscripts: “to seize weapons.”]

It tells him to consider how many people, and how great their number, have been able—and still are able—to accomplish what he despairs of being able to accomplish. From where they were able, he should firmly believe that he too can be able. With certain hope, he should place spiritual things before carnal things, heavenly things before earthly things, and future things before present things.

## CHAPTER XVII. By what steps those who have converted ascend to the summit of perfection

[Col. 0500B] 1. When someone, enticed by the persuasion and beauty of virtue, has withdrawn even slightly from his former way of life, another temptation immediately confronts him, against which he must struggle.

[Note: [Col. 0499D] Six manuscripts: “But if he has been persuaded.” One: “If he has been persuaded.”]

[Note: [Col. 0499D] One manuscript: “by the beauty.”]

[Note: [Col. 0500C] One manuscript: “a struggle.”]

For the person whom carnal pleasure, once overcome, has left will be seized by the vanity of the world. This is shown by those who forbid themselves the pleasure of their own sensual lust but allow the license of empty vanity to govern their pleasure.

[Note: [Col. 0500C] One Colbertine manuscript: “the pleasure of his own lust.”]

[Note: [Col. 0500D] One Colbertine manuscript: “they prefer the pleasures.”]

They oppose the shamefulness of sexual intercourse but yield to ambition. They use delicacies and carefully fashioned clothing for luxury, long-haired boys for display, and powerful horses for pomp; they use hawks and fattened dogs for the hunt and frequent hunting for extravagance. They falsely claim that the ostentatious display of an ambitious establishment is necessary adornment.

[Note: [Col. 0500D] One Colbertine manuscript: “and they yield to the desire for greed and ambition.”]

[Note: [Col. 0500D] Two manuscripts: “boys”; one: “girls”; another: “with little animals,” perhaps “with youthful long-haired attendants.”]

[Note: [Col. 0500D] This is the reading of four manuscripts. The printed editions instead have “and for the boastful display of an ambitious establishment.” One Colbertine manuscript: “and the boastful display of an ambitious establishment.”]

[Col. 0500C] 2. They laugh immoderately, raise their voices in shameless guffaws, gladly listen to disgraceful jokes, and make other people’s suffering their own amusement by wearing them down. They indulge every sort of urbane person, however disgraceful, in pleasures; they reject serious people in need of necessities; they build very large and ornate houses; they continually increase their possessions; and, if opportunity permits, they yearn to seize what belongs to others.

[Note: [Col. 0500D] One Colbertine manuscript: “They raise an uncontrolled voice in shameless guffaws.”]

[Note: [Col. 0500D] Six manuscripts have this reading. The printed editions have “servos” (“slaves”). But the earlier reading seemed preferable to those who had added “serios” (“serious people”) in the margin; it is also read this way in the Cambrai manuscript, which may have been the only one available to them.]

They do not consider the object of their greed, but some obscure usefulness, to be the issue. Thus they not only gladly pursue the practices I have mentioned, or many others like them, but also mock those who rebuke them for doing so, believing that those people are foolish because they condemn as the crime of ambition things that are permitted and customary among the nobility.

[Note: [Col. 0500D] One Colbertine manuscript: “calling foolish those who condemn as ambition things permitted and customarily granted to nobles.” Shortly afterward, five manuscripts and the Lyon edition have “defame.”]

[Col. 0501A] But whoever, aided by God, has overcome this evil as well, and, strengthened by the power of spiritual continence, has trampled everything by which he can be held back from perfection, inclines his mind toward holy virtue through the earnestness of a good will. Then, with delight and devotion, he observes in himself every command of the queen virtue reigning within him. Thus, having become one spirit with his God, he always does and thinks nothing other than how he may become more distinguished and noble, and overcome the pleasures of all vices with pure delights.

[Note: [Col. 0501D] Four manuscripts have this reading. Another manuscript: “inclines.” The printed editions: “will have inclined.”]

[Note: [Col. 0501D] Three manuscripts: “or more noble.”]

## CHAPTER XVIII. What perfection should be attributed to the number four, and that the four virtues called principal, bestowed by God upon those who live by faith, justify them

1. Let us now see whether that philosophical opinion is true by which philosophers define four virtues as certain sources of all virtues, and also four vices as certain origins of all evils. Philosophers are not the only ones who hold that there are four principal virtues; our own teachers agree with them. But why there are four, and what the works of each are, we must briefly demonstrate, with the Lord’s illumination.

[Col. 0501B] Almost no one is unaware that the number four is consecrated to perfection.

[Note: [Col. 0501D] One manuscript: “in perfection.” Another: “The number four is hallowed to the perfection of number.”]

Indeed, the whole world is found to be bounded by four regions or corners: East and West, North and South.

[Note: [Col. 0501D] Two manuscripts omit “and,” which is found in other codices.]

[Note: [Col. 0501D] Two manuscripts: “bounded.”]

Adam himself, who is the father of the human race—or the general name “human being,” which is “homo”—is expressed in four letters. The body too, constructed from four elements, contains within itself the mystery of the number four.

[Note: [Col. 0501D] One manuscript: “equipped.”]

The ancients also carefully discovered that the soul itself has four affections, by which we employ it either for good or for evil; and later generations, approving their discoveries, accepted them.

2. The four rivers proceeding from the fountain of paradise (Gen. 2:10), the four Gospels, the four wheels of the divine chariot, and the four living creatures, their four wings and four faces (Ezek. 1:5 and following), also abundantly commend the dignity of this number.

[Note: [Col. 0501D] One manuscript: “these virtues.”]

Therefore we must carefully consider these virtues, which contain so much perfection in their number: how much holiness they confer upon the Christian soul, and how there is nowhere any perfection that is not found in these virtues.

[Note: [Col. 0501D] Four manuscripts: “that there is never any.”]

For if temperance makes a person temperate, prudence prudent, justice just, and fortitude strong, what could be more perfect than one who acts temperately, justly, prudently, and courageously? It is indeed difficult for us to display the names of the virtues that arise from the four we have called principal. But when their properties and actions begin to be disclosed, it may perhaps become clear from the affections of each which virtues arise from which.

[Col. 0502A]

[Note: [Col. 0501D] One Regius manuscript: “from the affections.” Another and one Colbertine manuscript, together with the Cambrai manuscript: “from the effects.”]

3. Nevertheless, we must first know and hold firmly that these four virtues, and all those that arise from them, are gifts of God; and that no one has had, has, or will have them unless God, who is the nature and source of all virtues, has conferred them.

For all who, at whatever time and among whatever people, believed in God and lived by faith were certainly able, through his gift, to become temperate and prudent, just and strong.

[Note: [Col. 0502D] Two manuscripts: “or strong.”]

But those who lived without faith, not knowing God or even blaspheming him, must be considered incapable of receiving or possessing any of these virtues from God.

## CHAPTER XIX. On the character and work of temperance

[Col. 0502B]

1. But let us now see what the nature of each virtue is. Temperance makes a person temperate, abstinent, frugal, sober, moderate, chaste, quiet, serious, and modest.

[Note: [Col. 0502D] The word “serious” is absent from two Colbertine manuscripts.]

[Note: [Col. 0502D] One Colbertine manuscript: “when this virtue dwells in the soul, without ‘if.’”]

When this virtue dwells in the soul, it restrains lusts, moderates emotions, multiplies holy desires, disciplines vicious ones, orders everything confused within us, strengthens what is ordered, removes evil thoughts, implants holy ones, extinguishes the fire of lustful pleasure, kindles the soul’s tepidity with desire for future recompense, composes the mind in peaceful tranquility, and always defends it entirely from every storm of vices.

[Note: [Col. 0502D] One Colbertine manuscript: “and always defends it safely from the power of every vice.”]

Temperance reduces our intemperance to an honorable moderation in food and drink themselves, so that we are content with what is set before us. We should not shamelessly ask for something that the person being asked perhaps does not have, or offend others by seeking what pleases our desire, or display the intemperate appetite of our gluttony. Nor should we condemn those who wish to abstain from the foods that we ourselves eat, nor shame those who perhaps partake of what we abstain from and give thanks to God. We should be certain that it is sufficiently pitiable to condemn anyone for consuming food or drink, or to claim holiness for ourselves on account of abstinence.

[Note: [Col. 0502D] One manuscript: “or lest we offend others, etc.” These words are absent from one Regius manuscript.]

2. It belongs to temperance that we show reverence to our elders, honor our equals as brothers, and extend to our juniors the grace of fatherly love.

[Note: [Col. 0502D] One manuscript: “of pure love.”]

It belongs to temperance that we grant a speaking elder silence; that we await his command to speak; that in conversation we do not raise our voice excessively; that we do not allow laughter to burst into loud guffaws; that we disparage no one; and that we do not patiently tolerate those who disparage others.

[Note: [Col. 0503D] Three Colbertine manuscripts: “that we do not allow laughter to burst forth.” Another: “that we do not allow ourselves to burst into laughter.” One Colbertine manuscript and the Cambrai manuscript: “that we do not dare burst into laughter.”]

[Note: [Col. 0503D] One Regius manuscript: “nor those who disparage.” One Colbertine manuscript: “and those who disparage.” Another Regius manuscript: “nor do we consent to one who disparages, nor endure him with equanimity.”]

We know that both those who disparage others and those who consent to their disparagement are corrupted by the disease of vanity. They want others to appear worthless so that they themselves may be commended by comparison with those whom they criticize, and so that they may seem not to possess the vices they maliciously rebuke in others.

[Note: [Col. 0503D] Three manuscripts: “because they want others to appear worthless for this purpose.”]

Temperance removes this evil. Whoever wishes to serve it looks not for something to criticize in his brothers, but for something for which to praise God. Accordingly, it belongs to temperance that we are moderate not only in the functions of all our members, but also that we willingly observe everything that makes us moderate and sober.

But let these remarks about temperance suffice, so that we may discuss fortitude.

[Note: [Col. 0503D] One manuscript: “now let us discuss fortitude.”]

## CHAPTER XX. What those whom strength of mind ennobles ought to be like

[Col. 0503B]

1. Strength of mind must be understood as that which not only remains unshaken when struck by various troubles, but also does not become relaxed and succumb to any enticements of pleasure.

Otherwise, if it breaks the assaults of raging evils, withstands whatever calamities are inflicted, persists untiring amid the savagery of injuries, amid storms of oppressive afflictions, amid present enmities and losses, and amid persecutions of every kind, yet boasts about its very endurance of its adversaries and does not rejoice in the gift of God by which it is enlightened, but takes carnal delight in the favor of the crowd by which it is praised; if it rejoices more in being praised than in possessing something for which it may be praised; and if, by this means, it places human praise before divine gifts—who could doubt that this disposition of mind cannot be called virtue?

[Note: [Col. 0503D] One manuscript: “by which he is enlightened.”]

[Note: [Col. 0503D] One manuscript: “who is enlightened.”]

[Note: [Col. 0503D] The Regius manuscripts and the Cambrai manuscript: “works.”]

If it were virtue, it would also bravely resist such flatteries, and would not yield to soft things when, with the Lord’s help, it had overcome things hard and harsh. The desire for the world makes some people invincible in harsh sufferings; in their case it is not patience that should be praised, but hardness that should be marveled at.

[Note: [Col. 0503D] One manuscript: “to be pitied.”]

2. But those whom love of God makes strong for enduring sufferings are corrupted by no fleshly delight and no pleasure that falsely entices.

[Note: [Col. 0503D] Three manuscripts add “evil.” One: “no pleasure.”]

For it makes a great difference not what we suffer, but why we suffer. Patience is not found in those who endure oppressive things with equanimity, but only in those whom justice makes able to endure them courageously.

Finally, the Lord did not say, “Blessed are those who suffer persecution” (Matt. 5:10), and then remain silent; rather, he added “for the sake of justice,” clearly showing that true patience is produced not by punishment but by its cause. Therefore he promised blessedness not to those who suffer persecution, but to those who suffer for the sake of justice.

[Note: [Col. 0503D] The word “Blessed” was absent from the printed editions; it is restored from five manuscripts.]

If this is so, endurance of evils to be overcome—or of evils already overcome—is true patience only if it is just.

[Note: [Col. 0503D] All manuscripts here add “or of evils already overcome”; the printed editions omit it.]

And patience is just in those whose steadfastness of unconquered mind yields neither to pains nor to pleasures.

[Note: [Col. 0503D] The Cambrai manuscript: “falls.”]

But this strength of mind comes to us from him to whom, with the prophet, we sing: “The Lord is my strength and my praise, and he has become my salvation” (Ps. 117:14).

[Note: [Col. 0504D] The Cambrai manuscript: “we sing.”]

[Note: [Col. 0504D] Four manuscripts: “and my praise.”]

He is our strength because he strengthens us against every vice with unconquerable protection, so that neither flatteries dissolve our spirit nor adversities cast it down.

[Note: [Col. 0504D] Three manuscripts: “which is thus.” Two manuscripts: “who is thus.”]

And he becomes our praise if we desire not to have ourselves praised for God’s gifts, but to have the divine gifts praised in us. Nor can those boast of their own virtue for whom the Lord has become salvation.

3. Therefore the person for whom the Lord is strength of mind must yield to no carnal desires, consent to no pleasures, and conquer ambition and popular glory. The love of money must not enslave him, nor the bitterness of sufferings and losses subject him.

[Note: [Col. 0504D] One manuscript adds “of another’s.”]

[Note: [Col. 0504D] One manuscript: “must not cast him down from the suffering of losses.”]

Let God be his entire praise, perfect glory, pure love, certain hope, firm security, sound ability, and incorrupt health.

[Note: [Col. 0504D] Five manuscripts: “pure affection.”]

Then whatever pleases the carnal must displease him in this world; whatever seems precious must become worthless; whatever shines must grow sordid through contemplation of future things; and he must not allow himself to be crushed by those vices which he has already crushed through God’s grace.

[Note: [Col. 0504D] One manuscript: “by comparison.”]

[Note: [Col. 0504D] One manuscript: “by God’s grace.”]

For it appears more disgraceful for the mind to be conquered by vices that it had conquered. It profits him nothing to have overcome some things if he submits to something else that he has neglected to overcome.

[Note: [Col. 0504D] Four manuscripts: “the mind.”]

[Note: [Col. 0504D] One Colbertine manuscript: “it profits nothing”; the others: “it should profit nothing.”]

[Note: [Col. 0504D] One manuscript: “is subjected.”]

For a person is not usually considered strong merely because he has distinguished himself in undertaking labors and dangers, or has devoted himself to restraining and subduing pleasures. Rather, that person must be judged great and exalted, powerful and worthy of the name “fortitude,” who has permitted no vice to rebel against him or dominate him.

[Note: [Col. 0504D] One manuscript: “in restraining.”]

[Note: [Col. 0504D] This word, “now,” was inserted in the Cambrai manuscript, which reads: “Therefore let there be absent.”]

Let cowardice be absent, lest we despair of being able to do what we can do.

[Note: [Col. 0504D] One manuscript from Colbert: “miserable cowardice, inactivity, and sloth, so that we do not…”]

Let vicious presumption be absent, lest we attribute to ourselves what we can do through God’s grace.
