[Col. 0505A] For whether we despair of the gift of God by which we are made strong, or boast of our own ability, we cannot be capable of resisting vices. Strength of mind must therefore both shake off the sloth of despair and oppose boastfulness.

## CHAPTER XXI. On justice, or the faith that proceeds from it

Until now we have discussed the virtue called fortitude.

[Note: [Col. 0505C] The words “we have discussed” are absent from four manuscripts; another has “we have treated.”]

Let us now see what protection justice also offers us in this life, and how it too cannot be overcome by any assaults of the vices in the hearts of those who have entrusted themselves to it.

[Note: [Col. 0505C] Two manuscripts omit “also.” The Cambrai manuscript has it later: “offers.”]

For faith, which is the foundation of justice, which no good works precede and from which all good things proceed, cleanses us from every sin, enlightens our minds, reconciles us to God, and joins us to all who share our nature. It inspires in us hope of future recompense, increases holy virtues within us, and confirms us in their possession.

[Note: [Col. 0505D] Two Regius manuscripts and one Colbertine manuscript have: “but from which all good things proceed.” The printed editions: “and from which all things proceed.” These words are absent from two Colbertine manuscripts.]

[Note: [Col. 0505D] Three Colbertine manuscripts: “reconciles.”]

## CHAPTER XXII. On equity; that the welfare of human society belongs to it

From justice flows equity. It makes us say that the needs of all human beings are our own, and makes us believe that we were born not only for ourselves but also for the human race. Whatever can harm any person, we avoid as though it harmed us.

[Note: [Col. 0505D] One manuscript: “that, as though…”]

For, since we are human beings, we ought to consider nothing human foreign to us.

[Note: [Col. 0505D] One manuscript from Colbert: “because we are human beings—whence the term ‘humanity,’ by which, as mortals, we protect one another; nothing human…”]

For it is characteristic of beasts to live for themselves and not contribute their advantages to the common good.

[Note: [Col. 0505D] One manuscript lacks the word “for themselves.”]

[Col. 0505C] We differ from such creatures not only by the prerogative of mind, but also by preserving the equality of right, if, considering the advantages and disadvantages of all, we live for the benefit of all who share our nature just as we do for our own advantage.

[Note: [Col. 0505D] One Colbertine manuscript: “from them we differ not only by the privilege of merits, grace having gone before, or by the privilege of our own dignity, but also… in equality.” Three manuscripts and the Lyon edition: “we differ in equity.”]

[Note: [Col. 0505D] One manuscript: “in all profits and advantages,” etc.]

[Note: [Col. 0505D] The printed editions insert the word “advantage,” which is absent from all manuscripts; its omission improves the proper sense of this passage.]

Furthermore, if pursuing, tearing apart, or destroying one another is characteristic of beasts, who could doubt that it belongs to human excellence to help, instruct, and build one another up, and to care for the common good as though it were one’s own?

[Note: [Col. 0505D] One manuscript: “Finally.”]

From this it becomes clear that those who persist in oppressing and deceiving human beings, though they were born human, degenerate into beastly ways not by a change of nature but by a change of life.

[Col. 0506A]

[Note: [Col. 0506C] Three manuscripts: “or.”]

[Note: [Col. 0506C] The Lyon edition lacks the word “human beings.” It is found in all the other manuscripts.]

[Note: [Col. 0506C] One manuscript: “not by nature but by vice.” Another: “not by nature but by life.”]

## CHAPTER XXIII. That there are two kinds of injustice

1. There are two kinds of injustice: one by which we inflict injuries, and the other by which, when we can, we neglect to repel injuries inflicted by others.

[Note: [Col. 0506C] Two manuscripts: “one by which… the other by which…”]

In a certain sense we oppress ourselves when, although we can defend the oppressed, we disdain to rescue them from oppression.

[Note: [Col. 0506D] One manuscript: “the most wretched.”]

It does me no good that I do not deceive or circumvent anyone if I permit someone to deceive or circumvent another.

[Note: [Col. 0506D] Three manuscripts: “if I permit the deceiver to circumvent him.” Another: “that I do not circumvent or deceive, but allow myself to be deceived,” etc.]

The same may be understood concerning sins. If I see someone sinning and not only do not rebuke him but also consent to him in his sin, I make myself a participant in his condemnation. I sin in all who sin when, through a kind of cruel malice of mind, I do not rebuke those whom I know to have sinned or to be sinning.

[Note: [Col. 0506D] Four manuscripts: “must.”]

2. Nor should we listen to those who say that they cannot rebuke delinquents lest they make enemies of those who do not wish to amend themselves.

[Note: [Col. 0506D] One Colbertine manuscript: “rebuke or admonish.”]

While they spare the will of such people, they do not spare their salvation.

[Note: [Col. 0506D] One Colbertine manuscript: “And if.” Another: “If not.” Another: “Or if.”]

But if we correct them not out of boastfulness but out of mercy, and with a certain compassion of a sympathetic spirit; if they perceive that we are no less moved by their sins than by our own; then either, restored to a good state, they give thanks to God with us,

[Note: [Col. 0506D] Two manuscripts: “so that they…”]

[Note: [Col. 0506D] Two manuscripts: “they give thanks to God.” One Colbertine manuscript: “or at once in the good, with us.” Another: “or they immediately give thanks to God for the good.”]

or, if the sweetness of sin still holds them in sin and, seeing that we are concerned for their salvation, they wish to return evil for good, we ought to prefer incurring the enmity of those who refuse to amend themselves to incurring God’s offense by flattering sinners.

[Note: [Col. 0506D] The Lyon edition has this reading. Other editions: “we should be more willing to…” One Colbertine manuscript: “we ought rather to incur the enmity of those who refuse to amend themselves.”]

But since we have already said more about these matters in the second book (chapters 1 and 2), let us continue, as we began, with the remaining parts of justice.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On generosity, and how the work of beneficence ought to be practiced

1. From the remaining source of justice proceed generosity, beneficence, charity, and other things of this kind, by which human beings can be helped in many ways.

[Note: [Col. 0506D] One manuscript: “But from the remaining source of justice.”]

[Col. 0507A] Generosity is that which overflows even toward those who appear to need nothing; and in generosity there is a breadth of personal means.

[Note: [Col. 0507D] Four manuscripts add “is,” which was absent from the printed editions.]

Beneficence has many forms of action by which merciful aid is given to those struggling in need, and by which the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom is acquired from earthly wealth—provided that the work of beneficence is performed without any display, and that a shameful love of popular glory does not drive us to show mercy.

Some people have been found who certainly came to the aid of different people’s different needs, but were compelled either by a desire to acquire a reputation, or moved by carnal affection, or constrained by the hope of receiving back what they gave, or by the necessity of returning what they had received.

[Note: [Col. 0507D] Two manuscripts: “they were constrained.” Some have “certain people,” etc. The Lyon edition also has this reading. Another: “they were constrained.” Others: “there are some who…”]

[Col. 0507B] 2. There are others whom crafty greed alone moves to give something to the poor; they give something for this purpose, that they may receive greater things here. Whatever is given to them, as though to pastors of the poor, for distribution—while those for whose support they receive it are hungry—they spend all, or nearly all, that they have received on their own pleasures. And, what is worse, they shamefully desire to be regarded among the generous and merciful, or even to be praised above them.

[Note: One Regius manuscript reads, “for this reason … that greater things may come from here.” Another manuscript and one Colbertinus manuscript read, “for this purpose … that greater things may come.” Two Colbertinus manuscripts read, “for this purpose … that greater things may come from here.” One Cambridge manuscript reads “fathers” (*patribus*) for “pastors” (*pastoribus*) of the poor. One manuscript reads, “for distribution.”]

Those people are entirely different from all these and their like who desire not themselves but God to be praised in their works; whom the hope of future reward leads to good work; and who wish to have him alone as the witness of their work, from whom they firmly believe, with complete faith, that they will receive their reward.

[Note: One manuscript reads, “other people who.”]

## CHAPTER XXV. On the differences among kinds of love, and how far perfect love differs from them

[Col. 0507C]

Therefore, since the subject requires it, I shall also touch briefly here on charity, concerning which I have discussed many things earlier in this book. I say nothing about carnal love, which, beginning with marriage, flows to children, because we share this kind of love with cattle and beasts. I likewise pass over the love of relatives, because it too still seems to belong to flesh and blood. Nor do I speak of that love by which we love friends, although it too is directed toward some temporal advantage.

[Note: Seven manuscripts add “also.” One manuscript reads, “they themselves are also referred to” a temporal advantage.]

This is not because these loves are dishonorable, since they are natural to everyone, but because that love by which we love God freely, and a friend, is incomparably superior to all of them.

[Note: Two Colbertinus manuscripts read, “by an incomparable necessity,” one of them continuing, “when we love friends and others freely.”]

But whoever loves a friend for any advantage is shown to love not the friend but the advantage. Indeed, whoever loves someone for any temporal thing will cease loving him when that thing, being temporal, has ceased to exist.

[Note: Six manuscripts read “since it is temporal”; one of these reads “as it were.” The printed editions lack this phrase.]

But whoever loves on account of God will love his friend eternally, just as God is eternal.

[Note: One manuscript lacks the substantive verb “is.”]

And therefore God, than whom there is nothing greater or better for which he should be loved, is perfectly loved for his own sake.

[Note: One Colbertinus manuscript reads, “because there is nothing greater or better for which he may be loved.” Another Colbertinus manuscript, together with the Lyons and Louvain editions, reads, “than whom there is nothing greater or better for which he should be loved.” Two Regius manuscripts read, “for which he is loved; he is perfectly loved for his own sake.” The printed editions read, “for what reason he is loved”; others, “for which he should be loved?”]

If he is loved even for the sake of the things he bestows, he is not loved freely, since what is loved on his account is then preferred to him—something which it is even impious to say.

[Note: One manuscript reads “for the sake of those very things.”] For he himself is the blessed life, eternal salvation, the kingdom, and everlasting joy of all who love him. Those who love God will receive these things, because he alone will be everything to them when he himself is all things in all.

## CHAPTER XXVI. What it means to give each his due

Therefore, if in this life we strive to fulfill justice, whose proper work is to give each his due, let us render ourselves to God, by whom we were made; and let us not permit those things over which we have naturally been placed to rule us. Let reason rule the vices; let the body be subject to the mind, and the mind to God—and the whole perfection of the human being is complete.

[Note: One Colbertinus manuscript reads, “and every perfection.” Another reads, “and the whole perfection in us will be complete.”]

Thus, having been made participants in justice, we give each his due if we subject lower things to better things, and bodily pleasures to the virtues.

[Col. 0508C] [Note: Four Colbertinus manuscripts read, “so that, just as …”]

And just as by reasoning we place living things above things without life, things endowed with sensation above living things, intellectual things above things endowed with sensation, and immortal things above mortal things, so by living well we place useful things above pleasurable things, honorable things above useful things, holy things above honorable things, and perfect things above all holy things.

[Note: One Colbertinus manuscript reads, “and let us place more perfect things above holy and perfect things.”]

Nevertheless, neither will the body be able to obey the spirit, nor desire reason, unless God—who created both the spirit and the body—delights in our thoughts, rests in us, and, like a true farmer in his field, causes growth in our heart.

[Note: Seven manuscripts read, “in the field that is our heart.” The printed editions read, “thus in our heart.”]

Whatever faith plants in it and devotion waters, may he himself bring to the increase of complete maturity.

[Note: Six manuscripts read, “and whatever …”]

And may he so subject evil desires to us, who willingly subject ourselves to him, that our very actions may reveal who our inhabitant is and whose will is being done in us.

[Note: Three manuscripts read, “that his will may be done.”]

## CHAPTER XXVII. That active life is brought to completion by three virtues—temperance, courage, and justice—and that prudence, the fourth virtue, supplies the mind with knowledge of hidden things

[Col. 0509A]

This is the order of nature and justice. Whoever wishes to hold and observe it will fulfill the perfection of the active life. The three virtues of which I have spoken, God granting it, contribute to this active life.

[Note: One manuscript reads “if anyone” (*si quis*). All manuscripts read, “as seemed appropriate.” One of them presents the passage as follows: “When those three virtues perfect the active life …”]

For temperance, courage of spirit, and justice constitute spiritual action, without which the knowledge that appears to belong to prudence is entirely useless. For it will profit us nothing to have learned what must be fulfilled unless we strive to fulfill what we have learned.

Therefore the power of the mind, which is divided between desire and reason, is assisted by these four virtues—about which we have been discoursing for some time—in fulfilling the perfection of good action and attaining knowledge of hidden things.

[Col. 0509B] [Note: Two manuscripts read, “the power of the soul.”]

The desire itself is formed for action by three of these virtues, namely temperance, courage of spirit, and justice; but prudence illuminates reason, which is the mind’s sharp vision, so that reason may govern desire and desire obey reason.

[Note: All manuscripts read, “whence, behold, we have now long been discoursing.” Three manuscripts read, “By which three.”]

For every virtue, as the ancients maintain, is concerned with approximately three things.

[Note: The printed editions read “truly”; six manuscripts read “approximately.” Three manuscripts read “in each matter”; one reads “in every matter”; the printed editions read “in what matter.”]

One is discerning what is true and genuine in each matter, which is the proper task of prudence; we shall examine this in its proper place.

[Note: One manuscript and the Lyons edition read *de qua* (“concerning which”) rather than *de quo* (“concerning which,” referring grammatically to the preceding masculine noun).]

The second restrains and moderates the mind’s disturbed emotions, which the Greeks call πάθη (*pathē*, “passions”), so that it makes all the impulses, which they call ὁρμαί (*hormai*, “appetites” or “impulses”), obedient to reason.

[Note: One manuscript reads “call” (*vocant*) rather than “say” (*dicunt*) πάθη; another reads “they say *pathos*.” One manuscript reads “they call *ormas*” for “which they call ὁρμαί.”]

The third is that we should wish to make use of those with whom we associate in order to attain their welfare and our fulfillment.

[Note: One manuscript reads “those with whom we meet” (*congredimur*). One manuscript reads, “for their salvation and our fullness.” Another reads, “for their salvations and our fullness.”]

All these duties seem to belong to the remaining three virtues. Temperance and courage are especially effective in restraining and curbing the mind’s disturbances, which some call passions and others afflictions.

[Note: One Colbertinus manuscript omits “disturbances,” reading simply “which some call passions.”]

When these disturbances have been moderated and ordered by a certain law of temperance and courage, all the virtues reign in a person subject to his Creator, without any opposition from the vices.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On social virtue, and that those who, though able, contribute nothing to human society do not act rightly

[Col. 0510A]

1. Justice, by which those who practice it are made just, is regarded as a certain social virtue, because it is increased by the benefits it confers on others.

[Note: One manuscript reads, “it is increased”; two manuscripts read, “it is joined to the benefits it now confers on others.” Two manuscripts read “some people withdrawing themselves” (*aliqui se removentes*).]

For who does not advance by the very fact that he wishes another to advance? Who does not make God merciful toward himself by being merciful toward those who labor or go astray? Or how will anyone not increase all his own goods if, inspired by God, he not only does not begrudge them to those who possess them, but also, insofar as he can, shares them with those who do not?

[Note: One manuscript reads, “which he not only …”]

It must therefore be considered whether those act justly who withdraw from every occupation and devote themselves to spiritual studies, yet contribute nothing to human society; and who, preferring their own desires to the advantage of all, disregard the common good by choosing the leisure they desire.

[Note: One manuscript reads “to all advantages” (*commodis omnibus*).]

For plainly, to refuse help to those who labor when one is able, and, with the common good put aside, to wish to enjoy idle repose, has nothing just about it.

[Note: One manuscript reads, “when one is able.” Another reads, “when they are able.” The word “to wish” is absent from the Lyons manuscript.]

Those who serve justice live wholly for the good of all, and, as though born for one another, protect and love one another’s welfare.

[Note: One manuscript reads, “in this way, as though …”]

Therefore those act against justice who, chosen on account of the merit of their way of life or learning, prefer idle study to the fruitful usefulness of governing a multitude; and who, although they can assist the laboring Church, avoid the labor of active administration by contemplating the enjoyment of repose.

[Note: One manuscript reads, “although they could.”]

2. But since there are many who know themselves unequal to so great a burden, such people rightly do not offer themselves even when sought, lest they seem unwilling to undertake ecclesiastical labors but eager for honors.

[Note: One manuscript reads, “but eager for honors.”]

For ecclesiastical office is neither to be sought ambitiously nor avoided. Those, however, who are able to preside over and benefit peoples, if they are not sought out, rightly devote themselves to the pursuit of acquiring wisdom.

Nevertheless, if both those who grow through the gains of people who progress by their efforts, and those who, under their God, advance in themselves through the acquisition of spiritual wisdom, remain in their purpose, they travel by different roads but head toward one homeland; and, serving in different offices, they arrive at one kingdom, called by Christ, the King of all.

[Note: One manuscript reads, “serving in different military duties.”]

For who does not know that just as studious leisure pours the ineffable sweetness of heavenly wisdom into those who are free from carnal occupations, so spiritual engagement in holy labors brings manifold fruits to those occupied with the needs of human society?

[Note: All manuscripts read, “studious leisure”; the printed editions read, “idle study.” Two manuscripts read “brings”; four read “will bring.”]

Who could adequately enumerate how greatly ecclesiastical men can advance even in spiritual studies? By teaching those beneath them, they exercise themselves; by conferring with those equally learned, they become more cautious in many matters; and by listening to the more learned, they lay aside mistaken convictions, hold what is right more firmly, learn what was hidden, and are strengthened in matters about which they had been wavering.

[Note: Four manuscripts read, “about which they were doubtful.”]

But since the order of discussion requires us to say a little also about prudence, which is placed as the fourth principal virtue, what we have said about justice may suffice.

## CHAPTER XXIX. That those who fervently devote themselves to acquiring knowledge drink from the fountain of prudence and wisdom a knowledge of all things

1. Most people place prudence and wisdom in the investigation and discovery of truth. I believe this is because no one can properly be called wise without prudence, nor prudent without wisdom.

[Note: Three manuscripts add “rightly.” Four manuscripts omit “without prudence” in the first clause and read, “nor prudent without wisdom.”]

Therefore, if the task of prudence and wisdom is understood as nothing other than the inquiry into and comprehension of truth, whoever has been able prudently to seek the truth and wisely to discover it will rightly be called prudent and wise.

[Note: Four manuscripts read the future *poterit* (“will be able”) rather than the perfect *potuerit* (“has been able”).]

I have prefaced this so that whatever is discussed about prudence may also be understood as having been said about wisdom. For these two virtues are so interwoven and united that neither can exist without the other: wisdom cannot be called imprudent, nor prudence foolish.

[Note: Three manuscripts read, “so that neither of them can exist without the other; one cannot be called wise without prudence, nor prudent without wisdom.”]

If, then, the whole perfection of human life consists in action and knowledge, just as we have shown that action is fulfilled by the completion of temperance, courage, and justice, so let us establish that knowledge of things comes through the attainment of prudence.

[Note: This is the reading of the Cambridge manuscript, two Regius manuscripts, and one Colbertinus manuscript. Another Colbertinus manuscript reads, “just as we have proved that action is fulfilled by the completion of temperance, courage, and justice.” Another Colbertinus manuscript and the printed editions read, “just as in many matters we have proved the action of temperance and courage, and the completion of justice.”]

2. The knowledge of things that proceeds from the fountain of prudence and wisdom illumines all spiritual people cleansed from carnal vices; and, turning them away from every delight in harmful curiosity, inflames them with the desire to contemplate virtue.

[Note: Seven manuscripts read, “the knowledge of things that is imparted from the fountain of prudence.” One manuscript reads, “it proceeds.” The manuscripts vary considerably: one reads “illumines spiritual people rather than carnal people”; another, “illumines all spiritual people cleansed from all carnal vices”; two read, “it illumines all carnal people cleansed from carnal vices”; another reads, “vain curiosities”; another, “from the love of harmful curiosity, as is cited below.”]

Thus, having attained knowledge of human and divine things, they truly become prudent and wise. They foresee and at the same time avoid impending evils; they do not consider anything evil except what makes people evil; nor do any disturbances, as though they were ignorant of their nature, shake from them a measure of self-control or tranquility. They distinguish between deceptive goods and solid goods. They prudently understand that nothing in this world happens by chance or unjustly, but that all things occur by God’s will or permission.

[Note: Two manuscripts read, “by God’s will or by his permission.”]

They either teach those who think otherwise wisely or correct them. They understand that the various pains and different infirmities that afflict mortal people do not always follow upon preceding sins, but often arise, as corruptible beings are born, from the very condition of mortality.

[Note: Two manuscripts read, “come upon them.”]

And, knowing that they are not condemned by present adversities but tested by them, they courageously seize from the endurance of suffering an opportunity to acquire patience. They neither harm others nor permit others to harm them.

[Note: One Cambridge manuscript reads, “and they know.” One Colbertinus manuscript omits “present.” Two manuscripts read, “nor permit harm to be done to themselves.”]

3. The Lord commanded such people to become like this in the Gospel, saying: “Be prudent as serpents and innocent as doves” (Matthew 10:16).

[Note: One manuscript reads, “he commands.”]

For the innocent cannot deceive others, nor do the prudent permit themselves to be deceived. But if, in any transaction, conversation, or other matter, a person does not allow himself to be deceived while he himself deceives another, he does not possess prudence—which is a cause of salvation rather than destruction—but only pretends to possess it.

For this virtue differs from vice in that vice corrupts what is healthy, whereas virtue heals what has been corrupted by the addition of vice. Thus the truly prudent person hastens to benefit all whom he can, so that the fruit of all those whom he acquires for God through himself may increase through his merits.

[Note: One Regius manuscript reads, “this virtue.” One Colbertinus manuscript reads, “whom he can benefit, he benefits quickly and truly, so that the fruit of all those acquired for God through him may increase according to his merits.” Another Colbertinus manuscript reads, “he hastens to be truly prudent.”]

But if he thinks about someone’s destruction or rejoices in the fall of one who is perishing, he himself must perish before he destroys another; and the destruction by which he wishes another to perish must begin with him.

## CHAPTER XXX. That the prudent neither harm others nor permit themselves to be harmed; and that their completed prudence, without any admixture of error, exists where life will be perfect and without sin

[Col. 0512C]

1. Those, therefore, who have become prudent through participation in prudence and draw near to their God not on foot but by holy conduct, insofar as they are prudent by God’s gift can perish neither through their own sin nor through another’s sin.

[Note: One Regius manuscript reads, “If therefore those who …” One Colbertinus manuscript adds, “nor can they endure their own sins or the sins of others.”]

But because their prudence is not yet as perfect as it will be in that life where no error can at all creep upon those who live perfectly, even the prudent sometimes yield to sins that deceive them—not depraved by the will, but falling, as human beings do, through human error—and they are not yet perfected in the full perception of prudence and wisdom.

[Note: One Cambridge manuscript reads, “in perfection.” Four Colbertinus manuscripts read, “where error will no longer be able to creep upon those living perfectly.”]

They will be perfected there, where they will no longer be able either to be ignorant of anything or to sin.

2. Here, if what is rightly done could be perfectly distinguished from sin, that man would never pray to be cleansed from his hidden faults who says: “Cleanse me from my hidden faults, O Lord, and spare your servant from the sins of others” (Psalm 18:13).

[Note: Three manuscripts read, “he would never pray to be cleansed from his hidden faults.”]

By these words he sufficiently shows that even those who live holily through the gift of the Holy Spirit nevertheless, because they carry certain human weaknesses, sometimes yield either to their own sin or consent to another’s sin, whether knowingly or unknowingly.

[Note: The manuscripts vary between “certain weaknesses” and “the remnants of weaknesses”; one reads “of human life”; another, “which they attribute.” Another reading is “to some extent.”]

In this life, therefore, where sin is committed either by the will, through error, or through weakness, all who, aided by God, do not sin by their will live irreproachably. But because error or weakness can involve them in sins, let them faithfully ask to be illumined and healed by him to whom that man joyfully cried out in the Spirit: “The Lord is my illumination and my salvation; whom shall I fear?” (Psalm 26:1).

[Note: One manuscript reads, “let them ask.” Two manuscripts read, “through the gift of knowledge and wisdom.”]

When the illumination bestowed through the gift of prudence and wisdom has removed blindness, and salvation poured out through God’s grace has healed sickness,

[Note: The Douay and Cologne editions read, “salvation poured in and sickness”; one Colbertinus manuscript reads, “with sickness driven away.”]

then the mind, divinely illumined and healed, will not be deceived by human error in those things that must be avoided or desired, so as to defend falsehoods as truths or reject truths as falsehoods.

[Note: One manuscript reads, “retain truths as falsehoods.”]

And without any obstacle of weakness it will be able to accomplish the good that it has chosen.

3. The salvation of this life, in which we live mortally, is one thing; the salvation of that life, in which our mortality will be endowed with immortality, is another. We have been saved here in hope; there we shall be saved in reality. Here we have been saved in such a way that we can still perish; there, whoever has been saved will no longer be able to perish.

Therefore, the knowledge that grants us knowledge of things while we live in the night of this age must be regarded, in comparison with the fullness that is to come, as a part of knowledge, not the whole of it. Hence the holy Apostle says: “For we know in part and we prophesy in part; but when what is perfect has come, what is partial will be brought to an end” (1 Corinthians 13:9–10).

[Note: Six manuscripts read as translated above. Another reads, “Here he asserts that it is brought to an end, that is, completed.” One of those manuscripts reads, “From this he asserts that it is brought to an end.” The printed editions read, “Here he asserts that it is brought to an end, there completed,” although “there” seems superfluous in view of what follows.]

He says that what is partial is brought to an end because the part of knowledge that is to be perfected is not to be taken away from the perfected, but fulfilled.

[Note: The Lyons edition alone reads, “the part of knowledge is to be perfected; once perfected, it is not to be taken away but fulfilled.”]

Therefore, where the salvation of all faithful Catholics will be complete, where there will be no corruption and blessed immortality, there will be the true perfection of prudence and wisdom, and complete knowledge of all things, when knowledge has been brought to perfection by the completion of what is partial.

[Note: The printed editions read, “of prudence and knowledge.” Four manuscripts read, “of wisdom and knowledge”; two others, “of wisdom and prudence.”]

## CHAPTER XXXI. On the four emotions: that they should not be counted among the vices if their use proceeds from a good will

1. Let us now see what careful discussion discovers concerning the four emotions that the foolishness of the wise men of this world considers vices.

[Note: Two manuscripts read, “for if … they cannot”; one reads, “if they can.”]

For if it were impossible to fear, grieve, desire, or rejoice except for sinners or the lost, these would rightly be called not emotions but diseases. But when such movements of the soul are found in holy apostles and prophets, who would be so foolish as to believe them to be vices, when those who resisted vices more than other people pleased God through them?

Thus the Apostle Paul speaks in this way about fear: “But I fear that, as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, so your minds may be corrupted from the chastity that is in Christ” (2 Corinthians 11:3).

Again, concerning desire, he says confidently: “I desire to depart and to be with Christ” (Philippians 3:23, as printed).

[Note: Three manuscripts read, “The same thing.”]

And concerning sadness, which others call grief, the same chosen vessel and teacher of the Gentiles says: “For I have great sorrow and continual grief in my heart for my brothers, who are my relatives according to the flesh” (Romans 9:2).

[Note: Four manuscripts add, “And when, writing to the Romans, he had said …”]

And when, writing to the Romans, he had said, “Your obedience has been reported everywhere,” he says, “I rejoice in you. But I want you to be wise in what is good and innocent in what is evil” (Romans 16:19).

[Note: Two manuscripts add “now” after “but.” Two read, “in every place.” Three read, “I rejoice in you.” One adds, “yet I wish you to be wise.”]

Whoever wishes to condemn this fear, this grief, this desire, and this joy condemns the Apostle himself, who not only pleased God through such emotions but also condemned certain people among the guilty because they were without feeling.

[Note: One manuscript reads, “let him condemn.” One Regius manuscript reads, “because they were without emotion.” The Lyons edition reads, “because they were without fault, he condemned them as being at fault.”]

The prophet likewise commends such joy and grief when he says, “I rejoiced at the things that were said to me” (Psalm 121:1), and, in the person of the Lord, “I looked for one who would grieve with me, but there was none” (Psalm 68:21).

[Note: One manuscript reads, “one who would grieve with me at the same time.” Another reads, “one who would grieve with me.”]

When another says, “The fear of the Lord drives out sin” (Sirach 1:27), and, “Desire for wisdom leads to the kingdom” (Wisdom 6:21), he does not merely refrain from condemning the emotion of spiritual desire and divine fear; he praises it.

2. We do not sin, then, by having these emotions, but by using them badly. For the nature of human emotions indicates the Creator of the human being; their quality signifies a good or evil will.

[Note: One alternative reads “creature” rather than “nature,” though “nature” is preferable. Four manuscripts read, “a good or evil.”]

Thus these movements, which in human beings are emotions, become virtues in those who use them well, and in those who live badly they become passions, disturbances, or, as some prefer, afflictions.

[Note: One manuscript reads, “in all people, and not badly.”]

Nor should we listen to the Stoics, who insist that these emotions can and ought to be eradicated.

[Note: Three manuscripts read, “can and ought to be completely eradicated.”]

For there is no sensation at all when no emotion of fearing, grieving, desiring, or rejoicing is present. Finally, as though they themselves regretted their position, excepting sadness—which they deny can enter the mind of the wise—they say that the other three emotions are present in the wise, though under altered names: they substitute caution for fear, joy for rejoicing, and will for desire.

[Note: Two manuscripts read, “the remaining three emotions.” One reads, “they say that all emotions are present in the wise.”]

It is as though the wise person does not fear but is cautious, wills but does not desire, and does not rejoice in this life but experiences joy. They do not believe that his mind can be saddened because sadness, which ordinarily arises from a committed sin, cannot, they think, trouble the wise person, whom they suppose to have no sin.

[Note: One Colbertinus manuscript reads, “from a committed sin … some recollection of sin cannot occur.” Another reads, “no recollection of sin can occur.”]

Our Lord, born according to the flesh, showed how utterly empty this is: he was sad and wept (Matthew 26:37; Luke 19:41; John 11:35), yet the sadness by which he was sad did not arise from his sins, since he was conceived and born without sin, not only did not sin, but could not sin.

[Note: One manuscript reads, “from his own sin.”]

3. To refute from their own writings the foolishness of those who think that the wise person cannot be saddened or grieve, let them read what their most learned authority says: “To feel no grief at all does not come about without paying a great price: inhumanity in the soul and numbness in the body” (Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations*, Book III, *On Freedom from Pain*).

Concerning the fear that they classify as evil, our Scripture says: “The fear of the Lord is holy, enduring forever and ever” (Psalm 18:10).

[Note: One manuscript reads, “enduring.”]

But, as must honestly be acknowledged, this is distinguished from that other punitive fear of which the Apostle says: “There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear” (1 John 4:18). The former restrains those who wish to sin from evil and keeps the unwilling in what is good. The latter—the fear of which the prophet says, “Whoever is without fear cannot be justified” (Sirach 1:28)—increases rather with the growth of love.

[Note: Five manuscripts read “love” rather than “truth.”]

A person fears in one way lest he incur an evil by which he may be punished, and in another way lest he lose a good in which he delights. Not every fear, therefore, is to be considered a vice, but only that of which it is written: “Fear has punishment” (1 John 4:18).

But this fear of which it is said, “The fear of the Lord drives out sin”; “Whoever is without fear cannot be justified”; and “The fear of the Lord is holy, enduring forever and ever,” is not to be counted among the vices, but rather understood to be an enemy of vices.

4. As for what they say—that the good will, while the bad desire; or that the good rejoice, while the bad are joyful—what sane person would accept this? Indeed, who in his right mind would not refute it?

For our Scripture rebukes a person of evil will, saying, “Do not wish to utter every lie” (Sirach 7:14). And the distinguished orator Tully places desire among good things when he says: “I desire, conscript fathers, to be merciful” (Tully, *Invective against Catiline*, Book I).

And among them Virgil condemns joy, saying:

> Hence they fear, desire, grieve, and rejoice.

(Virgil, *Aeneid*, Book VI, line 732.)

Likewise, whereas among us the joys of an evil mind are assigned to evil and joy to good, the prophet says: “Rejoice in the Lord and exult, you righteous” (Psalm 31:11).

[Note: The Louvain edition reads “of an evil people” (*malae gentis*). The Lyons edition reads, “Likewise, whereas the joys of an evil mind are assigned among us to evil and joy to good.” This passage is absent from the Regius manuscript. One Colbertinus manuscript reads, “Likewise, the joys of an evil mind.” Another reads, “Likewise, there are both joys of an evil mind and, among us, joy assigned to good.” Two manuscripts add “to good”; one of them reads “is assigned to good.”]

[Col. 0516C] 5. Accordingly, all the righteous and all who are perfected in holiness, without any needless Stoic distinction, fear and take care, will and desire, rejoice and experience joy, are saddened and grieve. But it matters greatly what they fear or guard against, what they will or desire, what makes them rejoice or experience joy, and what saddens or grieves them.

They fear losing the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom; they desire to reach the heavenly homeland; they grieve when tempted and rejoice when freed from temptations. Thus a sound mind has rightly ordered emotions, while a perverse mind has perverse ones.

[Note: One manuscript reads, “the evil that they fear, the good that they will.” Four manuscripts and the Lyons edition read, “these people have rightly ordered emotions.”]

6. Saint Augustine the bishop—keen in intellect, pleasing in speech, learned in secular literature, diligent in ecclesiastical labors, distinguished in daily disputations, composed in all his conduct, Catholic in his exposition of our faith, acute in resolving questions, circumspect in refuting heretics, and cautious in explaining the canonical Scriptures—

[Note: One manuscript reads “adorned”; two, “pricked with remorse”; one, “convinced.” The printed editions read “in his exposition,” while four manuscripts omit “his”; two of them read, “in the exposition of the holy faith.” Three manuscripts read, “in explaining”; one, “in examining.”]

—I have followed him, insofar as possible, in these little books. He determines the question under discussion in this way, saying:

> “If these movements, these emotions, arising from love of the good and holy charity, are to be called vices, then let us allow what are truly vices to be called virtues. But when these emotions follow right reason, whenever they are employed as they ought to be, who would dare call them diseased or vicious passions?” (Augustine, *City of God*, Book XIV, chapter 9.)

[Note: One manuscript reads, “arising from good love.” The printed editions read, “true vices”; one Regius manuscript reads, “what are truly vices.” Four manuscripts and the Lyons edition read, “when these emotions follow right reason”; one Colbertinus manuscript reads, “who would then dare call them diseased or vicious according to their own disorder?”]

To show that these emotions are ours as a consequence of mortality and are necessary for this life but not for the future one, the same teacher adds after a little further discussion:

> “Even when we have these emotions rightly and according to God, they belong to this life, not to the life that we hope will be future” (*ibid.*).

[Note: Three manuscripts read, “even when we possess these emotions rightly.”]

## CHAPTER XXXII. That the emotions without which one cannot live rightly in this life will not exist in the future blessedness, which will have neither fear nor grief
And so, unless these affections were present in us because of the condition of our weakness, we would very often never yield to them unwillingly through grieving or weeping. [Note: Thus five manuscripts. One has *concederemus* (“we would concede”). The printed editions have *crederemus* (“we would believe”). The words “or weeping” are absent from the single Colbertine manuscript.] But for this reason we perceive that they are necessary to this present life: because in this mortality we cannot live rightly at all without them. For if no one fears or takes care lest either he himself, as long as he lives in mortality, [Note: Two manuscripts read *non vivitur* (“one does not live”).] or another whom he loves in Christ, [Note: The particle *a* (“from”) was absent from the printed editions; it is supplied by five manuscripts.] fall away from his faith; if he is not saddened by his own sin or that of his neighbor, nor grieves, nor rejoices and is glad at his progress; if he does not wish for or desire anything good—he not only does not live rightly, but also loses the very sense of humanity.

But in that blessed life to which all who are destined to be there will attain, [Note: One manuscript reads *perveniet* (“will attain,” singular); all the others read *pervenient*.] after all corruption and mortality have been consumed, [Note: Five manuscripts omit *istud* and “and mortality.”] where there can be neither any weeping nor sighing, [Note: One manuscript reads *ibi nec* (“there not even …”).] all the saints will possess perfect love, no fear, and everlasting joy. There [Note: Four manuscripts lack *eis* (“for them”).] their will shall be right and there shall be no desire, because, enjoying the heavenly goods which they wished to attain, they will lack nothing further to desire; and in that region of perpetual security and peace, perfectly blessed, they will suffer neither the goads of fear nor of pain. [Note: One manuscript has “nor pains.”] Yet that fear—not the fear which love casts out, but the fear which love nourishes—will perhaps remain forever and ever, because forever and ever will remain those things to which that very fear has led.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. How the four virtues called principal either defend us from sin in the present life or remain with us eternally without any sin.

1. Those four virtues of which I have said a little, [Note: Two manuscripts read *et ibi erunt* (“and they will be there”).] even if they will exist there, will nevertheless exist in a very different manner from that in which they exist in this life, where they fight without interruption against vices and, because the outcome of the struggle is uncertain and precarious, sometimes abandon those who are negligent and unwilling to obey them; sometimes, when the Lord has mercy, they approach others [Note: Two manuscripts read *Domino miserante* (“when the Lord has mercy”).] who are displeased with their sins, or return to them. [Note: The Lyon edition has “of the conduct.”]

For there, although temperance will exist, it will not be present in order to restrain or conquer evil desires or vices, but in order to perfect those whom here it defended from the assault of intemperance. [Note: One manuscript has “and conquer.” Another has “in order to conquer.” Another manuscript reads “whom here it defended from the disease of intemperance when it attacked”; a single Colbertine manuscript has “from the assault of the disease of intemperance.”] Thus, for those perfected in every respect, the blessed enjoyment of their reward will be perfectly sufficient. [Note: Two manuscripts have “in the receiving of it.”]

2. [Note: The printed editions read *Ibi enim* (“for there”); five manuscripts, *Ibi erit* (“there will be”); one, *Ibi et* (“there also”).] There, too, will be courage of soul—not in order to drive away any evils or bear them with equanimity, but in order to keep the blessed courageously within eternal good, without any evils. There will be perfect justice in all who are perfect—not in order to distinguish between virtues and vices, where even the bodies themselves will no longer be subject to vice, [Note: Two manuscripts have “where even the bodies themselves will no longer exist.”] but in order to bestow everlasting rewards upon those who are perfect.

This will take place when all carnal desire has been consumed, and neither the spirit will desire against the flesh nor the flesh against the spirit (Galatians 5:17); but the mind, subject to God, will reign in everlasting peace together with the flesh subject to it, and will happily cleave to its Creator forever.

Now prudence, which is considered illustrious even here, where it enlightens the prudent in a certain riddle, what will it be there, where it will show the truth without any deceptive figures to those perfected whom its inquiry delighted here? [Note: A Cambrai manuscript has *veritate perfectos*, “those perfected by truth.”] Divinely illumined by the full possession of prudence and wisdom, they will recognize without any impediment of corruption or mortality all those things which here they desired perfectly to know but could not; and they will behold, with unveiled face, not only the rational principles of all creatures, [Note: The printed editions have “the principle.” All the manuscripts have “the principles.”] but also the very majesty of their Creator. [Note: A Cambrai manuscript reads *perfectione* (“perfection”) for *perceptione* (“receiving” or “apprehension”).]

## CHAPTER XXXIV. Where the speaker excuses himself concerning the whole work.

1. And so, if it pleases you, let this little book now come to an end, lest, having been extended beyond what is proper, it displease not only because of its own roughness, [Note: One manuscript has “because of its own squalor.”] but also because of its excessive length. This, indeed, I solemnly declare to all [Note: Three manuscripts read *omnibus* for *omnes*.] who may perhaps [Note: In one manuscript *forte* (“perhaps”) is absent.] read these things, and I beg them: whatever in the matters themselves, arranged as they are in some fashion, they find worthy of criticism, [Note: One Colbertine manuscript reads *reprehensionis invenerint* (“find [something] of criticism”); the other codices read *reprehensione dignum invenerint* (“find worthy of criticism”).] let them attribute to the defect of my rusticity and kindly pardon me. For, while striving [Note: One manuscript reads *dum studui* (“while I strove”).] to fulfill the command of the one who ordered me, I presumed to undertake even tasks greater than my strength.

But whatever they approve as having been said according to the Catholic faith, let them ascribe to God, who gives generously to all and reproaches no one (James 1:5); and for all these things, let them give thanks to him together with me. [Note: The word “to him” is absent from the printed editions; it is present in all the manuscripts.]

2. As for the careful refinement of polished diction, I do not trouble myself; nor am I ashamed [Note: One Regius manuscript reads *pudor est* (“it is a shame”); the printed editions have *pudoris est*.] if my discussion, which perhaps is approved in its substance, offends certain devotees of empty words by the harshness of its unadorned speech. For what I did not learn through study from a learned teacher, I was unable to display in my speaking.

And yet, when deliberately cultivated speech weakens the vitality of ideas, [Note: These words are absent from the Cologne edition and from four Colbertine manuscripts.] and elaborated brilliance empties out the entire force of what is said, who would not judge that I ought to have despised affectation of composition, even if, as an expert speaker, I had been able to fulfill it? [Note: Five manuscripts have “affection” rather than “affectation.”]

Therefore, that composition seemed to me sufficiently adorned which conveyed the conceptions of the mind with a certain necessary clarity, not one that served the allurements of the ears. For, unless I am mistaken, that is regarded as good Latin which states what is to be understood briefly and clearly, while observing the proper meanings of customary words; not that which luxuriates in the beauty and charm of flourishing eloquence. [Note: A Cambrai manuscript has “crafty”; one Regius manuscript has “with crafty”; another has “with practiced eloquence,” and so forth.] Nor do embellished expressions please prudent men, but strong ones, since words were established not for the sake of words instead of things, but for expressing things.

# At the End of the Fifth Century. Two Anonymous Authors.

## Baluzius’s Notice Concerning the Following Little Books

The little works which I present here were supplied to me by a manuscript codex of the library of the most illustrious chapter of the major church of Lucca. It was written in square letters, which they call Lombardic, and copied in the age of Charlemagne, as P. Mabillon, an eyewitness, once recognized while he was at Lucca; I also demonstrated this in a commentary on that manuscript, written and published among the little works of P. Calogera, volume 45.

I judged them worthy of public attention both on account of their antiquity and because I considered them to contain material useful either for discovering the truth of events or for illuminating and confirming what has already been discovered. I now undertake in this preface to indicate how useful I think each of them may be.

I assigned the foremost place to the little work on the genealogy of the ancient patriarchs and of the others down to Jesus Christ, and from Jesus Christ to Saint Cyprian, and from him to the author’s own time. The author was writing in Africa under Genseric.

In this matter P. Mabillon must be corrected. In his *Italian Itinerary*, while identifying this very codex and the little work from it, he tried to decipher something from its final page, which had been very badly worn and almost obliterated by age and rubbing. He read what appeared as *erici* and, being unable to recover the preceding syllables, inserted in the margin, by conjecture, *Theoderici*. But *Genserici*, or, as it is written there, *Geiserici*, must be read. This is demonstrated both by the letter-traces, examined more carefully in daylight and sunlight, and by the fact that the same name recurs several times where the letters are preserved intact. Indeed, the author carefully specifies the very year of Genseric in which he was writing this: the twenty-fourth year of that king. Who this Genseric was, and in what year of the common era he began to reign, I shall investigate below.

The author’s failure to consult the Hebrew text, and his lack of proficiency in Hebrew, are demonstrated by interpretations of names that correspond very poorly to Hebrew, as is especially clear in the word *Laminir*, rendered by the Vulgate as “hot waters,” but retained here. The word is expressed in the Septuagint, where, however, it is not *Laminir*, as here, but ἰαμεὶν (*iamein*). From this it follows that our historical author consulted the Septuagint rather than the Hebrew text; for in Hebrew it is *Haciemim*.

Indeed, I do not think that he had even the Septuagint before his eyes, since he has retained that version less exactly. He therefore follows some Latin version, of the kind of which Saint Jerome warned that several had existed, derived from the Septuagint. The same may also be demonstrated from his computation of the years, in which he follows the Septuagint rather than the Hebrew text, although he does not adhere consistently even to the Greek interpreters, as is sufficiently apparent from the computation of the years.

Since it is therefore clear from these points that this anonymous author consulted some Latin version, he may be useful to those who are concerned today with the Latin Vulgate.

I also judge it worthy of notice that several passages from the Third Book of Esdras are brought forward here. They will easily be worthy of the readers’ reflection, both because of the author’s antiquity and because it is understood that some Latin version of this book already existed at that time. Moreover, I do not know whether there is another older author who mentions this book.

Since the letters of Artaxerxes are read here from a version different from that which now exists in our Bibles, it can rightly be inferred from this that a new version of this book had been prepared, just as happened with other books of Holy Scripture. It also follows from all this that another interpretation of the Hebrew names existed at that time, different from the one published by Saint Jerome.

Nor do I readily believe that this interpretation was first introduced by the anonymous author himself. Rather, he received it from his Latin version or from some other ancient writer who had not learned from Saint Jerome. Perhaps, therefore, Saint Jerome should by no means be regarded as the first source from whom these interpretations became known to Latin speakers, although the same holy doctor asserts this about himself in the preface to his little work *On the Interpretation of Hebrew Names*.

But where that chronology which our author follows was derived from, I openly confess that I am entirely ignorant. I suspected that it came from Julius Africanus, since he was a writer from the same region; but when I compared the material concerning Julius Africanus that survives for us with this author, I found that the two do not sufficiently correspond, unless perhaps this discrepancy arose from the carelessness of the scribe of this codex—a carelessness that is certainly great and utterly incredible.

The final page of this little work would be more pleasing to the reader’s taste, where, drawing closer to his own times, the author would have offered matters still more credible and deserving of approval. But it is lamentable that this page has been so worn away by age and the negligence of its former possessors that even the letters have been completely erased, with no traces of them remaining.

I carefully applied labor and diligence to deciphering something, and succeeded in recovering certain portions, so as to bring out what is represented here by me. Nor was this without benefit, for from these fragments we learn on what particular day the persecution of the Donatists began at Carthage. The date of the law of Honorius is also corrected. In the Theodosian Code its subscription is marked “the day before the Ides of February”; here, however, we have that it was published at Ravenna on the very Kalends of February. Perhaps, nevertheless, the law was sealed by the emperor on the Kalends of February but publicly announced on the day before the Ides of that same month.

In this very page the chronological method is more accurate, and it is reckoned not from the day of the Lord’s birth but from his Passion, as was customary among the ancients before Dionysius Exiguus. Accordingly, beginning from the Passion of the Lord—which these ancient writers placed under the consulship of the two Gemini, in the twenty-ninth year of the common era—and since this was the established custom in Africa, as will become clear from the following work, the author marks the year in which he was writing as 434 from the Passion of the Lord. The year in which this work was committed to writing was therefore the year 463 of our era.

When he connects this same year with the twenty-fourth year of Genseric, a correct calculation leads us to recognize that Genseric began to reign in the year 439 of the common era. Yet this does not agree with the epoch more commonly accepted by chronologists for the beginning of the reign of Genseric who first occupied Africa; they place his accession in the year 429.

We shall not solve this difficulty unless we suppose that this Genseric was the successor of the earlier Genseric, and perhaps the same person whom the ancients call Hunneric, the son and heir of Genseric. The African author of the following little work agrees with this chronology. He connects the year 426 from the Passion with the sixteenth year of Genseric; these two dates, when properly calculated, likewise place Genseric’s beginning in the year 439.

There are therefore two Genserics, father and son, who must be carefully distinguished, lest, if only one be admitted, confusion be introduced for readers.

From this we also learn about the author of the second little work which I present here, and about the time when he was writing. Its author says that he committed his work to writing in the sixteenth year of King Genseric, which is the year 455 of the common era.

It was therefore at that time that this Paschal computation was produced, when the disputes between the Africans and the Romans concerning the Paschal date of the year 444 had scarcely ceased. The Romans contended that Easter for that year ought to be assigned to the ninth day before the Kalends of May, while the Latins assigned it to the seventh day before the Kalends of April.

On this matter one should read the letter of Saint Cyril of Alexandria to Saint Leo, together with the notice prefixed by the Ballerini to that letter, or rather to the fragment of the letter. I judge that this Paschal computation, now published by me for the first time, as I believe, will be of great use in clarifying that fragment.

I have little doubt that many writings were produced on both sides on that occasion. The same Paschal cycle of eighty-four years was also debated. Some detected an error in it, while others devised various calculations by which they might reconcile it with the truth.

Among these writers was that African, Agriustas of Thimida, the champion of the cycle. Our anonymous author wrote against him and defended the cycle in such a way that he acknowledged that it contained some error, which he himself corrected.

The codex from which I took this work is extremely corrupt, with the result that at times the meaning of the writing itself does not appear. Nevertheless, I refrained from correction, lest I force readers to read my words rather than those of the author. The rules of grammar are observed not at all, or scarcely at all; yet I restored them where no doubt could intrude concerning the author’s intention.

Finally, I do not think it should be passed over that the author of the eighty-four-year cycle, otherwise unknown, as I believe, first emerges into the light from this little work. For here we read that he was a certain Augustalis. The learned are aware, therefore, that the cycle of eighty-four years was then especially prevalent among the Latins.

The work mentions a certain Hilarianus, to whom, the author says, a treatise *On the Paschal Computation* had been addressed by a certain Agriustia, a citizen of the municipality of Thimida in the region. This municipality was situated in Caesarean Mauretania, since among the bishops of that province at the Carthaginian conference we find Securus, bishop of Timida.

I have read nothing whatsoever about Agriustia. Hilarianus may easily be the same as Quintus Julius Hilarianus, who, when Caesarius and Atticus were consuls—that is, in the year 397 of Christ—wrote a little work *On the Paschal Cycle*. The librarian Pfaff of Tübingen extracted it from the Turin shelves and published it at Paris in 1712. Enough has now been said about this little work.

# An Anonymous Little Book on the Genealogies of the Patriarchs

## The Genealogy of the Whole Library, Collected from All the Books of the Old and New Testament, in Which the Prophecies Are Set Out Together with the Names and Times of All the Prophets Down to the Most Blessed Cyprian; and What Was Done Down to Our Own Age Is Shown with Complete Clarity: Collected from Histories of Legal Commands. (C, S)

### At the Beginning: From Where the First Man Is Known to Have Appeared in the World

Let us hear. If he was born, he has parents; if he was made, he has matter; if he was brought forth, he has an author.

The wisdom of almighty God, taking clay from the earth, conceived by paternal command to make man. And when he had been seen as solitary and alone by the Lord himself, his maker and creator, God took a bone from his side and made a woman for him as a helper.

For death, fashioned through the serpent’s poisons by the envy of the devil, entered the world and began to reign from Eve to the Virgin Mary, united in the chastity of the Lord. For just as death was born through a woman, so also the resurrection of the dead was born through a woman.

This is Adam, who knew his wife Eve after being expelled from paradise, in the land of Naid. She conceived and bore Cain from the seed of accusation, mourning, and vapor; and she continued to bear and bore his brother Abel, who became a shepherd of sheep, while Cain was a farmer.

After some days, when Cain had reached the proper age, he brought an offering to God from the fruits of the earth, while Abel brought from the firstborn of his sheep and from their fat. The Lord looked upon Abel and his gifts, but upon Cain and his offering he did not look, intending the one for the glory of martyrdom and appointing the other as the chief of murderers.

For since the devil, who had excluded their fathers from paradise, was destined also to lead their sons into danger of death, he then entered Cain’s heart. Cain said to his brother, “Let us go out into the field.” And while they were in the field, Cain rose up against his brother Abel and killed him.

Adam again knew his wife, and she conceived and bore him a son in place of Abel, who is called Seth. His name in the Latin language means “resurrection,” because through him the Lord raised up a righteous seed, from whose descendants we shall reach our Lord Jesus Christ through successive generations following one another.

This is Seth, who fathered Aenas; for *Aenas* in the Latin language means “forgetting.” From him Chainan was born, whose name is called “birth of God.” Chainan fathered Malelel, whose name is said to mean “change of God.” Malelel fathered Jaret, whose name is said to mean “descent.”

From him Enoch was born, whose name in the Latin language is interpreted as “renewal,” because through him God will renew the world in those days when Antichrist will cause great devastation. Then he and Elijah will prophesy together for 1,260 days, and Antichrist will kill them where their Lord was crucified.

But lest anyone say that they will be crucified in Jerusalem, where Christ the Lord was crucified, the text says “where their Lord was crucified,” that is, in the Roman kingdom.

Enoch fathered Matusalam, whose name in Latin is interpreted as “sent.” From him Lamech was born, whose name, by interpretation, we call “of good mind.” He is the one who prophesied concerning his son, saying, “This one will give us rest from all our works.” For he is called Noah, that is, “rest.”

## Here Begins the Origin of Cain

Let us pass to the origin of Cain, and then return to the generation of Noah.

After Cain had been cursed by God, he received a wicked sign so that no one would kill him. Whoever now receives this sign on his forehead or on his right hand will drink of the wine of God’s wrath, mixed in the cup of his wrath, and will be punished in the presence of his chosen angels.

For his name in the Latin language is said to mean “increasing forever.” He had received this very name because, until the coming of Christ, the sons of Cain, his associates, would kill Christians, following the footsteps of their brother Abel.

This Cain fathered a son named Enos. Cain, when he is recognized as having been born from the serpent, is known to have fathered Lothus. Then he built a city and gave it the name of his son, Su . . . . nos. [The supplied text is materially lacunose or corrupt here.] This is the city of blood, which even now pours out Christian blood. This city is known to have been built in the land of Naid, and it is alive.

That land is interpreted as pursuing Christians to the end, those who are called by the name of the faithful.

Enos fathered Geda. He possessed knowledge of walls. From him Malelel was born, whose name is interpreted as “strong hearing.” From Malelel was born Matusalan, who fathered Lamech, the man who had two wives: one named Ada, which is interpreted as “testified,” and the other named Sella, which is interpreted as “overshadowing herself.”

This is the Lamech who said to his wives:

“Hear my voice, wives of Lamech, and receive my words with your ears, because I have killed a man in my wound and a young man in my labor.”

By “man” he means Christ, and by “young man” he means the Christian people: Christ is killed by the Jews, and the Christian is killed by pagans and heretics. Or, as we see in reverse, a guilty person is killed, so that Cain is spoken of in place of Abel, the one who is torn apart for the name of Christ.

He continues, saying: “For Cain shall be avenged sevenfold, but Lamech seventy-sevenfold.” From this it appears that he killed Cain.

Adam, from his wife, fathered Hobel, who is the father of those dwelling in tents, and another named Jubal. This is Jubal, who displayed the psaltery and the lyre.

From Sella he fathered Thobel, who had been a worker in iron and bronze, and his sister was Noema. She was the one who sang with her voice, not with an instrument.

Through these generations the multitude of human beings increased until a dreadful catastrophe came upon them; the cataclysm covered them and destroyed them, because the sons of God had mingled with the daughters of men and had not attended to his commands. Their wickedness had blinded them, and they had not expected that destruction would come upon them.

## Here Begin the Generations of Noah

Let us therefore return to Noah, who before the flood fathered three sons, and they took wives. There were eight persons in his household. The Apostle deemed it worthy to mention them, saying: “Eight persons were saved through water, just as baptism now saves you.”

Thus, from Adam the first-created man up to Noah—that is, up to the generation of Shem, the same Noah’s son—there are 2,142 years; and from the generation of Shem up to the cataclysm—that is, up to the generation of Arphaxad, the son of Shem, who was born immediately after the cataclysm in the hundredth year—there are altogether 2,242 years. For *cataclysm* in the Latin language is called “judgment,” according to the interpretation.

## Here Begin the Generations of Shem, the Son of Noah

Noah fathered Shem, whose name is called “name” in Latin, and Shem took a wife named Norea. From her Elam was born. Elam is interpreted as “age.” From him came the Elamites.

His second brother is called Assir. Nebrod the giant, the grandson of his paternal uncle Cham, drove him out from the land of Sennar—that is, from the land of servitude. Then, fleeing, he founded Nineveh, the city of Roboth, Chalech, and Dassen, between Nineveh and Chalech. This is that great city of theirs which the prophet Jonah circled in a journey of three days.

From Assir came the Assyrians, who had come to assist the Chaldeans against the children of Israel at Jerusalem. Their region is bounded in the following manner: from India to the island of Malicus, it is said to be 1,500,000 paces; Malicus, however, to Scenio, 225,000; from there to the island of Madano [sic], across the open sea, 1,875,000, apart from regions inaccessible to the human race.

Solinus asserted this, and they extend as far as Ethiopia through 127 satrapal regions. These are the dwelling places of the Persian and Median peoples.

Another was Arphaxad, the third son of Shem, who was called “the coming Lion”; the fourth was Lud, who is called “being born”; the fifth was Aram, who is called “high.”

From Aram four sons were born. The first was named Obs, who is called “chorus.” The second was El, who is called “forever”; for El is called God, that is, “everlasting.” The third was Gatera, who is called “surpassing.” The fourth was Mosoch, who is also “the archer.”

The sixth son of Shem, called Chanaam, is interpreted as “birth of God.” These are the six sons of Shem and Norea together with their descendants.

Arphaxad, the third son of Shem, was called “the coming Lion.” He received this name because from him the true Lion, the Lord Jesus Christ, was destined to come.

From Arphaxad, Sala was born, who is called “messenger.” From Sala, Eber was born, who is called “across the river.”

This Arphaxad, the son of Shem, lived 165 years and fathered Sala. After he fathered Sala, he lived 430 years and fathered sons and daughters, and he died in the fifth generation.

## Here Begin the Generations of Cham, the Son of Noah

Let us return also to Cham, the son of Noah, who was called “cunning.” He took a wife named Ause, from the seed of the giants, and fathered a firstborn son named Chus.

He took possession of Ethiopia against Egypt, and from him six sons were born. These are their names:

The firstborn was Saba, interpreted as “Tote”; from him came the nation of Saba, from which came that queen of the South who had come to hear Solomon’s wisdom.

The second was Evilad, who is called “giving birth.”

The third was Sabata, that is, “you take.”

The fourth was Regina, that is, “called out.” He had two sons: the firstborn, Sabam, that is, “condemned,” and the second, Judas, that is, “he confesses.”

The fifth son of Chus was Sabacatha, which was his name, that is, “adorned.”

The sixth was Nebrot, that is, “rebelling.” This is Nebrot the giant, who was a hunter before the Lord. From him the Chaldeans were born.

He is the one who drove out Assyr, the son of Shem—that is, the son of his father’s brother—and built Babylon, Orech, Archad, and Chalane in his land, within the borders of Canaan.

Babylonia extends for 60,000 [units]; its walls are 200 feet high and 70 feet wide. Solinus asserted this, for he described the entire circuit of the world.

The second son of Cham was named Mestrem, that is, “grinding everything.” He took possession of Egypt. Six sons were born to him, and these are their names:

The firstborn was Ludin, that is, “a man of his own business.”

The second was Emimegim, that is, “he has been prophesied.”

The third was Latisin, that is, “angry.”

The fourth was Neptabin, that is, “inflated.”

The fifth was Patrosin, that is, “raw.”

The sixth was Caslonin, that is, “horned.”

From Caslonin were born the Philistines and the Chapterini.

The third son of Cham was named Phut, that is, “perfect.” He appeared nowhere.

The fourth was Chanan, that is, “worshiping iniquity.” Eleven sons were born to Canaan:

The firstborn was Sidona, that is, “she went out to judgment, a huntress.” From him came the Sidonians, among whom was Jezebel, who worshiped the idol of the Sidonians, Baal.

The second was Cettheus, that is, “sinning.”

The third was Jebuseus, that is, “confused.” He built Jerusalem; for this reason it was called Jebus, after his name.

The fourth was Amorreus, that is, “full of gall.”

The fifth was Gergesseus, that is, “believed.”

The sixth was Evveus, that is, “serpent.”

The seventh was Aruceus, that is, “darkened.”

The eighth was Asenneus, that is, “he is not his.”

The ninth was Azirius, that is, “angry.”

The tenth was Samareus, that is, “he heard the accused.”

The eleventh was Amattheus, that is, “offending.”

These are the eleven sons of Canaan.

After this the tribes of the Canaanites were dispersed, and the borders of the Canaanites extended from Sidon until one comes to Gerar, Gaza, Ascalon, Azotus, and Geth; and until one comes to Sodom, Gomorrah, Adama, and Seboin; and as far as Laban, which is called Segor, where Lot had taken refuge, and throughout all the land of Canaan.

They had built a tower from baked bricks, and bitumen had served them as mortar. There God confused their languages, so that what one person requested he did not receive.

This happened in the days of Eber, from whom the Hebrew language was named, according to the Hebrews.

## Here Begin the Generations of Japhet, the Son of Noah

The third son of Noah was named Japhet, which is interpreted as “delay.” He had a wife named Ruth. From her he fathered Gamer, the firstborn, that is, “measure.”

He had three sons:

The firstborn, named Agganaz, that is, “burning fire.”

The second, Rifat, that is, “burning vision.”

The third, Zhargam, that is, “abundance.”

The second son of Japhet was named Magog. He took possession of Pamphylia.

The third was Madias. He took possession of Parthia.

The fourth was Lotham. He took possession of Greece. He is the father of the Syrian Palestinians.

From him four sons were born:

The firstborn was Elisa, that is, “come to me.”

The second was Tharsis, that is, “gladiator.” He built a city named Tharsus, after his own name, in which Jonah wished to flee from the presence of the Lord.

The third was Citi, that is, “I shall trample you.”

The fourth was Rodi, that is, “condemned.”

From these the islands of the nations in their land were designated, and each made a language for himself according to his own kind and among his own nations.

The fifth son of Japhet was called Elisa, that is, “you came to me.”

The sixth was Thober, that is, “abounding.”

The seventh was Moise, that is, “the archer.”

The eighth was Thiras, that is, “the spearman.”

These took possession of Carthage, according to the author’s statement. The Tyrians held it as settlers. Carthage was an ancient city, certainly belonging to the Tyrians.

These are the eight sons of Japhet, the grandsons of Noah. They took possession of Pamphylia, Parthia, all Greece, Rhodia, and Citia; from them came the Rhodiciti, the Mazianites, the Carthaginians, and the Tharsensians.

## Here Begins the Recollection of Sala, the Grandson of Shem, the Son of Noah

Let us return to Sala, the grandson of Shem, the son of Noah.

This is Sala, who lived 157 years and fathered Eber. After he fathered Eber, he lived 430 years and died.

Eber lived 144 years and fathered two sons. The firstborn was named Falech, that is, “divided.” Why “divided”? Because under him the sons and grandsons of Noah were divided.

The second son of Eber was called Jecta, that is, “small.”

He had twelve sons:

The firstborn, named Elmodam, that is, “agitated.”

The second, Salef, that is, “alienated.”

The third, Sarmoth, that is, “house of death.”

The fourth, Seruch, that is, “visible.”

The fifth, Odorrem, that is, “high enough.”

The sixth, Azaer, that is, “light.”

The seventh, Declax, that is, “across this.”

The eighth, Abimelech, that is, “cloudy.”

The ninth, Soba, that is, “take, come.”

The tenth, Ufer, that is, “light of healing.”

The eleventh, Evilath, that is, “show this.”

The twelfth, Jobab, that is, “loving God.”

These are the twelve sons of Jecthan.

Their commemoration extends from Massa until one comes to Gofer, from the death of Salma. Saul reigned in his place, from the city of Roboth, which is beside the river.

Saul died, and Ballenon, the son of Agnobor, reigned in his place. Ballenon died, and Arad, the son of Barad, reigned in his place. The name of his city was Fogor; the name of his wife was Metebel, daughter of Matrab, son of Mezob.

These were their leaders: Theman, Galla, Jephte, Telimas, Elas, Pynon, Genethz, Themna, Mazer, Magediel, Eram, and Fazoin.

These are the leaders of Edom in the land of their possession.

This is Esau, who was called Edom because of his eagerness for food, on account of which he lost his birthright when he ate lentils cooked in a frying pan; from this he received the name.

This is the nation that drove out the Horites.

And this is the nation of the Horites.

For there were seven sons of Seir the Horrite and twenty-two grandsons. These are their names: the first, Lotan, and his sons Heman and Chorri. The second, Shobal, and his six sons: Golla, Manachacat, Geba, Sofan, and Onan. This is Onas, who discovered Laminir in the wilderness of Elas while he was tending the beasts of his father Sebegon. The fourth was Aunam, and his two sons were Deson and Elibath. The sons of Deson were four, and these are their names: Emadan, Asban, Thasra, and Chorram. The fourth was Aran, and his four sons were Emadan, Asban, Thasra, and Chorram. The sixth was Asam, and his four sons were Balam, Zucam, Juscha, and Juschan [Col. 0528C]. The seventh was Rison, and his two sons were Oe and Arranh. These are the seven sons of Seir the Horrite, and their sister was Thamna, and their grandsons numbered twenty-two.

This was the nation of the Zozomim, whom Esau drove away from his presence from the land of Seir, so that he might possess it; and they became Gibeonites while fleeing from his presence. This occurred in Jesus—that is, “saved.”
