These are the four sons of Issachar. The sons of Zebulun were as follows: the first, Seder, that is, “learned”; the second, Allon, that is, “everlasting”; the third, Sem, that is, “cloudy.” These were the three sons of Zebulun. And no sons were born to Dinah.

The sons of Gad were seven, and these are their names: Sofan, Anges, Saunis, Soban, Ismaelis, and Ariolis. These were the seven sons of Gad.

The sons of Asher were these, and these are their names: the first, Semna, that is, “counted”; the second, Sesua, that is, “requested”; the third, Zievi, that is, “my honor”; the fourth, Baria, that is, “requesting,” and his sister Sara, that is, [the meaning is not supplied]. These were the four sons of Asher and their sister.

The sons of Baria were two, and these are their names: Chober, that is, “surpassing”; and the second, Melchiel, that is, “sent by God.” These were the two sons of Baria.

Now the sons of Joseph by Aseneth, the daughter of Petefres, were these, and these are their names: Manasses, that is, “forgetfulness,” and Ephraim, who is called “fruitful.” From Manasseh were born Machir, that is, “sold,” and Gaad, that is, “testimony.” From him was born Susi, and from Susi was born Gaddi, who had been sent by Moses to spy out the Promised Land.

From Ephraim were born Hisuthalan, that is, “apostolic dignity,” and Thaan, that is, “cloudy”; and from Suthalan was born Edem, that is, “temple” [Col. 0529A]. He begot Ause, and Ause begot Navve, who was called Jesus.

The sons of Israel carried Joseph’s bones with them out of Egypt—that is, from the land of Shechem—and placed them at Shechem, in the portion of the field which Jacob had acquired from the Amorites who inhabited Shechem, for one hundred lambs. We read this at the end of the Book of Jesus son of Nave; and since it says that Joseph gave it as a portion, and since we can establish the location of his burial, we bring forward Genesis and find that Jacob came to another city of Shechem, which is in the land of Canaan, when he had come from Mesopotamia of Syria. He set up his tent before the city and bought a portion of the field from Emmor, the father of Shechem, for one hundred lambs. There he erected an altar to God and invoked him as the God of Israel.

Lest anyone say that Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Sarah were buried in the same tomb, the Book of Genesis teaches us fully, as we read written: “And Abraham buried Sarah his wife in the double cave which is opposite Mamre.” This is Hebron in the land of Canaan. The field, together with the possession and the cave in it, became Abraham’s property for a burial place, acquired from the sons of Heth for forty didrachmas of silver from Ephron son of Saar the Hittite, opposite Jericho. This is their burial place.

The sons of Benjamin were these, and these are their names: the first, Bellach, that is, “gluttonous”; the second, Chober, that is, “firstborn”; the third, Asibel, that is, “fire from God.” These were the sons of Benjamin.

The three sons of Bellac, the firstborn of Benjamin, were these: the first, Adar, who is called “hospitality”; the second, Noeman, that is, “singing willingly”; the third, Jachim, that is, “my brother”; the fourth, Roos, that is, “initiator”; the fifth, Afim, that is, “likeness”; the sixth, Afim, that is, “according to my face.” These were the six sons of Bellac.

His grandson, born from Arad, was called Arad, that is, “descent.” He had one son, named Dannomine Ason, whose name is interpreted in Greek from the Chaldean language as “bishop,” but in Hebrew into Latin as “watchman.” Through a subtle deception the name is concealed, for the Antichrist also watches for evil. For we read in the secret traditions that he is announced as having come from this tribe.

The sons of Naphtali were these, and these are their names: the first, Masiel, who is interpreted as “strong God”; the second, Guni, that is, “strength”; the third, Enzer, that is, “everlasting”; the fourth, Sillem, that is, “debt.”

These are the names of the sons and grandsons of Israel who entered Egypt together with their father Jacob, seventy-five persons [Col. 0529D].

His fourth son, Judah, was a man powerful in strength. He begot Fares, who is interpreted as “divided.” Fares begot Esrom, that is, “high”; Esrom begot Aram, that is, “nation.” Aram begot Aminadab. Aminadab is interpreted as “loving desire.” Aminadab begot Naasson, who is called “refreshment,” and his sister Elisaphat, who was called “the grace of God.” Aaron took her as his wife, and priests were born from her.

Naasson begot Salmon, that is, “strength.” Salmon begot Booz, that is, “perfect,” by Rahab. And why is he called perfect? Because in him the Lord accomplished what we read in Deuteronomy: “And you, Moab, you shall appear to me in my house”—that is, through Ruth [Col. 0530A], the daughter-in-law of Noemi, who was the wife of her son Chellon.

This was Ruth the Moabite. By her he begot Obed, that is, “serving.” Obed begot Jesse, that is, “forgetting.” Jesse begot seven sons and two daughters, and these are their names: Eliab, Aminadab, Sama, Nathanael, Jadeum, Asomum, and David, the seventh; and their sisters Sarvia and Abigea.

The sons of Sarvia were Abessa, Joab, and Elagel. This is Joab, who counted the people from Dan to Beersheba. The number of Israel was eleven hundred thousand men who drew the sword, and of Judah four hundred seventy thousand men who drew the sword. But he did not count Levi and Benjamin among them, because the king’s command had overruled Joab; and this matter was evil in the sight of the Lord. Because of it, he struck Israel.

David said to the Lord: “I have sinned greatly, because I have done this thing; and now take away the iniquity of your servant, for I have acted very foolishly.” And the Lord spoke to Gad the seer, saying: “Go and speak to David. Thus says the Lord: I decree three things against you; choose one of them, and I will grant it to you: either three years of famine, or that for three months you flee from the presence of your enemies while they pursue you, or that for three days the sword of the Lord spread destruction throughout all the borders of Israel. And now see what word I shall answer to the one who sent me to you.”

David said to Gad: “I am in great distress. Let me rather fall into the hand of the Lord, for his mercies are very great; let me not fall into the hand of man.”

And the Lord sent death upon Israel from morning until the hour of dinner, and seventy thousand men of the people died. Abdanus [died] at Beersheba seventy thousand men, and God sent an angel to Jerusalem to destroy it; but as soon as he was ravaging it, the Lord repented. He said to the archangel, “It is enough; withhold your hand.” And the angel of the Lord was standing at the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite.

David saw the angel of the Lord standing between earth and heaven, with his sword stretched out over Jerusalem. David and the elders, covered with sackcloth, fell upon their faces. David said to the Lord: “Was it not I who said that the people should be counted? I am the one who sinned and acted wickedly. But these sheep—what evil have they done, Lord my God? Let your hand, then, be against me and against my father’s house, but let it not be against your people for their destruction.”

The angel of the Lord said to Gad: “Tell David to set up an altar at the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite.” David did according to what the Lord had commanded him. Then the Lord said to the angel: “Turn back your sword”; and he returned his sword to its sheath [Col. 0530D].

For this Jerusalem was formerly called Jebus, and Judah received it by lot. He went against the Canaanite dwelling in Hebron, and Sessi, Achiman, and Thalmi, descendants of Anak, who was born from Canaan, cut him down. The Jebusites dwelt among the sons of Benjamin and Judah in Jerusalem until they were expelled, after fifteen hundred years, by Jonathan son of Mattathias.

Abigea, David’s sister, bore Amessa. And the father of Amessa, Aeter the Ishmaelite, was counted with the people of Israel. When kings were given to that people, Saul became the first king, because the Lord was angry. Then the Lord said: “You will cry out to me because of your king, and I will not hear you, because you yourselves asked for a king.” And again he says: “I will give you a king in my anger.”

Under that anger he reigned forty years and was killed on Mount Gilboa. Then David said in his grief: “Mountains of Gilboa, let neither dew nor rain fall upon you, where the blood of the Lord’s anointed was poured out.”

This is David, who is called “merciful.” He reigned forty years and begot Solomon, who is called “peaceful.” Solomon also reigned forty years.

These are the names of David’s wives: Achima, Abigea, Agal, Habital, Agla, Bathsheba, and Michal. But when he returned from Hebron, Michal rejected him, and he gave her to another man, because he hated her greatly.

Solomon was born from Bathsheba. Solomon begot Rehoboam by Naamah, daughter of Anna, king of the sons of Ammon. Rehoboam is interpreted as “multitude of nations.” In his time King Shishak, king of Egypt, took the golden weapons—that is, spears and three hundred shields—which David had taken from Arazar, king of Syria; and Rehoboam, son of Solomon, made bronze ones in their place. He reigned eighteen years.

Rehoboam begot Abiud, that is, “to the Father God,” by Maacah, daughter of Ariel from Gaba; and he reigned three years. Abiud begot Asaph, that is, “he flies,” by Anna, and he reigned forty-one years. Asaph begot Jehoshaphat, that is, “judge,” by Gazuba, daughter of Selthi; and he reigned twenty-five years.

Jehoshaphat begot Joram, that is, “visible,” by Fache his wife; and he reigned eight years. Joram begot Ahaziah, that is, “strength,” by Athaliah, daughter of Ahab and Jezebel. Athaliah, a widow, reigned eight years, while he reigned one year.

Ahaziah begot Joash, that is, “gentle,” by Chobodda; and he reigned forty years. Josiah begot Amessias, that is, “asking,” by Jode; and he reigned twenty-nine years. Amessias begot Odiah, that is, “loving,” by Jeccelia; and he reigned sixty-one years.

Odiah begot Jonathan, that is, “perfect,” by Darbia, daughter of Zadok; and he reigned sixteen years. Jonathan begot Ahaz, that is, “holding,” by Saba; and he reigned sixteen years.

Ahaz begot Hezekiah, that is, “kingdom of God,” by Rabbuti, daughter of Zechariah; and he reigned twenty-nine years. Hezekiah begot Manasseh, that is, “forgetfulness of sorrow,” by Hephzibah; and he reigned fifty-five years.

Manasseh begot Amos, that is, “bashful,” and Masthelamitaba; and he reigned two years. Amos begot Josiah, that is, “asking,” by Jedidah, daughter of Uzziah; and he reigned thirty-one years.

Josiah begot Jehoahaz, that is, “like,” by Jecora; and he reigned ninety days. Examital begot Joash and Zedekiah. Nebuchadnezzar blinded Zedekiah’s eyes in the presence of his sons, bound him in bronze fetters, ordered him to be taken to Babylon, and placed him in a mill; there he died. In the eleventh year of his reign, Jerusalem was plundered by Nebuchadnezzar the king.

The years of the kings came to an end: five hundred fifty-five years, six months, and ten days. The people were carried away to Babylon, and Nebuchadnezzar appointed Jeconiah, son of Jehoiakim, as king; he was called “preparation” and reigned one hundred days.

Then he too was taken to Babylon. In the thirtieth year of the captivity Jeconiah was shaved, when Ulemadar brought him out of prison. This is Ulemadar, who became Nebuchadnezzar’s successor while Nebuchadnezzar was living among the beasts of the field.

Then Ulemadar spoke kindly to Jeconiah, set his throne above the thrones of all the kings who were with him in Babylon, changed his garments, and ate with him at table all the days of his life. His ration was assigned to him, and Ulemadar was his counselor throughout all his days.

Jeconiah begot Salathiel, that is, “God has sent.” Salathiel, in Babylon, begot Zerubbabel, who is called “victory of God.”

At this time Cyrus, king of the Persians, obtained the kingdom. In the fifty-second year of the captivity, Astyages the king was gathered to his ancestors, and Cyrus, king of the Persians, received his kingdom. In the second year of his reign he subjected Babylon to Nineveh, a Median city.

At that time he promised to return the sacred vessels which Nebuchadnezzar had taken from Jerusalem and from the temple of the Lord and had placed in his idol-temple. Cyrus, king of the Persians, brought them out and assigned them to Mithridates, the keeper of his treasures; through him they were handed over to Salmanasar, the prefect of Judea.

Their number was: one thousand golden libation vessels; five hundred silver vessels; twenty-nine silver cups; fifty golden bowls; two thousand four hundred ten silver bowls; and one thousand other vessels. All the golden and silver vessels together numbered four thousand nine hundred seventy-nine. They were carried by Salmanasar and by those who returned from the Babylonian captivity.

Cyrus reigned nineteen years and was killed by Miride in Massa Jada, in the sixty-eighth Olympiad. He was buried in the fortress held by the Magi, called Thiasarcis. This is the tomb of Cyrus.

After Cyrus died, as we have said, in the sixty-eighth Olympiad, King Darius succeeded him in the kingdom. This Darius was the son of Asieri, born from Bastin in the city of Susa, and he reigned over the Chaldeans. From the third year of his reign Daniel’s weeks begin, at the beginning of the second cycle.

At that time the Romans were growing in greatness under Tarquinius Superbus, who was the eighth Roman king from the foundation of the city and reigned twenty-four years. Rome was founded by the sons of Martius and Ilia on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May, on a Thursday. From that time until the twenty-fourth year of King Geiseric there are, to the present day, one thousand two hundred seven years.

At that time, in the tenth year according to the Roman reckoning of the months, Uzziah son of Amaziah was reigning in Judea, in the twenty-fourth year of his reign. From then until the completion of the seventy years of the captivity, the succession of the individual Roman kings accounts for two hundred fifty-eight years, beginning with the twenty-fourth year of Uzziah son of Amaziah.

But in order that the times of the Jewish and Roman kings might be brought into correspondence, the number of years of the Roman kings must be sought and recited in order, beginning with Remus and Romulus, the founders of the city.

For these two first reigned together at Rome for thirty-eight years. After them Titus Tatius, leader of the Sabines, reigned forty-one years; then Numa Pompilius forty-three years; Tullus Hostilius thirty-two years; Ancus Marcus Fili[p]pus twenty-eight years; Tarquinius Priscus thirty-eight years. In the sixth year of his reign, Jerusalem is shown to have been taken captive by King Nebuchadnezzar.

Servius Tullius, born of a slave woman, reigned thirty-six years [Col. 0533A]. Altogether, these make two hundred fifty-six years up to the first year of Darius, in which Cyrus died. At that time Tarquinius Superbus had begun to administer the Roman kingdom.

In his second year, the years of the kings of the city reached two hundred fifty-eight, up to the completion of the seventy years of the captivity, with the seven weeks of Daniel also succeeding, during which he himself reigned twenty-two years. Thus the years of the kings of the city amounted to two hundred eighty.

After these kings, consuls, tribunes, and aediles governed for four hundred eleven years, up to Gaius Julius Caesar. From Gaius Julius Caesar until the final shipwreck of Valentinian’s life there are five hundred eight years. During this period, although clay was mixed with iron like pottery, the Roman empire nevertheless stood continuously by divine providence.

Let him who reads understand Daniel’s interpretation of the statue which Nebuchadnezzar had dreamed.

And at the very beginning of the one thousand two hundredth year, when the boundaries of time had run their course, the kingdom of the Romans came to an end. For this reason, now almost throughout the whole circuit of the earth, murders and torments increase; the crashing of wars and the plague of punishments follow one another in doubled succession. Lamentation, deceit, wounds, and mourning are poured out everywhere. When all these things are thus repeatedly inflicted upon this world, each comes immediately to an end together with the killers and the slain.

[Note: [Col. 0533D] The material here and following is taken from Book III of Esdras.]

Meanwhile Zerubbabel, son of Salathiel—the man who was declared wiser than the others by King Darius—was of the house of David, from the lineage of Fares, of the tribe of Judah. At his request the king ordered the temple to be built and all the vessels to be restored.

This is the Darius who, according to the Chaldeans, was called Artaxerxes, but according to the Medes was called Darius. He held a great banquet for all who were under his authority, for all his household and for all the governors of Media and Persia, from India to Ethiopia, over one hundred twenty-seven provinces.

When they had drunk and eaten their fill, they returned. King Darius went up to his chamber, slept, and became insensible. Then three young men who guarded the king’s body said to one another: “Let each of us state a proposition which will prevail. To whichever one of us has the wiser saying, King Darius will give great gifts: he will be clothed in purple over his victory, drink from gold, sleep upon gold, receive a gilded chariot, a linen tiara, and a golden necklace around his neck; he shall sit second to Darius because of his wisdom and shall be called Darius’s kinsman.”

Then each wrote down his saying and placed it beneath Darius’s pillow. They said: “When the king rises, we shall give him the writings. The king and the three chief men of Persia shall judge, and victory shall be given to the one whose saying is the wisest, as it is written.”

One wrote: “Wine is mighty.” Another wrote: “The king is mighty.” The third wrote: “Women are mighty, but above all things truth is mighty.”

Then the king arose [Col. 0534A], and they gave him the writings. He read them, sent for, and summoned all the governors and chief men. All the princes also sat down, and the writing was read before them. He said: “Call the young men; they themselves will explain their sayings to us.”

They entered, and he said to them: “Tell us what you wrote.”

The first began, speaking about the power of wine, and said:

“Men, how quickly wine prevails over all the people who drink it! It leads astray the king’s mind and makes the minds of orphans, slaves and free persons, poor and rich, foolish. It changes every mind into merriment and joy, and makes one forget all sadness and debt. It makes every soul rich, and one remembers neither king nor governor; it makes everything speak through talents. When they drink, they do not remember the friendships of friends and brothers; shortly afterward they seize swords, and when they rise from the wine, they do not remember what they have done.

“O men, does not wine prevail, since it compels people to act in this way?” And he was silent.

After he had spoken thus, the second began to speak, the one who had written about the power of the king:

“O men, do not human beings rule the earth and the sea and everything in them? Yet the king prevails and dominates them, and whatever he says to them they do. If he sends them against enemies, they go and demolish mountains, walls, and towers; they kill and are killed, and they do not transgress the king’s command.

“If they conquer, they bring the king whatever they have captured. Those who do not serve or fight but cultivate the land, when they have plowed and harvested, bring the produce to the king. He alone is supreme. If he says, ‘Kill,’ they kill; if he says, ‘Release,’ they release; if he says, ‘Withdraw,’ they withdraw; if he says, ‘Lay waste,’ they lay waste; if he says, ‘Build,’ they build; if he says, ‘Cut down,’ they cut down; if he says, ‘Plant,’ they plant. Every people and all his power belong to him.

“While reclining in his pride he eats, drinks, and sleeps, while these men keep watch around him. They cannot go away individually to do their own work, nor can they disobey him. O men, how could the king not prevail?”

The third, who had spoken about women and truth, was Zerubbabel, son of Salathiel, of the house of David, from the lineage of Fares, of the tribe of Judah. He began to speak:

“O men, is not the king great, and are not there many people, and is not wine strong? Who, then, rules them? Are they not women? Women have given birth to the king and to all the people who rule the sea and the lands, and from women they have come. They also nourished those who planted the vineyards from which wine is made.

“They make garments for all people, and they bring glory to men. Men cannot be separated from women. Even when men have acquired gold and silver and every beautiful object, if they see one woman beautiful in appearance and form, they abandon all these things and gaze at her. They stare at her with open mouths, and all praise her more than gold, silver, or any precious work.

“A man leaves his father who nourished him, his own land, and clings to his wife. With the woman he leaves his soul, and he remembers neither father nor mother nor land.

“And you ought to recognize that women rule over you. Do you not labor and suffer and bring and give everything to women? A man takes up his sword and goes wandering, sails in a ship, crosses rivers, sees a lion, and walks in darkness; and when he has stolen and committed robbery, he begins to bring the spoils to his beloved.

“Again, a man loves his wife more than his father or mother. Many have been touched by despair because of women; they have become slaves because of them; many have perished, been killed, and sinned because of women.

“And now you do not believe me, because the king is great in his power and all the provinces fear to approach him. Yet I saw Debanna, the concubine of the king, the daughter of Emen, daughter of that remarkable man Bezzachi, sitting beside the king, taking the diadem from the king’s head, placing it upon her own, and striking the king with her left hand. Through all this the king, like a dull-witted man, gazed at her with open mouth. If she smiled at him, the king laughed; if she became angry, he flattered her until she again became gracious toward him.

“O men, how can women not be strong, when they act in this way?”

Then the king and his power looked at one another, and he began to speak about truth:

“O men, are not women strong? Great is the earth and lofty is heaven; the sun, swiftly running, turns back in the circuit of heaven and again returns to the same place in a single day. Is not the one who made these things great? And truth is great and stronger than all.

“All the earth invokes truth; heaven blesses it, and all things that move tremble. There is no injustice in it. Wine is unjust, the king is unjust, women are unjust, and all the children of human beings are unjust; all their works are unjust, and there is no truth in them. In their injustice they will perish.

“But truth remains forever; it lives and endures for ever and ever. With it there is no accepting of persons; it carries out equity. It keeps away from all the unjust and evil, and there is no unjust person in its judgment. To it belong strength, kingdom, power, and majesty throughout all ages. Blessed is the God of truth.”

And he ceased speaking.

All the people cried out and said: “Great is truth, and it prevails.”

Then the king said to him: “Ask whatever you wish, beyond what was written, and I will give it to you, since you have been found wiser. You shall sit next to me and be called my kinsman.”

Then he said to the king: “Remember the vow that you vowed: to build Jerusalem on the day when you received the kingdom, and to release all the vessels that were taken away, which King Cyrus separated when he captured Babylon.”

And he vowed to return them to Jerusalem.

“And you vowed to build the temple which the Chaldeans burned when Judea was laid waste. Now this is what I beg of you, lord king, and what I ask; this is your majesty, which I beseech you to carry out: the vow which you vowed to the Lord, the King of Heaven, with your mouth.”

Then King Darius arose and kissed him. He wrote letters to all the stewards, leaders, and governors, ordering them to escort him, and ordering all who were with him to go up and build Jerusalem. He also wrote to all the governors of Coele-Syria, Phoenicia, and Lebanon, commanding that cedar wood from Lebanon be transported to Jerusalem.

When the young man had gone out from the king’s presence, he looked toward heaven in the direction of Jerusalem, blessed the Lord, and said: “From you comes victory, from you wisdom, and yours is the glory; I am your servant. Blessed are you who gave me wisdom, and, Lord Father, to you I give thanks.”

He received the letters, departed for Babylon, and reported everything to his brothers. They blessed the God of their fathers, because he had granted them permission to go up and build Jerusalem and the temple in which his name had been invoked.

The number of those who returned from the Babylonian captivity to the land of Judah and Jerusalem, from twelve years of age and above, apart from boys and girls, was forty-two thousand three hundred sixty.

The boys and girls numbered seven thousand three hundred twenty-seven; singers, male and female, two hundred forty-five; camels, four hundred thirty-five; miscellaneous pack animals, five thousand seven hundred seventy-five [Col. 0536B].

When they departed from the region of Babylon, Ezra the prophet and teacher of the law also went up with them. King Artaxerxes sent him a letter, of which this is the text:

“King Artaxerxes to Ezra the priest and reader of the law of the Lord, greetings.

“Since I judge with goodwill, I command that those of the race of the Jews, and of the priests and Levites who are in our kingdom, who wish to go up with you to Jerusalem, may do so. Let all who are considering going depart, as seems good to me and to my seven friends and counselors, so that you may inspect everything that is in Judea and Jerusalem.

“According to the law which you possess, take gifts for the Lord God of Israel. I and my friends have offered these gifts, because God dwells in Zion. All the gold and silver that may be found in Babylon shall be restored to the temple of God and to Jerusalem.

“You, Ezra, according to the wisdom of God, appoint judges of the causes of the congregation throughout all Syria and Phoenicia. You shall teach all whom you know, and whoever transgresses the law of your God and of the king shall be diligently punished, whether by death, penalty, monetary loss, or exile.

“Farewell.”

And Ezra the scribe said:

“Blessed is the Lord, the God of my fathers, who put this in the king’s heart, to glorify his house which is in Jerusalem, and who honored me in the presence of the king and his counselors. I was strengthened in courage according to the help of the Lord my God.”

They departed and came to Jerusalem, and celebrated Passover on the ninth day before the Kalends of April, on a Thursday, one thousand one hundred seventy-six years after Moses’ Passover in Egypt [Col. 0536D].

Then the foundations of the temple of God, laid by Zerubbabel, were restored. The temple was built over forty-six years. For he did not loosen his belt, nor cut the hair of his head, nor even remove his shoes, until, through Ezra the prophet and priest and renewer of the law, after the completion of Daniel’s seven weeks, the dedication of the temple took place.

This is Zerubbabel, who begot Abiud, who is called “Father of confession.” Abiud begot Eliachin, that is, “rising again.” Eliachin begot Azzor, that is, “killed.” Azzor begot Saddoc, that is, “commanded.” Saddoc begot Achim, that is, “prepared.” Achim begot Eliud, that is, “the Lord is strong.” Eliud begot Eliazar, that is, “God is helper.” Eliazar begot Matham, that is, “gift.” Matham begot Jacob, that is, “beloved.” Jacob begot Joseph, that is, “he gathers,” whose son, as it was thought, the Lord Christ was according to the flesh.

The genealogies which Matthew the Evangelist describes as far as Joseph, to whom Mary was betrothed, are completed.

Here begin the others which Luke describes as far as Mary; but, retracing the course from her back to the first man, he returns.

Let us return to Exodus and set forth the generations of the Levites. Levi begot Kohath, Gershon, and Merari. Kohath begot Amram, whose name is said to mean “love,” and Izhar, interpreted as “strong toward the strong,” and Hebron, interpreted as “eternal friend,” and Uzziel, interpreted as “God is strong.” Uzziel begot Mishael, interpreted as “visitation,” and Elzaphan, interpreted as “petition of God,” and Sithri, interpreted as “hidden.”

Gershon, the second son of Levi, whose name is said to mean “settler,” begot Libni, that is, “white,” from Shimei, whose name is interpreted as “hearing.” Merari, the third son of Levi, begot Mahli, interpreted as “change,” and Mushi, interpreted as “my fountain.”

Amram, the son of Kohath, begot Aaron, Moses, and Miriam, whose name is interpreted as “mistress,” by Jochebed, who was called “the dignity of the Lord,” the daughter of his father’s brother. Izhar, the second son of Kohath, begot Korah, whose name is interpreted as “bare.” Korah begot Assir, interpreted as “one who asks,” and Elkanah, interpreted as “zeal,” and Abiasaph, interpreted as “my father.”

These are the sons of Korah. From this family came those who, in the time of David, sang before the ark of the covenant with the other Levites and priests, in twenty-four divisions by lot, together with Asaph, Jeduthun, Heman, and Ethan.

The second son of Izhar was called Nepheg, which is interpreted as “impiety”; the third was Zichri, interpreted as “love”; and the fourth was Mishael, interpreted as “God has sent.”

Aaron is interpreted as “the seeing chest,” or “vision of the Most High.” Aaron begot Nadab, whose name is interpreted as “desire,” and Abihu, who was called “friend of God.” Nadab and Abihu died while they were offering strange fire before the Lord God in the desert of Sinai. Their number was twenty-three thousand. Every male from one month old and above was counted among them, for they were not reckoned in the midst of the children of Israel, since no inheritance was given to them among the others. “Strange fire” means fire from a common source, not divine fire coming from heaven.

Eleazar, the third son of Aaron, whose name means “my God is helper,” begot Phinehas, whose name is interpreted as “persecutor,” by one of the daughters of Putiel. This is the Phinehas of whom Matthias spoke in the Books of the Maccabees, saying: “While Phinehas was zealous for the law, he obtained the priesthood.”

The fourth son of Aaron was called Ithamar, interpreted as “rancid.” He begot Elisheba, whose name is interpreted as “the grace of the Lord.”

Moses, the second son of Amram, begot Gershom, interpreted as “guest,” and Eliezer, interpreted as “the strength of God,” by Zipporah, whose name is interpreted as “beautiful visitation,” the daughter of Jethro of Midian, the priest. Gershom begot Jonathan. He and his sons offered sacrifices in the tribe of Dan until the day of the land’s deportation.

Aaron and Moses were buried on this mountain at Geth, near the house of Peor. This tribe did not receive a lot, because the priests who serve at God’s altar come from it: the Lord is their lot. Therefore, tithes ought now to suffice for the priests, so that those who desire to dwell upon other people’s possessions may be free from the pleasures of the world.

Moses is interpreted in the Egyptian language as “taken from the water,” and in the Hebrew language as “he preserves for the Lord.” He begot Gershom and his brother Eliezer by Zipporah, whose name means “visitation.”

This Moses was in the desert of Sinai for forty years. When, at the Lord’s command, he ascended from the plains of Moab upon Mount Nebo, to the summit of Pisgah, which is opposite Jericho, the Lord showed him the whole land of Naphtali, Ephraim, and Manasseh, and the whole land of Judah as far as the western sea, and the desert and the surrounding region of Jericho, the city of palms, as far as Peor. And the Lord said to Moses:

“This is the land which I swore to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, saying, ‘I will give it to your descendants.’ I have shown it to your eyes, but you shall not enter it.”

And Moses, the servant of the Lord, died in the land of Moab, according to the word of the Lord. They buried him at Geth, near the house of Peor, and no one knows his burial place to this day, lest they should worship him as God, just as they abandoned him at Horeb.

Here the four hundred and seventy years are completed, from Abraham’s call and Israel’s sojourn to the time of the wilderness and the end of Moses’ life.

After him Jesus son of Nun, who was called “Savior,” judged Israel for thirty years; his whole life lasted one hundred and ten years. They buried him within the boundaries of his allotted inheritance, at Timnath-serah on Mount Ephraim, beyond Mount Gilead. They placed in his tomb the stone knives of circumcision, after Israel had conquered twenty-nine kings.

At this time twenty-nine kings and peoples held Africa, which in ancient times was called an island. From the beginning of its habitation until the sixteenth year of the king, there are two thousand and seventy-six years.

After Jesus, when the people had transgressed God’s commandments, they served Chushan-rishathaim, king of Mesopotamia, for eight years. Then the people repented, and Othniel judged them for fifty years.

The origin of Othniel was as follows: he was the son of Kenaz, the brother of Caleb, the brother of Jephunneh. Othniel began the city of letters, and Caleb gave him Achsah his daughter as wife. This is Debir, the city of letters.

Then Eglon judged them for eighteen years. He was king of the Moabites. At that time the people did not serve the Lord, because they sacrificed to idols, and they were handed over to King Eglon.

Afterward Ehud son of Gera judged them for eighty years. He took a dagger made for the palm of the hand and said to Eglon: “I have a word for you, O king.” When they had entered the chamber, he killed him, shut the door, and escaped through the midst of the army unharmed.

In the twenty-fourth year of Ehud, Job died in the land of Edom. Then they served King Shamgar for twenty years. He killed eight hundred men of the foreigners with an ox-goad and defended the children of Israel.

Afterward they served Jabin, king of the foreigners, for twenty years. This king of Canaan reigned in Astaroth, and his army commander was Sisera. He had nine hundred iron chariots.

Then Deborah judged them for forty years. In her time Sisera fled into the house of Jael, and Jael herself killed him with a tent peg, while Barak, the commander of the army, pursued him.

Afterward the Midianites possessed them for seven years, and their leader was called Zalmunna. Under him the children of Israel fled into caves and hid themselves in clefts of the mountains, while the Lord was angry.

Then Gideon judged them for forty years. He was the son of Jerubbaal. Only three hundred men went with him into battle against Midian, those who lapped the water like dogs. Then the Lord said: “By the three hundred men who lapped the water like dogs I will save Israel.”

Afterward Abimelech judged them for three years. He killed a thousand foreigners with fire in the tower of the Shechemites, when they had fled from him into the citadel. Then, struck by a woman with a millstone, he died.

Afterward Puah son of Haran judged them for twenty years. He lived on Mount Ephraim, and during his time peace abounded; there was no war in Israel.

Then Tola judged them for twenty-two years. Then Jair judged them for twenty-two years. He had thirty sons who rode thirty horses, and they possessed thirty cities, which were called the Villages of Jair in Gilead.

Afterward the Philistines and Ammonites possessed them for eighteen years. Under their oppression the children of Israel cried out to the Lord, not once but repeatedly, and only with difficulty did he free them from their dangers.

Then Jephthah of Gilead judged them for seven years. From Aroer to the place reached by going toward Marathaim, as far as Abel-keramim, he overthrew twenty cities of Ammon with their peoples. When he returned to his house, he offered his daughter.

Afterward Ibzan, an Israelite, judged them for seven years. He was from Bethlehem. He had thirty sons and thirty daughters whom he sent outside, and he took thirty wives for his sons. He died and was buried at Bethlehem.

Then Elon judged them for ten years. This Elon was a Zebulunite; therefore he was buried in the land of Zebulun.

Afterward Abdon judged them for eight years. He was a Pirathonite. He had forty sons and thirty grandsons who rode seventy horses. He died and was buried at Pirathon, in the land of Ephraim, on Mount Eliath.

Then foreigners possessed them for forty years, because they had provoked the Lord, and they were handed over to the Canaanites who inhabited Ashkelon, Gerar, Gaza, Azotus, and Gath—the five cities which Inathen son of Mattathias conquered.

Afterward Samson son of Manoah and his wife Delilah judged them for twenty years. His strength could not be overcome; he killed more at his death than during his life.

Then Samir judged them for one year. He struck down six hundred men of the Philistines, apart from their animals, and saved Israel.

Afterward they had peace for thirty years. In those days there was no leader in Israel, and each person did whatever he wished.

Then the tribe of Benjamin had committed an act like that of the Sodomites, and they were destroyed by the children of Israel. Six hundred men remained, who had fled in order to escape.

Afterward Eli the priest, who had been at Shiloh, where the ark of God had been established, judged them. His sons Hophni and Phinehas were priests of the Lord. Phinehas begot Ahitub and Beriochabel; Ahitub begot Abimelech, and he begot Abiathar, who in turn begot Ahimelech, banished by Solomon into exile. Eli was very old, and both his sons were sinners in the sight of the Lord.

At this time Samuel was born. Hannah, the wife of Elkanah, asked for him when she was barren, and the Lord heard her. She conceived and bore a son, and called his name Samuel, saying: “Because I asked him from God Almighty.”

Eli was ninety years old. His eyes were covered, and he could not see. He judged the people for twenty years. When he heard the report that the ark of the Lord had been captured by the Philistines, he fell from his chair and died.

Then Samuel succeeded him and judged Israel for twenty years. Samuel begot sons, one named Joel and the other Abiathar.

In his time, after the ark had been captured by the Philistines, when Phinehas and Hophni, the sons of Eli, had been killed, he too died upon hearing the report, and the ark had been plundered by the nations.

After its return, four sanctified places existed, which Samuel visited: Bethel, called Luz, where God appeared to Jacob; Gilgal, where Jesus circumcised the people opposite Jericho; Mizpah, where Jephthah offered his daughter; and Ramah, at his own house, where he had made an altar to God.

For he was priest, judge, and prophet. But for this reason he was not included by us among the priests, nor was Eli, because they are counted among the Judges.

Here are completed the five hundred and sixty-one years of the Judges, from the beginning of the captivity of the foreigners.

After him Saul became king, whom the Lord in his anger had given to the people of Israel. He was anointed by Samuel while he was seeking the donkeys of his father Kish. Saul reigned over Israel for forty years. Bamah is the name of the city where this Saul was anointed.

Saul had a wife named Ahima. By her he begot Jonathan, Jesui, Ishbaal, Mephibosheth, and their sisters Merab and Michal. Jonathan’s son Mephibosheth begot Micah.

After him David reigned over Israel for forty years and six months. Between Samuel and David there were forty years.

In their time there were twelve thousand two hundred and sixty priests of the tabernacle of testimony, and one hundred and twelve thousand Levites. There were twenty-four chief priests, who are the twenty-four elders. Their names are these. They were descended from Eleazar and Ithamar, the sons of Aaron:

The first lot was Jarim, from whom Mattathias came; the second, Bidae; the third, Choreb; the fourth, Seroib; the fifth, Michae; the sixth, Beniamin; the seventh, Choos; the eighth, Abia, from whom Zechariah came; the ninth, Jesu; the tenth, Jecchenir; the eleventh, Enasib; the twelfth, Jachib; the thirteenth, Chobra; the fourteenth, Isba; the fifteenth, Banne; the sixteenth, Emmer; the seventeenth, Chezir; the eighteenth, Afesor; the nineteenth, Phaner; the twentieth, Ezechiel; the twenty-first, Achin; the twenty-second, Samuel; the twenty-third, Dalea; the twenty-fourth, Mazia.

These are the twenty-four whom David appointed as chiefs over the priests.

When he brought the ark of the covenant from the house of Abinadab and placed it in Zion, in the house of Aminadab, and afterward transferred it and placed it in his own house, he appointed these as chiefs over the priests, so that they might go before the people before the ark of the covenant.

There were also twenty-four Levites who commanded the Levites. They were descended from Kohath, Gershon, and Merari. Four were set over them, whose names are these: first Heman, second Asaph, third Jeduthun, fourth Ethan.

Their number, together with their brothers who were trained to sing to the Lord—every one who understood—was two hundred and eighty-eight. They also received daily lots for their appearances, according to great and small, the perfected and the learners.

The first lot fell to the sons and brothers of Asaph: Joseph himself, and his sons and brothers, twelve. The second was Godolias, his sons and brothers, twelve. The third was Zacchur, his sons and brothers, twelve. The fourth was Jesdri, his sons and brothers, twelve. The fifth was Natanias, his sons and brothers, twelve. The sixth was Bocia, his sons and brothers, twelve. The seventh was Israel, his sons and brothers, twelve. The eighth was Ageas, his sons and brothers, twelve. The ninth was Matthanias, his sons and brothers, twelve. The tenth was Semei, his sons and brothers, twelve. The eleventh was Esdriel, his sons and brothers, twelve. The twelfth was Asabias, his sons and brothers, twelve. The thirteenth was Sabael, his sons and brothers, twelve. The fourteenth was Matthatias, his sons and brothers, twelve. The fifteenth was Jarimoth, his sons and brothers, twelve. The sixteenth was Ananias, his sons and brothers, twelve. The seventeenth was Jesbachas, his sons and brothers, twelve. The eighteenth was Ananias, his sons and brothers, twelve. The nineteenth was Misael, his sons and brothers, twelve. The twentieth was Eliath, his sons and brothers, twelve. The twenty-first was Etth, his sons and brothers, twelve. The twenty-second was Gotholias, his sons and brothers, twelve. The twenty-third was Mazoth, his sons and brothers, twelve. The twenty-fourth was Ramagi, his sons and brothers, twelve.

These are the two hundred and eighty-eight who went before the army of the children of Israel and sang a song to the Lord.

At that time David too, filled with the Holy Spirit, prophesied the one hundred and fifty psalms together with them. There were four appointed as leaders of those who sang to the Lord, as we said: first Heman, second Asaph, third Jeduthun, fourth Ethan. They had seventy-two each, answering one another with cymbals, harps, and lyres.

They did not sing whatever they wished, but what the Spirit announced through them.

The ark was in captivity for twenty years; it was in the house of Abinadab for forty years; and it was in the house of King David for twenty years. David reigned over Israel for forty years and six months. From his house Zadok son of Ahitub took the horn, and he anointed Solomon as king in place of David his father.

David reigned seven years in Hebron and thirty-three years in Jerusalem. In Hebron he begot seven sons, whose names are these: the firstborn, Amnon, whom Absalom killed after he had violated Tamar; the second, Caleb; the third, Absalom; the fourth, Ornias, who was killed by Solomon because of Abishag the Shunammite, since Ornias had asked to take her as his wife.

Then Abiathar was banished because he had anointed him king. Abiathar was the son of Ahimelech, who alone escaped and was saved when three hundred and fifty priests were killed by Doeg the Syrian, whom King Saul had sent.

David said of him to Saul:

“You loved wickedness more than goodness, and iniquity more than you speak justice.”

He condemns the cunning of Doeg the Syrian, who presented himself as righteous in his words but practiced iniquity against the innocent.

And again:

“You loved every word of destruction, a deceitful tongue.”

By these words he means that he suddenly cast the unwary into death.

This Abiathar, who had then escaped death, was banished by Solomon because of Ornias, so that, in accordance with the Lord’s judgment, no one from the seed of Eli should administer sacrifice in the house of the Lord.

The fifth was Aphatias; the sixth, Ethoram; and Tamar was the sister of Absalom.

In Jerusalem, of Bathsheba [and] Uriah the Hittite, Saman and Soban are sons of David, brothers of Solomon and Nathan, from whom Luke the Evangelist demonstrated Mary’s descent.

Similarly Matthew the Evangelist demonstrates Solomon’s descent to Joseph, so that it may appear that they came from one tribe and thus came to Christ according to the flesh, fulfilling what is written:

“Behold, the lion has conquered, from the tribe of Judah, the root of David.”

The lion is from Solomon, and the root from Nathan. Solomon begot Rehoboam, and Nathan begot Mattan.

Then Jeroboam son of Nebat obtained the kingdom; his wife was named Sorum, and she remained a widow. After a long time, the servant of Solomon rose up against Rehoboam, the son of Solomon; the servant acquired a kingdom against his master. In the first year of his reign he made two golden calves, placing one in Dan and one in Bethel.

Then he said to the people:

“It is enough for you to go up to Jerusalem. Behold your gods, O Israel, who brought you out of the land of Egypt.”

This Jeroboam reigned in Samaria for thirty-four years. There was a schism between Rehoboam son of Solomon and Jeroboam son of Nebat, and there was war between them throughout all their days, just as now there is war between true Christians and false Catholics.

Jeroboam begot Nadab by a wife named Anna, and Nadab reigned for two years. Baasha son of Ahijah succeeded him and reigned for twenty-four years. After him Elah son of Baasha reigned for two years. After Elah, Zimri reigned for eighteen years with Thamni, and alone for twelve years.

This is the Zimri who begot Ahab. Ahab had Jezebel, the daughter of Ethbaal, king of the Sidonians. Ahab reigned for twenty-one years and begot Ahaziah, who reigned for two years. Another son of Ahab, named Joram, reigned for twelve years.

After him Jehu son of Nimshi reigned for twenty-eight years.

At that time Jehosheba, daughter of the king of Judah—that is, daughter of Jehoram and sister of Ahaziah—hid Joash, the son of her brother Ahaziah, king of Judah, from Jehu for eight years in the house of the Lord, under the priest Jehoiada.

Under Jehu, Hazael king of Syria left from the army of Israel fifty horsemen, ten chariots, and one thousand men, according to the prophecy of Elisha.

Jehu was succeeded by Jehoahaz his son, who reigned for seventeen years. Jehoahaz begot Joash, who reigned for sixteen years. Joash begot Jeroboam, who reigned for twelve years. Jeroboam begot Zechariah, who reigned for six months. After him Shallum son of Jabesh reigned for one month. After him Menahem son of Gaddi reigned for ten years. Menahem begot Pekahiah, who reigned for two years. Pekahiah was succeeded by Pekah son of Remaliah, who reigned for twenty-two years.

When the book was consulted, [lacuna] [ru?] it was found that in the time of Pekah son of Remaliah Tiglath-pileser, king of the Assyrians, came up and deported the tribe of Gad and half the tribe of Manasseh as far as the borders of Naphtali, and scattered them throughout the land. [lacuna] [son of] Remaliah, Hoshea reigned for nine years.

Salmanasar, king of the Assyrians, humbled him, and he offered him tribute. [lacuna] In the fifth year Salmanasar discovered that Hoshea himself was sending to Egypt and preparing an ambush for him. [lacuna] In the eighth year of his reign he bound him and sent him to prison. In the ninth year he deported him with the people of Israel to the river Gozan, in the cities of the Medes, [lacuna] and scattered them there.

This occurred in the first year of the reign of Ahaz, king of Judah. At that time Tobias also [lacuna].

This Salmanasar begot Sennacherib. He is the one whose angel of the Lord killed, in a single night, one hundred and eighty-five thousand living men. Between the captivity of Samaria and Nineveh, and Jerusalem and Babylon, there are one hundred and forty-four years, six months, and ten days. Both received indulgence from captivity at the same time and, through Ezra and Zerubbabel, ascended to their own land.

The Samaritans remained in captivity at Nineveh for twenty-two years, while these were in Jerusalem for seventy years and in Babylon.

Let us return to Nathan, Solomon’s brother, from whom Mary derives her origin. Nathan begot Mattan. Mattan begot Enan. Enan begot Eliakim. Eliakim begot Joram. Joram begot Josram. Josram begot Judah. Judah begot Simeon. Simeon begot Levi. Levi begot Mattathias. Mattathias begot Joram. Joram begot Eliezer. Eliezer begot [lacuna]. [He] begot Eren; Eren begot Eldam; Eldam begot Cosam; Cosam begot Addi. Addi begot Melchi. Melchi begot Neri. Neri begot Salathiel. Salathiel begot Zerubbabel. Zerubbabel begot Resa. Resa begot Anna. Anna begot Judah. Judah begot Joseph. Joseph begot Semei. Semei begot [lacuna] Messen. Messen begot Mattathias. Mattathias begot Nahum. Nahum begot Jose. Jose begot Janna. Janna begot [lacuna] Levi.

Levi begot Nathan. Nathan begot Eli. Eli begot Joseph. Joseph begot Joachim. Joachim begot Mary.

This is Mary, the Mother of the Lord, from whom the Savior was born in the forty-first year of the reign of the emperor Augustus.

Augustus lived fifteen years beyond the year in which the Lord Christ was born. Tiberius Caesar succeeded him. In the sixteenth year of Tiberius, the Lord Christ suffered, when Annas and Caiaphas were priests.

Here are completed the five hundred and seventy-four years [lacuna] from Cassius [to] Ganiel, up to the passion of our Lord Jesus Christ, beginning from the eleventh year of Joachim the king—that is, from the first year of the captivity of Jerusalem and of Jeconiah his son.

From the Lord’s passion until the apostles Peter and Paul, twenty-eight years elapsed. They suffered under Nero twice. [lacuna] This was the first, and Nero’s second persecution is still to come under Enoch and Elijah.

This Nero is the one whose name is Labanius [lacuna] is called six hundred and sixteen. Here wisdom is required, so that the name of the one called

**Antichrist**

may be reckoned:

I. XIII. XVIII. VIIII. III. XVII. VIII. VIIII. XVII. XX. and XVIIII. [lacuna]

After the [lacuna] is taken away, the collected number becomes six hundred and fifty-four. Those who are involved in this [lacuna] the name of Antichrist. For we also read in secret that [lacuna] of Nero, and it is said to be a city in the West where he is still held [lacuna] by which [lacuna] the stars, when Antichrist will come.

But now many [lacuna] have been driven away. [lacuna] from us [lacuna] would have been and would certainly have remained with us.

From Nero onward [lacuna] seventy-three years. He was a false apostle who became the second fiercest opponent of the Christians. [lacuna] of Nero [lacuna] and the portion of the bishop, namely one hundred and fifty-three. [lacuna] twenty-eight. Nor was he himself an immoderate persecutor in the time of the Gospel’s persecution. [lacuna] Under whose persecution very many prophets suffered, whom [lacuna] glorious throughout the world [lacuna] preside from him [lacuna].

And there is a tolerable persecutor at Athens, while Labianus is presiding as bishop in the city. [lacuna] another ruin [lacuna] The bishop of Carthage was [lacuna].

Under Decius, at Rome, Sempronius, Julius [lacuna], the father Montanus, suffered up to Valerian; the years number seven. [lacuna] and at Carthage Cyprian. [lacuna] up to Maximian, the years number forty-five. These are the seventh most savage persecutors of Christians. [lacuna] of the city, and Ensurius of Carthage, Siranus, and Cassianus [lacuna] deacons of the city. [lacuna] they burned the homily.

From them until Stilicho’s second consulship there are one hundred and two years. In that consulship the persecution against the Donatists came on the sixth day before the Kalends of July; it was issued at Ravenna on the day before the Kalends of February. [lacuna] up to twenty-four years of King Geiseric, there are fifty-eight years.

This is the number of years [lacuna] from the passion of the Lord Christ to the present year; that is, as written above, there are four hundred and thirty-four years.

Now, in order to run through the years of the world in order, let us read the law. [lacuna]

From Adam to the Flood there are two thousand two hundred and forty-two years. From that time to Abraham’s call there are one thousand one hundred and eighty-eight years. From Abraham’s call until the children of Israel entered Egypt with their father Jacob there are two hundred and fifteen years. And with Moses [lacuna] he judged them, and they were from the children of Israel for four hundred and fifty years.

After God was offended, until [lacuna] foreigners ruled them for one hundred and eleven years. They had kings for five hundred and [lacuna] months, six days, and ten days. They were in the Babylonian captivity for seventy years.

Daniel’s seven weeks, during which the temple of God was restored, amount to forty-nine years. The other sixty-two weeks, during which the priests of the temple ruled over them up to the birth of Christ the Lord, amount to four hundred and thirty-four years.

From the Lord’s birth until his passion there are thirty-one years. From the Lord’s passion until the twenty-fourth year of King Geiseric there are four hundred and thirty-four years.

Altogether, from Adam, reckoned in the order of the law up to the present year, there are [lacuna] nine hundred and eighty-four years.

[Col. 0546A] Here ends the Genealogical Book, in which the conclusion of the aforementioned years [lacuna].

[Col. 0545]

**THE LITTLE BOOK OF THE ANONYMOUS AUTHOR ON THE COMPUTATION OF EASTER** (C, S)

**BOOK ONE.**
[Col. 0545B] While the inquisitive mind labored with particular zeal upon so weighty and highly desirable a matter, and, reading with prolonged eagerness, persisted for a long time in pursuit of that which purifies a human being, held fast in mortal snares, by fasts from sins, and joins him to the choir of the blessed; which receives the baptismal garment, sprinkled with scarlet stains and another’s redness, and displays it white as snow; which also receives [him] into the wedding-feast of the Lamb—[the following sense is uncertain]—when he is swollen with long-standing sins;

[Note: [Col. 0545D] The sense is confused.] which raises up by the prayers of the priests the temple of the Lord that has fallen and collapsed in ruin; and which, shining with the splendor of mercy, rose up and flashed forth into the light of knowledge, so that those things which appeared obscured by certain clouds to the one seeking and desiring them might be disclosed, and every hidden matter revealed to him; by this means the lunar courses might be established in their entirety, and the paschal cycles, consonant with one another [Col. 0545C] and with the lunar years and the reckoning of the embolisms, might be known without any error by those who were ignorant of them. In these cycles the years of the octads and hendecads are marked out, investigated and completed by divine providence, so that they seem in no respect whatever to waver.

The Creator’s providence is recognized as having fixed so great a designation upon them that, in the tenth year of King Geiseric, four hundred and twenty years from the Lord’s Passion were completed at the beginning of the first octad, and a Passover was found such as had then been celebrated by the Lord with his disciples, by both Jews and Christians. Meanwhile he suffered for us on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, on the sixteenth day of the moon, on the sixth day of the week; and he rose from the dead on the sixth day before those same Kalends, on the eighteenth day of the moon, on the first day of the week, as is undoubtedly shown to our truthful eyes in the first year of the first octad of the work begun [Col. 0545D] in that year. For the present year is the four hundred and twenty-sixth from the Lord’s Passion in the first octad, in the sixteenth year of the King. The beginning of the second cycle, however, has the year in the seventeenth consulship of Theodosius and of Festus; at the end of that year, the two thousand one hundred years were completed from the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt, and a Passover was found such as had first been sacrificed in Egypt by the Fathers. In the sixteenth year of the King, two thousand one hundred and sixteen were recorded, in the twenty-sixth cycle, in the seventeenth year of that same cycle; in that year the Lord’s Passover is celebrated on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May, on the seventeenth day of the moon.

But so that one as (= unit) may be found added in this cycle and the reckoning may revolve again from the second day of the moon [Col. 0546A] to the beginning, the lunar fractions produced it, because, in order that we might pronounce the paschal days as a complete reckoning over twelve years, one as of the accents and unciae will plainly be found in addition, apart from that as of the weekdays, which is very often inserted among the four years for the leap year. Therefore, when the eighty-four years have been enclosed by unciae and seven [uncertain term], you have eighty-four years, in which Augustalis of holy memory marked six of the seven asses in his octads and hendecads, not in their proper places and positions. The annual unciae discovered these over eighty-four years.

For this reason an error is sometimes found in those cycles, when insufficient attention is paid to the number of years and the courses of the elements, although one of the seven asses is always deducted over eighty-four years and is never admitted at all into the paschal computation. That as, unless I am mistaken, he improperly introduced into the lunar course; rather, by complete assertions he turned it aside as superfluous. It is this which is recognized as generating paschal errors, as the written sequence of the years shows.

To enable you to find the as that is excluded, you must use this [perhaps: the following] calculation. Eighty-four times [a] tenth of an uncia make 931 days for you; divide by thirty, and you will find 31. These are the thirty-one embolisms that every calendar table is known to contain. There remains that one as, which is always deducted from the seven at the end of the eighty-four years, and which, as we have said, the lunar fractions produced as superfluous.

[Col. 0546D] Agriustia of the municipality of the royal Thimidenses, writing also to Hilarianus concerning the paschal reckoning, tried by a certain technique to exclude this same as through scruples. He relied upon eleven days and not unciae for each year, but upon eleven days, half-uncia, two selae, his own scruple half a half-uncia, two selae, less by one uncia two scruples, [and] five cincunselae. These make, over eighty-four years, two hundred and four scruples, a sixth, which are eight hours, half-points, and two [uncertain term]. They are divided and excluded externally. Therefore, to exclude a full day from the number seven, there remain three hours, eleven scruples, and ten points too few. For this reason he was unable, in his assertions, to determine a certain number of years in their entirety.

[Col. 0547A] Since, therefore, it is evident in every respect that this as must be set aside—and if Augustalis had inserted the six asses, as I have said, into the parts of the calendar table with their proper numbers, he would in no way have incurred a defect in the lunar course and the paschal years—he nevertheless appears, through the excess produced by this error, to have assigned this as superfluously and variously in his lunar course. In the smaller element, however, the lunar course is concluded in the twenty-fourth year of the thirtieth year of the third cycle.

This also agrees with these paschal cycles of eighty-four years: when they have been completed, you return to the beginning, whether in the lunar tables or in the paschal years. Their seventeenth year therefore corresponds to the sixteenth year of the King. But in the lunar course, as we have said, among twelve years you insert one as into the first, second, and third squares, above whatever has been absent at the Kalends of January; and in this way the years are supported one by one in truth.

When, therefore, you have reached the twenty-fourth year in the third square, you return after eighty-four years, with one day excluded from the number seven, a day arising from the lunar increments. You will find at the head of the squares the second day of the moon. From A through K ten letters are counted there, which [each] add six days, so that the menstrual number may be set in motion. These same [letters] are fixed outside through the twelve months, and from them you observe the [letter] for each individual day. Thus, descending year by year in the squares, you will follow in a straight line opposite that same [letter] line; and which day of the moon you can find more accurately will be known to you by a sound knowledge of the matter.

In the weekday squares, the indication sought is supplied by the number seven. From A through G [Col. 0547C] seven letters are marked, in which the seventh year is conducted. When, in the leap-year sequence, you insert one as after three four-year periods—that is, one year, K—and in the order of the months you wish to seek a particular day, you will find the [letter] marked at the head, as you observe it day by day; opposite it, in the same squares, you will find the fixed weekday.

In the leap-year column, which is joined to the lunar squares and associated with them at a fixed boundary, the seventeenth year is therefore a Tuesday. But where you find the day of the Kalends of March marked, there you have the leap year, with the inserted weekday indicated. When you reach the twenty-eighth year, you return to the first year; and so, by recapitulating one by one until the end of the world, you will find marked both the paschal and leap years, as well as the lunar years and the weekdays.

But so that you may recognize the leap day itself in its entirety [Col. 0547D], you must follow this method and know that you will not alter this leap day. The Hebrews, taught from the beginning by God’s wisdom rather than by their own, could not err concerning the course of the moon. Therefore, when at the beginning, in Egypt, on the day before the Ides of April, on the fourth day of the week, with the moon fourteen days old, they sacrificed the Passover—[with the measures] bessicilicus, two selae from a scruple, three-tenths, half an uncia, sicilicus—they said: “Twelve waning and twelve waxing,” because they discovered that the moon, when it had been made, began from diminution, not from increase.

From this it is understood that the eighth day before the Kalends of April was found to be the first day, and that on the fourth day, which is the fifth day before the Kalends of that same month, Almighty God said: “Let there be two lights in the firmament of heaven, so that they may shine upon the earth, and divide between day and night, and be for signs, seasons, days, and years, and let them shine in the firmament of heaven so that they may shine upon the earth”; and so it was done. “And God made two great lights: the greater light for the beginning of day, and the lesser light for the beginning of night,” and so forth.

Almighty God therefore made the sun the beginning of day, and it ran for eleven hours and a quarter of an hour before the moon was made. Immediately he commanded the moon to be made and to follow it, since it had obtained so great an office in heaven alongside it. It was therefore established as full on the fifteenth day, since the Creator’s power has produced nothing that is not full and perfect.

[Col. 0548B] For this reason it was said: “Twelve waning and twelve waxing.” For the moon diminishes through twelve half-months and grows through twelve half-months, so that what the sun is recognized to have traversed short of a full day, the moon is found by the wise to have diminished according to divine instruction. Thus the Lord commanded it to grow by quarters and to diminish by quarters, as the calculated division itself shows.

Fifteen quarters, decases, make a quarter. But because he said “twelve waning and twelve waxing,” the twelfth decas makes a quarter for you, a deunsicilicus. The lunar year has 354 days. In one month of that year you will find twenty-nine and a half days; to these you add a deunsicilicus, and they make thirty days for you, a cincunsicilicus.

Twelve times a triescincunsicilicus make, according to the course of the Romans, 365 days and a quarter. You reduce that quarter over a period of four years, and it makes one leap-year as for you—that is, four quarters of an as. This is one weekday.

Concerning the columns that are depicted at the head of the cycles with their own lines, the following arrangement is shown, set out in a shield-like figure for anyone who wishes to understand it. Whatever the day of the moon is at the Kalends of January, you will find it by following the straight line opposite it. In the second column, that of the first month, you will find the particular day on which the first moon is fixed before your eyes. In the third, fourth, fifth, and sixth columns, you will see the tenth moon, pertaining to the fourth, fifth, seventh, and tenth months. Looking along this line, you will observe that it is arranged through four columns.

[Note: [Col. 0547D] I found this sign in the manuscript.]

It is marked as serving the legitimate fasts, [Col. 0548D] just as the most holy Moses testifies concerning the fast of the seventh month at the Lord’s command:

“Thus says the Lord: From the ninth of the month,” he says, “to the evening of the tenth of the month you shall keep your Sabbaths; and everyone who does not humble himself in that fast, I will destroy that soul from his people.”

Likewise, through Zechariah, the glory of all the prophets, the Lord spoke after the periods of captivity concerning these sacred and legitimate fasts, saying:

“The word of the almighty Lord came to me, saying: Speak to the people of the land and to the priests: If you fasted and mourned in the fifth or in the seventh fast—and behold, for seventy years, did you fast for me, O house of Israel? And if you ate and drank, were you not yourselves eating and yourselves drinking? Are these not the words which the Lord spoke by the hands of those prophets who were before us? When Jerusalem was inhabited and prosperous, and its cities round about, and the mountain country and the lowlands were inhabited.”

And the word of the Lord came to Zechariah, saying:

“Thus says the almighty Lord: Judge with just judgment; show mercy and compassion, each one to his brother, and to the widow, the orphan, and the stranger; and do not let the poor be oppressed, nor any one of you preserve the evil of his brother in your hearts.”

And a little later:

“Thus says the almighty Lord: The fourth fast, the fifth fast, the seventh fast, and the tenth fast shall become for the house of Judah joy, gladness, and good festivals; and you shall be joyful, and you shall love truth and peace.”

Behold, the Lord announces how the legitimate fasts ought to be observed. But why they are designated in these months, we shall show to those who wish to know.

The fourth fast is for the first fruits and the months. We fast the fifth fast for preparing the threshing floors and offering the tithes. The seventh fast is for gathering the vintage, and the tenth fast is for the sowing of seed and also for the first-fruits of the oil.

During the four weeks of these fasts you will observe the tenth day of the moon without any error, clearly. From the Lord’s Passover, you count eighty-four days for each year. At their conclusion you will find the Sabbath days, that is, the end of the week, [Col. 0550A] which contains the tenth day of the moon of the fourth month, and after the sacrifice you will complete the fourth fast.

The fifth fast is at 112 [days]; the seventh fast at 175; the tenth fast at 266. By reviewing each item in order, the master and teacher of this art will be able to find them, provided that the sleepiness of the heart—which wise people avoid—has not oppressed his understanding.

To the columns mentioned above, seven others are joined. In them the moon of the Kalends of January and the days of the Lord’s Passovers are marked. For the lunar number of thirty, divided by the number seven of the weeks, separates 210 spaces by number.

To find the day of each Passover, you will observe what the moon and weekday are at the Kalends of January, so that, keeping to the course of the moon in the same column, you may find the day of Passover that appears to belong to the weekday written above. The same is confirmed in the thirty following fastenings, in which you will find marked, by the number seven, the moon and weekday of the Kalends of March, with 210 spaces of thirty days of the moon, announcing with complete certainty the fixed Lord’s Passover of each year.

Three other columns follow the number of these fastenings as attendants. In them the titles of the embolisms and the lunar years are displayed by extended lines, showing more plainly to the curious and attentive which day from the Kalends of January each one is. Thus the truth of these cycles, adorned with all its ornaments, may be displayed.

[Col. 0549]

## BOOK TWO, WHICH CONTAINS WITHIN IT ALL THE ORNAMENTS OF THE CYCLES

[Col. 0549C] We also demonstrate clearly another calculation concerning the twenty-fifth cycle, because it contains 2,100 years, reckoned from the most sacred day of Passover sacrificed in Egypt, with the Lord’s consent. Thus you may observe that, at the Kalends of January, the second day of the moon; the fourteenth day of the first month, on the day before the Ides of April; and the fourth day of the week were all fixed in their entirety at the head of the second cycle. You, most diligent investigator, must find this by calculation in the following manner.

Eighty-four times 354 make 29,736 lunar days for you. Eighty-four times a tenth of an uncia make 931 embolismic days for you. Add these to the preceding total, and you have 30,667 days. From this you deduct one day, which, as we explain in what follows, was produced by lunar losses, and whose removal we demonstrate most clearly.

One cycle therefore has eighty-four years, which contain 30,665 nights. Since the twenty-fifth cycle was completed from that same Passover in the sixteenth consulship of Theodosius and of Faustus, when you reckon the elapsed time, you will find that it contains 766,625 nights. When you divide these by the sixtieth part, you will find 12,777 and an uncia. Add this total to the preceding sum, and the result is 779,402 nights. Divide these by thirty, and you will have 25,908, with an excess of a dipundius and an uncia. This, I say, was the second day of the moon at the Kalends of January.

Behold, thanks be to God, how worthily and rationally the second day of the moon was found at the Kalends of January: it is found everywhere to generate the fourteenth day of the first month together with the title of the embolism.

Therefore, from those very Kalends of January, in order to find the fourteenth day on the day before the Ides, count to the third day before the Ides of April; you have 101 days. To these days add the second day of the moon, which was found to occur at those very Kalends of January, and they make 103 days for you. Divide by the sixtieth, and you have a bessicilicus, two selae of a scruple, a third, uncia, sicilicus. Add this to the 103 days, and they make 104 days for you: a bessicilicus, two selae of a scruple, a third, half an uncia, sicilicus.

Divide by thirty; you will find three in addition, and a tenth of a fourth, a bessicilicus, two selae of a scruple, a third, half an uncia, sicilicus. Thus you have the fourteenth day of the first month, and what follows, on the day before the Ides of April, which is the first and most sacred day of Passover.

But so that you may find the fourth weekday of that fourteenth day of the moon, the day on which the children of Israel departed, pay attention. The twenty-fifth cycle is found to have been concluded at the end of the second calendar table, when the children of Israel were departing from Egypt, as the history of the law indicates by the number 6 × 25.

If, therefore, eighty-four make 2,100 Passovers, and in the twenty-sixth cycle, at its beginning, 2,100 years are completed twice, then 365 and a quarter times 2,100 make 767,025 days for you. Divide these by seven, and you have 109,575 and four-sevenths.

Begin counting from the first weekday, which occurred at those very Kalends of January in the first year of the Passover sacrificed in Egypt, from the first as among the seven asses. You will find the day before the Kalends of January to be the seventh weekday, and the Kalends of January themselves to be the first weekday. From that day of the Kalends you count to the day before the Ides of April, and you will find 102 days.

Divide these by seven, and you have a tenth of a fourth plus four-sevenths. This is the fourth weekday of the fourteenth day of the moon of the first month in the first year, as we have said, at the head of the second cycle, in which we find that the most sacred Passover was then sacrificed by the Fathers in Egypt.

But when you have followed these cycles attentively in order, you will find the true days of Passover marked within the columns; those outside, written with certainty falsely upon the borders of the columns, were undoubtedly fixed in error. You see, therefore, dearest ones, that Almighty God denies nothing to any one of us. But to whoever faithfully desires to know how much he may presume upon God, he generously grants it.

Thus he commanded these mysteries to be revealed, so that in the four hundred and twentieth year from the Lord’s Passion, in the tenth year of King Geiseric, we might find the day on which the Lord ate the most sacred Passover with his disciples. In that same year the 2,110 years were also completed from that yearling lamb without blemish sacrificed in Egypt, as the headings of the second cycle show in their ordered sequence.

Let us therefore begin, brothers, with the reading from Exodus concerning that lamb sacrificed in Egypt, recalling it to the memory of those who know, so that we may demonstrate to those who wish to know the likeness of both lambs.

In that reading we recognize that God himself, our Lord, said to Moses and to his brother Aaron in the land of Egypt:

“This month,” he says, “shall be for you the beginning of months; it shall be the first among the months of the year. Speak to the whole congregation of the children of Israel, saying: On the tenth day of this month let each person take for himself, according to the houses of his tribes, a sheep for each household. If they are too few in a household to be sufficient for a sheep, let him take with him his nearest neighbor; each shall calculate, according to the number of persons, what will be sufficient for a sheep.

“The sheep shall be without blemish, perfect, male, and a year old. You shall take it from the sheep or the goats, and it shall be kept by you until the fourteenth day of this month. Then the whole assembly of the congregation of the children of Israel shall kill it at evening. They shall take some of its blood and put it on the two doorposts and on the lintel of the houses in which they shall eat it. In those houses they shall eat its flesh that night, roasted by fire, and unleavened bread [Col. 0552A] with [lacuna] they shall eat it. You shall not eat it raw or cooked in water, but roasted by fire. Its head with its feet and its entrails; you shall leave nothing of it until morning, and you shall not break a bone of it. Whatever remains of it until morning shall be burned with fire.

“Thus you shall eat it: your loins girded, sandals on your feet, and staffs in your hands. You shall eat it hastily, for it is the Passover of the Lord.”

Almighty God therefore commanded through Moses the whole congregation of the children of Israel, in the month of new things—which is the beginning of the months and the first among the months of the year—in what manner they should eat the Passover. He did this so that he might manifest his own divinity to us who believe in Christ, and then demonstrate their crime: how, from the first Passover celebrated in Egypt, they went out at evening—that is, at the final period of the age—girded and shod, against the immaculate Lamb of God, on the first day of Unleavened Bread at evening, with swords and clubs, and committed against him everything that had been foretold concerning him by all the prophets.

Therefore we, who now celebrate the Passover in remembrance of the Passion of the Son of God, not according to the image, as they did, but according to the truth, ought above all else to seek diligently with the full strength of our faith concerning the coming of that same Lord of ours, and then proceed through the sequence of the cycles.

The first to rule at Rome was Gaius Julius Caesar. He ruled for ten years, four months, and six days. After Gaius Julius Caesar, Augustus the emperor succeeded him; he ruled at Rome for fifty-six years, four months, and one day.

While he was reigning, John, son of the priest Zechariah, came, sent by God, preaching a baptism of repentance. In accordance with the preaching of the law and of all the prophets, he showed that Christ, the Son of God, had come into this world, that is, into the region of Judea, saying:
