“This is the Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world. This is the Savior of the world. This is the one of whom I said: ‘A man has been made before me, whose sandal strap I am not worthy to loosen.’”

After this Jesus began to teach the people and to perform mighty works and great signs such as no one else had performed. After his baptism he manifested himself to the whole human race, to the children of God, sent by God the Father to establish, restore, and reconcile to himself the people he had formed. To those chosen twelve disciples power was given in the Holy Spirit, and he sent them among all nations, teaching them to teach.

After arranging them for the office of preaching the grace of God accomplished through his name—the forgiveness of sins, the resurrection of the flesh, and eternal life for the dead when they rise—he foretold to them how much he would suffer from the Jews, even to death, the death of the cross; that he would remain in the heart of the earth for three days; that on the third day he would rise from the dead; and that after his resurrection he would ascend to heaven.

Next Tiberius Caesar ruled for twenty-two years, seven months, and twenty-two days. While he was reigning—that is, in the sixteenth year of his rule—when Pontius Pilate was procurator of Judea, under the priests Annas and Caiaphas, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, with the two Gemini as consuls, the sixteenth day of the moon fell on the day of Preparation, when our Lord and Savior of the human race, Jesus Christ, the Son of God, suffered.

Having therefore endured everything that had been written concerning him, in accordance with the preaching of the law, all the prophets, and his Gospels, he suffered, as we have said, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, on the day of Preparation. On the third day he rose from the dead, on the Lord’s Day, the sixth day before those same Kalends. He then lived with the Apostles and disciples for approximately forty days and was received into heaven, surrounded by a cloud.

From that time onward, while the grace of God reigned, people who believed in his name began to be enlightened. Therefore, in all these matters, let us give thanks to the one who arranged everything for our salvation. The Lord God almighty, Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, calls us to divine knowledge. To him be honor and glory, through the same Lord Christ, in the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

Thus, from the first-formed Adam to the sixteenth year of Tiberius Caesar—that is, to the day of the Lord’s Passion—there are 5,500 years; and from the Passion of the Lord to the tenth year of the King there are 420 years. In that year you will also find the most sacred day of Passover, on which our Lord, the Lamb of God, was sacrificed for us. That day is fixed at the head of the first cycle, in the tenth year of the same King, marked with a complete number.

In these years Augustalis, the author of his calendar table, although he was equipped with knowledge of letters and skilled in the art of calculation, is recognized to have incurred an error, particularly in the number of years in his lunar course, since one additional as is shown to have arisen from that deceptive number of years.

For he says that, in the 186th year from the Lord’s Passion, on the day of that same Passover, one day coincided with the day, although he ought to have found that same day in the 169th year from the beginning of the third cycle. He is known to have fixed it in his cycles in the sixty-ninth year. That day, without its parts, designated by its name, is shown among us in the seventeenth year to have been marked at the head of his cycles with an uncertain number. For this reason he appears to have fallen into error, as he himself admits in his statement:

“What was not arranged and discovered from the year in which the Lord suffered, the usefulness of the abbreviated calculation is this: from the two Gemini, in whose consulship the Lord suffered, to the consulship of Antoninus for the fourth time and Albinus—the first year in this work—186 years are counted. Since in that same consulship it happened that the day of Passover coincided in every respect with the day of the Lord’s Passion, the usefulness of the abbreviation ought not to have been rejected through tediousness.”

From that consulship, in which the beginning of the first octad commenced, to the year in which the eighty-fourth year is concluded with its signs of embolisms, it is very easy for those who inspect it to confirm with their own eyes the truth of Kosmuta’s calculation: how he promises to prove himself in this reckoning, although he neither fixed the day of the Lord’s Passion in its entirety at the head of his first octad nor brought the certain number of years to a truthful conclusion.

As the text of our following cycles indicates, at their head you find at the Kalends of January the twentieth day of the moon and the second weekday; the seventh [uncertain reading], the fourteenth day of the first month, on the tenth day before the Kalends of April, on the fourth weekday; the Lord’s Passover on the sixth day before the Ides of April, on the eighteenth day of the moon. In his cycles, however, at their head are found at the Kalends of January the twentieth day of the moon and the sixth weekday; the fourteenth day of the first month on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, on the fifth weekday; and the Lord’s Passover on the fifth day before the Kalends of April, on the seventh day of the moon.

He thinks that the Lord’s Passion occurred on this day, which in no way agrees with the truth. Thus also the lunar course itself, shining with a bright light, indicates to our eyes the truth, and likewise the number of years fixed in its proper place.

Agriustia, however, the first cultivator of perversity, lover of his own error, and most unskilled teacher of his own assertion, even attacks himself. Although we said that he must be set aside, he attempts to scatter the years one by one through scruples, so that his falsehood may be exposed as evident and he may be recognized as alien to the truth.

He is then more foolishly harassed by questions: by what argument of consolation, or for what reason, in the course of the year and in his own tables, did he wish to extend the lunar increase by eleven asses, half an uncia, two selae, one and a half scruples of an uncia, and two selae, rather than by eleven asses and an uncia? The moon itself undoubtedly bears witness, in that annual separation, that it increases by the same increment.

By that uncia the calculator could have had seven asses in eighty-four years. Of these he ought to have recognized and fully turned aside one as, which runs after thirty-one years in the time of Moses.

Eighty-four times, therefore, as he says, a half-uncia, two selae, one scruple, one and a half unciae, and two selae: he himself answered, “six asses, a quarter, eleven scruples less a destans” [uncertain reading]. That is what he asserts.

The other says: “Six asses are six days, and the quarters are three hours; the eleven scruples are shown to be less than a semis, because ten points are plainly contained in a destans.”

What could be clearer in this questioning, or more persuasive in his answer, than that the inept man was defeated by his own fuel? He tried, according to his own suppositions and practice, which alone had admitted eight hours, to exclude only two points according to his own arbitrary judgment, and was entirely unable to set aside a full as.

[Col. 0554D] For this reason he taught that all the heretics [reticos, sic] had departed from the rule of truth, and, like blind men after the event, could no longer find the door of light. But, once the matter has been grasped, let no one delay in turning away from the sound understanding by which it is set out in certain numbers for the prudent.

Eighty-four times 354 are 29,736 days. Again, eighty-four times a tenth of an uncia make 931 days for you. Add these to the preceding total, and they will make 30,667 days. These days are known to be determined by the octads and hendecads in such a way that they also exclude the one day which they contain as superfluous and assign within themselves a certain number set apart.

For there are five octads and four hendecads. These five octads contain fifteen embolismic and twenty-five lunar years, 495 months, which contain 14,614 days. The hendecads contain [a number omitted or corrupt in the source] embolismic years and twenty-eight lunar years, 544 months, which yield 16,056 days. Add the total of these days, and they make 30,666 days.

Behold, from the 30,667 days, the one as excluded among the octads and hendecads is truthfully confirmed by the division of the days; and then it is dissipated in disputes between the unlearned and the diligent.

Likewise, in the following cycle, when it is harmonized with the preceding one by means of embolisms and common years, you will find that same as, in its entirety, quickly set aside. For in the second cycle, as in the first, there are thirty-one embolismic years and fifty-three common years.

Thirty-one times 384 gives you 11,904; and fifty-three times 354 makes 18,762 days for you. These two small totals, joined to one another, produce 30,666 days, and that aforementioned as has been set aside.

Let us return also to that total mentioned in the preceding statements concerning that year, by which you learned that Easter was first celebrated in Egypt on the Kalends of January, with the moon in its second phase. If you wish to apply your attention to this, you will reduce this same unit completely. For in the aforesaid total there are 766,625 units, from which you subtract 365 units, namely, those of the final year of the cycles, so that it may appear that this unit, through this total, was excluded from the septenary number, born from the increase of the ounces. But learn also that the twenty-first moon, entirely bare and without ounces, belongs to the eighty-fourth year. When you have again brought back the aforesaid days of the higher total and divided this same quantity, you will find the second moon, which, as we have said, was marked by hand on the Kalends of January at the beginning of the second cycle.

After subtracting these 365 units, 766,260 units remain. Divide these by sixty, and you will have 12,771; add this to the aforesaid total, and there will be 779,301 units. Divide these by thirty: you will find 25,967, with a remainder of twenty-one units. These are the twenty-first moon of the eighty-fourth year.

When the aforesaid 365 units have likewise been brought back to that higher total, there will be 766,625 units, as above. Divide these by sixty, and you will find 12,777 units and an ounce; add this to the stated total, and you have 779,400 units, two-pence and an ounce. Divide these by thirty, and you will have 25,980, with a remainder of two-pence and an ounce, just as the moon is designated at the beginning of the second cycle; and you will reduce to the same point that unit which, as we have very often said, must be reduced at the end of the cycles.

For whoever you are, wounded by the deceit of folly or ignorant of this calculation, recognize that, through this lofty and profound division of the total—or, to speak more truly, through the fact that it has been demonstrated with complete clarity—this unit was excluded from the septenary number. You will not be able to reduce the whole of it in your calculation; in both cases you will be found [in an uncertain or corrupt condition: *neutericus in veniris*].

Cease, I beg you—cease now—to mislead wretched peoples through deceit with your little distortions. At last submit your stubborn neck to the truth, you who, through clouds and illusions, continually proclaim that the most sacred day of Easter is to be celebrated without a fixed time, as though it were coming to you from Egypt, from unknown expanses of the provinces and through the long intervals of the lands. For when you have glued the lunar course of these cycles to the understanding of your heart, then you will find the true foundation established from the first year in which the Passover was offered in Egypt. You will recognize that it agrees sufficiently with the true lunar tables and with the paschal designations.

For from the Kalends of January, on which, according to the preceding statements, you know that the second moon was found and held at the beginning of the cycles, you will calculate to the day before those same Kalends of January in the following year. There will be 365 days; to these you will add the second moon, which was on those same Kalends, as he said—recognize, if you can, the method of proceeding—and there are 367 days. Divide these by sixty: you will find six-pence and two *selae*. Add these to the aforesaid total, and you have 373 days, an ounce and two *selae*. Divide these by thirty: you will find ten and two-pence; ten, three-sixths and two *selae* remain.

You must calculate similarly in the following year, which is called the third in order. Twice 365 make 730 days. You insert, as above, the second moon of the first year, and you will have 732 days. Divide these by sixty: you will find ten and two-pence. Two *selae* remain; add this to the aforesaid total, and there will be 744 days. Two *selae* remain; divide these by thirty, and you will find four days and four *vies*; two *selae* remain.

In this way you will calculate each year up to the eighty-third year; you will recognize the eighty-fourth, marked at the end of the cycles, so that in each of these years you may appear to insert eleven units and an ounce, and may be known not to have erred at all through the winding paths of the tables or the lunar designations.

For our Lord Christ, obedient to the Father’s command, brought forth the nourishing star of this moon in such a way that, from the light of night, you will find the solid darkness weakened by clouds; carried along in its clear course, it seemed to have passed through no errors, while hidden causes were at work. Now, when full, it withdraws what must be fulfilled, and again, through revolving courses, is brought to its completion.

These, therefore, are the beginnings of the moon and its offices, divinely instituted for perpetual service; these were made for signs, times, days, and years. Through this chaste and pure fabric, and by the foreshadowing of his majesty, the Lord signified the Church: she is very often diminished by various misfortunes and is always reduced through her decline, yet, supported by the brightness of splendor, she grows among the saints.

Thus, in particular, I say: the same Church speaks of herself: “I am dark and beautiful, O daughters of Jerusalem.” And the Lord, through the Prophet, answered with a resonant voice and said: “You are altogether beautiful, like the sun, and perfect like the moon.” And again: “Once I have sworn by my holy one: if I lie to David, his seed shall remain forever, and his throne shall be before me like the sun, and like the perfect moon forever.”

This entire sacrament remains in the Church in Christ and is fitting for her. For we most appropriately represent the moon’s perfect course, so that you may know it to have been completed, as it were, in its own tables on each successive day.

From the Kalends of January, I say, you will calculate to the day before that day on which you are asking what phase the moon is in. But perhaps you say: Why do you indicate the day before, and the lunar phase on the following day? Because you gather the total from the Kalends of January and add the lunar phase that was present on those Kalends? Can you in any way count one day as divided or doubled and still treat it as a single number? Therefore divide these by sixty, and place what you have divided above the number of days; likewise divide them by thirty, and on whichever day, as I said, the moon will be found, you will designate its phase with the greatest precision by days and years, down to the smallest unit.

Nevertheless, the beginnings of each Easter are generated only by the new moon of the first month. But so that it may be shown by a definite and ordered calculation that this first month is generally said to extend from the third day before the Nones of March to the fourth day before the Nones of April, and so that the paschal birth may be disclosed within these twenty-nine days and demonstrated more clearly by trustworthy evidence through the first annual cycle, let us proceed as follows.

From the creation of the sun and moon, which took its beginning on the fifth day before the Kalends of April, we calculate that 340 free days have elapsed up to the coming fifth day before the Nones of March. To these days we add the fifteenth moon, in whose fullness the Lord had established the fifth day before the Kalends of April toward evening. There are therefore 355 days. Divide these by sixty, and you have five *deunces*. Add these to the preceding total, and there are 360 days. Divide the *deunx* by thirty, and you will find ten and two-pence, with a remainder of ten and a *deunx*.

Since, as we have said, the fifteenth moon, full, had been made on the fifth day before the Kalends of April, it was the day before the Ides of April that, with its horns growing thinner, it completed its first month. For this reason the new moon was commanded to be observed by the Jews up to the present day. It completed the second month on the fourth day before the Ides of May, the third month on the fourth day before the Ides of June, the fourth month on the sixth day before the Ides of July, the fifth month on the sixth day before the Ides of August, the sixth month on the seventh day before the Ides of September, the seventh month on the day before the Nones of October, the eighth month on the Nones of November, the ninth month on the day before the Nones of December, the tenth month on the third day before the Nones of January, the eleventh month on the Kalends of February, and the twelfth month on the fifth day before the Nones of March.

Thus you have 355 days, which the first year contains, together with fifteen days of the moon, which had indeed become full and perfect. For the calculation from the fifth day before the Nones to the fourth day before the Nones of March declares the moon to be [in a phase] midway between the fifth and the third [days], on which day the moon was found to be a *deunx* and a ninth of an *as*, constituting one full day.

Therefore the first month cannot begin on that very day, but from the third day before the Nones of March to the fourth day before the Nones of April. On the day before the fourth day before the Nones—that is, on the day of the Kalends of April—we calculate from the fifth day before those same Kalends, which belonged to the preceding, that is, the first, year. On that day both luminaries had been established by the Lord in signs, times, days, and years. We shall find 370 days. To these we add the fifteenth moon, in which state it had meanwhile been made, and there are 385 days.

Divide these days by sixty, and you have six [*sexis cincun*: corrupt]. Add these to the aforesaid total, and there are 391 days and a *cincun*. Divide by thirty, and you will find a *decus* and three [*tresis*]; [*ascincunt*: corrupt] remains.

Therefore, from the third day before the Nones of March to the fourth day before the Nones of April, we must seek the first moon, because on whichever day within these twenty-nine days the first moon occurs, from that point the first month begins. In this month the almighty God commanded the most sacred Easter to be celebrated, as Exodus testifies and says:

“You shall observe the feast of Passover; for seven days you shall eat unleavened bread, as I commanded you, at the time of the month of new things, for in it you came out of the land of Egypt.”

Likewise, in Leviticus the Lord commands and says:

“In the first month, on the fourteenth day of the month, between the evenings, is the Lord’s Passover; and on the fifteenth day of this month is the feast of unleavened bread for the Lord.”

Likewise, in Numbers:

“The Lord spoke to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai, in the second year after they had departed from Egypt, in the first month, saying: Say that the children of Israel are to celebrate the Passover at its appointed time, on the fourteenth day of the first month, toward evening. According to its appointed times, according to its law, and according to its ordinance, you shall celebrate it. And Moses spoke to the children of Israel, telling them to celebrate the Passover in the wilderness of Sinai, just as the Lord had commanded Moses; so the children of Israel did. Shortly afterward the Lord commanded with a threat and said: The person who is clean and is not on a journey, yet ceases to celebrate the Passover, shall be cut off from his people, because he did not offer the offering to the Lord at its appointed time; that person shall bear his sin.”

In Deuteronomy Moses spoke to the people and said:

“Observe the month of new things, and celebrate the Passover to the Lord your God, because in the month of new things you came out of the land of Egypt by night, and you shall sacrifice the Passover to the Lord your God.”

Likewise, it is written more clearly in the First Book of Ezra: Osias celebrated the Passover to God in Jerusalem and sacrificed the Passover (*phasec*) on the fourteenth moon of the first month toward evening.

Behold, the day of the fourteenth moon—from the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April to the seventeenth day before the Kalends of May—is recognized as legally fixed by true calculation. Likewise, from the third day before the Nones of March to the tenth day before the Kalends of April there are nineteen days; while the moon is born during these, they are unquestionably assigned to lunar years. From the ninth day before the Kalends of April to the fourth day before those same Nones there are ten days; while the moon is born during these, they are plainly marked as belonging to embolismic years, as is confirmed by the ancient register of the cycles.

Six months divide the year; in an embolismic year, one month of thirty days is added as an extension. Thus six times twenty-nine make 174 days for you; and seven times thirty make 210. Add the two totals, and they give you 384 days. This is an embolismic year.

A lunar year likewise is divided into six months. Six times twenty-nine therefore give you 174 days, and six times thirty give 180. Joined together, the two totals make 354 days—not calculated from Sunday to the Sunday of Easter, but from the fourteenth to the fourteenth moon of the first month of the coming year. In this way, throughout all eighty-four years in their proper order, you will undoubtedly find the days gathered into definite months, just as the appearance of the moon’s birth shines before the eyes in each successive month.

From the first moon of the Kalends of January to the eighth you will find embolismic years; from the ninth through the twenty-seventh you will certainly find lunar years. Likewise, from the twenty-eighth through the thirtieth you will find embolismic years.

You will observe all these things with the greatest care and will find the days of Easter complete. You will not labor: behold, with the Lord’s approval, everything is shown clearly and perfectly. By these things the deceit of the slanderers is now refuted, so that the clever simplicity of the innocent may be recognized as subject to all, while the errors of hypocrites are avoided; for boasting belongs to the unlearned, whereas the virtues mentioned above are full of modesty.

## At the same time. An uncertain author.

[Note: From the Marianus, Br. Codex Regularis, volume II.]

## Critical Observation

Anyone even slightly acquainted with Scottish history must recognize that the first Christian teachers of religion in what is now Scotland were practitioners of the monastic life. Hence the famous statement of Fordun in the *Scotichronicon*, book XIII, chapter 8, page 184, where, speaking of Saint Palladius, who was sent as bishop to the Scots already believing in Christ around the year 430, he says:

“Before his arrival, the Scots had teachers of the faith and ministers of the sacraments, merely presbyters who were monks, following the rite of the primitive Church.”

By these words that sincere historian of Scotland seems to imply only that Saint Palladius was the first bishop sent by the Roman supreme pontiff to govern the Scottish Church, which was rising again from its beginnings, since before his arrival it had still been imperfect and rudimentary, instructed by presbyters ordained by other legitimate bishops and for the most part monks. It was nevertheless already prepared to receive the Church’s supreme hierarchy, just as other peoples converted to Christ were first instructed by presbyters before being endowed with episcopal jurisdiction.

Yet the writers of Scottish history, and Fordun himself, acknowledge that Saint Ninian, bishop of Candida Casa; Saint Palladius; Saint Fernanus; Saint Servanus; Saint Kentigern; and other bishops of the primitive Scottish Church were true monks and vigorous defenders of discipline. They established monasteries as a kind of Christian military camps, from which emerged so many most holy soldiers, trained to defeat the army of demons and fully equipped to spread the faith of Christ.

A vivid example of this is provided by the following monastic Order, observed by the ancient Scottish monks at the beginning of their adoption of Christianity. Since it is the oldest surviving monument of all Western monks and has a considerable connection with the rules of the Egyptian Fathers, it rightly deserves its proper place among these additions after the Institutions of Saint Cassian and the Rule of Saint Pachomius, since it embraces the strictest observance of Eastern discipline, except for those frequent immersions in water that were peculiar to the Scottish monks.

Since, therefore, monasteries existed in what is now Scotland long before the arrival of Saint Palladius, and since their inhabitants were called *Kiledei* or *Kildei* after the cells that they inhabited, not after the worship that they practiced there, it seems consistent with the truth that this Monastic Order was observed even before the spread of the Institutions of Saint Cassian by those *Kiledei* or *Kildei*, later and corruptly called *Culdees* by more recent writers.

For this monastery of Kilros, commonly called Culros, was founded by Saint Servanus, apostle of the Orkney Islands and disciple of Saint Palladius. He did not introduce a new monastic discipline, but cultivated the ancient discipline common to the earliest Scottish monks. This monastery was situated in the estuary of the Forth, or Bodotria, on the northern bank of the river and six miles below Stirling Castle. There the ebb and flow of the tide may still be seen, which the author of the life of Saint Kentigern, in Bollandus under 13 January, designates by the rivers Malena and Ledon. Following the custom of certain ancients, he understands by Ledon the sea’s flood and tide, while by Malena he denotes the ebb or retreat of the sea. He therefore mistakenly considered them two separate rivers, since at Kilros no other river appears besides the Bodotria. Nevertheless, although that place lies twenty miles from the river’s mouth, a great ebb and flow of the sea is still observed there.

Saint Kentigern, commonly called Mungo, the first bishop of Glasgow in Scotland and father of many monks, was educated in this monastery. When he withdrew from Kilros toward the southern regions, he necessarily crossed the Forth estuary at the time of Malena, or the ebb of the sea. Then, settling at Glasgow, he erected a notable monastery inhabited by 950 monks, to whom he prescribed the observance of the monastic discipline practiced by their master, Saint Servanus.

The monastery of Kilros was therefore very famous, and perhaps was built before the arrival of Saint Palladius by the Scottish monks themselves, or *Kiledei*, from whom it seems also to have received its name, since it is entirely clear from what has been said that monks had long flourished among the Scots.

For experts in Scottish antiquity observe that in the old Scottish language *kil* denotes a cell, while *ros* or *ross* signifies a promontory. Thus Kil-ros was the true promontory of the *Kiledei*, whose cells built there rose to an exceptional height above the surrounding plain, especially on the northern side of the estuary.

But as the seventh century passed, this notable monastery of the *Kiledei* was reduced to utter ruin by the Danes and Norwegians while they were devastating northern Britain, and it did not begin to be restored before the year 1217. In that same year Malcolm, Earl of Fife, restored the devastated monastery, enriched it with extensive lands and gifts, and granted it to the sacred Cistercian Order. Its most devout inhabitants adopted Saint Servanus, formerly the most holy abbot of the place, as their titular saint, and annually celebrated his sacred memory with solemn festivity on the first day of July.

Indeed, although sumptuous monasteries had gained a footing among the Scots by the year 717, the strict monastic discipline observed by Scottish monks throughout Germany, Gaul, and Belgium, even after they had adopted the Benedictine Rule as the primary standard of life, testifies that this Monastic Order was preserved for a long time in certain places. We are instructed in this by various records of Scottish monasticism.

Therefore there should be no doubt about the authenticity of this ancient monument, since, before the fatal dissolution of the monasteries in Scotland, many ancient monuments were preserved especially in the *Kiledei* monasteries of Dunblane and Dunkeld. These two monasteries seem to have retained some trace of the ancient discipline until the twelfth century, when they were erected into separate bishoprics.

The Rule of Saint Benedict was first introduced, and in later centuries many new monastic orders were established there. From the archives of the Church of Dunblane, this present Monastic Order was transcribed by the religious man Servanus Thomson, a Scot, a Benedictine monk professed in the celebrated monastery of Dunfermline. He brought it with him to Regensburg, together with other ancient documents, while the orthodox and Catholic religion still flourished among the Scots.

For in the year 1526 our most devout father Servanus, together with other monks of Dunfermline, was summoned by the excellent uncle, Lord John Thomson, most worthy abbot of the monastery of Saint James of the Scots at Regensburg. There he was appointed conventual prior and led a most devout life, a vigorous defender of stricter monastic discipline, until the year 1544, when he returned his religious soul to God.

## The Monastic Order Formerly Observed in the Ancient Scottish Monastery of Kil-Ros (C, S)

Servanus, a disciple of Saint Palladius, built the monastery of Culros around the year 448. There he gathered a large community of monks, whom he kept in the fear of God and in great continence. By the common people they were called *Culdees* or *Colidees*, but properly they were called *Kiledei*, so named from the cells that they inhabited. They were true monks, imitating the Egyptian monks and leading a life like theirs.

First of all, they observed perpetual fasting, taking food once a day: in winter, when the stars appeared in the firmament; in summer, after sunset. This meal was called supper among them. At table they did not serve dishes of various flavors or especially rich foods, but, according to the number of diners, as many pieces of bread (*paximacia*) as there were diners, together with cooked vegetables seasoned only with salt.

They never ate meat or fish, nor did they allow cheese or butter, except on Sundays and feast days, when they took two meals, namely dinner and supper. For drink they had pure water, sometimes mixed with milk; wine and beer were unknown to them. Some more pleasant foods were nevertheless given to the sick, to the elderly, and even to those fatigued by a long journey, but they never ate meat.

At table they maintained profound silence, intent upon the reading of divine writings and the exhortations of the spiritual father. In this way they relieved their weary limbs through the refreshment of the supper they had received, but never to satiety. For excessive fullness, even from bread alone, produces lust. Nevertheless, according to the differing condition of bodies and ages, each person could take supper.

They all slept in one place, but in separate beds, and indeed clothed and girded with a leather belt, so that when awakened they might rise more readily. At the first crowing of the cock, all had to be present in the oratory, roused at every season of the year by the ringing of a bell, so that they always rose at midnight to perform the nocturnal vigils.

These vigils lasted for three full hours, because twenty psalms were assigned to each hour, and at the end of every psalm they deeply bent the knee, prostrating themselves upon the ground. When the three nocturnal vigils had been completed, all had to leave the oratory with one accord of voice and intention of heart. The monastery’s father alone poured out a secret prayer to God for the state of the Church, while the others devoted themselves to meditation, genuflections, and other pious works until dawn.

Then, at a given signal, all were to approach the oratory to offer the morning praises. When these were finished, the monastery’s father, overflowing with daily fountains of tears, fragrant with the incense of prayer-offerings, and burning with the fire of charity, consecrated the due offering of the Lord’s body with pure hands, and thus proceeded to the angelic address.

When the sacred assembly was over, some sought cold water, remaining in it for a longer time to bathe the body and subdue every heat of the flesh. While they were praying in the oratory, no one was permitted to yawn, sneeze, or spit.

Then all prepared themselves to work at home or in the fields, so that, sweating through their daily labor, they might complete their common life through the work of their hands. They knew well that carefree rest and idleness are the mother and fuel of vices, and therefore they placed their shoulders beneath divine labors. With the greatest zeal they worked with hands and feet, and thus cheerfully completed all the community’s tasks through their own strength.

When equipped for rural work, they placed the yoke upon their shoulders and drove mattocks and spades into the earth with unconquered arms. They carried hoes and saws in their holy hands for cutting, and by their own labor performed everything that rural people commonly accomplish with the aid of oxen and horses.

Among them there was no supply of oxen, horses, or other animals for cultivating the fields or completing any task, because each person was himself an ox and a horse for labor. Only the old abbot had a little horse for traveling and a few cows for the sake of milk; they also kept sheep for wool and skins. They rejected all other possessions and detested riches.

When the rural work lasted longer, they performed the customary allotment of psalms in the fields at the proper times, according to each of the canonical hours. They were intent on reciting the entire Psalter devoutly every day. While they worked, no murmur was heard and no conversation was permitted except what was necessary; each person completed the assigned task either in prayer or in right meditation.

When the rural work, or any other assigned labor, had been completed, they returned to their own cells. There they spent the entire day until evening either writing or praying, except when the time came to pray the canonical hours in the oratory.

As evening approached and the ringing of the bell was heard, each person abandoned his study or labor. As soon as the ringing sounded in anyone’s ears, they rose quickly, even if they had written only the tip of a letter or half of its form, brought their duties to an end, and went to the oratory in silence and gravity, without any frivolous talk.

When the psalmody and songs had been completed, each person devoted himself to private prayers and genuflections with one accord of heart and voice, until the stars seen in the sky closed the finished day; in summer, because of the shortness of the night, they continued until sunset.

At last they gathered at table to relieve their weary limbs with the refreshment of supper. There they paid more attention to spiritual reading than to the taste of food, for, as has already been said, the entire meal consisted of nothing but common bread seasoned with salt.

Moderately refreshed, they went with thanksgiving to the oratory. After pouring out a prayer for a short time, at a given signal and after receiving the blessing of the spiritual father, they all went to the dormitory, elders and younger alike, according to the cloister’s order. No muttering of voices was heard; they rested until the first crowing of the cock.

In this way they served their Creator through all the days and nights of the year, except that from Saturday night until the first light of dawn—that is, until the first hour of the Lord’s Day—they devoted themselves to vigils, prayers, and genuflections. One hour after the morning praises was excepted, when they prepared themselves to examine the innermost secrets of their hearts.

When this had been completed, and they were truly contrite, they approached the spiritual father and disclosed their thoughts to him. Without his command they could do nothing; they obtained his permission even for the necessities of nature.

They cultivated poverty above all and possessed no property except what they could work with their own hands. For this reason they rejected the gifts of the wicked and detested riches. If one of the great men of the land wished to grant something as alms, they immediately distributed it among the poor. They likewise gave the offerings of the faithful to the poor.

For they had a hospice nearby, where they nourished the poor and infirm, the lame and blind, the elderly and orphans. Saint Servanus took particular care of them, supplying them with everything necessary and serving them with pious exhortations.

They wore cheap garments, especially garments of fur, but white in color, so that they might appear white in both character and clothing. Their inner garment, woven of white wool, descended to the knees; they used it for work, since they never wore linen garments.

The outer garment was a *birrus*, also called an *amphibalus*, covering both body and head. They fastened it with a leather belt and thus went about each day to pray and work; in the same way they also slept.

Among those ancient monks, or Culdees, therefore, shone perfect uprightness of conduct, poverty of life, perpetual continence in all their actions, and unfailing obedience to the command of the spiritual father. All had to obey not only the monastery’s father but also the elders appointed by him to keep watch; those who resisted were subjected to severe penances.

For every fault, even the smallest, a strict punishment was imposed. Thus, if anyone claimed anything for himself and said, for example, “My book,” and so forth, he had to remove his clothing and immerse himself in water up to the neck, remaining there for a longer time in order to extinguish every perverse desire of self-will.

If anyone did not fulfill the commands of the spiritual father or of the other elders cheerfully and eagerly, he was separated from the company of the brothers and had to live on bread and water until he came to his senses. If he remained obstinate in disobedience and refused to acknowledge the fault committed, he was punished by the filthiness of imprisonment.

For small faults committed publicly, they performed penance before the whole community, struck with dreadful blows. These lashes were called penitential scourges.

The *Kiledei*, or ancient monks of Culros, undertook this harsh and difficult way of life with great joy, so that they might seize the kingdom of heaven by force. Nor was entry easily granted to anyone wishing to undertake such arduous monastic discipline, although many came together for the reform of their conduct.

Whoever desired to preserve the holy purpose and sincerely sought fellowship with the brothers had first to remain for ten days outside the monastery gates, as though rejected, and to endure verbal insults. He knocked repeatedly but found no entrance.

If he used patience well and persisted until the tenth day, then the cloister gate was opened, and the new entrant had to serve the elder appointed at the gate. There he labored for a long time and was tested by many adversities of spirit; at last he earned the right to enter the fellowship of the brothers.

Whoever wished to share the brothers’ way of life also had first to distribute all his possessions to the poor. For the spiritual father would accept nothing from him for the monastery’s use—not even, so to speak, a single penny. He was received into the community naked, as though escaping from a shipwreck; before entering, he also had to remove his secular clothing and give it to the poor.

The new member was required to do all these things so that he might choose voluntary poverty there and not exalt himself above the brothers; nor, supported by his own possessions, might he avoid undertaking the same labor as the brothers, or bring with him the habit of religious life and forcibly reclaim what he had left to the monastery, thereby provoking the brothers’ patience to anger.

The ancient *Kiledei* practiced these and many other harsh and difficult observances. The brevity imposed by the plan of this compendium prevents us from setting out the rigor of their discipline, although it is necessary for imitation. In all things they imitated the Egyptian monks and led a life like theirs.

[Note: In this series we have placed those authors who wrote wholly or principally in metrical language and who, especially under the title of poets, have until now been published and known as such. In addition, we may include Avitus and Sidonius, edited in this and the preceding volume, whom it perhaps would not have disgraced to place among the poets of this century. EDITOR.]

# Poets of the Fifth Century

## In the Year of Our Lord 405. Aurelius Prudentius

*(According to the edition of Arevalus.)*

## Dedicatory Letter

To the Most Blessed Father and Lord, Our Lord Pius the Sixth, Supreme Pontiff:

Faustinus Arevalus.

## Dedication

I have resolved to publish for the common light of day, dedicated to your name and majesty, most blessed Supreme Pontiff, Pius, the monuments of Christian poetry—indeed, the finest of all that now exist or that we know ever to have existed—the poems of Marcus Aurelius Prudentius, revised and corrected with the greatest diligence possible.

Permit me, most gracious Prince, to approach not only humbly and reverently, as is fitting, toward that throne of yours and the kisses of your blessed feet, but also to declare freely that the gift I offer you is not without value, and openly to explain what kind of value it possesses. For although you alone bear so many and such great responsibilities—as may most truly be said of you—and devote yourself with extraordinary zeal and wisdom to the government of the Catholic Church, while you look after the happiness of the peoples subject to you with incredible vigilance and foresight, nevertheless, amid so vast a burden of affairs, you are so devoted to letters and the liberal arts that in this sphere too your outstanding merits are celebrated with the unanimous voice and praise of all; nor will posterity ever be silent about them so long as letters and humane learning retain their proper honor.

For the splendid museum that you have furnished with every kind of distinguished monument, whether for the admiration—or even the envy—of the present and of posterity; the many and immense benefits that you have most generously bestowed upon letters, upon men of letters, and upon the other arts that derive their name from liberality; the fact that you have made your library especially remarkable for its abundance and selection of books, and have enriched the Vatican Library with great additions; the fact that you continually discuss letters and the study of the best arts with the greatest delight of mind and with a polished and subtle judgment—these and other things of this kind sufficiently reveal your vehement and ardent love of refined learning, joined to learning itself.

Since, moreover, knowledge of ecclesiastical matters is for you more sacred and more ancient than other branches of study—for you were nourished in these studies from adolescence and have won the highest praise through your treatment of them—I trust that for this principal reason this new edition of Prudentius will be not only pleasing but also welcome to you.

For you understand very well, most wise Pontiff, that Prudentius is a most authoritative defender of the Church of Jesus Christ, whose place on earth you occupy, with all good people applauding, against the impious heretics of this age. He was exceptionally learned in secular letters, trained in forensic eloquence, and had held the highest offices in the Roman state; yet he most successfully turned his delightful talent and poetic wit toward adorning, illuminating, and defending the cause of the Christian faith.

To pass over other matters—for Prudentius left nothing unattempted in these ecclesiastical studies—he contributed greatly to that sublime gravity and dignity which shines forth in the prayers of the Church and in the hymns sung to God, and in which you, Pius, most deeply delight. He also embraced Christian antiquities for the most part, but described with particular care those rites that now incur the criticism of certain people. In particular, he clearly demonstrated by his own example the religious worship by which the heavenly saints ought to be venerated: lying prostrate on the ground at the martyrs’ tombs, pouring forth abundant tears, fixing kisses upon the marble, and clinging so closely to the tombs that his mouth warmed the altar and his breast the stone, he experienced those dispositions of soul that, as we all know, you, Pius, share with Prudentius.

For it is well known with what constancy you perform such offices of piety, and how accustomed you are, with a devout mind and with the reverent posture of face and body, to visit the glorious tomb of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and almost daily to venerate and kiss his venerable image.

More weighty still are the matters in which Prudentius defended the most exalted mysteries of our religion against the sophistical arguments of heretics by a learned and rigorous mode of philosophical reasoning. He attacked the Altar of Victory and the whole worship of idols with such force and vigor that afterward the pagans scarcely dared to write or object anything further.

If we wish to consider not only what concerns the common good of the Church but also what relates more particularly to your apostolic see, Pius, although what is there that belongs to the Roman Church—which is the teacher of faith and morals and the mother of all the churches—that is not most closely connected with the common cause of the Catholic religion? Yet whatever pertains more specifically to that first chair, Prudentius proclaims its dignity, majesty, and authority in such a way that he believed nothing else had been accomplished through the Roman Empire’s many and various successes except that a road might already be prepared for Christ’s coming, that peace and Rome might hold human hearts bound together by a single bond, and that these chief summits of affairs might be united under one rule and one mind in sacred matters.

Indeed, Prudentius not only describes in the most elegant verses the tombs of the martyrs—he testified that he had seen their countless ashes at Rome—and not only celebrates with the highest praise the crowds of peoples gathering at their relics and to observe their feast days; after returning home, he also worked with great zeal to introduce among his fellow Spaniards many of the practices that he had seen and learned at Rome in this sphere.

Therefore, I resolved to bring to the light of day Prudentius—a man and writer of such great learning and piety, always useful and salutary, but especially necessary in our most calamitous times—vindicated, insofar as I could accomplish and attempt it, from the faults that had crept in through the injury of time, the ignorance of copyists, or their negligence. I exerted all my strength to surpass the industry and labor of all those who had toiled in this field before me; and, unless my own judgment deceives me, I have surpassed them.

I must not keep silent about this, and I consider it an honor to profess that, through your permission and favor, Pius, the most ancient Vatican codices were freely open to me whenever I wished, so that I could bring more easily and more fully to completion what I had undertaken.

Would that what I judged ought to be added for the elucidation of Prudentius may not appear of so little value and so slight an effort that Prudentius himself should therefore approach you less acceptably and gratefully! Yet this too will be a mark of your graciousness, most blessed Father: that you may kindly and benevolently, as is your custom, pardon Prudentius for whatever is not sufficiently approved in me, and, if not the perfection of my commentaries on Prudentius, at least receive favorably some attempt and diligence of mine.

For me, nothing more welcome, nothing more desired, nothing more in accordance with the deepest wish of my heart could happen than that the Catholic poet Prudentius, revised by me as you see, and honored by the prerogative of your judgment—which ought to be most weighty for all—might arrive not unpleasantly before the Catholic king Charles III, Pius, Felix, Augustus, my most gracious lord, to whose sole benevolence I must acknowledge that I owe the ability to devote myself to these studies according to my own wishes.

[Col. 0571]

# PRUDENTIANA, OR PROLEGOMENA TO THE ROMAN EDITION OF THE WORKS OF MARCUS AURELIUS CLEMENT PRUDENTIUS

[Col. 0571A]

## CHAPTER ONE. The Plan and Division of the Whole Work

### 1. 1.

The praise that Gaspar Barthius bestowed upon Prudentius—I know no one more diligent or more learned than Barthius in reading and elucidating poets—I shall not labor very hard to wrest from others if they resist it. But certainly I would most gladly receive such a judgment from the mouth of an ecclesiastical man who loves the Christian religion—and, I add, the Roman Catholic religion—alone and above all.

Thus Barthius, in book IX, chapter 1 of his *Adversaria*, after saying that the commentaries of the blessed soldiers of Christ are filled with accounts of the punishments inflicted upon Christians on the wheel, added:

> “I consider Prudentius the first herald of these matters, a most sweet, devout, and learned poet, whom, if I possess, I shall not deny that I disdain the writings of all Greek and Latin poets.”

### 2.

Those very heterodox writers who raise this divine poet to the highest praise and who have applied greater diligence than our own scholars in preparing editions of his works are compelled to admit that, concerning free will, the innocence of the flesh, good works, and especially the invocation of martyrs and other saints, the blessed Virgin, and other matters of the same kind—in short, concerning nearly everything about which they themselves hold erroneous opinions—Prudentius agrees with Catholics.

I know that heretics excuse Prudentius, who openly disagrees with them, either on the ground that he spoke poetically or because, as they claim, the seeds of superstition had already begun at that time to be scattered among Christians. I shall explain elsewhere how perversely, or rather shamelessly, they abuse these responses.

Certainly Prudentius not only attacks the insane superstition of idolatry with force, not only brilliantly defends the foundations of our religion against the pagans, not only vigorously demolishes the faithlessness of the Hebrews, and not only argues carefully against the heretics who preceded him; he also adds much by which the heretics of our own times may easily be refuted.

Moreover, he describes the rites of the ancient Church—concerning the use of lights, altars, the adornment and wealth of temples, the veneration of relics, images of the saints, and other matters of this kind—so vividly and so clearly that one is tempted to ridicule the ignorance or perversity of certain people who, fearing superstition in every matter as though it were lurking there, do not hesitate to scorn and reject the most holy ceremonies, even those customary from the earliest centuries of the Church, as monastic inventions.

For why should I speak of the countless tombs of the martyrs that Prudentius saw at Rome; of the pilgrimages of Christians, or their gathering to celebrate the martyrs’ festivals; or of the crypts, which I understand more clearly while reading Prudentius than while surveying them with my own eyes?

### 3.

When Prudentius celebrates the crowns of the martyrs, traveling through places whose soil no one before him had trodden, with what acuteness and abundance of genius, with what inspiration, does he represent and set before our eyes the strength of Christ’s soldiers, their steadfastness, their unconquered words addressed to tyrants, their endurance in suffering punishments, and the astonishing variety of tortures!

In the hymns for the hours of the day, what beauty of invention! In his exposition of the battle of the soul, how certain is the doctrine drawn from the very source of mystical theology! In all his works, finally, how brightly the ardor of piety shines forth!

Although he left us many and varied writings, you will not be able to find even a single verse of his that does not tend either to strengthen religion or to foster piety, as many have already observed.

### 4.

If anyone seeks in Prudentius, beyond his sublime genius and the nobility of his subject matter, other gifts as well, I would especially point to his singular eloquence in *Laurentius*, *Romanus*, *Against Symmachus*, and all his poems. You can easily recognize that the man who composed those poems was thoroughly practiced in the study of eloquence.

For, as Antony says in Cicero (*De Oratore*, book II, p. 52, Aldine edition, 1554):

> “Men of the other arts speak more ornamentally in their own manner if they have learned anything from this art”—that is, eloquence.

To these qualities, if you wish, you may add his finely turned verses and rhythms flowing smoothly in every kind of meter, as well as the gravity of his thoughts and the uncommon elegance of his language, generally drawn from the best authorities of Latin literature.

Some people accuse Prudentius of very many errors in prosody and of words insufficiently Latin. We must refute this in a separate chapter, where it will become clear that those who think Prudentius sometimes followed, merely through ignorance of the subject, a usage different from that of others in certain syllables and words are seriously mistaken. He did so neither without a definite method and art nor without the authority and example of the ancients.

There is no need for me now to weave together Prudentius’s praises. So many and such weighty encomiums have later been brought forth about him by the most learned men of every age and every rank that nothing fuller could be desired in this respect.

[Col. 0573A]

### 5.

Since these things are so, who would not be astonished that this distinguished writer—who ought to occupy an eminent place both among poets and among the holy Fathers of the Church—has not yet had commentators and editors capable of satisfying the wishes of prudent men in every respect?

Yet, if any writer does, Prudentius certainly needs clear and learned commentary—not because he suffers from the fault of obscurity, as some wrongly suppose, but because poets speak, as it were, another language and are not easily understood by those unfamiliar with their idiom, especially when they deal with new subjects that others have not touched.

Moreover, we often assign the blame for obscurity to authors who excel in hidden learning and unfold their subjects subtly, when instead we ought to accuse our own slowness, ignorance, and blindness.

[Col. 0573B]

> Porcius Latro once gave an acute reply to his teacher Marillius in the *Controversies*, a work now usually attributed to Seneca the philosopher, Marcus by name, in the preface to book I.
>
> When we were students under the rhetorician Marillius, a rather dry man who spoke very little, but in a style that was elegant though not commonplace, he blamed the sparseness of his own speech on the difficulty of the subject and said: “It is necessary for me, as I walk through a thorny place, to place my feet cautiously.” Latro replied: “By Hercules, it is not that thorns are pricking your feet; rather, you possess them.”
>
> Latro immediately proceeded to deliver maxims that could very appropriately be inserted among the arguments of Marillius, who was then declaiming.

### 6.

To offer one outstanding example among many: in the preface to the *Psychomachia* there is a famous riddle—for that is what it is called—which some have thought Prudentius deliberately proposed, around the number 318 of Abraham’s household slaves, to exercise the ingenuity of others and to suggest their mystical significance. Most have denied that it could be explained without an Oedipus or a Sphinx.

[Col. 0573D]

The reference is to the story in Genesis, chapter 14, where Abraham is said to have counted 318 of his trained household slaves, with whom he rushed upon the enemies and recovered Lot. Turning this into an allegory, Prudentius sang:

> Let us know that we are richly endowed  
> With household slaves,  
> If three hundred, with twice nine added,  
> Can signify something mystical.

I shall clearly demonstrate, in a separate chapter, that this is not a riddle but an allegorical explanation of that story, an explanation very commonly found at that time on the lips and in the books of many people. I shall cite the authorities of the holy Fathers who understand Christ’s cross and the name of Jesus in Abraham’s 318 household slaves: through the Greek letter Τ (*tau*), which has the form of a cross, and the letters ι and η, with which the name “Jesus” begins, the number 318 is expressed in Greek.

Prudentius therefore wished, in accordance with his rights—or with poetic convention—to indicate only an interpretation already familiar to the public, following Horace:

> He always hastens toward the outcome and carries  
> His hearer into the midst of things,  
> As though they were already known.

Perhaps he also followed the remainder:

> And what he despairs of being made to shine  
> By treatment, he leaves aside.

### 7.

These and infinitely many other matters of this kind, which lie hidden in this author, require a most diligent interpreter who has devoted no less effort to theological learning than to humane letters. For Prudentius is a kind of inexhaustible treasury of deeply hidden secular learning, and even more of ecclesiastical learning, which is displayed most broadly in every aspect of his work.

I shall not deny that several very learned men have applied themselves to this work. But some adapted their editions to the use of schools—or, what amounts to the same thing, to the use of the Dauphin—while others possessed no theology at all, or, worse, possessed a bad theology, although theology is utterly necessary for an exact interpretation of this poet.

For this reason we must strive and labor all the more to place the poems and doctrine of our poet in a favorable light.

“But what?” someone may object. “Do you think you can accomplish what you declare that so many distinguished interpreters have altogether failed to achieve?”

Indeed, if I thought so—if I were so foolish as to claim for myself the complete ability to explain Prudentius—I would not be undertaking to select the best material from all the commentaries and join it together into a single body. Rather, I would be attempting to raise a new building from its foundations, thereby obstructing the light shed by the others.

[Col. 0574D]

After I had long and seriously considered what path I ought chiefly to follow, and had consulted several learned and prudent men, what happened to me was exactly what happened to Demipho in Terence’s *Phormio*, act II, scene 3. After he had consulted three lawyers about his son’s marriage and heard them giving different opinions, he said:

> “You have done very well: I am much more uncertain than I was before.”

As another poet said:

> Three guests seem almost to disagree,  
> Each demanding very different things  
> According to his varied palate.

### 8.

Now, since I thoroughly understand the great difficulty of the undertaking and clearly feel how slight my own powers are, I have decided to follow the easier path: to examine and freely present all the studies on Prudentius that have so far been published; then, if anything should occur to me by which I could explain passages passed over by others, or confirm or refute the interpretations of others, I would bring it forward—not as though discovering it anew, but as though adding something to what had already been discovered.

I saw that in our own age especially several authors, both sacred and secular, were being printed in this fashion, with great apparatus and the most elegant typography. I would not deny that they deserved such labor, and, if you like, that they were endowed with refined learning; but they had contributed nothing to Prudentius.

I also saw that, shortly after the beginning of the preceding century, an edition of Prudentius’s works had been prepared by Weitz, together with the commentaries of all who, as he believed, had written on Prudentius. But Weitz had not seen all the commentaries of those who preceded him; and after him many writers interpreted Prudentius, illuminated by a fuller light than the ancients and striving with no less industry.

### 9.

Therefore no one will blame me—and I hope I shall even please many people—if I publish Prudentius in the form in which many ancient writers have appeared, indicating the notes of all the others and adding my own observations.

I shall not say what those observations will be like or how far I have advanced beyond the discoveries of the other interpreters—not only lest I seem to promise golden mountains, but also because anyone will easily be able to judge for himself if he has the commentaries before his eyes and compares them here and there.

I shall say only this: in the two branches of knowledge that I previously identified as necessary for the explanation of Prudentius—namely, theological and philological knowledge, especially poetic knowledge—I have, from childhood, applied myself with no little diligence under outstanding teachers, if only in a more favorable age. Whether I was impelled toward these studies by some natural inclination or whether the conditions of life undertaken from my earliest years demanded it, I mention this not to arouse expectation but to dispel the suspicion of arrogance.

[Col. 0575B]

### 10.

Another scruple must now be removed. I hear that an edition of Prudentius’s works based on the Vatican manuscript codices was begun at Parma some time ago. Why, then, is it useful now to print Prudentius in Roman type?

I shall state the truth. If I had heard anything about the Parmese edition before applying my mind to this labor, perhaps I would not have thought at all about publishing Prudentius. But since an idea concerning any matter should either not be undertaken or, once undertaken, should not be abandoned without cause, I began to wonder whether I ought to desist from my purpose on account of the Parmese edition. I preferred to rest my decision on the counsel of wiser men rather than on my own judgment.

The most serious men, who asserted that they knew the matter thoroughly, said that no hope remained that the edition begun at Parma would be brought to completion. They also agreed that, even if it were completed, it could in no way obstruct my work.

### 11.

Certainly, two points seemed certain to me. First, it was not superfluous for two editions of Prudentius to be completed at the same time if each were furnished with different commentaries. Second, the edition being prepared at Parma could suffer no harm from this Roman edition.

Copies of Prudentius’s works, especially copies with commentaries, are so rare that I have nowhere found them offered for sale. On this matter I appeal to the testimony of those who possess sufficiently well-stocked private libraries, who examine those possessed by friends, who visit booksellers’ shops, or who finally are accustomed to run through the catalogues of libraries offered for sale each day.

[Col. 0575D]

I shall say nothing about the edition prepared for the use of the Dauphin, and how much it is sold for whenever an opportunity arises. I know that the price of such things is often increased intolerably, because certain people establish some peculiar kind of learning by assembling a single series of editions. This luxury in the furnishing of libraries has now proceeded so far that what that satirist said can sometimes be repeated of a book and its author:

> Perhaps a fisherman  
> Could have been bought for less  
> Than the fish.

[Col. 0575D]

### 12.

That this Roman edition of ours cannot harm the Parmese edition is readily apparent. Who, at the present time, would not prefer Bodoni’s types—not to my own ineptitudes, but even to the commentaries of the most serious men?

I pass over what will be added to the Parmese edition through the editor’s industry and diligence, especially material drawn from the Vatican manuscript codices, which he can use most conveniently. I am so far from wishing anything to be taken away from his learning that I rather hope, when permitted, to irrigate my own little gardens from that source, adding an appendix if no other means is available.

[Col. 0575D]

The Parma Prudentius, which Bodoni’s presses had been bringing forth for many years, has just now been published under the auspices of a man of great name, eagerly desired by the wishes of many, especially my own. I had nothing more at heart than to seek out everywhere as many editions and elucidations of Prudentius as I could, and to extract their kernel for the public benefit.

I have not yet seen the Parma edition; but, knowing the new editor’s diligence and zeal, I hope that our interpretations will thereby be opportunely elucidated. When I received news of it, I judged that I ought to delay; yet I do not think it permissible to withdraw altogether, since my word has already been given. Yet it will certainly not be because of me if others are unwilling to remain bound by the commitment that I have undertaken concerning them; this I openly declare.

### 13.

Since, then, there is no reason why I should abandon what I have begun, I shall explain the order in which I intend to publish Prudentius’s works.

First, I have decided to place these *Prolegomena*, which I have already begun to write, under the title *Prudentiana*, borrowing the title and, for the most part, the model of the work from others who have made titles such as *Gersoniana*, and especially from the distinguished Daniel Huet, who prefixed *Origeniana* to the works of Origen.

No one should demand or expect me to follow the meager method of division that he adopted, indulging the customs of his fellow citizens, who cut matters into small pieces rather than divide them. In these prolegomena, therefore, I shall pursue the subject in the simple order in which the matters themselves present themselves and in the manner that anyone can understand for himself.

For who, even without my saying so, would not perceive that I must discuss Prudentius’s life; the works that survive, those that have perished, and those doubtfully or falsely attributed to him; manuscript codices; editions; and published and manuscript commentaries?

I shall defend Prudentius’s doctrine against heretics and against certain Catholics. I shall explain more distinctly and fully from the poems of the sacred Poet certain notable passages concerning ecclesiastical dogma and discipline: the veneration of relics, the invocation of the saints, the adornment of temples, Christian tombs, the use of lights, and other matters of this kind.

### 14.

I shall also try, with the greatest diligence, to construct something like a new poetic art, according to whose rules I believe that the first poets of our most holy religion composed their poems. Although I shall sow in an uncultivated and abandoned field, I shall nevertheless do so with some hope of fruit.

This knowledge can be useful for selecting, among the various readings of manuscript codices—not only in Prudentius but also in the poems of other holy Fathers—those words that appear most suitable to the laws and usage of the meters commonly accepted at that time.

[Col. 0576D]

I truly believe that such an art will also prove very useful to many learned men who labor to publish the poems of the ancient Fathers and who sometimes, while trying to restore their works, corrupt them and thereby—sadly—expose themselves to the mockery of grammarians.

For grammarians, as is characteristic of that arrogant class of men, commonly ridicule learned men who excel in every other kind of learning if they see them judging freely contrary to their own canons. They do not consider how much knowledge others have acquired in different fields; instead, they shamelessly exaggerate what those men lack in grammar.

### 15.

Nor shall I omit the testimonies of the ancients and of certain more recent writers by whom Prudentius has been praised.

Only then shall I begin to print the works of the Christian Poet, in the following order. First I shall place the book of the *Cathemerinon*, together with the preface to all the poems, “For five years now, ten times over,” and so forth. Then I shall place the *Apotheosis*, the *Hamartigenia*, the *Psychomachia*, and the *Dittochaeon*, which in most printed editions is called the *Handbook of Sacred Scripture*. These poems will be contained in the first volume.

In the second I shall include the books *Against Symmachus* and the book of the *Peristephanon*, together with many extensive indexes of subjects and words.

### 16.

I shall place glosses and commentaries beneath the poems: the glosses drawn from Master Iso and from the most ancient Vatican and other manuscript codices; the commentaries drawn from my own judgment, together with variant readings.

Who that Iso, or Ison, was is explained by Mullerus in the preface to his Cologne edition of Prudentius of 1701. He was a monk of Saint Gall, flourished around the year 900, and was a man celebrated for learning and holiness. Concerning him, one may consult Ekkehard the Younger, book I and II of *The Disasters of the Monastery of Saint Gall*, in Goldast, volume I of *Germanic Matters*, pp. 12 and 22, and the author of the *Glossary of Latinity*, in the preface to his work, p. 35.

I have no doubt that he is the same Iso whom Notker the Stammerer says was his teacher in the preface to his sequences. Notker died in the year 912. See further about Iso below, sections 113 and 114.

### 17.

As prolegomena to the second volume, I shall place two discussions. The first will concern the Altar of Victory in the Julian Curia and its successive removals; the second will concern Prudentius’s reliability and his accuracy in narrating the histories of the martyrs, to which anonymous or more recent acts ought to yield.

I shall provide engraved illustrations in both volumes, both to adorn the work and to elucidate its subjects. Especially in volume II, I shall offer more images so that the deeds and monuments of the martyrs may be known more fully, and I shall reproduce all those that Gallonius inserted in his work *On the Crucifixions of the Holy Martyrs*. To these I shall add other new illustrations drawn from the cemeteries, as well as certain observations from Gaspar Sagittarius and others concerning the torments of the martyrs.

There would be no great need to ask why I have arranged Prudentius’s poems in a different order from that of other editions, since all the principal editors have followed their own different paths and there is great disagreement among the ancient manuscripts. Recent editors wished to follow Heinsius, yet they have not succeeded in doing so.

For in his additions Heinsius noted that the ode which most people place as the preface to the book of the *Peristephanon* ought to be referred to the whole work as an epilogue. This was neglected in his edition, and likewise in the later editions of those who boast that they most closely imitate Heinsius.

I wished to retain the order prescribed by Prudentius in the preface to his poems, where he clearly sets forth the subjects of his little works, as I shall explain in the commentaries.

Someone may object that it is not certain whether Prudentius listed his books in the order in which he published them. But I shall ask why, in setting forth his work, he would have reversed the order that he had decided to observe.

“Because,” you will say, “he wished rather to accommodate the meter.”

But surely you do not know how easily Prudentius brought everything he wished, and in whatever manner he wished, within the laws of poetry.

Besides, even when poets set forth their subject, they strive to state it in the order demanded by nature. Thus Virgil skillfully indicated the four books of the *Georgics* at the beginning of the first:

> What makes the crops glad, under what star  
> It is fitting, Maecenas, to turn the earth  
> And join the vines to the elms;  
> What care is required for cattle,  
> What cultivation for keeping sheep,  
> And how great the experience needed  
> For thrifty bees—  
> Of these things I shall begin to sing.

Prudentius, after mentioning the book of the *Cathemerinon*, immediately lists the *Apotheosis*, although he could have designated the book of the *Peristephanon* with a similar verse. For he says:

> Let the day continue with hymns,  
> And let no night be empty of singing praise to the Lord;  
> Let it fight against heresies  
> And examine the Catholic faith.

He could have placed first:

> Let the song be devoted to the martyrs  
> And praise the apostles.

By this verse he indicates the book of the *Peristephanon*, which we have placed last because Prudentius himself lists it last.

Although Prudentius separated the daily hymns from the hymns of the *Peristephanon*, it was nevertheless easy for both works to be joined together in manuscript codices and printed books. In former times, when people copied works by an author, each person transcribed what pleased him most, sometimes without any order. Many, when seeking hymns, joined together all the hymns of Prudentius and gave them the title *Hymnary of the Seasons and of the Saints*, as I shall say in the commentary on the preface.

Anyone who carefully considers the editions and manuscript codices of Prudentius, as well as the different order in which the poems are arranged—a matter that we shall discuss in chapters 4 and 5—will, I think, conclude that the order demonstrated by the author himself in the preface and presentation of his works is to be preferred.

But let these matters, spoken thus far in place of a preface, suffice.

# CHAPTER TWO. The Life of Prudentius

### 18.

As I begin to write the life and achievements of Prudentius, I do not know whether I should wish more strongly to discover his certain homeland or whether that uncertainty is more glorious for him. Just as several cities of Greece once claimed Homer for themselves, so now two especially distinguished cities of Spain contend over Prudentius’s birthplace: Caesaraugusta and Calagurris.

Anyone who sets aside partisan zeal and carefully weighs the force of the arguments will easily judge that the matter should rather be left before the judge than awarded to either side.

But since many others have set forth and compared the arguments presented on both sides, we shall not omit doing the same, since this is the most appropriate place. I shall mention that two dissertations have been published on the controversy: one of which Johann Albert Fabricius makes mention, and another, written in Spanish with great learning by the distinguished Emmanuel Risco in volume XXXI of *Sacred Spain*.

[Col. 0579D]

I have not seen the first of these, but I shall quote Fabricius’s words about it, from the Venetian edition of the *Bibliotheca Latina Vetus*, 1728, volume II, chapter 2, book IV:

> “A discussion by G. L. concerning Calagurris Nasica, the homeland of the Vasconian Prudentius, is presented in the German literary journal published at Halle, *Neue Bibliotheke*, XXVI, p. 475. I suppose that the purpose of this dissertation, or discussion, is to prove that Prudentius’s homeland was Calagurris, which was formerly called Calagurris Nasica and later Calagurris Julia, after Julius Caesar. Concerning this place, see García de Loaysa, *Collection of the Councils of Spain*, p. 159, and Ferrari’s *Lexicon*, following Strabo, Pliny, and others.
>
> “Pliny, book II, chapter 3, reports that the inhabitants of Calagurris were called Nasici; but Ludovicus Nonius, chapter 90 of *Spain*, believes that this was a different Calagurris, of which not even traces remain today. Consult him.”

### 19

Others who wrote Prudentius’s life in dictionaries and bibliographies likewise investigated his homeland carefully. The first of all these is said to have been Aldus Manutius of Rome, who, in his edition of Prudentius’s works, began to inquire from what particular town Prudentius originated, although the people of Zaragoza had already claimed Prudentius for themselves in their breviary (see no. 51). The other editors and commentators touched on the same controversy more briefly.

Peter of Mantua, in order to establish an unusual opinion, treated the question at length in his little work *Advertencias a la Historia del P. Mariana* (*Observations on the History of Father Mariana*). To refute Mariana, Lupercius and Bartholomew Leonardo Argensola, a distinguished pair of brothers, contended for Zaragoza as Prudentius’s homeland. [Col. 0579D] Two letters by Lupercius, one by Bartholomew, and another by Mariana, in which he defends his opinion in favor of Calahorra, have recently been published by the distinguished Juan Antonio Pellicer y Saforcada in his work *Ensayo de una Biblioteca de Traductores Españoles* (*Essay toward a Library of Spanish Translators*), which is prefaced by *Noticias para la vida de Lupercio Leonardo y Argensola* (*Notices for the Life of Lupercio Leonardo y Argensola*).

Thomas Tamayo de Vargas attempted to dissolve the arguments of Peter of Mantua and Lupercius Leonard in his defense of the Spanish history of John Mariana.
