Moreover, Martín Carrillo, in his *History of Saint Valerius, Bishop of Zaragoza*, published in 1615, and Luis Díez de Aux, in the preface to his Spanish translation of Prudentius’s *Hymns*, [Col. 0579C] maintained that Zaragoza was his homeland. Those who debated Prudentius’s homeland should rightly be joined by Nicolás Antonio, *Bibliotheca Hispana Vetus*, book II, chapter 10, and Bayle in the *Dictionnaire critique*, under “Prudence.”

### 20

John Peter Ludewig, whom Rodríguez, in the *Biblioteca Hispana*, preferred to call Luis, must not be passed over in silence. He published a *Life of Prudentius* separately in March 1692; it was reprinted in volume II of Ludewig’s *Opuscula Miscellanea*, column 494, Halle an der Saale, 1720, where I read it, although Fabricius gives the year of publication as 1719 and the place as Halle in Saxony, unless there were two editions.

Therefore, even if it were not a task of great importance, I could nevertheless be impelled by such a major controversy to discuss Prudentius’s homeland, and all the more because the same undertaking will also shed some light on several of Prudentius’s poems. Before, however, I examine the two opinions into which the authors are chiefly divided, I shall bring less celebrated views back under examination.

George Fabricius (*Preface to the Commentary on Certain Hymns of Prudentius*) asserts that Prudentius was from Numantia, or, as more recent writers say, from Zaragoza. [Col. 0580D] Ludewig adds, in the place cited, that Numantia—“a city famous to the Romans because of its countless wars, now called Amuza”—is well known to lie not far from Zaragoza. Indeed, scholars are more persuaded that Numantia is the city now called Soria, or another called Zamora. For although Pomponius Mela, book II, chapter 13, says:

> Of the inland cities in Tarraconensis, the most distinguished were Pallantia and Numantia; now there is Zaragoza.

one should not therefore conclude that Numantia was Amuza, or some town not far from Zaragoza, as may be seen from the case of Pallantia, which lay far away.

Whatever the location of Numantia may ultimately have been, no convincing reason appears why Prudentius should be called Numantine, except that this city was situated in the province of Tarraconensis—a fact equally applicable to every town in that province. I suppose Fabricius inferred from Mela that the city of Numantia was the same as Zaragoza; for John of Gerona attributes this error to the same Mela, whom he did not understand, in volume I of *Hispania Illustrata*, [Col. 0580B] page 33.

### 21

We ought to be more extensive in refuting the opinion of Peter of Mantua, whom Nicolás Antonio, contrary to his usual practice, harshly rebuked in the place cited:

> In preference to the genuine reading and sense, merely in order to detract from John Mariana, he, to the poet’s great injury, attributes to him—I do not know what—some statement about Salia, a river of Hispania Tarraconensis near the Cantabrians.

Risco, in the place cited, asserts that this absurd interpretation of Mantua’s first arose in 1613, perhaps because he had seen an edition of Mantua’s pamphlet completed in that year. In fact, Mantua had already published his observations against Mariana in 1607; and although I have not seen the first edition, I have seen another, enlarged Milanese edition of 1611, in which Mantua certainly claims this new opinion as his own.

[Col. 0580C] “These are the opinions concerning Prudentius’s homeland that have been found to date; I shall follow neither of these two.” (He is speaking of the opinions in favor of Zaragoza and Calahorra.) What if others had discovered this opinion before Mantua? Tamayo de Vargas, in the place cited, maintains that Mantua stole from others the opinion which he marketed as his own. For when Mantua had cited Giselinus’s authority up to these words, “The old manuscript which I used has *ME SALIAE*,” he omitted the words that immediately follow, from which some thought they could extract a convenient opinion: namely, that Salia was a river of Hispania, and they conjectured that there had been a city of that name.

Nor in the 1564 edition with Giselinus’s commentaries, nor in the later Weitz edition with the same commentaries, have I found these words.

[Col. 0581A]

### 22

It must nevertheless be considered whether either Giselinus, in another edition, or others had thought of Salia as Prudentius’s homeland before Mantua. Ferrari, under “Salia,” gives the following from Mela:

> Salia, Riba de Silla or Sella, a river and town of Hispania Tarraconensis, on the coast of the Astures. (According to Pintianus, the river is called Saia, and by others Silla.) The homeland of Prudentius, who wrote much in verse and was raised by the emperor Theodosius to the prefecture; a town of no little importance, six leagues from Lanas to the east and from Veca to the west. The Salini people . . . Prudentius: “I, forgetful of old Salia, the consul,” etc.

Under “Calaguris” he writes:

> Calaguris, which Livy calls Calaguris and Ptolemy Calagorina . . . The homeland of Clement Prudentius, the most distinguished poet, according to Mariana; but, as he himself seems to indicate, the town of Salia on the Cantabrian coast alone was his birthplace.

The geographical lexicon appeared after Ferrari’s death; but in 1605 he had published an *Epitome Geographica*. I believe Ferrari drew his opinion from an old edition of Giselinus. For Mantua himself quotes these words from Giselinus:

> This passage has tormented many people and has not yet been sufficiently clarified. Nebrissensis comments on it in these words: “Forgetful of the old consul of Messalia,” namely, the one under whom Prudentius seems to have been born. Aldus, in the *Life of the Poet* published by himself, says that he was a jurist and consul of Messalia, apparently led to this conclusion by this passage, if I am not mistaken. The old manuscript which I used has *Me Saliae*. Remus attributes the same interpretation to Giselinus.

Giselinus certainly indicated it in the words reported above by Tamayo, in the Paris edition of 1562, adding immediately:

> I really do not know what I ought to say here; I have thought it enough to provide others with material for reflection.

Mantua included the opening words of the sentence up to *me Saliae*, but omitted the rest, which explains the antiquity of the conjecture.

### 23

I shall now state what is established concerning Salia from the ancient authorities. Mela described the location and name of the river in book III, chapter 1:

> On the coast of the Astures there is the town of Noega, and three altars called the Sestian Altars sit on a peninsula. They are sacred in the name of Augustus and illuminate lands previously obscure. But from the river called Salia the coasts begin gradually to withdraw, and the broad spaces of Hispania contract more and more.

Pliny, book IV, chapter 20, calls the same river Sada, or Sanga, as Mantua thinks. Pliny’s words are:

> The region of the Cantabrians; the river Sada.

In an old manuscript, however, *Sanga* is read. The river is now called Salia by the Spaniards, Saya according to Mantua, or, according to Risco, Sella.

Mantua therefore thinks that Prudentius was born near the river Salia, and perhaps in a town of the same name, since towns commonly either give their names to rivers or receive their names from them. He argues this from the words of the preface to the works, or of the book *Cathemerinon*, which he incorrectly calls a hymn:

> While this fleeting life was carrying on these things,
>
> Gray hair suddenly crept upon me in my old age,
>
> Rebuking me for having forgotten the consul of ancient Salia,
>
> Under whom my first day [—].

[Col. 0581D] Here is his Spanish interpretation:

> While life, which goes flying, does these things, the whiteness of the hair suddenly entered my already old person, reproaching me for having forgotten the year in which my first day of life occurred in ancient Salia.

The syntax, however, is this: “rebuking me, forgetful of the consul”—that is, of the year—“under whom my first day [was] of ancient Salia”—that is, in ancient Salia. It is unnecessary to pursue at length how absurd this is and how far it departs from common sense, especially since Tamayo de Vargas treated the matter carefully in the place cited, with John Mariana’s approval, as it is useful to explain.

### 24

It is commonly reported that Mariana absolutely refused to read either Mantua’s attack against him or Tamayo’s defense on his behalf. [Col. 0581D] Nicolás Antonio, *Bibliotheca Nova*, under “John Mariana,” reports the following:

> With a great display of learning, Peter of Mantua attacked Mariana’s history; Doctor Thomas Tamayo de Vargas defended it. He asserts, on sufficiently reliable testimony, something resembling a prodigy: that Mariana refused to read either Mantua’s criticism or the apology of Tamayo, his most devoted friend, even before the author had offered it to him for careful examination and correction. Posterity will scarcely believe this.

Bayle, in the article “Mariana” of his *Dictionnaire critique*, eagerly seizes upon this account and, as is his custom, interprets it in the least favorable sense.

The truth is partly as reported and partly otherwise. For as soon as Mantua published his observations in 1607, he sent a copy to Mariana. Mariana not only read them but also added suitable replies in the margins, and returned to Mantua the copy illuminated with these notes.

When Mantua continued to set his pamphlet in type and reprint it in an enlarged form, undeterred by Mariana’s replies, Mariana, who had greater matters in mind, decided to say nothing further or waste further effort, so that, without a rival, either he alone might cherish himself and his own work, or Mantua might do so with a few supporters.

When Tamayo wished to defend Mariana’s cause, he showed Mariana what he had written about Prudentius’s homeland, as though engaged in another matter, and demonstrated his arguments. Later, when he had completed the entire apology, he offered it to Mariana for examination and correction. Mariana refused to do this, trusting Tamayo’s strength and ability, although it seems to me that he was also moved by another consideration: namely, that Mantua might in some respect attribute Tamayo’s writing to Mariana himself.

[Col. 0582D] I have reported all this from Tamayo’s work in the appendix, or *Razon de la historia del P. Juan de Mariana: de las advertencias de Pedro Mantuano: y de la defensa del doctor D. Thomas Tamayo de Vargas* (*Account of the History of Father Juan de Mariana; of the Observations of Pedro Mantuano; and of the Defense of Doctor Don Thomas Tamayo de Vargas*). In the work itself, while discussing Prudentius’s homeland, he says:

> This paper was written long before I determined to respond to the rest, and was communicated, among others, only to Father Mariana, the oracle of our age, etc.

### 25

The explanation was already generally accepted: Prudentius was saying that he had forgotten the consul of ancient Salia, under whom he had first seen the light of day. Nevertheless, Mantua stubbornly denied that this was true, because there had not been two consuls of Salia, so that one could be called “old.” He failed to understand that Prudentius was merely implying that Salia had held the consulship long ago.

He added that this consul was called not *Salia* but *Sallea* in an inscription cited by Onuphrius Panvinius, *Commentary on Book III of the Fasti*, page 408:

> QVIESCIT . IN . PACEM . DEPOSITUS . DIEM QVAR TVM . NONAS . AVGV STAS . FLAVIO . PHILIPPO ET . FLAVIO . SALLEA . CON SVLIBVS . PATER . SERBA TIVS . FECIT

“Here rests in peace, buried on the fourth day before the Nones of August, when Flavius Philippus and Flavius Sallea were consuls. Father Serbatius made [this].”

As though it were not possible for the name to be written either *Salia* or *Sallea*, or, if it was written *Sallea*, for the poet to remove one *l* to accommodate the meter, especially in a proper name. The Greek *Fasti* and Cassiodorus in his *Chronicle* have *Sallia*. Glandorpius, in his *Onomasticon Romanum*, restores the name *Salia* from ancient monuments.

### 26

Having rejected Mantua’s opinion, we must inquire into Tarragona. Prudentius says the following about the three martyrs Fructuosus, Augurius, and Eulogius in their hymn:

> O triple honor, O threefold summit,
>
> By which the head of our city is raised,
>
> Surpassing all the cities of Iberia!

Even those who assert that Prudentius was from Zaragoza or Calahorra do not ignore this. They say that he called Tarragona “the head of our city” because it was the capital of Hispania Tarraconensis.

I shall not object, although one might be led by some conjecture to think that Prudentius is praising his own city when he immediately mentions all the others:

> Surpassing all the cities of Iberia!

But if Prudentius, because he was from Hispania Tarraconensis, calls Tarragona “our city,” why could he not have used the same expression when he named other cities of that same Hispania Tarraconensis, even if he had not been born in them?

Nicolás Antonio thinks that Prudentius composed the hymns of the *Peristephanon* (“On the Crowns”) in the name of those in whose towns the saints were celebrated. I shall investigate the force of this shortly. For now I shall observe that this hymn suggests that Prudentius’s birthplace was situated in the Pyrenean lands. For after the verses quoted above he continues:

> It is a joy to exult in three protectors,
>
> Under whose protection we are all cherished,
>
> The peoples of the Pyrenean lands.

The reading must be *fovemur* (“we are cherished”), not *foventur* (“they are cherished”), as I shall demonstrate from ancient books in the commentaries.

### 27

I do not dare to determine which lands Prudentius calls Pyrenean. Mela, book II, chapter 13, says:

> The Pyrenees first extend from here toward the British Ocean; then, turning their front toward the land, they burst into Hispania. With their smaller portion excluded on the right, they draw out their continuous sides in an unbroken chain, until, sent through the whole province along a long boundary, they reach those shores which face the west.

Risco, *Hispania Sacra*, volume XXXIV, pages 191 and following, observes that the ancient geographers called all those mountains Pyrenean which spread out like branches between Fuente Rabida and Cabo de la Cruz. He interprets these words of Bishop Pelagius concerning the mountains of León:

> Certain citizens of León, however, lifted the body of Saint Froilan, bishop, below the Pyrenean mountains and placed it upon the altar.

[Col. 0583D] I would rather read “beneath the altar,” since it is customary for the bodies of saints to be buried beneath the altar, as I shall explain more distinctly elsewhere.

It is clear from this that Tarragona, Zaragoza, Calahorra, and countless other towns could have been called Pyrenean.

[Col. 0584B]

### 28

It remains for us to discuss the two most famous opinions in this matter: whether Zaragoza or Calahorra should be considered Prudentius’s homeland. [Col. 0583D] I previously gave, in no. 21, the praise of Zaragoza from Mela. Saint Isidore says something more significant in *Etymologies*, book XV, chapter 1:

> Zaragoza, a town of Hispania Tarraconensis, was both established and named by Caesar Augustus. It surpasses all the cities of Hispania in the pleasantness and delights of its location, and flourishes more gloriously in the tombs of holy martyrs.

These words, especially the final ones—that it “flourishes in the tombs of martyrs”—agree most closely with our Prudentius’s hymn concerning the martyrs of Zaragoza.

Aldus of Rome, in the *Life of Prudentius*, and many others, especially the commentators, maintain that Zaragoza was Prudentius’s homeland. [Col. 0583D] These include Aelius Antonius Nebrissensis, in the prefatory epigram to Prudentius’s works and in his commentary on the hymn of the eighteen martyrs of Zaragoza; Jacobus Spiegelius, in the preface to his commentary; Georg Remus, in a letter to Weitz; Sixtus of Siena, *Bibliotheca*, book IV, under “Aurelius Prudentius”; John Vasaeus, *Chronicon*, under the year 351; Antonio Possevino, *Apparatus*, under “Aurelius Prudentius”; Alfonso García Matamoros, *On the Spanish Academy*; Luis Nonius, *Notes on Hispania*, chapter 82; John Henichius, *History*, part 2, fourth century, chapter 3, page 23; Lucas Osiander, *Epitome of Ecclesiastical History*, century 4, book I, chapter 26; the Centuriators, volume I, century 4, chapter 10, page 681; Quenstedius, *On the Homelands of Illustrious Men under Zaragoza*; Étienne Chamillard, in the edition for the use of the Dauphin; Martín Carrillo, *History of Saint Valerius*; Luis Díez de Aux, in the Spanish translation of Prudentius’s hymns; Lupercius and Bartholomew Leonardo y Argensola, in their letters concerning this controversy; Emmanuel Risco, *Hispania Sacra*, volume XXXI, in a separate dissertation; Carlo Agostino Ansaldo, in the preface to his Italian translation of the books against Symmachus; Andreas Mollerus, in his commentary on the hymn for the eighth day before the Kalends of January; and the distinguished prelate Stefano Borgia, in his singular and learned work *The Vatican Confession of Saint Peter*.

The arguments by which Prudentius is thought to have been from Zaragoza are drawn solely from Prudentius’s works, indeed almost solely from the hymn of the eighteen martyrs of Zaragoza. These are the verses usually adduced:

> Twice nine, our people, beneath one tomb,
>
> Preserves the ashes of the martyrs;
>
> A matter of such great importance.

Risco notes that Prudentius calls Zaragoza “our people” before naming it explicitly, as though this favored his opinion. On the other hand, Rodríguez de Castro observes that the term “people” fits very well with the entire judicial district of Zaragoza. He also observes that Prudentius could say “beneath one tomb” even while speaking of martyrs belonging to the same judicial district, which extended over all Aragon, part of Catalonia, Navarre, Rioja, Guadalajara, Alcalá, and Ágreda—much as Lucretius, book V, verse 26, spoke of “the common tomb, the earth.”

But neither side is helped by this. In the hymn of the holy martyrs Hemeterius and Celedonius, Prudentius nowhere mentions Calahorra, although he calls it “our town.” Here, after saying “our people” and “beneath one tomb,” he immediately adds:

> We call it the city of Zaragoza,
>
> A matter of such great importance.

From this one understands that the tomb existed in the city itself. He continues concerning the same city:

> The house, full of great angels,
>
> Does not fear the ruin of the fragile world,
>
> Bearing in its bosom so many gifts
>
> To be offered together to Christ.

And when he had celebrated other cities—not only those of the judicial district of Zaragoza but also those of the rest of Hispania and beyond Hispania—indiscriminately for the exceptional distinction of their martyr-patrons, he returns to Zaragoza:

> You bring back ten saints and eight,
>
> Zaragoza, devoted to Christ,
>
> Your summit bound with golden olive branches,
>
> In honor of peace.
>
> You alone prepared to meet the Lord
>
> More numerous throngs of martyrs.

Thus he continues, proclaiming Zaragoza’s unique glory.

### 29

When he wished to praise other martyrs of Zaragoza besides those eighteen in whose honor he composed the hymn, he first mentions Vincent:

> From this, Vincent, your palm is renowned.

And afterward:

> No fury here ever departed without praise,
>
> Nor did the number of martyrs,
>
> Never lacking illustrious blood,
>
> Fail to grow beneath every storm.
>
> Did you not, Vincent, a martyr destined to die abroad,
>
> Mark in these lands, with a slight dew of blood,
>
> An image of what was to come
>
> When death was near?
>
> The citizens worship this place, as though its own turf
>
> Enclosed the very limbs and, embracing them,
>
> Preserved in its ancestral tomb
>
> The bones of the blessed martyr.
>
> He is ours, although he suffered far away
>
> In an unknown city; victorious, he gave glory
>
> To the tomb near the shore of lofty Saguntum.
>
> He is ours, and as a boy in our arena,
>
> Anointed with the olive of virtue and faith,
>
> He learned by his strength to subdue
>
> The dreadful enemy.
>
> He knew that in this temple
>
> Eight times and ten times palms had been won;
>
> Trained by the native laurels, he ran
>
> The same course to the same glory.

Anyone can observe in these poems that Vincent was born in Zaragoza; that the people of Zaragoza are called “ours”; that “these lands” means Zaragoza; that “the ancestral tomb” indicates the same city; and that the expressions “our Vincent” and “our boy in the arena,” who had known the renowned palms won eighteen times in this temple and had been trained by his native laurels, clearly demonstrate that Zaragoza was his homeland.

Therefore Risco rightly refutes Thomas Tamayo de Vargas for thinking that Saint Vincent is called “ours” by Prudentius because he was a Christian. Bayle similarly rightly refutes Peter of Mantua, who interprets “our arena” as referring to Valencia.

### 30

After Vincent, Prudentius praises Saint Encratia. Concerning her he says:

> Since no one of the martyrs, remaining alive,
>
> Was granted the privilege of dwelling in our lands,
>
> You alone, surviving your own death,
>
> Live in the world.

And later:

> Christ himself granted this new title
>
> To be enjoyed by our Zaragoza,
>
> So that the perpetual house of a living
>
> Martyr might be consecrated.

In the notes I shall show that one cannot infer from this that a temple was dedicated to Saint Encratia while she was still alive, but only that Saint Encratia was regarded as a martyr, although she had survived martyrdom, or the punishments.

For now we may merely observe that “our lands” and “our Zaragoza” seem to imply that Prudentius was born in Zaragoza.

From this position Bernard Ibáñez de Echavarri must be rejected. In his *Life of Saint Prudentius, Bishop of Tarazona*, page 26, he asserts that, of all the cities of the province of Tarraconensis—Tarragona, Gerona, Calahorra, Barcelona, and Zaragoza—Prudentius calls none his own city except Calahorra.

For in no. 26 we read that Prudentius says of Tarragona:

> By which the head of our city is raised.

And although he nowhere uses the expressions “our city,” “our town,” or “our stronghold” of Zaragoza in precisely these words, he often calls the people of Zaragoza “ours,” and speaks of “our Zaragoza,” “our lands,” and “our people.” Therefore Bernard Ibáñez is either mistaken or playing a foolish game in a foolish matter. [Col. 0585D] I do not understand why Risco speaks of him in this way, calling him “an author under the name of Don Bernard Ibáñez de Echavarri.” For I know that a man of great and keen intelligence bore this name and committed the life of Saint Prudentius, bishop of Tarazona, to writing.

If someone nevertheless maintains that Prudentius uses the possessive pronoun “our” of Zaragoza because he himself was from the province of Tarraconensis or from the judicial district of Zaragoza, I do not see how he can be dislodged from that position. For those who wish to make him a native of Zaragoza assert, by essentially the same reasoning, that he called Tarragona “our city” and Calahorra “our town.”

### 31

Risco also took another route to support the Zaragoza side, drawing on what Theodoric Ruinart notes in the *Acts of Saint Hippolytus*. Prudentius addressed the hymn of Saint Hippolytus to Bishop Valerian, whom he addresses as follows:

> In Rome, the city of Romulus,
>
> We saw countless ashes of saints,
>
> O holy Valerian of Christ.

At the end of the hymn:

> Thus, when I remain at last in the grassy field,
>
> As a careful shepherd, bring back the sick sheep.

Prudentius therefore came from the city, or diocese, over which Valerian presided.

Ruinart remarks on this passage:

> This appears to be Valerius, bishop of Zaragoza, who took part in the Council of Zaragoza in the year 381.

Risco, who more correctly reports that Valerius subscribed to the council in the year 380, thinks that this bishop was the same as Prudentius’s Valerian. But before Risco and Ruinart, Paul Albinianus de Rajas, S.J., had discovered this argument. Tamayo, in the index of the work cited, reports that he wished to prove in a manuscript history of Zaragoza that Prudentius was from Zaragoza, on the basis of the hymn of Saint Hippolytus, in which he calls himself Valerian’s sheep. Tamayo had learned this from Paul’s own letters.

[Col. 0587C] Those who constructed the *Chronicle of Dexter* and similar works were certainly not unaware of this; therefore they confidently reported that Valerius was also called Valerian. It must nevertheless be noted that, in the Spanish councils published by Cardinal Aguirre, Valerius subscribes to the Council of Zaragoza in ninth place, but it is by no means declared that he was the bishop of Zaragoza. Loaisa did give Valerius this title in his collection of the Spanish councils, but, as I believe, solely on the basis of a probable conjecture.

Risco says that it makes no difference that Prudentius writes *Valerianus*, not *Valerius*, in the hymn:

> Either because the vocative of *Valerius* cannot be fitted into the pentameter verse, or because there he was not using it as a proper name but as an appellative, agreeing with the word *sacer*.

These arguments are unsatisfactory, especially the first. [Col. 0587C] For what is there to prevent the vocative *Valeri* from fitting into a pentameter verse? If he had said this of the vocative *Valeriane*, I would agree: its first three syllables are short, and Prudentius lengthens the first by necessity. But there would have been no fault if he had shaped the pentameter verse in this way:

> *Vidimus, o Christi praesul amans, Valeri*

“We saw [them], O Valerius, loving bishop of Christ,” or something similar.

Nor will I interpret *Valeriane sacer* as “O priest from the family of the Valerii.”

### 32

Nevertheless, I have no intention of denying that some conjecture in favor of Zaragoza can be drawn from the hymn of Saint Hippolytus. For it is clear from the hymn of the eighteen martyrs of Zaragoza that several bishops of Zaragoza belonged to the family of the Valerii:

> Here is the mitred house
>
> Of the Valerii.

Therefore a bishop from this family could have been called Valerianus, just as among Roman families names were frequently derived in this way: Constans, Constantius, Constantinus. The Valerius who took part in the Council of Zaragoza could also have been called Valerius Valerianus, like Claudius Claudianus and others formed in a similar manner; or some may have called him Valerius and others Valerianus.

[Col. 0587D] I shall not omit the fact that Glandorpius, in his *Onomasticon*, indicates that Valerius and Aurelius—the latter being Prudentius’s name—are the same name of the same family, supposedly composed anagrammatically. I consider this ridiculous.

Nothing further can be extracted from the catalogues of the bishops of Zaragoza after that second Valerius in the year 380, until the year 458, when an unnamed bishop presided. In the catalogue of the bishops of Calahorra, the first bishop with a certain name is Silvanus, around the year 457.

Nicolás Antonio, on the basis of the preconceived opinion that Prudentius was from Calahorra, asserted that the hymn of Hippolytus was published at Calahorra under Bishop Valerianus. But even if it were plainly established that Valerianus held either the see of Zaragoza or that of Calahorra, could one safely conclude that Prudentius was from Zaragoza or Calahorra? I certainly do not think so. For why could he not have called himself that bishop’s sheep after fixing his residence for some period in the bishop’s diocese? Yet Prudentius had such a course of life that he seems to have spent long periods in many different places.

### 33

It is certainly established from the hymn of the eighteen martyrs that Prudentius was at some time resident in Zaragoza, and especially that he was there when he composed the hymn. [Col. 0587D] Hear his words concerning Saint Encratia:

> We saw a piece of her liver torn away
>
> Lying far off beneath the pressing claws.

Hear other words at the end:

> Grant that we may wash with pious tears
>
> The furrows of the marble beneath which
>
> Hope is covered, so that I may release
>
> The bonds of my restraints.
>
> Stretch yourself out, noble city,
>
> With me over the holy tombs.

To this we may add that the Clement family existed at Zaragoza, as Henry Flórez proves in volume I of *Numismatics*, plate 9, no. 9. He admits that Prudentius belonged to this family, although he otherwise believes that Prudentius was born at Calahorra.

These are approximately the considerations which, even if they do not establish a certain opinion, can at least produce a probable conjecture that Prudentius should be called a native of Zaragoza.

[Col. 0587D] I almost forgot to mention that Zaragoza is called *Zaragoza* by the Spaniards, not *Saragoxa*, as Remus says in his letter to Weitz, nor *Saragossa* or *Caragoca*, as Ludewig writes in the *Life of Prudentius*, unless a cedilla is placed beneath the second *c* in *Caragoca*, as Spaniards do when they do not write *z*.

I do not wish thereby to detract anything from Ludewig or from the others who, while illuminating our affairs, often fall into errors of this kind. Rather, I favor and applaud them because, although foreigners and constrained by certain difficulties, they nevertheless celebrate the praises of our countrymen. Such is Ludewig here: when he planned to write the lives of Christian poets, he began, as he says, with the most honey-sweet Prudentius; but there he also stopped, entangled in other studies and occupations.

### 34

Now it must be explained why Calahorra—called *Calahorra* by us—claims Prudentius as its citizen. [Col. 0588C] This is the judgment of García Loaisa, *Collection of the Spanish Councils*, after the Council of Lugo; John Mariana, *History of Hispania*, book IV, chapter 7; John Marieta, book XXI, page 23, as cited by Nicolás Antonio; Thomas Tamayo de Vargas, in the place cited; Nicolás Antonio, *Bibliotheca Hispana Vetus*, who gave considerable weight to this cause; Goldastus, in the preface to the *Manuale Biblicum*; George Fabricius, in his commentary on certain hymns of Prudentius, Weitz’s edition, page 308; Rivet, *Sacred Criticism*, book III, chapter 26; the author of the dissertation mentioned in no. 18; Fabricius, *Bibliotheca Latina Vetus*, volume II, book IV, chapter 2; Joseph Moret, *Annals*, book I, chapter 4; Henry Flórez, volume XV of *Hispania Sacra*, page 328, and volume XXIX, page 292; Arnaud Oihenart, *Notitia utriusque Vasconiae*, chapter 7, page 139; Joseph Rodríguez de Castro, volume II of the *Biblioteca Hispana*, pages 213 and following; Tillemont, *Ecclesiastical History*, volume X, page 560; Christoph Cellarius, in the preface to his edition of Prudentius, who understands Calahorra Násica; Bernard Ibáñez de Echavarri, in the place cited; and Ludewig, who considers it probable that Prudentius was born at Calahorra and held public offices at Zaragoza.

Those who establish Calahorra as Prudentius’s homeland have no slight support in the hymn of the holy martyrs Hemeterius and Celedonius—not because he celebrated those martyrs before all others. For the conjecture of Moret and Flórez is weak: namely, that Prudentius preferred the patrons of his own homeland to other martyrs and for that reason placed their hymn first.

The more substantial point lies in the very words of the hymn. After Prudentius had related the miracles performed at the tomb of the holy martyrs, he added:

> The Savior himself granted us this good,
>
> For he consecrated the martyrs’ bodies
>
> In our town;
>
> They now bring healing to the inhabitants
>
> Whom the Ebro waters.
>
> Let this day be a festival for us;
>
> Let it be a sacred joy.

### 35

Lest these words be understood in this way merely because Calahorra belonged to the judicial district of Zaragoza, other verses are brought forward from the hymn of Saint Laurence. There, speaking of Rome, Prudentius continues:

> The Basque Ebro divides us,
>
> Set far apart by two mountain ranges,
>
> Across the ridges of the Cottian Alps
>
> And the snowy Pyrenees.

Loaisa thought that in this passage Prudentius was asserting that he was from Calahorra. Mariana more cautiously considered that a probable conjecture could be drawn from it.

In reality, although the Ebro separates the people of Zaragoza from Rome, that part of the country is not Basque; nor can the river near Zaragoza properly be called Basque. Calahorra, on the other hand, is situated in the territory of the Vascones.

### 36

Other words from the hymn of the holy martyrs Hemeterius and Celedonius can be referred to the same interpretation:

> This fortunate Iberian land is powerful throughout the world
>
> By this distinction.
>
> Do you now believe that the once-savage paganism of the Vascones,
>
> Which cruel error had sacrificed sacred blood,
>
> They now bring healing to the inhabitants
>
> Whom the Ebro waters.

For these words, which are spoken of Calahorra, confirm that the statement “the Basque Ebro separates us” is to be understood of the same place.

Nevertheless, this argument is not entirely convincing. The Ebro could have been called Basque because it flows through the territory of the Vascones. And even if it had been demonstrated that Prudentius lived at that time in Calahorra or in the territory of the Vascones, it would not yet have been established that he had first seen the light of day in that same place. For the subject is a man

> Who saw the customs of many people and cities.

[Col. 0589D] Luis Nonius, volume II of *Hispania Illustrata*, page 832, although he otherwise believed Prudentius to be from Zaragoza, says that in this passage the poet implies that he was living at Calahorra at that time. I read this in Tamayo, but I have not found it in Nonius.

Writers are certainly less sharp in refuting the opposing opinion than in strengthening their own. For they clearly see that Prudentius called several cities his own; yet, as they refute one another, they say that Prudentius used this designation because Tarragona was the capital of Hispania Tarraconensis, or Zaragoza the capital of the judicial district, or because Calahorra belonged either to the province of Tarraconensis or to the judicial district of Zaragoza. They fail to notice that, while destroying the opinions of others in this way, they destroy their own as well.

[Col. 0590A]

### 37

Nicolás Antonio attempted to meet this difficulty. From the hymn of the eighteen martyrs of Zaragoza, he seized upon these two verses in favor of Calahorra:

> My Calahorra will carry both,
Those whom we venerate. Giselinus, in his commentary on the hymn of Saints Hemeterius and Celedonius, brought forward the same two verses, but was not at all deterred. “By these words,” he says, “he makes Calagurris his own, since, as Pliny testifies in Book III of his *Natural History*, the people of Calagurris are counted among the jurisdictional district of Caesaraugusta.” Nic. Antonius, however, takes it as certain that in the hymns of the *Peristephanon* Prudentius speaks in the name of those among whom the saints were being celebrated, on the basis of Gennadius’s words concerning Prudentius: “He also composed a work in praise of the martyrs under the names of others.”

He further observes that Prudentius called Calagurris his own not only when he sang of Saints Hemeterius and Celedonius, but also when, under the auspices of others, he praised the eighteen martyrs of Caesaraugusta; and he concludes that it is clear that his homeland has thereby been demonstrated. This does not seem so clear to us.

First, Ernestus Salomon Cyprianus, in the edition of Gennadius, annotated Gennadius’s words, “under the names of others, an exhortation to martyrdom,” with this note (in Fabricius’s *Ecclesiastical Library*): “These words are omitted in our manuscripts, and rightly so. Accordingly, I would more willingly read in Gennadius: ‘He also composed one book in praise of the martyrs, and another of hymns.’”

Furthermore, there can be no doubt that Prudentius often speaks in his own name alone [Note: As in the hymn to Saint Laurence:

> Hear kindly the suppliant,
>
> Prudentius, guilty before Christ.

In the hymn to Eulalia:

> But I shall carry, in the midst of the chorus,
>
> garlands woven in dactylic measure,
>
> poor and withered, yet festive.
>
> 
> In the hymn for the eighteen martyrs of Caesaraugusta:
>
> 
> Hope that I may loosen
>
> the chains of my bonds.
>
> 
> Stretch yourself, noble city, wholly over the holy
>
> tombs together with me.
>
> 
> In the hymn to Saint Fructuosus and his companions:
>
> 
> Perhaps, with Christ prospering,
>
> he will deign to grant healing even to my torments,
>
> while turning over sweet hendecasyllables.
>
> 
> In the hymn to Saint Cassian:
>
> 
> Here, when I was seeking.
>
> 
> In the hymn to Romanus:
>
> 
> I wish that, as I shall be among the goats on the left,
>
> I might be recognized from afar.
>
> 
> And, not to be more lengthy, this is so in almost all the hymns of the book.] 

### 38

If Prudentius were speaking in those hymns in the name of others, the following verses would have been uttered in the name of the citizens of Caesaraugusta:

> Our Calagurris shall bear both,
>
> those whom we venerate.

But if at one time he speaks in his own name and at another in the name of someone else, no argument—except a weak one—can be constructed from his having called now one city and now another his own.

Indeed, I hold this firmly: the pronoun *our* is often understood by Prudentius in different ways. Thus, in the hymn to Saint Cyprian:

> He is a martyr belonging to his homeland, but by love and speech he is OURS.

Here “ours” unquestionably means “Spanish,” as I shall explain more fully in the commentary. Prudentius himself, because he was a Christian poet, is called “ours” by Saint Gregory of Tours.

I also observe that he never used the expressions “my city,” “my town,” “my settlement,” or anything similar by which his homeland might have been declared more distinctly. Therefore, if I may add my own conjecture to those of others, I would suppose that Prudentius’s homeland could have been located in some town or small town somewhere in the province of Tarraconensis, or even in the jurisdictional district of Caesaraugusta, which he never named.

What prevents this? If you object, I shall reply that he may have been born either in one of the towns that he called his own, or in others that he could equally well have called his own because they were in the same province and the same jurisdictional district.

To seek his homeland in other Spanish cities far from the regions of the Pyrenees is wholly without foundation, since so many of the verses cited above protest against it—especially because, although he celebrated several other saints and mentioned their towns, he never called those places his own, even when passage 23 itself seemed to demand it [Note: As at the end of the hymn to Saint Eulalia:

> Give these gifts, O virgin and boy,
>
> from the leafy foliage:
>
> but I shall carry, in the midst of the chorus,
>
> garlands woven in dactylic measure,
>
> poor and withered, yet festive.
>
> 
> Thus I delight to venerate the bones,
>
> and the altar placed upon the bones:
>
> that one, set beneath the feet of God,
>
> looks upon this one and, having been appeased
>
> by song, cherishes its peoples.] 

Most amusing, however, is the statement of Petrus Crinitus in his *Life of Prudentius*: “Some believe that he was Spanish by birth.” Is that really so? Both the books of Prudentius themselves cry out that he was Spanish, and Walafrid Strabo, Bede, Dungal, and others emphatically affirm it, in addition to several manuscript codices—for example, the Oxford manuscript, where he is called “the Spanish one” in the inscription of the *Dittochaeon*, which may be seen in the commentary at that passage, and Vatican manuscript 2868, no. 77.

### 39

With these matters established, we must now discuss the year of Prudentius’s birth. That year can be securely deduced from the preface to his works, once the interpretation of Petrus Mantuanus, discussed above in section 21 and following, has been rejected:

> You accuse me of having forgotten the consul of old, Salia,
>
> under whom my first day [was].

The first verse was formerly read differently:

> You accuse me of having forgotten the consul of old, Messalia.

From this reading there arose great obscurity in arranging the facts of Prudentius’s life, for many inferred that Prudentius had held the consulship at Messalia or Massilia.

Andreas Resendius revealed the true reading and pointed out that mention was made of the consul Salia [Note: I shall report this in the words of Joannes Vasaeus in his *Chronicle* under the year 351:

“Aurelius Prudentius Clemens was born at Caesaraugusta in the consulship of Philippus and Salia, as he himself testifies concerning himself in the preface to the book of the *Cathemerinon*, where he says: ‘Suddenly old age crept upon me, reminding me—rather, accusing me—of having forgotten the consul of old, Salia.’ This must indeed be read in this way, not as it had hitherto been corruptly read even by learned men. This restoration of the passage, candid reader, is not owed to me, but to L. Andreas Resendius, who, with his customary courtesy, communicated this passage and several others to me. I rightly attach the greatest importance to his highly refined judgment in these matters, as you will discover in fact if at some time he is able, amid his serious occupations, to publish the commentaries on Prudentius that he has been polishing.”

Glandorpius, in his *Onomasticon*, published after his death in 1589, claims this correction for himself: “We see this passage corrupt in all printed copies . . . All learned men, I know, will gladly acknowledge that the genuine reading is *me Saliae*, correctly discovered by us from these ancient records.”] 

Theodorus Pulmannus received the true reading and explanation from Vasaeus, and Giselinus from Pulmannus. Before then, as he honestly admits in his commentary on that passage, no one had thought of a way to avoid the obstacle into which Aldus, Nebrissensis, and all the others had run. Nic. Antonius complains that Pulmannus did not give Resendius credit for the correction, and that Giselinus, having been warned by Pulmannus [Note: Ludewigius is much mistaken when he writes: “Georgius Fabricius restored *me Saliae*.” Giselinus published the poet in the same year, 1564, with this correction. I would not dare to assert which copied the other, since each says that he was the first to notice the reading. Fabricius has only this: “This last verse, corrupt in all the Italian, French, and German editions up to the present, gave rise to the error.”].

### 40

As for the manner of interpretation, it must be pointed out that, although Nebrissensis read *Mesaliae*, he nevertheless understood the sense correctly. For he did not understand this as referring to a consulship held by Prudentius, but to the consulship under which he had been brought into the world. “Under this consul,” he says, “Prudentius appears to have been born.”

The manuscript codices have various readings: in some one finds *Mesaliae*, in others *Messaliae*, in one *Messalae*, and finally in others *me Saliae*. As is clear from the glosses, the passage was already corrupt in antiquity, and *Mesaliae* or *Messaliae* was being read.

Iso the Master, in the ninth or tenth century, noted *me* beside the word *arguens*. But why would he have added this if the text already read:

> You accuse me of having forgotten the consul of old, Salia,

and so forth? Yet the true sense did not escape Iso. For beside the word *Saliae*—or, as I think, *Messaliae*—he added “of that consul.” Thus Iso and Nebrissensis believed that Prudentius had been born under the consul Messalia.

But there are many reasons for believing that the reading must be *me Saliae*, and therefore that the consulship of this Salia is indicated. Philippus and Salia were consuls in the year 348, approximately the time in which Prudentius is otherwise known to have been born. Moreover, around that time there was no consul—at least no ordinary consul—named Messalia, Mesalia, or Messala.

Further, Prudentius contains many errors of this sort, caused by the ignorance of copyists who joined wholly different words into a single expression. These may be seen in Giselinus’s commentary on the thirteenth hymn of the *Peristephanon*. Finally, the manuscripts favor this reading, as I shall indicate in its proper place.

It must therefore remain fixed and certain that the year of Prudentius’s birth fell in the consulship of Philippus and Salia. That year was A.D. 348, as Petavius notes in the *Rationarium temporum* in his succession of the Roman consuls; it is also so read in Panvinius’s consular *Fasti*, although others prefer the year 350 or 351.

This is wonderfully confirmed by the following verses from the *Apotheosis*, verses 449 and following:

> Yet among all the rulers there was one who was not lacking,
>
> when I was a boy, as I remember: a commander most powerful in arms,
>
> a founder of laws, most renowned in word and deed,
>
> an adviser to his country—but not an adviser in establishing
>
> religion, a lover of three hundred thousand gods,
>
> that treacherous man toward God.

Here he means Julian the Apostate, as will be clearer from the commentaries. Julian held imperial power from the year 361 to 364. In Petavius’s lists of the emperors, this seems to be indicated in such a way that nevertheless, in the *Rationarium temporum* itself, he is said to have died in the year 363, which is also established elsewhere from history.

Furthermore, Prudentius published his works, including the books against Symmachus, in the fifty-seventh year of his age, as is clear from the preface to the poems:

> For ten periods of five years now,
>
> if I am not mistaken, we have lived; and, in addition, the seventh year
>
> turns the year upon its hinge while we enjoy the revolving sun.

Since this occurred approximately in the year 405, as I shall say below in section 25, it follows that the consulship of Salia is also indicated in the same preface.

### 41

Nothing certain has come down to us concerning Prudentius’s ancestors or family. Yet it is reasonable to conjecture from the offices he held that his family was most distinguished, and many ancient writers also confirm this.

Joannes Glandorpius, in his *Onomasticon historiae Romanae*, has much to say about the Aurelii and something about the Clementes. Of the three Prudentii whom he names, he treats our poet with a great encomium. Concerning the family of the Clementes of Caesaraugusta, see section 33.

His three names, in the order usually transmitted, are Aurelius Prudentius Clemens. In the most ancient manuscript codices, from the sixth century onward, he is called Aurelius Clemens Prudentius, as may be observed in chapter 4, section 96, apart from Vatican codices Alexandrinus 1439 and 1838, no. 78, and Colbertinus 1682, no. 83.

The first editions—one of uncertain date and the other the Daventer edition of 1495, which most people incorrectly assign to the year 1472—have *Aur. Clemens Prudentius*. This order of the names was changed without any adequate reason in all the editions that followed. Trithemius, Ferrarius, Ruinartius, and others preserve it.

Bede names him twice in *The Art of Meter*: first as “Prudens in the *Psychomachia*,” and again as “Aurelius Prudens Clemens.”

That Clemens is sometimes placed before Prudentius or Prudens is not unprecedented. Thus Sulpicius, surnamed Severus, is called by others Severus Sulpicius, as Rosweidus observed in his note on Epistle 1 of Saint Paulinus, citing Franciscus Sylvius, who teaches in the second century of his *Progymnasmata*, chapter 41, that the cognomen was often placed before the name.

Sirmondus, in his preface to his notes on Apollinaris Sidonius, admirably proves that the names of the Middle Ages had, in a certain sense, a twofold rule: first, that they placed each person’s proper name last; second, that they imposed both this proper name and the other names, sometimes arbitrarily from elsewhere, but usually derived from the affections of relatives.

One may also consult the distinguished Marquis Scipio Maffei in his dissertation *On Roman Names*, where he proves that Cassiodorus’s praenomen was Marcus, his gentile names Aurelius Cassiodorus, and his proper name or cognomen Senator; this appears after the *Historia theologica* and the *Complexiones* of Cassiodorus, published at Trent in 1742.

Riscus observes that Prudentius is called Quintus by Dupin in volume III of the *Bibliotheca*, and by Joannes Ferreras under the year 406. That name is absent from the manuscript codices and ancient writers. I would suppose that the error could have arisen because Symmachus, whom Prudentius attacked, was called Quintus Aurelius by certain ancient authors.

Nevertheless, there is nothing to prevent Prudentius from similarly having been named Quintus Aurelius Clemens Prudentius. Indeed, Alexander ab Alexandro, in Book I, chapter 9 of the *Genialium dierum*, proves that among the Romans males often had four names: praenomen, cognomen, agnomen, and nomen—and that this indicated nobility.

If one wishes to add a praenomen to Prudentius, let it be Marcus. He is indeed so called in a certain manuscript codex, no. 89. He should therefore be called M. Aur. Clemens Prudentius: the first is his praenomen, Aurelius and Clemens are gentile names, and Prudentius is his proper name, according to the naming law of the Middle Ages.

There were many Marcus Aurelii, such as Marcus Aurelius the emperor; Marcus Aurelius Valerius Flavius Claudius Constantinus; Marcus Aurelius Claudius Gothicus; and Marcus Aurelius Claudius Quintillus. Many think that Saint Maurelius was named from Marcus Aurelius, just as Agellius was named from Aulus Gellius.

### 42

Because Carolus Sigonius, in *On Roman Names*, shows that Roman names were sometimes derived from the founder of a family, from wisdom, or from an art, Ludewigius thinks that those who turned Prudentius’s names into praises of him were not wrong [Note: Such are Aleimus Avitus; several manuscript codices of Prudentius’s works; the author of the *Catalogue of Witnesses to the Truth*, Book IV, p. 185 of the later edition; Taubmannus, in his *Culex of Virgil* and in his letters to Weitzius; and Zacharias Victor, *Topica*, dissertation 11, inquiry 2. Compare chapter 4.].

Nevertheless, although his names can not absurdly be turned into praise of the poet, as is often done with other names, no prudent person will judge that they were derived from prudence, clemency, and golden character. They were imposed before those virtues began to exist or become prominent in Prudentius.

Another name is also commonly attributed to Prudentius, certainly bestowed long after his death. For Prudentius Major is called by that name in an ancient, learned, parchment manuscript on prosody preserved by Barthius, *Adversaria*, Book XXXVII, chapter 13:

> *Macera* and *maceries* lengthen the *a*, although they come from *macer* . . . and Prudentius Major:
>
> “Although the *maceries* surrounds the flowering fields.”

Likewise Joannes Balbus, or de Janua, in the *Catholicon*, under the word *SPERA*:

> “Hence Prudentius Major:
>
> ‘At whose command the noble and rounded sphere . . .’”

The latter verse is read in the *Apotheosis*, verse 210; the former in the *Hamartigenia*, verse 226.

Someone might suspect that this name came to Prudentius from a larger manuscript from which those verses were taken, since works were sometimes divided among several codices of different sizes. In this sense Ovidius was called “the Great,” as were Claudianus Magnus and Theodosius Exiguus, as one may read in Barthius, in the work cited, Book VI, chapter 1.

Children and teachers alike know that this elegance also adhered to our own customs in the case of books used in the schools of grammarians.

### 43

Our Prudentius is believed to have been called “Major” in order to distinguish him from the others.

Melchior Goldastus distinguishes five Prudentii in the Weitz edition, p. 319: a bishop of Turiassus around the year 300; our poet; another bishop of Troyes in Gaul; the author—so he thinks—of the hymn *Virgo Dei genitrix* (“Virgin Mother of God”), which the manuscript codices attribute to Prudentius (see section 98); and, fourth, a German monk, the teacher of Walafrid Strabo, the author of the hymns on the Nativity of the Lord, *Corde natus ex parentis* (“Born from the Father’s heart”), and on the Passion, *Vidit anguis immolatum* (“The serpent saw [him] sacrificed”).

“This,” he says, “is he in distinction from whom Prudentius Clemens began to be called Major.” To these he adds a fifth Prudentius through his own generosity and courtesy: Prudentius Amoenus, equal or not far inferior to Prudentius Clemens.

Nevertheless, it will be demonstrated, when we discuss his *Dittochaeon*, that this Amoenus is in no way different from Prudentius. That name was given to him because of the pleasantness of his talent, or for some other reason.

Nic. Antonius rightly censures Tarrafa, Trugillus, and Ferrarius for confusing the sacred poet Prudentius with the bishop of Turiassus.

Consult the continuators of the Bollandists under 28 April, in the preliminary commentary on the life of Saint Prudentius. They join Bernard of Lucca to Tarrafa and the others, and determine that scarcely anything certain is known about the age of Prudentius of Turiassus except that he lived before the year 846 of the Lord. The opinion that he lived around the year 300 is probable.

### 44

Come now, let us hear from Prudentius himself the course of his life up to the fifty-seventh year of his age, from the preface to the poems:

> For ten periods of five years now,
>
> if I am not mistaken, we have lived; and, in addition, the seventh year
>
> turns the year upon its hinge while we enjoy the revolving sun.
>
> The limit approaches, and God is already bringing near
>
> the day adjacent to old age.
>
> What useful thing have we done during so great a span of time?
>
> My first age wept beneath
>
> the resounding rods; soon the toga taught me
>
> to speak falsehoods infected with vices, not without guilt.

By “the first age” I understand late boyhood and, if you wish, the beginning of adolescence, extending to approximately the twentieth year. At that time, he accuses himself—with the humility of spirit in which he especially excelled—of the little falsehoods with which that age is generally infected.

Unless one prefers to interpret “to speak falsehoods” as rhetoric and dialectic, disciplines to which the expression “to speak falsehoods” in a certain sense corresponds. This interpretation seems preferable, since it has pleased the best recent commentators and is also found in the ancient glosses.

Riscus reasonably conjectures that Prudentius devoted himself to literature at Caesaraugusta under the rhetorician Petrus, on the basis of Saint Jerome’s *Chronicle* under the year 356:

> “Petrus, a distinguished rhetorician, teaches at Caesaraugusta.”

[Note: If the *Chronicle* published under the name of this Petrus should happen to reach your hands, know that I would very much like you to understand it as having been fabricated by those who, in order to sell their own dreams, appropriated famous names from antiquity.]

Prudentius continues:

> Then wanton insolence
>
> and petulant luxury—alas, I am ashamed and regret it—
>
> stained the young man with the filth and mud of depravity.

These are the words on which every accusation against Prudentius’s youthful crimes rests. For all those who have narrated his life in recent centuries portray him as a wicked and ruined adolescent.

Ludewigius compares him with Saint Augustine, in whom there is nothing similar. Augustine confessed certain very serious sins not merely in general terms, but specifically and individually.

Riscus greatly expanded the same vices in Spanish:

> “He allowed himself to be dragged along by vices . . . staining his heart and loving the shameful pleasures of the flesh.”

And who does not speak in approximately this way? Fabricius went further still and asserted that, while wearing the toga, Prudentius conducted unjust cases; he likewise deduced this from the present preface.

### 45

I shall undertake Prudentius’s defense—not from any desire to commend him, nor carried away by the custom of our own times, in which apologies multiply and even the most desperate causes find bold advocates, but impelled by love of truth.

For I am convinced that he said nothing which could not ordinarily fall from the mouth of a just man endowed with Christian humility. When I say “a just man,” I mean the kind of justice that can belong to human beings while they live in this world.

“For although,” says the Council of Trent, session 6, *On Justification*, chapter 11, “in this mortal life even the holy and just may sometimes fall into at least light and daily sins, which are also called venial, they do not thereby cease to be just.”

And Proverbs 24:16 says:

> For the just man falls seven times and rises again.

[Note: Although the words “in a day,” which many add, are not found there, the truth of the saying could nevertheless be confirmed by the authority of many. For from the time of Cassianus this addition is recorded. “Scripture plainly declares,” he says in *Conference* XXII, chapter 13, “the just man falls seven times in a day and rises again.”]

These sins, then, into which the just often fall, and that law which the Apostle himself experienced in his members, resisting the law of his mind and taking him captive under the law of sin, are fully sufficient to allow Prudentius’s words to have been spoken both truthfully and humbly by a just man.

I am glad to use this Christian term, since the ancient Latins did not bestow a proper name upon that virtue—indeed, they did not even recognize it.

Certainly Saint Jerome notes this about Saint Paula in her epitaph, volume I of his works, no. 15:

> In her you would have thought there were fountains of tears.

She wept over light sins in such a way that you would have thought her guilty of the gravest crimes. The mystical books are full of examples of this kind, as are the acts of the saints. There is no time to list them individually. One may read what the most innocent virgin Saint Teresa relates about herself when she explains what she did before entering the monastery.

### 46

No one should be disturbed by those grave words that Prudentius used: “wanton insolence,” “petulant luxury,” “filth,” and “the mud of depravity.” For, apart from the fact that some saints who lived innocent lives used similar or even harsher expressions, these words are not as serious as many may suppose.

Everything ultimately turns on explaining what the Latins understood by the word *depravity*.

Christianus Becmanus, in *On the Origin of the Latin Language*, under the word *Aequor*, argues against Perottus, who derives *nequam* (“worthless,” “wicked”) from *ne* and *queo* (“not” and “I can”). That derivation might be tolerated if it did not also conflict with Varro, who in Book IX of *On the Latin Language* derives it from *ne* and *quidquam* (“not” and “anything”).

Becmanus believes that *nequam* is most correctly derived from *ne* and *aequum* (“not” and “equitable”), so that *nequam* means Greek *adikos, kakos, achreios* (ἄδικος, κακός, ἀχρεῖος; the source prints ἄρχειος): “unjust,” “bad,” or “useless.” This suggests that *nequitia* (“depravity”) was derived from *nequus*—for which we use *nequam*—just as *malitia* (“wickedness”) comes from *malus* (“bad”).

But what if the ancient Latins also derived *nequitia* from *nequicquam* (“to no purpose”)? Cicero, in the Aldine edition of the *Tusculan Disputations*, p. 194, says:

> *Nequitia*, although this may seem somewhat harsh, comes from what is of no use in such a person; hence the same person is called *nihili*, “worthless.”

Accordingly, he frequently uses *nequitia* almost in the sense of inactivity or idleness. In *Against Catiline*, p. 98:

> Now I condemn myself for idleness and worthlessness;

and on p. 103:

> Idleness and worthlessness.

This accords with what Prudentius says:

> What useful thing have we done during so great a span of time?

And below, concerning the good and bad things of fortune:

> Will such things be of any benefit
>
> after death to the flesh, whether good or bad?

Thus Prudentius could lament and grieve in the verses cited over leisure, idleness, and activities that contributed nothing toward attaining eternal salvation—sins, although not grave ones, into which he had fallen especially during his youthful years.

It is rightly inferred that there was nothing in him that could indicate a criminal life or a life devoted to paganism, as is read in a later Vatican manuscript. This follows from his humility, which shines most clearly in all his works:

> What useful thing have we done during so great a span of time?

Riscus says that this was spoken out of humility, because Prudentius had already written the books against Symmachus and had performed other good works, namely:

> We administered civil justice to the good;
>
> we terrified the guilty.

Barthius, Book VIII of the *Adversaria*, chapter 11, notes the modesty that shines in the trochaic preface to the book of the *Peristephanon*. He says that this was a particular virtue of Prudentius, who at the end of the hymn to Saint Romanus, saying that he would be a goat joined to the goats on the judge’s left, withdrew even farther from the true mediator through excessive humility. We shall discuss this elsewhere.

For now I observe only that Riscus and Barthius, who acknowledge such great humility in Prudentius, ought not to have exaggerated the crimes of his youth on the basis of his words while at the same time admitting the man’s modesty [Note: Barthius continues in the passage cited:

“So loudly does this trochee proclaim Prudentius as its author that in so many centuries, among so many poets who later professed Christ, no one has written anything comparable to him. At the beginning he separates himself from the choir of the devout, evidently because of the sins of his youth, when he lived as a pagan and a soldier, in a military and pagan manner.”]

### 47

I do not see how these things cohere. If Prudentius proceeded so far in excessive humility; if in the hymn to Saint Laurence, and indeed throughout his poems, he repeatedly says similar things, acknowledging no period of his life as having been spent usefully, there is no reason why all such statements should not be attributed to humility.

For it is well known with what devotion he visited the tombs of the martyrs [Note: In the hymn to Cassian:

> Stretched upon the ground, I used to crawl toward the tomb,
>
> which the holy martyr Cassian adorns
>
> with his dedicated body.

In the hymn to Hippolytus:

> As I examine these things with my eyes, and wherever by chance
>
> the hidden beginnings of events may lie,
>
> I follow them through the monuments of the ancients.

In the hymn to the apostles Peter and Paul:

> It is enough for you to have learned these things at Rome.
>
> When you return home, remember to celebrate
>
> this twofold day in this way.]

I omit for now the fact that all or most of the poems preceding the preface seem to me to have been composed earlier, as I shall explain later. Whether they were written before or afterward, the humility of a devout and just man is evident throughout them all [Note: In the epilogue to the *Peristephanon*:

> We dedicate swift iambics
>
> and rolling trochees,
>
> though lacking holiness.
>
> Christ fits me, in his Father’s court,
>
> like a worn-out little vessel,
>
> for uses destined to perish.

And similar verses in the passion of Laurence, at the end:

> Among these, O glory of Christ,
>
> hear the rustic poet
>
> confessing the sins of his heart
>
> and revealing his deeds.
>
> 
> I acknowledge and know myself unworthy
>
> of being heard by Christ himself,
>
> but through the patron martyrs
>
> he can obtain healing.
>
> 
> Hear kindly the suppliant,
>
> Prudentius, guilty before Christ,
>
> and release from the bonds of the world
>
> him who serves the body.
>
> 
> In the hymn for the eighteen martyrs:
>
> 
> Let us, I beg, wash with devout tears
>
> the grooves of the marble beneath which
>
> hope is buried, so that I may loosen
>
> the chains of my bonds.
>
> 
> At the end of the hymn to Fructuosus:
>
> 
> One day will come, when the world collapses,
>
> when Fructuosus, covering you, Tarragona,
>
> will release you from the harsh punishment of fire.
>
> Perhaps, with Christ prospering,
>
> he will deign to grant healing even to my torments,
>
> while turning over sweet hendecasyllables.
>
> 
> At the end of the hymn to Romanus:
>
> 
> I wish that, as I shall be among the goats on the left,
>
> I might be recognized from afar.
>
> 
> And what follows in the hymn to Hippolytus:
>
> 
> Thus at last, when I remain in the grassy field,
>
> may you, diligent shepherd, bring back
>
> the sick sheep.
>
> 
> I pass over other examples, including the prayer at the end of the *Hamartigenia*:
>
> 
> O God, parent of all,
>
> of whom there will be further discussion below, in chapter 17.]

Nor shall I mention how inferior he considered himself to Symmachus in eloquence in the preface to Book I: “I am altogether rash,” and so forth. Enough has been said to establish what I intended: the verses of the preface in which Prudentius confesses his sins indicate his humility, not a pagan or notably wicked life.

I shall offer an example from Saint Eugenius, bishop of Toledo, who at the end of a prayer confesses that he did not deserve the crown of eternal glory:

> When the final day of death shall have opened the urn,
>
> grant pardon to him whose guilt removes the crown.

“This is a modesty customary among the ancient Christians,” says Barthius in Book LV, chapter 11 of the *Adversaria*. “You will find it in several places even in Prudentius.” At that passage Barthius undertook to emend several poems of Saint Eugenius.

### 48

Having described his youth, Prudentius narrates the rest of his life:

> Thereafter quarrels armed
>
> my turbulent spirit, and the ill-advised, obstinate desire
>
> to win was subjected to harsh reverses.

No one doubts that the office of a lawyer is meant here. Since Bede and Walafrid Strabo call Prudentius a *scholasticus*, it is reasonable to judge that this title was given to him because he was a jurist.

Although in earlier times the word could mean a student, sophist, rhetorician, or learned man, it was also used of a jurist and an advocate. I shall omit its other meaning, by which after Charlemagne *scholasticus* meant one who presided over schools, or, from the twelfth century onward, one who taught Aristotelian philosophy. On this subject one may consult the distinguished Bartholomaeus Pavius, a writer of the most refined judgment and style, *Institutes of the History of Philosophy*, Book IX, chapter 1 [Note: Saint Macarius, in Homily 15, says:

“Then, when he has become a *scholasticus*, he is a novice and the last among all advocates.”

Saint Augustine understood *scholasticus* in this same sense in Tractate 7 on John, as did the Theodosian Code, Book VIII, *On Extortion by Advocates*, title 10, law 2:

“Our Clemency is not unaware that very often *scholastici*, after receiving their fees, have been accustomed to accept both provisions and expenses beyond measure in the defense of every case.”

The commentary of Jacobus Gothofredus there deserves to be read.

Merobaudes, whose poem on Christ appears in the *Bibliotheca Sanctorum Patrum*, is commonly called “the Spanish Scholasticus.” In the Theodosian Code two Merobaudes are named: one a consul, the other master of the infantry in Gaul. Compare Antonius Zirardinus, p. 168, in the *Novels of Theodosius*.]

In the general Council of Sardica, canon 10, it was decreed:

> If anyone from the forum, whether rich or a *scholasticus*, is judged worthy to become a bishop, he shall not be appointed before he has fulfilled the ministry of lector, deacon, and presbyter.

This is how it is rendered in Latin in the Paris edition of the collection of councils, 1671. It could be translated more accurately:

> If anyone rich or a *scholasticus* from the forum is judged worthy to become a bishop.

The Greek is:

> Ἐάν τις πλούσιος, ἢ σχολαστικὸς ἀπὸ τῆς ἀγορᾶς ἀξιοῖτο ἐπίσκοπος γίνεσθαι.
>
> “If a rich man or a *scholasticus* from the forum should be considered worthy to become a bishop.”

“Innocent I,” in his letter to the Council of Toledo, no. 4, complains that certain men in Spain had been admitted to the priesthood who, after receiving the grace of baptism, had engaged in forensic practice and had undertaken *obtinendi pertinaciam* (“persistence in obtaining their ends”).

Prudentius used this same phrase of himself and his own office shortly afterward when he wrote:

> And a stubborn desire to win.

### 49

After serving as an advocate, Prudentius was advanced to the administration of cities:

> Twice, through the governance of laws,
>
> we held the reins of noble cities;
>
> we rendered civil justice to the good and terrified the guilty.

From there the emperor advanced him to the rank of palace service and to the next order:

> At last, having been raised in the rank of service,
>
> the piety of the emperor elevated him,
>
> ordering him, once taken up, to stand nearer
>
> in the next order.

Since Prudentius described the offices he held poetically—that is, in an elevated and figurative style—we can indeed conjecture what they were, but cannot define them with certainty.

In a manuscript of the Vatican Library, no. 3859, which appears to have been written in the ninth or tenth century, the following is written at the beginning:

> This Aurelius Prudens Clemens was partly in the consulship and partly in the emperor’s intimacy, and thus he advanced. For fifty-seven years he devoted himself to secular studies, but afterward abandoned them entirely and turned to composing divine meters.

Michael of Saint Joseph, in his *Bibliography*, under “Prudentius,” reports from Tirinus that Prudentius was a palace poet, and from Gennadius that he was a palace soldier.

Barthius, Book LIV, chapter 18 of the *Adversaria*, observes that the description of the gates of a military camp in the following verse of the *Psychomachia*:

> The double-hinged barriers grant entrance through the threshold,

was composed, he says, by a man who had once been a soldier in his own right and, by Gennadius’s testimony, therefore a palatine soldier, after the model of Roman gates.

Ansaldo, in the preface to his Italian translation of the books against Symmachus, relates that Prudentius held the first rank in the army after the emperor and had twice been praetor.

### 50

Thus each person judges the offices of Prudentius more or less according to his own preference. From the Theodosian Code the following points may be gathered that are relevant to our subject.

There were governors of Baetica; the year is uncertain for the law dated in 337, Book II, *On the Sale of Pledges*, which, as I noted on p. 48, in the note, should be read as referring to the year 324. Julian is named as governor of Tarraconensis in the year 316, in connection with the law *On the Course of Time*, where his title is added: *V. C.*, that is, *vir clarissimus*, “most illustrious man.”

In some laws, however, and in similar designations, the governors of provinces are meant by the title *rectores*. Thus the governors of provinces—who were also called ordinary judges and provincial judges, and were sometimes counts of the first order—possessed the right of the sword and the authority to administer justice in the provinces.

Above the governors of a province or provinces were the vicars, who administered several provinces in place of the prefects. Throughout that period no prefect of the Spains appears, but there was a vicar, frequently mentioned in the Theodosian Code, whose title was *PP. Hispaniarum*, that is, “proprefect of the Spains.” He is also called a *vir clarissimus* in law 4, *On the Custody of Prisoners*.

There was also a certain dignity called *proximatus*, “the honor of the next rank,” or “the splendor of proximity,” through which men advanced by order and by the merit of their service.

Specifically, after the masters of the bureaux, who served in the first three bureaux, came others next to them, who were called the “next men of the bureaux.” After laying down their service, or after the completion of their term, they were enrolled among the *clarissimi*, ranked on an equal footing with the vicars, and could come to the emperor’s court without an official travel warrant [Note: One may consult Book VI of the Theodosian Code, the entire title 26, *On the Next Men*, and so forth. Law 2, issued in the year 381, says:

“We join the most illustrious men, the next men of the bureaux, and the masters of dispositions to the order of the vicars.”

And law 14:

“To these men themselves—the next men—we grant free and perpetual permission to come to the emperor’s court, and we do not order that an imperial summons be awaited in their case.”

This law was issued in the year 407. The imperial court is the place where the emperor resides; the emperor’s summons is his calling of someone to him. Concerning this, see title 23, law 3, namely, the permission to come to the imperial court.

Rigaltius, in his note on Epistle 24 of Saint Cyprian, where certain men are called “next to the clergy,” reasonably concludes that there was in the Church a dignity of proximity to the clergy analogous to the proximity of the bureau officials.]

[Col. 0601A] **51.** From these facts we may infer that Prudentius was twice governor of the province of Tarraconensis, unless he was governor or administrator once of this province and once of another. His duty, accordingly, was to hold the reins of the great cities by the administration of the laws, to render civil justice to the good, and to terrify the guilty. From there he was promoted to a higher grade of service—namely, civil, palatine, or provincial service, not military, camp, or cohort service. For those who perform the offices of legal advisers, governors, administrators, and similar officials are commonly said in the *Theodosian Code* to serve and to advance to higher services.

That grade of civil service was either vicariate authority in Spain, or the rank of comes of the first order, or finally the dignity of *proximatus*, together with the emperor’s summons, that is, the imperial command or permission [Col. 0601B] to approach the imperial court. For this is what Prudentius’ words indicate: that, promoted by the emperor in the grade of service, he was ordered to stand nearer, in the rank of *proximus*. Where, besides the emperor’s command, the *proximus* rank is expressed, it seems to be none other than the rank of *proximatus*. There is therefore no reason for us to think of Prudentius’ consulship, or to imagine that he was praetorian prefect, of which offices there is not the slightest trace.

Ludewig asserts that, after Aldus, almost everyone calls our poet a *vir consularis*; but at the time when he was writing, scarcely anyone said this, since many had already observed, after Alciatus, that the marks **V. C.**, which are appended to Prudentius’ name, signify not *vir consularis* but *vir clarissimus*. For in Prudentius’ age the title *vir consularis* was not in use.

From Valerius Probus’ *On Interpreting the Abbreviations of the Romans*, and from other sources, it is clear that **V. C.** signified either *vir consularis*, *vir clarissimus*, or *quinta cohors*. We have already seen that Prudentius’ service was not military; but that the title *vir consularis* was not in use in his time is not altogether true [Note: From the *Theodosian Code*, book III, *On the Property of Proscribed Persons*, it is clear that certain men were called *consulares*, including, in Spain, Caelestinus in the year 357. They were ordinarily called *consulares* or *exconsules*, not *viri consulares*. It is, however, absolutely certain that these letters very often indicate *vir clarissimus*, and that they were sometimes appended to those who held the consulship, so that consuls were called *viri clarissimi*—a fact that could be confirmed by many inscriptions and legal enactments. On the *consulares*, see more in Guido Pancirolus, *Notitia dignitatum*.].

From manuscript codices and from the *Breviary of Zaragoza* it may be gathered that, even before Aldus, the opinion had already become established that Prudentius was a consul or *vir consularis*. For Tamayo de Vargas, in his *Defense of the Marian*, reports that in the old office of Zaragoza the lessons of the eighteen martyrs were identified as drawn from Aurelius Prudentius, a man of consular rank at Zaragoza.

From Dungal in the ninth century he was called *vir consularis*, as may be seen below, no. 243; and Isone, in his glosses on Prudentius’ preface, asserts his consulship at verse 17. Some have thought that Prudentius held the consulship not at Rome but at Massalia, or at Salia in Spain—unknown cities—or finally at Massilia, if *Massiliae* should be read instead of *Massaliae*, or *Mesaliae* in the verse:

> accusing the consul of having forgotten ancient Messalia.

But since the true reading and interpretation of that verse have already been established and demonstrated above, no. 39, there is no need to dwell longer on the matter.

Some, however, offer a weak argument when they deny that Prudentius was consul because, in the West, there were no consuls except at Rome. The distinguished Emmanuel Martinus seems to have followed them in book II, letter 53, where he plainly teaches that there were no consuls outside Rome. Ausonius refutes them in his poem on Bordeaux, as most interpreters explain it:

> This is my homeland; but Rome has surpassed all homelands.  
> I love Bordeaux; I revere Rome: in this city I am a citizen,  
> In both a consul. Here are my cradle, there the curule chair.

**52.** Others inferred from the fact that Prudentius was taken up by the emperor “nearer, in the nearest rank” that he had been praetorian prefect or prefect of the City [Col. 0602B]; but I have already shown that the passage must be understood otherwise.

Ludewig tries to demonstrate that Prudentius held no dignity at Rome because he came to Rome at an advanced age and was therefore overwhelmed with admiration for a city he had scarcely seen before. He bases this on Cassian’s hymn:

> Cornelius Sulla established the Forum; from him  
> The Italians call the City by the founder’s name.  
>   
> Here, when I was seeking you, greatest of things, Rome,  
> Hope arose in me that Christ would prosper.

And below:

> The sacristan, when consulted, says: “What you behold, stranger,  
> Is no empty or old woman’s tale.”
