Moreover, Ludewig says that Prudentius would not have dared to contend with Symmachus, whom he calls an apostate, perhaps on the basis of what he intends to say at verse 450 of the *Apotheosis*, if he had held office in the City. For although Saint Ambrose, when preparing to dispute against Symmachus, also asks pardon for the harshness of his language, Ambrose himself, though bishop of Milan, was far inferior to Symmachus, a man of consular rank, prefect of the City, and pontiff of ceremonies.

Ludewig concludes that Prudentius seems to have possessed the highest authority in Spain rather than at Rome, and therefore to have been prefect of the Spains.

**53.** Many things in this argument are unsatisfactory. First, it is not clear that Prudentius came to Rome at a very advanced age. For who can discover the year in which he visited Saint Cassian? Who would dare to assert that at that time he was visiting Rome for the first time, or seeing the Forum of Cornelius for the first time?

As for the claim that Prudentius was afraid to contend with Symmachus, that pertains only to Prudentius’ singular modesty: he placed Symmachus’ eloquence far above his own [Note: In the preface to book II *Against Symmachus*:

> I am utterly rash,  
> Who do not fear to entrust to the waves  
> My vessel, conscious of the night  
> In which I pass my life,  
> Against so great a man—  
> Than whom no one now is more eloquent—  
> Who leaps, rages, thunders,  
> And swells with the winds of eloquence;  
> It would be easy for him to sink  
> A craft unskilled in handling,  
> Unless you, powerful Christ,  
> With your propitious power, extend your hand.

See also Ausonius’ letter 17 to Symmachus, where Ausonius says: “Who shines so brightly that, compared with you, he does not appear sordid?”].

It is likewise false that Symmachus, when he was attacked by Saint Ambrose [Col. 0603A], had attained all those honors, since he had not yet been proclaimed consul before the year 391.

I shall not admit that the prefecture of the Spains was granted to Prudentius unless Ludewig means the vicariate dignity of a prefect, which at that time existed in Spain. I gladly agree with Ludewig that Vossius and others who say that Prudentius was a suffect consul rather than an ordinary consul [36] rely on no foundation whatsoever. The names of those who were substituted in place of a deceased consul were indeed not recorded in the consular annals; but if we are to believe that someone was a suffect consul, a plausible argument must be supplied.

I have discovered nothing about the year in which Prudentius came to Rome, or whether he came only once. Nor do I see on what grounds Nicolaus Antonius thought that he exercised the office of advocate at Rome and remained there until the reign of Honorius and Arcadius. He likewise infers that Prudentius was present in the City in the year 405 because, when writing his preface in that year, he did not yet add anything about his departure from Rome, though it would have been appropriate to do so. This conjecture seems to me extremely weak.

Riscus believes that Prudentius was promoted by Theodosius in the grade of service to the palace officials called *admissionales*. The *Theodosian Code* and Jacobus Gutherus, book III *On the Offices of the Imperial Household*, discuss these officials, who adhered to the emperor’s side in the year 388, when Symmachus, in a panegyric delivered before Theodosius, hypocritically requested the restoration of the altar of Victory and was immediately punished with exile. New edicts were issued promoting the Christian religion, and from that time arose the remarkable piety of all the Romans, about which Prudentius writes in book I *Against Symmachus*: “By such edicts,” and so forth.

Riscus maintains that Prudentius undoubtedly assisted these imperial policies, and attempts to prove it.

**54.** These claims are difficult to reconcile with Prudentius’ life and chronology. For in the year 388 he was forty years old; and when he recalls that after his youth he had practiced as a legal adviser, had then twice held the reins of the great cities, and finally, he adds, had been promoted in the grade of service, he seems to indicate a man more than forty years old. Even if one could prove that these things might have happened, one would still not persuade me that they actually did.

A similar difficulty concerns the statement that in 405, after renouncing public offices, Prudentius withdrew to Spain to devote himself to God; that he was forced to return from there to Rome, where he honored the martyrs Cassian and Hippolytus; and that, after returning again to Spain, he celebrated them.

I think that Prudentius wrote *Against Symmachus* around the year 404 and published his poems in 405, though he had composed them earlier and at different times. The preface to the book *Cathemerinon* is more appropriately understood as applying to all the works that he was then publishing, as is clear from several old codices.

Although he urges himself to compose sacred poems:

> Yet at the final end,  
> Let my sinful soul cast off its folly;  
> Let it at least celebrate God with its voice,  
> If it cannot do so by its merits,

these are not the words of someone just beginning to sing, but of someone placing a preface before poems already completed—a preface sometimes written after the work itself has been finished.

**55.** Thus I think that he composed the books against Symmachus at Rome. At Rome also he composed the hymn on the holy apostles Peter and Paul, which ends:

> It is enough that you have learned these things at Rome; when you return home,  
> Remember to celebrate the twofold feast in this way.

The following verses suggest that the hymn to the holy martyrs Hemeterius and Celedonius was written at Calagurris:

> The Savior himself granted us this good, that we might enjoy it,

and so forth.

I believe that our poet was at Emerita when, celebrating Saint Eulalia, he sang:

> But I shall bring garlands, woven in the midst of the choir,  
> With the dactylic foot—  
> Poor and withered, yet festive all the same.  
> Thus I desire to venerate the bones,  
> And the altar placed upon the bones.

No one will deny that the hymn concerning the eighteen martyrs was composed at Zaragoza.

As for the reason why, and the place where, he celebrated Saint Cassian, he himself relates:

> Then I review all the secret details of my labor;  
> Then I murmur what I sought and what I feared;  
> And the home I had left behind under uncertain fortune,  
> And the hope of future good, wavering in uncertainty.  
>   
> I am heard; I approach the City; my undertakings prosper;  
> I return home; I proclaim Cassian.

As I said earlier, he praised Saint Lawrence and Hippolytus in Spain [Note: In the hymn to Saint Hippolytus, the piety of the sacred poet is noteworthy. He addresses the bishop Valerianus in these words:

> If I remember rightly, most beautiful Rome honors him  
> On the Ides of August, as she herself calls  
> The day according to ancient custom. I should like you also, holy master,  
> To count him among the annual festivals.  
>   
> Believe me: he will bring health-giving dawns to those who venerate him,  
> Restoring the rewards of honored light.  
>   
> Among the solemn days of Cyprian, or Celedonius,  
> And of Eulalia, let this day also run for you.

Saint Hippolytus’ insertion into the Isidorian *Breviary* perhaps derives from these prayers of Prudentius. From the festivals of Cyprian, the holy Hemeterius and Celedonius, and Saint Eulalia, some infer that the passage concerns the bishop of Zaragoza, since these are foreign saints, as Hippolytus was, for whose festival Prudentius was praying. Others, on the contrary, recognize the diocese of Calahorra, whose patrons were the holy Hemeterius and Celedonius. To me neither interpretation is clear.].

I shall discuss Prudentius’ works individually and at greater length in the following chapter.

[38] **56.** It is uncertain in what year and where he died. But, I do not know by what fate, the life of Prudentius has become so entangled in the suspicions and conjectures of many that even where nothing at all can be known or determined, our discussion must pause for a while, lest anyone suppose that what others put forward is probable and unknown to us.

Some say that Prudentius died before the year 413, when Stilicho suffered the penalty for treason. For, unless Prudentius had already died by then, they argue, he would have removed the praises of Stilicho from book II *Against Symmachus*, verses 695 and following:

> Gelicus attempted …

What could be weaker than this conjecture? As though it had been within an author’s power to recall a book once issued [Col. 0605A] [Note: Horace did not think so. In *Epistle* 20 of book I he addresses his book in these words:

> You seem, my book, to look toward Vertumnus and Janus,  
> So that you may be displayed, polished by the pumice of the Sosii.  
> You hate keys and seals pleasing to the modest,  
> You groan at being shown to a few, and praise what is common.  
> You were not nourished in such a way: flee wherever you wish to go.  
> Once released, you will have no return.].

Much more decisively must we reject what Joseph Rodríguez de Castro says in the cited place: that Prudentius heard nothing about Stilicho’s conspiracy because he does not mention it.

Riscus, on the contrary, appears to judge correctly when he gathers Prudentius’ virtues from his works: that he lived sparingly and piously, and that he ate only once a day. See his hymns *Before Food*, *Of Those Who Fast*, and others in both the book *Cathemerinon* and *Peristephanon* [Note: This does not, however, mean that he should be called a saint. Antonius Raymundus Pasqual of the Cistercian order, in his work *Illustration of the Astonishing Favor of Her Heavenly Milk, by Which Most Holy Mary Distinguished Father Saint Bernard*, etc., printed in the workshop of Don Ignacio Sarra y Frau, 1782, octavo, as I believe, in the city of Palma de Mallorca, p. 111, proposition 2, quoting verses from Cassian’s Prudentius apud Mabillon, openly calls Prudentius a saint.

In the *Roman Journal* of 2 December 1786, it was accidentally stated that Prudentius should be called a saint, when my little work *Hymnodia Hispanica* was announced; yet in that work I certainly never attach this title to our Prudentius.

In manuscripts at no. 96, the name **Blessed** is said to have been applied to Prudentius only once. He is likewise called a saint by a certain Italian translator of the hymn to Saint Cassian, no. 121, and by Father Liberius of Jesus, volume I of the posthumous works, col. 763; and apparently also by Mabillon in his work *Memoirs Serving to Clarify the History of the Holy Tear of Vendôme*, where he says, “the holy poet Prudentius.”

This passage of Mabillon deceived Antonius Raymundus Pasqual. These statements could perhaps be maintained by those who wish this poet Prudentius to have been the same person as Saint Prudentius, bishop of Tarazona; but I warned above, no. 43, that this is false.].

**57.** Up to this point I have explained certain matters that are clear, others that are controversial, and many that rest on conjecture. The remaining matters, which are certainly fabricated, are less necessary to clarify; nevertheless, they must be exposed—first, so that no one may adopt such narratives either from Dexter’s *Chronicle* or from those who followed it, as I think Chamillard did in his brief and inaccurate *Life of Prudentius*; and second, so that it may be evident what opinions or conjectures were embraced by those who delighted in discovering similar fictions. For some invented stories adapted to genuine histories as far as they could and knew how.

Flavius Lucius Dexter, therefore, writes the following with Franciscus Bivarius’ commentary under the year of Christ 388:

> “Flavius Prudentius flourishes, born at Zaragoza of a father from Zaragoza and a mother from Calahorra (Salia being consul), at Zaragoza.”

The name **Flavius** and the other details are inventions, except that he was born when Salia was consul [Note: Bivarius says in his commentary that Prudentius is rightly said, from this passage of Dexter, to call Zaragoza and Calahorra his own, and Tarragona because he was its governor.].

Likewise, under the year 388:

> “Prudentius, having governed Toledo, Córdoba, and Zaragoza in Spain with distinction, becomes a commander and is regarded as a most celebrated orator and remarkable poet. In the year 400 he seeks Rome.”

[Note: Bivarius wishes to confirm this fiction from the preface to the poems, and thinks that *Twice by the administration of the laws* should be corrected to *Three times by the administration of the laws*. Likewise, in the printed Dexter, he thinks one should read at Zaragoza: “In his fortieth year he seeks Rome.” For Dexter writes under the year 396: “Prudentius, the lyric poet of Zaragoza, writes at Rome.”

Bivarius explains this as referring to the book *Psychomachia*, as though that book were composed in lyric verse. For he maintains that the books against Symmachus were written in 407, after the victory over Radagaisus and the Goths gained in 406, in the consulship of Arcadius VI and Probus, as he explains in his commentary under the year 417.].

Finally, the fictitious Dexter narrates Prudentius’ death under the year 424:

> “Prudentius, returning from Rome to Zaragoza, after reaching the see of Zaragoza of Saint Mary, full of days and illustrious works, and after waging many struggles against all the heretics of his time, dies peacefully.”

[Note: Nicolaus Antonius fully refutes the fiction of the pseudo-Julian the archpriest, according to which Prudentius was bishop of Zaragoza from the year 410 to the year 424, in his *Bibliotheca Hispana vetus*. You will find other absurdities in certain Vatican manuscripts, chapter 4.].

The temple of the Blessed Virgin of the Pillar is implied.

[Col. 0606A] **58.** Bivarius wished to appear clever here, contrary to the rules of prosody. He says that *Enchiridion* was the last of Prudentius’ works, and suspects that in its preface [Note: That is, in the ode *Immolat Deo*, which in the Arevalian edition is headed with the title *Epilogue* and is read on p. 1225; in some copies, however, *Dittochaeum* or *Enchiridion* precedes it in place of a preface. EDIT.] one should read:

> **Me materno in atrio**  
> “In my mother’s hall,”

instead of:

> **Me paterno in atrio**  
> “In my father’s hall,”

not seeing that the poem proceeds correctly with *paterno*, but not with *materno*. He thought that this would confirm Dexter’s claim that Prudentius lived in a corner of the temple of Christ’s mother.

Observe his extremely foolish interpretation. Prudentius, counting himself among the worthless vessels of the house of God, says:

> In my father’s hall,  
> Like a worn-out little vessel …  
>   
> He permits me to remain in a part of the corner.  
>   
> Behold, we undertake an earthen office  
> Within the palace of salvation.

“What,” Bivarius asks, “does it mean to enter within the palace of salvation, unless it means to write within the house of God?”—in whose corner he declares that he remains.

The following also concerns us, which Dexter reports under the year 430:

> “Cyril writes to Valerian” (or “to Bishop Valerius”) “of Zaragoza.”

The commentator Bivarius wishes this to be the Valerian bishop whom Prudentius addresses in the hymn to Hippolytus. He is uncertain whether this was the same Valerian who was bishop of Iconium [40], to whom Saint Cyril of Alexandria dedicated his exegeses.

Someone may object that these are trifles and dreams. I admit it; but this very point had to be noted, as I said above, lest someone else suppose them true or probable.

From such writings, even in our own century, Carolus Augustinus Ansaldus constructed the life of Prudentius in the preface to his Italian translation of the books against Symmachus. After asserting that Prudentius held the first rank after the emperor in the army and had twice been praetor, he adds that in his forty-eighth year, exhausted by service, he returned home; in his fiftieth year he began composing verses; in the year of Christ 404 he published the book *Cathemerinon*; and at the beginning of the reign of Honorius and Arcadius he published two books against Symmachus.

He further invents that in his sixtieth year Prudentius returned to Rome to venerate the tombs of the martyrs [Col. 0607A] and, having returned to his homeland, composed the book *Peristephanon*. What could be more contrary to Prudentius’ own works? [Note: It is absolutely certain that when he came to Rome he venerated the tombs of the martyrs; but the passion of Cassian shows that he was moved to undertake this journey for another reason:

> Here, when I was seeking you, greatest of things, Rome,  
> Hope arose in me that Christ would prosper.

And at the end:

> Then I review all the secret details of my labor,

together with the remaining verses that I transcribed above, no. 55.

It is also clear that already in his fifty-seventh year he counted the book *Peristephanon* among his works:

> May the poem be devoted to the martyrs; may it praise the apostles.

].

Finally, Ansaldus asserts, without any witness, as with the rest, that Prudentius died at Zaragoza.

To an educated writer who was so greatly pleased by the books against Symmachus, Prudentius ought not to have been so unknown—or known in a manner so different from what was proper.

We found a likeness of Prudentius, long sought, in an Urbinate codex of the Vatican Library. It is painted in the initial letter of the preface beginning *Per quinquennia*, and we reproduce it in the form in which it appears. I think it was copied from an older codex, for certain traces of it appear in the same initial letter of an ancient Vatican codex. In both, the garment is red; in the old Vatican codex, the features of the face have faded [Note: Ancient scribes often attached an image of the author to the first letter of a work. Virginius Valsechi, a Cassinese monk, discusses this practice learnedly in the preface to his dissertation on John Gerson as the Benedictine author of the book *The Imitation of Christ*. He lists several codices with portraits of authors in the initial letter that he himself had seen, including works of Saint John Chrysostom, Saint Basil, Saint Jerome, Saint Eucherius, and other ancient writers.].

## CHAPTER III. The Works of Prudentius

[41] **59.** I shall now explain more fully which books Prudentius wrote and at what time, adducing his own words and those of others. Thus, when I produce the testimonies of learned men concerning Prudentius, I shall merely identify those whom I mention here.

In the preface to his works Prudentius enumerates and explains them as follows:

> Yet at the final end,  
> Let my sinful soul cast off its folly;  
> Let it at least celebrate God with its voice,  
> If it cannot do so by its merits.  
>   
> Let it continue the days with hymns,  
> And let no night be free from singing the Lord;  
> Let it fight against heresies and examine the Catholic faith;  
> Let it trample the sacred rites of the nations,  
> And, Rome, bring reproach upon your idols;  
> Let it devote a poem to the martyrs and praise the apostles.

When Prudentius says that days and nights should be continued with hymns, he unquestionably means the book *Cathemerinon*, which Gennadius and Theodulf of Orléans, together with many manuscript codices, call the **Book of Hymns**.

Fighting against heresies and examining the Catholic faith pertains to the *Apotheosis*, the *Hamartigenia*, and, as I think, the *Psychomachia*. Trampling the sacred rites of the nations and bringing reproach upon the idols belongs to the books against Symmachus. The praises of the martyrs and apostles are contained in the book *Peristephanon*.

Chamillard and others incorrectly infer from this passage that Prudentius composed no other works. While publishing these works he could have omitted others; after publishing them he could have undertaken new ones. This is what must now be examined.

**60.** I shall present Gennadius’ eulogy from chapter 13, *On Illustrious Men*, using Aldus, Giselinus, and manuscript codices, together with the notes of Aubertus Miraeus, Ernest Salomon Cyprianus, and Johann Albert Fabricius. Gennadius writes as follows:

> Prudentius, a man learned in secular literature, composed the *Dittochaeum* (*Διττοχαῖον*) on selected persons from the Old and New Testaments. He also composed, after the manner of the Greeks, a *Hexaemeron* (*Ἑξαήμερον*) on the making of the world, up to the creation of the first man and his transgression.  
>   
> He also composed little books which he entitled with Greek names: *Apotheosis* (*Ἀποθέωσις*), *Psychomachia* (*Ψυχομαχία*), and *Hamartigenia* (*Ἁμαρτιγένεια*), that is, *On Divinity*, *On the Conflict of the Soul*, and *On the Origin of Sins*.  
>   
> He also produced, in praise of the martyrs and under the names of certain persons, one book called the *Invitation to Martyrdom* and another of hymns. In particular, against Symmachus, who defended idolatry, he composed two highly praiseworthy books; from reading them it is recognized that he had been a soldier of the palace.

Thus far Gennadius [Note: Fabricius’ notes are as follows:

“Prudentius, a man”: the word *man* is absent in the Corbie manuscript.

“*Dittochaeum*”: the same manuscript has *trocleum*, corruptly. But one should read *Diptychon*, following Gifanius’ emendation.

“*Hexaemeron*”: *Exemeron* … “up to the creation of the first man”: the same manuscript.

“little books”: “books,” the same manuscript.

“he entitled”: “he prefixed as a title,” the same manuscript.

“on divinity”: “on diverse matters,” corruptly, the same manuscript.

“For from their reading …”: Fabricius notes that Prudentius refers not to the books against Symmachus but to the preface of the book *Cathemerinon*: “Finally, promoted in the grade of service,” etc. Gennadius could perhaps be answered that the words “from reading them” may include not only the books against Symmachus but all of Prudentius’ works.

Likewise, I shall explain elsewhere why I do not approve Fabricius’ proposed reading *Diptychon* instead of *Dittochaeum*.

Aubertus Miraeus observed little beyond the fact that manuscript copies rightly place the preface to *Cathemerinon* at the very beginning, as the prologue to the entire work. He also says that Prudentius wrote these poems in the year 405, on the basis of the verse “Having forgotten ancient …,” etc.

Salomon Cyprianus writes: “*Exceptis*: thus all manuscript codices, but Miraeus reads *excerptis*.—The codices have ‘the conflict of the soul’; Miraeus has ‘of the mind.’—‘An invitation to martyrdom under the names of others’: these words are omitted in our manuscripts, and rightly so.”

I need add nothing at present to the observations of others, except perhaps that Gennadius said that Prudentius’ *Hexaemeron* was written after the manner of the Greeks because certain Greek writers, such as Gregory of Nyssa and Basil, used the same title and subject.

I shall give several glosses on Gennadius from Vatican manuscripts in the following chapter.

The variant readings are from Vatican A and Rat.; from the whole text of the Old Testament in Rat.; from Rat. “on the conflict of the soul”; from the same manuscript, “of those invited to martyrdom.” In the printed editions one finds “learned in secular literature … under the names of others … nevertheless with special intention against.” From Giselinus I adopted: “he composed two highly praiseworthy books.”].

[Col. 0608C] **61.** Let us now hear Honorius of Autun, who flourished in the year 1120 and largely reproduces Gennadius, except when he occasionally goes astray. In book II, chapter 13, he writes:

> Prudentius, a man learned in secular literature, composed the *Dittochaeum* on selected persons from the whole Old Testament. He also composed, after the manner of the Greeks, a *Hexaemeron* on the making of the world. He also composed little books which he entitled in Greek *Ἀποθέωσις*, *Ψυχομαχία*, and *Ἁμαρτιγένεια*, that is, *On Divinity*, *On the Conflict of the Soul*, and *On the Origin of Sins*. He also produced one book in praise of the martyrs and another against Symmachus.

**62.** Trithemius is more expansive. He had examined many codices and often made several works out of a single work, distinguishing them under different titles. Thus he writes in chapter 90:

> Aurelius Clemens Prudentius, a Christian poet, a man learned in secular literature and sufficiently skilled in the divine Scriptures, excellent in meter and prose, was held for fifty-seven years by the loves of the world. He read and expounded many little works of the poets, and from his own vein wrote many profound poems.  
>   
> Finally, in old age, rejecting the vanity of the world, he turned to the sacred Scriptures and, in verse and prose, expounded many obscure passages from both Testaments. He also wrote many distinguished little works. Among them I found the following, arranged according to their metrical form [Note: He lists the following:

*Against Symmachus the idolater*, book II: “Paul, herald of God,” etc.

*On the Conflict* (a), book I: “The faithful old man,” etc.

*On Divinity*, book I: “God is the highest Trinity” (b).

*Against the Patripassians* (c), book I: “There are many things,” etc.

*Against the Sabellians* (d), book I: “Yield, profaner.”

*Against the Jews* (e), book I: “If these things [are said] to the Jews,” etc.

*Against the Homuncionites*, book I: “There are those who, in Jewish fashion,” etc.

*Against the Phantasmatists*, book I: “It is worthwhile,” etc.

*On the Origin of Sins* (f), book I.

*On the Hexaemeron*, book VI.

*On the Holy Trinity*, book II.

*Various Hymns*, book II: “The winged herald of day” (g).

*Praises of Saint Vincent*, book I: “Blessed martyr, prosper.”

*Praises of Saint Lawrence*, book I: “Ancient parent of shrines.”

*Praises of Romanus against the Gentiles*, book I: “Strong Roman of Christ,” etc.

*Histories* (h), book I: “Eve was a dove.”

*On the Nature of the Soul*, book I: “The doubting one encounters” (i).

*On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, book I: “I claim what is mine in Christ” (k).

*On the Martyrs*, book I: “They are written in heaven” (l).

*On the State of the Soul* (m), book I: “Everyone’s soul goes astray.”

*Hamartigenia*, book I: “Brothers, young men, the digger” (n).

*On the Hope of Forgiveness*, an oration or book I: “O God, parent of all things” (o).

*Against the Marcionites*, book I: “Whither does rage hurl you?” (p).

*Peristephanon*, book I: “Pious, faithful, innocent” (q).].

He also wrote not a few letters. He published several other works that did not come into our hands. He flourished under the emperor Gratian, in the year of the Lord 380 [Note: Fabricius added the following notes to Trithemius:

(a) *Psychomachia*.

(b) The preface to the *Apotheosis*.

(c) *Apotheosis*.

(d) *Against the Sabellians*. In the printed editions it is entitled *Against the Unionites*, verse 178 of the *Apotheosis*.

(e) Verse 321 of the *Apotheosis*.

(f) It does not appear to differ from the *Hamartigenia*, which he mentions again below.

(g) The beginning of the book *Cathemerinon*.

(h) The *Enchiridion* of both Testaments.

(i) *Apotheosis*, verse 783.

(k) I do not find this in the printed editions.

(l) The beginning of hymn 1 of the *Peristephanon*.

(m) In the printed editions it is entitled *On the Integrity of the Vision of the Soul*, verse 867.

(n) The preface to the *Hamartigenia*.

(o) Verse 931 of the *Hamartigenia*.

(p) Verse 1 of the *Hamartigenia*.

(q) In the printed editions the beginning is: “Immolated to God the Father, pious, faithful, innocent, chaste.”].

**63.** From Fabricius’ notes anyone can readily recognize how freely Trithemius multiplied Prudentius’ poems. It is useful to add a few observations.

When Fabricius says that he did not find the book *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, beginning “I claim what is mine in Christ,” he failed to notice an error in Trithemius. It should read: “I know what is mine in Christ,” which is verse 1131 in the Weitz edition and verse 1063 in our edition, at the end of the *Apotheosis*, where the title *On the Resurrection of Human Flesh* is prefixed.

Trithemius says that Prudentius read many little works of the poets and wrote many profound poems from his own vein before turning to the sacred Scriptures. He further says that Prudentius expounded many passages from both Testaments not only in verse but also in prose, and wrote many letters [Col. 0610A]. Trithemius may perhaps have had some reliable witness. To us, however, Trithemius is not a reliable witness [Note: See the commentary on verse 26 of the hymn *Before Food*:

> Reject, Muse, the light ivy  
> With which you are accustomed to gird your temples.

].

Did Trithemius, just as he made several little works out of one work of Prudentius, conversely compose one work out of several works of Prudentius?

We may conjecture that the six books *On the Hexaemeron* are the very work praised by Gennadius.

Finally, I shall observe that Prudentius should more properly be said to have flourished around the year 400 than in 380. Bayle had already noted this in his *Critical Dictionary*, criticizing both those who asserted that he flourished in 380 and those who placed him in 430. The latter date is found in the *Bibliotheca Hispanica*, attributed to Andreas Schottus [Note: Prosper Marchand, in the article “Peregrinus” of his *Dictionary*, tries to persuade us that Andreas Schottus was not the author of the *Bibliotheca Hispanica* under the name A. S. Peregrinus.

I shall examine his arguments if I ever manage to publish Nicolaus Antonius’ *Bibliotheca Hispana vetus* and *nova*, arranged in one continuous order, expanded, continued, and corrected. Raymundus Diosdado, Joannes Arevalo, and I have long been preparing it by comparing our materials. It is a work of great magnitude, and cannot be completed without some great Maecenas—or, shall I say, Augustus.].

**64.** In addition to all the works of Prudentius that survive, and the book *On the Hexaemeron* mentioned shortly before, Trithemius records two other books *On the Holy Trinity*. Philippus Bergomensis confirms this in book IX of his *Chronicle* under the year of Christ 400:

> He also wrote two books on the Trinity, one of which may be the preface to the first *Apotheosis*, which is usually entitled “Verses on the Holy Trinity”; the other may perhaps be some portion of the books we possess.

Nicolaus Antonius thinks that the book *Invitation to Martyrdom* has perished. But, as I said in no. 60, those words do not appear certainly to belong to Gennadius; and even if they do, it is not clear whether he intended to distinguish that book from the book *Peristephanon*, since the latter contains exhortations to martyrdom under the names of others. There seems to have been no reason why Prudentius in his own age should invite Christians to martyrdom, whether under the names of others or under his own.

In Montfaucon’s *Bibliotheca bibliothecarum* of manuscript codices, a codex 227 from the Cassinese library is cited with the title:

> “The poems of Saint Prosper, etc. Prudentius’ book *On Doves*. Poems of a witty poet, etc.”

Should it perhaps be read *Book on Crowns*? Anyone who has noticed the errors occurring everywhere in that work of Montfaucon will not strongly object.

But since the *Dittochaeum* is entitled *On the Dove* in several Vatican codices, as I shall explain in chapter 4, it is clear that someone judged that the *Dittochaeum*, whose first verse is “Eve was a dove,” ought to be entitled *Book on Doves*—just as ancient scribes were generally as ignorant as they were bold.

The same Montfaucon cites, from the library of Saint-Germain, codex 540 with the following title:

> “Prudentius’ verses against Symmachus … Other metrical works by the same author: *On the Ocean*. *On Saint Hippolytus the Martyr*.”

Who would dare to guess what sort of work, or what work in particular, that *On the Ocean* might be? May we conjecture that it is an error for *On Cassian*?

45 65. I shall speak with confidence about another codex mentioned by Montfaucon from the library, or manuscript codices, of Saint-Martin of Sées, no. 13: *A Treatise on the Aedificium of Prudentius*. “This piece” (says someone—I do not know who—in that place) “is of little consequence: the question is whether Prudentius the poet or the bishop of Troyes composed a work entitled *Aedificium*, upon which this anonymous writer produced an allegorical explanation of the description of the House of God in the Apocalypse.” The answer is easy and straightforward. Our Prudentius, the Christian poet, at the end of the *Psychomachia* described the building of the house of God from the Apocalypse, verses 823 and following:

> When the Queen had spoken these words, she leaped down  
> From her proud steps, and Concord, the partner of so great a work,  
> Was about to build a new temple upon the foundation she had cast.

Here the title *Aedificium Fidei et Concordiae* (“The Building of Faith and Concord”) is prefixed. This, therefore, is the *Aedificium* of Prudentius about which that anonymous writer composed his treatise.

[Note: I would nevertheless point out that, in this catalogue of Montfaucon’s library, all the works both of Aurelius Clemens Prudentius and of Prudentius Galindo, bishop of Troyes, are listed under the single name Prudentius, as though Prudentius had been one and the same person. I should not omit to mention that a few verses of Prudentius from the *Psychomachia* are somewhere cited as though they were a work of his distinct from the others and entitled *The Combat of David with Goliath*. More will be said about this at the place in the *Psychomachia* where that battle is described.]

66. It follows that I should speak of the *Dittochaeum* and its author. The title of the work in Gennadius and in Honorius of Autun is *Dittochaeum*, as though meaning “double nourishment.” Most manuscripts agree at chapter 4, but through the error of scribes it is sometimes called *Dirochaeum* or *Ditrochaeum*.

[Note: In one manuscript, no. 80, chapter 4 calls it *Diptychon*; but, as I conjecture, this was added by a recent hand after Gifanius’s conjecture. I can testify to the same thing regarding a similar title in Codex Vaticanus Alexandrinus 1702, which I shall review below.]

Gifanius was the first to judge that there was an error and to assert that *Diptychon* should be read; most have readily followed him. I have no doubt that, through the ignorance of copyists, errors of this kind have often crept into manuscripts in Greek words. Yet, apart from the fact that the word *Diptychum* is very common, when the oldest manuscripts, which will be reviewed at chapter 4, give the title *Dittochaeum* and explain it as “a double refreshment,” and when the title *Dittochaeum* is by no means absurd, a correction is not especially necessary here. And if some correction is to be made, why shall we assert without further examination that *Diptychon* should be read?

I do not deny that this name can fit the work to some extent, since diptychs are double tablets, or tablets folded in two; on this subject one may consult those who have published books about sacred and secular diptychs. For Riscus does not interpret *dittochaeum* correctly when he says that it is almost the same as *diptychum*, namely, a doubled book.

Rosweydus devised another title, one that pleases me much more, in his notes on Paulinus, poem 30, p. 869. “Before Paulinus,” he says, “Prudentius also used this expression. For in his *Diteuchum*” (thus, he teaches, it should be read in Prudentius instead of *Dittochaeum*, and so forth) “Rosweydus wishes *Diteuchon* to be understood as a double book, just as *Pentateuchon* is a fivefold book: for Prudentius includes in that work a summary of the Old and New Testaments.” It would have been easier for copyists to turn *Diteuchum* into *Dittocheum*, and then into *Dirocheum* or *Ditrocheum*, than to derive those forms from *Diptychon*.

Nevertheless, I retain the ancient title, and I suspect that Prudentius composed those tetrastichs so that they might be placed beside images representing stories from the Old and New Testaments in churches. Paulinus of Nola composed many such poems, as did Walafrid Strabo, whose work consists of “Pictures of the Stories of the New Testament for a Church,” in hexameter verses of one or two lines, in the *Biblical Manual* published by Goldastus at Frankfurt in 1610, p. 85. There was also Rusticus Helpidius, an illustrious Roman citizen and former quaestor, whose work consists of “Pictures of the Stories of the Old and New Testaments,” in the same volume, p. 17, in three hexameter verses for each story. Compare Paulinus’s Letter 12 to Severus and *Natale* 9 to Nicetas.

To omit for now what could be said about the various titles of this little work, the arguments establish with the greatest certainty that Prudentius must be regarded as its author. Gennadius counts the work among Prudentius’s books, and most manuscripts attribute it to Prudentius. Why, then, should it be taken away from him? Some object to the difference in style; and because one manuscript bears the name *Amoenus*, Barthius, in Book VIII of the *Adversaria*, chapters 11 and 12, undertakes to prove that no one other than this divine Pindar, Prudentius, wrote the *Dittochaeum*.

[Note: He demonstrates this from the very phrasing, comparing many passages with one another, and concludes: “Once these matters had come to my attention, I was glad to write them down; but I do not doubt that anyone who wishes to investigate will find that each and every expression and story handed down in this little book is scattered throughout Prudentius’s works and formed in the same ways.… It seems, however, that Prudentius wrote this little book for the purpose of being able thereafter to use, as circumstances required, the more notable passages of Scripture, reduced in verse to brief titles and chapters; and perhaps the title *Amoeniorum* arose from this.… It is no different from the way that certain passages are titled *Florida* in Apuleius, Vestius [or Vettius] Valens, and several others, although the former are excerpts from larger works, while the latter were, for the sake of fuller treatment, conceived and sketched out beforehand. In Roman poetry several such passages exist in Claudian: *Ports*, *Sirens*, and so forth.”]

67. Although I agree with Barthius, who asserts, as though it were something new, that the *Amoenus* whom antiquaries call by that name is Prudentius himself, that very poet than whom no one has ever written more divinely about Christian subjects, I do not entirely agree that the poems of the *Dittochaeum* are passages prefigured and sketched out in advance for the sake of fuller treatment. For all those epigrams are deliberately concluded in four verses, and not one of their verses appears intact anywhere else in Prudentius’s complete work, although he often discusses the same subjects.

It is therefore more likely that Prudentius either arranged those tetrastichs for the explanation of paintings in churches, as I said earlier, or reduced the more notable passages of Scripture to brief titles and chapters in order to produce a work distinct from his others, in which he remains everywhere true to himself and often uses the same expressions, as will become clearer in the commentaries.

[Note: Barthius himself, in Book VI, chapter 1, explains the origin of the name *Amoenus* as follows: “Thus the most illustrious prophet of Christ, Prudentius, was called *Amoenus* by ancient copyists because, among all Christian poets, he is by far the foremost in the charm and variety of lyric poems. For those who deprive Prudentius of that brief work entitled *Amoenus* display no sound judgment whatsoever.” He adduces examples of others who received surnames through the generosity of copyists: Plautus Asinius, Ovidius Geta, Statius Aquilinus, Ausonius Paeonius, Propertius Nauta, Caelius Apitius, Martialis Cocus, Petronius Arbiter, Persius Severus, Sallustius Liberalis, Ovidius Magnus, Claudianus Magnus, Sidonius Modestus, Theodosius Exiguus, Abbo Cernuus, Radulfus Ardens, Saxo Grammaticus, Sulpitius Rhetor, Prosper Rhetor, and Juvenalis Ethicus.]

68. If one wishes to suppose that the *Dittochaeum* was first entitled by someone *Amoeniora* or *Amoena Prudentii*, from which one person made *Amoenus Prudentius* and another called him simply *Amoenus*, one may indeed judge this not unreasonable. But Philippus Brietius rashly conjectured, in Book IV *On Poets*, that there was another Spanish poet called Amoenus, distinct from our Prudentius, who elaborated the *Dittochaeum*.

Michael of Saint Joseph, in the *Critical Bibliography*, under the entry “Amoenus,” says that Amoenus was a certain Greek poet, but that the work published among the Christian poets under his name belongs to Prudentius. Melchior Goldastus, in the preface to the *Biblical Manual*, boasts that he was the first to add Prudentius Amoenus to the four other Prudentiuses. He thinks this poet was Spanish and nearly contemporary with Prudentius of Tarazona and with Aurelius Clemens; in this way he joined the two names Prudentius and Amoenus, and did not hesitate to assert that Gennadius, deceived by the homonymy of writers of equal standing, could not distinguish their writings.

Emmanuel Riscus does not differ greatly from Dupin, who thinks that the *Dittochaeum* is a certain epitome of the Prudentian work praised by Gennadius, compiled by Amoenus.

[Note: You will find different titles of this little work at chapter 4, in the manuscripts. Mariettus transcribes the following from a Vatican codex: “For he made many books: one which he entitled *Dirochaeum*, that is, calling it ‘a double refreshment,’ concerning the Old and New Testament; and others which we have at hand, if one wishes to examine them.” Compare our commentaries on the title of this work.]

48 69. It is not clear in what year Prudentius began to write, although most have asserted that in the fifty-seventh year of his life he turned his attention to composing sacred poems. For from the preface, on which they base their argument, one may infer only that in the fifty-seventh year of his life he published his small works, most or all of which, as is more likely, he had composed earlier at different times.

There is scarcely any doubt that he wrote the two books against Symmachus before the year 404. Theodosius issued a law in the year 392 by which the sacrifices of idols were prohibited:

> Let absolutely no one, from any class or order of persons, of any rank, whether holding office or having completed a term of honor, whether powerful by the fortune of birth or humble in lineage, condition, or fortune, in any place whatsoever or in any city, slaughter a harmless victim to senseless images, or, by a more secret act of atonement, venerate the household god with fire and the genius with wine [read: “the household god with fire, the genius with unmixed wine”], honor the household gods with smoke, light lamps, offer incense, or hang garlands, and so forth.

See Book XVI of the Theodosian Code, title 10, law 12; and compare in the same place law 11, by which sacrifices and access to temples throughout Egypt were forbidden, under the consuls Tatianus and Symmachus, in the year 391. I have followed the orthography of the code.

[Note: Since the Theodosian Code has been mentioned, I shall not delay in pointing out that shortly before no. 50, when two governors of Baetica were supposed to be reviewed, one was omitted. It should therefore read: “The governors of Baetica were: an uncertain person in the year 324, to whom law 1 *On the Sale of Pledges* was addressed; and Egnatius Faustinus, to whom law 2 *On the Sale of Pledges* was addressed in the year 337.”]

70. I judge that in Book I against Symmachus Prudentius had these laws of Theodosius in mind rather than the exile of Symmachus, as Riscus supposes, at verse 507:

> Informed by such edicts, the City recoiled  
> From ancient errors and scattered the dark clouds  
> That rose from her withered mouth; now prepared by her nobility  
> To attempt the eternal roads, and to follow Christ  
> Who calls her, with a great-hearted leader, and to place her hope in the age to come.

Riscus wishes to persuade us that Symmachus, after his return, made some new attempt to recover the altar of Victory. I believe that neither is this necessary nor can it be demonstrated by any argument. Even if one does not wish to agree with Nicolaus Antonius, who asserts that after the year 403 Prudentius wished to take up a new subject for his poem from Symmachus’s report, in order to exercise his style, one may nevertheless maintain that Prudentius attacked Symmachus’s report not only to exercise his style but also to overthrow the worship of idols completely.

It often happens that a work is refuted by several people, one sooner and another later; and Symmachus’s report, requested and read by many—as is highly probable—from a man who was then most eloquent, could have delayed some people’s efforts to embrace the Catholic faith unless it had been refuted more fully than Ambrose had refuted it. Thus, as I conjecture, Prudentius arrived in Rome around the year 403 and either saw Symmachus’s report then for the first time—for books were not circulated then with the same ease as now—or noticed that it was a favorite of the pagans and was being exalted with excessive praise; and he undertook to attack it.

The distinguished Emmanuel Riscus infers that Symmachus had made some new attempt from the fact that, when Symmachus says that he was once again an envoy of the senate, Prudentius replies at verse 610 of Book I:

> Behold how, with the senate in full attendance, our benches  
> Decree that Jupiter’s infamous shrine and every idol  
> Must be driven far away from the cleansed City.

[Note: Riscus wisely observes that Joan Albert Fabricius should be corrected in the *Bibliotheca Latina Antiqua*. Fabricius argues from Prudentius’s verses, truncated in this manner, that there were not a few in the senate who agreed with Symmachus:

> Behold how, with the senate in full attendance, our benches  
> Decree Jupiter’s infamous shrine.

Rodriguez de Castro did not notice this error in the *Bibliotheca Hispanica*, although he wrote after Riscus and rendered the whole passage of Fabricius into Spanish.]

71. Yet these verses do not rightly prove that Symmachus had again attempted to erect or request the altar of Victory. For Prudentius, addressing Symmachus at the end of the first book, presents the example of the other senators in order to bring him back to the right path. Similarly, what Prudentius adds at verse 624:

> You yourself conferred upon yourself the office of consul,  
> You yourself gave yourself the tribunal and granted yourself  
> The golden garment that wraps the toga—  
> You who defend the gods whose religion displeases you,  
> O advocate of the doomed gods.

This, I say, does prove that Symmachus remained of the same opinion after his consulship, but it does not prove that he again attempted to obtain the altar of Victory from the emperor.

Sigebert of Gembloux, who flourished in the twelfth century, relates that when Radagaisus the Scythian invaded Italy in the year 407, Symmachus attributed those disasters to the Christian faith. Against these blasphemies Saint Augustine wrote the books *On the City of God*, Orosius his history, and Prudentius the books against Symmachus. The last claim, however, does not at all agree with the chronology or with Prudentius’s verses about the battle of Pollentia.

[Note: Riscus observes that Sigebert confuses the chronology, insofar as Prudentius is concerned. He therefore asserts that Symmachus, without any new occasion having arisen, renewed his old complaints shortly after the battle of Pollentia and before the year 404. But since Prudentius replies with precisely the arguments found in Symmachus’s report, I do not dare assert that the complaints were renewed, especially without any new cause. Prudentius says in Book II, verse 683:

> And there are those who do not hesitate to reproach us  
> With disastrous wars.…  
>   
> Let those who again press upon me  
> The past defeat and ancient sorrows  
> See that, in your time, I now suffer nothing of the kind.

All this concerns the overthrow of Symmachus’s report, in which it is asserted that the world, reduced to Roman law by the worship of idols, had driven Hannibal from the walls and the Senones from the Capitol. Thus Prudentius, comparing the ancient times under Hannibal and the Senones with the present, continues:

> Recently a Gothic tyrant attempted  
> To destroy Italy.…  
>   
> The ever-watchful goose did not drive away those clouds of cavalry.

The verses that follow concern the victory achieved in the battle of Pollentia. It is therefore perfectly clear that Prudentius wrote after the battle of Pollentia, but not long afterward, because when Honorius returned to Rome at the beginning of the year 404, he had not yet returned when Prudentius was writing; this is clearly shown by verses 725 and following of Book II:

> Into what embrace shall I receive you, bravest prince?  
> What flowers shall I scatter?]

72. Another argument confirming our view is drawn from the poems in which Prudentius attacks the gladiatorial games and asks that Honorius prohibit them, at verse 1113 and following:

> So that golden Rome may no longer know this kind of crime,  
> I beg you, most august leader of the Ausonian realm,  
> Order this grim ritual, like the others, to be abolished.  
> Consider: is this place not empty of your father’s merit?

These verses are among the other very beautiful lines with which Book II against Symmachus concludes. The gladiatorial games were in fact prohibited in the year 404 or afterward, on the occasion of the death of the monk Telemachus, who openly condemned that cruel spectacle and was pelted to death by the spectators.

When the emperor learned of this, Theodoretus says in Book V, chapter 26 of his *History*, he enrolled the admirable Telemachus among the number of the unconquered martyrs and completely abolished that cruel kind of spectacle. Gothofredus, in his commentary on law 1 of Book XV, title 12 of the Theodosian Code, *On Gladiators*, corrects from this passage of Theodoretus and from Prudentius’s verses several errors of Baronius and others.

I do not see on what grounds Riscus denies that the killing of Telemachus under Honorius is established, and consequently denies that the prohibition of the gladiatorial games should be attributed to the poem of Prudentius, to which it is clearly to be attributed. The account of Theodoretus is clear and authoritative; nor is it shown from any other source than Theodoretus and those who followed him that Honorius prohibited that criminal spectacle. I shall also readily believe that the emperor was moved by Prudentius’s exhortation, although this is less clearly established.

[Note: Baronius relates the death of the martyr Telemachus under the year 395, on the basis of the Roman Martyrology, on January 1: “At Rome, Saint Almachius the martyr, who, when he said, ‘Today is the eighth day of the Lord’s Day; cease from the superstitions of idols and from polluted sacrifices,’ was killed by gladiators at the command of Alypius, prefect of the City.” Baronius maintains that this Almachius was none other than Theodoretus’s Telemachus, and that the event occurred under Theodosius, not Honorius. In this matter neither Baronius nor Bollandus satisfies me; I am more inclined to refer the martyrdom of Almachius to the time of Domitian than to suppose that Theodoretus was mistaken about Telemachus and his time. I do not find Alypius in the catalogue of the prefects of the City published by Corsinius. Several writers report that Almachius attained the palm of martyrdom under Domitian, as may be seen in Bollandus, volume I, January, under January 1. I shall speak more fully in the prolegomena to volume II about the other matters relating to the destruction of the altar of Victory.]

73. We have spoken sufficiently of the works of Prudentius that survive and those that have perished. For the various titles of each work will be recorded partly among the manuscripts, partly among the editions to be discussed, and partly in the commentaries. I shall now describe no poems that either appear to be doubtful works of Prudentius or are spurious.

Barthius, in Book I of the *Adversaria*, chapter 3, produces an iambic poem on the sending of the Holy Spirit, which he thinks should be attributed either to Prudentius or to Paulinus. It comes from ancient parchment manuscripts containing Lactantius’s poems on the Passion of the Lord, several elegies of Venantius Fortunatus, and songs of Paulinus and Ausonius written in hexameters. Among the last is found the following iambic poem:

### On the Sending of the Holy Spirit

> When the renewed course had brought  
> Ten times five festival days to completion,  
> And the promised coming of the Spirit drew near,  
> Who would deliver the truth,  
>   
> Christ himself had promised this to his own,  
> Before he departed to the Father—  
> Whom he had loved from the beginning  
> Unto the final end.  
>   
> When the twelve apostles had gathered  
> And were saying their prayers,  
> So that, as they were about to go forth into all the world,  
> They might first be anointed with heavenly chrism,  
>   
> Suddenly the house, shaking as its hinges were stirred,  
> Trembled and swayed far away.  
> A wind driving the four-sided blocks  
> Moved the towering mass;  
>   
> Zephyr flies from the front, Eurus from behind,  
> And beats his discordant wings;  
> From either side Notus and Aquilo rush together,  
> And fight to shatter the roofs.  
>   
> The air surges in divided tumult,  
> And the struck walls roar.  
> You might say that, when the foundations were torn away,  
> The whole structure would fall to the ground in an instant.  
>   
> Amid these things they sat, stricken in mind  
> Like priests struck by lightning.  
> Without delay, with loosened tongues,  
> They sang to God, taught foreign songs.  
>   
> The Jewish crowd, knowing nothing except how  
> To move the plectrum with Hebrew sound,  
> Heard Greek, Latin, Parthian, Babylonian,  
> Egyptian, and Persian;  
>   
> And, singing together in a thousand languages,  
> It resounded with the mighty deeds of God.  
> Filled with the Spirit of God, it sang of God,  
> Who, keeping the promise made to the fathers,  
>   
> Sent, through the womb of the Virgin in childbirth,  
> The child born for himself before the ages.  
> Begotten before time within time,  
> He came as salvation for all nations.  
>   
> Now, when the hour had come, with its appointed limits fulfilled,  
> The life-giving Paraclete descended upon us,  
> So that we might be borne as witnesses of the new life  
> To the nations.  
>   
> That day fulfilled the vows of the Fathers,  
> Awaited through so many ages.  
> In this hope the first father Abraham  
> Instructed his Isaac.  
>   
> In this hope Israel, through twelve tribes,  
> Drew forth blessed offspring.  
> All that glorious company of kings  
> And prophets lives forever.  
>   
> They announced this to our fathers,  
> And we hand it on to our descendants,  
> To whom the blessed days have now come,  
> So that we may be their interpreters.  
>   
> We saw, before the foundations of the world,  
> The things appointed by God.  
> We are witnesses of what we see,  
> And we proclaim it so that every people may hear.  
>   
> This trumpet, proceeding from Zion,  
> Filled the world with the mighty deeds of the Messiah.  
> By it the sun, having abandoned evening, brings back the dawn,  
> And changes morning into evening.  
>   
> Here the sound will be heard throughout the kingdoms of the world,  
> And the ends of the earth will learn Christ.  
> Nothing lies hidden beneath the frozen north;  
> Nothing human is oppressed beneath the south,  
>   
> That does not, when this trumpet-call of the voice is heard everywhere,  
> Adore upon the mountain of Israel.  
>   
> New ages are present, the idols having been abandoned,  
> And the demons flee, defeated.  
> The royal power of hell has been cut down  
> By the sign of the cross, which bears the standards of Christ.  
>   
> The armies rebellious against God lie hidden  
> Beneath the Stygian night, never to be freed.  
> Victorious, Christ brought his trophies to heaven,  
> To the right hand of God the Father.  
>   
> These things having been spoken, tongues of flame  
> Seemed to hang above them from heaven;  
> And as the Spirit of Christ had filled each one,  
> So the soul of each burned.  
>   
> The Jewish crowd, ignorant of the mysteries,  
> Laughed with profane gestures;  
> And the company of foreigners, visiting the festivals  
> Within the walls of Jerusalem,  
>   
> Heard each of these speakers in his own voice,  
> In his own language.  
>   
> The man whose mind was struck, whose reason was powerless,  
> Evaded the miracle with a jest.  
> But Peter, keen, with multilingual song,  
> Preached with his mouth set free.  
>   
> They heard him speak of God the Father, the Son, and the Spirit,  
> From the very beginning of the world.  
> Though a thousand peoples were present with discordant tongues,  
> Uneducated multitudes,  
>   
> Each heard him speaking in his own sound,  
> And very many believed.  
>   
> This is the first light of the gathered Church;  
> From this beginning it remains forever.  
>   
> That same Spirit, who appeared above the witnesses  
> Flying with tongues of flame,  
> Will preserve her until the trumpet, with its final sound,  
> Awakens the dead.  
>   
> Then, translated, she will depart into Abraham’s bosom,  
> There to behold Christ forever.

74. After copying this hymn, Barthius says: “Let someone trained in the readings of Prudentius and Paulinus judge whether anything could be more like their writings.” If I must answer Barthius, I shall say openly that Prudentius and Paulinus are very unlike each other, and that this iambic poem comes closer to the style of Paulinus than to that of Prudentius.

For Paulinus too wrote hymns, as he himself indicates in Letter 45 to Alypius: “Write this to me also: which hymn of mine you have come to know.” Gennadius reports that Paulinus composed a *Sacramentary* and a *Hymnary*. Some interpret this badly as referring to only one hymn, although a *Hymnary*, like a *Sacramentary*, is an ecclesiastical book containing several hymns.

Nevertheless, Barthius suspects that many works bearing Paulinus’s name are actually by Prudentius.

[Note: Thus, in Book VIII of the *Adversaria*, chapter 12, he argues: “The Lament of Babylon beside the Rivers. Paulinus used the same words in Psalm 136, unless that poem too is Prudentian, as we suspect many works now bear other titles. Since, because of his learning and subject matter, he was easily the foremost of all Christian poets, everyone added many works by others to his books, and from this there ultimately arose a mixture and confusion of authors. Besides, among the certain works of Saint Paulinus there is a poem to Cytherius about the shipwreck of Martinianus, which is so like this iambic poem on the sending of the Holy Spirit that an egg is not more like an egg.”]

In the iambic poem quoted above, he conjectures that at verse 7 one should read *vitae* (“of life”) or *summum* (“the highest point”) instead of *finem* (“the end”).

In the Gothic, or Isidorian—also called Mozarabic—office, a hymn of Saint Vincent is recited from the hymn composed in his honor by Prudentius, with eight additional strophes prefixed. Joseph Blanchinius asserted in his notes on the Veronese codex of the Isidorian office that these appeared to be by Prudentius, certainly unaware how different those strophes are from Prudentian style and how full of metrical errors they are.

[Note: Here they are:

> A wondrous passion is present,  
> Of the holy martyr Levite,  
> For whom, blazing with glorious virtue,  
> A crown is given to Vincent.  
>   
> Blessed is that spirit  
> Which, after the triumph of battle,  
> After the dreadful bonds of prison,  
> The heavenly court received.  
>   
> Everyone forever marvels  
> At the martyr after the blood was touched,  
> Whom they wound with a sharp sword  
> By fragments of pottery.  
>   
> He is broken by no pain,  
> Conquered by no punishment;  
> Bearing flames upon his nails,  
> His steadfast faith remained.  
>   
> Thereafter they lay down  
> Christ’s faithful soldier on soft ground;  
> His body having been left behind,  
> His spirit migrates to the stars.  
>   
> The mad emperor orders  
> The body cast to wild beasts;  
> With a raven as guardian,  
> Wolfish hunger is driven away from the body.  
>   
> A grave madness rouses the tyrant,  
> And he orders the martyr,  
> Sewn into a small boat,  
> To be plunged into the deep sea.  
>   
> The highest honor is rendered:  
> At Christ’s command, to the shore,  
> Through restored and gentle waters,  
> He arrives before everyone as a rower.  
>   
> You alone, O twice-renowned one, and so forth.

In the Isidorian Breviary, stanza 5, verse 3 clearly reads *Carnis relicto pondere* (“the weight of the flesh having been left behind”) instead of *corpore* (“the body having been left behind”); and stanza 8, verse 4 reads *remiges* (“rowers”) instead of *remigeo*, which Blanchinius did not notice. Instead, for a different spelling, he reads *suscipit* for *suscepit*, *factum* for *tactum*, and *fragmina* for *fragmine*.]

I shall speak in chapter 4, in connection with Vatican Codex Alexandrinus 334, about the *Flowers of the Psalms*, which is a work of Prudentius of Troyes but is attributed by some to Clemens Prudentius. What sort of hymn to the Blessed Virgin Mary, attributed to our Prudentius in the catalogue of the Paris library, I certainly do not know; but I think it is the work of another Prudentius. See no. 98.

I do not distinguish the *Poem on Faith*, mentioned in the same catalogue, from the *Psychomachia*. Compare the same no. 98.

Joannes Christophorus Ritterus, in his dissertation *On the Water Flowing from Christ’s Side*, part 2 of the *Theological-Philological Treasury*, Amsterdam, 1702, says that Aurelius Prudentius, a poet not without standing in the Church, expresses the size of this wound—the wound in Christ’s side—in the following manner:

> If you have a stained heart,  
> Look upon a wound so wide:  
> From his heart there flows  
> A wave that washes away filth.

He does not explain where he took these verses from. But anyone who believed them to be Prudentius’s would know little of Prudentian style. Nor do I find in Prudentius the verse attributed to him by Barthius, Book XLI of the *Adversaria*, chapter 27:

> Now I seem to myself to be among crags and resounding groves.

Perhaps Barthius accidentally wrote the name Prudentius for that of another poet.

## Chapter IV. Manuscript Codices of Prudentius’s Works

56 75. In this chapter I shall collect, from various catalogues and other documents, information about the manuscript codices of Prudentius, where they are hidden, and also the manuscript notes and interpretations concerning him. It is laborious, certainly, but not useless work, since through it the divine poet may be increasingly illuminated.

Fabricius, in the *Bibliotheca Latina Antiqua*, praises a very ancient codex of Prudentius existing in the Ambrosian Library at Milan. Montfaucon testifies in his *Italian Diary*, p. 18, that he had seen no manuscript of more remote antiquity, and assigns this one to the seventh or eighth century. See no. 80 concerning this codex.

In a letter about the supports or spits of Diana of Ephesus, Holstenius explains an obscure passage of Minucius Felix and restores the true reading from another similar passage of Prudentius in a very excellent codex of the Urbino library, transferred to the Vatican. Fabricius also mentions this codex; we shall speak of it later.

Edmund Martene, in the *Literary Journey of Two Maurists*, published anonymously in French, part 2, p. 138, lists among the codices of the monastery of Münster poems of Prudentius written in the tenth century.

Joannes Aloysius Mingarellius, in the preface to the *Fascicle of Anecdotes*, describes a codex of the poems of Saint Paulinus preserved in the library of San Salvatore at Bologna, written, as he thinks, in the fourteenth century by Lippo Platesius. After thirteen poems of Paulinus, the following works of Prudentius occur:

> *Apotheosis*, that is, *On the Divinity*, by Prudentius, the most illustrious poet.  
> A poem or book of the same Prudentius against the Patripassian heretics.…  
> A book against the Unionists.…  
> A poem or book against the Jews.…  
> A poem or book against the heretics and unbelieving Homuncionites.…  
> A book *On the Nature of the Soul*.…  
> A book against the Phantastics.…  
> *Marciogenia*.…  
> A book against the Marcionites.…  
> A book called the *Psychomachia*.

Our friend Rochus Menciaca communicated to me the various readings of this codex. Together with our other friends, he has diligently undertaken to illuminate the whole of ecclesiastical history. The Bolognese codex contains only the *Apotheosis*, the *Hamartigenia*, and the *Psychomachia*; it is corrupt and perhaps has been altered according to Platesius’s judgment.

76. Nicolaus Antonius reports the following concerning a certain Vatican codex in his *Bibliotheca vetus Hispana*: “In the Vatican Library there is a codex of sufficiently ancient character, numbered 5821, containing all the works of Prudentius. On its first leaf we read a note in a more recent hand:

‘Joannes Antonius Mariettus, priest of the Society of Jesus, received this book as a gift from the most learned man Christophorus Colerus when I was living in Prague. Since I compared it with several manuscripts very carefully in various places, and especially with that famous and exceedingly old manuscript preserved at Regensburg in the library of St. Emmeram (Nicolaus Antonius writes “Emerianus”), I judge it to be of excellent quality and to have been written many years ago by a highly accomplished antiquarian. 1618, on the Ides of July.’

That Mariettus carefully compared the Aldine edition of Prudentius of 1501 with this codex and others, and added various readings in the margin, which we shall record when occasion permits. The book is preserved in the library of the Roman College; from it we have already given some material above, nos. 49 and 68.

I am uncertain whether this was Mariettus himself, or someone else, who compared the Cologne edition of Prudentius of 1589 and 1594, prepared from Giselinus’s first recension and preserved in the same library, with Sichard’s edition and with a certain manuscript. At the end of that manuscript he also copied verses by Constantina, the daughter of Constantine, and others by St. Damasus in honor of St. Agnes, which, I suppose, were excerpted from a Prudentian codex after the hymn of St. Agnes.

[Note: [Col. 0620D] He added the following note:

‘This edition of Sichard, Antwerp 1536, in octavo, with the commentaries of Nebrissensis, is of such a kind that it contains many annotations in the margin of the book, distinct from those in the text, so that it is not easy to know what belongs chiefly to Sichard. Sometimes what is written in the margin agrees with our manuscript, sometimes what is in the text, and sometimes neither. Therefore an edition with only the commentaries of Nebrissensis should first be sought, and then compared with this one, so that it may be seen what Sichard restored; finally both editions should be compared with our manuscript, so that we may see which readings in ours differ from all the others. From what I have noted, however, it is easy to recognize which of our readings Sichard had previously recorded and which he had not seen. For, as we said elsewhere, the book which he says was brought from Strasbourg does not appear to differ greatly from ours.’]

[Col. 0621A] In this codex the book *Cathemerinon* contained only the hymn for the eighth day before the Kalends of January and the following hymn of Epiphany, as far as the stanza “Among kindred blood.” Yet in the preceding hymns I notice some variant readings marked with the letter P. Whether this indicates a Palatine codex, a Prague codex, or another, I do not know; for it does not mean *potius*, although that word is sometimes written, just as the manuscript itself also has P.

The book *Peristephanon* in the same codex began with verse 107, “This restrains, torments, burns; this rattles chains.” In the hymn of St. Fructuosus, the anonymous person who collated the codex observes that his own codex is older and better than Sichard’s, and that most of the readings approved by Sichard are marked in his own manuscript, though by a more recent hand.

All the remaining works of Prudentius were present in this codex, except that in Book II against Symmachus a mark had been placed at verse 264, with the remainder lacking all the way to the end. The same anonymous annotator sometimes explained certain words of Prudentius, whether he himself interpreted them or took the explanations from another codex; we shall reproduce these interpretations in their proper places.

I am almost certain that this was Mariettus’s codex, which we shall mention again among the Vatican manuscripts.

In the Angelica Library at Rome, among the Augustinian Fathers, I saw and collated a manuscript of the *Psychomachia*. The codex was written by a certain Cistercian monk in 1472 from a very ancient exemplar, apparently, though not without errors.

[Note: [Col. 0621D] This codex contains the preface to the works, “For five years,” the preface to the *Psychomachia*, and the *Psychomachia*. Certain verses follow, said to be Philelphus’s *Symbolum*, then poems by Lactantius and Sedulius’s *On Easter*.]

I shall call this codex Angelicum, or simply Aug. in its initial letters.

The place of a codex may be taken by Weitz’s edition of Prudentius, with various manuscript readings from an old codex belonging to the distinguished bishop Joseph Antonius Reggius. He communicated to me with singular generosity not only this edition but also all the Vatican codices of Prudentius and certain observations of his own, collected through profound learning and constant reading. Thus, in gratitude, I willingly acknowledge that this Roman edition of Prudentius owes very much to the learned custodian of the Vatican Library.

77. In the Vatican Library I saw and examined all the codices that exist there, which I shall describe in their order.

[Col. 0622A] Among the Vatican codices—for in the Vatican Library some manuscripts are called Vatican, others Alexandrian, others Urbinat﻿e, and others Otthobonian, having been transferred to the Vatican from various libraries by order of several popes—is:

1. Codex no. 2766, page 81, parchment, in octavo, believed to have been written in the twelfth century. Among other poems by various authors it contains the *Psychomachia*, or *The Battle of the Soul*, with red initials and marginal annotations, but only at the beginning; it has no titles such as occur in the others, and no diphthongs. Thus it writes *hostentatrix*, *hictibus*, and so forth. At the end: “The book ends.” It is full of very many errors. We call this codex E.

2. Vatican Codex 2868, page 51, parchment, in quarto, of the thirteenth century. It contains the *Psychomachia* among other poems by various authors. The titles are absent, including the first title of the work.

[Note: [Col. 0621D] In the margin there is an observation about the poem and its author, whose elegance may be sampled from these words:

‘At the beginning of this book the matters investigated at the beginnings of other books are investigated, namely how many causes there are and of what kinds,’ and so forth.

He then distinguishes four causes: material, formal, efficient, and final. Of the efficient cause he writes:

‘The efficient cause was Aurelius Prudentius, a layman, a Spanish scholar; he was married.’

This may perhaps have been taken from the end of the hymn of St. Cassianus. The annotator adds that Aurelius is derived from gold, Prudentius from prudence or providence, and Clemens from the mind of heaven; that he came to Rome and gave himself over to the Church; and that he first wrote the book of the Martyrs, second the Hymns, and third the *Psychomachia*.

At the end of the codex: “The book of Prudentius on the *Sichomachia* ends.” “The Slav concerning Varus begins.” “The Slav’s harmonious sayings concerning Varus begin, fashioned in verse by Jacob of Benevento.”

In the same codex there is a work by Henricus Florentinus in elegiac verse.]

Its script approaches the fourteenth century. Its orthography includes *tempto*, *honero*, *glorie*, and so forth. How little care was taken may be learned from the first verse: “The faithful old man is the first path of believing.” We call this codex F.

3. Vatican Codex 3267, page 34, parchment, twelfth century, in octavo. The *Psychomachia* is in an ancient script, with glosses largely erased. Its orthography includes *seuientis*, *fallerata*, *temptes*, *connisa*, and *honero*. Certain poems of Ovid precede it; the *Life of Prudentius* by Gennadius follows, in which *Dirocheum* is read for *Dittochaeum*. There are also the preface “For five years,” with its interpretation, and commentaries on the *Psychomachia*, which appear more recent. We have given this codex the name C.

4. Vatican Codex 3859, parchment, eleventh century, in quarto. It contains the books *Cathemerinon*, *Peristephanon*, *Apotheosis*, *Hamartigenia*, and the books against Symmachus, written with extreme carelessness; the *Dittochaeum* is without any title for the poem, although some titles occur in the tetrastichs, written in a childish manner. The *Dittochaeum* ends with these verses:

> The baskets are filled with an excess of crumb-like morsels,
>
> Twelvefold: such is the abundance of the eternal table.

The *Psychomachia* is also missing, as is the conclusion of the poems:

> He offers sacrifice to God the Father,
>
> Pious, faithful, innocent.

[Note: [Col. 0622D] The order of the book *Peristephanon* is as follows:

1. Saints Hemeterius and Celedonius;  
2. St. Vincentius;  
3. The eighteen holy martyrs of Zaragoza;  
4. Saints Fructuosus and his companions;  
5. St. Quirinus;  
6. Concerning the place where the martyrs suffered, now a baptistery at Calagurris (I shall discuss this title in its proper place);  
7. Cassianus to Valerianus the bishop (there is an error here as well);  
8. Hippolytus (rather, “to Valerianus the bishop” should be added here);  
9. Saints Peter and Paul;  
10. St. Cyprianus;  
11. St. Agnes;  
12. St. Laurentius;  
13. St. Eulalia;  
14. The book concerning the blessed martyr Romanus;  
15. The Nativity of the Lord;  
16. The Epiphany.]

[Col. 0623A] Montfaucon also cites this codex under the same number, 3859, in his *Bibliotheca bibliothecarum manuscriptorum*. He calls it elegant and thinks it was written in the tenth or ninth century. In the catalogue shown to me from the Vatican Library it is said to have been written in the eleventh century.

This is Vatican Codex A, whose glosses and variant readings we cite. Mariettus collated it very carefully with the Aldine edition, from which we have benefited; nevertheless, we did not entirely spare ourselves the labor, since we ourselves collated the principal passages, even after testing and fully examining Mariettus’s great diligence. We had a representation of this codex’s script engraved in copper.

5. Vatican Codex 3860, also of the eleventh century, parchment, in quarto. Mariettus likewise collated this exemplar with Aldus’s edition and considers it older than the preceding codex. We call it codex B, and we have shown in copper an image of its script.

[Note: [Col. 0623] A specimen of this codex and of several cited below appears at the front of the volume. There the reader will also find copper engravings of the images repeatedly mentioned, apart from a few to which we ourselves have added references. Editor.]

Montfaucon likewise asserts that this codex is elegant and was written in the ninth century, in the place cited above. But it contains only the book *Cathemerinon*, and that incomplete; the book *Peristephanon*; the *Titles of the Stories*; and the *Apotheosis*. The remaining poems of Prudentius are missing. There are, however, poems in praise of St. Agnes by Constantina, daughter of Constantine, and by Pope St. Damasus.

6. Vatican Codex 4318, page 52, thirteenth century, paper, in octavo. Its title in the catalogue of the Vatican Library is: “Commentaries on Prudentius, *On the Dove*, the stories of the Old and New Testaments.”

[Note: [Col. 0623D] On page 52 of the codex the commentaries begin together with the tetrastichs of the *Dittochaeum*, and the title is said to be: “The author Prudentius’s book on the new dove”—perhaps it should be read “on Eve the dove”—“of the stories of the Old and New Testament.” It ends with the tetrastich on the Apocalypse.

On page 63 another exposition of the stories by Aurelius Prudentius follows. It is noted that the author had three names: Prudentius, because he was prudent; Aureolus, because he led a golden life; Clemens, because he was [perhaps: “as if”] “the mind of heaven,” since he had his mind on heavenly things.

It is added: “This book is called *Dittochaeus*, that is, the refreshment of the Old and New Testament . . . Its title is: ‘Prudentius begins his treatment of the Old and New Testament.’”

The script belongs to a later age; the etymologies are ridiculous, and the commentaries are useless to us, even when a hand written in the margin commands the reader to attend carefully. We therefore pass over this codex without assigning it any name. Why the *Dittochaeum* is usually entitled “On the Dove” I explained above, no. 64.]

7. Vatican Codex 5356, parchment, in quarto, thirteenth century. In the catalogue of the Vatican Library it is entered as: “Prudentius’s book on certain men of the Old Testament.”

The codex itself has the title: “The book on Adam and Eve begins.” At the end: “The book of Prudentius ends.” The initials are in various colors; the titles of the tetrastichs are written in red. In the New Testament, however, there is only the first title: “On the New Testament and Gabriel, the messenger of Christ.”

Its orthography includes *sopnus*, *archa*, *cratherem*, *fauille*, and *nuptu* for *nutu*. Many errors occur. We have named this codex D.

8. Vatican Codex 5821, extremely ancient, written in the ninth or at least the tenth century, as I find noted in the catalogue of the Vatican Library.

This is Mariettus’s codex, discussed above under no. 76. The note of Mariettus reported by Nicolaus Antonius belongs to the Ides of July in the year 1618. It had indeed been written by the first hand “in the library of St. Emeretianus,” but this was corrected to “St. Emeram,” which is the monastery’s true name.
