We frequently cite this codex, but under the name Mariettus, or Mar., rather than distinguishing it by a letter, as we do most of the other Vatican codices. We reproduce its script in copper. What it contains, and in what order, we shall state more distinctly in the commentaries.

78. From the Alexandrian Library of the Vatican:

1. Codex 58, formerly 1225, containing hymns; thirteenth century, parchment. The codex contains the book *Cathemerinon*, excluding the final two hymns, on the Nativity and Epiphany of the Lord, and the poem *Psychomachia*.

[Note: [Col. 0624D] There are no titles either in the book *Cathemerinon* or in the *Psychomachia*. Only at the end of the *Psychomachia* is it noted: “Here ends the book of the poet Prudentius: Faith, idolatry [sic], chastity, lust, patience, anger, humility, pride, sobriety, extravagance, kindness, greed, concord, discord.”

At the end of the book *Cathemerinon*: “The book of Prudentius ends.”]

There are no diphthongs. It writes *horis* for *oris*, *tempto*, *alumpnus*, and so forth. We assign this codex the name O.

2. Alexandrian Vatican Codex 74, parchment, in octavo, eleventh or twelfth century, containing poems. These are the books *Cathemerinon* and *Peristephanon* as far as the hymn of St. Romanus, at the verse “What is that disgraceful pomp?”—namely, “the ignoble.”

The preface has no inscription. After the preface: “The hymn before dawn begins,” and in the initial A a cock is depicted. Then: “Morning hymn.”

In the hymn “Good leader, inventor of the ruddy light,” there is no title. In the hymn “Give me the plectrum, boy, that I may sing to the faithful in dances,” the title has now vanished. The hymn “O fiery source of souls” bears the inscription:

[Col. 0624C] “Hymn for the funeral rites of the dead.”

The hymns of the Nativity and Epiphany of the Lord are missing. The book *Peristephanon* follows without a title.

[Note: [Col. 0624D] The order of the hymns is:

1. Saints Hemeterius and Celedonius, without a title;  
2. The Passion of St. Vincentius;  
3. The Passion of the eighteen holy martyrs;  
4. The Passion of St. Fructuosus;  
5. The Passion of St. Quirinus;  
6. Without a title: “The place chosen for Christ,” and so forth;  
7. The Passion of St. Cassianus;  
8. Without a title, the hymn of St. Hippolytus;  
9. The Passion of the holy apostles Peter and Paul;  
10. The Passion of St. Cyprianus;  
11. The Passion of St. Agnes (so it is written);  
12. Without a title, the hymn of St. Laurentius;  
13. The hymn of St. Eulalia, without a title;  
14. The hymn of St. Romanus, without a title.]

There are few diphthongs. The orthography includes *sollepnem*, *lauachrum*, and *hyemps*. In the initial letter of the preface “For five years,” an image of Prudentius had been painted, as far as I can determine, in the same kind of clothing as in the Urbinate codex; the features of the face have been completely erased. See no. 58, chapter 1 of the *Prolegomena*. This codex is designated P in our commentaries.

3. Alexandrian Vatican Codex 321, parchment, in a large folio, written approximately in the tenth century.

[Col. 0625A] At the beginning there is a eulogy of Prudentius: “This Aurelius Prudentius Clemens, partly during his consulship,” and so forth, almost as I quoted above under no. 49 from Vatican Codex 3859.

Then come the inscription and list of the works.

[Note: [Col. 0625B] “The books, nine in number, of Aurelius Prudentius Clemens, a man of consular rank: *Cathemerinon*, *Apotheosis*, *Hamartigenia*, *Psychomachia*, *Against Symmachus*, Book II *Against Symmachus*, *Romanus*, *Peristephanon*, *Titles of the Stories*.”

Before the preface “For five years already ten” there is an inscription, “Preface,” and nothing else.

After Book II *Against Symmachus* one reads: “Concerning his own little works, Prudentius: ‘He offers sacrifice to God the Father,’” and so forth, with the final verse “By whose governance we live.” “*Against Symmachus* ends.”

Then: “The *Titles of the Stories* begin.” After the titles, in the same ancient script: “Epilogue, that is, the conclusion and end of the book: ‘Pious, faithful, innocent,’” with the final verse, “By whose governance we live.”]

This is the only complete codex among so many Vatican manuscripts in which this conclusion of the poems is written: first after the books against Symmachus, as though it were their epilogue, and then after the *Titles of the Stories*, or *Dittochaeum*, as though it were the conclusion of all the poems.

We provide an engraving in copper of the codex’s script. Its variant readings are recorded under the name Alexandrian Codex, or Alex.

[Note: [Col. 0625C] We also benefited from the labor and diligence of the distinguished Father Peregrinus Chiesa. He had formerly been preparing an edition of Prudentius and had carefully collated this codex; with great kindness he supplied us with the notes he had taken from it for transcription. I also owe it to him that I can make leisurely use of the edition prepared for the use of the Dauphin, which I have already noted is extremely rare.

In the Alexandrian codex I observed certain matters worthy of a special note. The titles of the hymns are:

“Hymn at cockcrow”;  
“Morning hymn”;  
“Hymn at the lighting of the lamp”;  
“Hymn concerning the funeral rites of the dead”;  
“Hymn for the eighth day before the Kalends of January”;  
“Hymn on the Epiphany”;  
the others, as in the common editions.

After the book *Cathemerinon*: “The *Apotheosis* begins,” “God is threefold and supreme,” and so forth, with the following titles:

“The book begins against the heresy that asserts that the Father suffered”;  
“Against the Unionites”;  
“Against the Jews”;  
“Against the Homuncionites”;  
“On the nature of the soul”;  
“Against the Phantasmaticists, who deny that Christ had a true body.”

“*Apotheosis* ends.”

[Col. 0625D] Then: “The book *Hamartigenia* begins.” At the end: “Book III of *Hamartigenia* ends.”

Then: “Book IV of the *Psychomachia* begins.” After the preface, titles are attached in the margin; at the end: “Book III of the *Psychomachia* ends.” I shall discuss this variation in the numbering of the books more fully in the commentaries.

After the *Psychomachia*: “Book I against the speech of Symmachus begins.” After this: “Book I against the speech of Symmachus ends. Book II begins, successfully, amen.”

At the end: “Book II against Symmachus ends, by Aurelius Prudentius Clemens, a most illustrious man.”

“The same author’s *Romanus* against the Gentiles begins.”

After the hymn of St. Romanus: “*Romanus* of Aurelius Prudentius Clemens ends. The book *Peristephanon* begins.”

The order and titles of the hymns are:

1. “Hymn in honor of the holy martyrs Emeterius and Chelidonius of Calagurris.”  
2. “The Passion of the most blessed martyr Laurentius begins.”  
3. “Hymn in honor of the passion of the most blessed martyr Eulalia.”  
4. “The Passion of the martyr Vincentius begins.”  
5. “Hymn in honor of the eighteen holy martyrs of Zaragoza.” At the end: “The Passion of the eighteen holy martyrs ends.”  
6. “The Passion of St. Agnes begins.” Afterwards: “The Passion of St. Agnes ends.”  
7. “Hymn in honor of the most blessed martyrs Fructuosus, bishop of the Church of Tarragona, and the deacons Augurius and Eulogius.”  
8. “Hymn in honor of Quirinus, the most blessed martyr and bishop of the Church of Siscia.” “The Passion of Quirinus ends.”  
9. “The Passion of Cassianus of Forum Cornelium begins.” “It ends.”  
10. “The work concerning the place where the martyrs suffered, now a baptistery, begins.”  
11. “To Valerianus the bishop, concerning the passion of Hippolytus, the most blessed martyr.”  
12. “The Passion of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul.”  
13. “The Passion of the blessed martyr Cyprianus.”]

4. Alexandrian Vatican Codex 334, written in the tenth century: “Flowers of the Psalms, with a preface to a widow.” This is the catalogue of Prudentius’s works that I received from the officials of the Vatican Library.

In the codex itself I read: “The *Flowers of the Psalms* of Prudentius, with a preface to a widow, in Lombard script.”

And on the first page: “The Vatican Codex has as its title: ‘The *Flowers of the Psalms* of Prudentius, with a preface to a widow.’ This author is certainly extremely ancient, since the name ‘widows,’ or ‘deaconesses,’ has long since fallen out of use in the Church. Perhaps this Prudentius should be assigned to the time of St. Jerome, unless we should rather say that he is the same as the Christian poet himself, who flourished at the beginning of the fifth century.”

And afterwards: “Found among the books of L. Zaccagni.”

The title of the work is: “The Psalter of Prudentius begins: ‘Lord, most merciful king.’”

I have included this codex because I found it listed among the Prudentian codices in the catalogue of the Vatican Library. The author, however, is not Aurelius Clemens Prudentius, but another Prudentius, namely Prudentius Galindo, a Spaniard by nationality and bishop of Troyes. Nicolaus Antonius may be consulted concerning him in the *Bibliotheca vetus Hispana*.

[Note: [Col. 0626C] His *Flowers of the Psalms* appears in the edition of the works of Cardinal Thomasius, prepared and edited by Joseph Blanchinius, volume II, page 464. Blanchinius published this little work from the celebrated Royal Vatican Codex 334, adding a preface and variant readings from another Vatican codex numbered 84. He thinks both codices belong to the tenth century.

The preface begins: “When a certain noble matron …” No other mention is made of deaconesses. The title is: “The prologue of Prudentius the bishop concerning the *Flowers of the Psalms* begins.”

In Vatican Codex 191 there is another work by the same Prudentius, entitled: “This Prudentius the bishop of Tricasia collected from both the Old and New Testament and ordered to be committed to the memory of those hastening toward holy orders; these are also called *Precepts*.”

Compare what will be said on page 221, in the note beginning with the words “I said, no. 78.”]

5. Alexandrian Vatican Codex 348, parchment, in octavo, ninth century, without any title. It begins: “For five years already ten.” At the end: “The preface ends.”

Then comes this inscription: “The book of the Hymns of Aurelius Prudentius Clemens, the most noble and eloquent poet, begins.”

[Col. 0626B] There are some glosses and explanations of the meters, and titles written in red.

[Note: [Col. 0626D] Among these I shall transcribe the following:

“Hymn at cockcrow.” In the initial A a cock is depicted with a green branch hanging from its beak.

“Morning hymn.”

“The hymn at the lighting begins.” It is not sufficiently clear whether it is written “at the lighting of the light” or “of the lamp.”

“Hymn for every hour.”

“Hymn concerning the funeral rites of the dead.”

After this hymn: “The first book of hymns ends. The second book, *Peristephanon*, begins: hymn in honor of the martyrs Emeterius and Chelidonius of Calagurris.”

But this entire hymn and those that follow are missing, the leaves having been torn out as far as verse 1110 of the *Passion of St. Romanus*. When that poem ends, one reads:

“Romanus of Aurelius Prudentius Clemens ends.”

“The hymn for the eighth day before the Kalends of January begins.”

At the end: “The hymn for the eighth day before the Kalends of January ends,” that is, the Nativity of the Lord.

“The *Cathemerinon* of Prudentius Clemens ends.”

“CV. CV.”

“Concerning his own little works begins: ‘He offers sacrifice to God the Father.’”

At the end a second hand added the verse: “By whose governance we live.”

After this ode: “The *Titles of the Stories* through Adam and Eve begin. Tetrastichs.”

This is not placed as a title, but as an explanation of the meter, or as a name.

When the *Dittochaeum* has ended: “The *Titles of the Stories* end.”

“*Apotheosis* begins,” that is, “On Divinity.”

The leaves after the two prefaces to the *Apotheosis* are missing.]

This codex must be held in high esteem. If only it were not mutilated and shortened! Its orthography includes *ymnus*, *inrepsit*, and similar forms with diphthongs. This codex is called I in our commentaries.

[Col. 0627A] 6. Alexandrian Vatican Codex 1439, in octavo, parchment, eleventh century. Its inscription is: “The book of Aurelius Clemens Prudentius’s *Psychomachia* begins.”

There are some glosses in the margin and between the lines. There are scarcely any titles. At the end: “The book ends.”

“Aurelius Prudentius Clemens, learned in the art of verse, engaged the battles of virtues against vices.”

There are some corrections by a recent hand, which on the first page wrote “Nicolai Heinsii,” as though he had owned the book.

Its orthography includes *onore*, *haut*, and no diphthongs. This codex is fairly correct, and we call it G.

7. Alexandrian Vatican Codex 1702, parchment, in quarto, twelfth century. It contains poems. The book *Cathemerinon* is incomplete, for it begins at verse 45 of hymn 5: “But the king of the Nile shore, envious …”

Afterwards: “The hymn before sleep begins,” and similarly other titles. But in the hymn “For every hour” and in “For the funeral rites” the title is missing.

In this book *Cathemerinon* there are some glosses. After the hymns of the Nativity and Epiphany of the Lord have been omitted, the book *Peristephanon* follows without an inscription; titles have been added to the hymns by a recent hand.

[Note: [Col. 0627D] The order of the hymns is:

1. Saints Hemeterius and Celedonius;  
2. St. Vincentius;  
3. St. Laurentius;  
4. St. Hippolytus;  
5. St. Cyprianus;  
6. Saints Peter and Paul;  
7. The eighteen holy martyrs of Zaragoza;  
8. St. Agnes;  
9. St. Eulalia;  
10. St. Fructuosus;  
11. St. Quirinus;  
12. St. Cassianus;  
13. St. Romanus;  
14. On the Nativity of the Lord;  
15. On the Epiphany.]

Afterwards: “Pious, faithful, innocent,” with the final verse “By whose governance we live.” A title has been added to this poem by a recent hand: “The conclusion of the remaining works.”

The *Dittochaeum* follows, with a recent marginal inscription: “The Diptych of the Old and New Testament, which some attribute to Amoenus and others to Sedulius.” Concerning this inscription, see no. 66.

Then comes the *Apotheosis*. When it ends, the following verse is written by a hand unknown to me: “Cheese ought to have a place before the hearth.”

Then follows the preface to the *Hamartigenia* as far as verse 6. The remainder is missing.

It writes *perhennis* and similar forms; many diphthongs are absent. Most of the glosses are like those in Vatican A and I. We have named this codex Q.

8. Alexandrian Vatican Codex 1835, in quarto, parchment, thirteenth century. The *Psychomachia* is accompanied by annotations, most of which have been worn away. The titles are missing. At the end: “The book of Prudentius ends.”

Its orthography includes *temptes* and *horis* for *oris*, without diphthongs. At the beginning it is noted: “This codex belonged to the library of St. Sylvester,” I think on the Quirinal Hill. This codex is called L in our commentaries.

9. Alexandrian Vatican Codex 1838, paper, in quarto, written in the fourteenth century, containing the *Dittochaeum*. Its title in the list of the codex’s works is: “Prudentius’s *Dove*, with commentary.”

[Note: [Col. 0627D] The commentary says:

‘The author here was Clemens Aurelius Prudentius … Clemens from clemency, Aurelius from gold, Prudentius from prudence … He wrote a book on the Dove, which we now intend to discuss.’]

This codex was written in 1472, as appears from a note on the first page, and therefore belongs to the fifteenth century, not the fourteenth, as had been stated in the catalogue shown to me.

The codex is erroneous, its commentaries are of no use, and the titles are missing. We call it codex N.

10. Alexandrian Vatican Codex 2078, ninth century, small folio, parchment.

[Col. 0628A] “Aurelius Prudentius Clemens. The Contest of the Virtues against the Vices.”

It begins without a preface: “Christ, who has always pitied the grievous labors of men.”

Much is missing from the verse “From this there arises unexpectedly” to the verse “We know the uncertain things.” The final verse, “Eternal …,” and so forth, is also missing.

Nothing, however, is torn or erased. Perhaps it was copied from another incomplete codex.

Its writing includes *adgreditur*, *sulphoreus*, *thoracha*, and no diphthongs. There are quite a few errors. This is codex H.

[Col. 0628B] 11. Vatican Palatine Codex 235, parchment, in folio, approximately eleventh century. Page 45 of this codex reads: “Glosses on Prudentius begin.”

[Note: [Col. 0628D] To the eulogy of Gennadius on Prudentius these particular glosses are added:

“Distinguished”: noble or famous.  
“Ditrocheum”: double refreshment, that is, concerning the Old and New Testament.  
“Excepted”: separated from one another.  
“Apotheosis”: deification.

I affirm again and confirm that in no Vatican codex have I found *Diptychon* written by an ancient hand in this way. Someone else reports that the most approved Vatican codices support this title, *Diptychon*. But perhaps he took recent catalogue titles for ancient ones.]

Most of the glosses are like those in I and Vatican A. I shall insert some peculiar to this codex in their proper places.

After the hymn concerning the funeral rites: “The book of the Hymns ends.” The hymns on the Nativity and Epiphany follow. Afterwards comes the *Peristephanon*, or “On the Crowned,” that is, the martyrs, but there are no glosses. Immediately follows the *Apotheosis*, with titles written in red.

At the end: “The *Apotheosis*, on Divinity, ends.”

“*Hamartigenia* begins, that is, on the origin of sins, against the Marcionites, who assert that there are two gods.”

The *Psychomachia* and the two books against Symmachus follow, but the glosses do not continue to the end of the second book.

It should be noted that this codex contains only glosses, not poems.

[Col. 0628C] The codex is written in a bright, elegant script. We call it T.

79. 12. Vatican Palatine Codex 242, in duodecimo, approximately twelfth century. “On Prudentius and his works.”

This little work is only a preface to the poem *Psychomachia*.

[Note: [Col. 0628D] Certain things are related about Prudentius that are either false or insufficiently established: that he studied literature at Rome, that he attained the consulship, and that, finally receiving the faith, he became a Christian.

It is added that the book bears the title: “The book of Aurelius Prudentius Clemens.”

“The book of the *Psychomachia* begins.”

It is also said that he wrote certain books on Divinity, among which he composed this one, calling it the *Psychomachia*.]

In fact, after other little works by other authors, the *Psychomachia* occurs at the end of this codex, although it is not mentioned in the index; but it ends at verse 683, “He inflicted this wound,” and so forth.

The script appears to belong to the eleventh or tenth century. Much has already vanished; some titles are present and others absent.

Its orthography includes *lues*, not *luis*, in the nominative case, but later *famis*, and above it *fames*, as well as *seuientis*, *glorie*, and *harenas*. We assign this codex the name R.

13. Vatican Palatine Codex 1715, parchment, in octavo, written approximately in the eleventh century. It begins: “The gloss of Aurelius Clemens Prudentius.”

[Col. 0628D] This little work consists of thirty pages.

[Note: [Col. 0629D] It begins as follows:

“*Kyrocheum*: that is, manual.  
*Exameron*: of six days.  
*Apotheosis*: that is, on Divinity.  
*Hamartigenia*: that is, the origin of sins.  
*Psychomachia*: the battle of the soul,” and so forth.

These are glosses on the life of Prudentius written by Gennadius.]

There are few glosses, some of which we shall give in their proper places; nothing else is present apart from the glosses.

Its orthography includes *effebi*, *frenesis*, and *ymnus*, with diphthongs. The glosses are chiefly concerned with explanations of stories. This codex will be called S.

14. Vatican Urbinas 666. “Little works of Prudentius.”

Another title, written with great magnificence, reads: “This most splendid codex contains the works of Aurelius Prudentius Clemens, a most learned man.”

A list of the poems preceded it. The inscription of the preface is: “The preface of Aurelius Prudentius Clemens to the following little works: ‘For five years,’ and so forth.”

In the initial letter P an image of the author is depicted, as we said in the *Prolegomena*, no. 58.

At the end of the codex: “Book II against Symmachus, on the restoration of the altar, ends. Antonius Sinibaldus transcribed this in Florence, in the year of Christ 1481, 20 November.”

The codex is a folio, on smooth, bright parchment, written in an elegant script and richly ornamented with many golden letters and excellent images of the saints whom Prudentius praises, as I can confirm on the judgment of experienced men.

[Note: [Col. 0629D] In the arrangement of the works this codex resembles the Florentine codex, which will be discussed below under no. 85 and following. In my opinion, the Florentine codex was copied from the Urbinate, or both were copied from some extremely ancient exemplar.

In the book *Cathemerinon* most things are as in the Florentine codex and the printed editions, but these distinctive titles occur:

“At cockcrow”;  
“At the lighting of the lamp”;  
“At every hour”;  
“Concerning the funeral rites of the dead”;  
“On the Nativity of the Lord”;  
“On the Epiphany.”

In the book *Peristephanon* the title of the book and hymn 1 are missing. It reads: “The Passion of the thirteen holy martyrs of Zaragoza,” instead of “the eighteen holy martyrs.”

Likewise: “The Passion of St. Fructuosus, first bishop of Tarragona, and his companions.”

And: “Verses in praise of the baptistery made illustrious by the blood of two martyrs.”

The remainder is as in the Florentine codex.]

We call this the Urbinate codex, or simply Urb. in its initial letters. For Holstenius’s judgment concerning it, see above, no. 75.

15. Vatican Otthobonian Codex 237, paper, in octavo. “Prudentius on Blessed Cassianus.”

This codex contains the *Legend of St. Cassianus the Martyr*, compiled by Brother Jacobus of the Order of Preachers. Franciscus Ferrus, a canon of Imola, dedicates it to Hieronymus Dandino, bishop of Imola. Jacobus wrote it at Bologna in the year 1282.

On folio 27: “The poet Prudentius sang as follows about Blessed Cassianus: ‘Sylla,’ and so forth.”

At the end: “Prudentius, as is well known, a man of faith, commending religious doctrines also through the pleasure of poetry,” and so forth.

This will be the codex called X.

16. Vatican Otthobonian Codex 1193, paper, in quarto, formerly among the codices of Joannes Angelus, duke of Altaemps. The *Dittochaeum* is without any inscription. There are some interlinear glosses.

The *Dittochaeum* occurs on page 108 of this codex, as we have said, and the same work occurs again on page 113 with a longer commentary; but in this second instance only the first two tetrastichs are present.

At the beginning of the second commentary it is said:

“Among the works composed by Prudentius, this is the most useful. Its subject is the double refreshment of the New and Old Testament, and its title is: ‘The tetrastich of Aurelius Clemens Prudentius on the Dove begins.’”

This codex is extremely erroneous. We have called it Y.

17. Vatican Otthobonian Codex 1220, in quarto, paper. It contains the *Dittochaeum* with commentaries, as above in codex Y. Here, however, the work is complete. At the end: “The book of Prudentius ends.”

This codex will be called Z in the commentary.

### 18. Codex Vaticanus Otthobonianus 1297

A parchment codex in folio, from the thirteenth or fourteenth century, elegant and ornamented with titles written in red, which had belonged to the books of John Angelo, Duke of Altaemps. It begins: “The book of Prudentius,” that is, the *Columba* of the New and Old Testament. In the commentaries it is said to bear the title: “Here begins the book of the *Dittocheus*”—a name arbitrarily chosen, from Greek *dia*, in Latin “refection” or “refreshment.” From this you may learn the other absurdities of the commentaries. At the end: “Here ends the *Columba* of the Old and New Testament.” The titles differ from the ancient ones, having been spun out of the interpreter’s own invention. The codex is faulty, but we shall call it AA.

### 19. Codex Vaticanus Otthobonianus 1502

A parchment codex in quarto, elegantly written with multicolored titles. It begins: “The book concerning the Two Testaments.” Immediately thereafter: “Eve, the dove.” Other titles are recent. At the end: “Here ends Prudentius’ book concerning the Two Testaments.” The *Dittochaeum* begins on folio 12 of this codex; on folio 39 the *Psychomachia* is found, though it is not noted at all in the catalogue of the Vatican Library. There is no inscription either in the preface or in the work, which ends with the verse “We render eternal …,” etc. The age of the codex is approximately the thirteenth century; we designate it BB.

[Col. 0630C] **20.** Codex Vaticanus Otthobonianus 3325, in quarto, on paper. The *Dittochaeum* lacks its first title; there are other titles in the tetrastichs, but they are recent. In nearly all these copies the same variants of the *Dittochaeum* occur, and their authority should not be considered great.

So much for the Vatican codices. If you compare the catalogue I compiled with what Montfaucon reports about these same manuscripts, you will easily recognize how imperfect the “Library of Libraries” of manuscripts is. Nevertheless, the work of that learned and most diligent man should not be despised, since those who have no opportunity to inspect the manuscripts and libraries themselves can be greatly assisted by it.

Now I shall say a few words about the Regensburg, Prague, and Vienna manuscripts, whose variant readings I borrowed from Marietti’s *Adversaria*.[^c0063-1]

[^c0063-1]: [Col. 0630D] Concerning the Regensburg manuscript Marietti notes the following: “The manuscript of the monastery of Saint Emmeram is the best of all those I have seen, and plainly a good one, except that some utterly incompetent person substituted much of his own text for the earlier readings, erasing them so thoroughly that no trace whatever of the ancient reading remains; we have noted this in the proper places. For this reason I do not think that Prudentius can still be corrected exactly and restored to his former purity unless we obtain another ancient manuscript besides those we have used, by which the passages erased here might be restored. We compared it with our own manuscript with the greatest care, and there was nothing different in it that we had not noted in ours, although we did not always record the places where ours agreed with it. Thus, whenever nothing particular is noted in our manuscript, it will be a sure sign that the same reading is found in that one as in ours. Giphanius also used this same book, and we obtained our knowledge of it through the efforts of Father Gorradus Viterius. In the same library of Saint Emmeram there is an excellent Lucan, a fairly ancient grammar of Donatus, and, in the sacristy, a New Testament written entirely in elegant majuscule letters about eight hundred years ago. I believe this to be the New Testament whose variant readings were published in 1786 under the title *Dissertation on the Golden and Very Ancient Manuscript Codex of the Holy Gospels of the Monastery of Saint Emmeram at Regensburg*, by Father Colomann Sanftl, printed by Johann Michael Englerth, 1786, in quarto. This codex had been preserved in the church of the monastery of Saint Emmeram for nearly nine hundred years, as the author of the dissertation explains in his preface.

“The order of the Regensburg codex as reported by Marietti is as follows: preface, ‘For five years’—the ten hymns of the *Cathemerinon*, as in the printed editions, with the last two transferred to another place—the twelve hymns of the *Peristephanon*, as in the Florentine codex, no. 85, with the verses of Constanti[na] and Saint Damasus in praise of Saint Agnes. After the hymn of Saint Romanus, hymns for the Nativity and Epiphany of the Lord. — Ode: ‘Pious, faithful, innocent.’ — *Dittochaeum*. — *Apotheosis*. — *Hamartigenia*. — *Psychomachia*. — Two books against Symmachus.

“Concerning the Prague and Vienna manuscripts Marietti observed nothing distinctive. He says that the Vienna manuscript is faulty; it contains only the *Psychomachia*, and even that not complete, as we shall note in the work itself. The variant readings of the Prague manuscript are taken from the book of the hymns of the *Cathemerinon*, the *Apotheosis*, the *Hamartigenia*, the *Dittochaeum*, and the books against Symmachus; but in Book II, from the verse ‘When he had spoken these words,’ the remainder is missing.”

[Col. 0631A] Besides these manuscripts, Marietti also collated the Vatican manuscripts A and B, and most carefully entered the variant readings in the margin of the Aldine edition. I gladly acknowledge that I have been assisted by this edition, enriched through the diligence of that exceptionally curious man—not only to avoid the fault of ingratitude, but also to commend my own edition.

Nevertheless, I did not on that account evade any labor; indeed, a vast effort was required to read through and compare with one another so many manuscript codices not seen by Marietti, and also fully to understand what Marietti had written in extremely small characters and to decipher the abbreviations he used by comparing them across very many passages. To speak frankly, Marietti’s notes were for me a kind of gold mine, but one from which extracting the gold was laborious, and the trouble greater than the profit.[Col. 0631B] Nor can anyone easily believe, unless he has experienced it, how burdensome it is to examine manuscript codices in order to recover the true reading. Often, when only a tiny result appears, the greatest diligence has been expended, and sometimes even when no result appears at all; for it was necessary to investigate whether some new reading could be extracted.

Some will accuse me of misplaced diligence because I have pointed out manifest errors in the manuscripts. But since I followed the footsteps of those who preceded me, especially Weitzius and Heinsius, I did something more useful by declaring which readings were errors and by being much more sparing in introducing new ones.

### 80.

Now I shall list other manuscripts. In Montfaucon, at the place cited, from the Casinensis Library, codex 222: “The poems of Saint Prosper, etc. Prudentius’ book concerning the Doves.” “The poems of the facetious poet, etc.” (Concerning that inscription about the Doves, see no. 64.) In the same place, codex 374: “Poems of Prudentius.”

In the Laurentian Medicean Library, Pluteus 23, codex XV, parchment: “The poems of Prudentius, the Christian poet.” In the same place, Pluteus 34, codex L: “Certain poems of Prudentius”; the ending is missing.

In the Florentine Benedictine Library: “A recent codex of Prudentius concerning the New and Old Testament,” that is, the *Dittochaeum*.

From the same Montfaucon, in the Patavine Library, or the museum of Lorenzo Pignorio: “Prudentius’ *Diptychon*” (see no. 66).

In the Ambrosian Library at Milan: “The works of Prudentius; parchment, bombazine.” “A codex of Prudentius,” says Montfaucon, “of the seventh or eighth century; scarcely could you see another manuscript of this author of such remote antiquity.” Prudentius of the royal library, however, appears still older (Montfaucon means the Parisian Library). Concerning the Milanese codex, see nos. 75 and 100.

The same Montfaucon lists several separate works. In the Royal Library at Paris, codex 6016: “Prudentius’ *Stichomachia*” (correct to *Psychomachia*).

These are the items I excerpted from Montfaucon. In his catalogue I again warn that under the single name “Prudentius” he included both Prudentiuses: Prudentius, bishop of Troyes, and our Aurelius Prudentius.

The work of Prudentius of Troyes, *Precepts from the Old and New Testament for Those to Be Ordained*, which occurs once and again in Montfaucon, must be distinguished from Aurelius Prudentius’ *Tetrastichs on the Old and New Testament*.

### 85.

Angelo Maria Bandini, in his catalogue of the manuscript codices of the Laurentian Library at Florence, lists Prudentius’ works more clearly and distinctly. From him I draw the following.

Volume I, column 720 and following: Pluteus 23, codex 15, on parchment, in folio, from the fifteenth century, with the initial letters of the books beautifully illuminated in gold. In it Bandini observed very many readings of no small importance that differ from the editions he had at hand. Its title is: “The poems of Prudentius the Christian.” It should nevertheless be added that it contains “the poems of C. Vettius, Juvencus, Proba Falconia, Sedulius, and Arator.”[^c0063-3]

[^c0063-3]: [Col. 0633D] Page 1 of the codex: “The book of the lyric poems of Prudentius the Christian poet. Poem 1: ‘For ten five-year periods now,’” which is the preface, as in the edition with the notes of Christoph Cellarius, Halle-Magdeburg, 1703, in octavo. In the margin of the codex the meter is identified in red.

Pages 25 and following contain other hymns without titles belonging to the book *Peristephanon*, in this order:

1. The first, without a title, is also first in that edition and is entitled “The Passion of Emeterius” (correct to Emeterius, or Hemeterius) and Chelidonius.
2. The second, fifth in the edition: “The Passion of Saint Vincent the Martyr.”
3. The third, second in the edition: “The Passion of Saint Lawrence the Martyr.”
4. The fourth, eleventh in the edition: “The Passion of Saint Hippolytus the Priest.”
5. The fifth, thirteenth in the edition: “The Passion of Saint Cyprian the Martyr.”
6. The sixth, twelfth in the edition: “The Passion of the Holy Apostles Peter and Paul.”
7. The seventh, fourth in the edition: “The Passion of the Eighteen Holy Martyrs of Caesaraugusta.”
8. The eighth, fourteenth in the edition: “The Passion of Saint Agnes the Virgin.”
9. The ninth, third in the edition: “The Passion of Saint Eulalia the Virgin and Martyr.”
10. The tenth, sixth in the edition: “The Passion of Saint Fructuosus, Bishop of Tarragona, and his Companions.”
11. The eleventh, seventh in the edition: “A Hymn in Honor of Saint Quirinus the Martyr.”
12. The twelfth, ninth in the edition: “The Passion of Saint Cassianus the Martyr.”
13. The thirteenth, eighth in the edition: “Verses in Praise of a Baptistery Illustrious with the Blood of Two Martyrs.”
14. The fourteenth, tenth in the edition: “The Passion of Saint Romanus the Martyr.”
15. The fifteenth is a poem entitled “Prudentius Offers His Little Works to God,” beginning “Pious, faithful, innocent.” In the edition this is the preface to the book *Peristephanon*.

### 86.

In this same codex, after the hymn to Saint Agnes, are appended verses by Constantina, the daughter of Constantine, in honor of Saint Agnes, and verses by Saint Damasus concerning her, beginning in the manuscript: “Fame tells that the saints, long ago restoring the laws …” Both are found in the Paris edition of the *Bibliotheca Sanctorum Patrum*, 1644, where the first verse of Saint Damasus reads: “Fame tells that the saints were once born of parents.”

Two verses by Constantina are missing from the edition:

> Still bearing the name, the body, and all its limbs,  
> Raised from the darkness of death and the blind night,

These are read in the codex after the verse “Invincible alone,” etc. (correct to “Invictus in heaven”).

Both epigrams occur in Weitzius’ edition among the glosses of Master Iso, from the codex of Carolus Widman. We shall transcribe them there, together with the variant readings from the codex of the Roman College, concerning which I spoke at no. 76.

Although the distinguished Gaetano Marini, prefect of the Vatican archives, endowed with exceptional judgment and learning, has long been preparing to publish these and other ancient Christian inscriptions, illustrated by his own scholarship—and will include among them the poems of Saint Damasus, most of which experience has shown to have been composed and used for this purpose—perhaps time will make us equally certain about the remainder.

[Col. 0634A] **87.** In the same codex, on page 81, follows: “Prudentius’ book *Ditrocheus*, which is contained in the Historical Titles”; in the editions it is called the *Diptychon*.

On page 86: “The book *Apotheosis against the Heresies*,” preceded by two prologues:

1. With the title “Verses on the Holy Trinity.”
2. “An Invective against All Heresies.”

The codex makes no division into chapters, but at the chapter which in the edition is entitled “Against the Phantasmatic Heretics,” it has only this title: “Here ends the *Apotheosis against All Heresies. Here begins the work against the Manichaeans.”

Page 106: “Against Those Blaspheming That There Are Two Gods,” or rather, as it is entitled in the edition, *Hamartigenia*, with a prologue entitled “Prologue against the Marcionites.”

### 88.

Page 124: “Two books against Symmachus,” with a prologue to each. Symmachus’ report is presented in the codex divided into chapters, or sections, of Book II.

At the end this subscription is read in red letters:

> Here ends the second book against Symmachus, concerning the restoration of the altar. Thanks be forever to God. Written at Florence in the year of salvation 1489, on the twenty-fourth day of November. May praise, honor, dominion, and glory be to almighty Jesus Christ and to his holy mother, ever-virgin Mary, throughout endless ages of ages. All things undergo change.

Bandini firmly believes that this codex was copied from some very ancient and excellent exemplar. See note b, page 66, no. 79 (Col. 629, note b).

### 89.

In volume II of the same catalogue, column 166: Pluteus XXXIV, codex L, written by the hand of Pietro Crinito, though very rapidly. On page 26 another hand has added: “The *Cathemerinon* of Marcus Aurelius Prudentius Clemens,” namely the preface [Col. 0634C] of the work and the following six hymns, up to the verse “And in various forms,” which is verse 31 of the hymn *Ante Somnum*.

In the index of the catalogue Bandini calls our poet Marcus Aurelius Prudentius Clemens, perhaps influenced by the authority of this codex, and because the praenomen Marcus was quite common in the Aurelii family. See no. 41.

In the same place, column 747, Pluteus XCI of the Gaddian Library, codex IV: an untitled *Enchiridion of the New and Old Testament*, as in the *Bibliotheca Sanctorum Patrum*, Paris, 1644. The codex is on paper, faulty, and from the fifteenth century.

In the same place, without any title: the *Psychomachia*, as in that same library of the Fathers.

In the catalogue of the manuscript codices of the Riccardian Library at Florence, I find only the following. Page 330: “Prudentius, sacred epigrams.” M. IV, a paper codex in quarto, nos. XX and XXXIII. M. II, a paper codex in quarto, no. XIII.

The author of this index or catalogue is Giovanni Lami, who does not explain what those sacred epigrams are. I suppose they are the *Dittochaeum*, or *Enchiridion*.

### 93.

Ludewig states in his *Life of Prudentius* that Giselinus used a manuscript from Deventer in editing Prudentius’ poems, in addition to the old Deventer edition; but I do not find this in Giselinus.

He likewise says that Hübner, the bookseller at Dresden, possesses Bunchner’s manuscript notes on Prudentius.

Heribert Rosweyde, in his notes on Paulinus, page 814, mentions that he too possessed notes, or a commentary, on Prudentius, which he intended shortly to commit to print.

Nicolaus Antonius, in his *Bibliotheca vetus*, praises an ancient scholiast on Prudentius, of a genuinely early period and containing much documentation. Barthius seems to have seen him in Book X of the *Thebaid*, verse 657, although that work is nowhere to be found.

Since Antonius says this at no. 448, shortly afterward, at no. 450, he lists in Weitzius’ edition the continuous ancient glosses of Iso. I believe this to be precisely the ancient scholiast cited by Barthius.[Col. 0635D]

Concerning the commentary on Prudentius that Resendius was preparing, reread no. 39.

Some praise Giphanius’ manuscript notes, perhaps because they have been misled by the fact that he corrected many passages in Prudentius from manuscript codices in his index to Lucretius, as we shall often explain in the commentaries.

### 94.

Whatever Barthius observed in ancient manuscripts, especially in the *Psychomachia*, in the hymn to Saint Eulalia, in the hymn for the Dead, in the work *On the New Light of Holy Saturday*, and in the hymn to Saint Hippolytus, we shall collect carefully. He himself often hints that he was considering illuminating Prudentius with a continuous commentary.[^c0063-5]

[^c0063-5]: [Col. 0635D] At the end of Book IX of the *Adversaria*, chapter 20, he says: “These things, encountered in the manuscripts and not altogether unworthy of notice, we were recording for the sake of the most learned poet and by far the sweetest of all.” He adds that he does not [devote anything] to that work which they have vowed to Christ’s swan, the sole most holy, sweetest, and most eloquent of all.

[Col. 0636A] We shall publish the glosses that he found in ancient papers.

I know that some people regard Barthius’ reliability in citing manuscript codices as somewhat unstable. But they provide no sound reason why this most learned man should be branded a falsifier. As far as Prudentius is concerned, he often conjectures what ought to be read, and often states and explains what is actually read in the codex. Why, then, would he attribute variant readings—especially useful ones—to spurious papers rather than to himself?

From the catalogue of the manuscript codices of the Royal Library at Paris, part 3:

### 96.

In the same catalogue and part 3, codex 8084, on parchment, formerly Puteanus, apparently written in the sixth century. It contains only:

1. Aurelius Clemens Prudentius’ book *Cathemerinon*;
2. his *Apotheosis*;
3. his *Hamartigenia*;
4. his *Psychomachia*;
5. five hymns from his book *Peri Stephanon* (*Περὶ στεφάνων*): the first to the martyrs Hemeterius and Chelidonius, the second to Blessed Lawrence, the third to the virgin Eulalia, the fourth to the eighteen martyrs of Caesaraugusta, and the fifth to Blessed Vincent. The ending is missing.

Concerning this codex, see no. 100. Mabillon, in *De re diplomatica*, Book V, offers a specimen of it in Plate 6, no. 2, from the beginning of the hymn *Ante Somnum*. He notes that this codex is not far removed from the earliest period of Roman script, and that it has a distinctive form of the letter *h* in *Hymnus* and *Christus*, in which the letter is transposed after *r*; this form resembles the letter *k*. The earliest period of Roman script flourished through the fifth century.

In the same place, codex 8085, on parchment, formerly Colbertinus, apparently written in the tenth century, contains only “the poems of Aurelius Clemens Prudentius”; some material is missing toward the end.

Codex 8086, apparently written in the tenth century, contains only “the poems of Aurelius Clemens Prudentius with scholia.”

Codex 8087, on parchment, formerly Colbertinus, apparently written in the tenth century: “The poems of Aurelius Clemens Prudentius.”

Codex 6088, formerly Colbertinus, on parchment, apparently written in the twelfth century, no. 1: “The poems of Aurelius Clemens Prudentius”; glosses occur frequently between the lines and scholia in the margin.

This is what the catalogue of the Royal Library at Paris, published with the greatest elegance and magnificence, revealed to me in its index. I have no doubt that some other items lie hidden in that catalogue, omitted by the index, which I know was not prepared with the greatest accuracy.

### 99.

I shall now report, from the same sources, which manuscripts other editors of Prudentius used.

Aldus had only one exemplar at hand, and that one extremely ancient.[^c0063-9]

[^c0063-9]: [Col. 0637D] I do not know whether, when he wrote the following, he intended to indicate that exemplar or something else: “Prudentius, the first of the Christian poets to come into our hands, summoned from as far away as Britain, after he had lain hidden for eleven hundred years and more, emerges into public view, printed by our presses, so that he may benefit his fellow Christians.” If that codex had lain hidden in Britain for eleven hundred years or more when it was printed by the Aldine press, it would have had to be written before the year 400—a very difficult supposition, and one inconsistent with the *Life*, deeds, writings, and circumstances of Prudentius.

Sichard published Prudentius from, as he says, older manuscripts, one of which Werinherus Woflinus had sent from Strasbourg.

Giselinus restored much in Prudentius to its original purity from two apographs from Ghent; another manuscript, not so old but extremely well corrected, belonging to Luca Maera, jurisconsult; four manuscripts of Theodore Pulmannus; and three others from Antwerp—one from the Library of Arts, another from the Buslidian Library, and a third from the Martinian Library.

Concerning Spiegel, who used Peutinger’s manuscript, of worn-out antiquity, see the commentary on the inscription of the hymn *Omni Hora*, *Cathemerinon* IX.

At verse 10 of that same hymn he cites another codex, but one less reliable.

Fabricius collated a codex that Gaspar Bornerus had obtained from the Library of Naumburg. From it, Fabricius says, he restored an entire verse in the hymn on the baptistery and corrected many passages. But that verse was already read in earlier editions:

> Here two men, purple [with blood], slain for the Lord’s name …

It is missing from Aldus.

Weitzius used parchment manuscripts in which Prudentius was complete. He had received them from D. Hoeschelius, and Hoeschelius from D. Carolus Widmanus. Weitzius followed the order of this codex, except that he placed the hymns on the Nativity and Epiphany of the Lord—which Widman’s codex places after the book *Peristephanon*—at the end of the book *Cathemerinon*.

Weitzius also possessed the codex of D. Jacobus Bongarsius, in which there were extensive lacunae.[^c0063-10]

[^c0063-10]: [Col. 0638D] In the *Cathemerinon*, hymn 11, it proceeds as far as verse 100; the remainder and the following material are missing, and in the Passion of Vincent it begins only at verse 539. In the *Psychomachia*, verses 283 through 531 are missing; at verse 531 the text resumes and continues to verse 641, while everything else is entirely absent. In this manuscript of Bongarsius the *Psychomachia* was illustrated with figures; the other codices seen by Weitzius lacked this illumination and the tessellated emblem.

Gruterus communicated to Weitzius variant readings from an ancient manuscript of the monastery of Egmond.

Rittershusius obtained for Weitzius’ use, from the monastery of the Fountain of Salvation, or Hailsbronn (also Heilsbronn), parchment manuscripts containing the *Hymnary for the Seasons and Saints* throughout the entire year.

From the Ampelonian College at the Gate of Heaven, located at Erfurt, Weitzius obtained for his use a very ancient exemplar of the *Psychomachia*.

From the Fulda Library, M. Joachim Zehnerus collated a manuscript of the *Psychomachia*. The variant readings from that codex in Weitzius are owed to him.[^c0063-11]

Goldastus gave Weitzius parchment manuscripts containing the book *Cathemerinon* and the *Manual of Amoenus*. I do not know whether this is a recent title; I shall discuss it further in connection with the *Dittochaeum*.

Christianus Becmanus had obtained the Palatine codex from Gruterus and supplied variant readings from it for Weitzius’ edition.

[^c0063-11]: The printed page marker reads “77.”

[Col. 0639A] **100.** Heinsius collated the Bodleian manuscript at Oxford in Britain, copied approximately six hundred years ago (now seven hundred) [Note: [Col. 0639D] Its age was proclaimed by this inscription: “Leofric, bishop of the Church of Saint Peter the Apostle at Exeter, gives this book to his episcopal see, for the remedy of his soul and for the benefit of his successors. But if anyone should remove it from there, may he be subject to perpetual damnation. So be it.” Leofric presided over the see of Exeter around the year 1060 or 1070.]. Bernard Rottendorphius, or Rottendorfius, offered Heinsius the complete works of Prudentius in parchment manuscripts written approximately in the twelfth century, as well as two further codices of the same period, one containing the books *Against Symmachus*, the other the *Psychomachia*. He also received from the distinguished Isaac Vossius the Nomsian manuscript, neither very old nor complete, and mutilated through a large part of it.

The exemplar of the Putean brothers was of particular use to Heinsius: it was extremely ancient and written in large Roman letters. In it, the books *Against Symmachus* and most of the *Peristephanōn* were missing. Concerning this manuscript, see Mabillon’s judgment, no. 96. Next to the Putean manuscript in excellence and antiquity stood the Thuan manuscript, written approximately in the ninth century. It bore the name of Hildegarius, bishop; Heinsius had no opportunity to investigate more precisely the period in which he lived. In the *Gallia Christiana* of the Sammarthani I find three Hildegarii in Gaul: the first, bishop of Meaux in the ninth century; the second, bishop of Limoges in the tenth century; the third, bishop of Beauvais, likewise in the tenth century. But from the mere name of Bishop Hildegarius nothing certain can be determined about his age.

Emericus Bigotius supplied Heinsius with excerpts from the *Psychomachia* from his own parchment manuscripts, and from the *Cathemerinōn* and *Peristephanōn* from the Altinian manuscripts, as well as a considerable portion of the same hymns from a Milanese manuscript in the Ambrosian Library. This manuscript, Heinsius says, was mutilated and truncated precisely in its better part, but nevertheless extremely ancient, so that in the form of its script and the ductus of its letters it rivals the highly praised Putean manuscript.

At Antwerp, among the fathers of the Society of Jesus, he collated the discrepancies of three manuscripts whose readings Laevinus Torrentius of Lyon had added to the margin of his edition. But Torrentius had not carried this labor beyond the hymns of the *Cathemerinōn* and *Peristephanōn*, and the manuscripts themselves which he had used did not appear to be of great importance. According to Torrentius, the first belonged to Saint Lawrence, the second to Saint James—both were from Liège—and the third, according to Torrentius, belonged to Abbey 78 at Groenendael [the numeral is as printed]. From Joannes Georgius Graevius, Heinsius obtained the manuscript notes of Joannes Cauchus, as well as the Antwerp edition of 1536, [Col. 0640A] illustrated with the scholia of Joannes Sichardus. That edition was faulty and strangely corrupt, but Cauchus had written into it in his own hand various readings from an old book, together with many conjectures of his own that were not to be despised. He also obtained the Basel edition of Henricus Petrus, four years more recent than the Antwerp edition but equally defiled by errors; Claudius Salmasius had added to it variant readings from the parchment manuscripts of the Thuan and Putean libraries.

Heinsius also examined the Egmond manuscript, whose readings Weitzius had reproduced from Janus Gruterus with insufficient fidelity, and two manuscripts from the Dijon library of President Joannes Boherius, one of which was very old. Heinsius had heard—but had not seen—that a manuscript of remarkable antiquity was kept at Cambridge in Britain, in the college of Saint Benedict.

He reports, moreover, that Everardus Elmenhorstius and Franciscus Juretus had considered emending Prudentius. Juretus testifies that he used five parchment manuscripts in his notes to the *Life of Saint Martin* by Paulinus, and that, according to rumor, the unpublished notes of Obertus Gifanius were still extant. On this point I am doubtful at verse 444 of the *Psychomachia*.

For the recently published Parma edition, about which more will be said in the next chapter, the distinguished Teolius used only the Vatican manuscripts, and not all of them [Note: [Col. 0639D] It will not be unwelcome to hear his very judicious opinion of these manuscripts from chapter 4 of his preface. It is now clear from this evidence that none of the editors of Prudentius had yet seen or collated the Vatican codices, apart from one or two, which were brought there after the time of Weitzius and Heinsius. Nevertheless, we may rightly and deservedly assert that they are most worthy of consideration. For if one attends to their number, there are sixteen; if to their antiquity and fidelity, then, with four or five exceptions—either written in a later age or by a less careful hand—all the rest are of the highest quality both in age and in diligence, and of great value.

He names five principal manuscripts: the Alexandrian, Vatican 321, perhaps of the eighth century, or certainly of the following century, as he believes; Vatican manuscripts 3859 and 3860, approximately of the same age; Vatican 5821, which was collated by Marietto; and the Urbinate, Vatican 666. Concerning these, compare what we have said, and, if you wish to judge, examine the form of the script of the first four manuscripts. Observe also, I ask, that Vatican 3859 does not contain all of Prudentius.].

## CHAPTER V. Editions of the Works of Prudentius, Interpreters, and Translations

**79 101.** Since so many editions of Prudentius’s poems have been produced, as I shall now enumerate, what reason, I wonder, can there be for his works to be so rare that scarcely any copies are offered for sale, and that they are lacking even in many libraries of no mean standing belonging to religious families? Whoever interprets this as a compliment to the poet will, I think, judge not incorrectly: for it may be inferred that copies sold successfully and that many were worn out through use, while those who acquired them held on to them eagerly. I shall list the editions in chronological order.

**1. In an uncertain year.** An old edition of Prudentius’s works, seen by Fabricius and discussed in the *Bibliotheca vetus Latina*, without indication of year or place, in quarto [Note: [Col. 0640D] At its end one reads: “You will find, prudent reader, the works of Aurelius Clemens Prudentius printed in this order. First, the *Tetrasticha* on both Testaments. Then the book which he wrote on the Divinity and entitled the *Apotheosis*. The *Psychomachia* follows. The *Hamartigenia* is added in its proper order. The *Peristephanōn* follows, for thus in Greek the book is entitled *For Martyrdom*. The book of Daily Hymns—also called the *Cathemerinōn*—and the work which he wrote against Symmachus, defender of idolatry, complete the whole work in a beautiful and proper order. The book *Against Symmachus* is presented as though it were one, although there are two; I believe the reason is that one book is understood as a work containing one or several books.”] This edition is perhaps older than all the others.

**2. In 1470.** Ludewigius states that the ending of the *Hamartigenia* and the *Psychomachia* appeared at Augsburg.

**102. 3. In 1472.** The quarto Deventer edition is frequently praised by Fabricius, by Michael Maittaire in *Annales typographici*, volume I, page 99, and by others. But it is certainly they who are mistaken, since Giselinus reports as follows in the preface to his commentary on the 1564 edition: “Meanwhile, however, this good fortune befell me: by chance I happened upon an edition published at Deventer approximately seventy years ago.” Accordingly, the Deventer edition mentioned by Giselinus belongs approximately to the year 1495.

**4. In 1475.** Prosper Marchand, following Beughem and Oudin, reports that the works of Prudentius were published at Deventer. The abbot of Saint-Léger rightly doubts this in the supplement to Marchand’s *History of Typography*, assigning the beginning of printing at Deventer to the year 1477. All these authors were unaware of the genuine Deventer edition of Prudentius’s poems.

**80 5. In 1495.** That Deventer edition so often praised by Giselinus, which, as he says, helped him as much as any other manuscript. It is listed in the catalogue of the Royal Library of Paris as follows: *Poetic works of Aurelius Clemens Prudentius, from the edition of Rodolphus Langius. Deventer, 1495, quarto.* Ludewigius, who had read this edition—apart from Giselinus, seen by no one—assigned its date to 1494.

Besides Giselinus, Spiegelius mentions the same edition once and again in his commentary on the hymn *Omni hora*, and Erasmus in his commentary on the hymn *Eight Days before the Kalends of January*. In the *Annales typographici*, Maittaire, apart from that fictitious Deventer edition of Prudentius’s works dated 1472, records nothing else printed at Deventer until 1481, when he gives the following entry: “At Deventer, the book of *Examples*, by Richard Pafraed, quarto.” I have not yet discovered what order the Deventer edition follows.

**103. 6. In 1498.** At Leipzig, in quarto, three hymns of Prudentius were published at the end of Dares Phrygius’s *History of Troy*: (1) *On the Passover of the Israelite People*; (2) *On the Miracles of Our Savior*; (3) *On Rest and Sleep, a Divine Gift*—according to Fabricius’s *Bibliotheca vetus Latina*. I conjecture that the first hymn is *On the New Light of the Easter Sabbath*, in which the journey of the Israelite people is described: “This fire, the people of illustrious blood …” For the second is certainly the hymn *Omni hora*, and the third the hymn *Ante somnum*.

[Col. 0641D] **104. 7. In 1499.** The *Enchiridion* was published at Leipzig by Jacob Thanner, in quarto, according to Ludewigius and Rodriguez de Castro.

**8. In 1501.** *The Works of the Poet Prudentius*, in quarto, Venice, from the press of Aldus, January 1501. Certain works of Damascus and others, in Greek and Latin, were printed and bound together at the same time. Hence I found this edition ridiculously described in a catalogue as *The Greek and Latin Works of Prudentius*.

Why did the very learned Niccolò Antonio regard this edition as the first? I should be less surprised if he himself had not acknowledged and praised the Deventer edition so often celebrated by Giselinus. Fabricius also complains unjustly that Prudentius was omitted from the collection of Christian poets printed at Venice in 1502, in quarto. He was not omitted by Aldus, but placed first; Aldus clearly asserts this in his preface.

In the copy possessed by the Barberini Library, however, the Christian poets are arranged in this order: first Sedulius, Juvencus, and others; Prudentius is last, and at his end is written: “Venice, from the press of Aldus, January 1501.” That Prudentius appeared first is clear from the preface to the same volume: “Juvencus besides, Sedulius, Arator … whom our types have for so long been travailing to produce … will give birth very shortly.”

A different order was therefore followed in assembling the volumes, and perhaps in some copies the year 1502 was added to the edition of the Christian poets, while in others it was 1501 [Note: [Col. 0641D] When Aldus first published Prudentius, he added the epigrams of Prosper of Aquitaine on the sentences of Saint Aurelius Augustine, together with these verses:

“Come now, I beg you, companion  
of my affairs, never to be parted,”

which nevertheless seem rather to belong to Paulinus than to Prosper. In this edition of 1501, several variant readings based on conjecture by Aldus are placed at the beginning; we shall examine them in their proper places.].

Heinsius wonders why Giselinus mentions two Aldine editions, when he himself had seen only the edition of 1502. But if Aldus published an edition of Prudentius in 1502, we must admit that there were two, for I myself have seen the edition of 1501 in the Roman libraries of the Sapienza, the Barberini, the Angelica, the Casanatense, and the Roman College.

In the commentaries I shall often point out that there appear to have been two editions of Aldus, since variant readings are sometimes presented in the same passage as though they came from Aldus. Recently someone distinguished three Aldine editions: two in the same year, 1501, one of which was published separately and the other together with the other Christian poets; and a third, seen by Heinsius, said by him to have been produced in 1502.

But the existence of those two editions of 1501 is by no means established, since a single edition of Prudentius is found in some copies joined to the other Christian poets and in others separated from them [Note: [Col. 0641D] The order of the Aldine edition is as follows:

1. The book of the *Psychomachia*.
2. *Verses on the New Light of the Easter Sabbath*—which are repeated again in hymn 5 of the *Cathemerinōn*.
3. The book of the *Cathemerinōn*, namely the preface and the hymns:

   1. At the cockcrow.
   2. At morning prayer.
   3. Before food.
   4. Ode after food.
   5. Ode for the lighting of the lamp.
   6. Before sleep.
   7. For those who fast.
   8. After fasting.
   9. At all hours.
   10. At the funeral rites of the dead.
   11. On the eighth day before the Kalends of January.
   12. On Epiphany.

Then follows the *Apotheosis*: a hymn on the Trinity; a hymn against unbelievers. The *Apotheosis* begins: “Against the heretics who assert that the Father suffered: ‘There are many things …’” Against the Unionists, that is, the Sabellian heretics: “Yield, profaner …” Against the Marcionites, who asserted that there are two gods: “Whither are you rushing …”—which is the *Hamartigenia*. The *Romanus* follows.

Then comes the book of the *Peristephanōn*, without a preface:

1. The first hymn, in honor of the martyrs Hemeterius and Chelidonius of Calahorra.
2. The second, in honor of the passion of the blessed martyr Laurence.
3. The third, an ode in praise of the martyr Eulalia.
4. The fourth, an ode in praise of the eighteen holy martyrs.
5. The fifth, an ode in praise of the holy martyr Vincent.
6. The sixth, an ode in praise of the blessed martyrs Fructuosus, bishop of the Church of Tarragona, and Augurius and Eulogius, deacons.
7. The seventh, the passion of the martyr Hippolytus, addressed to Bishop Valerianus.
8. The eighth, an ode in praise of the martyr Quirinus, bishop of the Church of Siscia.
9. The ninth, the place where the martyrs suffered, now called the Baptistery. One hexameter is missing: “Here two purple …”
10. The tenth, the passion of the martyr Cassianus.
11. The eleventh, the passion of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul.
12. The twelfth, the passion of the martyr Cyprian.
13. The thirteenth, the passion of the martyr Agnes.

The two books *Against Symmachus* follow. After the title “On Hercules,” the other titles are missing until “On the Power of the Cross: ‘By this sign, unconquered.’” Then comes “The Roman Senate Converted to Christ: ‘The fathers rejoice.’” “The Roman people have believed in Christ”; thereafter, “To the people.” The title “He addresses Symmachus” is missing. In Book II the report of Symmachus is inserted.

The *Dittochaeum* follows; we shall note its variant titles in the work itself. At the end of the *Dittochaeum* is an ode in which the poet speaks of himself: “Pious, faithful, innocent”; its final verse is “It will delight [me] to have sounded forth Christ with the mouth.”

[Col. 0644C] In the *Psychomachia*, without any other title, the beginning is: “O Christ, the grievous [things] of men …” The final title is “The Battle of Concord and Discord,” and in the titles the word *pugna*—“battle”—is always used for conflict or contest. In all other respects this edition agrees with Weitzius’s edition concerning order and titles.].

[Col. 0643A] **82 9. In 1502.** We infer with probability from Giselinus that Aldus published Prudentius’s works again. In his commentary on verse 379 of the *Psychomachia*, Giselinus praises Aldus as “the most diligent,” if anywhere else, certainly in this author’s edition, especially the second.

And since Heinsius says that he frequently consulted an Aldine copy published in the year *CIDICII* [1502], a new edition must have been produced by Aldus in that year. I suspected that in it Aldus inserted the readings which in the first edition he had corrected separately on his own authority.

Indeed, Giselinus used these words in order to point out that in the second edition Aldus had lengthened the middle of the word *idolum* whenever this could conveniently be done through transposition of the words—something Aldus had accomplished in the corrections to the first edition.

But because I have observed that errors of the first Aldine edition are cited by Heinsius without his having paid attention to the corrections, I remain doubtful. I suspect that the Aldine edition praised by him belongs to 1501, while by “second edition” Giselinus means the corrections; and that the variant readings attributed to Aldus should be blamed on the error of those citing them, since it often happens that one person’s name slips out instead of another’s without the speaker noticing.

**10. In 1502.** Of the many, almost innumerable, breviaries in which some hymns of Prudentius were printed, it is sufficient to mention only one, namely the Isidorian or Gothic breviary—either because it contains very many hymns, or because it is wholly Spanish and therefore useful for extracting certain readings that differ from those of the others.

It contains the hymns *Jejunantium*, *Saint Eulalia*, *Saint Vincent*, *Agnes*, *Fructuosus*, *Hemeterius and Chelidonius*, *The Eighteen Martyrs of Zaragoza*, *Laurence*, *Romanus*, *Omni hora*, *Concerning the Funeral Rites*, *On the New Light*, and *Before Sleep*. From some of these only particular stanzas are selected, as we shall state for each one.

The breviary was published in 1502 by order of the celebrated Cardinal Ximénez. I would also believe the claims of some that it was produced at his expense, unless I read at the end:

“To the praise of almighty God, and of the Virgin Mary, his mother, and of all the saints, this Breviary according to the rule of blessed Isidore, called Mozarabic, has been completed with the greatest diligence, and corrected by the reverend master Alfonso Ortiz, doctor of both laws and canon of Toledo, by order of the most reverend father in Christ, the lord Don Francisco Ximénez, archbishop of the same city. At the expense of the noble Melchior Goricius of Novara. 83 Printed by Master Peter Hagembach, a German. In the year of our salvation 1502, on the twenty-fifth day of October.”

Nevertheless, Ortiz mentions the expenses of Francisco Ximénez in his preface:

“May the clergy attribute to your diligence and care the fact that, after a long and careful revision, I have made the more distinguished [parts] still more illustrious. For previously it is well known among the learned that almost everything lay confused in the old books and hitherto unknown. But now you will find each office restored to its proper place and suitably arranged, distinct in characters and punctuation, clear in words and meaning. Through your industry and expense, therefore, the offices of Isidore, long endangered by age, will be read. When they reach the knowledge of all posterity, they will record your devotion to charity and my labors. The diligence of the noble Melchior Goricius of Novara will also be seen, through whose most exact work this laborious book was printed in the royal city of Toledo.” [Note: [Col. 0644D] He repeats nearly the same thing in the preface to the Missal, where he says of Melchior Goricius: “Through whose work and expense the art of printing has been greatly honored in that city [Toledo].” Of himself he says: “You did not hesitate to entrust this most difficult task to me, the least among your servants, so that with the greatest diligence I might first revise the solemn rites of the Masses and, through sleepless study, restore those things which had long been dismissed because of the roughness of the type, without changing the style, and preserving the dignity of the words, guard the majesty of the ancients. For you had ordered that whatever bore the appearance of antiquity should remain untouched, and so it was done. After arranging in order what had been scattered, erasing defects, examining doubtful matters by bringing the truth to light, and repairing much as though it had been obliterated, I illuminated everything, as far as I was able, at your command.”].

As for the expenses, perhaps Cardinal Ximénez bore part of them and Melchior Goricius part, so that the truth on both sides may stand. I wished to record what Ortiz did in his own words, in order to counter the opinions of certain people who loudly assert that there is a great difference between the manuscripts and the printed Gothic offices.

The fidelity of Ortiz is confirmed by the distinguished archbishop of Toledo, Don Francisco Antonio Lorenzana, whose work produced a second edition of the Isidorian Breviary and Missal, much more magnificent and accurate. In an erudite preface to the Breviary—which I use as a gift from him—he says openly:

“We recognize some, though slight, difference in the transposition of certain words between the Isidorian Breviary printed by Cardinal Ximénez and the aforementioned manuscript codices. It may therefore be conjectured either that Alfonso Ortiz, canon of Toledo, had before his eyes other autograph copies, now lost, or that Alfonso himself, strengthened by the authority of Cardinal Ximénez, resorted in obscure passages of the psalms, where he was hard-pressed, to the Vulgate or another version, and added certain words in accordance with it.”

This was entirely unknown to the abbot of Saint-Léger, director of the Library of Saint Geneviève in Paris. He published, as I believe, in Paris in 1787, on a quarto leaf without indication of year or place, the following work: *Literary Particulars concerning the Mozarabic Liturgy, Drawn from the Manuscript Letters of Father Burriel, a Spanish Jesuit, by M. the Abbot of Saint-Léger*. The abbot of Saint-Léger, relying on Burriel’s letters, which he had not sufficiently understood, asserts that the Gothic office published by Cardinal Ximénez differs in reality and substance from the Toledo manuscripts.

He did not know that two letters of Burriel which he cites had already been printed: one addressed to Father Francisco Ravago and translated into French at Paris, the other addressed to Don Pedro de Castro and printed in the *Biblioteca Hispana* of Pedro Rodríguez de Castro, under the article “Isidore of Seville” [Note: [Col. 0645C] The same abbot of Saint-Léger says that he saw at Brussels, among the gentlemen of Santander, several literary documents, some written by Burriel’s own hand, others copied at his command and under his supervision. I mention this because I have heard that a collection of Burriel’s letters is to be published at Madrid.].

**105. 11. In 1505.** I read in Ludewigius that the *Enchiridion* was printed at Leipzig.

**12. In 1507.** *The Poem on the Roman Martyr*, with the commentary of Joannes Murmellius, Cologne, 1507. After the restoration of letters, I would call this the first interpreter of Prudentius. Fabricius and another recent writer, in the collection of commentaries to Weitzius’s edition, list Joannes Murmellius’s explanation, which indeed appears in the index of interpreters but is absent from the work—perhaps because he hoped to obtain it but could not.

The title is as follows:

“The renowned contest against the Gentiles of Saint Romanus, hero and most valiant martyr of Christ, composed in noble verse by Aurelius Prudentius Clemens, a man of consular rank and distinguished poet; in it all the sacred rites of the gods and the customs of the pagans are most vehemently censured and refuted. With the commentary of Joannes Murmellius of Roermond, full of various matters and expressions.”

At the end:

“This little work was printed at Cologne in the printing house of the noble free-born Quentell family. In the year of Christ’s birth 1507, on the tenth day before the Kalends of June.”

It is in large octavo rather than quarto, in the semi-Gothic type so called. In the catalogue of the Casanatense Library the year of the edition is incorrectly given as 1510. Some say it is quarto. See Giselinus’s judgment of Murmellius, no. 117, in the note (Col. 653, n. a).

[Col. 0646A] **106. 13. In 1509.** The *Psychomachia* was published at Deventer, according to Ludewigius.

**14. In 1512.** *The Little Books of Aurelius Prudentius Clemens, a man of consular rank, with the commentary of Antonius Nebrissensis.* At the end of the book one reads:

“This work was printed in the city of Logroño by Arnaldus Guillermus de Brocario, and was completed on the second day of September, in the year from the birth of Christ 1512.” [Note: [Col. 0645D] The distinguished Gregorius Maiansius, who describes it, possessed this edition. See his *Specimen of the Maiansian Library*, Hanover, 1753, page 26. Maiansius adds: “For understanding Prudentius, the most learned of Christian poets, no clearer or more convenient notes could have been devised. In certain places my copy was emended by Vincentius Pons of Valencia, a man of astonishing learning, and by the distinguished Joannes de la Torre y Guereña, a man of most agreeable talent.” Rodriguez de Castro also mentions the same edition, saying that it is octavo in format, and gives in Spanish the Life of Prudentius explained by Nebrissensis in the dedicatory letter to Diego Ramírez de Villaescusa, bishop of Málaga. Read the judgment on Nebrissensis’s interpretation at no. 107, in the note below, n. d.].

It is greatly to be regretted that Nebrissensis left unexplained the books *Against Symmachus*, the *Apotheosis*, the *Hamartigenia*, and certain hymns of the *Peristephanōn*, namely those of Cassianus, Hippolytus, Peter and Paul, Cyprian, and Agnes. He did not even give the *Dittochaeum* a place among the poems.

When copying Nebrissensis’s notes, Weitzius asserts that hymns 5 and 6 and the beginning of hymn 7 of the *Cathemerinōn* are missing. Perhaps he obtained a mutilated copy, for in mine these hymns and their notes are complete.

Nebrissa appears to have had only Aldus before him: he sometimes corrects Aldus’s errors, but more often copies them. I am uncertain whether the edition I saw is different from the one I am now mentioning; I am inclined to believe that it is.

Niccolò Antonio, who thought that Nebrissensis was the first commentator on Prudentius among the printed editions, failed to notice the glosses of Ison and the commentary of Murmellius. Cellarius rather absurdly calls our Antonius—named from his birthplace Lebrixa, Nebrixa, Nebrissa, and Nebrissensis—“the bishop of Nebrissa.” I wish that another writer had not copied the same error [Note: [Col. 0645D] It is a certain fate of our Spain that its most celebrated writers are commonly unknown or poorly understood by foreigners, even when these are learned men. The same man who, misled by Cellarius, honored Nebrissensis with the title of bishop, did not dare to name Father Ignatius Como when attacking him; and in the same passage he seems to have taken the distinguished Francisco Pérez Bayer—famous from here to the stars and already for a long time director of the Royal Library at Madrid—for some monk or friar. When discussing the homeland of Saint Laurence, he called him “Father Pérez.” I do not think he was criticizing anyone other than the author of the learned dissertation *Laurence and Damasus Asserted and Vindicated for the Spaniards*, Rome, 1756. In its proper place I shall explain and defend Bayer’s response to the argument drawn from Prudentius’s silence in the hymn to Saint Laurence.].

[Col. 0646C] **107. 15. In 1512 or shortly afterward.** *The Little Books of Aurelius Prudentius Clemens, a man of consular rank. With the commentary of Antonius Nebrissensis. With privilege.* Nothing else is printed on the title page, nor at the end or elsewhere is the year and place of publication given. The edition is quarto, in semi-Gothic characters. Before it, in place of a preface, stands only an epigram of Aelius Antonius Nebrissensis addressed to Prudentius, returned from Britain, alluding to Aldus’s preface.

This edition exists in the Roman Library of the Sapienza [Note: [Col. 0646D] I suspect that the place of publication was Zaragoza, on the basis of Nebrissensis’s epigram. In Zaragoza, in 1515, Georgius the printer published Nebrissensis’s exposition of the hymns of the Breviary, and printed Sedulius together with Nebrissensis’s paraphrase. The epigram I mentioned is:

“Aurelius Clemens, Prudentius, tell me, I beg you,  
Who sent you into exile, so harshly?  
Did you desire to see the Britons, divided  
From the whole world, and the monsters of the Caledonian sea—  
Whales, killer whales, and panting sperm whales,  
And great sea creatures as large as trees?  
Was it not better not to leave the Celtiberians,  
And never to abandon your ancestral hearths?  
Here are the lands called by Caesar Augustus’s name,  
Where Liber and kindly Ceres pour forth their riches;  
Here abundance gives grain from her reversed horn,  
And Pomona gives her fruits, and Minerva her gifts.  
But now, unless you are foolish, you must go straightway,  
So that by the right of restoration you may reclaim what was left behind.  
So that you may drive out the unjust possessors,  
Who now tear apart and plunder your goods.  
‘Who are they?’ you will say. ‘They are barbarians and solecists;  
They are their offspring and a numerous band.’  
Therefore hasten swiftly; come to the aid of your tottering house.  
For the property of an absent man, and a just cause, are perishing.  
If your fellow citizens perhaps cannot recognize you,  
To them your speech will be foreign.  
I shall come as interpreter; if they try to drive you from your home,  
I shall come as your defender and bring assistance.”

Its order is:

1. The book of the *Cathemerinōn*.
2. The *Romanus*.
3. The book of the *Peristephanōn*.
4. The *Psychomachia*.
5. The *Apotheosis*.
6. The *Hamartigenia*.
7. The two books *Against Symmachus*.

The *Dittochaeum* is missing. The edition is faulty, and its pages are unnumbered.].

86. On the title page is depicted the arms of Spain, with the motto “Tanto monta” (“It amounts to the same”). Jovius, in the work translated into Spanish by Alfonso Ulloa, *Dialogue on Devices*, 1558 edition, page 30, reports that Nebrissensis devised this motto, *Tanto monta*, for King Ferdinand the Catholic. It is an expression associated with Alexander, who cut through the Gordian knot.

Later the famous alternative motto *Plus ultra* (“Further beyond”), invented by Ludovicus Marlianus of Milan, physician to Charles V and bishop of Tuy, became attached to the arms of Spain.

**108. 16. In 1513.** Ludewigius assigns an edition of the hymn *For the Lighting of the Candle* to Wittenberg.
