**17. Also in 1513.** The same Ludewigius reports that the hymn to Saint Romanus was published at Leipzig in quarto. This may perhaps be the copy now before me, at whose end one reads:

“Prudentius on the martyr Romanus ends here, printed by the industrious printer Melchior Lotter in the year of the Lord 1513.”

It is in quarto, a handsome edition. Much of the title on the title page has been worn away by age. The copy preserved in the Angelica Library has glosses written between the lines by hand.

**18. In 1520.** Ludewigius states that the *Enchiridion* was published at Leipzig in quarto.

**19. In the same year, 1520.** *The Interpretation by Jacobus Spiegelius of the Hymn on the Miracles of Christ in Aurelius Prudentius Clemens of Zaragoza, a Man of Consular Rank, “At All Hours.”* Small folio, 142 pages. At the end: “At Sélestat, in the house of Lazarus Schurerus, 1520.” Spiegelius will be mentioned again below. This edition exists in the Alexandrian Library, that is, the Sapienza.

[Col. 0647C] **87 20. In 1522.** Rodriguez de Castro reports that the book of the *Cathemerinōn* was printed at Leipzig.

**21. In 1527.** All the works were published at Basel in octavo, with Sichardus’s commentary. The catalogue of the Royal Library of Paris lists it as follows: *The Works of Aurelius Prudentius Clemens, with Certain Scholia of Joannes Sichardus*, Basel, Andreas Cratander, octavo, 1527. The copy is marked in the hand of Guillelmus Postellus. This is Sichardus’s first edition, which I used in preparing the second volume.

**22. In 1536.** *The Works of Aurelius Prudentius Clemens, a man of consular rank, much more carefully corrected than before; further, illustrated with the not-unworthy commentaries of Aelius Antonius Nebrissensis, to which are additionally attached the scholia of Joannes Sichardus. All these are now printed for the benefit of lovers of literature for the first time.* Printed at Antwerp by Martinus Caesar, in the year of human salvation 1536, octavo, 563 pages. I saw this edition in the library of the Roman College.

[Col. 0648A] **23. In 1537.** Niccolò Antonio mentions notes by Jacobus Meyerus on two trochaic hymns, *On the Miracles* and *On the Holy Martyrs Hemeterius and Chelidonius*, omitted by Weitzius. He says that they were published at Louvain in octavo together with Meyerus’s verses. Other bibliographers confirm this. I have not yet found these notes.

**24. Also in 1537.** Ludewigius notes that the *Enchiridion* was published at Basel together with Juvencus and Arator. The catalogue of the Tellerian Library lists it as follows:

*The Enchiridion of Aurelius Prudentius on the Old and New Testament*, Basel, B. Westhemerus, 1537.

It exists in Rome in the Angelica Library. Its title is:

“Three books of Juvencus, a Spanish presbyter, on Gospel History, corrected and purged of many errors. Two books of Arator, subdeacon, comprising the Acts of the Apostles, previously not printed in Germany. *The Enchiridion of Aurelius Prudentius Clemens, a man of consular rank, on the Old and New Instrument.* Necessary books for the Christian school. Basel, from the presses of Bartholomaeus Westhemerus and Nicolaus Brylingerus, in the year 1537.”

Small octavo. A similar edition is found in the year 1542.

**110. 25. In 1540.** The works of Prudentius, with the commentary of Nebrissensis and the scholia of Joannes Sichardus, who had used six manuscripts, were published at Antwerp in octavo, according to Fabricius. Ludewigius testifies that this edition is full of errors.

**26. In the same year, 1540.** *The Works of Aurelius Prudentius Clemens, a man raised to the dignity of consul because of his exceptional natural gifts and learning, and distinguished in knowledge of divine matters, the Christian religion, civil law, and military affairs, with the commentaries of Sichardus and Erasmus.* Basel, from the press of Henricus Petrus, duodecimo. I received this edition from the distinguished physician Franciscus Petraglia. Heinsius rightly called it contaminated with errors. See no. 100.

88 **27. In 1542.** The *Enchiridion* at Basel, together with Juvencus and Arator, according to Ludewigius. Perhaps in a format similar to that of 1537. See no. 109, edition 24.

**28. In 1546.** The distinguished Teolius reviews in the preface to the Parma edition an Antwerp edition of this year which Bailius had possessed. I have already begun to praise that preface, having received it immediately after its publication as a most welcome gift from a very distinguished man. I would gladly name him as a mark of honor, were he not himself unwilling to be known.

**29. In 1553.** *The Works*, with the scholia of Sichardus and the short commentary of Erasmus on two hymns, *On the Birth of the Child Jesus* and *On Epiphany*, Lyon, octavo. Erasmus’s short commentary is found in Weitzius’s collection and was reprinted in his works. In the catalogue of the Royal Library of Paris the edition is said to be duodecimo, printed by Joannes Tornaesius at Lyon in this year, 1553. Others call it octavo. Gallandius praises this edition.

**30. In 1562.** *The Entire Sacred Poems Extant of Aurelius Prudentius Clemens, a Man of Consular Rank.* To the whole work were added the concise scholia of Joannes Sichardus, and to certain hymns the commentaries of Erasmus of Rotterdam and Jacobus Spiegelius. Basel, from the press of Henricus Petrus, in the year of human salvation 1562, in March, octavo, 719 pages. This edition exists in the library of the Roman College; it is rather poorly corrected.

31. In the same year, 1562. In the collection of Christian poets, edited with study and notes by Georg Fabricius, Basel, [Col. 0649B] in quarto. Thus Johann Albert Fabricius in *Bibliotheca Latina vetus*. Some assign the edition to 1563, others to 1564. Ludewig calls this edition learned and rare. See below, no. 111, where we describe it.

32. In 1562. *The Works of Prudentius*, octavo, Basel, with the notes of Erasmus and Sichardus (from a certain catalogue).

33. In 1562. The first, faulty edition of Giselinus, as he himself acknowledges in the second edition. Title: *The Works of Aurelius Prudentius Clemens, a man of consular rank, corrected by Victor Giselinus and illustrated with annotations. Dedicated to Hippolytus d’Este, cardinal*, Paris, at the shop of Jérôme de Marnef, duodecimo, 494 pages. Errors in this edition were repeated in many others. Someone incorrectly asserted that Giselinus had undertaken this edition after obtaining ten manuscripts of Prudentius, having been misled by the title-page [Col. 0649C] of the second edition of 1564. The first edition of Giselinus is held in the Angelica Library, where I saw it.

34. In 1564. *Aurelius Prudentius Clemens, emended through the work of Theodor Pulmann of Cranenburg and Victor Giselinus on the authority of ten manuscript books, with a commentary by that same Victor Giselinus*. Antwerp, from the press of Christopher Plantin, 1564. Octavo. ^89 After Giselinus’s commentary there follow the opposing letters of Symmachus and Ambrose on religion, illustrated with notes by Peter Nannius of Alkmaar and Victor Giselinus. Erasmus’s commentaries on two hymns of Prudentius are added; see no. 109.

[Col. 0649D] Ludewig rightly declares this edition to be the most carefully corrected and most beautifully printed; and although he likewise says that the Weitzian edition is considered the best, Heinsius nevertheless preferred Giselinus’s edition to the Weitzian one. It must be observed, however, that in some copies Erasmus’s commentaries are lacking, having been torn out for religious reasons. Consequently, Giselinus’s revised work was torn apart at the same time: that revision removed many errors and added several observations. Barthius unfairly attacks Giselinus, whom he calls, in *Adversaria*, book IX, chapter 20, “a man of such presumption that he wished to entitle his notes a commentary.” Barthius gives his reason in book XXI, chapter 4:

> But in both cases he ought not to have caused Giselinus so much trouble, a respectable and learned man—of the one quality we know from the report of learned men, of the other publicly and universally—if only he had not been too high an estimator of his own labors, making so much of those few pages when he says that he wrote a commentary on Prudentius. A commentary on Prudentius must necessarily be the work of many years, in which even the most ingenious, learned, and industrious man could spend all his energy for the best part of a lifetime.

Nicolaus Antonius places Giselinus’s notes before the interpretations of all who preceded him. Giselinus truly rendered excellent service to Prudentius; even theological controversies, with few exceptions, he handled not unsuccessfully for a physician. See no. 117 for Chamillard’s judgment in his preface. A copy of this edition of Giselinus is held in the Royal Library at Paris; it was collated by hand with a very ancient manuscript of the Royal Library.

111. 35. In the same year, 1564. Georg Fabricius published Prudentius together with other Christian poets, and placed him first. The title is:

*The Christian Works of the Ancient Ecclesiastical Poets, together with the Remains and Fragments of their Works: a Treasury of the Catholic and Orthodox [Col. 0650A] Church and of Religious Antiquity, for the Benefit of Scholastic Youth; collected, emended, arranged, and also explained in a commentary through the diligence and scholarship of Georg Fabricius of Chemnitz.*

At the end: Basel, from the press of Johann Oporinus, 1564. Quarto. On the title page, the indication of place and year had been torn off; Fabricius himself dates his preface 17 February 1562. In some copies the commentaries are absent at Rome, since they were occasionally impiously composed by a heretical author and were therefore torn out. He dates the preface to the commentaries 19 June of that same year, 1562.

36. In the same year, 1564. An edition of Prudentius together with other Christian poets, Basel, by Johann Oporinus, octavo, is praised by the distinguished Teolius, though, so far as he knew, no one had noticed it. But since he himself did not mention [Col. 0650B] the quarto Basel edition by Johann Oporinus, which I saw and which several people have described, it must be considered whether this is the only edition and whether someone mistakenly reported it as octavo.

37. In 1566. *The Works of Prudentius, corrected by Victor Giselinus and illustrated with annotations*. Paris, Marnef, 1566, sextodecimo, 140 pages. ^90 Fabricius says: “From the recension of Giselinus.” This edition is entirely conformed to Giselinus’s first edition of 1562. See no. 110. Erasmus’s little commentaries are also present. If you find it stated anywhere that this edition was prepared by Giselinus, do not accept the claim.

38. In 1568. Georg Fabricius’s *Commentaries on Certain Hymns of Prudentius*, Leipzig, 1568, octavo (from Johann Albert Fabricius). They are found in the Weitzian collection [Col. 0650C] and in Fabricius’s works.

112. 39. In 1574. *The Poems of Aurelius Prudentius Clemens, a Man of Consular Rank and a Most Ancient Christian Poet; the Epigrams of Prosper of Aquitaine; and the Little Works of John of Damascus, Cosmas of Jerusalem, Mark, Bishop of Taluontis, and Theophanes.* Cagliari, 1574. Printed by Vincent Sembenio of Salò, printer to the Reverend Lord Nicola Canyelles, vicar general during the vacancy of the see. Octavo, 552 pages. This edition follows Aldus’s edition and is not very carefully corrected. It is preceded by Aldus’s preface and by another on meters, together with a Life of Prudentius written by Aldus; but it does not contain the variant readings mentioned by me in no. 104. The distinguished Teolius saw this edition in the library of the Minim Fathers on Monte Pincio; I saw it in the Alexandrian and Angelica libraries, and I know that it exists [Col. 0650D] in the very rich library of the Most Sacred Prince Pius VI.

[Col. 0651A] 40. In 1580. The books *Against Symmachus* were included in the edition of the letters of Quintus Aurelius Symmachus, edited and studied by François Juret, Paris, quarto, p. 317: “The two books of Aurelius Prudentius Clemens against Lucius Aurelius Avianius Symmachus,” etc. On the title page Symmachus is called Quintus; here he is called Lucius. Page 98, in the notes: “Juret’s notes on Prudentius’s books against Symmachus, which Juret calls most elegant and illustrates from a very ancient manuscript.” These notes of Juret were unknown to Weitz.

41. In 1585. The Cologne edition of this year, octavo, is praised by Nicolaus Antonius and Rodriguez de Castro; perhaps it is not distinct from the one that follows.

42. In 1588. An edition of the books *Peristephanon* and [Col. 0651B] *Cathemerinon*, octavo, Cologne, which Ludewig calls faulty—and faulty it is. The title is: *The Hymns of the Daily Hours [Καθημερινῶν] and On Crowns [περὶ Στεφάνων] of Aurelius Prudentius Clemens, a Man of Consular Rank*. Cologne, from the Birckmann press, at the expense of Arnold Mylius, 1588.

43. In 1589. *The Works of Prudentius*, Paris. This is from the catalogue of the Bodleian Library, where nothing else is specified. See no. 114 in edition 52.

44. In 1591. The Leiden edition of Prudentius, sextodecimo. From Nicolaus Antonius.

45. In 1594. An octavo Cologne edition of the works (from Nicolaus Antonius and Rodriguez de Castro). The title is: *The Works, corrected by Victor Giselinus ^91 and illustrated with annotations. Dedicated to Hippolytus d’Este, cardinal and most illustrious prince.* Cologne, from the Birckmann press, at the expense of Arnold Mylius, 1594. In the copy I use, only the *Psychomachia*, *Apotheosis*, *Hamartigenia*, and *Dittochaeum*, with Giselinus’s notes, are present. The rest has been sewn and bound together from the Cologne edition of 1588. This edition corresponds to Giselinus’s first edition and is therefore faulty.

46. In 1596. *The Works of Aurelius Prudentius Clemens, V. C., from the recension of Victor Giselinus.* Leiden, from the Plantin press, at the shop of Franciscus Raphelengius, 1596. Vigesimo. There are no notes. “From the recension of Giselinus” means according to the standard of his first edition, whose errors were repeatedly reprinted through the intolerable ignorance and negligence of printers and editors. I am therefore surprised that anyone should assert that Giselinus supervised this edition, since Giselinus himself warned in the preface to his second [Col. 0651D] edition that the first, of 1562, had been produced in haste and that innumerable errors had crept into it.

47. In 1603. *The Life and Works of Prudentius*, Lyons. From the catalogue of the Bodleian Library.

48. In 1610. *The Works of Prudentius*, Lyons. In the catalogue of the Bodleian Library.

49. In the same year, 1610. Andreas Wilchius published *Heortographia*, or *Commentaries on the Hymns of Ancient and Modern Poets*, octavo (from Fabricius). I have not seen these commentaries. Andreas Wilchius’s *Exposition [Col. 0652A] for the Feast of the Three Kings*, drawn from certain verses of the *Apotheosis*, is found in the Weitzian collection.

50. In the same year, 1610. The distinguished Teolius reports that the works of Prudentius appeared at Antwerp in twenty-fourmo, without any notes; but since he says that this occurred after the Weitzian edition, perhaps he intended to give another year.

113. 51. In the same year, 1610. Prudentius’s *Dittochaeum* appears in the work *A Biblical Manual, or Handbook of Holy Scripture, Compiled from the Fathers of the Catholic Apostolic Church of Antiquity, and Now Collected for the First Time from Ancient Manuscript Parchments, and Dedicated to the Venerable Religious Father Lord Johann Myntzenberg, Prior of the Carmelites in the Frankfurt Convent*. Frankfurt, 1610, at the shop of Egenolph Emmel. Octavo. The editor, writing under the initials M. H. C., as I gather from Weitz’s preface to the *Dittochaeum*, is Melchior Goldast of Haiminsfeld, from whom Weitz received the parchments containing the book *Cathemerinon* and *Amoeni Manuale*. Yet Weitz does not seem to have read this work; he omitted the fuller glosses of the master Ison, which Goldast had supplied. I am surprised, however, that he took from Goldast’s preface what concerns Prudentius, unless Goldast also wrote the same words elsewhere.

In this ^92 *Biblical Manual*, therefore, p. 1 contains Prudentius’s *Amoeni Diptychon*, or *Titles of the Histories of the Old and New Testament*. Two other similar works are included in the same collection: that of Rusticus Helpidius on p. 17, and that of Walafrid Strabo on p. 85. I shall record Goldast’s variant readings in their proper place. On Ison, see nos. 16 and 114, in the note.

[Col. 0652C] 114. 52. In 1611. The works of Prudentius in the collected works of all poets, Geneva, quarto, reprinted in all editions of this collection, as also in the editions of the *Library of the Holy Fathers*. Specifically, in the collection of ancient poets, Orléans, 1640; London, 1713—not to mention the edition of Pesaro and other more recent ones. In the *Library of the Holy Fathers*, Paris, 1589, volume 8; Lyons, 1677, volume 5. In the *Library of the Holy Fathers* compiled in our own time by the learned Andreas Gallandius, the works of Prudentius are published with notes, especially from Chamillard; Gallandius himself added some brief notes. He follows the order of his own published edition—perhaps the Tornoesian edition—as follows: *Peristephanon*, *Apotheosis*, *Hamartigenia*, *Psychomachia*, the two books against Symmachus, *Cathemerinon*, *Dittochaeum*. [Col. 0652D] These works appear in volume VIII of his *Library*, Venice, 1772, where he prefaces them with a Life of Prudentius arranged with insufficient accuracy.

53. In 1613. *The Works of Aurelius Prudentius Clemens, V. C., newly reviewed according to manuscripts, interpolated, purged of countless errors, and illustrated with notes and a careful index by M. Johann Weitz, P. L. To these have been added the notes, scholia, and observations of all learned men who have written on Prudentius, together with ancient glosses.* Hanover, from the Wechel press, through the heirs of Johann Aubry, 1613. Octavo.

[Col. 0651D] In one volume: its first part contains Prudentius’s poems with variant readings, 382 pages; the second, a *Collection of Annotations, Scholia, Observations, and Notes on the Works of Aurelius Prudentius Clemens*, collected, arranged, and organized with exceptional care by M. Johann Weitz, P. L. [Col. 0652D] The index of interpreters includes Nebrissensis, Sichardus, Erasmus, Spiegelius, and Georg Fabricius, whom we have already discussed; also the *Scholidia* of Adam Siber, the explanation of Johann Murmellius on the *Romanus*—on which see no. 105—Victor Giselinus’s commentary (see no. 110), Adam Theodor Siber’s little commentary on three hymns, Andreas Wilchius’s exposition of certain verses from the *Apotheosis* (see [Col. 0653D] no. 112), Johann Weitz’s notes and observations, and the glosses of the master Ison, excerpted from the codex of Karl Widman and another of Jacques Bongars by M. Johann Weitz.

Ludewig considers this the best of the editions he had seen. Compare, however, no. 110 and Heinsius’s preface, no. 100. I ask you to observe that Goldast, who had excerpted fuller glosses of Ison from ancient parchments for the edition of the *Dittochaeum*, asserts that Ison was a monk in the monastery of Saint Gall and the teacher of Solomon III, bishop of Constance, around the year 900. Compare no. 16. I do not know why someone else calls Ison “Isonius.”

[Col. 0653A] 115. 54. In 1614. *Commentaries on the Two Books of Aurelius Prudentius Clemens against ^93 Symmachus in Defense of the Altar of Victory, dedicated to Caesar de Vendôme, Duke of Vendôme*, by Isaac Grangaeus, headmaster of the school at Vendôme. Paris, at the shop of Robert Fouet, 1614. Octavo, 240 pages, apart from the index. The edition is extremely faulty. At the end are added Symmachus’s *Report*, with notes by Jacques Lectius and François Juret. Also two books of Ambrose against Symmachus. Grangaeus’s commentaries are learned. I received this edition for use from the distinguished bishop Joseph Antonio Reggio.

55. In 1624. Various poems of Prudentius, Paris. From the catalogue of the Bodleian Library.

56. In 1625. *The Works of Prudentius from the Latest Recension of Learned Men.* Amsterdam, at the shop of Willem Jansz. Caesar, 1625. Thirty-secondmo, 261 pages. It is false that this edition derives from the latest recension: it contains the errors that were read before Giselinus’s second edition.

57. In 1631. *The Works of Prudentius*, Amsterdam, at the shop of Johann Janssonius, 261 pages. This is perhaps the same as the preceding edition of 1625: the title is not different, and the number of pages is the same in both. I have seen this edition; I possess the other.

58. In 1643. Franciscus Weitz published, in octavo, *Heortologium*, or *Festal Hymns Illustrated with the Notes of Ancient and Modern Authors*. From Fabricius, *Bibliotheca Latina vetus*.

59. In the same year, 1643. *The Hymn of Aurelius Prudentius Clemens on the Nativity of Christ the Lord and Our Savior.* Augustus Buchner published it separately and illustrated it with a short commentary. Wittenberg, at the expense of Balthasar Mevius, [Col. 0653C] bookseller, from the press of Johann Haken, 1643. Small octavo, 130 pages. On Buchner, see no. 93 and the commentaries.

116. 60. In 1646. *The Hymn of the Lord’s Nativity, of the Epiphany, and “At Every Hour.”* Görlitz. From Ludewig.

61. In 1648. *Prudentius for the Use of Schools*, Lüneburg, duodecimo (from Fabricius). Some wish Prudentius to be published for this use.

62. In 1655. *The Hymn Before Fasting*, with the disputations of Calixtus [Col. 0654A] and Hepf, Hanover, quarto. From Ludewig.

63. In the same year, 1655. Two hymns of *Cathemerinon* with notes. Hanover, quarto. Catalogue of the Bodleian Library.

64. In 1659. *The Hymn of Christ’s Nativity*, with Mollerus, Freiburg, octavo, which Ludewig praises, and which I received for use from the distinguished bishop Joseph Antonio Reggio. The title is: *The Commentary of Andreas Moller of Pegau on the Prudentian Hymn for the Eighth Day before the Kalends of January*. Freiberg, from the press and at the expense of Georg Beuther. At the end is a German paraphrase of this hymn rendered in verse. This commentator is heterodox but learned.

65. In 1667. *The Extant Works of Aurelius Prudentius Clemens*, reviewed from the oldest exemplars and supplied with observations by Nicolaus Heinsius, son of Daniel. Amsterdam, at the shop of [Col. 0654B] Daniel Elzevir, 1667. Sextodecimo. A handsome and especially well-corrected edition. No one has deserved better of Prudentius than Heinsius, at least with respect to the selection of variant readings. He scarcely touched anything else, since he had planned fuller notes on Prudentius but was unable to carry them out. Therefore, if the subject is commentators on Prudentius, the Heinsian edition should not be preferred to the *Edition for the Use of the Dauphin*, nor even compared with it—

66. In 1670. The distinguished Teolius lists another Heinsian edition, following Moreri’s *Dictionary*, and states as a certainty that another exists at the Soncinos’, although he did not see it. I must observe that the Heinsian edition praised in the corrected 1740 edition of Moreri’s *Dictionary* is the one completed in 1667, not another from 1670.

117. 67. In 1687. *The Works of Aurelius Prudentius Clemens, Illustrated with an Interpretation and Notes*, by Stephanus Chamillard of the Society of Jesus, for the use of the Dauphin. Paris, at the shop of the widow Thiboust and Pierre Esclassan. Large quarto. A rare, learned, and sufficiently correct edition; its interpretation, or paraphrase, is less pleasing. Compare Le Clerc, volume XII of the *Bibliothèque*.

[Col. 0653D] I shall now transcribe Chamillard’s judgment on the interpreters he had seen. “There are,” he says in his preface, “I admit, some interpreters of Prudentius: Antonius Nebrissensis, Giselinus, Weitz, and Nicolaus Heinsius. But Giselinus followed only what was easiest for everyone and least necessary to know; he also stumbled and was mistaken in many things. Nebrissensis is more deeply engaged with Prudentius, but he is briefer and is content merely to touch on each matter. He omits what is required for understanding the story, the history, and the author more profoundly. Why, he did not touch the *Apotheosis*, the *Hamartigenia*, or the two books against Symmachus, although these are among the works most deserving of being read. Heinsius remains: his variant readings on Prudentius, interspersed with occasional choice little notes, are extremely learned and accurate, so that one readily recognizes them as having come from Heinsius. Therefore, I think no one will criticize me for following him as far as I could, just as I followed Weitz, who, after collecting the notes on Prudentius previously published, added his own as well, and ones by no means to be despised. In this respect he surpasses the others: he identifies passages in ancient authors, especially those of Holy Scripture that Prudentius wove into his work.

“I pass over Jacobus Spiegelius, who published a short commentary on Prudentius’s ode entitled *Omnis hora*. His notes on it are not only wearisome because of their excessive length, but are also filled with certain petty and almost childish trifles drawn from grammar itself. I also pass over Adam Siber, Georg Remus, Adam Theodor Siber, and Andreas Wilchius: some of them occasionally offered six or seven words on three or four hymns; others only one word. They therefore deserve to be struck from the number of Prudentius’s interpreters. A different judgment must be made of Ison’s scholia, which, although very brief, nevertheless resolve every more serious difficulty. Honor must also be paid to Georg Fabricius’s notes on the ecclesiastical poets and on the five hymns of Prudentius that he illustrated.

“Erasmus will bring up the rear of the interpreters. Although he worked on only the last two hymns of *Cathemerinon*, he was nevertheless a man who, if anyone of his age was, possessed keen and polished judgment, did work not to be regretted, and can serve as evidence that Prudentius should not be despised by learned men.”

You see that Chamillard had heard nothing of many interpreters of Prudentius: of Murmellius, Juretus, Grangaeus, Buchner, Mollerus, and others whom I pass over. His judgment against Giselinus is not universally accepted. Giselinus himself judges Nebrissa differently: he grants Nebrissa and Murmellius the highest praise for diligence, especially in explaining historical matters, although he wishes Nebrissa to possess greater knowledge of poetic art and Murmellius to have supplied more observations.

Chamillard’s statement that Weitz identified passages from ancient authors is true, but he should have added [Col. 0656D] that Weitz often identifies both the authors and the passages incorrectly; Chamillard, following him carelessly, occasionally goes astray. Chamillard criticizes certain petty and almost childish trifles in Spiegelius; but perhaps it is no less petty and childish that he himself, in the preface to Prudentius, appended to the word *Rome* the note: “A sufficiently well-known city.” In his edition it often happens, through I know not whose negligence, that one reading is printed in the poems and another defended in the notes. I pass over several typographical errors, and occasional violations of the meter, which at least ought to have been indicated and corrected.

It must nevertheless be admitted that Chamillard far surpasses the other commentators in explaining theological questions. He might perhaps have been a better interpreter if he had not prepared his edition for the use of the Dauphin. Nor do I doubt that this edition should be preferred to all those that preceded it, as Johann Albert Fabricius prefers it, although Heinsius fulfilled the critic’s task more fully in explaining the variant readings.

[Col. 0655A] 95 68. In 1701. *The Works of Aurelius Prudentius Clemens, V. C., with the Notes of Nicolaus Heinsius, son of Daniel, and of Various Learned Men, Especially Those Most Necessary.* At the end there is an extremely full index of subjects and words. Cologne, at the shop of Johann Christoph Stoissel, 1701. Octavo, 978 pages. A faulty edition. Besides Heinsius’s notes, it contains the commentary of Nebrissensis and the glosses of Ison.

69. In 1703. *The Extant Works of Aurelius Prudentius Clemens*, edited and illustrated with notes by Christoph Cellarius, who also added extensive indexes of subjects and words. Halle in Magdeburg, at the expense of the orphanage, 1703. Octavo, 559 pages. At the end is an index of expressions that Prudentius used more freely than usual; in this index Cellarius himself often transgresses even more freely, as I shall later demonstrate. Worse still, he sometimes defends his own heresy.

70. In 1739. A second edition with Cellarius’s notes, in the same place and in the same format as the first. Octavo, 501 pages.

71. In 1750. *The Works of Aurelius Prudentius Clemens, V. C., from the Latest Recension of Nicolaus Heinsius, Son of Daniel, and Various Learned Men.* Cologne, 1750. Octavo (from Rodriguez de Castro). It must be determined whether this edition is entirely identical with the edition of 1701, and whether someone received the year 1701, printed somewhat obscurely, as the year 1750; for I suspect this may be the case.

72. Finally, in 1788. *The Complete Works of Aurelius Prudentius Clemens, V. C., Now for the First Time Collated with the Vatican Manuscripts, Enlarged and Illustrated with a Preface, Variant Readings, Notes, and a Very Full Index of Subjects and Words.* Parma, from the Royal Printing House, 1788. [Col. 0655C] Large quarto, volumes I and II. A handsome, splendid, and sumptuous edition, worthy of our poet and of his Maecenas. It was dedicated to the most distinguished knight Joseph Nicholas Azara, ambassador extraordinary and plenipotentiary of the King of Spain to the Holy See. The interpreter’s name is indicated by the initial letters I. T., that is, Joseph Teolius. In the Roman journals of 19 April of that year there is an exceptional eulogy of this edition.

The editor collated Prudentius’s poems with twelve or more Vatican manuscripts; he would have pleased many readers if he had taken care to state from which manuscript he had drawn each individual variant reading. He arranged the works in the order that he thought had been approved by Heinsius: *Cathemerinon*, [Col. 0656A] *Peristephanon*, *Apotheosis*, *Hamartigenia*, *Psychomachia*, the books against Symmachus, and *Dittochaeum*, which he prefers to call *Diptychon*.

He was nevertheless mistaken in thinking that, according to Heinsius’s view, the ode *Immolat Deo Patri* should properly be placed at the beginning of *Peristephanon*. Heinsius says explicitly in his additions:

> Most of the ancient manuscripts make the epilogue of the volume the preface that is now read before the book *On Crowns* … From this, you will readily recognize, I think, that it too ought to be referred to the whole poetic work of our Clemens as an epilogue … Therefore, by right of restoration, let that ode return to its former place, from which it had been unjustly exiled.

But that the better-quality Vatican manuscripts support the order preserved in the Parma edition, or the order that Heinsius wished to preserve, I do not see on what grounds can be asserted. In the preceding chapter I explained what order each Vatican manuscript followed in arranging the poems; let others judge the matter as a whole. Certainly the manuscript Vat. Alex. 321, of which I treated in no. 78 and in the notes, the only one among the twenty-seven Vatican manuscripts that contains all the poems of Prudentius, comes much closer to our method than to Heinsius’s.

For the rest, I rejoice that this beautiful edition has been brought to me at an opportune time, so that I may benefit from the diligence of a learned commentator. He indeed aimed at brevity and seems to have followed the advice of Father Francesco Pozzo, or da Puteo, who, in his work *Memoirs of the Life of Saint Lawrence*, offered this recommendation: when preparing a new edition of Prudentius of the kind he desired, one should attend both to brevity in the observations and to convenience in the physical form of the volume. [Col. 0656C] The printer’s magnificence, however, ensured that the volume was not as convenient as Francesco da Puteo wished.

Teolius candidly acknowledges that he was greatly assisted by the writings of Father Francesco da Puteo and Father Joseph Blanchini, priests of the Congregation of the Oratory. This ought to be mentioned by us, lest we pass over in silence those two distinguished men, who deserved well of Prudentius. ^97 Now, if Teolius has attained the highest praise in his manner of interpretation, I shall not neglect, if I can, to attain a little praise in another manner—namely, a fuller, more complete, and, if you will, freer one.

[Col. 0656D] I shall willingly attribute to the modesty of the distinguished Teolius—though perhaps others will not praise it—that, after examining so many Vatican manuscripts, he scarcely dared to depart from Heinsius by even the breadth of a fingernail, although he could sometimes justifiably have preferred them. Chamillard and Cellarius deserve less criticism on this point: they examined no manuscripts personally, yet seem to me freer in their judgments.

Teolius also reproduced from Heinsius a certain antiquated orthography: *urguet*, *tinguit*, *temptat*. From the same source he might likewise have adopted *labsa*, *inpar*, *loquella*, and similar forms. In Heinsius I would rather imitate something else: the fact that he cites ancient manuscripts is not a sufficient reason for him to maintain one spelling himself while adopting another in writing out the poems of Prudentius. Heinsius says in his preface:

> Pulmannus had reproduced the orthography of the ancient exemplars neither inelegantly nor foolishly; nevertheless, here and there we have altered it on the oldest parchments and improved it as far as we could, giving greater weight to the more harmonious agreement of the most ancient manuscripts than to the rules of grammarians, which generally display less truth and reliability than ingenuity.

> I would not deny that I could have altered many more orthographic forms if I had had the right and duty to follow in every respect the venerable antiquity displayed by the parchments; but it seemed that something ought to be reserved for a second revision.

For my part, in the most ancient manuscripts I find nothing except the greatest diversity in orthography and countless errors. Nor do I understand why the poems of Prudentius should be restored to the orthography of manuscripts from the seventh, eighth, or ninth centuries more than the works of Cicero. But I shall discuss the different spelling practices of the manuscripts and of some editions of Prudentius more fully in a note at the end of this chapter. In the commentaries I shall point out certain typographical errors in the Parma edition in Prudentius’s poems—where, that is, the sense is deficient or the rules of meter and Latin are not maintained. I have decided to do the same with the best other editions, so that no one will think these are variant readings.

Someone may one day count it to the credit of our poet that scarcely had the Parma edition been completed when another edition was begun. For whoever thinks that the subjects concealed in Prudentius have already been so fully illuminated that they could be exhausted by one or two scholars has either not read Prudentius or has understood him in no way.

[Col. 0657D] I shall now list many hymns of Prudentius that were printed separately. Among Theodoric Ruinart’s *Genuine Acts of the Martyrs* are the hymns of Eulalia, Cassian, Agnes, Laurence, Hippolytus, the eighteen martyrs of Zaragoza, and Quirinus. In the catalogue of the Casanatense Library, a hymn of Saint Dionysius, bishop of Alexandria, is attributed to Prudentius; but there is no hymn of Saint Dionysius in the Verona edition that I use, from 1731. In the same *Acts* there is the *Passion of the Infant*, taken from a hymn of Saint Romanus.

Among the Bollandists there is, in volume II of April, the hymn of the eighteen martyrs of Zaragoza; in volume I of March, that of Saints Hemeterius and Celedonius; in volume II of August, that of Saint Laurence; and in volume III of the same month, that of Saint Cassian—to pass over other works splendidly illustrated by the continuators of Bolland from the works of Prudentius. The *Passion of Saint Eulalia* appears in the *Hagiologium* of Georg Vicelius, Mainz, 1541. That of Saint Cyprian appears in his works; those of Saints Hemeterius and Celedonius and Saint Leocadia appear in Surius.

In the *Lives of the Fathers*, collected by Aloysius Lippomano, there are hymns of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, Laurence, Agnes, Vincent, Cyprian, the eighteen martyrs, Romanus, Cassian, Hippolytus, Fructuosus, Quirinus, Eulalia, and Hemeterius. Others are found in the *Hymnary* of V. Thomasius.

98 118. I shall not give as many examples as I would like of Prudentius translated into vernacular languages, although perhaps more are hidden away. Certainly translations of the Christian poet are not as readily available as those of pagan authors, from whom sometimes no benefit, and more often the greatest corruption of human morals, may arise.

Rodriguez de Castro had seen a Spanish translation of the *Psychomachia*—made in verse, as I infer—by the bachelor Francisco Palomino, a priest of the Order of Saint James at the convent of Uclés, published at Uclés in quarto. He praises it in his learned *Bibliotheca Hispanica*.

[Col. 0658D] *Battle or Combat of the Soul, composed in Latin verse by the poet Aurelius Prudentius Clemens, newly translated from Latin into Castilian.* Under this title the year 1259 is given instead of the publication year 1559, as Castro seems to infer conjecturally. It is dedicated to Alfonso Manrique, son of García Manrique, Count of Osorno, president of the orders. If I could inspect the book myself, I would try to determine whether the year of publication, with the numerals arranged differently, was 1529. García Manrique, Count of Osorno, was already flourishing at the beginning of the sixteenth century. Rodriguez writes “Dosorno,” and shortly afterward “Huartanet.”

[Col. 0657B] 119. He also reports another translation:

*Translation of the hymns Aurelius Prudentius composed for the most illustrious martyrs Saint Laurence, Saint Vincent, Saint Engratia, Saint Lupércus, and the countless others who suffered in the imperial city of Zaragoza, together with the birth and homeland of Aurelius Prudentius himself. By Luis Díez de Aux, son of that same city, to whom it is dedicated.*

Zaragoza, by Juan de Lanaja and Quartanet, 1619. Octavo. Following the fictitious chronicle of Dexter, Luis Díez wrote a Spanish verse Life of Prudentius. I have likewise heard from the distinguished Pedro García de la Huerta that he rendered the hymns of Prudentius into Spanish verse, and some time ago I read, carefully prepared, his translation of the hymn *On the New Light* for Holy Saturday.

[Col. 0658A] 120. Antoine du Verdier, *Bibliothèque française*, Lyons edition, 1685, p. 95, records the following:

*Aurelie Prudence Clement. The Passion of Saint Quirinus, martyr and bishop of Siscia, taken from the seventh hymn of Prudentius, the Christian poet, in his book of crowns, and translated into French verse, stanza by stanza.*

It was published among the *Lives of the Saints* in Paris by Nicolas Chesneau. In the same work, p. 1025, Pierre de Montchault translated into French two hymns of Prudentius, on the Nativity and the Epiphany—into verse, I believe. On p. 521, Guy Le Fevre de la Borderie published in Paris, through Robert Le Maignier, *Ecclesiastical Hymns and Canticles, Partly Translated and Partly of His Own Composition*, octavo, 1582, second edition. There are, according to Verdier, fourteen or fifteen hymns of Prudentius, elegantly rendered by Guy into French meter.

[Col. 0658B] On p. 939, Paschal Robin rendered into French—I believe in verse—the second hymn of *Peristephanon*, on Saint Laurence, and the third, on Saint Eulalia.

99. **121.** I have the following Italian translations of Prudentius’s poems: *I due libri di Prudenzo contro Symmaco* [The two books of Prudentius against Symmachus], translated into Italian verse by Fr. M. Carlo Agostino Ansaldi, Dominican. Venice, printed by Pietro Valvasense, 1754, octavo. In his preface Ansaldus says that few have illustrated this work of Prudentius with commentaries, and that only Heinsius did so successfully—an entirely false claim, since Juretus and Grangaeus illustrated those books with learned commentaries, not to mention others who published commentaries on all the poems. The edition is teeming with errors in the Latin verses.

[Col. 0658D] Having completed this and the preceding chapter on the manuscripts and editions of Prudentius, I shall now gather together some observations concerning the differing orthography of the manuscripts and editions, although I have already said something about this when discussing the individual manuscripts. The Marietti codex writes *Kerastae* for *cerastae*, *conicio, deicio, proicio, harena, frutecta, virecta*, *Adlantis* for *Atlantis*, *haut* for *haud*, *dispero*, and *fervos* for *fervor*, *clodus* for *claudus*. Aldus writes *obmutisce, deminuo, holuscula*. Vaticanus A has *obmutisce, police, milia* for *millia, disuesco, subfodit, obicio, asscitur* for *adscitur, vagantis* for *vagantes*; others have *vaganteis*. Weitzius has *police, tonica, ymnus, inrepsit, atquin, saltim, vendico, ora* for *hora*, and *sevus* for *saevus*. The Puteanus codex has *dispuite*, *solporeus* for *sulphureus*, *vertex* rather than *vortex*, *marsuppium*, and *Solomonia*. The Codex Alexandrinus has *ferrugeneus*, *totiens*—as does the Marietti codex—*neglegat*—likewise with that codex—*luis* in the nominative, *fatesco, nichil* and *michi*, and *tempto*. It should be noted that this spelling, *tempto, condepno*, and similar forms, was especially prevalent in the eighth, ninth, and tenth centuries. The Egmondanus codex has *postlimineo, distructum, futtile, elegitur,* and *ligumine*. The Pragensis codex has *disparsa, hii* for *hi, dispoliare, assit* always for *adsit*, and *haut* for *haud*. The Ratisbonensis has *disparsa, conicio, deicio, proicio, harena, virecta, frutecta, nothus* for *notus*—*nothus* being the African, or southern, wind—*holuscula, clodus, coagola,* and *conubium*. All or most of the Heinsian manuscripts have *Abessolon, atquin, setius* for *secius, cruminae* for *crumenae,* and *verticibus* for *vorticibus*. The Viennensis has *conicio* and *frutecta*. The Widmannianus has *atquin, hora* for *ora, fraglat* for *fragrat,* and *alitus* for *halitus, sevus* for *saevus*. The Bongarsianus has *atquin, saltim, flagrat,* and *fraglat* for *fragrat*.

These and other similar forms are found everywhere in the ancient manuscripts of Prudentius, no less than in those of other ancient authors. They arise partly from a certain established spelling customary to a particular period or copyist, and partly from negligence or error. One may consult Gifanius’s index to Lucretius, in which he wished to restore several words from old books in Prudentius: read *pignera, praestringo, suboles, linguo, pulcer, conluces,* and *volnera*, on pages 378, 382, 412, 419, 438, 440, and 445. In the commentaries we shall note other matters. For now I shall merely observe that those are completely mistaken who think they are following an author’s orthography if they imitate every word and letter-stroke of an ancient manuscript written two or more centuries after that author. They are doing nothing then except presenting us with the errors of some unlearned copyist—or, if one prefers, the orthography customary in that later age.

It is nevertheless not useless to record such variant spellings, since in obscure passages the true reading is often recovered from the alteration of a single letter. In this matter I have been neither as diligent as the painstaking Dutch intellects usually are, since I have claimed for myself some freedom to judge and select, nor as sparing as many perhaps would wish who are afflicted with an extraordinary weariness of such matters. Indeed, I took great care that nothing which Johannes Mariettus had conjectured in this field in his *Adversaria* and written in the margins of Aldus’s edition should be missing from my edition, except when I plainly judged a variant reading superfluous.

As for the Aldine edition, enriched with Mariettus’s manuscript notes, I should mention once and for all that it was first brought to my attention by the distinguished Laurentius Hervas, already well known for the abundance and variety of his writings and especially accomplished in mathematical studies. While examining the manuscripts of the Roman College, he came upon this edition of Aldus; from it I conceived the idea of illustrating Prudentius. Hervas added that he had once seen some mathematical writings by the same Mariettus among the manuscripts. I have learned nothing else about Mariettus except what the distinguished Vitus M. Giovenazzi pointed out: a passage in Juvencius’s *History of the Society of Jesus*, book XVII, sections 36 and following, where it is related that Antonius Mariettus of Rome returned in 1616 from a certain sacred mission to which Pope Paul V had delegated him together with another companion. I am very willing to believe that this was our Johannes Antonius Mariettus.

[p. 100] The translation is pure and polished.

[Col. 0659A] Ansaldus had seen a manuscript Italian translation of the *Peristephanon* at Milan, said to be by Salvinius. I read the matter differently in Argelatus, *Biblioteca de’ volgarizzatori*, vol. III, p. 302: he names the translator Marcus Antonius Mozzius, while saying that Salvinius added the preface. Argelatus had this translation in his possession and intended to publish it in a collection of old translations of Latin poems; but I think he never carried the project through. Certainly Johannes Lamius was mistaken in volume I of the *Memorabilia Italorum eruditorum*, p. 120, Florentine edition of 1742, when he asserted that Mozzius’s translation had been made public at Milan after Mozzius’s death.

From the manuscript papers of a certain friend I extract the following:

*The passion and death of St. Cassian, martyr and bishop of Imola, translated into ottava rima from the Latin verses of St. Prudentius*, Ferrara, 1585. The translator appears to have been a certain Ludovicus Napoli, who dedicates the work to Musottius, bishop of Imola, and placed the initials L. N. at the beginning of the translation. By the same judgment with which he calls St. Cassian a bishop, he also calls Prudentius a saint.

See no. 56: *Hymn of Aurelius Prudentius Clemens, a man of consular rank, to St. Cassian the martyr, with a paraphrase in ottava rima and annotations by the Rev. Giuseppe Antonio Cavalleri of Comacchio, an Argonaut Academician of Ferrara and public teacher of grammar at Bagnacavallo*. Venice, 1772, printed by Bartolo Barucchelli. Cavallerius, a grammarian, preferred to follow the forebears’ interpretation of the initials *V. C.* and call Prudentius a man of consular rank, rather than to consider what learned men in this century, the preceding one, and the one before that had observed. I have discussed above, under no. 116, the paraphrase in Germanic rhythm of Hymn VIII for the Kalends of January, composed and published in 1659. Under no. 91 I said that a Greek manuscript translation of the *Psychomachia* existed—unless someone inferred the translation of the entire work merely from its Greek title.

## CHAPTER VI. The Magdeburg Centuriators’ and Other Heretics’ Judgment of Prudentius’s Doctrine

101. **122.** If I explain how many doctrines of our religion Prudentius defended, established, and confirmed, and how learnedly and vigorously he did so, in the words of heretics rather than in my own or those of another Catholic, I think no one will be angry with me, provided he carefully considers the purpose I have in view. My aim is to show how much weight Prudentius’s authority deserves against recent heretics and other bad Catholics, whom he openly opposes. I shall accomplish this if, besides the man’s renowned piety and outstanding integrity, universally commended, it is also established that he explained the most difficult theological questions and the most serious doctrines of the Christian faith with an exceptional store of learning and singular judgment.

Accordingly, the Magdeburg Centuriators, in century 4, chapter 10, as reported by Ludovicus Lucius, say that Prudentius was gifted, serious, disciplined in character, devoted to literature in his youth, and that he went from Spain to Rome to venerate the martyrs (see no. 58). In his books against Symmachus, they say, he displayed no ordinary learning and intellectual power.

Concerning his doctrine they say approximately the following: he held correctly that there is one divine and eternal essence, distinguished in three persons, as at the beginning of the *Psychomachia*: “For we worship one God under a threefold name”; and in the hymn *Before Sleep*, verse 1: “Be present, supreme Father.” Likewise concerning Christ, *Hamartigenia*, verse 51: “The true Son of the true Father stands.” Concerning Christ’s incarnation, in the hymn *Before Meals*, verse 136: “Behold, a new offspring has come”; and again in the hymn *At Every Hour*: “Born from the Father’s heart”; and in Hymn VIII for the Kalends of January: “But he did not endure that devastation.”

**123.** Concerning creation, in the same hymn, verse 22: “Heaven and day, and the rest.” Concerning God’s not being the author of evil, *Hamartigenia*, verse 159: “God is not the inventor of vice.” Concerning the corruption and destruction of created things, in the same work, verse 504: “For whatever the sun beholds is vain,” and so forth.

Concerning the angels, he rightly says that they were created in great number and are preserved by God for his purposes, book II against Symmachus, verse 233. He calls them “airy ministers,” *Hamartigenia*, verse 166, and teaches at length that the devil fell from their number and rank through his own wantonness.

He held correctly that man was created perfectly and that he fell and was restored through Christ, both elsewhere and especially in book II against Symmachus, verses 260 and following, and in *Hamartigenia*, verse 665: “It is the work of God to save fallen man.” He relates at great length that man possessed an entire and upright power of will before the Fall, *Hamartigenia*, verse 673: “Fool, you do not know the power of your freedom, given by the Creator himself.” What the Magdeburg Centuriators assert here—that Prudentius taught that the power of the will was wholly destroyed by original sin and transformed toward every evil—we shall shortly see for what it is worth. They go on to say that he held correctly concerning original sin, *Apotheosis*, verse 908: “This is the soul’s first nature.” Concerning the distinction between the Law and the Gospel, in the same work: “But the people fall on their face, not destined to see the depths,” verses 330 and following.

**124.** They add that Prudentius refuted several heresies, especially those that blasphemed Christ’s person and office. In the preface to the *Apotheosis*, against the foolish disputes and questions of the pagans concerning God and religion, he rightly says: “Therefore God chose the foolish things of the world.”

In the following poem he vigorously attacks the Patripassians. Against them he asserts that it was the Son, not the Father, who became man, suffered, and died; likewise, that it was the Son, not the Father, who was seen by the patriarchs. He expressly says in verse 111: “The Father is he whom no one is permitted to see.” Then he argues with great force against the Sabellians and concludes: “This is our salvation,” and so forth. Afterwards he attacks the Jews most fiercely: “Behold Christ, God, for you, wretched Judaea.”

**125.** He fights in an extensive poem against the followers of Ebion, Artemon, Paul of Samosata, Photinus, and Marcellus, whom he calls *Homuncionites*, and he concludes that discussion with memorable doctrine, saying: “He himself bears the work which he constructed,” and so forth.

Again, in a poem of the same work, he attacks the heresy of Cerdo, Apelles, and the other Fantasists. There he also mentions by name the Manichaean who attributed an airy body to Christ: “And first observe whether he teaches that anything fictitious should be ascribed to God.” It appears that he composed the final poem of that work specifically against those who denied the resurrection of the body; in it he says beautifully: “I know that my body will rise in Christ.”

In the extensive book *Hamartigenia* he refutes the heresy of Marcion. Finally, he enters into combat with Symmachus, refuting all his arguments by which he had attempted to persuade people to restore the ancient rites.

**126.** The Centuriators also frequently praise Prudentius’s doctrine, listing him among the eminent and illustrious teachers from whom one may chiefly learn what form doctrine took in the fourth century. Thus, in chapter 4, they say that Prudentius taught that God is everywhere, *Apotheosis*: “But God, immense and poured throughout all things.” That three persons exist in one divine essence, preface to the *Apotheosis*: “God is threefold in his supreme unity”; and in the *Apotheosis* itself, verse 238: “This is our salvation.” That the Father is eternal and immeasurable, *Apotheosis*, verse 111: “The Father is he whom no one is permitted to see.”

He carefully explains what the Son is in respect of his substance, properties, and offices, *Hamartigenia*, verse 346: “Therefore the Father is the creator of good, and Christ together with the Father.” The doctrine of the two natures of Jesus Christ appears in the *Psychomachia*, verse 74: “An unwedded woman conceived God Christ, a man from a mortal mother.” That all good things were created by God, *Hamartigenia*, verse 338: “In the beginning of things.” Concerning the cause of the Fall, *Hamartigenia*, verse 184: “But he was made good from a good stock.” Concerning man’s Fall and his condition after the Fall, book II against Symmachus, verse 260: “I had created man perfect”; and *Hamartigenia*, verse 697: “Go,” said the first parent.

Concerning free will before the Fall, *Hamartigenia*, verse 673: “Fool, you do not know the power of your freedom given by him.” Concerning the matters in which the human will is free or enslaved, *Hamartigenia*, verse 269: “Behold for you a clear proof of freedom.” Concerning the distinction between the Old and New Testaments, *Apotheosis*, verse 330: “But the people fall prostrate, not destined to see Christ, written in the image of the profound Law through riddling figures.”

**127.** Moreover, concerning the proper works of Christians, to be performed with a willing and eager spirit, hymn *Fasting*, verse 211: “For this too is a great kind of virtue.” Concerning the dwelling-place of souls, hymn *Funeral Rites*, verse 149: “But the dissoluble body.” Concerning the resurrection of the dead, the same hymn, verse 33: “For that the body should rest.” And *Apotheosis*, verse 1062: “I know my body in Christ.” Concerning eternal life, hymn *For the Dead*, verse 97: “These things, which now in pallid corruption…” Concerning hell, book II against Symmachus, verse 185: “The inner man who breathes—he shall pay eternally.” Against vain philosophy, astrology, and magic, book II against Symmachus, verse 470: “Whoever thinks that there is a place for fate.”

**128.** Let us now see what the Magdeburg Centuriators and other heretics accuse Prudentius of saying less appropriately. In chapter 4 they criticize Prudentius for invoking the saints in the hymns to St. Lawrence, St. Vincent, and St. Cassian. Yet in this doctrine they give Prudentius as companions Athanasius, Basil, Gregory Nazianzen, and Ambrose, shamelessly asserting that an evil spirit inserted into the writings of such men many statements of the sort concerning the invocation of departed saints.

They add that Ambrose—or whoever was the author of the funeral oration on the death of Theodosius—recounts many superstitious matters concerning the cross discovered by Helena, which are insulting to Christ’s merit, such as Prudentius’s statement in the hymn *Before Sleep*, verse 133: “The cross drives away every sin,” and so forth. They also seem to think that Ephrem attributed too much to the sign of the cross, and that the Church was burdened with many unnecessary and useless things if, at that time, the penitential canons of Peter of Alexandria were in use within it.

Concerning purgatory, they note that Prudentius’s doctrine in *Hamartigenia*, at the end—“Be thou in a cavernous …”—agrees with Lactantius, book VII, chapter 21, and Jerome, book IV of his commentary on Isaiah, chapter 4, and book XVIII of his commentary on Isaiah.

**129.** Concerning ecclesiastical rites, they observe that, as superstition increased in the fourth century, funeral ceremonies were heaped together from both paganism and Judaism. They cite, in chapter 6, Prudentius’s verses from the hymn *Funeral Rites*: “Shining with bright whiteness,” and “We shall cherish the bones beneath the roof.”

They admit from the histories of that age—those of Socrates, Sozomen, Theodoret, and others—that there were altars in the churches, but they say that this custom had passed over from the Jews. They report that Prudentius indicates that images representing the sufferings of the martyrs were customarily placed in churches, but that Jerome disapproved of paintings in churches in his letter to John of Jerusalem.

They concede that Prudentius mentions wax candles in the hymn to St. Lawrence, and that Jerome, in his work against Vigilantius, asserts that throughout the churches of the East, when the Gospel is to be read, lights are kindled even while the sun is shining—not indeed to drive away darkness, but to display a sign of joy. But they reply that these things too originated in Judaism.

Finally, in chapter 10, they count among Prudentius’s blemishes that he does not speak sufficiently appropriately about the freedom of the human will, *Hamartigenia*, verse 769: “Behold for you a clear sign.” They also fault him because, in the same work, verse 509, he adopted what seems to them a forced interpretation of Paul’s statement in Ephesians 6: “He errs who says that our struggle is with flesh and blood.” Likewise, because he wrote that the merits of the martyrs would benefit the cities in which they had fallen asleep, hymn XVIII, *The Martyrs of Zaragoza*: “Alone, in greater numbers, to meet…” Nor does his statement in the *Cathemerinon*, hymn *Before Meals*, verse 146, seem sufficiently cautious: “This was that ancient hatred.”

Lucas Osiander also brings some of these charges against Prudentius in *Ecclesiastical History*, century 4, book I, chapter 26: “We do not doubt,” he says, “that the Lord himself forgave him these errors.” Yet he admits that Prudentius held correct views concerning most parts of the Christian religion, attacked and condemned certain heresies with pious zeal and sound judgment, and refuted Symmachus admirably.

In this poet, he adds, Christians should especially commend and imitate the fact that he neither invokes pagan gods nor mixes them into his poems, nor defiles theology with impure pagan fables; rather, he treats divine matters seriously and yet with sufficient elegance in holy language. Thus the heretics add great weight to the cause of the Catholic religion when they praise Prudentius so highly and freely admit that he was alien to their own opinions.

I shall add to these Johannes Clericus, who perhaps would not strongly disagree with them. In volume XII of the *Universal Library*, he charges Prudentius with suspicion of Pythagoreanism on the basis of hymn 3 of the *Cathemerinon*, verse 58: “Far from us be that hunger which delights to tear bloody feasts from the slaughter of cattle.” He also chatters at length about the prayer in *Hamartigenia*: “O god, father of all,” and about Prudentius’s calling the soul a liquid.

Strangely enough, Clericus is no better a critic in poetic matters than in sacred ones. He asserts that Prudentius sometimes crawls along the ground precisely when he tries to fly into the heights; nevertheless, he does not deny that Prudentius’s work is useful for learning about ecclesiastical antiquity.

Bayle, in the *Critical Dictionary*, under “Prudence,” partly follows Clericus and partly disagrees with him. He maintains that the prayer of the *Hamartigenia* can be defended and praised, and testifies that Prudentius explicitly affirms the immortality of the soul. Bayle is more concerned with the heresy of the Manichaeans, and denies that Prudentius sufficiently dispelled their objections, stubbornly asserting that he nowhere found an adequate response in Prudentius.

## CHAPTER VII. The Worship and Veneration of the Saints and Their Relics, from the Poems of Prudentius

[Col. 0664C]

**130.** To vindicate Prudentius’s doctrine methodically and in proper order, I shall first discuss the matters in which Prudentius agrees with Catholics and differs from heretics; then I shall explain those points which seemed to some people to depart from the truth of the Christian faith.

Prudentius affirms the invocation of the saints and the worship of relics. But is Prudentius alone in affirming this? “No,” they say, “others do so as well,” because this superstition had already begun to enter the Church.

[Col. 0663D] Fabricius says in his commentary that the invocation of the saints had already infiltrated the Church in Prudentius’s time, and wishes to defend his error against Prudentius by the authority of Joachim Camerarius, who asserts that Prudentius was too much of a poet in these matters and departed from simple truth while pursuing musical charm. But Camerarius should not be heeded here—that old man who deserved far better of Plautus than of religion. I rightly found the following written by hand in the margin of one of Fabricius’s copies: “Prudentius often speaks historically, and no differently from the other holy Fathers.”

What if I demonstrate that this was done throughout the Christian world, with the bishops approving and applauding? Shall we say that those ancient Christians were in error while the innovators hold the truth? Let Prudentius’s poems be reread, and it will clearly appear that Prudentius is not proposing some private opinion of his own, but recounting the practice of the universal Church.

[Col. 0663D] *Peristephanon*, hymn 1, verse 7:

> Here, stained with a double slaughter, he drank the hot waters;  
> Now the inhabitants throng the sands marked with holy blood,  
> Entreating with voice, with prayers, and with offerings.  
> Foreigners too, settlers from across the world, come here,  
> For the report, spreading the news, has struck every land:  
> Here are the patrons of the world whom worshipers encircle.

Those verses in the *Passion of Lawrence*, verse 513, are splendid:

> Whatever the Quirites were accustomed  
> To pray for with Numa’s ladle,  
> The crowds frequenting Christ’s halls  
> Echo in hymns to the martyr.  
> The very lights of the Senate,  
> Once luperci or flamines,  
> Kiss the thresholds  
> Of apostles and martyrs…  
>   
> Thrice, four times, and seven times blessed  
> Is the inhabitant of the City  
> Who celebrates you and, close at hand,  
> The seat of your bones.  
> To whom it is permitted to fall prostrate before you,  
> Who sprinkles the place with tears,  
> Who presses his breast upon the ground,  
> Who pours out his vows in murmured prayer.

And in hymn 3, on Eulalia, verses 191 and following:

> Here, where the kindly brightness  
> Illuminates the courts with shining marble,  
> The revered earth keeps in its bosom  
> The sacred relics and ashes  
> For both stranger and native.  
> Here it is pleasing to venerate the bones;  
> An altar is set upon the bones,  
> And she, placed beneath God’s feet,

[Col. 0665A] In Hymn IV he celebrates the patronage of the martyrs toward the cities that venerate their bones, verse 13:

> Raised up as a head from the great world,  
> Each city will hasten eagerly  
> To meet Christ, carrying precious gifts  
> In baskets.

He then lists, one by one, Carthage, Córdoba, Tarragona, Gerunda, Calagurris, Barcelona, Narbonne, Arles, Mérida, Complutum, Tingis, and especially Rome and Zaragoza.

In the *Passion of Vincent* one may observe the care with which those ancient Christians gathered the relics of the martyrs, so that they might be a protection for themselves and their descendants, verses 333 and following.

> You would see a faithful crowd  
> Gathering from the whole city,  
> Softening the bed prepared for him,  
> Drying the raw wounds.

> Of the claws with kisses;  
> Another rejoices to lick

> In the blood as it drips,

[Col. 0665D] And in the same hymn to St. Vincent, verse 509:

> While pious care, lamenting,  
> Adorns the mound,  
> And the body entrusted to the tomb  
> Reserves it for a future life.

In the *Passion of Hippolytus*, verses 135 and following:

> Stunned with grief and searching with their eyes, they went about,  
> Filling their bosoms with the mangled limbs.  
> One embraces the snow-white head  
> And tenderly cradles the revered gray hair.  
> Another gathers the shoulders, severed hands, arms, forearms,  
> Knees, and the bare fragments of the legs.  
> The absorbent cloths too dry the blood-soaked sands,  
> So that no drop remains upon the stained dust.  
> If any blood still clings to the stakes  
> In their hot spray, the pressed sponge  
> Carries it all away.

You see why vessels containing blood are so often found in the tombs of martyrs. The heretics themselves have established by experiments that this is genuine blood; therefore no sane person will deny that such vessels are a sure sign of martyrdom. What else could they indicate? Consult Boldetti, *Observations*, book I, chapters 28 and following, where he explains this argument learnedly.

[Col. 0666C] Concerning the holy martyrs Fructuosus and his companions he relates the following in hymn 6:

> Then ashes from the sacred bodies  
> And bones soaked with wine are gathered,  
> Which each person hastily claimed for himself.  
> So great was the brothers’ love to carry home  
> The dedicated gifts of the saints’ ashes,  
> Or to wear a faithful pledge in the bosom.  
>   
> But lest they divide the relics to be raised again,  
> And soon to be with the Lord together,  
> Among separate tombs, they are seen  
> Clad in white robes.

> And enclosed in a hollow,

>

The words of Braulio in his letter to the priest Jactatus, volume XXX of *Sacred Spain*, appendix 3, are relevant here:

[Col. 0666D] “Concerning the relics of the venerable apostles which you demanded should be sent to you, I faithfully report that I possess none of the martyrs’ relics in such a way that I can know which relics belong to whom. The judgment of my predecessors and lords was that, since the relics which people possessed were everywhere, or secretly, or even unwillingly and under compulsion, demanded either to be given away or surrendered through the affection of many, the labels should be removed so that no indication of anyone’s identity might be available to all, and they should be placed together in a single chamber. About seventy have nevertheless been preserved and are used for various purposes; among them are not those which you seek. I would suspect that the feast of the innumerable martyrs of Zaragoza arose from this, unless their acts were more reliable than to be shaken by any suspicions.”

The other hymns of the *Peristephanon* contain statements by Prudentius concerning the worship and invocation of the saints that are substantially to the same effect.

**131.** From this great care of Christians in collecting the bones of the martyrs—a practice not only affirmed by Prudentius but also abundantly confirmed by authentic acts of the martyrs—we rightly conclude that the custom of venerating the relics of the saints prevailed everywhere not only in the fourth century but also in earlier times. This also explains why these precious memorials have been preserved down to our own age.

Indeed, Prudentius asserts that the couch on which St. Vincent lay still existed in his own time, verse 553:

> By that fragment of earthenware,  
> Through which his glory grew,  
> By that couch which trembling descendants  
> Kiss,  
> Have mercy on our prayers,  
> So that Christ, appeased on behalf of his own,  
> May incline his favorable ear  
> And not charge all our offenses against us.

**132.** This practice is confirmed not only by Prudentius’s testimony but also by the statements of many others. To omit the rest, I shall cite St. Paulinus of Nola, because he commonly embraces opinions very similar to those of Prudentius and gives an excellent account of the miracles performed at the tomb of St. Felix.

[Col. 0666D] *Natalis* 3:

> Then one may see everywhere breasts cleansed  
> By the sacred remedy lying prostrate at the threshold,  
> Their minds already restored,  
> Already giving thanks with their own voices.  
> A trembling crowd of open-mouthed people gathers…  
>

> So many throngs driven together by a single prayer.  
> The peoples of Lucania gather…

> For, as though the chambers were joined beneath sacred roofs,  
> They look through all the windows from above  
> Upon the altars, beneath which inside  
> The bodies of the saints have their dwelling…

He then mentions the relics of several saints, including:

> Here too is the martyr Nazarius, whom  
> By the faithful gift of noble Ambrose  
> I received with a submissive mind.

*Natalis* 11, among Muratorius’s *Anecdota*, verses 46 and following:

> The Lord, healer of all things, has given holy physicians  
> To suffering mortals throughout the various nations,

>

> In the Roman city.

>

> Libya received Lebbaeus (Thaddeus), Phrygia Philip,

> And Mark was given to you, Alexandria…  
>

I shall encompass much in a few words of St. Augustine, who says in his *Expositions on Psalm XLIV*: “Let the temple of Romulus be shown to me at Rome in as great an honor as I shall show the memorial of Peter there. In Peter, who is honored, if not he who died for us?”

In Paulinus, *Aquitania* should perhaps be read *Aquitanica*. The distinguished Giovenazzius conjectured this, having noted several passages in ancient authors in which Aquitania is presented as a province distinct from Gaul. Giovenazzius preserves many more such conjectures concerning St. Paulinus in his papers; it would be desirable for them to be published. Paulinus’s poems especially need an experienced physician to restore them to health, and Muratorius and Mingarellius were not such men.

109. Paulinus reports in many places how great was the gathering of peoples to venerate the body of St. Felix of Nola, as in *Natalis* 11, verse 305:

> And the throng, gathered continually  
> From various lands, venerates  
> The brief throne of the great confessor.

St. Augustine also confirms this admirably in letter 78: “Many people know the holiness of the place where the body of Felix of Nola was buried. I wanted them to go there, because from there it can more easily and more reliably be reported to us whatever may have been divinely revealed to any one of them.” Here Augustine alludes to the friendship he had formed with Paulinus, with whom he was most closely united. In Paulinus’s verses, *throne* means a tomb, as one customarily says “the throne of blessed Peter.”

## CHAPTER VIII. Sacred Images, the Adoration of the Holy Cross, and the Primacy of the Roman Pontiff

[Col. 0667B]

**133.** From these considerations it is clear that Hospinian, Bingham, and others are wrong to assert that the practice of venerating relics became established only after Augustine’s time. I also conclude that paintings in churches were not disapproved by St. Augustine—as Peter Martyr and others allege. Augustine knew very well what was happening at Nola, and he praises the letters of St. Paulinus, in which paintings are mentioned, most highly in letter 27 to Paulinus.

Nor was Paulinus the first to introduce this custom, as some heretics chatter. He himself indicates that it had also been practiced elsewhere, though rarely, *Natalis* 9:

> Perhaps someone may ask by what reasoning  
> This decision concerning the manner of practice  
> Has been made by us: to paint holy dwellings  
> In the likeness of living creatures, though rarely.

The images of which our Prudentius speaks in the poems on Cassian and Hippolytus were certainly older: one was at Forum Cornelii, the other at Rome. Barthius, *Adversaria*, book II, chapter 32, thinks that the following verses in the poem *On the Passion*, among the works of Lactantius, plainly mention a painted image of the Lord at the entrance to a temple:

> Whoever you are who draw near and enter  
> Beneath the temple’s central threshold,  
> Pause a little, and look upon me, innocent,  
> Suffering for your crime;  
> Look upon me, enclose me in your mind,  
> Preserve me in your heart.

In the time of the Council of Elvira this custom already seems to have been introduced in some regions. For this reason canon 36 appears to have been enacted: “It has been decided that there should be no paintings in churches, lest what is worshiped and adored be depicted on the walls.”

That canon could wisely have been established at that time, since the churches of Christians were not safe from the incursions and mockery of pagans. Moreover, from the example of the pagans, Christians could easily have learned idolatry, and especially could have worshiped the images rather than God, whom the images represented.

Theodoret, chapter 16 of his *History*, in his *Life of St. Simeon Stylites*, testifies that images of that saint had commonly been erected in the porticoes of workshops at Rome, so that people might add his protection and defense to their own. This sufficiently shows what the Roman Church’s attitude toward images of the saints was in Theodoret’s age. Compare Petavius, book XI, chapter 13, volume IV, part 2.

**134.** Prudentius’s doctrine concerning the veneration and power of the cross is especially illustrious. *Cathemerinon*, hymn 6, verse 129:

> Grant that, when summoned by sleep,  
> You seek a chaste bed,  
> The forehead and the place of the heart  
> May be marked with the figure of the cross.  
>   
> The cross drives away every sin;  
> Darknesses flee the cross;  
> When the mind is dedicated  
> To such a sign, it does not waver.

*Cathemerinon*, hymn 5, verse 96:

> For, fixed upon the cross,  
> The hope of mankind flourishes.

*Cathemerinon*, hymn 9, verse 82:

> Release your resonant voice, release your nimble tongue;  
> Speak of the trophy of the Passion, speak of the triumphant cross;  
> Sing of the standard that shines upon marked foreheads.

In the *Romanus*, verse 586:

> This is that cross, the salvation of us all;  
> Romanus says: this is mankind’s redemption.

*Apotheosis*, verse 446:

> Now the purple robe, submissive,  
> Is spread before the halls of Christ,  
> The ruler of the Aeneads;  
> And the supreme ruler adores  
> The standard of the cross.

Many other passages may be found in *Cathemerinon*, hymn 11, verse 113; *Peristephanon*, hymn 10, verses 621 and following; *Psychomachia*, verse 347; and book I against Symmachus, verses 465 and following, where he describes Constantine’s victory over Maxentius, observing that:

> Then that Senate  
> Adored the title of avenging warfare  
> And the revered name of Christ,  
> Which shone brightly upon the weapons.

Book II, verse 711, concerning Christian soldiers:

> With the cross inscribed  
> Upon their foreheads, the trumpets sounded;  
> The first spear bore dragons…

What follows surpasses it, elevating Christ’s summit even higher. Certainly the heterodox do not deny these things; indeed, many of them acknowledge that several other of the holy Fathers both spoke and acted in this way. But they loudly proclaim that the Fathers spoke and acted wrongly and superstitiously. Nor, I think, could the Magdeburg Centuriators be refuted more effectively than by collecting from their History all the passages in which they do not hesitate to accuse the Fathers of the fourth century—when Catholic religion and doctrine flourished most vigorously—of error [Col. 0669B] and superstition. For they know very well that most of those Fathers agreed with Catholics of our own time both in words and in actions; and consequently it cannot be doubted that all the peoples whom they taught and governed lived in the same manner [Note: [Col. 0669C] It is not my intention now to harass those who, dazzled by the splendor of the light [Col. 0669D], wished to close their eyes altogether and dared to corrupt the explicit testimonies of the holy Fathers. Such was George Fabricius, who, in his poem on the Passion of the Lord, among the works of Lactantius, substituted these lines for the words:

> Bend the knee, and adore with reverence the venerable wood of the cross,

> Weeping,

> Bend the knee, and, seeking with humble mouth the earth drenched in innocent blood.

> It would have been preferable, says Jo. Albert Fabricius—although himself heterodox, in *Bibliotheca Latina vetus*, book IV, chapter 2—that G. Fabricius had not shown himself so ingenious, here and elsewhere, in tampering with works not his own, which he published.].

### 135

Among the holy Fathers whom they say never spoke of the primacy of the Roman pontiff—and with whom we are not presently concerned—they also number our Prudentius. Yet the matter is entirely the reverse. Here are the words of the most courageous martyr Laurence, *Peristephanon* 2, lines 413ff.:

>
> One, called to the nations;

And at line 660, Rome speaks of herself:

> Of Novatus; return yourselves to the Catholic peoples.

## CHAPTER IX. Prudentius is unjustly criticized concerning the doctrine of freedom and his interpretation of the Apostle to the Ephesians, chapter VI

### 136

Prudentius does not deserve criticism for having defended what is called freedom of indifference, unless all the holy Fathers without exception are to be criticized. His verses are from *Hamartigenia*, lines 769ff.:

> Here you have a marked proof of freedom,  
> By which God wished us to know that whatever must be followed  
> Is placed under our control and everywhere left open,  
> So that we may tread either path. The two are ordered to depart  
> From Sodom: one rushes out, the other lingers.
>
> The one hastens his step in flight; the other resists.  
> Each possesses a free mind, but differing desire  
> Divides them, as their own impulse drags each one  
> This way or that.
