Marchese Scipione Maffei, in his *History of Gratian*, places Prudentius among the other Fathers who transmitted the Catholic doctrine concerning grace and free will. Daniel Huetius, in the *Origeniana*, book II, question 7, magnificently defended Origen’s position concerning freedom of indifference against Cornelius Jansenius on the basis of St. Augustine, whom Jansenius wishes to be the sole judge of this controversy. I am glad that these most learned men have said what I would have had to say on behalf of Prudentius [Col. 0670C], so that I may not become entangled in an irksome question or repeat here, to the point of nausea, the same stale cabbage, although I shall have to add certain things in the notes.

Nor can Prudentius be said to give a bad exposition of the Apostle’s passage in chapter VI of the Epistle to the Ephesians:

> Put on the armor of God, so that you may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil. For our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in heavenly places.

Prudentius, *Hamartigenia*, lines 509ff.:

> He errs, says he, who thinks that our struggle is with blood  
> And flesh, and hot veins, and corrupt gall,  
> And believes that the soul sins through heated marrow.
>
> It is not the mind’s own limbs that oppress it, nor does earthly strength  
> Attack the fluid senses or challenge them in battle.  
> Rather, night and day we engage in combat  
> With dark spirits.
>
> It is easy to restrain  
> The rebellious passions of the flesh.
>
> There is a greater force within man, which breathes in  
> Its poisonous vapor and strikes the delicate mind  
> With a delicate air.

Nor does Prudentius assign all blame to the demon; rather, to a considerable extent he refers it to the rebellious movements of the heart and mind, line 553:

> But why do I turn every evil of the world and of mankind  
> Against the malice of the hostile enemy, when our evils,  
> Arising from our own minds, derive their origin, source, and power—  
> What they are and what they can do—from the heart that gives them birth?
>
> He indeed is the tinder and cause of our evils.  
> But he can disturb or deceive only as far  
> As we ourselves are willing . . .
>
> We generate all our evil from our own body.

Most interpreters understand the Apostle’s words, “against flesh and blood,” to mean human beings. St. Jerome refers Prudentius’s interpretation to those words, and does not appear to condemn it [Note: [Col. 0671D] Someone may say: “This statement, ‘Our struggle is not against blood and flesh,’ and so forth, is made in order to teach us that even those vices which we think are supplied to us by the flesh are not of flesh or blood, but are suggested by certain spiritual wickednesses . . . Since, therefore, the Apostle wishes to teach us, they say, that these kinds of vice do not arise from the nature of the body or from the material of flesh and blood, but from the impulse of demons, he says, ‘Our struggle is not,’ and so forth. For this reason we have now brought forward examples of those who unhappily serve magical arts and are said to perform such things, in order to blunt the opinion of those who think that all vices are of flesh and blood and that demons have no power to incite us to sin.” [Col. 0672D] And after much else: “Perhaps we have discussed this chapter more fully than the reader would have wished; but I ask him to pardon the difficulty of the passage itself and the circumstances of the Ephesians, who, after their magical practices, ought to have known by whom they had once been deceived.””].

The distinguished Teolius, in his commentary on this passage of Prudentius, noted that Estius used no other commentary on St. Paul’s meaning than these verses of our poet. He especially commends Prudentius because “the world of these darknesses” is said to be this lower world, turbulent and gloomy, over which demons have been appointed on account of human transgression, whether to test human beings or to harm them. [Col. 0671C] Certainly Estius strengthens this part of his interpretation by Prudentius’s authority and calls him a theological poet. But in the first and principal part he differs from Prudentius, wishing the words “with flesh and blood” to be understood not of concupiscences but of human beings.

## CHAPTER X. The reading of the Vulgate edition at Genesis 3:15, “And she herself shall crush your head,” strikingly confirmed by Prudentius

### 137

Prudentius is further accused of having read at Genesis 3:15 the words that are now in fact found in the Vulgate edition:

> I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed: she herself shall crush your head, and you shall lie in wait for her heel.

Prudentius, *Cathemerinon* 3, lines 121ff.:

> Conscious of her guilt and fearing God,  
> She is driven far from the holy dwelling.  
> The woman who had been unmarried  
> Receives her husband’s command,  
> Ordered to endure the sorrowful covenant.
>
> The serpent itself, author of the deceit,  
> Is punished in its wickedness, so that the woman  
> May crush its threefold tongue with her heel.
>
> Thus the serpent looks up at the woman’s sole,  
> And the woman at the man.
>
> Behold, a new offspring comes,  
> Another man, brought forth from heaven,  
> Not of clay, like that first man,  
> But God himself bearing humanity,
>
> Free from bodily faults.  
> The living Word of the Father becomes flesh,  
> Whom, bearing the radiant divinity,  
> The undefiled maiden gives birth to  
> Neither in a marriage chamber, nor by the law of wedlock,  
> Nor through marital pleasures.
>
> This was that ancient hatred;  
> This was the deadly conflict  
> Between the asp and mankind,  
> When the serpent, bending its head,  
> Is trampled beneath a woman’s feet.
>
> For the maiden, worthy to bear God,  
> Subdues every poison:  
> Through its endless coils, the sluggish serpent  
> Vomits forth its harmless venom,  
> Green like the verdant grass.

[Col. 0672B] What could be more illustrious for confirming the reading of the Vulgate? What could be clearer for establishing the immaculate conception of the Mother of God? The heretics say that Prudentius read some corrupted copy of the sacred books. But why was that copy corrupted? Clearly because he read in it words which they themselves would not wish to have written. Thus they can defend the claim that the reading of the Vulgate is corrupt in no other way than by asserting that already in the fourth century Prudentius had used one or more corrupted copies.

Moreover, does not Prudentius’s interpretation sufficiently persuade us not only that this passage was then commonly read in this manner, but also that it was applied to the Blessed Virgin, who subdues every poison because she was worthy to bear God—that is, because she was conceived without stain? You cannot invent—or, if you invent it, you cannot persuade me—that Prudentius seized these words from one or another corrupted copy in order to establish his own novel interpretation upon them.

Why, then, do those especially who defend the undefiled conception of Blessed Mary in so many volumes not press Prudentius’s perfectly clear authority? Alva, who devoted himself extensively to that cause, brought forward in the *Militia of the Conception* scarcely a few verses of Prudentius, which he had found in Eusebius Nieremberg [Note: [Col. 0672D] Plaza and others do not even mention Prudentius. This omission is especially regrettable in Plaza’s work entitled *The Case of the Immaculate Conception of the Most Holy Mother of God, Mary Our Lady, Argued and Concluded from the Sacred Testimonies Arranged Chronologically on Both Sides and Referred to Theological-Critical Examination*, by Benedict Plaza, S.J., Palermo, 1747.].

Melchior Canus, in book VII of *Theological Places*, chapter 3, could by this route have refuted Erasmus’s so-called Achilles argument. Erasmus does not think himself overwhelmed by the testimony of all the saints whenever he opposes them all; for, as Erasmus boasts, all the saints who happened to mention the matter asserted with one voice that the Blessed Virgin was conceived in original sin. Canus replies that this matter, otherwise of the greatest importance, has no significance in the Christian religion. “I frankly confess,” he says, “that no other path was open to me for evading that argument of Erasmus, by which he indeed cleverly attempted to evade the authority of the saints.”

But in Prudentius one may see a pious doctrine, not merely as theologians explain it, but also as painters express it in vivid colors: the image of the Mother of God is depicted with a bowed serpent trampled beneath her feet, vomiting forth its harmless venom through winding coils.

### 138

Canus likewise counts among the errors which have entered Sacred Scripture through the carelessness of printers or the incompetence of copyists that passage of Genesis, “And she herself shall crush your head,” instead of “And he himself”—namely, the seed, or “he”—which he thinks was written by the first translator, who rendered “seed” in the masculine gender after considering the sense of the thing signified, as Jerome states in the *Hebrew Questions*. Others share this opinion, among them Natalis Alexander in his dissertation on the Vulgate translation of Sacred Scripture.

But they do not notice that the Hebrew text itself could have been corrupted, since Bellarmine, in book II of *The Word of God*, chapter 12, actually read a manuscript in which the Hebrew word was written in the feminine form, “she herself.” And that the Hebrew word rendered “he himself” can also mean “she herself,” although it is less frequently taken in that sense, is taught by authors most skilled in the Hebrew language.

St. Augustine approaches the reading of our edition in book XI of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapter 36:

> I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed. She herself shall preserve your head, and you shall preserve her heel.

And in book II of *Genesis against the Manichaeans*, chapter 6:

> She herself shall watch over your head, and you shall watch over her heel.

Likewise St. Ambrose, *On Flight from the World*, chapter 7:

> She herself shall watch over your head, and you shall watch over her heel.

Claudius Marius Victorinus, in the fifth century, in his *Genesis*:

> You shall crawl on your feet and with your breast bowed low,  
> And a woman shall destroy you with her seed;  
> You shall cunningly lie in wait only for the extremities of her feet,  
> So that, trembling, she may even set her footsteps upon your head.

In the same period Alcimus Avitus, bishop of Vienne, followed the reading of the Vulgate and the interpretation of Prudentius in book III of his *Genesis*:

> In time to come, you shall bow before the female sex,  
> Though you will lie in wait for the ankle of her who is afraid.  
> At last the victorious woman alone shall crush your head,  
> And the offspring to be born from such a stock.

I omit more recent authors. These examples sufficiently refute Abraham Costerus in his little book, *Defender of the Passage of Sacred Scripture at Genesis 3:15 against the Faulty Interpretation Concerning the Blessed Virgin Mary, Which Has Long Prevailed in the Bibles of the Roman Church*, contained in volume II of Thomas Crenius’s *Thesaurus of Philological and Historical Books*.

Costerus confidently says in chapter 5: “This reading, ‘SHE SHALL CRUSH,’ had not yet been discovered in Augustine’s time”; and in chapter 15: “Although some of the Fathers retain ‘SHE,’ they neither acknowledge nor explain the predicate ‘SHE SHALL CRUSH THE HEAD.’” He says this because some read, “she shall watch over.”

Nor does he more truthfully attack Francis Brugensis in the same chapter, although Brugensis proves that the reading “SHE SHALL CRUSH” does not conflict with the Hebrew text. In the same place Costerus denies that the Vulgate reading can be accepted in the convenient interpretation offered by Bellarmine, Brugensis, and others. Yet the heterodox Grotius frankly admits that a sufficiently suitable meaning can be drawn from that reading.

I shall concede this much: I have seen no one older than our poet who clearly read “SHE SHALL CRUSH”; but I do not doubt that others preceded him. The hymn of Prudentius, celebrated in many churches, sufficiently proves [Col. 0674B] how common the belief then was that the Virgin crushed the serpent’s head—that is, original sin—as the holy Fathers and interpreters explain it. Mazochius, in his additions to Junius, volume III of the *Calendar*, page 990, admirably explains Ambrose’s passage in sermon 22 on Psalm 118 in support of this pious doctrine.

## CHAPTER XI. Ecclesiastical rites now in force that were practiced in the Church in the age of Prudentius: the use and abundance of lights

### 139

Heretics—and would that they alone were guilty of this!—are accustomed to despise almost all ceremonies, especially those employed by the Roman Church. When venerable antiquity is brought forward against them, they either deny that these ceremonies were practiced at the very beginning of the nascent Church or reply that they derive their origin from paganism and Judaism [Col. 0674C]. In this they show little discernment, whether because they are altogether blind or because they are leaders of the blind.

As for their appeal to the first three centuries, first, many documents have perished from which the very practices they seek could have been elucidated. How many things have come to our knowledge from only one surviving book—things which, had that book perished, would now be denied with equal right? In addition, where public worship is concerned, especially matters involving churches, altars, and their decoration and splendor, the norm of religion should more appropriately be sought in the fourth century, when peace was restored to the Church, than in the preceding three, during which Christians certainly could not carry out everything they might have wished [Note: [Col. 0673D] Luther, Calvin, and other reformers of this kind do not know better than those holy Fathers, teachers, and bishops what the custom and mind of the Church were during the first three centuries, nor what was more fitting after peace had been restored to the Church—those Fathers through whose counsels and doctrine the Church itself flourished so greatly in the fourth century.

Joannes Marangoni published a book entitled *On Pagan and Profane Things Transferred for the Use and Ornament of Churches*. Pietro Lazzeri, a distinguished authority in theology and ecclesiastical history, disliked the opinion of Marangoni and others. In a dissertation or discussion entitled *On the False Derivation of the Rites of the Ancient Christians from Pagan Rites*, delivered by Pietro Rinaldi at the Roman College in 1777, he proves: first, that no argument is brought forward by which the origin of our rites from pagan rites is truly demonstrated; second, that no ancient ceremony commonly observed by the Catholic Church is identified which could not be derived elsewhere much more suitably and conveniently; and third, that, in view of the teaching of the holy Fathers and the ancient discipline of the Church, the origin they propose cannot in any way be assigned.

He is speaking of the first four centuries and insists that the law of nature itself, together with the instinct toward certain ceremonies, has led human beings by the hand at all times to such practices no less than to other actions, such as eating, drinking, and clothing themselves.].

Since worship of God must be carried out through certain external rites and ceremonies, and since the number of such rites is in some sense limited, while nature has arranged that signs of obedience and reverence be displayed—signs that are generally the same among nearly all peoples [Col. 0675A]—it is not surprising, and much less blameworthy, if certain customs were introduced into the Catholic Church even from the time of the apostles, customs resembling those practiced by pagans.

That the Gentiles derived almost their entire method and manner of worshiping their gods from the Hebrews was demonstrated in a dissertation in volume VII of Gronovius’s *Greek Antiquities*, page 1: Daniel Clasen’s *Theology of the Gentiles*, or a demonstration proving that the theology of the Gentiles—its “darkness”—and their gods, sacrifices, and other practices derived their origin from the source of Scripture—its “light.”

Finally, the Hebrews had been taught by God by what rites they ought to venerate him. The first Christians therefore acted wisely when, in accordance with the authority that Christ granted his Church to establish new laws as circumstances and times seemed more suitably to require, they established certain of their ceremonies upon the ancient discipline of the people of Israel [Col. 0675B].

### 140

These arguments vindicate Prudentius, whom non-Catholics and semi-Catholics accuse because he graphically described ancient ecclesiastical rites which they themselves now reject. The piety of this most noble man, who lived amid secular affairs, and who himself used to prostrate himself before the tombs of the saints, invoke the martyrs as his patrons with fervent prayers, and promote their veneration, ought to have deterred these innovators from their position altogether. They extricate themselves only by rashly and inappropriately applying the word “superstition.”

Nor would I deny that ignorant people sometimes incline toward superstition. But, apart from the fact that the customs of our own age suffer much more from the vice of impiety than from superstition, the superstition that sometimes creeps into these rites is not a fault of the laws but of human beings, who find it difficult to remain at the mean of virtue.

I remember reading in Linguet’s *Annals* that, while he was staying in London, he was greatly astonished at the superstition of the people. He had previously believed that superstition reigned only among Catholics, but discovered that it triumphed equally, or even more, among the English.

The inconsistency of the reformers may be noted in another, though not very different, matter. In Rome we often see—and in other cities others will see—the men whom they themselves have and call bishops and preachers, or pastors, excelling greatly in no other respect, nor striving to excel in any other, than in riding well and dancing skillfully, and in being indistinguishable from secular men [Col. 0675D], neither in dress nor in conduct [Col. 0676A]. Yet this was originally the principal pretext offered by the heretics themselves for their dissension from the head. They claimed that the Roman clergy were corrupt and in need of reform. But, while wishing to avoid Charybdis, they fell into Scylla—or, better, they fell into Scylla without avoiding Charybdis.

It would be easy to construct the whole of this controversy against certain recent innovations. Even now there are those who search for novelty in antiquity, as Maldonatus aptly said of the heretics of his own time in his commentary on John, chapter I, verse 1 [Note: [Col. 0675D] “Perhaps someone in our own memory translated ‘SERMON’ instead of ‘WORD’ . . . All heretics followed novelty . . . I would grant some indulgence if they had followed antiquity, in which, as we shall immediately indicate, many translated it in that way. But I am indignant at the ingenuity of the heretics, who pursue evasive paths and call it ‘SERMON’ for no other reason than that we call it ‘WORD,’ and who ‘SEEK NOVELTY IN ANTIQUITY.’ For although that usage was at some time ancient, since it had already become obsolete it is now new.”].

But the matter speaks for itself, without my intervention. I shall offer one example concerning the use of lights, so that I may not depart from our Prudentius.

### 141

Benedict XIV, in book I, chapter 3, *On the Sacrifice of the Mass*, attempts to demonstrate against Vert and Joachim Hildebrand that, in the first centuries of the Church, Christians used lights not only to dispel darkness but also for a symbolic reason indicated in both the Old and the New Testament [Col. 0676B]. Hildebrand admits that Christians retained the use of lights in the fourth century, but claims that only toward the end of that century do monuments exist showing that lights were accustomed to be kindled even after daylight had already appeared.

That lights were kindled in the Old Law for a mystical reason rather than merely to drive away darkness may rightly be inferred from the temple’s lampstand. In fact, lighting was regarded among the ancients as an honor. In 2 Maccabees 4:22, Antiochus, magnificently received by Jason and the city at Jerusalem, entered “with the lights of torches” and praises. Cicero, *On Duties*, book III:

> Marius went straight from the benches to the rostra; and what had been commonly arranged he alone proclaimed. And this, if you ask, brought him great honor. Statues were erected in every street; incense and candles were offered before them.

Why, then, should this honor not be rendered to God? It may be granted that in the first centuries of the Church there was no established custom of lighting lamps during the day. But even if the existence of such a custom cannot be proved, you will never establish that it did not in fact occur whenever Christians gathered at church during the day.

Indeed, from what Prudentius says in hymn 5—without now mentioning the golden lampstands during the time of persecution, to which I shall return at no. 152—I infer that, even when lights were kindled at night, they were used not merely to dispel darkness but chiefly to render honor to God, whether one considers their multitude or the rites associated with them [Note: [Col. 0675D] Read again the hymn on the new light of Holy Saturday:

> Author of the gleaming light, good leader of light,  
> Restore light to your faithful, Christ.  
>
> Yet by the striking of flint you show us  
> To seek lights from the stone-born seed,  
> So that man might not fail to know  
> That the hope of light is hidden  
> In Christ’s solid body.
>
> The living flame burns strongly, whether the hollow vessel  
> Supplies its fuel to the thirsty wick,  
> Whether the pine provides its pitchy nourishment,  
> Or the heated wick drinks smooth wax.
>
> Therefore, Father, your gifts make your halls shine  
> With moving flames;  
> The light, rivaling the absent day,  
> Drives it onward, while night, defeated, flees  
> With its torn cloak.
>
> But who would not perceive the lofty origin  
> Of the swift light, flowing from God? . . .
>
> Lights hang from moving cords,  
> Fixed lights gleam along the ceilings,  
> And, nourished by little floating wicks,  
> The flame pours light through transparent glass.
>
> You might think that above there stood  
> A starry expanse adorned with twin constellations,  
> And that, wherever the plow turns its Bosporan yoke,  
> Purple evening stars were scattered everywhere.

Would you like to hear the reason for lights of such number and such varied kinds? Prudentius continues:

> O thing worthy, Father, for your flock to offer you  
> At the beginning of dewy night:  
> The light you give, than which nothing is more precious;  
> The light by which we see all other gifts.
>
> You are true light to our eyes, light also to our senses;  
> Within, you are a mirror; outside, you are a mirror.  
> Receive the light which I, your servant, offer,  
> Dyed with the oil of peaceful chrism.

In St. Jerome’s time this was the objection of Vigilantius and the heretics against Catholics: that they lit lights according to an ecclesiastical rite. See no. 162.].

## CHAPTER XII. The celebrated Easter vigil among the ancient Christians; Prudentius’s verses on the new light of Holy Saturday; the true title of the fifth hymn of the *Cathemerinon*

### 142

Since Prudentius describes in the celebrated fifth hymn of the *Cathemerinon* the vigil for the Lord’s resurrection, I shall derive and defend its true title. The manuscripts of Heinsius have *For the lighting of the lamp*, a title that pleases him because the rite of the Paschal candle was unknown in Prudentius’s age. The title is the same in the Regensburg manuscript. Most recent editors follow this heading in their printed editions, except that some write *For the kindling* or *lighting of the lamp*.

Rudolph Hospinianus, in *On the Origin of Christian Festivals*, when discussing Holy Saturday, cites Naogeorgus, book IV of *The Papal Kingdom*, who describes the rite of blessing the Paschal candle and calls it superstitious. Hospinianus likewise attributes this rite to Pope Zosimus around the year 420, on the authority of the *Pontifical Book*, Alcuin, Amalarius, Rabanus, Walafrid, Micrologus, Rupert of Deutz, and others. From other authorities—who are in no way comparable with the preceding ones—he assigns it to Theodatus, whom they call Theodorus or Theodotus, around the year 615, or to Honorius I around the year 622.

He notes that around the year 627 it was not the custom in Galicia to consecrate a lamp and a candle, since canon 8 of the Fourth Council of Toledo decreed that, for the sake of the unity of peace, the rite of blessing them should also be instituted in those churches. From this he concludes that the fifth hymn of the *Cathemerinon* should not be entitled *For the lighting of the Paschal candle*.

### 143

He employs these arguments because Zosimus held the pontificate forty years after Prudentius; but here he is seriously mistaken. Zosimus was elected pontiff in 417, whereas Prudentius was writing in 405, and it is not established in what year he died.

Furthermore, Hospinianus says that all the hymns of the book *Cathemerinon* were written not for any particular day of the year but as general hymns, and that they correspond to the title of the book *Cathemerinon*, or *Daily Hymns*. But here too he is no less mistaken. The hymn *Of Those Who Fast*, *After Fasting*, *At Every Hour*, *At the Burial of the Dead*, *The Eighth Day before the Kalends of January*, *On the Epiphany of the Lord*, and others correspond no more to the title *Cathemerinon* than does a hymn sung only on Holy Saturday.

Another argument, drawn from the order in which this fifth hymn is placed between the hymn *After Food* and the hymn *Before Sleep*, may appear stronger; consequently, it ought to be referred to the hour of the lighting of the lamps. Riscus, in volume XXXI of *Hispania Sacra*, regards this opinion as established, asserting that this hymn is an evening hymn for daily use, since the hymns are arranged in order through the seventh. He says that it makes no difference that Prudentius mentions certain matters concerning the Paschal night, because in hymns one is accustomed to recall events that occurred at the hours when the hymns are sung, as well as events known from Sacred Scripture.

And, to cut my own vines, I myself had stated in the *Hymnody of Spain*, in the notes on the hymn of St. Laurence, that some people wrongly entitle this hymn *For the lighting of the Paschal candle*, and that it speaks not of the Paschal candle but of the candle that was lit every day, just as the Greeks had a hymn recited every night when the first light was brought in, a hymn discussed by St. Basil in *On the Holy Spirit*.

This opinion could be confirmed by the fact that in this hymn too Prudentius expresses the doxology of the Holy Trinity—“Through Christ begotten”—which Basil praises in the Greek evening hymn. Nevertheless, although I still do not approve the title *For the lighting of the Paschal candle*, I hold an entirely different view of the matter itself.

I know that certain features of this hymn fit extremely well the ecclesiastical office once called the lighting of the lamps, which St. Ambrose, in book III of *On Virgins*, chapter 4, calls “the hour of kindling,” and Cassian, in book III, chapter 3, calls “the lamp-lighting hour.” In the First Council of Toledo, chapter 9, we read: “Let the lamp-lighting office not be performed except in a church.” See the note of García de Loaysa, who wishes to prove that the lamp-lighting office corresponds to our Vespers. The tenth hymn of Ennodius, which is called an evening hymn, was unquestionably composed for the lamp-lighting office.

### 144

Although Prudentius’s hymn is placed in the position in which the daily evening hymn ought to stand, you should not therefore infer that it was a daily hymn. For since many things in that hymn fit the evening hymn quite well, and since it was moreover sung at the beginning of the night of Easter Saturday, it was not without reason assigned that place—whether by the author, or, as I rather believe, by those who later assembled his works and placed this hymn separately among the other *Cathemerina*. In Aldus’s edition it was printed twice: first immediately after the *Psychomachia* and before the book of the *Cathemerina*, and then between Hymns IV and VI of the *Cathemerina*. From this it is clear that Aldus found these verses separately, although they had also been inserted in the book of the *Cathemerina*.

I have already noted in no. 103 that this hymn was published under the title *On the Passover of the Israelite People*. In the hymn books of Cardinal Tommasi it is now entitled *For the Lighting of the Lamp*, now *For the Blessing of the Paschal Candle*, according as Churches employed it for one or another use. In the ancient Roman Ordo one reads: “Order for Holy Saturday during the day.” Some, however, sing here Prudentius’s hymn:

> Inventor rutili, dux bone, luminis.

> Discoverer of the radiant light, good leader of the light.

In the Mozarabic office the same hymn is sung in part at Vespers on the first Sunday after the octave of Epiphany. Blanchini, in his annotations on the Verona manuscript, retains the title *For the Incensing of the Lamp*, but argues at length that Prudentius composed the hymn for the blessing of the paschal candle. Although I agree with him to some extent, I cannot refrain from observing that the matter should not be judged from ideas and customs introduced later, but should be restored to its original principles.

For most people judge ancient practices by new ones, and imagine that the former were such as the latter sometimes are under the same names, although they are performed in a different manner.

[Note: Adamus Siberus, in his *Scholia* on this hymn, gives the title *For the Lighting of the Candle*, adding: “which was lighted as evening approached on the night preceding the feast of the Lord’s Resurrection; and Christians customarily passed that night without sleep for the sake of religion, not superstition.” These words strongly support our view.]

Prudentius’s hymn, whatever its eventual purpose may have been, could have been used either for the blessing of the lamp and candle, which the Mozarabic Christians had introduced into practice, or for the blessing of the candle, which had already become customary in the time of St. Ennodius and of which two blessings survive, composed in the same terms, or finally for the hour of the *lucernarium*. Hence the various titles arose, none of which I approve.

[Note: In the Parma edition the title *For the Lighting of the Lamp* is retained, and it is defended from the order of the hymns: this fifth hymn is to be understood as concerning Vespers, at which in Prudentius’s age it was customary for lamps to be lighted daily in solemn fashion. The author of the *Constitutions* emphatically calls Psalm 140, which used to be recited at that service, the “LUCERNAL PSALM.” From this the distinguished Thomassin, in his *Treatise on Feasts*, translated into Latin by Carlo Guietto, book II, chapter 24, concludes that this hymn was composed for lighting the lamps at the *lucernarium*, that is, at daily Vespers. Carlo Guyet, S.J., published in 1657 a Latin treatise on feasts composed by himself; Thomassin published another work in French under this title in 1683. These two works, later printed together, must be distinguished. See the ritual bibliography of the distinguished Zacharia.]

What title, then, shall I give it? I do not altogether dislike the title *For the Lighting*, without anything further being added, or *For the Lighting of the Light*. But I prefer Aldus’s heading—not the one he places among the *Cathemerina*, where it is called “Ode for the Lighting of the Lamp,” but the one he gives from some separate manuscript:

> Verses of Aurelius Prudentius on the new light of Holy Saturday.

You see that this heading is neither monastic, nor taken from any breviary, nor devised by later authors. Sixtus of Siena retained it in book VI, chapter 47, of his *Bibliotheca sancta*; on this see below, no. 183.

### 145

Now observe how aptly the title suits the subject. “On the new light,” it says; for this is what Prudentius says:

> Yet you show us to seek lights  
> by the striking of flint, from a seed born of stone.

This rite is still observed in the blessing of the paschal candle. He does not add “of the candle” or “of the lamp,” because at the feast which Prudentius celebrates it was not only a candle, nor only a lamp, but torches as well that were lighted.

[Note:]

> Lest a man fail to know that the hope of light  
> is hidden for him in Christ’s solid body:  
> he who wished to be called the steadfast rock,  
> from whom our little fires derive their origin.  
>   
> These we feed in lamps  
> drenched with the rich dew of oil,  
> or in dry torches.  
>   
> Indeed, we fashion even rushen wicks,  
> gathered beforehand from flowering reeds  
> and pressed in rich honey.  
>   
> The living flame burns strongly, whether  
> a hollow vessel supplies its fuel  
> to a thirsty linen wick,  
> or a pine tree provides pitchy nourishment,  
> or heated flax drinks in smooth wax . . .  
>   
> Therefore, Father, your gifts shine  
> in moving flames throughout the halls.

It is rightly added to the title: “of Holy Saturday.” Nor is it a minor error to deny that the hymn was composed for the celebration of the Paschal vigil. I myself once fell into this error, and other, more learned men have done so as well. For thus he says in verse 125 and following:

> There are also, beneath Styx, renowned holidays of punishment,  
> often harmful to spirits,  
> on that night when the holy God returned  
> from the Acherontic pools to the realms above.  
>   
> Not as Lucifer, rising from the ocean,  
> bathes darkness in bright torchlight,  
> but the Lord, from the cross,  
> greater than the sun, restores a new day to sorrowing lands.  
>   
> Tartarus languishes beneath its gentle punishments,  
> and the people of the shades rejoice  
> in the leisure of their prison, freed from the fires;  
> nor do the rivers boil with their customary sulphur.

> We draw out the night amid festive celebrations  
> through holy rejoicing and assemblies,  
> and eagerly heap up favorable vows  
> in vigilant prayer,  
> offering sacrificial offerings in the sanctuary that has been prepared.

The vigil of Holy Saturday is clearly described: its night was spent by Christians in festive assemblies, amid holy rejoicing and favorable vows. Accordingly, instead of “on that night when the holy God returned,” I would gladly read “on this very night,” if the manuscripts permitted it. The meaning, however, is always the one I have explained: the passage does not concern the hour of the *lucernarium* on each successive night, but the vigil of Holy Saturday.

### 146

And lest you doubt it, you should know that during these Paschal vigils Christians customarily refreshed themselves with the sacred Eucharist, as is clear from the words of St. Gregory Nazianzen to be cited in no. 149. This is the origin of the precept of Paschal communion. To this belongs the cause of the martyrdom of St. Hermenegild, narrated by St. Gregory the Great in book III, chapter 31, of the *Dialogues*:

> When the day of the Paschal festival arrived, in the silence of the dead of night the treacherous father sent an Arian bishop to him, so that from his hand he might receive communion of sacrilegious consecration.

Prudentius also recalls this rite. After describing the journey of the Israelite people, he says:

> Such rewards once the illustrious devotion  
> of the one God bestowed upon our fathers,  
> by whose help we too are nourished,  
> feeding our hearts with mystical banquets . . .

> We draw out the night amid festive celebrations  
> through holy rejoicing and assemblies . . .

> And in the sanctuary we have built  
> we perform our offerings.

Thus, even from Prudentius’s hymn alone, this feast ought to be recognized as existing in the ancient Church, since traces of it still remain in the blessing of the paschal candle. For these verses of his demonstrate that in Prudentius’s time a certain rite of blessing and consecrating the light was customary:

> Receive the light which, as your servant, I offer,  
> dyed with the oil of peaceful chrism.

This further confirms that the hymn was not intended to be sung in the evening on every night, or composed for that purpose.

### 147

Moreover, many further proofs can be offered that this was a solemn custom of celebrating the Paschal vigil in the ancient Church, and therefore that Prudentius’s hymn fits it perfectly. Tertullian, in book II, chapter 4, *To His Wife*, speaking of a pagan who had married a Christian woman, says:

> Who will calmly tolerate a wife remaining awake through the solemnities of Easter?

Eusebius, book VI, chapter 34 of his *Ecclesiastical History*, with the notes of Valesius, mentions the prayers held during the final vigil of Easter under the emperor Philip. Lactantius, book VII, chapter 19, writes:

> And this is the night which we celebrate by a vigil because of the coming of our King and God. This night has a twofold rationale: on it he received life when he suffered, and afterward he is to receive the kingdom of the world.

[Note: Isidore had this passage before his eyes in the *Etymologies*, book VI, chapter 17:

> “The night of Easter is therefore kept as a vigil because of the coming of our King and Lord, so that the time of his resurrection may find us not sleeping but awake; and this night has a twofold significance, either because in it he then received life when he suffered, or because afterward, at the same hour at which he rose again, he will come to judge.”

This deserved our notice, because in the notes on Isidore’s *Etymologies* Lactantius’s passage is not identified, although other authors’ passages are commonly identified in one another’s works.]

### 148

St. Jerome, in book IV of his commentary on Matthew, chapter 25, at the words “But at midnight there was a cry,” etc., teaches that the custom of observing this vigil has persisted from apostolic tradition:

> Suddenly, as though in the dead of night, when all are secure and the deepest sleep prevails, the coming of Christ will resound through the cry of angels and the trumpets of the powers that go before him.

Let us say something that may perhaps be useful to the reader. It is a Jewish tradition that Christ will come at midnight, in imitation of the time of the Egyptians, when Easter was celebrated, the destroyer came, the Lord passed over the dwellings, and the doorposts of our foreheads were consecrated with the blood of the lamb. Hence I think that the apostolic tradition was also handed down (perhaps read *permanasse*, “was handed down”), namely, that on the day of the Paschal vigils it was not permitted to dismiss the people before midnight, while they awaited the coming of Christ. After that time had passed, they were all to celebrate the feast with confidence. Hence the Psalmist also said:

> At midnight I rose to give thanks to you  
> because of the judgments of your righteousness.

This is why Prudentius sings in several strophes of the liberation and departure of the Israelite people from Egypt:

> Moses indeed saw God,  
> flaming in the thorn-bearing bush  
> with conspicuous light.

The holy Fathers likewise compare the Israelite people liberated from Egyptian tyranny with the righteous summoned into heaven by the risen Lord, as does St. Gregory Nazianzen in his oration on Easter and on delay:

> Today we flee Egypt completely, and that bitter Pharaoh.

[Note: Hence Prudentius, verse 109:

> He calls the weary across the straits of the world,  
> guiding the people through torn-apart whirlwinds,  
> and commands souls tossed by a thousand labors,  
> the righteous, to climb into their homeland.  
>   
> There every land, covered with purple rose gardens,  
> exhales fragrance, etc.

The sermons of St. Zeno of Verona belong to the same subject, as does the treatise of St. Gaudentius, bishop of Brescia, on Exodus, delivered during this vigil; and nearly the whole blessing of the Paschal candle:

> This is the night on which our fathers, the children of Israel, were first led out of Egypt, etc.

All these ideas are found in Prudentius.]

### 149

St. Gregory Nazianzen speaks splendidly about the lighting of lamps during the Paschal vigil in Oration II on Easter:

> This is for us the festival of festivals and the celebration of celebrations . . . Yesterday’s carrying of TORCHES AND LIGHTS was indeed splendid—a rite which nearly every class of people performed both privately and publicly, and all who were distinguished by office and rank, illuminating the night with A GREAT FIRE, etc. But today’s celebration is more splendid and more excellent. For YESTERDAY’S LIGHT was a herald of that great light which was to rise, and a kind of preliminary joy of the soul.

And in the oration in praise of his deceased father, which is XIX, page 304:

> He was suffering from illness, and it was the season of illness: holy and solemn Easter, the king of days, and THAT SPLENDID NIGHT which dissolves the darkness of sin, in which we celebrate the feast of our salvation with A GREAT ABUNDANCE OF LIGHT . . . The time of the mystery had arrived.

[Note: Nicetas, in Oration II of Nazianzen on Easter:

> Yesterday’s celebration of lights was also splendid, that is, the assembly held toward evening on the great Sabbath. For they spent the night in vigil until the seventh hour, singing and lighting lamps, and awaiting the approaching resurrection of our Savior.

These words accord with Prudentius’s hymn.]

Eusebius, book IV, chapter 22, of the *Life of Constantine*:

> He himself, as a participant in the sacred mysteries . . . during the very days of the saving festival, intensifying the vigor of discipline and exercises, and gathering together all the powers of soul and body, fulfilled the office of priest and revealer of the sacred mysteries. He himself led all the others in the celebration of the feast. He had transformed the sacred vigil INTO THE BRIGHTNESS OF DAY, with certain pillars of candles lighted throughout the whole city by those who had been assigned that task. Lamps too, once lighted, illuminated every place on every side, so that this mystical vigil became brighter than any day, however splendid.

Valesius notes that Christians were accustomed to light a very large number of candles only inside the church, whereas Constantine, in honor of so great a festival, ordered candles to be lighted outside the church as well. He thinks those candle-columns designate the Paschal candle, about which Barnabas Brissonius wrote a separate book.

St. Zeno of Verona indicates the lights of this same vigil in his First Sermon to the Newly Baptized:

> After the most devout chaste fasts of sacred purification had been completed, after the sweet vigils of THE BRIGHTEST NIGHT, with its own sun . . .

[Note: Compare the sermons of the same Zeno on Exodus, as well as the treatise of St. Gaudentius, bishop of Brescia, on Exodus, on the night of the Vigils, and on the observance of Easter. There, in Treatise IV, he calls the night of the vigils “the most splendid night.” In the *Apostolic Constitutions*, book V, chapter 18, the vigil of the great Sabbath and the day of the resurrection are discussed; there too it is prescribed that the sacrifice be offered before the fast is broken. Aldhelm, *On the Praise of the Virgin*, chapter 16:

> During the Paschal vigils, when the Lord’s resurrection is customarily celebrated in the recurring cycle of the years with the rejoicing of the accustomed solemnity, it happened by chance that the suitable supply of thick oil for the lamps was lacking.

See Chrysostom, on Genesis, chapter 11, Homily XXX.

Nebrissensis agrees with our view. Although he entitles the hymn *For the Lighting of the Lamp*, he nevertheless says:

> This hymn ought to be sung at the beginning of the night, when the lights are lighted; or RATHER, AND ESPECIALLY, ON HOLY SATURDAY, when new lights are kindled, or ought to be kindled.

And on the verse “That night when the holy God,” he confirms that among the ancients it was customary on the night of Holy Saturday to set out many lights in the houses, made from every material capable of providing fuel for fire.]

### 150

These matters are so clear that anyone who continues to doubt whether Prudentius composed the hymn *On the New Light of Holy Saturday* for the celebration of the Paschal vigil seems to be blinking in broad daylight. Although the origin of the blessing of the paschal candle must be sought here, the terms “paschal candle” and certain rites used in the blessing may perhaps be of later origin. This would explain why the blessing has been attributed to this or that Roman pontiff, as though he had prescribed some formula or wished to extend this ancient institution to the universal Church.

I also believe that the sermon entitled *On the Paschal Candle*, placed among the works of St. Jerome, is later than the times of St. Jerome and Prudentius. There the author observes:

> Read the Pentateuch; run through the Old Testament: nowhere will you see honey in God’s sacrifices, nowhere the use of wax, but the lights of lamps and little flames fed with oil . . . Run through the New Books . . . Is there a candle anywhere?

Drepanius Florus composed a poem on the Paschal candle. He was not, as Baronius calls him in the entry for 8 May in the *Roman Martyrology*, the oldest of Christian poets, but flourished only in the ninth century. He also celebrates the Paschal vigil:

> So that we may carry this through the whole night,  
> we bring bright fires to the sacred altars.

I further observe that some trace of the new light, kindled by the striking of flint, seems to survive in the eastern regions, in Liberius a Jesu, volume III of the *Controversies from the Posthumous Works*, columns 712 and following. He discusses the fire which schismatics call miraculous and pretend to be so, reporting that a genuine miracle once occurred when, on Holy Saturday, fire descended from heaven in the church at Jerusalem. In the same work, columns 600 and following, he explains and attacks the Armenian story and rite in which, early in the morning of the day of the Resurrection, they light candles from a certain light which, as they claim, they have received divinely.

I have gladly gathered all this together, not only to elucidate Prudentius’s hymn and its title, but also for the sake of the excellent and most religious prince Ferdinand of Bourbon, Duke of Parma. From suitable authorities I have learned that, with the willing consent of Pope Pius VI, he celebrated the Paschal vigil according to ancient custom, following the example of Constantine the Great, although in a different manner.

### 151

From these matters the piety of the most ancient and most fortunate times in their use, abundance, and ceremonies of lights has been clearly demonstrated.

[Note: I do not wish to pass over the conjecture that already in Prudentius’s age the light at the Paschal vigil seems to have been offered by a deacon, as the paschal candle is offered today, on the basis of the verse:

> Receive the light which, as your servant, I offer,  
> dyed with the oil of peaceful chrism.

Since Prudentius also speaks of fragrant tears, and Paulinus, in verses to be cited shortly, mentions not only painted candles but also fragrant lights, although another interpretation may be adopted, I have a strong suspicion that the origin of the five grains of incense inserted into the paschal candle by the deacon is to be sought here. He continues singing:

> Therefore, in the grace of this night, receive, holy Father, the evening sacrifice of this incense, which in this solemn offering of the candle your holy Church renders to you through the hands of its ministers from the works of bees.

Some critics of higher standing also accuse the rubricists of error because they believed that incense was mentioned at this point and consequently prescribed the insertion of grains of incense at these words. Nevertheless, I think that “the evening sacrifice of incense” is to be understood as referring to frankincense, and that it is distinguished from the solemn offering of the candle, made through the hands of the ministers from the works of bees. Thus, shortly before, in the blessing of the incense:

> May there come, we ask, almighty God, upon THIS INCENSE a rich outpouring of your blessing.

And whenever incense is burned before the Gospel in the sacrifice of the Mass:

> Let my prayer be directed, Lord, as incense in your sight;  
> the lifting of my hands is AN EVENING SACRIFICE.

Compare St. Isidore, *On the Explanation of the Mysteries of the Sacred Sacraments*, chapter 58, on compounded incense, and Rupert of Deutz, book VI of *On the Divine Offices*, chapter 31, “Why he also carries incense for the blessing of the candle.”]

But in order to rebuke the impiety of our age, I wish still to bring forward several verses of St. Paulinus of Nola. In *Poem 9*, on the arrival of Nicetas, bishop of Dacia, who had come for the fifth birthday feast of Felix:

> Behold, you see how great a splendor smiles,  
> as though from a renewed temple;  
> the coffered ceiling, carved with curling designs,  
> feigns ivory in the middle;  
> above the roof, hanging lamps  
> are held by bronze spirals.

Paulinus has much more in other places.

[Note: *Poem 3*:

> Now the golden thresholds are adorned with snowy veils,  
> the bright altars are crowned with dense lamps.  
> Fragrant lights burn in waxen reeds;  
> THEY SHINE NIGHT AND DAY, and thus night glows  
> with the brightness of day;  
> and day itself, bright with heavenly honor,  
> shines more brightly, doubling its light  
> with innumerable lamps.

*Poem 6*:

> Let others light lamps in painted wax  
> and attach many-branched lamps to hollow ceilings,  
> so that hanging torches may throw trembling flames.

*Poem 11*, among Muratori’s *Anecdota*, verse 407:

> These things which you see there, ready every day,  
> or spread around all sides in ordered array,  
> stand like candelabra about the columns;  
> they bear painted waxes upon their points,  
> so that fragrant lights may be produced  
> within enclosed papyrus wicks.  
>   
> In the middle space, fixed to the lofty ceilings,  
> hollow lamps hung from bronze supports.  
> In tree-like form, extending arms on flexible, vine-like branches,  
> at their highest summit they bear glass cups  
> as though these were their fruits.  
> They bloom like springtime with kindled light,  
> and with their many-branched flames imitate  
> the crowded stars,  
> distinguishing the deep darkness with abundant light.]

It is useful to add Paulinus repeatedly to Prudentius in these controversies, since no one can object that Paulinus’s opinions were prejudices absorbed in childhood among ecclesiastical men.

## CHAPTER XIII. A Reply, from Prudentius, to Those Who Ask with Persius, *Satire* 2, verse 69: “Tell us, priests, what is gold doing in the sanctuary?”

### 152

At the end of the hymn *On the New Light of Holy Saturday*, Prudentius gives an excellent reason why lights ought to be kindled in God’s honor:

> O thing worthy, Father, for your flock to offer you  
> at the beginning of the dewy night:  
> the light, than which you grant nothing more precious;  
> the light by which we see the other rewards.

This argument applies perfectly to the adornment and wealth of temples. To those concerned with civic affairs who repeat Persius’s verse, “Tell us, priests, what is gold doing in the sanctuary?”, the proper answer is:

> O thing worthy, Father, for your flock to offer you.

I know what they answer to this: that it would be better if these riches were distributed to the poor. Let them decide for themselves whether they make this claim because they are concerned about the needy or for some other reason. I, for my part, see that the Savior rejected the words of Judas Iscariot, John 12:5:

> Why was this ointment not sold for three hundred denarii and given to the poor?

When St. Laurence suffered martyrdom, there was valuable church property in the Church. Serious and learned men infer this from the words of the prefect addressed to St. Laurence in *The Crown of Martyrs*, hymn 2, verse 57:

> You are accustomed, he says, to complain  
> that we rage more harshly than is just,  
> when we cut Christian bodies  
> with more than bloody violence.  
>   
> The burning judgment has withdrawn  
> from its more savage movements;  
> gently and quietly I demand  
> what you ought willingly to undergo.  
>   
> This has been revealed as the custom  
> and art of your ceremonies,  
> this the discipline of your covenant:  
> bishops delight in gold.  
>   
> They say that sacred blood smokes  
> in silver cups,  
> and that golden candles stand fixed  
> at the nightly rites, etc.

Nevertheless, there were very many poor people in the Church at that time, verse 157:

> Such people he seeks out in every street,  
> accustomed to be fed from the storehouse  
> of Mother Church;  
> the steward himself had known them,

or, as most correctly write,

> whom he himself had first known.

You can see that these two things are entirely compatible: that wealth should abound in the church and that the poor should be assisted from it. Indeed, one scarcely sees anyone who contributes to the splendor of churches who is not also, and especially, moved by compassion toward the poor.

### 153

I shall use Paulinus, mentioned shortly before, as an example. How generously he distributed alms among the poor can be read in his life, elegantly written by Francisco Sacchini, S.J., and published anonymously in the Antwerp edition of the works of St. Paulinus, 1622.

[Note: Paulinus himself, in letter 11 to Sulpicius Severus, composed the epigram requested by Severus to be attached to images of St. Martin and Paulinus himself, in these words:

> Rich in possessions for Christ, poor for himself, Severus  
> built a beautiful lofty structure at sacred springs.  
>   
> And because he was building a hall for heavenly works,  
> where human beings might be renewed by the spring for God,  
> he painted, in a double image worthy of the sacraments,  
> so that the reborn human being might learn the gifts of life.  
>   
> The venerable image of the man bears witness to Martin;  
> the other likeness represents humble Paulinus.  
>   
> The former arms faith with examples and powerful words,  
> so that through merits he may carry undefiled palms.  
>   
> The latter teaches that, by redeeming his sins  
> with money poured out,  
> a man should regard wealth as less valuable  
> than his own salvation.]

Paulinus himself relates in letter 12, and explains repeatedly in his poems, how diligently he worked to enlarge and adorn the basilica of St. Felix.

[Note: *Poem 9*:

> Behold, you see this portico, where the first doorway receives you.  
> Previously it had been buried beneath a dark roof.  
> Now the same structure has grown with new colors and a roof, etc.  
>   
> Three groups of craftsmen, working with varied ornament, embellished it:  
> builders with its double coffered ceiling and marble,  
> and a painter with images bearing divine faces, etc.

*Poem 10*:

> In his buildings this work has been newly born,  
> which you see shining forth with equal splendor  
> amid masses raised high on every side.

And *Poem 11*:

> For many other things were present, as you know,  
> in that very place—ornaments which he might employ  
> so that he could spare the gold of the cross;  
> for inside lay hidden mystical vessels  
> entrusted for the celebration of the sacred rites . . .  
>   
> When he saw them, likewise skillfully varied  
> with different little stones . . .  
>   
> A small crown lies beneath, surrounded by various gems . . .  
>   
> There is a continuous silver cup, suitable for use.]

He also mentions a tomb long ago covered with silver, in *Poem 13*, verses 524 and following:

> He also revealed to us the secrets of his own sacred tomb . . .  
> a certain page of marble, clothed with an attached covering  
> of silver metal.

Those who study antiquity report that the actual coffins of tombs were customarily made of silver, and provide examples of them.

### 154

Nor are there lacking in Prudentius certain proofs of the wealth and splendor of temples. In *Eulalia*, verse 191:

> Here, where the nourishing brightness illuminates  
> the halls with gleaming marble,  
> the earth revered in its bosom preserves  
> the sacred relics and ashes  
> of the foreigner and the native.  
>   
> Above, the glittering roofs shine  
> from their golden coffered ceilings;  
> the cut stones vary the floor,  
> so that you might think red meadows  
> were blooming with many kinds of flowers.

[Note: In the Passion of St. Fructuosus and his companions, concerning their church:

> From here, let gilded roofs resound in the citadel.

In *Hippolytus*, verse 183:

> The little shrine itself, which within contains  
> those mortal remains,  
> gleams with SOLID SILVER.  
>   
> A wealthy hand set up shining panels  
> with a smooth surface,  
> like a hollow mirror gleaming within.  
>   
> Nor content merely to cover the entrance  
> with Parian stone,  
> he added bright talents of wealth  
> to adorn the work.

And verse 215:

> Nearby stands another building, to which at that time  
> such a great multitude throngs,  
> noble in royal splendor.  
> It rises high with lofty walls,  
> powerful in proud majesty  
> and rich in gifts.  
>   
> A double row of columns, set beneath gilded beams,  
> supports the coffered roof.  
>   
> Slender recesses, under a lower roof, are added  
> and continually open the series of the side walls.  
>   
> Through the middle runs a broader passage  
> beneath the lofty roof,  
> rising to a higher summit.  
>   
> Opposite the front, a lofty tribunal  
> is raised by steps,  
> from which the bishop proclaims God.  
>   
> The full house scarcely receives the surging crowds,  
> and the narrow entrance seethes with the throng, etc.

In the hymn of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, verse 31:

> On the right, the royal building receives Peter  
> beneath golden roofs . . .  
>   
> Within the tomb there is a chamber  
> where, with melodious falls,  
> a pool rolls in snowy depth.  
>   
> Above, multicolored painting tints the glassy waters;  
> mosses shine back, gold grows green,  
> and blue water casts the shadow  
> of the purple fabric hanging above . . .  
>   
> On the other side, the Ostian road preserves  
> Paul’s inscription . . .  
>   
> The place has royal splendor:  
> the good Prince consecrated these halls  
> and lavishly adorned their circuit  
> with great wealth.  
>   
> He raised little sheets of gold beneath the beams,  
> so that the whole interior would be golden light,  
> like the radiance at sunrise.  
>   
> He also placed Parian columns beneath  
> the golden coffered ceilings;  
> a fourfold row distinguishes them there.  
>   
> Then arches of splendid glass ran in varied curves:  
> thus meadows gleam with spring flowers.]

### 155

Much more can be brought forward on the same subject from writers contemporary with or earlier than these. Eusebius, *Life of Constantine*, book IV, chapter 58, describing the church of the holy Apostles at Constantinople, says:

> Having raised the entire church to immense height, he made it splendid with various kinds of stone, covering it from the floor to the ceiling with marble slabs. Then, covering the ceiling with coffered work of the finest workmanship, he overlaid the whole with gold. Above, in place of tiles, there was bronze . . . which likewise gleamed, covered with a great quantity of gold.

Theodoret adds much more in book I, chapter 31, of his *Ecclesiastical History*, concerning the dedication of the church at Jerusalem under Constantine:

> The most holy altar was adorned with wholly royal hangings and with votive offerings, precious stones, and gold.

St. Augustine, book III, chapter 29, *Against Cresconius*, reports from the proconsular records that in the year 320, during the persecution, Silvanus and others handed over two golden chalices and likewise six silver chalices . . . After the place had been opened, it was discovered that there were empty cupboards in the library. There Silvanus produced a silver *capitulata* [the exact vessel is uncertain] and a silver lamp.

From the *Pontifical Book*: St. Sylvester gave to the Church of the title of Equitius a silver paten weighing twenty pounds, a gift of the emperor Augustus Constantine. He also gave two silver cups, each weighing ten pounds; a golden chalice weighing two pounds; two silver ewers (*amas*), each weighing ten pounds; and a silver chrismal paten, enclosed in gold, weighing five pounds.

Among the apostolic canons, in the translation of Gentianus Hervetus, canon 72:

> No one shall convert a golden or silver vessel, or a consecrated veil, to his own use.

Optatus of Africa, book I, *Against Parmenianus*, concerning the time of persecution:

> The churches had very many ornaments of gold and silver, which the bishop Mensurius could neither bury in the earth nor carry away with him.

[Note: There is an outstanding testimony of Paulus Orosius concerning the golden and silver vessels used in the basilica of the Apostle St. Peter at Rome, as well as concerning the reverence that moved even the barbarians to leave them untouched when they destroyed Rome under Alaric in the year 410. He says in book VII, chapter 39, of his *History*:

> As the barbarians were running through the city, one of the Goths, a powerful man and a Christian, happened to find in a certain ecclesiastical house a sacred virgin already advanced in age. When he honorably asked her for gold and silver, she, with faithful confidence, promised that she had a great quantity in her possession and would immediately bring it out—and she did so.  
>   
> When she had displayed the treasures, and perceived that the barbarian was astonished by the size, weight, beauty, and unfamiliar workmanship of the vessels, Christ’s virgin said to the barbarian: “These are the sacred vessels used in the service of the Apostle Peter. Take them, if you dare; you will see what you have done. Since I cannot defend them, I dare not retain them.”  
>   
> But the barbarian, moved by reverence for religion, fear of God, and faith in the virgin, reported these matters by a messenger to Alaric. Alaric immediately ordered all the vessels to be carried back to the apostle’s basilica as they were, and ordered the virgin, together with all who joined her, to be escorted there under protection.  
>   
> That house, as they say, was far from the holy shrines, with a considerable distance lying between it and the middle of the city. Thus, to the great spectacle of all, the vessels were arranged one by one, each carried openly above a head; golden and silver vessels were borne aloft, and a pious procession, protected on every side by drawn swords, advanced for their defense.  
>   
> Hymns were publicly sung by Romans and barbarians together in praise of God. The trumpet of salvation rang widely amid the destruction of the city; it invited and knocked upon even those hiding in secret places. From every direction people hastened to Peter’s vessels, the vessels of Christ. Many pagans joined the Christians in outward profession, if not in faith, and thereby escaped for a time, only to be more thoroughly confounded later.  
>   
> The more Romans gathered in flight, the more eagerly the barbarian defenders surrounded them. O sacred and ineffable discernment of divine judgment!

This is what Orosius says. In his words, “These are the sacred vessels used in the service of the Apostle Peter,” the phrase is understood, according to ancient ecclesiastical usage, as referring to a collection of sacred vessels.]

I shall relate an event belonging to a later period but very noteworthy. Ado, in his *Chronicle* under the year 519, says the following concerning the capture of Toledo:

> Childebert, among the rest of the treasure, carried away sixty most precious chalices, fifteen patens engraved with marvelous workmanship, and twenty Gospel-book cases of purest gold with gems; all these he distributed among the churches.

So ancient is the piety of the Church of Toledo in the precious furnishings dedicated to divine worship.

## CHAPTER XIV. The practice Christians followed in Prudentius’s time for burying the bodies of the dead. The different reason is shown why the holy Fathers condemned certain rites among the pagans but approved them among Christians.

133 156. From the care customarily bestowed on tombs among all peoples, Cicero and other pagans everywhere infer the immortality of the soul. Prudentius likewise argues for the resurrection of the dead from this in the hymn concerning funerals, verses 37 and following:

> The ages will soon come when at last  
> The kindred warmth revisits the bones . . .  
> Hence the greatest care is bestowed on tombs;  
> Hence the final honor receives  
> The limbs released from life,  
> And adorns the procession of the funeral.  
> It is customary to spread over them  
> Linen shining with bright whiteness,  
> And, sprinkled with Sabaean myrrh,  
> To preserve the body with medicinal ointment.  
> What do the hollowed stones mean?  
> What do the beautiful monuments signify?  
> Unless it is because people believe  
> That the one entrusted to them is not dead,  
> But has been given over to sleep.  
> This is what the provident devotion  
> Of Christ’s worshipers diligently practices, etc.

And at the end:

> We shall warm the bones we have covered  
> With violets and abundant foliage,  
> And we shall sprinkle the inscription  
> And the cold stones with liquid fragrance.

Some who call themselves wise would like the entire ritual of burying the dead to be abolished. Lactantius refuted them long ago, book VI, chapter 12:

> We, however, are not saying what a wise man ought to endure, but what he himself ought to do. Therefore, we are not now asking whether the whole manner of burial is useful or not; but even if it is useless—as they think—it must nevertheless be performed, if only for this reason: among human beings it is seen as right and humane. For the disposition of the mind is what is sought, and the intention is weighed.

Nevertheless, the manner of burying the dead was not the same and uniform among the ancient Christians. In Minucius Felix’s *Octavius*, the pagans raised among other objections against Christians:

> You do not honor the body with perfumes, reserving ointments for funerals, and you even deny wreaths to tombs.

Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 42:

> We certainly do not purchase incense. If Arabia complains, let the Sabaeans know that their merchandise is expended more abundantly and at greater cost on burying Christians than on fumigating the gods.

Regarding wreaths, Minucius replies to the pagans:

> Nor do we crown the dead. In this I am all the more astonished at you: how do you assign a torch to one who is conscious, or a wreath to one who is not conscious?

[Note: I do not know why Meursius and Heraldus call this passage corrupt. The latter wishes to restore it as follows: “How do you assign to the lifeless one a torch, as to one who is not conscious, and a wreath, as to one who is conscious?” The former: “How do you assign to the lifeless one, or to one who is not conscious, a wreath, as to one who is conscious?” Minucius says that the pagans act inconsistently when they burn the dead and judge them worthy of wreaths, as though they enjoyed these things. Therefore he adds: “Since the blessed person has no need of them, and the wretched person does not rejoice in flowers.” But we adorn funerals with the same tranquility with which we live.]

157. Later Christians adorned with flowers the tombs of the dead whom they wished to honor especially, as appears from Prudentius’s verses:

> We shall warm the bones we have covered  
> With violets and abundant foliage, etc.

And at the end of the hymn of Saint Eulalia:

> Take up purple violets,  
> And gather blood-red crocuses.  
> Generous winter is not without these;  
> The warming ice loosens the fields,  
> So that it may heap baskets with flowers.  
> O virgin and boy, give these gifts  
> From the leafy foliage in bloom, . . .  
> Thus it is pleasing to venerate the bones,  
> And an altar is placed upon the bones.

Among Roman writers there is frequent mention of flowers with which tombs were decorated, but in such a way that one understands this was not a custom necessarily practiced.

[Note: Virgil, book VI:

> Give lilies with full hands;  
> Let me scatter purple flowers,  
> And with these gifts at least let me heap offerings  
> Upon the soul of my descendant,  
> And perform an empty duty.

Cicero, *For Flaccus*, p. 518: “The tomb of Catiline adorned with flowers.” Suetonius, in *Nero*, at the final chapter, says that Nero himself was honored after death in this way and with other honors:

> Yet there were still some who for a long time adorned his tomb with spring and summer flowers; sometimes they brought out his images dressed in the *praetexta* on the Rostra, and sometimes they published edicts as though he were alive and about to return shortly, to the great harm of his enemies.

Indeed, Vologases, king of the Parthians, when he sent ambassadors to the Senate to renew the alliance, earnestly requested this as well: that his memory should be honored.]

Christians, therefore, honored in a similar way those dead toward whom they were well disposed. Saint Jerome, *To Heliodorus*, letter 3, chapter 1:

> Whenever I try to break forth into words and scatter flowers over his tomb, my eyes are filled with tears.

And more clearly in the *Consolation to Pammachius on the Death of His Wife Paulina*, letter 26, volume I, chapter 2:

> Other husbands scatter violets, roses, lilies, and purple flowers over the tombs of their wives, and by these services console the grief of their hearts. Our Pammachius waters the holy ashes and venerable bones with the balsams of almsgiving; with these perfumes and fragrances he cherishes the resting ashes.

Saint Paulinus likewise reports this in letter 38 to Pammachius. You did not accompany her—Paulina—not devoid of tears, as most mortals do, nor with the empty honor of vain processions, as those accustomed to lack hope do; rather, you followed her with saving remedies and living resources, that is, with almsgiving. You paid the proper rites to the dear dead in due order, and, drenched in devout tears and the abundant dew of charity, you honored her funeral with greater religious devotion.

158. It must be observed, however, that these same holy men, who prefer other works of piety, do not reject the veneration shown to the tombs of martyrs through the use of flowers and foliage. Saint Jerome, in the epitaph of Nepotianus:

> He shaded the meeting places of the martyrs with various flowers, the crowns of trees, and the tendrils of vines.

Saint Paulinus, *Natale* 3:

> Bring praise to God, boys; fulfill your pious vows.  
> Likewise offer festive songs with chaste dances.  
> Scatter flowers over the ground; cover the thresholds with wreaths.  
> Let purple spring breathe even in winter; let the year be flowery  
> Before its time; let nature yield to the holy day.  
> Earth, you owe crowns at the tomb of the martyr.

At Rome even today the use not only of flowers but also of foliage continues in the celebration of the feasts of the saints. Some outsiders detect I do not know what rusticity in this custom. I, however, judge that whatever is done at Rome with public authority and according to the rule of ancient times is especially refined.

There are further testimonies concerning this same rite among the Romans and other peoples. I shall cite one passage from Virgil, *Aeneid* II, verse 248:

> We wretched ones, for whom that day was to be our last,  
> Veil the shrines of the gods throughout the city  
> With festive foliage.

Saint Paulinus also shows that this was customary at weddings, in the *Epithalamium for Julianus*:

> Let no one cover the ground and thresholds only with leaves.

[Note: Some corruption or empty superstition introduced in Spain is noted in canon 73 of the ancient codex published by Dominicus Lopez de Barrera: “It is not permitted to practice wicked observances of the calendars, to devote oneself to pagan leisure, or to encircle houses with laurel or the greenery of trees. All this observance belongs to paganism.” From the Council of Laodicea, canon 31. On the first day of the month the pagans performed sacrifices.]

159. It was also the custom of the ancients to wash the bodies of the dead with wine or water, no less than to anoint them, and to pour wine and ointments into the tombs. Virgil, *Aeneid* VI:

> They wash and anoint the body of the cold man.

In the same work, when describing the honors paid by Aeneas at the tomb of Anchises, book V:

> Here, duly pouring an offering of unmixed wine to Bacchus,  
> He spills two cups upon the ground; two more of fresh milk, two of sacred blood,  
> And casts purple flowers.

Ausonius, in the *Epitaphs*, poem 36, says this at the tomb of a fortunate man:

> Sprinkle the ashes with unmixed wine, and wash them  
> With fragrant nard, stranger,  
> And add balsam to crimson roses.

Some have thought that Martial alludes to this, *Epigrams* XIII.126:

> Leave no ointment to your heir, nor wine;  
> Let him have the money, but give all the latter to you.

Acts of the Apostles 9:37: “When they had washed her”—Tabitha, who had died—“they laid her in an upper room.” Prudentius touches upon this custom at the end of the hymn on funerals: “We shall sprinkle [the stones] with liquid fragrance,” although there I understand ointments rather than wine. Thus in book I, ode 5, Horace says, “Perfumed with liquid fragrances,” that is, “anointed with ointments.” But the matter is clear in the hymn of Saint Fructuosus and his companions, verse 13:

> Then the ashes from the sacred bodies  
> And the bones drenched with wine are gathered.

[Note: Barthius interprets the following passage in Saint Vincent, verse 517, in this way:

> Placed beneath the shrine,  
> And enclosed below the altar,  
> They drink in the heavenly breeze  
> Of the gift poured upon them.

The subject is the bones of Saint Vincent. “The bones of those who were burned,” says Barthius, “or their ashes, were sprinkled with wine.” But it is better to interpret the passage from a similar place in Saint Paulinus, quoted below, where an ancient sarcophagus of Saint Felix is described.]

Martinus Roa, in *On the Sacred and Profane Birthday*, chapter 19, thinks that Prudentius’s words, “And the bones drenched with wine are gathered,” should not be understood according to the pagan rite described by Virgil, *Aeneid* VI:

> They washed the remains with wine and the thirsty ashes,

but should be explained in this way: “washed, in order to cleanse the remains of the fire and ashes.”

160. Besides, even if this rite was pagan, there is nevertheless no reason to deny that Christians used it differently. It is certain that both pagans and Hebrews used spices in burying the dead. Concerning the spices with which Jesus’ body was anointed, see John, chapter 19, verse 30. The first Christians retained the same custom, and there is no doubt that they poured balsams into the tombs of martyrs. Prudentius, *Hymn on Hippolytus*, verse 193:

> They press kisses upon the shining metal,  
> They pour out balsams and water their faces with tears.

[Note: Saint Paulinus, *Natale* VI:

> Let them strive to drench the martyr’s tomb with nard,  
> And bring medicinal ointments back to the devoted sepulcher.

*Natale* XIII, concerning the ancient sarcophagus of Saint Felix, verse 537:

> This surface of the slab is open on two sides,  
> Providing beneath it openings into which nard has been poured.  
> Coming from the hidden seat where the sacred ash rests,  
> It sanctifies, as it heals, with the mysterious breeze of the spirit.]

What reason, then, could Saint Paulinus have had—since he frequently praises this honor shown to the tombs of the saints—to appear to condemn either the same or a similar rite in *Natale* IX? For he writes:

> But would that they performed these celebrations with sound vows,  
> And did not mingle their cups with the holy thresholds.  
> Although the fasting crowd here resounds  
> With a better service,  
> And sounds hymns to the saints  
> In chaste voices,  
> And offers to the Lord the sober praise  
> Sung to him,  
> Nevertheless, I think such things must be forgiven—  
> The joys they derive from small feasts—  
> Because error has crept into unsophisticated minds.  
> Simplicity, unaware of such great guilt,  
> Falls through piety,  
> Mistakenly believing that the saints rejoice  
> At tombs drenched with fragrant wine.

161. Heretics abuse these and a few other similar statements, in which the holy Fathers criticize either pagan superstition, Christian corruption in religious rites, or depraved human practices—things sometimes tolerated but never approved—in order to bring the whole class of such customs into disrepute and condemn them under the name of idolatry.

[Note: Paulinus’s intention is plainly declared in the verses immediately following:

> Do the dead, then, approve what their teachers condemned?  
> Does Peter’s table receive what Peter’s doctrine rejects?  
> Everywhere there is one cup of the Lord, one food,  
> One table and one house of God.  
> Let them sell their wines in taverns;  
> The church is a holy house of prayer.  
> Depart from the sacred thresholds, serpent:  
> Such wicked sport is not owed to you in this hall,  
> But punishment.

Paulinus says that he was moved by this to adorn the church with paintings, so that he might recall the people from feasts to these spectacles.

Saint Augustine speaks of such feasts in book VI of the *Confessions*, chapter 2, where he says of the blessed Monica:

> When she had brought to the memorials of the saints, as she had been accustomed to do in Africa, dishes of porridge, bread, and unmixed wine, and was forbidden by the doorkeeper, she embraced the prohibition with such piety and obedience, etc.
