Thus, when she learned that the distinguished preacher and bishop Ambrose had prescribed, as a matter of piety, that these things should not be done—so that no opportunity for drunken gluttony might be given to drunkards, and because such practices were almost identical with the pagan custom of honoring the dead—she very willingly abstained. Instead of a basket full of earthly fruits, she learned to bring to the memorials of the martyrs a heart full of more purified vows.]

A careful distinction is therefore necessary. Among pagans, certain rites were criticized by the holy Fathers because they were performed in a perverse manner and were not referred to the true God. Christians were rebuked for a similar reason, because, by following pagan custom, they corrupted otherwise pious works either through empty credulity or through a depraved disposition.

Saint Jerome magnificently refutes Vigilantius, who objected to Catholics:

> These people pay great honor to such blessed martyrs, whom they think must be illuminated by the most worthless little candles, although the Lamb who is in the midst of the throne illuminates them with all the splendor of his majesty.

Jerome replies:

> Whoever lights candles according to his faith receives a reward . . . And because once we worshiped idols, are we not to worship God, lest we seem to venerate him with an honor like that given to idols? That was done for idols, and therefore it must be detested; this is done for martyrs, and therefore it must be accepted.

See the letter to Riparius and *Against Vigilantius*.

Saint Augustine, book XXI *Against Faustus*, chapter 10:

> Virginity among consecrated women is not therefore to be despised or detested because there were also Vestal virgins; nor are the sacrifices of the Fathers therefore to be criticized because there are also sacrifices of the pagans. For just as there is a great difference between those kinds of virginity, although the only difference is what is vowed and rendered to whom, so there is a great difference between pagan and Hebrew sacrifices, precisely because the only difference is to whom they were sacrificed and offered: the former to the proud impiety of demons, but the latter to the one God.

162. Therefore, when certain statements occur in the holy Fathers by which some rite appears to be rejected universally, one must examine against whom those statements were directed. Thus Lactantius—whose authority is nevertheless not held in high regard—praised the celebration of the Paschal Sabbath, as I said in no. 147, and certainly knew the manner in which it was observed. Yet in book VI, chapter 1, at the end, and chapter 2, he cannot tolerate this custom and others among the pagans:

> The same blindness presses upon the wretched: just as they do not know who the true God is, so they do not know what true worship is. Therefore they slaughter rich and fat victims to God, as though he were hungry; they pour out wine as though he were thirsty; they light lamps as though he were living in darkness . . . Is a man, then, to be thought in possession of his mind if he offers the light of candles and lamps as a gift to the author and giver of light? . . . Thus they attribute to the gods not a heavenly but rather a human understanding, and therefore they believe that the things necessary and pleasing to us are necessary and pleasing to them: food to us when we are hungry, drink when we are thirsty, clothing when we are cold, and light when the sun has gone away so that we may see . . . This is true worship: that the mind of the worshiper present itself to God as an undefiled victim.

Lactantius, therefore, rebukes the pagans because they offer created things to God as though he needed them, and because they fail to understand that the worship of God consists chiefly in the virtues of the soul. None of this overturns the Catholic worship—or even the worship of all Christians and Hebrews—prescribed by God.

Saint Augustine, *On the Morals of the Catholic Church*, book I, chapter 34:

> Do not follow the crowds of the ignorant, who are either superstitious even within the true religion, or so devoted to lusts that they have forgotten what they promised God. I know that there are many worshipers of tombs and paintings; I know that there are many who drink most luxuriously over the dead, and, offering feasts to corpses, bury themselves over the dead, and count their gluttony and drunkenness as religion.

Here he chastises corruption. The same Augustine commends pious religious observances in book I of *The City of God*, chapter 12, and in *On the Care to Be Taken for the Dead*, to Paulinus, chapter 3:

> The Lord himself, who was to rise again on the third day, praised and commended the good work of the devout woman, because she had poured precious ointment over his limbs and had done this for his burial. And those are deservedly remembered in the Gospel who carefully and honorably received his body from the cross and covered and buried it.

He himself also praises the miracles that occurred at the memorials of the martyrs, both at Milan and at Nola, in letter 78:

> Nevertheless, regarding these things that are known to human beings through visible signs, who can investigate his purpose, why these miracles occur in some places and not in others? For many people know very well the holiness of the place where the body of the blessed Felix of Nola was buried.

In book XXII of *The City of God*, chapter 8, he says:

> While the body lay there and the funeral rites were being prepared amid the groans and lamentations, one of his friends, in the midst of the consoling words, suggested that the martyr’s head be anointed with oil. This was done, and he revived.

163. Further evidence in confirmation of the same point can be drawn from other writers: for example, concerning the scattering of flowers in churches, from Saint Gregory of Tours, in the *Life of Sulpicius Severus*, chapter 50, where he says:

> He was accustomed, when lilies are in bloom, to gather their flowers and hang them along the walls of this building.

And from Fortunatus, book VIII, epigram 9, addressed to the lady Radegund, whose title is “To the Same Woman, Concerning Flowers upon the Altar.” Another poem had preceded it, “Concerning Violets”:

> But you bring fragrances not for yourselves but for Christ,  
> And you offer these first fruits to the pious temples.  
> You have woven festive crowns of many kinds around the altars,  
> So that the altar is painted with new flowers like threads.

Concerning oil from the tombs of martyrs, Paulinus of Périgueux should be read in the *Life of Saint Martin*, book V:

[Note: For, as the faithful often do with prudent hearts, they fill vessels with oil, brought either to offer to righteous men or to store in holy places as a religious observance, places where the present working of the martyr reveals patrons who have earned their honor through their power, etc. In the Bibliothèque de Lyon edition of the Fathers, these verses are read somewhat differently.

At a later time, the monk Iotsaldus, at the funeral of Odilo in the year 1048:

> A flowered and snow-white bed is brought for him,  
> Covered by kindly cedar and adorned with fragrant cypress.  
> Violets are scattered, and every kind of lily is laid out.  
> Then you might see him painting roses for himself,  
> And gazing kindly upon various herbs.  
> Balsams are not lacking, nor many spices are ground;  
> Nard, myrrh, storax, and great quantities of cypress are present.  
> There are a thousand kinds, and the fragrances vary still more;  
> A nectar-like savor fills heaven itself above.

Paul Aringhus gathers many further details concerning the funeral rites of Christians in book I of *Subterranean Rome*, especially from chapter 17 through chapter 31, where he repeatedly praises our poet and calls him a witness.]

I omit many others.

# CHAPTER XV. In what sense Prudentius called the soul “liquid” and an “element”

164. I shall now dispel the objections raised against Prudentius, whether by heretics or by Catholics, as though they were contrary to the Christian religion. Bayle, in the *Dictionary*, after Clericus, volume XII of the *Universal Library*, thinks that Prudentius calls the soul corporeal in these verses of the tenth hymn of the *Cathemerinon*:

> But when these two are torn apart,  
> They dissolve and destroy the human being.  
> Dry earth receives the body;  
> The air carries away the soul’s fluid.

And in book II *Against Symmachus*, verse 184:

> “He will not perish,” he says,  
> “The inner man who breathes;  
> He will suffer everlasting punishment  
> Because he badly governed the limbs entrusted to him.  
> Nor is it difficult for me to surround with flames  
> A liquid nature, although it is borne along in the manner of the south wind:  
> I shall nevertheless seize it and apply torments.”

Bayle would have written “in the manner of the breeze” if he had paid attention to the meter. Prudentius certainly has it that way.

Two answers can be given. First, when Prudentius speaks of the soul’s fluid and of the soul as liquid, he does not attribute matter or body to the soul, but indicates its purity and heavenly origin. Second, this meaning of “liquid” is not absurd and should not be criticized. Prudentius sometimes understands by “fluid” and “liquid” the spirit and the spiritual, as in the *Apotheosis*, concerning the demon, verse 411:

> Driven away, depart, airy fluid:  
> Christ commands; come out.

In *Cathemerinon* III, verse 190, speaking of our soul, he asserts that it does not die because it possesses “the power of liquid reason.” And in the *Apotheosis*, verse 87, concerning the divine nature:

> Pure, serene, shining,  
> Set free in liquid motion.

And in the same work, concerning the divine spirit, verse 694:

> But after the liquid spirit, from the heavenly mouth,  
> Sprinkled the virgin earth,  
> It became healing.

165. That Prudentius speaks in the passages under discussion in this sense is so evident that nothing more is needed. For he frequently distinguishes the soul most clearly from the body and from matter. In the *Apotheosis*, verse 830:

> It is indeed the Lord’s breath; but the spirit and power  
> Is not the fullness of God,  
> Sent forth with such restraint  
> As the one who breathes wished to preserve  
> The measure of breathing.  
> It is impossible for a human being to behold  
> The depths of Sabaoth;  
> But man is the mirror of the Godhead.  
> In the body, learn, with Christ as interpreter,  
> The reality that is not bodily,  
> For he displays the Father himself  
> In a mortal body.

One might think that Prudentius had the Athanasian Creed before his eyes—if it had truly belonged to Athanasius, or if it already existed at that time:

> For just as the rational soul and flesh are one man,  
> So God and man are one Christ.

In *Cathemerinon* III, verse 196:

> I believe—and my faith is not vain—  
> That bodies live in the manner of the soul.

The passage in the *Passion of Romanus*, verses 432 and following, is especially evident:

> Let them see that light of eternal hope,  
> Not flowing into eyes filled with bodily moisture,  
> Nor flashing through bodily windows,  
> But shining within pure minds.  
> The thick pupil of the flesh sees what is thick,  
> And sees a perishable thing,  
> Something destined to be dissolved.  
> The soul’s fluid is suited to see things clearly;  
> Its nature, ardent by itself,  
> Receives the flashing power  
> Of the most ardent divinity.  
> May the emperor learn of this light.

The distinction between the substance of the soul and the substance of the body is explicitly asserted in the *Psychomachia*, verse 905:

> Nor is human nature simple:  
> It rages with discordant arms.  
> The entrails formed from clay press down the soul;  
> But the soul, born from serene breath,  
> Burns within the black prison of the heart  
> And rejects filth amid its narrow bonds.  
> Light and darkness contend with differing spirits,  
> And a twofold substance animates  
> Their divergent powers.

In the *Peristephanon* X, verse 533, concerning the soul:

> The spirit, poured back from heaven, will soar upward.

In the *Hamartigenia*, verse 527:

> For the mind is far superior,  
> Since it was sent down from the highest ether;  
> If it wishes, it can shake the limbs subject to it  
> With heavy command, etc.

I pass over many other passages of this kind.

166. To make the insolence of intemperate critics more evident, I shall demonstrate from the very two passages in which they claim that Prudentius calls the soul corporeal that the matter is actually the opposite. *Cathemerinon* X, verses 5 and following:

> Both are yours, Ruler, yours;  
> Their union is joined by you.  
> While they remain joined together in life,  
> Both spirit and flesh serve you.  
> But when they are torn apart,  
> They dissolve and destroy the human being.  
> Dry earth receives the body;  
> The air carries away the soul’s fluid.

Clericus would like these words to express the opinion of the Epicureans, who asserted that the soul is mortal, and he cites verses of Lucretius expressing that view.

[Note: Book II:

> Finally, we are all born from heavenly seed.  
> The same father is the source of all,  
> From whom the life-giving mother, earth,  
> Receives drops of flowing moisture;  
> Pregnant, she gives birth to shining crops,  
> Joyous trees, and the human race;  
> She gives birth to every generation of wild animals . . .  
> Therefore she has rightly acquired the name of mother.  
> Likewise, what was previously from earth  
> Returns backward into earth;  
> And what was sent forth from the regions of ether  
> Is carried back upward and received  
> By the temples of heaven.]

First, however, it must be observed that the words of any author should not be considered in isolation, but in accordance with what precedes and follows them and with the author’s mind as more clearly expressed elsewhere. I shall judge that Clericus or Bayle intended one thing, and a man who thinks well of religion another, even though both pronounce the same ambiguous words.

[Note: Bayle himself agrees that in similar words Epicharmus had a different intention, according to Plutarch, *On Consolation*, p. 110:

> “It was compounded,” says Epicharmus, “and it has been separated; it returned to the place from which it came: earth downward, spirit upward.”

“What is unjust in all this?” Nothing.]

Next, what could be more unlike Prudentius’s position than the verses of Lucretius? Lucretius represents earth as the common mother of crops, trees, human beings, and wild animals, all of which are born in the same way and perish in the same way.

[Note: He continues:

> Nor does death destroy things in such a way  
> As to annihilate the bodies of matter;  
> It merely disperses their combination.  
> From there it joins one thing to another,  
> And brings it about that all things  
> Change their forms and alter their colors.]

But Prudentius says at the very beginning of the hymn, “God, fiery source of souls,” verse 21:

> So that, while noble things are bound to perishable ones  
> As though enclosed in a prison,  
> That more powerful part may remain,  
> Which drew its origin from ether.  
> If an earthly will happens to savor clay  
> And seeks what is heavy,  
> The mind too, overcome by weight,  
> Follows its limbs downward.  
> But if, remembering its fiery origin,  
> It rejects sluggish contaminations,  
> It carries its bodily host with it  
> And likewise bears it back to the stars.

Verse 129:

> This was once the dwelling of the soul,  
> Created from the Maker’s mouth.  
> Fiery Wisdom dwelt in these things,  
> With Christ as its chief.

Verse 149:

> But when you recall and restore, O God,  
> The dissoluble body,  
> In what region will you command  
> The purified soul to rest?

Prudentius explains and defends the immortality of the soul in many other passages, which there is no need even to indicate. Bayle admits that the words “the air carries away the soul’s fluid” do not deny the immortality of the soul, which Prudentius acknowledges shortly afterward. Clericus seems merely to wish Prudentius to have said more than he intended to say. But he neither intended nor said anything other than that, at death, the pure soul departs, migrates, and flies out of the body received by the earth.

167. Other verses were raised from book II *Against Symmachus*, where the soul is called a liquid and permeable nature, “in the manner of the south wind.” But since Prudentius is speaking there of the punishment with which the souls of sinners are to be punished, he must be understood to affirm that God can surround with flames a nature that, although liquid and permeable like the lightest breeze, is nevertheless able to be seized and subjected to torments. In this way he signifies that the soul is spiritual and cannot be affected by fire in any way except through a wondrous power of God.

This becomes clearer if the whole sentence is cited:

> Nor is it difficult for me to surround with flames  
> A liquid nature, although it is carried along in the manner of the south wind.  
> I shall nevertheless seize it and apply torments,  
> I myself, incorporeal and alone,  
> The one creator of spirits.  
> Indeed, I shall decree for bodies as well  
> A punishment corresponding to that of their companions,  
> Since I can renew the ashes  
> Into their former form,  
> And my power must not be despaired of:  
> I who was able to form what was new  
> Shall restore what has been destroyed.

Here not only is the body distinguished from the soul, but God is said to be able to punish the soul—that is, a spiritual and noncorporeal thing—with fire because he possesses supreme power, is incorporeal, and is the one father of spirits.

For this reason Saint Augustine affirms that demons, though bodiless, and the souls of the damned are to be tormented by fire, book XXI of *The City of God*, chapter 10:

[Note: Why should we not say that, although in wondrous ways, nevertheless by true means, incorporeal spirits can be afflicted by the punishment of bodily fire, since the spirits of human beings are themselves certainly incorporeal and yet have been able to be enclosed in bodily limbs, and then will be able to be bound inseparably by the bonds of their bodies? On this question the theologians may be consulted. For me it is enough to note that Prudentius acknowledges corporeal fire and raises the difficulty of how incorporeal souls can be affected by corporeal fire. Since Prudentius argues in this way, when he calls the soul “liquid,” it follows that by that word he did not understand it to be “corporeal.”]

168. It would now be superfluous to ask whether Prudentius properly called the spiritual soul “liquid” and a “fluid”; that is a question about terminology. Barthius, book XXI, chapter 4, considers the expression elegant:

> “The air carries away the soul’s fluid.” He elegantly called the soul’s fluid a fluid because its nature is liquid, pure, bright, and heavenly.

In the *Apotheosis*:

> These, joined together, made the rough clay live,  
> Since from the liquid seed of nature  
> It received its first forms,  
> Imprinted from the serene realm above.

These are verses 902 and following.

Properly speaking, the meaning of *spiritus* derives from the origin of the word: a breath of air, from the verb *spiro*, “I breathe.” From there the term was extended to the rational soul. Prudentius himself often calls the soul a breath, as in the *Hamartigenia*, verse 920, “a breath without a body.”

Since water is an element joined to air, poets often confuse the epithets of the two. Air is commonly called “liquid,” and Lucretius calls the waves “aerial.” The same Lucretius, as well as Virgil, calls fire “liquid,” indicating that it is ethereal and pure and opposed to the heaviness of earth.

Among the Hebrews, under the name “liquid,” or “heaven,” everything is understood that the Greeks call *aēr*, *aithēr*, and οὐρανός (*ouranos*, “heaven”). Hence Prudentius did not improperly use “the soul’s fluid” and “the liquid soul” for the soul’s spirit and purity, for the spiritual and heavenly soul, or one that draws its origin from heaven. He insists on this very frequently.

[Note: See Saint Augustine, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book VII, and his exposition of Psalm 136:

> As Scripture says in a certain passage, “He flew upon the wings of the winds”—that is, upon the powers of souls. Hence the soul is also called God’s breath, like wind—not so that it should be understood as the wind that we perceive propelling the body, but so that by this name something invisible may be signified, etc.

Among Latin authors, *liquidus* is often used for “pure,” as in “liquid speech” and similar expressions. Catullus, in the poem on Attis, verse 46: “And with liquid mind he saw.”]

For another reason the ancient Christians could have called the soul a fluid: namely, because they called the body the vessel of the soul. See the commentary on hymn VII of the *Cathemerinon*, verse 190.

169. Some raise another dispute about the term, because Prudentius called the soul an “element” in the same hymn on funerals, verses 1 and following:

> God, fiery source of souls,  
> You who join together two elements,  
> Father, you fashioned the living  
> And the dying human being as one.

They do not deny that Lactantius also used this term, book III, chapter 6:

> Knowledge comes to us from the mind, which arises from heaven; ignorance from the body, which is from earth. Hence we have something in common both with God and with animals. Since we consist of these two elements, one of which is endowed with light and the other with darkness, one part of us has been given knowledge and another ignorance.

Barthius, in the passage cited, says that Prudentius used *elementa* in the sense of “principles,” following the pagan usage found in Alcinous, Epictetus, and Euripides. I would rather say that the expression is Latin. Cicero, *Academica*, p. 44:

> Therefore, those first beginnings—or, to translate it from the Greek, “elements.”

Thus people commonly speak of “the elements of children,” “the elements of speech,” and “the elements of dialectic.” Why, then, should the beginnings or principles of a human being not be called “elements”?

Therefore, to defend Prudentius, there is no need to resort to the arguments made by Huetius in the *Origenian Questions*, book II, chapter 2, question 6, no. 14. There he wishes to excuse Origen’s error—his attribution of bodies to souls—on the grounds that the truth had not yet been defined by an ecclesiastical decree. The same opinion was apparently held by Tertullian, Saint Hilary in his commentary on Matthew, chapter 5; Ambrose, book II *On Abraham*, chapter 8; Cassian, *Conferences* VII, chapter 13; Theodotus, in the excerpts appended to the end of Clement of Alexandria; Methodius, in Photius, codex 234; Faustus of Riez; and others.

The manner in which Prudentius calls the mind fiery and fire will be explained in the commentaries. There is no particular difficulty in this, since he often calls God himself fiery. Some of the ancients actually thought that the soul was fire, and therefore said that a human being was extinguished when he died, and that someone punished by exile was deprived of water and fire. By these words they meant a lesser, or intermediate, diminution of civil status, as though the body consisted of water or moisture and the soul of fire. Others added the madness that dying in a shipwreck was especially grievous because the soul was fire and therefore most opposed to water. How far Prudentius is from these ravings is clearly evident from all his poems.

# CHAPTER XVI. Did Prudentius favor the Pythagoreans and Manichaeans concerning abstinence from meat? Or did he decisively overturn the Manichaeans’ arguments concerning the two principles?

170. Here again is Clericus, who contends that Prudentius approached the Pythagorean and Manichaean error concerning abstinence from meat. In *Cathemerinon*, hymn 3, “Before Food,” verse 56, Prudentius writes:

> This abundance serves Christ’s worshipers  
> And supplies them with everything.  
> Far from us be that hunger  
> Which would make us delight  
> To tear apart bloody feasts  
> In the slaughter of cattle.  
> Let the peoples who are untamed  
> Have banquets from the killing of four-footed beasts;  
> Let us be nourished by harmless feasts  
> Of leafy greens, of pods,  
> Of produce rich in many kinds of legumes.

[Col. 0698B] It commonly happens that those who readily embrace errors themselves, especially in matters of faith, try diligently to detect errors in others, as though they were seeking and adding companions for themselves. Prudentius does only this in the present hymn: he urges Christians to follow a practice that at that time was very common among them—namely, to be content with harmless foods and abstain from the flesh of four-footed animals—not because he denies that it is lawful to eat such flesh, but because it is better not to eat it.

He had already indicated clearly enough in verses 11 and following that no food is forbidden to Christians:

> Without you, Lord, nothing is sweet,  
> Nor does it please me to desire anything with my mouth,  
> Unless your favor, Christ, has first imbued  
> My cups and foods,  
> SANCTIFYING EVERYTHING BY FAITH.

By the final words he alludes either to Acts 10:11:

[Col. 0697D] “And he saw heaven opened, and a certain vessel descending, like a great linen cloth let down by its four corners from heaven to earth. In it were all four-footed animals, and reptiles of the earth, and birds of the air. And a voice came to him: ‘Rise, Peter; kill and eat.’ But Peter said: ‘By no means, Lord, for I have never eaten anything common or unclean.’ And the voice came to him a second time: ‘What God has purified, do not call common.’”

or to Romans 14:20:

[Col. 0697D] “Do not destroy the work of God for the sake of food. All things indeed are clean; but it is evil for a person to eat through giving offense. It is good neither to eat meat nor to drink wine, nor to do anything by which your brother is offended, or scandalized, or weakened. Do you have faith? Keep it to yourself before God . . . But whoever discriminates, if he eats, is condemned, because it is not **from faith**. Everything that is not **from faith** is sin.”

171. Prudentius’s meaning is understood more clearly from the reason he adds for why we ought to give thanks to God:

> He himself, because he gave everything to man,  
> Which we receive under his ruling hand—  
> Whatever sky, earth, or sea  
> Produces through air, depths, or fields—  
> He subjected these things to me, and me to himself.

Among the things God subjected to human beings, he selects birds and fish as food for Christians:

[Col. 0698D]

> Cunningly he ensnares the birds:  
> Either deceit with traps or with snares;  
> Twigs smeared with sticky bark  
> Entangle the feathered line  
> And prevent it from departing.  
> Behold, through the waters  
> Nets with winding folds drag  
> The flocks that wander through the waves.  
> The fish likewise follows the rod,  
> Seized by the wound-inflicting point,  
> Its trusting mouth injured by the bait.

Then he adds the fruits of the earth and of trees, as well as milk and the many things commonly made from milk.

Such was the madness of the Syrians that, for religious reasons, they abstained from fish and pigeons. Hyginus, *Fabula* 195:

> For this reason the Syrians do not eat fish or pigeons, which they count among the gods.

The ancient Christians placed birds and fish in the same category, since Genesis 1:20 teaches that both birds and fish were produced from the waters:

[Col. 0698D] “And God also said: ‘Let the waters bring forth the creeping creature having a living soul, and the bird upon the earth beneath the firmament of heaven.’ And God created the great sea creatures, and every living and moving creature that the waters had produced according to their kinds, and every bird according to its kind.”

Hence Saint Ambrose, in his hymn for Vespers on Thursday:

[Col. 0699A]

> God of great power,  
> Who causes those born from fertile water  
> To remain partly in the depths  
> And partly to rise into the air,  
> Marking those submerged in the waters  
> And raising those borne aloft to the heavens,  
> So that, produced from one stock,  
> They may fill different regions.

Rabanus Maurus, *On the Instruction of Clerics* II, chapter 27, says that the eating of birds and fish is permitted because birds were created from the same element from which fish were created; nor, he says, is the eating of other meats forbidden in the monastic rule, except that of four-footed animals. I believe he has in mind chapter 39 of the Rule of Saint Benedict:

[Col. 0699D]

> The eating of the flesh of four-footed animals is to be abstained from by everyone, except those who are entirely weak or sick.

[Note: Nicephorus, *History* XII, chapter 35, recounts various practices of those who fast:

> Some do not touch living creatures; others touch them, but only fish. There are some who also taste birds along with fish, saying that these too were produced from the waters, as Moses says. Some abstain from eggs and nuts or berries. Others eat the fruits of trees. Some eat only dry bread; others do not even touch that.]

172. Prudentius’s words could also be understood as referring by “to tear apart bloody feasts” to the practice of abstaining from blood and from strangled animals, which persisted in the Church for a long time.

[Col. 0699B] Tertullian, *Apology* 9:

> Let your error be ashamed, since we do not even have the blood of animals among our edible dishes, and for that reason we also abstain from strangled animals and animals that have died of themselves, lest in some manner we be contaminated by blood, even when it is buried within the organs.

The Second Council of Orléans, held in 533, chapter 20:

> Catholics who engage in the worship of idols, and so forth, are to be excluded from the assemblies of the Church. Likewise, those who eat animals killed by the bites of beasts, or strangled in any way or by any accident.

But Saint Augustine already held a different view in his own time, *Against Faustus the Manichaean* VI, chapter 32:

> When the Church of the nations has become such that no physical Israelite appears in it, what Christian now observes this rule, that he does not touch thrushes or smaller birds except those whose blood has been poured out, or that he does not eat hare if it has been killed by a blow of the hand to the neck without a bloody wound? And those few who still happen to fear touching such things are mocked by the rest.

Since Prudentius admits birds and fish among the foods of Christians but rejects four-footed animals, he was not referring to this practice of the few, which was mocked, but to the praiseworthy custom of the many, concerning which Saint Augustine says in *On the Morals of the Catholic Church* I, chapter 33:

> Thus many neither eat meat nor superstitiously consider it unclean . . . Therefore those who are able exercise restraint; they are nevertheless **innumerable**, and abstain both from meat and from wine for two reasons: either because of the weakness of their brothers, or because of their own freedom.

[Note: Petrus Castellanus, who published four books on the eating of meat, explains in book I, chapter 1, the custom of human beings in the earliest period of abstaining from meat. Plato, *Laws* VI, page 782, volume II, says:

> Our ancestors abstained from meat, as though it were not pious to eat it, and they did not pollute the altars of the gods with blood.

Castellanus himself, in chapter 2, proves against others that meat, above all foods, provides the best and greatest nourishment. Compare Clement of Alexandria, *Paedagogue* II, chapter 1; Tertullian, *On Jewish Foods*; and Saint Jerome, *Against Jovinian* I.

In an ancient codex of the Spanish Church, edited by Lopezius de Barrera, canon 58 appears, taken from the thirteenth canon of Ancyra:

> If anyone abstains from food not for the sake of abstinence but out of abhorrence for food, it has pleased the holy council that he first taste it and then, if he wishes, abstain. But if he rejects it to such an extent that he will not even taste vegetables cooked with meat, let him be deposed from the clerical order, since he neither obeys nor removes the suspicion of heresy from himself.]

146

173. Bailius must now be refuted. In his *Dictionary* and other works he repeatedly insisted on this point: that Catholics had never adequately refuted the Manichaean arguments concerning the origin of evil.

Jacobus Georgius de Chaufepié, in the article “Manichaeans” in the *New Historical and Critical Dictionary*, learnedly and forcefully refutes Bailius and lists his other opponents on this point: King, Clericus, Bernard, Jaquelot, Leibniz, Clarke, La Placette, and de Crousaz.

I shall explain only briefly what Bailius objects against Prudentius, matters which Chaufepié does not remember as having been raised against him.

“Whatever prince,” says Bailius, “can prevent evil and does not prevent it, wills that evil.” He calls this an evident proposition. But when Prudentius responds that human beings sin freely, Bailius says that this is a begging of the question, because Prudentius offers the disputed thesis itself as his answer.

Following Clericus, Bailius also supposes that Prudentius would answer that only a few are damned. For in hymn 6 of the *Cathemerinon*, verse 93, Prudentius says:

[Col. 0700A]

> Yet the same merciful Avenger  
> Blunts his anger  
> And does not allow the few of the ungodly  
> To perish forever.

Bailius replies that this answer is inadequate. If the damnation of all human beings would be an act of cruelty amounting to eight, then the damnation of a few would be an act of cruelty amounting to four, or two, or one. Thus he enjoys playing the scholastic against the cause of religion.

But anyone who reads Prudentius attentively, without some prejudiced opinion, will see through Bailius’s empty subtleties. First, why does he suppose that Prudentius would answer that only a few are thrust down into hell? Prudentius presents the Manichaean and Bailian argument to himself, and far from answering in this way, he plainly asserts the opposite in that passage.

*Hamartigenia*, verse 819:

[Col. 0700B]

> Thus nature pours souls of one color  
> From the fountains of heaven into the earthly soil;  
> But there they are held fast by pleasant enticements,  
> And only a few return and climb to the ether;  
> The sticky feast ensnares many  
> And does not allow them to pass through to the upper air.  
> Therefore the all-knowing Father sets the livid Tartarus  
> Ablaze with liquid lead  
> And digs out the pitch-filled trenches  
> Of infernal water beneath dark Avernus.

147

174. Prudentius had already expressed the Manichaean objection cleverly, and even more subtly than Bailius, although Bailius strains every sinew of his intellect. Read verse 640 and following.

[Col. 0700C]

> “If God does not wish evil to exist, why does he not forbid it?” he says.  
> It makes no difference whether he was the author and maker of evils.  
> Shall the fairest works be turned into wicked crime,  
> When he can prevent it, yet permits it? If, being almighty,  
> He should wish all to act innocently,  
> And his holy will should not degenerate,  
> Nor his hand stain itself with any deed,  
> Then the Lord created the evil which he beholds from above,  
> And permits and approves its being done, as though he himself had created it.  
> For he himself created what, although he can shut it out,  
> He does not abolish, but allows to spread through long practice.

What does Prudentius reply to this?

[Col. 0700D]

> Take away, merciful Father, my ears, and close the passages  
> Of my dull head, lest its winding interior receive  
> Such sounds . . .

And after he had emphatically established that the Lord does not will evil and does not approve beforehand what he later washes away, he introduces Marcion pressing the objection again:

[Col. 0701A]

> “Can anyone sin against the Thunderer unwillingly,  
> When it is easy for him to arrange the thoughts in a human heart,  
> To animate every fiber with whatever impulses he wishes,  
> And pour honesty throughout the veins?”

Prudentius meets this objection not by simply answering that human beings sin freely, but by showing that the force of freedom consists in the fact that a human being can sin, and that humanity had to be created with this freedom in order to be praiseworthy and worthy of reward. This is by no means a begging of the question.

[Col. 0701B]

> Do you not know, fool, that the force of your freedom  
> Was given by the very one who formed you? Do you not know  
> How great a power was granted to you, his servant, over the world? . . .  
> What would it have been for a human being, chosen to be king  
> Of the great world, not to be king of himself,  
> Disgraced by curtailed honor?  
> What praise, then, or what merit belongs to a human being  
> Who lives justly without a definite distinction  
> Between the two paths? . . .

Therefore, since that Providence is better in which human beings can act freely and consequently sometimes sin than that Providence in which not a single person possesses freedom, everything collapses that Marcion, Clericus, or Bailius may allege.

For even a mortal prince—whose laws are otherwise constituted—would not be said to will evil merely because he did not remove a Providence that was otherwise good and useful, although he knew with certainty that certain evils would follow from it. Nor do I see why Bailius sells as a self-evident notion a thesis fabricated by himself, by which he would bind even God.

150

175. If Bailius, or someone arguing on his behalf, should nevertheless object that God could have made human beings always act both well and freely, I shall first reply with Saint Augustine that God judged it better to bring good out of evils than to permit no evils to exist at all. Moreover, one must not ask only what God could have done, but whether what he did is compatible with his goodness.

[Col. 0701C] There can be no doubt that God must be judged good even if he permits human beings to sin. Finally, whatever may be the case concerning whether some Providence could be conceived under which all human beings would always use their freedom well, the present order of things entails that human beings sometimes sin unless God impedes the natural course of causes—a thing he ought not to do. For it cannot happen that freedom, moved by so many contrary impulses, should constantly pursue the good.

Whether Prudentius believed that the number of the damned was small has no bearing on this question. Bertius, and with him Riscus in *Hispania Sacra*, volume XXXI, interpret Prudentius as not holding the opinion of certain theologians concerning a greater number of the predestined, but merely asserting that few of the impious perish in comparison with those who would be damned unless God came to their aid through his grace and kindness.

That interpretation seems capable of being drawn from the verses cited in section 174, unless Prudentius is declared plainly self-contradictory—something which some people wrongly deny to be absurd in Prudentius and other poets.

Theologians discuss at length whether the number of the predestined is greater than that of the reprobate. If the comparison is between angels, it is probably asserted that the predestined were more numerous. If the question concerns all human beings whatsoever, both those who have existed and those who will exist, the more common and truer opinion is that the reprobate are more numerous.

It must likewise be maintained that among Christians, including heretics, more are damned than saved. Among those who die within the Catholic Church, learned and devout theologians believe that the predestined are more numerous than the reprobate, and I do not dare oppose them.

There exists the work of the distinguished Petrus Franciscus Fogginius, entitled *The Remarkable Agreement of the Fathers of the Church Concerning the Small Number of Adult Believers Who Will Be Saved, When Compared with the Believers Who Will Be Rejected*. Rome, 1752.

Fogginius ought to have distinguished the passages of the Fathers in which all adult Christians, including heretics, are included from the other authorities that concern Catholics alone. He should then have transcribed and explained the other testimonies of the Fathers that seem to favor the contrary opinion. Otherwise no secure judgment can be made in support of that remarkable agreement which he asserts.

I shall speak in the following chapter about the distinction between the godly and the ungodly, and will say something further in the commentary.

## CHAPTER XVII. The Prayer at the End of *Hamartigenia* Explained and Defended

176. After Prudentius had discussed at length in *Hamartigenia* the rewards of the godly and the punishments of the ungodly, he turns in verse 931 to a prayer addressed to God. The following verses are chiefly subjected to examination:

[Col. 0702C]

> I do not ask for a home  
> In the blessed region . . .  
> For me it is enough if no face  
> Of a Tartarean minister should meet me,  
> Nor the flame of greedy Gehenna  
> Devour this soul plunged into the deepest furnaces.  
> Let a gloomy fire, because this is necessary  
> For bodily defilement, consume me  
> In hollow Avernus;  
> At least let the slow flames breathe forth  
> Mildening vapors,  
> And let their heat grow gentle as their ardor fades.  
> Let immense light, and brows bound with crowns,  
> Glorify others;  
> Let a light punishment mercifully burn me.

Most Catholics are harsher in attacking this prayer than certain non-Catholics. The latter acknowledge that it defends a purgatorial fire; although they themselves consider that doctrine false, they nevertheless admit that it was held by certain ancient writers and is now held by the entire Catholic Church.

I have discussed the Magdeburg theologians in section 128. Nicolas Antonius, in *Bibliotheca Hispana Vetus*, says that an explicit mention of another fire, distinct from the fire of hell, occurs at the end of *Hamartigenia*. He says this passage deeply torments the heretics who oppose purgatorial fire, and he cites Osiander, *Epitome of Ecclesiastical History* IV, book I, chapter 26.

[Col. 0702D] Osiander indeed praises Prudentius in that chapter; but in Weitzius there is no mention of purgatorial fire, although he does bring certain blemishes against Prudentius.

177. In the Venetian edition of Fabricius’s *Bibliotheca Veterum Latinorum* of 1728, book IV, chapter 2, I read in a note that prayers are appended at the end of *Hamartigenia* in which the author says that it is enough for him not to be thrust into Tartarus, even if punishments must be endured in purgatory.

152

Bailius attempts by another route to defend Prudentius against Perkins. Prudentius, he says, could have considered himself unworthy of blessedness and worthy of punishment; such humility is not impious:

[Col. 0703A]

> Is this humility impious? By giving the matter a favorable interpretation, might it not be called an offering of oneself to the justice of God?

By these words Bailius sufficiently reveals that he does not know what humility is. For what sort of humility would it be if a person, when he could beseech God to erase his crimes in this life and free him from eternal damnation, instead offered himself to God to be tormented by everlasting flames, eternally deprived of heavenly blessedness and of God himself?

Petrus Wesseling, *A Single Book of Probable Opinions*, chapter 22, replies to Guilielmus Caveus, who maintained that the statement “I do not ask for a home in the blessed region” was impious and unworthy of Prudentius:

[Col. 0703B]

> But what if the poet is indicating that, conscious of very serious errors, he does not aspire to that most blessed station into which the martyrs and virgins will be transferred?

This is suggested by the words that precede and follow:

> There are many dwellings of Christ in the Father’s treasuries,  
> Distinguished by unequal places. I do not ask for a home  
> In the blessed region. Let the chaste companies of men be there,  
> Who, scorning the wealth of dust, sought their own riches;  
> Let virginity, white with unfading blossom, be there,  
> Having cut away and castrated the heart.

Wesseling adds that the rest of what Prudentius says is not something to be praised in a Christian, but is so framed that it does not wholly disagree with the opinions of the ancient teachers who held that all who would eventually become participants in blessedness must pass through fire and be purified by it.

Wesseling, of course, rejects purgatorial fire, although he nevertheless says that “hollow Avernus” is a poetic expression and tolerable in a poet for unremitting fire.

At first sight the final verses seem harsher to him:

[Col. 0703C]

> Yet I would not have you think, he continues, that by the words “Let a light punishment mercifully burn me” the poet inserted himself among the company of the damned. These words too are to be explained from the opinions of the ancients.

[Note: Ludewigius, in his *Life of Prudentius*, wishes to excuse Prudentius in other doctrines which he shares with Catholics—free will, the innocence of the flesh, good works, the worship and invocation of the martyrs, and the blessed Virgin—both because of corrupt manuscripts and because a poem should not be confined within the narrow barriers of its words.

[Col. 0703D] But he calls the passage “I do not ask for a home in the blessed region” a foolish invention worthy of old women’s tales. Nevertheless, he says that Prudentius is excused here by the fact that he said it was necessary to suffer for bodily defilement, since he believed that the holy martyrs had already paid the penalties for the torments they endured for Christ.

In this respect, nearly his equals in error were those cited in the Centuries, century 4, chapter 4, although our theologians believe that they should be interpreted according to a sounder understanding than that of today’s Roman Catholics . . . .

Nevertheless, Prudentius may have held a private and personal error: conscious of the crimes of his youth, he may have believed himself unworthy of eternal life immediately after death.

Thus Ludewigius testifies that Catholics say the same thing as the ancients, except that he strives to discern in the ancients some sounder understanding. In Prudentius he finally censures the belief in the temporal punishments of purgatory. See below, section 184, where similar prayers, uttered by the mouth of certain persons, are brought forward by Saint John Climacus.]

153

178. Many either deny that this prayer belongs to Prudentius or at least cast doubt upon it. Andreas Rivetus, *Sacred Criticism* III, chapter 26, says that the prayers appear to have been falsely attributed to Prudentius and contradict ode 7 of the *Cathemerinon*; Perkins, he says, held the same opinion. Guilielmus Caveus likewise judges them spurious for the same reason.

[Col. 0704A] Giselinus provided the occasion for this opinion. In his commentary he reports that he saw this prayer printed separately with other material, without the author’s name being indicated—perhaps because the copyist did not know it. He infers this from the two verses appended at the end, which are wholly contrary to the author’s intention and meaning and conflict with the epilogue of the hymn to Saint Romanus.

[Note: On verse 963, “At least let the flames breathe forth mildening vapors,” Giselinus exclaims:

[Col. 0704D]

> Is this so, Prudentius—that anyone should be so abject in spirit? Surely the gentle words of the Gospel promise us something else. Once the means of obtaining divine grace have been set before us, they strictly command us to make our calling certain and confidently and assuredly await the glory of eternal life. Conversely, they teach that to pray for the fire of hell or for a more severe punishment is characteristic of servants who are always fearful and almost despairing, since there is now no condemnation for those who remain in Jesus Christ, who has been made for us by God wisdom, righteousness, and so forth.

The Belgian Appendix to the Roman Index, in Labbe’s *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, orders that these words of Giselinus be deleted—or rather corrected according to the recension published by the author himself, lest the heterodox be excessively inquisitive in another person’s work. I have not seen Giselinus’s recension.]

Ludewigius reports that Giselinus’s opinion is expressed in Flaccus’s catalogue, but he does not agree that the prayer is spurious, on the grounds that writers—especially poets—can more readily forget themselves.

179. For my part, I see no adequate reason why prayers of this kind should be denied to Prudentius. Apart from the agreement of all the manuscripts, Iso the Master explains this prayer with glosses among Prudentius’s other works, and Theodulfus of Orléans likewise attributes it to Prudentius in his book *On the Holy Spirit*:

[Col. 0704B]

> Thus Prudentius demonstrated with marvelous truth the perfect and singular nature of the Holy Trinity in his heroic-meter book against the Marcionists:
>
> O God, father of all, giver of the soul, O God Christ,  
> From whose mouth God the one Spirit proceeds.

The interpretation adopted by Riscus is not wholly displeasing: Prudentius did not dare ask for blessedness immediately after death and appears content with the punishments of purgatorial fire. Riscus also cites verses from the end of the *Apotheosis*:

[Col. 0704C]

> Drive fear from your hearts, my limbs, and believe that you  
> Will return with Christ your God, for he carries you  
> And recalls you with himself. Laugh at threatening illnesses,  
> Scorn the disasters inflicted upon you,  
> And cast off the dreadful tombs. Rise and go  
> Where Christ summons you.

154

As for Ludewigius’s reply that writers, especially poets, sometimes forget themselves, that may have force when they clearly say contradictory things. But when the words are clear in one place and doubtful in another, fairness demands a favorable interpretation in matters of the greatest importance; it is not necessary to have recourse to forgetfulness.

And lest we believe that Prudentius despaired of attaining eternal life, ode 7 of the *Cathemerinon* is readily available. Some say that it contradicts these prayers; with better reason, we maintain that the interpretation should be drawn from it.

[Note: In this ode, concerning the Ninevites, verse 96:

[Col. 0705C]

> But while a little day for repentance is granted,  
> If perhaps they should wish to tame and break  
> Their wicked desire and their old follies,  
> Forgiving terror suspends the blow,  
> And the pronounced sentence pauses for a little while.

And verse 171:

> Softened by these and similar things,  
> God restrains his brief anger,  
> Tempering a favorable oracle’s dark pronouncement.  
> For ready mercy does not find it difficult  
> To release the guilt of supplicating mortals  
> And become the helper of those who weep.

There are many other passages at the end concerning fasting and other works of piety by which God is appeased.

To these I add from the preface to book I of *Against Symmachus*, verse 80:

> Savior of the Roman race, I pray to you,  
> Who grant pardon to all who perish,  
> Who declare that no mortal is excluded  
> From your work, whom you may raise with an easy hand:  
> If you can, have mercy now upon this person, and so forth.]

Since Prudentius’s understanding of divine mercy, easily appeased, is so openly and repeatedly expressed that even before section 175 it was necessary to labor lest he appear to have embraced an excessively favorable opinion concerning the greater number of the predestined, it follows that the prayer in *Hamartigenia* must be explained in light of what he said elsewhere and according to the teaching presented by other holy Fathers, such as Saint Hilary in his exposition of Psalm 1:

[Col. 0705A]

> For there are some between the ungodly and the godly . . . For the fear of God holds many within the Church; nevertheless, the allurements of the world entice these same people toward worldly vices . . . They are not ungodly, because the name of God is honored among them; but they are not godly, because they pursue things foreign to godliness . . . Judgment therefore awaits them—judgment that has already been carried out against unbelievers and is not necessary against believers.

[Note: Also, in chapter 2 of his commentary on Matthew:

[Col. 0705C] “The Lord indicates the time of judgment for our salvation when he says: ‘He will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire,’ because after those baptized in the Holy Spirit it remains for them to be perfected by the fire of judgment.”

Saint Cyprian, in letter 52 to Antonianus, says that only on the day of the Lord will wooden vessels be consumed in the fire of divine ardor, and earthen vessels be broken by him to whom the iron rod has been given.

[Col. 0705D] Saint Ambrose, in his exposition of Psalm 36:

> Therefore the sons of Levi will be purified by fire, Ezekiel by fire, David by fire. Yet although these will be tested through fire, they will nevertheless say, “We have passed through fire and water” . . . Although the Lord will save his servants, we shall be saved through faith, yet saved as through fire.

Sixtus of Siena, *Bibliotheca* VI, note 345, adducing many testimonies of the holy Fathers, especially Prudentius’s hymn *On the Burial* and the eighteen martyrs of Zaragoza, and Daniel Huet, *Origeniana* II, chapter 2, question 11, demonstrate that, down to the Florentine synod, nothing certain had been prescribed by the Church concerning the manner and place of the blessedness of the saints, so that the Fathers adopted differing views.]

155

180. Therefore I judge that in the final verses of his prayer Prudentius intended nothing other than to say that he would be tormented lightly by purgatorial fire, if it were necessary for the soul to be purified from bodily defilement before the final day of judgment. For he clearly speaks of a person’s death:

[Col. 0705B]

> Grant this to my soul at some time, when it has left  
> The lodging of this body . . .  
> When the mournful hour  
> Has closed these eyes, and the body, after the death-call, lies there,  
> And the mind, stripped bare, enjoys its own sight,  
> Let it not see some savage robber  
> From the race of brigands, pitiless and raging,  
> Terrible in face and threatening in expression and voice,  
> Who might drag me, stained with the spatter of my character,  
> Headlong like a bandit,  
> And plunge me as I fall into black caverns,  
> Exacting every last quarter and smallest fraction  
> Of the debt owed for a life marked by stains.

He is therefore not speaking of the eternal punishments of hell, in which bodies too must be tormented. Concerning those punishments he says in this same poem, verse 827:

[Col. 0705C]

> And beneath the Phlegethontian flood he decreed  
> That devouring worms should grow old  
> In everlasting punishments for crimes . . .  
> He gave an immortal age  
> To worms, flames, and tortures.

And in book II of *Against Symmachus*, verse 191:

> I shall also decree for bodies  
> Punishments joined in equal fellowship.

[Col. 0706A] The words “Let a gloomy fire, because this is necessary for bodily defilement, consume me in hollow Avernus” therefore convey this meaning: if it is necessary that I, since I have not merited a place among the godly and holy, be consigned to purgatorial fire, at least may I be affected by a mild burning; and while immense light and brows bound with crowns glorify the holy martyrs and virgins immediately after death, may a merciful punishment burn me.

The other words, “I do not ask for a home in the blessed region,” point in the same direction. He means: I do not dare ask for a home in that blessed region where, immediately after death, the souls whose holiness in this life was outstanding are received.

For he always has in mind the time immediately following death:

> When the mournful hour has closed these eyes.

In fact, he very frequently hopes to attain eternal blessedness at last and invokes the patronage of the martyrs for that purpose. To avoid going further afield, in this very prayer he says:

[Col. 0706B]

> With you as judge I tremble, pale with fear;  
> With you as the same judge I take hope  
> That whatever I do or say, however unworthy of pardon it may be,  
> Will be pardonable before you.  
> I confess it—willingly forgive and spare one who confesses.  
> I have deserved every evil; but you, good judge,  
> Take away what I have deserved;  
> Favorably grant better things to one who prays.

Those who say that the poet, having forgotten himself, despaired of God’s mercy plainly show that they themselves have forgotten what the poet embraced in this prayer.

[Note: Johannes Lamius, in *Deliciae Eruditorum*, volume XIII, page 314, when transcribing Prudentius’s prayer, imagines that he asked for a milder place in hell because he considered himself unworthy of paradise. He then adds the impious testament of Filippo Strozzi, asserting that it was composed with a different intention:

[Col. 0706C]

> So as not to come again into the power of my enemies . . . I, Filippo Strozzi, have resolved to end my life with my own hands by whatever means I can, however harsh this may seem to my soul. I commend my soul to God’s supreme mercy, humbly praying him that, if he does not wish to give it anything better, he will at least give it some place where Cato of Utica and other virtuous men who met such an end may be found.

What connection is there between this prayer and Prudentius’s?]

## CHAPTER XVIII. Prudentius’s Opinion Concerning the Mitigation of the Punishments of the Damned During the Vigil of Easter Saturday, and Whether It Occupied the Minds of Others

181. Prudentius expressed a distinctive opinion in *Cathemerinon* hymn 5, verse 125:

[Col. 0706D]

> There are also, for the often-harmful spirits,  
> Celebrated holidays from punishments beneath the Styx,  
> On that night when the holy God returned  
> From the Acherontian pools to those above . . .  
> Tartarus grows weak under gentler punishments,  
> And the population of the prison rejoices  
> In the leisure of its confinement, freed from the fires.

[Note: Clericus wrongly understands this passage and draws an even worse argument from it:

> He says that every year, on the night when Jesus Christ rose again, the damned feel no punishments. This implies that Jesus Christ had descended to that place and had removed the damned from it on that night.

See the commentary on *Cathemerinon* hymn 3, verse 196.]

Bellarminus, *On Purgatory* II, chapter 18, when dealing with the question whether suffrages benefit the damned, answers concerning Prudentius’s passage:

[Col. 0706C]

> I say nothing other than that Prudentius played poetically.

But he could have said something else; and certainly, if he had said something else, he would not have given Hospinian an opportunity for mockery. Hospinian, in his book *On the Origin of Christian Festivals*, on the festival of Saint Hippolytus, says that Prudentius, in describing the martyrdom of Saint Hippolytus, played poetically—something which, he adds, Bellarminus says Prudentius also did in a more important matter.

What else, then, could Bellarminus have said? He could—and perhaps should—have said that certain ancient writers held the opinion which Saint Augustine did not dare condemn in chapter 112 of the *Enchiridion*:

> Let them suppose, if they wish, that the punishments of the damned are mitigated to some extent at certain intervals, provided that they understand that God’s anger remains in them—that is, the damnation itself.

157

To this passage Bellarminus replies that Augustine is not dealing there with prayer for the dead, but merely saying that it is not erroneous to concede that the damned are punished less than they deserve; he teaches this more clearly in *The City of God* XXI, chapter 24.

Why, then, should the same not be said of Prudentius? It cannot be denied that Augustine indicates Prudentius’s opinion when he leaves it free to believe, if one wishes, that the punishments of the damned are mitigated to some degree at certain intervals.

[Note: Saint Augustine taught nothing different in *The City of God* XXI, chapter 24:

[Col. 0707D]

> But those who wish to extend this opinion even to the torments of the ungodly should at least understand it in this way: while God’s anger remains in them—an anger announced in the eternal punishment—God does not contain his mercies within that anger, but causes them to be tortured not with punishments as severe as their deserts, but with punishments less atrocious and lighter than they deserve. Thus God’s anger will remain, and within that anger he will not contain his mercies.]

[Col. 0707B] **182.** Compare what he added in the place cited from the *Enchiridion*: “For this is called the wrath of God, not a disturbance of the divine spirit, so that in his wrath—that is, while his wrath remains—he nevertheless does not withhold his mercies, not by bringing eternal punishment to an end, but by applying or interposing relief amid the torments.” Saint John Chrysostom embraced this opinion in Homily 3 on the Epistle to the Philippians, though Bellarmine attempts to draw him into another meaning:

“Let us therefore mourn for these” (he is speaking of the damned), “and let us bring them aid according to our ability; let us procure some help for them, small indeed, but nevertheless capable of helping . . . And this, indeed, concerns those who departed in the faith. But catechumens are not deemed worthy even of this consolation, except one. What is it? It is permitted to give something to the poor on their behalf, and from this they receive some refreshment.”

Passing over John of Damascus—whether the work is genuine or not, or whether it was written by another under his name—Saint Paulinus of Nola, whose prayers for Nicetas I shall produce in note 185, and Innocent III, from whose authority Bellarmine does not extricate himself sufficiently, the passages I shall transcribe from the Mozarabic Missal for the Wednesday after Easter are clearer and come closer to Prudentius:

“The infernal regions saw you, O God; they saw and trembled at the voice of your thunder, saying: ‘Death is swallowed up in victory. Where is your victory, O death? Where is your sting, O death?’ Therefore the punishments of the wretched stood stunned for a little while. Nor should the bloody torments have thought themselves to have conquered, when they saw the crucified one; even punishment itself trembled before its judge.”

[Col. 0707D] **183.** Sixtus of Siena, *Bibliotheca sancta*, book VI, chapter 47, reports the opinions of the theologians Praepositivus, priest of the Church of Liège, Gilbert, William, and Rupert. On the basis of the cited words of Saint John Chrysostom and other passages—also Homily 33 on Matthew, likewise John of Damascus, [Col. 0708A] Saint Gregory the Great, and Prudentius in the hymn “On the New Light” of Holy Saturday (for this is how he titles it), together with similar statements of illustrious Fathers—they inclined toward this opinion; others explain it differently. For Saint Thomas seems to acknowledge in the damned only a certain empty appearance of deceptive joy and a pleasing delusion of the grieving mind, such as is said to exist in demons, who, when they lead human beings into sin, are affected by a kind of vain joy, without their punishment decreasing. The scholastic theologians discuss this matter.

**184.** In an eleventh-century manuscript in the Riccardian Library there is a missal, and in it a Mass for a soul concerning which there is doubt, mentioned by Lamius in volume XIII of the *Deliciae eruditorum*, pages 311 and following. The prayers aim precisely at what we are investigating:

“And if we cannot obtain full pardon for that soul, at least let it feel, even amid the torments which it perhaps suffers, refreshment from the abundance of your mercies . . . so that, if perhaps on account of the gravity of its crimes it does not deserve glory, through these offerings of the sacred oblation the torments themselves may at least become tolerable for it.”

Among the Bollandists, volume III for May, under May 14, page 336, Saint Pachomius says of a certain damned person:

“For this reason I ask you: if you desire to make the sufferings of the deceased lighter, commit him to burial without psalms. For since God is good and merciful, he might grant him some rest.”

See the notes of the Bollandists.

Saint John Climacus, in step 5 of the *Ladder of Paradise*, reports similar prayers from the mouths of certain persons:

“Others, at once weighed down by the burden of conscience and imploring relief from eternal punishments, nevertheless sincerely proclaimed themselves unworthy of heaven, and said: ‘Provided that this is done, it is enough for us.’ I saw there humble souls, weighed down beneath the burden, who . . . [Col. 0708C] kept saying . . . ‘It is enough for us if we are delivered from your most grievous threat and from the unutterable and hidden punishments. We do not dare to ask that all punishment be entirely remitted to us and pardon granted.’”

This perhaps pertains more properly to Prudentius’s prayer at the end of the *Hamartigenia*, discussed in chapter 17, since the two matters are contained in and connected with one another by a certain resemblance.

I shall not omit the fact that this hymn of Prudentius was sung in many churches at the lighting of the paschal candle. For this reason that opinion was not ill received in those churches. These considerations perhaps moved Dionysius Petavius, when, after having transcribed the verses of Prudentius in volume III, book III of *On the Angels*, chapter 7, he added:

“Nothing certain has yet been decreed by the Catholic Church concerning this breathing-space, at least for damned human beings. Therefore this opinion of the most holy Fathers should not rashly be rejected as absurd, although at the present time it is foreign to the common Catholic understanding.”

I know that Petavius’s freedom of judgment is defended by many and attacked by many. But I think that Prudentius is better understood by Petavius than by those who defend the view that Prudentius spoke not dogmatically but poetically; I wish they would explain this distinction themselves. I find a partial explanation in the index of books to be expurgated compiled by Father John Maria of Bracichelli, master of the Sacred Apostolic Palace. There, on page 257, [Col. 0709A] these words from volume VIII of Margarini’s *Bibliotheca Patrum* are expunged under Aurelius Prudentius:

“Against the words of the text, ‘THEY ARE ALSO FOR THE SPIRITS,’ place in the margin: ‘READ WITH CAUTION,’ for according to the principles of theology there is never any true refreshment for the souls of the damned in hell. Perhaps Prudentius merely wished to play poetically, in order to indicate the joy of the day of the Lord’s resurrection. Let others defend this interpretation if they wish; I would rather believe that Prudentius, together with others, was mistaken, if it can nevertheless be established with certainty that the opinion of certain ancients was an error.”

[Note: [Col. 0709D] The index cited is believed to be rarely encountered. Its title is: *The First Volume of the Index of Books to Be Expurgated, Compiled for the Benefit of Students, in Which the Books of Fifty Authors Especially Sought After Are Corrected*. Rome, from the press of the Reverend Apostolic Chamber, 1607. A copy belonging to the distinguished bishop Reggio bears, at the beginning, a handwritten note:

“Had we followed the series and customary style of the other indexes of this kind, we would have been compelled to expunge certain matters which, although learnedly observed, ought nevertheless not to have been inserted in the purpose of this book, since it is enough to indicate what must be deleted and what must be read with caution. Nevertheless, it seemed useful at the beginning of certain books to touch briefly on certain matters concerning their authors, so that the reader might readily learn what sort of author he is, whether Catholic or heretical, and finally of what reputation.”

From this I infer that not everything which Thomas Malvenda, the most distinguished ornament of Spain and of the Dominican Order, noted in the *Bibliotheca Patrum* was entered into the index. Nicholas Antonius writes of this:

“His task for that year, lasting two months, was the review of the *Bibliotheca of the Ancient Fathers*, entrusted to him by the sacred purple Fathers of the Index. Thus, through the observations of our Thomas, the kind and age of each author’s doctrine, and the authority or rank to be assigned to each of the writers included in it, were entered into the Roman Index, which appeared in 1607 under the name of John Maria of Bracichelli, master of the Sacred Palace. The Parisian printer also admitted those very annotations into the *Bibliotheca* revised by him in 1605.”

In Nicholas Antonius, however, “the year 1605” should, in my opinion, be read as “the year 1624.]

## CHAPTER XIX. Why did Prudentius pray to be transferred to the Judge’s right hand on the day of the final judgment?

[Col. 0709B]

**185.** It is also liable to the criticisms of certain people that Prudentius concluded the hymn of Saint Romanus with these verses:

“I would wish, though I am destined to be on the left among the flocks of goats,  
to be recognized from afar as I shall be;  
and while I pray this, may the excellent king say:  
‘Romanus prays; transfer this goat to me; let him be a right-hand sheep,  
let him be clothed in fleece.’”

And at the end of the *Passion of Saints Fructuosus and his Companions*:

“There will one day be a time, when the world collapses,  
when Fructuosus will release you, Tarraco,  
from harsh punishment, sheltering you from the fire.  
Perhaps, with Christ prospering, he will also deign  
to grant healing to my torments,  
as he turns over these sweet hendecasyllables.”

Since in the sacred Scriptures that final and terrible day is described with great solemnity, the prayers of Christians, especially of the ancients, are directed toward this: that at the time when the whole world is judged, they may avert from themselves the wrath of the supreme judge—not because they thought it uncertain before that day what destiny each individual would undergo, but because then the sentence must be pronounced before all.

[Note: [Col. 0709D] The notable passage is in Matthew 25:31 and following:

“When the Son of Man comes in his majesty, and all the angels with him, then he will sit upon the throne of his majesty. And all nations will be gathered before him, and he will separate them from one another, as a shepherd separates sheep from goats. And he will place the sheep at his right hand, but the goats at his left.”]

Saint Paulinus of Nola confirms exactly the same thing in his *Natalia*:

“When you too, happy portion of the holy,  
will accompany the reigning Lamb,  
ask that we be placed among the flock of sheep, so that the sentence  
of the highest Judge may once again grant us to you as this gift,  
lest he assign us, because we have badly given thanks,  
to the goats on the left,  
but rather join us, placed on the right in the portion of salvation,  
to the generous flock, to the praised lambs.”

[Note: [Col. 0710C] And concerning the return of Bishop Nicetas to Dacia:

“Separated from you by place, as we are by merit,  
we shall look upon you from afar, humble before exalted patrons,  
as your companion among the sacred companies.  
Who will grant us this on that day,  
that we may stand beneath the shadow of your side,  
and that the breeze of your rest  
may temper the fire for us?  
Then, I pray, remember us exceedingly,  
and, reclining in the lap of the holy Father,  
with your dew-moistened finger  
disperse the raging flame for us.”]

This was the opinion of the holy Fathers: that at the final judgment God, on account of the merits and prayers of the saints, would call more people to the right-hand side. By this they intimate that while human beings are alive, through the intercession of the saints, they obtain the ability to perform good works and attain eternal salvation.

**186.** Saint Cyprian should be interpreted in this way in his book *On the Lapsed*:

“We indeed believe that the merits of martyrs and the works of the righteous can have great influence with the Judge; but when the day of judgment comes, when, after the passing of this age and of the world, his people have stood before the tribunal of Christ . . .”

Venantius Fortunatus, book IV of *The Life of Saint Martin*:

“You too will be ordered to sit upon the right-hand seat.  
Then, I pray, conceal my frailty with your sacred veil,  
and may your lamp defend me, trembling, from the fire.  
For I know that Christ can yield any guilty person to you.”

[Note: [Col. 0710D] An imitator of Prudentius in this and other passages, as Barthius observed in book XLV, chapter 9, is Hericus of Auxerre, book VI of the *Life of Saint Germanus*:

“Therefore, holy father, then have pity on your poet,  
and when from afar you see me joined to the foul goats—  
the memorials of my sins promise this to me—  
remember to appeal to the king with kindly prayers.  
He will surely be moved, and, once moved, will say to his minister:  
‘Germanus prays; it is not right to reject one who prays.  
Transfer this goat as quickly as possible among the snowy lambs;  
let him go as a right-hand lamb, adorned with beautiful fleece.’”

Barthius, who by these passages confirms that it would lie in the power of the martyrs to remove from the number of the damned whomever they wished, if credence is to be given to writers who are otherwise not ill disposed toward our religion—he says that he read this in his beloved author Prudentius, at the end of the *Passions of Fructuosus and Romanus*—is nevertheless rather inconsistent with himself. For in book VIII, chapter 11, he notes that in the conclusion of the *Romanus* Prudentius, through excessive humility, withdrew himself too far from the true Mediator by joining himself as a goat to the goats on the left side of the Judge. If Barthius understands this to mean that it would lie in the power of the martyrs to remove from the number of the damned those whom they wished, so that those who are truly already damned might be freed from the punishment of damnation, he has understood neither the mind of Prudentius nor that of the others.]

**187.** Fabricius, driven by a heretical spirit, addresses Prudentius at the end of his commentary on *Romanus*:

“If this opinion is yours, most distinguished Prudentius, it is contrary to prophetic doctrine . . . and likewise contrary to apostolic doctrine.”

Clearly Fabricius thinks that the merits and prayers of the saints avail nothing with Christ.

Georgius Remus says in his notes: “The prayer for the left side of an excessively timid and superstitious author.” Nicholas Heinsius observes that Fabricius and the others had not sufficiently understood the author’s meaning. He says:

“This passage must be distinguished. He says that he wishes to be placed even among the flocks of goats, but on this condition: that he should be recognized from afar for what he will be, and that Romanus should pray for him, whom he firmly persuades himself Christ will hear.”

This interpretation, which Chamillard transcribed word for word, does not greatly please me. For Prudentius in no way wishes to be placed among the flocks of goats; he merely prays that, from the left side, which he believes is owed to him on account of his sins, he may be transferred to the right through Romanus’s prayers—or rather, he prays that he not be left on the left side with the goats when the sheep are separated from the goats.

Heinsius is right, however, that the following passage of Alcimus Avitus, book III *On the Supreme Judgment*, is not unlike this passage of Prudentius:

“Then, when the shepherd has separated the undefiled lambs,  
the unlike goats having been placed on the opposite side”

—and also this passage from *On the Praise of the Virgin* (perhaps elsewhere):

“Where, seated upon the heavenly throne,  
the arbiter of the world will divide the human race into parts,  
washing the lambs on the right,  
and scorning the left-hand ones as goats.”

And Tertullian, book IV *Against Marcion*:

“Those whom the Lord himself also said in the Gospel  
would be seen as goats apart from the sheep,  
standing on the left side,”

where “to be seen” means “to be distinguished.”

But Juvencus and Eugenius of Toledo support Prudentius more clearly. Juvencus, in the preface to his books *On the History of the Gospel*:

“Nor is there fear that the fires of the world will carry this work away with them;  
for perhaps this will rescue me from the fire,  
when Christ, the glory of the high-throned Father,  
will descend gleaming from a flame-vomiting cloud,  
the Judge.”

I transcribed the verses of Eugenius in which he expresses the same opinion in number 47.

[Note: [Col. 0711D] In the catalogue of the Laurentian Library, volume I, column 339, Bandini lists among the manuscripts an eighth-century Psalter, which ends with a certain prayer whose title is:

“Hymn which King Gildus sang for the soul of his father, who was in hell.”

“Whoever sings this every day throughout the whole year for the soul of his friend, even if he is in hell, will be rescued and led into the kingdom of God. But if he forgets on one day of the year, let him begin again from the beginning and complete the whole year in this manner: ‘To the Lord, when I was troubled,’ through ‘Praise the name of the Lord.’”

It begins:

“O most high God of peace, holy Father of heaven,  
almighty, eternal God.”

It ends:

“May he himself deign to grant this, who is to come to judge the living and the dead, and the world by fire.”

This prayer is foolish, superstitious, and contrary to true theology and Christian doctrine; it must in no way be attributed to the martyr Saint Hermenegild, as seems to be done in the catalogue index, since Hermenegild died before his father, having been killed by him.

Prayers of this exceedingly foolish kind derive their origin from words of certain Fathers badly understood, and are usually composed by the common people and by the most ignorant women.]

**188.** Others in subsequent ages maintained the same manner of speaking. In volume XXXIV of *Hispania sacra*, page 440, there is a charter of donation in which King Ordoño, shortly after the year 916, offers many things for divine worship and the support of ministers. He says:
