“For when, at the time of judgment, we shall appear standing before the Redeemer, may we, through the intercession of those who faithfully serve God and receive support from this, deserve to escape in soul and body from the *VULGARIS* and from the recesses of Avernus, and be rescued from those who shall receive the sorrowful rejection of the Judge; then, indeed, may we, safe on the right and clothed in the fleece of consolation, be able to be joined with the clean sheep.”

In another charter of Ordoño III, from the year 955, the same sentence occurs; but instead of *vulgaris* it reads *vulgalis*.

[Note: [Col. 0712C] This word derives from *vulga*, which among Nonius’s authorities signifies a capacity or hollow space with breadth. In Dante’s *Comedy* the *malebolge*, or *malebolgie*, are the receptacles and dwelling places of hell. The Spanish call the hot baths in the city of Ourense *burgas*. In the *Diccionario académico* of Spanish, the etymology is derived from the sound of boiling water. But the Latin origin of the word *vulga* must not be overlooked.]

From these sources another charter of Fruminius II, from the year 917, can be supplied, with almost the same sentence:

“And in the future . . . to merit eternal [life]”—namely, “to merit the right hand.”

Finally, to conclude Prudentius’s defense in this matter, his opinion is entirely similar to that which we sing in the prose or sequence of the Mass for the Dead:

“Grant me a place among the sheep,  
and separate me from the goats,  
placing me on the right-hand side.”

Bellarmine, *On Purgatory*, book II, chapter 5, discusses several matters acutely in order to explain the prayer after the Gospel in the Mass for the Dead:

“Deliver, Lord, the souls of all the faithful departed from the punishments of hell and from the deep pit; deliver them from the mouth of the lion, lest Tartarus swallow them, lest they fall into darkness,” and so forth.

But he offers nothing that cannot be transferred to Prudentius.

Lest these prolegomena become longer than is appropriate, the other objections made against Prudentius’s doctrine will be dissolved in the commentaries; we shall now pursue other matters.

## CHAPTER XX. The ignorance of certain people who thought that the interpretation of sacred Scripture employed by Prudentius in the preface to the *Psychomachia* was an enigma

**189.** I promised in chapter 1, number 6, that I would demonstrate that the obscurity charged against Prudentius sometimes arises from ignorance of antiquity, in which many people are involved, rather than from any fault in the author. I proposed as an example a passage from the preface to the *Psychomachia*.

In that preface Prudentius embraces the history from Genesis, chapter XIV, verse 14.

[Note: [Col. 0712D] “When Abraham heard that his brother Lot had been taken captive, he counted his trained household servants, three hundred and eighteen, and pursued them as far as Dan. And dividing his companions, he rushed upon them as far as Hoba, which is on the left of Damascus. And he brought back all the wealth, and his brother Lot with his possessions, together with the women and the people.”]

Then, embracing an allegorical interpretation, he adds in verse 56:

“We are rich in household servants in abundance,  
if we understand what the three hundred,  
with twice nine added, can accomplish  
through mystical symbolism.”

This passage has tormented interpreters extraordinarily. Antonius Nebrissensis says:

“Three hundred and eighteen. But what that number signifies—one ought to consult some Pythagorean who is occupied with such numerical calculations. But I see no other mystery signified by Abraham’s companions than those three hundred and eighteen bishops who were present at the Council of Nicaea, where many matters concerning the Christian religion were established, but especially concerning the faith for which Abraham is reckoned righteous. For there the Nicene Creed was composed.”

Giselinus is not satisfied.

[Note: [Col. 0713C] Antonius Nebrissensis thinks that the number should be applied to the 318 bishops summoned to the Council of Nicaea; but I do not see what the mention of them has to do with the allegory. For that reason I am awaiting some Oedipus or Pythagorean here.]

Sichardus, however, adopts an interpretation which he thought had been clearly transmitted by no one.

[Note: [Col. 0713C] “What the mystery means—this is what Prudentius calls it—of the three hundred and twice nine armed servants of Abraham has not, so far as I know, yet been explained by anyone. I suspect, however, that it signifies the Council of Nicaea, at which, by the authority of 318 bishops, certain boundaries of our faith were, so to speak, marked out, whereas previously most matters had been uncertain and had been twisted here and there according to the pleasure of heretics’ calumnies. Both this and other considerations, but above all certain traces in the very ancient manuscript which we used, led me to this opinion. Nevertheless, I would not object if someone referred it elsewhere, although I do not see what else could occur to anyone here.”]

**190.** I suspect that Sichardus had seen the glosses of Iso, in which not merely traces but the interpretation itself is clearly expressed. Thus Iso writes in the Bongarsian manuscript concerning verse 10 of the preface:

“Three hundred and eighteen household servants signify the faith established at the Council of Nicaea by 318 bishops. But the ten may pertain to the Decalogue, and the eight to the eight beatitudes. Whoever lacks all these things will never attain the aforesaid beatitudes.”

And concerning verse 57:

“IF THE THREE HUNDRED CAN: These three hundred signify a mystery, namely the cross. For Tau, which has the form of the holy cross, signifies three hundred; if you wish to know about the ten and the eight, by arithmetic you will count the lesser number within nine.”

This is from the Widmanian manuscript. But the Bongarsian manuscript reads:

“It signifies that in the temple of Constantine 318 bishops defended the Church of God against the Arian heresy.”

Chamillard follows the same interpretation concerning the 318 bishops:

“IF THE THREE HUNDRED CAN: These two verses explain nothing other than the Council of Nicaea, at which the faith was confirmed by the authority of 318 bishops. For there the Nicene Creed was composed.”

Weitzius and Drusius, however, refer these words to the letter T, which resembles a cross. Weitzius, indeed, concerning verse 57, “IF THE THREE HUNDRED CAN,” transcribed Barthius’s opinion.

[Note: [Col. 0713D] Barthius explains this exceedingly ingenious enigma in book I of the *Adversaria critica*, chapter 5, as follows:

“He says that *prosint* should be read instead of *possint*. The three hundred, moreover, signify nothing other than the Lord’s cross, enclosed in the letter—or in the Greek character by which teachers of the language supplied that number . . . It remains for us to show what is to be understood by twice nine. It is well known that the letter Θ is the deadly mark of the praetor, as Martial says, because the ill-omened word for death, *thanatos* (θάνατος), begins with it. It is now familiar even to children that the same character expresses the number nine in Greek. Therefore, by two thetas, or signs of nine, the poet alludes to two deaths, specifically the deaths of those who died with the Tau-bearing Lord . . . Knowledge and consideration of these robbers is of the greatest benefit,” and so forth.]

**191.** Since Weitzius gave Barthius’s passage in full, I do not know why he immediately says, concerning verse 58, “Let us understand by mystical symbolism”:

“This is more obscure than the leaves of the Sibyl and more recondite than the numbers of Pythagoras; scarcely anyone can bring it forth and play the part of Oedipus, except John Drusius,” book II of *Questions and Answers*, whose words are:

“The learned man who recently illustrated Prudentius with a commentary desires some Oedipus here. There is no need for an Oedipus: I, Davus, will solve the riddle, if there is one. It is easy to understand, provided we know that the letter Tau represents the shape of the cross.”

[Note: [Col. 0714C] For Drusius continues, explaining the first part of the riddle:

“The same letter in numbers denotes three hundred. Isidore, *On Etymologies*: ‘Among the mystical letters, Tau is third, displaying the figure of the Lord’s cross.’ Jerome, in his commentaries on Ezekiel 9:4: ‘In the ancient Hebrew letters, which the Samaritans still use today, the final letter Tau resembles a cross, which is painted on the foreheads of Christians and marked by the frequent inscription of the hand.’ What you wish will become clearer from the ordinary gloss, where, at Genesis XIV, in the place where it illustrates this history in the allegorical sense, we read:

‘Let each person wage war for his soul against spiritual wickedness with three hundred and eighteen household servants—that is, with the aid of the holy cross. For the letter Tau, which has the shape of a cross, signifies CCC.’”]

The remaining difficulty concerns the greater number:

“BY WHICH I AM ENTIRELY UNABLE TO EXTRICATE MYSELF.”

Unless the explanation is the one I suspect: because among the Hebrews the letter Tau is written with two consonants, namely T and V, the latter of which is worth six, the ancients may have thought that, just as Tau is repeated three times as one hundred, so Vau should be repeated three times as six. Three is also a mystical number. Thus there emerge three hundred and three times six household servants.

In any case, although I would not wish to affirm this latter point with certainty, I am as certain of the former—that Prudentius had the allegory mentioned above in mind when he wrote these verses—as I am of anything at all.

**192.** It is therefore clear that Drusius had not yet solved the riddle. Barthius himself, in favor of Drusius, testifies in book XXIX, chapter 15 of the *Adversaria* that he is undertaking to explain it:

“At the beginning of their works the highest authors are accustomed to fix something which, although it may seem to demand little at first sight, requires more careful attention. Thus Plato did not change without reason the beginning of his books *On the Republic* so many times, nor did Maro, the prince of poets, enclose two enormous Homeric volumes in a single verse of the divine *Aeneid*. It is not worth the effort to pile up examples. Who has examined Prudentius, the Christian poet par excellence, without finding difficulty in the exceedingly ingenious riddle which he deliberately inserted into the preface of the *Psychomachia*?”

Barthius then explains the riddle for the sake, or at least in honor, of John Drusius, a most learned man, who had pronounced it more obscure than Pythagorean and Sibylline numbers. He denies that it can be understood of the 318 Fathers of Nicaea, because the mystical figure indicates a type of some inanimate thing; then he adds the interpretation which Weitzius transcribed from another work. Barthius says that this passage, hitherto most obscure in an excellent poet inspired by the living Spirit of God, had baffled every intellect.

[Note: [Col. 0714D] Teolius’s interpretation is obscure to me, at least as it now stands. Almost all the Fathers, both Greek and Latin, sought a mystery in this number, 318 or the round number 300, and either think that the cross and the name Jesus are signified by it, or the 318 Fathers assembled at the Council of Nicaea against Arius. This much is clear: the Lord’s cross and the name, because Greek T has the shape of a cross and signifies 300, while L and N signify eighteen, express the name Jesus, Ἰησοῦς. This is exactly what he says. But it must be understood that the letter A—that is, L—represents 30 among the Greeks, and the letter N 50; therefore I do not understand how they signify 18 or express the name Jesus. There is reason to suspect that Teolius’s words have been corrupted by a copyist or printer, for he is pointing his finger toward the sources.]

[Col. 0715A] **193.** In the explanations of Barthius and Drusius, the first part concerning the three hundred, indicated by the figure of the cross, is expressed not only in the ordinary gloss on the passage from Genesis but also in the glosses of Iso on Prudentius.

[Note: [Col. 0715C] Barthius also cites, in the places mentioned, Tertullian, book III *Against Marcion*:

“For this is the Greek letter Tau, while our letter is T, the form of a cross.”

And in poem 3:

“For by this sign he laid low heaps of robbers,  
engaging the people of Christ without a large army;  
with three hundred horsemen—the number of the Greek letter T.”

There he is speaking of Gideon. He also adds Paulinus, Epistle 2, of whom I shall speak later.]

In explaining the second part, however, neither Barthius nor Drusius satisfied the others; Drusius did not even satisfy himself, while Barthius, who speaks more confidently, adopted another opinion in book XLIII, chapter 7. He says that we are guilty of a double death; therefore there are two Θs. The poet had in mind two books: one, an account of our sins, which many have traditionally said Satan possesses; the other, the book mentioned in Exodus 32.

Concerning military notation, Isidore says in book I of the *Etymologies*, chapter 33:

“In the little tablets containing the names of soldiers, the ancients had a particular mark by which it could be observed how many of the soldiers remained and how many had perished in battle. A T placed at the beginning of a line designated a survivor, while Θ was added to the name of each deceased man.”

“If, therefore,” Barthius adds, “we can distinguish true life from true death by a mystical figure—namely, through the cross of Christ—we shall be rich in household servants sufficiently and more than sufficiently.”

**194.** A very obscure riddle would indeed lie hidden in Prudentius’s verses, unless there were another explanation. I say that this is the most common allegorical interpretation, which still occurs in very many volumes of the Fathers: namely, that Abraham’s 318 household servants signify the Lord’s cross and the first two letters of the name Jesus, ι and η, because among the Greeks Tau, which is the figure of the cross, signifies three hundred, ι ten, and η eight; from these the total 318 is obtained.

As for the number three hundred, the holy Fathers often say that it signifies the Lord’s cross, including those who have no thought of the history of Abraham.

[Note: [Col. 0715D] Among others, Saint Augustine says in sermon 36 of the appendix:

“Gideon chose three hundred men for battle, to show that the world would be freed from the attack of grievous enemies not through the multitude of numbers but through the mystery of the cross. For three hundred, according to the Greek T, displays the likeness of the cross . . . And because three hundred, according to Greek reckoning, forms a cross, so Gideon at that time delivered the people of the Jews from the most savage nations through three hundred men, just as afterward Christ, through the mystery of the cross, liberated the whole human race from the power of the devil.”

Saint Ambrose, explaining in book VI, chapter 7 of his commentary on Luke the words of John, “It could have been sold for three hundred denarii,” says:

“The three hundred bronze coins reveal the emblem of the cross.”

Saint Gregory the Great, book XXX of the *Moralia*, chapter 17:

“The number thirty is contained in the letter Tau, which bears the appearance of the cross. If to it were added above the transverse line what projects in the cross, it would be not the appearance of a cross but the cross itself. Therefore, since this number three hundred is contained in the letter Tau, and through the letter Tau, as we have said, the appearance of the cross is displayed, it is not without reason that in these three hundred followers of Gideon those are signified to whom it was said: ‘If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me.’”

Isidore, *On Genesis*, book VII:

“Indeed, in these three hundred cubits of the ark the sign of the wood of the Passion may also be displayed. For the number of the letter T demonstrates the sign of the cross,” and so forth.]

Clement of Alexandria taught that the cross and the abbreviated form of the name Jesus, or its first two letters, are signified in Abraham’s 318 household servants; this had already been taught by others, in book VI of the *Stromata*, page 656:

“Just as in astronomy we have Abraham as an example, so also in arithmetic we have the same Abraham. For when he heard that Lot had been taken captive, he attacked the enemies after counting his own three hundred household servants, and defeated their very great number. They say, therefore, that the element which signifies three hundred is a type of the Lord’s sign with respect to its figure; while iota and eta signify the saving name. Thus Abraham’s household members and companions are signified as those who, with respect to salvation, have taken refuge in the sign and name of the Lord and have overcome those who were carrying them away captive, together with the many unbelieving nations that followed them.

Now the number three hundred is three in the hundreds. Ten, without any controversy, is complete in every direction. Eight, which is the first cube, is equality in all dimensions,” and so forth.

The Latin version which I use, Paris, 1647, should be amended to read “three hundred and **eighteen** household servants,” for the Greek has τιὴ.

[Note: [Col. 0716C] Clement of Alexandria frequently cites the Epistle of Barnabas, or of another person writing under the name of Barnabas. The same interpretation is found in that epistle, although it is less appropriately applied to the history of circumcision:

“Learn, therefore, children, fully about everything. Abraham, who first gave circumcision, looked forward in the spirit to the Son—more correctly, to Jesus, as the Latin version reads—and circumcised, having received the document of the three letters. For Scripture says that Abraham circumcised three hundred and eighteen men from his household. What, then, was the knowledge given to him in this matter? Learn: first, the eighteen, then the three hundred. The ten and the eight are expressed by ι (ten) and η (eight): you have the beginning of the name Jesus.” (I punctuate this period in this way; others punctuate it differently.) “But since the cross was to possess grace in the figure of the letter T, which designates the number CCC, he says, ‘and three hundred.’ Thus he displays Jesus in the two letters and the cross in the third. He knows this who placed the implanted gift of his teaching in us. No one has received from me a more genuine discourse; but I know that you are worthy.”

The notes of Hugh Menard, John Davies, John Baptist Cotelier, Edward Bernard, and the Oxford edition may be consulted at this passage.]

Saint Ambrose, book I *On Abraham*, chapter 3:

“Abraham counted three hundred and eighteen, so that you may know that not the quantity of the number but the merit of election is expressed . . . For the Greek letter T signifies three hundred, while ιη expresses eighteen. Abraham therefore conquered by the merit of faith, not with a numerous army.”

Some read: “The sum ιη expresses the name of faith”; others: “The sum expresses the name Jesus.”

And in the preface to book I *On the Faith*:

“For you know that victory is usually sought through the faith of the commander rather than through the strength of the soldiers. For Abraham too led three hundred and eighteen into battle and carried off trophies from countless enemies; and by the sign of the Lord’s cross and the name . . . he avenged his kinsman,” and so forth.

195. Eucherius, too, should be added, in his Commentary on Genesis, whom Saint Isidore of Seville praises in his book On Illustrious Men:

“But whereas he (Abraham), not by the multitude or strength of his legions, but only with the three hundred and eighteen who accompanied him, defeated hostile kings, it was already then represented in the mystery of the sacred cross—whose figure is expressed by the Greek letter tau (Τ), in the number three hundred—and in the name of Jesus, which is written with the Greek characters iota and eta (ιη), and which means ‘Savior,’ expressed in the number three hundred and eighteen: namely, that the passion of Christ would free us from the domination of the five bodily senses, which had previously overcome us by taking us captive through various vices.”

After “is expressed,” *imaginabatur* (“was prefigured”) must be supplied, so that it reads: “that we,” and so forth. Saint Isidore, in his Genesis, On Abraham’s Victory, chapter 11, repeats Eucherius’s passage with some variation in the later Madrid edition:

“Already then it was represented in the mystery of the cross (whose figure is expressed by the Greek letter tau in the number three hundred), that we,” and so forth.

From this Rosweyd restored *imaginabatur* (“was represented”) in Eucherius, in his note on Paulinus’s second letter. Moreover, in Eucherius one should read either “who [writes] iota and eta in Greek characters” or “who [writes] iota and theta in Greek characters.” Rosweyd writes: “who [writes it] by the Greek characters ι and η.”

Saint Maximus the Confessor, volume I of the Paris edition of the works edited by Father François Combefis, page 170, among the Questions on Sacred Scripture:

“Perhaps relying on this figure of the cross together with the name of him who for our sake was fastened upon it, the great patriarch Abraham, leading forth three hundred and eighteen men—that is, with the figure and name of Jesus—routed the hostile powers symbolized by the kings. For it is Scripture’s custom not infrequently to disclose its own aim even through the figures of letters, so that, purified, we may attain it.”

Faustus of Riez, in his book On the Holy Spirit:

“We call it a sacred number, because three hundred, in Greek notation or calculation, displays the sign of the cross, while eighteen displays the name of Jesus, which is to be adored.”

In his letter On Penance to Felix the pope and Patricius, he follows the same interpretation and applies it to the struggle against vices, imitating Prudentius:

“And therefore, just as Abraham, the father of faith, conquered those five kings through three hundred and eighteen, with a mystery concealed within the letter, so let us also fight against those chief leaders of the vices in the name of Jesus and under the sign of the cross—for this is what the two figures express.”

Thus it is read in the rare work *Writings of Certain Ancient Theologians of Gaul*, Paris, 1586, which is held by the distinguished Giovenazzi.

Hincmar of Reims, in his response to certain questions about why he had placed the mystical Nicene Synod in a particular writing, says much about this same interpretation. There he explains that in Greek and Latin books names are written by means of signs: sometimes by the first and last letters, with a line placed above and extending equally to the right from the left, as in DS, NR, and VR; sometimes by the first, middle, and last letters, with a line placed above and extending equally to the right from the left, as in XPS and DNS.

In a similar way Rupert of Deutz explains the matter in book V of his Commentary on Genesis, chapter 15. He notes that the name of Jesus, with an I and H written beneath a line above it, is expressed in the genitive case, so that the number XVIII is completed.

Others observe that the ancients were accustomed to designate proper names by their first two letters, as CN for Cneus and TI. for Tiberius.

196. Saint Paulinus had touched upon the same allegory near the end of his second letter to Severus:

“But just as he (Abraham), not by the multitude or strength of his legions, but already then in the mystery of the cross—whose figure is expressed by the Greek letter T in the number three hundred—defeated hostile kings, by the power of whose mystery the ark, woven from three hundred cubits lengthwise, overcame the flood,” and so forth.

Rosweyd rightly observes that Eucherius and Isidore transferred these words into their commentaries, and that Eucherius also explained the number eighteen, which Paulinus omits here—unless this portion was omitted by scribes because of the difficulty of the Greek number-signs ι and η, which constitute the abbreviation of the name Jesus. This seems to me highly probable. For in Eucherius, too, I detect a familiar scribal error; and in Ambrose there is great variation among the readings because of the difficulty of the Greek numerals ι and η.

Rosweyd himself says that the passage in Ambrose mentioned shortly before should instead be read as follows:

“For three hundred is signified by the Greek letter T, while eighteen expresses the name by means of the sum represented by ιη.”

Barthius judges that Paulinus had Prudentius in mind here. But there is no need for Paulinus to have had Prudentius in mind, or Prudentius Paulinus. The interpretation had already long been known from earlier sources.

[Note: For the rest, Barthius, in book XXIX of his *Adversaria*, chapter 15, finally judged Paschasius’s interpretation in the preface to his book On the Holy Spirit to be probable. There he simultaneously names the three hundred and eighteen Nicene Fathers and understands the number three hundred as the cross, and the eighteen as the first letters of the name of Jesus among the Greeks. Thus says Faustus of Riez, whom I cited above—or rather, as Barthius and others maintain, Paschasius, following Saint Ambrose, *On the Faith*, book I, chapter 18:

“Among these words also, the sacred number of three hundred and eighteen priests condemned the errors of Arius and Macedonius. For although through this number the weakness of a few withdrew, it did not dissolve the mystery of the universal number. And therefore we called it a sacred number: three hundred, by mere Greek calculation, displays the sign of the cross, while eighteen displays the name of Jesus, which is to be adored. In this number and mystery, in which holy Abraham also triumphed over innumerable nations, the piety of the elders confounded the enemy of faith under the single proclamation of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.”

These words are read in a less correct form among the works of Faustus.]

Although some interpret the cross of the Lord and the name of Jesus mystically in the number 318 of the Nicene Fathers, the allegorical explanation of Abraham’s 318 servants as referring to the Lord’s cross and to the first letters of the name of Jesus had already been applied to the cross itself before the Council of Nicaea; other Fathers followed it after the council. I have no doubt that many more examples could still be collected with greater diligence. But those I have cited are more than sufficient for anyone to understand, without a Sphinx or an Oedipus, what Prudentius intended to express when, after relating the story of Abraham’s victory, he added:

> Let us know ourselves to be richly endowed  
> With the wealth of servants,  
> If three hundred, with twice nine added,  
> Can accomplish anything through mystical figure.

## CHAPTER XXI  
## How much the designation of the Catholic faith and the Catholic Church owes to Prudentius and the other ancient Spaniards

197. Prudentius often used the word *catholicus* in his poems, even when the meter resisted it—not in the common sense in which *catholic* means universal, but in the more particular sense in which someone is called Catholic because he is not a heretic and is distinguished from one.

In the preface to all his works, verse 39:

> Let him fight against heresies; let him examine the Catholic faith.

In *Peristephanon*, hymn 11, verse 24:

> Enriched by the gift of the Catholic faith.

A little later he explains what the Catholic faith is, verse 30:

> Restore yourselves to the Catholic peoples.  
> Let one faith flourish, founded in the ancient temple,  
> Which Paul preserves, and which the chair of Peter—

[Note: In this description of the Catholic faith, one should observe the poet-theologian’s precise manner of expression. He names Paul and Peter, but attributes the chair only to Peter. He is everywhere consistent with himself in the poem on Laurence, verse 460:

> The one, called to the nations,  
> The other, possessing the first chair,  
> Unbars the doors of eternity  
> Entrusted to his keeping.

Likewise, in the preface to book I Against Symmachus, which concerns Saint Paul:

> Paul, the herald of God, who first  
> Subdued the savage hearts of the nations  
> With his sacred pen.

But concerning Saint Peter, in the preface to book II:

> Simon, whom they call Peter,  
> The supreme disciple of God.

The distinguished scholar Francesco Antonio Zaccaria treated this subject learnedly, as was his custom, in his dissertation *On the Primacy of Saint Peter*, Rome, 1776.]

In *Apotheosis*, verse 2:

> Lest dreadful doctrines, badly proclaimed,  
> Stain the Catholic tongue.

There, verse 291:

> If you doubt these mysteries of Christ’s birth,  
> Wretched man, you are not of the Catholic people.

In *Psychomachia*, verse 107:

> He consecrates it in the Catholic temple  
> At the altar of the divine spring.

In the first preface Against Symmachus, verse 59:

> The Catholic ship.

The word *catholicus* began to be used from the earliest centuries of the Church by Irenaeus, Clement of Alexandria, and others. But none expressed earlier or more clearly this particular meaning, by which heretics are excluded from the number of Catholics, than the Spanish writers.

198. In canon 16 of the Council of Elvira we read:

“If heretics refuse to transfer themselves to the Catholic Church, Catholic girls are not to be given to them.”

Ferdinand Mendoza, in book II of his *On the Confirmation of the Council of Elvira*, observed that subsequent councils, whether general or provincial, adopted from this canon the other provisions that barred access to such marriages.

Pacian, bishop of Barcelona, to whose son Dexter Saint Jerome dedicated his catalogue of ecclesiastical writers, died in extreme old age under the emperor Theodosius. Saint Jerome describes him as distinguished for chastity and eloquence, and renowned both in life and in speech. He wrote a letter against a certain Novatian concerning the name “Catholic,” a name over which the Novatians had raised a controversy.

“If it is a good name,” he says, “it does not admit hatred; if it is a bad one, it is free from envy.… But, you will say, under the apostles no one was called Catholic. Granted; let even that be conceded. When heresies arose after the apostles, did not the apostolic people demand a surname by which it might distinguish the unity of the uncorrupted people? … Suppose that I entered a populous city today and found Marcionites, Apollinarians, Cataphrygians, Novatians, and others of that kind, all calling themselves Christians: by what surname would I recognize the assembly of my people, unless it were called CATHOLIC?”

He adds many other excellent statements, but one must not omit the following, which is repeated in the books of many authors:

“Do not be agitated, brother. CHRISTIAN is my name, but CATHOLIC is my surname. The former names me; the latter displays me. By this I am approved; by that I am identified.”

Nothing could have been said more clearly.

199. The title of book XVI of the Theodosian Code is *On the Catholic Faith*. Our most illustrious emperor Theodosius issued to the people of Constantinople, in the year 380, the second law of title 1 in these words:

“We wish all the peoples whom the moderation of our clemency governs to live under that religion which the religion introduced to the Romans by the divine apostle Peter himself declares that he delivered, and which has remained so until now; and which it is clear that the pontiff Damasus follows, as does Peter, bishop of Alexandria, a man of apostolic holiness. In accordance with apostolic discipline and evangelical teaching, let us believe in one divinity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, under equal majesty and in the pious Trinity.

“Following this law, WE ORDER THAT THEY EMBRACE THE NAME OF CATHOLIC CHRISTIANS. But judging the others to be demented and insane, we order that they bear the infamy of heretical doctrine, that their assemblies not receive the name of churches, and that they be punished first by divine vengeance and afterwards by the retribution of our authority, which we shall assume by heavenly judgment.”

Justinian wanted this law to be the first law of his Code and of its first title, *On the Supreme Trinity and the Catholic Faith*. Although the names of the emperors Gratian, Valentinian, and Theodosius are prefixed, it is nevertheless clear from the Theodosian Code and from Gothofred’s commentary that the law was enacted by Theodosius the Great alone.

I observe in passing that the religious intolerance which certain innovators so call, and loudly proclaim to have arisen in the barbarous centuries, was established by solemn edicts of the earliest Christian emperors themselves. Anyone who now wishes to defend it may invoke authorities of no small weight—or, I do not know whether I should say, of the greatest weight—illustrious in war and piety: Constantine, Theodosius, and the other ancient emperors. Their laws against pagans, heretics, and Jews are preserved in ecclesiastical history and throughout book XVI of the Theodosian Code. Other laws may be added from the Justinian Code.

[Note: In the Justinian Code, law 2, title 1, from a constitution of Theodosius the Great:

“No place for the mysteries is to be allowed to heretics—otherwise, but less correctly, ‘no opportunity for the exercise of their stubborn insanity is to be opened.’”

Law 3 of the same title orders the writings of heretics, specifically those of Nestorius, to be burned:

“Those who endure having or reading such writings or books are to suffer the ultimate punishment.”

Book I, title 5, *On Heretics and Manichaeans*, law 2:

“Those are included under the name of heretics, and must submit to the sanctions enacted against them, who are discovered, even on slight evidence, to have departed from the judgment and path of the Catholic religion.”

Law 5 lists twenty-nine heretical sects individually. They are nowhere permitted to assemble or reside within Roman territory. The Manichaeans are also to be expelled from the cities and handed over to the ultimate punishment, since no place must be left to them in which even the elements themselves might be subjected to injury.]

I shall not pursue lesser matters. What I have brought forward sufficiently proves that the title of Catholic king and Catholic kingdom was rightly and deservedly attributed to the Spaniards, since they had distinguished the designation of the Catholic faith and Catholic Church with exceptional excellence from ancient times. I say nothing now of the fact that Reccared was acclaimed Catholic king by the Third Council of Toledo, or—what is more relevant here—that in Spain war was especially and perpetually declared against heresy.

Nor was it without reason that our Prudentius, who occasioned this discussion, is called by Christopher Brower, in his notes on book V of Venantius, page 141, “the most chaste and truly CATHOLIC POET OF CHRIST.”

## CHAPTER XXII  
## Two notable transpositions of certain verses of Prudentius reconsidered

200. It often happens that, through the carelessness of scribes, transpositions of words and verses enter manuscripts. Critics customarily notice them, not without some benefit, and restore each word to its proper place. I shall give two striking examples in Prudentius: one from Barthius’s correction, the other from the conjecture of the distinguished Vito Maria Giovenazzi.

Barthius, in book V, chapter 21 of his *Adversaria*, observes from a parchment manuscript sheet in the *Passion of Eulalia* that beginning with verse 56 there is an obvious transposition of two verses. “Since,” he says, “we owe their correction to this sheet, it deserved, even by that help alone, to be taken into account.”

In all the printed editions and manuscript codices that I myself have examined, and that other interpreters have seen, the verses read as follows:

> Thus the noble band of the fathers  
> Possessed the column-bearing ray,  
> Which, powerful to cleave a path  
> Through the dark night with shining torch,  
> Provided a way while chaos perished.  
>  
> In the same way the devout virgin,  
> Following the way through night, deserved the day;  
> Nor was she covered by darkness  
> When she fled the Canopic realms  
> And prepared a path above the stars.  
> She, swift with vigilant step,  
> First traverses many miles,  
> Before the eastern region opens  
> The expanse of heaven, and so forth.

The noteworthy restoration from Barthius’s sheet is:

> Provided a way while chaos perished,  
> Nor was she covered by darkness  
> When she fled the Canopic realms  
> And prepared a path above the stars.  
>  
> In the same way the devout virgin,  
> Following the way through night, deserved the day.  
> She, swift with vigilant step, and so forth.

Barthius says that the transposition of the two verses produced the difficulty, whereas the reference to Egypt suits the girl’s flight, since most Christians understand Egypt as darkness, as Gaudentius does in treatises 1 and 2.

201. No one should be surprised that transpositions of this sort occurred in all, or nearly all, copies. Scaliger, in the preface to his third edition of Manilius’s poems, notes innumerable errors and the transposition not merely of one but of many verses in Manilius. Barthius himself, in book VI, chapter 28, observed the fault of transposition in the work of Chalcidius, sometimes requiring correction, to pass over other examples.

In the present matter, the restoration is supported by the manuscript cited by Barthius. Even if someone considers Barthius’s reliability in citing parchment manuscripts uncertain—on which point see section 94—the restoration may nevertheless be defended by the prudent conjecture of a learned man.

I would not deny that the old reading can be retained with some advantage of meaning, and I too shall follow it because of the authority of the ancient codices. But certainly the verses restored from Barthius’s sheet, or by his judgment, permit an interpretation more fitting than that of Chamillard:

“Thus formerly God, by night, showed the Israelites, the illustrious descendants of the patriarchs, the way by means of a fiery column, whose exceptional brightness drove away the darkness. Therefore Eulalia, while traveling in the middle of the night so as to depart from this world and seek heaven, is clothed in a light as clear as day, and sees nothing darkened by shadows.”

The verse “And prepared a path above the stars” seems to refer to the journey that the Israelite people made by night.

[Note: Exodus 13:21–22:

“The Lord went before them to show them the way, by day in a column of cloud and by night in a column of fire, so that he might be their guide at both times. The column of cloud by day and the column of fire by night never failed to stand before the people.”]

202. The other passage is one which the distinguished Giovenazzi conjectures to be affected by transposition, in the *Passion of Vincent*, verses 37 and following:

> We shall confess the Father,  
> The author of light, and his Christ the Son,  
> Who alone is true God,  
> Datianus.

Giovenazzi thinks it should be read:

> We shall confess the Father,  
> The author of light, who alone is true God,  
> And his Christ the Son,  
> Datianus.

I would insert here his words, drawn from a manuscript commentary on Saint Hilary’s hymn *Let the Assembly of the Brethren Sing the Hymn*, had he not himself anticipated me.

It will nevertheless be useful to make two observations. First, these verses of Prudentius, as they are found in the printed books and manuscripts—and as we shall read them, so as not to depart from our rule—can indeed be produced as proof of the divinity of Jesus Christ. But Prudentius contains so many other exceptionally clear arguments for this Catholic truth that there would be no reason for regret if these verses, arranged differently, could no longer be cited in confirmation of it.

Moreover, Giovenazzi rightly argues that from this single verse of Prudentius, “and his Christ the Son,” the divinity of Christ is proved not only in meaning but also in wording: for the true Son of God must necessarily be God.

Second, it should not be surprising if some less suitable transposition has entered Prudentius’s poems despite the unanimous agreement of all the manuscript codices that we have so far been able to consult; perhaps its error will one day be exposed.

In *Apotheosis*, verse 248, we may see with what agreement of all editors and several manuscripts, before Heinsius, the following verse was transposed:

> I shall say how exceedingly ridiculous it is,

The glory was greater in a more trivial matter for Latinius. In the preface to book I Against Symmachus, verse 74, everyone had printed:

> Unaccustomed hope approaches, to creep in winding ways,  
> And to brandish the keen head of eloquence.

Latinius, having detected a transposition of letters, restored *seps* (“asp”), to the applause and subsequent acceptance of everyone.

Chamillard attributes this restoration to Sirmondus. Heinsius says that Latinus Latinius, Jacobus Sirmondus, and Laurentius Pignorius had long ago advised that it be corrected in this way. I certainly esteem both Sirmondus and Pignorius highly. But if part of the glory of this correction is to be shared with them, it would be necessary to show that they knew nothing of Latinius’s correction, since he was much earlier in age.

The report spread widely through the conversations of many people around the year 1581. Latinius had composed a riddle for Cardinal Guglielmo Sirleto. Since I believe it has not yet been published, I shall reproduce it here from the manuscript papers preserved by the distinguished bishop Reggio:

> If a sure hope, long sealed in the hands  
> Of the nobles’ tablets, were suddenly transformed  
> And should creep, while a wild asp sought  
> Broad hiding places in the bosom,  
> Who would not, if he considered it soundly,  
> Bewail the dangers of such a dreadful and sudden event?  
> And think it scarcely possible  
> That immediately all the powers  
> Of body and mind, and proud strength,  
> However great-hearted, should not collapse?  
>  
> I therefore, bolder than the rest,  
> Alone and fearless embrace the friendly monster,  
> And at the same time bid Hope flourish;  
> I compel it at once to restore  
> The alien rights furtively appropriated  
> To their rightful owners.

“I shall resolve, Sirleto, what this obscure riddle means.” Then follows a letter dated 12 October 1581, which has already been published. After it comes this epigram, which also explains the riddle:

> Perhaps beneath the dark shadow of a hedge (*sepis*)  
> Prudentius had woven the dreadful poisons  
> Of your genius, Symmachus,  
> You who trusted too greatly in the splendor  
> Of your proud name and the powers  
> Of your brilliant eloquence.  
>  
> Unaware of history, an antiquarian,  
> And at the same time a bold grammarian,  
> Places hope upon the throne of the asp.  
>  
> For nine centuries, an age poorly conscious of the theft,  
> Has retained another’s hope,  
> Although the asp itself is not a thief.  
>  
> No one dared defend the cause of the exile;  
> No one, when it cried out, was asked to bring aid.  
>  
> At last, my mind suffused with divine light,  
> Seeing the unjust exile of the unhappy one,  
> I order HOPE to go out  
> And restore its seat to the ASP,  
> Fearing no sharp brow of any man.

There follows Giulio Giacoboni’s interpretation, who explained the riddle as concerning hope, which had deceived the aged Latinius. Others interpreted it differently.

In 1594, Joseph Castalio’s *Various Readings* was published at Rome; it was later reprinted more than once. In chapter 12 this reading is drawn from Latinius and preferred to the other reading, *spes*, which also appeared in a manuscript of remarkable antiquity that Federico Rainaldus had purchased and placed in the Vatican Library.

One may also consult what is recorded in Latinius’s *Selected Library* from Ulysses Aldrovandi and others. Finally, Weitzius found *Seps insueta* (“an unusual asp”) in the Egmond manuscript.

## CHAPTER XXIII  
## The metrical faults charged against Prudentius. A manuscript work of Ludovicus Cavallus against the hymns of the Roman Breviary refuted

203. Since Prudentius is commonly said to have violated the rules of meter, whether through ignorance or negligence, I had collected a great many examples—not so much to defend him as to establish a method by which the poems of the Fathers of the Church might be restored, while observing the practice of the ancients rather than corrupting it, as many have evidently done.

From this immense forest I shall select only a few, chiefly those that seem more directly relevant to Prudentius, and explain them in a better order, so that matters closely connected and entangled with one another may be arranged. From these examples, however, it would not be difficult to sketch an outline of the poetic art of the ecclesiastical poets of the earliest period.

Chamillard, at the beginning of his edition, provided a catalogue of the syllables in which Prudentius erred. I shall reproduce it here, with others added from Cellarius.

[Note: The following syllables are wrongly shortened by Prudentius, according to Chamillard:

- First syllable of *aenigma*, *Apotheosis*, verse 331;
- third of *allophylus*, *Hamartigenia*, verse 500;
- second of *Arius*, *Psychomachia*, verse 794;
- first of *Beryllus*, *Psychomachia*, verse 855;
- third of *calceamentum*, *Peristephanon*, hymn 6, verse 74;
- third of *Chalcedon*, *Psychomachia*, verse 857;
- *cui*, a monosyllable, *Cathemerinon*, 3, verse 167;
- second of *daemon*, *Against Symmachus*, book II, verse 888;
- second of *dispar*, *Hamartigenia*, verse 26;
- second of *elutus*, *Peristephanon*, hymn 5, verse 362;
- third of *energima*, *Apotheosis*, verse 400;
- first of *enervatus*, *Against Symmachus*, book II, verse 143;
- second of *eremus*, *Psychomachia*, verse 371;
- first of *fio*, *Peristephanon*, hymn 13, verse 59;
- first of *ganeo*, *Hamartigenia*, verse 322;
- first of *haeresis*, *Psychomachia*, verse 710;
- second of *idolium*, *Apotheosis*, verse 186;
- second of *idololatra*, *Hamartigenia*, verse 404;
- second of *idolum*, *Psychomachia*, verse 379;
- second of *imbecillus*, *Apotheosis*, preface 2, verse 31;
- second of *impar*, *Symmachus*, book I, verse 168;
- third of *involucrum*, *Symmachus*, book I, preface, verse 54;
- fourth of *Lacedaemon*, *Symmachus*, book II, verse 247;
- second of *mathesis*, *Symmachus*, book II, verse 478;
- second of *phrenesis*, *Hamartigenia*, verse 125;
- second of *poesis*, *Symmachus*, book II, verse 52;
- first of *pugillaris*, *Peristephanon*, hymn 9, verse 15;
- third of *Pyreneus*, *Peristephanon*, hymn 6, verse 147;
- third of *quadrupes*, *Apotheosis*, verse 212;
- second of *romphaealis*, *Cathemerinon*, hymn 7, verse 93;
- first of *rubigo*, *Psychomachia*, verse 105;
- first of *socors*, *Cathemerinon*, hymn 1, verse 35;
- first of *sphaera*, *Apotheosis*, verse 210.

Syllables improperly lengthened:

- first of *cui*, a disyllabic word, *Hamartigenia*, verse 105;
- second of *Cyaneus*, *Psychomachia*, verse 859;
- second of *delibutus*, *Psychomachia*, verse 312;
- first of *Duita*, *Hamartigenia*, preface, verse 37;
- second of *hecatombe*, *Peristephanon*, hymn 10, verse 1051;
- second of *margarita*, *Psychomachia*, verse 874;
- second of *redimitus*, *Psychomachia*, verse 688;
- second of *Sardinia*, *Against Symmachus*, book II, verse 945;
- first of *smaragdinus*, *Psychomachia*, verse 863;
- second of *sophia*, *Against Symmachus*, book I, verse 34.

Prudentius uses the same quantities when he repeats these words, namely: *allophylus*, *Dittochaeon*, verse 71; *daemon*, *Peristephanon* 2, verse 505, and there 10, verse 1088; *dispar*, *Hamartigenia*, verse 775; *enervans*, *Cathemerinon* 8, verse 64; *eremus*, *Cathemerinon* 5, verse 89, and *Dittochaeon*, verse 45; *fiam*, and so forth, *Peristephanon* 6, verse 83; *Symmachus* I, verse 223; *Peristephanon* 10, verse 855; *ganeo*, *Psychomachia*, verse 343, and *Hamartigenia*, verse 322; *heresis*, *Cathemerinon*, preface, verse 39; *Hamartigenia*, verse 64; *Psychomachia*, verses 710 and 725; *Dittochaeon*, verse 72; *idolum*, throughout; *imbecillus*, *Cathemerinon* 4, verse 2; 11, verse 99; 12, verse 207; *Peristephanon* 10, verse 721; *Cathemerinon* 7, verse 90; *impar*, *Peristephanon* 10, verse 565; *Psychomachia*, verse 549; *involucrum*, *Cathemerinon* 5, verse 36; *Hamartigenia*, verse 868; *mathesis*, *Against Symmachus* II, verse 893; *socors* and *socordia*, *Peristephanon* 10, verse 810; *Apotheosis*, verse 126. I shall discuss *cui* later; *Cyaneus*, *Peristephanon* 12, verse 41; *Against Symmachus* I, verse 302; *margarita*, *Peristephanon* 10, verse 648; *sophia*, *Cathemerinon* 1, verse 34.

Cellarius adds the following:

- *Asclepiades*, with the second syllable long, *Peristephanon* 10, verses 42, 108, 392, 548, 687, and 921;
- *charisma*, with the first syllable long, *Apotheosis*, preface 1, verse 11; *Symmachus* II, verse 94; *Peristephanon* 13, verse 61;
- *idolium*, with the second *i* short, *Peristephanon* 11, verse 52; *Apotheosis*, verse 186; *Symmachus* I, verse 611; 2, verse 79;
- *Iesus*, with the first *i* elided, *Peristephanon*, verse 756; *Apotheosis*, verse 417; *Psychomachia*, verse 777; *Dittochaeon*, verse 142; *Cathemerinon*, verse 181; *Apotheosis*, verses 222, 502, and 770; *Dittochaeon*, verse 102; *Cathemerinon* 7, verse 178; 12, verse 173; *Apotheosis*, verses 935, 992, and 1058; *Peristephanon* 6, verse 74;
- *Hadrianus*, with the second *a* short, *Symmachus* I, verse 274, although he lengthened it in *Peristephanon* 12, verse 61;
- *homo*, with the first syllable long;
- *Marcion*, with the *i* long, *Hamartigenia*, preface, verse 36; verses 56, 124, 129, and 502;
- *Paraclitus*, with the *i* short, *Cathemerinon* 5, verse 160; *Peristephanon* 10, verse 430;
- *Magia*, with the *i* long, *Symmachus* I, verse 89;
- *utraque*, plural, with the *a* long, *Cathemerinon* 10, verse 5; *Peristephanon* 3, verse 80; *Apotheosis*, verse 320. In this verse Chamillard incorrectly says in his index that *utraque* is singular ablative.]

204. Cellarius further notes that Prudentius formed words ending in *-es* from the third declension for the sake of brevity, such as *famis* in the nominative, *luis*, and *pubis*. He also shortened second-conjugation verbs as though they belonged to the third, such as *extorque*, *percense*, and *collucis*.

More often in Prudentius than in other poets, a short syllable is lengthened at the end before the doubled consonant of the following word, as in *Cathemerinon* 7, verse 152, and often elsewhere.

Casaubon, in his commentary on Trebellius, page 214, asserts that Prudentius shortened the first *i* of *Spiritus*. But, I think, he meant Sedulius. For Sedulius, in order to sing aloud the glory of the holy and undivided Trinity, neglected the rule of grammatical arrangement:

> Great glory to the Father always, glory to you, O Son;  
> With the Holy Spirit, great glory to the Father.

This was observed by the Venerable Bede in his book On the Art of Meter.

If Casaubon truly had Prudentius in mind, perhaps he was referring to *Cathemerinon* hymn 10, verse 8:

> Spirit and flesh alike serve.

But it is certain from the commentary that this verse must be read differently. Prudentius uses this word very frequently and always lengthens the first *i*.

Ricciolius, in part 8 of his *Prosody*, appendix 5, says that Prudentius lengthened the *a* in *criminaque*, deceived by the accent. Ricciolius, however, was more deceived: Prudentius never lengthened the *a* in *crimina*. He did indeed lengthen the *a* in *ridendaque*, *Against Symmachus* I, verse 361:

> Mimic and laughable to his own people,

but this was because of the caesura, as I shall explain shortly, or rather because of the enclitic *-que*.

205. Barthius, in book XI of his *Adversaria*, chapter 20, observes that Agobard, in a Phalaecian poem after the death of Charles and Ledradus, placed the first syllable of *propitius* as long, following Prudentius in the *Passion of Agnes*.

Prudentius certainly has this in verse 130:

> I shall be purified by the propitiating mouth.

And in the *Passion of Eulalia*, verse 215:

> She cherishes him, having been appeased by song.

Agobard may nevertheless have followed a legitimate principle, since in words of this kind, where more than two short syllables occur together, one of them may be lengthened so that the word can enter a pentameter or hexameter. This occurs in *religio*, *reliquiae*, *Italia*, *Priamides*, *catholicus*, and *pupugerat*.

Moreover, why should the *o* in *propitius* not be long?

[Note: Becman, in *On the Origin of the Latin Language*, admits that *propitius* derives from *porro* or *prorsus pius*, according to the opinion of certain ancients, although he himself prefers to derive it from *prope* with the common ending *-itius*, as in *fictitius* and *commentitius*. If we accept the first opinion of the ancients, it is clear from the origin of the word that the *o* should be long. Before Prudentius, Juvencus also lengthened it, in book I at the beginning:

> For the one Father of all things, propitious, from on high.

Ricciolius first indicates this quantity and then gives another example from Seneca and Plautus; but the verses of Plautus are ambiguous.]

Ludovicus Cavallus, in his observations on the new hymns, which survive in manuscript in the library of the Roman College, objected to the revisers under Urban VIII that they had shortened the *y* in *azyma* together with Prudentius, observation 39; likewise that they had made the *a* in *Judaicus* long together with Prudentius, observation 40; that they had shortened the *i* in *sempiternus*, following the same Prudentius, observation 41; and that they had pronounced *Paraclitus* with a short *i* on Prudentius’s authority, observation 42.

[Note: Here I cannot refrain from transcribing the words of observation 42:

“Although the holy Fathers and ancient hymn-writers placed this name at the end of an iambic dimeter in their hymns, it does not follow that they shortened it. Rather, they preferred to place a spondee and disregard the law of meter than to shorten and corrupt this distinguished epithet of the Holy Spirit, which is naturally long.”

I wonder why he excluded Prudentius from the number of the other Fathers and ancient hymn-writers; why he did not defend him by the same argument with which he defended the others; and finally, why he opposed the authority of recent writers alone to Prudentius and the other ancients.]

206. I remember citing this work of Cavallus, praised by others, in my dissertation *On Ecclesiastical Hymns*, sections 159 and 160, and again in *Hymns of the Spaniards*, page 267. I had thought that the learned man’s intention was different, and that he had other arguments with which to attack the Urbanian correction.

Later I came upon the manuscript book and found only a few matters that seemed worthy of an answer. But what was omitted in its proper place I shall not hesitate to say here, if this should nevertheless be judged an unsuitable place in which to defend both the corrected hymns of the Roman Breviary and our Prudentius.

In the hymn for Saturday Vespers during the octave of Easter, *Ad regias Agni dapes*, he criticizes the phrase *Sinceritatis azyma* (“the unleavened bread of sincerity”), in which the *y* of *azyma* is shortened, although Prudentius shortened it in *Apotheosis*, verse 353:

> To revel in choirs, to be the unleavened bread of fine flour.

Ricciolius, in the second index of disputed syllables, lists this very word. He admits that Nicander lengthens it in the *Alexipharmaca*, but adds that in pronunciation we may follow, according to established custom, the Greek accent, which falls on the antepenultimate syllable.

What if that custom had already become established by at least the fourth century of the Church? Paulinus writes in his poem to Citherius On the Shipwreck of Martinianus:

> In the unleavened bread of truth;

and in *Natale* 8:

> Therefore, mindful even now of their flight, they take unleavened bread.

Casimir Sarbiewski, S.J., who alone corrected that hymn, therefore rightly judged that the verse *Sinceritatis azyma* should not be changed.

I had not previously known that Sarbiewski, the outstanding lyric poet, was among those who worked on the correction of the hymns at the command of Urban VIII. I now affirm it with certainty, having been informed by the eminent Cardinal Giovanni Carlo Boschi. Being exceptionally well versed in many matters, and especially in ecclesiastical affairs, he most courteously brought this to my attention and showed me a splendid Paris edition of Sarbiewski’s works, whose preface contains this account of the Urbanian correction.

207. A similar answer is given for the word *Paraclitus*, on the basis of usage and the Greek accent. Although Cavallus admits that the Fathers placed *Paraclitus* at the end of an iambic line—as in St. Hilary’s “When the Paraclete Spirit shone upon the disciples”—he foolishly argues that they thereby used a spondee in place of an iamb. They were more likely to violate the meter in other positions than at the end of an iambic line, where they always used an iamb.

[Note: In the hymn on the Holy Spirit which I transcribed in no. 73, and which I conjecture to be by Paulinus of Nola, *Paraclitus* is pronounced with a short *i*. Sidonius likewise pronounced *Heraclitus* with a short *i*: “Whatever Pythagoras, Democritus, and Heraclitus . . .” Hermolaus attacks him for this, but Ptolemy of Hispaniola defends him in the *Corollary on the Licences of Poets*, vol. IV of the works of Baptista Mantuanus, his brother, p. 167.]

The correctors likewise retained what Prudentius had written in *Cathemerinon* 12, line 42: “And king of the Jewish people” (*Populique rex Judaici*), in the Vespers of the Transfiguration. Cavallus, by contrast, adduces nothing except Juvenal’s doubtful example, *Satire* 14, line 101: “They learn, preserve, and fear the Jewish law” (*Judaicum addiscunt, ac servant, et metuunt jus*).

Prudentius used the word similarly in *Apotheosis*, line 552: “There are those who regard a doctrine akin to Jewish madness” (*Sunt qui Judaico cognatum dogma furori*), and in line 321: “If these things, so understood, had watered the Jewish [people]” (*Haec si Judaicos sic intellecta rigassent*). But in all these lines there is room for a spondee through synaeresis in *Judai*; in the first line cited an iamb is required in the final position: “And king of the Jewish people” (*Populique rex Judaici*). Likewise, a dactyl is required in Alcimus Avitus’s line on the origin of the world: “When the Jewish people hardened the name” (*Quando induratum plebes Judaica nomen*).

To establish that the *i* in *sempiternus* is long, the authority of Joseph Scaliger alone is entirely insufficient. It is not certain that the word is derived from *semper* and *aeternus*; and even if that were certain, derived words do not always follow the rule of their primitives—especially since, just as *ae* changes into *i*, so it may also be converted into a short *i*. Paulinus likewise shortened the *i* near the end of his poem to Cytherius on the shipwreck of Martinianus: “That the glory of eternal life may shine” (*Ut sempiternae clara vitae gloria*). Huetius, in his *Origeniana*, defends the same quantity against Scaliger’s opinion.

These points are shared by Prudentius and the Urbanian correctors. I omit the rest, since they are either less important, do not concern us, or, if they do concern us, are not relevant to this time or this place.

## CHAPTER XXIV  
### Rules observed in meter by Prudentius and other ancient Christian poets

180. 208. To continue the defense of Prudentius, and to reduce the whole defense to definite headings, I shall set out certain rules by which the quantities of syllables used by him may be vindicated.

[Note: From the three lists of syllables which Prudentius is said to have lengthened or shortened more freely than usual—lists compiled by Chamillard, Cellarius, and Teolius—I shall select certain words in which these authors seem to judge contrary to the common and widely accepted rules of poetic art.

Chamillard and Teolius note that Prudentius lengthens the first syllable of *Duitas* in the preface to the *Hamartigenia*, line 37: “He teaches that the *Duitae* differ from the spirit” (*Docet, Duitas discrepare a spiritu*). You see that this is a senarius, in which the first syllable of *Duitas* must necessarily be short.

Cellarius observes that Prudentius lengthens the second syllable of *magia* in book I of the *Symmachus*, line 89: “And that most learned man of Thessaly in magic” (*Necnon Thessaliae doctissimus ille magiae*). I do not see why it ought to be shortened, since the Greek is *μαγεία* (*mageia*), and the writers on prosody commonly assign it no other quantity.

In his own list, Cellarius also conjectures that Prudentius lengthened the first syllable of *homo*, from hymn 5 of the *Peristephanon*, line 157. He reads: “There is another inner man” (*Est alter homo intrinsecus*). But since Aldus alone printed the line in this form, while all other printed editions and manuscripts have “There is another; there is an inner one” (*Est alter, est intrinsecus*), whereas Fabricius has “Another man is within” (*Homo alter est intrinsecus*), Cellarius foolishly preferred that reading without offering any reason. Besides, why should a tribrach not be admitted in the second position of an iambic dimeter? Thus Horace has in *Epode* 2: “To see them hurrying home” (*Videre properantes domum*). In Prudentius’s line, “There is another inner man,” a hiatus ought to be admitted; it is not unusual either for Prudentius or for other poets.

Teolius alone adds from his own store *excit-us*, with the second syllable short, from *Peristephanon* 3, line 96: “Roused by such things into madness” (*Talibus excitus in furias*), and *noverimus*, with the third syllable long, from the preface to the *Psychomachia*, line 58: “Let us recognize the mystical figure” (*Possint, figura noverimus mystica*).

But the grammarians teach that *excit-us* may come either from *excio*, in which case the second syllable is long, or from *excieo*, in which case it is short; hence *excito, excitas*. The same applies to *percitus* and *concitus*.

As for *noverimus*, the following little verses from the grammatical art of Juan Luis de la Cerda, published under the name of Nebrissensis, still remain in my memory:

> The *ri* of the subjunctive may vary in poetry;  
> Let the learned usage of the country’s orator not be despised.

Indeed, most Spaniards lengthen the *ri* of the subjunctive in prose. Some ancient grammarians agree that the penultimate syllable of the subjunctive in *-rimus* and *-ritis* is long; I have read that Vossius and Emmanuel Alvarez also incline somewhere to this view. They think that, by metrical necessity, the penultimate syllable of the subjunctive in *-rimus* and *-ritis* is shortened. This defense is sufficient to vindicate Prudentius; examples are not necessary to confirm the rules.]

### First rule

Certain words used in the Roman Church from the very beginnings of our religion, translated either from Greek or from Hebrew, have acquired a special interval of shortness or length. Learned men rightly pronounced them with that quantity, attending not to their origin but to usage: they allowed the people their customary practice while reserving knowledge for themselves.

Following Vossius, book IV, part 2 of the *Institutiones oratoriae*, chapter 1, section 3, Ludewig says of Prudentius:

> In any case, it is absurd to wish to blame words which were discovered in the more divine assembly of Christians, and which our poet received and used.

He likewise observes that Christian poets shortened on the antepenultimate syllable the words *ecclesia*, *mysterium*, *psalterium*, and other words accepted in the Roman Church—words which no one could alter without danger of false doctrine and which had therefore also become common among the people.

Yet in these examples the usage does not seem to have been uniform. Prudentius lengthens the antepenultimate syllable in *ecclesia* and *mysterium*, while St. Paulinus often likewise made that syllable long.

By this rule the following forms in Prudentius may be defended: *Allophylus, Arrius, eremus, heresis, idolum, daemon, Iesus* with the *i* or *e* elided, *Paraclitus, Azymon, Iudaicus*, and other similar words. Nothing prevents the same words from being defended by different reasons and rules, as will be clear from the rules that follow.

### Second rule

In words derived from Greek whose accent conflicts with their quantity, the ancient Christian poets disregarded the quantity and followed the accent on the antepenultimate syllable, because that was how they then pronounced the words.

That there was once a different manner of pronunciation, and that learned men held various opinions about it, we learn from Quintilian, book I, chapter 5:

> Thus *Atreus*, which in our lifetime the most learned old men were accustomed to pronounce with the acute on the first syllable, so that necessarily the second was grave.

Indeed, Plautus not only makes a dactyl of *Phoedromus*, whose *o* is an omega, but also shortens the penultimate syllable of *Philippus*, because in both cases the words are written and pronounced in Greek with the accent on the antepenultimate syllable.

Thus, by usage, we pronounce the penultimate syllable of *antiphona* as short, although its *o* is long. In Italian we say *Otranto* and *Taranto*, and in Spanish *Fromesta*, placing the accent on the antepenultimate syllable.

By this rule several syllables in Prudentius are defended: *eremus, phrenesis, idolum, poesis,* and *mathesis*, with the second syllable shortened. Conversely, he lengthened the *i* in *sophia*, because the Greek accent falls there; for the same reason, and because of usage, many now pronounce the second syllable of *Andreas, Matthias,* and *idea* as long.

209. I establish a third rule. Many things can be defended by the authority of Prudentius and his contemporaries, especially when no examples or precepts of earlier writers stand against them.

Prudentius often shortened the *e* in *imbecillus*. Why is he criticized by Vossius, book II of the *Grammar*, chapter 17, Chamillard, and others? *Imbecillus* is formed from *baculus* or *bacillus*, as though it meant “without a staff.” They say that Horace and Lucretius lengthened it in hexameters. But in hexameters it had to be lengthened by metrical necessity. Accordingly, Becmannus, in *On the Origin of the Latin Language*, under *baculus*, rather accuses Horace of lengthening it while disregarding its origin—unless one excuses him by a figure such as occurs in *reliquiae* and in the example of Prudentius and J. C. Scaliger, who shortened it. He himself, however, lengthens it.

Prudentius shortened the *u* in *involucris*. Why is he criticized? They say that the word comes from *involutum*, and that Prudentius was deceived, as though he had thought it came from *volucris*. But what if it is derived from *involvo*, as some suspect, and *involucrum* is formed as though it were *involvucrum*, with the consonantal *v* worn away?

[Note: Ricciolius defends Prudentius in *Controversial Syllables* as follows:

> Those who think that the word is formed from *involutum* blame Prudentius for shortening its penultimate syllable. But if it can readily be formed from *involvo*, as *molocrum* from *molo* and *pollubrum* from *polluo*, it is not necessary to derive it from *involutum*. Nor would I judge Prudentius so foolishly as to think that he was deceived by the adjective *involucris*, meaning “slow.” Rather, I would strengthen his opinion from this very fact, if I suspect that *involucrem* was said because it makes the one whom it has enveloped *involucrem*. But let this be mere conjecture.]

But that *involucrum* was formed from *involvo* or *involvendo* is confirmed by Iso in his glosses on line 36 of hymn 5 of the *Cathemerinon*: “Lest he profane the holy place with coverings” (*Ne sanctum involucris pollueret locum*). He explains *calceamentis* as deriving “from rolling” (*a volvendo*). I do not approve this etymology, but the ancient usage is certain: they also shortened *simulacrum* and *lavacrum*, as Fabricius observes from Prosper of Aquitaine and other verses by authors of uncertain identity in the *Index of Christian Poets*.

The learned Teolius testifies that in St. Prosper’s poem *Against the Ungrateful* the word *involucris* occurs with its penultimate syllable shortened; the passage did not come to hand when I searched for it. In old manuscripts I find it written *involucla*, as though derived from *involuculum*. I find no notice elsewhere that Prudentius shortened the first *u* in *lugubri*, line 79 of hymn 9: “The sun retreats, foul with mournful rust” (*Sol refugit, et lugubri sordidus ferrugine*). Against this there are examples from the best poets, and in *lugeo* the *u* is long.

Nevertheless, since the quantity of certain syllables has varied, and since derived words often depart from the quantity of their origins, Prudentius should not immediately be accused of error. His example may defend the possibility that, at least in the period when he wrote, the first *u* in *lugubre* could be shortened. St. Damasus likewise shortened it in his verses on St. Agnes:

> Tradition tells that the holy parents once wept  
> For Agnes, when the trumpet had sounded mournful songs.

[Note: The old grammarians’ rules also state that the *u* in *palus* is long. Yet since we know that Horace made it short in the *Art of Poetry*—

> The work of a king, or a sterile marsh long unused,  
> And suitable for oars—

the authorities on prosody teach that it is common. Suppose that Horace’s line had perished: would Prudentius or his contemporaries be condemned if they used that syllable as short, even though they had themselves seen Horace’s line? How many poems by ancient poets Prudentius read which time has denied to us!]

The following examples in Prudentius can more or less be referred to this rule: *propola* with its first syllable lengthened—this word is absent from the lists of Chamillard and Cellarius—along with *berillus, calceamentum, cui, pugillaris, frustra* with a short *a*, *dispar, ganeo, impar, Pyreneus, delibutus, smaragdinus, charisma,* and *redimitus*. In *redimitus*, although Prudentius shortened the first *i* several times, he lengthened it only once; it is a fairly plausible conjecture that *redimitus* entered the manuscripts in place of *coronatus*.

In *berillus* Venantius Fortunatus also shortened the *e*, book III of the *Life of St. Martin*:

> This mantle, with chrysoprase mingled with beryls,  
> [*Quae palla ex humeris mixto Chrysoprase berillis*]

This is how I read it. Others print incorrectly, “with mixed chrysoprase” (*mixto Chrysopraso*), or “with chrysoprase-beryls” (*Chruso prasoberillis*).

### 210. Fourth rule

There was great freedom among ancient poets in proper names, either because some believed that their syllables were common or because they followed the example of others; and there was much greater freedom in names they received from foreign and barbarian peoples.

To this class belong *Allophylus, Lacaedemon, Pyreneus, Cyaneus, Sardinia, Asclepiades, Hadrianus, Arrius, Marcion, Marcionita, Iesus*, and other Hebrew names, although several of these can be defended by better arguments—for example, *Hadrianus, Marcionita,* and *Iesus* through synaeresis.

I know that some poets preface their use of proper names with an apology when they pronounce them against what the customary interval of their syllables seems to require.

[Note: Ovid does this in book IV of *Letters from Pontus*, elegy 12. He denies that *Tuticanus* can enter a verse, yet playfully introduces it twice:

> And shame on me if, at the point where a syllable delays you,  
> I should address you more closely and call you Tuticanus.  
> You cannot enter the verse in the manner of Tuticanus,  
> unless the first syllable, long by nature, becomes short;  
> or unless the second syllable, which now comes out too short,  
> is drawn out and made long by a prolonged delay.  
> If I should dare to corrupt the name by such faults,  
> I would be mocked, and rightly thought to have a black heart.

Martial does the same with the name *Earinus*:

> I wished to utter a noble, soft, delicate name  
> in verse that was not rough.  
> But you, rebellious syllable, resist.  
> Yet poets say *ἐάρινον* (*earinon*);  
> they are Greeks, to whom nothing is forbidden,  
> and whom it suits to sound out *ἄρες, ἄρες* (*ares, ares*).  
> We are not permitted to be so eloquent,  
> for we cultivate stricter Muses.

Barthius, book VIII, chapter 18, observes poetic frivolity in Martial, who in book I, epigram 104 (in my numbering, 105), made *cui* out of two short syllables and placed the same word as a monosyllable, although elsewhere, when criticizing the Greek *ἄρες ἄρες*, he claims that he and his Latin companions cultivate stricter Muses.

But the two cases are very different. It is one thing to make synaeresis from two vowels, or to dissolve an ordinary or extraordinary diphthong; it is another thing to shorten or lengthen the very same syllable. Martial could be refuted by another example: for Latins commonly pronounce the name of Mars, *Gradivus*, with the first syllable either short or long, as with many other proper names. Thus the following line would proceed correctly:

> Romans may say *Gradivum* or *Gradivum.]

211. I have no doubt that poets often played with the difficulty of pronouncing a proper name, as Horace does in *Satire* 5:

> We shall remain in a little town which cannot be spoken in verse,

although, had he wished, he could have introduced the name either by poetic licence or by metrical necessity.

Ausonius begins Epistle 20 to Paulinus as follows:

> Ausonius to Paulinus: the meter persuaded me  
> that you should come first and precede my name.

Yet the meter could have been maintained, even if Paulinus came first, if the line had been formed in another way.

[Note: Some infer from this that it was then customary to place after the name of the recipient the name of the person to whom the letter was sent. But in Paulinus’s own letters I often see the opposite: “Paulinus to his brother Severus” (*SEVERO FRATRI PAULINUS*).]

Our own Prudentius likewise said that the meter resisted including the name *Saturnini* in a Sapphic poem, line 161 of hymn 4 of the *Peristephanon*:

> Four men remain thereafter,  
> Their name refusing to be raised by the meter,  
> Whom ancient times remember as having been called  
> Saturnines.

[Note: Iso thought that the names of the Saturnines were being deliberately suppressed because they were barbarian names and therefore could not be placed in the meter. Nebrissensis thought the same: “The meter refusing,” because certain syllables of those names conflicted with the rules of the Sapphic poem. Ambrosius Morales followed Nebrissensis, but Riscus properly refuted them. Prudentius, he says, declares that the very name *Saturnini* cannot be included in the meter.]

I understand Prudentius to have said this because of some difficulty, not because the Sapphic line could not be composed in this way:

> Thus four Saturnines go forth together, secure,

or in some similar form.

Sidonius imitated Prudentius in book IX, letter 16:

> After Saturninus, I wish the lyres to sing . . .  
> Those men whom now, one by one, pious speech  
> Cannot contain within verse,  
> Yet whom the strings cannot sound—  
> The hearts will sound.

Sirmondus gives many similar examples, p. 103, in his notes on Sidonius.

In Sedulius, Arator, Venantius Fortunatus, and Prudentius I find *Arrius* written in the Latin manner, with the second syllable shortened. Why should I condemn this? Why should I not rather acknowledge a common pronunciation of the word? Christian poets pronounced proper names with common syllables more freely than the ancients, especially those who wrote in or after the Iron Age.

Fortunatus, book VIII, poem 4:

> Among these companions, united Caesaria shines.

After quoting the line, Barthius says in book LXVI of the *Adversaria*, chapter 3:

> One should not demand from this author’s poetry exact care with proper names.

I shall therefore conclude that even the best poets used a certain licence in varying the syllables of proper names, but with moderation and restraint where Latin and Greek names are concerned.

As for those who investigate with excessive care the interval of shortness or length with which the Hebrews pronounced their words, or who tell us, on the basis of the Masoretic discipline, how those words must now be pronounced, they seem to me to be wasting labor and oil—not to say, Judaizing.

If they finally persuade me that the opinion of Rabbi Moses is to be preferred to that of Rabbi Solomon; that some word is written with *chateph patach*, namely with an extremely short *a*, or with *patach*, which is a short *a*, or with *kamatz*, namely with a long *a*; and that a more Hebrew rather than Arabic or Syriac origin should be considered—when, I say, they have established all this, then, with their permission, I shall answer that I prefer to follow the judgment of Tertullian, Juvencus, Prudentius, Paulinus, and the other ancient Fathers.

They, who were not ignorant of the usage of their own age and language, either knew and disregarded the pronunciation of the Hebrews, or did not even take the trouble to learn it. I would rather imitate their negligence than the obscure diligence of those others.

### 212. Fifth rule

Prudentius and the other ancient ecclesiastical poets should not be accused of error because they sometimes use poetic licence and the figures of synaeresis, crasis, and other devices of this kind.

Since this rule is established, the following words must be removed from the catalogue of Prudentius’s metrical errors: *cui*, treated as a short monosyllable; *ganeo*, whose *a* may be long through synaeresis in the final two syllables; *delibutus*, where the *i* becomes long through metrical necessity—as Ricciolius also concedes in *General Rules of Prosody*, part 2, rule 9; *margarita*; *Iesus* with the *e* elided; *Hadrianus*; and *Marcionita*, with *ia* and *io* joined through synaeresis, since the *i* in *Marcion* is long.

The learned Giovenazzi mentions a book by Christophorus Wasius, *The Senarius, or On the Rules and Licences of Ancient Poets*, Oxford, from the Sheldon Theatre, 1687. It is rare in our regions.
