In it the author discusses, somewhat obscurely but learnedly, the figures of poets, hiatus, ectasis, diaeresis, and other subjects, and adduces much that applies to Prudentius, except that Prudentius did not use as much licence as the ancient poets, especially comic poets, claimed for themselves.

[Note: Hispaniolus, in his book *On the Licences of Ancient Poets*, says of synaeresis:

> The Greeks also use this licence, and among them it is called *synecphonesis* . . . They turn either two long syllables into one long syllable, or a short and a long syllable into one long syllable; or two short syllables into one short syllable, or two short syllables into one long syllable.

Thus two short syllables may be turned into one short syllable in *cui*, and a short and a long syllable into one long syllable in *Iesus*.

In Lucretius, book VI, p. 218, Gifanius reads: “Should it rather be the gate of Orcus in these regions?” (*Janua ne potius his orci regionibus esse*), so that it is a disyllable with a short final syllable. Similar examples occur everywhere among the comic poets: *sua, tua, mea*, as though they were *sa, ta, ma*. Add *bobus* and *subus*, from *bovibus* and *suibus*.

I find no example in which *cui* is a short monosyllable, but figures of this kind are rare. Moreover, *cui* often occurs in places where it could be either short or long, without our being able to determine the exact interval used by the author.

In St. Paulinus’s poem to Cytherius I would gladly read, “To whom a hundred cells are named” (*Centum cui Cellas nomen est*), so that the iambic line would receive an iamb in its second position, with *cui* as a short monosyllable. The text now reads, “To whom Centumcellas is named” (*Cui Centumcellas nomen est*), formerly, “To whom Centumcellis is named” (*Cui Centumcellis nomen est*).

Fronto Ducaeus corrected an error introduced by printers who did not understand the usage of that age: city names that were indeclinable were sometimes pronounced in the fourth case and sometimes in the sixth—*Colonia Veios*, “Colonia [called] Veii”; *Fundis oppidum*, “the town Fundi.”

But I would venture to decide nothing, since I know that Paulinus sometimes admitted a spondee in the second position of an iambic dimeter. Julius Caesar Scaliger notes that Ausonius did this twice in book VI of the *Poetics*, though he could have noted that Ausonius did it much more often.

That in *Iesus* synaeresis is made from one short and one long syllable is no more reprehensible than Lucretius’s making *eicit* from *ejicit*, or his making a spondee from the last three syllables of *oriundi in semine*, or Virgil’s making *reice* from *rejice*.

In the synaeresis of *Iesus*, the pronunciation of the ancients seems to have expressed the *i* more than the *e*: even today, among some eastern peoples, *Isa* is pronounced instead of *Iesus*.

*Ysus* was once sung instead of *Iesus* in a certain hymn which I believe has not yet been published. The hymn is found in a parchment codex now belonging to the Church of Velletri, formerly to Besançon, written around the year 1030, as is clearly established by the preceding catalogue of the bishops of the Church of Besançon.

For permission to use it I am indebted to the learned prelate Stefano Borgia, who is exceptionally well versed in such sacred antiquities and who very courteously allowed me to consult the codex. I shall give the entire hymn:

**Tuesday after Easter**

> Now let the blessed choir of the Lord sing the names of the Most High:  
> Messiah, Soter, Emmanuel, Sabaoth, Adonai.  
> He is the Only-Begotten, the Way, the Life, the Hand, consubstantial;  
> The Beginning, the Firstborn, Wisdom, and Power.  
> He is called and is Alpha, the Beginning and the End, and is Omega (*Ο*).  
> The Source and Origin of Goodness, the Paraclete and Mediator.  
> The Lamb, sheep, calf, serpent, ram, lion, and worm.  
> The Mouth, Word, Splendor, Sun, Glory, Light, and Image.  
> Bread, flower, vine, mountain, gate, rock, and stone.  
> Angel and bridegroom, shepherd and prophet, priest.  
> Immortal Lord God, ruler of all, Jesus (*Ysus*).  
> May he save us; to him be glory throughout all ages.

In the most ancient manuscripts Prudentius has *IHV* and *IHM* for *Iesu* and *Iesum*. We saw above, no. 193, that Christians regarded the first two letters of the name *Iesus*, *ι* and *η*, as the whole or abbreviated form of the name Jesus.

In inscriptions and other ancient monuments this august name is often written *IHS*, as may be seen in the anonymous dissertation of the commendator Vittorio on this most sacred name.

It seems quite probable to me that Christians not only wrote the name *Iesus* in abbreviated form but sometimes also pronounced it in that way, since it was so often on their lips. Similar examples exist among the Romans: *in Hercle, Mecastor, Aedepol*.

Prudentius may therefore have followed this common pronunciation and made a spondee of *Iem* and *Ieu* for *Iesum* and *Iesu*. In the illustrations of Walahfrid Strabo, published in the *Biblical Manual* at Frankfurt in 1610, where the New Testament is briefly narrated in hexameter verse, a spondee is likewise made from *Iesus* and *Iesu*, which are written *IHC* and *IHV*.

Heinsius testifies that in the very old Putean manuscript of Prudentius one reads *Hisum* and *Hisu* for *Iesum* and *Iesu*; in the Egmond manuscript, *Hiesum*. Juvencus and the other ancient Christian poets always write *Iesum*, shortening the *i* and lengthening the *e*.]

186. 213. Sixth rule. Poets of the third and fourth centuries, especially Christian poets, lengthened short syllables by reason of the caesura more frequently than the ancients did. Many people, failing to notice this, undertook to correct ecclesiastical poems and thereby corrupted them.

Christophorus Cellarius, although not an unlearned grammarian, in his later *Observations on Barbarisms* alters a line of Juvencus from the prologue:

> May the sanctifying Spirit be present with me, the author of my song.

He reports it as follows, adding: “Unless perhaps the law of meter requires that *SANCTIFICANS* be read.” This conjecture is utterly foolish.

Cellarius likewise notes that Prudentius more frequently than others lengthens a short syllable at the end because of the doubled consonant of the following word, as though this were worthy of criticism. But Prudentius could not merely do this correctly; he ought to have done so if we wish to uphold the judgment of several learned men.

[Note: Barthius, book IX, chapter 9 of the *Adversaria*, reports that Hericus, like most Christians, failed to observe what the most learned men teach concerning letters: that *st* and *sp* lengthen the preceding syllable.

Hericus, line 229:

> And he marvels that he still survives for himself.

Line 209:

> Now the eyes breathe light.

Sedulius, book IV:

> Christ is present, bread; and the Holy Spirit too, fire,  
> Victorinus,  
> And the splendid axis of the moon.

Guilielmus Brito does the same frequently.

The same Barthius, book XXXVII, chapter 13, cites the following from an ancient parchment manuscript on prosody:

> A vowel before *z* is found short in the preceding word, as in Juvenal:
>
> “If your archives should be opened to the jealous adulterer.”

This is as though it violated some rule because *z* has the force of a double consonant.

If one consults the ancients, Priscian seems to have held precisely this view in book II:

> It must also be understood that not only before *l* or *r*, but also before *m*, as we have taught above, and *n*, mute consonants placed in these positions make syllables common . . .

Ovid, book X:

> And fish-rich Gnidus, and Amathus, rich in metals.

Nor should we omit the fact that a common syllable may result when three consonants follow, whenever at the beginning of the following syllable, after a shortened vowel, *s*, a mute, and a liquid occur; for in meter *s* is customarily suppressed according to ancient usage, as Horace has in the *Satires*:

> We leave behind, laughing at the rewards of the mad scribe.

Becmannus, under the letters *ST* in *On the Origin of the Latin Language*, raises the question whether *sc, sp,* and *st* lengthen the vowels immediately preceding them.

It is indeed difficult to reject all the examples cited from Lucretius, Virgil, Propertius, Ovid, Lucan, and other excellent poets, in which the vowel remains short although the following word begins with *sp, sc,* or *st*: in Virgil, “Place your hopes” (*Ponite spes*); in Ovid, “That Scinis perished” (*Occidit ille Scinis*); in Catullus, “the wave of the Scamander” (*unda Scamandri*).

What Becmannus says—that it is well known that the ancients were often not especially concerned with proper names—may confirm what I said in no. 210. But it has no place in the present matter, since the vowel under discussion precedes a proper name; and even if one supposes that the point does apply, there are many examples in other words.

I therefore think that it is permissible to construct a verse with the vowel shortened in this way, though it is more fitting for it to be lengthened. From this one can see the foolishness of those who ventured to correct certain lines of Prudentius for the sole reason that he had lengthened a short vowel when two consonants at the beginning of the following word seemed to require it to be long.

Thus Aldus and others read, from some manuscript, “having flowed from the stomach” (*cessisse e stomacho*) instead of “having flowed from the stomach” (*cessisse stomacho*), at line 904 of the *Psychomachia*.]

The more difficult question is whether a syllable can be common by reason of the caesura alone, even when the vowel at the caesura is not closed by a consonant belonging to the same word. In *his, pectoribus, oratis, Eurialus, caput, tuus, obruimur*, and similar cases, there is no reason for doubt.

Servius, at least, criticizes line 164 of book III of the *Aeneid*:

> Then he seized gifts heavy with gold and carved ivory,

because *gravia* is lengthened by reason of the word-ending, but his criticism is rather harsh, since the word ends in no consonant.

Other examples are also commonly produced from Lucretius, Ovid, Statius, and Virgil. In my *Censure of the Hymns of Santolius after the Spanish Hymnodist*, p. 440, I have shown that they are not established and do not settle the matter.

Scaliger, against certain grammarians—perhaps he means Servius—says in book II, chapter 17 of the *Poetics*:

> Every caesura is indifferent; nor is this without reason, for the rhythm comes to a stop there.

In dances, too, they struck the ground with the foot at the caesuras.

To this reasoning I shall add the authority of Prudentius and his contemporaries, if that authority has any weight—and why should it not? It at least establishes that it was the practice of Christian poets to use an indifferent caesura more frequently than the ancients.

### 214. Seventh rule

The earliest ecclesiastical poets, because of some Greek dialect or because of the usage of their own time, converted *ω, η,* and *αι* in certain Greek words into short vowels, not without precedent among the ancients.

In Prudentius the following words are repeatedly criticized for shortening Greek syllables long by nature: *aenigma, Berillus, Chalcedon, daemon, energima, eremus, heresis, idolum, Lacedaemon, mathesis, phrenesis, poesis, Pyreneus, romphealis,* and *sphera*.

But why are the earlier poets, who used similar licence and provided the example, allowed to escape without criticism? I shall collect some instances, partly from Hispaniolus and others, partly from my own observations.

*Ionius* is written with an omega; nevertheless Virgil has “in the great Ionian sea” (*Ionio in magno*), and others likewise shorten it.

*Orichalcum* contains the diphthong *ei*. Horace shortens its *i* in the *Art of Poetry*:

> The pipe, not as now joined to brass, and the trumpets.

Virgil and others do the same.

*Sithonius* is written with an omega, yet Virgil and others likewise shorten it, as they do *Haemonius*.

*Orion* too has an omega. Servius, however, reports that it was formerly written with *ου*, and that when the *υ* was worn away, the remaining letter was *ο micron*. Ovid, book IV of the *Fasti*:

> Since Hyreus called him Orion because he was born in this way,  
> The first letter lost its ancient sound.

Horace shortens the omega in *Origenes*. Virgil, in the *Ciris*:

> To waste away equally in filth and scoria.

In Greek, *scoria* has an omega.

Latins shorten the *η* in *hepar*, and Catullus and Persius do likewise in *crepida*, which also has an eta.

It is well known that the *η* in *mater* and *pater* is shortened. In *aer* it is sometimes lengthened, but Claudian shortens it:

> The lucid air will mingle with shadowy Avernus.

Valerius Flaccus, book VI:

> Nor lighter than iron, nor a spear to wood.

Tibullus pronounces *chorea*, and Catullus *platea*, with a short *e*, although the Greek spelling has the diphthong *ει*.

The Greeks write *ptissana* with two *s*’s, and *grabbatum* with two *b*’s. Horace says *ptisana* with a short *i*, and Virgil in the *Moretum* has *grabatum* with the first syllable short.

This is a line of Quintus Serenus:

> And furious phrenesis is stirred by an ailment of the head.

In *Aeneadae* the second vowel is *ει*, yet Virgil shortens it.

[Note: Hispaniolus, p. 167, refutes Hermolaus, who had accused Sidonius Apollinaris of shortening the first syllable of *Phonascus*, the penultimate syllable of *Paraclitus*, the first syllable of *Ctesiphon*, and the penultimate syllable of *diastema*. He concludes:

> If the ancients are found to have shortened eta and omega, and even a diphthong—for example, in Virgil and Persius, authors of great authority—why is this imputed to modern writers?

Julius Caesar Scaliger, book VII, part 1, chapter 6, observes that *enim* comes from the Greek *ἦν, ἦνι* (*ēn, ēni*). Nor is the long vowel an obstacle; we have demonstrated this in the books of the *Origins*, just as in *crepida*, from Greek *κρηπίς*, and in *venio*, from *βαίνω*.

Joseph Scaliger, in his *Notes on the Greek of the Eusebian Chronicle*, p. 102, observes that formerly in Ionic Greek the *ο* was also written with *ο* alone.

It is clear from Plato’s *Cratylus* that the ancient Greeks did not have the letter omega, but only *ο*, nor eta, but only *ε*.

The name of the vowel *ο* was *ου*, which has the force of negation. From this one understands the line of Ausonius and others:

> There was only one answer with which the Spartans could reply,
The letter *o*, and they pleased the angry king by answering in the negative. For they replied not with *οὐ*, which consists of two letters, but with *ο*; among the Greeks this was called *οὐ*, meaning “no.” Muretus, *Variae Lectiones*, book XVIII, chapter 1, adds that it is entirely correct to say in the Apocalypse, “I am Alpha and O,” without Latin speakers’ needing to say “O mega.” Indeed, in Prudentius, Paulinus, and others, “alpha and omega” is written; and if the verse were to be composed in Latin from the ground up, one would write “alpha and o,” since “o mega” is incompatible with the requirements of the meter.

[Col. 0736C] It must nevertheless be observed that the short *o* and the long *o* were pronounced differently by the ancients. Casaubon, in his notes on Trebellius, p. 214, says that in many ancient texts one finds *sepulcrum* with a diphthong, as in the epitaph of Aureolus, one of the thirty tyrants:

> Donat saepulcro victor post multa tyranni.  
> “The victor gives to the tomb after many tyrants.”

This is contrary to Prudentius, who shortened the *e* in *sphera*. [Col. 0736D] Salmasius, pp. 129, 169, and 213 of his notes on the *Historia Augusta*, discusses *sphera* and the related question at length and promises a commentary on the faults of recent poets. He shows that writers of that period wrote *sphera*, like *machera* and *macera*, with a short *e*; and that Ausonius wrote *Citheron* with a short *e* instead of *Cithaeron*. In Maximianus, book of *Elegies*, we find:

> Me pedagogus adit  
> “My tutor approaches me,”

instead of *paedagogus*. Nor did only the Latins write and pronounce words in this way; the Greeks did so as well, as Salmasius proves from ancient Greek inscriptions. He notes that Prudentius and Ausonius shorten the final syllable in *fames*, *lues*, *maiestas*, and *colluces*. Ausonius, however, may not have shortened the second syllable of *maiestas*, but may have used a spondee for an iamb, as he often did elsewhere, in the second position of the iambic dimeter.

*Fames*, *lues*, and *colluces* have a short *e* according to the ancient spelling tradition of *famis*, *luis*, and *collucis*, third-conjugation forms, like *rido, -is*; *strido, -is*; *fervo, -is*; *fulgo, -is*; and others, which Priscian discusses more fully in book X. All these things ought not to be called faults of the poets.

Many recent writers go astray when they summon the writings of the ancients to judgment. They think that the age of the Latin language must be confined to the Augustan century, or at any rate judge as though anything not found written by some author of that century were less Latin. They speak of Prudentius, Paulinus, Ausonius, and their contemporaries as though they were people of our own time, who learn Latin—now a dead language—through labor and study from books alone. Thus they rashly assert that those most distinguished men, who moved in the public forum and in the full light of society, erred in the pronunciation and usage of certain very common words, and were deceived or misled.

They unfairly wish to measure the poetry and Latinity of Prudentius and men like him by the rules or usage of the so-called Golden Age, while at the same time defending not only Terence, whom Cicero held in very high esteem, but also Plautus, Ennius, and others, although the prosodic liberties taken by Terence and the others depart farther from the age of Augustus than do the poems of Prudentius. Finally, scarcely any syllable can be detected in Prudentius that cannot be excused by some poetic figure—figures that Lucretius, Catullus, Virgil, Horace, Ovid, and their contemporaries used in similar words, though some people regard them as errors and faults.

## Chapter XXV. Prudentius corrupted by some, wrongly corrected by others, defended by others. Special observations on his prosody

### 190 [215]

If one sets aside what Prudentius did either by reason or on the example of others, one will find very few things that can be called metrical errors. In this respect he would have as his companions the most excellent poets—Horace, Virgil, and others—of whom, nevertheless, one may often say what Terentianus Maurus said of comic poets:

> In metra peccant arte, non inscitia.  
> “They offend against meter by art, not through ignorance.”

Scaliger, *Poetices*, book II, chapter 31, speaking of faults in quantity, says: “You could demand many examples from Homer, for he was exceedingly negligent.” Aristarchus noted Homer’s errors with such moderation that he never said that Homer had erred; rather, whatever he did not approve, he denied to be Homer’s. Cicero, *Letters*, book III, letter 11, writes:

> Ut enim Aristarchus Homeri versum negat quem non probat: sic tu (libet enim mihi jocari) quod disertum non erat, ne putaris meum.  
> “As Aristarchus rejects a verse of Homer that he does not approve, so you—for I may jest with you—should not suppose that what was not eloquent was mine.”

Understand Ausonius’s reference to the same Aristarchus in letter 18:

> Quique notas spuriis versibus apposuit.  
> “He who placed marks upon spurious verses.”

I shall incidentally correct another passage of Ausonius that Scaliger the Younger overlooked in his *Ausonian Readings*, in the preface to *The Contest of the Seven Sages*:

> Maeonio qualem cultum quaesivit Homero  
> Censor Aristarchus, normaque Zenodoti.  
> Pone obelos igitur, spuriorum stigmata vatum,  
> Palmas, non culpas esse putabo meas.

> “Such adornment as Aristarchus the censor  
> And the rule of Zenodotus sought for Maeonian Homer—  
> Set down your obeli, then, the marks of spurious poets;  
> I shall regard them as palms of victory, not as my faults.”

Read, at my own risk, *spuriorum stigmata versuum*, or *versum*.

[Col. 0737C] **Note:** In my commentary on the hymn to Saint Eulalia I shall refute an error of that same Scaliger, who, in the epigram with which Ausonius celebrated Hispalis, adopted *Emerita* against the ancient reading, although reason suggests that *Hispalis*, not *Emerita*, ought to be read.

What Aristarchus did with Homer’s poems could therefore, with greater justice, be done with Prudentius: we could say that verses were spurious when it was clear that they had been infected by some fault.

[Col. 0737C] **Note:** I shall not pass over Barthius’s words, *Adversaria*, book XXI, chapter 4:

“The ancient Christian writers did not disdain that acquired learning from the books of the wise which the common people today, with great confidence born of their supposed learning, habitually reject. Although such learning lay outside the innermost precincts of the Church, they nevertheless often agreed with it in a remarkably thorough way. I think that both the other interpreters of such matters, and especially those who have undertaken to illuminate Prudentius for the public benefit, ought to have paid attention to this. For in that poet there is hidden learning, rare elegance in his words, and an undefiled Latinity in his phrasing—except where, by imitating sacred speech, he deliberately violated the rule, and where he was often forced by the barbarity of the monks who copied him to write otherwise than he intended. It must nevertheless be said that thanks are due to the monks, because they preserved for us not only Prudentius but also other ancient writers; their ignorance should not be blamed so much as the adversity and difficulty of the times.”

### 191 [216]

Excellent are the observations brought forward by Barthius, book LXI, chapter 23. After showing that *aer* and *aether* are correctly used in the neuter gender, he says:

[Col. 0737C] “There are many more such examples among the Christian poets, which we condemn because of our ignorance of antiquity, since the loss of so many outstanding—indeed, apart from one or two, almost all the greatest—founders of Roman eloquence has left us unable to understand them. Above all, this applies to their chief, Prudentius, whom I consider, in this group, to be by far the most suitable writer for explaining many customs and practices. Yet he still lies pierced and disfigured by many blemishes, for no other major reason than that he wrote things most welcome to everyone, and in a manner of expression such as could scarcely have been more desirable.”

[Col. 0737D] **Note:** Barthius again tries, to some extent, to stir up resentment against the monks; but his praise of Prudentius, which he adds, must not be omitted:

“Hence, being especially familiar with cloistered men, he received many wounds as the reward of his learning.” Let the eloquence of so great a man be attested even by the single *Coronation of Romanus*, which, though it is still defiled by a few blemishes—belonging not so much to the author as to the copyists—can otherwise challenge all iambic poets from Horace onward.

[Col. 0738C] Again Barthius attacks the copyists of Prudentius in book LIV, chapter 18. In the title he says that the division of the chapters of the *Psychomachia* is monastic, and afterward explains it:

“To me, that entire division and inscription of chapters does not seem to belong to the author but to schoolmasters, with whom, to his great misfortune, that excellent Christian author was so familiar, at least as far as poetry was concerned.”

Gronovius and others teach that many faults must be attributed not only to manuscript codices but also to the editions of Prudentius. We shall note this at the individual passages when we examine the variant readings. Some confusion may also have arisen from two editions of Prudentius’s poems published while he was still alive, as Heinsius suspects. There are ancient examples showing that authors published their works again in more carefully corrected form. I think it probable that Prudentius composed and published his hymns and shorter works separately and at different times, and finally, in the fifty-seventh year of his life, gathered them into one corpus and issued them publicly, correcting some passages.

### 217

As an example of errors introduced by printers, I shall cite *idolum*, which Prudentius consistently uses with a short *o*. The elder Aldus, thinking this an error in the manuscripts, often wished to correct it, as in *Psychomachia*, verse 379:

> Quosque viros non ira fremens, idolaque bello  
> “And the men whom raging anger does not [overcome], and idols in war”

instead of:

> Quosque viros non ira fremens, non idola bello.  
> “And the men whom raging anger does not [overcome], not idols in war.”

Aldus followed the rule and did not fall into error. Muratorius, however, did not do so in the case of Saint Paulinus. Daring to correct the same syllable, he himself committed a much greater fault: contrary to every rule, he shortened the *i* in *idolum*, although the word is Greek *εἴδωλον* (*eidōlon*), and without any supporting example, in the final poem, *Against the Pagans*, verse 203:

> Nec se paganus laudet, si vitat idola.  
> “Nor let the pagan boast if he avoids idols.”

Muratorius adds this note: “In the manuscript it read *si qui idola vitat*. I corrected it.” You did not correct it, Muratorius; you corrupted it.

The same Paulinus writes in the *Epithalamium for Julian*:

> Absit, ut idolici videatur filia templi.  
> “Far be it that she should appear to be the daughter of an idolatrous temple.”

It is clear that Paulinus shortens the *o* in *idolici*.

[Col. 0738C] **Note:** Barthius, book XXXIV, chapter 4:

“Our Prudentius uses *idola* in a dactylic position; in this all the other Christian poets are found following him as their author. Tertullian, book III *Against Marcion*, though Prudentius rather follows him: *Idola vana sequi*, ‘to follow empty idols.’ Sedulius, book IV: *Idola dilexit*, ‘he loved idols.’ Arator, book I: *Idola quaerens*, ‘seeking idols.’ Yet Prudentius did this deliberately, for elsewhere he is found using the same word in its proper order, as we shall note elsewhere.

Barthius is mistaken in believing that Prudentius lengthened the *o* in *idolum* somewhere. He identifies the passage in book LX, chapter 7: ‘That same most learned poet, when he encounters Greek syllables, does so not through error but by judgment, constraining them by Latin rules. How often did he place *IDOLUM* with a short medial syllable? Yet he knew that it ought to be lengthened.’ The verse is 424, whose true reading is:

> Caeruleasque animas, atque idola nigra volare.  
> “And the dark-blue souls and black idols to fly.”

Add also Venantius Fortunatus, *On the Contest of the Blessed*, who says:

> Idola dum cuperet Martinus sternere.  
> “While Martin wished to overthrow idols.”

I greatly commend the learning of Joseph Blanchini, which others have praised so highly. I particularly appreciate his diligence in having illuminated our Isidorian work. But I wish that this learned man, unprepared in poetic ability or in the knowledge of it, had not undertaken to correct Prudentius’s hymns in the Mozarabic Office. I observed in number 74 how he tried to attribute abnormal verses to Prudentius. I shall now touch upon certain passages that, in wishing to correct them, he corrupted, lest new errors at some time creep into the poems of Prudentius.

In *Saint Eulalia*, verse 64, *Mane superba tribunalia adit* (“In the morning she proudly approaches the tribunals”), he makes no correction, although it should read:

> Mane superba tribunal adit.  
> “In the morning she proudly approaches the tribunal.”

In verse 209, *Texta feram pede datilico* (“I shall bear woven things with a dactylic foot”), he corrects it to *dactylo* or *dactylico*. It should read *dactylico*, since the other form conflicts with the meter.

In the *Hymn of Those Who Fast*, verse 7:

> Quo fibra cordis expiatur vividi.  
> “By which the fiber of the living heart is purified,”

he corrects it to *expiamur lividi*, “we are purified, pale”—wrongly, for *fibra* is nominative and its *a* is short.

In verse 24, he changed *Liberque flatu* (“and free by breath”) to *libet*; I do not know why. In verse 98, *Veteresque nugas condomare ac frangere* (“and to tame and break old trifles”), he printed *condonare et frangere* (“to forgive and break”), contrary to sense and meter.

With a similar error, in place of the true reading in verse 134, *Impendit, inquit, ira summi judicis* (“‘The wrath of the supreme judge hangs over [him],’ he says”), he substituted *Impendet, inquit, ita* (“‘It hangs over,’ he says, ‘thus’”), contrary to both sense and meter.

In verse 161, *Nullus vivendi* (“No one of living”), the correction should have been *Nullus bibendi* (“No one of drinking”). Blanchini, unless the printer erred, wrote *Nullus habendi* (“No one of possessing”).

I pass over many other passages that he corrected badly, and many that he failed to correct when he should have done so. Gallandius, otherwise a most learned man, also fell into some errors of this kind in his edition of Prudentius.

[Col. 0739D] **Note:** Certainly it is neither beautiful to master the intricacies of poetic art nor disgraceful to be ignorant of them. Yet Horace’s advice on a similar or related matter should not be disregarded, *Epistles*, book II, letter 1:

> Navem agere ignarus navis timet: abrotonum aegro  
> Non audet, nisi qui didicit, dare: quod medicorum est,  
> Promittunt medici, tractant fabrilia fabri.  
> Scribimus indocti, doctique poemata passim.

> “The man ignorant of ships fears to steer a ship;  
> No one dares give southernwood to the sick unless he has learned how—  
> What belongs to physicians, physicians promise; craftsmen handle craftsmen’s work.  
> Learned and unlearned alike write poems everywhere.”

He repeats the same point in the *Art of Poetry*:

> Ludere qui nescit, campestribus abstinet armis,  
> Indoctusque pilae, discive, trochive quiescit,  
> Ne spissae risum tollant impune coronae.

> “He who does not know how to play keeps away from the field’s weapons;  
> Untrained in ball, discus, or hoop, he remains at rest,  
> Lest the crowded spectators raise laughter at his expense.”

The man who does not know how nevertheless dares to compose verses.

Prudentius needs neither these aids nor these defenders. Scaliger undertook his defense in his *Ausonian Readings*, p. 207, edition of 1588. Latin poets, especially in the age of Ausonius, also possessed this distinctive habit: they not only neglected Greek declensions in Greek words and brought them under Latin rules, but also overturned quantity, measuring it by accent.

Thus, on p. 104, he shortens the *e* in *Thales*, just as Sidonius does in *Lyristes*:

> Alcaeo potior Lyristes ipso.  
> “Lyristes, superior even to Alcaeus.”

It is as though they pronounced not *Thales* and *Lyristes*, but *Thalis* and *Liristis*. Likewise Quintus Cicero writes:

> Conditur Oceani ripa cum luce Bootis.  
> “He is buried on the shore of Ocean with the light of Boötes.”

As Servius notes in his little book *On Accents*, Latins pronounce Greek names with the same accent the Greeks use. *Idola* is always a dactyl in Prudentius. Sidonius lengthens the penultimate syllable in *Euripides*, following not quantity but accent:

> Orchestram quatit alter Euripidis.  
> “Another of Euripides’ [characters] shakes the orchestra.”

He lengthens the second syllable in *Marsyas* … but, by contrast, shortens the second in *Aratus* … Finally, inspect all of Sidonius, all of Prudentius, and the others: you will find that they consistently followed not Greek syllable quantity but Greek accent.

[Col. 0740D] **Note:** Scaliger continues to confirm the same point with other examples. Thus Ausonius shortens the penultimate syllable in *trigonos* and *tetragonos*. Who would dare say that Ausonius did this through ignorance of Greek letters? No sane person, I think. But in those times it seemed foolish not to lengthen the syllable where the accent fell, because that is the custom of the Latin language. So much so that Plautus followed popular judgment in this respect.

Conversely, in Plautus’s time, just as they admitted Latinisms in syllable quantity, so they admitted them in declension. They said *Nestorem* and *Hectorem* as they said *rectorem*, *mensorem*, and similar forms.”

### 218

Barthius, book XXIII, chapter 14, adheres to these observations. He says that those who object to the most learned, elegant, and thoroughly Christian poet Prudentius because he handles the rhythm of syllables too carelessly are fighting with ghosts. Prudentius does this deliberately and does not wish to quarrel with grammarians on that account, since he knowingly committed solecisms. Nor, however, are his practice and reasoning without examples. Both objections are frivolous and amount to nothing.

Ausonius committed the same fault in letter 1:

> Et festinato tempore utraque daret.  
> “And that each might give herself at the hastened time.”

And elsewhere. Whatever you read in this most learned poet Ausonius, I advise you, at my own risk, to judge as though you were reading it in Lucilius, Ennius, or writers of that kind. He then notes many more examples in Ausonius that are not even found in Prudentius.

Beckmann, discussing the verb *video* in *Origins of the Latin Language*, says that, because Prudentius always shortens the medial syllable of *idolum*, some excuse him by *systole*, while others explain it in another way. He says that the grammarian Tryphon explains it by *ἔνδεια* (*endeia*), meaning a deficiency or reduction of a letter or letters—namely, *εἴδολον* (*eidolon*) in place of *εἴδωλον* (*eidōlon*).

Ludewig, in his *Life of Prudentius*, vigorously defends him against those who call him barbarous because, for metrical reasons, he wrote *famis*, *luis*, *pubis*, and *Joannis* instead of *fames*, *lues*, *pubes*, and so forth. “Why,” he asks, “do we read in Plautus and Virgil *lea* for *leo*, *hospita* for *hospes*, *vallis* for *valles*, *felis* and *vulpis* for *feles* and *vulpes*? Prudentius used *intereceptus* for *interceptus* and *interefectus* for *interfectus*—see the following number—and Virgil likewise used this license.”

Poetic figures are nothing other than errors wearing a cloak. If all that Homer, Virgil, and the other ancients dared to do had been said by a later poet, with no precedent to support it, he could scarcely have endured the criticisms of men.

Clericus plainly displays his ignorance in the *Life of Prudentius*, arguing from lists of syllables in which Prudentius is said to have erred and from supposedly un-Latin words noted in him, and concluding that he made many mistakes in meter and Latinity. Similar lists can be compiled against any excellent author, and have been compiled in the editions of many, so that obsolete, archaic, and uncommon words may be identified, without thereby detracting anything from their reputation.

I do not deny that Prudentius was devoted to antiquity. But Cicero is right, *On the Orator*, book III, p. 123:

> “Unusual words are generally ancient and old-fashioned, long since withdrawn from the usage of daily speech; they belong more freely to the license of poets than ours do. Yet even in prose a poetic word rarely fails to possess dignity.”

This was much more permissible for Prudentius, who was imitating the example of the most learned men of his own time.

For this reason *fames*, *lues*, and *colluces* with a short final syllable can be defended, as I argued against Salmasius in number 214. Plautus was freer still. As Muretus observes, *Various Readings*, book XVI, chapter 14, he shortens the final syllables of imperative verbs whenever he wishes, even when they belong to the first or second order, as in *ama*, *vide*, *tace*, and *cave*. Christopher Wasius, chapter 15, proves with many examples that the ancients generally shortened the final syllable of imperatives of the first, second, and fourth conjugations in verse.

Ausonius, the celebrated grammarian and rhetorician, did not hesitate to call a short second syllable a solecism, even while writing against the grammarian Auxilius, whose little red-marked tablets—or rather his rods—he might have respected:

> Auxilium te nempe vocas, inscite magister,  
> Da rectum casum, jam solecismus eris.

> “You call yourself Auxilius, foolish schoolmaster;  
> Give the correct case, and you will already be a solecism.”

It should perhaps be written *solicismus*, so that the first vowel may be removed from the diphthong *οι*, for in pronunciation there was little or no difference between the diphthong *οι* and *iota*.

### 219

The following is also by Ausonius, *Idyll* 11:

> Qui bipes, et quadrupes foret, et tripes omnia solus.  
> “He who alone would be two-footed, four-footed, and three-footed in every respect.”

He has a short *e* in *bipes* and *tripes*, just as elsewhere *quadrupes* is treated by Saint Paulinus, *Nature*, book XII, verse 383:

> Constitit ignoto pro limine quadrupes hospes.  
> “The four-footed guest stood before the unknown threshold.”

Again Ausonius, epigram 9:

> Suasisti Venus ecce duas dyseros ut amarem,  
> Odit utraque: aliud da modo consilium.  
> “You advised me, Venus—look, I loved two difficult women;  
> Each hates me. Give me another piece of advice.”

And in *To His Father*:

> Et placuisse reor geminis aetatibus, ut se  
> Non festinato tempore utraque daret.  
> “And I think that I pleased two generations, so that each  
> Might give herself at an unhurried time.”

Scaliger excuses this by appeal to accent.

[Col. 0741C] **Note:** Ausonius follows the custom of his own age, lengthening the syllable wherever the prosodic accent lay. The accent fell on the same syllable in the feminine noun as in the masculine *uterque*. Ausonius did the same in the same word in the *Funeral Oration for His Father*:

> Victum, habitum, mores semper eadem habuit.  
> “She always had the same food, dress, and customs.”

When Barthius had noted this, book V, chapter 11, he said: “Ausonius seems to have indulged his age; but I rather believe that he followed the authority of some ancient writer, having often discovered that he used almost nothing without such authority.”

Prudentius’s critics, Chamillardus and Cellarius, did not include in their catalogue the following expression from *Peristephanon* hymn 1, verse 3:

> Sanguinis notis eadem scripta terris tradidit.  
> “She handed down the same writings to the lands in marks of blood,”

where the *a* in *eadem* is long by reason of accent.

Servius, on *Aeneid* I: “For the sake of pronunciation, contrary to Latin usage, an accent is assigned to the final syllables to which particles are attached, as in *Musaque*, *illene*, and *cuique*.” Martianus Capella likewise reports this in book III, in the chapter *On the Acute Accent*. It follows that the accent was placed on the medial syllable of the nominative plurals *utraque* and *eadem*.

Scaliger the elder notes of the ancient comic poets, book VI, chapter 5, that they pronounced their verses in such a way that not even the position of consonants prevented a syllable from remaining short. Thus they pronounced *tempestivum* with a short second syllable, because, just as the medial syllable of *temporis* is short, so is its comparative form in the derivative.

The difficulty is greater in the case of Prudentius’s lengthening of the first syllable of the trisyllabic *cuique*. I do not approve either of those who correct Prudentius’s passages to:

> Suus est mos cuique genti, sua cuique dextra est, sua cuique jura.  
> “Each nation has its own custom, each its own right hand, each its own laws,”

or of Gifanius, who says that Prudentius lengthened the *e* in these passages, as though he had forced a spondee into the fifth position in place of a dactyl. Prudentius wished to dissolve the diphthong in such a way as to lengthen its first element; this is customary in *aquai*. It is also well known that the ancients wrote *quoi* for *cui*.

Nor do I agree with those who think that every time *fio* or *fiat* occurs with a short first syllable, Prudentius’s verses should be corrected. Although this can sometimes be done without bad results, and although Prudentius did not shorten the syllable as often as Chamillardus thought, it is nevertheless unfair to oppose the oldest manuscript codices when they agree.

I shall therefore say that Prudentius followed the Greek origin, from *φύω* (*phyō*), from which come *fuat* and *fio*. Arator and Tertullian used the forms similarly.

I judge differently concerning the *a* in *ratus*. Prudentius often shortened it:

> Esse rati, etc.  
> “Thinking that it was so, etc.”

*Symmachus* I, verse 295; *Cathemerinon* 9, verse 32:

> Mando, ut abluantur, inquit: fit ratum, quod jusserat.  
> “I command them to be washed,” he says; “what he ordered becomes fulfilled.”

And *Cathemerinon* 3, verse 99:

> Utque foret rata materies.  
> “So that the material might be duly established.”

*Peristephanon* 5, verse 15:

> Supplicium sibi dulce rata.  
> “Considering punishment sweet for herself.”

Giselinus therefore did not correct without reason in *Peristephanon* 10, verse 911:

> Ergo ratus Praefectus elinguem virum.  
> “Therefore, the Prefect, judging the man speechless,”

instead of:

> Praefectus ergo ratus elinguem virum.  
> “The Prefect, therefore, judging the man speechless,”

whatever Vossius may have thought in *On the Art of Grammar*, book II, chapter 22.

Salmasius explains in his notes on Aelius Spartianus, p. 61, Prudentius’s making the first *e* of *enervo* short.

[Col. 0742C] **Note:** At that time they wrote no differently. They wrote *INORMIS* and *INORME* for *ENORME*, and therefore the first syllable of the word was pronounced short by the poets of that age; it would have remained long if the word had been written with *e*. They therefore said *INORMIS*, like *INANIS*, and similar forms.

Not long ago I observed from very ancient books that this occurs twice or three times in Prudentius (Salmasius is mistaken); but the passages are not now at hand. Prudentius likewise uses *enervare* for *enervare*, with a short first syllable. Thus the old book reads. Aldhelmus, *On the Praises of the Virgin*:

> Flammis combussit inormem.  
> “He burned the enormous one with flames.”

Thus it was also written in an old book. Add Sedulius, book III:

> Et septem panibus agmen  
> Pavit enorme virum.  
> “And with seven loaves he fed an enormous multitude of men.”

A similar example is found in Tertullian, book IV *Against Marcion*:

> In cataclysmo enecans.  
> “Destroying in the cataclysm.”

And in Fortunatus:

> Corrigit ipse prius quod poscit, ut alter emendet.  
> “He first corrects what he asks another to amend.”

Nevertheless, I suspect that Prudentius coined a new word, *inermo*, *inermas*, from *inermis* or *inermus*. Others correct the passage differently.

I shall present other corrections in the commentary, such as reading *erutus* for *elutus*. I shall also read *interfectus* and *interceptus* with the manuscripts, not *interefectus* or *intereceptus*, which Bede seems to have read, with Ludewig’s approval.

### 196 [220]

I omit other, less important matters that can more easily be sought in works on prosody, especially concerning Hebrew names, from Ricciolius’s *Index of Controversial Syllables* I and II, although I would not wish you always to adhere to his authority.

From what I have taught, it may be gathered that Prudentius can be defended by men skilled in poetic art not only on the basis of the usage of his own age but also by reason and the example of the ancients, even in syllables that seem to be exceedingly anomalous. It is also clear what rules should be followed by those who undertake to purge the poems of Christian poets of the third or fourth century from errors, or to pass judgment on one of their poems.

In Edmund Martene’s *Collection of Ancient Writers*, Paris, 1733, volume IX, columns 13 and following, there is a book on Genesis attributed to the presbyter Juvencus in the manuscript from which it was extracted. Its first four chapters had long ago been published with Tertullian and Cyprian; the remainder, extending to chapter 50, was taken from a Corbie manuscript written more than nine hundred years ago.

Pamelius attributes the work to Tertullian; Elias Pinius, by conjecture, attributes it to Salvian of Marseilles, on the basis of what Gennadius says of Salvian:

> “In the manner of the Greeks, from the beginning of Genesis to the creation of the first man, he composed one book in verse, as a kind of *Hexaemeron*.”

It would be surprising if someone wished to attribute this book to Prudentius as well, for Gennadius also says in his eulogy of Prudentius:

> “He also composed, in the manner of the Greeks, a *Hexaemeron* on the creation of the world, extending to the creation of the first man and his transgression.”

I would not, however, wish this to occur to anyone. First, the book proceeds far beyond the creation and transgression of the first man; consequently, it cannot rightly be assigned to Salvian of Marseilles, who extended his own book only to the creation—that is, the making—of the first man. Moreover, the verses are for the most part entirely lawless and unworthy of Juvencus, Prudentius, or their contemporaries. I have no doubt that many are corrupt through the carelessness of copyists, and I have corrected several of them conjecturally in my notes.

Usually the ablative ending in *-a* is shortened, even though some correction has been made in the printed editions against the manuscript codices. But what can one do with verses 43 and 44?

> Viritim cunctis nomen quod permanet, indit  
> Adamus, donata sibi prudentia solers.

> “Adam, skillful in the wisdom granted to him,  
> Gives each person individually a name that endures.”

You must change four or five words, and even that will scarcely suffice.

[Col. 0743D] **Note:** I shall extract a few similar passages:

> Femina fraudiferis misere decepta suadelis.  
> “The woman, miserably deceived by deceitful counsels.”

> Cui junctus Abelus.  
> “To whom Abel was joined.”

> Innocuas multa servabat cura bidentes.  
> “With great care he preserved harmless two-year-old sheep.”

> Qui tibi ceu Domino subjectus colla praebebit.  
> “Who, subjected to you as to a lord, will offer his neck.”

> Nam malo promeritus signo fit notus inusto.  
> “For, having deserved evil, he becomes known by a mark branded upon him.”

To include more examples briefly: in *daturus* the *a* is lengthened; in present forms the *ae* is shortened; in *aemulus* the *a* is shortened; in *praesentant* the *a* is shortened; in *laturus* the first *a* is lengthened; in *carentia* the first *a* is lengthened; in *acumine* the *a* is shortened; in *columbas* the *o* is lengthened; and there are six hundred other such examples encountered everywhere.

Anyone who thinks that poems of this sort could have been composed by Juvencus, Prudentius, or the first Christian poets will resemble a man who, wishing to judge paintings, attributed a picture made by some bad painter from the common people to Raphael of Urbino.

[Col. 0743C] Barthius thought that among the ancients there were some who composed verses in a kind of macaronic fashion, partly according to the laws of meter and partly in prose. Of this kind, he says, are the comic *Testament* of Sergius Polensis and, as some think, the Anacreontic poem of Annaeus Florus to Hadrian and *Querolus*, the drama modeled on Plautus’s *Aulularia* and composed by Gildas the Wise.

As for the verses of Sergius Polensis, parasite and actor, it has already been established that they were composed in the fifteenth century, not fabricated and passed off as ancient, as some had believed. Florus’s verses to Hadrian observe the law of meter; this would easily be demonstrated against Barthius, Muratorius, and others. A more suitable example is found in that celebrated comedy with a crippled foot, *Querolus*.

Others composed verses according to no metrical law, restricting themselves to a fixed number of syllables, as Commodianus under Constantine did in his *Instructions*, in something resembling hexameter:

> Praefatio nostra viam erranti demonstrat  
> Respectumque bonum; cum venerit saeculi meta, atque ita reliqua.

> “Our preface shows the wandering man the way  
> And the good direction, when the world’s limit has come,”

and so forth.

But the book on Genesis, of which I have given a specimen, belongs neither to the first nor to the second class. It belongs rather to a later period, when similar license in syllable quantity had prevailed without reason or precedent. Abbo and others of his age used this kind of composition.

## Chapter XXVI. Prudentian Meters

### 198 [221]

The first kind of meter is the three-membered, three-stanza ode. Its first verse is a Glyconic consisting of a spondee, a choriambus, and a pyrrhic or spondee, followed by two dactyls. The second is an Asclepiad, consisting of a spondee, two choriambi, and a pyrrhic—or, as it is now commonly scanned, a spondee, a dactyl, a long syllable, and two dactyls. The third is a choriambic Callimachian, consisting of a spondee, three choriambi, and a pyrrhic or iamb.

The preface to the works before the book *Cathemerinon* belongs to this genre:

> Per quinquennia jam decem, etc.  
> “For ten periods of five years now,” etc.

Prudentius used this very sweet meter only once, and I know of no one else who used it, except Wandelbertus, who imitated both its meter and its thought, as I shall say in the commentary. All these verses may be called choriambic; but the whole matter comes down to the same thing.

In Vatican manuscript 1715 there is a gloss saying that the second verse is called Asclepiadic because the inventor of this meter was Aesculapius, the son of Apollo. But although Aesculapius is *Asclepios* in Greek, the author of the poem was the poet Asclepiades.

In a Glyconic the first foot is sometimes a trochee, rarely an iamb. The scheme of measurement is as follows:

1. Verse: *Per quin-quennia jam-decem*  
2. Verse: *Ni fal-lor fuimus-septimus in-super*  
3. Verse: *Annum-cardo rotat-dum fruimur-sole volubili.*

### 222

The second kind is the one-membered ode. The verses are iambic dimeters, with iambs in the even positions and either iambs or spondees in the odd positions. This kind includes hymns 1, 2, 11, and 12 of *Cathemerinon*, and hymns 2 and 5 of *Peristephanon*. The even feet are sometimes tribrachs; the odd feet may be anapaests or tribrachs. They are scanned as follows:

> Ales-die-i nun-tius.  
> “The winged messenger of day.”

Unless longer feet, as I have said, require something else, as in:

> Vigila-te jam-sum pro-ximus.  
> “Keep watch; I am already near.”

### 223

The third kind is the one-membered ode, an Alcmanic dactylic trimeter hypercatalectic, consisting of three dactyls and one syllable. The hymn is *Cathemerinon* 3, cited by Ricciolius as an example, where verse 28 reads:

> Sertaque mystica dactylico  
> Texere docta liga strophio.

> “Bind the mystical garlands, skilled  
> To weave them with a dactylic foot around the fillet.”

Also belonging here is the hymn to Saint Eulalia, *Peristephanon* 3, which ends:

> Texta feram pede dactylico.  
> “I shall bear woven things with a dactylic foot.”

Its scansion is:

> O cruci-fer bone-lucisa-tor.  
> “O good bearer of the cross, maker of light.”

### 224

The fourth kind is the one-membered ode. Its verses are hendecasyllables properly so called, or Phalaecians, containing a spondee, a dactyl, and three trochees. Prudentius calls them hendecasyllables in *Peristephanon* 5, together with Catullus and other ancient poets:

> Dulces hendecasyllabos revolvens.  
> “Turning over sweet hendecasyllables.”

This kind includes *Cathemerinon* hymn 4 and *Peristephanon* 5. Its scansion is:

> Pastis-visceri-bus ci-boque-sumpto.  
> “With the entrails fed and food consumed.”

There are examples of a dactyl, trochee, and iamb in the first position.

### 225

The fifth kind is the one-membered ode: Asclepiadic verses, as in the second verse of the first kind. This includes *Cathemerinon* hymn 5:

> Inventor rutili, dux bone, luminis.  
> “Inventor of the radiant light, good leader,”

and the preface to book I *Against Symmachus*.

### 226

The sixth kind is the one-membered ode. The verses are Anacreontic iambics, that is, catalectic iambic dimeters consisting of three iambs and one syllable. They admit a spondee in the first and third positions. This kind includes *Cathemerinon* hymn 6:

> Ades, Pater supreme.  
> “Be present, supreme Father,”

which is scanned:

> Ades, Pater, supre-me.

[Col. 0745B] **Note:** Chamillardus does not appear to admit a spondee in the third position, although Aldus recognized one. Ricciolius observes that Prudentius admitted an anapaest in the first position. He did so quite often; and since the acatalectic iambic dimeter admits an anapaest in the first position, there is no reason to deny it to the catalectic iambic dimeter—especially since the author of the poems, Anacreon, often uses an anapaest in the first position.

I do not think, however, that he placed a spondee in the third position. For verse 142:

> Qui mille per maeandros.  
> “Who, through a thousand winding channels,”

does indeed have a spondee in the third position; but who could assert with certainty that Prudentius did not shorten the *ae* in *maeandros* because of the following vowel? For he did this in *romphaealis*, and in the same word *Maeandros* in *Cathemerinon* hymn 7, verse 124:

> Ventris maeandros circuibat tortiles.  
> “He moved around the winding channels of the belly,”

although the manuscripts vary at this point. But it is certainly very common for a diphthong in Greek words to be shortened before a following vowel.

### 227. Seventh type: a single-form ode

The verses are iambic senarii, that is, iambic trimeters without catalexis. If they are pure, they require iambs in every position; if mixed, they admit in the odd-numbered positions a tribrach, spondee, anapaest, dactyl, and, rarely, a proceleusmatic. In the even-numbered positions they generally have iambs, but they admit a tribrach in the second, fourth, and sixth positions. Of this type are Hymn 7 of the *Cathemerinon*, Hymn 10 of the *Peristephanon*, the preface to the *Hamartigenia*, and the preface to the *Psychomachia*. The scansion is:

> O Na-za-re-ne, lux Beth-lem, Ver-bum Pa-tris.

[Note: [Col. 0745C] I do not understand what Chamillard intended when he explains this type. All the verses are Hipponactean iambic trimeters without catalexis, though a spondee is admitted in the odd-numbered positions. The Hipponactean poem is usually called an iambic trimeter catalectic, as in “Three ancient gallons of Falernian.” But, leaving aside this question of terminology, iambic senarii admit not only the spondee, nor do they admit feet other than the iamb only in the odd-numbered positions. This should be noted, lest anyone think Prudentius has erred in his iambic senarii when he finds other feet. It is well established that the comic poets were freer: in the first five positions they inserted spondees, dactyls, anapaests, and occasionally proceleusmatics. Ausonius more often inserted a spondee in the fourth position in the *Game of the Seven Sages*, for which reason Scaliger calls him to account in Book VI of the *Poetics*. Yet Ausonius might be excused on the ground that in that poem he speaks in a quasi-comic manner, bringing the Sages onto the stage; and Scaliger himself, against Erasmus, states in Book VII, p. 926, that in many senarii of Seneca the rules were observed no more strictly than in comedies or plays. As for Prudentius, there is no doubt that he observed the rules customary among tragedians. Bede takes an example of an iambic senarius from him. See no. 242.]

### 228. Eighth type: a two-form, four-stanza ode

The first three verses are Sapphics, and every fourth verse is an Adonic. In the Sapphic verses, the first position contains a trochee, the second a spondee, the third a dactyl, and the fourth and fifth a trochee. The Adonic consists of a dactyl and a spondee. Of this type are Hymn 8 of the *Cathemerinon* and Hymn 4 of the *Peristephanon*. Its metrical pattern is:

> Christe, ser-vo-rum re-gi-men tu-o-rum.

In the Adonic:

> Le-ge co-er-ces.

Prudentius bound himself to these rules, although some have admitted a trochee and a dactyl in the second position; Seneca, however, admitted a spondee, dactyl, and anapaest in the first position, and an iamb in the second.

### 229. Ninth type: a single-form ode

Chamillard less appropriately calls it “three-stanza,” for there are not here several poems of different kinds. The verses are Archilochian trochaics consisting of seven feet and one syllable. The feet are trochees, also called chorees; in the even-numbered positions a spondee is admitted. Of this type are Hymn 9 of the *Cathemerinon* and Hymn 1 of the *Peristephanon*. It is scanned as follows:

> Da pu-er ple-ctrum cho-re-is, ut ca-nam fi-de-li-bus.

Prudentius observes this rule.

[Note: [Col. 0745D] It will not be superfluous to ask whether, in this poem, there is room for the other feet which Prudentius occasionally used. They say that the ancients very rarely placed a tribrach in the odd-numbered positions, and that they rarely used, in the even-numbered positions, feet equivalent to the spondee. Terentianus Maurus, in his poem on letters and feet, gives several examples:

> η and ω, which submit two time-units to the feet—  
> Just as one; before the number gave the second—  
> Such is the form of the lesser, when we say “soul”—  
> For four times number and double time recur—  
> It will be an ἀνάπαιστος [anapaest]; you see that this foot consists of time-units.

In Hymn 9 of the *Cathemerinon*, Prudentius either admitted a spondee in the third position or shortened the first *u* in *lugubri*; I have shown in no. 209 that the latter is more pleasing to me. But in the same hymn, verse 40, a spondee is inserted in the fifth position:

> Extimum vestis sacratae furtim mulier attigit.  
> The woman secretly touched the outer edge of the sacred garment.

In verse 103, there is an anapaest in the sixth position:

> Post, ut occasum resolvit, vitae et hominem reddidit.  
> Then, when he had undone death, he restored life and the human being.

Likewise, there is a dactyl in Hymn 1 of the *Peristephanon*, verse 63:

> Tempus est Deo rependi, quidquid est proprium Dei.  
> It is time to repay to God whatever belongs to God.

In the same poem, verse 70, there is a tribrach in the fifth position:

> Et chalybs attrita colla gravibus ambit circulis.  
> And the rubbed steel encircles the neck with heavy rings.

Of these examples, the only one contrary to the rules is the spondee in the fifth position, in *furtim* in the verse:

> Extimum vestis sacratae furtim mulier attigit.

Perhaps the copyists transposed the words and, instead of *mulier furtim attigit*, without eliding the *m* in *furtim*, produced the reading now found. If the Gospel expression is to be retained, I would emend it more satisfactorily to:

> mulier furtim contigit.  
> the woman secretly touched.

Someone might doubt whether Prudentius wrote *mulier attigit*, or perhaps *mulier attigit* is correct; but *furtim* accords better with the Gospel narrative. Wasius, chapter 1 of *On the License of Ancient Poets*, states that among the ancients the spondee, or its substitute the anapaest, occupied any position in a trochaic poem except the last, without distinction. By this ancient rule or practice, *furtim mulier attigit* may be retained in Prudentius.

These trochaic verses are complete catalectic tetrameters and should be written out whole, although formerly even ordinary poets divided them in the middle, as Salmasius noted in his commentary on Flavius Vopiscus. Hence, I think, Christian poets who commonly presented their hymns for singing divided these verses already in Bede’s time.

See also what I have discussed concerning this type of metre in my dissertation *On Ecclesiastical Hymns*, nos. 221 and following. There, in the note to no. 223, please correct an error, whether typographical or scribal: Meyerus says that it is known that the spondee is admitted only in the odd-numbered positions; read “in the even-numbered positions,” as can be understood from the surrounding discussion. Through a similar error, on p. 199, no. 255, “iambic trimeters” has been printed instead of “iambic dimeters.” These two errors were pointed out by the most prolific poet and my very dear friend, the distinguished Dominicus Naxera; I neither wished nor ought to pass them over.]

### 230. Tenth type: a single-form ode

All the verses are anapaestic catalectic dimeters. Chamillard calls them catalectic trimeters; perhaps he wrote, or intended to write, “dimeters” or “hypercatalectic trimeters.” They consist of three feet and one syllable. The feet are anapaests, with a spondee admitted in the first position, as Chamillard maintains; Aldus adds that in Prudentius a spondee is also introduced in the second position, which is true. Of this type is Hymn 10 of the *Cathemerinon*, which is scanned as follows:

> Deus igne-e, fons anima-rum.

[Note: [Col. 0747D] Barthius, in Book XXI, chapter 4 of the *Adversaria*, observing the metre of this hymn of Prudentius, notes that it is suited to funeral songs and is very ancient, as may be seen in the Greek verses of Timotheus quoted by Macrobius, Book VII, chapter 16. Among the Latins, Varro celebrated its use in the *Margopoli*; those who followed, whose works still survive, include Martianus Capella in Book II, Terentianus in his treatment of the catalectic anapaestic metre, who inserted several such verses of Serenus, and Boethius in Book III of the *Consolation of Philosophy*, metre V. Boethius also uses a spondee in the second position:

> Foedis submittat habenis.  
> May he submit to foul reins.]

### 231. Eleventh type: a two-form, two-stanza ode

The first verse is a catalectic Euripidean trochaic dimeter, consisting of three chorees and a syllable, with a spondee admitted in the second position. The second verse is a catalectic Hipponactean iambic trimeter, consisting of five iambs and one syllable, with a spondee admitted in the first and third positions.

Of this type is the ode in which Prudentius speaks about his own little works. For us it is the epilogue of the work; for others, the preface to the *Peristephanon*. The first verse is scanned in this way:

> Immo-lat De-o Pa-tri.

The second as follows:

> Pius fide-lis in-no-cens pu-di-cus.

[Note: [Col. 0748D] Chamillard wished to call these verses something else: the first an acatalectic Archilochian iambic verse consisting of an amphimacer and two iambs, and the second a catalectic Archilochian iambic trimeter consisting of the feet mentioned above. I prefer the name we have given, following Manutius more or less closely. Prudentius himself says:

> Nos citos iambicos  
> Sacramus, et rotatiles TROCHAEOS.  
> We consecrate swift iambics  
> and rolling TROCHEES.

I take this as referring to the verses of this ode, whatever others may say to the contrary.]

### 232. Twelfth type: a single-form ode

The verses are Glyconics, like the first verse of the first type. Of this type are Hymn 7 of the *Peristephanon*, “Insignem meriti virum,” and the preface to Book II *Against Symmachus*, “Simon, whom they call Peter.”

### 233. Thirteenth type: elegiac verses

Of this type are Hymn 8 of the *Peristephanon*, concerning the place where the martyrs suffered, and Hymn 11 of the *Peristephanon*, in praise of Saint Hippolytus. Since its explanation is obvious and well known, we may safely omit it.

### 234. Fourteenth type: a two-form, two-stanza ode

The first verse is a hexameter; the second is an iambic senarius, discussed above under the seventh type. Of this type is Hymn 9 of the *Peristephanon*, concerning Saint Cassianus.

### 235. Fifteenth type: a two-form, two-stanza ode

The first verse is a dactylic Archilochian heptameter, as some more recent writers call it; the ancients more accurately called it an odd-syllabled heroic hexameter, consisting of seven feet, of which the first four are dactyls and the last three trochees. Spondees may be substituted for the dactyls.

The second verse is a catalectic iambic trimeter, discussed under the eleventh type. Of this type is Hymn 12 of the *Peristephanon*, in honor of the holy apostles Peter and Paul. The first verse should be scanned as follows:

> Plus soli-to coe-unt ad-gaudia, dic a-mice quid sit.  
> They gather together more than usual for rejoicing; tell me, friend, what it is.

Prudentius observes this rule: he always uses a dactyl in the first, second, and fourth positions, and always a spondee in the third.

### 236. Sixteenth type: a single-form ode

The verses are acatalectic dactylic Archilochians, which I explained under the fifteenth type. Of this type is Hymn 13 of the *Peristephanon*, concerning Saint Cyprian:

> Punica terra tulit, quo splendeat omne, quidquid usquam est.  
> The Punic land produced him, so that everything existing anywhere might shine.

### 237. Seventeenth type: a single-form ode

The verses are dactylic Alcaians, consisting of a first foot that is either a spondee or an iamb, a second iamb, a long caesura, and two dactyls. Of this type is Hymn 14 of the *Peristephanon*, concerning Saint Agnes. Its scansion is:

> Agnes-sepul-crum-romule’-in domo.  
> Agnes’s tomb in the Roman house.

### 238. Eighteenth type: a two-form ode

The first verse is an iambic senarius, discussed under the seventh type. The second is an iambic dimeter, discussed under the second type. Of this type is the preface to the *Apotheosis*:

> Est vera secta? te, magister, consulo.  
> Is this the true sect? Master, I ask you.

> Rectamne servamus fidem?  
> Are we preserving the right faith?

The remaining poems are heroic, in hexameter verse: the *Apotheosis*, *Hamartigenia*, *Psychomachia*, the Books *Against Symmachus*, and the *Dittochaeum*. The measure of the hexameter is too well known to require explanation from us.

## CHAPTER XXVII. The Latinity of Prudentius

### 239

Horace’s judgment is well known:

> Mediocribus esse poetis  
> Non homines, non dii, non concessere columnae.  
> Neither men, nor gods, nor columns have permitted poets to be mediocre.

If the best Latin poet is one who does not rise above the elegance of the Latin language in the Augustan age, I might perhaps concede that Prudentius was a mediocre poet. But I shall set against Horace’s judgment a passage of Cicero from the beginning of the *Orator*:

“For among poets there is room not only for Homer (to speak of the Greeks), or Archilochus, or Sophocles, or Pindar, but also for those below them, and even below the second rank. Nor did the greatness of Plato deter Aristotle from writing philosophy; nor did Aristotle himself, with his remarkable knowledge and abundance, suppress the studies of others. Nor were outstanding men deterred from the best pursuits alone; even craftsmen did not withdraw from their arts because they could not imitate the Jalysus, which we saw at Rhodes, or the beauty of the Coan Venus. Nor, deterred by the statue of Olympian Jupiter or the Doryphorus, did the rest become less experienced in discovering what they could accomplish or how far they could advance. Their number was so great, and the praise awarded each in his own field so considerable, that although we admired the highest achievements, we nevertheless approved the lower.”

Some may think that Cicero sought a place for his own poems when he declares that there is room for poets below the second rank. But the matter stands thus: although Prudentius possesses everything that makes an outstanding poet, if the purest language customary in the Augustan age is lacking, this does not justify those who delight in poetic talent in arguing that he should not be read with profit. First, if anyone wishes to treat a Christian subject in verse, he could find no better model elsewhere. Moreover, in other matters many things are found in him expressed with the greatest elegance and drawn from the best authors, so that one can reject scarcely a few—and, if ecclesiastical terms are excepted, fewer than are found in Ausonius and his other contemporaries. Furthermore, since Prudentius treated the most difficult theological questions, he was obliged either to devise many technical terms or to use terms devised by other Christian writers.

### 240

Giselinus placed in an appendix all the words which Cornelius Valerius, public professor of the Latin language, judged to be as far as possible from the purity of Latin speech, and rendered them with Latin words so that younger writers would not be misled in imitating them. Petrus Rodriguez de Castro reports that Antonius Nebrissensis made a similar catalogue. I have not seen Nebrissensis’s Lucronian edition of the commentaries; in another old edition, mentioned at no. 107, this catalogue is missing. I shall append Giselinus’s catalogue so that others may judge:

[Note: [Col. 0749B–0750D]

- *Aenipes*: having bronze feet.
- *Altrinsecus*: on the other side, reciprocally.
- *Amasio*: lover, paramour.
- *Arula*: diminutive of *ara*, altar.
- *Audientia*: hearing, the power of hearing.
- *Aurulentus*: shining from the reflection of gold.
- *Bifestus*: a day sacred twice over, as though one said “twice a festival.”
- *Bractealis*: gilded with gold leaf.
- *Bustialis*: he coined it from *bustum*, pyre or tomb.
- *Cantamen*: enchantment.
- *Carceralis*, *carcereus*: from a prison.
- *Carnalis*, *carnaliter*: from flesh; carnally.
- *Carnulentus*: devoted to flesh and the world.
- *Centuplicatus*: hundredfold.
- *Collumino*: I illuminate.
- *Comperpetuus*: equally eternal.
- *Complices*: accomplices in crimes.
- *Congregatim*: in a dense mass, in a troop.
- *Congrex*: unanimous.
- *Conspicabilis*: conspicuous.
- *Corporalis*: bodily.
- *Creamen*: creation, or a created thing.
- *Cruciamen*: torment.
- *Defuga*: deserter, fugitive.
- *Digestim*: distinctly, in due order.
- *Dilancinare*: to tear apart.
- *Discruciatus*: various pains and torments.
- *Disparilis*: unequal, unlike.
- *Excruciabilis*: tormenting.
- *Excruciatus*: torment, pain.
- *Exfibulare*: to remove, undo, or release brooches or clasps.
- *Exsequialis*: used in funeral rites.
- *Exsimulare*—read *exsinuare*: to unfold in the manner of folds or bosoms and extend more widely.
- *Exsibilare*: to drive out by hissing. He combined it very well in “He hisses out serpentine words.”
- *Fabriliter*: in the manner of a craftsman.
- *Factura*: work, a created thing.
- *Falsificatus*: falsified, corrupted.
- *Fidelis*: endowed with the Christian religion, faithful.
- *Figmen*: work, a product.
- *Flabralis*: capable of being blown, emitted with a breath.
- *Forare*: to pierce.
- *Fotus*: fomentation.
- *Fulgidus*: shining, brilliant.
- *Frugescere*: to be fertile in crops.
- *Fundalis*: an adjective from *funda*, sling.
- *Funerare*: to bring to a funeral; read “to carry out for burial.”
- *Genealogus*: author of genealogies, tracing each family back to its origin.
- *Hydrinus*: an adjective from *hydra*, serpent.
- *Hymnire*: to sing hymns.
- *Ignire*: to burn, brand.
- *Impassibilis*: incapable of suffering.
- *Impiatum*: impure.
- *Incapax*: entirely incapable.
- *Incentivum*: inciting, kindling.
- *Incerare*: to coat with wax.
- *Incircumscriptus*: ἀπεριγραπτὸς, unlimited, without bounds.
- *Incorporatus*: clothed with a body and, so to speak, incarnate.
- *Indages*: investigation, pursuit.
- *Indomabilis*, *indominus*: undominated.
- *Innatus*: never born, unbegotten.
- *Inspatiari*: to walk about.
- *Insubjectus*: subject to no one, independent.
- *Intemporalis*: eternal, bounded by no time.
- *Interminus*: the same.
- *Irremotus*: unmoved.
- *Irritamen*: incitement.
- *Liquabile*: easily melted.
- *Litamen*: sacrifice.
- *Malefabrum*: unlucky, unskilled, imprudent.
- *Mammoneus*: greedy; derived from *Mammon*, the Pluto of the Syrians.
- *Manceps carceris*: superintendent of a prison. Thus Pliny calls the keeper of a cobbler’s workshop its *manceps*.
- *Mediator*: intermediary, μεσίτης.
- *Melodum*: sweet-sounding.
- *Mitificus*: mild, gentle.
- *Muculentus*: mucous.
- *Monstruosus*, *monstrosus*: monstrous.
- *Mortificatus*: dead, lifeless.
- *Multicolora*: multicolored.
- *Multinodus*: knotty, having many knots.
- *Mundialis*: worldly.
- *Nemo dies*: no day.
- *Nescienter*: ignorantly, as though from *negligenter*.
- *Noxialis*: owed to the guilty or harmful person.
- *Oblacterare*: to bleat against someone like a sheep.
- *Oblivialis*: forgetful, causing forgetfulness.
- *Obludere*: to lure with a deceptive appearance.
- *Obsequela*: obedience.
- *Obstrangulatus*: strangled, suffocated.
- *Occidualis*: setting, western.
- *Omniformis*, *omniparens*, and *omnipollens* are of the same kind.
- *Opulens*, *opulentum*: opulent, wealthy.
- *Orarium*: a sweat-cloth drawn from the mouth.
- *Palpamen*: touching, stroking.
- *Palpebralis*: projecting at the eyelids.
- *Parricidialis*: stained by parricide.
- *Passibilis*: capable of suffering.
- *Passio*: affliction, suffering.
- *Peccamen*: crime, sin.
- *Plasmatus*: formed, created.
- *Praenuncupatus*: announced beforehand.
- *Primitivus*: first-born, original.
- *Propitiabilis*: propitious, favorable.
- *Prosperatus*: granted in response to prayer.
- *Pudescit*: it shames, one is ashamed.
- *Resculpere*: to imitate, reproduce.
- *Resultare*: to celebrate together.
- *Romphaeale*: something that supplies the use of a *romphaea*, a sword.
- *Ructamen*: belching.
- *Rosulentus*: rosy; he coined it on the model of *rorulentus*, dewy.
- *Sagus*, *praesagus*: prophetic, presaging.
- *Saporum*: savory.
- *Segrex*: separated, divided into two parts.
- *Separ*: the same.
- *Sensualis*: capable of reason.
- *Sequestrare*: to commit something to someone’s custody.
- *Spurcamen*: filth, uncleanness.
- *Speculamen*: sight, the power of seeing.
- *Stigmare*: to brand with a mark.
- *Strictura*: liquefaction.
- *Subjectio*: obedience, submission.
- *Sublidere*: to crush or suppress slightly.
- *Sublimare*: to raise aloft.
- *Subternus*: subterranean.
- *Sufflabilis*: fashioned by breath or spirit.
- *Suggillare*: to suggest, supply.
- *Superfio*: I surpass, I rise above.
- *Terrulente*: thickly, densely.
- *Terrulentus*: earthen, made of earth.
- *Tripictus*: painted with a threefold tongue.
- *Tutaculum*: protection, safeguard.
- *Ululamen*: a howl.
- *Vaporus*: vapor-bearing.
- *Vegetamen*: growth, movement.
- *Veniabile*: deserving pardon.
- *Ventilari*: to be whirled about, to be inconsistent.
- *Versicolorus*: multicolored; he reduces this compound only once to the second declension.
- *Veternus*, *veternosus*, *inveteratus*: sluggish; long-standing, inveterate.
- *Vians*: traveler.
- *Vitiabilis*: corrupted, corruptible.
- *Virginal*: ὑμὴν, a virgin membrane or bond.
- *Viscereus*: created, arising from the viscera.]

Thus others may judge.

Ludewigius, as he says, would scarcely approve every item marked as impure in Giselinus’s catalogue, since some may be thoroughly Latin and merely uncommon. Macrobius, in Book VI, chapter 4, brings forward many rare words used by Virgil:

> “Which,” he says, “the neglect of antiquity makes seem NEW TO US.”

Prudentius used certain words of Lucretius and the older writers out of love for antiquity, a practice that particularly becomes a poet when done sparingly. Others used by him may once have been obsolete but had revived in his time—something Horace both predicted and did not disapprove:

> “Many things will be reborn that have already fallen,” and so forth.

Giselinus placed several ecclesiastical terms in his catalogue, such as *fidelis*, *mediator*, and *passio*. Others have suitable authority among the ancients, such as *fulgidus* and *omniparens*. Still others cannot confidently be called Prudentian, since the manuscripts vary, such as *nescienter* and *insubjectus*. Most can be defended by the authority of Prudentius’s contemporaries or of earlier writers.

Certainly, among the words criticized in Prudentius, none is less Latin or more deserving of avoidance than the word used by the author of the catalogue:

> *Sufflabilis*, spiritu EFFORMATUS.  
> “Fashioned by breath or spirit.”

I know that more recent writers commonly use *efformo, efformas*, but it is not found among the ancient Latins. Jacobus Facciolatus—or whoever is the author of the dictionary published under his name—places it among barbarous words, and nevertheless uses it more than once in compiling the dictionary.

But if Giselinus was eager to identify every word found in Prudentius and occurring rarely or never in the books of the Augustan age that have come down to us, he could have produced a much longer catalogue. In the commentaries we shall point out some matters useful for this purpose, and at the end of the second volume we shall present an index of the rarer words occurring in Prudentius that may in some way become subjects of controversy.

I shall summon ancient Latin writers to confirm the use of a word in such a way that I shall sometimes neither quote the words nor indicate the passages, when these can readily be found in the accurate dictionaries of Facciolatus, Forcellini, and others; or in Christophorus Cellarius’s later work, revised for the third time, *On Barbarisms and Idioms of the Latin Language*; in Olai Borrichius’s *Analecta*; or in Andrea Borrichius’s appendix to Cellarius’s *Later Work*, namely, his observations concerning the Latin language, to which Cellarius opposed a discussion of the Danish appendix.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Testimonies of Certain Ancient and Modern Writers Concerning Prudentius. His Ancient Imitators

### C. SOLLIUS APOLLINARIS SIDONIUS

(*Book II, Letter 9*)

### 241
