### 242. SAINT ISIDORE OF SEVILLE

(*In his Library*)

> Si Maro, si Flaccus, si Naso, et Persius horret,  
> If Maro, Flaccus, Naso, and Persius weary you,
>
> Lucanus si te, Papiniusque tedet:  
> if Lucan and Papinius bore you,
>
> Par eat eximio dulcis Prudentius ore,  
> let sweet Prudentius, with distinguished utterance, go alongside,
>
> Carminibus variis nobilis ille satis.  
> noble enough in his varied poems.

[Note: [Col. 0751C] Muratorius, in Volume II of the *Anecdota*, p. 208, describes these poems under the title: “Very ancient verses once read in the library of Saint Isidore of Seville,” from a very ancient codex. Muratorius thought these poems had never been printed; but Joannes Tamayus de Salazar had already published a large part of them in the *Hispanic Martyrology*, on April 4. Muratorius has forty-six couplets, Tamayus thirty-two, most of them identical, though some differ.

It is of great importance that Muratorius published them, for if only Tamayus’s name appeared, everyone would doubt their authenticity. Now, because both Muratorius and a very ancient codex are named, no one will call the truth into question. Nor shall I oppose anything, provided the codex really was very ancient; otherwise the Milanese Library would arouse some suspicion in me, since it is known that several monuments brought from Spain were formerly introduced there.

Nor is it clear to me whether Muratorius subjected the codex’s antiquity to examination and, if he did, whether he applied all the diligence required in such a matter. Muratorius does not seem to have sufficiently recognized the frauds that had become widespread in the previous century in fabricating writings by Spanish authors. Evidence of this suspicion appears in Volume IV of his *Inscriptions*, p. 1953, no. 2, where he produces the epitaph of Wistremirus, archbishop of Toledo, “with Julian, archdeacon of Saint Justa at Toledo,” as he says, “from my notes.” After raising and resolving a difficulty concerning the Leonine verses of which the epigram consists, he adds:

“What perhaps presents itself to me with greater difficulty: in this title, insignia seem to be designated (we now call them *le armi*, coats of arms) . . . Were such insignia in use in the ninth century? I do not think so. I therefore leave this knot for learned Spaniards to untie.”

Muratorius had not, therefore, read what Niccolò Antonio had extensively discussed concerning the forged writings of that archdeacon Julian in Book VII of the *Bibliotheca Hispana Vetus*.

But, to return to the verses of Saint Isidore: in the latest Madrid edition of Saint Isidore’s works, the same couplets are presented in an expanded form from manuscript codex B of the Royal Library. Petrus Crinitus, Book V of *On Latin Poets*, chapter 90, says that Isidore testifies that Prudentius was trained in Latin literature with great diligence and equal zeal; but he does not state where he read this, and I cannot find it myself.]

### THE VENERABLE BEDA, PRIEST

(*On Metrical Theory*)

An iambic senarius admits an iamb in every position, a tribrach in every position except the last, and a spondee, dactyl, or anapaest only in the odd-numbered positions; it admits a pyrrhic only in the final position. In this metre the most distinguished Spanish scholar, Aurelius Prudentius Clemens, wrote the preface to the *Psychomachia*, that is, the book which he composed in heroic verse about the struggle between virtues and vices. Thus he begins:

> Senex fidelis, prima credendi via.  
> Faithful old man, the first path of belief.

[Note: [Col. 0752D] Weitzius, and even more Chamillard, corrupt this passage in such a way that one cannot understand what Bede intended.]

[Note: [Col. 0752D] He lists him among the books he habitually read. He more than once employs his authority to confirm doctrines of the faith. Rabanus borrowed from this same Theodulf the words that I shall shortly quote. For Agobard, see the commentary on Hymn 7, verse 160; for Lupus of Ferrières, see *Hamartigenia*, verse 2.]

>

> will lay the power of idolatry overturned to its foundations;
>
> Ac penitus tetri lingua teretur hydri.

> Inclytus hic martyr elingui concinet ore,

>
> Heroumque acer rite canetur agon.

>

>

> the concluding Muse rings out in varied song.
>

>

> turn it over in your mind, and hold fast to it in your conduct.

>
> Pro me, proque meo, qui notat haec, famulo.  
> for me, and for my servant who records these things.

[Note: [Col. 0753D] I compared this epigram, copied by the distinguished Teolius, with the manuscript itself. In the first verse I change nothing, although in the manuscript I found *dinoscere* instead of *noscere*: this is evidently a metrical error made by the servant who recorded the verses. In verse 9, Teolius omitted the word *libri*; in verse 11, the word *frequens*—both of which are in the manuscript and without which the verses are defective. Teolius read *In aliis* in verse 10; I read *Finalis* from the manuscripts, which metre and sense require. The first pages of the book precede it, and *Finalis musa* corresponds to them.

All Prudentius’s poems are indicated in the order in which they occur in this codex: 1. “Hymns of Christ’s followers,” that is, the book of the *Cathemerinon*; 2. the *Apotheosis*; 3. the *Hamartigenia*; 4. the *Psychomachia*; 5. the Books *Against Symmachus*; 6. the *Romanus*; 7. the *Peristephanon*; 8. “The concluding Muse in varied song,” which is the *Dittochaeum*.]

### NOTKER BALBULUS

(*On Illustrious Men*, chapter 7)

If you seek metres as well, you do not need the myths of the pagans; rather, in Christianity you have the very wise Prudentius, singing most sweetly about the origin of the world, the martyrs, the praises of God, and the fathers of the New and Old Testaments; presenting the conflict between virtues and vices with the sweetest allegorical charm; and fighting most fiercely against heretics and pagans.

### BRUNO, BISHOP OF COLOGNE

(*From Georgius Fabricius, on the hymn for the eighth day before the Kalends of January*)

### 244

Prudentius deservedly holds—and formerly held—a place in the libraries of learned men and in the minds of the devout. Bruno, bishop of Cologne, duke of Saxony, and brother of the emperor Otto I, gave his volume to all the churches and himself always held it in his hands.

In the *Life of Bruno*, written by his contemporary and household companion Rotgerus, preserved by the Bollandists under October 11, we read:

“When he had received the first rudiments of grammar, as we learned from Bruno himself, who often recalled this in praise of almighty God, he began, at the direction of his teacher, to read the poet Prudentius. Since Prudentius is Catholic both in faith and intention, outstanding in eloquence and truth, and most elegant in his metres and books, he soon pleased the palate of Bruno’s heart with such sweetness that Bruno drank in not only the knowledge of external words but also the innermost marrow of meaning and, so to speak, its most limpid nectar, with an eagerness greater than can be expressed. Later, there was no branch of liberal studies in all Greek or Latin eloquence that escaped the keenness of his intellect.”

[Note: [Col. 0754D] The distinguished Joseph Petiscus, an excellent judge in such matters, argued from this and other evidence that the tenth century was not as dark and ignorant as many proclaim. Most of those who everywhere denounce the ignorance and darkness of the tenth century cannot be compared with him, whether one considers the serious sciences or every branch of more attractive literature.

In the same century the poet Roswitha also flourished, learned in both Latin and Greek. She composed in heroic verse a panegyric of the emperor Otto, Bruno’s brother, and described in the same metre the martyrdom of Blessed Pelagius, a Spanish boy. The Bollandists present this poem among the authentic acts of Saint Pelagius the martyr, no less than the hymns with which Prudentius celebrated other martyrs.]

**GEORGIUS FABRICIUS**

*(Commentary on the Christian poets, p. 17.)*

247. Caesarius attributes to Prudentius seriousness and elegance in certain passages; Rivius, piety and a genuinely Christian spirit. Vives considers him the one poet who should be read (I do not find this statement, nor does it agree with what Vives teaches elsewhere). Some attribute to him Roman eloquence, or at least something close to it. We would not have known the name of Leonard Quercetanus, an obscure man, had he not judged Prudentius badly. Lilius ascribes to him extensive and varied learning, but says that in eloquence and purity of language he was either of little ability, or rather neglected these qualities. We grant neither point to a man who is himself neither eloquent nor elegant enough to judge eloquence and purity of expression.

[Col. 0756B]

[Note: [Col. 0755C] Also in the preface to his *Exposition on Certain Hymns of Prudentius*: “The obscure men Leonard Quercetanus and Petrus Summontius deprive Prudentius of learning, leaving him nothing but bare religion, with which we are content; and we consider that man, outstanding in nobility and learning, greater than those shadows perceived him to be, and possessed of more of the ancient Roman elegance than they themselves either understood or attained.” Again, in the preface to the hymn for 8 Kalends of January: “As a young man I heard from the most learned men Andrea Comitiano and Gaspare Bornero, and I remember their approval, that the writings of Aurelius Prudentius had once been proposed in the public examination to those seeking the customary honors of the liberal studies.”]

**GISELINUS**

*(In the dedicatory letter of the first edition.)*

212 248. Aurelius Prudentius Clemens is uniquely worthy of admiration for his incredible devotion to piety and his profound knowledge of the most praiseworthy sciences. Although the excellence and variety of his subject matter are remarkable and extraordinary, he nevertheless depicts and pursues each matter, however serious and difficult, in a harmonious and polished manner, with embellishments and lights partly discovered by himself and partly drawn from the most abundant source of antiquity, while continually keeping himself within the bounds of sacred religion.

[Note: [Col. 0755D] And at the end of the annotations: “Once the style had been sufficiently examined, there was no great need to labor over the subject, since it is easy and familiar to everyone. For, to speak freely on this point also, I still cannot agree with Erasmus in a certain apology against Latomus, where he denies that Prudentius ought to be read aloud to children because only theologians can understand him. What, after all, are those obscure matters, [Col. 0756C] hidden from the common understanding of children? I have not yet been able to discover them. If he is speaking of the *Apotheosis* (as he certainly is), I admit that some matters lie somewhat beyond the customary knowledge of children, namely those dealing with disputed questions concerning the essence of the divine Trinity. But how small a part is that, I ask? Indeed, if we required nothing in the very art of expression, with how much greater ease and with how much richer a benefit to the Christian commonwealth would children learn these things than those empty histories—or rather fables—of the poets, in which no small portion of time is miserably wasted. There would also be other much greater advantages, which it is neither the place nor the purpose of this work to enumerate.

“To return, then, to Prudentius: although there is no sound reason why he should be in everyone's hands except that he provides no slight encouragement to undertake whatever is most honorable, surely even this one reason ought to carry sufficient weight. For, if I may digress briefly, what chaste, what pious, what holy thing is not found in him? He is wholly occupied in giving thanks to God and magnifying His munificence; even the smallest matters he turns to His praise. Moreover, he adorns the martyrs with his praises. What could be more religious? What could more worthily be taken as an example? Finally, whenever he has to deal with enemies, whether internal enemies of the body—I mean vices and the desires of the soul—or external enemies, namely heretics or nations devoted to idols, good God, with what liveliness of spirit he attacks them! With what ardor he fights and lays them low! You would say he is still a soldier, not a poet.

“And in the preface to the second edition: ‘I am even more amazed that the vein of so fruitful a breast, in treating subjects so varied, so new, and so exceedingly difficult, has never run dry or failed. Certainly, among all posterity I have not yet seen anyone who has equaled him.’”]

**MARCUS HOPPERUS**

*(In the preface prefixed to Prudentius, addressed to Johann Rudolf von Erlach.)*

[Col. 0757A]

249. I do not think it necessary to say much about this author, whom I wish to be yours, or about his works, since he has always been held by pious and learned men in the same rank as any other poet, however famous. Indeed, he deserves so much greater esteem and honor because the subjects with which he deals are considered nobler, holier, and more useful than those of any pagan poet: for nearly all of them are drawn from the sources of sounder theology and provide both the material and the occasion for every kind of pious exercise.

[Note: [Col. 0757C] Hopperus proceeds to explain the subject matter of the individual poems. “For, so that I may present to you, almost word for word, the outlines of the individual little works, so that you may know them: Do you wish to be armed against the desires of the flesh? Exercise yourself in the *Psychomachia*, which comes first. Do you wish to know and sing the miracles and immeasurable benefits that our Lord Jesus Christ bestowed upon the human race? Read again the *Cathemerinon*. Do you wish your faith and constancy in the Christian religion to be strengthened by the examples of the holy martyrs? Examine the *Peristephanon*. Do you wish to avoid the false doctrines of heretics? Read the *Apotheosis* and the *Hamartigenia*. Do you wish to contemplate with abhorrence the dreadful superstitions and idolatries of the pagans? Learn what he wrote against Symmachus. Finally, do you wish to commit to memory, in abridgment (*ἐν ἐπιτομῇ*), the sacred histories of both Testaments? Unroll the *Enchiridion*, which is the last work.”]

**JACOBUS SPIEGELIUS**

*(In his commentary on the hymn “At Every Hour.”)*

250. Among the Greeks the leader of the lyric poets was Pindar, among the Latins, Horace, both of them pagans; among those who composed hymns filled with piety in honor of the true God, it was Prudentius.

**NIC. HEINSIUS**

*(In the dedicatory letter of his edition of Prudentius to Ferdinand, Bishop of Paderborn.)*

Aurelius Prudentius Clemens, than whom none of the ancients cultivated Christian poetry with greater success or commended it to fame and posterity by a more praiseworthy example, etc. You had been familiar with this poet from your earliest youth; and your Lucas Holstenius, that man of most illustrious name, admired him with you so greatly that, when already at the point of death and dying, he wished a hymn from the *Cathemerinon*, the one appointed for the funeral rites of the dead, to be recited to him by you; and in this way, with his mind raised in consolation toward the better life and filled with God, he breathed his last.

**CHAMILLARDUS**

*(In the dedicatory letter to the Dauphin.)*

251. Prudentius was held in the highest esteem by Arcadius and Honorius because he offered them an example to follow in describing those heroes of the Catholic religion. That same example is now offered to you by that supreme poet. You will, I think, favor him, and you will kindly receive, as you customarily receive other men, one flourishing in the glory of talent and piety who, through the injustice of earlier times, has lain neglected for a while.

[Note: [Col. 0757D] In his preface Chamillard praises in Prudentius his distinguished devotion to religion, his astonishing variety of learning, and those great spirits with which poets are inspired. He says that whatever is scattered and dispersed among the Greek and Latin poets, Prudentius gathered together and represented in a compendium. He says that Erasmus and Heinsius borrowed from Prudentius forms and beauties of Latin expression for their own imitation. He also says that three very wise men appointed to educate the most serene Dauphin in good arts and letters—Charles de Sainte-Maure, Duke of Montausier; Jacques-Bénigne Bossuet; and Pierre-Daniel Huet—formed an excellent judgment of Prudentius and judged him worthy of being illustrated with commentaries for the Dauphin’s use.

I once considered reprinting this edition of Chamillard, prepared with such elaborate apparatus and now sought by many, because a man of universal learning had judged that this ought to be done. But many considerations deterred me from that plan. First, that Paris edition is chiefly sought in order to complete a series of similar editions; if it were repeated with different type, it would lose its value. Moreover, the translation is often obscure and sometimes incomplete; where it is best, it is useful only to children. Many of the notes concern matters that are common and worn out; and the critical notes taken from Heinsius ought not to be copied by us, who have consulted manuscript codices, but should be subjected to examination. Finally, Chamillard generally transcribed passages of Sacred Scripture and the holy Fathers from sources that were not very clear.

If all these matters were passed over in silence at their individual locations by anyone reproducing Chamillard’s edition, others would accuse him of negligence; if they were noted, the repetition of so many things would produce intolerable boredom in the reader.]

And in the *Life of Prudentius*: “You may wonder that, although he said much about various heresies, he nevertheless wrote nothing that could be interpreted in a worse sense or be accused of error. Indeed, we can draw from his writings, as from a pure spring, all the doctrines of the holy Roman Church, and especially those concerning the mystery of the Trinity, the birth and divinity of Christ, the virginity of Mary, the veneration of the saints, and their grace and power before God. Hence all learned men who have lived have considered the authority of Prudentius by no means negligible.”

**M. D. MULLER, S.J., P.R.**

255. Finally, I shall give the names of other men who have accompanied Prudentius with their praises. Michael Piccart; Christian Becmann; Joannes Franciscus Mirandulanus; Christophorus Mylaeus; Andreas Tiraquellus, jurist; Obertus Gifanius; Hadrianus Turnebus; Christophorus Colerus; Melchior Goldastus Haiminsfeldius; Gaspar Barthius; P. Christophorus Brower; Bernardinus de Bustis; the *Catalogue of Witnesses to the Truth*; Caesar Baronius; Joannes Ludovicus Vives; Matthaeus Dresserus; Henricus Beberius; and Zacharias Victor.

Barthius, in his *Adversaria*, which Weitzius does not cite, very frequently names Prudentius, and scarcely ever without the greatest praise. I have presented some of these praises when occasion arose, and I shall present others in the commentaries. I have scattered further eulogies throughout the prolegomena, and I shall often freely transcribe elsewhere the words of others by which Prudentius is celebrated.

You may also consult the writers of ecclesiastical history, who almost all commend Prudentius’ learning, talent, and eloquence. Add the theologians who confirm the dogmas of the Catholic religion by means of his poems, especially Dionysius Petavius, who frequently cites Prudentius and, while discussing the Holy Trinity in book V, chapter 9, no. 17, composed an uncommon eulogy of Prudentius in these few words:

“Finally, what we have so far traversed in a longer discussion concerning divine generation, Prudentius has gathered together in a few verses, which it will be best to quote here: ‘This alone we know,’ etc.”

He quotes twenty-two verses from the *Apotheosis*, beginning at verse 268.

Very many interpreters of Sacred Scripture also quote verses of Prudentius, with the highest praise of the author, to explain difficult passages. Someone asserts that Estius regarded Prudentius as the best interpreter of Sacred Scripture and frequently preferred Prudentius’ understanding to the sense of all the other Fathers, both Greek and Latin, in his commentary on the apostolic epistles. For the sake of both Prudentius and Estius, I wish and judge this to be false. Read no. 136.

[Col. 0760C]

“More than anyone else, however, the never-sufficiently-praised Prudentius bears clear witness to this.”

Likewise, all those who have published libraries in which Prudentius might have had a place, especially those who have composed special works on ecclesiastical writers—among whom the most learned Ceillier stands out—have celebrated him with the greatest praise. Nor should the authors of liturgical writings be omitted, since they often accompany our poet with some exceptional eulogy, especially the most pious Cardinal Bona.

[Note: [Col. 0760D] One may consult Thomas Pope Blount in *Censura of Celebrated Authors* and Adrian Baillet in *Judgments of Wise Men*. The latter rejects the comparison between Prudentius and Horace made by Sidonius; the former does not dare to place Prudentius among the good poets. 256. Most of the ancient Christian poets who wrote after Prudentius imitated him, as though they recognized him as the father of Christian poetry. Although the reputation of some of them is obscure, this detracts nothing from Prudentius’ glory, just as it does not detract from the glory of Virgil and other ancient writers whose verses Christian poets of a later age often reproduced. Indeed, these poets owe Prudentius in large part whatever lights cause their poems to shine, since they drew from the Prudentian source those elements that most brightly stand out in their works. I shall present more examples of this kind in the commentaries; for now I shall list the names of some of them: Apollinaris Sidonius, Alcimus Avitus, Fortunatus, Theodulf of Orléans, Dudo, Hericus, Arnulfus, Dares or Joseph Devonius, Corippus, Hartmannus, and Wandelbertus.

## CHAPTER XXIX  
### On the selection of variant readings, and the symbols by which editions and manuscript codices are indicated in the commentaries

[Col. 0761B]

218 257. To make the use and understanding of the commentaries easier, certain matters must first be explained. We willingly set out the probable conjectures of learned men, but we adopt them rarely, or never, when they conflict with old books and ancient editions, especially when a satisfactory sense and the rule of meter observed by Prudentius can be maintained.

By “the reading preferred by us” we mean the reading presented in the poem, even though in the commentaries we may produce several codices against it, or declare that another reading seems equally good, [Col. 0761C] or perhaps better. In selecting readings, we considered the sense, the meter, the poet’s usage, and other similar passages, whether Prudentius himself imitated them or other ancient writers reproduced them from him. More often we prefer a larger number of very old codices to a smaller number of recent ones; sometimes, however, we prefer a few to many, and recent witnesses to ancient ones.

When we argue nothing against a variant reading found in others, we consider that it may be retained. When I speak of “our codices,” I mean chiefly the Regensburg, Prague, Angelica, Alexandrian, Marietti, Vienna, Vatican A, and Vatican B manuscripts. For I have sometimes not recorded a reading from other sources that differed from the common and established reading because it was corrupt or plainly superfluous. Often, too, the letters, almost worn away by age, escaped the eye so completely that it would have been dangerous to judge with certainty what had been written.

I distinguish the first hand of the copyist from the second hand, which I indicate by the abbreviations *m. pr.* and *m. sec.*, in such a way that by “old hand” I understand both the second and the first hand, unless I explicitly call it recent.

I usually designate manuscript and printed books that are mentioned more frequently by their initial letters only. So that the reader may easily recognize them, I shall append their catalogue.

**ALD.** The edition of Aldus Manutius, discussed above at no. 104.

[Note: [Col. 0761C] Another copy of this edition exists in the exceptionally select private library of His Holiness Pope Pius VI. Its beginning is missing, but its ending agrees with the other Aldine editions of Prudentius that I have seen. To make that question—which I touched upon at no. 104 and following, concerning three, two, or, as I think more accurately, one Aldine edition of Prudentius—easier to resolve for those able to examine other copies, I shall add some observations.

Aldus printed the Christian poets in 1501 but published them in 1502. He dedicates them to Daniel Clarius in June 1511, addressing him as follows: “At last, my Clarius, we are issuing the Christian poets, printed a year ago in our baths.” The pages are not numbered. Sedulius begins with gathering *a*, which continues through *bb*. All are gatherings of four sheets, except *d*, a gathering of two, and *bb*, a gathering of three. At the end: “Venice, at the house of Aldus, January 1501.”

In the two copies that I have seen, other works in prose and the Homerocentones of Proba Falconia follow, but with a different gathering sequence, and the year of the edition is not recorded at the end. Anyone who takes up this volume without observing the matter carefully will readily think that it was printed in 1502. If the poems of Prudentius, printed and published in 1501, were bound together with it—as can be seen in the copy in the Barberini Library—one will suppose that Prudentius too was published in 1502.

All the Aldine editions of Prudentius that I have examined have this gathering sequence and no page numbers. They begin with *ff* and end with *yy*, the last gathering being a gathering of five sheets. Aldus indicated this sequence at the beginning, and perhaps intended Prudentius to be read immediately after Arator, since Arator ends with *ee*. Aldus also prefixed the gathering sequence of the Greek works of Damascus and others, and of the poems of St. Prosper. Yet this sequence proceeds in a different order, and these works were printed separately, so that they could also be bound separately.

Thus, in some places I have seen Aldus’ Prudentius alone; elsewhere with the Greek works at the beginning and the verses of St. Prosper at the end; elsewhere with these verses first and the Greek works at the end; and elsewhere with all the other Christian poets together.]

258. I shall now briefly explain which Vatican codices are cited for the individual poems of Prudentius. I examined a total of twenty-eight Vatican codices under the name of Prudentius. Twenty-six codices therefore remain. Seven of them contain only the *Psychomachia*, namely Vatican Codices 2766, 2868, and 3267; Vatican Alexandrian Codices 1439, 1835, and 2078; and Vatican Palatine Codex 242.

Another seven codices contain only the *Dittochaeon*, namely Vatican Codex 5356; Vatican Alexandrian Codex 1838; and Vatican Otthobonian Codices 1193, 1220, 1297, 1502, and 3325.

Two Vatican Palatine codices contain only the ancient glosses: those numbered 235 and 1715.

Vatican Otthobonian Codex 237 contains only one hymn.

Nine codices therefore remain in which several poems are found. Only Vatican Alexandrian Codex 321 contains the complete works of Prudentius.

In Vatican Codex 5821, formerly Marietti’s, the book *Cathemerinon*, or the first ten hymns, is missing; several verses from the book *Peristephanon* are missing; and most of book II against Symmachus is missing.

I shall name more distinctly several manuscript codices often cited by other writers, especially critics, when the occasion arises. Perhaps commentaries on Prudentius lie hidden at Zaragoza, or in some Spanish library—commentaries which Vincentius Joannes de Lastanosa reports that Bartholomaeus de Morlanes composed—in his celebrated work *Museo de las medallas desconocidas españolas*, Huesca, Juan Nogues, 1645. In its preface he praises several persons by whose assistance he was helped, among them Doctor Bartholomaeus de Morlanes, a chaplain, as they call him, in the Church of Our Lady of the Pillar at Zaragoza, concerning whom he says: “And his studious piety applied no less diligence to commenting on certain Catholic poets, such as Aurelius Prudentius of Zaragoza,” etc.

It would be worthwhile for someone to consult those commentaries, if they are preserved anywhere; for he seems to have been exceptionally experienced in this kind of literature. According to Lastanosa, he wrote commentaries and notes on Claudian, Virgil, Martial, Valerius Flaccus, Papinius Statius, Silius Italicus, Claudius Rutilius, Alcimus Avitus, Marius Victor, Juvencus, Sedulius, Arator, Petrus Apollonius, Corippus, Justin, Boethius, Titus Alexander, Crispus Sallustius, and Lucius Florus. Joannes Mariana, Joannes Ludovicus de la Cerda, Thomas Tamayo de Vargas in the index of his *Defence of Mariana’s History*, and others celebrated his learning. He was omitted by Nicolás Antonio in the *Bibliotheca Hispana*.

At Ferrara there exist manuscript notes on the poems of Prudentius by the distinguished Father Angelo Maria Peverati, about whom Father Vezzosi gives further information in volume II of *Writers of the Order of Clerics Regular of Saint Cajetan*. Peveratus died in 1741; his notes on Sallust have been printed. In letters sent to me, the distinguished Lucianus Gallisa, prefect of the public library of Ferrara—a man fully entitled to pass judgment—praised Peveratus’s sharp judgment and uncommon learning in his notes on Prudentius. Although I was informed of this only late, I nevertheless took pains to have all Peveratus’s notes, or at least the principal ones and those most distinctly his own, sent to me. Through them, I hope, our Prudentius will be increasingly illuminated.]

In the book *Peristephanon*, however, there is some discrepancy concerning the placement of the hymns.

4. The martyrs of Zaragoza  
5. Saint Vincent  
6. Saint Fructuosus

9. Saint Cassianus  
10. Saint Romanus  
11. Saint Hippolytus  
12. Saints Peter and Paul the Apostles  
13. Saint Cyprian  
14. Saint Agnes

This same order appears in the first edition of Heinsius and in the second, prepared by others in 1701, with Heinsius’s notes, the commentary of Nebrissensis, and the glosses of Iso.

[Note: [Col. 0766C]

Here I should observe that the first edition of Heinsius was completed in 1667, as is proved by the dedicatory letter. It is therefore necessary that Remigius Ceillierius was mistaken when he claimed to possess an edition of Prudentius prepared by Heinsius at Amsterdam in 1631 and 1667. I should add that the second edition of Heinsius mentions Iso, a reference that can be elucidated from Mabillon, *Annales Benedictini*, under the year 871, no. 29. Iso was prefect of the external schools at the monastery of Saint Gall; from there he was summoned by the duke of Burgundy to educate the monks of Grandval. He died in that monastery at an advanced age on 14 May 871, not without a great reputation for holiness. He left several illustrious pupils—Notker, Ratpert, Tutilo, and others—from whom he received the surname “the Master.”]

The more recent editions preserve the same order. I shall not omit the warning that there is also variation among editions in the very numbering of the verses. Weitzius was the first to begin numbering the verses in the *Apotheosis* from the prefaces and to continue the numbering through the end of the poem; other editors do not continue the numbers of the prefaces together with those of the poem. Moreover, some admit certain verses which others reject as spurious. In addition, through the carelessness of printers the numbers frequently go astray; the Heinsian edition is sometimes infected by this defect, and the distinguished Paris and Parma editions are not free from it either. It is indeed difficult to avoid all errors of this kind; nevertheless, I shall diligently take care first that no error enter, and then that, if one does enter and might mislead others, the reader is suitably warned of it.]

[Col. 0767]

## The Poems of Marcus Aurelius Clemens Prudentius. (C)

[Note: [Col. 0767A]

Verse 1. “Through ten periods of five years,” that is, fifty years: Iso. “For fifty years”: Vatican codex A.

2. “We have been, we have lived”: Iso and Vatican A.

3. “Pivot,” that is, “year.” Here “pivot” is used for rotation; for properly speaking, a pivot is the piece of wood on which a door turns, and it is called *cardo*, as though “the heart of the door”: Iso. A wagon wheel is also called *cardo*: Vatican A. “With the revolving sun,” that is, with this life, which is always turning: I.

4. “Limit,” the limit of life: I.

5. “Old age”; he applies it to old age: I.

6. “We have spent,” namely, nothing: I.

[Col. 0767B] 7. “Age”; he describes each period of life, showing what it has done: Vatican A. “Resounding,” echoing: I.

8. “With rods”: properly, a *ferula* is the rod used by schoolmasters, with which they strike the hands of pupils. Hence Juvenal says, “And we too have withdrawn our hand from the rod.” They are called *ferulae* from their heat, because they make pupils “boil,” that is, tremble; schoolmasters carried rods for striking pupils. Properly, however, it is a kind of tree whose sap is called *thapsia*: Iso.

Properly, *ferula* is a kind of tree whose sap is called *thapsia*. Schoolmasters carried rods for striking pupils. Hence Juvenal: “And we too have withdrawn our hand from the rod”: Vatican A.

“With the toga,” the garment worn by the Romans. Before the age of fifteen, boys wore the *praetexta*; afterward, under discipline, the toga, when they had reached youthful strength. For the toga is the garment worn only by freeborn persons: I.

The *toga praetexta*, worn by the noble boys of Rome until their fifteenth year, was so called because a broad purple band was woven along its border: Vatican A.]

“Here begins the preface.” Thus Vatican codex A and, in Heinsius, the Egmondanus. Most call it the preface of the *Cathemerinon*. In Vatican A, after that first heading, the words “The book of the *Cathemerinon* begins” are repeated twice; this is how it is written. Weitzius, from the Hailsbronn codex, gave: “Here begins the hymnary for the seasons and saints throughout the year.”

Verse 1. Concerning the first letter P, on which an image of Prudentius has been engraved, see the *Prolegomena*, no. 58.

2. What Prudentius says, unless I am mistaken, is not a doubt but a cautious formula of affirmation. Someone therefore conjectured ineptly that one should read *nil fallor* (“I am not mistaken”), because later he reports that he was born when Salia was consul; I found this conjecture in some manuscript papers.

3. Peveratus wished, in his manuscript notes, “the seventh sign of the zodiac” to be understood by “the seventh pivot.” Neither Prudentius’s life nor his words permits this explanation. “The seventh pivot” means “the pivot rolls the seventh year” by metonymy. “To roll” and “to turn,” concerning the cycle of the year, occur frequently among poets and often in our author, as immediately below: “with the revolving sun.” Anacreon, Ode IV:

> For life, like the wheel of a chariot,  
> runs on, rolling forward.  
> We shall lie down for only a little while,  
> dust, when our bones have been dissolved.

6. Teolius rightly rejects the reading *Utile quid tanti* (“What useful thing of such [worth]”), found in one Vatican manuscript, since the meter opposes it. Dudo, dean of Saint-Quentin, expressed Prudentius’s words and meaning in Book III of *On the Customs of the Normans*, p. 159:

> Through five decades I have been turned in miserable life,  
> and fear of Stygian punishment presses upon me.  
> For I remember that I have done nothing good,  
> and nothing useful in so long a span of time.

That is, understand *haud quid bonitatis*: “nothing good.” Wandelbertus—or, as some write, Wandalbertus—also imitated the meter. In 842 he published a metrical martyrology:

> Behold, through three decades  
> I have lived my miserable life; and in addition the fifth  
> circuit of the age is present and moves along.  
> Now, remembering no good  
> that I have done, I am exceedingly shaken.

[Col. 0767D] 8. A gloss of Iso is similar to the gloss in Vatican A. Compare Isidore, *Etymologies*, Book XVII, chapter 9, on the *ferula*. Juvenal’s verse became proverbial. Martial calls the rod of pedagogues their scepter in Book X, epigram 62:

> And the grim rod, the scepter of pedagogues.

Ausonius likewise writes in his *Protrepticus on Juvenile Study*, addressed to his grandson Ausonius:

> The scepter that the rod brandishes, and the abundant  
> supply of switches.

For this period of Prudentius’s life and the succeeding ones, see the *Prolegomena*, no. 44 and following. By “toga,” Nebrissensis understands the manly toga, which boys assumed in their eighteenth year, at which time, as Terence says,

> The freedom of living was greater.

And Persius:

> And the now-white hem  
> permitted the eyes to scatter through the whole Subura with impunity.

The gloss of Vatican A says: “The *toga praetexta*, worn by the noble boys of Rome until their fifteenth year, was so called because a broad purple band was woven along its border.” This interpretation is supported by the fact that Prudentius seems afterward to distinguish youth: “Then wanton insolence . . . disgraced the young man.” Yet when no qualification is added, *toga* generally means the manly toga. It was usually given at the end of the sixteenth year; under the emperors sometimes later, sometimes earlier. It was also called the *libera*, because for boys it marked a certain beginning of freedom. See more in Joannes Rosinus, Book V of *Roman Antiquities*.]

9. Nebrissensis interprets this as the vice of flattery, when flattering companions, etc., drawing on Persius; or he understands by “the toga” the life of those who wear the toga and flatter kings. 10. Iso’s gloss is not pleasing: the subject is the vices of youth, not of judges. From the expressions “wanton insolence,” “petulant luxury,” and “in the filth and mud of wickedness,” Nebrissensis infers sins of lust; I do not reject this, if one understands a tendency toward those vices and keeps in view what I stated in the cited passage of the *Prologue* concerning Prudentius’s Christian humility. I argued there not as though I had established that Prudentius’s innocence was beyond doubt, but merely to show that those very serious crimes are by no means proved.

11. Read *Et luxus*, against Giselinus and Weitzius, who have *ac luxus*; below we find *sordibus ac luto*, whereas in Hailsbronn it is *et luto*. Thus *ac luxus* is not inappropriate. 14. Innocent I, in his letter to the Council of Toledo I, notes among jurists the persistence of seeking to obtain something; this is what he calls what Prudentius terms “the badly persistent desire to conquer.” They wrote at nearly the same time, but Prudentius composed this preface after that letter. Innocent indeed sent his letter to the Council of Toledo in 402 or not long afterward. Hence different opinions arose concerning the year in which that first Council of Toledo was held. Most assign it to 400; others say that it began then and continued into the following year; others again say that it was convened under Innocent; still others assert that Innocent wrote to a council that had already assembled.

In the dedicatory letter of the *Hymnody of Spain* I casually said that the council was held at the end of the fourth century, or rather at the very beginning of the fifth, that is, in the year 400. Some learned men and my friends took notice of this. But, to pass over other reasons why I could have spoken in that way, the question itself is whether the year 400 belongs to the end of the fourth century or the beginning of the fifth. Joannes Petrus Ludewigius presents the issue in these words, volume II of his works, treatise 9, Book II, column 760: “In what year did the century end—its ninety-ninth or its hundredth? This is now a common but fruitless question. For the year of Christ’s birth, and still more the endpoint of the year, remains uncertain to historians, who all argue against Dionysius Exiguus.”

16. I rejected Bivarius’s suspicion that *ter* should be read instead of *bis* in *Prolegomena*, no. 57. Chamillardus and others think that the verse indicates how many cities Prudentius governed. Incorrectly: it expresses how many times, not how many cities, he governed.]

[Col. 0770C] 17. Iso hints that Prudentius had been consul. See the *Prolegomena*, no. 51.

18. He touches on two branches of law: one concerning the adjudication of lawsuits, the other the punishment of crimes. The interpretations of others are not satisfactory. Observe that *jus reddere* (“to administer justice”) is also said of one who judges unjustly, *Digest*, Book I, title 1, law 11: “The praetor is also said to administer justice even when he decides unjustly”—the reference being not to what the praetor has actually done, but to what the praetor ought to do.

The good are called those who are not defendants in criminal cases, whether they seek something in court or whether another seeks something from them; for in this sense the plaintiff is the one who seeks, and the defendant the one from whom another seeks. Indeed, Cicero, *On the Orator*, Book II, folio 75 of the Aldine edition, says: “I call defendants not only those who are accused, but all whose case is under discussion; for that is how people formerly spoke.” But Prudentius clearly indicates defendants whose crimes are at issue and distinguishes them from the good; thus in the Theodosian Code, Book XVI, title 5, laws 9 and 13, all who are not heretics are called “good.”

22. Heinsius would prefer *volens* (“willing”) to *volans* (“flying”), against Iso, all the manuscript codices, and the editions, except the Thuaneus. The examples he accumulates, which concern something else, accomplish nothing. Prudentius does not say that life willingly performed these offices, but that it passed quickly; therefore he adds, “Gray hair crept in suddenly.” Poets frequently speak of the shortness and speed of life: “fleeting age,” “fugitive years,” “life hastens with rapid course,” “the hour flies, changeable on uncertain wings,” “life flies,” and similar expressions. Read the verses of Juvenal, which I shall now quote.

Hailsbronn, Egmondanus, and Palatine incorrectly have *Messaliae*; Vatican O, *Mesaliae*; Vaticani I and P, Widmanstadius, Bongarsius, and Goldastus, *Messaliae*; the Angelicanus, *Messalae*; others, *Massiliae*. See the *Prolegomena*, no. 39 and following.

In Vatican A the gloss is ridiculous. The distinguished Gallandius observes that the reading *me Saliae* was also approved by Almeloveen in the *Roman Consular Fasti*, p. 162; on p. 354 he arranged the years in which the Messalae were consuls differently from Chamillardus.

Peveratus rightly calls the reading *me Galliae*, which he had seen in some copies, inept. Latinius in the *Select Library* reads *me Suliae*. But since that work is posthumous, I think Latinius wrote *me Saliae*. Muratorius, in the *New Treasury of Inscriptions*, volume I, class 5, p. 379, wrote the consul’s name differently: “Filippo and Salio, consuls.” But the inscription in Muratorius is not accurately transcribed. It exists in the monastery of Saint Paul Outside the Walls and is written as follows:

> MIRI BONITATI ATQ. SANCTITATI ESVBIAE IANVARIAE CONIVGI QVE VIXIT MECVM ANNOS XVIII. M. V. D. XXV. ARRADIVS MELISSVS MARITVS ET SIBI FECIT O DEPOSITA. IN. PACE. III. KAL. APR. FILIPPO ET SALLIA COSS.
>
> “To the wondrous goodness and holiness of Esubia [reading uncertain] Januaria, my wife, who lived with me eighteen years, five months, and twenty-five days. Arradius Melissus, her husband, made this also for himself. Buried in peace, 30 March, in the consulship of Philippus and Sallia.”

Muratorius published it as:

> Mire bonitatis . . . L. Subie. Ianuarie . . . D. XX. Varadius . . . Filippo et Salio coss.
>
> “Of wondrous goodness . . . L. Subia Januaria . . . twenty days . . . Varadius . . . in the consulship of Philippus and Salius.”

I owe the correction of this inscription as printed by Muratorius to the distinguished Aloysius Galletti, bishop of Cyrene, whose name is celebrated in so many volumes of inscriptions formerly printed. When he was still a private monk, he collected with extraordinary diligence a large quantity of ancient stones from the pavement of the basilica of Saint Paul, the monastery, and the neighboring estates, placed them in the monastery cloister, and arranged them systematically, skillfully distinguishing Christian from pagan inscriptions. Others imitated this example in decorating the entrance to the Vatican Museum, which in our own time Pope Pius VI, that most munificent prince, advanced and enlarged to the admiration—and envy—of other nations.

Among the Christian inscriptions collected in that cloister is the inscription cited by Muratorius, where *Sallia* is indeed read. Yet the inscription should rather be corrected from Prudentius than Prudentius from the inscription that happens to confront us at the very threshold: “Miri bonitati.” Aldus Manutius, son of Paulus, cites an ancient inscription in his work on orthography: “C. SALLIO ARISTENETO V. C.” (“To Gaius Sallius Aristenetus, a man of consular rank”). On the other hand, it is certain that the Romans wrote *Salii* and *Saliare* with a single l.]

33. The Prudentianus has *fluunt* (“they flow”) instead of *studuit* (“it cultivated”), incorrectly. *Cujus* may be a Greek usage in the genitive, meaning “by whom you will be considered,” or it may be a nominative, as in Virgil’s “whose flock,” which someone maliciously mocked in this parody:

> Tell me, Damoetas, whose flock is it? Is it Latin?  
> No, it is Aegon’s; that is how our people speak in the country.

Cicero also uses *cuja res* (“whose affair”) in the *Verrine Orations*, 13. Plautus frequently employs *cuja*, *cujae*, and *cujum*. See Servius’s commentary on Virgil’s *Eclogue* 3 and Vossius, *On the Faults of Language*, Book I, chapter 1.

If *cujus* is understood as a genitive, it is a Greek construction similar to Juvencus, Book IV: “they rule over them,” a phrase drawn from Holy Scripture.

35. Tertullian uses the expression “sinful” in chapter 15 of *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*: “sinful flesh.” The word “sinner” is extremely common in the Church, but is not easily found among pagan writers. “To cast off folly,” as in Virgil, *Georgics* 2:

> They would cast off their woodland disposition.

36. As for the addition “if it cannot by merits,” understand this of other heroic or excellent works. For praising God, etc., if done rightly, is not without merit.

37. I discussed at greater length the most ancient Christian custom of singing hymns day and night, based on Christ’s example and apostolic tradition, in the special dissertation prefixed to the *Hymnody of Spain*: “On Ecclesiastical Hymns, Their Correction, and Their Best Arrangement.”

38. This verse and the preceding one express the purpose of the book *Cathemerinon*, which includes hymns to be sung throughout the day and night. Therefore Rat is incorrect in reading *vox ulla* (“any voice”) instead of *nox ulla* (“any night”).

39. The Egmondanus has *puget*, erroneously, instead of *pugnet*. Teolius notes here: “HERESIES,” with the middle syllable lengthened; he meant to say that the first syllable is short. It is appropriate for the *Apotheosis* and the *Hamartigenia* to fight against heresies and examine the Catholic faith. It is also appropriate for the *Psychomachia*, in which the Catholic faith takes the leading role against idols and heresy, and in which the poet attacks the Photinian heretics, the Antidicomarianites, and likewise Carpocrates, Ebion, Cerinthus, and Tertullian, as we shall note from Chamillardus at verse 79 of the *Psychomachia*. Why should the same not be said of the *Dittochaeum*, which survives, and of the *Hexaemeron*, which is lost? Is not the Catholic faith examined in this kind of poetry?

“To examine” means to investigate, arrange systematically, and illuminate, as Barthius observes from this passage of Prudentius in *Adversaria*, Book LXIX, chapter 5. Forcellinus, in his very comprehensive dictionary, recognized only *discussus*, *discussor*, and *discussio*; yet for these words he does not produce authors superior to Prudentius. In the Theodosian Code, under the title *On the Examiners*, the verb *discutio* occurs more than once; Prudentius also repeats it elsewhere. On the designation “Catholic faith,” see *Prolegomena*, chapter 21.

40. This and the following verse indicate the two books Against Symmachus.

41. Properly, *labes* means damage or destruction; hence, as some think, *labor*, “I am ruined,” and *labor*, “I struggle.” “To bring ruin upon the innocent” is Cicero’s phrase in the speech for Caelius, p. 46. In ecclesiastical usage, an “idol” is a fictitious god.

42. The book *Peristephanon* is indicated by this verse; in its twelfth hymn the passion of the Apostles Peter and Paul is celebrated. Observe that Prudentius neither named nor praised holy confessors, because in his time either martyrs alone, or martyrs especially, were celebrated.

Much later than Prudentius, in the year 632, only hymns in praise of God, the apostles, and the triumphs of the martyrs are mentioned in canon 13 of the Fourth Council of Toledo: “And because it is known that certain hymns composed through human effort in praise of God and the apostles and the triumphs of the martyrs exist, such as those which the most blessed teachers Hilary and Ambrose published,” etc.

Saint Gregory the Great, in the decree of the Roman Council of 597, restraining the people who readily paid veneration to recently deceased Roman pontiffs, says: “And although many coverings from the sacred bodies of apostles and martyrs are present, that which is reserved with great reverence is taken from the body of sinners.”

Nevertheless, it is established that the public cult of confessors began in the fourth century. Although Saint Martin may perhaps have been the first to receive worship through more solemn festivals and ecclesiastical office in various dioceses and regions, I am certain that before him certain confessors had been honored publicly and religiously.

Saint Jerome, in his *Life of Saint Hilarion*, reports that Saint Antony ordered his body to be buried in an unknown place, lest Pergamius, who was extremely wealthy in those regions, carry the saint’s body to his estate and build a *martyrium* there. Why would he have done this if no example had preceded him? I pass over Saint Hilarion, Saint Ephrem the Syrian, and others.

In any event, the *martyrologies* took their name from the martyrs, who were the largest group, and I do not doubt that in former times the term “martyrs,” when saints were being discussed, sometimes included confessors as well. Saint Isidore explains this in Book VII, chapter 11, of the *Etymologies*.

Saint Jerome called a small shrine or altar that Pergamius was going to build after removing Saint Antony’s body a *martyrium*. In the epitaph of Paula, chapter 13, he says: “Your mother, crowned by a long martyrdom.” For not only the shedding of blood in confession is counted as martyrdom; the service of a devoted and undefiled mind is also a daily martyrdom.

Martyr is understood in nearly this sense in Ammianus Marcellinus, Book XXVII, chapter 7: “Those whom you order to be killed as harmful persons, Christian religion honors as martyrs, that is, ACCEPTABLE TO THE DIVINITY.” Compare Benedict XIV, *On the Beatification*, Book I, chapter 5.]

44. Prudentius calls the body itself the “chains of the body,” because it is the soul’s bond. I know that some excessively scrupulous theologians dislike calling the body the prison or bond of the soul. I shall remove their scruples in the hymn *On Funerals*. For now I shall cite only the Apostle, Romans 7: “Who will free me from this body of death?” And Philippians 1:23: “Having the desire to depart and be with Christ.” Saint Ambrose refers to this in Book II of his *Commentary on Luke*, chapter 2, speaking of the old man Simeon: “Desiring to be released from the bonds of bodily frailty,” etc. See also: “Just as though enclosed in a bodily prison of material mass, he wishes to be released, so that he may begin to be with Christ.”

45. In the Rat manuscript: “The preface ends.” Our old heading and the poem itself sufficiently demonstrate that this preface belongs to all the little works Prudentius was then publishing. Dungalus, writing against Claudius of Turin, called it the preface of the book. See the *Prolegomena*, nos. 51 and 243.

Scaliger, Book VI of the *Poetics*, thinks that before Claudian the first and only person to attach a preface to his poems was Persius. The distinguished Michael of Saint Joseph followed Scaliger in the *Critical Bibliography*, under “Claudianus.” But Scaliger ought not to have been unaware that others besides Persius, and before Persius, had done this. To omit our Prudentius, who was a contemporary of Claudian, Catullus begins with a preface addressing Cornelius Nepos: “To whom shall I give this charming new little book?” Martial regularly attaches prefaces to his books, not only in epigrams but also in prose, which he calls a letter, as in the prefaces to Books I and II: “Why do we need a LETTER, you ask?” . . . “I see why tragedians receive a LETTER, since they are not permitted to speak for themselves. Epigrams . . . on whatever page one wishes, they make a LETTER.”

Among Christian poets, Prudentius also had Juvencus to imitate; Juvencus added a prologue to his books on Gospel history. I shall speak of epilogues in their proper place.]

Cathemerinon, genitive plural: that is, “daily,” or “of consecrations” or “dedications,” I.

Verse 1. “The bird”: through the cock, which announces the day by its crowing, Christ is signified, who calls our minds from unbelief to true life, to true light, I.]

[Note: [Col. 0775A]

**Cathemerinon.** Thus most manuscript copies and editions; Gennadius, Theodulf of Orléans in his book *On the Holy Spirit*, Bergomensis in the *Chronicle* under the year 400, and Trithemius call the book of hymns. Yet I do not doubt that *Cathemerinon* is a Prudentian title: for Iso reads it so, as do manuscripts older than Iso. Iso’s gloss is: “*Cathemerinon*, etc.” Weitzius, I do not know from what manuscript, gives this title: “Here begins the book *Cathemerinon* of Aurelius Prudentius Clemens, a most noble and eloquent poet.” In Rat. it is: “Here begins the book of hymns of Aurelius Prudentius Clemens, a most noble and eloquent poet. Book One: *Cathemerinon*.” In Prag.: “The book of hymns of Aurelius Prudentius Clemens, a most noble and eloquent poet, who flourished under the emperor Theodosius in the year of the Lord 387. He wrote the *Dirocheum*, the *Sichomachia*, against Symmachus, etc.” In the old edition seen by Fabricius: “The book of Daily Hymns, which is also called *Cathemerinon*.” As for the fact that some move the last two hymns from their proper place, they do not do so correctly unless they also move the hymn *On the Dead*, *On Those Who Fast*, *After Fasting*, and also *At Every Hour*, which fit the title *Cathemerinon* no more than do the last two. [Col. 0775D] Trithemius made two books of hymns out of one, perhaps in order to distinguish the daily hymns, or *cathemerina*, from the others. In truth, all the hymns that are not about the saints can appropriately be gathered into this book, called *Cathemerinon* from its principal and largest part. I do not agree with Heinsius, who thinks that Prudentius borrowed the title *Cathemerinon* from Acts of the Apostles, chapter VI, where the phrase καθημερινὴ διακονία—“daily ministry”—occurs; for a very different matter is presented there: “Now in those days, as the number of the disciples increased, there arose a murmuring of the Greeks against the Hebrews, because their widows were being neglected in the daily ministry.” Georgius Remus, who said in his notes that Ausonius’s *Ephemeris* and Prudentius’s *Cathemerinon* have the same subject, does not seem to have read Ausonius’s *Ephemeris*, whose subject is [Col. 0776C] the business of the entire day.

**At cockcrow**, so Vatt. A and I, and Weitz. Others: “at the cock’s crow”; Vat. P: “before dawn.” On cockcrow, see Apuleius and Isidore, *Etymologies*, book V, chapters 30 and 31, together with Grialis’s notes. The hours at which prayers were to be offered to God are expressly given in *The Apostolic Constitutions*, book VIII, chapter 34: “Pray in the morning, at the third hour, the sixth, and the ninth, and in the evening, and at cockcrow. In the morning, giving thanks because he has enlightened us, removed the night, and restored the day. At the third hour, because at that hour Pilate pronounced judgment against the Lord. At the sixth, because at that hour he was led to the cross. At the ninth, because then all things were shaken and trembled when the Lord was crucified, since they shuddered at the Jews’ audacity and could not bear the Lord’s insult. In the evening, because he gave the night for rest from the labors of the day. At cockcrow, because at that hour it announces the coming of day for the performance of works of light.” Yet you should not suppose that all these hours were prescribed in the Church by public and universal law for prayer; they served only private religious exercises, although in the time of the apostles and shortly afterward, following Jewish custom, three hours in particular were assigned to prayers, as I shall say in hymn 3, verse 86. Teolius wishes “cockcrow” in this hymn to be understood not as the first crowing in the middle of the night, but as the last crowing at the approach of light, which is properly called *gallicinium*, because at this time the birds make a noise shortly before the light breaks. Contrary to these is St. Isidore, in the passage cited, chapter 30: “The day begins, among the Romans, at midnight. Hence cockcrow also occurs then, that is, the crowing of the cocks, whose voice displays the day’s proclamation, when the midnight breath has also been breathed.” On this passage Grialis learnedly comments: “And because the better part of the night has passed, and the sun is already bending toward us, this world is said to be breathed upon by its rays.” “Breathed upon” is a word of the magicians, who believed that, as the sun approached, nocturnal apparitions fled at once. Hence Philostratus, book III of the *Life of Apollonius*, says that Achilles’ apparition did not await cockcrow. To this also belongs Anchises’ line:

“Now farewell: humid night is driving through the middle of its course,

and the rising sun has breathed upon me with his fierce panting horses.”

Servius interprets the same way the passage in *Aeneid* VI:

“But behold, beneath the light and rising of the first sun”—

so that “the first light of the sun” means the middle of the night. Moreover, Prudentius recalls things that generally occur at midnight and afterward. Teolius agrees that the ancient Christians were accustomed to rise for prayer not only before sunrise but also during the night itself. Some place cockcrow after midnight, and the silence of night after cockcrow. See the commentary on the title of the following hymn. Barthius discusses cocks at greater length in *Adversaria*, book XXXV, chapter 7, drawing on Theognis’s *Gnomology* and Heliodorus, book I of the *Aethiopica*, as well as Martial, Antipater of Thessalonica, and Peter the Venerable, book V *Against the Jews*. The commentators on the hymns of the Roman Breviary may also be consulted—Michael Timotheus, Gregory of Valencia, and others—for part of this hymn is sung at Lauds on Tuesday.]

**HERE BEGINS THE BOOK CATHEMERINON.**

5. From the *Apostle to the Romans* XIII, 11 and following: “And know this, that the hour has already come for us to rise from sleep. For our salvation is nearer now than when we believed. The night has passed, and the day has drawn near. Therefore let us cast off the works of darkness and put on the armor of light. Let us walk honorably as in the day.”

6. Heinsius, together with others, reads: “the sick, drowsy, sluggish beds.” Becmanus, chapter 6 of his *Guide to the Latin Language*, supports the same reading from the Palatine manuscript; it also appears in Thomasii’s *Hymnarium* 5 and was adopted by Teolius. Aldus, Nebr., Vat. P, and others: “the sick beds, sluggish slumbers”; Widm., Bong., Rat., Prag., Gis. in the text: “the beds, sick, sluggish through sleep.” I prefer “the beds, sluggish through sick sleep,” with Vat. A, Weitz., Gold., Gisel. at the margin, and the correctors of the hymns of the Roman Breviary under Urban VIII; for the adjective “sick” attaches more smoothly to “sleep” than to “beds,” and the verse runs more agreeably. Vat. I has “sluggish through sick sleep,” but above it “slumbers”; and in *sick* the *s* seems to have been erased. I also understand *desides* as a vocative: “O you sluggish through sick sleep.” Iso does not seem to have understood it otherwise in his gloss. The same people who are called “sluggish through sick sleep” when asleep are called “chaste, upright, and sober” when awake. An illness of the soul is indicated, as below and in the hymn of St. Ambrose for Wednesday at Matins:

“Free us from harmful rest,

sunk in sleep.”

And in Cato’s distichs:

“For prolonged rest supplies nourishment to vices.”

In the first edition of Gis., verse 4 of stanza 1 is *Castique*; verse 2 of stanza 2 is *Jam Christus*; verse 3 of that stanza is *Aegros*, a typographical error which many later followed.

7. Weitz., Gold., Widm.: *Casteque recti*; but in Widm. above: *Castique*. Prag.: *Casteque*, correctly. Rat.: *Casteque*, correctly, “upright and sober.” Thus Vat. I in the first hand: above, *Castique, recti, ac sobrii*.

8. The verb “to keep watch” frequently occurs in sacred Scripture. First Letter of St. Peter V, 8: “Be sober and watchful.” Matthew XXIV, 42: “Watch therefore, because you do not know at what hour your Lord will come,” etc.

[Col. 0778C] 9. The word *fulgidus* is thought to have become obsolete in Lucretius. It was revived by Lampridius, Solinus, Arnobius, and Juvencus. We shall return to it later.

13. Teolius, for a different spelling, has *Vox illa*. For more on the sound of birds, drawn from this passage of Prudentius and other writers, see the Burmannian edition of Propertius, which the distinguished Laurentius Santenius, an exceptionally elegant poet, completed and published in 1780, at verse 46 of book I, elegy 16: “And it makes a din among the morning birds.”

14. St. Paulinus, *Natalis* 6: “the roof’s rooflines.” Virgil, *Eclogue* 1: “the roof piled up with turf,” and “the roofs of the farmhouses smoke”; and *Aeneid* VIII, verse 456: “and beneath the roofline the morning songs of birds.”

15 and 16. In Iso I would read “to rise from the beds,” not “from the trumpets.” In Vat. P these two verses are read as follows: “Before the light breaks forth, / he is the figure of our judge.” The first is not absurd; the second, however, violates the meter. Vat. O: “He is the figure of your judge.”

19. Teol. at the margin: “He admonishes rest.”

[Col. 0778D] 21. Nebrissa interprets it as “with flames” or “with breezes that blow beneath the dawn.” Chamillardus suspects that *fletibus* (“with tears”) should be read. Change nothing. “To scatter the sky with flashing breaths” means to fill it with light. Here *flatus* is the breath of the mouth, as in *Symmachus* I, preface, verse 86: “Unwittingly he breathes with sacrilegious breaths.” Cicero, in the *Aratea*, on the constellation of the Dog: “With mighty blasts he bursts forth with heat-bearing fires.” So Ovid’s horses of the Sun, *Metamorphoses* II: “vomiting fire … they fill the air with flame-bearing neighs.” Virgil speaks of dawn in a similar phrase: “And now the first dawn was scattering the lands with new light,” *Aeneid* IV, verse 584.

22. The final part of Vat. A’s gloss is taken from Isidore, *Etymologies* V, chapter 31. In the first part read *aurarii* instead of *aurati*: for *aurarii* were called supporters, not from *aurora* (“dawn”), as the author of the gloss thinks, but from *aurae* (“breezes” or “popular favor”), which those who showed support aroused with a gesture, as Servius explains on Virgil’s line: “Now also rejoicing too much in popular favor.” He explains: “*Auris* means favors, and hence supporters are called *aurarii*.” Thus *orarium* would be almost the same as *aurarium*. Casaubon thinks that *oriarii* were named from *orarium*, and *aurarii* for the sake of euphony; *orarium* was a linen cloth prepared for wiping the mouth. See the notes on Aurelianus in Vopiscus, who reports that Aurelian was the first to give the Roman people *oraria*, which the people used to show approval. Previously, at games and in theaters, they had been accustomed to show approval by waving the toga.]

26. Put. has *Mortis imago est perpetis*, which conflicts with the meter; from this Heinsius conjectures *Imago mortis perpetis*. It should be retained, with all the others, as *Est forma mortis perpetis*: for *forma*, from the Greek μορφή, means appearance, figure, or idea. Thus Cicero repeatedly says *forma reipublicae* (“the form of the state”); and in *On Divination* II: “Have you ever noticed in the clouds the form of a lion or a hippocentaur?” In *Tusculan Disputations* I he calls sleep “the image and likeness of death.” Prudentius, *Apotheosis*, verse 309: “Christ is the form of the Father; we are the form and image of Christ.” Weitzius confirms at greater length that sleep is an image of death, which will occur to you whether you seek it or not; so I am surprised that interpreters say Prudentius was referring to Naso’s line: “Fool, what is sleep except the image of chilly death?” Why not to other similar passages?

29. Ald. has *vox*, with the top removed, from a transposition of letters, instead of *ab alto*. Vat. A has *ab alato*, incorrectly.

Peveratus thinks the sense may be: “Let God not serve sins through the sluggishness of sleep,” in accordance with Jeremiah’s words, “You made me serve my sins”; since, that is, God is called “mind” by the Platonists, as by Virgil in *Aeneid* VI: “Mind moves the mass.” This interpretation is subtle but should not be accepted.

34. Egm., in a second hand, and Vat. P have *socordes*, incorrectly. The first *o* is shortened—an unusual example—for the poet does not admit a spondee in the second foot. Some think *socordia* was so called as if from *sine corde* (“without heart”), others from the separating particle *se* and *cor* (“heart”); some therefore write *secors* and *secordia*. One Vat. manuscript cited by Teolius incorrectly reads *mentes socordes*.

35. “The breast buried in crime,” as people are said by Virgil to be buried in wine and sleep.

37. St. Ambrose, *Hexaemeron* V, chapter 24, is cited by Weitzius for this passage; but Ambrose says nothing there about demons, only about nocturnal birds, especially the song of the nightingale brooding over its nest, the owl, the bat, and the cock. St. Augustine, *City of God* VIII, chapter 22, says that demons inhabit the air, a point he often repeats elsewhere; and St. Gregory the Great confirms it in *Moralia* II, chapter 24. The same Augustine, *City of God* XIV, chapter 3, teaches that the demon is destined to eternal punishment in the prisons of this gloomy air. And in sermon 103: “Those demons seek to lead souls astray; but where the sun has not risen, there is darkness.” Perhaps St. Ambrose understands demons in the hymn for Sunday Lauds: “This whole troop of wanderers abandons the way of harming.” On St. Isidore and Grialis’s notes I spoke in the title of the hymn.

40. Although above he said that the demons wander, he now correctly asserts that they fear and retreat “here and there,” because they wander joyfully in the darkness in troops, but when light arrives they flee, scattered. Someone had conjectured *passim*.

42. Vat. A has *numinis*, elsewhere *numini*, that is, “to the demon.” I do not agree. For it is unheard-of, so far as I know, for ecclesiastical writers simply to call a demon *numen*, although Scripture calls the devil “the god of this world.”

43. Virgil, book VI, describing Aeneas’s journey through the jaws of Avernus to the underworld, says: “Through places rough with decay.”

50. Matthew XXVI, 34: “Truly I say to you, in this night, before the cock crows, you will deny me three times.” Luke and John say the same. Mark XIV, 30, however: “Truly I say to you, today, in this night, before the cock has crowed twice, you will deny me three times.” Vossius thought that this word, *salvator* (“savior”), was invented after Tertullian’s time. Its antiquity is shown by this inscription in Gruter: “To Jupiter Custos, Quirinus, Savior, for the safety of Caesar Nerva Trajan Augustus, the Sarmizian colony.” Yet there will be those who doubt whether this inscription is genuine. Cicero did not dare use this word when he wished to translate *soter*. P. Castus Innocens Ansaldus is rightly criticized, since in his commentary on the forensic trumpet of the Jews he maintained that the cockcrow in the Gospels might perhaps mean the blast of the forensic trumpet. See the distinguished Cancellierius in the passage cited shortly.

53. Ald., Gis. in the first edition: *peccator* (“sinner”). The same Gis. in the second edition has *peccatum* (“sin”), and falsely says that others have *peccator*, because shortly afterward he says that Peter’s mind remained sound and that, recognizing the cockcrow, the righteous man ceased to sin. I do indeed read *peccatum* from the manuscript copies, but I do not approve Giselinus’s reasoning: for Peter truly sinned [Col. 0781B] and recovered righteousness only when he repented and ceased sinning, as will soon become clear. Chamillardus errs in several ways here: he places the note under verse 57 and says that Nebrissa reads *negator* (“denier”), which is false of this verse 53. He adds that he himself writes *peccator*, whereas the text has *peccatum*. Gallandius, misled by this error, printed at verse 57, contrary to the metrical rule, *Flevit peccator* (“the sinner wept”), and praises Chamillardus as the author of this correction—or rather corruption. It is useful to point out such lapses, especially in distinguished writers, just as those who draw maritime routes on a chart mark reefs and shoals.]

59. Some try in vain to accuse Prudentius of error, as though he had denied that Peter sinned; among them is Cellarius, who did not understand the poet when he said that Peter’s mind sinned more than his tongue. Clericus had preceded him, volume XII of the *Bibliothèque universelle*, who thinks that Prudentius said more than he intended and associates with him St. Cyprian, page 127 of the Oxford edition, concerning those who yielded under torture: “The weakness of the viscera felt it; not the spirit, but the body failed through pain.” Calmet more correctly confirms from this passage of Prudentius the truer opinion: Peter was implicated in the sin of outward denial, which is truly sin and makes a person a sinner, but he preserved faith inwardly, since Christ prayed that his faith might not fail. St. Augustine, *Against Lying*, chapter 6: “In that denial he held the truth inwardly; outwardly he uttered a lie.” Prudentius repeatedly makes the sin of outward denial clear: “foretelling that he would deny him three times … For sin first comes to pass … Finally the denier wept, the wickedness having slipped from his mouth … He ceased to sin.” Compare St. Ambrose, book X on Luke’s Gospel, with the notes of the Maurists.

62. Gis., Bong., Wid., Vat. I, Iso, Cell., and others read *lingua lubrica* (“with a slippery tongue”), not badly. Rat. likewise has *Lingua locutus lubrica est* (“he spoke with a slippery tongue”), but above *locutus* was written with an *a*, so that it would be feminine, *locuta*, and indeed by the same hand. The meter does not permit *lingua* in the nominative case. Prag. or another manuscript—for the annotator of the Cologne edition that I am using does not distinguish them clearly—has *Lingua proloquitur lubrica* (“the slippery tongue speaks”), incorrectly. Our reading is more elegant and consistent with Prudentius’s style, and is held by the best and oldest manuscripts; it also seems to have been in Hail., and was written above in Gold. Vat. O has *Linguae locutus lubrico* without *est*.

[Col. 0782B] 63. In the hymn *Aeterne rerum conditor* for Sunday Lauds, St. Ambrose beautifully describes Peter’s conversion when admonished by the cockcrow: “This very rock of the Church, when the cock crowed, washed away his guilt,” etc. In such a multitude of books—not to say a crowd—in which Matthew XVI, 18 is examined, “And I say to you, you are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church,” etc., I do not know whether others have noticed that the Catholic interpretation is demonstrated especially by this passage. “This interpretation,” says St. Augustine, *Retractations* IX, chapter 21, “is also sung by the mouths of many in the verses of the blessed Ambrose, where, speaking of the cock, he says: ‘This very rock of the Church, when the cock crowed, washed away his guilt.’” Since the Ambrosian hymns spread to all, or nearly all, the churches of the West, it follows that the interpretation by which Peter is called the rock of the Church must be regarded as established by the common consent of the churches. In the Isidorian office, too, the hymn for the Chair of St. Peter begins: “O Peter, rock of the Church.” Therefore, since the matter concerns the interpretation of sacred Scripture, St. Augustine’s rule, and that of the theologians, applies here: “The law of prayer establishes the law of belief.” Any one or another of the holy Fathers who adopts a different explanation should, if possible, be brought back to this interpretation of the Catholic Church; if that is not possible, his interpretation may, in our view, be considered probable, since the same passage of Scripture can have two meanings—but in such a way that the second does not undermine the certain interpretation.

65. That Christ rose from the dead while it was still dark is clear from the Gospel. Formerly Christians believed [Col. 0782D] that Christ would come at midnight to judge human beings, as you can see in the prologue, no. 148. Hence the poet recalls not only the Resurrection but also the final judgment, as will be clear from what follows; earlier, too, he said: “He is a figure of our judge.” In hymn 2 for morning he likewise recalls the final judgment.

69. **Vigor**: Teol., Ald., Weitz., Gis. first edition, Rat., Prag., Vatt. A, I, and P, and other very old witnesses. Chamillardus, with Gis. second edition and Heins., has *rigor* (“severity”). But it is better to say that death’s force, power, or vigor is overcome than its severity. The poet likewise says below, in hymn 2, verse 8: “It lost the vigor of guilt.” In Vat. A, *expressus* appears incorrectly for *oppressus*. Note that the first three verses of this stanza begin with *Tunc* (“then”), corresponding to the first three verses of the following stanza, which begin with *Jam* (“now”).]
