82. Sichard. has *sobrios* instead of *sobrii*, incorrectly. Vat. O: *sobrie*. The Christian practice especially characteristic of the worship of God—praying to him with tears—should be noted by those who pursue ecclesiastical antiquities, since it has either been entirely overlooked or insufficiently explained. The poet says in hymn 2, verse 49: “We learn to beseech you with a pure and simple mind, with voice, with pious song, bending the knee, weeping and singing.” Judith urged the people to pray with tears for deliverance from the siege of Bethulia, chapter VIII, 7: “Let us speak to the Lord with tears, that according to his will he may show us his mercy.” Other examples occur in the Old Testament, involving David and Hezekiah, and in the New Testament, involving St. Peter and Magdalene. Others can be read in the *Lives of the Fathers* collected by Rosweyde, for example in the life of Abbot Paul of Nazarbe and of Abbot Thalleleus of Cilicia. Histories of more recent saints frequently mention the gift of tears; I infer that Prudentius was distinguished by it from the *Passion of Cassian*, verse 99: “I obey, I embrace the tomb, and I also shed tears; the altar grows warm from my mouth, the stone from my breast.” St. Maximus of Turin, homily 3, praising St. Peter’s tears, says: “Tears, I say, are in a certain way silent prayers; they do not ask for pardon, and yet they obtain it; they state no cause, and yet they receive mercy.” See Raynaudus, volume XV of *Heteroclita spiritualia*, page 151, and Benedict XIV, *On the Beatification*, book III, chapter 26. In both kinds of penance—of baptism and of the fallen—tears were formerly accustomed to be shed, and they are commended by the holy Fathers when they are constant and flow from the inmost heart.

84. Ald., Gis., Chamil., Vat. P, O and I in a second hand, together with other editions and manuscripts and the Roman Breviary, have *vetat* (“forbids”). *Vetet* (“may forbid”) better suits the sense, with Prag. and Gold. (in which *vetat* is written above), and is approved by Heinsius in his notes. “May rest,” “may fall asleep,” “may wither,” “may keep watch,” and “let us call” all require *vetet*. Thomasii’s Venetian *Hymnarium* has *vetat*, which I retain.

88. In Teolius, one Vat. manuscript has *vacuis* (“empty”) instead of *vanis* (“vain”), not badly.

90. Aldus had printed *Quae mundi alit gloria* (“which the glory of the world nourishes”), but corrected it. Tertullian, *On the Soul*, chapter 54: “the stain of worldly filth.” Sulpicius Severus, *Sacred History* II, chapter 14, calls profane historians *mundiales* (“worldly”). The use of *mundus* (“world”) for the wicked, for vanity, and for profane pomp was introduced by ecclesiastical writers.

95. Gisel. in the first edition has *instant* (“press upon”), perhaps referring to Iso’s gloss. All the others have *inflant* (“inflate”). Vat. A incorrectly has *mala* (“evil”) for *male* (“badly”). I accept the common reading and understand those things to be called “evils” that others call the goods of fortune: gold, pleasure, joy, wealth, honors, prosperity—things of which he had said: “They are false and trifling things, which we have done through worldly glory,” etc. And now: “Whatever evils inflate us are all nothing.” See what is noted in the preface, verse 29, on whether the things are good or evil.

96. Vat. A has *nihil* instead of *nil*. Teolius adds a question mark: “Does morning come?” and repeats this in his note. Was this deliberate, or a typographical error?

[Col. 0784C] 97. Heinsius, with the oldest manuscripts, and Weitzius have *dissice*. Rat. likewise has *dissice*, but after one *s* was removed by a corrector it became *disice*. Franciscus Juretus, book III of Paulinus’s *Life of St. Martin*, and Casperius in *Select Readings*, page 61, discuss this verb at length and insist that *dissice* should be read. I am not moved. I write *disjice* with some Vulgate copies and Thomasii’s *Hymnarium*, as in Virgil and others, from the verb *disjicio*, which Prudentius also used in the present tense in the hymn to St. Lawrence, verse 209: “when disease scatters the limbs.” Therefore the verb is not defective, possessing no forms beyond *disjice* or *dissice*. The whole controversy is orthographic, and I follow the customary spelling. In the Vulgate and the Roman Breviary, *discute* (“scatter”) appears instead of *disjice*, which is the gloss of the older manuscripts, as we have seen. Aringhus praises this hymn and its elegance in book VI of *Subterranean Rome*, chapter 37, which concerns the cock. From his book VI, chapter 37, I present the following monument. [Col. 0785B] “For the ancient Christians habitually represented the image of the cock as a symbol of vigilance, and also of Christ the Lord and the heralds of the divine word; and its image frequently appears not only in connection with the apostle Peter but also in other cemetery locations, such as sarcophagi and lamps, and in the more elevated views of the underground chambers, on vaults and in apses. From this it began to be represented on the lofty gables of our churches. In the Vatican manuscripts Alexandrinus 74 and 348, a cock is painted in the first letter of this hymn. See the prologue, no. 78. But the distinguished Franciscus Cancellierius has recently published more about cocks; in four learned and elegant volumes he has exhausted the new subject of the *Secretaries of the Vatican Basilica*. He discusses the matter at length in book I, chapter 14, section 4 and following: why ancient Christians placed cocks on bell towers; Christ’s words, ‘Before the cock crows’; and the symbol of the cock among Christians.”

**Morning hymn**, another title of Ald., Rat., Gold., and Weitz. “For Matins” seems to have entered the manuscripts from the breviaries. Alex., Vat. I, and others: “Morning hymn.” From the learned preface of the most excellent archbishop of Toledo to the new edition of the Isidorian Breviary, I gather that this hymn may be called “At the Crowing of the Chicks,” following an old Spanish custom. “At the end of our codex,” says the most learned prelate, “you will find not only the morning hours and those of Lauds, but also hymns for the first watch of the night, AT COCKCROW, WHICH WAS AROUND MIDNIGHT, and AT THE CROWING OF THE CHICKS, which was around the rising dawn; they called this second hymn THE CROWING OF THE CHICKS in order to distinguish it from the cockcrow at midnight.” These things agree excellently with St. Isidore’s words in book V, chapter 21 of the *Etymologies*: “Morning is between the departure of darkness and the coming of dawn.” Part of this Morning hymn is sung on Wednesday at Lauds in the Roman Breviary: “Night, darkness, and clouds”; the remaining part on Thursday at Lauds: “Behold, golden light rises,” for which verse Prudentius has: “Behold, the fiery sun rises.” Ricciolius, part VIII of the *Prosody*, chapter 6, rule 2: “What,” he says, “is more elegant than that Boethian hymn sung at Wednesday Lauds, ‘Night, darkness, and clouds,’ etc.?” I would think that “Boethius” had slipped in for “Prudentius.” But shortly before he had said: “In the hymns composed by St. Ambrose, Boethius, or Prudentius, the Catholic Church uses iambics of this kind, arranged in four-line stanzas, at the canonical hours.” Yet this is not a Boethian hymn, nor do I know of any other iambic dimeter composed by Boethius that is used by the Catholic Church.]

1. Egm. has *jubila* (“shout for joy”) instead of *nubila* (“clouds”), incorrectly. Below, verse [Col. 0786B] 65, *Nox mundi* (“the world’s night”), as here, *Nox, tenebrae, nubila mundi* (“night, darkness, clouds of the world”): all of these differ from one another.

3. An old manuscript in the Cologne edition has *micat* (“sparkles”) instead of *intrat* (“enters”), incorrectly and apparently from some gloss. Thomasii’s *Hymnarium* V requires correction in many places, as in this third verse: *intrat, albescit polus* (“[light] enters; the sky grows white”), where *lux* (“light”) is missing.

4. *Discedite* (“depart”) is a formula by which the profane are ordered to leave sacred places, as in “Away, away with you, profane ones”; and below, hymn 6, verses 136 and following: “Away, away, wandering / apparitions of dreams; / away with your obstinate / magical practice … Depart: Christ is here; / Christ is here—melt away.” When emperors dismissed soldiers in disgrace, they used the formula: “Depart, Quirites, and lay down your arms.” See Brissonius, *On Formulas*, book IV.]

6. *Spiculum* properly means “arrow.” Chamillard, following Fabricius, says that *spiculo* is improperly used for “rays,” and that elsewhere *radiorum spicula* is more correct, *Hamartigenia*, verse 87. Gifanius, however, in his index to Lucretius, under *Tela diei*, observes that the sun’s rays are elegantly and learnedly called “the weapons of day,” just as Varro called them “the darts of the sun,” and Prudentius “arrows.” Gifanius adds the reason: in Latin, a *radius* is nothing other than a shaft or spear, whether made of iron or wood. This explanation does not satisfy Becmann, *On the Origin of the Latin Language*, under *Radius*; nevertheless, he agrees that *spiculum* may likewise be used of sunlight, as *radius* is. You may consult him.

8. Hailsius reads *nitenti* instead of *nitentis*, which adheres better to *sideris*, so that the sun is indicated, as Iso correctly interprets it. Nevertheless, *vultu nitenti* is well formed.

9. Prag. has *hic* for *sic*, incorrectly.

12. Aldus, Rat. (where the gloss is *fulgescit*), Gis., Fabricius, Weitz, manuscripts I, O, P, and others read *pallescit*. Vat. A and Alex. have *pallescet*, which the sense seems to require. The poet is speaking of God’s final judgment and therefore adds: “Then it will not be possible to conceal . . . But at the new morning they will grow bright.” Nebrissensis has *pallescat* for *albescat* and alludes to the morning hour when the dawn is pale. In Nebrissensis’ text, however, one reads *pallescit*. Dawn is first pale, then rose-colored, and finally white or bright. These words, properly belonging to the dawn and the morning hour, are poetically transferred by Prudentius to the final day of judgment, when the sun of righteousness will appear.

15. Vat. I and Gold., in the first hand, have *clarescunt*, which may be defended if *pallescit* is read above.

17. Beware of the error in the Aldine edition: *Furante* instead of *Fur ante*. The poet wonderfully embellishes the thought that one who acts wickedly hates the light. Similar statements occur among the holy Fathers. St. Ambrose, *On Cain and Abel*, book II, chapter 8: “The robber flees the day, as though it were a witness to his crime. The adulterer blushes before the light, as though it were conscious of the adultery.” The poets imagine Fraud and Falsehood born from Night, to indicate that night is suited to deceit. Pagans charged the early Christians with nocturnal gatherings. Minucius Felix, in the *Octavius*: “There, after many courses, when the banquet had grown heated and the frenzy of unlawful lust had been inflamed by drunkenness, a dog tied to a candelabrum is provoked to charge and leap by throwing a morsel beyond the distance of the line by which it is bound. Thus, once the witnessing light has been overturned and extinguished, shameless darkness envelops the bonds of abominable desire in the uncertainty of chance.” Tertullian refers to this in his *Apology*, chapter 7: “We are called the most criminal of men because of the sacrament of infanticide and the food derived from it, and because of the incest after the banquet—which those who overturn the lights, namely the procurers, arrange, along with darkness and the shamelessness of impious lusts.” And in chapter 8: “Moreover, there are candelabra and lamps, and certain dogs, and morsels which stretch them out toward the overturning of the lights.” Christians dispelled this tale and slander above all because they believed and worshiped God as always present and before whom nothing is hidden. Prudentius explains this throughout almost the entire hymn, as will become clear.

21. Oxon. has *frons* for *fraus*, but *fraus* is far better.

29. He refers to the custom of almost all peoples, especially the Jews and, thence, Christians, not to drink wine in the morning. By this custom St. Peter, in Acts of the Apostles, chapter II, repelled from himself, the apostles, and the other one hundred and twenty persons upon whom the Holy Spirit had descended, the suspicion of drunkenness: “For these are not drunk, as you suppose, since it is the third hour of the day.” It was not credible that so many devout and sensible men together should, contrary to custom, the common way of life, and the prescribed law, have drenched themselves with wine before the third hour. Chamillard and Teolius preferred another interpretation: that the reference is to cups taken on the preceding day or night. I do not approve it, nor does Iso seem to approve it.

He takes *nugator* to mean “libidinous,” as in hymn 7, verse 98: “to subdue and break the old frivolities,” and in the *Psychomachia*, verse 433, jesting, wantonness, pleasure, and desire are called the “frivolous battle-line.” Prudentius readily uses *castum* for *caste*, and similar forms: thus *severum* and *ludicrum* in the two verses immediately following. A little earlier he uses *turpia* for “shameful things,” and shortly afterwards *inepta sua* for “his own foolish acts.”

But he has not seen clearly enough: for forensic glory can be applied to all who are occupied in the forum, and verse 46, which corresponds to this passage—“utterly ignorant of speaking”—declares that orators in particular are meant here.

42. I have some suspicion that these verses have been transposed, so that “The mournful trumpet-call carries off this man” ought to come first, and then “Forensic glory [carries off] that man.” For in this order the soldier, the civilian, and the merchant are first enumerated, and then the same occupations are indicated in reverse order: “But we [are ignorant] of petty gain and interest,” etc. The poet observes that many people do not choose a fixed mode of life, but seize upon one by chance or recklessness: this is what *raptat* means. Compare the first satire of Horace, book I:

“How is it, Maecenas, that no one lives content with the lot which either reason has given him or chance has thrown in his way?”

He then adds things about the soldier, merchant, farmer, and jurist:

“The expert in law and statutes praises the farmer.”

45. Would you like to hear another etymology of *foenerator*—or, as others write it, *fenerator*—from Varro? Here it is: “*Fenerator* is so named from *fenus*; but *fenus* is said from *fetus*, as though from a certain offspring of money that bears and increases. Therefore Marcus Cato and the other men of his age pronounced *fenerator* without the letter *o*, just as they called *fetus* itself and *fecunditas*.” From Aulus Gellius, book XVI, chapter 12, Nonius, and Marcellus. For the same reason, Greek *τόκος* means both “offspring” and “interest.” Cicero uses the word *lucellum*.

[Col. 0789A]

52. *Canendo*, “by praising,” I.

58. *Dispice*, “look carefully,” “look downward,” I. “Inspect carefully,” Vat. A.

59. *Fucis*, “sins,” or “dark colors.” *Fucus* is used of every color, which is why we call garments *fucatae* when they have been dyed in any manner; “darkened by sins,” I. *Fucus* is a black color, but the word is used for every color, Vat. A.

[Col. 0789B]

46. Someone may ask from whose point of view Prudentius speaks here, for he cannot include all Christians, among whom there were soldiers, civilians, sailors, craftsmen, farmers, and tradesmen. Therefore, when he says, “By this art alone we live,” namely by praising God, this applies only to the clergy, and perhaps also to associations and communities of Christians in which religious orders were already taking shape. This may be seen in St. Augustine, *On the Morals of the Catholic Church*, book I. Besides anchorites and cenobites gathered into common life and living in prayer, reading, and discussion, and besides women separated into residences and kept as far as possible from men, Augustine adds another praiseworthy class of Christians who live in cities but are very far removed from ordinary life. “I myself,” he says, “saw at Milan a dwelling of holy men—not a few people, under one excellent and most learned presbyter. At Rome, too, I came to know several, and so forth.” This was not confined to men, but also existed among women, over many widows and virgins living together and earning their livelihood from wool and weaving, each community being directed by a woman of the greatest seriousness and proven character. Perhaps Prudentius had withdrawn to some dwelling of this kind.

49. These four verses contain the principal forms of worshiping and supplicating God. The first is inward, in spirit and truth, with a pure and simple mind; the second is with the voice, without singing; the third with a devout song; the fourth with a bent knee; and the fifth with weeping. Others have written frequently about restrained ecclesiastical singing from the earliest beginnings of the Church, and I have discussed it to some extent in my dissertation *On Ecclesiastical Hymns*, section 9 and following. On weeping during prayer, see above, on hymn 1, verse 82. Kneeling was so common among the first Christians that in the *Acts of St. Thecla* kneeling is used as a term for prayer itself. Bingham, *Ecclesiastical Antiquities*, book XIII, chapter 8, reports that this practice was customary in morning and evening worship on ordinary and station days, that is, days appointed for fasting. Tertullian, at the end of *On Prayer*: “The station gave its name to the military service; prayer gave it its practice.” Stations were customarily held every Wednesday and Friday, during which the fast was ended together with the station, as I shall say in the hymn to St. Fructuosus and his companions. On these days Christians also knelt in prayer. St. Justin, or another ancient author, explains on which days they did not kneel in *Questions to the Orthodox*, question 115: “If kneeling in prayers commends one more to God than praying while standing, why do they not kneel on Sundays and from the weekdays of Easter until Pentecost? From where did such a custom enter the Church?” He answers: “Because it was always necessary to preserve the memory of both our fall through sin and Christ’s grace, by which we rose from our fall. Therefore, kneeling for six days signifies our fall into sin. But not kneeling on Sunday signifies the resurrection, through which Christ’s grace freed us both from sins and from the death that accompanied them.” From the time of the apostles, this custom began, as blessed Irenaeus, martyr and bishop of Lyons, says in his book *On Easter*. He also mentions Pentecost, during which we do not kneel, because it has equal authority with Sunday, for the reason given concerning Sunday. Traces of this practice remain in the ecclesiastical office: at its conclusion, the antiphons to blessed Mary are recited kneeling, except on Sundays and throughout the Easter season. The same practice is observed when the ringing of bells summons us to greet the Mother of God. On kneeling, see, among others, Caesarius of Arles, homily 34. Regarding kneeling in prayer, he reproves those who, when the deacon cries, “Let us kneel,” remain standing upright like columns; for, he says, this is wholly neither permitted nor appropriate to Christians while prayer is being offered in church. When Christians prayed standing, they often extended their hands in the form of a cross. I shall explain this practice in the hymn to St. Fructuosus.

56. The ancient Christians not only offered prayers to God at sunrise but also prayed facing east. St. Justin, in the passage cited, question 118: “Why, although every place is suitable for worshiping God with a pure mind, do we offer hymns and prayers with our eyes fixed on the region of the rising sun? And who handed this down to us?” He answers: “We dedicate the most excellent things to the honor of God. The east is more excellent than all creatures; therefore we turn our faces toward the east.” Jacob Thomasius wrote a dissertation on praying toward the eastern region. Christians also once built their churches facing east.

58. Gold., Widm., Bong., one Vatican manuscript cited by Teolius, and Weitz read *despice*. Prag. has *despice*, with *dispice* in the margin; Rat. has *despice*, corrected to *dispice*. Juretus wished to restore *dissice* in book III of *The Life of St. Martin*. The reading should be *dispice*. Catullus, speaking of Berenice’s hair: “You who surveyed all the lights of the great world.” John Antonius Vulpius gathers several passages relevant to this in his edition of Catullus, much of which you will also find in the lexicons. In his very extensive commentaries on Catullus, Vulpius repeatedly mentions our poet with great praise.

59. Giselinus insists that *fuscis* should be read in the second edition, from a very ancient book, since the poet had already said, “Whatever each person thinks dark,” a reading approved by Heinsius, the *Hymnary of Thomasius*, Alex., and others. The other reading is more common and should not be rejected. It is found in the excellent manuscripts I and P, as well as in Aldus, Weitz, the correctors of the hymns under Urban VIII, and most editions, including the Egmond manuscript, which Weitz incorrectly cited for *fuscis*, since it plainly has *fucis*, as Heinsius observed. In Vat. O: “There are many things smeared over”; *fucis* or *fuscis* is absent. Teolius says in his notes that Cellarius, following Weitz, has *fucis inclita*—read *inlita*—and that Heinsius has the same if one attends to what he says in his additions. But Heinsius did not alter his opinion in the additions. His words, connected from the note and additions, are: “Good: *FUSCIS* in the Egmond manuscript cited by Weitz. But he intended to designate another manuscript. For the Egmond manuscript itself, which I examined, clearly has *FUCIS*; nevertheless Giselinus has *FUSCIS* from a very ancient exemplar.” Teolius, with most editors, reads *fucis*. This reading is confirmed by a similar phrase in the hymn to St. Hippolytus, verse 123: “The wall bears the pattern of the crime, on which multicolored pigment arranges every wickedness.” Nebrissensis accepts and explains both readings: “Spotted with vices. *Fuscis* is also read, that is, stained with darkness, and this fits better with the following word, when he says, ‘May they be cleansed by your light’; or he alludes to another property of the sun, which not only illuminates but also cleanses.”

[Col. 0792A]

61. *Durare*, “to persevere,” I.

63. *Nitere*, “to shine,” I.

64. *Jordane flumine*, “by baptism,” I, Vat. A.

[Col. 0792A]

63. Prag. incorrectly has *prius* for *pridem*.

64. Rat. incorrectly has *Jordanis* for *Jordane*. Christians of old greatly praised the waters of the Jordan because Christ had been baptized in them. Juvencus, using an unusual but devout invocation, says:

“Come then: may the sanctifying Spirit, author of my song, be present and refresh my mind with the pure stream of the sweet Jordan as I sing, so that we may sing things worthy of Christ.”

Paulinus of Petrocoria, book IV of *The Life of St. Martin*:

“Let thirsty hearts seek Castalian waters; other cups befit men reborn in the Jordan.”

The custom of which St. Jerome bears witness in *On Hebrew Places* is also relevant here: “Across the Jordan, where John baptized for repentance, even to this day many of the brethren—that is, from the number of believers wishing to be reborn there—are baptized in the life-giving flood.” Valesius, in his notes on chapter 62 of book IV of the *Life of Constantine*, where Constantine is said to have wished to be baptized in the Jordan, observes that St. Jerome translated Eusebius’ words from *On Hebrew Places* in such a way as to explain them of catechumens who eagerly desired baptism in the Jordan; but they may be understood of a simple washing, which Christians especially practiced at the feast of the Epiphany after the baptism of infants, according to the *Itinerary of the Martyr Antoninus* and the *Journey of St. Willibald*, published by Canisius. That water from the Jordan was sometimes carried to distant regions so that the children of princes might be washed in sacred baptism is proved by the learned commendator Franciscus Victorius in his commentary on an ancient Christian bronze coin, which we too have presented so that the memory of that ecclesiastical antiquity might spread more widely.

[Col. 0793B]

65. *Dehinc*, “after this,” that is, after baptism, I.

66. *Infecit*, “stained,” “defiled with sins,” I.

67. *Rex*, “King,” that is, Christ. *Eoi sideris*, “of the eastern star,” that is, of the sun rising in the east, I.

69. *Picem*, “pitch,” that is, sins or the sinner, I.

70. *Candore*, “with righteousness,” I. “You who make the stained and sinful white and righteous,” Vat. A.

71. *Ebenoque*, “and ebony,” a tree of the blackest kind and with black wood. Ebony is a kind of black wood, or a tree whose wood, once cut and thrown into water, hardens there through a kind of coagulation and becomes a black stone. Useful implements are later made from it to distinguish good and evil works, I. Ebony is a kind of black wood which, once cut, turns into stone; from it, it is said, there was an altar in the house of the Lord where a fire was always burning, Vat. A. *Crystallum*, “transparency,” I.

72. *Livida*, “stained,” “filthy,” I.

74. *Luctator*, “wrestler,” not with the arms but in prayer, so that he might bless him, I.

75. *Eousque*, “up to that point”; Iso says that it means as much as *usque*.

76. *Sudavit*, “wrestled,” “labored,” I.

77. *Jubar*, “the sun,” “the splendor of day,” I.

79. *Femur*, a figurative expression, that is, “having the means of victory.”

80. *Culpae*, “of lust,” I.

81. *Inguen*, a synecdoche.

82. *Quae*, “where.” *Vilior*, “is more lowly,” I.

83. *Cordis*, “of the mind,” I.

[Col. 0793B]

67. For *rex*, Prag., Bong., and Sichard have *lux* in the text, and Gis. in the first edition; Gallandius did not dislike this reading when he found it in the *Hymnary of Thomasius*. I understand *vultu* as referring to the face of the eastern star. Chamillard distinguishes the passage differently: “You, King of the eastern star, illumine [us] with a serene face.” The Parma edition punctuates less well: “You, King, illumine with the serene face of the eastern star.” The Roman correctors under Urban VIII substituted another verse: “You, true light of the heavenly beings.” Ricciolius says in the cited passage that Urban VIII did this because the first syllable of *eoi* is usually long. Neither reasoning nor examples will readily persuade me that the first syllable of *eoi* is usually long. In the first edition of the corrected hymns, the reading is “You, light of the eastern star,” which was changed to “You, true light of the heavenly beings,” perhaps for greater clarity. The correctors themselves observe in their preface that they left several passages that could have been improved, such as “You assumed form by being born”; among poets, *nascendo* is more often lengthened than shortened. Thus *eoi* should not have been changed, even if it were true that its *e* is more often lengthened than shortened. Moreover, the correctors were inconsistent when they introduced *dicendo* for *dicens*, with the *o* shortened, in the dominical vespers for the Passion of the Lord: “By saying to the nations: God reigned from the tree,” whereas the earlier reading was, “Saying, among the nations, God reigned from the tree.” Since Prudentius often shortens the final *o* in gerunds, I note in passing that the rule commonly taught—that this *o* is more often long, as though this were its natural quantity—is not so certain. Servius, commenting on Virgil, *Aeneid* IV, verse 413, “To go again into tears, again to attempt by pleading,” says that in *precando* and *cantando* the *do* is naturally shortened. Terentianus uses it similarly: “While renewing various pains, uncertain of life.” Below, Prudentius shortens it in “wrestling with the lame and wasted man.” I omit Catullus.

69. Weitz and Marietti observe that the poet alluded to Ovid, book III of *Letters from Pontus*, elegy 3: “Nor is milky fluid changed into black pitch, nor does what was white become terebinth or ivory.”

71. See Pliny, book XII, chapter 4. *Ebenus* and *ebenum* are both used, and *hebenus* is also written. Pliny says that there are two kinds of ebony, but the better is the tree with a knotless trunk and wood of black brilliance. On crystal, see the same author, book XXXVII, chapter 2, and others who write about minerals. Prudentius’ thought is taken from Isaiah 1:18.

72. In Vat. A and Alex. the reading is *tergens* instead of *terge*; so also Bong., and Hailsius in the second hand. The others have *terge*. The old manuscript in the Cologne edition incorrectly has *tegens*. Observe that Prudentius uses interchangeably *tergere*, “to wipe away,” *illuminare*, “to illumine,” *purgare*, “to cleanse,” and *inficere*, “to stain,” with night, dark clouds, pitch, and ebony, to signify the removal of sins by God. So above, according to the more common reading, “There are many things smeared with pigments, which your light may cleanse.”

73. This story is narrated in Genesis 32, and Hosea 12 also mentions it. Prudentius interprets it allegorically. St. Ambrose, in book II of *On Jacob and the Blessed Life*, chapter 7, pursues a similar interpretation. The conclusion of Prudentius’ poem at verse 90 is relevant here. Teolius printed *caerulea* instead of *caerula*, unless this is perhaps a typographical error. Retain *caerula*. Below, in the fifth hymn, verse 41, there is also *caerulae noctis*.

74. Against Iso, most interpreters explain that the struggle was fought both with the arms and in prayer.

75. Aldus reads “until the eastern light should rise,” omitting *dum*. Fabricius separates the words as *Eo usquedum*. Iso handles it differently. One may also write *Eo usque dum*. Oxon. has *quousque* as a variant reading. Heinsius suspected *Eoa dum lux surgeret*.

76. Rat., Widm., Bong., Aldus, Nebr., manuscripts I, O, P, and the Vulgate read *impar praelio*. Giselinus, however, very properly emended it to *praelium* from his manuscript and from the manuscript at Deventer; Heinsius confirmed this from his own manuscripts and from the poet’s style, since he often uses *sudo* with the accusative, as Claudian does: “What battles do you sweat through?” *Praelium* is also found in Vat. A and other very ancient manuscripts, together with Alex.

78. Weitz conjectured and read *luxante*, arising from the error *laxante* in Gold., which is also found in Vat. I. But why reject *lapsante*, which all the manuscripts have? This is a Virgilian word with the same meaning.

80. I would rather say “of stubbornness,” by which he resisted God, than “of lust,” with Iso.

81. *Inguen* is used for *coxendix*, the hip. The thigh’s sinew is said to have been touched and to have withered—namely, the sinew that binds the head of the bone inserted into the socket or acetabulum.

93. *Fatescat*, “may depart,” “may withdraw,” I.

2. *Verbigena*, “begotten by the Word,” I, Vat. A. “Begotten by the Word”: masculine only, because Christ alone is begotten, Vat. A. *Verbo genitum*, Vat. B.

90. *Cui* is disyllabic and forms an iambic foot.

92. Fabricius says: “He places blessedness in abstinence and chastity, by which we struggle against intemperance and lust.” But this is not the poet’s true and more immediate meaning. Fabricius himself does not express another interpretation. Prudentius follows the interpretation of Sacred Scripture, namely Genesis 32:31: “The sun rose upon him immediately after he had passed over Penuel, but he limped.” He understands night and darkness as sin, and the rising of the sun as the grace of Jesus Christ; hence he calls blessed the person whom Christ has illumined after subduing his desires. The following verses strongly confirm this interpretation.

93. Iso, Weitz, and Wid. read *fatescat*, or *fatiscat*; Wid. has *facessat* above. Gis., in the margin of the first edition, has *fatiscas*, followed by “and then, you dragged [me] through a wandering error.” Georgius Remus seems to have read *fatescas* or *facessas*, since he advises that verse 94 should read “You drew [me] through a wandering error.” Vat. I has *fatiscat*; Prag. and Rat. likewise. I follow manuscripts A and O, Heinsius’ older copies, Aldus, Nebr., and others, which read *facessat*.

96. Those who read *fatiscas* or *facessas* write here either “You have dragged [me] through a wandering error” or “You have drawn [me] through a deviating error.” See verse 93.

102. Rat. has *nec manus*. So do manuscripts I and P.

103. Vat. A, Egm., and Bong. have *oculine*. Others more correctly have *oculive*. Vat. P has *nec peccent*.

105. Christians always kept before their eyes the thought that God is present everywhere and observes hearts, and they inserted it most wisely into the ecclesiastical office. Ouzelius, Woverus, Elmenhorstius, and others collect many passages on this subject in their notes to Minucius: “How much more does God, author and observer of all things, from whom no secret can exist, dwell in darkness—dwell in our thoughts as though in other darknesses?” Our poet’s words are regularly cited by writers on ecclesiastical antiquity and by others when they discuss this subject, and they are particularly striking.

107. *Actus*, “deeds,” for *actio*, “action,” is common among ancient Christian writers.

108. Teolius has *e luce* in the margin.

Before food. This is an ancient Christian custom: to pray to God before eating. Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 39: “No one reclines at table before prayer to God has been tasted first.” In the published code of the Spanish Church by Dominicus Lopez de Barrera, canon 65 from the Council of Carthage 12: “Clergy or devout laypeople should not begin banquets before the sacred hour of the third hour of the day, nor should clergy ever eat bread unless a hymn has been recited, and after meals they should offer thanks to God the Author.” Lopez gives this canon in that form; but in the *Collectio maxima conciliorum Hispaniae* of Sylvester Pueyo, page 150, the margin reads: “Canon 12, distinction 44.” It is also in the fourth supplement to the *Capitularies of the Frankish Kings*, chapter 69, Paris edition of 1677.

[Col. 0796C]

1. Aldus first had *primum lucis sator*, later corrected to *lucisator*. Rat. likewise has *lucis sator* in the first hand; Pal. has *lucis auctor*. Burmann, in book IV of Propertius’ elegy 3, on the verse *Lucis et auctores*, cites this passage of Prudentius and says that Egm. reads *lucis auctor*, with *lucis sator* in the margin. The true reading is *lucisator*. Other readings arose falsely from the novelty of this word. Prudentius formed this expression, like *omniparens*, *verbigena*, and earlier *crucifer*, by imitation of similar compounds, although Virgil also used *omniparens* in *Aeneid* VI, verse 595. St. Prosper coined *omnitenens* in epigram 39 and *omnicreator* in epigram 61.

2. Vat. A has *omnipotens* for *omniparens*. Chamillard is mistaken here: he denies that the poet’s meaning is that *verbigena* should be understood as “begotten by the Word,” and instead explains it as “the Word begotten.” Du Cange likewise asserts in his *Glossary* that Iso incorrectly explained it as “begotten by the Word,” and he cites verses from the *Mamotrectus* on 2 Kings 25, taken from the *Graecismus*: “Words compounded from those terms are of common gender. Except *VERBIGENA*, which applies only to Christ.” But there is no doubt that the poet’s meaning is “begotten by the Word,” since in hymn 11, verse 17, he repeats the same thought: “From the Father’s mouth, however you were born, and brought forth by the Word,” where Chamillard interprets it: “And brought forth when the Father addressed us.” In what theological manner the Son can be called the Word begotten by the Word, Petavius explains in book VI, chapter 8: “Nevertheless, it does not seem strange that these things should be expressed in this way, so that the very wisdom of the Father, by which he is wise, should be called the Son . . . and that the term *logos*, used by the ancients not only insofar as it signifies reason but also insofar as it signifies word, should be applied in the same way.” And in chapter 3, section 5: “For the Word, as a person, arises from the Word who is the Father, that is, from reason or understanding.” Weitz, in his note on this passage of Prudentius, cites St. Augustine, *Confessions* XI, chapter 7, and St. Cyprian in his *Exposition of the Creed*. Chamillard thought that they had used the word *verbigena* and asserted this confidently. But neither Augustine nor Rufinus of Aquileia, to whom that *Exposition* is attributed, offers anything that could explain Prudentius’ expression, much less do they use the word *verbigena*. Lamius, defending Prudentius against Le Clerc, thinks that both here and in hymn 11 the poet speaks of the second generation, by which the Word became flesh. I shall examine this opinion in hymn 11.

[Col. 0797B]

14. *Favor*, “praise.” *Imbuerit*, “may bless,” “may sanctify,” I.

16. *Fercula*, by the figure in which the container stands for what it contains: “dishes” for the foods, Vat. A.

17. *Pateras*, “tables.” *Patena* is so called from *patere*, “to be open.” A *patera* is a vessel suitable for receiving drink, I.

18. *Seria*, “of old men.” *Serium* means seriousness; hence *seria*, in the plural, means serious or honorable things. *Ludicra*, “of young men.” *Jocos*, “of children,” I.

19. *Quod sumus*: “May the heavenly piety govern both what we are and what we do.” *Agimus*, “we do,” I.

[Col. 0797C]

4. One manuscript of Vat. cited by Teolius has *manens* for *potens*.

14. Origen prescribes similar prayers to be said before food, volume II, page 36, book II on John.

15. In the prolegomena, section 170, I explained the meaning of “sanctifying all things by faith.”

16. Prudentius urges that our dishes should taste of God, and he seems to indicate what St. Cyprian says at the end of his book to Donatus: “Let psalms sound through the sober banquet; and since your memory is tenacious, undertake this duty according to custom with a melodious voice. You will feed those most dear to you more abundantly if there is spiritual hearing among us, and religious sweetness delights the ears.” Other holy Fathers have similar statements. Weitz says that St. Bernard, book II, letter 2, produced words from St. Cyprian that we have quoted; but I find nothing of the kind in Bernard.

[Col. 0798B]

21. *Spolia*, “spoils,” as the ancients used to do, I.

22. *Aromate*: this aroma is nominative singular, I.

23. *Ambrosius*, “sweet,” “divine”; it is used for “divine.” *Ambrosia* is the food of the gods, I.

24. *Nectaream*, “pure,” I.

25. *Ab usque*: *abusque* and *adusque* are also used freely, I.

26. *Camoena*: *camoenae* is said to derive from *canenae*, from *canendo*, “singing.” *Leves*, “empty,” Iso.

27. *Queis*, *quibus*, “by which,” Iso.

17. In *Miscellaneous Observations Published on Ancient Authors by Learned Britons*, vol. III, part III, [Col. 0797D] p. 320, it is conjectured that one should read *Spiritus influat in pateras* (“May the Spirit flow into the cups”); but there is no adequate reason to abandon the old reading.

18. If you wish, distinguish them in this way: *ludus* (“play”) applies to action, *jocus* (“jest”) to words. The poet asks that both actions and words be directed by God, whether those pertaining to self-restraint or those pertaining to *eutrapelia*—that is, a certain relaxation of the mind. The theologians discuss this virtue with St. Thomas, *Summa theologiae* II–II, question 168, article 2.

20. Heinsius prefers *superne* (“from above”) instead of *superna* (“heavenly”), following Put., Alt., and Egm.; Alex. agrees with them, and more recent printed editions follow, because *superne* shortens its final syllable. I do not deny that this syllable may be common, but I retain *superna*, with Iso, Hincmar, Gottschalk, the oldest manuscripts Vat. A, I, O, P, Urb., Rat., Prag., Ald., Gis., Weit., and most others. The learned Britons, in the work cited, suspect that *deitas* (“godhead”) should be read instead of *pietas* (“piety”). Nothing should be changed. Gottschalk, in order to prove against Hincmar that it is correctly said *trina deitas* (“threefold godhead”), brought forward these words of Prudentius along with others. Hincmar, in his book *On the Non-Threefold Godhead*, replies that Prudentius, under the compulsion of metre, said *trina pietas* (“threefold piety”), and elsewhere—in the conclusion of the hymn *On the New Light of Holy Saturday*—*numine triplici* (“with threefold divinity”), or, as it is read in certain manuscripts, *nomine triplici* (“with threefold name”); and again, in the preface to the *Apotheosis*: *Est tria summa Deus, trinum specimen* (“God the Highest is threefold, a threefold manifestation”). Hincmar himself disapproves these expressions. Nevertheless, he concedes that Arator says *trina potestas* (“threefold power”), *trinum nomen* (“threefold name”); Prosper, *trina majestas* (“threefold majesty”); and Sedulius, *trina fides* (“threefold faith”), as well as: *Quod simplex triplicet, quodque est triplicabile, simplet* (“May what is simple make threefold, and what is capable of being threefold make simple”). He adds an appropriate explanation: “It is enough to have said this: Prudentius, by *threefold piety*, Arator, by *threefold power*, Prosper, by *threefold majesty*, placed the substantial names *piety*, *power*, and *majesty* for the persons of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, who are spoken of relatively in the Holy Trinity.” See the commentary on verse 2 of the *Psychomachia*.

21. This was indeed the custom of the pagans; but the early Christians abstained so completely from ointments and perfumes at banquets that the pagans reproached them for it, as is clear from the words of Minucius Felix: “You do not bind flowers around your head, nor adorn your body with perfumes; you reserve perfumes for funerals.” See Clement of Alexandria, *Paedagogus* II, chapter 8, and St. Chrysostom, vol. II, Homily 1 *On Lazarus*. Instead of *rosae* (“of roses”), Prag. has *rosea* (“rosy”) in the margin, incorrectly.

22. Some write *flagrat* or *fraglat* (“burns/fragrances”).

24. As ambrosia is the food of the gods, so nectar is their drink. The words Prudentius uses—*liquor ambrosius* (“ambrosial liquid”), *redolet* (“is fragrant”), *fusus* (“poured”)—perhaps suggest ambrosial ointment, about which Facciolatus may be consulted.

25. *Usque* is usually placed first; Virgil, however, said *ab usque Pachyno* (“from Pachynus onward”).

26. Macrobius, *Commentary on the Dream of Scipio* II, chapter 3, reports that *Camoenae* (“Muses”) is formed as though from *canenae*, from *canere* (“to sing”). Poets also placed crowns of ivy upon themselves, because the divinities of Bacchus and Apollo were considered equal. Horace, book I, ode 1: “The ivy, reward of learned brows, joins me to the gods above.” Ovid, book I, elegy 6: “Take the Bacchic ivy garlands from my hair. These happy signs become joyful poets; a crown is not suited to my circumstances.” Compare Charles Paschal, *On Crowns*, 1610 edition, p. 60, book I, chapter 18, who cites this passage of Prudentius in praise of the devout poet.

27. From this verse someone might infer that Prudentius was accustomed to indulge in composing profane poetry. [Col. 0799C] I do not judge it so. For he addresses poetry in general, so that it may sing the praises of God rather than other foolish things. See the *Prolegomena*, no. 63. Someone explains it as follows: “O my Muse, skilled at weaving mystical garlands, with which you have been accustomed to encircle the temples—now bind them with a dactylic fillet.” For previously she had bound them with an iambic, Sapphic, or other fillet.

Here understand *strophium* as a crown, with Nebrissensis; for *strophium* is anything that is bent around and encircles, such as a crown or belt. Pliny, book XXI: “The ancients used thinner crowns, calling them *strophia*.” The meaning is: “Muse, skilled at weaving mystical garlands, bind the temples with a dactylic fillet, because this poem is dactylic.” Chamillardus interprets it almost this way, except that he adds “O my Muse,” which I do not approve.

[Col. 0797A]

**Brought forth from a virginal body,**

**but previously powerful in the Father,**

**before the stars, the earth, and the sea came into being.**

To this place, I pray, with shining gaze

turn your saving face,

serene upon your brow; and shed your light,

so that under the honor of your name

I may partake of these feasts.

Without you, Lord, nothing is sweet;

nor does it please me to desire anything with my mouth,

unless your favor first has imbued

the cups and the foods,

with faith sanctifying all things.

[Col. 0798A]

May our dishes taste of God,

and may Christ flow into the cups.

May the serious, the playful, words, jests—

in short, what we are and what we do—

be governed by the heavenly Trinity.

**259**

Here I have no spoils of roses,

no fragrant scent burns from perfume;

but an ambrosial liquid flows,

and faith smells of nectar,

poured forth from the Father’s embrace.

Muse, reject the light ivy

with which you are accustomed to encircle your temples,

[Col. 0799B]

28. *Sertaque mystica* (“mystical garlands”), a crown. I.

29. *Strophio* (“with a fillet”), with a golden belt; *strophium* is a belt. For *strophos* in Greek means “to turn”; hence *strophium* is so called because it is turned from the back toward the front. I. *Strophium* is a belt so called because it is turned from the loins toward the front; for *strophe* means “turning.” Vat. A.

30. *Redimita* (“crowned”), a figurative construction. *Comas* (“the hair”), through the hair. I.

31. *Generosa* (“noble”), nobly created by God. Iso.

32. *Indigena* (“native”), inhabitant. Iso.

34. *Data* (“given”), namely, given to him by the Lord. I.

35. *Artificem* (“maker”), Christ. I.

36. *Ipse* (“he himself”), the maker. I.

39. *Aere* (“by air”), in the air. I.

40. *Haec mihi* (“these things to me”): he subjected all created things to human power, and subjected the human being to himself. I.

41. *Callidus* (“crafty”), ingenious. I.

42. *Pedicis* (“by snares”): snares are impediments to walking; a snare is a noose by which birds are caught. *Maculis* (“by meshes”), nets. I.

[Col. 0800B]

43. *Glutine* (“with glue”): glue is made from bark. I.

44. *Vimina* (“twigs”), bushes. I.

46. *Fluctivagos* (“wandering through the waves”), wandering through the waves. I.

47. *Texta* (“woven things”), nets. I.

48. *Calamum* (“the reed”), the hook. I.

65. St. Jerome, letter 43, formerly 18, commends these foods together with those mentioned in the following stanza: “There, bread for food, and a vegetable watered by our hands, and milk—the delicacies of the countryside—provide foods indeed humble, but innocent.”

66. Nebrissensis says that *mulctra* means vessels for receiving milk, also called *mulctralia*, from Virgil, *Georgics* IV: “The cows will fill the milk vessels.” In that passage some read *mulgaria*, others *mulctraria*, but with the same meaning, namely vessels for receiving milk. In Egm. *mulctra gerit* appears, not improperly, as a different reading; for *mulctra* is also feminine.

67. The udder also belongs to goats and cattle, which have two udders. Sows, dogs, and other animals nourish more offspring and therefore possess more udders.

68. *Coagulum* (“curdling agent”) comes from *coactum* (“what has been forced together”), because it compels and thickens; hence he calls the curds *coagula* from their effect. Peveratus says that *coagula* are vessels in which milk is curdled. Among the ancients, however, *coagulum* is what is mixed into milk so that it may curdle. A *calathus* is something else.

[Col. 0801C]

70. Three kinds of milk are distinguished here: one for drinking, carried in milk vessels; another thick, forced into solid form by curds; and another pressed in a basket. *Calathus* is Greek; in Latin it is *fiscina*, a basket in which milk is usually pressed. Milk pressed in this way is distinguished from milk curdled into cheese. I think pressed milk is the kind of soft cheese that Italians call *raviggiuolo*; I understand Virgil’s passage in *Eclogue* 1, “and an abundance of pressed milk,” in the same way.

71. Attic honey is especially famous; Cecrops founded Athens.

74. In Bong. *liquet* (“is clear”) appears instead of *liquat* (“melts”), incorrectly. Nectar is said to smell of honey because honey itself is fragrant with thyme.

75. Virgil, Pliny, and others frequently teach that bees do not engage in intercourse to produce offspring. Some now maintain, and assert that it has been observed, that bees also mate in order to produce young. They distinguish female bees, which are very rare; males, which are not so rare; and the common, sexless bees, workers of honey, of which the largest portion consists. That honey was once food for abstainers is apparent from St. John the Baptist, who was accustomed to feed upon it.

76. Aldus has *hic* (“here”), which is not altogether displeasing. Here is another food of those fasting: the mild gifts—ripe, as *mitia poma* (“mild fruits”) in Virgil—of trees. Moreover, Christians sometimes practiced *xerophagy*, that is, dry nourishment, rejecting even juicy fruits. Tertullian, chapter 1 *On Fasting*, already entangled in heresy, removes from his followers the charge of novelty because “we observe xerophagies, drying food of all flesh and all broth, and of every more watery fruit, so that we neither eat nor drink anything containing wine”; he adds abstinence from bathing, appropriate to dry nourishment.

81. He includes both heroic and lyric poetry, in each of which genre the ancients had excelled.

82. Most read *inclyta*, *inclita*, or *incluta*, all of which amount to the same thing. Vat. A has *incita* above in smaller letters; in Rat. and Egm. *incita* has been corrected from *inclita*. The same occurs in Gold. as a correction. Bong., Urb., Ald., Gis., and other common editions have *incita*, which could be defended even though *incita* follows shortly afterward. Gallandius preferred *incita*.

85. Heinsius writes *aequiperare* (“to equal”).

86. Some think that these five verses designate acts of thanksgiving that ought to be offered to God whenever food is taken—namely morning, midday, and evening—while banquets are omitted, as wholly unbecoming to Christians. I disagree with them as strongly as possible. Here Prudentius expresses the Holy Scriptures and the custom of the early Christians. Psalm 54:17–18: “But I cried to God, and the Lord will save me. Evening, morning, and midday I will declare and proclaim, and he will hear my voice.” These are the three times at which Daniel prayed daily, chapter 6:10. From the Acts of the Apostles, Clement of Alexandria, and Cyprian it may be inferred that the Apostles devoted those same three hours to prayer, which they call the third, sixth, and ninth hours.

In volume III of Muratori’s *Anecdota* there is the complete book of Tertullian *On Prayer*, where in chapter 25 he says: “As for the time, there will not be a useless external observance even of certain hours. I mean those common hours which mark the divisions of the day: the third, sixth, and ninth, which are found to be more solemn in the Scriptures. The Holy Spirit was first poured out upon the disciples gathered together at the third hour. On the day when Peter experienced the vision of the universal community in that vessel, he had gone up to the upper rooms at the sixth hour for the sake of prayer. The same man, together with John, went to the temple at the ninth hour, where he restored the paralytic to health.” See Muratori’s notes.

From Tertullian’s passage, the distinguished Giovenazzius pointed out to me that another passage of St. Isidore, *Etymologies* VI, chapter 19, should be corrected. Isidore, copying Tertullian, says: “On the day when Peter experienced the vision of the community in that vessel, he had gone up at the sixth hour for the sake of prayer.” One should read, “the vision of the universal community.” Tertullian may also be emended from Isidore: for *PRIMUM* (“first”) the Holy Spirit was poured out upon the disciples gathered together at the third hour. So Isidore has it. Therefore in Tertullian read *PRIMUM Spiritus sanctus* (“the Holy Spirit first”), not *PRIMUS* (“the first [male]”).

90. Vat. A's gloss belongs to the explanation of the following stanza. Weitzius reads *canit* instead of *canet*, with Widm., Hails., and Gold.; but all our witnesses have *canet*, as do Ald., Gis., Put., Oxon., Heins., and Pal.

93. Aldus has *resonat*, incorrectly.

96. Instead of *sancte*, which the best and most witnesses have, Prag., Rat., Weitz., Gis. in the first edition, and Vatt. I and O read *sancta manus*, less well.

97. The poet used *cespitem madidum* (“moist turf”) for clay. Festus says: “A *cespes* is earth cut in the shape of a brick, with grass; or a crop cut and shorn.” Isidore, *Etymologies* XVI.6, says: “*Cespites* are shrubs.” See *Psychomachia*, verse 904: “For entrails fashioned from mud oppress the soul,” and so forth.

100. In the margin of Vat. A is: “He gave the soul from his own mouth,” a verse which Put. and Vat. O have in the text itself and which Heinsius calls more elegant than the received reading. Perhaps it is a variant reading by the same author arising from two editions of his works. He alludes to Genesis 2:7. You may read the rest of what is here narrated in the same place.

101. Vat. A has *hunc* instead of *tunc*, less well, and *directa* instead of *vireta*, incorrectly. Its glosses, and those of Iso, are not satisfactory. *Viretum* is a fixed noun, or substantive, not an adjective. Virgil, book VI: “They came to the joyful places and pleasant green groves.” The poet describes Paradise similarly in hymn 5, verse 113, and in the *Hamartigenia*, verse 856.

107. In the margin of Vat. A, *nisibus* (“efforts”) appears instead of *usibus* (“uses”), a reading that must certainly be retained.

110. Rat. has *medico* instead of *medio*, but the *c* has been erased, rightly; for Genesis 2:9 says: “The tree of life also in the midst of Paradise, and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.”

111. Nebrissensis understands *indocile* either as “uneducated” and “rude,” or as “incapable of the good arts,” which, according to Aristotle, are not found in a woman. I understand Eve's disposition as unwilling to learn God's command not to eat the forbidden fruit, by which Adam and Eve were bound. For the command *Ne comedas* (“Do not eat”) is put in the singular, by enallage, for *Ne comedatis* (“Do not eat, plural”), as the Septuagint has. Some teach that Eve was created before this command, although her formation is related afterward.

112. Prag. has *allicit* instead of *illicit*.

116. Aldus punctuates thus: *Corpora mutua nosse nefas. Post epulas inoperta vident Lubricus error et erubuit.* Rat. is better, where *videt* instead of *vident* is read: *Post epulas inoperta videt Lubricus error, et erubuit* (“After the meal slippery error sees them uncovered, and blushed”).

122. Aldus incorrectly has *sede propria* (“from her own dwelling”).

123. Nebrissensis correctly explains that Eve is called *innuba* because *nubere* is for a woman of lower status to give herself to her husband, and she had not yet been told: “You shall be under the power of your husband, and he shall rule over you.” Consider also whether the proper meaning of *nubere* is relevant: it means “to veil” or “to cover,” and *nubere* or *nubi* properly belongs to women, who, when about to be married, covered their head and cheeks to conceal their modesty beneath the bridal veil. Lucan, book II: “The saffron bridal veils did not cover the lowered faces of brides, lightly concealing modesty that was not timid.” Others write *flammeum*. Thus Eve, though given by God to Adam as wife, was not married in this sense, nor did she need a bridal veil to hide her modesty. This rite is suggested in Holy Scripture at Genesis 24:65, where Rebecca, on seeing Isaac, quickly took up a veil and covered herself . . . “He brought her into the tent of Sarah his mother and took her as his wife.” Covering, or veiling, the head in women is a sign of subjection, from 1 Corinthians 11:5 and following: “Every woman praying or prophesying with her head not veiled dishonours her head . . . A man indeed ought not to veil his head, since he is the image and glory of God; but woman is the glory of man. For man is not from woman, but woman from man.” For this reason a man is not properly said to marry his wife, except in jest. Martial said: “I do not wish to marry my wife.”

28, 129. *Solum* (“sole”) for the foot, or the lowest part of the foot, is frequent. In the hymn of St. Agnes, verse 116: “Now subdued by the virginal sole, [the dragon]”; and Lucretius: “I traverse places previously trodden by no sole.” Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations*, p. 246, in Anacharsis’ letter to Hanno: “My clothing is a Scythian covering, my footwear the callus of my soles, my bed the earth.” From *solum* (“sole”) comes *solea* (“sandal”), as well as the Spanish *suela* and similar words in other languages.

It may also be questioned whether the Latin expression *vertere solum* (“to change one’s ground”) belongs here, used in the sense of changing one’s position. One says, “Where shall I turn?”, “Where will you turn?”, “Where will they turn?” Strictly speaking, it is the feet that turn elsewhere, not the earth, when someone withdraws from it. Cicero, however, understands it differently, *Pro Caelio*, p. 69: “Those who had changed the soil of a certain state by changing their citizenship”; for him *vertere solum* and *mutare solum* mean the same thing.

By these verses and those that follow I have shown particularly clearly that the Vulgate reading, “She herself shall crush your head,” and the conception of the Blessed Virgin without the stain of original sin, which according to the opinion of the holy Fathers is signified in the serpent, are supported. Since this interpretation is especially clear among the ancients in the Spanish poet, I shall indicate a very recent testimony from Spain in its support: the address of the royal assembly of theologians, *For the Defense of the Mystery of the Immaculate Conception of the Virgin Mary*, to Charles III, concerning the present-day worship of this holy mystery and the pious opinion concerning it, rightly to be advanced to a greater degree of certainty. It was published at Madrid in 1778 and dedicated to the Catholic king Charles III by the Archbishop of Toledo, Francisco Antonio Lorenzana.

130. In Prag. the earlier reading was *suspic[i]atque* (“and may he suspect”), with the gloss above, *timeat* (“may he fear”). Widm. has *suspic[i]atque*; Gold. has *suspicit, utque* (“he looks, and so”).

131. Add to the gloss *Adamum*, whom Eve had compelled to eat from the forbidden things. When Prudentius says that posterity rushed into sin under these leaders and imitated its untaught ancestors, he does not agree with the Pelagians, whose heresy St. Prosper explains in his poem *Against the Ungrateful*, verses 20 and following. Prudentius explained original sin in clear terms in the *Apotheosis*, verses 911 and following. Observe also that Laurentius Berti, *On Theological Doctrine* XIII, chapter 2, proves original sin to belong to the foundations of the faith from Prudentius’ verses in the *Apotheosis*, 909 and following: “This is the soul’s first nature.”

133. Statius uses a similar phrase, *Silvae* III.3: “You cultivated untaught peoples and golden kingdoms.” Prudentius often uses *rudis* (“untaught”) for “new” and “recent.”

136. From Virgil’s *Eclogue* 4: “Now a new generation is sent down from high heaven.”

[Col. 0806C]

137. Christ is called the second man and the new man, just as Adam is the first man and the old man. St. Paul, 1 Corinthians 15: “The first man was from the earth, earthly; the second man was from heaven, heavenly.”

138. All printed editions and most manuscripts have *prius* (“before”). Rat. has *primus* (“first”) instead of *prius,” contrary to the metre. *Prior* (“the former”) is better, corresponding to the Apostle’s words, “The first man was from the earth, earthly.” Urb. likewise has *prior*, and it alone is worth following.

142. Rat., Weitz., Thuan. in a second hand, Gis., and Iso read *quem* (“whom”). Heinsius, together with his best witnesses, Ald., Vat. A, Prag., most Vatican manuscripts, and others, has *quam* (“which”): namely, “which flesh.” *Quem*, referring to “the Word,” is more pleasing.

144. *Genialis* (“marital”) is often applied to matters connected with marriage, as in Horace, Virgil, Martial, and others: *lectus genialis* (“marriage bed”), *torus genialis* (“marriage couch”). The *genius* was regarded by the ancients as the god who receives and protects a person at birth. They also called water, earth, fire, and air *genial* gods, for these are the seeds of things.

148. Most write *discidium* (“separation”). Gis. has *dissidium*, not improperly. It is preferable, however, to retain *discidium*, not derived from *dis* and *caedo*, as Becmanus thinks—for then the second *i* would be long—but from *discindo*, with the perfect *discidi*, just as *excidium* comes from *exscindo*. Gifanius, in his index to Lucretius under *discidium*, says that *dissidium* applies to the mind, *discidium* to the body, and that the word *discidium* has been corrupted in all good writers: Catullus, Plautus, Tibullus, Terence, and Cicero at least seven times, while it has remained intact in the Florentine *Digest* and in Tacitus. He himself restores many passages of the authors.

151. Many holy Fathers affirm that the Blessed Virgin deserved to give birth to God, including Augustine, Ambrose, Jerome, and many others. Hence theologians ask whether the Blessed Virgin deserved, in the strict sense of merit, to be the Mother of God—or, as they themselves put it, whether she merited the divine motherhood. Many affirm this with sufficiently probable reasoning, because the holy Fathers use the same words to prove that the just merit eternal life by good works and that the Virgin Mary merited to become the Mother of God. Francisco Suárez discusses and illustrates all this admirably, vol. I, *On the Third Part*, question 2, disputation 10, sections 7 and 8; he admits merit *de congruo* (“according to fittingness”).

153. The poet vividly depicts the serpent as it is usually represented by painters in the mystery of the Conception: *tractibus inexplicitis*, that is, compressed and entangled into coils and knots.

154. I do not see where the meaning “harmful” in the Vat. A gloss on *inerme* (“harmless”) came from, unless here too one says that *in-* intensifies the meaning, as the same Vat. A gloss stated above at verse 3. The true sense is that the serpent’s venom is *inerme* (“harmless”) as far as the Blessed Virgin is concerned, since she tramples the bowed viper underfoot and conquers all its poisons—that is, because she is free from original sin. Hence it is a sluggish serpent, that is, a weakened one.

155. The serpent is called *concolor* (“of the same color”) in the green grass because Horace, Virgil, and other poets frequently give snakes the epithet *viridis* (“green”).

He calls Christians the “little white flock” because of the custom of wearing white garments when they were cleansed in baptism, as though they were candidates for Christian life, and to signify the purity of the soul. A similar phrase occurs in hymn 1 of the *Peristephanon*, verse 67: “Christ presides there over companies clothed in white.”

Although every day belongs to the Lord, as Tertullian says in *On Baptism*, chapter 19—every hour and every time being suitable for baptism—“if the matter concerns solemnity, it does not affect grace”; nevertheless, the solemn period for conferring baptism was the fifty days from Easter to Pentecost, as may be gathered from that passage of Tertullian: “Easter provides the more solemn day for baptism, since the Lord’s Easter, into which we are immersed, has been fulfilled.” Those baptized walked about for eight days in white clothing. From the white garments of the baptized, the ancients called the week immediately following Easter *in albis* (“in white garments”). The name now remains attached to the Sunday *in albis*.

Nevertheless, on all the weekdays of that Easter week the ecclesiastical office contains several things pertaining to baptism, as in the hymn for Saturday Vespers: “Clothed in white robes for the royal banquets of the Lamb.” St. Ildefonsus, *On the Knowledge of Baptism*, chapter 140, has a prayer for removing the white garments, and chapter 142 has a sermon to be delivered to infants on the third day after Easter for the removal of the white garments.

Perhaps Prudentius also alluded to the symbol of Christian believers as just persons: the snowy lamb or white sheep, signifying purity of soul, in accordance with Matthew 25: “As a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats.” St. Paulinus, letter 12 to Severus, concerning a painting in the apse—or *absida*, for Paulinus hesitates whether it should be called *absida* or *abside*—says:

“Two pairs of contrasting goats surround the throne among the lambs; the Shepherd turns the goats away to the left and embraces the worthy lambs on the right.”

There is also a very ancient custom of depicting on sacred chalices the parable of the shepherd carrying the sheep back to the fold on his shoulders. Tertullian, *On Modesty*, chapter 7, although he had already fallen into heresy, attests to this matter in striking words: “Let the very paintings on your chalices come forward, if even in them there will shine through an interpretation of that sheep—whether it is meant to restore a Christian or an ethnic sinner.” [Col. 0808A] And in chapter 10: “To whom that shepherd whom you paint on the chalice may perhaps lend his support … concerning whom you drink nothing more willingly than the sheep of the second repentance.” [Col. 0808B] In the following verse Prudentius calls Christians fearless sheep.

158. Here the wolf is the devil. Teolius refers it to Isaiah 11:6: “The wolf shall dwell with the lamb,” and so forth. I do not agree.

159. Prag. has *rapidum* (“swift”), less well.

160. Ald. has *sanguis* (“blood”), erroneously.

161. Since the paschal lamb in the Old Law was a type of Christ, who was also called the LAMB OF GOD by St. John the Baptist, early Christians very often represented Christ by the figure of a lamb. Jacobus Bosius, book VI of *The Triumphant Cross*, chapter 12, presents an ancient image of this sort: a lamb standing beneath a cross upon a rock and emitting five springs, to signify Christ’s five wounds—one from its breast and one from each of its four feet. St. Paulinus, *Letter 12 to Severus*: “Christ stands as a Lamb; the Father’s voice thunders from heaven, and through the dove the Holy Spirit flows.” And later: “Beneath the bloody cross Christ stands in a snow-white Lamb.” See Aringhi, book VI of *Roman Subterranean Things*, chapter 20, where, from the custom of the earliest Christians, he derives the practice of the Roman Church of making waxen images of lambs in the manner of coins; Panvinius had already taught this.

165. The Holy Spirit appeared in the form of a dove over Christ when he was baptized (Matthew 3). Hence the devout custom of the faithful, who placed golden and silver doves, as figures of the Holy Spirit, above fonts and altars; of this the Council of Constantinople of 536 speaks in its fifth session. Christians themselves, however, were also represented by this symbol. Paulinus, in the passage cited: “A crown surrounds the cross with a shining orb; the apostles are crowns of that crown, whose figure is in the choir of doves.” And, omitting many other passages: “Make us also, O Christ, doves pleasing to you, if your peace flourishes in pure hearts.” He refers to Christ’s command in Matthew 10: “Be simple as doves.” St. Augustine, on this passage, teaches that the unity of the Church is signified by the dove, concerning which it is said, “My dove is one” (Song of Songs 6); and on Psalm 54 he likewise says that the dove is used as a sign of love. At the beginning of *Against the Valentinians*, Tertullian writes that the dove was customarily used to show Christ, a statement which Petrus Lazzeri, *Dissertation on the Rules of Criticism*, interprets for our purpose. Some also understand Christ in what Tertullian says in chapter 3: “The house of our dove is simple, always on high and open, and toward the light.” Sedulius, of Christ: “The dove alone returns, which circles the whole world; let the ravens depart, the dove alone returns.” In the *Wood of Allegories*, under “Dove,” Lauretus identifies the holy Fathers who recognized a type of Christ in the dove carrying an olive branch, and likewise Christ’s wrath in the wrath of the dove, often mentioned in the sacred writings. It is therefore clear that Prudentius may rightly call Christ a Dove; perhaps the ancients sometimes represented Christ in that form, as when St. Basil enclosed the Eucharist in a golden dove and suspended it over the altar, or when others painted doves perched on crosses or flying above them. Yet it is far more probable that even then the Holy Spirit was signified. Tertullian’s passages too clearly indicate that the dove is a figure of the Holy Spirit. Among the symbols which Clement of Alexandria says Christians should engrave upon the bezels of rings, he includes a dove: “Let our seals be a dove, or a fish, or a ship borne on its swift course by the wind, or a musical lyre such as Polycrates used, or a nautical anchor such as Seleucus engraved.” Rosweydus there explains the mystical meanings suggested by these symbols: baptism, Peter the Apostle as a fisher of men, David’s lyre, the Church, and so forth.

178. Teolius seems to infer from this passage that the precept of abstaining from meat had already prevailed, at least in Spain, in Prudentius’ time. Yet Prudentius neither explains what those forbidden foods are nor designates any particular day. In any case, the custom of fasting on Saturday in Spain, Rome, and other Churches is established by ancient records, namely the Council of Elvira and the testimony of many holy Fathers. The origin of fasting, or semi-fasting, on Wednesday and Friday is much older and more distinguished, and must therefore be traced back to the apostles themselves.

180. That fasting benefits the healing of souls and bodies, and likewise moderation in food, is a common declaration of everyone; the Church sings it as well.

182. Nebrissa interprets *liba* as cakes offered to demons before Christ’s birth. Chamillardus says that Prudentius used *liba* for any fruit. I understand by the impious *liba* only the forbidden fruit of paradise, whatever that fruit may have been, since the word derives from *libo*, “to take a little, pluck, taste,” as in Lucretius, Virgil, Varro, and others. The entire stanza concerns the punishment of death inflicted because of original sin.

199. Prudentius says *gradu facili* (“by an easy ascent”) because Virgil, *Aeneid* VI, had said: “The descent to Avernus is easy. … But to retrace one’s step and escape to the upper air—this is the task, this the labor.” Clericus rebukes Chamillardus in the *Life of Prudentius* because he interpreted, according to the now customary manner of speaking, that Christ returned from limbo. Clericus himself infers that Prudentius held Christ to have descended to the place of the underworld where the condemned are tormented. See the preface, no. 181.]

203. I do not know what the final words of the gloss mean, unless, as I think, they are to be referred to the following verse, *parili*. A tomb is called a sarcophagus, as though it devoured flesh. See what Isidore, *Origins* XVI.4, takes from Pliny, where he says that a sarcophagus was a stone from which tombs were made because it consumed the bodies of the dead. In another sense, *sarcophagus* means a bier or coffin; what others say, I cannot make out.

204. Aldus and Gis., in the text of the first edition, with Urb. and Vat. P, read *Dux parilis redivivus homo*. Nebrissa likewise. Put. has *Dux parili redivivus homo*; Oxon., *Dux parili redivivus humo*. The rest read *Dux parili redivivus humo*, including Egm. as a variant spelling.

After Food. Aldus entitles it: “Ode after food.” Janus Parrhasius: “Hymn of divine Prudentius after food has been taken.” As prayers should be offered to God before food, so also after food. Tertullian, *Apology* 39: “One does not recline before prayer to God has first been tasted. … Prayer concludes the banquet.” St. Basil, Letter to St. Gregory the Theologian on the Life to Be Lived in Solitude: “Let prayers before food worthily concern God’s gifts, both those which he now gives and those which he has laid up for the future. Let prayers after food contain thanksgiving for what has been given and petition for what has been promised.”

4. Parrh. has *cubile sacrum*. Nebrissa says that *cherubim* and *seraphim* are either plural accusatives (for *cherub* and *seraph* are singular), so that cherubim and seraphim are understood to be the seat upon which God rests, or plural genitives, because God’s seat consists of cherubim and seraphim. St. Jerome, *Commentary on Isaiah* 6, says that those err who customarily say in prayers, “Who sit above cherubim and seraphim,” because Scripture has not taught this. In his letter to St. Damasus on the seraphim and related matters, he calls it a pious error in those who dare to say this in their prayers and offerings (see the gloss). Hence it is clear that already in Jerome’s time there were prayers in which this was asserted. Indeed, if it is said as though expressed in explicit words by sacred Scripture, Jerome rightly calls it an error. For Psalm 79:1 says only, “You who sit above the cherubim, reveal yourself.” Prudentius, however, merely affirms that God, supported by his highest throne, holds and governs the cherubim and seraphim, his seat. This is true, provided that both belong to the adornment of God’s seat and attend upon it. Isaiah 6:1–2 reads: “I saw the Lord seated upon a throne high and lifted up; and those things which were beneath him filled the temple. Seraphim stood above it; each had six wings, and the other six; with two they covered his face, with two they covered his feet, and with two they flew.” The Septuagint translates, “They were around him,” and interpreters rightly observe that this fits the context. Cornelius a Lapide explains it plainly thus: “Beside or around the throne, namely upon the foot or pavement of the throne; for it was fitting that they should be in a lower rank than God’s own seat and throne.” These seraphim surround the throne as cherubim surrounded the mercy-seat in Exodus 25. In short, this is more than enough to defend the poet from the foolish gloss.

[Col. 0812C] 7. Rat. has *Deum Sabaoth* for *Sabaoth Deum*, incorrectly. From this infer that the poet looked to Isaiah 6, where the seraphim cried, “Holy, holy, holy, the Lord God of hosts.” We write these Hebrew names as we find them in the Vulgate edition, though we are by no means unaware of the objections often raised. Nor do we wish to defend Prudentius at length for sometimes disregarding, in these names, the quantity of syllables prescribed by experts in Hebrew; this was discussed in the preface.

10. God as “fountain of life” occurs everywhere in sacred Scripture and the holy Fathers, and often in Prudentius. So too “fountain of souls,” “fountain of good,” “fountain of all goods,” and similar expressions.

[Col. 0812D] 13. Weitzius, alone with Hailsb. against the Vulgate and the rest, wished to read *omne*. Why, when it conflicts with the rules of the phalaecian verse, which Prudentius plainly observes? Of the Vatican manuscripts only one has *omne* in Teolius; of Heinsius’s older manuscripts only Altinius has *omne*; of ours none. Gisel., Gold., and Weitz. have *ac vigemus*. Aldus, our manuscripts, Wid. above, and Heinsius with Put. have *aut vigemus*.

16. The Spirit is called radiant-white either because he appeared and is represented in the form of a dove, or because of the brightness which he pours into souls. The procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son is not obscurely suggested by these verses, specifically by the verb of sending used in sacred Scripture. Chamillardus asserts that, at the Council of Toledo by Leo’s command, the phrase *Filioque* was added to the creed of faith, whereas the Nicene Creed says only, “Who proceeds from the Father.” He means Leo I and either the Council of Toledo or the Spanish council of 447. The learned Henricus Florez, volume VI of *Sacred Spain*, dissertation 1, discusses at length the First Council of Toledo in 400 and the rule of faith inserted in its acts, in which the phrase *Filioque* is found. He seeks to prove that another council met at Toledo in 396 before it; that the compiler of the acts of the council held in 400 flourished at the end of the fifth century; that the rule of faith was made at that council; and that the addition *Filioque* is not spurious, since all manuscripts and printed books have it and that council dealt with Priscillianists who erred concerning the Holy Spirit. These points might be confirmed from these poems of the Spanish poet, in which the procession of the Spirit is expressed, as though he had before his eyes the rule of faith and its clause, “Who proceeds from the Father and the Son.” Nevertheless, I judge that the matter is not clear, and the mention of Pope Leo which occurs in the title of the rule of faith plainly indicates that it is much later than the Council of Toledo of 400, or at least that the compiler of the acts did not know to what time it should be assigned.]

37. Parrh. has *praenitens* for *praecluens*. The verb *cluo* was used not only by the older Latins—Ennius, Plautus, and Lucretius—but also by Cicero. Lucretius uses *cluo, -es*; Prudentius uses *cluo, -is*, as may be observed elsewhere. It is one of those verbs which belong equally to the second and third conjugations. From *cluo* comes *inclytus*, or *inclitus*, or *inclutus*.

52. The practice of praying to God with extended hands; see the note on the hymn of St. Fructuosus.

54. Prag., Rat., Weitz., and Gis. read *victu*. Ald., Vat. A, Put., Oxon., Egm., Alt., Pal., Heins., and others read *victus*.

57. Parrh. has *dissilit*. St. Isidore, *Etymologies* II.29: “The world is that which consists of heaven, earth, and sea, together with all the stars.” See also his book XIII, chapter 1, and the notes of Grialis.
