[Col. 0815C] The poet alludes to Virgil’s phrase, “he loaded the tables with unbought provisions,” likewise said of the farmer in *Georgics* IV. Horace too, in praise of country life, *Epode* 2.48: “Unbought banquets he displays.”

59. The manuscripts differ remarkably in writing the name *Habacuc*. Some have *Abacuc*, others *Abbacuc*, *Abbacum*, *Ambacum*, or *Ambacuc*. On this name see the second index of Riccioli, where he defends Prudentius against Ludovicus Cavallus for lengthening the first *a* in this hymn according to a Syriac or Persian root. Although Prudentius calls Habakkuk a prophet, it cannot be inferred with certainty that he is the same Habakkuk whose prophecy survives. Read this question in the preliminary remarks of Jacobus Bonfrerius, section 11.

61. Widm. has *cujus caesarie* from the first hand.

62. This expression, *sicut erat*, seems to bear the flavor of ecclesiastical style, but it was used by the best and most ancient Latin authors.

68. In this speech of Habakkuk, Prudentius introduces Christ by anticipation; for the Word had not yet become flesh, and therefore had not yet become Christ, as Nebrissa notes. Clericus raises some quibbles in his *Life of Prudentius* concerning such expressions.

69. Ald. has the erroneous *libatibus*. Nebrissa copied the error and interpreted it as “for your taste.” The sense and meter require *liba tibi*, “cakes for you.”

70. Scripture does not explicitly say that Daniel gave thanks to God after receiving the food. The poet infers it from the thanksgiving that preceded it in verses 36–37.

71. Parrh. has *ciboque functus*, “and having partaken of food.”

72. Parrh. has *Evieque dixit*, which is corrupt. The word *amen* was customarily used in responses in the Old Testament, meaning “certainly,” “truly,” “this will be,” “truth,” or “so be it.” Deuteronomy 27:15: “All the people shall answer and say, Amen.” In the Christian Church the practice of saying *amen* after the priest’s prayer seems to have been introduced from the very beginning. The Apostle says, 1 Corinthians 14:15–16: “What then? I will pray with the spirit, and I will pray with the mind; I will sing with the spirit, and I will sing with the mind. Otherwise, if you bless with the spirit, how will the one who fills the place of the unlearned say ‘Amen’ over your blessing, since he does not know what you are saying?” Justin Martyr, *Apology* 2—or, as others hold, 1—says: “When he [the presiding minister] has concluded the prayers and the Eucharist, the entire assembly of the people applauds with favorable acclamation, saying ‘Amen.’” St. Paulinus, *Natale* 11: “And when the devout crowd offers ‘Amen’ to the holy shepherds,” and so forth. On the word *alleluia*, consult Riccioli’s second index, though his view should not be accepted that Prudentius should not be imitated because he shortened the *e* in this verse; Orientius likewise shortened it. St. Justin, *Questions* 50 to the Orthodox, testifies that Christians already used the words *alleluia* and *hosanna* when singing praises and hymns, as had formerly been done by children. See St. Jerome’s letter to Marcella, St. Augustine on Psalm 106, and Loaysa’s notes on canon 11 of the Fourth Council of Toledo: “On not singing *alleluia* during Lent.”

74. This verse is included, with altered wording, in the prayer of St. Rose of Lima: “Almighty God, giver of every good thing.”

77. Cauchius emended *antro conclusos regis*—“confined in the king’s den”—ingeniously, but against the manuscripts. Nebrissa interprets *actum* as the actions of the world, that is, of one excessively powerful and raging; for this is what *impotens* means in Latin. Heinsius understands *actum* either as the wandering and uncertain movement of human affairs or as what human beings do. Prudentius used the word elsewhere in this sense.

79. Having described the lions’ den, the poet, following Scripture in his customary manner, represents the devil as a lion, drawing on 1 Peter 5:8.

81. Ald., Nebr., Rat., Widm., Gold., and Hails. have *tunc te*. Gis. and Weitz. have *cum te*. Parrh. has *nec te*. Vat. A, Prag., Put., two Torrentian manuscripts, and others have *cur te*, which Heinsius favors because it frequently occurs in Cicero. Horace, *Epistles* I.8: “I shall be angry with my friends: why should they hasten to shut me out with deadly lethargy?” Aldus in his corrected edition has *summe Deum*.]

82. Aldus’ punctuation is preferable: *premimur malis, alii premimur, malis rotamur*—“we are oppressed by evils; others read, ‘we are oppressed, we roll amid evils.’” Alex. agrees with Aldus. But Vat. I, O, and P, along with others, have the latter arrangement. A similar passage occurs in St. Augustine, *Enchiridion* 26: “The condemned mass of the whole human race lay in evils, or was even rolled about, and was hurled from evils into evils.” Therefore I prefer *malis rotamur*.

84. Nebrissa explains it thus: “Let faith be, or let it be applied.” Giselinus seems to have understood it as “faith grew through punishments.” Chamillardus: “Faith was subjected to unjust punishments.” I prefer the latter.

91. In Rat., *hinc* instead of *hic*, but the *n* has been erased. Beware the error found in some editions: *sociatus* instead of *satiatus*. The meaning is “satisfied with the food” that the prophet Habakkuk—or someone else—brings. The poet adheres to the same story and understands by the harvesters, for whom Habakkuk had prepared food, righteous men such as the apostles and other laborers whom the Lord sends into his harvest.

101. I conjectured *Deum loquemur*. Parrhasius printed this, but the reading should be *loquamur*, with *feramus* in the following verse. If this reading is accepted, the unity of the divine nature in Father and Son is elegantly expressed. See Aldus’ correction at verse 81.

“Again,” and so forth. We have explained this title and almost the entire hymn at length in chapters 12 and 18 of the preface. I shall now add that the learned Father Mamachi treated the miracle of the light called that of the Holy Sepulchre much more accurately than Father Liberius of Jesus, in volume II of *Christian Antiquities*, chapter 1, page 65, where he defends the truth of the miracle against Mosheim. I printed Drepanius’ verse in the hymn *On the Paschal Candle* as I found it in certain editions: “That we may be able to carry him through the whole night.” But in Fabricius’ *Christian Poets* I found another reading, which is more correct: “That we may be able to speak him through the whole night.” Brissonius, in his *On Spectacles*, page 351, discusses at length the vigil of Paschal Saturday and gives this hymn the title *On the Lights of Paschal Saturday*. In Cardinal Thomasius’ *Hymnary*, part of this hymn is inserted twice, first under the title “For the lighting of the paschal candle,” and then under the other title “For the lighting of the lamp.”

1. Giselinus explains this hymn at greater length than usual and, following Georgius Cassander, holds that it belongs to the custom of that age, when on Holy Saturday, as the day was inclining toward evening, before the solemn celebration of baptism, a candle was customarily consecrated by the deacon and lit with a new fire, either produced by striking flint or drawn from the sun by means of a crystal held before it. From this candle the candles of the newly baptized—those, namely, which they carried in their hands—were lit. [Col. 0818C] That same candle was carried before the newly baptized as they proceeded to the sacred rites during the seven following days, which were called the days of the newly baptized.

But I fear that this whole practice of consecrating the paschal candle, together with its other accompanying features, belongs to a period later than Prudentius. Gaspar Barthius also devoted some effort to explaining this hymn in book IX, chapter 20 of his *Adversaria*, from a parchment manuscript sheet:

“Which,” he says, “I immediately compared with the author, whom I hold dearest of all, with great delight: the complete fifth hymn on the paschal candle is written in it.”

Although we judge that this hymn was not a daily one, we nevertheless place it here because it was certainly sung at that hour, namely after the meal and before sleep. In the Mozarabic Breviary, some stanzas of it are read at Vespers on the first Sunday after the octave of Epiphany: specifically the first, seventh, thirty-fifth, thirty-eighth, and the three following stanzas. From this source I shall indicate various readings.

Concerning Nebrissensis’s annotations on this and the two following hymns, I made some observations in the prolegomena, no. 106, against Weitzius. The opening is drawn from the subject itself. God is the inventor of light, as above in hymn 4, verse 9, “the discoverer of the world.” Claudianus, or rather Merobaudes, in the *Eulogy of Christ*:

“and discoverer of light, parent before your own birth and your mother’s.”

Barthius, book I of the *Adversaria*, chapter 7, would prefer to read:

“and discoverer of light, O Son,  
parent of your own mother.”

One may also punctuate the words as follows: “and discoverer of light, before your own mother’s parent.”

The Mozarabic Breviary has, incorrectly, *rutilis*.

4. Theodulfus of Orléans read this verse in this way in his book *On the Holy Spirit*. Barthius likewise reads it so in his parchment manuscript sheet, as do Vatican manuscripts A and P and the Thomasian Hymnary when Giselinus first copied this hymn into the margin of the second edition. Others read differently: Aldus, Rat., Prag., Giselinus in the text of the second edition, Heinsius with his manuscripts, Vatican manuscripts I and O, and Weitzius:

“Restore light to your faithful, Christ.”

Bongarsius, Giselinus in the text of the first edition, the Thomasian Hymnary in its second position, and the Mozarabic Breviary have:

“Light, Christ, restore to your faithful,”

which Fabricius also retained. Giselinus, however, in the margin of the first edition, has:

“Light, Christ, restore to your faithful.”

On the word *faithful*, used in the sense of “Christian,” Christopher Cellarius and both Borrichii—Olaus and Andreas—argue among themselves. They say that ancient pagan authors used the word in this sense, against Cellarius, who maintains that *Christo* should be added, “faithful to Christ.” For us, it is enough that this meaning is ecclesiastical.

8. Rat. has *monstrans*, but the *n* has been erased, and rightly so, since it is superfluous. After this verse Aldus, Sichardus, and Fabricius insert these four lines:

“You signify by this work, illustrious Creator,

That all minds should constantly seek

The true light in Christ the Lord,

Whom the eminent teacher calls the rock.”

They are absent from our parchment manuscripts and from those of others. Barthius says that they are obscure in meter and wording, contaminated with solecisms, and rightly rejected by Giselinus. I would agree with him rather than with Gallandius, who doubts which of the two sets of verses ought to be admitted into the text, since both seem to him not unworthy of Prudentius; or with Teolius, who thinks it possible that Prudentius wrote the rejected verses in the first edition of the work and corrected them later. I shall never believe that Prudentius made two dactyls out of *doctor egregius*. Rupertus, in book V of *On the Divine Offices*, chapter 34, did not recognize those verses:

“Prudentius,” he says, “in the hymn sung on Holy Saturday, after saying, ‘Yet you show us how to seek lights from seed-bearing rock,’ to indicate that this is done in commemoration of the fire of the Holy Spirit proceeding for us from Christ the stone, immediately added, ‘So that man might know,’ and so forth.”

In the Roman Order, a very ancient book, those spurious verses are likewise omitted; perhaps Rupertus derived the other verses from it. He titles that chapter *On the New Fire*.

11. Christ is the steadfast rock, from 1 Corinthians 10:4: “The rock was Christ.”

[Col. 0819D]

12. In Barthius’s very ancient manuscript:

“From our little fires, whence comes the store of food.”

Barthius calls this “a most elegant reading,” and says that he would defend its acceptance at any wager. Consider, he says, those inexhaustible seeds of flame which the rock supplies: they show that it contains a store of fires and sparks. Nothing more poetic or more pleasing could have been devised. “I change nothing,” he says, “for both the expression and the word *genus* are elegant, and all our manuscripts, as well as those of others, have *genus*.”

13. Giselinus, first edition, has *pingui* instead of *pinguis*. The Alexandrian manuscript incorrectly has *quoque* instead of *quos*. On the bronze and earthen lamps of the Christians, see Bosius, Aringhus, Severanus, Fortunius Licetus, Casalius, and others. Saint Paulinus, *Natalis* 7, gives a lengthy description of a glass lamp, whose verses are especially suitable for explaining Prudentius:

“Close by, in the middle,” and so forth.

From among the many ancient Christian lamps that can be observed in writers on Christian antiquities, I have selected one to be engraved, since it may be useful for explaining many other matters. It is presented by Dominicus Georgius in his dissertation *On the Monogram of the Lord Christ*, Rome, 1738, p. 11. It was preserved at Pesaro in the museum of Giovanni Battista Passerius, and Georgius calls it a distinguished monument of sacred antiquity, more precious than gold, in which Eusebius’s account of Constantine’s vision is reproduced with exact precision and defended against the innovators. On other lamps, consult Victorius in his *History of the Seven Holy Sleepers*, p. 54, and Pietro Sante Bartoli, *The Ancient Figured Funerary Lamps*.

14. The glosses disagree with others who derive *fax*, “torch,” more correctly from Greek φάος, “light.” Vatican A, Egmondanus, Hailsbrunner, and Widmann, by a second hand, have *ac* instead of *aut*, which is not objectionable. In favor of the reading *ac*, Gallandius cites the Thomasian Hymnary, and Teolius two Vatican manuscripts.

15. In fact, *scirpus* is the reed that grows in marshy places, light and tall, from which mats are also made. It was formerly called *sirpus*.

20. I do not adequately understand whether the gloss says *fontem* or something else. Rat. incorrectly has *bibat*, “let him drink.”

21. Barthius says that the method of making lamps here described differs from that of our own age, and he thinks that it is not found so vividly and truthfully anywhere else in antiquity. It was an ingenious construction. The fire heats the wax or oil hanging above it and makes it liquid; this drips drop by drop through a carefully arranged narrow opening, feeding the flame, which thus obtains its own fuel through heat. Anyone could make such a lamp without difficulty from any material. The ingenuity of the ancients is noteworthy in their effort to save the continual labor that would otherwise have been required to pour in the liquid drop by drop.

Gronovius, *Ecclesiastical Observations*, chapter 5, ridicules Barthius’s admirable and imaginative interpretation, and says that Prudentius is merely singing of what we see every day in our wax or tallow candles. In Barthius’s manuscript there was *vortice*, as though some pool of the suspended liquid were being indicated. The first two verses were also transposed:

“For the fiery force, having burned it, makes

The rain weep from its moist summit;

From the liquid whirlpool the boiling nectar

Drips drop by drop in fragrant tears.”

22. Aldus, Palatine, Giselinus, Iso, Urbinate, and Vatican manuscripts O and P have *alentibus*, “nourishing”; *olentibus*, “fragrant,” is far better. Wax has an odor, and this epithet is sometimes applied to candles. Prudentius, hymn 3, verse 62: “The honeycomb sweats fragrant nectar.” It should also be noted that in both places *nectar* is used in imitation of Virgil, *Aeneid* I: “and they fill the cells with sweet nectar.”

Giselinus and, with him, Chamillardus want the other liquids—those from oil and pine—to be understood by synecdoche from the one dripping liquid of wax. But it is not necessary for this stanza to speak of anything besides the wax. Barthius explains it of wax and oil and says that fragrances were added by the ancients to make its use more pleasant. I believe that from this arose the custom of inserting incense into the paschal candle. Saint Paulinus, *Natalis* 3, mentioning lamps and candles, attributes fragrance to the candles:

“Fragrant lights are burned on waxen papyrus.”

Prudentius calls them “tears,” as he will soon say “to weep.”]

58. *Pelusiacis*: Egyptian; Pelusium is a city of Egypt, I.

60. *Rubris*: thus the Red Sea is called—not because it is red in itself, for water has no color in itself, but because it has red shores. Water derives its color from the surrounding objects and from the sky. Vatican A.

62. *Praelia*: from pressing upon the enemy; hence also *praeligna*, the wooden instruments by which grapes are pressed, I.

66. *In faciem*: “in the likeness of,” Vatican A.

Properly, *justitium* is a stoppage of law, like *solstitium*, a stoppage of the sun; it is used for mourning because mourning can occur when justice is abandoned, Vatican A.]

53. It should read *densetur*, from *denseo, densere*, a verb that must also be restored in other passages. Heinsius, with his manuscripts, follows our Vatican manuscripts A, B, I, O, P, the Alexandrian, Pragense, and Rat., in which *a* has been made from *e* by an inept corrector. Aldus, Chamillardus, and Giselinus in the first edition read *densatur*, which occurs in the Urbinate. Gifanius, in his *Index to Lucretius*, under *densere*, notes that in certain passages of Virgil *densare* is incorrectly read for *densere*. Horace, Ovid, and often Lucretius use the same verb *densere*. All manuscripts have *turba* in this verse of Prudentius. Gronovius conjecturally restored *turma*, a reading that pleased Heinsius. But since all the manuscripts oppose it, I would dare change nothing. For what if Prudentius deliberately wrote *turba* to signify the crowd’s disorder and a makeshift army?

54. The same Gronovius, *Ecclesiastical Observations*, chapter 5, conjectures:

“Part of the chariots and horses, and the birds of the wheels,

Swiftly mount,”

namely, “they mount the chariots, the horses, and the wheels that fly.” Heinsius likewise approved this. The old reading should be retained: it possesses poetic elegance and expresses the Egyptians’ panic. Heinsius made no change; Cellarius adopted Gronovius’s conjectures.

56. The dragons, which after Trajan’s time were used by the Romans on military standards, the poet transfers to the Egyptians, in a trope familiar to him, says Giselinus. He uses *dragons* for the insignia of the standard. On this use of dragons, see hymn 1 of the *Peristephanon*, verse 35.

57. Our manuscripts have *hinc*, except that Rat. seems to have *hic*. Bongarsius, Aldus, and Giselinus have *hinc*. But Heinsius, with his better manuscripts, and Weitzius have *hic*. Rottendorphius, for a different reading, has *libera* in place of *nescia*, perhaps from a gloss.

59. Vatican B has *purpurea*, incorrectly.

60. In Greek this sea is called the Erythraean. Some think it was called Red from its reddish sand; Agatharchides, as quoted by Photius, derives the name from a king Erythras. Others say that this was Esau Rufus, named from his reddish hair.

62. In the gloss I correct *prela ligna*.

63. Heinsius notes that his better manuscripts have *suos praecipit*; I do not know who read otherwise. The precision of the adverb *porro* is noteworthy: it indicates a further extension toward the end. Hence the verb *porricio* comes from augural usage. “To extend *porro* into the sea” means to advance far and onward into the sea.

[Col. 0824B]

65. Damascenus and Cosmas begin several hymns with this marvelous event. Saint Damasus used the verb *viandi* in his hymn on Saint Felix, as did Juvencus and others.

66. Vatican B incorrectly has *pervias* instead of *pervia*.

67. From the old Roman Order and other monuments it is clear that this triumph of the Israelite people was once sung in the Church on Holy Saturday. Avitus confirms this at the end of book V:

“The renowned leader describes in solemn song

When guilt, cleansed by sacred baths, is wiped away.”

68. Here too Heinsius notes that Rot. reads *dum permeat*, which is found in all the manuscripts.

76. Vatican A and Prag. by a second hand have *refluo* instead of *confluo*. Among Weitzius’s manuscripts, Egm., Pal., and Hailsb. seem to have *refluo* in the first hand; Teolius cites two Vatican manuscripts for this reading.

79. Rat. adds *in* above *nare*, giving *innare*, which Vatican A has. The meter opposes it.

80. Aldus adds *ut*, namely *justitium ut triste*, but this is truly superfluous. Barthius’s parchment manuscripts most ineptly have *inscitium* instead of *justitium*. Barthius spends much time explaining this passage and generally agrees with the glosses. He says that *arx* means a palace, or, as we barbarously say today, a royal state; *justitium* means vengeance or a mournful overthrow. Lucan, book II: “the deadly mourning through the city.” The whole point is that among the ancients *justitium* meant public mourning.

81. An anonymous author of a ninth-century hymn for martyrs at Vespers reproduced this passage. See Hincmarus, *On the Non-Trinal Deity*.

82. Fabricius and Giselinus, first edition, have *domitum Pharon*. Vatican B has *domitam Pharaon*. Rat., Gold., and Widm. have *domitum Pharaon*. Heinsius with his manuscripts, Gifanius, and Cauchius have *domitam Pharon*; so too Aldus, Giselinus, second edition, Prag., Vatican A, Egm., Palatine, Fabricius, Hailsbrunner, and Weitzius, who writes *Faron*. The poet uses Pharos, the island near Alexandria, for Egypt. Lucan, book X:

“Then he seized Pharos, the barrier of the sea:

An island that once stood high in the midst of the sea,”

and so forth. On the same island stood a very tall tower from which torches lit at night guided the course of sailors; this too was called a *pharos*.

83. Fabricius and Giselinus have *praesidi*; others, *praesuli*. This is Moses, the overseer of justice. Giselinus wants the “right hand of justice” to be understood, rather than “the overseer of justice.” I prefer this, as in hymn 11, verse 115: “whom you, as leader of fury, …”]

[Col. 0823A]

The crowd is massed in marching wedges;

Some swiftly mount chariots, horses, and wheels that fly, and the famous military standards

Display their swollen dragons.

From this point, the people, now ignorant of their former slavery,

Scorched by the Pelusian heats,

At last, guests of the purple flood,

[60] Wearied, settled beside the Red shores.

289 The dreadful enemy arrives with his treacherous leader

And brings battle with powerful forces.

Moses then commands his people

To advance into the sea with steadfast, fearless steps.

[65] The broken waters offer a passage to travelers;

Passable in the likeness of shores; the surrounding wave

Is held fast in glassy waters,

[Col. 0823B]

While the people pass beneath the divided sea.

[Col. 0824A]

Even the dark-skinned youth,

[70] Provoked by fierce hatred under an impious king,

Thirsting to pour out Hebrew blood,

Dares entrust himself to the hollow sea.

The royal ranks went, driven by headlong force,

Through the midst of the waves:

[75] But then the confused water turns back,

Flying upon itself in a united flood.

Then chariots, horses, and shipwrecked weapons,

290 The princes themselves and the wandering bodies

Of the black attendants—you could see them floating—

[80] The sad public mourning of the tyrant’s citadel.

What tongue could finally recount

Your praises, Christ, who by your avenging right hand

[Col. 0824B]

Compel conquered Pharos, through many plagues, to yield to the guardian of justice?

[Note: [Col. 0825B]

92. *Axe*: “by the sun,” I. *Sub perusta plaga*, “beneath the scorched region,” that is, through Arabia, Vatican A.

94. *Ligni*: “of the wood,” that is, of the cross. — *Venia*: “by favor, benefit,” Vatican A. — *Atticum*: that which is found sweeter than every honey, I.

97. *Ninguidus*: snowy, I.

102. *Alites*: quails, Vatican A.

[Col. 0826B]

106. *Numinis*: “of the Son of God,” Vatican A.

109. *Freta*: storms, I.

113. *Rosariis*: roses; *rosarium* and *rosetum* mean the same thing, namely a place where roses grow, I.

114. *Calthaque*: precious pigments; *caltha* is a shrub in Egypt from which balsam flows. — *Pinguia*: herbs, I.]

[Note: [Col. 0825B]

85. Vatican A has *pontum rabidis*. Heinsius with his manuscripts, Aldus, Rat., Giselinus, Weitzius, and the Vatican manuscript O have *pontum rapidis*. Barthius’s sheet has *rabidis*.

86. Prag. and Giselinus, second edition, have *persulcare*; Aldus, Vatican B, Prag., Weitzius, and Vatican O have *persultare*, which Vatican A seems to have intended, where it reads *persultetre*. Barthius’s sheet has *sale* instead of *salo*, a word Virgil used.

88. Palatine, Aldus, and Weitzius have *devoret*. Our manuscripts and those of Heinsius have *ut voret*. Giselinus in the margin has *devoret*. So do two Vatican manuscripts cited by Teolius.

89. Aldus and Giselinus in the text of the first edition have *viae* instead of *eremi*. This was done because the second syllable of *eremi* is long. But the poet’s usage, and that of his age, should be noted, as I explained more fully in the prolegomena. Teolius says: “He shortened the second syllable of *eremi*; elsewhere he lengthens it,” and cites verse 39 of the preface. But I already noted there that the second syllable in *haereses* is shortened, not lengthened; I thought Teolius had said this through a slip of the pen. *Eremus* is an ecclesiastical word in Jerome and his contemporaries. In Heinsius I believe there is an error when he says that ecclesiastical writers frequently shorten the first syllable of *eremus*. No doubt a man skilled in prosody meant the second syllable, for the first is certainly short. Giselinus in the text of the first edition and Fabricius have *madentibus* instead of *loquacibus*.

93. *Tristificus* here means “bitter,” and in the thirteenth tetrastich of the *Dittochaeon*:

“He held the bitter liquids in a pool of gall.”

See the other passages there. Nebrissensis noted *tristes lupinos* and *tristes succos* in Virgil with the same meaning. Hence, in the *Apotheosis*, verse 344:

“To make the hair bitter with ointment.”

[Col. 0825D]

94. Becmanus, *On the Origin of the Latin Language*, under *venio*:

“*Venia* is what comes to one who desires it, or by which it is permitted to come.”

Prudentius uses the word plainly according to its origin:

“There is favor from the wood,”

that is, by the wood’s intervention or arrival, when the wood comes upon the scene. Barthius, book VIII of the *Adversaria*, chapter 20, interprets it as “by the wood’s aid, remedy, correction, or help.” Prudentius rightly asserts that the wood signifies the cross. The passage occurs in Exodus chapter 15. *Mel Atticum*: as above, *Cecropium*, in hymn 3, verse 71.

97. Giselinus, first edition, has *cibus pinguidus*, “fat food.” He corrected it to *ninguidus*, “snowy.”

99. Hailsbrunner has *ac* instead of *hac*, less correctly.

101. Barthius observes that the breaths of winds are called “souls” by Arnobius, book I: “Have the winds breathed out their souls?” He adds that Prudentius in this verse used *anhelitus*, “breath,” for souls. He understands “souls of the wind”; but why not rather say that Prudentius used *anhelitus* for “breath,” just as Arnobius used *animae* for “breaths”?

103. Aldus, Vatican A by its first hand, O, P, Weitzius, Widmann, Hailsbrunner, Palatine, and others have *conflata*, “massed together,” which he adopts from his manuscript. Barthius explains this by saying that the wind drove the birds, compacted into a mass, down upon the earth. Vatican B, Rat., Prag., Bongarsius, Widmann above, and Giselinus have *difflata*, “scattered by the wind.” Some have *deflata*, which would mean something like “dispersed and scattered.” Teolius claims that *conflata* is read in Heinsius’s text, although Heinsius noted that *difflata* occurs in two older manuscripts. Giselinus, whom Heinsius generally follows unless he notes something contrary, has *difflata*, and *difflata* is clearly printed in Heinsius’s own text. Vatican A has *in unum*, “into one,” correctly corrected above the line in smaller characters to *in humum*, “to the ground.”

104. Heinsius would prefer *revolent*, “will fly back.” But the manuscripts are not wrong in reading *revolant*, “they fly back.” Barthius has *referunt*, “they carry back.”

106. In Vatican A, *vel nominis* is written above *numinis*; the latter should be retained.

108. From the food by which the Israelites were restored, the poet hastens to the mystical food by which Christians were nourished during the vigil of Holy Saturday. See the prolegomena, no. 146.

109. *Saeculum* is commonly used by ecclesiastical writers for the world and worldly affairs.

110. Some have *discussis* instead of *discissis*.

111. Giselinus, first edition, in the text has *raptatasque*; in the margin, *jactatasque*. Virgil, book I of the *Aeneid*, verse 3: “tossed upon land and sea.”

114. Gronovius, in *Ecclesiastical Observations*, says that *culta* should be read, so that a cultivated field may be indicated; Heinsius attempts to support this with some conjecture. Iso seems to distinguish *caltha* from *pinguia*, but this is unnecessary. Chamillardus says that the poet erred in using *caltha* in the neuter gender, since among all ancient writers it is feminine, namely a flower of yellow or saffron color. This is Gronovius’s reason for preferring *culta*, following Virgil, *Aeneid* X, where he has *pinguia culta*, and so forth. Nebrissensis had observed from Virgil and Columella that *caltha* should rather be feminine. Nor do I find anyone who used *calthum* except Prudentius; but I do not condemn him.]

[Col. 0825A]

[85] You forbid them to leap across the impassable sea

With its rushing tides, so that, when the flood ebbs,

A safe passage may open under your leadership,

And soon the rapacious wave may devour the impious.

291 For whom the barren rocks of the wilderness

[90] Overflow with babbling springs,

And from the split flint you pour out fresh waters,

Giving drink to thirsty peoples beneath the burning sun.

Water, like gall in a bitter lake,

By the wood’s favor becomes honey sweeter than Attic honey.

[95] By the wood, the harsh waters taste sweeter;

For hope, fastened to the cross, flourishes for humankind.

Then food, snowy and thick as cold hail,

Fills the camp,

As it falls from heaven’s starry firmament.

With these delicacies and this food they set their tables,

[100] [Col. 0826A]

Which Christ gives from the starry heavens.

Moreover, with rain-bearing breath,

The wind carries light birds upon a heavy cloud,

292 Which, once the flocks have been blown down to the ground,

Do not fly back again in returning flight.

[105] In former times the distinguished loving-kindness of the one God granted these rewards

To the fathers:

By whose help we too are nourished,

Feeding our hearts on mystical dishes.

He calls the weary across the storms of the world,

[110] Guiding the people through storms that have been torn apart,

And commands souls tossed by a thousand labors

To climb into the homeland of the righteous.

There every stretch of earth, roofed with purple roses,

Sends fragrance;

And marigolds and rich herbs [Note: [Col. 0827B]

115. *Crocos*: a kind of pigment, I.

116. *Fugacibus*: “swift, lively, flowing, or living streams,” I.

118. *Rara*: precious, I.

119. *Folium*: an excellent pigment, a kind of spice, I. *Folium* is a very precious herb said to come from paradise, from which a costly ointment is made. Juvenal:

“To me comes the prostitute anointed with *foliatum*.”

Vatican A.

120. *Praelabens*: flowing, Vatican T.

[Col. 0828A]

122. *Suave*: “sweetly,” Vatican A.

123. *Melos*: “praise,” neuter singular, I.

126. *Styge*: the river Styx of the underworld, interpreted as “sadness, mourning.” — *Feriae*: festivals, Iso.

128. *Acheronticis*: “without joy.” Phlegethon is fiery; *phlox* is Greek for “flame,” I.

130. *Imbuit*: drives out, propels, or illumines, I.

133. *Mitibus*: made gentle, I.

135. *Umbrarum*: of the dead; alternatively, “of those who have been made,” I.]

[Note: [Col. 0827B]

115. Paschalis, *On Garlands*, pp. 145, 147, 187, and 190 of the Paris edition of 1610, cites and repeats these verses. Virgil called the violet “soft”; Ovid, the crocuses “delicate.”

116. Prag. has *viventibus* in the text, taken from the gloss; in the margin it correctly has *fugacibus*. I prefer *uda* to *unda*, following Put., Thuan., Egm., Alt., Hein., Urbinate, and Alexandrian, as does Gronovius in *Ecclesiastical Observations*. Elegantly, “the earth, wet with little springs, pours forth violets.” Likewise, with Thuan., I think *terra uda* should be read in the *Peristephanon*, hymn 8, verse 14.

118. Barthius found *prataque* in his sheet, as though cinnamon grew commonly “through the meadows.” But if some change were to be introduced, I would rather read *grataque*—“and pleasing cinnamon.” *Rara* is a suitable but uncommon epithet for cinnamon. Martial, book IV, epigram 13:

“So well does rare cinnamon mingle with its own nard.”

119. In that same sheet of Barthius it is noted that *spirare* refers to an uncommon fragrance, and *folium* is explained as a spike. Barthius understands “leaves” that, added to various ointments, altered their taste and value; even today, in French and Belgian vernacular usage, *folia* means the flowers of nutmeg trees. Juvenal, satire 6: “ointments containing *folia* are prepared for adulterers.” The scholiast: “ointments full of leaves or other spices.” Claudianus, book I *Against Eutropius*:

“Let the Arabs enrich you with leaves, let the Seres enrich you with fleece.”

Lactantius, or whoever wrote the poem *On the Phoenix*:

“Then he gathers cinnamon, and at the same time the air

Of fragrant amomum, and balsams mixed with leaf.”

Giselinus says that medical writers give innumerable examples. He thinks *folium* may mean either the bdellium tree or the *malobathrum*, which floats without roots in the marshes of India.

120. Rat., Fabricius, the Alexandrian, Urbinate, and Giselinus in the text have *praelabens*. Vatican Q likewise. The others have *praelambens*, and in Vatican I there is a gloss, “drawing from the shore,” which seems to imitate Alcimus Avitus, book I of the poem *On the Ganges*:

“Whenever he, rising from his fragrant summit,

Steals the falling treasures

Which the rivers scatter through the beautiful grove,

Gently skimming them.”

Horace, book I, ode 21:

“or the places which legendary Hydaspes

Washes.”

122. Put., Alexandrian, and Rottendorphius have *pariles* instead of *parili*. Thuan. and Egm. have *pariles suavisonantibus*, which pleased Heinsius. Compare Lucretius: *suaviloquus*, *suaviloquens*, *suavidica verba*; and Prudentius: *flavicomantes*, *milliformis*, *multinodis*. See Gifanius’s *Lucretian Index*.]

124. To tread on flowers is especially an expression for happiness among poets. Martial, Book VIII, 77: “Worthy to live forever in the eternal rose.” Persius likewise: “Whatever he shall tread upon will become a rose.” By metaphor from the pebbles placed in an urn, by which happy days were formerly marked, *candidus* is taken for “fortunate.” Hence *pede candido* (“with fortunate foot”).

[Col. 0828B] 125. We explained the question that arose here in the *Prolegomena*, chapter 18. Giselinus declares this to be a poetic fiction, although the Ethiopians, as Damianus Goes reports in his *History of Their Customs*, still believe that souls—not indeed the damned, but those undergoing purification—are freed from every punishment on each Sunday and Saturday. Chamillardus certainly says that the poet is mistaken, whether he is speaking of the damned or of souls undergoing purification, although some of the holy Fathers judged that the punishments of the damned are at times mitigated; among them is St. Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 112. Georgius Remus likewise holds this to be a poetic fiction with no basis in the word of God. Georgius Fabricius asserts that he has found it nowhere else and that it appears to be a Spanish invention. See the cited chapter. It must be considered whether such holidays under the Styx can be explained so that only the souls assigned to purgatorial fire experienced relief, and not those eternally damned. For formerly they included even the place of purgatorial fire under the name “hell,” where demons also inflicted torments upon souls being purified. Compare St. Caesarius of Arles, to be cited shortly, on verse 129.

126. The true origin of *Styx* is from Greek *stygeō*, “I hate.” Hence Virgil, Book VI: “And the hateful marsh binds them with its gloomy water, and the Styx, flowing between nine times, restrains them.” *Inamabilis* (“hateful”), because it is hated by everyone.

129. Vatican B divides the words as *Non sicut*. Lucretius also used the word *fulgidus*, which some reject as belonging to the declining age of Latin. Cicero says *fulgens*. St. Caesarius of Arles seems to have imitated this passage in Homily 3 on Easter:

“This God shone more brightly from the tomb than he had flashed from the sun . . . Therefore, immediately, when Christ descended, the eternal night of hell shone brightly. The groan of the mourners fell silent; the burdens of the chains were loosed; the broken bonds of the damned fell apart. The torturers stood amazed in mind. The whole impious workshop trembled at once when it suddenly saw Christ in its own dwelling.”

130. I find no similar example of *imbuere tenebras* (“to saturate the darkness”) in the sense of “dispel,” “put to flight,” or “drive away.” The better gloss is *illuminat* (“he illuminates”).

135. Iso seems to have recognized this alternative reading, *functorum* (“of the dead”) instead of *umbrarum* (“of the shades”). Thuan., Rot., Alt., Noms., Sich., two Torrentian manuscripts, Boher., and Egm. have *functorum* in the text; Pal. and Hailsbr. in the first hand also have *functorum*. Aldus, Gis., Weitz., Rat., and Vatican B have *umbrarum*. In Vatican A, *functorum* appears above, with *umbrarum* in smaller characters. Puteanus likewise has *umbrarum*, as does Egm. in the margin. I prefer this reading with the oldest witnesses, and because *functorum* appears to be a gloss or the correction of an incompetent copyist. Prudentius freely uses here the words of pagan poets, as other ancient Christian poets also did.

[115] [Col. 0827A] 293

And soft violets and delicate saffrons

the damp, fleeting springs pour forth.

There, too, balsam flows, sweating from

a slender stalk,

and rare cinnamon breathes its fragrance,

and the leaf which a river from a hidden

spring, lapping at it, carries to its outlet.

The blessed souls sing sweet melody

through grassy meadows,

with voices sounding in harmonious measure,

with the gentle rhythms of hymns,

294 and tread upon white lilies with white feet.

[125] There are also, for spirits often harmful,

[Col. 0828A] famous holidays from punishment beneath the Styx

on that night when the holy God returned

from the Acherontian pools to those above,

not as the morning star, rising from the ocean,

[130] filled the darkness with light from its radiant torch,

but, greater than the sun, restoring a new day to the sorrowful lands from the Lord’s cross.

295 Tartarus grows faint beneath gentler punishments,

and the people of the shades rejoice

in the leisure of their prison,

freed from the fires;

nor do the rivers boil with sulfur

as they normally do.

[Note: [Col. 0829A]]

140. *Agimus liba*: “we perform the sacred cakes,” that is, “we offer sacrifices.” I.

*Sacrario*: “sanctuary,” “sacrifice,” Vatican A.

141. *Mobilibus*: “loosenable,” “pliant,” or “soft.” I.

142. *Laquearia*: structures that cover and adorn a ceiling, which we also call *lacūnāria*. Properly, however, *lacus* means a basin or recess; its diminutive is *lacunar*. From this comes another diminutive, formed by a change of letter, *laquearia*. Iso.

143. *Fota*: “nourished.”  
*Natatibus*: *natatus* is used of oil in which papyrus floats. Vatican A.

145. *Desuper*: “in the temple,” Vatican A.  
*Aream*: “a level surface,” I.  
*Planitiem*, that is, “the flooring of the temple,” Vatican A.

146. *Geminis*: “the lights hanging from the ceiling shine in such a way that you might think them to be the twin Bears,” that is, the two constellations, Helice and Cynosura, which have very bright stars. Vatican A.  
*Trionibus*: “wagons,” I.

[Col. 0830B] 147. *Bosphoreum*: “the Morning Star” or “Boötes.” We say *Bosphoreum* or *Phosphoreum*, that is, “bearing fire,” for *phōs* means “fire.” I.

148. *Hesperos*: “stars.” I.

149. *O res*: sc. “it is,” I.

[Note: [Col. 0829B]]

139. In the *Hymnarium of Thomas* and in the Mozarabic Breviary, other verses are inserted in place of this verse and the next:

“With harmonious song and sweet-sounding hymnody

we open our mouths.”

In the Mozarabic Breviary the reading is *suavisonantibus* (“sweet-sounding”). The poet says that vows are gathered together to indicate the power of prayer, which is customarily made by many assembled as one. Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 39: “We are a body through the consciousness of religion, the unity of discipline, and the covenant of hope. We come together before God, as though by forming ranks we were surrounding him with prayers.” This force is pleasing to God.

140. Barthius, in his manuscript, reads: “Having prepared the sanctuary, we offer the sacred cakes,” and considers *agere liba* (“to perform the cakes”) rather harsh. What if one reads: “Having prepared the sanctuary, we eat the sacred cakes”? Then *sacrarium* would be the altar or table of sacrifice, about which Prudentius speaks in *Peristephanon*, hymn 11, verse 171. This, I think, is what Prudentius intends, since he is speaking of the sacrament of the Holy Eucharist. The word *exstructo* (“prepared,” “laid out”) is appropriate, for Virgil uses it more than once in describing a banquet, *Aeneid* III, verse 224: “And we prepare the couches”; XI, verse 66: “and the couches prepared.” The verb *ago* was customary in connection with sacrifices, and even now we say of the sacrifice of the Mass, “What we perform in the mysteries.” Perhaps here *agimus* means “we bring forward” or “we present.”

142. Iso’s gloss is taken from Servius on Virgil’s phrase *laquearibus altis* (“with lofty ceilings”).

143. Latinius reads, “And nourished by rich little flowing streams”; perhaps Latinius wrote *manatibus* (“flowing”), and Frontinus certainly used the noun *manatio* (“outflow”). But the verse would not scan with *manatibus*, and there is no reason to remove *languidulis* (“sluggish,” “gentle”). Macrus attempts to confirm the reading *namatibus*, which he himself printed in Latinius’s *Bibliotheca selecta*. Macrus says that Greek *nama* means liquid, water, or a flowing stream, and that in corrupt manuscripts of Prudentius *natatibus* is found. This may indicate that *namatibus* was written by Latinius either deliberately or by mistake. In any case, this reading cannot be approved: besides the fact that I have seen no manuscript in which it occurs, *natatibus* is sound, and Prudentius uses the word elsewhere as well. I do not find *nama* used by Latin authors.

145. In Barthius’s manuscript stood: “You might think the star-bearing fiery heaven above, adorned, stood with twin Bears.” I understand *ornatum* to be a substantive noun. In Hailsbr. the reading is: “You might think the star-bearing air above, adorned, stood,” and so forth. Nothing should be changed.

147. The subject here is the yoke carried by oxen; therefore *Bosphoreum* should be written. Some write *Phosphoreum*, others *Vosforeum*, others *Bosforeum*, and others *Bosporeum*, which Heinsius does not dislike in his notes, although he printed *Bosphoreum* in the text. The matter itself is clear. But what Teolius says—that in Greek it should be written *Bosporeum* without aspiration, from the Cimmerian Bosporus—I do not fully understand. For the Bosporus, whether Thracian or Cimmerian, is written *Bosphorus* by most authors. Nor do I agree with Cellarius, who maintains that the yoke should be called *Bosporeum* from the Cimmerian Bosporus, which was chiefly northern for the ancients. The interpretation of the gloss is more satisfactory.

148. Vatican A incorrectly has *sparsim* instead of *passim*.

149. Puteanus has *Pater* (“Father”), which pleased Heinsius and others, and does not displease me. Alexandrinus has *Deus* (“God”), with *Pater* in the note. In the Mozarabic Breviary, replace *residuae* with *roscidae*.

150. Rat. and the Mozarabic Breviary have *offeret* (“will offer”), but *offerat* (“may offer”) is better. From this verb, repeated below in *quod famulans offero* (“which I, as a servant, offer”), one may correctly infer that, according to ecclesiastical custom, light was then offered not only in candles but also in lamps and, as I believe, in torches made from pine. The custom of blessing and offering candles has remained throughout the universal Church; in the Gothic rite, however, the blessing of the lamp is likewise practiced.

151. This is a figurative construction: *O res digna lux, quam ucem* (“O thing, worthy light, which …” [the source is damaged or elliptical]), much as in Virgil, “The city which I found is yours.” The Mozarabic Breviary has *luce* (“light”) here and in the following verse, incorrectly.

152. Barthius’s codex adds a gloss to the word *RELIQUA*, namely, “promised.” Barthius says that perhaps the author of the gloss had in mind eternal rewards. Prudentius is speaking of the rewards or gifts of this life, and admirably asserts that no gift has been granted by God more precious than the light by which we see the remaining rewards. The word *praemia* (“rewards”) is absent from the *Hymnarium of Thomas*.

155. I do not know why this verse was changed in the *Hymnarium of Thomas* into another: “Receive the light which your people, serving, partake of.” The Mozarabic Breviary is also corrupt: “The light too for the senses, within you the mirror, the fountain: receive the light which your people partake of.” Chamillardus says that almost everyone has interpreted this passage as referring to the offering of candles, whereas Giselinus interpreted it as referring to any kind of light. He is mistaken. Giselinus says that this passage is more fertile than any richly productive soil, whereas others had interpreted it, with complete sterility, as referring to the offering of candles. He then undertakes to explain it by adducing a similar passage from elsewhere, in which Romanus says that he will pray for Caesar and his soldiers: “That they may reject the darkness of idols and behold that light of eternal hope.” Giselinus adds nothing, but it is clear that he is speaking of the inward light of the mind or reason. I nevertheless do not follow his view; I interpret the passage as referring to the offering of candles and lamps. I argue that lamps are indicated by this verse from what follows: “stained with the oil of peaceful chrism.” Chrism is oil, and it is called “peaceful” because the olive is the emblem of peace. *Peristephanon*, hymn 12, verse 33: “the everlasting branch, rich in chrism.” Unless one prefers to understand *unguen pacifici chrismatis* (“the ointment of peaceful chrism”) as indicating some more sacred rite by which the light of Holy Saturday was customarily offered. St. Paulinus also used the word *unguen* (“ointment”) in *Natalia* 8 when describing a lamp: “When its light, thirsty, had been exhausted, it failed for want of oil.”

We draw the night through sacred assemblies

in festive, holy joy,

and eagerly gather favorable vows

in watchful prayer,

[140] and perform the sacred cakes in the prepared sanctuary.

The lights hang from flexible cords,

and, fixed throughout the ceilings,

they shine;

and nourished by gentle, flowing currents,

296 a flame casts light through transparent glass.

[145] You might think that the star-bearing expanse above,

adorned with the twin Bears,

stood there,

and that, where the shaft guides the Bosphorean yoke,

purple Evening Stars were scattered far and wide.

O thing worthy, Father,

which your flock may offer to you

[150] at the beginning of the dewy night:

the light through which you grant nothing more precious,

the light through which we behold the remaining rewards.

157. *Genitus* (“begotten”) is regularly used by Christian poets as a substantive noun meaning “son.” Fortunatus, Book I, *On the Birth of the Virgin*: “Your begotten son, O Virgin Mary, cared for [you].”

158. Pliny uses *visibilis* (“visible”) in the sense of *visivus* (“pertaining to sight”). Cicero’s phrase is *res quae sub aspectum cadunt* (“things that fall under sight”).

160. The procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son is asserted here and repeated at the beginning of the following hymn. See Petavius, volume II, Book VII, chapter 8. 163. Prag. has *contineat* (“may contain”) instead of *continuat* (“continues”). Rat. has *contineat*, but *continuat* is written above it. Widm. and Gold. have *contineat*. Rat. reports that Theodulfus has *nomine* (“in name”), while others have *numine* (“by divine power”). Alexandrinus, Vatican A, O, P, and Q have *numine*. Vatican I, together with Urb., has *nomine*. The Mozarabic Breviary has this here and elsewhere, but incorrectly reads *tu et contines* instead of *tua et continuet*. Hincmarus recognized both readings. See *Psychomachia*, verse 2. Aldus adds *Amen. Finis* (“Amen. The end”) to this hymn, something found nowhere else.

[Col. 0831D] Before Sleep. We said in the note on the title of Hymn 1, from the *Apostolic Constitutions*, that prayers should be offered at various hours, including evening, because the Lord gave the night for rest from the labors of the day. This hymn belongs here, as is clear from verse 9 and those following: “The labor of the day has flowed away; the hour of rest returns.” Compline now occupies the place of this kind of prayer. Theodulfus cites this hymn in his work *On the Holy Spirit*, where he proves the procession of the Holy Spirit from this and other passages of Prudentius, together with the passages cited from the other holy Fathers. The final seven stanzas of this hymn are found in the Mozarabic Breviary among other hymns for Compline. St. Gregory of Tours, Book I of *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 162, extracts several verses from this hymn. According to Prudentius, “the cross drives away every sin,” and so forth. I noted in the *Prolegomena*, number 103, that this hymn is elsewhere entitled “On Rest and Sleep, a Divine Gift.”

3. Against the unrestrained licentiousness of innovators who read *sermo* (“discourse”) instead of *Verbum* (“Word”) in the Gospel, because some of the holy Fathers spoke in this way, as Prudentius does here, one should consult Joannes Maldonatus, an especially weighty theologian, some of whose words I quoted in the *Prolegomena*, number 140. Among other holy Fathers, Maldonatus cites this very passage of Prudentius.

6. In the margin of Vatican A there was added, alternatively: “One strength and one power.” The same appears in Puteanus, in the second hand of Alexandrinus, and in the Graevian papers. Salmasius also wished this reading, adding a passage of Ausonius: “The majesty of one kind, joined to the holy spirit,” so that the *a* in *potestas* should be shortened, just as the final *a* in *majestas* is shortened by Ausonius. But Salmasius accomplishes nothing by this. Ausonius often introduces a spondee into the second position of an iambic dimeter. In this same iambic poem, *Ephemeris*, he says: “There is abundance for the divine rite.”

6. In Rat. *et* is absent, but there seems to be space left by an erasure. Alt. has *rediit* (“returned”). Fabr. and Gis. have *redit quietis* (“the hour of rest returns”), without *et*, which all the others have, except the two Vatican manuscripts cited by Teolius. He also asserted that the character of this poem does not tolerate the particle *et*. But an anapest is often placed in the first foot of this hymn, which is not at all incompatible with the meter.

12. Virgil, Book V: “Scarcely had unexpected rest relaxed their first limbs.” Similar expressions are common among poets. Cicero, *On Divination*: “the mind relaxed by sleep.” The description of sleep that our poet unfolds in his verses is remarkable. Joannes Baptista Gandutius collected descriptions of Sleep and his dwelling among poetic descriptions. Compare also Lucretius, Book IV. Nor should the hymn of St. Ambrose, “God, Creator of All,” be omitted.

14. Instead of *sauciata*, I would prefer *vulnerata* (“wounded”) or *fessa* (“wearied”) in the gloss, rather than *tuta* (“protected”).

16. Aldus and Nebrissensis have *poculum* instead of *poclum*, although the meter requires the latter. Horace, *Epode* 14: “cups bringing Lethean sleep.” This was taken from the myths. But the most holy poet was permitted to continue the metaphor and, since he had said *bibit* (“drinks”), to add *poclum* (“cup”) for sleep. In the gloss one should perhaps read *laboris sensualis* (“of bodily labor”).

19. Fabricius understands *dolor* to mean distress. But why should we not say that it is true pain, whose sensation is absent in the sleeper? So shortly afterward, “healing pleasure,” because sleep sometimes also brings health. In Hails. *aegris* (“for the sick”) appears instead of *aegri* (“of the sick”).

24. Vatican B, Prag., Widm., and Gold. have *medicalis*, contrary to the rules of meter. Sleep is *medicabilis* (“healing”) because it either restores bodily health or preserves it. Ovidius uses this word for something to which medicine can be applied, in the letter of Oenone to Paris: “Love cannot be healed by herbs.”

29. Vatican B and I, Rat., Gold., Fabr., Widm., and Bong. have *vacat* (“is empty”); Vatican A, O, P, Q, two Torrentian manuscripts, and three Heinsian manuscripts have *vagas per auras* (“wanders through the empty airs”). Aldus, Heinsius, Weitz., Puteanus, Thuan., Prag., Gis., and others have *vagat* (“wanders”), a reading also defended by Gifanius in his *Index to Lucretius*, page 423, and by Latinius in the *Bibliotheca selecta*. Priscian, Book VIII, may be consulted; he discusses at length such verbs as the ancients once used, including *auguro*, *opino*, and *exsecro*. So too Nonius, who cites Plautus, Attius, Pacuvius, Ennius, Turpilius, Pomponius, Varro, and the much later Serenus concerning the verb *vago*.

35. The poet calls God the fiery source of souls in the *Hymn for the Dead*, verse 1. Rat. has *ab aethere* (“from heaven”), but the intervening *e* was correctly inserted so that the phrase would be *ab aethra* (“from the bright sky”), which the corrector seems to have intended.

37. The mind is said to form many different shapes for itself because dreams are diverse. Although the cause of dreams is not only internal but also external, as St. Thomas explains from the holy Fathers, *Summa* II–II, question 95, and Thomas Hurtado, volume I, *Various Treatises*, treatise 5, chapter 6, resolution 56, numbers 1155 and following, the mind itself forms the shapes, figures, and phantasms for itself, for the soul acts even then. The poet seems to be speaking of all dreams, although in verse 40 he says, “may enjoy a subtle activity.”

41. Rat. has *somniantium* (“of those dreaming”) in the first hand.

42. I conjecture that *error* (“wandering”) should be read instead of *horror*, however much no one may have doubted the matter. For *error* properly means wandering, as in Virgil, *Eclogue* 1: “to let my cattle wander,” and as our poet says in the following verse, “Now splendor wanders through.” Although you may wish some element of fiction to be expressed by *error*, you can recognize it in a dream: above he says *fingit* (“forms”), below *intererrat* (“wanders through”); “the lying image, with truths dispersed, deceives by entanglement,” and “the play sees fearful forms with much terror.” See verse 118, “whom frequent error fills.” But why should *error* rather than *horror* be preferred? I draw the reason from the dreams of Pharaoh’s ministers themselves. Nothing terrifying appeared in them, although they showed sadness in their faces because there was no one to interpret them. Their interpretation, however, struck one servant with terror and filled the other with joy. Thus Prudentius distinguishes between the two dreams, and never uses words of terror concerning the first:

“Now splendor wanders through,

which grants knowledge of things to come . . .

Whom rare fault in conduct

has not often polluted,

him serene, flashing light

teaches hidden things.”

But concerning the second:

“By dark entanglement

it deceives minds saddened by fear . . .

With much terror the play

shows fearful forms.”

43. It is clear that dreams are sometimes sent by God, and there are many examples in the Old and New Testaments, collected by Durandus, *Treatise on Visions*, chapter 9. It is equally certain that dreams which sometimes prove true may also arise by chance. For how few wise men have recognized the truth of a future event while asleep? Yet everyone commonly dreams. What wonder, then, if in so great a number something true should occur? Cicero rightly says, *On Divination*, Book II, chapter 59: “Who is there who, throwing darts all day, does not sometimes hit the mark?”

51. *Vibrare* (“to flash”) in the sense of “to shine.” Virgil, Catullus, Cicero, and others use it thus.

Thus someone who had read *ministris* (“servants”) corrected it to *magistris*, although the latter, taken simply, is inept.

Puteanus, Oxford, several other Heinsian manuscripts, Weitz., Vatican A, B, O, Q, and I above the line, Prag., Rat., Sich., and Giselinus, together with the oldest edition of Daventer, have *monuit* (“warned”). Aldus and the first edition of Gis. have *novit* (“knew”). Fabricius not ineptly adopted *movit* (“moved”), that is, “impelled by moving,” “compelled by persuasion,” and this is found in Vatican O. I have no doubt that *monuit* is the true reading. Some corrupt editions of Plautus retained the opposite error, *monuit mihi* (“warned me”) instead of *movit*, *Truculentus*, Act IV, Scene 1: “One thing moved my spirits,” although others read, “One thing my spirit warned me.” It is surprising that the author of the Turin dictionary should have presented it as established from this passage of Plautus that *moneo* (“warn”) admits the dative case. On that authority, others, without consulting the best editions or the notes of commentators repeated ever since Camerarius, have tried to impose on me an obscure dispute and to prove that the verb *moneo* can be defended as taking a dative just as easily as the second vowel in *potitur* can be treated as common. If they wish to attempt any defense, they must take another path; even so, they will not attain what they desire.

77. Fabricius notes that Prudentius says the evangelist saw obscure and sealed things in clear light, with the clouds removed, whereas John himself says that he was “in the spirit,” or, as later writers say, “in ecstasy.” Sedulius, whom Fabricius names, says that John himself saw these things in dreams, as Nebrissensis had earlier noted. But Prudentius also affirms that the vision occurred during sleep, as is perfectly clear from the preceding stanza. And Sedulius, whom Fabricius mentions, is Prudentius himself in the *Dittochaeon*, which Fabricius attributes to Sedulius. I understand Prudentius to be speaking mystically and to call ecstasy sleep. See St. Bernard, Sermon 52 on the *Song of Songs*, “On Ecstasy,” which is called contemplation, in which the bridegroom makes the soul rest, and so forth.

86. The passage is from Revelation 1:16: “And he held seven stars in his right hand, and from his mouth came a sharp two-edged sword.” Chamillardus wonders why Prudentius says that the hand was armed with a sword, since John says that the sword came from the mouth. But Prudentius has touched upon the sword’s movement from the mouth to the hand. Christ carries the sword in his mouth so that it may signify the word of God, or the sentence at the final judgment; in his hand, so that its advance in punishment may be shown. Psalm 7: “He will brandish his sword.” Exodus 15: “I will draw my sword; my hand shall destroy them.” See the commentators.

[Col. 0836D] 89. Rat. has *quaesitus* (“sought”), incorrectly. Virgil, Book VI: “Minos, the judge, moves the urn.”

92. Taken from Revelation 20:14: “And hell and death were thrown into the lake of fire. This is the second death.”

95. Nebrissensis explains *paucos* (“the few”) as those who are incurable. I interpret it as referring to those between the righteous and the impious, namely, those who neither excel in holiness nor are burdened by the crime of unbelief or by other very serious faults. The poet therefore says that God allows few among those who are Catholic to perish, and that if they fall into sins, they grieve over them and strive to repent. Prudentius was permitted to hold this view concerning the Catholic Christians of his own time, since it was evident that most of them were earnestly striving for eternal life, although many did not stand out through remarkable and heroic piety. Gravina, in his book *On Paradise*, added a chapter on the greater number of the saved; it was rightly suppressed because it exaggerated the favorable opinion too greatly. See the *Prolegomena*, number 175.

100. In some manuscripts and in Widm., in the second hand, *super* (“above”) appears instead of *supra*. The meter requires the former, while the latter comes from the Vulgate edition, Philippians 2:9: “And he gave him the name that is above every name.”

101. Becmanus, *On the Origin of the Latin Language*, argues from the verb *potior* (“I prevail,” “I possess”) that it is better to use of God either *potens* (“powerful”), as in Luke 1 and elsewhere in Holy Scripture, or even *omnipotens* (“almighty”), rather than *praepotens* (“very powerful,” “more powerful than others”). Nor is he moved by Cicero’s authority, for Jupiter is *praepotens* in Cicero; but Cicero was a pagan. To pass over other considerations, Christ is appropriately called *praepotens* here, since the subject is the victory won over Antichrist. Nor is the comparison inappropriate, since he is understood as powerful above Antichrist. See 2 Thessalonians 2:8 and following.

103. In Vatican A, *de* is absent from an old hand.

105. Rat. has *rapacem* (“ravenous”), but *capacem* (“receptive”) seems to have stood earlier. Hails. in the second hand, Weitz., and Gis. have *rapacem*, which is not displeasing. The others have *capacem*. Gallandius printed *rapacem* with Aldus and Tornaesius, but my Aldus has *capacem*. Gallandius is wrong to suppose that Chamillardus wrote *capacem* by mistake.

107. Vatican A incorrectly has *sanguini* (“to blood”) instead of *sanguinis* (“of blood”). The poet is referring, I think, to Revelation 17, where the harlot is described as sitting upon a scarlet beast, drunk with the blood of the saints and the blood of the martyrs of Jesus. Aretas, in his commentary on Revelation 11:7, calls the beast Antichrist because of his cruelty, savagery, and thirst for blood. Puteanus and others read *charybdem* (“Charybdis”).

108. Puteanus has *Joannis* (“of John”), a reading preferred by Heinsius and others to satisfy the meter. But the meter is sufficiently accommodated if one accepts that an ending in *-es* may more often be shortened than is commonly believed. See Gifanius, *Index to Lucretius*, page 440, under *Is terminata*. Alexandrinus writes *Joannes*; so do Vatican O and P, together with two others cited by Teolius, who nevertheless followed the Putean or Heinsian reading.

109. The more authoritative Heinsian manuscripts, Aldus, Alexandrinus, Vatican B, and Egm. have *hanc* (“this,” feminine). Others have *haec* (“this,” neuter), and in the following verse *ausa est* (“has dared”). Teolius thinks *haec* the smoother reading, and later likewise read *ausa* without *est*. I and others do not agree.

110. Iso seems to have read *haec* in the preceding verse instead of *hanc*. The first edition of Gis. has *ausa est*, namely because he read *haec*. Concerning Antichrist, 2 Thessalonians 2:4 says: “He who opposes and exalts himself above everything called God or worshiped, so that he sits in the temple of God, displaying himself as though he were God.” Thomas Malvenda, Book VIII, chapter 2, proves through a collection of testimonies from the holy Fathers that Antichrist should be understood as calling himself Christ. Lactantius, Book VII, chapter 19, is especially relevant here: “He is the one who is called Antichrist; but he will falsely claim to be Christ himself and will fight against the TRUE one.”

112. Gallandius seems to approve the restoration that Heumannus wished to make to this verse: “Christ, slain by the word,” because Christ will kill Antichrist by the breath of his mouth. But in that form the elegance of the antithesis between the true Christ and the one who will falsely claim to be Christ, as Lactantius says, is lost.

114. Among the pagans, *heroes* were called demigods and men endowed with some outstanding virtue. Hence Christian heroes were called saints, and their virtues heroic. St. Augustine, Book X of *The City of God*: “If ecclesiastical usage permitted it, we would call these martyrs, much more elegantly, our heroes.” Ancient usage consecrated this designation among the saints. Avitus, with a rare meaning, called Pharaoh an “impious hero” in Book V.

118. Widm. and Vatican O have *herror* instead of *error*. Perhaps, because of a similar manner of writing, *horror* entered in verse 42 instead of *error*. This verse should also be understood as indicating again the error of the mind wandering in dreams.

123. Vatican A has *Sat est, si nil* (“It is enough if nothing”), which the meter rejects.

124. Rat. has *minetur* (“may he threaten”), but above it correctly has *minentur* (“may they threaten”).

127. Vat. B: “sacred,” above “holy.” Chamillard understands this as immersion into the baptismal font itself. Propertius used “dew” for the sea, and thus the word can be applied both to sprinkling and to immersion. Although in the earliest periods of the Church baptism was generally administered by immersion, it must nevertheless be acknowledged that those who could not be immersed, whether because of age or because of poor health, were cleansed through baptism by sprinkling. The case of the sick, who were baptized in bed, is well known, as is that of those who postponed baptism until the final moments of life. I will be even less persuaded that immersion was practiced everywhere in such a way that the baptized—whatever their sex or age—entered the water completely naked. For that was not necessary, just as it certainly is not now; and if such a custom had been common among Christians, the pagans who reproached them with the kiss of peace would not have remained silent about such nakedness. Certain statements of the ancients do not establish this matter as clearly as many suppose. Whatever that nakedness may have been, I have no doubt that modesty was provided for either by separate baptisteries for women and men, or by curtains, or by some other arrangement. See Lupus, Dissertation 1, no. 23 and following, and the author of the Life of Saint Otto in Surius under 2 July, where he says: “The priest, who was standing beside the font, heard rather than saw that someone was in the water; after the veil had been moved aside a little, he completed the sacramental mystery by immersing that person’s head three times.”

[120] For evil things corrupts us.

It is enough to cherish

307 Threaten the tranquil sleeper.

131. “Forehead,” etc.: these are the two lintels that seemed to be sprinkled with the blood of the lamb. Thus the forehead is the lintel of the head, and likewise the heart is the lintel and chief part of the breast. Vat. A.

139. “Pervicaci”: “stubborn,” “persistent,” “persevering.” Iso.

[Col. 0839B] 140. “Praestigiator”: “deceiver”; *praestrigium* is said of a monster, from *praestringere*, that is, from suddenly deluding the eyes. “Astu”: “by cunning,” “by trickery.” I.

142. “Maeanders”: the Maeander is a river of Caria that makes many winding turns. Here, however, the river itself is introduced to represent the serpent’s winding coils. I.]

128. Although Heinsius found *innotatum* marked in the Put. and other older manuscripts, he nevertheless adopted the altered reading *innovatum*, together with five manuscripts, the Oxford manuscript in the margin, and Gronovius in *Observations Ecclesiastical*. Rat., Sich., and Hailsb. likewise have *innovatum* above; it is also found in Urb. and Vatt. I, O, and Q, whose gloss is *signatum* (“marked”). Teolius followed this reading so as not to depart from Heinsius. I read *innotatum* with Heinsius’s oldest witnesses, Ald., Vatt. A, B, and P, Alex., Nebr., Prag., Gold., Bong., Fabr., Gis., and others; it fits this passage wonderfully. Prudentius is speaking of the sacrament of confirmation, which here and elsewhere he clearly distinguishes from the sacrament of baptism. The sacrament of confirmation was called *chrisma* because it was performed through sacred anointing. That this *chrisma*, enclosed in a small vessel, was customarily preserved in the Church may be gathered from Optatus, *Against Parmenian*, book II. Tertullian, Cyprian, Augustine, Cyril of Alexandria, and many others call the sacrament of confirmation by this name. Since the forehead of the person being confirmed was marked by the bishop with sacred chrism, with the figure of a cross inscribed upon it, the sacrament was therefore also called the “mark” or “seal”; Cyprian, Pope Cornelius, Ambrose, and others used this designation. Thus Prudentius, combining both names in two words, expressed himself excellently: “marked with chrism,” and below he explains why he said “marked”: “the sign that you yourself know.” The same subject is treated in *Psychomachia*, lines 358 and following; *Apotheosis*, lines 487 and following; hymn 9, *Cathemerinon*, line 84; and book I *Against Symmachus*, line 587: “Whence he may bear back the sacred sign with royal chrism.” Beware, therefore, of Cellarius, who not only prefers *innovatum* but falsely states that some manuscripts have *innotatum* and more have *innovatum*. I nevertheless concede that *innovatum* occurs in certain ancient manuscripts and also in the Mozarabic Breviary. See Baronius under the year 55, pages 248 and following, who expressly proves that this anointing performed by bishops on the forehead is a sacrament. Bellarmine and other theologians explain how this anointing differs from the other one that priests apply to the crown of the head while baptizing. The distinguished Bertius, book XXXII of *Theological Disputations*, chapter 10, uses these verses appropriately when discussing the slap by which the confirmed person is lightly struck: “Worshiper of God, remember,” etc. The following verses confirm our reading *innotatum*, where the figure of the cross is commended.

129. Mozarabic Breviary: *somnum*; correct to *somno*.

132. The very great honor paid to the cross in the ancient Church is attested by the oldest monuments and inscriptions. See Aringhi in the many places of subterranean Rome, and the other writers on Christian antiquities. On the custom of signing the heart, forehead, and mouth, consult Gretzer, *On the Cross*, book IV, chapter 31, and elsewhere throughout that distinguished work. Saint Athanasius, at the beginning of his *Oration Against the Idols*: “For if, after the coming of the cross, all worship of images has been removed, and all the demons’ illusions are driven away by this sign,” etc. Shortly afterward Prudentius calls the demon a “deceiver.” Among the writings of several ancient theologians of Gaul, published at Paris in 1586, there is a bucolic poem by Severus Sanctus, or the Rhetor, *On the Deaths of Cattle*, where this miracle is recounted: “This sign, added to the middle of their foreheads, was the sure salvation of all the herds.”

133. In one of the most ancient Vatican manuscripts, someone heterodox wrote in the margin in a recent hand: “Not well.” For the holy Fathers who celebrated the Lord’s cross with these and similar praises, see Gretzer, *On the Cross*.

135. Mozarabic Breviary: *tales*, incorrectly, instead of *tali*.

137. Aldus: *Procul*, *procul*, omitting the *o* found in the others. Alex.: *vagantium* instead of *vagantum*. It should be retained for the meter. Saint Eugenius, bishop of Toledo, seems to have imitated Prudentius, epigram 29, page 32, among the works of the Holy Fathers of Toledo, published through the efforts and at the expense of Don Francisco de Lorenzana, archbishop of Toledo: “Verses above a bed: The almighty commands: Far away, far away, flee, demon,” etc. Compare the same Eugenius’s verses above a bed, part 2 of his works, epigrams 3 and 4, where he says: “I bear the life-giving sign of the cross: flee, demon.”

140. Heinsius is not displeased with the origin and spelling of the gloss *praestrigiator*. Others write *praestigiae*, as though *praestegiae*, from *tego*, “to cover,” because they delude and cover the eyes. Heinsius likewise defends *actu* instead of *astu*, with Put., Egm., and Noms. I prefer *astu*, with Ald., Weitz., Nebr., Gis., Alex., Vatt. A and B, Rat., Prag., and others. The sense is coherent: “deceiver, winding serpent, your twisting frauds require the reading *astu pertinaci* (‘with persistent cunning’).” Chamillard and Cellarius followed Heinsius. In the Mozarabic Breviary, *aestu* seems to derive from *astu*. Teolius prefers *actu*, based on manuscripts, not *astu*. But even the oldest manuscripts have *astu*.

141. Several holy Fathers call the devil a winding serpent. Philip the priest, Saint Jerome’s disciple, on Job 26: “The winding serpent,” namely that serpent “which is more cunning than all the animals upon the earth.” Saint Gaudentius, addressed to Germinius, or rather Serminius: “The winding devices of that serpent.” Phoebadius, in his book *Against the Arians*: “The light-fleeing serpent, unfolding its course through winding passages and proceeding in a twisting manner.”

142. The first syllable of *Maeander*, since it contains a diphthong, is ordinarily long. Prudentius shortens it, a fact overlooked by his critics. I write *maeander* with the diphthong, because even so the first syllable can be shortened before the following vowel.

145. Aldus: *lux est* instead of *hic est*, contrary to both meter and sense. On this formula, see hymn 2, line 4.]

150. Fabr. and Vat. O have *reclive*, a reading that greatly pleased Chamillard, although nearly all manuscripts have *recline*. Nebrissa rejects it because Chamillard cited a verse of Ovid’s *Metamorphoses*, book X, in place of *recline*, which Chamillard reads as: “And, his neck placed in the young man’s lap, reclined”; he asserts that he has never found *reclinis*. Giselinus, who preferred *recline* from a manuscript, says that he followed Lambinus’s judgment, since Lambinus read it that way in his Horace. The passage did not present itself when Giselinus was looking for it. Fabricius produced from Virgil: “with his neck placed, reclining.” He intended to refer to Ovid, where, with the others, I read *renidens*; in Prudentius, Martial, Tacitus, *reclinis*; just as Lambinus has *acclinis* in Horace, *Satires* II, 2, and elsewhere, not *acclivis*. I think Giselinus had read that. Seneca, letter 26: “Sleep is accustomed to steal upon someone leaning against a support.” Isidore, book I of *Differences*, says: “The difference between *decline* and *declive* is that the sun is *declinis*, while a place is *declivus*.” The same is to be understood of *accline* and *acclive*: a person is *acclinus*—read *acclinis*—and a place *acclivus*. I would say the same of *reclinis* and *reclivis*. In Isidore I would read: “a person *acclinis*, a place *acclivis*,” and “this is called *acclivum*,” not “from this it is called *acclivum*.” Above he likewise has “a *declivis* place.” In the Mozarabic Breviary there is an error that confirms our reading: *reclinet paululum* instead of *recline paulum*. Nebrissa explains it as “reclined in bed”; Chamillard does the same in hymn 5, *Peristephanon*, line 365, where he reads *recline*, though he is inconsistent with himself. For *paulum*, Ald., Vat. A, and Rat. have *paulo*. Gold. recognizes both. Prag. has the incorrect *paululum*.

152. Rat.: *meditatur*, ineptly, instead of *meditabimur*, which the verse also requires. Meditating on Christ during sleep itself is characteristic of those who meditate on him while awake—those whose heart remains awake even when they sleep. Teolius copied from a later Vatican manuscript, in a note, the conclusion of this hymn, which has nothing of Prudentius in it: “Glory to the eternal Father, and to Christ the new King, and to the holy Paraclete, both now and forever.” In the preface to the appendix of the works of Saint Zeno, the Ballerinii produce another ending for this hymn, but it is clumsily assembled from its first stanza: “Praise be to the supreme Father, whom no one has ever seen, to the Father’s Word, Christ, and to the gracious Spirit.” The treatise *On the Sign of the Holy Cross*, attributed by some to Saint Zeno, consists of this conclusion and the final seven stanzas of this hymn of Prudentius.]

*On Those Who Fast.* The Mozarabs sing this hymn, distributed among the weekdays, though it is corrupt in many places. I think it was composed by Prudentius for all days of fasting, especially the Lenten fast.

1. Ald., Vat. P, and other common witnesses have *dux* instead of *lux*. Most of our manuscripts and the better Heinsian witnesses have *lux*, which Weitz retained. Giselinus followed Aldus; Nebrissa not ineptly confirms Aldus’s reading from Matthew 2:6: “And you, Bethlehem, land of Judah, are by no means least among the princes of Judah. For from you shall go forth a leader,” etc. See hymn 12, line 78.

[Col. 0842C] 4. Sichard: *accipe* instead of *aspice*. To look upon someone in God is to have mercy, as even the pagans observed. Why the fast is called a feast, see the commentary on line 13 of the following hymn. *Festum* used substantivally is rare among the writers of the golden and silver ages in prose. They said *festus dies*.

5. Some derive *litare*, with Varro, from *luere*; others from the Greek λιτή, “prayer” or “supplication,” whence also *litania*, which is rendered in Latin as *rogatio*. Iso’s explanation does not always hold.

He likewise reads *vividi*, found in Sich., Alex., Weitz., and Gis. in the margin, and in all the Heinsian witnesses except Rot., who reads *lividi* with Aldus, Heinsius, and others; this reading also appears in Thomasius’s Hymnary and Fabricius’s edition. Vat. P has *lividi*. Vatt. A, I, O, and Q and the Mozarabic Breviary have *vividi*. Vat. B, Prag., and Rat. have *uvidi*.

VII. HYMN OF THOSE WHO FAST.

O Nazarene, light of Bethlehem, Word of the Father,

Whom the birth from a virgin’s womb brought forth,

And look serenely upon our feast, O King,

[5] While we offer the victim of fasting.
