By which the living fiber of the heart is purified;

By which the unrestrained entrails are subdued,

So that fat, exuding its foul indigestion,

[10] May not oppress the powers of the strangled mind.

Thus luxury and shameful gluttony are subdued;

The degenerate sluggishness of wine and sleep,

Sordid lust, shameless pleasure,

And the various plagues of languid senses

[15] Feel the sparing discipline to which they are subjected.

For if, freely overflowing with drink and food,

You do not restrain your limbs through proper fasting,

Then it follows, through frequent indulgence,

[20] And the spirit snores within its sluggish breast.

Let the desires of the body therefore be restrained, [Note: [Col. 0843B]

27. “Priest,” “prophet.” —“Of the dry countryside,” “of the wilderness.” I. Jephthah, when he was going to war against the nations, vowed that he would sacrifice to the Lord whatever first met him on his return victorious from battle. Having won the victory and returned home, he found his daughter coming to meet him with tambourines, and he wished to sacrifice her to the Lord. Phinehas, the priest, being unable to defend her, abandoned the priesthood and went into the desert. The Jews therefore suppose—Vat. I has “believe”—that he was Elijah. Hence Prudentius calls him “the old priest,” as do Vat. A and I.

30. The primary meaning of *Syrtis* or *Syrtium* refers to the two extremely dangerous gulfs of the Libyan Sea; from there the word extends to the inland deserts of Libya. Horace indicates these in book I, ode 22: “Whether through the burning Syrtes,” unless one prefers to think that Horace intended to include any deserted places, especially sandy and waterless ones. Prudentius, having earlier called it “dry countryside,” now calls it “the Syrtes.” See *Apotheosis*, line 443.

As he said above that Elijah fled from the multitude of crimes because crimes are usually committed amid a multitude of people, so now he says that he was carried away lest he contract any filth from nearby contagion. See Wisdom 4:10 and following. The Essenes, whom Philo undertook to praise, withdrew into solitude, believing that just as contaminated air harms bodies, so association with the crowd harms the soul.

Victor, book II: “By the motion of the sevenfold axis.” Isidore derives the phrase from Ambrose, *Hexaemeron*, book II, chapter 4. The philosophers, however, introduced seven heavens of the world—that is, the planetary spheres—moving in harmonious motion. Philosophers now teach other things about heaven.

40. See Exodus 34:28. From this and the preceding chapter it seems possible to infer that Moses saw the Lord’s back before he had completed the forty-day fast. The opinion that Moses observed only two periods of forty days is both more probable and more common.

57. Vatt. B and I, Prag., Rat., Widm., and Gold. have *vigeto* above *vieto*. Bong. has *vigeto in corpore* instead of *vieto in pectore*. Terence, *Eunuchus*, act IV, scene 4: “Here is a weakened, old, decrepit old man.” Varro, book IV *On the Latin Language*: “*Viere* means ‘to bind’; from this comes Ennius’s phrase in *Asoto*: ‘They went in the morning to bind a garland of Venus.’ Hence *vietus* properly means bent, and figuratively languid. Some think the second syllable of *vieto* is short, based on Horace’s verse, ode 12 of the *Epodes*: “What sweat for weakened limbs, and how harmful everywhere”; but Ricciolius correctly notes in index 2 that it is lengthened by Plautus, Terence, Lucretius, and Prudentius, since it comes from *vieo, vies, vievi, vietum*. Horace can be excused on account of synaeresis, so that the second foot is a spondee. Quintianus Stoa considers it common.

69. Giselinus had earlier printed *parum* with Aldus, as he himself says, ineptly. He later corrected it to *parvum*, somewhat harshly, as it seemed to him, and conjectured that *parcum* might be read, a reading not displeasing to Heinsius. Vat. P and the Mozarabic Breviary have *parum*. Heinsius, with only Put., chose *rarum* instead of “infrequent nourishment.” Teolius copies Heinsius, although he admits that nearly all the Vatican manuscripts have *parvum*. But since all the other Heinsian witnesses except Oxford, which has *parum*, read *parvum*, and since the Latin manuscripts and Weitz’s witnesses adhere to it, we retain this reading. Sedulius likewise has it in his alphabetic hymn: “And he was fed with little milk,” for correctors of hymns introduced *modico* instead of *parvo* without necessity. Two controversies arise here: first, whether the locusts on which Saint John fed were a kind of bird or plants; second, whether John ate genuine honey. Most of the ancients believed that these locusts were plants. Saint Paulinus, poem 5 on John the Baptist: “The wild honey supplied easy nourishment, and fruits, and herbs growing on uncultivated rocks.” I omit others. Anyone who observes that the small creatures called locusts are listed among the clean animals in Leviticus 11:21–22, and that they were also food among other peoples, will scarcely doubt that Saint John lived on these animals. John Maldonatus, commenting on Matthew 3, attacks certain heretics because they interpreted the locusts as sea crabs—unclean by the law, but, according to their interpretation, clean and permitted, so that John might eat them and already teach evangelical freedom. “For who,” he says, “doubts that John the Baptist was a Calvinist or a Lutheran?” Although some, following Euthymius and Theophylact, thought the locusts were plants; others, wild pears; and others, the tops of trees and leaves, as Nicephorus preferred, Maldonatus himself, with Origen, Hilary, Ambrose, Augustine, Chrysostom, and nearly all the ancient interpreters, understands them as the animals—or little birds—I mentioned. As for the other question, he explains wild honey as the honey that bees, flying into the forests, produce in tree trunks or cracks in the rocks; this must certainly have happened in Palestine, the land flowing with milk and honey, as it is called in Holy Scripture. He does not accept, however, that such honey was bitter and unpleasant to the mouth, much less that it was not real honey but some sort of dew by which John was nourished, as the people of old had been in the wilderness. Rabanus Maurus holds that the honey on which Saint John fed consisted of the white and tender leaves of trees, which, when rubbed and crushed in the hands, gave off a honeyed smell and taste. Others think it was moisture collected from tree leaves; still others, heather honey, mentioned by Pliny, book XI, chapter 16, from the heather shrub flowering in autumn. Compare Cornelius à Lapide on Matthew 3, and lines 117–118 of the *Dittochaeon*.

70. Aldus’s *corporis vetus* is an error.

72. Giselinus found in the manuscript of Deventer a reading that he considered equally suitable or better than the common one, namely: “That first exhorter and teacher of the new salvation, and teacher of new grace.” In the Maeran manuscript, which guided Giselinus in his emendations, this passage was mutilated. This variant reading was reported neither by Weitz nor by Heinsius nor by later editors.

73. Ald., Nebr., Urb., Vat. Q, and the Mozarabic Breviary have *veterum pietas*. Vatt. B and I, Prag., Rat., Gold., Vidm., and Weitz have *pie vetustas*; Hailsb., against the meter, has *vetustas pie*. The reading must be *veterum piatas* with the Heinsian witnesses, Bong., Wid. above, and Gis.; I find it also in Alex. and Vatt. O and P. Nebrissa suspected *vietus*, as above in *vieto in pectore*, or *pietas* used interjectively, as in Virgil: “Alas, piety! Alas, ancient faith!”

Baronius and the Bollandists, against Franciscus Combefis, reject Amphilochius’s account in the *Life of Saint Basil* that the Holy Spirit had also descended in the form of a dove at the Jordan. See Victorius’s commentary *On the Ancient Bronze Mirror of Christ*.]

76. Teolius approves the opinion of the Vatican glossator against Prudentius. But Prudentius spoke no differently from many other holy Fathers, who explicitly say that John’s baptism was different from Christ’s baptism, and nevertheless affirm that the stains of sins were washed away by John’s baptism. Maldonatus wisely says against the heretics who acknowledge no distinction between the two baptisms, commenting on Matthew 3:11: “Let someone object to us the poets Prudentius and Juvencus, both of whom seem to equate John’s baptism with Christ’s baptism. For they say that they remitted sins. I could answer that they spoke not subtly but poetically; yet there is no need to excuse the statement by poetry, since we can interpret it favorably. For many ancient authors spoke in the same way, although they nevertheless deny that the baptism of Christ and that of John were the same.” Among them he lists Basil, Chrysostom, Augustine, Gregory the Great, Bede, and Theophylact. Saint Luke 3:3 says of Saint John: “And he came into the whole region of the Jordan, preaching a baptism of repentance for the remission of sins.” The holy Fathers had this in mind when they asserted that sins were remitted through John’s baptism, insofar as it stirred people to repentance, through which sins would be remitted, and prepared them for Christ’s baptism, through which, as theologians say, the stains of crimes are completely washed away *ex opere operato*, “by the work performed.” Juvencus, book I, on Mark 3: “Now I have begun to wash away former stains in the pure river; but another, stronger than I, will come,” etc. Saint Paulinus, poem 5 on John the Baptist: “He washes away the crimes of believers with poured-out waters, absolves human fears and remits punishments, extinguishes fire with water; he urges forgetfulness of errors and grants new bodies to a new life.” Basil, *On Baptism*: “As soon as anyone approached and confessed his sins, whatever their number or character, he was baptized in the river Jordan and immediately received remission of sins.” Chrysostom teaches the theological distinction in sermon 137: “With John there was forgiveness, but not without repentance; there was remission, but obtained through lamentation.” In the same sense the Spirit, or gift of grace, flowed invisibly from heaven, shining forth—thus refuting Nebrissa and Giselinus, who criticize this in Prudentius. Indeed, the distinguished Bertius, book XXXI of *Theological Disputations*, chapter 2, proves that Prudentius’s verses, “This from the washing,” etc., should be understood as remission in hope, which did not accompany John’s washing but followed it, because in the same passage he sang: “But after the limbs had been purified, the Spirit flowed in, shining from heaven.”

81. Vat. A had *stema*. Should *schema* be read? *Stemma* is indeed a crown, from στέφω, “to crown”; and because the Romans arranged images of their ancestors in their halls in the form of a crown, the insignia of families were therefore called *stemmata*. Here *stemma* may signify an image, or nobility and antiquity, and, as it were, a sequence of fasting. Others interpret *stemma* as an illustrious example.

82. I do not understand how Iso’s gloss belongs here. Perhaps it has been moved from its proper place, as often happens in such matters, and should be read after *stemma* as a separate gloss: “the figure concerning the people of Nineveh.”

84. In *mansuefactum*, a diaeresis is customarily made in *sue* so that the verse may scan. Teolius found in one Vatican manuscript *benignae mansuefactum dextrae*, “tamed by the kindly right hand”; the law of the meter does not permit this.]

88. Nebrissa, better than Iso, explains it in the ordinary, common, and widespread sense; he also interprets *fluentem* wickedly as “fallen into lust.” The verb *fluere* and *diffluere* are often used of lustful persons.

89. Hails reads *fastigio* for *fastidio*.

90. Egm. and Vat. A, in the first hand, read *vultum* for *cultum*; the latter is much better.

93. A *romphaea* is a kind of Thracian weapon: some call it a spear, others a sword.

94. Rat. wrongly reads *fragrosas*.

95. Ald. mistakenly reads *nubem* for *nube*.

96. Donatus, in *Andria* IV.2 and *Eunuchus* IV.5, interprets *brevem moram* as “a little day,” that is, a short interval. Teolius confirms from a marginal note in one Vatican manuscript that this was said according to the Septuagint, since the Septuagint assigns only three days to the conversion of the Ninevites. Saint Augustine, *City of God* XVIII.49, attempts to reconcile this reading with the Vulgate’s forty days. It should nevertheless be observed that a period of forty days could also have been called short, or “a little day,” when the matter was extremely serious—namely, repentance for long-standing crimes.

98. See the preface, no. 217, on the verb *condomare*, which Blanchinius wrongly changed to *condonare*. Prudentius regularly uses *nugae* for lust or wantonness.

99. *Continuit manum* with Nebrissa is better than *elevavit* with Iso.

105. There is no single agreement among interpreters concerning what city this was. Some interpret it as a city of Cilicia, others as Carthage, Africa, the Mediterranean Sea, a region of India, or Tartessus in Spain. Bonfrerius’s opinion in his notes on the *Onomasticon* of the cities and places of Sacred Scripture seems probable to me: that this name universally signifies places that can and ordinarily do be reached by ships, whether they are islands or overseas regions.

114. Some interpreters confidently assert that the sea creature was a whale; others object that a whale’s throat is too narrow to swallow a whole human being. A little later Prudentius speaks of teeth and molars, which some deny are appropriate to whales. Others maintain that whales are not all of one species, and report that some have no teeth, others one, and others several. It is commonly stated that the name *cetus* includes all fish of a certain considerable size. Many think that the great fish that swallowed Jonah was the creature called the *carcharias*, whose likeness Aldrovandus gives in *On Fish* XIII.12.

B, *desecarent*. *Offa* is ordinarily used for any shapeless mass thrust into the mouth. Its diminutive is *ofella*.

Weitz. and Heinsius, with Put., Oxon., Nom., Rot., one Torrentian manuscript, Vat. Q, and Alex. in the margin, read *maeandros*, which seems preferable. *Recessus* appears to be a gloss or correction by someone who knew that the first syllable of *maeandros* was long but did not notice that Prudentius shortens it in Hymn 6, verse 142. Egm. has *ventris recessus tortilis*, as though one should say “a twisted belly”; this is not satisfactory. For *circumibat*, some editions print *circuibat*.

129. The error *cadens* in Vat. A has been corrected to *candens*. In Minucius Felix some read: “There the gentle wave, pouring over the outer sands as though spreading them for a walkway, extended itself.” Others restore *tundebat* (“beat”). Elmenhorstius cites Saint Jerome’s authority, since Jerome uses the same verb, and cites this passage of Prudentius; but he corrupted the meter by changing one word: “And the shining foam beats the salt pumice stones.” Ouzelius copied the error. What wonder, then, if, in the days when monasteries were flourishing, such blemishes clung to Prudentius and passed from one copy to another? Ouzelius has much to say there about the gray and shining foam of the waves, and poets have nothing more common than descriptions of storms.

136. Ald. reads *deinde*, less suitably; the others read *deinceps*. Teolius—I do not know whether intentionally—has *deinde*, for he cites no manuscript.

137. Prag. reads *turbidum*; others have *turbidae*.

139. Weitz., Gis., Teol., Vat. B, I, P, Q, Urb., Rat. read *multinodi*, which Cellarius adopted because it is more pleasing in pronunciation, and because Apuleius uses *multinodis voluminibus* and *multinodis ictibus*. Vat. O wrongly has *multimodi*, also found in the Mozarabic Breviary. Codex Alex. and Put. have *multinodis*, with forms *a multinodis*, *multinode*, like *trinodis*, *enodis*. Egm. and Pal. likewise have this reading, and Ald. and those who read with him wrongly print *multimodis*. The meter does not permit it, nor does it permit *multimodi*, which occurs in Prag. Cellarius, and with him Teolius, criticize Heinsius because he denied that *enodus* and *trinodus* could be said. Heinsius, however, printed *multinodi* and merely stated in his notes: “Thus poets say *trinodis clava*, not *trinoda*, and *enode lignum*.” See Jonah IV.6. The more probable view seems to be that the plant called in Hebrew *qiqayon* grew only in Palestine; hence the Greeks, who did not know this shrub, translated it as “gourd,” while Saint Jerome translated it as “ivy,” to which it is more similar. Ancient pictures showing Jonah sleeping beneath a tree, such as one formerly in Victorius’s collection on an ancient glass vessel, prove only that the artist held this view, whether in this passage or elsewhere. See Victorius’s dissertation on the Seven Sleepers, in which he vainly attempts to persuade us that the question can easily be settled by the authority of his ancient glass, on which Jonah is represented beneath a gourd.

140. Prag. wrongly reads *perfruente*. The Mozarabic Breviary has *hic et repente*.

142. The Mozarabic Breviary wrongly reads *auxit* for *hausit*.

152. Rat. reads *turma*; *turba* is better.

153. Vossius and Borrichius had proscribed the word *bestialis*; Cellarius restored it from Prudentius in the “bronze age.”

154. Vat. A has *nigranti* as a variant reading. The meter requires *nigrante*. Compare *nigrante sub velamine* in *Peristephanon* II.379.

156. Vat. B, Prag., Rat., Sich., Gold., Hails., Bong., and Widm. in the margin read *Chios*. Others read *Coos*, which is correct, for the exceptionally fine garments made on the island of Cos were famous. See Ovid, Propertius, and other poets. Prag. indicates *Choos* in the margin, thereby pointing to *Coos*. Vat. A has *murice*, but a later hand changed it to *murices*. I think *Coo aestuantem murice*, which Torrentius found in his copies and judged in need of correction, should be emended to *Coo exaestuantem murice*. I do not dislike that reading even without emendation. Prudentius sometimes, as Virgil does with Greek words, does not elide the final vowel through diaeresis; and here he seems to have imitated *Tyrioque ardebat murice laena* in *Aeneid* IV. Nevertheless, Heinsius strives to defend the reading consistently supported by the manuscripts, adducing numerous examples from Prudentius and others in which *aestuare* is followed by *sitim*, *cursum*, *aestum*, *annum*, and similar words. I think these differ somewhat from our *aestuare murices*; and even if one grants that the expression can be used, I shall always doubt whether Prudentius preferred it to *Coo aestuantem murice*. Alcimus Avitus imitated this passage in Book IV: “From here he throws down his scepter, abandons his lofty tribunal, unfastens the scarlet cloaks, rejecting gold, and despises silk.” On the garment clasp, see Pignorius, *Commentary on Slaves*, p. 78.

Agobardus cites these verses in his book against Amalarius and praises Prudentius’s interpretation: “From the greatest to the least.” That is, down to the nursing infant, as those understood it who wished to write about this praiseworthy repentance; among them was Prudentius, a learned man: “No one,” he says, “remembered drinking …”

Whether one writes *pubes* or *pubis* matters little, provided it is understood that the final syllable is shortened here. Cellarius advises reading *jejuna*, not *jejunās*; I know of no one else who has made the latter reading.]

Teolius says that the manuscripts read *derogat* and that the printed books have *denegat*. Yet both readings occur in both printed books and manuscripts. 186. Here one sees the origin of the Lenten fast, for below, verse 196, we read, “Let each of us follow this.” Binghamus, who in *Antiquities* XXI.1 maintains that originally the fast lasted forty hours, not forty days, refused to apply his attention to these and similar words of the Fathers. The imperial laws that we cite at verse 14 of the following hymn testify that it lasted forty days. I would rather believe that some relaxation was introduced into the fast than that forty hours were transformed into forty days.

187. He is speaking of the forty days during which Christ the Lord fasted. All this is found in Matthew IV and Luke IV.

188. Nebrissa interprets *gratia ciborum* as “the pleasantness of food.” Here it means a gift, favor, or benefit bestowed upon us. See Hymn 11, verse 5: “Alas, how fleeting is grace.”

190. He calls the body the soul’s vessel, as Saint Paulinus does concerning the death of Celsus: “The flesh alone, which was the rational soul’s vessel, will receive the power of rising again.” Compare 1 Thessalonians 4:4: “Let each of you know how to possess his vessel in sanctification and honor.” Lupius, volume I, dissertation 11, pp. 203ff., proves by many examples that souls are depicted on Christian tombs in the form of doves near a vessel, since the vessel is a symbol of the body and the dove a symbol of the soul. See *Apotheosis*, verse 1025, and *Hamartigenia*, verse 281. Lupius also conjectured that the body might be represented in a wine jar, as though the soul were expressed through wine. See the commentary on Hymn 9, verse 28.

191. Prudentius more than once calls the human body *limus*, because it was made from clay.

194. Vat. A mistakenly has *sit recertus*. By the marvelous providence of God, the mystery of the Incarnation was concealed from the devil, and the birth of the Virgin who bore God remained unknown to him. Petavius and other theologians explain and defend the reasoning of Saint Ignatius the Martyr and other Fathers: Christ was conceived by a betrothed woman so that his birth from a virgin might be hidden from the devil. This was the sign given of the coming Messiah. Isaiah 7:11ff. says: “And the Lord continued to speak to Ahaz, saying, Ask for yourself a sign from the Lord your God … Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign. Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son.” Someone may ask what kind of sign this could have been if, in order to conceal the Virgin’s childbirth from the devil, she had been betrothed to Joseph. For how could the Hebrews have known that Jesus was born of a virgin? Someone has stated and resolved this question in two couplets:

“God wished the virgin birth to be a sign and pledge  
Of the salvation promised to the Hebrews.  
Who could know it? Surely those who looked upon Mary’s face  
And observed the character of the Virgin.”

I have inserted this epigram, once composed in honor of the distinguished Joseph Bustinzuria—whom his friends mourn, recently carried off by an untimely death—for this reason also: that I might dedicate at least this modest memorial to one who deserved well.]

[Col. 0853A] Moreover, when milk was denied to the wailing infants,

The cradles of the little ones grew wet with their tears:

[165] 324 The sparing nurse withheld the nourishment of her breast.

Even the flocks he shuts up, under the vigilant care

Of the herdsmen, so that the wandering animals

May not touch the dewy grass with their mouths,

Nor drink the water of a babbling spring;

[170] Empty stalls resound with lamentation.

Softened by these and similar things, God

Restrains his brief anger, tempering

The favorable yet threatening oracle;

For ready mercy easily releases

[175] The guilt of suppliant mortals and becomes the helper of those who weep.

But why should I speak of the example of an ancient people?

Long ago, when he was weighed down with mortal limbs,

[Col. 0853B] Jesus fasted with a devoted heart:

[Col. 0854A] He who, announced beforehand by the prophetic voice,

[180] 325 Is Emmanuel, or “God with us,”

Who made this body, naturally weak,

The liberator of the enslaved body,

[185] The conqueror of the desire that had previously reigned.

326 The inquisitor investigates by cunning questioning,

[Col. 0854B] Whether God has entered earthly limbs:

201. This means: so that the spirit itself may triumph over the flesh; the fast. *Livor*: envy, I.

203. *Altaris aram*: the altar’s altar, the altar of faith. *Aram*: a level place, I.

204. *Fidem*: offering, I.

205. *Limat*: files smooth, purifies, cleanses, I. *Pectorum rubiginem*: the contagions of the body, Prag.

206. *Amne*: with water, I.

207. *Calente*: burning, I.

208. *Scabra*: rough, Vat. A and Iso.

[Col. 0856B] 210. *Largitas*: almsgiving, Vat. A.

5. *Impeditum*: greatly burdened, I.

6. *Tuleris*: you would endure, I.

195. Mazochius, volume III of the *Spicilegium Biblicum*, judged that Prudentius here affirmed the devil’s actual fall backward, and not merely that the devil left Christ. Teolius does not accept this, but I find it unobjectionable. Some manuscripts read in Matthew, “Go behind me.”

196. Prag. wrongly reads *sequamur unusquisque*.

197. Ald. has *tum* for *tu magister*.

199. Heinsius prefers *vicerint*, with only Ambr. supporting it, and Cellarius and Teolius followed him. But *vicerit* is correct, with *spiritus* understood as its subject.

203. The ancients said that *altaria* belonged only to the higher gods, their name deriving from height, while *arae* belonged also to the gods below. Prudentius seems to imply that the *ara* is the more sacred part of an altar. See Berthaldus, *On the Altar*, chapter 2, who uses Prudentius to show that the *ara* was the foundation of the altar.

205. Vat. A has *corporis*; in the margin: “Others have *pectorum rubiginem*.” Oxon., Noms., Rottend., Egm., and Pal. have, not altogether badly, *corporis libidinem*; Oxon. marks it as a variant, and the Mozarabic Breviary has *pectorum rubiginem*. Amb. and Hails. have *corporis rubiginem*. Thuan. has *peccati rubiginem*, which fits the meter.

209. The Mozarabic Breviary wrongly has *alvo* for *almo*.

214. He rightly places this among the virtues: to consider all human beings equal by nature and to avoid what is called acceptance of persons.

216. Giselinus replaced *quisque* with *quisqui*, as though it were *quisquis*, not knowing that poets regularly use *quisque* for *quisquis*. Ausonius has in the *Sayings of Pittacus*: “Obey the law that you have enacted.” Other examples occur in Cyprian, Sidonius, and similar authors. Lexicographers also cite several passages from Plautus and Terence, although the reading in Terence is not equally certain and consistent. In the Theodosian Code, *quisque* frequently occurs for *quicumque* or *quisquis*. See the glossary at the end of volume VI of Gothofredus.

217. Why does the poet here say “the right hand greedy for praise,” and immediately afterward, following Matthew VI, “Let not your left hand know what your right hand does”? Because almsgiving must not be performed as hypocrites perform it, so that they may be honored by human beings; nevertheless, praise always arises from it, and, as Matthew continues in verse 4: “That your almsgiving may be in secret, and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you.”

220. This too is taken from Matthew XIX.29: “He shall receive a hundredfold and possess eternal life.” The reference is to the enduring riches of the preceding verse. Some manuscripts have *centiplex*, as Alex. does. In Plautus most read *centuplex*.

In Parrhasius’s edition the title of this hymn, Hymn 8, is: “Hymn of the divine Prudentius after the fast.”

3. Prag. wrongly has *leviter*, apparently from a gloss, for *leniter*. Parrh. has *septus*, less suitably. Matthew XI.30: “My yoke is easy.”

5. Vat. A and Prag., in a second hand, read *portas*, which could be defended if *toleras* were read in the following verse.

6. Vat. A has *toleras labores*. Christ, it says, bore hard labors and treated his servants gently under a relaxed doctrine, among other reasons because of the law of fasting. Christ fasted for forty complete days; for us, during the period of fasting, food is permitted after a fixed hour. He is therefore greater than we are by his examples, since he did not command us to do everything that he himself did.

7. Parrh. has *exemplo*.

8. Iso’s gloss is derived from the etymology: *palpo* means to touch lightly with the palm or hand.

9. This passage shows at what hour the ancients broke their fast. Just as they divided the night into four watches, they divided the day from sunrise to sunset into four parts, naming them successively the first, third, sixth, and ninth hours. Thus, after three divisions of daylight—that is, three parts of the day—had passed, the fourth followed, called the ninth hour. At the beginning of the ninth hour assemblies were held and the fast was broken. Binghamus, *Christian Antiquities* XIII.9 §2 and XXI.3 §3, distinguishes between fasts that continued until evening and stations, or semi-fasts, that were broken at the ninth hour. He understands Prudentius to be referring to these stations and notes that *festum* denotes the station at which religious gatherings were observed in church. This explanation is extremely foolish, for in the preceding hymn, verse 4, Prudentius likewise says, “And look upon our feast, serene King,” where he is certainly speaking of the Lenten fast. I think that in Prudentius’s time not everyone observed a distinction based on duration between the Lenten fast and the stations, and that when the ninth hour arrived it was permissible either to break the fast or to continue it, as can be inferred from verse 65 and those that follow in this hymn.]

[195] [Col. 0855A] But, when his deceit was rebuked, he fell backward.

Let each of us now follow this according to our strength,

Which you, Christ, teacher of the consecrated doctrine,

Gave to your followers,

So that when the appetite for devouring has been conquered,

[200] The spirit, the ruler, may triumph far and wide.

This is what the dark enemy’s envy begrudges,

What the governor of the world and heaven approves,

What makes the altar’s altar favorable,

What awakens the faith of the sleeping heart,

[205] 327 What files smooth the sickly rust of the breasts.

A flame is not so extinguished when water is poured over it,

Nor do snowdrifts melt so beneath the burning sun,

As the crop of murky faults vanishes,

Crushed beneath the nourishing fast,

[210] If generous almsgiving is always joined to it.

[Col. 0855B] For there is also that great kind of virtue:

To cover the naked, feed the needy,

[Col. 0856A] To bring gracious aid to those who beg,

To regard the lot of human beings as one and equal

[215] Among the powerful and the poor.

Everyone is sufficiently blessed who extends a right hand

Greedy for praise, lavish with money,

Whose left hand does not know the sweet deed.

Immediately enduring riches fill him,

[220] And the hundredfold fruit enriches him who lends at interest.

328 VIII. HYMN AFTER THE FAST.

Christ, ruler of your servants,

You who govern us with gentle reins,

Gently bridle us and restrain us

With an easy law,

[5] Although you yourself, bearing the burden

Of the body, have endured harsh labors,

10. *Vixdum*: still, not yet. *Tribus*: hours, out of twelve hours, I.

14. *Solvimus*: broke, ended. *Festum*: fast, praise, I.

15. *Affatim*: abundantly. *Imbuatur*: may be filled, refreshed, restored, I.

17. *Favor*: mercy, I.

19. *Lactat*: caresses, charms, I.

21. *Invenusto*: indecent, I.

[Col. 0858B] 22. *Lacerare*: to soil, I.

24. *Comat*: adorns—read *ornet*, “may he adorn,” I.

27. *Luteus*: saffron-colored, ruddy. *Tingat*: colors, I.

29. *Pudore*: chastity, I.

33. *Morbo*: with sickness, in sickness. *Residem*: sluggish, I.

35. *Vellus*: it is called so from *vellere*, “to pluck,” because the ancients did not shear sheep but plucked the fleeces from them, I.]

[Note: [Col. 0857C]

12. Juvencus likewise has in Book III: “The remaining portion of the waning daylight was left.”

13. In Rat., *vindicata* has rightly been made from *vindicatae*. Chamillardus interprets it as “with prepared food.” To vindicate something is to make it one’s own. During the fast Christians are forbidden food, which is restored or permitted when the fast has been ended.

14. Understand “the feast of a brief vow,” that is, of a brief fast. See above, Hymn 7, verse 4, where the day of fasting is called a feast because the victim of fasting is offered. I think Prudentius also had in mind the fourth law of Emperor Theodosius, *On Questions*, in the Theodosian Code: “During the forty days which, by the observance of religious rites, anticipate the Paschal season, all judicial examination in criminal matters is suspended.” And the fifth law: “During the sacred days of Lent, let there be no bodily punishments, when the absolution of souls is awaited.” Many think that games and spectacles were also forbidden during the days of fasting, as on other feast days.

15. Because Prudentius shortens the middle syllable of *affatim*, Barthius concludes in Book XL, chapter 11, that *affatim* is derived not from abundance of speech but rather from *fatigare*, “to weary.” There is no doubt that the syllable is short, whatever the origin of the adverb may be. Whether it can be lengthened on the example of Arator, Book II of the *History of the Apostles*, Ricciolius discusses in Index 2 of his *Prosody*.

16. Hails. and Widm. above have *voluntas*. Nebrissa calls the pleasure *prona*, because we are inclined toward it. It may be understood as pleasure inclined toward food.

19. Prudentius uses the verb *lactare* more than once in a sense unnoticed by others. In one sense *lacto* derives from *lac*, “milk,” but here it derives from *lacio*, from which come *allicio*, *pellicio*, and the frequentative forms *oblecto*, *delecto*, *illecto*, and *prolecto*. Thus *lactat* means “he attracts by alluring.” In Avitus, Book V, I read and understand the line as: “Immediately, with the word alluring amid loosened poisons.” In this sense I shall defend *lactantibus horis* in *Apotheosis*, verse 613. In Sacred Scripture the verb *lacto* is used with a similar meaning. Proverbs 1:10: “If sinners entice you”; and 16:29: “An unjust man entices his friend,” where the Hebrew word means “to allure.” The words *levis obsequela* likewise indicate the shortness of the prescribed fast. By repeating so often God’s kindness, which does not impose a heavy burden on us, he makes it sufficiently clear that fasting must be observed as a necessity and binding commandment, contrary to the chatter of heretics who claim that the early Christians fasted freely. If what the piety of the first Christians freely practiced were the point at issue, all these references to the ninth hour, the relaxed doctrine, the brief vow, and the light observance would be superfluous. For, as Eusebius reports from Irenaeus, *Ecclesiastical History* V.25, some fasted one day, others two or three, and others measured their fast by forty daylight and nighttime hours. See what I noted from Saint Augustine in the preface, no. 172.

21. Aldus wrongly has *adit* for *addit*, and *in venusto*. Hails. has *in vetusto*, where above we have *invenusto*. Nebrissa has *invenuste*, an adverb. The poet explains the Savior’s saying in Matthew 6:17–18: “But when you fast, anoint your head,” and so forth.

22. Aldus reads *cultum*; the sense requires *cultu*. Some Heinsian manuscripts and Gis. first edition have *sordibus* for *sordidus*, which is much better. Nebrissa reads *macerare* for *lacerare*, but the *a* in *macero* is long.

23. In Prag., *plexum* was made from *pexum*. But *pexum* is correct. Understand the hair.

26. Matthew 6:16: “When you fast, do not become like the hypocrites, sad.”

27. I think there is an error in Iso’s gloss. For the color *luteus* is not “ruddy.” Perhaps *croceus*, “saffron-colored,” should be read, not *rubicundus*, “reddish.” Ovid, Book XV of the *Metamorphoses*, called sulfur “yellow.”

31. Parrh. has *cernat*, and in the following verse *munere ditet*. Heinsius considers Gronovius’s conjecture clever and ingenious, *patenti munere donat*, although Heinsius himself found *latente* in Noms. Egm., Pal., and our Vat. A also have *latente*. I much prefer *latentem*, however, which is found in Ald., most of Heinsius’s manuscripts, Weitz., Vat. B, I, O, P, Q, Urb., Alex., Prag., Rat., and Gis. The poet is insisting on evangelical words, such as are now read in the Vulgate and formerly stood in the Greek Gospel of Saint Matthew: “And your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you.” There is no mention there of an open gift, but of one who fasts in secret.

34. With Vat. B, Rat., Put., Thuan., Rot., and Weitz., one should read *sano*, that is, “to the herd,” and the sentence should be allowed to continue through the following stanza. Others have *sanat*.]

35. Rotterdam and one Vatican manuscript. Teolius has *affixum*, quite suitably, which appealed to Caucius. Rat., less well, has *affixit*. Isidore’s etymology of *vellus* (“fleece”) is drawn from Varro, Book IV of *On the Latin Language*; others say that *vellus* was so called because it veils the sheep.]

39. *Revehens*: carrying back, bringing back. — *Aprico*: sunny, summery, warm, clear; as though from *Africo*, that is, a place without cold, I.

42. *Vibrat*: grows. — *Impexis*: bristling, I.

43. *Sudibus*: thorns, I.

45. *Frequens*: dense, thick, Iso.

46. *Vernat*: blooms. — *Tum*: also, I.

49. *Hisce*: in place of *istis*, I.

51. *Compensant*: repay, return, I.

54. *Confectos*: constricted, afflicted, I.

71. *Tu*, namely *dum*: while, I.]

[Note: [Col. 0859C]

38. *Gravatos* is an error of Aldus. *Gravatos* likewise appears in Egmondanus and Hailes. In earlier writers *u* was sometimes written for *o*, as *servos* for *servus*.

39. Understand Isidore’s gloss in this way: *apricum* is as though from *Africum*, that is, without dread or cold, from φρίκη (“shivering,” “horror”). Hence some think Africa was so called; others derive the name from Apher, Abraham’s grandson.

41. Aldus has an error, *patris*. Prudentius seems to have alluded to Psalm XXII, verse 2: “He placed me there in a place of pasture.” See Barthius, Book XXXII, chapter 2, who explains this passage of the meadow and dew of Psalm XXIII, as also the poem *On the Passion*: “They will refresh you with heavenly dew, and the good meadows will feed you with their sweetness.” Barthius correctly changes *pacti* to *prati*. This parable of the lost sheep, which the shepherd, after finding it, places joyfully upon his shoulders, is related in Luke, chapter XV, verses 4 and following. A similar description of the heavenly meadow occurs above, in Hymn 5, verses 113 and following.

42. Aldus has *implexis*, less correctly. *Lappae* are plants commonly found in meadows that cling to clothing. Virgil, *Georgics* I: “The rough forest rises, and burs and thistles.”

43. *Sudes* are stakes of any kind of wood, sharpened like points, set against the trespass or climbing of those wishing to leap over. Prudentius uses *sudes* for thorns, or the prickles of the thistle.

46. Widmann has *dum*; *tum* is better.

47. Fabricius and Gisbertus’s second edition have *vivi*. Then *fluenti* could be read.

58. He calls God “Father,” as often, in the evangelical manner.

59. Vat. B has *frangat*. The others, and the sense, require *frangit*.

64. Why *enervans*, with the first syllable shortened, is pronounced in this way, I explained in the *Prolegomena*, no. 219. In Heinsius’s older manuscripts, and in the Ambrosian papers, Parrhasius and Alexandrinus have *inervans*, and the same form occurs in a very ancient manuscript of Althelmus’s *On the Praise of Virginity*, formerly held in the Bodleian Library at Oxford. Gellius attests, and ancient copies confirm, that in words such as *innitor*, *innecto*, and similar forms, the *n* is expressed only once; some think *inervans* was formed by analogy with these, as though it were *innervans*. Heinsius once conjectured *inerrans*. If conjecture were necessary, I should prefer *inermans*, from *inermis* (“unarmed”). Festus mentions the verb *inermo, -as*, “to strip of weapons.” Salmasius wants *inervans* to stand for *enervans*, with *e* changed to *i* so that the syllable may be shortened; thus in *Apotheosis*, verse 400, some have *inergima* for *energema*.

65. This passage by no means asserts the freedom to fast in the manner defended by heretics. It merely says that a measure has been prescribed in fasting, beyond which everyone is free to extend abstinence. For the poet adduces as an example the very food they took after fasting, which he trusts will be healthful. Bingham, together with Jeremy Taylor, wrongly uses these verses to support complete freedom in fasting. See the remarks above, and observe that the poet is consistent throughout the hymn. “Lest a more extensive practice of labor break the body’s clay lattice, and lest relaxed strength abandon fragile earth”—with these words he concludes that a loose and free *measure* of abstinence has been assigned to all, that is, that excessively long fasts have not been prescribed.

69. It is a pious and constant Christian practice to invoke God for every action, so that they always begin through God, and that what has been begun through him may be completed through him. 1 Corinthians X, 31: “Whether you eat or drink, or do anything else, do all things to the glory of God.” See the note on Colossians, chapter III, verse 17. At banquets, lest the memory of God slip away amid food and drink, the ancient Christians decorated the vessels used at meals with images of Jesus Christ and the saints. Consult Buonarroti’s most learned work *On the Cemetery Glasses*.

71. Prag. has *mensas*. Heinsius, with all his copies, Aldus, our manuscripts, and also Alexandrinus, Urbanus, and Vatt. O, P, Q, and Gisbertus’s second edition, have *renuas*. Widmann has *renues*. Weitz, Sichard, Bongarsius, Goldastus, and Gisbertus in the margin of the first edition have *renoves*, which is also found in one of Torrentinus’s manuscripts and in Vat. I; and thus correctly in Vat. I: *cibumque*, not *cibumve*. From this Heinsius once conjectured *removes*, and in the following verse *tentas*—in vain, as he later admitted, since the true reading is *renuas*. In his older manuscripts he likewise found *cibumque*, in the more recent ones *cibumve*. The latter is supported by the sense in our copies. The meaning is: whether you reject the table or take food, in the words of the Apostle. Teolius reads *renoves, cibumve sumere temptes* with one very ancient Vatican manuscript and Weitz. Yet Weitz clearly has *cibumque*, and so does the very ancient Vatican manuscript, if it is Vat. I, as I think it is. Nor do I approve his reading *temples* for *temnas*, since *temptes* is the same as *tentes* in the old orthography, not a frequentative formed from *temno*. Parrhasius supports us, but he incorrectly printed *tentas* for *tentes*.]

[Col. 0859A]

Its fleece, caught upon the brambles

Of the rough forest’s pathless places,

The tireless shepherd calls back,

And, keeping the wolves away,

Carries it upon his burdened shoulders.

Then, bearing it back, he cleanses it

[40] And restores it to the sunny fold.

He restores it also to the meadows and green field,

Where no thorn bristles with clinging burs,

Nor the fearsome thistle arms

Its shoot with stakes;

[45] But a dense grove, with palms,

And the bending crown of grasses, blooms:

Then the perpetual laurel shades

A glass-clear stream of living waters.

For such gifts to you, faithful Shepherd,

[50] [Col. 0859B]

What service could be repaid?

No vows of those who pray can equal

The price of salvation.

[Col. 0860A]

However much, despising customary food,

We willingly keep our limbs exhausted,

And entreat you with banquets refused,

By night and day,

[55] The care of those who obey is always surpassed;

Nor does any gift equal that of the Father.

And a more severe practice of exertion breaks

the body’s clay lattice.

Therefore, lest relaxed strength

[60] Abandon fragile earth, and lest watery moisture

Rule in the pale veins,

Weakening the sick body,

333 A loose and free measure of abstinence

[65] Is assigned to all; nor does severe

Terror drive us on. The power of choice

Compels each person to will his own course.

Whatever you do, first begin it

[70] After calling upon the will of the Godhead,

[Col. 0861A]

Whether you reject the table or attempt

To take food.

The favorable God gives his assent,

And prospers it with a favorable countenance,

[75] Just as we trust that this food

Which we have dedicated and consume

Will be healthful for us.

May it be good, I humbly pray,

And bring healing to our limbs,

And may the food scattered through the veins

[80] Nourish the spirit of those who beseech Christ.

IX. HYMN FOR EVERY HOUR.

[Col. 0862A]

Give me, boy, the plectrum, that I may sing with faithful songs

335 A sweet and melodious poem, the glorious deeds of Christ.

Let our Muse sing of him alone; let the lyre praise him.

It is Christ whom the king and priest, wearing the priestly fillet,

[5] Had sung of as soon to come, with voice, string, and drum,

[Col. 0863A]

Drawing in through his marrow the Spirit flowing from heaven.

336 We sing of deeds accomplished and now proven:

The world is witness, nor does earth itself deny what it saw;

God, manifested openly to mortals for their instruction.

[10] Born from the Father’s heart before the world’s beginning,

Called Alpha and Omega: himself the source and conclusion

Of all things that are, that were, and that afterward will be.

He himself commanded; he spoke, and created things came to be:

[Col. 0864A]

earth, heaven, the hollow of the sea,

[15] and whatever thrives within these beneath the high sphere

of the sun and moon.

He assumed the form of a perishable body,

limbs subject to death,

lest the human race perish through the offspring of the first-created man,

whom the guilty law had plunged into deep Tartarus.

[20] O blessed birth, when the virgin mother

bore our salvation, pregnant with the Holy Spirit,

77. He had said that what we consume as dedicated food would be healthful, as he trusted; he prays that it may actually be healthful, good, and auspicious. This derives from the formula used when beginning anything under favorable auspices: “May it be good, fortunate, and prosperous.” In Alexandrinus and Urbanus, *amen* is written after this hymn.

The inscription of Hymn 9 is not the same in all copies. Aldus: “For all hours.” Vatt. B, I, Rat., Bongarsius, and Thuanus: “For every hour.” Oxoniensis: “For all hours.” Rottendorf: “A hymn always to be sung.” Gisbertus: “A hymn for every hour and day,” with “On the miracles of Christ” in the margin. Spiegelius, who found *for every hour* in the Peutinger manuscript and in another copy *A poem on the deeds and miracles of Christ*, while in other copies he found *A hymn for all hours on the miracles of Christ*, placed this last title before his extensive commentary on the hymn. To complete it he used the Peutinger manuscript, of what he calls obsolete antiquity. See the *Prolegomena*, no. 103, for another title: *On the miracles of our Savior*. Vat. A, Put., Ambrosianus, Weitz, and others have *A hymn for every hour*, as the expression commonly runs, “a man for every hour.” Since Prudentius had previously written hymns to be sung at fixed hours, he offers this one for any hour of the day. The Mozarabic rite recites this hymn at the Lord’s resurrection and on the following weekdays; in the recent edition of the Isidorian Breviary it appears on page 385 and page XCIX among the hymns, with the order of the stanzas somewhat reversed. We shall record the variant readings, including corrupt ones, so that a more accurate text may someday be produced. John Louis Vives inserted almost the whole hymn into his little work *The Sacred Daytime on the Sweat of Christ*, but from an erroneous edition, such as were then in use.

1. Giselinus attributes to Jacobus Meyerius the restoration of this hymn and the first hymn of Book *Peristephanon* after changing the metrical form. They had been divided into Alcmanic and Euripidean lines. I discussed this division in the *Prolegomena*. Aldus also printed complete trochaic lines, and that form is likewise preserved in certain manuscript copies, which seems to have been Prudentius’ intention. For after the final syllables of an Alcmanic line he never concluded the verse as though it were a separate unit; rather, he continued the Alcmanic and Euripidean forms as a complete verse, without any collision of vowels. See also Hymn 1 of Book *Peristephanon*. Crinitus, among the hymns of Prudentius that he says were celebrated, lists the hymn *On the Deeds and Miracles of Christ*. In expounding this hymn, Fabricius titled it *A Paean on the Life and Death of Christ*, and later added, “For every hour and day.” A paean is a song of thanksgiving for some victory won, which is especially appropriate to Christ.

Perhaps no one has thought of interpreting the gloss “BOY, Christ.” Prudentius, in the manner of lyric poets, calls the servant who brings the plectrum a *puer*. Fabricius says that he alluded to the custom of antiquity whereby boys sang to the lyre, or whereby some sang while a boy played the cithara; this is confirmed by Athenaeus. Among the ancients *puer* means a servant or attendant, much as today in Italian and Spanish those who serve are called *giovine* and *mozo*. Horace, Book I, Ode 38: “I hate Persian preparations, boy”; and Book I, *Satires* 10: “Go, boy, and quickly write this beneath my little book.” Propertius, Book III, Elegy 19: “Go, boy, and quickly place these words upon some column.” This same meaning can be inferred from civil law. The same usage is found in sacred Scripture.

By contrast, I think that older men are called *signori* and *señores* in Italian and Spanish because they are masters. Since formerly the senior member of a household or family was master of its possessions and was called *senior* by distinction, the word passed from there to all who possessed means. Thus wealth completely reverses nature, causing old men to be designated by the term for boys and boys to take pride in the title of elders.

In some copies of the Vulgate, *fidibus* is incorrectly printed for *fidelibus*. *Chorei*, or trochees, are the feet proper to this poem, or songs marked by these feet. The trochees are called faithful, as Fortunatus—or whoever was the author of the hymn *The Banners of the King Advance*—said: “David in a faithful song”; and Prudentius in Hymn 7: “Revealed in a faithful volume”; and below, verse 26: “faithful pages.”

2. Alexandrinus has *melodios*, perhaps *melodon*. Vat. A has *ac* for *et*. Iso drew the etymology of *lyra* from Isidore, Book III, chapter 22: “The lyre is called from the Greek *lyrein* (‘to play the lyre’), from the variety of sounds, because it produces different sounds.” Some believe that the lyre received its Greek and Latin name from the sharp thinness of that sound, *lyr, lyr*. See J. C. Scaliger, Book I of the *Poetics*.

4. Some believe this priest to have been Melchizedek; but they do not know that the poet gave this name to prophets, as in Hymn 7, verse 27, “the ancient priest” concerning Elijah.

5. David is called *infulatus* either because, girded with a linen ephod, he danced before the Lord’s ark, or because he was king and a *infula* is a band shaped like a diadem. Lucretius beautifully describes the *infula* in Book I: “Around her head, a fillet, with its ornaments, was spread from either side of her cheeks.” Vatt. A, B, and Q read *corde* for *chorda*. Goldastus has the elision *et*.]

7. Some have it incorrectly; so do we.

8. Alexandrinus, Vat. B, Aldus, and Weitz have *Testis est orbis*, which is smoother than *Testis orbis est*, found in Vatt. I, O, P, Gisbertus, Heinsius, Teolius, and others. Vat. A has *Testis orbis terrae, nec ipsa*. The meter resists it. Hailes and Vat. Q have, with a similar error, *Testis est orbis, terra nec ipsa*.

10. Heinsius thinks *fusus* more harmonious and more in Prudentius’ style with Ambrosianus, although the other copies he consulted have *natus*, as Aldus, Weitz, Gisbertus, and all our manuscripts. The learned Teolius acknowledges that *natus* is the more genuine reading, but retains *fusus*. “I would restore,” he says, “*natus*.” Yet it contributes nothing to the sense. He should have used greater freedom. For whether the meaning is the same or not, what the author most probably wrote should be printed. Spiegelius found *fusus* in Conrad Peutinger’s manuscript and another, though less reliable, but himself followed Aldus and the Daventry edition because of the authority of ecclesiastical usage. Alexandrinus and Thomasii’s Hymnary also have *natus*, along with Urbanus and Vatt. I, O, P, Q. In the Veliternian manuscript, discussed in the *Prolegomena*, no. 212, there are verses by Fortunatus in praise of chrism, which P. Michael Angelus Luchius, Benedictine, noted among others in a new edition of Fortunatus. In that hymn he transcribed Prudentius’ half-line: “Born from the Father’s heart, filling the virgin’s womb.” See *Prolegomena*, no. 43, concerning the other hymn, “Born from the Father’s heart.” The poet expresses Psalm CIX, 3: “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you.”

11. Vat. B, A, and ω have *cognominatur*, “is called,” above, *cognominatus*, “called.” Others have *Alpha et ω*. Weitz, Gisbertus, and several more recent manuscripts have *cognominatur*. Vat. I has *A et ω cognominatur*. Revelation XXI, 6: “I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end.” Therefore it is not necessary to add “Omega,” as most do. These letters were greatly used among ancient Christians. Saint Paulinus, in *Natale* 11, describes a cross with the letters α and ω placed on either side, verse 645: “Alpha surrounds the cross, and Omega … Alpha likewise is Christ to me, and Omega.” Compare the hymn on the names of Christ, which I edited from the celebrated Veliternian manuscript in *Prolegomena*, no. 212. Coins of emperors inscribed with α and ω are found. At Constantinople there once stood two columns, and on their bases were shields bearing these signs, α and ω. The same signs are frequently carved upon Christian tombs. See the ancient monument of the Seven Sleepers and the commentary of Victorius, who adorned it with this type of decoration. On account of these letters, Marcus and Colobarsus based their heresy upon the Greek alphabet, as Tertullian reports in Book *On the Prescription of Heretics*, chapter 50. Compare Rosweidus’s notes on Paulinus, as well as Gretzer, Lipsius *On the Cross*, Bosius, Aringhus, and other writers on Christian antiquities.

[Col. 0864B] 12. Virgil, *Georgics* IV, verse 392: “For the prophet knows all things, what is, what has been, and what is soon to come.”

13. Genesis I, 3: “God said, ‘Let there be light,’ and there was light.” And similarly elsewhere. Psalm XXXII, 9: “For he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created.” Some suspect that Pythagoras learned his “He himself said it” from the Egyptian prophets; this manner of speech is frequent among the prophets.

14. *Fossa ponti*, “the hollow of the sea,” may seem an inelegant expression for the sea. Others have not hesitated to say “the pools of the deep.” Spiegelius takes the threefold structure of things as a triple principle according to the opinion of the Peripatetics, who believe that there are three principles of things: matter, form, and privation. Nonsense. The poet means the three parts of the world that he has enumerated: heaven, earth, and sea. Fortunatus imitated him: “Whom earth, sea, and ether” (we now read *stars* in the ecclesiastical office) “worship, adore, and proclaim, him who rules the threefold structure; the womb of Mary bears him in confinement.” Prudentius alluded to Psalm CXLV, 6: “Who made heaven and earth, the sea and all that is in them.”

16. He used the Apostle’s expression when he says “the form of the body.” But lest anyone distort this into an empty bodily appearance, he added “limbs subject to death.”

17. Alexandrinus and our copies, with Aldus, as well as Heinsius’s older manuscripts, Weitz, Gisbertus, and others, have *primoplasti*. This is not foreign to the practice of ancient Christians, who formed a single word from one Greek and one Latin word. Such Greek-Latin words are called hybrids. Others write *hybridas* or *ibridas*. It is clear from Quintilian and others that profane authors also used them. The Sicilians are said to have used a speech that was mixed, as it were, like a *cinnus*, from Latin and Greek. Rottendorf, two manuscripts of Torrentinus, Fabricius, and Spiegelius have *protoplasti*, which appealed to Nebrissensis and especially to Jacobus Meyerius. The Mozarabic Breviary has the erroneous *primo plausti*.

[Col. 0864D] 18. Aldus, Weitz, Spiegelius, Gisbertus, and others have *quam*, that is, “the race.” Vat. B, Rat., Prag., Fabricius, Egmondanus, Bongarsius, Put., Thuanus, Ambrosianus, Alexandrinus, and others have *quem*, that is, “the first-created man.”

19. Hailes and Prag. have *partus ille*, “that birth.”

22. Aldus has *psallant te omnes angeli*, “let all angels sing praise to you.” Vatt. A, B, I, O, P, Q, Urbanus, the Mozarabic Breviary, Rat., Weitz, and Gisbertus have *Psallant omnes angeli*, “let all angels sing.” When Meyerius saw that this reading conflicted with the meter, he restored *Psallat omnis angelus*, “let every angel sing,” followed by Fabricius and Spiegelius from uncorrupted manuscripts. I prefer *psallite omnes angeli*, “sing, all angels,” with Alexandrinus, Ambrosianus, Put., Thuanus, and one manuscript of Torrentinus. Some think *psallant omnes angeli* was produced by ecclesiastical usage. But Thomasii’s Hymnary has *psallite omnes angeli*.]

30. *Rex*: the master of the feast; he calls the master of the feast “king.” For *architriclinus* means the chief of the couches; *cline* is Greek for “bed.” The ancients had three couches: one for the master, a second for the mistress, and a third for the guest. 24. The Mozarabic Breviary punctuates and reads it this way: “Let no voice of languages be silent, but let every voice sound together.”

25. Spiegelius wants *vates* to mean the Sibyls. I do not think this is clear. Our copies, Aldus, Weitz, and Gisbertus have *concin[e]bant*, “they sang together”; two copies of Torrentinus have *praecinebant*, “they sang beforehand”; Rottendorf has *praecinebat*, “he sang beforehand”; Thuanus and Vat. I in the first hand have *concinebat*, “he sang together.” If one accepts *praecinebat* or *concinebat*, understand David, whom he praised earlier. The Mozarabic Breviary has *concin[e]bant*, and in the text *quam*, with *quem* in the margin.

27. One manuscript of Torrentinus has *collaudent Deum*, “let them all praise God.”

28. He begins to relate Christ’s miracles from the Gospel history. Jesus changed water into wine, John II. This miracle was frequently carved on the sarcophagi of ancient Christians together with other scenes signifying the resurrection of bodies. Lupius, volume I, dissertation 2, conjectures that a wine jar sometimes represented on Christian tombs signifies the body, at times to be joined to the soul, whose figure is wine.

29. Thuanus has: “You announce, steward, that wine is ready from the jar.” Ambrosianus has *sumptum* for *promptum*. Saint Ambrose used *minister vini* and *ministerium vini* in Book I of *On Duties*, chapter 29, and in chapter 6 concerning Joseph.

30. I would readily read *colore tinctis poculis*, “cups colored with wine,” if all the manuscripts did not oppose it. The Gospel passage also expresses flavor: “When the master of the feast tasted the water made wine,” and so forth. Sedulius joined both the color and flavor of wine. Concerning the king of the feast, Horace, Book I, Ode 4: “Nor will you draw the kingdom of wine by lot,” where he means a banquet celebrated by pooled contributions. Ausonius, in the *Ephemeris*, and at the place concerning a banquet: “I invited five; for six make a proper banquet with the king; if there are more, it is a quarrel.” The king of the feast is, as some think, the one who provides the banquet; or, as others believe, the steward of the feast; or even the priest who presided over a Jewish banquet. More generally, a master of anything is sometimes called “king,” as in Virgil, *Eclogue* 1, “my kingdom.” Saint Paulinus, *Natale* 6, on the rustic man: “And, at the very threshold, they joyfully recognize as king the one offered to them”—meaning the oxen. Cicero, *On the Orator*, page 11: “If we were not in your kingdom, we would not have endured this,” referring to Crassus’ Tusculan villa. The author under Claudian’s name, Juvencus, Sedulius, and others celebrate this miracle of Christ and those that follow in verse.

31. In Matthew VIII Jesus cures a leper and sends him to the priests. In the Parma edition I think *membra mortis* is a printer’s error. Correct it to *morbis*, “diseases.”

[Col. 0866B] 33. Giselinus has *ulcerum* in the margin for *vulnerum*. The cited passage, Matthew VIII, verse 4: “Show yourself to the priest, and offer the gift that Moses commanded, as a testimony to them.” These are the *piamina*. Correct the Mozarabic Breviary, where *repugnans* appears.

34. In John IX Jesus restores sight to the man blind from birth. “Perpetual darkness” means blindness from birth, or from the first moment of life. Elmenhorst, in his 1610 Hamburg edition of Arnobius, page 72, cites these verses for Arnobius’ phrase “the mobile orbs of the eyes,” and confirms through examples from several poets that the eyes are called *orbes*.

35. *Apotheosis*, verse 675: “He anointed the blind eyes and restored light to them with mud.” See other passages there concerning Christ’s miracles, and in the *Dittochaeon*. The Mozarabic Breviary has *odoris*; read *et oris*, “and of the mouth.”

36. Ovid, *Metamorphoses* I, has *luminis orbis*, “the orb of light,” of the eye. The sockets in which the eyes lie may be understood, as in Hymn 2 of *Peristephanon*, verse 146: “Bearing hollowed orbs.” Correct the Mozarabic Breviary’s *ac medulla* and read *hac medela*, “by this healing.”

37. In Hailes and the Mozarabic Breviary, *increpans* is an error. Spiegelius conjectures that Prudentius read in Matthew VIII: “Then, rising, he rebuked the winds,” which Erasmus, annotating this passage of Matthew, thinks may originally have been written. Certainly, from Prudentius, this conjecture is empty, since he rather expressed Luke VIII, 24: “But he rose and rebuked the wind and the storm of the water, and it ceased; and there was calm.” Prudentius uses the words of Saint Matthew in *Apotheosis*, verse 650: “I see waters struggling with mighty whirlwinds stretched out upon a tranquil surface at Christ’s command.”

38. Fabricius and Hailes have *verrat*. The others have *vertat*, which Heinsius alone approves. Vat. A has *summo*, “top,” and, in a different writing, *fundo*, “bottom.” Vat. B has *fundo*, with *summum* in the margin; this is not wholly displeasing. The more common and truer reading is *fundo ab imo*, “from the bottom upward.” In Vat. A, *et* was missing after *vexet*; it was correctly added, apparently by another hand. It was also missing in Vat. P. Asconius Pedianus, Probus, Gellius, and Macrobius explain the force of the verb *vexo* against Annaeus Cornutus, who had noted in Virgil “to toss the Dulichian ships,” as though a slight word had been used to describe so great a calamity.

39. The Mozarabic Breviary has the error *ille jussit obsecundans*, “he commanded, obeying.”

40. Jesus frees a woman from a flow of blood, Matthew IX, 20; Mark V, 25; Luke VIII, 44. *Extimum* for “outermost edge” is Latin and elegant. Concerning the spondee admitted in the fifth place in *furtim*, I spoke in the *Prolegomena*, no. 229. Georgius Remus, in his notes on this hymn, says that the metrical rule shortens the final syllable of *furtim*, as in Ovid’s “of the circling sheep.” But who would not immediately perceive that the cases differ? For after *circum* a vowel follows in Ovid, whereas after *furtim* a consonant follows in Prudentius. Remus likewise conjectures that perhaps one should read …]

59. Ambrosian, Altinian, Nomsian, and Daventrian editions read *refecta*; most, and more correctly, read *referta*. Chamilard, Cellarius, and Teolius retain *refecta*. The poet seems to have intended *referta*, as in the *Apotheosis*, concerning the same miracle: “the satiated … the raw guest sweats out the mass of his belly.” Aldus has *accumbentum* for *accubantum*; the Putean and Oxford manuscripts have *adcubentum*, incorrectly. Unless one reads *accumbentum*, admitting a spondee in the fifth foot, as at verse 40.

61. Ambrosian has *et perennis*, less well. John 6:56: “My flesh is truly food”; and there, verse 51: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven.” And again, verse 59: “Whoever eats this bread will live forever.” From the same chapter, where the miracle is narrated, this beautiful apostrophe has been taken, although Saint John does not report these words immediately in this form.

[Col. 0869C] 63. The Mozarabic Breviary has *lacuna*, incorrectly.

65. The Putean, Oxford, Nomsian, and Vatican A manuscripts have *clausa* for the different reading. I prefer *crassa* with the others, including the Mozarabic Breviary, where *grassa* is written incorrectly: for *clausus* is read in the immediately preceding verse, and “the thick obstructions of hearing” is more appropriately said than “the closed obstructions.” The story is found in Mark 7:32.

66. The Mozarabic Breviary has *susurris praevius*.

67. Matthew 15:30–31.

68. *Veternus* means “grown old,” from *vetus*, “old.” It is usually said of idleness, laziness, and excessive sleep. Perhaps one should read *veterno vinxerint silentia*, “the silences of lethargy have bound.” But *veternus* as an adjective is graceful, although it is more commonly used substantivally. The Mozarabic Breviary has the faulty *lingua vatur*.

69. The Hailsbrunn, Mozarabic Breviary, Widmanstetter, and Goldast manuscripts above have *orbem* for *urbem*.

70. The Prague manuscript, not badly, has: “And even Tartarus itself he enters graciously, lest they should be deprived of salvation below.”

71. The Prague manuscript has *tartara*. Others have *tartarum*, which suits the poem better. Certain heretics denied that Christ truly descended to the underworld; Bellarmine, volume I, and Petavius, volume IV, part II, set forth and refute their differing opinions, and praise these verses of Prudentius. It is probable that Christ’s soul descended to all the regions of the underworld. The Mozarabic Breviary has *facta* instead of *fracta*, correctly conjectured by its editor. In the following verse it has, incorrectly in the text, *refulsis* for *revulsis*.

72. Aldus, Egmondanus, Oxford, Nomsian, Altinian, Rotterdam, and the Vatican A, B, O, and P manuscripts, as well as the Alexandrian and Urbinate, have *indissolubilis*; I rather like this reading. I think Prudentius occasionally admitted a spondee in the fifth foot, to make the rolling trochees somewhat heavier. See verses 59 and 40. Vatican I has *dissolubilis*, which the others also have, and I retain it because the sense and meter proceed correctly. The hinge is *dissolubilis*, as though “loosened,” just as above *fracta janua*, “the broken door,” and below *dissolutis vinculis*, “the chains being loosed.”

73. See Hymn 3, verse 199, and the note. Tasso uses a similar phrase in *Jerusalem Delivered*, canto 7, stanza 46: “For that fortress, by wondrous contrivance, is always open to those entering, closed to those departing.” The Mozarabic Breviary has the faulty *ac revertentes*.

74. Aldus first printed *obice retrorsum repulso*, later correcting it to *obice retrorsum pulso*. Both are wrong. The Putean, Torrentian, and Vatican A manuscripts have *obice extrorsum repulso*. The Prague and Ratian manuscripts, the two Torrentian manuscripts, Spiegel, together with the Peutingian, Sichardian, and Vatican B, I, O, P, and Q manuscripts, have *objice extrorsum recluso*, which the Mozarabic Breviary perhaps intended by its *objice extorsus recluso*. Teolius, following Heinsius’s Putean manuscript against five other Vatican manuscripts and the others, wrote *obice extrorsum repulso*. The Alexandrian and Thuanean manuscripts have *objice extrorsum reclusa*, which can be defended, since *obex* occurs in the feminine gender in the manuscripts of excellent authors and often in Alcimus Avitus. In the Alexandrian manuscript, however, *repulso* stands in the margin. The Oxford reading, *objice extrorsum excluso*, should not be followed. To make the first vowel long, the word is usually written *objice*. The Urbinate has *introrsum*.

75. The Mozarabic Breviary needs correction: read *vestra lege, et limen atrum*. Weitz reads: “The law restores the dead, and the threshold,” *porta reddit mortuos lege versa, et limen*. Heinsius has: “the dead: the law being turned, the threshold.” Cellarius and Teolius have: “the dead: the law being turned, and the threshold.”

76. The Prague manuscript has *antrum*. Heinsius thinks *furva* should be read, so that it may refer to the tombs. But *luce fulva*, “with tawny light,” that is, “reddish-golden,” is not bad. Thus we find tawny gold, tawny stars, and tawny jasper in the best poets.

78. The Mozarabic Breviary incorrectly has *polluerunt*. At the edge, correctly, stands *palluerunt*.

79. In the third foot he perhaps placed a spondee instead of a trochee, unless one prefers to say that he shortened the first vowel of *lugubri*. Aldus, Vatican B, and most others have *sordidus*. Vatican A has *sordibus*, with a *d* added above. I find it noted somewhere that Sichard restored *sordibus*. But *sordidus* is the more credible reading, as is *moerens* below. Prudentius describes the darkness that occurred during the Lord’s Passion, imitating Virgil at the end of Book 1 of the *Georgics*. Juvencus and Sedulius treated this subject in much the same way. Some have questioned whether there was a true eclipse of the sun. Spiegel thinks that Prudentius did not acknowledge a true solar eclipse, but in reality asserts that the sun withdrew and abandoned the sky; and that Juvencus, Sedulius, and Saint Jerome spoke in the same manner, so that the prophecy might be fulfilled: “The sun shall go down at noon, and the light shall be darkened over the earth in the day.” Spiegel adds that the darkness occurred only over the whole land of Judaea, and discusses the matter at length from this standpoint. Augustin Calmet published a dissertation in volume VII, *On the Darkness at Christ’s Death*, in which he learnedly investigates the causes, effects, duration, and extent of this most celebrated prodigy, also adducing the testimony of pagan writers, Phlegon and Thallus. Three explanations of the phenomenon are commonly proposed: first, that the sun drew back its rays and its light into itself; second, now the more usual explanation, that the moon came between the sun and the earth and prevented the sun’s rays from illuminating the earth, as happens in eclipses; third, the explanation that seemed more convenient and easier to Calmet, especially if “the whole earth” means Judaea alone, namely, that the sun’s rays were blocked by the intervention of some dense cloud. I see no reason why “the whole earth” in this passage should be referred only to Judaea. Prudentius clearly suggests that the whole world shuddered at the chaos of eternal night. He seems to have imitated Hilary, *On the Trinity*, Book III, chapter 11: “The sun did not set, but withdrew. What do I mean by saying that it withdrew? It was not received into a cloud, but failed from the course of its work.” Both Prudentius and Hilary seem to allude to the first of these explanations of the miracle.
