81. “Chaos,” “darkness.” *Chaos* and *melos* are neuter in gender and singular in number. Iso.

[Col. 0871B]

81. The Mozarabic Breviary has *horruisse mundum*, “that the world shuddered.”

82. Aldus has *solve lingua*; Alexandrian, Mozarabic, Vatican A and B, I and O, Ratian, and others have *sonora*, which Heinsius also found in the Putean and several others; but in the Oxford manuscript: *Solve mens voce sonora*. From this he conjectures: *Solve voce mens sonora, solve linguam mobilem*. Weitz has *Solve vocem mens sonora, solve linguam mobilem*. We followed Giselinus, the Urbinate, and others; but perhaps the reading more faithful to the manuscripts is: *Solve vocem, mens, sonora; solve lingua, mobilem*, so that *sonora lingua* is ablative and *mobilem* refers to *vocem*. We may also conjecture: *Solve vocem mens sonoram, solve lingua mobili*, or *Solve vocem mens sonoram, solve lingua mobilis*. Vatican Q has *Solve mens voce sonora*, with the same error as the Oxford manuscript.

83. Fortunatus had seen this passage of Prudentius, for he sang: *Pange lingua gloriosi praelium certaminis*, “Sing, tongue, the battle of the glorious conflict,” which we now say as *Pange lingua gloriosi lauream certaminis*, “Sing, tongue, the crown of the glorious conflict.” The word *passio*, “Passion,” was known to few pagan writers but commonly used by ecclesiastical authors; it also occurs in the Theodosian manuscript.

84. The banner of the cross shines upon marked foreheads, because in the sacrament of confirmation the foreheads are marked with a cross. See Hymn 6, verse 128. Gifanius, in his *Annotations on Lucretius*, under the word *PANGO*, says that Prudentius used *pangere* in a novel sense for “to sing,” since *pangere* properly means “to write” or “to fix in wax.” Fortunatus, as we saw in the preceding verse, used *Pange lingua* with the same meaning. For my part, I do not find this meaning in the older writers, nor do the most celebrated lexicographers note anything about it.

85. Aldus, the Urbinate, Vatican A, B, P, and Q, the Putean, Oxford, Nomsian, Rotterdam, Giselinian, and others read this way, and I approve it. The poet calls the soldier’s piercing of both sides a “dreadful slaughter,” as he supposes. The two Torrentian manuscripts and the Alexandrian have *caede in stupenda*, where *in* is superfluous. Indeed, the *e* in *caede* is lengthened by the *st* of the following word. Ratian, Prague, the marginal Giselinian, Sichard, Weitz, and Vatican I have *caedis stupendae*, which Heinsius rejects. The Mozarabic Breviary agrees with us, except that its text incorrectly has *miracula*. In Hailsbrunn there is an erasure indicating that *caede stupenda* once stood there. In the Ambrosian notes: *O novum caedes stupenda vulneris miraculum*, so that by epexegesis “dreadful slaughter” and “miracle of the wound” are said. I do not know why this has pleased the more recent editors so greatly: it is not “a dreadful slaughter” that is a new miracle of the wound; rather, the new miracle of the wound inflicted by dreadful slaughter, or piercing, is that blood and water flowed—blood from one side, water from the other—as the following verse makes clearer. Teolius reproduced Heinsius’s Ambrosian reading and cited the older Vatican manuscripts for the same reading. I wish he had named them more distinctly. The other interpreters did not notice the particular novelty of the miracle. Chamilard was the first to observe that Prudentius clearly intended both sides to have been pierced, differing from the Evangelists, who write that the soldier opened the Lord’s side with only one thrust of the spear. But he did not grasp Prudentius’s meaning: Prudentius does not assert that both sides were opened by two thrusts, and it could have happened that one thrust pierced both, which the Evangelists do not deny; not to mention that the Gospel does not explicitly state that there was only one thrust of the spear. Cornelius a Lapide, more skilled than Chamilard in interpreting Scripture, embraced the opinion of our poet. Prudentius repeats this view a second and third time in Hymn 7 of the *Peristephanon* and in the forty-second tetrastich of the *Dittochaeon*. Raynaud, volume of the *Philological Works*, page 103, says that Prudentius may be understood as referring to the piercing of one side so deeply that it reached the heart and even extended somewhat into the left side, although outwardly only one side had been pierced. Gretzer, Book I *On the Cross*, chapter 35, wonders whether Prudentius held that opinion—that the soldier, driving the spear through, pierced both sides, as is customary among the Japanese. But he more truly thinks that Prudentius indicated the depth of the wound: the spear was driven so deeply into the right side that it reached the left as well, and therefore wounded the heart, which is on the left, so that both sides were wounded in some sense, though the spear did not pass completely through. Yet neither Gretzer nor Raynaud considers the part of Prudentius’s statement that says: “from here blood, from there water flowed.” In the sermon *On the Passion of Christ*, among the works of Saint Cyprian, there is a similar opinion: “From your side a spring goes forth … water and blood flow out along divided channels.” Cornelius a Lapide, in his commentary on John 19, teaches that the spear seems to have been driven through Christ’s right side and to have passed through the heart and pericardium, so that its point came out through the left side near the breast; he confirms this from Prudentius, Cyprian, and Theophylact, who calls this wound *τύπους* (*typous*, “wounds” or “marks”) in the plural, and because the wound in the right side alone was so large that Thomas could insert his hand. He thinks Prudentius implies that blood burst forth through the larger or more powerful wound, and water through the smaller wound, nearer the pericardium. Franciscus Xaverius de Idiaquez—whose name is great threefold in piety, learning, and nobility of birth—collected, with tireless industry and refined scholarship, very much, almost everything, that the holy Fathers and other ecclesiastical writers have committed to writing concerning devotion to the Sacred Heart of Jesus and the wound in his side. Some of his notes have been shared with me, and they could illuminate this subject. Many explicitly state that the side was pierced; the force of that word makes it not unreasonable to argue that the spear passed through the whole body from one side to the other. Omitting these witnesses—for so great a matter should not be settled by a single word—Saint Gregory of Nazianzus says in the tragedy *Christ Suffering*: “See … how a double fountain gushes from his side.” Saint Eustathius, bishop of Antioch, in Theodoret’s *Dialogue 2, The Inconfused*, volume II, page 329 of the Cologne edition, says: “Presenting to their eyes … the pierced sides … he showed them.” I later came upon G. Sagittarius’s dissertation *On the Spear by Which Christ’s Side Was Pierced*, where he cites Saint Leo the Great, Letter 98, chapter 3, who speaks of “the wounds of the side,” and Eustathius in Theodoret’s *Dialogue 1*: *τὰς τετρωμένας πλευρὰς*, “the wounded sides.” He denies, however, that *perforata latera*, “pierced sides,” is read in *Dialogue 2*. I read in *Dialogue 2* *τὰς τετρωμένας πλευρὰς*; but the translator renders it “side” rather than “sides” in the Paris edition of 1642, volume IV, page 90. Nevertheless, I would not deny that the more common and more consonant opinion with the Gospel words is that the Lord’s one side—whether right or left—was opened by a single thrust, from which water and blood flowed together, without understanding that water flowed from one side and blood from the other through separate channels.

[110] You, the crowd of mothers and virgins, and the innocent little girls,

[Col. 0875A]

111. “They resound,” “they ring out.” — “With songs,” “singing together,” I.

1. “Fiery,” which the Greeks call *pyrinoeron*, “the sensual fire,” I.

2. “Joining,” “touching the body and the soul,” Vatican A.

[Col. 0876A] 3. “Living,” etc., “the soul and the body,” I.

4. “You fashioned,” “you formed,” Iso.

6. “To you,” “by you,” Iso.

7. “Given life,” “strengthened,” Iso.

[Col. 0875A]

111. Iso, Ambrosian, Ratian, and Vatican B and I have *perstrepunt*, a reading Weitz found in Goldast, Hailsbrunn, and Widmanstetter above. Aldus has *perstrepent*. Vatican A, O, P, Q, and Egmondanus have *perstrepant*. The Mozarabic Breviary corruptly has *pestrepent*. Giselinus, Weitz, and Heinsius with their manuscripts have *perstrepant*. I approve this, since *concelebrent* follows below. The thought is taken from the Psalms, especially Psalm 148: “Praise the Lord from the heavens,” etc., and from the song of the three children in Daniel 3. Iso turned *concentibus* into a participle, as though it meant “singing together”; incorrectly.

113. Ratian, Prague, and Widmanstetter have *arva*, less well, for *aura*. One must also beware of Giselinus’s *aura, silva*. In the first edition he had printed *silva, et aura*.

114. Saint John of Damascus, Book II, chapter 1 of *The Orthodox Faith*: “The reason why ages of ages are spoken of is that the seven ages of this world comprise many ages, or human lives. And that one age contains all the ages within its embrace; it is therefore called ‘the age of the age,’ meaning the present and the future.” This is according to the edition of John Lequien.

[Col. 0875C] The title of the hymn is given by Vatican A and B, Ratian, Putean, and Thuanean: *In exsequiis defunctorum*, “At the funerals of the dead.” Aldus has *In exsequiis defunctorum*. Fabricius has *Ad defunctorum exsequias*, “For the funeral rites of the dead.” Oxford and Rotterdam have *Circa exsequias defunctorum*, “Concerning the funeral rites of the dead.” Alexandrian has *Circa requies*, “Concerning rest.” Adam Theodorus Siberus illustrated this hymn, along with a few others, with a short commentary, and Barthius explained part of it in Book XXI, chapter 4. He calls this hymn wholly divine; and in Book XLII, chapter 10, praising Prudentius, he says: “Hence Prudentius is far more elegant, whose words—or rather that entire funeral hymn—cannot adequately be described by any abundance of verbal ornament or learning.” Crinitus understood this same hymn when he said that Prudentius’s poems “On the Nativity of the Lord,” “On the Purification of Souls,” and so forth were to be commended. Some stanzas of this hymn are found in the Office of the Dead of the Mozarabic Missal, second edition, page 149: the first four, the twelfth, the fifteenth, and the two following, the fortieth, and the two following. We shall extract the variant readings from there.

1. Prudentius calls God the fiery source of souls, not in the sense in which pagan philosophers asserted that God and souls were fire, but in the proper language of Sacred Scripture, where God is compared with fire and is said to dwell in fire. He says the same in *On Saint Lawrence*, verse 393: “Thus God is eternal fire,” for Christ is the true fire. And in the eighth tetrastich of the *Dittochaeon*: “FIRE IN THE BUSH: The fiery God, flashing with a radiant mouth, flies among the thorns.” Malachi 3:2: “For he is like a refiner’s fire and like fullers’ soap.” Deuteronomy 4:24: “Your God is a consuming fire.” God is called the source of souls because he is the source of life. See Hymn 4, verse 10. Arnobius, Book II *Against the Pagans*: “Because the souls of all of us flow down from one source.” Perhaps Prudentius wished to reject the error of those who invented some source of souls from which God would draw souls, rather than creating them when he infused them into bodies. See Saint Augustine, Book X *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*. Barthius observes that, to understand this hymn, Christian doctrine concerning the soul should be drawn from Gregory Thaumaturgus’s special treatise on the subject, from Nemesius’s commentary *On Man*, and from the works of others.

2. I explained in *Prolegomena*, number 169, in what sense the elements are said of body and soul. Understand “principles.” The Mozarabic Breviary incorrectly has *socias*.

3. Weitz, Goldast, and Widmanstetter in the first hand. Vatican B and I, Prague, and Ratian have *vividum*, which Barthius claims is found in a good part of the manuscripts, but it is coarse and contrary to the law of the poem. See *Prolegomena*, number 230. Ratian incorrectly has *morbidum* for *moribundum*. Here *vivus* means immortal, *moribundus* mortal. Thus God is called “living” in Sacred Scripture, and in nearly the same sense by Virgil, Ovid, and others. Virgil, Book VI, verse 732, uses *moribundum* for perishing or mortal: “And earthly limbs grow dull, and dying members.” Cicero and others use *moribundum* for one near death. The Mozarabic Breviary incorrectly punctuates *moribundum hominem, pater effigiasti*.

4. *Effigiare* means to form in the likeness of something. Apuleius, Sidonius, and our Prudentius often use the word; Barthius says it is elegantly employed, as though the poet had in mind artistic workmanship and care.

5. I gave the reason why the *a* is lengthened in both places in the *Prolegomena*. Giselinus found in some Vulgate manuscripts *Tua sunt, tua recta utraque*, contrary to the testimony of the manuscript codices. God, who is the source, is himself the ruler.

6. Barthius approves Iso’s gloss, and I do not altogether dislike it. But the ending could also be understood in the word *tibi*, so that the meaning is immediately: “for you, while they remain joined in vitality.” Thus in the Office of the Dead: “The King for whom all things live,” etc. Barthius adds that someone might bring Aristotle’s *entelechy* into this passage, as discussed by Nemesius. Someone else will understand the passage more clearly as referring to the union, or that wonderful conjunction and interaction, of body and soul.

8. Following a copy of Manilius, Giselinus corrected the text to *Animus simul, et caro vivit*, “The soul together with the flesh lives.” Barthius agrees and says that others print *spiritus* barbarously. See verse 3. Aldus, Weitz, and others read *spiritus*. Heinsius found in his older manuscripts *Et spiritus, et caro servit*, “Both spirit and flesh serve,” which he approves because it suits the meter and occurs in the Alexandrian and Urbinate manuscripts, although the latter has *vivit* for *servit*. Vatican A, B, I, O, P, and Q have *Spiritus simul, et caro servit*, together with the Mozarabic Breviary. In other passages Prudentius lengthened the first *i* in *spiritus*, and therefore the reading *Spiritus simul, et caro servit*, in which it is shortened, must be rejected. Cauchius conjectured *flatus* for *animus*. In Thomasius’s Hymnary: *Spiritus simul, et caro servit*. Vatican A, Prague, Widmanstetter above, Palatine, Bongarsius, and Sichard have *servit* for *vivit*, as do many others.

9. We print the following verses in the order in which they occur in Vatican A and Q, Aldus, Giselinus, and the Alexandrian. In the margin of Vatican A there is this note: “Other books have:

‘But when these things have been separated,  
They are recalled to their proper origins.  
The fervent breath seeks the air;  
The earth receives the body from the air.  
Because all things,’ etc.”

For *aere* one should read *aera* in the verse *Petit halitus aera fervens*, “The fervent breath seeks the air.” In the following verse the different reading noted there is the true one: *arida* for *aere*. Vatican P has our printed text, but in the margin: “Other books have: ‘But when these things have been separated,’” etc. And in the margin of the stanza beginning *Quia cuncta* it gives, as a variant, *Sic cuncta*, etc.

[Col. 0877A] Vatican O has:

“But when these things have been severed below,  
They are recalled to their proper origins.  
The fervent breath seeks the ether;  
They dissolve the man and destroy him;  
The dry earth receives the body;  
The air snatches away the soul’s liquid.  
All created things must necessarily,  
Once weakened, grow old at last,  
And what has been joined be separated,  
And woven things be woven anew,  
And endure the final death,  
So that, the seeds having been separated,  
Their origin may absorb them again.”

Vatican B reads:

“But when these things have been cut apart,  
They are recalled to their proper origins.  
The fervent breath seeks the ether;  
The dry earth receives the body;  
Thus all created things must necessarily  
Endure the final death,  
So that, the seeds having been separated,  
Their origin may absorb them back into itself.

But when these things have been separated,  
They dissolve the man and destroy him;  
The dry earth receives the body;  
The air snatches away the soul’s liquid.  
Because all things,” etc.

The Ratian manuscript has the same, and, as I think, the Ambrosian. These are better arranged and more correct than Vatican O: in Vatican O *cuncta* is an error for *quia cuncta*, and *texi* for *retexi*. The Putean manuscript has, after the verse *Et spiritus, et caro servit*, immediately:

“But when these things have been separated,  
They are recalled to their proper origins.  
The fervent breath seeks the air;  
The dry earth receives the body.  
Thus all created things must necessarily  
Endure the final death,  
So that, the seeds having been separated,  
Their origin may absorb them again into itself.  
You, best God, this,” etc.

The Urbinate and Vatican I agree with the Putean, but in them *rescissa* appears for *resoluta*, and in Vatican I *sibimet sumat* for *sibi sumat*. The Egmondanus follows our text. But in the margin, as a different reading, it has *Resoluta sed ista seorsum* and the following three verses as in the Putean. Weitz reads as in Vatican B, but for *sibimet sumat origo resorbens* he better has *Sibi sumat origo resorbens*. Weitz has the error *arma* for *aura* in the verse *Animae rapit aura liquorem*. Verses 13 through 21 of Weitz’s edition are absent from Nomsian and Rotterdam; in the Oxford manuscript some are given as in Weitz, others not, as Heinsius attests. Weitz cites Fabricius for his reading, who has *rescissa* for *resoluta*, and Widmanstetter, Bongarsius, and Goldast. From such great disagreement among the manuscripts Heinsius concludes that Prudentius produced two editions of his poems, with some alterations in each. Accordingly, some editors adopted one reading, others another, and some combined both in this hymn. Even among the verses I have retained there is some variation in the readings. In this verse Vatican A has *recisa*, together with Goldast and Widmanstetter; but in Goldast above, *relicta*. *Rescissa*, with Aldus, Bongarsius, and others, is much better.

The falling streams and the shores of the waves,

Rain, heat, snow, frost, forest and breeze, night and day,

Let all things celebrate you together through the ages of ages.

15. “Joined,” “connected,” I.

16. “Woven anew,” “dissolved,” I. Vatican A has “loosed.”

19. “You display,” “you displayed,” I.

11. The reading *excidit* in Vatican A is an error; it should be *excipit*.

12. The Mozarabic Breviary has the faulty *Anima rapit aurae liquorem*.

14. Fabricius reads *tabefacta*, less well, for *labefacta*. In the margin of Vatican A is the note: “Others have: *Obitum tolerare supremum*.” Hericus, imitating Prudentius in his poem, says *labefacta senescere*.

16. Sichard has *ut dissona*. Cicero, *On the Orator*, Book II, page 72, says *detexta retexere*, “to weave again what has been unwoven.” Hericus, *On the Resurrection of the Dead Man*: “By what power can he weave again what has been unwoven?” I shall briefly touch upon what Barthius comments on these verses and on the others omitted. He says that Weitz’s stanza, *Rescissa sed ista seorsum / Proprios revocantur in ortus*, etc., may be retained for the sake of its antiquity, although Fabricius rightly omitted it. He explains the verse *Proprios revocantur in ortus*, “They are recalled to their proper origins,” by other verses of Lucretius, Book II: *Cedit item retro*, etc., which you may read in *Prolegomena*, number 166. He adds that the most recent edition, Weitz’s, inserted an unnecessary stanza with a monastic flavor. Understand this to be the stanza *Sic cuncta creata necesse est / Obitum tolerare supremum*, “Thus all created things must necessarily endure the final death.” In the verse *Petit halitus aethera fervens*, he found in the older books *Petit alter aethera fervens*, “The other fervent ether seeks,” and does not hesitate to say that it should be written *Petit aether aethera fervens*, “Ether seeks the fervent ether”; for Ovid also lengthened the final syllable: *Ipse meas aether accipe summe preces*, “Receive my prayers yourself, highest ether.” The final syllable of *aether* may indeed be lengthened in Ovid and Prudentius, if the verse is read this way, at least by the rule of the caesura. Gallandius, from Tornaesius, transcribes the verse *Petit alter aethera fervens*. *Alter* may be understood of the spirit. Barthius continues by observing that *senescere* indicates the decay of all things; that the body is called *texta*, “woven fabric,” as elsewhere *crates*, “a framework”; and that *compacta* is used by Arnobius at the end of Book II for the bonds by which the skin and limbs are attached to the true human being.

18. To abolish death is proper to God alone; this often occurs in Sacred Scripture and in the prayers of the Church.

[Col. 0878C] 19. Aldus, Egmondanus, Putean, and Oxford have *monstrans*; Rotterdam has *monstra*. All the others, and the sense itself, require *monstras*.

22. That the body can be called the prison of the soul is established partly by what I said on verse 44 of the Preface and on verse 190 of Hymn 7, and partly by what I shall add. Plato discusses this idea at length on the authority of the doctrines of Socrates and the Egyptians, and other philosophers repeat it from him, as may be seen in Barthius’ *Adversaria*, book XLII, chapter 5, and Martinus de Roa’s *On the Birthday*, chapter 3. Christian philosophers and the holy Fathers spoke in nearly the same way: Nemesius in *On the Nature of Man*, Theophridus the abbot in *On the Veneration of the Saints*, Arnobius in book II, and Saint Paulinus frequently. In the common hymn for the office of one martyr we read these verses: “Now the bonds of your consecrated body have been loosed.”

Accordingly, although pagan philosophers called the body a prison, bond, cave, tomb, or vessel of the soul, misusing these expressions so as to deny the soul’s true and intimate union with the body, such expressions, commonly used by the holy Fathers and approved by ecclesiastical usage and indeed by the authority of Holy Scripture, ought by no means to be rejected. Among Christians the true meaning is agreed upon: namely, that while the soul is united to the body, it cannot exercise all its functions fully and freely. Saint Ambrose aptly says in book V, letter 21: “Every soul, seeing itself shut up in this bodily hovel—though it has not become degenerate through sharing this earthly dwelling—groans, weighed down by its union with this body.”

Nevertheless, one must observe the error condemned by canon 6 of the Second Council of Braga: “If anyone says that human souls sinned previously in a heavenly dwelling and, on account of this, were cast down into human bodies on earth, as Priscillian said, let him be anathema.” I shall refute Martin Luther’s quibble on verse 45 of Hymn 11, “He put on a mortal body.”

45. An argument for the resurrection of the dead is drawn from the honor bestowed upon tombs, an argument advanced by Tertullian and others. The *Novella* of Theodosius and Valentinian, title 5, “On Tombs,” says: “We know—and our faith is not vain—that souls released from their limbs retain sensation and that the heavenly spirit returns to its origin . . . . It is excessively barbarous and insane cruelty to begrudge those deprived of light their final gift.” Pignorius, *On Slaves*, page 230, cites these verses to prove that white coverings were customarily spread over the tombs even of Christians, following, as he thinks, the custom of the Hebrews, among whom whitewashed tombs were seen; Paul perhaps alluded to this when in Acts XXIII he called Ananias a “whitewashed wall.” Sedulius, book V of the poems, on Judah: “Like every tomb, bearing on its exterior coverings of white appearance, but within full of filth and a foul corpse.” See below, verse 49.

The poet lists nearly all the rites that were customarily performed so that honor might be shown to the dead. Candles were also used, and, as is clear from this hymn, hymns or psalms. Saint Jerome, in his letter to Eustochium on Paula’s epitaph, says: “While some bishops carried lamps and wax candles before them, others led choirs of singers.” And in the *Life of Paul*, near the end: “Also singing hymns and psalms according to Christian tradition.” Victor of Vita, book I, and others attest the same custom. Canon 22 of the Third Council of Toledo states: “The bodies of all the religious who depart this life by divine calling must be carried to the tombs only with the voices of singers chanting psalms. For we altogether forbid the funeral song which is commonly sung for the dead, or the beating of oneself, one’s relatives, or one’s household upon the breast.” Compare the Council of Valencia, A.D. 524, chapter 4; the First Council of Braga, chapters 16 and 17; and below, verse 113.

47. The funeral together with the tomb constitutes the final honor. In the ancient epitaph of Popilia: “Since I am compelled to render you the final service.” Virgil, book VI, verse 213: “and he bore final gifts to the ungrateful ashes.”

49. We have said more about these matters in the Preface, numbers 156 and following. Repeat what was said at verse 45, and compare Jacob Gretzer, book I of *On Christian Burial*, chapter 3, not to mention many others who wrote generally on funerals and praised these verses of Prudentius.

56. In Holy Scripture, in ecclesiastical prayers, and in the volumes of the holy Fathers, the dead—especially the saints and those who will rise gloriously to eternal life—are called “sleeping.” Hence *coemeterium*, or *cemeterium*, Greek *koimētērion* (κοιμητήριον), from *koimaō* (κοιμάω), “I sleep.” Iso’s gloss must therefore be corrected, since he writes “cymitron” and “cymiterion.” From this expression very learned men believe that the story of the Seven Sleepers arose: they had “slept in Christ,” that is, had truly died, and were found as though sleeping. Compare Baronius under 27 July in the *Roman Martyrology*, Cuperus, *Acta Sanctorum*, page 393, volume VI, and Petrus Lazzeri, *On the Rules of Criticism*, section 7.

The most learned knight Victorius published at Rome in 1741 the history of the Seven Sleepers, reproduced from casts in the Victorii Museum, illustrated with a dissertation and ancient monuments. In chapter 12 he observes that Prudentius disclosed the mystical meaning in these verses and adds the epitaph of Saint Alexander the martyr, which seems doubtful to me: “ALEXANDER IS NOT DEAD, BUT LIVES ABOVE THE STARS.” He adduces much else to prove that those holy Sleepers were called so because they had truly died and had been crowned with martyrdom.

Although Victorius professed that he was presenting the story accurately delineated and engraved from casts in his own museum, the illustrious bishop Stephanus Borgia, an exceptional lover of such antiquities, observed from the original preserved in his richly furnished museum that the letters by which the names of the holy martyrs were inscribed in Victorius’ image were not represented in the same ancient form as they appear on his own glass. Nor did he merely point this out to me with great courtesy: he also arranged for the same story to be carefully drawn from his original, so that it might be faithfully engraved by me and represented here.

I later learned, however, that Victorius’ cast, now preserved in the Vatican Museum, corresponds exactly to the original in the Borgian Museum at Velletri. It should also be noted that the instruments of martyrdom were formed by an ancient artist: knotted clubs, axes, nails, burning torches, and hooks. The names are Constantinus, Maximianus, Martinianus, Joannes, Malchus, Sarapio, and Danesius, who may perhaps be Dionysius.

Victorius says that his cast was made from sulphur poured many years ago, taken from an ancient gem; he assigns the age of the gem—or of the original, which he suspected had perished—to the eighth or ninth century. It is surprising that a man commended for diligence took so little care to make the image engraved on copper correspond to the cast that he himself possessed.

Pignorius, in his commentary on *On Slaves*, page 234, observes that the celebrated memory of the Seven Sleepers derives not only from ecclesiastical speech but also from the fact that Roman pontiffs appointed members of the Roman clergy as guards for the tombs of the apostles; these guards are called *cubicularii*, “chamberlains.”]

Lactantius eloquently develops this whole idea in book VI, chapter 12 of the *Divine Institutes*: “That final and greatest duty of piety is the burial of strangers and the poor . . . . We shall not therefore permit the image and handiwork of God to be cast as prey to wild beasts and birds, but shall return it to the earth from which it arose . . . . For where is the principle of justice more clearly present than in this: that what we provide for our own out of affection, we should provide for strangers out of humanity? This is all the more certain and just when it is no longer offered to a human being, who feels nothing, but is a most acceptable sacrifice to God alone, a just work.”

Nebrissa suspects “schemata” [“forms”], a reading pleasing to Chamillardus, because man is so perfect a figure and image of God that “enigma” could in no way suit him unless everything that represents something else is called an enigma. I, on the contrary, think that man is rightly called God’s enigma. For an enigma is, as Giselinus says, an image of a less-known thing. If you wish an enigma to be an image that is somewhat obscure, as most assert, man will most aptly be called God’s enigma, since he does not represent God clearly and distinctly. See the hymn of Saint Laurence, verse 118: “the enigmas of silver.”

141. “Cariosa senectus” [“worm-eaten old age”] occurs in Ovid, book I of the *Amores*, elegy 12.

142. Christians did not burn the bodies of the dead. Nevertheless, they called the remains kept in tombs “ashes” and “cinders,” as can very often be observed in ecclesiastical writers, including Prudentius and Paulinus. Nor are there lacking older examples in which “cinder” is used of any minute dust into which human beings were reduced after death, whether consumed by fire or in some other way, the word being transferred from the ordinary practice of burning bodies.

143. Nebrissa notes that “dry” is a proper epithet of ash. Thus Virgil said “absorbing ash,” because it is dry.

144. Barthius, book V of the *Adversaria*, chapter 10, defends this passage against G. Agricola, G. Fabricius, and others who attack it because a handful is not a unit of measure. In fact, among physicians a handful really is a measure, as is shown by Pliny, book III, chapter 26, and other writers. Apicius, book III, chapter 10: “To make mature leeks, mix a handful of salt, water, and oil, and cook them in it.” The poet therefore meant that a little ash of a human being could be contained in a fist. Propertius touched on this in a way, and Burmannus compares Propertius with Prudentius and adds others in book IV, elegy 11, verse 14: “Behold, I am a burden lifted by five fingers.” There Cornelia speaks of her ashes, or of the funerary urns, which were generally small vessels. Ecclesiastical writers often used the expression “to enclose” or “contain in a fist,” as in the poem on the resurrection attributed to Lactantius: “whose entirety is enclosed in a fist.” And Venantius Fortunatus: “holding the world in a fist.”

145. Prag.: “inepte” [“foolishly”], and “nec si flamma vaga” [“nor if wandering flame”]. Gis. first edition in the text; Fab. and Bong. have “vaga flumina” [“wandering streams”], less well.

148. Vat. A has “perisse” [“to have perished”], but the meter requires “periisse.”

149. The *Index of Prohibited Books*, which I mentioned in the Preface, number 184, orders the following warning to be placed in the margin of this passage: “Read cautiously, for he seems to teach that the souls of the pious, which bring nothing requiring purification, after leaving the body are detained in that earthly paradise from which Adam was expelled.”

Perhaps by the paradise of delight and the bosom of Abraham Prudentius understands nothing other than the essential glory of the soul before the glorification of the body. This explanation is confirmed by what Prudentius said earlier: “Let the appointed times now come, when God fulfills every hope.” In the *Hamartigenia*, verse 839, he similarly describes paradise and understands it as heaven.

In the prayers by which the soul about to leave this world is commended to God, similar expressions are used to indicate heavenly glory: “May the embrace of blessed rest in the bosom of the patriarchs hold you fast . . . . May Christ, the Son of the living God, place you within the ever-green delights of his paradise. Do not refuse to introduce you into the bosoms of your patriarchs . . . . May angels lead you into the bosom of Abraham.”

It was the opinion of certain ancient writers that after death the souls of the pious are received into the bosom of Abraham, the father of believers. Paulinus, in his poem on the death of Celsus: “And may he set them down rejoicing in the bosoms of the patriarchs, from which hell rages far away with yawning chaos.”

These stanzas of Prudentius are sung in the Mozarabic rite. See Saint Ildefonsus, chapter 90 of *On Knowledge of Baptism*; Rigaltius’ notes on chapter 13 of Tertullian’s *On Idolatry*; Isaeus on Lactantius, book VII, chapter 21; Bellarmine, volume I, controversy 7; and Malvenda, *On the Paradise of Delight*, chapter 90 and following, where he cites the authors who thought that the souls of the pious are detained in the paradise of delight and that this paradise is the bosom of Abraham.

These authors include Tertullian, Origen, Saint Justin in the *Questions to the Orthodox*, our Prudentius, Theophylact, Euthymius, Moses Bar-Cepha, Saint Athanasius, Saint Augustine, Saint John Chrysostom, and Peter Comestor. Malvenda partly rejects their authorities and partly explains them by saying that they spoke allegorically. He refutes John Maldonatus, who understands Christ’s words to the thief in Luke XIII, “Today you will be with me in paradise,” as referring to the bosom of Abraham or the limbo of the Fathers.

Rigaltius, in the passage cited, says more openly that in that age very many people were still greatly uncertain and doubtful about these matters; he also cites Irenaeus’ opinion that the resurrection is awaited in Abraham’s bosom, from the *Questions of Justin* at the end of the book. The error of those who assert that holy souls do not enjoy the vision of God until the day of judgment has now been condemned.]

152. “Requiescere” [“to rest”]: until the resurrection, I.

172. “Odore” [“with fragrance”]: with fragrance, or with *adodore*—read *adore*. *Ador* is a kind of grain placed in sacrifices to the gods; it comes from the verb *adoro*, and therefore its final syllable is long. But another rule conflicts with this, since all neuter nouns ending in *-or* shorten the *o*, such as *marmor, marmoris* and *aequor, aequoris*. Since these rules conflict with one another, *ador* remained indeclinable, Vat. A.

The others, and Gis. first edition itself, have “fronde frequenti.” One might conjecture “recenti” [“fresh”], which also occurred to Burmannus, volume I of the *Anthology*, page 733; but perhaps the poet implies that this honor was frequently and repeatedly bestowed upon tombs. On these funeral rites see the Preface, numbers 157–158; Baronius, volume I of the *Annals*, page 238; Kirchmannus, *On Funerals*, page 581; Carolus Paschalis, *On Crowns*; and countless others.

[Col. 0888B] In the very oldest copies—Put., Ox., Mar., and Vat.—the title of this hymn is “VIII kal. Jan.” [“the eighth day before the Kalends of January”], which Aldus and others reproduced. Vat. A, Eg., and Rott. have “Hymnus natalis Domini” [“Hymn for the Nativity of the Lord”]. Others combine both titles, namely Weitz. and Fabr.

In Vat. B, after the preceding hymn, the text continues as follows: “The first book of the hymns ends. The book of the *Peristephanon* begins. After the hymn of Saint Romanus, of Aurelius Prudentius Clemens. The hymn for the eighth day before the Kalends of January begins.” The same appears in the Marietti codex, in which the other hymns of the *Cathemerinon* are absent except this one and the following, since they were preserved in another place, separate from the *Cathemerinon*. In Vatt. A and Q these two hymns likewise occur after the hymn of Saint Romanus.

In Rot. and Noms. they close the series of the book of the *Peristephanon*, after the passion of Saint Romanus. I think that this was done by copyists who, when dividing the hymns “of the Seasons,” as they called them, from the hymns “of the Saints,” judged that these two hymns, which celebrate the feasts of the Nativity and Epiphany of the Lord, belonged more properly among the hymns of the Saints than among the other seasonal hymns.

Nevertheless, I shall not strongly oppose anyone who argues from the authority of the old copies that these two hymns were separated from the *Cathemerinon* by the author himself. Crinitus commends this hymn only briefly, while Erasmus and Augustus Buchnerus illustrated it with separate commentaries.

Buchnerus gives the following assessment of the poem: “That outstanding and wholly divine poem—one lacking nothing in elegance of diction, harmony of meter, acuity of invention, or genius; and one that, like most of the others, easily asserts for our poet the primacy which the greatest men of the Christian age long ago attributed to him.”

After Buchnerus, Andreas Mollerus Pegavius commented on this hymn. He devotes much attention to explaining the title, “For the eighth day before the Kalends of January,” but he ought rather to have written *a. d.*, that is, *ante diem* [“before the day”], since from these abbreviations some people came to write *ad*. Buchnerus likewise maintains that one should write *calendae*, not *kalendae*; many others discuss this orthographical controversy.

Baronius, in the *Martyrology*, page 2, under 1 January, praises the opening verses, saying that it happened by an entirely divine plan that at nearly the same time each of the two suns shone upon the world with a different light. Scaliger thought that no one older than Ambrose and Prudentius had assigned the Lord’s birthday to the eighth day before the Kalends of January, that is, 25 December.

Yet Victorinus, bishop of Poitiers, who is said to have flourished before Constantine, mentions the same birthday in his poem *On Jesus, God and Man*. Petavius refutes Scaliger, and after Petavius, Antonius Maria Lupius; in Lupius’ dissertation, with the notes of the distinguished Zacharias, several differing opinions on this subject and the arguments advanced on both sides may be found.]

3. Saint Peter Chrysologus, Sermon 159: “The days began to increase because the true Day had dawned.” Saint Augustine and others develop the same idea.

4. Egm. has *augit*, an error.

5. Juvencus, Book IV, *History*, p. 507, Fabricius’s edition: “The moon’s gracious light will lose its course.” Above, in Hymn 7, line 188: “the grace of foods.”

9. Erasmus reads *nitescit* (“grows bright”), not improperly. The others have *nitescat* (“may grow bright”), as though in the prophetic manner.

10. Erasmus has *gratatur*. In the Marietti manuscript, *gratet* seems to have been written first.

13. Fabricius says that the transposition of these lines, which occurred in the manuscripts, caused obscurity. I do not know which manuscripts he means, since the order of the lines is the same in all those I have either seen or read after they were collated by others. The obscurity will be explained in the lines that follow. Arator, Book II, col. 601, Fabricius’s edition: “In whom the Mother, without a husband, is present; and the one born from the Virgin’s womb, God’s Son, flashes forth, and the Mediator completes man in all things.” Thus *emerge* has the same meaning as *emica* (“flash forth”), as above in Hymn IX, line 27: “He flashes forth,” etc.

14. Buchner notes that the construction is not sufficiently well connected and is somewhat confused by obscurity. The construction, he says, ought to be: “sweet little child, whom the chastity of his parent-mother brings forth, and [whom] the mediator, without a husband, [brings forth], and [who is] of twofold nature.” Nebrissa, Erasmus, and Chamillard became entangled in nearly the same difficulty. When Nebrissa found in Aldus, at line 15, *Parens et Christus conjugis* (“Parent and Christ of a husband”), and noticed the metrical error, he corrected it to *Parens et ipse conjugis* (“Parent, and he himself, of a husband”) and explained it as “he who is both son and father of his mother, but *conjugis* meaning ‘eternal with the Father,’ formed from *con-* and *jugis*, ‘everlasting.’” Yet he himself violates the meter no less, for the *u* in *conjugis*, *conjuge*, is long, whereas in the genitive *conjugis* from *conjux* it is short. Once the reading offered by Aldus in line 14 is restored—*Quem mater edit castitas* (“whom mother-chastity brings forth”)—anyone can easily understand that all obscurity disappears. In the Heinsian manuscripts, Vat. A and B, Urb., Alex., and others, the reading is *mater castitas*, not *matris castitas*. In the preface to the *Psychomachia*, line 12, we find *matre virtute* (“with virtue as mother”); so here *mater castitas* means “mother, who is not merely chaste but chastity itself,” much as a vicious or criminal person is called “vice” or “crime.”

[Col. 0890B] 15. Aldus’s error, *parens et Christus*, is not rightly corrected by Nebrissa to *parens et ipse*, as was just noted. In Marietti another error, written by the first hand, is *parcens*.

16. Some say that the Latins did not know the word *mediator*. Yet the earliest Latin Christians knew it, and did not hesitate to call the Lord Jesus Christ “the mediator of God and human beings.” Indeed, it cannot be said better in Latin. Moller observes that in the common edition of Apuleius, Book IX, one reads *mediatorum*, but that the passage is corrupt and was long ago corrected by Wower, who substituted *metatorum*. Petavius, vol. IV, part 2, Book XII, chapter 2, asserts that Christian writers—indeed, elegant and eloquent ones—used this word, including Lactantius, Prudentius, and many others.

17. In later Latin writers, *quamlibet* is more often, or even always, placed after its governing word. Prudentius places it before, as other authors of his period likewise did. I find no example in earlier writers, nor did Erasmus.

18. Prag. has *genitus* (“begotten”) instead of *editus* (“brought forth”), contrary to the meter. How the Word can be said to have been brought forth by the Word I discussed in Hymn 3, line 2, under the word *VERBIGENA*. Buchner in his commentary and Giovanni Lami in *On the Correct Faith of the Nicene Fathers*, chapter 22, offer another interpretation: namely, that Prudentius is speaking of the generation by which the Word became flesh. Moller explains it more fully: Christ was announced by the Father through the prophets in the Old Testament, and afterward by the angel Gabriel, who announced his birth; then, when the appointed time was complete, he was finally brought forth as man. There is no doubt that in both hymns—and especially in the present one—the poet intends to praise the generation of the Son of God in time. Since John’s Gospel makes clear that all things were made through the Word and that nothing was made without him, Prudentius inferred that the Word itself was made flesh through the Word and was brought forth, yet in such a way that it first lived in the Father’s heart, for, as he says, “the Word was God.” Prudentius himself often expresses the same idea, as in the *Apotheosis*, line 524. Ennodius of Ticinum agrees, Book II, Hymn 10: “By hearing she conceived the Son … What the tongue cast forth is seed.” Sedulius, in the alphabetic hymn, has “She conceived the Son through the Word,” which was altered, for metrical correction, to “She received the Son through the Word.” Prudentius seems to have had in mind Ecclesiasticus 24:5: “I came forth from the mouth of the Most High, the firstborn before every creature.” From this and similar passages the eternal generation of the Son must be acknowledged and demonstrated, although some of the holy Fathers occasionally understood them of the generation by which the Word became flesh. Clericus, against whom Lami argues, cavils pointlessly and claims that Prudentius believed the Word to have been produced by generation shortly before the creation of the world, whereas previously its nature, not yet existing, had lain hidden in God in some ineffable manner; he says that other pre-Nicene Fathers likewise taught this. Prudentius’s Catholic doctrine is set out in the *Prolegomena*, no. 126. Clericus’s entire difficulty rests on the single word *prius* (“before”) in line 20: “You had wisdom before.” But that difficulty is wholly dissolved both by the priority of origin, as theologians call and explain it, and by the different ways in which we consider the divine Word—one way as it is in the Father, another as the Word uttered toward created things—and finally by recognizing the temporal generation of the Word by which it became flesh. See Tournely, *On the Trinity*, question 4, article 2, section 2, and the Ballerinis’ dissertation against Petavius in defense of Saint Zeno and the pre-Nicene Fathers.]

20. Vat. B has *pollebas* (“you were powerful”) instead of *callebas*. Weitzius, Widm., Vat. I, Gold., Hails., and Bong. have *calebas*. This does not satisfy the meter. In Weitz’s edition, in the copy belonging to the distinguished bishop Reggio, someone seems to have corrected it to *callebat* from some manuscript. Tertullian, *Against Praxeas*, chapter 6: “This power and this arrangement of the divine meaning is also shown in the Scriptures under the name of Wisdom. For what is wiser than God’s reason, or Word? Therefore listen also to Wisdom, as the second person created.” Saint Zeno, Sermon 5, *On the Eternal Generation of the Son*: “In the depth of the secret place of his holy mind.” The passage may also bear on what theologians discuss concerning the mutual indwelling of the divine Persons in one another, or circumincession, as they call it, from John 14:10: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me.”

21. Wisdom, or *sapientia*, is called *prompta* (“ready”) because it was manifested when it created the world, from *promo* (“bring forth”). Tertullian, in the passage cited, chapter 7: “Then the Word itself also takes on its form and adornment, sound and voice, when God says, ‘Let there be light.’ This is the Word’s perfect birth, when it proceeds from God … It appears that the same power is present now under the name Wisdom and now under the designation Word.”

22. Erasmus and the Daventria edition have *noctem* (“night”) instead of *coelum* (“heaven”). The Alter edition, contrary to the metrical rules, has *coelum, noctemque, et tartara* (“heaven, night, and Tartarus”). Heinsius conjectures *solum diemque, et tartara* (“earth, day, and Tartarus”), as in the Roman hymn, lines 325–326: “One power created heaven and earth.” The reading accepted in all the other manuscripts needs no correction.

[Col. 0892B] 28. John 1:18.

32. The holy Fathers readily use the words *visendi* and *visitandi* (“seeing” and “visiting”) when explaining the mystery of the Incarnation, borrowing them from Holy Scripture, as in Zechariah’s song, chapter 1: “He has visited,” etc.

33. Not only poets but also prose writers use *vis* (“force”) to mean a multitude, as Cicero and others do.

34. He calls idols *naenias* (“dirges”), as in Laurentius, line 496, and Hymn I *Against Symmachus*, line 433, *nugas* (“trifles”); and, according to the probable reading of certain manuscripts, in line 515 of the Hymn to Saint Laurence: “To pray to Numa’s dirges.” Cicero, Book II of *On the Laws*, chapter 24: “Let the praises of distinguished men be commemorated in the assembly, and let them also be accompanied by singing and by the flute-player, a practice called *naenia*, a word by which the Greeks likewise designate mournful songs.” Properly, too, *nugae* were songs sung in praise of the dead. The poet therefore rightly calls the worship of people whom others, after their death, had enrolled among the gods both *naenias* and *nugas*. *Nugae* and *naeniae* can also mean the fables and superstitious inventions to which idolaters gave credence. Numa’s ideas about the worship of the gods are well known.

35. Egm. and Palat. wrongly have *vel aere, vel fixa* (“whether bronze or fixed”). Some heretics and semi-Catholics deny that pagans descended into such madness as to believe that wood or bronze were gods. They would abolish the honor and worship offered to statues of God and the saints, as though the true idolatry charged against pagans consisted in this, rather than in attributing divinity to inanimate objects. Yet they are refuted by the clearest testimonies of Holy Scripture. Isaiah, chapter 44, offers many arguments to prove that God is not an idol fashioned by human hands and openly exposes the vanity, indeed the stupidity, of the craftsmen who make idols. There are hundreds of other passages of this kind. Prudentius, not only here but in many other places, condemns the same madness of the pagans. Among the Gentiles there were certainly some who recognized that images received worship insofar as they represented the divinity and power of the gods. The defenders of our religion attacked these people with other arguments. The whole matter is made clear in the words of Athenagoras, *Apology for the Christians*, p. 17: “To put the matter briefly, all images everywhere have been made by human beings. If these gods did not exist at the beginning, will they be later than those by whom they were made? Or why, in order to exist, did they need human beings and human skill? These are earth, stones, material, and elaborate workmanship. But since there are some who say that these are nothing more than images, while the gods in whose honor they were dedicated, and to whom all the revenues and sacrifices offered to them belong, are real gods; and that human beings cannot meet the gods in any other way (and the sight of a god is formidable, as the poet says); and to prove this they recount certain stories about the works of some idols—come, then, let us inquire what power and efficacy those who are called gods possess.”]

45. Sedulius imitated this in his alphabetic hymn: “He put on a servile body,” etc. Luther, vol. I, fol. 415, says that there were no Fathers or teachers who did not occasionally speak improperly, if one wishes to quibble over their statements; and he asserts that nothing more heretical can be said than that Christ put on a body, for a garment and a body do not constitute one person. But since the Apostle and most of the holy Fathers used a similar manner of speaking, that expression has now been consecrated by ecclesiastical usage itself and conveys a correct meaning. Thus the body is called a prison, the vessel of the soul, and the like. See Hymn 7, line 190, and Hymn 10, line 22.

51. Erasmus, against the testimony of all manuscripts and editions, substituted: “He gave life and clothed [him] in clay.” The critic thought that one could not say “the Father breathes forth the Son,” and had made it his fixed practice to change and correct at his own discretion whatever he did not understand. This is the true cause of his innumerable emendations in sacred and theological matters—emendations that might perhaps be tolerated in other authors, but are in no way to be endured in Holy Scripture. No one will deny that God may be called spirit. Our poet himself, in the *Apotheosis*, line 666, says: “The spirit that once, breathed forth from the Father’s mouth, was flying over the waters not yet divided,” where he understands the Son. Paulinus, in his final poem: “This is God from the heart of God, this the spirit of his mouth, the holy Father’s Word.” Muratorius thought that the first line was metrically defective and failed to notice a hiatus like Virgil’s: “Having preferred to cultivate Samos, this man’s weapons.” Hugo Grotius, commenting on Mark 2:8, “Jesus, in his spirit,” etc., proves from the words of Prudentius and other holy Fathers that the Word is called spirit not only *διὰ τὸ ἀσώματον* (“because of its incorporeality”), in which sense the name applies to the Father, but also because they used the word spirit in a broader sense for any kind of emanation. This manner of speaking continued not only after the controversy with the Arians but also after the conflict that arose with Macedonius.

[Col. 0894B] 52. Chamillard interprets it as “joining the body together by the efficacy of his Word.” Others, as I think more correctly, understand it of the hypostatic union. Buchner considers *glutinans* (“gluing”) a coarse word for *copulans* (“joining”), although it is more effective than the verb *miscere* (“to mix”), which most of the holy Fathers use. Phoebadius observed that some people had craftily used the word *coagulare* (“coagulate”) to imply a confusion of the natures in Christ. It often happens that we regard certain words of the ancients as low and coarse because the corresponding words in our own vernacular have become low and coarse through usage and custom. In Holy Scripture, the word *conglutinare* (“to glue together”) is used more than once to signify serious and weighty matters, as in 1 Samuel 18:1: “Jonathan’s soul was joined to David’s soul.” In the Theodosian Code, arguments are said to be “glued together” when many conjectures are heaped up.

53. I do not agree with Fabricius, who asserts that this question has a negative force, for then it would deny that the honor of modesty increases. Teolius approved Fabricius. His words are: “This question has a negative force, as though he were saying: ‘You do not feel that loathing which other mothers feel.’” I therefore maintain that if the question had a negative force, it would have this meaning: “You do not feel the untouched honor of modesty growing through mature loathings”—which is contrary to the poet’s thought, as can be gathered from the context and the following stanza. Prudentius’s meaning is that the honor of modesty grows as childbirth draws nearer. Someone interprets it as meaning that the honor remained untouched through loathings, that is, that there were no loathings by which the honor of modesty was affected. Horace uses the verb “touch” with a similar meaning, Book III, Ode 13, on the spring of Bandusia: “You the fierce hour of the blazing Dog-star does not know how to touch”; and Ovid, Book III of the *Metamorphoses*, of a spring: “Which neither shepherds nor the goats grazed upon the mountain had touched, nor any other flock.”

54. Prag. has *fastigia* (“summits”), less suitably. Perhaps Iso also read *fastigia*, with the gloss *dignitates* (“dignities”). Buchner thinks that Iso’s gloss was transferred from line 56, where *HONORE* (“with honor,” “with dignity”) occurs; transferred to this line, it became *dignitates*. This is sufficiently plausible. No one explained these *fastidia* (“loathings”) better than Nebrissa: “Not,” he says, “that they happened to the Virgin, as they usually happen to pregnant women … Rather, he speaks according to the custom concerning other women, just as one says, ‘the woman in labor gave birth,’ and elsewhere, ‘the woman in labor gave birth to a king’—not because that person experienced the labor and pains that occur in other women, but because she gave birth while preserving her integrity.” See Francis Suárez, who in volume II on the third part of Thomas Aquinas, question 28, disputation 5, section 1, remarkably elucidates this matter from Saint Augustine, Fulgentius, and Bernard. Petavius adds others in Book XIV, chapter 6, calling this the common opinion of the ancients.]

77. Gis., first edition, and Weitz. have *tua* instead of *tui*. Aldus, the Heinsian manuscripts, and all ours have *tua*. Buchner observes that the poet, in accordance with the expectation of his own age, foretells the reverence that future ages would show to the Lord’s manger. Perhaps Prudentius merely indicates the veneration then shown to the Lord’s manger; nevertheless, his words can be applied to our own times. At Rome a wooden manger is now displayed and is held in great honor, in accordance with ancient tradition. Samuel Basnage foolishly attempts to undermine this in *Political-Ecclesiastical Annals*, five years before the birth of the Lord, no. 20, because Tertullian calls that manger “hard” and therefore concludes cleverly that it was not wooden (as though wood were soft), but stone; and because an anonymous writer quoted by Chrysostom on Luke 2 says: “For honor we took the manger, which was of brick, and made it silver”; and Brocardus, or Burchardus, says that it was cut out of a rock. These two testimonies contradict one another. Serry, in Exercise 30, rightly teaches that the structure containing the wooden manger was either stone or brick. An ancient monument in the Borgia Museum displays the wooden manger to us. Around the year 642, a cradle and manger were brought to Rome from the Bethlehem cave. See Bianchini, *Dissertation on the Manger and Cradle of Our Lord Jesus Christ*, and Gori’s preface to the Italian translation of Sannazaro’s poem *On the Virgin’s Birth*, where he discusses four ancient representations of the manger.

79. In Aldus, *saeculum* (“age”) is a metrical error.

80. Understand the ox and donkey as being at the Lord’s manger, as pious antiquity believed. In the poem *On the Passion* among the works of Lactantius: “Here, among senseless brutes, it gave me, first, a bed of dry grass in the narrow manger.” After the works of Claudian there are some Christian poems, which many attribute to Claudian, whether to that flatterer of Christian emperors or, finally, to someone who professed the Christian faith. Among them is a poem *On the Praise of Christ*, which certainly was not written by Claudian but by Merobaudes, a Spanish schoolmaster, under whose name it was published in the collection of Christian poets and in the *Library of the Holy Fathers*. Merobaudes therefore says in that poem: “The mother, conscious of the birth, knew you to be God your creator, and the frightened cattle perceived it.” Sedulius, Book III, on the ass on which the Lord sat: “Not unlike that creature, which, although Christ lay in an open manger, nevertheless recognized him to be God.” The passage is Isaiah 1:3: “The ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master’s manger; but Israel does not know me,” etc., to which Prudentius alludes. Hence this story has been doubted by those who thought the account was invented because of Isaiah’s words; conversely, if it is false, some have thought it was derived from the same words, believing that Isaiah spoke not allegorically but foretold a future event—which otherwise appears all the more credible because the Savior’s birth occurred in a stable and manger. But when Serry says in his *Exercises* that the Fathers who mention the ox and donkey spoke allegorically, he plainly contradicts their words and intention. Many holy Fathers also cite Habakkuk 3 in the Septuagint version for the same purpose: “You will be known between the two animals,” but Saint Jerome teaches that this version is not reliable. Very ancient images still exist in which the manger is shown with an ox and donkey. Erasmus reports that such a representation has come down to us from the earliest centuries. [Col. 0897B] We present an ancient monument from the Borgia Museum at Velletri, communicated through the generosity of the most learned bishop Stefano Borgia. An image not unlike it had previously been published from the reliefs of ancient glass in the Victorine Museum; Victorius illustrated it in his dissertation on a bronze coin, where he says that a similar monument exists among the lords of Trautson and another with Paolo Sabbatini. The monument in the Borgia Museum is either different, or at least is now displayed more accurately through the diligence of the distinguished bishop, from the original itself, which I compared.]

85. Fabricius, driven by zeal for the reform which they themselves call it, labors in vain to twist the pilgrimages praised here into a different meaning. He explains *fideli spiritu* (“with faithful spirit”) as “with faith kindled through the Holy Spirit.” He says that to hurry to Christ’s manger does not mean going to Jerusalem and treading those mute places, but grasping Christ by faith and hoping through him alone for the remission of sins and eternal life. Cleverly argued. [Col. 0898C] But who could persuade himself that Prudentius does not commend a pilgrimage to the Lord’s manger, undertaken in a faithful spirit—in precisely that piety in which it was practiced especially in his own time, under the encouragement, prompting, and example of Jerome, the greatest teacher of the Church? Is it not certain that the poet often recalls with praise such gatherings of people as were held at the tombs of the martyrs? Since Fabricius frequently dares to accuse Prudentius of impiety because, concerning the invocation and worship of the saints, he said and did what the other Fathers of the fourth century said and did, he should not have been deterred by any difficulty from granting us Prudentius also on this point. Among others who should be consulted on this subject is Gretzer, who also fights with the weapons of our poet.

112. “*Illis*”: the wicked. “*Gehenna*”: the name *gehenna* is found written in the Gospel. It is interpreted as “the valley of gratuity.” It was a most pleasant place near Jerusalem, watered by the spring of Siloam descending from Mount Moriah, where the Temple of the Lord stood. Because of that place’s pleasantness, the Jews abandoned the Temple and sacrificed there to idols. In that same place, by a double punishment [lacuna] at the hands of enemies, they were killed in body and punished also in soul. Hence *gehenna* is used for hell, in which sinners are punished in body and soul, namely by heat and cold, Vat. A.

113. “*Fulmen*”: power, Vat. A. “*Epiphania*”: *EPIPHANON*, “to appear.” Hence *EPIPHANIA*, an appearance or manifestation; *THEOPHANIA*, the appearance of God, Vat. A.]

97. Vat. B has *hunc, quem latebra obstetrix*, which may also be retained: the final syllable of *latebra* need not be elided, and it yields the plausible sense that no midwife other than concealment attended the Virgin’s childbirth. Egm. and Palat. likewise have this reading; Vat. Q points in the same direction with *latebrae obstetris*. The others have *et*. Rat. writes *obstitrix*. Heinsius, with Oxon., Rot., Alt., and two Torrentian manuscripts, has *latebra et obstetrix*. Chamillard, Teolius, and Cellarius, as is their custom, follow Heinsius. Urb. and Alex. have *latebrae et obstetrix*. The explanation of almost all interpreters is that the Virgin herself was the midwife. Saint Jerome, against Helvidius: “No midwife was there; no officious attendance of women intervened. Mary herself wrapped the infant; she herself was both mother and midwife: for she herself placed him in the manger; she herself wrapped him in swaddling-clothes.” Thus the inventions of the apocrypha are refuted. Teolius attributes the mention of discomforts and of a midwife to poetic fiction. Yet it cannot be denied that some ancients held the opinion that a midwife was present. For this was read in apocryphal books, namely in the Protoevangelium of Saint James, the Gospel of the Infancy, and the book *On Saint Mary and the Midwife*. See the gloss on Sephora at line 92. Clement of Alexandria mentions the same account in *Stromata* VII, p. 543, and Saint Zeno adopted it, Book II, tract 8. See the remarks on this passage by the most learned Ballerini. It will be no disgrace if we judge that Prudentius believed what other learned men believed.

98. Bartholomew, Book VIII of the *Adversaria*, chapter 12, says that Prudentius clings so closely to his own phraseology that in the *Dittochaeon*, tetrastich 28, he repeated *cuna* in the singular from this hymn. But I do not find anyone who uses *cunula* in the singular, except Giselinus in the first edition. In the margin of the second edition, the same Giselinus has *Virgoque*.

100. There is a lacuna at this point in the Bongarsius manuscript; consequently Iso’s glosses from that manuscript are lacking for the following lines of this hymn and for the next hymn. Weitzius produced a few glosses by the same Iso from Widman’s manuscript for the following hymn.

From the first advent, in which Jesus Christ deigned to appear in humility, the poet proceeds to recount the second advent, in which he will judge the living and the dead.]

[The supplied source ends here, incomplete.]

[Col. 0900C] **106.** That the world is to be consumed by flames at the judgment of the last day is known from both the Old and New Testaments, Daniel 7:9; 2 Peter 3:10. Lactantius, *On the Anger of God*, chapter 23, cites verses of the Sibyl, who said that, through God’s indignation against the unjust, the cataclysm had occurred in the former age so that the wickedness of the human race might be extinguished, and prophesied that a conflagration would later occur in a similar manner, by which human impiety would again be destroyed. This opinion therefore passed into pagan writers. In the gloss, read *celerēs occurrite vestrō*, so that there are two hexameters.

**109.** Some copies of the Vulgate have *praeeminens*. Better is *praeminens*, formed by contraction, as in Seneca and Avienus.

**110.** An evangelical sentence from John 5:28–29, with which the Apostle agrees in Romans 2:6. *Congruus* is the word used by Apuleius and Palladius; Solinus, as most read him, has *congrue*. Earlier writers said *congruens* and *congruenter*.

**111.** Rat. and Mar. have *perpetem*, not wrongly; but others more suitably have *perpetis*.

**113.** Matthew 8:30: “And then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven.” Saint Jerome, Chrysostom, Augustine, and others teach that this sign will be the cross; Prudentius follows them. Mollerus and others wrongly explain it as referring only to the power and majesty of Jesus Christ crucified, thereby excluding the sign of the cross.

**114.** Erasmus boasts that he restored this verse, corrupted by an ignoramus, since it had previously been read *Experta quae sit, senties*; perhaps it was so read in the Daventer edition. Aldus had already printed *Experta, qui sit, senties*, which Mar. retains. Heinsius followed him, along with Giselinus and, as I think, his best manuscripts, as well as Weitzius, who records no manuscript variation. Vat. B has, not incorrectly, *quis sit*. Vat. A and Erasmus have, less well, *quid sit*. In the Weitzian edition, which I use, *expertae* is noted in the margin from some manuscript, but that reading is rejected by the poem.

**115.** Gis. 1st edition, in the margin, has *praesidi*; Fabr. has *praeside*. Sichardus appended this note: “An old exemplar had not *praesule* but *praeside*, which suits Prudentius better.” Yet Prudentius used a similar phrase above, in hymn 5, verse 83: *praesuli justitiae* (“to the leader of justice”).

**116.** The best editions have *mox reddidit* (“immediately restored”), and Weitzius, Marietti, and Heinsius do not record variant readings. Nevertheless, Erasmus and Fabricius expressly read *Mors hausit et mors reddidit* (“Death swallowed, and death restored”), which is both harmonious and not without suitable meaning. In Alex., Urb., Vat. I, and others: *mox reddidit*; in Vat. Q: *Mors hausit et mox reddidit*. We should read *hausit*.

Heinsius titles it, from his old manuscripts, “Hymn of the Epiphany,” as do Aldus and other printed editions. Weitzius has “On the Epiphany.” So also Vat. A and B. Rat. has “Hymn on the Epiphany of the Lord”; Mar. has “Here begins the hymn on the Epiphany.” Part of this hymn is read at the Transfiguration of the Lord: *Quicunque*, etc. Another part is read on the feast of the Holy Innocent Martyrs: *Audit tyrannus anxius* and *Salvete, flores martyrum*, at Matins and Lauds. Another part is used at the Epiphany: *O sola magnarum urbium*. In the Veliternus manuscript, concerning which see prolegomena no. 212, there is a hymn which, I think, has not yet been published, containing certain passages taken from Prudentius:

“Pouring forth milk together with blood …  
How great ... wailing ... among your contemporaries ... [fragment]  
And the shining flowers of the martyrs.”

Clearly, this belongs to the feast of the Holy Innocents.

**5.** Baronius, volume 1 of the *Annals*, page 68, discusses this star carefully. It is said to surpass the sun’s wheel, not because it was larger than the sun, but because it shone with a purer light and indicated both the true God and the sun. For many things that the poet says about the star must be referred to Jesus. Baronius, on the authority of the letter of Saint Ignatius to the Ephesians—which is regarded as interpolated—proves that Prudentius was speaking not poetically but historically. Others have praised this star in a similar manner. See what Fabricius notes in *Apocryphal Codex of the New Testament*, volume 1, pages 115 of editions 1 and 2, and in the *Paralipomena*, volume 2, page 407, where he illustrates these verses with words from Glycas. Moreover, Trombellius discusses many questions about the star with learned care in his *Life of the Mother of God*.

**6.** Gold., Vat. I, Mar. have *aut* for *ac*.

**12.** The star guided the Magi, even when they were traveling by day.

[Col. 0902C]

**15.** The setting of the stars is their going down. The two Bears, or Ursae—the Greater and the Lesser—revolve around the pole and never set for us. Prag. has *abire*, incorrectly.

**17.** These things are partly understood of Christ and partly explained appropriately by saying that the star never set for as long as it was needed, or was covered by clouds.

**21.** This follows especially the common opinion of the ancients, who thought that comets always or usually foretold something gloomy. The edition of Saint Isidore’s *On the Nature of Things*, chapter 26, should be corrected: “A comet is a star that pours forth from itself something like a mane of light. When it appears, it is said to indicate either a change of kingdom, or wars, or the outbreak of pestilences.” Concerning it Prudentius says: “A gloomy comet intervenes.” Read *intercidat*.

**25.** Gold. and Mar., in the first hand, have *Persae*, incorrectly. That the Magi who worshiped the newborn God were Persians is taught, apart from Prudentius, by Juvencus and other ancient writers, as well as by not a few recent interpreters. Others more probably think that they came from the Desert of Arabia, Chaldaea, or Mesopotamia. The evangelist Matthew says that they came to Jerusalem from the East. Jeremias Felbingerus argues—or dreams—that they were Chinese.

**28.** In Egm. *vix illum* is an error for *vexillum*. On this history, Chalcidius should be heard, chapter 75 of his commentary on Plato’s *Timaeus*: “There is also another, holier and more venerable history, which relates that, at the rising of a certain star, not sicknesses and deaths were announced, but the descent of the venerable God for the sake of human fellowship and mortal affairs. When wise men of the Chaldaeans, thoroughly trained in the contemplation of heavenly things, had observed this star during a nighttime journey, they are said to have sought the newly appeared God; and, having found him in the majesty of a child, to have worshiped him and offered vows befitting so great a God—matters which are much better known to you”—he addresses Bishop Hosius—“than to others.”

Prudentius rightly called them “faithful interpreters,” wise men trained in the contemplation of heavenly things. Barthius, book 58, chapter 2, suspects that Chalcidius should read *nocturno icti sidere* (“struck by the star at night”) instead of *nocturno itinere* (“on a nighttime journey”), that is, as though they were stunned. But what Barthius adds—that the Magi thought God had descended through the star itself, and believed the star itself to be a divine power—has not persuaded me. He cites their words, “We have seen his star,” which, he says, Prudentius interprets in the *Apotheosis*, verse 218: “We have seen this child, they say, borne through the stars.” Nor does he omit verses from this same hymn: “We behold something glorious.” None of this is compelling. For “the star of the king of the Jews” and “the child borne through the stars” merely show that the star indicated the Savior’s birth. The Magi’s words in Prudentius, “We behold something glorious,” refer not to the star but to what the star signifies, as is clear from the sequence of the speech.]

[Col. 0901A]

“Death swallowed, and immediately restored.”

## XII. Hymn on the Epiphany

Whoever seek Christ,

Lift your eyes on high:

There you will be permitted to behold

The sign of everlasting glory.

[5] This star, which surpasses

379 The sun’s wheel in beauty and light,

Announces that God has come to earth

With earthly flesh.

It does not serve the nights,

[10] Following the monthly moon;

But, possessing heaven alone,

It regulates the course of the days.

Although the stars of the Bear

[Col. 0902A] Refuse to set

In their revolving movements,

They nevertheless usually lie hidden beneath clouds.

This star remains eternal:

This star never sinks;

Nor, hidden by the encounter with a cloud,

[20] Does it overshadow its covered light.

Let the gloomy comet perish,

380 And if any star burns

With the heat of Sirius,

Let it now fall, destroyed beneath God’s light.

Behold: from the bosom of the Persian world,

[25] Whence the sun takes its entrance,

The Magi, skilled interpreters,

See the royal standard.
