**68.** The theologians point out that the verb *praedestinare* means the same as *destinare*, though it implies antecedence. Many have taught that the word is scarcely Latin; but Cellarius, in his later *Cures concerning Barbarisms*, acknowledged that Livy used it, having been alerted by Olaus Borrichius.

**69.** That the Magi recognized and worshiped the divinity is an established fact. Sedulius, book 2:

“They poured forth golden gifts for the newborn king;  
They gave frankincense to God, and myrrh to the tomb.”

Helpidius, in his poem on the benefits of Jesus Christ:

“The Chaldaean race … gives gifts:  
Riches to the king, frankincense to God, and myrrh to the tomb.”

Juvencus, book 1:

“And immediately, having bowed down, they bring forth mystical gifts:  
They bring gold, frankincense, and myrrh  
For king, God, and man.”

These verses of Juvencus are praised by Saint Jerome, Alcuin, and other ancient writers. Barthius, book 58, chapter 2, found in a certain manuscript of Juvencus: “Gold, frankincense, and myrrh, for king, man, and God.” But then another order would have to be established: “Gold, myrrh, and frankincense, for king, man, and God.” In Saint Jerome, book 1 of his commentary on Matthew, chapter 2: “They bring frankincense, gold, and myrrh for king, man, and God.” Even in this form the order of the gifts is not preserved. Barthius says that Prudentius, in the learned and splendid poem *Apotheosis*, magnificently and with Roman grandeur called these gifts “dishes.” See *Apotheosis*, verses 609 and following. In the Church Office for the Epiphany it is sung: “In gold, recognize the king’s power; in frankincense, consider the great priest; and in myrrh, the Lord’s burial.” The great priesthood is signified by frankincense in such a way that divinity is understood to reside in that great priest himself.

**70.** In Put., *flagrans odos*. Others also have *flagrans* here and elsewhere for *fragrans*, as I said above. Isidore prefers *fragrans odor*.

**71.** Vat. B, Alex., and Rat. have *at myrrheus*, which is much more elegant than *ac myrrheus*. Heinsius too found *at* in Oxon. and approved it, although he printed *ac*; Put. has *ad*, which amounts to the same thing. In the others, including Vat. I and Q, *ac*. In the same place, correct the gloss to: “from *sèbein*,” that is, **ἀπὸ τοῦ σέβειν** (“from worshiping”).

**73.** Alex. has *hocem*, perhaps an error for *hocce*. Put. has *hoc, hoc est sepulcrum* (“this, that is, a tomb”). Heinsius corrects it to *hoc, hoc sepulcrum* (“this, this tomb”). But if the Putean manuscript is to be emended, it should be brought into agreement with the other manuscripts rather than with conjecture; for the others correctly have *hoc est sepulcrum* (“this is a tomb”). Chamillardus, Cellarius, and Teolius, with Heinsius, read *hoc, hoc sepulcrum*. In Mar., *quod* for *quo*, as corrected above. Erasmus and Gis. also read *quod* in the margin. Vat. B has, incorrectly, *hoc sepulcrum, quo Deus* (“this tomb in which God …”).

**77.** He uses the comparative for the superlative, *major* for *maxima*: nevertheless, *O sola magnis urbibus major* (“O you alone greater than great cities”) could easily be understood. He used this phrase elsewhere as well. See hymn of Saint Vincent, verse 294, *Fortissimorum fortior* (“stronger than the strongest”); *Psychomachia*, verse 530, *magnus discipulorum* (“great among the disciples”); hymn 14 of the *Peristephanon*, verse 110, *Et quod malorum tetrius omnium est* (“and what is more loathsome than all evils”). This is a Hellenism and a phrase from the Vulgate edition, Matthew 23:2: “Whoever among you is greater.” Compare Drusius, *Observations*, book 5, chapter 23. Curtius has: “Two ships greater than all.” The ancients sometimes also joined a genitive to the positive degree. Ennius, book 1, in Festus: *Constitit inde loci propter sos dia dearum* (“Then he stood there in the place beside the divine goddesses”). Virgil, *Aeneid* 4.576: *sequimur te, sancte deorum* (“we follow you, holy one among the gods”), rather than “whoever you are among the gods”; for he seems to have taken it from Ennius: *Respondit Juno Saturnia, sancta dearum* (“Saturnian Juno replied, holy one among the goddesses”). The Greeks say **δῖα θεάων** (“divine among the goddesses”) in the same construction. Ludovicus Cavallus criticized the correctors of the hymns of the Roman Breviary because, in the hymn of the Little Office of the Blessed Mary at Lauds, they printed *O gloriosa virginum* (“O glorious one among virgins”), which, he says, should be *O gloriosissima virginum* (“O most glorious among virgins”). Yet the examples I have cited can vindicate the correctors. Fortunatus had said *O gloriosa Domina* (“O glorious Lady”), despite the meter.

**78.** Mar. and Rat. have *Bethleem*; Wid., Gold., and Hailsb. likewise have *Bethleem*, which may be retained. Egm. has *Major Bethlem* (“greater Bethlehem”), and *cui contigit* (“to which it was granted”), not incorrectly. Drusius, in the place cited, prefers *Bethlem* according to the ancient usage of the Hebrews, as in hymn 5 of the *Peristephanon*, *Belzebulis*, not *Beelzebulis*. See his book 7, chapters 18 and 19. Here and elsewhere Prudentius shortens the first syllable of *Bethlem*, although in Greek it is written with eta. This is not surprising, for Saint Jerome, highly skilled in the Hebrew language, also shortened it in the epitaph of Saint Paula. Ricciolius says that he was momentarily inattentive, and that those who shorten it were misled by a mute and liquid consonant. But we should not prescribe rules to the ancients; rather, we should receive them from them. This verse and the following confirm that in verse 1 of hymn 7 we should read *dux Bethlem* (“leader, Bethlehem”), which has always pleased me, although, with most editors, I printed *lux* (“light”).

**79.** Prag. has *lucem* (“light”) for *ducem* (“leader”), and this is correct. The poet refers to Matthew 2:6: “And you, Bethlehem, land of Judah, are by no means least among the rulers of Judah; for from you shall go forth a leader who will rule my people Israel.” For the adverb *coelitus* (“from heaven”), Lactantius, Cyprian, Marcellinus, Orosius, Jerome, and Marius Victor are cited in its support.

**80.** Prag. has *incorporatam* (“incorporated”), so that it agrees with *lucem* (“light”), about which see the following verse.

**82.** Psalm 2:8: “I will give you the nations as an inheritance.” In Eg. there is the error *creator* (“creator”).

**83.** In Mar. there was *Tonanti* (“to the Thunderer”), but it was correctly changed by another hand to *Tonantis* (“of the Thunderer”). Gold. and Wid. also have *Tonanti* in the margin. Vat. I has *Tonanti*, but it seems to have been *Tonantis*.

**85.** He continues the same thought. Having called the Son, as man and God, the only heir of the supreme Father, he now calls the prophets witnesses, sealers, and the testator. The Father is the testator; the new and everlasting testament is the Gospel. The prophets are witnesses and sealers, or notaries of the divine promises.]

[Note: [Col. 0909B]

**126.** In the *Hours for the Use of the Diocese of Lyons*, published in 1778, this stanza was altered to avoid the meeting of vowels:

“Hail, flowers of the martyrs,  
At the very threshold of the light,  
Whom the savage sword reaped,  
Like a whirlwind [reaping] roses as they sprouted.”

Why were the verses not simply transposed?

“Hail, flowers of the martyrs,  
Whom the savage sword reaped,  
At the very threshold of the light,  
Like a whirlwind [reaping] roses as they sprouted.”

Other inept transpositions of verses pleased the reformer of that Breviary, as in the familiar closing:

“Jesus, to you be glory,  
Who were born of the Virgin.”

He transposed it to:

“Who were born of the Virgin,  
Jesus, to you be glory.”

Augustine seems to have read Prudentius in this way. In sermon 220, appendix, he has: “Whom the impiety of Herod snatched, infants, from their mothers’ breasts; they are rightly called flowers of the martyrs, whom, springing forth in the midst of the cold of unbelief like the first budding gems of the Church, a certain frost of persecution withered.”]

[Note: [Col. 0909B]

**128.** Statius, *Silvae* 3.3:

“Such as pale lilies bend their stems,  
And budding roses die at the first south winds.”

**131.** Ald., Sich., Weitz., Heins. with their copies, our manuscripts, and also Alex., Vatt. I and Q, the hymn of Thomas, Widm., Hailsbr., and Gold. have this reading. Erasmus, with Giselinus, has *aram ante cujus* (“the altar before which”); Fabricius reads *aram ante et ipsam* (“the altar before it also”); Egm. has *aram ante ipsam et*. Torrentius and Cauchius have *aram sub ipsam* (“beneath the altar itself”), from a similar phrase in Revelation 6:9; I would prefer that reading if the manuscript copies supported it. I read *aram sub ipsam* only in the recent Urb. manuscript. There is no doubt that the first reading is sound, with the *e* in *ante* not elided, as Prudentius sometimes did. Heinsius, Cellarius, and Teolius call this *synaloepha*; I call it *dialoepha* or hiatus, since the vowel is not absorbed, reserving *synaloepha* for cases in which it is absorbed.

**132.** Alex. has, not incorrectly, *corona* (“crown”).

**133.** Ald., Gis., and our copies have *quid*; Egm. has *qui*; Heinsius, with Pat., Amb., Thuan., Rott., the first Boh. manuscript, and Cauchii’s books, has *quo*. Teolius found *quid* in two Vat. manuscripts, but with two others and Heinsius read *quo*. He cites Erasmus and Weitzius for *qui*; perhaps he meant to name others, for I find *quid* in Weitzius and Erasmus cited by Weitzius. Rat., Prag., and Gis. in the margin have *profuit* for *proficit*. The meaning is the same: human beings accomplish nothing against God’s purposes; Jesus alone, amid so many funerals, is snatched from the hands of those seeking him.

[Col. 0910B]

**136.** Nothing else of this hymn survives in Marietti’s manuscript after this stanza. Immediately afterward comes *On the Little Works of Prudentius*, as in Vat. B. In Vat. B this hymn is preserved complete.

**137.** The blood of the Innocents was of the same age as Christ. Saint Jerome uses this word, not Cicero, as some thought who read *coquus* (“cook”) for *coaevus* (“of the same age”).

**139.** *Nurus* (“daughter-in-law”) is used for wives by Martial, book 4, epigram 75: *Atque inter Latias gloria prima nurus* (“And first in glory among Latin wives”). Poets sometimes call women or brides *nurus*.

[Col. 0910C]

**143.** Put., in a second hand, has *quadam* for *quondam* (“once”).

**144.** *Receptor* means restorer or liberator, as in Eutropius, Tacitus, and others. Read this history in Exodus, chapter 2. In Vat. B and Rat. *Moyses* is always written rather than *Moses*.

**145.** Ald. and Gis. in the text, Urb., Vat. Q, Weitz., have *jusserat* (“had ordered”). Gifanius restored *jus erat* (“there was a law”) from an old book in the *Collectanea* of Lucretius, from the word *jussa* (“orders”); Heinsius adopted this with Put., Amb., and Rotten. Giselinus had noted the same in the margin. Cauchius conjectured *Cautus statuto jusserat* (“the cautious one had ordered by statute”). Elsewhere there is the error *statum* for *statutum*.

**146.** Egm. and Pal. have *qui* for *quo*, as earlier *qui proficit* for *quo proficit*.

**147.** Aldus has the error *absolveret*.

**148.** Cauchius, against the authority of the manuscripts, corrects it to *virile*. *Puerile*, from *puer* (“child”), is correct. *Tollere* means “to raise,” that is, to educate.

**149.** Prag. and Widm. have *sedula*.

**153.** Moses is called a priest in a broader sense, as previously were Elijah and David, although the more common and more correct opinion is that Moses was truly a priest in the proper sense. But Prudentius sometimes calls a person who handles, discusses, foretells, or celebrates divine matters a priest. In this sense the poets of Phoebus and philosophers of nature are called priests. Propertius, *Elegies* 3.1: “I first enter as priest from the pure spring.” Lactantius, in chapter 2 of book 5 of the *Institutes*, mentions someone who professed himself an overseer of philosophy. Prudentius takes the word *praesul*, which was also proper to priests, to mean “leader.” See hymn 11, verse 115, and hymn 5, verse 83, where Moses is likewise called *praesul justitiae* (“leader of justice”). In this sense some explain the words of Psalm 98:6: “Moses and Aaron among his priests, and Samuel among those who call upon his name.” Lorinus gives five different explanations of this passage, although he himself holds that Moses truly and properly was a priest.]

155. Exodus 31 and 32.

159. Ibid., chapter 2. Vat. B has *ipse* for *ille*.

161. Egm.: read *at* for *ad*.

165. Exodus 13 and 33. Note that this is Jesus, whose figure Moses is. The poet narrates both the figure and the thing signified by the figure. Nebrissensis: “Here, namely Moses, who led the people across the Red Sea; by this was signified Christ’s baptism, which was afterward consecrated in the sweet waters of the Jordan.” Cellarius did not understand this: Nebrissensis refers it to the Jordan, across which the people were led; but here the deeds narrated are those of Moses, not Joshua. Hence I would prefer that it be referred to the sweet water at Horeb, Exodus 17. Cellarius is reproved by Teolius: “Cellarius, understanding this wrongly, criticizes this interpreter for saying, contrary to historical truth, that Moses led the people across the Jordan—something he never even imagined.”

I do not think Cellarius charged Nebrissensis with that error. For Cellarius appends a note to verse 167, “He cleanses with sweet waters,” which Cellarius explains of Moses, while Nebrissensis explains it of Christ.

170. Ald., Weitz., Heinsius, with their older manuscripts, read *nostri pansis*. Gifanius had restored this from ancient manuscripts as *dispansus*, as in *Psychomachia*, “with outspread horns,” and in the preface to Book I against Symmachus, “The canvas could scarcely run when spread,” and *retunsis* in the Roman manuscript instead of *retusis*.

171. Vat. A has *sublimem*, incorrectly.

172. Read Exodus chapter 17, and the holy Fathers and interpreters who explain this history.

173. Jesus is the Savior, and this is also signified by *Joshua*, with whom he now compares Jesus. For just as Joshua led the tribes of Israel into the Promised Land, so Jesus brought the human race, freed from the captivity of the demon, into its heavenly homeland. Christ, therefore, is a truer Jesus than Joshua. Iso, Chamillardus, Cellarius explain it as: “Joshua is a truer Jesus, or savior, than Moses.” This is not satisfactory. See the notes on verses 165 and 177.

177. Erasmus read *qui ter quaternis*, and below, at verse 179, *petris*, which Giselinus noted in the margin. But the sense proceeds correctly without correcting the manuscript readings: “He founded twelve stones, the lineages of the apostles,” by the explanatory figure of speech familiar to Prudentius—that is, stones which are lineages. The poet alludes to Joshua chapters 3 and 4, where it is related that the Jordan was turned backward so that a passage might be open for the Israelites; and that Joshua ordered twelve men, one from each tribe, to be chosen. They entered the Jordan again and each took one stone from the riverbed, to be set up as a memorial for posterity; Joshua also placed twelve other stones in the middle of the riverbed, where the priests carrying the Ark of the Covenant had stood.

The poet allegorically recognizes the twelve apostles in these twelve men and stones, as Tertullian says in Book IV against Marcion, chapter 13: “For just so many apostles were foreshadowed … solid stones in faith, whom the true Jesus chose from the washing of the Jordan,” and so forth. Cellarius interprets the twelve stones as having been placed on the bank of the Jordan. Teolius seems to recognize no other stones than those placed in the middle of the Jordan’s bed. In the passage cited, Joshua ordered both these stones and others at the site of the camp to be placed.

179. Prag.: *fecit petras*, less well.

180. What *stemma* means was stated above, Hymn 7, verse 81. Here too one might suspect that *schemata*, that is, “figures,” should be read.

181. Vat. B and Rat. have *Judaeae*, which the poem’s meter does not permit.

182. The Magi did not see the leader of Judah in the star, but the star indicating him. See the note above on verse 28. This is even clearer from the argument that follows. The argument is drawn from the deeds of the ancient leaders of Israel, which, as many think, were not unknown to the Magi.

183. Egm. incorrectly has *fracta* for *facta*.

184. In Egm. and Pal.: *Christo figuram finxerint*. Erasmus, Thuan., Noms., the first Boherianus, Gis. in the margin, and Teol. have *Christi figuram finxerint*. Ald., Weitz., Gis. in the text, Heins., Vat. B, Sich., and others, along with Mar. and others, have *pinxerint*. In Vat. A, *finxerint*, with *pinxerint* written above it as an alternative.

185. Vat. B and Prag., contrary to the meter, have *priscorum* for *priorum*. In Vat. I, *priorum* seems to have been made from *primorum*, which did not fit the poem. The meter is also violated by Put., *Hic rex prior est judicum*; otherwise this might be tolerated, as above at verse 77, “Bethlehem, greater than the only great cities.” Heinsius thinks from this error that Prudentius himself wrote *Hic rex priorum est judicum*. But since Heinsius so often defends explanatory constructions in Prudentius, there is no reason for rejecting this one, established by Aldus, Weitzius, Giselinus, together with Vat. A, Vat. B, and many other manuscripts. For Heinsius produced no dissenting witness.

186. Vat. B has *domus*, the corrected gender.

187. Cauchius had found *nostraeque* in his manuscripts; he himself preferred *geminaeque*. Our manuscripts and those of Heinsius, together with the printed editions, have *dominaeque*.

188. Ambr., Rat., Hails., and Palat. have *templi novelli* without *et*. The others have *templi et novelli*. Gis. in the margin has *templi novelli ac pristini*. The Church founded by Christ is the new temple, as above, Hymn 11, verse 59, he called it the “new age.” Solomon’s temple is the ancient temple, a figure of the new temple. The temple restored after the captivity is also included under the name “ancient temple.”

189. Erasmus, Nebr., Gis., Fabr. have *Ephraim*, as the Greeks speak. Heinsius, with his older manuscripts, and Aldus with others, have *Effrem*, so that there may be synaloepha, Heinsius says; rather, diaeresis, as I have said elsewhere. Egm. writes *Efrem*.

190. Heinsius prefers *Manassae* to *Manasse*. Giselinus does likewise. Aldus has *Manasse*, and our manuscripts do not differ; Weitzius likewise approved it, together with Widm. and Gold.

191. Ald., Nebr., Gis. in the text, and Heins. have *suspic­iunt*. Vat. A and B, Prag., Rat., Weitz. with Widm. and Gold. have *suscipiunt*. The verb seems taken from John 1:11–12: “His own people did not receive him. But to as many as received him, he gave power,” and so forth.

193. Vat. B has *qui et*, but this was corrected to *quin et*. Above he asserted that not only the tribe of Judah but also all the other peoples worship God; now he confirms the same concerning the Gentiles. “Degenerate offspring” are those who derive their origin from neither the patriarchs nor the ancestors and have turned to the worship of idols.

194. Prag. has *ritum incognitum*, less well.

195. Ald., Egm., Pal., Hails., Vat. A, and Rat. have *durum*; Vat. B, Erasmus, Weit., Gisel., and Heinsius have *dirum*.

196. Aldus has *cox­erant*. Baal is used for any idol.

197. “Smoky” because of antiquity, like Cicero’s “smoky images.” There is no reason to think here of the workshops of craftsmen in connection with stone and wood.

198. Vat. A has the error *stipem*.

199. Vat. A, I, and Weitz. have *sectilem*. I understand *numen sectile* with the remaining witnesses; nor does *sectile* refer to the stock, but to the stone. Erasmus says that three materials for the gods are mentioned: stone, bronze, and wood. The workmanship is likewise threefold: metal is scraped with a file, stone is cut, and wood is hewn.

203. Gisel. has *Persa et Scytha*. Others have *Persa, Scytha*, because the final syllable in *Persa* is lengthened before the *sc* of the following word. The manuscripts vary in spelling: *Scitha, Schita, Scyta, Scytha*. Aldus, incorrectly, has *Scythia*; Vat. A and B, less well, *Scytae*. Urb. has *Persa et Scythia*.

205. He invites every kind of human being to praise God: those whom adverse fortune oppresses, those who enjoy prosperity, those who are well, those who are weak, and those who are already dead. This is the common interpretation. Yet nothing prevents its being referred to moral conditions, so that all who are of good character and all who are morally lost are invited to sing praises to Christ—but in such a way that afterward no one is dead, and all, converted to the good harvest, rejoice in the life Christ offers.

208. The Church sings that Jesus Christ destroyed death by dying; in this sense no one is now dead.

[Col. 0915A]

Aldus gives the title: “The *Apotheosis* of Aurelius Prudentius Clemens, a man of illustrious rank. Hymn on the Trinity.” This is also the inscription of this preface in Egm. In Vat. A: “Book on the Trinity”; the rest is missing. Giselinus: “*Apotheosis. Preface*,” with “Confession of the Trinity” in the margin. Weitzius: “Here begins the *Apotheosis*, that is, concerning Divinity.” Vat. B and Mar.: “Here begins the book *Apotheosis* with an explanation, that is, concerning Divinity,” which I judge not to be from the author. In Mariet., however, this book is placed after the *Dittochaeum*. In Alex. and Aldus, the *Apotheosis* follows immediately after the hymn on the Epiphany. See in the prolegomena, chapters 3, 4, and 5, the different ordering of the works.

Regarding this title, Barthius says in Book XLI, chapter 24: “Prudentius’ book, which is entitled by the Greek title *Apotheosis*, should by no means be entitled *On Divinity*. For he does not dispute whether Divinity exists or what it is. Rather, the aim of this outstanding author is to demonstrate Christ’s divinity, that he should be worshiped with divine honor and is not inferior to the Father, although human nature has been received into divinity—this indeed is *apotheosis*. Nor do I entirely reject, indeed I am almost fully prepared to approve, the interpretation of our old Helvetic manuscript, *On Deification*. Although it is not expressed in precisely this form—for the manuscripts prefer *de divinatione*, ‘concerning divination’—I conjecture that it was conceived in antiquity in this way. For *divatio* corresponds to *apotheosis*, whereas Latin has no single word meaning ‘to enroll among the gods.’ Joseph Rodriguez de Castro, who says in the *Bibliotheca Hispanica* that the book should be entitled *On Divination*, if Barthius is to be believed, perhaps intended to say *On Deification*; for this is what Barthius opposes. Emmanuel Riscus, in volume 31 of *Hispania sacra*, observes that *apotheosis* should not be understood in the strict sense as enrollment among the deified, since Prudentius’ aim is to treat Christ’s divinity.

Vat. A, before the first preface of the *Apotheosis*, seems to interpret this word differently: ‘How,’ it says, ‘human beings are transferred into divinity.’ I readily agree that Prudentius composed this book and the following one in order to eradicate completely the error of the Priscillianists, which had struck deep roots in Spain. But this does not mean that he did not deliberately attack ancient errors already refuted by others. Indeed, I think that he explicitly refutes Sabellius, Marcion, and Manichaeus, while never naming Priscillian, to show by which authors those heresies had once broken out or been propagated. Therefore some people reason incorrectly on this basis that the titles of the books are not by Prudentius because he chiefly attacks the Priscillianists. See the note on the title of the *Apotheosis*.”

[Col. 0915D]

1. “In the Trinity there are three supreme things.” Saint Augustine, in the appendix *On Various Sermons*, sermon 30, says: “The Holy Trinity is one and alone in substance, alone, and three in persons.” And in Book VII of *On the Trinity*, chapter 4: “These three together are one God … Again, that they are not three something, he could not say, because of human inadequacy in speaking, what Sabellius said, and by saying it fell into heresy.” And in Book VI of *On the Trinity*, chapter 4: “Those three are one God.” That is, as theologians speak, three individual entities.

The Trinity of persons is also not incongruously signified by a threefold distinction, in the sense in which the Greeks call three entities “characters.” Saint Athanasius, in the second set of questions, question 7, says: “I confess three persons, three subsistences, three properties, three individuals, three characters.” This agrees especially with the Fourth Council of Constantinople, session 10: “One and singular according to the account of substance, but three—or threefold—when we predicate him according to the account of persons.”

Petavius explains many similar expressions from the Fathers in volume II, Book VIII, chapter 9. Their common reasoning amounts to this: the plural number signifies that the individual persons possess those qualities, if it is permissible to speak so, yet they are not divided in such a way that each has its own separate quality from which it receives its name; rather, the quality is one and indivisible in the three, just as the essence is.

Hincmarus says: “He did not approve ‘threefold distinction’ for a non-threefold divinity.” Arator speaks of “threefold power,” and Prudentius of “threefold piety,” because of metrical necessity. The same Prudentius, perhaps compelled by the meter, elsewhere writes, to demonstrate three persons of one substance: “God is three supreme things, a threefold distinction, one power.” But since, as Priscian says, *specimen* is derived from *species*, “threefold distinction” cannot be said of God in the Catholic sense, as Augustine says in Book VII of *On the Trinity*, because the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not three species of one essence.

Yet Hincmarus ought to have distinguished these matters. It is one thing to say “three species,” another to say “a threefold distinction,” just as “threefold divinity” is not the same as “three gods.” Marius Victor, in Book I, said: “God is threefold power.” Nor do I find anything in Augustine that in any way supports Hincmarus’ case. Dudo, Dean of Saint-Quentin, borrowed this verse from Prudentius in Book III of *On the Morals of the Normans*, page 102: “He who remains three supreme things, a threefold distinction, one power.”

2. After *genita*, *est* is absent from the Prague manuscript. Giselinus omitted *est* after *Filius ipse* in both editions, and Heinsius made no note, although he printed *ipse est*. The poet often expresses that the Son was begotten from the Father’s heart.

3. On the procession of the Holy Spirit, see Hymn 6 of the *Cathemerinon*.

4. Vat. B, Urb., Mar., Vat. I, and Rat. in the first hand have *nomine*. Aldus and other printed editions have *numine*, together with Alex. and Widm. in the first hand.

5. The eternal generation of the Word is explained here with complete clarity. See *Cathemerinon*, Hymn 11.

6. Vat. A and Prag. incorrectly have *semper erant*. Saint Cyril of Alexandria, in the *Treasury*, assertion 5, gathers much in support of this position, proving that the Father did not exist before the Son, although he is unbegotten.

8. Some theologians dislike this expression, “to assume” or “to receive a human being,” concerning the Incarnation of the Word. The Fourth Council of Toledo uses it, chapter 1: “One of the Holy Trinity, assuming a complete human being, soul and flesh.” See *Apotheosis*, verse 779. In Chamillardus, *peremptu* is an error.

10. The Bologna manuscript has *fidelis*, less well.

11. Fortunatus also lengthened the first syllable of *charisma* in Book IV of *On Saint Martin*.

12. Prag. has *corpore*; Widm. above has *tempora*. Others correctly have *corpora*. Chamillardus notes that Prudentius, about to dispute against heretics, wisely placed a profession of the Catholic faith at the beginning as a preface, so that if anything contrary to the faith should happen to escape him, it would be clear that it was not intentional. For my part, I see the poet indicating in these few verses whatever is explained more fully in the *Apotheosis*.

Vat. A attaches this title to the second part of the preface: “Book I of Prudentius’ *Apotheosis*.” Vat. B and Mar. have no title. Aldus has “Hymn against the unbelievers,” which Weitzius adopted; most have “Another preface.” I do not reject this inscription, although I maintain that there is only one preface, whose first part is in hexameters and whose second part is in another meter. In Paulinus and others one may see one and the same poem composed in different kinds of verse.

In this second part of the preface Prudentius asks: “Is there a true sect?” that is, “Is this rule of faith true, which I conveyed in the preceding verses?”

1. Giselinus added in the margin “Rebuke of the unbelievers,” perhaps to indicate another inscription, “Hymn against the unbelievers.”

3. Vat. A has *servamus* for *cavemus*, against the meter and sense. Horace, Book I, Ode 5: “Why does he avoid olive oil more cautiously than viper’s blood?” Heresies are viper-like because they harm like vipers and creep secretly like snakes.

4. Vat. A, B, I, Urb., Mar., Prag., Rat., Gis., and Weitz. have *nescienter*. Heinsius, with his older manuscripts, and Aldus with Egm. and Pal., have *nescientes*, which is both more Latin and more agreeable. Bonon. and Alex. agree.

5. Thuan. and Alex. have *distinguere* for *discernere*. Bonon. has the inferior reading *viam vix*.

7. The old manuscripts Vat. A and B, Mar., Prag., and Rat. write *competa*. The Vulgate has *compita*. Salmasius, in *Plinian Exercises*, chapter 17, page 212, notes that in the oldest manuscripts of Prudentius *competum* is always written. *Competa* are places where many roads or paths meet and converge. The ancients often changed *e* into *i* and said *compito, pertisus,* and *distisus*. From this arose *compitum* from *competum*.

9. In Vat. A, *Oblica*, corrected by a recent hand to *obliqua*. Vat. B, Put., Thuan., Rotten., and Prag. have *conserunt*. Ald., Gis., Fabr., and Weitz. with Mar., Vat. A, and others have *conferunt*. Heinsius adopted *conserunt*, to which he says the Vatican manuscripts and Teolius give support; he also says that Cellarius should not have altered anything. Torrentius had noted from his manuscripts *Obliqua qua se*. The others differ, except Fabricius.

11. Rott. and Cauchius, from their manuscripts, have *quae si quis errans*, namely “which separations”; the others have *quas si quis errans*, namely “which paths,” as Heinsius wishes, or rather “tracks.”

12. Alex. has *linquens*. The meter prevents this.

13. Bonon. has, less well, *ruit* for *ruet*. Vat. B, Mar., Rat., and Prag. have *cadet*. Mar. in the second hand, Vat. A, Alex., Heins., Ald., Gis., and Weitz. have *ruet*; Heinsius noticed no variation from his manuscripts.

15. *Viantes* for *viatoribus* occurs in Apuleius, Solinus, and others of the same class. Saint Ambrose says in the hymn *Eternal Creator of All*: “Nighttime light for travelers.”

16. Bonon. incorrectly has *iter insequentis*.

19. Prag., against the meter, has *omnipotentis* for *omnipollentis*. See the note on similar words at *Cathemerinon*, Hymn 3, verse 2.

20. A legal term for malicious lawsuits whose injustice is obvious. Among jurists, dishonest suits and actions are also called *calumniae*, “slanders.”

21. Vat. A has the error *mutis* for *minutis*.

22. Widm., Bong., Rat., Vat. B, Mar., Bonon., and Aldus, in remarkable agreement, admit the metrical error *quisquis*. On the word *quisque*, see *Cathemerinon*, Hymn 7, verse 216. In some manuscripts *est* is absent after *lingua*.

23. In Bonon. *ligantque* is missing; it reads *solvuntque quaestionum*.

24. Paschalis, *On Crowns*, page 38, thinks that Prudentius calls the deceptive method of drawing conclusions “woven syllogisms” in imitation of the Greeks. Dominicus Aulisius, Book II, chapter 30 of *The Sacred Schools*, elegantly says that Prudentius calls them “woven syllogisms,” not because they resemble woven crowns, of which Plautus speaks, but because they resemble nets, insofar as their function is to capture. Aristo of Chios, quoted by Laertius and Stobaeus, asserts that the reasonings of dialecticians resemble spiders’ webs, which display skill but ultimately accomplish or produce nothing.

they loosen and bind the knots of questions

through woven syllogisms.

25. “Deceptive”: liable to deceive or treacherous. — “Sycophants”: slanderers or false speakers. They say that sycophants were so called because young men once used to break into gardens and steal figs from them. For this reason it was established by law that whoever did this should be beheaded; one who prosecuted someone for such petty losses was called a sycophant. — “Turns”: tricks, frauds, reversals, I.

28. “Hostile”: burdensome or troublesome. — “Arguing”: speaking, disputing, contending, I.

32. “To believe”: belief; a verb used as a noun, the infinitive interpreted by a nominative, I.

34. “Vanity”: the blindness of heretics, I.

41. “By which”: asking a question, he pronounces those two verses; or *quis*, “for whom,” I.

43. “Who”: unless it is he, I.

45. “Intermixes”: mixes in or sows among, Vat. A. “Steals away” or “darkens,” Mar. “Intermixes,” derived from *polo*, “pole,” Iso.

46. “Rival”: hostile, barren, I.

48. “Farmer”: God, the Father, I.

49. “Fiber”: root, Vat. A.

51. “Deceitful”: defective or darnel. — “Wheaten”: grain-bearing, I. — “Defective”: darnel. — “Wheaten”: grain-bearing, Vat. Q.

[Col. 0919B]

25. Prag. has the incorrect *ut* for *vae*. In the Parma edition this and the following verse are marked as questions, although they should rather be marked as exclamations. Petavius, in the prolegomena to his *Theology*, calls these verses exceedingly elegant—a judgment by which this distinguished theologian, and not inconsiderable poet, often praises Prudentius.

Some reject Iso’s interpretation of *sycophant*, saying that a sycophant was a slave who had eaten the figs himself but falsely and slanderously cast the blame for the theft upon another innocent slave. Paschalis, in the passage cited, page 35, chapter 11, observes that a crooked and deceitful mode of speaking is called *strophai*, “turns,” because the first wreaths were called *strophia*.

26. Vat. A incorrectly has *astutia* for *astutiae*.

28. Bonon. incorrectly has *dissentantibus*. *Dissertator* and *disserto* are not easily found among the older writers. Pliny and Gellius nevertheless use the noun *dissertatio*, although the manuscripts vary. Cato, in Festus, has *disserto*.

29. Egm. and Ox. have *dilegit*. Pal. incorrectly has *diligit*. See the hymn of Saint Romanus, verse 609, and 1 Corinthians 1:27.

31. Vat. A and Pal. have *neque* for *deque*, which the sense requires. Barthius, Book XVII, chapter 17, *Adversaria*, confirms with many examples that *de* is often superfluous—not only in Prudentius, Tertullian, Symposius, Nemesianus, Cyprian, Alcuin, and other less accomplished Latin writers, but also in Lucretius, Catullus, and others of their kind. Often *de* also signifies an instrument, and that meaning suits this passage.

32. Teolius noted that Ammianus, a pagan author, calls the Christian religion “absolute and simple” at the end of Book XXI.

33. Weitzius, with Widm. alone, wrote *offensaclo*, without concern for the meter. Prag. has, less well, *offendiculo*. The fixed stone may be understood as a sign once placed at a fork or crossroads to show the way; afterward it was called a sign. The pagans worshiped Terminus, an unshaped and rough stone. When Tarquinius wished to build the Capitol, all the other gods yielded, but Terminus alone remained; Virgil alluded to this in Book IX, verse 448: “The immovable rock of the Capitol.” Terminus was the guardian of boundaries. The Sibyl compared the errors of the nations to a stone of stumbling. See Luke 20:17; Romans 9:32; 1 Peter 2:8.

34. Vat. A has the error *Impinguat in quem*.

35. Vat. A has *lignum* above *signum*. *Scandalum* is an ecclesiastical word. Hence *scandalizari* in Tertullian and Jerome, among others.

37. Aldus has *in certo*; correct to *incerto*.

39. Vat. A has *fax*, with *lux* as a variant reading. In Palat. I think *pax* is an error for *fax*.

41. Cauchius preferred *quos* (*gressus*). But they are written differently, as Heinsius notes. Bonon. nevertheless has *quos* for *queis*. The meaning is “by which [steps] those wandering in darkness.” Teolius rejects this interpretation in Cellarius; with the question mark, he explains it as “What enemy tramples?” Iso indicates both interpretations.

42. Some Vulgate manuscripts incorrectly have *et poterit*.

43. See Luke 8 and Matthew 13:25, where this parable is explained.

45. Bonon. has the incorrect *interpululat*. Gis. in the margin has *grana* for *culta*. Barthius, Book XXIV, chapter 41, says this is expressed with great elegance, but suspects that *furtim* should be read for *fur*. I prefer the reading of the manuscripts.

47. Ald., Weit., Gis., with most manuscripts, have *in herbam fertilem*. Heinsius thinks *in herbam fertiles*—that is, “fertile oats”—is elegantly expressed, together with Put., Thuan., Egm. in the second hand, and Cauchianus. Bonon. and Alex. likewise have *in herbam fertiles*. I do not dislike *in herbam fertilem*. Barthius, in the passage cited, calls it graceful to say that milk is the first growth of grasses: “whom he suffers to grow from the milk of poison.” He calls the harmful sap of oats “poison.”

48. Aldus has the error *colonos*.

49. Aldus has *inani*; read *inanis*.

51. Ald., Weitz., Gis., with most manuscripts, have *dolosa et farrea*; the manuscripts of Heinsius, Alex., and Weitz., Bong., and Wid. above have *vitiosa et farrea*; Bonon. has *vitiosa farrea*. Both readings conflict not so much with the laws of grammar, as someone has said, as with the laws of poetry—at least those that Prudentius observes in this meter. Heinsius once conjectured *otiosa et farrea*. There is no reason to abandon the commonly received reading. Egm. has *dolosa*; in the margin, *vitiosa*.

[Col. 0919A]

ripeness, boiling, cooks the harvest,

[Col. 0921A]

55. “It matters”: it is useful or necessary, I.

[Col. 0921A]

[Col. 0921B]

1. “Dreadful to relate”: harsh to say, Iso.

2. “Brought forth”: uttered, Iso.

3. “He”: Sabellius; hence the Sabellians, and from the error the Patripassians, because they affirm that the Father suffered, Vat. A.

8. “Easy”: “it is,” I.

9. “Renowned”: glorious or famous, I.

Most printed editions and manuscripts place the title *Against the Heresy Which Affirms that the Father Suffered*. Put. reads “says” for “affirms.” Aldus has *haeresem* (“heresy”), and in his second revision, “Against the Heretics Who Affirm that the Father Suffered.” I believe such headings were not supplied by the author: they are absent from Vat. Q and others. In his second edition Giselinus omitted them and wrote *Patripassiani* in the margin at this place. In the Florentine manuscript, prologue, chapter 4, no. 87, there is no division of the books except after verse 952: “[Col. 0921C] Here ends the *Apotheosis against All Heresies*. Here begins *Against the Manichaeans*.” The title of the poem is *Apotheosis*, that is, “deification of man”; for the pagans called it *apotheosis* when they enrolled someone among the gods. The poet therefore attacks the heretics who err in explaining the apotheosis of Jesus Christ.

In the first chapter, from verse 1 to verse 177, he refutes the Patripassians, who, recognizing only one person in God, affirmed that the Father had suffered. In the second chapter, from verse 178 to verse 320, he argues against Sabellius and the Unionists—that is, those heretics who agreed with the Patripassians in denying the Trinity of persons, but differed from them in not defending the claim that the Father had suffered. Thus Prudentius here chiefly demonstrates that the Son is a distinct person from the Father, so that he may establish that the Son became incarnate and that Christ, together with the Father, is God.

In the third chapter, from verse 321 to verse 551, he refutes the Jews, who do not acknowledge Christ. In the fourth chapter, from verse 552 to verse 781, he refutes Christians who Judaize, or Homuncionists, who said that Christ was merely human. In the fifth chapter, from verse 782 to verse 952, he overturns the different error that the soul is a particle of God. In the sixth chapter, from verse 953 to verse 1062, he attacks the Manichaeans and the Phantastics, because they denied that Christ had a true body. And since, for the purposes of this argument, he discusses Christ’s death and resurrection, in the epilogue, from verse 1063 to the end, he proves the resurrection of human flesh by the example of Christ.

Not everyone speaks of the heretics who embraced these errors in the same way. Nor is that surprising: the character and habit of heretics in altering their doctrines is well known. Hence it happened that the heresy of the Patripassians was attributed to Sabellius, although it was not his but that of the Sabellians. The latter denied the Trinity of persons with Sabellius, but acknowledged the hypostatic union, which Sabellius denied. See Petavius, book I *On the Incarnation*.

Nestorius, in Cyril, book II *Against Nestorius*, charged the Catholics with teaching that human nature had been raised to apotheosis, as though they believed that human nature itself had been changed into God. But by this expression the Catholics meant nothing other than the elevation of human nature to union with the Word. Conversely, the Catholics denied apotheosis in Nestorius’s sense: namely, that a man already constituted as such had been elevated by his merits to God’s status and majesty. Prudentius explains and defends the Catholic sense of apotheosis in this poem.

1. Bonon. and Vat. Q, in the first hand, less correctly, *loquor* (“I speak”), [Col. 0922C] instead of *loquar* (“I shall speak”). Vat. B, incorrectly, *ni* for *ne* (“lest”).

2. Egm., incorrectly, *male perdita* (“badly lost”).

3. Egm. has *illa*, namely, “heresy”; the others have *ille*, “the Patripassian heretic.” This poem is connected with the prologue; hence *plurima* (“many things”) refers to “the seeds of weeds,” while *ille* (“he”) refers to the enemy, the thief whose mention occurs in the prologue.

7. In Vat. A, *illa* is missing. Arnobius, book I, p. 10: “O greatest, O highest creator of invisible things! O yourself invisible and never comprehended by any natures.” Minucius Felix: “He cannot be seen, being brighter than sight; nor can he be grasped, being purer than touch; nor can he be measured, being greater than the senses—unlimited, immeasurable, and known only to himself as great as he is.”

Nevertheless, the communication of idioms taught and explained by theologians must not be denied. God may be called mortal and capable of suffering through the communication of idioms—not because the Divinity can suffer or die, but because Christ, being man and God, was capable of suffering and mortal. The poet here speaks of divinity, or of the divine essence, which in itself cannot be grasped by the senses, eyes, or hand. The force of the argument [Col. 0922D] lies in this: the Godhead did not suffer, and therefore the Father did not suffer, since it is established from Sacred Scripture that the Son, not the Father, assumed human nature. This is the certain rule: in himself and by his nature, the Son no less than the Father and the Holy Spirit is incapable of suffering and invisible. Rufinus, in his *Exposition of the Apostles’ Creed*, testifies that among his people “invisible” and “impassible” were added to the article “God the almighty Father,” so that the Patripassian heresy might be excluded. “For it is established,” he says, “that the Son, not the Father, became incarnate … But as regards that immortal substance of the Godhead, which is one and the same in him and in the Father, there neither Father, Son, nor Holy Spirit is believed to be visible or capable of suffering.”

8. That among Christian writers “majesty” sometimes means the same as “divinity” was noted by Barthius, book X of the *Adversaria*, chapter 5, from Prudentius and others.

9. John 1:18: “No one has ever seen God”; and 6:46: “Not that anyone has seen the Father, except the one who is from God; he has seen the Father.” See hymn 6 *Cath.*, verse 2, and the hymn of St. Romanus, verse 312. Very many of the holy Fathers teach that, especially in the Old Testament, only the Son presented himself to human beings to be seen; he is sometimes called an angel because he was sent by the Father. This is the view of Justin, Origen, Tertullian, Irenaeus, the Fathers who wrote the synodal letter to Paul of Samosata from the Antiochene council, Athanasius, Cyril of Jerusalem, Basil, Chrysostom, Cyril of Alexandria, Theodoret, Hilary, Ambrose, Pope Leo, and Isidore. It is therefore false that the other Fathers after St. Augustine preferred the view that all Old Testament appearances were made through angels, as someone recently asserted. Others believe that not only the Son appeared in all those appearances, but also the Father—sometimes alone, sometimes with the Son and the Holy Spirit—and sometimes angels alone. St. Augustine strengthens this opinion above all others in book II *On the Trinity*.

Heinsius, from his manuscripts, and Fabricius: “Who did not put on the form of a man.” Aldus and Weitzius: “Who did not put on the form of a man”; Mariettus records no reading differing from this. In Thuan. and Boher., “But it is nevertheless the Father’s likeness.” Egm. has *fas est* instead of *fas sit*. In Thuan.: “But it is nevertheless the Father’s likeness, which it is permitted to see.”

20. Egm. and Pal. have *clauso* (“closed”), incorrectly, instead of *glauco*. He placed *speculum* (“mirror”) for *pupula* (“pupil”) at verse 869. Hamart. has “and the observing pupil” in the same place, verse 308. From the Greek word γλαύξ (*glaux*, “owl,” “little owl”) come *glaucus* (“gray-green”) and *glaucoma*. 25. Ald., Alex., Urb., Vat. Q, and all the older manuscripts of Heinsius: “Through forms which a human being can …” Vat. A and Egm.: *quam* (“which,” singular). Cellarius, at least in the second edition: “An equal form which he can …” Perhaps one should read: “An equal form which a human being could comprehend by sight.” Yet *per species, quas posset*, or *possit* (“through forms which he could,” or “can”), is better. Vatt. A, B, and Mar. have *posset* (“could”).

26. “Pure majesty” is that which assumes no form distinct from its own nature. The Scholastics would say “majesty taken nakedly.” In the hymn of St. Fructuosus, verse 91, *calce mera* means “with a bare foot.” *Mera virtus* occurs in book II *Against Symmachus*, verse 744. Gifanius is mistaken when he maintains in his *Index to Lucretius* that *merus* is used by Latin authors only for “true,” “excellent,” “not feigned,” “not simulated,” “distinguished,” or “forceful.” These passages of Prudentius alone refute him. See also what Becmanus brought against him in *On the Origin of the Latin Language*. Prudentius continues on the same subject. The divine nature cannot be seen by bodily eyes unless it assumes some form. It is established, however, that God assumed human nature not in a unity of nature but in the singularity of the person of the Word.

27. Aldus has *aliquos* (“some”) instead of *aliquo* (“by some means”). A suitable sense may indeed be present. But the manuscripts have *aliquo*. Heinsius found *ni se* in his manuscripts, which Ald., Bong., Vat. Q, and the Vulgate retain. In our manuscripts, Weitz., Gis., and others have *nisi se* (“unless he”).

The three men are a triple figure. In the poem *On Genesis*, whose author I have shown not to be Juvencus in the prologue, verse 556: “While he feeds God set beneath a threefold image.”

53. “By the power of the Holy Spirit,” says Chamillardus in explaining the words “by the power of the Word.” I do not agree. The theologians assert that only the Son is the Father’s notional Word, and they say that St. Basil spoke in a looser sense when he wrote in book V *Against Eunomius*: “The Son is the Word of God; the Spirit is the Word of the Son.” Prudentius himself does not call the Holy Spirit the Word, nor is there any need for us to explain him in that way. He therefore says that the body was compacted by the power of the Word—that is, of the Son, or second person. See what I noted at the cited passage of hymn 11. Below, verse 114: “He sent the visible Word and received the one sent; when he wished, by the Word he enclosed the pure Virgin’s womb, and by the Word he built the infant limbs.” “All things were made through the Word, and without him nothing was made that was made.” Therefore, through the Word also it came about that the body God was going to assume was compacted.

54. Sich., Bong., and Wid., from another hand and from a gloss, have *simulabat* (“represented”) instead of *referebat* (“bore”). Barthius, book XLI, chapter 24, observes that Christian poets variously shifted the tenses, so that Prudentius’s *faciem referebat eamdem* (“he bore the same face”) means “he was going to bear it.” But *referebat* can and should be understood of the time when God presented himself to Moses to be seen, not of the time when he was going to assume a body. That is, God, who at some future time was going to assume a body, bore or represented that same face when he appeared to Moses.

55. The older manuscripts of Heinsius and ours, Weit., have *sentam*, namely, “the thorny bush.” Ald., Gis., and the Vulgate have *sentum*. Bonon. has *sentem*, incorrectly. Fabricius thought it was the syncopated form *sentum* for *sentium*. But shortly afterward the poet says *contorta rubus* (“the twisted bush”) and *sentum peccamen* (“the thorny sin”). In the hymn of St. Eulalia, verse 47, “through places thorny with decay,” and in book II *Against Symmachus*, verse 1039, “For we uproot the thorny brambles from the breast,” where he adds other details appropriate to the matter. Chamillardus thought that Prudentius did not sufficiently distinguish the fact that on Mount Sinai God gave Moses the law and that on Mount Horeb he appeared to him in the bush. I maintain, rather, that the poet distinguished these two things most carefully, although he did not preserve their chronological order. Up to this point he has spoken of the vision on Mount Sinai, by which, in the figure of a man not yet clothed in flesh, he marked out the image of our face. Now he proceeds to the vision in the figure of fire consuming the bush: “Yet the thorny bush also,” through verse 70. See Exodus 3.

57. Bonon. has *alebat* (“fed”), not entirely badly, instead of *agebat* (“drove”). See Sedulius, book I: “Once the bush appeared blazing with harmless fires, burning without being consumed,” and so forth. Prudentius interprets the fire in the burning bush as the Word and the thorns as humanity.]

[45] [Col. 0925B] Yet, when the same one wishes, though the Father has never been seen,

He gathers that nothing was seen even in the bush except the Word, God: for the same Word that fills the thorny bush with the sin of our body was represented in the harmless fire that moved among the sharp thorns. 72. The Son is called the image of God in Colossians 1:15: “Who is the image of the invisible God.” The theologians demonstrate that the Son is the image of the Father from this passage of the Apostle: for the invisible God is there understood to be the Father, as is clear from the holy Fathers. Indeed, the Son is the image of the Father alone: the notion of an image cannot exist without true procession, and the Son proceeds from the Father, not from the divine nature. Vat. A reads *numen* (“divinity”) instead of *lumen* (“light”); this is much better.

In this sense it is common among the Fathers to call the Father the fountain of divinity and Godhead, as Suárez demonstrates from the works of St. Dionysius and others in book VIII *On the Trinity*, chapter 3. But the Father is by no means the fountain of divinity as though he produced it.

In the edition of Isidore’s glosses published at Cologne in 1701, the glosses were transposed and a false interpretation entered, namely: “FROM THE FOUNTAIN,” from the Father; “GOD THE FOUNTAIN,” the Son, who is the fountain. In Aldus, too, these words are wrongly punctuated: “not the fountain of God himself, visible, can be seen, who is born.”

93. Cellarius notes two indecorous metaphors in his word index: this one, *patrio ructata profundo* (“belched forth from the Father’s depth”), and the one at verse 595, *evomuit* (“vomited forth”), and so on. I shall discuss the second in its proper place. The first ought not to be called indecorous, since Prudentius adapted the words of Psalm 64:1 to his own meaning: “My heart has poured forth a good word,” which the holy Fathers interpret of the eternal generation of the Word. Ambrose, book IV *On Virgins*, chapter 1: “He is the one whom the Father begot before the Morning Star, generated from the womb as Son, and poured forth from the heart as Word.” He said *patrium profundum* (“the Father’s depth”), as Zeno of Verona says in sermon 1 *On the Eternal Generation of the Son*, “the profound mystery.” See the note on hymn 11 *Cath.*, verses 18 through 20. What Prudentius has here was explained more fully by Theophilus of Antioch, book II *To Autolycus* [Col. 0929D].

131. He calls the three boys thrown into the fiery furnace brothers because of their common religion and mutual love. Ovid used the word *inadustus* (“unburned”). Boldettus, book I, chapter 39, reproduced the three boys tested by the Babylonian fire from an ancient glass vessel.

132. Vat. A and Put. write *tris* instead of *tres*, as in ancient manuscripts of Virgil.

135. See Daniel, chapter III, where the entire sequence of this event is set out. Prudentius gathers from the tyrant’s words in verses 91 and 92 that it was the Son of God who descended into the furnace under the appearance of an angel and drove back the flame [Col. 0931D] of the fire. “Then Nebuchadnezzar was astonished . . . and answered and said: Behold, I see four men unbound and walking in the midst of the fire, and there is no corruption in them, and the appearance of the fourth is like the Son of God.” In Urb., *fateor: quem evictus adoro*, “I confess: whom, overcome, I adore.” Ald., Oxon., *fateor, quem victus adoro*, “I confess, whom, vanquished, I adore.” Sich., *fateorque, et victus adoro*, “and I confess, and vanquished I adore”; this is also found in the Heinsian manuscripts, Gis. first edition, Vatt. A, Q, Mar., Alex., Rat., and Weitzius. There was therefore no reason why Gis. should have altered it in his second edition to the rather harsher reading, *fateor quem, et victus adoro*, “I confess whom, and vanquished I adore.” Weitzius asserts that Aldus read it thus; perhaps he meant to say Giselinus. Vat. B nevertheless agrees with Giselinus: *fateor quem, et victus*, “I confess whom, and vanquished.” Prag. has, not unsuccessfully, *fateor, et victus adoro*, “I confess, and vanquished I adore,” with the *o* in *fateor* lengthened.

137. *Subtrahite, friget*, “remove them; it is cold,” is found in Aldus and the two principal Heinsian manuscripts. Giselinus, however, introduced *en hoc pacio subtrahite, en friget* (the first words are corrupt or uncertain; “behold, remove them; behold, it is cold”), which is also found in Torn. It is customary for Prudentius to lengthen a short vowel before two consonants of the following word. Nevertheless, Weitzius retains *en* [Col. 0932B] on the basis of his manuscripts, as do Alex. above, Vatt. A, B, Q, Prag., Urb., Rat., and Mar.; it is preferable to follow them, despite the contrary testimony of Heinsius, Chamillardus, Cellarius, and Teolius, who incorrectly asserted that all the Vatican manuscripts except one read *subtrahite, friget*, “remove them; it is cold.”

138. Aldus’s reading *ait*, “he says,” is an error for *agit*, “he performs.” Interpreters dispute whether the Word truly descended into the furnace under the appearance of an angel. Browerus, in his notes on Book V of Fortunatus, proves from the opinion of several Fathers, and specifically from these verses of Prudentius, that this apparition in the furnace is to be attributed to the Word. He confirms this because the Church sings that Christ rose from the tomb, having delivered the three boys from the furnace of the burning fire. And in Theodore the Studite’s *Canon of the Holy Cross*, Ode 7, it is said: “He who rescued the three boys from the flames came to earth in the flesh he had assumed.”

143. Alex. has *tangere visa*, “seemed to touch,” less suitably. Chamillardus observes that poets use barbarian garments in place of precious ones. Here the “barbarian folds” are flowing garments, cloaks, or another kind of clothing—interpreters differ concerning the meaning of the word *sarabala* in Daniel III, 95—which was made in the manner of the barbarians and in which those three boys, living in Babylonian captivity, would have been dressed. The distinguished P. Simon de Magistris, in his *Daniel*, refutes Grotius for abandoning Jerome and the Vulgate in order to follow the rabbis. Grotius explains *saraballa*—corruptly *sarabara* or *saraba*—as *mantella*, “cloaks”; lexicographers explain it as “leggings” among the Persians. In the Daniel mentioned above, according to the Septuagint, Daniel is displayed in barbarian dress in the lions’ den, from the celebrated *Menologion* of Basil Porphyrogenitus.

144. Prag. has *percurrit amictus*, “the garment passes over.”

145. Prag. has *inde* for *ipse* or *ire*, that is, “thence” for “he himself” or “to go.” Ald., *Ipse per Assyrias metuit vapor ire tiaras*, “The vapor itself fears to pass through the Assyrian tiaras”; Mar. has this as a variant reading, as do the Heinsian manuscripts. Gis. likewise has it in the margin, while in the text he has *Ire per Assyrias vetitus vapor ipse tiaras*, “The forbidden vapor goes through the Assyrian tiaras itself.” Weitz. with Widm., Palat., Bong., our Vatt. A and B, and Mar. in its first hand, has *ipse per Assyrias vetitus vapor ire tiaras*, “The vapor itself, forbidden, goes through the Assyrian tiaras.” Sichardus has *Ire per Assyrias vetitus vapor ipse tiaras*, “To go through the Assyrian tiaras, the vapor itself is forbidden.” In Put. there is *Assyrios tiaras* in the masculine gender, as in Virgil and Claudian. Chamillardus interprets “Assyrians” as Jews, because Europeans confused Assyria with Judea. I prefer to take the word in its proper sense, as referring to the Babylonians, just as above with “barbarian folds.”

148. Chamillardus argues from what Isidore writes in chapter 20 of Book II, concerning the second division of music, which is called instrumental, that among the ancients instruments had the same form as among us. “Organ,” says Isidore, “is a general term for all musical vessels. This instrument, however, to which bellows are attached, the Greeks call by another name. But that it is called an organ is rather the common usage.” This practice therefore flourished at least in Spain, where organs are still especially celebrated. Perhaps there were also two kinds of organs, hydraulic and pneumatic, as I shall say at verse 392. Whether this practice existed in Gaul before the times of Pepin and Charlemagne is questioned by the distinguished Hieronymus Tiraboschius, volume III of the *History of Italian Literature*, Book III, chapter 1, section 11. He cites the words of an anonymous monk of Angoulême in the *Life of Charlemagne*: “Similarly, the Roman singers mentioned above instructed the singers of the Franks in the art of *organandi*,” that is, “in the art of organ-playing” or “organ-making.” From these words, he says, it is not sufficiently clear whether the Romans taught the Franks the art of making organs or the method of using them. The distinguished Stephanus Arteaga, in his excellent work *On the Italian Musical Theater*, volume I, chapter 3, explains the word *organandi* differently and shows from suitable authorities that it signifies there a particular system and rule of music. I shall say in passing that it was not my intention to condemn, in a few words, the work of Arteaga—which I have often praised, and publicly before many people—because of certain chronological trifles that slipped into his discussion of Spanish hymnody and which someone seems unjustly to have taken in a bad sense.

[Col. 0931A] *Visibilem, per quem valeat Pater ipse videri*:  
“Visible, through whom the Father himself may be seen:”

[125] “Not only to the eyes of the saints, but also by a light denied to the sightless,

I speak of the blind among the blind: their dark stupidity,

In their shadowy heart, does not know how to weigh the truth.

413. If you deny that he is evident to mortals,

[130] Wandering far away unharmed amid the flames,

Treading the raging fires with his brothers unburned?
