In the furnace’s panting fires;

Behold, a fourth, laughing, cuts through the smoking flames.

[135] That one is the Son of God, I confess, and, vanquished, I adore.’”

[Col. 0931B] “Remove the useless (*irritas*) torches and the lukewarm brands.”

[Col. 0932A] “Take them away: behold, the heat of the kindled sulfur is cold.

It is the Son—there is no doubt—who performs these wonders,

414 Him whom I see; God himself, the most certain offspring of God,

[140] Commands the immeasurable fires and subdues their rage,

Exulting over the obedient pyre, and restrains the pitch-black fury,

Forcing the madness of the flames to grow cold.

The warm air, commanded not to touch the barbarian folds,

Passes by and, hissing, runs across the delicate garments;

[145] The vapor itself is forbidden to pass through the Assyrian tiaras,

Lest the hair flowing over the shoulders be soiled by bitter smoke.”

He spoke these words and ordered the various songs to fall silent:

The organs, sambucas, zithers, reeds, and trumpets.

[Note: [Col. 0933B]

149. *Superstitio*: paganism, false religion. *Festa*: empty, festive.

150. *Conspicuae*: statues.

151. *Virorum*: evidently “of men,” that is, “were heard.”

152. *Concentu*: song. Isidore.

156. *Servando*: for saving the human being. Isidore.

159. *Animalis*: bestial. *Agebat*: led, was led.

160. *Heri*: of God.

162. *Obside*: so that he might appear as a hostage and witness for seeing God.

[Col. 0934B] 164. *Animalis*: unbelieving.

165. *Seminis*: of divinity.

167. *Materies*: Christ’s humanity. *Intercute flatu*: by an inward breath, Vat. A. *Intercute*: remaining within the skin, inward; *interiore spiritu*: by an inward spirit, Isidore.

170. *Spiramine*: the Holy Spirit, Isidore.

171. *Hominis*: of Mary.

175. *Compendia*: namely, “are.” *Summae*: of the numbers, Isidore.

177. *Cucurrit*: descended and ascended, I. and Mar. — *Contra Unionitas*, “Against the Unionites,” that is, against the Sabellians. The Unionites are those who said there was one substance and one person; they denied the Son and the Spirit, saying: “The same God is Father when he wishes, Son when he wishes, and also the Holy Spirit.” The Arians said that there were three persons and three substances in the Godhead; the Sabellians, on the contrary, one person and one substance. Catholic faith, avoiding the error of both, truly affirms one substance of the Godhead and three persons. [Col. 0935A] For the Arians rightly affirmed three persons but wrongly three substances; the Sabellians rightly affirmed one substance but wrongly one person, I.]

[Note: [Col. 0933D]

150. Understand “gold” to mean the golden statue that King Nebuchadnezzar made.

151. Mar. has *resonantia* with the gloss *erant*, “were.” In Vat. B the same reading seems to have existed, but it has been erased; a gloss added says *fiunt*, “are made,” suggesting that *resonantia* should be read. Isidore’s gloss pertains to the same point. The others have *resonant jam*, “now resound,” which is clearer.

152. Heinsius, with only Put., has *triplice concentu* instead of *concentu triplici*, “with triple song” instead of “with a triple song,” not ineptly. But I am surprised that Heinsius cited Apollinaris Sidonius to show that the first syllable of *triplex* can be lengthened. Who would deny it, or who not know that this syllable is common? Prudentius indicates the hymn of the three boys in the furnace of fire: “Blessed are you,” etc.

159. Ald., Thuan., Cauch., Rat. in its second hand, Mar., Egm., and Widm. have *quae tunc*, “which then.” Others have *quam tunc*, likewise “which then.” Prudentius offers a fitting reason why the Word, the Father’s speech, always appeared: namely, so that the flesh he was going to assume might change its degraded life and become accustomed to seeing a companion of earthly form.

160. This verse is absent from Put. In Thuan., *fragilesque per artus*, “and through fragile limbs.” Oxon., Rot., Noms., the three Torr. manuscripts, and Pal. have *similesque per actus*, “and through similar actions.” See hymn 4 of the *Cathemerinon*, verse 77. Ald., Weitz., and Gis., with the other manuscripts, have *similesque per artus*, “and through similar limbs.” Vat. B has *actus*, “actions,” as a variant reading.

164. “Spirit” may be taken as referring to the third person of the Trinity; but there is no reason why it should not be understood of the second, with whom the passage is chiefly concerned. See above, verse 53, and hymn 11 of the *Cathemerinon*, verse 51. Petavius, volume IV, part 2, Book II, chapter 9, confirms by these verses the theological view that Christ became our righteousness not only through an external efficacy but through a certain internal and substantial—as the ancients say—influx, through the substantial conjunction and application of the Holy Spirit, as a form sanctifying in its own manner, which is the proper function of Christ’s incarnation.

166. The ecclesiastical word seems to be *vivificare*, “to make alive.” Minucius Felix used it. Tertullian also has *vivificatio*, “vivification,” and *vivificator*, “giver of life.” In Ammianus one finds *vivificus*, “life-giving.”

168. Cham. has *male, tamen?*, “badly, nevertheless?” in the form of a question.

169. Vat. A, with *corruptae* written by the first hand, an error.

172. Ald. wrongly has *solum* for *solus*. The explanation of this word is drawn from what follows.

174. In Vat. A, *et* is missing after *mediator*, although the sense requires it. See Matthew XI, 27.

175. Vat. A had *comprehendia*, but this was altered to *cemprendia*; read *compendia*.]

[Col. 0933A] 415. “Foolish superstition fell silent; the festive voice came to rest,

[150] Which wrongly celebrated the gold of the conspicuous image.

Now only the songs of holy men resound,

Praising the King of heaven with triple song,

Who made the sea, the lands, and the shining stars,

And sheltered his unharmed servants amid the fires.

[155] The speech of the almighty Father always descended

For the saving of humankind: he always took care,

Out of his own love, to unite mortal things to himself,

So that the flesh, destined to be joined to and filled with its eternal Lord,

Might by yesterday’s example change the degraded life that it then led in animal fashion,

[160] 416 And through like limbs become accustomed

[Col. 0933B] To see its companion of earthly form,

To recognize its partner by sight as though by a pledge,

And gradually draw near to Christ, its blood-relative.

[Col. 0934A] Thus the human being, once animal-like, now the Spirit

[165] Transferred to the nature of the heavenly seed,

Pouring God himself into him, making mortal things alive.

Now a new substance, solidified by an inward breath,

Yet still our substance, drawn from the Virgin,

Cast off the corrupted beginnings of its former life,

[170] Receiving immortal good through its own breathing.

That one is the Son of man, but that one is the Son of the Thunderer;

Now he alone looks upon the Father’s face and sees him himself.

No one knows the Father except the Son,

And the one to whom the Son reveals him—the mediator of us and of the Almighty.

[175] Finally, I shall conclude briefly, as a summary of the highest matters:

[Col. 0934B] 417 The Father did not descend into flesh, but flesh, once assumed,

Ascended to the Father’s citadel: born through both, he passed through both.”

[Note: [Col. 0935B]

178. *Profanator*: a blasphemer, a contemptuous person; one is called *profanus*, “profane,” because he is removed from the *fanum*, that is, the temple of God—hence irreligious. *Cede*: withdraw, depart.

179. *Depositor*: denier.

180. *Violas*: you deny. *Natum*: the Son, Isidore.]

[Col. 0936A] 181. *Quandoquidem*: since he. *Genitor*: father.

183. *Patriae*: paternal, belonging to the father.

184. *Nomine*: namely, the name of procreation, Isidore.

185. *Generis vim*: the strength of the son, I.

186. *Idolio*: paganism, in the place of idols, Mar. — *Idolio*: in sacrilege, in the place of idols; that is, where an idol-offering (*idolothytum*) is sacrificed [the printed gloss is corrupt]. An *idolium* is the temple of an idol. — *Recubans*: namely, reclining, I.

187. *Cespes*: a turf is earth torn up with grass, from which they made altars, I.

189. *Saturnis*: he used the word for all the gods. — *Citheraeis*: Citheraea is Venus, I.

190. *Portentisque*: idols, I.]

[Note: [Col. 0935B]

178. Alex. places before this verse the heading *Contra Unionitas*, “Against the Unionites.” So do Weitz. and Vat. A. In Vat. B and Mar., *Contra Unionitas Sabellianos*, “Against the Unionites, the Sabellians.” In Rat., *Contra Sabellianos*, “Against the Sabellians.” In Ald. and Gis.’s first edition, *Contra Unionitas, id est Sabellianos*, “Against the Unionites, that is, the Sabellians.” In his second edition Gis. has *Unionitae* in the margin. See Browerus, page 223, on Fortunatus, where he praises the arguments of Prudentius against the Unionites as worthy of the most learned of Christian poets. I shall also say in the *Psychomachia* that headings of this kind—*Against the Unionites* and similar ones—were not added by the author but by others. Petrus Coustant, in his *Vindications of Manuscript Codices*, incorrectly asserts on page 274 that Prudentius here calls the Sabellians Unionites. Prudentius proceeds to explain that the Father and the Son in the Trinity are not two bare names but truly distinct persons; for the Patripassians affirmed that the Father had suffered because the Father was not distinct from the Son. These heretics are called Unionites because they asserted one person only in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. In Urb. one reads *Nam cede*, “For withdraw.” Ancient copyists often changed *jam* into *nam*.

179. Vat. B has *depositos*, incorrectly, or perhaps according to the writing practice by which the ancients sometimes used *s* for *r*, as in *honos* and *labos* for *honor* and *labor*. The poet calls Sabellius the “depositor” of the Father because he truly denied that the Father existed and asserted that the Son was not truly begotten. Quintilian uses the word *depositor* in the headings of his *Declamations*.

[Col. 0935D] 184. Mar. writes *dispoliare*, “to strip away.”

186. In Rat., an inept corrector, after erasing the others, substituted *quisnam idolorum*, “which of the idols,” so as to accommodate the meter. Vat. A and Egmon. have *ne quis* for *ecquis* or *et quis*: “lest anyone” for “is there anyone?” If *ne quis* is read, the question in verse 188 must be removed, and the sense will be: “lest anyone not think,” etc. Widm. has *ut quis*, “so that someone,” above *et quis*. Gifanius, in his *Lucretian Collection*, under the word *ET QUANTIS*, observes that certain expressions were spoken in two ways by the ancients, whereas later writers insisted on using only one: they said both *ecquis* and *et quis*. Thus Gifanius reads in Prudentius, on the basis of an old book, *et quis in idolio*, “and who in the idol-temple,” and similarly in other passages. Tertullian, Jerome, and others use the word *idolium*. Just as *Minervium* and *Dianium* meant the temple of Minerva and Diana, so *idolium* means the temple of idols. *Aesculapium* is also found for the temple of Aesculapius. Certain interpreters should be corrected who, at 1 Corinthians VIII, 10, understand *in idolio recumbentem* by taking *idolium* to mean a table or a banquet. The pagans reclined at a table in their temples, not on a table, and much less “in a banquet.” There were couches on which they reclined in order to eat. Barthius, Book XXXIV, chapter 4, explains *in idolio recubans* as “reclining in the idol-temple,” that is, devoted to paganism, as one says “to lie sick.” Cudworth, chapter 4 of the *System of Intellectualism*, section 542, cites these verses with great praise.

187. Vat. A has *rudiculos*, incorrectly, for *ridiculos*. I shall discuss the turf altar at the hymn of Saint Eulalia and Saint Vincent.

189. Bonon., against the meter, has *dis* instead of *Cythaereis*, “gods” instead of “Cythereas.” Urb. incorrectly has *Cythareis*. He uses the plural *Saturns*, *Junoes*, and *Cythereas*, or Venuses, contemptuously, as below at verse 292, *Deucalions*, or to indicate the various titles by which the same god was named and worshiped by the pagans. We shall discuss these false divinities and their worship more fully at the hymn of Saint Eulalia, verse 122; Saint Vincent, verse 50; Saint Lawrence; and especially Saint Romanus; and in the books against Symmachus.

191. Prag. has *imo*, incorrectly, for *uno*. Radulphus Cudworth, *System of Intellectualism*, chapter 4, understands “the reason of the virtues” here as the clothing and appearance of the persons, and the ministers as the demons who were also called gods and whom God used for his commands, according to the theology of the gentiles of whom Prudentius speaks. Cudworth thinks that many pagans believed their divinities to be nothing other than the perfections and virtues of one God, clothed in the names of persons. I shall examine this opinion in Book II against Symmachus, verse 58: “Incorporeal things,” etc. Minucius Felix writes: “For what can be so open, so acknowledged, so evident, when you raise your eyes to heaven and examine what is below and around you, as that there is some divinity of the highest intelligence, by which all nature is inspired, moved, nourished, and governed?” See what Wowerus, Elmenhorstius, and Ouzelius note there from our poet, Augustine, Jerome, Isidore of Pelusium, Lactantius, and Cicero; for this is a subject treated by many authors. This is that testimony concerning the one God belonging to the soul naturally Christian, which Tertullian ingeniously defended in his single book *Against the Gentiles*. See his *Apology*, chapter 17, and the book *On the Testimony of the Soul*.]

[Col. 0935A] “Withdraw, profaner of Christ, withdraw now, Sabellius,

Denier of the Father and mad denier of the Son.

[180] Do you not deny the Father when you refuse to acknowledge the Son?

Since there is no father unless a son exists:

Nor can you call him father whom you deprive of offspring.

But perhaps you wish to strip God of the honor

Of paternal affection, content with a bare name,

[185] [Col. 0936A] To take away the fact that he is God, and the dignity and power of fatherhood.

418. Is there anyone reclining in an idol-temple amid a thousand sacred things,

Worshiping ridiculous gods with salt, turf, and incense,

Who does not think that there is one supreme God above all things?

Even though he consecrates smoking altars

[190] To Saturns, Junoes, Cythereas,

And other monstrosities,

Nevertheless, whenever he looks up to heaven, in the one—”

[Note: [Col. 0937A]

192. *Jus*: religion.

193. *Ministris*: angels.

194. *Barbara*: foreign, belonging to an alien people, Isidore.

195. *Superstitio*: paganism. *Caniformem*: having the form of a dog, Isidore.

196. *Anubem*: the Egyptian god, that is, a monkey, having a dog’s head. In the Egyptian language Mercury is called Anubis, and he is said to be the god of eloquence. Hence he is depicted with a dog’s head, because among animals nothing is considered more perceptive than a dog. He is said to bark because of the abundance of his speech; hence orators are also called “barkers.” The Egyptian god having the likeness of a dog, I.

197. *Cloacinae*: Cloacina and Epona are rustic goddesses. Cloacina is the goddess of sewers. — *Epona*: goddess of gardens. Cloacina and Epona, rustic goddesses, Vat. T.

198. *Solidam*: full, rich, fetid, putrid, I. — *Olidam*: putrid, Vat. T. — *Acerram*: a vessel for incense, a censer, Isidore.

199. *Molam*: a sacrifice or a mark; *mola* is a kind of sacrifice made from spelt and salt, with which they sprinkled the fire, the ritual, and the victim. — *Rimetur*: let him turn over. — *Exta*: entrails, I.

200. *Barbati*: of the old man, Mar. *Illius senis*: of that old man, I. — *Deliramenta*: madness, lies, foolishness. — *Platonis*: Plato is said to have received his name from the breadth of his shoulders; first an undefeated athlete, he later turned to philosophy and surpassed all philosophers, I.

201. *Hircosos*: adulterous or dog-like, Vat. T. — *Hircosus cynicus*: Epicurus, Vat. A. — *Hircosus cynicus*: he gives the proper names of heretics, some of whom are called goats because of their impurity, while others are called dog-like and adulterous: for κύων (*kyōn*) means “dog” among the Greeks, I.]

[Note: [Col. 0937B]

193. “Powers of heaven,” or angels distributed into various orders of service. Saint Gregory, Homily 34: “We have spoken of nine orders of angels, because, as sacred Scripture bears witness, we know that there are angels, archangels, virtues, powers, principalities, dominions, thrones, cherubim, and seraphim.” The Hebrews distinguish ten orders of angels and assign various names to them. Petavius, volume III, Book II, chapter 1, refutes Erasmus and Beza, who understand the Apostle’s passage, Ephesians I, 21, “above every principality,” etc., universally of all created things, drawing on Ignatius, Irenaeus, Athanasius, Cyril of Jerusalem, Basil, Epiphanius, and others. The name “virtues,” like “angels,” sometimes refers to all the angelic orders, as is clear from Chrysostom, Theodoret, Hilary, Jerome, and others. In Greek, in the sacred Scriptures, they are called δυνάμεις (*dynameis*), “powers”; in Hebrew, *Sabaoth*, “Hosts.”

196. Ald. and Gis. have *Anubim*, “Anubim.” Weitz., with most manuscript copies, has *Anubem*, “Anubis.”

197. Ald., Ox., Vat. Q, and Noms. have *Tiphonae*; Urb., *Typhonae*. Gis. has *Hippo*, from *Hipponis*, as *Dido* from *Didonis*. For the goddess of horses should be called *Hippo* or *Hippona*, from the Greek word. Vat. A has *Ypone*. The better Heinsian manuscripts, together with two Torrentian manuscripts, Vat. B, Alex., Prag., Rat., and Mar., have *Eponae*, “Epona.” Elmenhorstius anticipated this true reading, and before him Gifanius, in his *Lucretian Index* under the word *SOLIDA*, found it in old books. Adrianus Turnebus approves the same reading, *Adversaria*, section 791, because Latins sometimes pronounce Greek words in such a way that they conceal their origin, and because he had found *Eponam* in the dusty libraries of Juvenal manuscripts. Giselinus found *Hippo* in the Buslidian manuscript and judged *Tipho* and *Eponae* to be corrupt readings, relying on Gyraldus, who in his *History of the Gods of the Gentiles* wrongly thinks that this goddess is called *Epona* by some, and because the middle syllable in *Epona* would have to be long. Barthius, Book XXVI of the *Adversaria*, chapter 11, insists that in Prudentius and others one should read *Equona*, because this goddess was responsible for horses; he says that Prudentius shortens the middle syllable in the Greek manner, as Prudentius often does in Greek names. The name *Epona* should be retained, since it occurs in ancient monuments and inscriptions. On Epona, goddess of muleteers, see Plutarch in the *Parallels*, Minucius in the *Octavius*, and Tertullian in the *Apologeticus*.

198. Ald., Weitz., Vatt. A and B, and Mar., as a variant reading, and Gifanius from five manuscript copies, have *solidam*, “full,” as in Virgil; Gifanius notes that Prudentius borrowed much from him: *Aeneid* V, “the full censer he reverently worships.” Isidore explains both readings, *solidam* and *olidam*. Heinsius with his manuscripts, Giselinus, influenced by a similar epithet in Juvenal, *Satire* 8, “a face smelling of the stable,” Bong. in its first hand, Mar. in its first hand, Prag., and Rat. read *olidam*, “fetid.” I prefer *olidam*: the epithet “fetid” suits the stable and is also appropriate to the censer, since incense gives off a smell. Giselinus found *solitam* in the Daventrian manuscript, “customary,” which is not objectionable.

199. Aldus divides the passage differently: *Sacrilegisque molam manibus rimetur, et exta*, “and with sacrilegious hands let him turn over the mola and the entrails.” Isidore likewise adds the gloss “*RIMETUR*, let him turn over,” as though *rimetur* governed *molam*. The meaning is: “let him discharge the censer, the mola, and turn over the entrails.” Chamillardus, however, interprets it as: “let him search with wicked hands through the lowest entrails and the lowest mola.” But if the mola was made, as he himself observes, so that the foreheads of the victims, the hearth, and the knife might be sprinkled with it, what, I ask, is meant by turning over or searching through the “lowest mola”? Festus teaches that *immolare* comes from *mola*, that is, from ground spelt and salt with which the victim was sprinkled and consecrated. Above, verse 187: “worshiping with salt, turf, and incense.” From the same Festus, *exta* are so called because those parts are cut out for the gods which stand out and project most prominently. Others think *exta* means something like “cut-out parts.”

201. Put., Gifan. under *SOLIDA* from an old book, Egm. in its second hand, and Urb. have *hircosus cynicus quos somniat*, “the goat-like Cynic whom he dreams of,” namely, “the sinews.” Thuan., Rot., the three Torr. manuscripts, Weitz., Ald., Pal., and Mar. as a variant reading, and Prag. have *hircosus cynicus*, “the goat-like Cynic.” Fab., Gis., Widm., and Mar. in its first hand have *quos somniat*, “those whom he dreams of.” Thuan., Rot., the three Torr. manuscripts, Veitz., Alex., Ald., and Mar. in its second hand have *quod somniat*, “what he dreams of.” Vat. B incorrectly has *hircosos cynicos quis somniat*, “what goat-like Cynics does he dream of?” and Vat. Q, *hircosos cynicos quos somniat*, “the goat-like Cynics whom he dreams of,” which also appears in the Tornaesian edition. Prag. has *quid somniat*, “what does he dream of?” In Vat. A, *et hircosus cynicus quod somniat*, “and what the goat-like Cynic dreams of,” or similar words, had been erased, and *somniat*, “he dreams,” was written above. Cynics are called “goat-like” because they are obscene and foul-smelling; they were also called cynics because of their dog-like obscenity, unless one prefers the explanation that they were so called because of their unrestrained license to rail and, as it were, bark. Others think—reasonably enough—that cynics are called goat-like because of their goat-like beard, which was characteristic of philosophers and became proverbial. In the immediately preceding verse Plato is called “bearded” not only because he was old, as the gloss says, but also because of his philosophical beard. Philosophers now enjoy living in a very different manner.]

[Col. 0937A] 419. “He assigned all authority to God, whom the mighty order

Of the Powers, equipped with various ministers, serves.

What nation is so foolish in mind, so barbarous in speech,

[195] Or what superstition so filthy that it would set

Anubis, dog-shaped and barking, above heaven’s throne?

[Col. 0938A] No one gives a throne above the stars to the goddesses Cloacina or Epona,

420. Though with sacrilegious hands he offers the fetid censer and sacrificial meal,

And examines the entrails.

[200] Consult the ravings of bearded Plato;

Consult also what the goat-like Cynic dreams, and those whom—”

[Note: [Col. 0939A]

202. *Torta*: by a twisted circumlocution. — *Nervos*: games, unknottable expressions, syllogisms, I. — *Vertigine*: by a turning, Vat. A.

203. *Labyrinthus*: winding. He also calls it *laborinthum*, meaning error; the labyrinth was an underground house with a hundred entrances, which Daedalus made for the Minotaur. If someone entered it once, he could not return because of the multitude of entrances. It is called *laborinthus* because of “labor within,” I.

204. *Agat*: harass; *ducat*: lead, I.

205. *Gallinam*: a hen is sacrificed to Aesculapius, who presides over those lying sick. — *Clinicus*: curved. *Cline* in Greek means “bed”; hence *clinicus* is the proper name of the god who presided over those lying in bed, or of the sick person himself, from lying in bed, I.

206. *Aequum*: appeased, Isidore. *Propitium*: favorable, Vat. A.

208. *Fragosis*: difficult, I.

209. *Modis*: syllogisms, I. — *In unum*: to one God, Vat. A.

211. *Suos*: their own. — *Vaga sidera*: the seven wandering stars; he means the seven planets, which are interpreted as “wandering,” not because they themselves wander but because they make human beings wander. Hence they are better called *planoficiae*, that is, “causing error,” I.

212. *Non recipit*: does not understand. — *Natura*: that is, a human being is called merely a quadruped when he lives irrationally in the manner of animals and, devoted to gluttony, cares nothing for heavenly things; for all mortal animals except the human being are inclined toward the earth. Hence a certain truthful poet says: “While the other animals look toward the ground with bowed faces, he gave the human being an uplifted face and ordered him to look upon heaven and raise his countenance erect toward the stars.” — *Modo*: only, merely. — *Quadrupes*: animal-like. — *Ille*: the human being, I.

214. *Pollere*: to have power, I.

215. *Numae*: Numa established sacred rites for the Romans. Numa was of Sabine origin, and after the death of Romulus the Roman people made him their ruler. Wishing to turn the Romans away from their love of arms, he devised the worship of the gods by magical art, saying that every night he was instructed by the nymph Egeria. After his death, when the Romans discovered his magical books, they committed them to the fire. Yet, although they saw that they had been deceived, they persisted in the worship of the gods. — *Haruspex*: priest, I.

216. *Cottus*: whence the Cottian Alps, I., Mar. — *Cane milite*: a Molossian dog, I.]

[Note: [Col. 0939C]

202. Widm. has *Aristotelis*, incorrectly, for *Aristoteles*. Teolius has *tota vertigine*, “with complete turning,” both in the poem and in the note, instead of *torta*. I would believe this to be a printer’s error, for he cites no manuscript in support of the reading. The poet correctly assigns to Aristotle the art of weaving the “sinews,” since Cicero and others call Aristotle powerful in expression and say that no one was more vigorous than he in speech. His dialectic is famous. Some explain *torta vertigo* as a sorites, others as the *pseudomenon*, by which disputants become entangled. I myself would certainly not be entangled. Suppose someone says, “I am lying”: is this proposition true or false? I deny that anyone can seriously and sincerely utter this proposition; I deny that anything can be understood by someone if another person utters it. I can understand someone who says, “I have lied; I shall lie”; but I have absolutely no idea what he means by “I am lying.” Something similar is the view of those who think that the foundation of knowledge must rest on the proposition “I think,” from which they infer, “Therefore I exist.” If this is so, I plainly confess that I know nothing; for I shall say emptily and without any meaning attached, “I think,” although I have never had, nor been able to attain, this thought.

205. Giselinus noted that the wise Socrates, when almost his entire body had grown cold after drinking the poison, said: “Crito, we owe a cock to Aesculapius, because he was departing from this life as though recovering from an illness.” Aesculapius is a god of the sickbed; for physicians are called *clinici* by Martial and others because they customarily sit beside the beds of the sick, or assist those fastened to their beds—for these are properly called *clinici*, from the Greek word κλινικός (*klinikos*). Hence come *clinice*, the practice of medicine, and among ecclesiastical writers *clinici*, those who, lying in bed because of illness, were washed with the water of baptism; many delayed this as long as they could, often until the very moment of death, and were rightly criticized for it by the holy Fathers.

207. Vat. B, Mar., Prag., Rat., Gis. in the margin, and Weitz. have *convertunt*, “they turn,” instead of *cum ventum*, “when one has come.” Weitzius distinguishes *convertunt turbidulos sensus*, “they turn their confused thoughts”; this works reasonably well. Prag. has *arcis*, “of the citadel”; in the margin, *artis*, “of art.”

[Col. 0940C] 208. Bonon. and Egm. have *turpidulos* instead of *turbidulos*. From *turpis* one would form *turpiculos*, rather than *turpidulos*.

209. Vat. A has *concludent*, “they will conclude,” less suitably.

211. Planets are wandering stars; therefore they are called planets, or wandering stars, because they are not fixed in the same manner as the other stars. You may disregard the gloss that argues otherwise, just as in the passage above, verse 203, where it derives *labyrinthus* from “labor within.” This is an inept eagerness to fabricate etymologies, common among ancient writers, even learned ones, such as Varro and others. See what Becmannus argues on this subject in *On the Origin of the Latin Language*, concerning the proper meaning of words, against those who derive *diabolus* from two “balls,” *locusta* from the fact that it has long legs like a spear—an etymology found in Isidore—*colossus* from “worshiping bones,” and countless inventions of this kind. For Zachaeus Faber’s impudence was intolerable: after shortening the *a* in *examen*, he dared to insist that *examen* came from ἐξ and ἀμήν, in order to conclude that the *a* in *examen* could be short. Certain posthumous works of the most celebrated Thomas Serrano, together with his life written with singular elegance and judgment by the distinguished Michael Garcia, have recently appeared, containing a sharp epigram on a similar matter directed against Ferrius.

212. In Rat., an inept corrector, after erasing the earlier words, substituted *quadrupes modo non sit ille sed*, “provided that he is not merely a quadruped, but.” He thought that the *e* in *quadrupes* could not be short: *modo quadrupes ille non sit, et*, “provided that he is not merely that quadruped, and.” See the prologue. In the Parmese edition this verse is defective, for it ends in this way: *Non recipit natura hominis, modo quadrupes*, “human nature does not accept it, provided he is a quadruped.” The word *ille* was omitted through the printer’s negligence.

214. Prag. has *regnum*, “kingdom,” for *regimen*, “governance.”

215. There is an error in Vat. A: *studet ipse*, “he himself studies.” Gis. in the margin has *suspexit*, “looked up,” for *sibi sensit*, “perceived for himself.”

216. Vat. B, Mar. in its first hand, Rat., Weitz., Widm., and Bong. have *Cottus* above, referring to Prag.’s error *Coitus*. Isidore likewise adopted the gloss, “whence the Cottian Alps.” Therefore Heinsius should not have been so displeased with this reading. Prudentius mentions the Cottians in the hymn of Saint Lawrence, verse 539: “across the ridges of the Cottians.” They were so called after Cottius, king of the Gauls under Augustus. Giselinus found *Gothus*, “Goth,” in the common editions, which he rejected because everyone unanimously shortens the first syllable of *Gothus*, and this entirely convinced Chamillardus. [Col. 0941C] Yet it is known that it can also be lengthened; for Latins sometimes call that nation *Guttones* and *Gotti*, “Guttones” and “Goths,” to say nothing of the Greeks, who vary no less in writing the word. *Gothus* is found in Mar. in its second hand, in Bongars. in its first hand, and in Fabr. But Heinsius with his manuscripts, together with Gis., Ald., Pal., Alex., Vat. Q, and Bonon., has *Scotus* or *Scottus*, “Scot.” Giselinus proves the ferocity of the Scots by the authority of Saint Jerome, Book II against Jovinianus; from this it is certainly clear that they were worse than a war-dog, that is, a Molossian or camp dog, as Chamillardus explains it. For camp dogs, since they are accustomed to feed on the flesh of those killed in wars, are generally cruel and savage. This ferocity may also be attributed to the ancient inhabitants of the Cottian Alps, which were notorious for brigandage. The Cottian Alps divide the Dauphiné from Piedmont. There was also a promontory in Mauretania Tingitana called Cottes or Cotes, known to the Spaniards as Cabo esparto.]

[Col. 0939A] 421. “Aristotle, by twisted turning, wove the sinews.

Although an intricate labyrinth and winding error

Drive all these men around, although they themselves are accustomed

[205] To promise a hen or a cock, so that the god of the sickbed

May deign to show himself favorable to the dying:

422. Nevertheless, when they have come to the standard of reason and art,

They conclude, by confused thoughts and contentious

Arguments in difficult forms, that the divinity is one:

[210] [Col. 0940A] That by whose will the mobile, rounded sphere

May revolve, and the wandering stars preserve their courses.

Human nature does not admit, provided that he is not merely a quadruped

And looks upon heavenly things with an uplifted face,

That he should deny the power of supreme governance.

[215] 423 This even Numa’s silent haruspex himself perceived.”

He considers the half-beast Cottus worse than a soldier-dog. [Note: [Col. 0941B]

218. *Coram*: in person, actually, I.

221. *Lacunas*: holes, cavities, caves, fissures, scars, pits; he inserts himself among the apostles. For in the Gospel of Thomas he is read to have said to the one who still scarcely believed: “Put your finger in,” etc.; but, gazing at the marks of the nails, he did not dare touch him, but said: “My Lord and my God.” He is therefore said to have put his hand into his side, although he did not do so, because, had the Lord commanded it, he could have done it, I.

223. *Abjurare*: to renounce, deny, remove.—*Titulum*: title, praise, or power, I.

224. *Regem*: the King, Christ, I.

226. *Summae*: of heavenly things; *mediae*: of earthly things; *imae*: of those below, in the underworld, I. The highest, lowest, and middle order, that is: the middle order is in man; the highest order is in angels; the lowest in the smallest animals. Hence Solomon [Col. 0942B], speaking of Christ under the figure of Wisdom, says: “Reaching from end to end,” that is, governing from the highest angel to the smallest little worm, Vat. A.

228. *Stygis*: of hell, I.

229. *Defluit*: descends.—*In se*: when he ascended to heaven; *in unum*: into one, I.

231. *Munia*: duties, offices.—*Pronae*: human, I.

232. *Replicata*: restored, brought back, repaired; or *artus*: limbs, I.

233. *Subvehat*: raise to heavenly things, to heaven, I.

234. *Organa*: voices, I.

236. *Heroum*: of the prophets.—*Orsa*: sayings, or the words of heroes or prophets, I. *Dicta*: sayings, expressions, Vat. A.]

[Note: [Col. 0941B]

218. Bonon. has, ineptly, *cordis* for *coram*. Nor is Pal. better, with *fidem* for *fide*.

219. Ald., Egm., and Vat. A in the first hand have *quinque* for *quique*; the latter reading must be retained.

220. Perhaps he hints at a thought expressed more clearly by himself elsewhere, concerning the twofold wound in the side.

221. Prag. has *atque manum*, perhaps *atque manu*, or it understands: “we thrust our fingers in, and our hand.” The common and correct reading is *et manuum*, that is, the gaps or fissures of the hands.

222. In Rat., some little pedant substituted *veneramur* for *cognovimus*, lest *Iesum* should be a disyllable beginning with a vowel. Enough has been said about this in the prolegomena. Ennodius likewise used it in Book II, Epigram 34: “He receives the offering, to whom Jesus granted forgiveness.” On the perpetual kingdom of Christ, see the holy Fathers everywhere, and Jerome most extensively in his Commentary on chapter I of the Epistle to the Ephesians.

223. Vat. A and Pal. have *Deum*, incorrectly.

226. Gifanius, in the Index to Lucretius under the word “PROVERBIA APUD LUCRETIUM,” corrects *regionis* for *rationis*, because, as he says, the words *regionis* and *rationis* are often corrupted into one another through scribal error [Col. 0942C]. Heinsius conjectured *stationis*, a word that often signifies authority. Chamillardus did not understand Heinsius: the latter asserted that the manuscripts consistently supported the reading *rationis*, whereas Chamillardus thought that the manuscripts supported *stationis*, and accordingly embraced *stationis*. Cellarius recognized that *stationis* was Heinsius’s conjecture; nevertheless, he followed *stationis* against the books. I make no alteration, since all the manuscript witnesses and editions resist it; and *rationis* is correctly used. The poet means nothing other than what he explains in the following verses: “He has the middle of flesh, the summit of the Father, and the lowest depth of Styx.” Here are the highest, middle, and lowest orders. Do you wish to hear another explanation? The same poet says shortly afterward: “He is God, and he is man, and he becomes dead, and the same is God; he traverses all the duties of submissive nature.” Now, to explain these three duties, *rationis* is a more suitable word than either *regionis* or *stationis*. Compare the glosses.

[Col. 0942D] 228. In Vat. A something has been erased, in place of which a later hand wrote *imum*.

230. Bong., Vat. B, Mar., and Rat. have *et fit*. Others omit *et*.

232. Ald. and Egm. have *et*. Others have *ut*. Heinsius, from Put., Thuan., Noms., and the second hand of Rott., restored *sursum* for *rursum* in the others, although the latter could also be defended with some justification: “for above and again he revolves into himself.” Urb. has *rursum*; Alex. and Vat. Q have *sursum*, together with Bonon.

233. He persists in the same thought. God brings back to heaven the restored duties—those that had been dead—or his body raised from the dead, or the bodies of other saints. He also raises the limbs themselves, namely his flesh; concerning it he said above, “he has the middle of flesh, and becomes man.”]

[Col. 0941A] But we, who have already seen the Lord twice, in books and in the body,

first by faith, then in flesh and blood, in person,

and who, with the cross as witness, have examined the books of the prophets,

[220] have thrust our fingers into the raw wounds of his ribs,

and, with sight uncertain, scrutinized the gaps in his hands,

424 have recognized Jesus as the eternal King.

We believe it impious to deny God the title

and paternal name of him who brought forth the King from himself,

[225] not the king of the Parthian people or of the descendants of Romulus,

but the King of the highest, middle, and lowest order,

and therefore Lord of all things and King over everything.

[Col. 0942A] He has the middle of flesh, the summit of the Father, and the lowest depth of Styx.

He descends through these degrees and again revolves into himself.

[230] He is God, and he is man, and he becomes dead, and the same is God.

He traverses all the duties of submissive nature,

425 so that he may bear back to the Father’s embrace above

those things that had been dead, once restored, and may also raise up the limbs themselves.

When the instruments of the ancient prophets had sung

[235] that these things would come to pass,

we experienced them with eyes, hands, encounter, voice, and speech,

and at last understood the utterances of the ancient prophets,

the oracles made plain when Christ was seen. [Note: [Col. 0943B]

243. Thus nevertheless, we follow.—Three names.—*Separe*: separate, set apart; *separ* is said like *compar* and *dispar*.—*Ductu*: by leading, by increase, or by being led, I.

244. *Tres*: substances.—*Tribus*: persons, I.

246. *Innato*: the Father.—*Sata*: born, I.

248. *Per quam*: insofar as, how greatly.—*Futile*: empty, vain.—*Natus*: born as if from himself; *natus quasi ut ex se*—that is, that he, the Son, should be, [Col. 0944B] I.

249. *Natus*: born from another.—*Ipse*: the Son, Iso.

250. *Nova*: marvelous, I.

251. *Ediderit*: begotten, I.

252. *Vocabula*: words, verses, I.

256. *Indiscreta*: undivided, I.

257. *Vim*: power, strength.—*Generosus*: noble, I.]

[Note: [Col. 0943B]

241. Note the very ancient custom of invoking the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit in the doxology of the Trinity: “Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit.” I discussed this doxology in my dissertation on ecclesiastical hymns, no. 229 and following.

243. See Preface 1, verse 1: “God is the threefold summit.” In Prag. and Mar., for the variant reading, there is *ut non* instead of *ut ne*. Prag. has *dictu* for *ductu*, which should be retained.

244. Prag. incorrectly has *faciat* for *faciam*. Jerome, Letter 57: “The one Godhead subsists in three persons.” Most theologians rightly deny a fourth subsistence in God. Petavius is of the same opinion; in Book IV, chapter 12, of *On the Trinity*, he discusses at length whether there is in God a certain fourth subsistence, and, in support of the denying position, cites these very words of Prudentius, no. 3. Tournely likewise, in his *Theological Lectures*, question 5 on the Trinity, article 1, asks whether three relative subsistences and one absolute subsistence common to the three persons are to be admitted in God, and states the question thus: “Some, with Cajetan, Part I, questions 29, article 4, and 39, article 43, and Suarez, Book IV, chapter 4, admit four subsistences, namely one absolute and three relative. Others … commonly acknowledge only three relative subsistences and no absolute one; to this opinion, as the more common, we subscribe.” Bertius too, although in reality he recognizes an absolute subsistence in God, nevertheless concludes, for a certain diplomatic reason, in Book IX, chapter 6: “We judge that those theologians think more correctly who, when asked about this question, answer that there are only three relative subsistences in God.” If someone now asks me whether there are theologians who defend, in addition to the three relative subsistences, some subsistence common to God, I shall first answer that even from these words alone, which I have cited in support of my position, it is sufficiently clear that not a few theologians think so. Then I shall produce the assertion of the most eminent Cardinal Gotti, *On the Trinity*, question 4, doubt 2: “In addition to the three relative subsistences, there is in God an absolute subsistence, by which God, conceived prior to the three persons, subsists in himself. Saint Augustine indicated this … but Saint Thomas taught it explicitly.” I could add a hundred other theologians, if I wished to spend an hour and a half sifting dusty volumes, so that one might now rightly doubt whether there are more theologians who deny that there is a fourth subsistence in God or those who affirm it. I would explain more fully what difference there is between the notion of subsistence and that of person, and why, although only three persons are admitted in the Trinity, a fourth subsistence can be defended, if I were writing theological textbooks. I ought not to omit these few remarks, so as to oblige those who, with a friendly disposition toward me, desired some explanation. For the voices of others would have moved me little—those who dare, in the street-corner gatherings of the most ignorant men, to chatter about the most holy mysteries of our religion, things they have never learned. Some among them are so ignorant that, as Ammianus said of similar people in Book XXX, they do not remember ever having possessed books, and if the name of an ancient author happens to arise in a circle of learned men, they suppose it to be the name of some unfamiliar fish or food.

248. Before Heinsius, the printed editions arranged the verses thus: *Sive Pater natus fuerit, sive ipse repente, / Perquam ridiculum est et futile, natus ut ex se / Nascendi nova materies, ac se Deus ultro / Ediderit, natumque sibi se fecerit ipsum*—“Whether the Father should have been born, or whether he himself should suddenly become, born from himself, a new source of birth, and God should freely have brought himself forth and made himself his own son.” Weitzius and Mariettus noted nothing against this from the manuscripts. Teolius says that three or four Vatican manuscripts favor Heinsius, the rest Weitzius. Heinsius found in all his manuscripts that *Perquam ridiculum* preceded *Sive Pater*. In Put. the latter stood as *Sive supernatus fuerit sibi ipse repente*. Heinsius therefore proposed: *Perquam ridiculum est et futile, natus ut ex se / Sive supernatus fuerit, sibi ipse repente / Nascendi nova materies*. For *supernasci* (“to be born over or above”) is an elegant verb used by Pliny, and the hiatus *sibi ipse* is familiar to Prudentius. Vat. A likewise has *sibi ipse*. Heinsius conjectures that *sibi et ipse* may also be possible. Cellarius followed Heinsius in retaining that hiatus, which I do not approve here. Alex. agrees with Heinsius’s manuscripts; Urb. and Vat. Q with the old editions. Vat. Q also has *sibi ipse*, but erroneously *per quem* for *perquam*. Bonon. erroneously has *sive et ipse*.

252. Vat. B has *ni* instead of the less suitable *nil*.

254. Teolius, against the metre, reads *Filius, auctore quod genitus sit Patre summo*, and claims that the better Vatican manuscripts have this; Heinsius’s notes say something slightly different. I think Teolius slipped and intended to write *Filius, auctore ut genitus quod*. With Put., Heinsius printed *Filius, auctore genitus*, which gives an adequate sense. Heinsius conjectures that Prudentius wrote *tum Filius ex hoc, Filius auctore ut genitus qui sit Patre summo*. Vat. A has the senseless *si* for *sit*. Aldus punctuates wrongly: *tum Filius ex hoc. Filius auctore ut genitus quod sit Patre summo*. Saint Hilary very often calls the Father the *auctor* (“source” or “author”) of the Son. Among jurists, an *auctor* is one from whom a right passes to us. See Petavius, vol. II, Book V, chapter 5.

257. In Weit., the error is *generosus patriae*.]

[Col. 0943A] This is our salvation; from this we live, from this we draw breath.

This we follow: never, with the name of the Son removed,

[240] to call the Father “Father”; and never, without the Father’s name,

to know the God who was born; never to call him Son or Father

unless the holy and one Spirit be present.

Yet these three are so constituted that I do not separate them by distinction

and make three; but in these three God remains one.

[245] Nor is the Father himself the Son: since we know

that the Son was born from the Unborn, he is truly Father,

and the offspring truly born; nor is the Son himself his own begetter.

[Col. 0944A] 426 It is utterly ridiculous and vain that the Father, born from himself, should have been born, or that he himself should suddenly become a new source of birth,

[250] and that God should of his own will have brought himself forth and made himself his own son.

No false or deceptive words invent divine names.

He who is Father is Father by begetting; then the Son from him

is Son, begotten by the highest Father as begetter;

[255] yet he himself is also highest: for he is neither lesser nor unlike the Father.

Thus in both there is an undivided form of operation,

unless the noble Son possessed the whole power of the Father’s majesty. [Note: [Col. 0945B]

259. *Ulterius*: farther, beyond what is permitted, I.

260. *Gignere*: spiritual generation.—*Fas*: right, just, I.

262. *Super*: beyond, above.—*Principium*: the world, Vat. A.

264. *Via*: method, reason, I.

265. *Semina*: beginnings.—*Mortali*: to man, I.

266. *Ultra*: before, beyond.—*Pacto*: by law, or manner, I.

268. *Traditur*: in the Scriptures, I.

271. *Retro*: eternally; here a verb in the past tense, I.

[Col. 0946B] 272. *Decisus*: cut off, shortened, or truncated, diminished, I.

273. *Extendens*: expanding, by dilation.—*Tractim*: gradually, little by little, I.

275. *Mutata*: changed, effected.—*Procudit*: or *producit*, “brings forth,” that is, generates or fashions; “begot.”—*Portio*: substance, I.

276. *Unquam*: ever—but certainly, I.

277. *Atqui*: but he, nevertheless, I.

280. *Proditus*: brought forth, distributed, or manifested, I.]

[Note: [Col. 0945B]

258. In most editions the question mark after *esset* is missing; as a result, the sense is confused.

259. Egm. and Vat. B have *quod*. *Quid* must be read. Petavius, in the cited place, chapter 6, says that the modesty of the ancient, most holy and learned theologians in investigating the causes of this mystery is to be praised and imitated, and he cites these verses of Prudentius, by which freer-thinking minds are chastened.

260. Weitz. with Egm., Pal., and Oxon. has *gressus* for the variant reading; Vat. B in the first hand. The others have *sensus*.

[Col. 0945C] 262. Vat. A and Pal. incorrectly have *sprevit* for *praevenit*.

264. Lucretius records that philosophers came to ruin over the principles of things, Book I. In our own age the same difficulty in knowing the beginnings of things is felt, whatever those who embrace certain new systems—or restore systems already antiquated and obsolete—may say.

265. Put. has *qui*, that is, “by what method,” for *cui mortali*. In either form the sense is clear.

268. Aldus reads *quod traditur esse Deumque / Non genitus genitor generaverit*. Fabricius and Giselinus, followed by Cellarius, read *quod traditur esse Deus, quem*; the better Heinsian manuscripts and ours read *esse Deum, quem*. Petavius himself acknowledged that the theological doctrine concerning divine generation, which he treated at length, is contained in these few verses; see his words at no. 255 of the prolegomena. Truly remarkable is our poet’s theology.

269. Rat. less suitably has *generaverat* for *generaverit*. Put. and Rot. have *generavit*, perhaps “he has begotten both one and the other.” But the common reading is better. Teolius printed *generavit*, but since the law of meter opposes it and he noted nothing from the manuscripts, I think it is a typographical error.

271. Weitzius, Vat. B, and Mar. read *Et comperpetuum retro Patri, sed Patre natum* (“co-eternal from eternity with the Father, yet born from the Father”). Giselinus and Bong. read *Et comperpetuum Patri retro, sed Patre natum*. Egm. reads *Et comperpetuum retro Patris, et Patre natum*. Weitzius and Heinsius cite Aldus for the latter reading; but my Aldus has *Et comperpetuum retro Patris, sed Patre natum*. Put., Thuan., and the other Heinsian witnesses agree with Egmondanus. Heinsius thinks the original was *Et comperpetuum Patri retro, et Patre natum*. All these readings may be admitted and have the same sense. *Comperpetuus Patris*, in the matter of begetting, is not inaptly said, just as the manuscripts below have *coaeternus Patris*. Urb. and Alex. likewise have *Patris*. Vat. Q erroneously has *cum perpetuum*.

273. Vat. A has *tractum*. Egm. has *tactim*; I correct it to *tractim*.

274. Rat. incorrectly has *minuit vel*. Some heretics taught that God was constituted from the three persons of the Trinity in such a way that each of them was not fully God but a portion of God. Lamius, in his work *On the Correct Faith of the Nicene Fathers*, using these verses of Prudentius and other passages by other authors, explicitly proves that the Son originated from the Father, but not through cutting off, division, or alteration of the same substance.

275. In the copy of Weitzius that I use, *portio* is written in the margin from an old book.

276. The First Council of Toledo, in the rule of faith mentioned elsewhere, canon 7: “If anyone says or believes that the divinity of Christ is changeable—or generable—or passible, let him be anathema.” These words then began to come into use for refuting heresies and explaining the sacred mysteries of religion without ambiguity. I know of no one older than Prudentius who used *demutabilis*.

277. Aldus has *atque*. Others have *atqui*. Vat. A has *atquin*.

278. In Vat. A: *totus ex toto*, against the meter. Read: *totus, et ex toto*. Corippus, Book IV: “Born, not made, full light from light.” Saint Methodius the martyr, or another confessor, in *On Simeon and Anna*: “You are true light from true light.” The words of the Creed are well known.

280. Gifanius, from an old manuscript, has *prodigus* for *proditus*, “a fire abundant, lavish, and copious.” Aldus and three more recent manuscripts of Heinsius likewise have it. Others have *proditus*, as in Ovid: “He who is always brought forth by his own light,” although Heinsius here interprets “the fire brought forth,” which is then extended, as Nonius explains the Vergilian phrase, “the race would spring from the high blood of Teucer.” Vat. Q and Alex., in a second hand, have *prodigus*. In Urb. the whole passage beginning *quando est* is missing, as is *prodigus ignis / Ignem diminuat*. Peveratus, following Gifanius, approves *prodigus* and thinks it is used in the same sense as “luxuriant crops” in Virgil.]

[Col. 0945A] The Son—and that he, God the begetter, should be a son?

427 They continue farther, examining what this very act of begetting is,

[260] if it is lawful for human minds to stretch

as far as the mystery that precedes all times and days,

rises above the very beginning,

and surpasses whatever man can ask.

Since the way to know the seeds of beginnings is difficult,

[265] to what mortal will it be granted to inquire what God did

before the beginning? Or by what manner

did he bring forth the Word that has no beginning at all?

This alone we know, as tradition hands it down: that there is a God

[Col. 0945B] whom the Unbegotten Begetter has begotten, one and one,

[270] [Col. 0946A] whole and whole, not begun, but nevertheless born,

and co-eternal backward with the Father, yet born from the Father.

428 Nor is the Father cut off, so that the Son might be a part of the Father;

nor did an extending substance gradually produce itself

or diminish anything from the full Godhead,

[275] when the changed portion brought forth the newly born.

God is neither convertible nor ever changeable,

nor does he take anything from himself by begetting; but, nevertheless,

he is wholly God and God from the whole, light from light.

When does light exist without light? When does shining

[280] light lack radiance? When is the fire brought forth— [Note: [Col. 0947B]

282. *Olim*: eternally, without beginning, Iso.

290. *Tu*: you, Sabellian, I.

292. *Thurifero*: burning incense.—*Deucalionum*: gods, idols. Deucalion and his wife sowed stones; hence men and women, I.

293. *Devotus*: bowed down.—*Cippo*: to a stump or to the god himself.—*Unctor*: worshiper, I.

296. *Scriptoris*: of Moses.—*Bardus*: foolish; from the elephant, *baburrus*, foolish.—*Augur*: one who observes the chatter or omen of birds.—*Bardus*: foolish; from the elephant, Vat. T.

[Col. 0948B] 297. *Nutrix*: old woman, I.

298. *Sago*: magical or prophetic; *praescienti*: magical or wise, I.

299. *Rem*: the divine state.—*Coram*: openly, publicly.—*Proditus*: manifested, I.

300. *Trepidum*: fearful.—*Mortalem*: Moses.—*Amico*: friendly, amicable, I.

301. *Retexit*: unveiled, unveiled previously, I.

302. *Meminit*: teaches, I.

305. *Condens*: creating, I.]

[Note: [Col. 0947B]

281. Aldus, with the others, writes *deminuat*.

282. Rat. arranges the words thus: “not the father of light, and he is God.” Giselinus, first edition: “not the God of light, but is he the Father?” Perhaps *aut pater*.

290. Mar., Widm., and Bong. have *dubites*.

292. He calls the pagans “from the incense-burning herd” in the sense in which Optatus used *thurificare* and Cyprian *thurificatos*. The gloss read: “Deucalion sowed stones, and his wife sowed them.” I restored the order of the words. He uses *Deucaliones* in the plural to express contempt. See verse 189. In the hymn of Saint Romanus there is likewise mention of Pyrrha, Deucalion’s wife. Thus the tyrant Asclepiades says at verse 410: “Do you wish to know the whole power of things? Consult Pyrrha.”

293. Oxon. and Ald. have *ficulni stipitis*. Pal. above has *auctor* for *unctor*: this is correct. On the rite of anointing idols, priests, lights, and sacred fires with oil, see Johann Wilhelm Stuckius, *Description of Pagan Sacred Rites*, folio 55 verso. Peveratus brings here from the hymn of Saint Romanus, verse 260, the phrase “sooty household gods,” since among the pagans the images of the gods formerly became blackened with smoke and perfumes.

295. Fabr., Alex., Prag., have *percurre et scrinia*, as Giselinus and other printed editions do, together with Urb. and Vat. Q. But Aldus, Weitz., Put., Vat. A and B, Mar., and most of the best witnesses have *percurre scrinia*. It was likewise in Rat.; but a recent corrector changed it to *percurrens scrinia*, falsely believing that the final *e* in *percurre* could not be lengthened.

296. Vat. B has *pardus*; Prag. *barrus*: both are false for *bardus*. Properly, *bardus* means slow-witted, foolish. Chamillardus, from Festus, notes that in Gaul a singer was called *bardus*, from the people of the Bards. The poet perhaps alludes to what he said earlier: “Numa’s half-beast haruspex, Cottus.” The gloss of Isidore, “from the elephant,” and afterward *baburrus*, indicates that he read *barrus*, which means elephant, and that *barrus* should be read for *baburrus*. Two peoples called Bards are recorded: some are the Bards or Lombards in Germany, where the Brandenburg March is now located; others are the Bards and Bardaic peoples in Gaul.

298. Giselinus, first edition, has *saga*, incorrectly. The ancients called the crow an augur of water because they thought that by its cry it not only foretold rain but summoned it. The poet ridicules such superstitions. *Sagus* as an adjective occurs in inscriptions.

301. Weitz., Vat. B, Mar., Rat., and Prag. have *eloquio*. Aldus and Giselinus have *alloquio*. Heinsius observed nothing concerning this word in his own manuscripts, following Giselinus.

303. Some printed editions have *ne sine* for *nec sine*, but the latter is required by the sense.

[Col. 0948C] 304. Prudentius often uses *factura* for “creature,” as Barthius notes can reasonably be done in *Adversaria*, Book XLII, chapter 8, although more refined writers reject such usage. Sedulius likewise, Book II: “Unless that merciful sower were ready to pardon sins, though slow to repay, lest his own creation perish.” Alcimus Avitus, Book I: “The creation itself pleases its watching craftsman,” and often elsewhere. Gregory of Baetica does so more than once; Tertullian calls it *factitamentum* in *On the Soul*, chapter 18.

305. He draws an argument for proving the mystery of the Trinity from Genesis, chapter I, where God created man in his own image and likeness. The theologians reason as follows: “When God says, ‘Let us make man in our image and likeness,’ he speaks in the plural number; therefore, by the word ‘let us make,’ a single divine person alone cannot be understood. But when he says ‘in the image and likeness,’ the unity of nature is declared.” Saint Basil forcefully concludes that there are several persons in his nineteenth homily on the *Hexaemeron*: “What craftsman, bronze-worker, woodworker, or certainly shoemaker, works entirely alone, without any other person cooperating with him, seated among the instruments of his craft—who, I ask, mutters to himself alone, saying, ‘Let us make a sword,’ or ‘Let us construct a plow,’ or ‘Let us prepare a shoe,’ rather than silently carrying out, when he wishes, the operation suited to his craft?” Saint Hilary, on Genesis: “‘Let us make,’ he says, ‘man.’ Tell me, excellent one, with whom are you now speaking? It is clear that even then the Son is seated beside you on a lofty throne.” Prudentius reaches the same conclusion by another route. God made man in the image of God. What else does this mean except that the Word is distinct from the Father, yet is God and the image of the Father? We explained at verse 72 that the Word is the form and image of the Father. Tertullian, *Against Praxeas*, chapter 12: “And God made man; he made him in the image of God. Why not his own image, if the one who made was alone and there was no one whose image he was making? There was, however, one whose image he was making—namely the Son.” And chapter 6 of *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*: “Thus that clay, already then taking on the image of the Christ who was to come in the flesh, was not merely God’s work but also a pledge.” Many of the ancients teach that man was formed in the image of the Word; Petavius cites them in Book II of *On the Work of the Six Days*, while observing that Augustine dislikes this opinion in Book XII of *On the Trinity*, chapter 6. See the commentators, some of whom hold that the image of God is the Son and the likeness the Holy Spirit.]

[Col. 0947A] 429 Does it diminish the fire? When is the Father, God, and light

not the God of light, and the Father? If once he was not Father

and begot late, after the birth of time,

he becomes new and advances into a new status. Away with the thought

[285] that the Full One should ever advance, who needs no increase.

He was always God, begetter, light, and glory;

nor did he later acquire for himself the status of Father.

Thus we believe Christ eternal with the Father,

begotten by him as author, who had no author before him.

[290] If you doubt these mysteries of Christ the Son,

wretched man, you do not belong to the Catholic people;

[Col. 0948A] rather, you are one of the incense-burning herd,

devoted to the pillar of the Deucalions,

an anointer of a fig-tree trunk.

Instead, search out the seals of God in the very

[295] source of antiquity; examine the archives of the first

430 writer, whom no foolish father or grandfather who was an augur,

no tale of ancient fame or garrulous nurse,

no babbling diviner with magical muttering, nor shrill crow,

taught about the matter of God; but God himself,

[300] revealed openly, gently imbued the fearful mortal

with friendly speech, and unveiled himself and his supreme nature.

Surely the most learned writer remembers that, at the beginning

of the world, the Father did not form the new image of creation

alone and without Christ.

[305] “God,” he says, “the Creator, made man and gave him”— [Note: [Col. 0949B]

306. *Ora*: face, countenance, image, Iso.

307. *Deo Deus*: God from God; the Son from the Father, I.

311. *Saecula*: at the end of the ages, I.

315. *Genealogus*: reckoner of descent, that is, Moses, the writer speaking about generation, I.

322. *Stupidas*: from *stupere*, to be astonished.—*Fibras*: the veins of the heart, I.

[Col. 0950B] 326. *Suo*: his own, I.

327. *Dux*: Moses.—*Monte*: Sinai, I.

328. *Alloquioque*: he shone from conversing with God, I.

329. *Incisas*: written, engraved.—*Caeca*: blind, unbelieving, I.

332. *Praestricta*: surrounded, I.]

312. An imitation of Virgil, *Georgics* I, verse 176: “I can recount many ancient precepts to you, if you do not shrink from them.”

313. Ald. incorrectly has *non Patre*.

315. Ald. has *ille ait*, namely, “that same genealogist.” But the *e* in *ille* must not be elided.

316. Heinsius found *flamma* in Cauchianus; in the other older manuscripts, *flammam*, which he considers more harmonious with the Vulgate reading *flammas*. The editions and our manuscripts have *flammas*. Chamillardus and Cellarius copy Heinsius: the passage from Genesis is chapter XIX, verse 24: “Then the Lord rained upon Sodom and Gomorrah sulfur and fire from the Lord out of heaven.” Many—Ignatius, Justin, Irenaeus, Tertullian, Cyprian, Athanasius, Ambrose, Augustine, and others, besides the Council of Sirmium against Photinus—taught Prudentius’s interpretation. See Browerus, page 140, on Fortunatus, Book V, poem 5, verse “The Son and the Father is from the Lord, Lord,” where he teaches that Fortunatus followed the traces of his predecessors, especially Prudentius, no less a Christian than a chaste poet.

320. Vat. A incorrectly has *flumen*. In Rat. a bold corrector inserted *sed idem sunt utraque fulmen* (“but both are one thunderbolt”). Prag. in the margin, and Cauchius, have *uterque*. Fabr. and Giselinus, first edition, likewise. The true reading is *sunt unum fulmen utraque*. Why the *a* in *utraque* is lengthened, see the prolegomena. Prudentius seems to interpret as lightning the sulfur and fire that the Lord rained down. Josephus, Book I, chapter 11, reports that God hurled lightning bolts at those cities; since they abounded in sulfur and bitumen, they could easily have been consumed by lightning and heavenly fire.

321. The manuscripts of Heinsius, Alex., Mar., Rat., Aldus, and others have this title: “Against the Jews”; others omit it. Giselinus in the margin has *Judaei*.

322. Vat. B, Mar., Weit., and Sich. have *aut possent*. Aldus, [Col. 0950B] Giselinus, Vat. Q, and several manuscripts of Heinsius have *ut possent*. Put., Noms., and Palat. have *ut possint*.

324. Matthew, chapter XV, verse 24.

325. Exodus XXXII, 2. Tertullian, *Scorpiace*, chapter 3: “Aaron is pressed, and orders the earrings of their women to be brought into the fire. For they were about to lose, as a judgment upon themselves, the true ornaments of their ears, the words of God.” In Vat. A, *et* was added after *caput* by a later hand, since it had been missing. Several authors report that the Hebrews fashioned only the head of a calf, not the entire calf, as may be seen in the dissertation of François Monceius on the golden calf, Book I, chapter 21; he rejects this opinion and holds instead that, in Aaron’s mind, the calf was a cherub in the form of a winged calf.

327. Exodus XXXI. See hymn 6, verse 36 and following, *Cath.*

330. The poet demonstrates the blindness of the Jews from many passages of Sacred Scripture. Exodus XX: the Jews, terrified and shaken with fear, refused to hear God speaking, but listened to Moses. Likewise, Exodus XXXIV: when they saw Moses’ horned face, they feared to approach, and Moses placed a veil over his face. Chamillardus astutely concludes that, if the poet had this narrative in mind, he was certainly mistaken: we read only that Moses veiled his own face. But Prudentius borrowed the interpretation of this passage from the Apostle, II Corinthians, chapter III, verses 13 and following: “And not as Moses put a veil over his face, so that the children of Israel might not look intently at the face of that which was passing away. But their minds were dulled. For to this day the same veil remains unrevealed in the reading of the Old Testament, because it is abolished in Christ. But to this day, whenever Moses is read, a veil lies over their heart. But whenever it turns to the Lord, the veil will be removed.” I think Prudentius also had in mind John, chapter XVIII, verse 6, where Jesus, sought by the Jews for execution, after Jesus said “I am he,” they went backward and fell to the ground.

331. Vat. A and Egm. incorrectly have *regis in effigie*.

332. In Vat. A the error is *luee* for *luce*. For *praestricta*, manuscripts Vat. A and B, as well as others, have *perstricta*. Giselinus in the margin has *perstrincta*.]

[Col. 0949A] 431 What else is “the face of God” than to say, “He was not alone”?

Was God assisting God as he worked,

when the Lord made the Lord’s image in the form of creation?

Christ is the form of the Father; we are the form and image of Christ.

[310] We are formed in the image of the Lord by the Father’s goodness,

for Christ would come into our image after the ages.

I can draw many examples from the sacred books,

if you do not shrink from them, to teach you that the power of majesty

was placed not in the Father alone, but that Christ with the Father

[315] is God—as the same genealogist says.

“The Lord rained flames from the Lord upon the people of Sodom.”

[Col. 0949B] 432 Which Lord? From which Lord? If the Father alone

[Col. 0950A] watches from the starry citadel, or blazes into anger,

the Son was the Lord who scattered the armed wrath

of the Lord Father with fires: the two together are one lightning bolt.

[320] If these things, so understood, had moistened Jewish ears

so that they could touch their senseless inner faculties,

they would have heard the Lord of hosts,

who had come to save the perishing sheep; but all ornament

[325] had flowed away from their ears, and they had already fashioned

the baked head of Baal and stripped their little ears

of their proper honor.

The leader of the sinful people comes from the mountain of flashing light,

shining from his conversation with God; and he carries the tablets,

engraved by a dreadful finger, to the blind tents.

[330] 433 But the people fall on their face, not destined to see

Christ written in the image of the profound Law through riddling figures.

Unhappy people, whose terrified eyes are dazzled by the light— [Note: [Col. 0951B]

333. Or he means the eyes of the mind and the veil placed over the heart; or he recounts what probably happened, namely, that the Jews themselves, terrified and confused by fear, also veiled their faces.

334. Ald., Gis., and Pal. have *rejecto*. Sich., Weitz., and our manuscripts have *detecto*; Heinsius made no observation concerning Giselinus’s *rejecto*, plainly following him. See the second Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter III, verse 18.

338. In the Parmese edition, a question mark is incorrectly placed at the end of this and the following verse. Virgil, Book II, verse 81 of the *Georgics*: “a tree with blessed branches.”

339. Virgil, in the same passage, verse 31: “an olive root.”]

340. The comparison expressed in the Epistle to the Romans, chapter 11, verse 17, is touched upon by Saint Augustine, *Exposition 1 on Psalm 58*: “The Jews therefore exist; they have not been killed; they are necessary for the Gentiles who believe. Why is this? So that God might demonstrate his mercy to us through our enemies. By grafting the wild olive into branches of pride that had been cut away, he demonstrated his mercy.” Saint Prosper, *On the Ungrateful*: “But you, O new people, who strip the stock of the old wild olive and grow into the branches of the sacred olive.”

342. *Pro se* is found in Vat. A, Mar., Rat., Egm., Pal., Widm., Bong., Sich.; but the sense requires *se*.

343. In Mar. the first hand has *sulculos*, incorrectly.

[Col. 0951D] “So that he might cover it, and veil his face with a tightly pressed garment!

But we, with the veil removed, behold Christ openly

[335] and contemplate God with an unveiled face.

Nor do we lie prostrate with downcast brow beneath the heavy law;

rather, with uplifted countenance we recognize the ray of the law.

Alas, once a leafy tree with fruitful branches,

alas, once an olive root rich in plump berries!

[340] Behold: now, with the wild olive grafted in, the trunk grows green again for you,

434 and is clothed with the bark of a foreign book.

Now take pity on yourself: let not the wild olive shoot,

exulting in another’s trunk, boast of itself;

but let it warn you, so that, mindful of your own stock, you may cease

[345] to sadden your branches with bitter oil,

[Col. 0951B] and not begrudge the shoots sent into the lofty treetops.

You blaspheme the Lord, most ungrateful people, Christ.

[Col. 0952A] Say, say: your Passover—whose blood makes the feast

so solemn for you? What lamb, at last, is slaughtered,

[350] a year old? That sacred one returns to you with the years;

but that the sacred thing is in an animal—such belief is foolish:

to touch the highest doorposts with the blood of a bleating creature,

to revel in dances, and to make unleavened bread of fine flour,

435 while your morals swell with the guilt of leaven.

[355] Do you not understand, foolish one, that you prefigure our Passover?

That every mystery is depicted in the prefatory furrows of the ancient law,

which the true Passion contains—

[Col. 0952B] the Passion that protects our forehead with blood

and anoints the bodily dwelling with a marked mouth?”

[Note: [Col. 0953B]

360. *Hanc*, “this dwelling,” I.

361. *Haec*, “this Passion.”—*Pharii*, Egyptians; sacrilegious. Egypt is called Pharos.—*Ferale*, poisonous, deadly.—*Resolvit*, because Christ’s Passion destroyed the devil’s power, I.

364. *In ore*, “upon the mouth,” [that is,] the forehead, I.

368. *Credens*, “believing”; *cernens*, “seeing,” I.

369. *Geris*, “you bear, you perform,” I.

371. *Feta*, “full of Christ’s mysteries,” I., Mar.
