345. Prudentius often uses *triste* in the sense of “bitter.” See *Cathemerinon*, hymn 5, verse 93. He warns the Jews not to look upon Christians with hostile eyes.

346. In Vat. A, *in* is missing. Put., first hand, has *caeca*, incorrectly. *Celsa* should be read.

349. You may read of rites of this kind in Exodus, chapter XII.

350. Vat. A has *agniculus*, incorrectly.

351. Gis., first edition, has *in pecude est*, with other common copies. Heinsius’s manuscripts and ours, as also Weitzius, omit *est*. Weitzius punctuates thus: *Sed sacer, in pecude stultum est sic credere sacrum*. Others: *Sed sacer in pecude, stultum est*. Giselinus corrected it thus in the errata of the second edition, observing that the Jewish Passover consists solely in an animal, since the lamb is no longer a type of the true Lamb. Put., first hand, has *Sed sacrum in pecude*. Elsewhere *Christum* is read for *sacrum*: *stultum est sic credere Christum*; this does not please me. Alex. has a question: *Sed sacer in pecude?*

353. Fabr. foolishly reads *Lascivire coris similaginis, azymon esse*. Mariettus says that Germans still call white bread made of fine flour *semel*. Chamillard thinks that Prudentius wrongly used *similaginis* for any bread, since *similago* is the finest and most highly esteemed part of flour, and unleavened loaves are neither pleasant to taste nor useful for nourishment. I am surprised that Chamillard failed to grasp Prudentius’s acuteness and excellent point. Prudentius attacks the practices of the Jews, who clung so obstinately to ancient rites that they committed many sins contrary to the spirit of the law: not only did they lead dances, but they also behaved wantonly; and although unleavened loaves ought to serve bodily affliction, they added luxuries by making them from fine flour. Thus Christians are rightly reproved when they seek luxuries in hair-shirts. The same custom belongs to modern Jews, who customarily make unleavened loaves not merely from fine flour, but sometimes make them more delicate, for the sick and for friends, by adding sugar, milk, and eggs. They call them *Mazab hascirab*, that is, “rich unleavened bread,” and sometimes share them with Christians. See Leo Modena, *De’ riti Ebraici*, and Calmet, *Dict. Biblic.*, under AZYMUS and PASCHA. Other holy Fathers described and censured the corrupted practices of the Hebrews in a similar manner.

354. *Fermentum* derives from *ferveo*; hence morals fermented by crime are rightly said to swell. Conversely, ecclesiastical writers commonly take *azymum* and “without leaven” to mean holy and without malice.

355. Ald. has *fingere*; others, *effingere*.

359. Vat. A incorrectly writes *collinitore* as one word for *collinit ore*. The poet speaks of the cross inscribed on foreheads in the sacrament of confirmation, though he chiefly commends the merits of the Passion of Jesus Christ. See *Cathemerinon*, hymn 3, verse 125 and following.]

[Col. 0953A] “This one escaped, when the Egyptian plague was driven away by scourging;

this one dissolved the deadly kingdom of the Pharian king,

and from the dense hailstorm of worldly power

rescued Abraham with his offspring and faithful people.

He is the true offspring of Abraham: in whose mouth blood

[365] 436 is believed to be present and glows when inscribed; for whom, throughout the world,

God is seen—God truly from the Father, without doubting faith.

He saw God and immediately believed what he had seen; but you,

offspring of the flesh, believing everything in a fleshly manner,

carry out the work of the flesh under the law, which the spirit

[370] within fulfills. For the fleshly law did not come down from heaven,

which you worship in the flesh; rather, it was pregnant with Christ,

and in its womb was to bear my Hope. What hope? None other than

the nourishing Light of Light, and the coming of the Lord, whom Abraham’s

[Col. 0954A] first faith had seen and the father had once promised to our eyes

[375] to behold and to be confirmed by the voice of the law.

Nor is it only the law: for what letter now exists that does not contain Christ,

or what storehouse of writings is not filled with praise of Christ,

celebrating new miracles in new books?

The Hebrew style composes; Attic eloquence composes;

[380] and the eloquence of the Ausonian tongue, a third language, composes.

437 Pilate, though ignorant, commands: ‘Go, scribe, and arrange’

in three written lines what power has been fixed there.

Let the title of the cross be threefold, in a threefold language.

Let Judea recognize it as she reads, and let Greece know it,

[385] and golden Rome, worshipping God, read it through.

Whatever the curved trumpet bellows, resounding in hollow bronze;

[Col. 0954B] whatever the mighty breath pours forth from its hidden intake;

whatever the chaste lyre, whatever the cithara, sends back an echo—”

[Note: [Col. 0953B]

360. Some Vulgate copies have *Aegypti*; Pal. has *Aegyptica*. Gis. in the text, Ald., Vat. A, Q, Thuan., Ox., Noms., Urb., and Sich. have *flagellis*. Some of Heinsius’s copies, Alex., and others have *procellis*, which Weitzius adopted. The scourges or lashes of Egypt are called *flagra* or *flagella* by Alcimus Avitus, book V, Gregory of Nazianzus, Fortunatus, and others; this supports the reading *flagellis*, especially since *plaga* requires “scourges.”

365. Thuan. and the two Torr. have *creditus*, “believed.”

366. Oxon. has *ex Patre vero*; read *verus*, “true.”

368. Vat. B, first hand; Mar., another hand; Widm. above; Bong. and some common copies have *cernens*, “seeing,” instead of *credens*, “believing.” Isidore’s gloss, *cernens*, is rather a different reading.

371. Ald. has, less well, *Christo fixa*, “fixed to Christ.”

372. Becman, chapter 6 of *Manuductio ad linguam Latinam*, notes that some copies wrongly read *sed Christo fixa, meamque Spem paritur* instead of *feta, meamque Spem paritura utero*. For *luminis*, all of Heinsius’s copies have that reading. Bong. above, Ald., and Gis. have *numinis*, which appears in Vat. A, first hand, and Mar., second hand. Weitzius, Vat. B, Prag., Rat., Widm. above, Vat. A above, and Mar., first hand, have *luminis*. Teolius agrees with Heinsius and acknowledged only that one especially excellent Vatican copy has *luminis*. Gifanius says that it should likewise be read from an old book: thus earlier, “light from light,” and in the creed, “light from light”; it is well known that scribes frequently confused *lumen* and *numen*.

375. Prag. has, incorrectly, *perficiendum oculis*, “to be perfected by the eyes.”

376. In Aldus there is a typographical error, *namque jam*.

377. *Armarium* is ordinarily used for bookcases or shelves in which books are placed, as appears from the commentators on Juvenal, Tertullian, Sidonius, and others.

378. Rat. has *laude refecta*, “restored by praise,” in the first hand; this is incorrect.

381. Aldus was the first to print *I, scriba*, “Go, scribe”; but when a typographical error had entered—namely *sicriba*—and he clearly corrected the error in the errata, later editors printed *tu scriba*, “you, scribe.” Nebrissa, however, copied the error *sicriba*. Heinsius did not notice the correction; but, following Salmasius, he asserted that a trace of the true reading remained in the Aldine edition in *sicriba*, and restored *I, scriba* from nearly all his old copies. From this I conclude that only one Aldine edition, completed in 1501, exists; for it is not credible that this error, noticed and corrected in the first edition, would have been repeated in a second. Our manuscripts vary. Prag. has *tu scriba*. Vat. A and Q have *inscripta*, “written.” Rat. has *scribenda*, “to be written.” Mar. has *scribenda*, with *inscripta* above it in smaller letters; in the margin it appears to have read *scriba*, although the letters have faded. I do not doubt that the true reading is *I, scriba*, as Alex. gives it; Urb. comes close with *o scriba*. The scribes, not understanding what that *I* meant, fabricated a new reading from their own ingenuity. See *Hymn 12 against Symmachus*, verse 99: “Go, attendant, seize the sword.”

383. Rat. has *triplici*, “in triple,” correctly emended above from *triplice*. In the Parma edition the word *triplex* is missing: “On the forehead of the cross”; the title should be “in threefold language.” The verse is not secure, as you see. On the title of the cross in three languages, see John, chapter XXIII, verse 38; Lipsius, *On the Cross*, book II, note 11; and others. On Gordian Augustus’s tomb, soldiers placed a title in Greek, Latin, Persian, Jewish, and Egyptian letters so that it could be read by everyone, as Capitolinus reports.

386. Ald. incorrectly has *canore boans* instead of *cavo reboans*. Fab. has *aere cavo quidquid reboans*. In my copy of Weitzius, *hausto* appears in the margin. These verses are used by many to prove that musical instruments may be used in church. See Baronius, volume I of the *Annals*, page 578, under the year 60, who shows from Prudentius’s authority that Christ was customarily praised with musical instruments. Gis. placed the following verse before this one.

387. Gis., first edition, has *in arcano* instead of *ab arcano*. Prag. has *haustus*; Gis., in the margin, *hausto*. Others have the better reading *haustu*, that is, “by a hidden or secret draught.”

388. Some think that *chelys* and *testudo* are the same thing. Some interpret *tympanum chelyn* as “the lyre-like drum.]
