389. *Disparibus*, “unequal, unlike,” I.

390. *Aemula*, imitating, corresponding, or resounding, I.

392. *Fidibus*, strings, sounds, I.

397. *Surda*, Judaic.—*Sibi*, for their own advantage.—*Praeconia*, praises, I.

398. *Elementaque*, meanings, because things speak through figures, I.

400. *Insanum*, insane.—*Bacchantis*, raging.—*Energima*, illusion, or image, frenzy, or sluggishness, or inactivity, or, better, illusion. *Energima* means imagination or fantasy; hence those who suffer the fantasies of demons are called *energumeni*, Iso, Vat. T.

402. *Credat miseranda*, “let the pitiable people believe,” that is, the pitiable Jewish people. *Judaea*.—*Suis*, their associates, monsters, or neighbors, I.

403. *Fulmina*, the terrors of the word of God, I.

404. The number of blows with which the priest repeats the words while adjuring the demons is the number of blows by which they are afflicted, Vat. A.

406. *Antistes*, every Christian who drives out a demon, I.

407. *Spiras*, coils, or cunning devices, or knots, I.

408. *Mancipium*, servant.]

[Note: [Col. 0955B]

391. *Concelebrat, sonat* is the true reading, for the meter rejects *sonant*. Vat. B, second hand, has *concelebrant, sonant*. Rat. and Mar., first hand, have *concelebrant*. Weitz., Fab., Gis., and Bong. have *concelebret, sonet*, and below *loquantur*; but Giselinus has *concelebrat, sonat, loquuntur* in both editions. Fabricius is cited correctly, and Gallandius agrees with him, as does Torn.

392. Conrad Samuel Schurtzfleisch, in *Ecclesiastical Antiquities*, chapter 19, discusses organs learnedly and denies that an organ was known in the West before the year 757. He objects to himself with this verse of Prudentius and another from the same *Apotheosis*, verse 148: “Organs, sambucas, citharas, reeds, and trumpets.” He maintains that Prudentius does not mean the organs now in use, which are constructed with lead pipes. But he could have cited, more suitably for ancient organs, verse 389: “Organs that blend harmonious sounds with unequal pipes,” where an instrument resembling our organs is described. See the note above on verse 148. The use of organs supplied with bellows is older than many learned men think. Saint Augustine, on Psalm 56: “An organ is what is large and inflated by bellows.” I understand Prudentius’s “organs with unequal pipes” and the organ of the Church of Paris in this sense; Fortunatus, book II, poem 19: “Here the boy tunes the organs with little pipes.” Claudian describes an organ very similar to ours, *On the Consulship of Mallius Theodorus*: “And he who, pressing down great murmurs with a light touch, controls countless voices of a bronze harvest, makes them thunder beneath a wandering finger, and drives the waves, laboring deep within under a beam-like lever, into song.” This seems to have been a hydraulic organ. Other organs were pneumatic, concerning which see Augustine, Isidore, and Pliny, book VII, chapter 37, who appears to distinguish pneumatic and hydraulic organs. Compare Du Cange’s *Glossary*.

395. The name of Jesus Christ is sweet: a gentle taste in the mouth, honey in the mouth, melody in the ear, joy in the heart, and similar expressions occur frequently in Saint Bernard, sermon 15 on the *Song of Songs*, and elsewhere. Teolius thinks Saint Bernard took this from Prudentius. He also writes *flagrans odor*, “burning scent,” unless this is an error for *fragrans*, “fragrant.”

399. Egm. has, incorrectly, *auras* instead of *aures*.

[Col. 0956B] 400. Put. has *inergima*; Pal., *inhergima*. Ald., Urb., Bong., first hand, and Torn. have *energia*. Mar. has *inergia*, with *inergima* in the margin; Sich. and Alex. have *energima*. Vat. Q has *inergia*, as do our copies. Bonon. has *inorgia*, or *in orgia*, incorrectly. The Greek word is pronounced ἐνέργημα (*energēma*). Tertullian used it in Latin for a work, effect, force, or efficacy. I explained in the prolegomena why the penultimate syllable is short. Mariettus notes that Gregory of Tours, book VII, page 414, seems to have referred to this passage: “Some, seized by a demon, raving through *energía*, declaimed against the martyr.”

402. When demons were formerly ordered to leave the bodies of the possessed, they professed that they bore the names of the gods whom the pagans worshipped. Lactantius, book II, chapter 16: “But they fear the just—that is, the worshippers of God—whose name, when adjured, drives them from the bodies of the possessed. Struck by their words as though by whips, the demons not only confess that they are demons but also disclose their names, those that are worshipped in the temples,” and so forth. Baronius supplies much more on this subject, volume I of the *Annals*, page 413, where these words of Prudentius stand out particularly; the learned cardinal maintains that they contain a sort of formula of exorcism. See Saint Paulinus, *Natalia* 11, verses 95 and following, and what Wowerus, Elmenhorstius, Heraldus, and Ouzelius note on this passage of Minucius: “Most of you know all these things: how often the demons themselves confess who they are when they are driven from bodies by us through tortures of words and the fires of prayer. Saturn, Serapis, Jupiter, and whatever demons you worship, overcome by pain, declare what they are.” People afflicted by evil demons are called *energumeni*; to this, I think, the word *energima* belongs in Prudentius, Severus Sulpicius, Gregory of Tours, and others. For an *energumenus* is a demoniac who imitates the operations of the devil.

403. Rat., first hand, has *nec flumina*, incorrectly.

407. Egm. has, incorrectly, *exui te* instead of *exue te*. Heinsius conjectures *et spira solve latentem*, that is, “release yourself from the coil beneath which you lie hidden.” The reading of the manuscripts is preferable: *spiras solve latentes*, “release the hidden coils”; for the demon is no more hidden than are his coils.

408. Gis., in the margin: “Why do you torment [him]?” More recent copies have: “Thief, why do you torment [him]?”]

[Col. 0957A] 440 “Stop: Christ is present, avenger of the human body.

[410] You may not seize as spoil one to whom Christ has attached himself.

Driven out, depart, airy vapor; Christ commands: come out.

Amid these words, the burning Cyllenian

howls, and Jupiter sighs for his familiar fires.

Behold, a savage legion rushes upon the Gerasene swine,

[415] after the repeated chains of punishment beneath the tomb-covered cliff,

and utters groans of punishment in long grunts.

But from the man’s mouth it had cried: ‘We know you, Jesus,

Son of God, born of royal scepters and David’s seed.

Who are you, and why have you come? By what power do you drive us away?’

[420] [Col. 0958A] 441 ‘We know—and in terror of your coming we lie prostrate.

Judea, has this voice not reached your ears?

It has reached them; but it has not penetrated your impoverished mind,

and, shut out from the first doors of light, it recoils.

It heard the coming of the Lord, whom the Iberian sunset

[425] of the sun possesses, and whom the new dawn receives.

The evangelical voice, penetrating by its word, loosened the Scythian frosts;

it also dissolved the burning Hyrcanian winters,

so that, stripped of ice, the river, now softer,

might flow from the Caucasian rock—the Rhodopean Hebrus.

[430] The Getae have grown gentle, and the bloody fierceness of the Geloni,

442 thirsty for bloodless cups, mixes pure milk—”

[Note: [Col. 0957B]

410. Put., first hand, has *Christus adhaesit*, “Christ clung to him.”

412. Mar., first hand, has *medius Cyllenias*, incorrectly.

413. The gloss says that *ignes* are “angers, rages”; but they may better be understood as the fires by which the demon burns. Likewise Mercury, or the Cyllenian, is called “burning,” unless the poet preferred to allude to Jupiter’s lust, about which the myths tell much. The truer interpretation is drawn from Minucius’s words cited at verse 402: “by the fires of words and prayer we drive them from bodies.” I would therefore restore our reading *ignes*. Cauchus conjectures *admotos ignes*, “fires brought near.” The matter is established by Lactantius, book V, chapter 22: “At the name of the true God they are driven away. When they hear it, they tremble, cry out, and declare that they are being burned and beaten.” And book II, chapter 16: “Thus, after often uttering the loudest howls, they proclaim that they are being beaten, burned, and are already on the point of departing.” In *Hymn 1 against Symmachus*, our poet joins the fires of prayers to the fire of Gehenna in which demons burn, verse 106: “In these ways the virtue of the martyrs chastises the foul robber; it restrains, torments, and burns him.” Finally, the demon flees while confessing that he burns, for he is an inhabitant of Gehenna.

414. Put. has *gerasinos*. The best parchment copies have *ruit*; Fab. and Gis. have *irruit*. Widm. above and Vat. A, first hand, have *obruit*, which is a gloss; for Heinsius observed that *ruit* is Virgilian. Prudentius lengthens the *a* in *gerasenos*, although Juvencus shortens it. The same story is set forth in *Hymn 9 of the Cathemerinon*, verses 55 and following.

417. Compare Matthew, chapter 8; Mark, chapters 1, 3, and 5; and Luke, chapters 4 and 8. Ald., Egm., Palat. have *Iesum*; others, *Iesu*.

418. Fab. and Gis. have *nate et sceptris*. *Et* is absent from the manuscripts and is genuinely superfluous. Urb. has *nate ex sceptris*; Vat. Q has *nec te sceptris*, incorrectly.

419. Ald., Gis., Urb., three of Heinsius’s older copies, and Vat. A have *quis sis, quid venias*, “who you are and why you come.” Rot., the three Torr., Fab., Cauch., have *qui sis, qui venias*. Prag. has *qui sis, quid venias*. Vat. B, Alex., Mar., and Weitz. have *quid sis, quid venias*. The sense is the same in any of these forms. *Qui sim* is Virgilian. Burmannus, volume I of the *Anthology*, page 417, prefers *quid sis* from Egm. and confirms that Ovid uses the phrase in this way. It is often asked whether the demons clearly understood the mystery of the Incarnation. Some thought that the demons recognized it, but that the prince of demons, the devil, did not; this is foolish. Others maintain that they did not know it before the preaching, but afterward knew it in such a way that they remained ignorant that the redemption of humanity would take place through death. Most hold that their knowledge was conjectural, not certain.

421. In Heinsius’s edition, an error entered—rare for him—*aureas* instead of *aures*. His notes also contain several errors, even against the sense, which not everyone would easily notice. We mention this so that others may not be deceived by the reputation of the Heinsian and Elzevirian editions. Mar. has, incorrectly, *diras mox*.

423. Prag. has *discussa*; others, *disclusa*. The gloss seems to have to be transferred to the word *foribus*.

424. Aldus alone has the error *solis* instead of *solis* [the reading is evidently corrupt in the supplied text].

425. Heinsius, with Put., Thuan., Rot., and the two Torr., has *Vesper roseos et qui novus excipit ortus*, which he considers absolutely necessary to read, because “rosy evening” is improperly said; that expression belongs to dawn. I prefer the reading of the others if the words are punctuated correctly: “whom the Iberian sunset possesses, rosy, and whom the new dawn receives.” That is, “the rosy new dawn.” Yet *qui novus excipit* is less correct unless *novus* means “first.” As he says *quem vesper habet*, so he says *quem excipit ortus*. In *roseus* the poet lengthens the final syllable according to his usual practice because of the caesura. In Alex., *roseus* has been erased, though it is clearly read in Urb., Vat. Q, and others. Bonon. and Teol. agree with Heinsius.

428. Noms. has *exutus glaciem*, which Heinsius calls an elegant Graecism. Gis. has *et exutus*.

429. He also used *cotem* instead of *caute* in *Hymn 11 of the Cathemerinon*, verse 72. Put. has *Hebros* instead of *Hebrus*, after the Greek manner, or perhaps that of ancient Latin writers. Gis. has *fluit*.

430. Prag. has *Gelonum*, as though it were *Gelonorum*. On the Geloni, see Savaro, page 224, on Sidonius’s words *equimulgas Gelonos*, that is, “those who milk horses and drink mare’s milk.”]

[Col. 0959A] “about to drink sacred draughts of Christ’s blood.”

The treacherous land of the Atlas-dwelling Moors long ago knew

[432] how to offer long-haired kings at Christ’s altars.

[435] From the moment when the Spirit overshadowed the mortal womb,

that Spirit of God, God, and clothed himself in his mother’s body,

and created a human being from virginity,

the Delphic caves fell silent over their condemned prophecies;

no *cortina* governs the tripods; no panting fanatic

[440] 443 foams forth fates published in the Sibylline books.

Deceitful Dodona has lost its mad vapors;

[Col. 0960A] now dead, the mute oracles of Cumae mourn;

Ammon gives no responses in the Libyan Syrtes;

the Romulan Capitolia themselves mourn that Christ shines as God to their own

[445] rulers, and that the destroyed temples have fallen

by the power of their leaders. Now the purple, as a suppliant,

lies prostrate at the thresholds of Christ, ruler of the Aeneadae,

and the supreme sovereign worships the banner of the cross.

Yet among all the rulers there was not lacking one,

[450] 444 when I was a boy, as I remember, a commander most powerful in arms—”

[Note: [Col. 0959B]

432. Here is clear testimony to the presence of the body and blood of Jesus Christ in the Eucharist. For it is well known that formerly Christians were accustomed to be nourished in the sacred assembly under both species.

433. Bong., Widm., first hand, and some common copies in Weitz. have *fervida*, “fiery,” not unreasonably, although the word has just appeared. Thus Avitus, book V: “the fiery plague of heaven.” But Aldus, Heinsius’s copies, our copies, Weitz., and Gis. have *perfida*, “treacherous.” Punic faith became proverbial.

435. Gifanius’s *Collection from Lucretius* explains this passage. Namely, *ex quo*, “from the time when, after”; *praestrinxit*, “occupied, besieged, overshadowed,” as Scripture says. The general meaning is that, once Christ had been born, the false oracles of the pagans vanished. Some write *perstrinxit*, others *praestrinxit*.

436. Heinsius, with Put. and Thuan., has *Spiritus ille Deus, Deus*. Others have *Spiritus ille Dei, Deus*. Here too the Word is called Spirit. See what I said above.

438. Vat. A has *sordibus*, less well, instead of *sortibus*. Gifanius, from an old book, has *jacuerunt*, “lay,” instead of *tacuerunt*, “were silent”; I do not approve this.

439. Bong., Widm., Ald., Mar., and Prag. have *regit*, with Alex., Urb., and Vat. Q. Others perhaps more correctly have *tegit*, which Gifanius defends: for the *cortina* was a covering and bronze casing of the tripod. Virgil, book III of the *Aeneid*: “when the *cortina* was opened in the inner shrine.” The *cortina* was also called the tripod, or that enormous golden vessel at Delphi, spread beneath the table on which the Pythia sat while uttering oracles. Interpreters of Virgil and others explain these matters more fully. Servius says it is the place from which the oracle emerges. In another sense, according to Isidore, book XIX, chapter 26, *cortinae* are hangings or curtains made of skins.

Someone may ask us whether it is true that the oracles of false gods became silent after the Word was made flesh. An anonymous book was written in French by Balthus of the Society of Jesus, *On the Silence of Oracles*, against Antonius Van Dale, an Anabaptist physician of Haarlem, and his defender D. Fontenelle; it was translated into Latin in 1725. Balthus, part 3, chapter 3, shows that Prudentius here agrees with the other holy Fathers, because, although he speaks of the Lord’s incarnation, he nevertheless joins to it the overthrow of idols and the collapse of paganism. Gifanius’s interpretation, which I explained—*ex quo*, “after”—confirms this; the poet does not assert that all oracles everywhere immediately became silent. Plutarch wrote a treatise *On the Silence of Oracles*, which Balthus discusses at length in part 3, chapter 9.

Since we are hastening to other matters, it is enough to have indicated this. But we must not omit the response that Augustus received from the Delphic oracle when he sent envoys to inquire about future events, as many report: “A Hebrew boy, God himself ruling the gods, orders me to leave my seat and enter gloomy Tartarus. Therefore depart henceforth silently from our altars.” Compare also book I *Against Symmachus*, verse 245, where Van Dale is again refuted.

440. It is not clear to me whether Prudentius here rejects the Sibylline poems that circulated among Christians, or rather affirms them. The Romans customarily resorted to the Sibylline books as to oracles. Prudentius reviews the most famous ancient oracles: the Delphic, Sibylline, Dodonaean—the oak in the Dodonaean forest of Epirus and the doves perched upon it delivered responses—the Cumaean, where the cave of the Cumaean Sibyl was located—and the Ammonian in Libya.

441. He calls the frenzied vapors “mad,” referring to fanatical frenzy, whose material physicians identify as a hot, burning vapor rising into the brain. The physician Giselinus explains it in this way; although not an unsuccessful interpreter in other passages, here he is excellent.

443. The poet should not be criticized as though he had placed the oracle of Ammon in the Marmaric region, where the Syrtes were. I have already discussed another meaning of *Syrtes* in *Hymn 7 of the Cathemerinon*, verse 30; Turnebus, item 506 of the *Adversaria*, may also be consulted, since he cites this verse.

444. Peveratus observed that “the Romulan Capitolia” is used for the Capitoline Jupiter, especially by our writers Augustine, Cyprian, and others.

446. *Purpura* is used for the emperor, as in Claudian, *On the Third Consulship of Stilicho*: “the purple garment, its pride now laid aside.” See Bulengerus, *On the Roman Empire*, book II, chapter 4.

449. Vat. A, in the old hand, incorrectly has *tamen cunctis*. Saint Gregory of Tours, book I *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 4: “As our Prudentius mentions in his book against the Jews,” and so forth, “yet from all the rulers,” continuing to the verse “He raises his face to heaven and invokes Jesus.” Many others who composed commentaries on the praises of the cross cite these verses of Prudentius and transcribe them with praise of the author. They were, however, omitted from the Spanish work of Pedro Ordóñez de Zevallos, Madrid, 1614, on this subject, *Forty Triumphs of the Most Holy Cross of Christ*, in which many things of this kind are collected.

450. Gregory of Tours reads *quem puero memini*, “whom I remember as a boy”; I think this is a manuscript error. The glosses should be disregarded which identify this “treacherous leader” mentioned by Prudentius as Symmachus. Perhaps for this reason one of the more recent writers called Symmachus an apostate. See the prolegomena, item 52. No one so foolish as to deny it will fail to see that the passage concerns Julian the Apostate. Mariettus seems almost to have accepted the glosses as speaking truthfully about Symmachus. Peveratus concludes from this that Prudentius was present at Julian’s sacrifice, which he thinks Prudentius describes in *Against Symmachus*, verses 1011 and following. I do not accept this.]

[Col. 0961B] 451. *Conditor*, founder, establisher, builder.—*Celeberrimus ore, manuque*, most renowned in speech and hand, most famous in eloquence and power, I.

453. *Relligionis*, Christianity, I.

455. *Augustum*, noble.—*Curvare*, he used to bend, or he bent, I.

456. *Soleas*, the soles of the feet, that is, the footprints.—*Lambere*, he used to lick, I.

457. *Advolvi*, he was rolled toward it, and bent down, I.

458. *Quin*, moreover.—*Gypso*, a stone image, I.

459. *Pollucis*, because he was a tamer of horses.—*Suffire*, to fumigate, smoke, or fill with smoke.—*Extis*, entrails, I.

460. *Hecaten*, Diana, I.

464. *Insertato*, inserted, introduced.—*Reserabat*, cut open, I.

466. *Trepidas*, trembling, palpitating, I.

468. *Callidus*, ingenious, clever.—*Fine*, what the end may be.—*Notabat*, he marked according to their custom, I.

472. *Cymbia*, elongated vessels. *Cymbia* are kinds of drinking cups, also called *carchesia*, named from their resemblance to a ship’s boat, I.

474. *Umbras*, images of demons, Iso.

475. *Thesiphone*, Diana or Persephone, I.—*Thesiphone*, Diana, Vat. T.]

[Note: [Col. 0961B]

451. Marcellinus reports that Julian corrected the laws for the better.

454. Put. and Thuan. have *orbi*; others, *Urbi*. More recent editors adopted *orbi*, which Gallandius does not favor; I do not dislike it.

456. Gregory of Tours has a different reading from the Colbertine manuscript, *plantas*, “soles”; this cannot be admitted. Observe that *soleae* are a kind of footwear proper to women, and that men were not accustomed to use them except rarely and at banquets; it was considered disgraceful if they walked about wearing them. Prudentius therefore rightly speaks of Juno’s *soleae*. See further on this subject Balduinus, *On Ancient Footwear*, chapter 11, where he cites these verses; Heraldus also discusses them, page 378, in his notes on Arnobius.]

457. Aldus, together with Urb., Vat. Q, and others, reads *incurvare* (“to bend down”). Alex., Put., Thuan., Oxon., and Gregory of Tours read *incerare* (“to smear with wax”), which I consider correct and borrowed from Juvenal, *Satire* 10: “to wax the knees of the gods.” Prudentius likewise says in *Hamartigenia*, line 404, “He waxes stones,” etc.; and in *Against Symmachus*, book I, line 203: “He had seen stones smeared with wax, and the black household gods moist with ointment.” Others understand *incerare* to mean hanging wax tablets before the statues, or repeatedly kissing the statues until the stones became dirty and seemed coated with wax. Neither interpretation pleases me, for Prudentius says elsewhere that the stones were smeared with wax and oil—something that describes a real practice. It was customary among the pagans to anoint statues of the gods with oil or wax. Arnobius, book I *Against the Nations*, writes: “Whenever I saw a slippery stone, fragrant with olive oil as though a present power dwelt within it, I flattered it, addressed it, and sought benefits from the senseless trunk.” Clement of Alexandria, book VII of the *Stromata*, says: “These are the very people who worshipped every piece of wood and every stone, provided it had been anointed or made slippery with oil.” See above, line 293. The pagans consecrated different parts of the body to different gods: “knees to Mercy.” Peveratus, from Apuleius’ *Apology* and Pliny’s letter to Trajan, concludes that vows made for someone’s safety were customarily recorded not only on tablets but also fixed in wax, usually on the thigh or knee of the gods and sealed with a ring; thus he explains *incerare*.

[Col. 0962C] 460. Gregory of Tours has *Achatem* for *Hecaten*, incorrectly; *sanguine multo* (“with much blood”) appropriately refers to Julian’s sacrifices, in which herds of cows were slaughtered. Consult the histories.

463. Carolus Paschalius, *On Crowns*, p. 256, book IV, chapter 17, chiefly proves from this passage that sacrificial victims were generally crowned with cypress, and collects much material about cypress.

464. Ald., Egm., and the Heinsian manuscripts read *reserarat*, which seems to have stood in Vat. B in the first hand. Others, with Weitz. and Gis., read *reserabat*. Paschalius, in the cited work, p. 245, chapter 13, discusses at length priests wearing fillets and crowns, on the basis of Prudentius and others.

469. Weitzius reads *tum*; others, *cum*.

471. Ald., Pal., and the Heinsian manuscripts read *numen, nescio, quod*; others, *nescio quod numen*.

472. From Virgil, *Aeneid* III, line 66: “We bring in foaming bowls of warm milk.”

473. Verbena was customarily used in sacrifices; some think that other herbs employed in the rites were also called by this name.

474. The old books, together with Gregory of Tours, read *accitas*. Weitzius wrote *ascitas*. Heinsius thinks that the ancient reading was *eccitas*, that is, *excitas* (“roused”), a verb especially appropriate to magical matters, as is clear from many passages.

475. In Thuan., *Thersisore*; Weitz., with Widm. in the first hand, and Vatt. B and Q, Prag., Rat., and Mar. in the first hand, read *Thesiphone* or *Tesiphone*. Cauchius conjectured *Tisiphone*. Others correctly read *Persephone*, that is, Proserpina, whose rites are being discussed here.

476. Rot. reads *fracto* (“broken”) for *tracto* (“dragged”), not implausibly; *tracto* is found in Egm., Heins., Cham., and Teol. Perhaps the reading is *torto* (“twisted”). Virgil has “with a twisted lash”; Valerius Flaccus, “with the twisted scourge of the Furies.”

[Col. 0961A]

The founder and guardian of laws, most renowned in speech and deed;

A counsellor of his country, but no counsellor in preserving

Religion, loving three hundred thousand gods,

That traitor to God, though not a traitor to the City,

[455] Bending the August head before the feet of earthen Minerva,

And licking Juno’s sandals,

Crawling at the feet of Hercules, waxing Diana’s knees;

[445] Yes, even lowering his forehead before Apollo’s plaster,

Or fumigating the horse of Pollux with burning entrails.

[460] Perhaps, while sacrificing, he appeased Hecate with much blood:

There stood herds of cows, destined to be struck by the axes

At the festivals of the priests; and twisted cypress shaded

The heifers, their foreheads bound with crowns.

Already, with the knife inserted, he was opening the entrails,

[465] [Col. 0962A] When the old man, filleted according to custom and with bloody hands,

Handled the trembling fibres, chilled by deadly cold,

And, as a skilled interpreter, marked the final pulses

Of the soul in the still-warm heart, and noted their outcome,

When suddenly, in the midst of the rites, the priest cried out,

[470] Pale: “Look what I am doing! Something greater, excellent king, greater—

I know not what godhead—has intervened at our altars,

Which foaming bowls of milk, the blood of Caesar’s victims, verbena, and crowns cannot withstand.

I see shadows summoned from far away dispersing.

[475] Terrified Persephone turns her steps backward,

Her torches extinguished, fleeing with her scourge dragged behind.”

---

[Col. 0963B]

477. Thessalian: magical. I.

482. *Elisa*: shaken, trembling. I.

483. *Flamen*: a priest of Jupiter; the word is said to derive from *filamen*, because he wore a red thread on his head. I.

484. *Frustratur*: frustrates, evades. I.

486. *Infula*: a priest’s garment. I.

487. *Pulvinar*: a place or arrangement for reclining. *Lotus*: washed, baptized, anointed with chrism. I.

488. *Proserpina*: Diana. I.

490. *Exerto*: thrust out, exposed, uncovered, or freed. *Fulmine*: sword. I.

[Col. 0964B] 494. *Zoroastreos*: Zoroaster is also called Mesraim, who became the originator of idolatry; or Zoroaster was the first of the Magi and king of the Bactrians, whom Ninus, king of the Assyrians, killed in battle. From him comes the adjective *Zoroastreus*, referring either to his followers or to the magical art itself. *Zoroastreos*: magical secrets. Jupiter struck Mesraim with a thunderbolt, and therefore they say that he was taken up among the stars; for this reason they call him Zoroaster, that is, “the living star.” I.

496. *Lateris*: of the side, or of the king. *Unus*: some; some wish Prudentius himself to be understood. Prag.

[Col. 0963B]

477. Ald., *hircanum*, less suitably, for *arcanum*. Sidonius seems to have imitated Prudentius in his *Panegyric to Anthemius*: “The Chaldaean priest, among the entrails of the priests, performed secret murmurs according to custom.” Elmenhorst, in his commentary on Arnobius, p. 31, has more on the secret murmur of magicians, or the utterance of words, as Arnobius calls it.

[Col. 0963C] 483. Paschalius, *On Crowns*, p. 247, book IV, chapter 13, says that he learns from Prudentius that the Roman flamen’s crown was made of laurel, after citing these verses.

485. Barthius calls these verses “very sweet” in book XLI, chapter 27 of *Against the Diverse*. The account seems different from the story Gregory Nazianzen relates about the same Julian the Apostate in Oration 1 *Against Julian*, concerning a cross crowned, or enclosed within a circle: there was another crowned cross, namely one on which a crown was placed above it. Rosweydus discusses both learnedly in his commentary on Paulinus’ letter 12. Lactantius relates a similar story in book IV, chapter 27: “When they sacrifice to their gods, if someone wearing a marked forehead is present, they cannot sacrifice successfully in any way. Nor can the prophet consulted give an oracle. This was often the chief reason why wicked kings persecuted righteousness. For when some of our servants stood near their masters while they were sacrificing, they drove away their gods by placing a sign on their foreheads, so that they could not portray the future in the entrails of the victims. When the diviners understood this, they complained—at the instigation of the same demons to whom they had offered sacrifice—that profane men were taking part in the sacred rites, and they drove the rulers themselves into a frenzy.”

486. Vat. A reads *hoc*; Vat. B and Mar., with others, *hic juvenum*. Aldus, however, does not distinguish the passage correctly: “of the worshippers of Christ. This class of young men, this kind of people, trembles at the fillet, and all …” Gis., second edition, reads *huc juvenum*. Fabr.: “huc juvenum: this kind of people trembles at the fillet,” a suitable sense. Heinsius printed *hic*, but did not say which manuscripts he followed, although he abandoned Giselinus.

487. Lucian, in *Alexander the False Prophet*, writes of the impostor Alexander: “On the first day, an announcement was made according to the Athenian custom as follows: ‘If any impious person, Christian, or Epicurean investigator of the mysteries has approached, let him depart. But those who believe in God and obey him may be initiated into the sacred rites with good fortune.’ Thereupon they were immediately driven out, while he led the proceedings and said, ‘Let the Christians be driven out.’” It is certain that the words “washed and anointed” express the sacrament of baptism and confirmation. See *Catholic Hymn* 6, line 128, and Baronius, volume I of the *Annals*, p. 249; compare also Malvenda, *On Antichrist*, book VII, chapter 10, who cites these verses, not to mention Gretzer, *On the Cross*, and innumerable others.

490. Consult Baronius at the cited place and Paschalius, *On Crowns*, p. 246, book IV, chapter 13, who teaches from this passage that the emperors, whenever they sacrificed, were conspicuous in their royal insignia.

491. In some Vulgate manuscripts: *examinis*, incorrectly, for *exanimis*.

492. Put. reads *circum inspicit*, a sound reading preferred by Teol. with Heins.; most, however, have *circumspicit*, which is also found in Gregory of Tours at the cited place. Vat. B has *nequis* for *et quis*, or *ecquis*. See above, line 186, where Gifanius comments on the expression *et quis*.

493. Rot. reads *signarit*, which pleased Heinsius. St Gregory of Tours at the cited place has *signaret*; but in a third manuscript it is *signarit*, as the editor notes. The Heinsian manuscripts, Mar., Sich., Urb., Alex., Vat. Q, Teol., Tornaes., the Basel edition in the text, Ald., Egm., and Widm. in the first hand read *ligno* (“with wood”), which fits *signaret* better than *signo* (“with a sign”). Yet elsewhere “the wood of chrism” is not very apt. Chamillardus falsely says that all manuscripts read *signo*; he himself reads *ligno* with Heinsius. Gallandius prefers *ligno* because *ac signum Christi* occurs below at line 498, but that reason is weak. I prefer *signo*.

494. Aldus’ error is *turbas et*. Prag. reads *turbarit*.

495. Noms. reads *armigero e cuneo* for *armiger e cuneo*. Fabr. and Gis., second edition, print *flammicomantum*, against the manuscripts, which consistently have *flavicomantum*, except Vat. Q, where *flammicomantum* occurs. Juvencus, book IV, wrote *taedarum flammicomantum*. See Bulenger, book III, chapter 39, *On the Roman Empire*, concerning standard-bearers, and Pignorius, *Commentary on Servants*, p. 119. Gifanius, in the *Lucretian Index* under *ET QUANTIS*, understands the blond-haired boys to have been Germans; thus Germania is called “blond” in book IV of Manilius. Horace, *Epode* 16, has: “Nor did savage Germany subdue us with its blue-haired youth.” For why he calls the attendants or bodyguards “boys,” see what we said at line 1 of *Catholic Hymn* 9.

499. Fabr. and Gis. read *prosiliit*; the manuscript codices have *prosiluit*, and Gifanius, at the cited place under *DISSILUI*, advises that this is how it should be written.

[Col. 0963A]

The secret murmur achieves nothing; Thessalian

Charms are of no use: no victim recalls the troubled shades.

Do you not see how, with the censers’ fires grown cold,

[480] The flame languishes, and the coal beneath the ashes grows sluggish?

Look: the palace attendant cannot hold the bowl;

His shaken right hand lets the balsam drip away;

The flamen himself marvels that his laurel is yielding

From his head, and the victim renders the uncertain blade ineffectual.

[485] “Someone—certainly, I know not which one of the young worshippers of Christ—has slipped in. This breed of men makes the fillet, and every couch of the gods, tremble. Let the washed one remain far away,

And the anointed one. Let beautiful Proserpina return

To the rites restored.”

[Col. 0964A] He spoke, and fell down bloodless; and as though he actually saw

[490] Christ threatening with an exposed thunderbolt,

The emperor himself, also bloodless, having laid aside his diadem,

Grows pale and looks around at those standing nearby, asking whether some attendant

Might mark his temples with a sign inscribed in chrism—

[448] One who had disturbed the Zoroastrian whispers with his forehead.”

[495] One standard-bearer from the band of blond-haired boys,

Guardian of the purple side, is discovered;

He does not deny it, and throws down his spear, ornamented

With twin iron points, and confesses that he carries the sign of Christ.

The frightened emperor leapt up, with the priest thrown down,

[500] Fleeing the marble chapel with no companion.

---

[Col. 0965B]

501. *Domini*: of the Lord, of the emperor. Vat. A.

503. *En*: indicating or pointing something out. I.

504. *Sabbata*: rest. I.

511. *Plectatur*: let it be punished, condemned, penalized. I.

[Col. 0966B] 517. *Recipit*: begins. I.

526. *Hoc tu*: this, namely this. Vat. A.

528. *Esto*: an adverb expressing concession or deliberation. I.

[Col. 0965C]

501. Ald. and Gis. read *dum*; the manuscript codices and other editions have *tum*, which is also found in Gregory of Tours at the cited place. In Rat., an inept corrector emended—or rather corrupted—this and the following verse: “With uplifted faces he raises himself to heaven and implores Jesus.”

502. Aldus first wrote *Isum*, then corrected it to *ipsum*. This correction escaped Gallandius, who asserted that Aldus had *Isum*. Read *Iesum*, as explained in the prolegomena.

506. Mar. in the first hand has *praefulgit* for *praefulsit*. The former, a third-conjugation verb, is not entirely unsuitable. Egm. and Vat. A have *Urbem* for *orbem*.

507. Fabr., Gis., second edition, and the Heinsian manuscripts read *cedere*, which Aldus also printed. Gis., first edition, Weitz., Vatt. A and B, Mar., and Rat. read *credere*. Elmenhorst, in his commentary on Arnobius, p. 41, illuminates the expression by which Rome is called “mistress of the empire,” drawing on Arnobius and others.

510. *Carnaliter*, and below *carnalis*, are words belonging to the language of the Bronze Age. St Jerome also used the adverb *carnaliter*.

[Col. 0965D] 511. Pal. and Vat. A have *virtus et* for *virtus te*.

512. Put. and Egm. write *solomonia*. Mar. in the first hand has *salmonia*.

515. Fabr. reads *caemento* for *caementum*. Heinsius punctuates as follows: “He built it with destructible masonry; by right it has been demolished, and it lies.” I follow this, together with Alex., Urb., and Vat. Q, although Fabricius thought the passage corrupt. Giselinus reads *caemento* with Fabricius and punctuates: “He built it with cement; capable of being undone, it has rightly been loosened.” Aldus and Weitz. do likewise, except that, with the manuscripts, they read *caementum*.

518. In Vat. B, *quid fieri* was incorrectly added by a recent hand.

523. The better Heinsian manuscripts, Sich., Weitz., and Gis. in the text, and Bong. above, read *super arte*. Aldus, *nostri*, Vat. Q, Gis., first edition, and in the margin of the second edition, and Widm. in the second hand, read *super arce*. Alex. and Urb. have *super arte*, with Cham., Cell., and Teol., following Heinsius. To me *arce* seems correct, and I think the poet had in mind the etymology of *arcus*. St Isidore, *Etymologies* XIV, chapter 2: “Citadels are the elevated and fortified parts of a city; for whatever places in cities are safest are called citadels from warding off the enemy; hence also *arcus* and *arca*.”

524. Vat. Q in the first hand has *voce serena*.

525. Others punctuate: “It was. The Word.”

527. *Expurgare* for *expugnare* is incorrect; I do not know from which manuscript it entered the Cologne edition.

529. Thuan. has *quo*; others, *quod*.

531. Put. has, less suitably, *divum lux*.

533. In Ald. and Vat. B in the first hand, *fervor* is an error for *servor*.

537. Vat. A and Vat. B in the first hand have *cumulant*, less suitably, for *tumulant*.

538. See Baronius, volume I of the *Annals*, p. 657. A splendid monument of the fall of Jerusalem is seen at Rome: the Arch of Titus, on which the Jews are represented bound, with the candlestick, the tablets of the Law, the table with the loaves, and other temple furnishings shown beside them. Most rightly deny that the Ark is depicted there, as I shall say at line 813 of *Psychomachia*. The arch bears this inscription: “The Senate and People of Rome, to the deified Titus, son of the deified Vespasian, Vespasian Augustus.” See Donatus, *On Ancient and Modern Rome*.

539. Compare Florus, book III, chapter 5, with the notes of Joannes Camerte, and Orosius, book VI, chapter 6.

542. The Heinsian manuscripts, with Gis., read *patria*; others, with Ald. and Weitz., *patriae*.

[Col. 0965A]

Then the shaken cohort, forgetful of its master,

Raises its suppliant faces to heaven and invokes Jesus.

“Are you already ashamed of your deed? Already repentant? Look: here is Christ for you,

Unhappy Judaea—the God who, abolishing earthly Sabbaths,

[505] Took mortals into eternal Sabbaths;

He shone upon the nations, shone before kings, possessed the world,

[449] And compelled Rome, the mistress of empire, to acknowledge him,

And subdued the Tarpeian images of the gods.

Learn from your miserable disasters how, at last, by what avenger,

[510] Empty superstition, the law, and what is practiced carnally

Are punished; whose avenging power crushes you.

Do Solomon’s stones, built by hand, lie destroyed by steel?

[Col. 0965B] Does that renowned temple lie there?

Why does it lie there? Because a craftsman’s hand constructed it

With destructible masonry; it has rightly been demolished,

[515] And it lies there, since everything polished returns to nothing.

Whatever can be made is at some time capable of perishing.

If you wish to learn what our temple is, in contrast to that one:

It is what no craftsman constructed by fitting it together,

What no fir or pine, cut and shaped, wove together,

What never grew from marble hewn out;

[520] Whose weight, supported by no columns, hung aloft

On a slender arch, curved into a vault,

[Col. 0966A] But was made by the Word of the Lord, not with a resounding voice;

[450] But by the Word that always was—the Word made flesh.

This temple is eternal; it has no end; this temple you,

Wishing to destroy it, attacked with scourges, cross, and gall.

Destroyed, it lay there under the torments that afflicted it—granted:

[525] For from his mother’s womb he possessed what was to be destroyed.

But what was loosened briefly by death, on his mother’s side,

The third day’s light restores alive by the majesty of the Father.

You saw my temple rise high, accompanied by angelic hosts—

[Col. 0966B] The temple under whose protection I am kept.

The summits of the eternal gates hang from it,

And through inaccessible towers of stairs the glory is raised;

A bright road shines at the highest steps.

But your piled-up ruins bury your holocausts.

[535] Titus taught what you deserve; the Pompeian ranks taught it by their plunder—

They carried your members, torn out, throughout all regions

Of land and sea.

The Jew wanders, drifting in exile from place to place,

After being torn away from his native seat,

[540] Paying the penalty for the slaughter and for Christ denied.”

---

[Col. 0967B]

546. *Delapsa*: degenerated. I.

548. *Susceptat*, that is, *suspectat*. *Captiva*: foreign, exiled. I.

552. Against the Homuncionites. A Homuncionite is one who calls the Lord merely a man. I. Against the Ebionites. The heretics called Ebionites are interpreted as “poor,” because they hold a poor view of Christ, affirming him to be a good man but not God, except in the sense in which other holy men are called gods. Prag. *Cognatum*: similar. I.

554. *Hoc*: this indeed. I.

555. *Pietate*: because he deigned to become man; this was piety.

[Col. 0968B] 556. *Majestate*: so that he is God, who possesses majesty. *Pro laude*: as though this were praise, though it is not truly so. Iso.

557. *Summa*: divinity. I.

558. *Egregium*: one is excellent who surpasses the flock, that is, the multitude. *Solertia*: skill in many arts; *sollon* in Greek means “much”; hence *solemnitas*, an assembly of many; hence an act is said to be performed solemnly when many are present. I.

559. *Ingenii*: of the mind. Iso.

565. *Labe*: seed. I.

566. *Illum*: Christ. *Ignis*: the Holy Spirit. Vat. A. *Ignis*: concerning the Holy Spirit. Iso.

[Col. 0967B]

545. Weitz., Pal., and Egm. read *ex quo*; the rest more correctly have *en quo*. Thus Virgil, *Eclogue* 1: “See to what misery discord has brought the unhappy citizens; see the fields in which we have sown.”

546. Put. and Rat. write *dilapsa*.

[Col. 0967C] 548. Put., Egm., Palat., Vat. A, and Heins. have *susceptat*; others read *suspectat*, which is less pleasing, and Teol. followed it after Cellarius.

549. Fabr. has *crudelitatis*, incorrectly, for *credulitatis*. Here *credulitas* means theological faith, as in Salvianus, book III *Against Avarice*: “I do not ask you to prove your faith in me by the deeds of your former life.” Conversely, *incredulitas* in Jerome and *incredulus* in Orosius signify a vice opposed to faith.

551. Put. reads *priores* for *fideles*, against Heinsius. In fact, *fideles* (“the faithful”) fits Christians very well. For it is clear that the Jews dispersed throughout the whole world, and largely subjected to Christian rule, are witnesses to their own iniquity and to our truth, as St Augustine calls them in his exposition of Psalm 58.

552. Ald., Put., Weitz., Mar., Rat., and Vat. A have *Homuncionitas* as the title; Tornaes., *Homuntionitas*; Thuan., *Homucionitas*. Vat. B has “Against the Homuncionites, that is, the Ebionites or Marcionites.” Rot. and others have *Homusionitas*; the Torrentian manuscripts, *Omusionitas*, incorrectly. For the Homousionites were called “Homousionites” abusively by the Arians because they said that the Son of God was consubstantial with the Father and defended *homoousion*. St Jerome mentions the Homuncionites in his treatise *On the Error of the Jews*, published by Claudius Menardus; Vigilius of Tapsus does so in book III *On the Trinity*; and the author published under the name of *Praedestinatus*, edited by Jacobus Sirmondus, does likewise. Marius Mercator reports that Photinus and his predecessors were called Homuncionites by the Roman Church, while the Sabellians, together with their earlier kindred group, were called Patripassians. The error attacked by Prudentius was taught around the year 70 by Ebion and others. The gloss seems to indicate Marcion or the Marcionites as patrons of this heresy. But the Marcionites, around the year 150, held a different error: that Christ the Lord had only an apparently real body, as will be clear in *Hamartigenia*. Prudentius chiefly attacks the Ebionites, whom Jerome, in his commentary on Galatians III, and Isidore, *Etymologies* VIII, chapter 5, call “semi-Jews.” Isidore says, drawing on Eusebius, that they think Christ became merely a righteous man through moral progress. Paul of Samosata, from whom the heretics called Paulianists took their name, and Photinus taught a similar error: that Christ took his beginning from Mary and became God through progress in virtue. Nestorius in some way agreed with them, distinguishing two persons in Christ. They thought that the man, the son of Mary, attained by his merits to become Christ. This was the pagan apotheosis by which human beings were transformed into gods. The pagans themselves knew how absurd this was, and Vespasian, at the first onset of his final illness, joked: “I think I am becoming a god.” Catholics may use *apotheosis*, or deification, in another sense: the elevation of human nature to union with the person of the Word, by virtue of which it is truly said that man is God, and—as many holy Fathers and theologians express it—that man became God. Thus the same assumption of human nature by which the Word became flesh is called the incarnation of the Word. The distinction is that the Word existed before the hypostatic union, whereas Christ’s human nature did not exist before it was united to the Word.

560. Put., *nostri*, Weitzius, Ald., and Gis. read *excellet*. Heinsius, with most of his manuscripts, has *excellit*. The sense requires the present tense; but many such verbs belonged to both the second and third conjugations, such as *fulgo, fulgeo* and *vido, video*.

561. Rat. has *hominis*. Prag. reads *vana* for *cana*, less suitably. Weitz. and Widm. punctuate: “It is mortal, but both are human; for hoary minds grow old.” In that case Rat.’s *hominis* is not unsuitable. Others punctuate: “It is mortal, but both are human; for hoary minds grow old.” The belief that wisdom flourishes in old men while bodily strength declines is common. Others say that in the same men tongue and mind grow senile and become confused. Extreme decrepitude must be distinguished from vigorous old age, and in this way the apparently contrary opinions may be reconciled.

564. Fabr. and Gis. read *terra*. *Terrae* is better.

565. Ald., Gis., and others have *germinat in mundum*. Mar., Weitz., and Heinsius have *germinat: immundum*, which is preferable: “it germinates; it is pure, not from male pollution.”

[Col. 0967A]

Having been sprinkled with blood, he paid the penalties for the sins committed.

[545] “See to what point the virtue of our ancient ancestors has declined!

The nobility descended from the ancient faithful serves,

But is no longer noble; captive, it embraces the new faith.

Such power resides in this novel credulity.

The formerly faithless nation triumphs by confessing Christ,

[550] While the defeated people that denied Christ is subjected

To the empire, having received faithful masters.

There are those who, following Christ halfway,

[452] Establish a doctrine akin to Jewish madness:

This alone—that he is truly man; but they assert

[555] [Col. 0968A] That he is not God from heaven. They confess him in piety,

Deny him in majesty; they celebrate him as sacred for the praise

Of his morals, but remove the supreme from his nature.

Every excellent work, by which skill shines forth,

Is a work of intellect or strength: the former flourishes

[560] In a keen mind; the latter excels in hard strength.

But both are mortal in man: hoary intellects grow old,

And the ages consume strong arms.

We do not follow these things in the Lord’s power

And everlasting glory; rather, we follow him who germinates from earth with no seed,

[565] Who takes no beginning from the stain of male seed; a gentle fire begets him,

---

[Col. 0969B]

567. *Caro*: matter, or, as others customarily render it, “to be born.” I.

568. *Intactam*: untouched, ignorant, or chaste. I.

569. *Maritat*: makes fertile and pregnant; rain “marries” the earth, that is, makes it fertile. I.

570. *Incomperta*: unknown, unfamiliar, undiscovered. Iso. *Ortus*: of birth; a genitive. I.

572. “She is joined to the Spirit,” not because the Holy Spirit was the Father of the Son of God, but because, with the cooperation of the Holy Spirit, the Father begot him and caused him to be incarnated in Mary’s womb. I.

573. *Pubertas*: youthful chastity, that is, virginity. *Signata*: closed, sealed. *Gravis*: pregnant. I.

576. *Non credule*: O unbelieving one, or Homuncionite. I.

577. *Hoc*: destined to be. I.

582. *Contemnit*: rejects. I.

[Col. 0970B] 583. *Bibit*: for “conceived.” I.

584. *Latebris*: inner places. I.

585. The angel says: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you,” etc. Iso.

586. *Concretus*: thick, hardened, or dense. *De sidere*: to descend into the heart. I.

587. *Conjuge*: husband Zacharias. I.

589. *Interceptus*: conceived. I.

590. *Ex ore*: because John did not speak but showed the Lord’s coming by a gesture of the body. I.

593. *Norat*: namely, to speak. *Garrula*: talkative. I.

594. *Fastos*: secret sayings, annals; *fastus* of the fourth declension means pride; *fasti* are annalistic books. I.

[Col. 0969B]

567. Ald. reads *non sanguis*.

569. Egm., Put., Vat. A, and Pal. have *flatu*; others, *afflatu*. Rott. and two Torrentian manuscripts read *affectu*; *flatu* seems more Prudentian.

[Col. 0969C] 571. In Vat. A *Christus* is absent through a copyist’s negligence. *Innuba*, as later at line 614, “at the unwedded breast,” means the same as “ignorant of a man,” or “without a husband.” Drepanius Florus, in his poem on the Paschal Candle, writes: “The unwedded mother, pregnant in an untouched womb, gave birth.” Some have noted that *nubere* can sometimes, by metalepsis, signify the conjugal act; hence: “May I perish if marriage is not sweet,” and “married words.” Hence the terms “unwedded mother of God” and “unwedded.” *Psychomachia*, line 74: “And an unwedded woman, a mother, conceived God.” Plautus, *Pseudolus*, act I, scene 3: “Tell me, did you never marry his father?” Many Fathers called the Blessed Virgin unwedded: Tertullian, Epiphanius, Augustine, Gregory the Great, and Bernard.

572. Vat. A has the error *subit* for *nubit*.

573. The Virgin’s virginity is demonstrated here in almost the same words used by Arnulfus: “Nor does childbirth open the sealed gates of modesty.” See his poem in Barthius, book LVI *Against the Diverse*, chapter 16.

576. Shaking the head is the gesture of one mocking—not only, according to the testimony of Scripture, moving the head, but also among the pagans, for whom it was regarded as a sign of anger and grief. See Delrio’s commentary on Seneca’s tragedies.

577. Heins., with Put., Thuan., Rot., two Torrentian manuscripts, and Cauchius, reads *fore nuntiat*. Our manuscripts and others have *pronuntiat*. Chamillardus departed from Heinsius and followed *pronuntiat*. Teolius printed *fore nuntiat*, but admitted that *pronuntiat* is equally good and appears in almost all the Vatican manuscripts. Read the angel’s words in Luke 1:28 and following.

579. Weitz., Gis., Rat., and Prag. read *monitis*. Fabr. has *monitus*. Egm., Bong., most Heinsian manuscripts, and our copies have *monitum*. Gallandius, with Ald. and Tornaes., follows *monitum credidit*, as at line 368, “he soon believed what he had seen,” and line 715, “now believe that he is God.” In Mar., a recent hand has *monitis*. Chamillardus reads *monitis* and asks in a note, “Is it not *monitum*?” For above we have “He saw God; he soon believed what he had seen,” and he adds other material borrowed from Heinsius.

583. Petrus Lucensis, deceived by a revelation from a woman—either false or wrongly understood—dreamed that the Blessed Virgin conceived Christ in her heart, not in her womb. Prudentius gives no support whatever to this error. Here he speaks figuratively, and elsewhere clearly embraces the true doctrine, as at line 58 of this poem: “She brought forth beneath the law of the womb.” Similar words occur in the fifth responsory of the Feast of the Circumcision: “The Virgin’s heart was confirmed, in which, when the angel announced it, she conceived the divine mysteries; then in chaste inward parts she received him beautiful in form above the sons of men.” Peveratus, in his manuscript notes, adds something even closer to Prudentius’ mind and meaning: that the Blessed Virgin conceived in two ways—first by faith and spirit, then in the flesh, when she enclosed Christ’s body in her womb—citing Augustine, *On the Trinity*: “Maternal kinship would have profited Mary nothing unless she had carried Christ more blessedly in her heart than in her flesh.”

586. Giselinus correctly explains *concretum* as “compacted from earthly mass,” adding a physical axiom: the external senses are especially dull toward a highly remarkable object, and their judgment is distorted.

587. Refer to Luke 1:42 and following, concerning St Elizabeth visited by the Virgin Mother of God.

593. Vat. A has *Deum*, incorrectly, for *Deo*.

594. I read *fastos* with Vatt. B—where *fastus* occurs—Q, Urb., Alex. in the second hand, Thuan., Egm. in the second hand, and the other Heinsian manuscripts except Put., which has *fatos*, and Thuan. in the second hand, which has *festos*. Aldus, Tornaes., Gallandius, and Bong. also have *fastos*. Widm. above has *fastus*. The *fasti* were tablets on which festival and working days were customarily recorded. Vat. A, Mar., Weitz., Gis., and more recent editions have *fatus*. Egm. in Weitz. has *fatos*; in Heinsius, *fastos*. Andreas Wilkius began his *Exposition for the Feast of the Three Kings* at this verse, composing it from certain verses of the *Apotheosis*; he too reads *fastos*. Bulengerus, *On the Roman Empire*, book I, chapter 20, has more on the *fasti*. Isidore, in *On Differences*, teaches that *fasti* is used of books, while *fastus* means pride.

[Col. 0969A]

Not flesh, nor ancestral blood, nor shameful desire.

Divine power joins the untouched maiden,

A virgin ignorant of the marriage chamber, to the pure breath

Within her chaste entrails.

[570] The unheard-of novelty of his birth commands that God

Christ, thus begotten, be believed to be God; the unwedded virgin

Is joined to the Spirit, and feels no pollution of love.

Her sealed virginity remains, pregnant within yet outwardly

[575] Unharmed, blooming with chaste fertility—

Already a mother, yet still a virgin; a mother ignorant of man.

Why do you refuse? Why shake your empty head, unbelieving one?

[454] With holy mouth the angel announces this: is it pleasing

To believe and open your ear to angelic speech?

[Col. 0969B] The holy virgin herself believed the message of the radiant minister,

[580] [Col. 0970A] And therefore, believing, conceived Christ.

For Christ approaches those who believe; he rejects with dishonour

The doubting breast that recoils in wavering faith.

Virginity, with ready faith, drank Christ in the womb

Of her heart and, about to give birth, lodged him in untouched hiding places.

“Believe what the angel sent from the Father’s throne says;

Or, if congealed hearing cannot receive a liquid voice

From the starry realm, hear at last, sober man, what the old woman,

Pregnant by her husband and believing, cries out.

[Col. 0970B] Wonderful faith! A boy conceived in an aged womb,

[590] The first, greets the virginal Lord from his mother’s mouth,

And, though still unborn, announces that the infant is already

Beginning to cry for us; for the little boy did not yet know how

To speak, yet opened his talkative mouth to Christ God.

[Col. 0970B] Bring forth the secret annals; give it, open the book.

---

[Col. 0971A]

596. *Percensere*: to investigate. I.

598. *Ite*: go, O wicked ones. I.

603. *Pacti*: we call brides *pactae* when they have been bound by a marriage agreement. I.

608. *Eous*: eastern. I.

609. *Lancibus*: dishes; from this, *bilances* are called scales because they are made in the shape of dishes. *Fercula*: gifts. Iso.

611. *Pennatus*: swift. I.

612. *Aurorae*: of the eastern region; eastern peoples. *Bactra*: a region near India. I.

613. *Lactantibus*: because at that hour she nursed the child. I.

[Col. 0971B]

595. In Cellarius’ index, two indecorous metaphors of Prudentius are identified, as I said above. For the first, see *Apotheosis* line 93. The second is “to vomit out the book,” which seems harsh even to Wilkius, since things that ordinarily make someone ill are vomited out, if they can be. Perhaps the poet had this in mind, for Isaiah himself condemned himself because he had previously kept silent, chapter VI, verse 5: “Woe is me, because I was silent.” The same verb is used of God concerning the bishop of Laodicea: “I shall begin to vomit you out of my mouth,” *Apocalypse* II, 16.

596. Gis., first edition, reads *resolvere sulcos*, incorrectly.

599. Mar. in the ancient hand has *lacrymis*; in a recent hand, *lacrymans*. The veneration with which ancient Christians received sacred books is described here: they bowed down before them, worshipped them, and kissed them. This pious custom has long since grown cold among Catholics, although the clearest traces remain among ecclesiastical ceremonies. Heretics have tried to restore it among themselves—not wrongly, if they did not do so with bad intentions. For because this practice of venerating, worshipping, and kissing the sacred Bible has been somewhat discontinued among Catholics, they constantly inculcate these external signs of veneration and at the same time mock Catholics for showing similar reverence toward sacred relics. Nor do I doubt that, if they had observed that this ancient custom flourished among Catholics, they would have called it superstition and idolatry, just as they now do what they believe Catholics have abandoned. When I speak of honouring, venerating, and worshipping the sacred Bible, I speak with the holy Fathers; I mean the very practice observed by the heretics, namely kissing it and showing similar signs of veneration. On this ancient rite, see Cardinal Bona, book I, *Liturgical Matters*, chapter 25, no. 10.

600. It is well known that tears often flow from joy; Wilkius confirms this with many examples from sacred and secular history.

602. This is Isaiah’s verse, chapter VII, verse 14: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive.” More on this is found in *Catholic Hymn* 7, line 194. The ancient sacred books were also divided into numerous titles and chapters. Matthew’s Gospel was divided into sixty-eight titles and 355 chapters. See Suidas under the names Matthew and Mark.

605. In Vat. A, the two words *Deus jam* were added by a recent hand after the earlier words had been erased.

606. *Emmanuel* means the same as “God with us.” That verse of Isaiah, mentioned at line 602, was obscure in the ancient ages.

607. Veitz. has *ore?*, asking a question.

608. Vat. A has *veneratur*, but a recent hand changed it to *veneratus*, which the sense requires.

610. Mar. has *virgineum*; in the margin, in a more recent hand, *virginis*. On this story of the Magi and the star, which he soon calls a winged messenger, compare *Catholic Hymn* 12.

[Col. 0972B] 612. From Virgil, Book VIII, verse 687: “and carries Bactra, the farthest lands, with him.” Bactra is the name of a city, region, or province in Scythia. The commentators say that Virgil calls Bactra “the farthest” because the empire of Mark Antony did not extend beyond it. Prudentius appropriated Virgil’s epithet and said “the farthest Bactra” because the Roman Empire was bounded by these regions.

613. The ancient books differ greatly from one another at this point. Giselinus, from his manuscripts; one Torrentian manuscript; and, with a different spelling, the Rotundus and Oxford manuscripts have *luctantibus*, “struggling,” with the Oxford manuscript adding a double interpretation:

*Luctantibus*, because from Christ’s birth the hours of the day somehow struggle with the hours of night, wishing the days to grow longer.

*Lactantibus*, because Christ was suckled.

Giselinus prefers *luctantibus horis*, “with the hours struggling,” as though the hours, in their incredible eagerness to see the Messiah, tried to outstrip one another, as in the similar amplification in the Epiphany hymn:

“What is this, that the returning Sun now abandons the narrow circle? Is Christ being born on earth, who enlarges the path of light?”

Considering these same verses, Heinsius at one time suspected *laxantibus horis*, “with the hours loosening,” namely, the day, because at Christ’s birth the sun abandons its narrow circle. But afterward he recognized that *lactantibus horis* was correct, that is, “fostering” and, as it were, “nourishing.” Thus in the hymn of Saint Laurence, verse 572: “with a nursing embrace”; or *lactentibus horis*, “with newly born hours,” as in Alcimus Avitus, Book IV, where *lactens orbis* means “the newly born world.”

The Vatican Q and Bologna manuscripts, together with Aldus, read *lactantibus oris*, “with nursing regions”; Gallandius inclines to this reading and explains it as “in the outermost regions of the East,” and Marietti did not record any variant reading. The Noms., and the first hand of the Rotundus and Oxford manuscripts, also have this reading. Weitzius, with Egmondanus, has *laetantibus horis*, “with rejoicing hours.” The same Weitzius cites Aldus, Fabricius, Widmanstetter, and Bongarsius for *lactantibus*, but does not distinguish whether they have *oris* or *horis*. Fabricius indeed has *horis*. In Heinsius, the Put. and Thuan. manuscripts have *lactantibus horis*, while one of Weitzius’s manuscripts has *luctantibus horis*. Yet I find no manuscript with this reading in Weitzius, only Giselinus’s edition. *Luctantibus* does occur in the Alexandrian and Urbino manuscripts.

Teolius prefers *lactantibus horis* on the authority, as he says, of four or five Vatican manuscripts. In one of them, in the commentator’s hand, appears: “When Christ was suckled”; and in the same hand, in the margin: “Some manuscripts have *luctantibus horis*, because at Christ’s birth the hours of the day somehow struggle with the hours of night.” Teolius understands these as the hours during which Christ hung at his mother’s breast.

I prefer *lactantibus*, but in the sense I explained at *Cathemerinon* hymn 8, verse 19, namely, “enticing” or “alluring.” Otherwise the expression *illuxisse diem lactantibus horis*, “that the day had dawned with suckling hours,” or *illuxisse diem luctantibus horis*, “that the day had dawned with struggling hours,” seems sufficiently obscure. Weitzius’s reading is clearer: *illuxisse diem laetantibus horis*, “that the day had dawned with rejoicing hours”; or, if we adopt *oris* from many manuscripts, that is, “lands,” “that the day had dawned over rejoicing lands.”

[595] [Col. 0971A]

“He uttered what the holy Isaiah  
had proclaimed, as God breathed upon him.”

I delight to review these things and turn over the furrows of my pen,  
which the golden hand traced with heavenly signs.

Go away from here, while I bow submissively  
and adore the radiant letters;  
while weeping I venerate them,  
and fix sweet kisses upon them.

[600] 456 “Joy conceives tears, and joy gives forth weeping.

The promised day has arrived, which that little verse  
had said would come, when the virgin, having borne a child,  
with her husband as unquestionable witness—  
he who guarded the pledged purity—  
[Col. 0972A] brought him forth and made me see my Emmanuel.

[605] Is God now our man? He moves among us and stands here,  
and proves his name: he illumines with his present face  
the verse long obscure to ancient ages.

Is this the God whose cradle the East,  
in reverence, beheld, and humbly offered  
royal dishes on golden platters  
[610] to the virgin’s lap, wrapped in infant clothing?

Who was that messenger, so swift and like the rushing south wind,  
who reached the peoples of the dawn, and Bactra, the farthest land,  
457 and announced that the day had dawned with nourishing hours?”

[Note: [Col. 0973B]

617. *Pernox*: “awake throughout the night,” Iso.

619. *Manco*: “curved,” Mar. — *Manco*: “contracted, weakened, crippled, mutilated, or diminished.” — *Cancrum*: “Cancer,” because the feet are depicted at the side of Cancer, I.

621. *Hircinum*: “Capricorn.” Capricorn is called *aegoceros* (“goat-horned”) in Greek. — *Laceris*: “torn.” — *Marcescere*: “to diminish,” I.

622. *Puer Hydrius*: “Ganymede, Aquarius.” In Greek it is called *hydrochoos* (“water-pourer”). — *Sagittae*: “Sagittarius,” I.

623. *Palantes*: “fleeing, scattering,” I.

624. By “the silent lovers” he means Helice and Cynosura, whom he calls harlots: they are Juno’s concubines in the heavens and never turn, as the other stars do; therefore he calls them silent. The vault of the world is called the pole, because the sphere turns there, and the curvature of heaven is called a vault. — *Fornice mundi*: “in the vault of heaven, or in its rounded surface,” I.

625. *Ignes*: “stars,” I.

626. *Lurida*: “pale, dark”; a pale color is called *luridus*, as is a leaden color, Iso.

[Col. 0974B] 627. *Haeret*: “doubts.” — *Excidium*: “the destruction at Christ’s Passion, at midday, when darkness fell after the Lord’s death from midday until the ninth hour,” I.

628. *Velandum*: “he understands it as something to be veiled.” — *Glauco*: “dark, pale,” I.

630. *Orbe*: “the circle of the sun,” Vatican A.

631. *Cumulem*: “honor.” — *Myrrhaeque et thuris et auri*: “By gold we understand the king, or the splendor of wisdom; by frankincense, when we believe in the Lord; by myrrh, burial, or when we mortify our flesh to its vices and offer it,” I.

632. *Rependam*: “I shall repay,” I.

633. *Coelo*: “through the star.” — *Humique*: “through the offering of the Magi,” I.

634. *Inventus*: “found, or visited,” I.

635. *Specimen*: “beauty.” — *Inferna*: “the infernal regions.” — *Refringens*: “breaking,” I.

637. *Intervenit*: “fills.” — *Abdita*: “hidden things,” I.]

[Note: [Col. 0973C]

614. The Prague manuscript has *pendebat* instead of *penderet*.

615. The child was not carried through the heavens by the star, as someone has thought this verse indicates; rather, his birth was announced by the star. Compare *Cathemerinon* hymn 12, verse 28.

616. There is an error in Heinsius: *sigorum*.

617. He calls the Magi Chaldeans. See the passage cited, verse 25.

618. The commentators praise these verses with extraordinary admiration. I shall cite one, Giselinus: “Nothing is more liberally conceived than this fiction, nothing more vivid, nothing more ingenious, especially if you bring here the praises of the same star, sung above with such elegance, and compare them with these. It is incredible how much force of intellect and elegance shines forth in both passages.” Concerning the stars he names, consult Manilius, Book I, and the astrologers.

619. In Vatican A, *ex laceris* has correctly been changed by a recent hand to *lateris*. Virgil, *Georgics*, Book I: “Scorpio himself, glowing, already contracts his claws for you.” Prudentius is speaking of Cancer.

621. Some write *Hirquinum*.

622. Giselinus has *Sagitta*. The old editions have *Sagittae*, correctly, since the sign is Sagittarius. Heinsius printed *Sagitta*, but noted that the manuscripts have *Sagittae*, not *Sagitta*, although Cauchius preferred the latter. Our manuscripts also have *Sagittae*. Chamillardus, Cellarius, and Teolius have *Sagitta* with Heinsius, perhaps because they did not notice his note.

623. Vatican A has *palentes*, perhaps *pallentes*, with Egmondanus and Paldamus. Others have the better reading *palantes*. In the same Vatican manuscript there is an incorrect *reparat* for *separat*. The Gemini brothers are Castor and Pollux. In the Parma edition I think *reparat* is an error against the sense and meter, unless some poetic license is assumed.

624. Why Virgo, a heavenly sign, should be called wicked, and what it means for her to betray “silent lovers in the vault of the world,” has not, in my view, been sufficiently explained by recent commentators. Chamillardus gives only this interpretation: “False Virgo abandons her silent suitors in heaven.” *Prodere* does indeed seem to be understood in the sense it has in Virgil, *Aeneid* II: “Nor do I now ask for the ancient marriage which she betrayed.” Her lovers, therefore, will be the other stars, which are customarily called silent; “the vault of the world” rightly means heaven here, for a vault is a vaulted structure, and *fornix* was also used for the place where women prostituted their chastity; hence *fornicari* and *fornicariae mulieres* occur frequently in the works of ecclesiastical authors.

Meursius, in his *Criticus* on Arnobius, page 2, cites these verses to prove that *world* often means *heaven*, but makes no further observation. We must therefore know, from the teaching of Manilius, Book II, and other astrologers, that some signs love one another and some do not. Taurus and the Archer love Virgo, who loves no one. Those, then, are the lovers whom fleeing Virgo abandons; she is perhaps called wicked because of the unworthy effects attributed to her by astrologers.

625. Aldus has the error *quinque* for *quique*.

627. In Vatican A, *et* is absent. Aldus has *sensit*; *sentit* is better.

628. Aldus and the first hand of the Put. manuscript have *velandam*, not inappropriately, referring to the sun’s wheel. Others have *velandum*, namely, the sun.

629. Paldamus has *perituro*, namely, “with the world about to perish.” The others more suitably have *periturum*.

634. Vatican B has *conventus* for *inventus*. The Prague manuscript has *utramque*, and in the following verse *speciem*. Others have *utrumque specimen*; Aldus incorrectly has *utrumque speciem*.

635. Fabricius has *regimen*. Iso seems to have read *speciem*. See the preceding verse concerning *utrumque*.

636. Compare the note on *Cathemerinon* hymn 9, verses 95 and following.

638. Saint Augustine, *City of God* XXII.29: “For when we say that God is both in heaven and on earth—for he himself says through the prophet, ‘I fill heaven and earth’—we do not mean that one part of him is in heaven and another part on earth; rather, he is wholly in heaven and wholly on earth, not at different times but both at once, something no bodily nature can do.” Wilkius’s exposition does not proceed beyond this verse.]

[Col. 0973A]

“Where Christ, still tender, would hang  
from an unmarried mother’s breast?”

[615] “We saw this child,” they say, “carried through the stars,  
and glowing above the ancient courses of the constellations.

The astrologer, trembling, stayed awake throughout the night  
on the Chaldean summit. He saw the serpent yield,  
the lion flee,

458 Cancer draw in the feet of its sideward-curving form,

[620] the bull, with broken horns, bellow in submission,  
and the Goat-star waste away with torn fleece.

From here the Water-bearer slips away, driven on;  
from there, Sagittarius. The fleeing Gemini  
are separated by flight; wicked Virgo  
betrays her silent lovers in the vault of the world.

[625] And all the other fires hanging in the terrifying clouds  
feared the new Lucifer: the sun’s lurid wheel  
[Col. 0974A] clings in place and already feels destruction impending,

and, at midday, expects to be covered  
with a gray veil,  
while the splendor of the heavens is destined to perish  
in a daytime night,

[630] when sudden darkness veils the sun’s head.

Shall I not heap upon him myrrh, frankincense, and gold  
as gifts? I know whom I see, and what gifts I shall repay.

Shall I not venerate him, who, seen in heaven  
and found on earth as king and God, governs both,

[635] the true form of nature, and, breaking open  
the infernal realms beneath the tomb, commands  
the buried dead to rise with him?

He dwells in heaven, enters among earthly things,  
bursts open the hidden Tartarus: true faith—  
God is the one who is wholly everywhere.”]

[Note: [Col. 0975B]

639. *Lingua*: “a star shall arise from Jacob,” I, Vatican A.

640. *Frustrantia*: “rendered fruitless in some sense,” I.

643. *Crepundia*: “gifts for a child, or rattles”; they are so called because a bronze ringing was added to the cries of infants, or because infants were entertained by that sound; “ornaments,” I.

[Col. 0975C] 645. *Divinis*: “by the Holy Spirit,” I.

648. *Gremium*: because he contained him in his lap, the one through whom the star shone, I, Mar. — *Face*: “by the light of Christ,” I.

650. *Insanos*: “stormy, turbulent,” Iso.

651. *Luctantia*: “struggling, contending,” I.

652. *Marmore*: “a level surface, smoothness,” I.

657. *Otia*: “tranquility,” I.

659. *Facessite*: “rest, or cease; depart, or withdraw; leave us alone,” I.

[Col. 0976B] 663. *Excitam*: “stirred up.” — *Verrunt*: “drag, sweep away.” — *Ridente sereno*: “with the clear sky rejoicing,” I.

665. *Spatiatus*: “lingering, or walking; having traversed the distance.” — *Udum*: “wet,” I.

666. *Pendulus*: “hanging,” Iso.
