640. Vatican B and Mar. in the old hand have *fortuitu*.

649. Egmondanus and Paldamus have *facturum*. On Christ’s miracles, see *Cathemerinon* hymn 9.

650. Some vulgar editions have *mutescere*, not inappropriately. Below, verse 658: “go, be silent in your prisons.”

[Col. 0975D] 656. Bongarsius, Vatican B, and Mar. in the first hand have *et*. Aldus and Fabricius, in Weitzius, have *et*; my Aldus and Fabricius, with others, have *ac*.

658. Others have *silete, carceribus*, and so forth.

662. Virgil, *Aeneid* I.84: “and maker of clouds and powerful over storms.”

663. The Rat. manuscript has *ridenti*; the meter requires *ridente*. “To sweep the sea, heaven, and clouds” occurs in Lucretius, Virgil, Cicero, and the best writers.

664. Paldamus has *calcaret* for *calcarit*.

666. *Sola* means “the soles of the feet”; Barthius says that Fabricius did not understand this, *Adversaria* XXVI.12. Fabricius’s interpretation is: “having beneath him the hanging ground.” Barthius rightly rejects it. See *Cathemerinon* hymn 3, verse 129, and the hymn of Saint Agnes, verse 116.

667. As I noted earlier, *spiritus* is a word. I do not agree with Petavius, who in *On the Work of the Six Days* I.3 explains Prudentius as speaking of the Holy Spirit. [Col. 0976C] The poet’s meaning contradicts this, as does what he adds: “poured over him by the paternal mouth.” That applies to the Son. In Egmondanus, by a second hand, *cui spiritus* appears, incorrectly.

668. Fabricius incorrectly has *volitabit in undis*.

669. In Vatican B there was another reading, but it was certainly added by a recent hand. In the Rotundus and one Torrentian manuscript: *et uno Torr., certo limite*.

670. Sichardus incorrectly has *axe* for *ac se*.

671. Vatican A has *obstrinxit ad usus*.

673. Although Giselinus had found these verses written and punctuated differently in the manuscripts and editions, he corrected them in this way so that the sense might emerge more conveniently, with Heinsius applauding. Aldus has:

“What different illustrious deeds of God and Christ should I recall?  
Those which, examined more deeply in majesty, are denied.  
You yourself, without hesitation, will confess that the man is divine.”

The disagreement among the ancient books is extraordinary. The Put., Noms., Vatican B, Rat., and the first hand of Widmanstetter have *quae majestate negator*. The Oxford manuscript agrees with Aldus. Mar. has *quae a majestate negator*. Prag. and Bong. have *qua majestate negator*. Some of Heinsius’s manuscripts have *qui majestate negatur*. The Cauchianus has *qui majestate negator*. The Alexandrian has *quem majestate negator*, with *negatur* written above it. The Urbino manuscript has *quae majestate negator*. Vatican Q has *quae majestate negatur*. Bologna has *quem majestate negatum*.

675. In the first edition of Giselinus, *caecis* appears, which pleased Heinsius. But the parchment manuscripts stand against it, consistently writing *caecos oculos*.

679. Vatican A has *quoniam*, incorrectly, for *quonam*. See the *Dittochaeum*, tetrastich 33, “The Pool of Siloam.”]

[Col. 0975A]

“Could either the minds or tongues of men have been deceived by vanity?

[640] 460 Could they have given gifts rendered fruitless by chance,  
or dedicated a vow under blind devotion?

What reason, or what motive, could there be for bowing the neck  
before Mary’s feet and offering the childish gifts  
of a little boy, if he was merely mortal  
and supreme power did not fill his tender limbs  
[645] with divine breath?

But now remove the Magi, the frankincense, gold, and myrrh—  
gifts which taught that he was truly God—  
the manger, the wrappings, the mother’s lap adored,  
the star’s blazing light.

Let the very power of God, and the wonders of his works, speak.

[650] I see the raging winds suddenly grow mild  
[Col. 0975B] when Christ commands; I see waters struggling  
with mighty whirlwinds stretch out in tranquil smoothness  
at Christ’s command; I see the same flood,  
when he allows himself to be trodden,  
solidify its liquid back beneath his feet.

[655] He himself walks over the flowing waves  
with shining feet and makes his footprints firm  
upon the compressed water.

He himself rebukes the winds and commands the blasts to rest.

Who could command the savage north winds,  
‘Go, be silent in your prisons,  
and withdraw from the broad sea,’  
[660] [Col. 0976A] unless he were the heavenly Power,  
himself also the creator of the north winds?

The snowy north recognizes him,  
and the rain-bearing east wind,  
the Lord of clouds and powerful over storms;  
they sweep away the stirred-up winter  
as the clear sky smiles.

Who could have trodden the waters of the sea?  
Who could have walked with pressing footsteps  
through the green shallows, traversing the wet path  
without being submerged, hanging over the ground  
and with dry feet,

[665] unless he were the maker of the watery sea?

Who is the Spirit who once,  
poured over the Father’s mouth,  
flew over the waters,  
not yet separated or enclosed by a fixed shore?

[670] The liquid upheld the Lord’s step,  
and, deprived of its mobility,  
made itself solid for his use.

Why should I recount the various illustrious deeds of God’s Christ?  
When you have examined his majesty more deeply, you, a denier,  
[675] will yourself, without hesitation, confess the man to be God.

He anointed blind eyes  
and restored sight by touching with his fingers  
the earth moistened by sacred spittle.

The hidden night possessed the clay-like medicine;  
the moisture that covered it removed the darkness;  
and, moreover, it showed in what bath  
[Col. 0977B] the darkness ought to be washed away.”

[Note: [Col. 0977B]

681. What he says here, “nor does it always breathe out a flood,” he expresses elsewhere, in the cited passage, in different words: “the liquid which the Spirit belches forth at varying hours.” Prudentius wishes the Pool of Bethesda, or Bethzatha, to be the same as the swimming pool of Siloam. Concerning the Pool of Bethesda, where a great multitude of sick people lay waiting for the movement of the water, see John, chapter V; concerning the Pool of Siloam, to which Jesus sent the blind man, the same evangelist, chapter IX.

Most recent writers distinguish them, but some of the ancients think that it was the same pool, into which the waters of the spring of Siloam flowed. Irenaeus, *Against Heresies* IV.19: “Siloam also often healed on Sabbaths, and for this reason many sat beside it on the Sabbath days.” Arator, Book I: “That paralytic, marked by so many years, lay there inactive, for nearby Siloam had been stirred. Alas, it offered no waters.” The poet therefore did not err, nor does he confuse and mix up the narratives, as some charge; rather, he follows the opinion of others.

684. The best Heinsian parchment manuscripts have *ablutura*; the Put. manuscript, *ablitura*. Aldus, Giselinus, Weitzius, Urbino, Vatican Q, and other manuscripts have *ablu­itura*, which I think should be restored in the Put. manuscript. The Alexandrian, by a second hand, has *ablutura*, which I retain because it is more Latin.

691. Mar. incorrectly has *adjecesse*.

[Col. 0977D] 694. Aldus has *coelestis* instead of *coelesti*, which should be preferred, unless one reads, with Cellarius, *liquido coelestis spiritus ore*, “with the heavenly Spirit’s fluid mouth”; I do not know where he obtained this. Perhaps he thought that *spiritus* and *liquidus* do not fit well together. I have shown this to be false in the prolegomena, number 164, and the gloss here explains *liquidus* as “spiritual.” As usual, the poet understands baptism allegorically in these passages of Scripture, as he explains in the following verses.

697. *Baptisma*, *baptismus*, and *baptizo* are ecclesiastical terms derived from Greek. Pliny has *baptisterium* in Book V, Letter 6. It is correct to understand “to pour in the day” as referring to the light and grace of baptism, which the ancients commonly call illumination. Saint John Chrysostom, *Catechesis* 1 to those being illuminated: “It is also called illumination, and Paul himself called this very thing”—namely, baptism—“by that name” (apparently Hebrews VI.4; X.32). The very baptismal font was called *phōtistērion* (φωτιστήριον), that is, “the place of illumination.” From this perhaps arose the custom that the baptized immediately after receiving baptism held lighted candles in their hands, so that the inward light with which they had been filled might be signified.

[Col. 0978C] 702. In Egmondanus, incorrectly, *purgamen in aquae*; likewise in Paldamus the erroneous *purgamina quae*. Aldus has *purgamina lymphae*. Our manuscripts and the older Heinsian manuscripts have *purgamen aquai*, which is the true reading. *Aquai* for *aquae* occurs in Lucretius, Maro, and others. Heinsius conjectures *purgamina aquai*, and Gallandius reports that this is the reading in Tornaes.

704. Bongarsius and Widmanstetter have *retexens*, and in the following verse *relegam*. Heinsius has *e multis*.

705. Heinsius, with his older manuscripts, has *relegam*, as do Mar. in the first hand and Vatican A; Weitzius, Aldus, Vatican B, Rat., Giselinus, and Fabricius have *relegens*; Prag. has *religens*. I do not know from whom Cellarius took *paulatim* for *summatim*, since the sense requires *summatim*. Teolius seems merely to have copied Cellarius; he does not cite manuscript witnesses for *paulatim*, and reads, with Cellarius, *paulatim relegens*.

Barthius, *Adversaria* XLI.24, inferred from this passage of Prudentius—whom he incidentally calls “a most learned theologian”—that the final words of Saint John’s Gospel should be understood not of the number of books but of the weight of the mysteries. Sedulius clearly explains the number of books at the end of his *Paschal Work*: “The whole world would not suffice to contain such dense books in so many volumes.”

706. Ecclesiastical writers use *desertum* as a singular noun, as do Tertullian and Saint Jerome; the older secular writers say *deserta*. The ancient grammarians teach that *duo* may be used for *duos*. Thus Fridericus Besselius, *Miscellanea*, syntagma, page 206, restored from the manuscripts in Vegetius: “Forty-two feet.”

708. The Prague manuscript has *nec* for *non*. *Undique septum* is from Virgil, *Aeneid* IX.733.]

[680] [Col. 0977A]

“it ought to be cleansed. At various intervals Siloam  
pours back its waters, nor does it always breathe out a flood,  
but at changing times receives abundant draughts.

Crowds of the sick thirst for the hope of the grudging spring,  
expecting that their bodily stains will be washed away  
by pure swimming.

[685] Meanwhile, in eager competition, they wait beside  
the dripping, rough stone for the noisy springs,  
and hang over the dry bank.

Christ commands that this clay, laid upon the eyes,  
be washed from the fountain,  
and that the face shine with the light poured into it.

463 For he knew that he himself had formed a figure from clay  
[690] before the darkness, and had added the medicine of his own mouth  
to the new Adam whom he had first fashioned.

For without the divine breath of the supreme Lord  
the dry earth was incapable of any healing.

But after the fluid Spirit from the heavenly mouth  
[695] sprinkled the virgin soil, it became medicinal:

From it he draws sap, and with gentle moisture  
anoints and pours in the day, washed in baptism.

The blind man appears, his eyes now uncovered  
by Christ’s spoken command;  
he proclaims that he has received light  
from the mud and the shining streams,

[700] and through the astonished towns points out the author.

The author of light and giver of days,  
who did not disdain to show, in his own body,  
the cleansing of medicinal water  
to the sick who had gone astray—

[705] From the many thousands I shall unfold only the very few,  
briefly rereading what the whole world cannot contain.

He commands five loaves and two fish  
to be set out as food for the peoples,  
who perhaps, with hunger not recalling itself,  
surrounded their teacher on every side,  
[Col. 0978B] forgetful of food, of the alleys, towns, markets,  
and meeting places.”

[Note: [Col. 0979B]

710. *Conciliabula*: “places where councils were held,” Vatican A; “where councils were celebrated,” I.

712. *Virum*: “of men,” I.

717. *Aggesta*: “heaped up,” I.

718. *Micarum molibus*: “with masses of fragments,” I.

719. *Crudus*: “full, satiated, undigested, rustic,” I.

720. *Congeriem*: “satiety,” Vatican A. — *Congeriem ventris*: “fullness of the belly.” — *Sub fasce*: “under the burden of the baskets,” I.

721. *Grandia*: “in such great quantities,” I.

723. *Existente*: “remaining,” I.

[Col. 0980B] 725. *Rudere*: “a mine in the earth, where bronze is extracted,” I.

726. *Semine*: “matter,” I.

727. *Procedere*: “to proceed from the place from which it had come forth,” I.

728. *Mox et grandescere*: not because everything God created had not been perfect in goodness—such is the gloss—but he speaks poetically, I.

735. *Consummata*: “perfected,” I.

736. *Calcata*: “fragments,” Vatican A.

739. *Appositi*: “namely, the baskets have been set out; that is, the apostles,” I. Understand this as referring to the apostles, Vatican A.]

710. *Conciliabula* are villages, or, as others say, places to which country people gather in villages and fields for buying or selling. The Alexandrian, by a second hand, and the Urbino manuscript have *mercatos*.

718. In Rat. there was *mollibus*, incorrectly, for *molibus*, unless one wishes *mollia micarum* to mean “soft pieces,” which is not absurd and is supported by the gloss. Chamillardus has *mollibus*, but in the interpretation, “with a multitude of fragments.”

719. In Mar., by the first hand, *coenas*; in Vatican A, a recent hand changed it to *coenam*, erasing the earlier letters. Others have *coenam*.

720. The Prague manuscript has *ministra*, incorrectly.

721. Cauchius conjectured *in prandia parvas* for *in grandia parvas*. Neither Heinsius nor I approve this.

722. Mar. and Weitzius have *omne*; others *omnem*. Heinsius suspects *pastum quoque corporis omnem*, or understands *omnem materiam*, since that word follows. If a change had to be introduced, I would prefer:

“Who, unless he who, forming body and all the body’s food from nothing, created the world when no matter existed?”

In Prudentius’s poems errors have often been introduced by those who did not know the poet’s usage and, wishing to take account of meter without sufficient knowledge of poetic art, corrupted the true reading. If *corpus* is read, the final syllable in *corpus* is lengthened by the caesura, something familiar in Prudentius. Cellarius and Teolius followed Heinsius’s conjecture.

724. Giselinus, with the Daventriensis edition, reads:

“not as a sculptor, from bronze,  
accustoms himself to make a raw and unbaked mass,”

because he thought *rudus aeris* was less properly said. Aldus, Put., Thuan., Oxford, Rot., the three Torrentian manuscripts, Egmondanus, Paldamus, Mar. in the first hand, and the best Vatican manuscripts have:

“not as a sculptor accustoms a mass, cooked from bronze ore, to live.”

That is, *consuescit* is used for *consuefacit*, as in Book I against Symmachus, verse 541, “he accustoms himself to excel in the heavenly kingdom forever,” and in *Cathemerinon* hymn 9, verse 95, “so that he might accustom the buried to return.” Heinsius says that Alcimus Avitus had earlier thought of this passage, forgetting that Prudentius is older than Avitus, unless Heinsius meant that Alcimus had imitated this passage of Prudentius. He says:

“It should be noted that Alcimus Avitus, in Book I of his poems, first conceived these words of Prudentius, although with a somewhat different meaning; for he is speaking of the creation of man:

‘Then, when the whole man had grown accustomed  
to live with perfected limbs.’”

*Aes rudus* means bronze not yet smelted. Thus in the hymn of Saint Laurence, verse 189: “The gold which the deeply dug mines produce eagerly produces ores.” Hence the Roman bronze gate was called *ra­uduscula*, because *rudus* or *raudus* properly means bronze. Heinsius confirms with many examples that *vivere* can be said of statues skillfully fashioned, and no one challenges this.

For *vivere*, Weitzius, Mar. by a recent hand, the oldest Rat., and Vatican Q read *fingere*, without any erasure. Chamillardus, as usual, almost copies Heinsius; this is not surprising, since he admits in his preface that he will follow Heinsius’s readings as far as he can. Teolius says that Heinsius’s reading is uniquely correct on the authority of the parchment manuscripts, and that the entire glory of restoring it belongs to Heinsius. It should be noted, however, that several manuscripts vary, as we have seen, and that even before Heinsius *consuescit vivere* was read in Aldus and other printed editions. Heinsius’s reading is not so certain that another cannot be defended: *fingere* is not absurdly said of a sculptor, and praising the artist’s skill does not fit this passage especially well. Since the body was made from existing matter, Prudentius often uses *fingere* to explain its formation. Thus *fingere massam* is not inappropriate here. Indeed, someone thinks *fingere massam* should be preferred altogether. In the gloss, *mina* for “mine” is a medieval word.

731. Prag. and Mar. in the first hand have *age* for *ego*.

732. In Mar. there was *elementa*, incorrectly.

736. Vatican A has *At ne*; the others *ac ne*.]

[710] [Col. 0979A]

“the towns, markets, meeting places, and cities,  
content to feed on his abundant teaching.

Many banquets of men boil upon the spread hay.

A hundred companions together recline,  
and pour themselves in crowds over countless tables,

[715] to be filled—now believe in God—by two little fish  
and a few crusts, with food increasing through fragments.

The dishes, piled high with food already bitten, overflow;  
twelve baskets are filled with masses of fragments after the meal;  
the glutted guest sweats out the heap in his belly,  
[720] and the servant groans beneath the burden.

Who can heap such great banquets from small things?

Who, unless he who, forming body, food,  
and all the body’s substance from nothing,  
created the world when no matter existed?

[Col. 0979B] Not as a sculptor accustoms a mass  
cooked from bronze ore to live.

[Col. 0980A] But almighty God fashioned the universe without seed.

Everything that exists was nothing:  
nothing was commanded to proceed, to exist,  
to become new, and soon to grow great.

At first the small thing came from nothing;  
then additions increased the whole by full stages.

[730] Therefore, when I see Christ make  
small human provisions grow in his hands,  
can I doubt that through him the small forms of things  
and the elements of the world first arose from nothing,  
small at first, and soon gradually grew large,

[735] so that what we see perfected came from small beginnings?

[Col. 0980B] And lest, after feeding the people, the fragments  
should be trampled and perish,  
or lie abandoned to wolves, foxes, or tiny mice  
as prey, without anyone to guard them:

the twelve set beside them, who heap up Christ’s good gifts ...

[Note: [Col. 0981B]

740. *Gravidis*: “full.” — *Procul ostentata*: “scattered nearby, prepared for storage.” — *Canistris*: “vessels, baskets,” I.

744. *Abdita*: “secret, hidden,” I.

747. *Charybdis*: According to the myth, Charybdis was a woman whom Hercules threw into the sea because she was a devourer, and she still performs that function, since she swallows approaching ships. In reality, however, it is a rock; here he uses it for hell, which draws all who approach it into an eternal whirlpool and destruction, I.

748. *Tenui*: “narrow,” I.

749. *Superis*: “the living.” — *Taenara*: “places of punishment, or the underworld; the lamentations of the condemned, or infernal places,” I.

750. *Praeceps*: “into a precipice.” — *Chao*: “a chasm,” I.

[Col. 0982B] 751. *Amnis*: “Cocytus.” — *Inexpletis*: “insatiable.” — *Incendia*: “fires,” I.

753. *Damnarunt*: “closed,” Iso.

754. *Ciet*: “calls,” Mar. — *Frigentis*: “he had been dead four days,” I.

759. *Nidorem*: “stench.”

763. *Fluidis*: “rotten, dissolved,” I.

764. *Fictilis*: “capable of being formed.” — *Ulvae*: “earth”; *ulva* is marsh grass, but here he uses it for the mud from which man was made or formed, Iso.

765. *Vena*: “blood.” — *Cui*: “from him, or through whom.” — *Tabida*: “sluggish,” Iso.

766. *Infecto*: “introduced,” I. Vatican A has *corrupto*.

741. *Sed quid ego haec autem* is from Virgil, *Aeneid* II.101. In Vatican A, *autem* is absent. In Rat., *audax* appears from a correction by another, though still an ancient, hand. I do not approve it.

742. Fabricius and Giselinus have *tanta*. The manuscript witnesses and other editions have *sancta*. Victorinus of Poitiers: “Proceed from the tomb, Lazarus, he cries.”

743. Prudentius lengthens the first syllable in *Lazare* and shortens the second, as he also did in *Cathemerinon* hymn 9, verse 47. Hence I confirm that Heinsius, Chamillardus, Teolius, and Cellarius were wrong to print *Lazari* for *Eleazar* at verse 154 of *Cathemerinon* hymn 10.

744. Rat. has *audieras*; the others *audieris*. Giselinus has *penetrarit ad*. Aldus has *intima*; others *abdita*.

749. Prag. has *ubi tristia tartara*. Vatican B, Widmanstetter, Bongarsius, Mar., Rat., and Urbino have *trenara tristia*. Others have *thenara* or *taenara tristia*. Iso seems to have read *threnara*, from *threni*, “laments.” *Taenari* is used for the underworld because on Mount Taenarus there was a cave with a deep opening.

751. Vatican B has *implexis*. Mar. has *inexpletis*, but by a recent hand, and *expletis*. The true reading is *inexpletis*, that is, “insatiable,” which is a characteristic epithet of the underworld.

753. Weitzius, Iso, Mar., Prag., and Rat. have *damnarunt*. Prag. and Egmondanus have *substracta* or *subtracta*. Rat. has *substricta*, less well, for *substructa*.

754. Chamillardus correctly notes from Festus that *ciere* means “to call,” as in Virgil, “to call forth the men with bronze.”

755. Vatican A has *funereis*; *funereus* is better.

757. He addresses Mary Magdalene and Martha, the sisters of Lazarus. See John XI.

759. Elmenhorstius, in his work on Arnobius, page 116, discusses at length *nidor*, a strong odor, especially of sacrifices, comparing this passage of Prudentius with *Peristephanon* hymn 2, verse 388, and other authors.

761. With plausible inference the poet reports that Lazarus saw his former beauty as in a mirror; unless one prefers to explain it as meaning that his eyes, restored to life, were again bright like a mirror.

762. Mar., by the first hand, has the erroneous *tincta robore*.

763. Aldus has *qui*; the others *quis*. Prag. and Widmanstetter above have *diffundere*.

764. Latinius, in the *Biblia selecta*, reads *fictilis urnae*, which is not an absurd reading unless the manuscripts stood against it. In the following verse some editions have *vestam* for *venam*, incorrectly; from this someone conjectured *vestem*, so that the body would be called the moist garment of the clay urn. Properly, an urn is a vessel used for storing the ashes of the dead, concerning which the poet says: “He is covered by heaven who has no urn.” This is from our Isidore, *Etymologies* XVI.26.

767. Giselinus has *auditis* in the text and *auritis* in the margin, which others also have. The sense seems more satisfactory with *auditis* than with *auritis*, for it was not the laws that heard death, but death that heard the laws of the commanding Lord. Vatican Q incorrectly has *haustis* for *auditis*. Teolius says that all the Vatican manuscripts have *auritis*, among them two with this interpretation: *auritis*, that is, “capable of being heard.” Perhaps the poet means that the laws of death were “eared,” that is, heard. Rat. has *mitis jam*; others *jam mitis*.]

768. Fabr. reads “wherever you are commanded [to go],” which Heinsius and I would prefer, if the manuscripts allowed it. Ald., Thuan., Oxon., and others read “wherever she is commanded.” Vat. B, Noms., Bong., “whatever things are commanded.” Rot. and Cauch., “wherever he is commanded.” I prefer, with Put., Prag., Rat., Vat. A, Mar., Weitz., Gall., Tornaes., and others, “whatever is commanded.” Gis. has in the text “whatever things are commanded,” in the margin “wherever he is commanded,” and elsewhere “wherever.” Sich. reads “whatever things are commanded.” Gallandius praises Aldus for “whatever is commanded”; but my copy of Aldus has “wherever,” and I read the same in Aldus’s copy preserved in the Sapienza Library.]

[740] [Col. 0981A] They might preserve [them], displayed from afar in pregnant baskets.

But why do I rehearse these things in a faltering voice,

Unworthy to sing sacred matters? Come forth from the tomb,

Lazarus; tell us whose voice you heard beneath the earth:

What power penetrated the hidden recesses of death?

[745] When Christ calls you, wholly submerged in the utterly black abyss,

And summons you to return, you hear as though you were close at hand,

And, without delay, you are present. What Charybdis so near

Joins the realms of darkness, separated by so narrow a boundary,

To the realms above? Where Tartarus, gloomy and cast headlong

[750] Into a vast chaos, and that hidden river,

Rolls its fires along banks that can never be filled?

Before the tomb’s doors, which enormous stones

Had sealed with their hard barrier, built up beneath hollow crags,

The Lord stands and calls by name his lifeless friend.

[755] [Col. 0982A] There is no delay: the funereal horror, when the rocks have rolled back,

Spews forth living obsequies as the corpse walks forth.

[468] Now loose, joyful sisters, your fragrant bonds;

The single scent of scattered spices breathes forth its fragrance,

Nor does a foul breeze from bodily corruption

Bring back an odor from the decaying flesh.

[760] His eyes, freed as pus drips from them,

Recover their former beauty in the mirror,

And purple gradually clothes his rotting cheeks

With a stain of red.

Who could pour a soul over those fluid limbs?

Surely he who gave the limbs: he who breathed through the moist channel

[765] Of clay; he for whom the decaying earth drew blood-red colours

From tainted moisture.

O Death, now gentle under laws that have reached your ears!

[Col. 0982B] O Death, formerly deaf, now taught to follow whatever is ordered,

773. “Taken captive,” “by Christ,” I.

776. “Carries,” “bears,” I.

780. “Had taken,” “upon himself,” I.

781. “This,” the body. “That,” the soul. “Abyss”: he calls heaven the abyss, because just as we say “the deep sea,” so also we say “the depth of heaven.” Thus too we call heaven the abyss. On the nature of the soul: Heretics say that the soul is a part of God. Every substance is divided in three ways, namely into God, soul, and body. Or, if God is the highest good, the soul is a great good, and the body a certain good: without these three nothing exists, I.

782. “Disputer,” “combatant,” “debater,” I.

783. “Sets before,” “opposes,” I.

784. “Inspired,” the soul. “By God,” “from God,” I.

789. “Painted,” “imagined,” I.]

769. Aldus had printed *convicta fetere*; in his corrections he changed it to *conjuncta fatere*, with a new error. Virgil, book VI: “How much power has he had over you?”

[Col. 0983C] 770. Weitz., Sich., Mar., Prag. read “that he alone is God, who.” Others read “that he is God, the only one who.” The exceedingly inept correction added to the Regensburg edition, after the earlier reading had been erased, is: “To be God, who alone snatches me away from you, Jesus,” as though otherwise the poem were not intelligible.

772. “Use your lot,” Virgil, book XII, line 932. Vat. A reads “the blasphemers holding [them] in perpetual night.” Ald., Vatt. B, Q, Mar., Rat., read “the perpetual people of the righteous, held by blasphemers in the night.” Weitzius follows this and punctuates: “Use your lot for the blasphemers held in the night! Release the perpetual people of the righteous, whom you have taken captive.” Weitzius acknowledges that Giselinus’s reading, “held by blasphemers in perpetual night,” is sound, but says that Ald., Fabr., Egm., and Widm. oppose it. In Egm. and Pal. there is *necte tenentis*. Heinsius stopped at this passage, following Giselinus and adding no note. I prefer the reading of Vat. A: “To the blasphemer holding them in perpetual night, release the people of the righteous whom you have taken captive.” Yet I do not reject the reading of Gis. and Prag., which I follow.

777. Mar. reads *animavit*; and instead of the variant reading, *animae vim*, which is preferable.

[Col. 0983D] 779. Prag. reads *assumpsit*. Others have *assumit*. Some of the holy Fathers were unwilling to use the term *assumption*, especially with the concrete noun “man,” as though it favored Nestorius. Others employed it. Augustine, *City of God*, book XI, chapter 2: “with man assumed, not God consumed.” See further examples in Petavius, volume IV, part 1, book II, *On the Incarnation*, chapter 1, and in the Fathers of the fourth and sixth Councils of Toledo, omitting more recent authorities.

781. Here “abyss” is understood as the dwelling-place of souls after death. It is an ecclesiastical term for the realms below. Isidore, *Etymologies*, book XIII, chapter 20, says: “The abyss is an impenetrable depth of waters, or a cavern of concealed waters.” St. Jerome, on Ecclesiastes I: “Plato in the *Phaedo* calls this womb the abyss of Tartarus.” Teolius explains “abyss” as heaven, with a gloss. I understand the body to be drawn from the tomb, and the soul from the abyss.

782. Ald., Mar., Rat., and Heinsius’s manuscripts, together with Weitz. and other printed editions, have the heading *On the Nature of the Soul*, which Heinsius thinks should be removed, because what follows too should properly be referred to the argument against the Homuncionites. Gis., in the margin, has “The nature of the soul.” In Alex. and others the same heading, *On the Nature of the Soul*, appears. See the following note and what I observed above on line 118. I discussed the word *dissertator* in preface 2 to line 28.

783. Prudentius often says that the soul was inspired by God’s breathing, that it is the work of the divine mouth, and similar things, to indicate that it is spiritual, since “spirit” and “breath” have the same meaning. By contrast, he asserts that the body was made by God’s fingers, so that it is clear that it was produced from preexisting matter and not created anew. He now therefore dissolves the arguments of his opponents, who said that it was impossible for a spiritual and incorporeal soul to be tormented by punishments in hell. St. Augustine and other Fathers and theologians debate this question. Prudentius seems to be arguing against the Gnostics, who asserted that the soul was a part of God; consequently, the different heading is not inappropriate, for the Homuncionites held a different error.

784. Weitz., Gis., Vat. B, Mar., Prag., Rat. read *atque*. Ald., Egm., Pal., and Heinsius’s old manuscripts, together with Alex., Urb., and Vat. Q, read *utque*.

[Col. 0984D] 786. Giselinus improperly wrote *credo* three times in these two lines instead of *crede*.

791. When he says that it is not generation, he means that the soul is not God’s son.

793. Editions before Heinsius read: “The Son sprang forth, that true God; but this [was bestowed on the soul],” and so forth. Alex. incorrectly has “the true, true God; but this [was bestowed],” and so forth. Heinsius, with Put. and Thuan., reads: “true, that true God.” *Collatum est*, and so forth. Teolius follows Heinsius and cites only one Vatican manuscript for the other reading. But Mar. and our other copies, as well as the old editions, have the former reading.

794. In Aldus’s copy preserved in the Sapienza Library there is a manuscript note: “The soul was fused together, namely its breath.” But the true reading is “was joined.”

795. Rat., Weitz., Bong., Gis., Patri. read *Patri*. Most manuscripts, and the older ones, have *Patris*. Bong. has *in ipso est*, which Gallandius retained together with Torn.]

[Col. 0983A] [469] “Who has been granted such power over you? Confess, vanquished one:

[770] “That Jesus alone is God, who snatches me away from you.”

Hide the deniers of Christ; no one begrudges you. Hide them.

Use your lot upon the blasphemers held in perpetual night:

Release the perpetual people of the righteous whom you have taken captive,

Those who know how to call Christ both man and God,

[775] So that the true and supreme God bears mortal things.

He himself bears what he fashioned, his own work,

And the Creator is not ashamed of what he begot: I speak of the body and the power of the soul.

God assumes the whole human being, because the whole comes from him,

[Col. 0984A] [470] Here the disputant, in doubt, comes forward and raises the objection:

“Can faith accept that a substance inspired by God’s breathing

Should feel torment and seek the lowest depths

[785] Of the infernal heaven, and be cooked in the abyss?”

Believe that the soul is not God; but believe that it is greater

Than all created things; believe also that it was itself created.

For it was formed by God’s mouth, though it did not exist before:

But it was formed in a most beautiful condition, adorned with divine

[790] Realities, full of God, and like its creator.

Yet it is not itself God, since it is not generation,

But God’s workmanship. Only the Son sprang forth from the Father’s heart:

That one is true God. But this was bestowed

[Col. 0984B] [471] On the soul, so that what did not exist suddenly came to be.

[795] He is coeternal with the Father and always in the Father:

798. Put. has *junctim*; others, *junctum*.

800. Thuan. and Gis. have *simulatio*; the others, *imitatio*. Giselinus thought that *imitatio* conflicted with the meter and sense; both judgments are false. Prudentius often lengthens a short syllable for the sake of the caesura. Who would deny that a shadow is a kind of imitation of a body?

801. Mar. has *at*, made by a later hand, and *atque*: Tertullian, *Against Marcion*, book II, chapter 9: “For just as an image, although it reproduces all the lines, nevertheless lacks the power of truth, since it has no movement, so the soul, too, is an image of the Spirit and could not reproduce its power alone, that is, the blessedness of not sinning.”

802. Bon. from the first hand, and Sich., read *quia*; the others, *quod*, with the same meaning. The poet places the image and likeness of God partly in the immortality of our soul. Faustus of Riez, *On Free Choice*, book I, chapter 1: “What else, indeed, is to be understood in the very image of God in which man was created, except the mark of perpetuity?” Add Maximus the Martyr, *Centuries*, 3.25.

803. Vat. A has *quo*; *quod* is better. The subject is the soul.

804. Gis. has *instat*; in the margin, *infit*. So does Iso. Gifanius, in the Lucretian Index, reads *antevidet* as one word from an old manuscript; this is preferable.

805. Weitzius found *rerumque* instead of *morumque* in certain printed editions unknown to me.

806. There is much discussion by authors, and by the poet in several passages, of the mind’s speed.

807. This word is explained by *effigio* in hymn 10 of the *Cathemerinon*, line 4.

808. Egm. and Pal. have *sumptum*, but I do not see in what sense it could stand for *promptum*.

809. Prag. has *ac* instead of *at*.

810. Consult Wowerus, Ouzelius, and Meursius on Minucius’ words, which I transcribed in the note to line 7 of the *Apotheosis*. Petavius, book III, chapter 9, volume I, gathers much in this sense and says: “And most beautifully Prudentius: ‘But God is immense, and poured over all things.’”

813. Vegetius used *mensurare*; Claudianus Mamertus, *mensurabile*; Salvianus, *immensurabile*.

819. Weitzius cites M. Berg. in support of *peccanti*. In Cauch., Bonon., and Rot. there is *peccando natura luti*; three Tor. copies have *peccando natura luto*. Cauchius insists that it should be corrected to *peccati natura luti*, with *peccati* as a past participle used with the force of an active verb. He gives the Terentian example from the *Hecyra*: *peccato mihi ignosci aequum*, “it is right that I be forgiven for my fault.” Cauchius indicates another correction, *peccantis natura luti*. The common reading should not be disturbed; its sense is straightforward. It becomes mixed, then, “the nature of sinning, with clay, with simple breath”—that is, from the conjunction of soul and body arises the nature of sinning, mixed from clay and simple spirit. This is the meaning of *mixta luto cum simplice flatu*. Iso interprets *simplice* as “without sin,” which I do not approve.

822. Iso renders *oblita* as “surrounded”; “stained,” from *oblino*, is better.

823. Giselinus says that he moved the adulterine expression *pressum* from this place; perhaps it stood thus in the Daventria edition, for Aldus expressly has *pessum*. Sich. and Fabr. should not have printed *pressum* after Aldus. Against the Gnostics and Manichaeans, who asserted that the soul was God’s substance, he has so far proved that the soul is not God, because it is encompassed by the body’s filth, which is alien to God, and because the soul was joined suddenly to what did not exist, so that it came to be in time. Now, since they could answer that the soul was at least a part of God, he refutes and disproves them on this point as well.

824. Vat. A and Egm. have *fit res*, which is not as good.]

[Col. 0985A] He is not made but born, and possesses whatever is paternal.

This [soul] is like God as a shadow is. Thus the Creator himself,

Planning to build in his own likeness a human being joined from a twofold formation,

[did so]; but a shadow does not possess

[800] What the solid body possesses, whose imitation is in the shadow.

One thing is true, another an imitation of the true.

It is like him in that no ages consume it:

It is wise, capable of justice, and, queen of things,

Commands; it foresees, weighs, takes precautions, presses forward;

[805] A maker of words and morals, equipped with a thousand

Arts, and taught to traverse heaven with its understanding.

[Col. 0985B] [472] With these qualities the creator fashioned the soul like himself,

But unlike him in other respects; for it is easy to comprehend this soul,

[Col. 0986A] Which limit and form determine. But immense God,

[810] Poured over everything, has nothing within himself

That is bounded, so that he could be confined or grasped by the senses.

His power remains incomprehensible, lacking

A final boundary, while immeasurable space extends it.

Therefore the soul, made and lesser than the great creator,

[815] Yet greater than other things and ruling over all,

Is received at its birth by the turbid corruption of decaying flesh,

And, poured through wasting limbs,

Is made to share in that corruption’s dregs; then the nature of sinning becomes mixed

With clay and simple breath.

[820] But perhaps, because the soul flowed from the Lord’s mouth,

You may deny that it is compounded and made, as though it were itself a part of God—

[Col. 0986B] [473] Which is a wicked thing to say—that, stained, it should drag along

Dark faults, rushing headlong into destruction; that it should enter covered chaos.

Let it be a thing of God; I do not reject that. Yet that part

830. Theodoretus, as Chamillardus notes: “By the name ‘Breath’ we do not understand any part of the divine essence, according to the madness of Cerdo and Marcion; rather, the nature of the soul is indicated by this, namely that the soul is a rational and intellectual spirit.” Chamillardus gives no location for the passage, nor did I find it when I searched.

832. Heinsius’s manuscripts have *quanto*. So too Vat. A, Bong., and Widm. above, and Pragen. Others, with Ald., Weitz., and Mar., have *quantum*. Gis. has *quanto*. In Widm. above, *tenore*.

833. The word *impossibile* is more Latin than most people think; Quintilian used it in book V, chapter 13, as did Apuleius and others.

835. Aldus has the error *soleres* instead of *solers*.

836. He refers to Christ’s saying, “The Father is in me,” and to what theologians say, which also appears in the Athanasian Creed: “Just as the rational soul and flesh are one man, so God and man are one Christ.”

837. Vat. A has *respice*; others, *perspice*; Weitz., Egm., Pal., and Widm. above also have *respice*.

839. At this point Chamillardus recognizes the natural rhythm of an animated voice. But Prudentius discusses musical matters a little later; here he merely mentions and distinguishes warm and cold breath.

841. Mar. has *ingelidum*; others, *in gelidum*. The subject is a cold or chilly breath. Gifanius, in the Lucretian Index, read *flabrare* with a long *e* from an old book and concluded that *e* is sometimes long at the end of words. But since a mute and liquid follow, the *e* in *flabrare* could be lengthened for this reason. Goldastus, in his notes on Columbanus, page 112, also read *flabrare* from two very old manuscripts of St. Gall. Weitzius followed him. Widm., from the first hand, has *flabrari*. Most manuscripts and editions have *flabrali*; so do ours and the better manuscripts of Heinsius. From *flatus* come *flabrum*, *flabellum*, and *flabralis*. Vat. Q, Egm., and Pal. have *fabrili*, incorrectly.

844. Ald., Vat. A and Q, Mar., Gis., and Weitz. have *modulamine*; this is not objectionable, although *modulos* occurs again later. Thuan. has *moderamine*, that is, “with moderation,” as at line 831. Prag. and Rat. follow Thuan. Put. has *paucus*; Prag. has *partus* instead of *parcus*. Fabricius discusses this variation in the sounds as follows: “Prudentius calls musical sounds harsh, gentle, thin, and sharp; he adds sparse, lofty, and small. But ‘sparse’ can be included under gentle, ‘lofty’ under sharp, and ‘small’ under thin.” Fabricius says this in his *Commentary*, under the heading “Musical Instruments,” noting that Prudentius numbers among them in different places the flute, the sambuca, the chelys, the lyre, the trumpet, the pipe, the drum, and organs. He lists the musicians who in his time had published melodies for Prudentius and other pious poets: Ludovicus Senflius, Martin Agricola, Joannes Mopsus, Joannes Reuschius, Lucas Hordisius, Sebastianus Forsterus, and Wolfgang Figulus. See Isidore, *Etymologies*, book III, chapters 5 and following, on music and its threefold division.

845. The verb *sublimare*, used by Ennius and Cato and considered obsolete, was restored by Vitruvius, Apuleius, Solinus, Lactantius, Mamertinus, Ammianus, and Macrobius.

854. Boher. has *pernoscere* instead of *prior*.]

[825] [Col. 0987A] It must by no means be called God, since it began in time;

Nor should it be thought prior or older than the first formed creature, Adam.

For I see that it was made then, when the sister of the beloved heart

Entered the house, a guest of fresh clay,

And herself, newly made, took her seat in the brother’s body.

[830] Indeed, she is the Lord’s breath; but she is not the spirit

And power of God in its fullness, sent with as much restraint

As the one breathing wished to preserve in the act of breathing.

It is impossible to behold the depths of Sabaoth:

But man is the mirror of the Godhead. In the body learn

[835] [474] Skillfully learn, with Christ as interpreter, of a nonbodily reality—

[Col. 0987B] Christ who displays the Father himself in mortal flesh.

Observe how many different vapors we pour from our mouths.

Whenever we breathe, we breathe out the soul’s breath.

[Col. 0988A] Now warmth breathes out a tepid breath,

[840] Exhaling dewy mists from damp throats.

When it pleases, a thin spirit emerges as a cold wind

With a chilly breath and whistles through the air.

Add also the distinct breath that the musical pipe receives:

Or it is restrained by compressed modulation,

[845] [475] Or it raises a swelling boom with abundant breath,

Or it breaks harsh melodies, or whispers gently,

Or, drawing out a thin sound, produces sharp notes,

Or utters a tender murmur in a fine voice.

When you see yourself able to do these things in a mortal body,

[850] Why do you not believe that the Eternal could have infused

Such a soul as he wished? Since, creating it according to prescribed

Modes, he breathed it forth and poured it out,

It must have been made.

Finally, our soul knows many things, but does not know everything:

Its power has been commanded to know and foresee certain things.

But our flesh is the workmanship of God’s hand. Therefore our soul too is the workmanship of God’s mouth.” Prag. supplies this place for the deduction of the consequence.

855. Prag. has, incorrectly, *posse* instead of *nosse*.

857. Vatt. A and Q, Rat., Egm., Palm., Urb. have *dissimilis*, namely: “Gather whether this workmanship is unlike”—that is, “Gather whether this workmanship is unlike its creator.” *Collige de simili*, “gather from likeness,” is better, as Iso explains. Vat. A has *futura* instead of *factura*, contrary to the rules of the poem. Rat. has *creanti*. In the same Rat. manuscript this line is repeated, as it is found in most excellent copies, by the same hand: “Gather whether this workmanship is unlike its creator.” “Gather from likeness” means: determine whether this workmanship created; and in this second instance *creavit* appears where *creanti* stood above. Alex. has “gather, unlike; read ‘from likeness.’” The argument from likeness is this: just as the body is said to be formed by God’s fingers—although God properly has no fingers—and is therefore a work, so the soul, which is said to be the work of the divine mouth, is a work by the same reasoning.

860. In the copy of the Aldine edition in the Sapienza Library, some pedant noted that *sola* should be read instead of *vola*, meaning “earth.” *Involare* is derived from *vola*, as Iso says; Isidore also transmitted this explanation in book XVII, chapter 7, of the *Etymologies*.

[Col. 0989D] 863. Put. has *incircuminscriptus*, which I do not approve. St. Jerome, on Lamentations I: “Human limbs, as well as human emotions, are metaphorically attributed to God, not literally, because uncircumscribed light and immeasurable majesty do not know how to be circumscribed by bodily outlines.”

864. Prag. has *oculis*; the others, *animis*.

869. Prudentius seems to take *rudis* to mean new or recent. See hymn 3 of the *Cathemerinon*, line 133.

871. Someone wanted *et* added after *anima* for the sake of the meter. The poem proceeds correctly without *et*.

875. Mar. seems to have *quid tam*.

877. Ald. has *triste*; correct it to *tristem*.

878. Ald., Vat. A, the better manuscripts of Heinsius, Fabr., Weitz., Egm. read *recidit in poenam*. Gis., Bong., Widm., Vatt. B and Q, Rat., Prag. have *decidit in poenam*. Mar. has *in poenam recidit*. *Recidit in poenam* is not bad. The prefix *re-* is often lengthened in *reducere*, *refugere*, *recidere*, *referre*, and similar words. See Gifanius in the Lucretian Index under *re* and under *recidere*, *reducere*, and *refugere*. Alex., Urb., and others read *reccidit*. I prefer *decidit*.

879. Weitz., the older manuscripts of Heinsius, Gis. in the margin, Mar., and Rat. have *animae*; others, with Alex., have *anima*, which I think better.

880. Ald. and many of Heinsius’s manuscripts have *mundat*; others, with Put., Thuan., Wid., Gis., and Weit., as I think, have *inundat*. Widm. above has *nudat*; Alex. has *mundat*. Vat. Q has *lavat*, against the meter. Prudentius’ statement that, after Adam’s fall, Christ’s new grace cleanses him can suggest that he believed grace had been granted to Adam as well. This not only agrees closely with St. Augustine’s principles, as Teolius says, but also belongs to the doctrines of faith. The grace of Christ is new and overflowing because it is greater, stronger, more effective, and more powerful than the grace granted to Adam before his sin. For although free will was not altogether lost and extinguished in Adam’s transgression, it remained weakened and inclined toward evil; consequently, greater grace is necessary in the state of fallen nature than in the state of integral nature. These matters are clear. Nor is the extremely difficult passage of St. Augustine from *On Rebuke and Grace* useful for elucidating Prudentius: “To the first man was given assistance by which he could persevere, and without which he could not persevere, if he wished—not assistance by which he would be made to wish; but now, through Christ, assistance is given without which we cannot persevere, even if we wish, and assistance so great and of such a kind that we may be made to wish.” I have never sufficiently understood this distinction between assistance without which one cannot persevere and assistance by which one is made willing, although I have spent many hours attempting to clarify it. Nor am I ashamed to admit this amid such divergent interpretations. Indeed, I think that in this passage “new grace” means baptism, by which man is reborn. Cyprian and others call baptism the grace of Christ. After this work had been published, a certain theologian publicly expressed an honorable judgment of it and approved this very interpretation of mine—that the subject was baptism, which the holy Fathers and the acts of the martyrs often call the grace of Christ. He added much about Augustine’s distinction between the assistance by which one is made willing and that without which one cannot persevere. He thinks that this distinction confirms my interpretation. But since Prudentius is speaking of baptism, or of the habitual grace infused in baptism, as he clearly explains in the following lines—“Christ’s new grace cleanses the needy soul; the Holy Spirit ennobles it, justified by baptism”—it would be necessary for St. Augustine, in that distinction of his, to have had habitual grace in mind, not actual grace. As I think, this theologian will not admit that. I had said that Prudentius’ words present no difficulty, whereas theologians disagree sharply among themselves in explaining Augustine’s distinction. The theologian replies that no difficulty or obscurity appears if Augustine’s words are read with a calm and composed mind and compared with other things the same holy doctor says in the same book, chapter 12. The core of this reply is that the many theologians who defend different systems concerning the nature of actual grace, and consequently offer different interpretations of Augustine’s distinction, either did not read Augustine’s words with a calm and composed mind or did not compare them with one another—except, of course, those who agree with the aforementioned theologian in constructing his system of grace. I do not envy him; I am rather amazed: “Everywhere the whole countryside is so greatly disturbed.” “What then?” you ask. “Did Augustine not explain the doctrine of grace clearly?” He certainly explained, more than anyone else and as clearly as possible, the Catholic doctrine concerning the necessity and efficacy of grace. But when so many Catholic theologians—not to mention heretics—draw from Augustine’s words consequences for constructing different systems of grace, while all loudly claim that Augustine evidently supports them, who could justly be angry with me if I deny that Augustine explained those systems clearly? If you ask me which interpretation of Augustine’s distinction seems clearer or more probable to me, I will answer that I find Petavius’ explanation convincing, although I do not despise those of other Catholics. Petavius, therefore, in the *Elenchus of the Theriaca of Vincentius Lenis*, chapter 22 and following, explains “assistance without which one cannot persevere” as perseverance alone, or persevering grace. He confirmed this interpretation with many weighty arguments in his dissertation on assistance without which one cannot persevere and assistance by which one is made willing, rescued from the Iprensian sophistries and restored to its true and genuine meaning. There he notes that Jansenius considered this passage of Augustine so important that he repeated it almost two hundred times and seems to have laid no other foundation beneath his opinion.]

[855] [Col. 0989A] Now, whatever possesses a definite limit, and whatever is denied knowledge of everything,

Is a work; for it is shown to have been created and increased.

Gather from likeness whether this is a work: surely the Lord’s hand

Created the mortal body and composed the clay with his fingers.

But is the Lord’s hand arranged joint by joint?

[860] Does it have a palm? Does it have flexible nails

[476] To close and open? Or to stretch out the open hand?

That is the form of our hand, which the uncircumscribed Lord

Does not possess in himself; rather, a form was given

[Col. 0989B] That would provide the human mind with a recognizable understanding,

[865] So that he might be said, through bodily form, to have fashioned

The figure of the body. Thus, in turn, a breathable thing was fashioned

By incorporeal breath, and is said to be the work of the mouth;

Through it the delicate form of the soul, having been constructed,

[Col. 0990A] Shone forth and felt itself made by a fresh gift.

[870] If our flesh is not the work of the hand, neither is the soul

The work of the mouth, begun by breath and inspiration

And brought into some place. For everything that the hour of birth

Brings forth is received by some place, and whatever a place

Can contain is limited and is not poured into everything.

[875] And whatever is so limited that it is located in a definite place

Can already falter; and whatever has faltered is within

The nature of fault. Finally, being faulty and wretched,

[477] It falls into punishment. Believe me, God is not this.

[Col. 0990B] Or, if the soul is majesty, show what it is

[880] That, fallen and lacking Christ, new grace cleanses,

[Col. 0991A] The Holy Spirit justifies by baptism and ennobles,

Adding to the servant-girl the honor that was lacking:

Because this is granted for merits and denied for merits,

It is absurd to say that God—or a part of God—receives

[885] The divine and supreme good from an everlasting source,

Now drinks it through obedience, now loses it through fault or crime,

And at one time receives punishment, at another tramples freely.

Do you wonder that the soul sins, though, compacted with flesh,

[Col. 0992A] It has been allotted habitation in a house, when the angel himself sins,

[890] Though he does not know how to enter a perishable dwelling—
Of the wasting framework. He sins because he too was made,

Not begotten; in whatever manner he was made, the Maker alone

Knows; let it be enough for me to believe that he was made.

The Creator of the world alone is free from the stain of sin,

[895] The unbegotten and begotten God, the Father and the one born from the Father.

896. In Vat. A, an ancient corrector, almost of the same period, erased the previous readings and wrote *Spiritus et sanctus* (“Spirit and holy”); above it, in extremely small letters, he added *solus et exceptus* (“alone and excepted”), with the gloss “separated, set apart.”

897. Vat. A has *sensit* (“felt”); *sentit* (“feels”) is better.

[Col. 0993C] 898. In the first hand of Egm., *disce* for *dic*.

899. In Ald., the *a* after *vacuamque* is absent. Although, because of the two consonants in the following word, *que* could be lengthened, the manuscript copies have *a crimine* (“from crime”).

900. Prag. has *Qui peccare* (“who can sin”); the others have *quae*, namely *anima* (“soul”), for *ipsa* (“she herself”) follows in the next verse.

901. Cellarius, second edition, has *conditor* incorrectly.

902. The better copies have *viviscere*; others have *vivescere*. He calls it “raw mud,” just as above, verse 869, *rudi munere* (“with a raw gift”) for “a new gift.”

907. *Volutabra* are muddy places where sows and boars wallow. He calls the soul’s purity and brightness “fire,” as often elsewhere.

914. He clearly explains and establishes original sin, which the Pelagians denied.

915. This marks the error of those who taught that original sin was transmitted to Adam’s descendants because not only the body but also souls were propagated from Adam. [Col. 0993D] On this controversy St. Augustine remained very uncertain, since it seemed difficult to him that the soul should be corrupted in the body as in a vessel unless it itself were drawn, already corrupted, from Adam. Now it is certain among all Catholics that souls are not transferred from Adam, but that original sin is contracted solely because human beings are born propagated from Adam’s seed, in which, as in their head, all sinned.

919. Sich., Gis. first edition in the margin, Vat. Q, Heins., Cel., Teol., Cham., Pal., and Bong. in the first hand have *quod*. All the Heinsian copies, as well as our manuscripts and printed editions, including Alex. and Urb., have *quo*. Teolius accuses Chamillard of having been misled by a typographical error in Heinsius’s edition and of seeing nothing here. I, on the contrary, think Chamillard correctly understood what is printed in Heinsius. [Col. 0994B] In the verses of Heinsius’s edition I detect no typographical error; in the notes, however, there is an error—*corpora* for *vascula*—which has no bearing on the matter under discussion. Heinsius himself says at the end of the note that in Thuan. *vincula* is read for *vascula*, a reading he rightly rejects. Now Heinsius’s practice in explaining notes is to place first the reading he found in Giselinus, and then either reject or defend it. Thus he says here:

“*QUO PARVULA ANHELENT*, so all our copies; but in two of Weitz’s copies, *QUOD ANHELENT*, and this occupied the margin of certain editions: rightly so, as above, *Variis Siloa refundit momentis latices, nec fluctum semper anhelat*, etc.”

Chamillard read and says that *quod anhelent* should be read, and that it occupied the margin of certain editions. Teolius says that Weitz intended *quo anhelent*, as several editions also have. Weitz certainly printed this, and it is also found in most old editions, but he identified two codices in which *quod anhelent* is read; it really did appear before Heinsius in the margin of certain editions. In any case, it is true that *anhelare* occurs with the accusative in Prudentius and others; but it is not equally certain that the poet intended the accusative here, for what follows is *vitalisque adsit scintilla coactis*—namely, “so that the vital spark may be present in the compacted [vessels].”

922. Cellarius discusses the word *figmentum* at length in *Restored Latin of the Bronze Age*, citing Apuleius, Ammianus, Cyprian, Aulus Gellius, Macrobius, Minucius Felix, Lactantius, Tertullian, and Spartianus. He observes that Prudentius used the word elegantly for a thing made and created. He also adduces the still earlier testimony of Asconius Pedianus.

923. Ald., Put., Oxon., Alex. have *dicitur*. Vat. A, Mar., Rat. in the first hand, Urb., and Weitz. have *ducitur*. Heinsius conjectures *diditur*. Gifanius, in the *Lucretian Index*, p. 436, speaking of a cut or incision, reads from an old codex *dicitur illata*, which he considers entirely correct. Mar. has *in loco*; Rat. has *in toto* for *in luto*, as Mariettus explains, since it often uses *o* for *u*. Egm. has *illuto*. Urb. and Alex. in the first hand have *in luto*. The meter rejects *in luto* in Alex. [Col. 0995C] The second hand has *illoto*. Vat. B had *ducitur in luto*, but *factum dicitur in luto* appears in Vat. Q; *illuto* is the reading I retain, from the verb *illuo*, from which *illuvies* also occurs shortly afterward, although more recent editors prefer *illoto*. Some write *inluto* for *illuto*. In Arnobius, book I *Against the Nations*, one reads: “He carried his foot unwashed through the deepest whirlpools.”

[Col. 0993A]

Alone and excepted, he admits grievous torment;

479 Unviolated, he acts and feels nothing harsh.

Say that the soul is exempt from the cross and pain

If you know it to be free from guilt and empty of crime.

[900] Whatever can sin can also succumb to punishment.

She herself was indeed pure when she was once created,

She who, joined to the raw earth, made the mud live;

Receiving, as it were, from the liquid seed of nature

Her first condition, and impressed from the heavenly serenity.

[905] Soon, when she was commanded to be fastened to the pregnant field,

She cooled, excessively beguiled by sweet enticements,

And polluted the precious fire in the wallows,

When, impiously transgressing, she trod upon God’s appointed law.

This is the soul’s first nature: thus created simple,

[910] It fell into vice through the foul compact of the flesh.

[Col. 0994A] Thereafter, stained by the evil sin of its head, Adam,

It infected the whole human race that springs from him;

And the infancy of souls at birth retains

480 The stains of the first man, and no one is born innocent.

[915] Yet an error must be avoided: one must not believe that, by transmission of the flesh,

The source of souls is transferred to offspring,

As blood is, in which the vein is woven by descent.

Souls do not give birth to souls; rather, by a hidden law,

Nature pours forth its work, by which the little

[920] Vessels may breathe and the vital spark may be present in compacted bodies.

Although, once infused, the new soul always enters a new

481 Creation, it is nevertheless drawn from the crime of the ancestors,

Because it has been compacted in a muddy lethargy.

[Col. 0995B]

924. He refutes the Pelagians, who denied original sin, from baptism, through which we are reborn—plainly, dead through the sin we contracted from Adam’s crime. See St. Augustine and the theologians.

927. The tinder of sin is in the flesh, and even after the cleansing water of baptism it remains in the flesh. Nevertheless, the soul itself sins, although it is drawn to sin by the allurements of concupiscence, because it sins freely and often intensifies and kindles the force of concupiscence. Hence punishment has wisely been established for body and soul.

928. Prag. has *sodale*; Rat. has *sodalis*.

929. In some editions, *impleat* (“may fill”); correct to *implicat* (“entangles”). [Col. 0995D] *Incentivum* is an adjective in Varro, but a substantive in the author of the panegyric addressed to Constantine, Jerome, Symmachus, and Ammianus.

931. The Fathers and theologians teach that the soul, although spiritual, is tortured by fire. Yet I do not know why the practice has prevailed of distinguishing theologians from the holy Fathers, and of not ordinarily including the holy Fathers under the name “theologians,” since they are above all true theologians. But, as I was saying, both groups discuss the fire by which souls are tormented, and we have said something about this matter in the *Prolegomena*, no. 167.

932. In Vat. A, *factum crucibus* (“made by crosses”) is correctly derived from *cruciatibus* (“torments”), which is a gloss. I shall discuss the use of *crux* and *affigi cruci* for “torment” and “to be tormented” in the hymn of St. Lawrence, verse 21. Heins. and Cham. have the error *nos librat*.

933. Gifanius reads *gestatur* (“is carried”) from an old codex instead of *gestator* (“bearer”). I do not follow him.

935. Prag. has *expositam contractibus*, as in verse 989. *Contactibus* (“contacts”) is better than *contagione* (“contagion”). In Rat., a recent little scholar replaced *Iesus* with *ipse*.

938. This verse is present in Mar., Vat. Q, Prag., and Rat., without erasure and in the same hand, as well as in most of Weitz’s copies, in Giselinus, and others. It is absent from Put., Thuan., Oxon., two copies of Tor., Ald., Pal., Urb., and Alex.

939. Alex. has *quidquid in membris*, perhaps *quidquid et in membris*.

940. Weitz., Gis., Gall., Tornaes., and Rat. have *homini*. Most and the older copies have *hominis*, which is much better.

942. Egm., Put., and Pal. have *conciderent steriles*, which I do not understand. Others have *concideret, sterilis, peccati fomite nullo*, that is, “it would collapse, barren, with no fuel of sin”; this is death, which is itself called barren, for what follows is “death is nourished by guilt.”

945. As above in the hymn of the Burial, verses 17–18, “to abolish death,” so now death is consumed in Christ’s body.

947. Vat. A and B have *suscipe* (“receive”). Mar., Ald., Weitz., Gis., and most have *suspice* (“look up to”), which seems more consistent with the sense.

948. Put. has *naturam* (“nature”) instead of *virtutem* (“power”). Alex., Urb., and others of ours, together with Vat. Q and the printed editions, stand against it.

950. All the older Heinsian copies, Gif., Alex., Urb., Vat. Q, Rat., and Weitz. have *abscidere*. Others have *abscindere*. I had least expected to have to speak here about the worship and feast of the Sacred Heart of Jesus, which is celebrated by public authority in Rome and in countless other dioceses, especially since the matter was settled long ago. Yet complete silence is impossible, since a recent interpreter misunderstood Prudentius and appended this note to the words *CUM CHRISTO ABSCIDERE QUIDQUAM* (“to cut off anything from Christ”):

“I would have some of the modern devotees of the Sacred Heart of Jesus take heed, lest, while they strive to arouse in themselves and in others a more fervent affection toward Christ Jesus, they should divide his body and flesh, cut them into pieces, and place them before the eyes, thereby carrying out an act involving violated unity and integrity.”

But I observe and see very clearly that Prudentius is not dealing with Christ’s body at all. By “Christ” he means the Word and divinity, as in verse 29 of the *Apotheosis*:

“This the prince of the noble seed, Abraham, saw—  
even then the guest of Christ, who had deigned to visit the earth in human form,”

and often elsewhere. Prudentius proves that the soul is not a portion of God:

“To cut off anything from Christ,  
and to cut away a part from God, or merely to seize  
the Godhead, is impossible; it is always complete in itself and for itself.”

For this was the error of certain heretics: that the soul was a part of God’s substance. They never dreamed of asserting that the soul was a particle of Christ’s body or flesh. Therefore either the recent interpreter failed to grasp Prudentius’s meaning, or his entire argument finally comes down to this:

“Prudentius says that the divine nature cannot be cut apart; therefore those who offer worship to the Sacred Heart of Jesus, and who paint, commission, or adore such images of it as are displayed in the churches of the faithful for veneration, divide Christ’s body and flesh, cut them into pieces, and place them before the eyes, and thus may be carrying out an act involving violated unity and integrity.”

No one, I think, will favor this inference unless he seeks even worse advocacy for a bad cause in some lawyer. For the theological teacher who joined his studies with those of the Advocate could hardly have taught his pupil this method of argument. But enough of this as far as Prudentius is concerned. Other matters—if it is worthwhile to stir up half-conscious questions—will be supplied by Tetamus and Marquezius. I would add Mozzius, who vigorously defended devotion to the Sacred Heart of Jesus in a work published under the auspices of the most faithful queen of Portugal, Maria, whose piety in promoting this devotion, attested by illustrious monuments and entrusted to the hands of the most distinguished artists, no oblivion will erase.

[Col. 0995A]

From there the second generation returns, and from there the defilement of nature is washed away;

[925] We are born again within, washed clean,

So that the shining soul may put off the old Adam.

Since, joined to the flesh, it draws from the flesh’s tinder

The material of sin, and at the same time itself

Becomes an incentive to sin for its companion,

It entangles both, the guilty pair,

[930] With avenging punishment, sinning under one mind,

And burns its partners in sin with equal torments.

482 From these torments Christ sets us free, the bearer

Of an incorrupt mother and an innocent body. Jesus alone

Put on a nature exposed to punishment, but not to vices;

[935] he did not put on a nature exposed to contaminating contacts.

Therefore he owed nothing to punishment: unstained,

[Col. 0995B] Free from deceit, liberated from every stain of guilt.

What lineage of sinners could exist in that body?

[Col. 0996A] What savage attendant of sin could punishment

[940] Do in Christ’s limbs? What could death do to a guiltless man?

Obviously, with empty efforts and without strength,

It would collapse, barren, with no fuel of sin.

Death is nourished by guilt; he who has no guilt,

By the very failure of its food consumes death, empty.

[945] Thus death was consumed in the Lord Christ’s body;

Thus it perished, since it did not have its customary arid food.

Look upon, therefore, the blameless Godhead alone,

483 The power of the Father and of Christ, and cease now

To forge an injustice against our soul, claiming that it is God,

Or that it is a small portion of God, so that it could cut off anything from Christ,

[Col. 0996B] And cut away a part from God, or merely seize

The Godhead—which is always complete in itself and for itself.

It is worthwhile to expose the shadow of the nebulous doctrine

484 Which slender atoms construct in a tiny structure:

[955] It collapses, empty, and dissolves like wind,

Unable to sustain itself in empty flux.

The Manichaean says that God, airy and without a true body,

Flew about, a lying phantom, assuming

A hollow image of a body possessing nothing tangible.

[960] First, consider whether it is fitting to assign anything simulated

To God, whose pure glory admits nothing false:

Would he, subtly adapting himself to deceptive limbs,

Pretend to be human by a windy art?

[Col. 0997B] Having lied so often, when he said:

[965] “I grant remission to diseases, and at the same time forgive sins.”

485 He is the Son of Man, who can drive away the plague of the flesh

And loosen and release the bonds of crimes.

“Rise, restored; rise, innocent; now take up your bed.

I command this as the Son of Man.” Does he seem worthy

[970] To testify concerning himself, knowing himself and his own flesh?

And what of the time when, already foreknowing in truthful speech,

He warned the disciples what the Son of Man would suffer?

Did he not confess himself to be truly human

With the Father’s power? If I do not believe this, he deceived me.

[975] If you ask, Manichaean, what God’s nature is:

Everything that he does is true; for if, in acting, he does something false,

[Col. 0999A] He is not God; divine practice does not admit falsehood.

You object to the eternal Lord that he came to us deceptively,

Pretending to be other than what he truly was.

[980] Be silent, madness! Bite your own tongue,

Shameless dog, consuming your words with your torn palate.

Matthew resists the barking voice and refutes its rage:

486 He records every kind of fleshly lineage, down to

The bodily Christ, descending through six groups of seven men,

[985] And weaving the channel of noble blood from ancestors

Through the genealogical lines by a long thread.

Christ came to add the seventh to the sixth week,

Completing the peaceful year,

[Col. 0999B] Which releases everything entangled by various sins,

[990] [Col. 1000A] And raises man from the death of man.

For at that time the mortal clay was imperfect:

487 The one perfect man appears, Jesus whole and entire,

From whom nothing was lacking of the seven times seven,

So that by everlasting power he might perfect mortal humanity.

[995] This is he who completes for us the seventh Sabbaths,

So that our flesh, at last joined to God, may rest,

The flesh which six Sabbaths tormented with evil offenses.

Let us run through the marked stages and follow the lineage of kings:

You will find that Christ flowed forth from human parents’ flesh,

[1000] That he is of David’s seed,

An heir of the blood, numbered in the recorded lineage.

[Col. 1000B] What of the time when holy-speaking Luke, having unfolded the line of descent,

1003. Aldus has *ait* (“he says”), incorrectly, for *agit* (“he proceeds”). Prag. incorrectly has *nepotes*; it should be read *nepotis*.

1004. In the margin of the Cologne edition, *per quae* (“through which”) appears; it should be read *perque* (“and through”). Mar., Vat. A, Prag., and Rat. have *cursu*; *cursum* is better.

1008. In the margin of the Cologne edition, *auctus ad usque* (“increased up to”) appears incorrectly.

1009. Ald. has *mixtum*; others have *mixtim*.

1010. Prudentius rightly calls Adam the son of God through Christ, for it is certain that he attained eternal salvation. Some defend this on the grounds that in certain Bibles Adam is called “son of God” in the account of Christ’s genealogy. But the true reading is “Adam, who was of God,” that is, created by God alone and not the son of another human being. Someone interpreted this verse as follows: “And through Christ he became the son of the Most High God”—namely, because the Word became flesh and human nature was raised to hypostatic union. But apart from the fact that the sense is involved, [Col. 1002C] Prudentius would have used *Adae* in the genitive of begetting, as elsewhere *Abra(e)*, *Abrah(a)e*, and *Adae*.

1011. In Ald., through an error, *est* appears for *ab*; in the text of Oxon., Ald., Gis., and other common editions, *pingas*; our copies, Weitz., and Heins. have *fingas*.

1012. Aldus has *Levi, Juda, Simeonem*. Mar. and others have *Levin, Judam, Simeona*.

1016. In some common editions, incorrectly, *sanguis perstabilis*.

1020. Widm. above has *aut quid* (“or what”).

1023. Rat. has *indignumque putet*. The gloss is foolish: *luteum* (“clay”) is derived from *lutum* (“mud”).

1025. Heinsius writes *pertractare*.

1026. Rat. in the first hand has *nondum corporeo*.

1028. Virgil, *Georgics* II, verse 301: “So great is the love of earth.” Weitzius points this out. It is indeed an elegant exclamation, but much more so if we consider it expressed in Virgil’s words, which were not originally composed for this purpose. Petavius is not entirely consistent about these verses of Prudentius. In volume I, book II, chapter 1, he says that Prudentius seems to hold that, in forming man, God assumed a human shape—a view maintained by Augustine of Eugubium. But in his work *On the Six Days of Creation*, volume III, book II, chapter 1, he better explains what is meant by man being fashioned by God’s hands, as many of the holy Fathers say, understanding “hands” and “fingers” tropically and figuratively. “Prudentius,” he says, “described this in the most elegant verses: ‘So great is the love of earth,’ etc.”

1029. Rat. has *praepignus*; Bong. has *molem*. Correct to *praepinguis*, *mollem*.

1031. *Jubeo ut* is not very common. Nevertheless, excellent authors do use it in this way; Barthius, *Adversaria* XXXVI, 16, observes that Prudentius, Victor, Juvencus, and Arator imitated it from Cicero.

1035. Ald., Gis., Rott., Widm. above, Torn., Alex., Urbinas, and Vat. A and Q have *flabro*. Most Heinsian copies, with Weitzius and Iso, have *fabro*. The former is not objectionable, and Chamillard approved it. At verse 778 I said that Prudentius often confirms that the body is the work of God’s right hand and the soul of his mouth: “He fashioned this with his fingers; he breathed the soul with his mouth.” Lactantius, book II, chapter 13: “For, having fashioned the body, he breathed into it a soul from the living fountain of his spirit.” [Col. 1003C] The entire passage, however, seems to concern only the making of the body; therefore *fabro* (“by a craftsman”) is more correct than *flabro* (“by a bellows”). The best older copies have *fabro*. See the glosses and below, concerning the mud: “the sacred work would be made honorable by art,” etc. Teolius also reads *fabro*, but he is wrong to say that all the Vatican copies except one have *fabro*.

[Col. 1001A]

Upward he traces the line, as the body of the grandson climbs,

488 And retraces its course through ancient ancestors.

[1005] Christ ascended through seventy and two births,

For he sent just as many teachers into the world:

He retraced on returning the stages descended through birth,

Back up to the summit of Adam’s earthly body.

From there the divine parent receives what is his, and what is ours in combination,

[1010] And Adam becomes, through Christ, the son of the Most High God.

Now you must imagine an airy race from its origin,

Airy chiefs: Levi, Judah, Simeon;

An airy David, the bodies of mighty kings

Airy, and the womb itself of the fruitful virgin

[1015] Swollen with deceptive air, mists, and cloud.

[Col. 1001B] Let the transient blood vanish; let the soft bones dissolve;

Let the texture of the flying sinews perish.

Let an ineffectual south wind carry away everything that has been done;

Let thin breezes scatter it; let what we all are be a fable.

[1020] [Col. 1002A] And what does Christ accomplish if he does not receive me? Or whom

Does he free, infirm, if he disdains to approach

The burden of flesh and shudders at the monuments of his own hands?

489 Does he consider it unworthy to assume a clay body,

Who once did not consider it unworthy to handle that very

Mud,

[1025] when he fashioned the vessel from earth,

Not yet made fleshly, but with the adhesive of inert mud

Drew forth the yielding limbs beneath his impressed thumb?

So great is the love of earth, so great the love he bears for us!

He deigns to grasp the soft clod of very rich soil

[1030] With divine fingers, and does not deem foul

The contaminations of the clinging mass. He had commanded that light

[Col. 1002B] Be made; it was made as he had commanded. At his commanding order

Everything brought forth drew on new forms.

Man alone earned from the Lord’s right hand

[1035] To receive a formable face, and to be born through the craftsmanlike fashioning of the Godhead.

[Col. 1003B]
