1038. Vat. A reads incorrectly *tactui nobilis* (“noble to the touch”) instead of *tactu iam nobilis* (“already noble through touch”).

1039. Rat. reads *decrevit quoniam* (“because he decreed”); Prag. has *Pater* (“Father”) instead of *Deus* (“God”).

1040. Bong. and Gis. read *velle* (“to wish”); the others have *vellet* (“he would wish”), which is preferable. The summary of the arguments by which Prudentius attacks the Manichaeans, or Docetists, is this: (1) Christ possessed a true body, as is demonstrated by the duties he performed and by the words in which he called himself the Son of man; (2) from Christ’s genealogies he argues that, on the same reasoning, one could assert that Christ’s parents had aerial bodies, if Christ’s body alone were aerial; (3) on the same hypothesis he concludes that Christ can likewise be denied to be our Redeemer and Savior; (4) from the special manner in which God formed man from clay, he infers that this happened because his eternal Son would at some time be clothed in human flesh; (5) from the resurrection.

1046. Ald. and Pal. read *nec iam* (“and no longer”); others have *ne iam* (“lest now”), which is more appropriate.

1047. From the Epistle to the Romans IV, 53: “Who was delivered up for our offenses and rose again for our justification.”

1048. Saint Ambrose, *On the Sacraments*, book II, chapter 6: “A remedy was given, so that man might die and rise again … but Christ found resurrection,” and so forth.

1050. Ald. reads *et tumulo* (“and from the tomb”) instead of *e tumulo* (“from the tomb”).

1052. Vatt. A and Q, Mar., Prag., Rat., Weitz., Alex., [Col. 1004B] in the first hand, Urb. and others have, incorrectly, *mendax in utraque necesse est sit Christus specie* (“Christ must be false in both forms”). Put., Ald., Pal. and others read *mendax in utroque necesse est sit Christus specie* (“Christ must be false in both forms”). But the reading is better with Egm.: *mendax in utroque necesse est sit Christus species* (“Christ must necessarily be a false appearance in both”). I prefer *in utraque specie* (“in both forms”), that is, in the appearance of man and of God, “false and a phantom”; Giselinus likewise approved this reading. Bonon.’s reading is not very suitable: “And a false phantom of God; Christ must necessarily be an appearance in both.” Gallandius cites Aldus for *utraque*, in which I read *utroque*. I myself have never found a difference of readings in the various copies of Aldus. But even if this variation existed in different copies, it would not thereby be certain evidence of two Aldine editions. Nothing is easier than for several words to be changed during printing, if desired, so that variant readings appear in copies of the same edition; I think this happened in the ancient Mainz Bibles.

1054. Prag. has *ipse* (“he himself”) incorrectly instead of *ipsa* (“she herself”).

1055. Vat. A incorrectly has *haec* (“this”) instead of *nec* (“nor”). In Teolius the meter is corrupted by transposing the words *Nec Deus verus est* (“Nor is he the true God”).

1058. Prag. has *ille* (“that one”) instead of *Iesus* (“Jesus”). See verse 992.

1059. Aldus incorrectly reads *et redit illa Dei iustus* (“and that righteous one of God returns”) instead of *et redit? illa Dei virtus memorabilis est, ut* (“and he returns? That power of God is memorable, namely, that …”).

[Col. 1004D] 1061. Rat. has *quique*; Gis. has *quisqui’*. The correct reading is *quisque* (“whoever”). Compare hymn 7, *Cathemerinon*, verse 216. Vat. A has *discere* (“to learn”) instead of *dicere* (“to say”), with the gloss “that is, to believe.”

1062. Vat. A corruptly reads *ne majestate* (“lest by majesty”).

1063. Boher. the elder, Put., Alex., Urb., and Vat. A do not recognize a title before this verse; Heinsius approves this, because all the following material is directed against the Docetists. Nevertheless, other witnesses assign one. Rat.: “On the resurrection of the flesh.” Mar.: “On the resurrection of human flesh.” Ald., Weit., and Gis. first edition have the same. In the second edition of Gis., in the margin, “Resurrection.” Egm., in the margin, “On the resurrection.” Trithemius lists these few verses as a separate book.

[Col. 1003A]

Why, then, did such great favor toward our clay

Come to it, that, handled by the Lord’s hands, it should become sacred

Through honorable art, already noble through touch itself?

Because God had decreed to mingle Christ

[1040] With incorruptible soil: what he wished to fashion

With holy fingers, he held worthy and chose to store as a beloved pledge.

Nature, indeed, abandoned the form of the constrained

Earth and yielded to death, to which it was subject;

But the nature of God, never to be dissolved, wished

[1045] That the perishable earth, originally corrupted by our use,

Should be his own, so that it might no longer be corruptible.

Christ is our flesh: for me it is dissolved, and for me it rises.

I am dissolved by my death; through Christ’s power I rise again,

When Christ dies, when he is mournfully buried,

[1050] [Col. 1003B] I see myself: when he now stands forth, able to return from the tomb,

[Col. 1004A] 491 I behold God. If he is a phantom of my limbs,

And is also a phantom of God, then Christ must necessarily be false

In both appearances, if Christ knows how to deceive.

If he is not truly man, whom death itself proves to be man,

[1055] Nor is he truly God, whose glory of achievement reveals him

To be God; either believe that he died, or reject his presence,

And deny the true Christ on both grounds.

For what is magnificent, if Jesus did not die,

And return? That power of God is memorable: that one who was

[1060] Slain should return to the heights and, buried, rise again.

Whoever wishes to call Christ God must say that he is likewise

Man, lest his majesty lose its strength.

1066. The poet shows that the resurrection of the flesh will take place in precisely the same body in which the human being lived. For, as is handed down in the sixteenth Council of Toledo, Christ rose after resuming in truth the same flesh in which he had fallen, offering us through his resurrection an example [Col. 1005C] so that we too may believe that we shall rise in the substance of true flesh in which we now are and live. Let us disregard the empty and condemned subtlety of certain people concerning the true resurrection, even if the body is not numerically the same.

1069. Ald., Vat. Q, and Mar. in the first hand; Cham. incorrectly reads *removet* (“removes”).

1076. Aldus has *voravit* (“devoured”); the others, more correctly, *vorarit* (“may have devoured”). Prag. incorrectly has *forarent* or *foraret*.

1078. Gisel. has *erit* (“will be”); the others, *erat* (“was”). Bong. and the better Heinsian manuscripts read *reddat* (“may restore”). Palat. has *reddit* (“restores”). Ald., Weit., Gis., Alex., Urb. and our other copies have *reddet* (“will restore”).

1079. Aldus’s error is *quodcunque*. Heinsius and others punctuate: “it had swallowed, in whatever manner.” Others, more correctly, punctuate as I have printed it.

1081. Ald. incorrectly has *meo* (“my,” masculine) instead of *mea* (“my,” feminine). Thuan. has *membra* (“limbs”), with *credite* (“believe”) and without *et* (“and”); I have said in the prolegomena [Col. 1006B] that this does not conflict with the meter. Spiegelius, in his commentary on the *Cathemerinon*, at “Omni hora,” verse 94, says: “In this weighty poem Prudentius confessed both the resurrection of Christ and that of human flesh.” Spiegelius also notes that Faber cites the same passage under the name of one of the saints in his first commentary on Paul [Col. 1006C]. Prudentius concludes the true apotheosis, or deification of man, after setting forth the resurrection by which Christ, true God and man, rose and carries human beings rising with him into heaven.

Among the printed editions I have found only Cellarius retaining *et atra*, followed by Teolius, although Teolius noted nothing from the Vatican manuscripts. Both usually follow Heinsius; but in this matter Heinsius agreed with the others and recorded no variant reading. I do not doubt that *tetra* is correct.

Heinsius maintains that the *Hamartigenia* is part of the *Apotheosis*, on the basis of both its subject matter and the titles of the manuscripts. In Thuan. it reads: “Here begins book II of the *Hamartigenia*.” In Put.: “Here begins book II, *Hamartigenia*,” and at the head of every page: “Book II of Prudentius, *Hamartigenia*.” Thereafter: “Book III of Prudentius, *Psychomachia*.” In Thuan.: “Book II of the *Hamartigenia* ends. Book III, *Psychomachia*, begins.” Egm.: “The *Apotheosis* ends. One book of the *Hamartigenia* begins.” At the end: “The second book of Prudentius’s *Hamartigenia* ends.”

In our manuscripts the titles are as follows. Vat. A: “Here begins one book against the Martigenia” (read *Hamartigenia*). Mar. and Rat., with Weitz.: “Here begins the *Hamartigenia*, that is, concerning the origin of sins.” Alex.: “The *Apotheoses* ends. The book *Hamartigenia* begins.” Urb.: “Here begins the prologue against the Marcionites.” In Rot.: “Here begins the *Hamartigenia* concerning the origin of sin”; afterward: “The *Hamartigenia* of Aurelius Prudentius Clemens, that is, the book concerning the origin of sin, ends.”

From all these titles I rather conclude that the *Hamartigenia* is entirely distinct from the *Apotheosis*, especially since a different preface is also attached to it. Nor do I agree with Heinsius or with the distinguished Risco, in volume XXXI of *Hispania Sacra*, who asserts that in certain manuscripts the *Hamartigenia* is part of the *Apotheosis*. The fact that it is called book II does not prove that it is part of the *Apotheosis*, but rather that it is part of some work whose books are: I, *Apotheosis*; II, *Hamartigenia*; and III, *Psychomachia*, as the titles indicate.

In my opinion, all three books belong to the work which Prudentius hints at in the preface to all his poems in these words: “Let it fight against heresies and examine the Catholic faith.” It may also be said that books I, II, and III were numbered by copyists who wished to distinguish the books they had gathered into a single volume.

In the old Alexandrian manuscript I find the following written after the *Hamartigenia*: “The *Hamartigenia*, book III, ends. Book IV, *Psychomachia*, begins.” At the beginning of the volume all Prudentius’s works are listed, said to number nine. Since the first book is established as the *Cathemerinon*, the *Apotheosis* immediately follows and is therefore book II; then comes the *Hamartigenia*, which is consequently called book III; and the *Psychomachia* follows, which in its proper order is book IV. Yet in the same manuscript after the *Psychomachia* one reads: “Book III, *Psychomachia*, ends,” whether this is an error or whether it is called III because it belongs to the books written against heretics and for the examination of the faith.

1. This book is directed against the Marcionites, who asserted that there were two gods. They could not understand from what origin sin proceeded unless it came from an evil god. Hence the Greek title *Hamartigenia*, that is, “concerning the origin of sin.” Theodulf of Orléans, in his book *On the Holy Spirit*, calls the *Hamartigenia* a book against the Marcionists. See no. 179 of the prolegomena.

Giselinus observes that the poet seems to have brought forth all the power and force of his intellect in refuting Marcion’s error. “For,” he says, “he treats the most difficult and intricate subject of fate and free will with astonishing dignity and weight of language and thought, adorning everything most beautifully with the very flowers of rhetoric, so that from this single little poem one could easily infer that he excelled in every field of knowledge and letters.”

That Manes followed Marcion, as Giselinus says, is contrary to the chronology. Marcion spread his errors around the year 134, and Manes around 277. To understand Prudentius’s book more clearly, one should read Tertullian’s books *Against Marcion*, written in prose, as well as other works in verse circulated under his name. Chamillardus is much more prolific than usual in his notes on the *Hamartigenia*, so that one might think him another interpreter [Col. 1008C]. *Ephebi* is written differently by different witnesses. Mar. writes *Ephobi*, Widm. *Ephaebi*, Egm. *Efybi*, and others *Aphoebi*.

2. Mar., in the first hand, has *proximos creat* (“creates those nearest”); Prag. has *proximos procreat* (“begets those nearest”), which conflicts with the verse. Earlier in the same Prag. manuscript is *primos* (“first”).

5. Saint Ambrose, in his book *On Cain and Abel*, among the reasons why Abel’s sacrifice was approved by God but Cain’s was not, gives this one also. “For,” he says in book I, chapter 10, “an animal is more than something earthly.”

9. Vat. A has *ille* (“that one”); *illam* (“that one,” feminine) is better.

11. Prag. has *nam*, which Weitzius incorrectly adopted together with Widm.; the laws of the poem oppose it. Instead of *recte*, Rat., in the second hand, has *recta*. Prudentius refers to Genesis 4:7: “If you do well, will you not receive?” Giselinus observes that these words are read differently in the commonly used sacred Bibles, although he himself read them in a certain manuscript history excerpted from Scripture. Giselinus and Mariettus likewise note that the wording follows the Septuagint.

Saint Isidore, *Questions on Genesis*, chapter 6: “God said to Cain, ‘If you offer rightly, but do not divide rightly, you have sinned … Be quiet; desire will be under you,’” and so forth. Saint Ambrose, *On Cain and Abel*, book II, chapter 6, likewise reads and explains the passage as meaning that Cain did not divide correctly, because above all he ought to have offered the firstfruits to God, so that he might begin from the grace of the author. Cain is commanded to be quiet because he had nothing with which to excuse himself.

12. Instead of *recta*, Ald., Egm., and Palat. read *recte*. Perhaps Widm.’s reading, *certa* (“certain”), is better [Col. 1009B]. Whether *recta* or *certa* is written, the meaning is “by a certain or right law,” in the ablative. The rivalry is indicated by which Cain offered gifts different from Abel’s. “To offer rightly” should be understood with a proper intention and with regard to the other laws of sacrifice.

16. Browerus notes that Venantius Fortunatus, as often elsewhere, here too, in elegy 2 of book IX, closely followed Prudentius’s traces, since he taught that Abel had been killed with a hoe. Others report that he was killed in other ways: by sword, sickle, iron, stones, hands, or bites. Since all these accounts rest only on conjecture, the poet reasonably says that Abel was killed with a hoe, the tool farmers use to pull up useless weeds. Several paintings in the cemeteries of the ancient Christians depict Abel killed by Cain. See the distinguished Mamachi, volume II of *Christian Antiquities*, page 30.

19. Vat. A reads less well *perempto* (“having been killed”).

20. Vat. A, Egm., one Torr., and Pal. in the first hand have *sors* (“fate”); the others *mors* (“death”). Bong. incorrectly has *vulneris* (“of the wound”).

21. The written and printed books have *cessit* (“yielded”). In Weitzius, M. Berg. read *cessat* (“yields”). *Cessit* is better.

24. Bonon. incorrectly ends the line with *et* (“and”).

31. Bonon. incorrectly has *immolator* (“sacrificer”); Cain was not a sacrificer of a living victim, but a rival. Prudentius says that this story of Cain, who, as a rival of his brother’s sacrifice, inflicted death upon his brother, signifies a future reality. What reality? The heresy of Marcion, who perversely divided the discipline of sacred things and separated the eternal divine nature into two.

But why those who divide God into two are compared throughout this prologue, and in the first verse of the poem, with Cain, the interpreters do not adequately explain. Prudentius either followed the wording of the Septuagint interpreters, according to which Cain did not divide rightly, or he simply charges the Marcionites with the division and schism characteristic of all heretics.

Lauretus, in the *Silva of Allegories*, demonstrates from the holy Fathers that Cain is a figure of sin, of the sinner, of the Jews, of the people of heretics who generate other heretics, of false doctrine, and of false understanding. Saint Ambrose, in book I of *On Cain and Abel*, chapter 1 [Col. 1010B], considers two sects under the names of two brothers, mutually opposing and contrary to each other. I think Prudentius imitated this passage of Ambrose.

32. Ald. has *quae* (“which,” feminine); the others, more correctly, *quem* (“whom,” masculine).

33. Alex., Ald., Gis., Fab., and Widm. above have *fratricida* (“fratricide”). Mar., Urb., Prag., Weitz., and Sich. have *parricida* (“murderer of a close relative”). [Col. 1010C] The Heinsian manuscripts and Vat. A have *fratricida*, which is more pleasing.

34. Fab., Bong., and Gis. have *dividit* (“divides”). The Heinsian manuscripts, Alex., Urb., and our copies, along with others, have *dividat* (“may divide”), as above.

36. Ald. and Urb. incorrectly have *Arii* instead of *arui*. Marcion is reported to have been of extremely corrupt morals. Chamillardus objects to the poet’s lengthening of the penultimate syllable in *Marcion* and cites an example from the books *Against Marcion* circulated under Tertullian’s name: “This to you through Marcion, with Cerdo as teacher.” But others who compile prosodic indexes argue instead that all three vowels in *Marcion* should be lengthened.

Certainly, the example from Tertullian can be understood so that the third foot is a spondee, through synaeresis of *cio*. Thus Prudentius below, verse 129, says *Marcionita*, where *Marcio* is a spondee. See the note there. If the matter had to be settled by authority, it would be Prudentius, not the spurious Tertullian, who should be preferred. The final vowel in *Marcion* is short, as in *daemon*. See the prolegomena.

37. Vat. A, Prag., Pal., and Egm. have *dueta*; Aldus and Alex. *duetas*; Mar., Rat., and others *Duitas*. He calls those who asserted that there were two gods by this name. Perhaps it is better written without a comma: “Duitas teaches that it differs from spirit.” The glosses are foolish.

41. The Heinsian manuscripts have *quieta* (“quiet”); Alex., Urb., and our other copies have *quietam* (“quiet”), together with Gisel., Ald., and Weitz.

42. Prag. has *fessa* (“wearied”). Vat. A has *virorum* (“of men”). Correct to *fassa* and *vivorum* (“of the living”).

43. A, Ald., Egm., Palat., and the Heinsian copies. Teolius, who denies that any Vatican manuscript recognizes this verse, does not seem to have noticed Marietti’s manuscript.

Giselinus agrees with Heinsius, and I do not dislike the reading. For *regna* and *divorum* conflict with the meter, while *duorum* has already been said in the preceding verse, unless one punctuates as follows: “Separating evil and good as though they were two, he entrusts two scepters to the realm of two.” Vat. A, Bonon., Prag., Mar. in the first hand, Rat., above, Egm., [Col. 1012B] Put., Rott., and three Torr. copies have *cadit perempta*, namely, “the mind of Marcion falls slain.” Thuan. has *cadit peremptor* (“the slayer falls”). Aldus has *cadet peremptor* (“the slayer will fall”). Widm., in the margin, has *mens perempta cadit* (“the slain mind falls”), against the meter. Teolius follows Heinsius: *Cadit perempta*, although he asserts that two Vatican manuscripts support it and that the others prefer *peremptor*, as in the printed editions.

63. Ald., Fabr., and Gis. have *illitus* (“smeared”). Thuan., Rot., Cauch., three Torr. copies, and Bonon. have *oblitus*, from *oblino* (“to smear”), which Heinsius adopted, followed by later editors. Most have *halitus* or *alitus*, with the ridiculous gloss “nourished,” as in Vat. A, Alex., Urb., Mar., Prag., Rat., and Weitz. The meter does not permit *alitus* in the sense “nourished.” I take it as *allitus*, from *allino*, a verb used by Cicero and Horace in the *Art of Poetry*: “He smears a black mark with a transverse brush.” The meaning is the same as *oblitus* or *illitus*, namely, “stained.” One of the two doubled consonants could easily have been omitted [Col. 1012C]. Isidore, book I of the *Etymologies*, chapter 27, says on Victorinus’s authority that the ancients did not double letters but placed them above the letters, as in *sella*, *serra*, and *asseres*. In ancient inscriptions one of two consonants that ought to be doubled is often missing.

Prudentius compares Marcion with Cain; in Marcion himself he again distinguishes between flesh and mind. By the name Cain he understands the flesh, because it has wickedly triumphed over the mind, dragging it headlong.

Lupus of Ferrara, in letter 20 to Altuinus, praises this verse and its author in these words: “A certain Greek, who was accustomed to assert emphatically that Greeks say *blasphemus* with the penultimate syllable shortened, told me … Yet Aurelius Prudentius, who is celebrated most enthusiastically by many, placed that name in this way: *DIVISOR BLASPHEME DEI* [‘Blasphemous divider of God’]. Hence it spread far and wide that *BLASPHEMUS* and *BLASPHEMO* should receive the accent on the penultimate syllable.” Lupus confuses accent with syllable quantity: the penultimate syllable in *blasphemus* is long, but the accent is on the antepenultimate. See the prolegomena.

39. I have no doubt that the reading should be, with Rat. and Mar. from the second hand: “Or anterior in number, he to whom the only Son belongs to the one.” The meaning is that the Son is not later than the Father, nor the Father earlier than the Son; rather, God is one, first in his power, first in him whom he generated before chaos, and the begetter and the begotten are one, free from distinction both in number and in time. Saint Fulgentius used Prudentius’s words in *On the Faith to Peter* and explained the meaning: “None of these is outside any of the others, because no one precedes another in eternity, exceeds another in greatness, or surpasses another in power; for, so far as the unity of the divine nature is concerned, the Father is neither anterior nor greater than the Son or the Holy Spirit,” and so forth. In Vat. A the reading *interior* is an error. In other manuscripts and editions: “Anterior in number is he to whom the one Son belongs as the one Son”; I do not know how this can be explained. Olaus Borrichius sufficiently defends the Latinity of the word *anterior* in his *Analecta* to the *Thoughts on the Latin Language*, against Vossius and Cellarius, citing Julius Caesar in the best manuscripts, Priscian, Symmachus, Sulpicius, and other contemporaries. Teolius rightly noted the idiom “the one Son belongs to the one” from Saint Thomas, part 1, question 31, article 2: “We call him the only Son because there are not several sons in the divine persons; yet we do not call him the only God, because divinity is common to several.”

42. A simple generation is an eternal generation through communication of the same nature, not through division or multiplication of essence; for the Son is begotten, not created or made. Therefore the theological poet asks what difference there can be in nature, power, or majesty between the begotten and the begetter through simple generation.

43. Egm., in the first hand: “will always be.”

45. Here we could quote more from the Athanasian Creed: not three eternal beings, but one eternal being; not three gods, but one God; one Father, not three fathers, and so forth.

47. “To split” is preferable with Mar., Rat., Weitz., and Urb., rather than “to cut away” with Put., Thuan., and Ald.

48. This is another Catholic doctrine: the Word, and therefore Jesus Christ the Son of the Father, is natural, not adoptive; on this basis Marcion could neither assert nor argue that one of a different kind or nature was superior to two in number, thereby introducing a double divinity. Prudentius speaks especially of Christ insofar as he is God, for he often takes Christ as referring to the Word. Hence theologians argue that Christ, even insofar as he is human, is not God’s adoptive son; for an adoptive son is a person foreign to the adopter. At that time it was customary for emperors to adopt someone of another kind as a son and admit him to a share in the empire. Perhaps Prudentius has this in mind. Above, the poet used “kind” for “nature”; many of the holy Fathers used the same word, a point that must often be repeated against Clerici’s sophistries. The word *adoptive* occurs in the First Council of Braga, chapter 15: “An adoptive woman, an outsider,” and in the *Collection of Canons* of Saint Martin of Braga. In the morning prayer attributed by many to Ausonius and by some to Saint Paulinus: “He is to be honored by the better offspring of an adoptive line.”

51. I mentioned in the *Apotheosis* that the Son is the form or image of the Father. From this it follows that the Son has the same nature as the Father; for such perfect likeness and the relation of image could not exist between two distinct natures. Compare the theologians who prove the unity of essence in the three persons. Petavius, volume IV, book II, chapter 11, and book IV, chapter 15, observes that Athanasius, Basil, and Cyril used a similar argument; but, he adds, one must also include the account of divine generation or substantial production, which requires that what is produced in the same way should possess not merely likeness but also identity of substance.

55. Bong., “recalled”; the others, “is recalled.”]

[Col. 1015A] For one is the first principle of number, and only one

Can be counted as one: so, since there is no Father and another God,

Nor is Christ likewise second to his Begetter,

503 Or anterior in number, he to whom the only Son belongs to the one,

[40] He is God, and deservedly God: because he is first and one;

First in his power, and then first in him

Whom he begot: for what difference can there be

In simple generation? The begetter will always be one,

And one is he who was begotten from one before chaos,

Free from distinction in number and in time.

[45] [Col. 1016A] Who would dare say that two rule under one majesty,

Each possessing his own power, and eternal from the beginning,

And divide the forces of one nature?

504 Did the Begetter take an adoptive son for himself, so that another

Of an alien kind should constitute a second in number,

[50] And introduce a second, distinct divinity?

The true Son stands as the true form of the Father,

And rightly proves himself one, while preserving the same form.

Neither an adopted love unites them, nor does a

Conspiracy of faith join the two; rather, a sure kinship—

[55] One nature, which is God, is reduced to one supreme whole.

[Note: [Col. 1017B]

60. Prag. writes *disparsa*.

64. Aldus, to accommodate the meter, attempted to alter this into *hanc heresin*. The copyist in Ratisbon likewise dared to record this. The true reading is *hanc heresin*.

68. Vat. A has the faulty reading *neque quis* for *nequis*; Prag. has *credens* for *credat*, which is not satisfactory.

69. This verse is absent from Pal., Egm., Ald., all the copies of Heins., one copy of Torr., and from Alex. and Urb. It is cited by Weitz., Gis., Mar., Prag., and Rat., and indeed without erasure by Bong., Fabr., and others. But in Fabr., Bong., and Mar., in the first hand, the reading is *vagas formas* rather than *vagis formis*. Giselinus states that this verse is absent from the Daventry edition. Teolius says that it occurs in only one Vat. manuscript, but was inserted by a second hand—that is, added. Marietti recognized that the same verse appears in his manuscript in the first hand. Alex. has this verse in a second hand and reads *vagas formas*.

70. Fabr., Gis., and Bong. have *resolutos*, incorrectly, for *revolutos*. See Becmann, *On the Origin of the Latin Language*, chapter 6, who defends and explains this reading from the manuscripts. “Revolving days” are days that repeatedly turn and return.

71. The manuscripts and editions read *texit*. Fabricius printed *rexit*, which is supported by the gloss. Alexander the Great used this example: “Neither can the earth tolerate two suns, nor Asia two kings.”

75. Saint Augustine, *On Knowledge of the True Life*, chapter 10, brings forward the example of light, splendor, and heat—which are three different words but one undivided substance—to explain the deepest mystery of the divine Trinity. In sermon 1, *On the Words of the Apostle*, he compares the Trinity with the sun and with fire: “Fire too has three things, and cannot be divided: movement, light, and heat.” Chamillard says that Prudentius incorrectly used *vegetamen* for *vegetatio*. Barthius, by contrast, in book X of the *Adversaria*, chapter 24, calls it an elegant word, though not very common, like *nutamen* in Silius Italicus: “with the trembling movement of its snowy wing.” “Prudentius,” he says, “fashioned many such words, rashly counted among barbarisms by excessively delicate critics.” To this class I refer *vegetamen* and other words of the same kind: *peccamen*, *creamen*, *ructamen*, *ostentamen*, *oblectamen*. See in Fabricius’s index to the Christian poets *affamen*, *conamen*, *exhortamen*, and *testamen*. There are many similar forms in Lucretius, which Gifanius noted in his Lucretian index.

76. Mar., Prag., Rat., Weitz., and Gis. read *indiscreti*, namely, of the sun. The Heinsian manuscripts, Vat. A, Alex., Urb., Ald., Egm., and Palat. read *indiscretis*, namely, “these three.”

78. Prag. has *ex tribus*; the others, *et tribus*. Ald. has *mixtum*; the rest *mixtim*, which is preferable.

[Col. 1018D] 80. *Famulus* occurs as an adjective more than once in Ovid.

86. Vat. A has *et si* for *aut si*; Mar., Rat., Weit., Gis., and Sich. read *suffundit*. Vat. A, Ald., Alex., Urb., and the Heinsian copies have *suffudit*. “A dark veil” for a cloud, just as poets speak of being covered by a cloud or clothed in a cloud. Virgil, *Aeneid* I: “And the goddess enveloped herself in a great cloud of mist.”

87. *Nimbus* for “cloud” occurs in Lucretius, Virgil, and others. “Darts of rays,” as in “a dart of the sun,” *Hymn* 2 of the *Cathemerinon*, verse 6.

88. Ald. has *mentitus*; the others, *mentitos*.]

[Col. 1017A] This path displeases you, Marcion; your sect condemns this faith,

Having divided heaven between two lords.

What mists confuse you? What slumber weighs upon your sluggish mind,

To which, through phantoms, a double appearance

[60] Comes divided along a heavenly fork?

505 If dull stupor besieges the power of your mind, at least look upon

The elements visible to earthly eyes, by which

The hidden reality of God has deigned to reveal itself through signs.

The Father’s majesty had foreseen long ago

[65] That this heresy would arise, which would split the ruler of light

And of the universe into parts, separating him into a doubled kingdom.

Therefore he placed before our sight a visible representation

And an example for our eyes, lest anyone believe that two divinities

[Col. 1017B] Rule the empty spaces of the world in shifting forms.

[70] A single flame, throughout the immense vault of heaven,

Provides revolving days and, as the one sun, covers the year.

Yet that one is triple, vigorous without distinction,

Supported by a threefold principle: it shines, flies, and burns;

[Col. 1018A] It is driven by movement, consumes with heat, and then gleams with light.

[75] For there are three together: light, heat, and growth.

506 Yet one and the same wheel of the sun, through undivided

Motion, performs these functions and, by one course, maintains so many offices;

One substance underlies all three things in combination.

I would not dare compare anything with God as his equal,

[80] Nor liken a servant—the sign—to the Lord.

But the Father himself wished human beings to conjecture his greatness

From the smallest things, since they cannot behold what is lofty.

We mark what is not understood by the mirror of small things,

And are permitted to seek the hidden truth through what is near.

[85] [Col. 1018B] No one has seen two suns except under glaucoma;

Or, if a dark veil has covered the clear sky,

Whenever an opposing cloud scatters the darts of its rays,

507 Reflected by fire, into deceptive circles.

The mind too has its own clouds: dense and heavy air.

[Note: [Col. 1019B]

90. Ald. incorrectly has *vellet* for *velet*, as do Oxon., Widm., Mar., Prag., Rat., and Urb. Vat. A, Alex., and most of the Heinsian copies have *velat*, along with Weitz. and Gis.

91. Ald., incorrectly, has *ne tetrum*.

93. Bong., Sich., and Gis., first edition, note in the margin *malefida intentio*.

95. Egm. and Gis. read as follows: “Are there two? Then why are there not many thousands of gods?” Giselinus also cites the Daventry edition. Other manuscripts read: “If there are two, then why should there not be many thousands of gods?” except that Rat. has *sunt multa*, as in Weit., Cham., and others. See Tertullian, book I *Against Marcion*, chapter 5: “First I shall ask why there are not more, if there are two.”

97. “To pour out a swarm of gods” is an ingenious expression, like a swarm of bees, although *swarm* is also used of other things.

101. Rat., in the first hand, has *divum* for *coelum*. It was rightly corrected by another hand.

105. Gis. reads *sua jura cuique*. The manuscripts and other editions have *sua cuique jura*, so that *cuique* forms a dactyl. Gifanius, in his Lucretian index, testifies that old books of Prudentius which he examined also have *sua cuique jura*, and elsewhere *sua cuique dextra est* and *suus est mos cuique genti*. Nevertheless, I do not agree with Gifanius that Prudentius lengthens the *e* in *cuique*, as though those verses were spondaic or had a spondee in the fifth foot. I think rather that the first *u* is lengthened and the word forms a dactyl. Becmann, contrary to the evidence of other manuscripts, orders the words to be transposed as *sua jura cuique*, adding that the manuscript did so. This codex was the Palatine manuscript sent from Hildeberg by Jan Gruter. See chapter 6 of *On the Origin of the Latin Language*. The codex of the abbey of Gronendahl, used by Torrentius, has one verse more: “To assign particular gods, and to allot the elements of the countryside individually to their divided lords.” Here Heinsius corrects *ruris* to *juris*, namely, “the elements of jurisdiction.”

107. *Duos* is preferable with Vat. A, Alex., Put., Thuan., and Rot. *Deos* is not bad in Mar., Prag., Rat., Bong., Widm., in the first hand of Urb. Aldus has *duos*, apart from Heinsius and the more recent editions. Sichardus, Weitz., and Gis. have *deos*.

108. Mar. incorrectly has *ditiones* for *ditionis*; in the first hand it has the less bad reading *gubernet*, while a later hand has *retentet*.

110. Gis., first edition, notes in the margin: “The error of Marcion.”

111. In the Vulgate, *ait* occurs in a similar passage; *ais* is better here.

114. Aldus writes *anguineo*; most copies have *anguino*. Some later editions agree with Aldus. Prag. has *meditans*, incorrectly, for *medicans*. The manuscripts and ancient editions have *succo*. Thuan. nevertheless has *fuco*, which Heinsius approved. I retain the reading of our copies, *succo*, or *suco* with one *c*, as Prag. always writes it.

[Col. 1020D] 120. Gallandius suspects that the reading should be *est alii*; but he printed *ast alii*, since *est* can be understood.

122. Marcion added this also to his heresy. Compare Tertullian, book IV *Against Marcion*, where he overturns this error and refutes Marcion’s antitheses—that is, the book composed by Marcion to prove that the two Testaments are mutually opposed. Some more fastidious scholars prefer to call it an *instrument* rather than a *testament*, because the word “testament,” used of Sacred Scripture, is farther removed from common usage.]

[90] [Col. 1019A] This is glaucoma, which veils the sharpness of sight

With a watery covering, lest unfettered thought penetrate the tender sky

And grasp the one God with swift senses.

An unsound intention is scattered into divided lights,

And constructs twin altars for twin authors.

[95] If there are two, then why are there not many thousands

Of gods? Why is divinity content with a double number?

Would it not have been better to pour out swarms of gods

Among the peoples and fill the spacious world

With demigod monsters scattered everywhere without distinction,

[100] For what savage barbarism would slaughter perishable deities?

If discordant divinities hold a divided heaven,

It would be fitting to assign their own rights to the clouds,

To springs, to the resounding Ocean,

[Col. 1019B] To forests, hills, caves,

Rivers, winds, furnaces, and metals,

[105] Let each have his own jurisdiction.

508 Or, if you disdain to worship pagan shades

And prefer that two be equal under allied scepters,

Tell me: who, by lot of dominion, holds the lands?

[Col. 1020A] Who rules the stormy seas by eternal law?

[110] Declare the distinct right of the co-inheriting lords.

“One,” you say, “sits aloft in a grim citadel,

The author of wickedness, the God of crimes, harsh and unjust;

Whatever evil burns in the diseased world,

He sows and, doctoring new seed with serpent juice,

[115] Drew the beginning of death from the source of things.”

He himself, the maker of the world, made earth, sea, and stars;

He himself formed humanity and joined together its muddy limbs,

Fashioning what disease would consume, what many crimes would defile,

And what a tomb would dissolve with hideous decay.

[120] But the other possesses love of holiness and a gentle healing nature,

[Col. 1020B] 509 Reviving human beings and preserving mortal life.

Two Testaments proceeded from the two rulers;

The harsher one delivered the old, the better one delivered the new.

This is your weighty and dialectical argument, Marcion:

125. Aldus attempted to alter the meter by printing *cerebri manifesta phrenesis*; the manuscripts have *phrenesis manifesta cerebri*. For why the second syllable of *phrenesis* is shortened by Prudentius, see the prolegomena. Teolius notes: “PHRENESIS. The middle syllable is long.” He intended, I think, to say that the middle syllable is short. Some prefer to write, following the Greek origin, *phrenitis*, *pleuritis*, *arthritis*, and so forth.

127. Vat. A has *haud nequaquam*, incorrectly. In the Parma edition *tamen* was omitted, and the verse became shorter by one foot: “By no means to be God, but rather a slave of hell.”

128. The poet says that the Marcionite god must be condemned to Avernus, either according to the opinion of those who think that demons are without punishment and fire until the final day of judgment arrives, as Chamillard explains, or rather because a demon, being worthy of punishment, ought to be judged by all. For he later adds: “whose serpent-bearing head is encircled by black clouds and surrounded by smoke and fire.” Perhaps the poet wrote *qui sit damnatus*.

129. Prudentius often lengthens the *i* in *Marcion*. Because of his license with proper names, he sometimes shortens and sometimes lengthens vowels, as Giselinus says below at verse 610 concerning *Beliade*, or rather because here he uses synaeresis and places a spondee, not a dactyl, in the first foot.

130. Rot. has *vertice sublimi*, which Heinsius prefers. I do not dare alter the reading, since all the others have *vertice sublimis*.

133. Giselinus reads and punctuates differently: *felle perusto invidiae, impatiens*. In the margin: *invidia* with the others. Some punctuate *felle perusto invidia impatiens*. Others: *felle perusto, invidia impatiens*, which I retain. Concerning the devil’s envy, Wisdom 2:24: “But through the devil’s envy death entered the world.”

136. Saint Bernard perhaps imitated this passage in sermon 1 on Saint Andrew’s Day: “For that most wicked one has snares, and he has arrows, being a most cunning hunter of human beings and thirsting only for the blood of souls. He attacks some with the weapons of every kind of malicious suggestion and wounds many of them, whose endurance is slight. He endeavors to entangle others in pleasures.”

140. Aldus’s reading *irretit ore plagis* is corrupt.

141. Vat. A has the error *indepressa locis*.

143. Most ancient copies have *Nebroth*; others *Nembroth*; others *Nemroth*; others *Nimroth*; others *Nemrod*, as in the Vulgate. See Genesis chapter 10.

144. The older Boher. and Gis. in the margin have *sinuosis* for *silvosis*. Teolius says that Heinsius preferred this reading in the additions, though I think he merely reports it. Fabricius believes that *silvosis* has four syllables. But the reading can stand if the verse admits a spondee in the fifth foot.

145. First Epistle of Peter, chapter 5: “The devil prowls around, seeking whom he may devour.”

146. Ald. has *innectit*. Rot. has *adorsus*. In other authors too, ancient manuscripts vary, with both *adorsus* and *adortus* being found.

[Col. 1022D] 147. He shortens the *o* in *luctando*, which I said in the prolegomena should not be criticized. Some wrongly think that all adverbs ending in *o*, such as *porro*, have a lengthened vowel. See Gifanius’s Lucretian index under short *e*.

149. The well-known and familiar line is Virgil, *Aeneid* III, verse 56: “To what do you not drive mortal hearts, accursed hunger for gold?”

153. Barthius defends this phrase, condemned by certain teachers for reasons unknown to me, in book III of the *Adversaria*, chapter 25—not only because it is an imitation of the Greeks, among whom one finds “myriads of examples,” but also because the Latins themselves did not shrink from it; for example, Virgil, book VI: “So far will he lead his ancestors by hope,” besides Velleius, Tertullian, and others. Juvencus at the end has: “And so great was the grace of Christ to me.”]

[125] [Col. 1021A] Rather, this is unmistakably the frenzy of a stunned brain.

We know that he is the father of crimes; but we know that he

Is by no means a god, but rather a slave of hell,

Who must be condemned to Stygian Avernus.

The Marcionite god, grim, savage, treacherous,

[130] Lofty in stature; his serpent-bearing head is encircled

By black clouds and surrounded by smoke and fire.

He suffuses his livid eyes with burnt gall,

510 Unable through envy to endure the joys of the righteous.

[135] While green cerastae lick his face.

[Col. 1022B] With giant arms in wrestling

To such an extent are the wretched captivated by the nectar of sin

157. Minucius Felix, in the *Octavius*: “Titius both discovered and worshiped Cloacina; Hostilius, Fear and Pallor; and soon afterward, I do not know by whom, Fever was consecrated.” There is an inscription that may seem spurious: “To Fever, the divine; to holy Fever; to great Fever. Camilla Amata, for her son who was ill.” Valerius Maximus, book II, chapter 5: “The other gods they worshiped in order to obtain benefits; Fever they worshiped in temples so that it might do less harm.” See what Elmenhorstius, Wowerus, and Ouzelius remark on Minucius. Weitzius and Chamillard observe that Prudentius alone mentions a shrine of the Itch. Someone conjectured that there was an error in Lactantius, book I, chapter 20, and that the mention of the Itch, or Pruritus, should be restored by correcting it. “If you forbid these things to be consecrated,” Greece will reply to you in the same way that it worships other gods: some so that they may help, others so that they may not harm. This is always the excuse of those who regard their evils as gods, as the Romans did Rust and Fever. He wished to read *Pruriginem*, “Itch,” since fever and itching are very closely related human ailments. Yet it is established from other sources that the god Robigus was worshiped by the Romans so that rust would not attack the crops; hence the festival called Robigalia, or Rubigalia. Indeed, Robigo was also a goddess.

159. Elmenhorstius, on page 58 of his *Arnobius*, after quoting these verses, notes that Arnobius did not extricate himself in his discussion of the nature of evil because he did not sufficiently distinguish between the evil of guilt and the evil of punishment.

[Col. 1023D] 161. The devil is called a formerly august star, like Lucifer in Isaiah 14:12, according to the common interpretation of the Fathers, partly literal and partly allegorical.

162. Angels, good and evil, were made from nothing, no less than the other creatures. Simon Magus was mistaken—or rather dreamed—that angels were procreated by him from Helen. The Angelici—this is the name of a heretical group—were mistaken in asserting that angels were certain divinities. See Saint Paul, *Epistle to the Colossians* 1:16, and the Third Lateran Council, chapter *Firmiter*, on the Supreme Trinity. In the letter of Leo the Great to Turibius of Astorga, chapter 6: “The sixth note indicates that they [the Priscillianists] say that the devil was never good, nor was his nature God’s work, but that he emerged from chaos and darkness, because he has no author of his being.” Rot. has *honorum* for *honore*, from which Heinsius conjectures that the reading should be *nutritum ardebat honorem*. I do not deny that such conjectures of critics, drawn from corruptions in the manuscripts, are often ingenious; but I judge them to be of no value when the widespread reading proceeds correctly. It ought not to be changed, even when contrary suspicions appear plausible.

165. The Third Lateran Council under Innocent IV uses a similar expression: “There is one supreme reality, indeed incomprehensible and ineffable, which is truly the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.”

[Col. 1024C] 166. He calls the angels “airy,” that is, spiritual, for in Prudentius *airy* and *liquid* mean the same as spiritual.

169. Nothing is more common among the holy Fathers and theologians than the assertion that the angels committed the sin of pride. They do not agree equally on what kind of pride it was or what thought caused them to swell with it. Prudentius seems to adhere to the opinion of those who say that the devil reached such wickedness that he wished to imitate God and display himself as a god. Petavius, book III *On Angels*, chapter 2, volume III, says that Prudentius explained the demon’s proud act through a kind of poetic exaggeration, as though he acknowledged no creator of himself—just as those devoted to luxury and the banquet are said to have their belly in place of a god. We may understand the same exaggeration in other passages as well; for, as Petavius observes in section 21, most say that the devil’s sin was his desire to be equal and similar to God, and in the following section he adds that this is not easy to explain. Cyril, book V on John: “The devil persuaded himself through a false opinion that a creature could rise to the nature of its creator.” Alcimus Avitus, book II: “As though he himself were the creator of himself.” Nazianzen, poem 6: “While he desires to be god, he is wholly overwhelmed by foul darkness.” More closely resembling Prudentius are the words of Ezekiel 28:2: “Because your heart was lifted up and you said, ‘I am God’”; these words, spoken of the prince of Tyre, some apply to the prince of darkness. Many theologians, with Saint Thomas, part 1, question 63, article 2, object that the demon knew through natural knowledge that he had been created by God. Prudentius would not deny this, but would say that the angel acted as though he had been persuaded that he was begotten by his own powers. For by natural knowledge too he knew that he could not possess power against God, and nevertheless he desired this. It may also be understood that the demon persuaded the Marcionite heretics that he was another god. They believed this, certainly having been taught it by the demon. Prudentius seems to suggest as much in verse 174.]

[Col. 1023A] It is sweet to die; such pleasure is there in the plague of darkness!

[155] He who begot evils in the beginning is thought to be a god,

512 Consecrated goddesses—Fever and the Itch—in shrines.

The inventor of vice is not a god; a degenerate angel

[160] Created it, conceived in an infamous mind;

He who once shone as an august and mighty star,

And great splendor blazed forth from nothing, increased in honor.

[Col. 1024A] But not from nothing came God, true Wisdom,

[165] And the Holy Spirit: an ever-living reality, never

Begun, yet they fashioned even the airy ministers.

One of these, the most beautiful in appearance,

Swells with pride and, puffed up with greatness, raises himself higher,

[170] 513 And vaunts his own fires more arrogantly than permitted.

He persuaded himself that he had been begotten by his own powers,

That from himself he had taken the matter by which

He might first begin to exist, and that his birth had begun

Without an originator.

182. Giselinus thinks the statement *nil factum absque Deo* is confused, since it means that nothing was made without God but everything through him. In John, chapter 1, this is specifically attributed to God the Son. Yet the poet wisely mentions God without expressing the Son. The issue here is not proving the distinction of the Son from the Father; rather, against the Marcionites it must be demonstrated that nothing was made without God but everything through God, and consequently that even the angels were made through God. For it is clear that the Word is God, and that the things made through the Word were made by God.

183. Gis. in the margin, and Prag. and Rat. through an old corrector, have *facta*. Others have *cuncta*.

184. The Manichaeans and Priscillianists taught that demons were evil by nature. Against them stands canon 7 of the First Council of Braga, in the year 561: “If anyone says that the devil was not first a good angel made by God, nor that his nature was God’s work, but says that he emerged from chaos and darkness and has no author of his being, but is himself the beginning and substance of evil, as Manichaeus and Priscillianus said, let him be anathema.”

191. Gifanius, in the index to Lucretius, reads *convaluisse* in the word *fac* from an old book. All our copies, together with those of Weitz and Heinsius, have *concaluisse*, except that Prag has *decaluisse*, which seems to have pleased Marietto, just as *deculcare* occurs in Pliny for *calcare*, *decontari* in Apuleius for *cunctari*, and *delitare* for *litare*. Aldus and Giselinus also have *dominum quoque conditione* with Oxford. From this Heinsius conjectures *dominum quoque conditione imposita*. Vat. A has *quem* for *quoque*. Urb. has *dominumque conditioni*. Prag. has *dominum quoque conditionis*. The best copies have *dominum quoque conditioni impositum*, which Heinsius and Chamillard explain as “imposed upon the construction of the world.” For Gennadius says that Prudentius wrote *On the Construction of the World* down to the creation of the first man. Indeed, in Ezekiel, chapter XXVIII, *condition* is used for creation in verse 15: “Perfect in your ways from the day of your creation, until iniquity was found in you.” Gallandius also defends *conditioni* in the sense of created things, on the basis of the old translator of St. Irenaeus and Tertullian. Giselinus interprets his reading *conditione impositum* in this way: that man was appointed lord on this condition, namely, that he abstain from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. After this verse Mar., Prag., Rat., Urb., and others insert the following verse:

> Who should govern the whole world by his own authority,

which Aldus more correctly placed after the verse beginning *Nosset*, and after *effusum terreno addicere regi*; others omit it entirely. That the demon burned with hatred and envy is taught by Irenaeus, Lactantius, Gregory of Nyssa, Methodius, Cyprian, Augustine, Anastasius of Sinai, and Tertullian; but other writers explain this sin of envy differently. Some recognize both sins in the demon—pride and envy—and our poet follows them.

193. Elmenhorst, in his commentary on Arnobius, p. 20, supports this expression in Arnobius, *utero fusus* (“poured forth from the womb”), with examples from Cicero, Juvenal, Lactantius, and others.

194. After this verse, as I said shortly before, Aldus places the other verse beginning *Qui cunctum*, etc. Teolius likewise assigned this passage to the same verse; and he declares that it is found in all the Vatican manuscripts, with this difference: some place it after verse 191, while others restore it here.

195. Prag has, incorrectly, *tumore*. *Fermentum* (“leaven”) derives from *ferveo* (“to boil”). Hence the correct reading is “swelling inflated by leaven.” Horace, Book I, Ode 13: “The liver, boiling with difficult bile, swells.” Since there is a remarkable connection between the stomach and the heart, the Latins use *stomachum* and *stomachari* for anger and being angry. Prudentius therefore aptly said *fermento animi stomachante* (“with the leaven of an angered spirit”).

197. Weitz, Giselinus’s second edition, Mar., and Prag. have *corde carens* (“lacking a heart”), namely, the beast itself. The manuscripts of Heinsius, Aldus, Vat. A, and others have *sorde carens* (“free from filth”), namely, wisdom.

[Col. 1027A] He makes it fold new coils within its sinuous breast,

[200] wrapping its shining belly in twisting spirals.

At first its tongue was simple; then it flashed with varied skill in speech,

and, split by deceit, echoed in a forked utterance.

Hence the native head of vices: from that ruler

516 the origin of evil flowed; he first

[205] learned to corrupt himself, and then man, with no teacher instructing him.

At last the world receives destruction when its ruler is overthrown,

and all the world’s possessions are shaken.

Just as, when a robber happens to attack an unwary traveler,

first forgetting the booty, he strikes the master himself

[210] with his sword—the obstacle and delay of the struggle—

[Col. 1027B] and, when he has fallen, the victorious robber drags away

the garments as captive spoil, the wealthy robber now no longer hindered by the body.

slid into easy ruin when its lord sinned,

[215] and already, then liable to corruption, received its master’s evil.

Then the wicked field dared to bear darnel and light burdock

among adulterated crops, in poorly fertile clods;

it violated the wheat-bearing harvest with barren wild oats.

Then, too, lions learned to feed on the blood of harmless calves

[220] and to tear with their jaws oxen already tamed beneath the yoke;

with the shepherd killed, fierce lions learned this.

517 Moreover, the wolf, provoked by the plaintive bleating,

Every animal, skilled in the dreadful cunning of theft,

[225] was imbued with it, and deceit sharpened its twisted senses.

Although a wall surrounds the flowering gardens,

260. “No better epithet could have been given,” says Giselinus. For by using adornment as a kind of lure, we seem to prostitute the modesty and chastity implanted in us. If God would grant that, under the impious Turks, we were sometimes held in less contempt for this reason! Others may judge whether these remarks can be applied to our customs and our own times. Weitz, by contrast, adduces other examples against women’s adornment from Euripides and from the law of Zaleucus in Diodorus Siculus, Book XI. The following passage of Tertullian, *On the Crown of the Soldier*, chapter 12, belongs to the same subject: “For what is a crown on a woman’s head except a procurer of beauty, the highest mark of wantonness, the final denial of modesty, the kindling of seduction?”

> and hands, and golden bonds shone upon snowy feet.  
> And lest material for such a gift be lacking,

Compare Tertullian, *On the Veiling of Virgins* and *On the Apparel of Women*; Ambrose, Book VI of the *Hexaemeron*, chapter 8, and Book I *On Virgins*; Jerome’s letter to Furia on preserving widowhood; Isidore of Pelusium, Book II, letter 53; Arnobius, Book II *Against the Pagans*; and Seneca, *On Benefits*, Book VII, chapter 9.

A, Prag., Rat., and the best manuscripts of Heinsius have *sutilibus* (“stitched”), as in the hymn of the eighteen martyrs of Zaragoza, *sutîle vinclum* (“a stitched bond”); for whatever is sewn is *sutîle*. Ald., Fab., and Gis. have, less well, *sculptilibus*. Weitz has *sutilibus* in the text, and therefore *subtilibus* in the variant readings is an error. Sichardus likewise printed *sutilibus*. Pignorius, *On Slaves*, p. 200, presents drawn instruments of women’s adornment that once existed at Rome in the collection of Laelius Paschalinus: golden hairpins, some plain and some jeweled; a bracelet made of small emeralds, suitable for the arm and neck; a bronze earring decorated with glass gems; a finely worked amethyst pendant; earrings, one entirely of gold and the other ornamented with pearls; and two *elenchi*, or elongated pearls. He illustrates the subject with these verses of Prudentius.]

[Col. 1029A] 518 The elements exceed their appointed bounds; they are swept away and rush,

shaking the whole world with law-breaking force.

The battles of the north winds shatter the shady groves,

[240] and the forest falls, uprooted by immense storms.

Elsewhere a violent river with rushing waters

leaps over the opposing banks, the prescribed barriers,

and, wandering, rules widely over the overturned fields.

Yet the Creator himself did not establish such fury

[245] in these things when they were coming into being; but relaxed license

of the elements disturbed the peaceful laws by breaking their restraint.

Nor is it surprising if the limbs of the world, shaken,

roll about; if the worldly structure, driven by its own vices,

labors; if plague, inciting evil, wears out the lands.

[250] Human life gives an example by which the rest may sin:

[Col. 1029B] human life, to which madness and error supply

whatever it does, so that wars roar, so that fleeting pleasure

[Col. 1030A] flows freely, so that lust seethes with impure fire,

519 so that the whirlpool of avarice swallows

[255] heaps of money with its wide jaws—its endless appetite for possession

sets no limit, adding wishes to accumulated talents.

For the hunger for gold grows greater through acquired gold;

from this comes the harvest of crimes, the sole root of evils,

while it liquefies all the springs of rivers and hidden metals

[260] into adornment, the procurer of dissolved modesty;

while useless desire searches the veins of the squalid earth,

digging out the hidden secrets of nature,

to see whether it might happen to discover radiant stones

in some cavities, for woman is not content with

[265] her inborn beauty and counterfeits an external appearance.

[Col. 1030B] 520 And as though the hand of the Lord, the craftsman,

had given an imperfect face that still required work,

or as though it were necessary to paint the summit of the adorned brow

with stitched hyacinths,
