[Note: [Col. 1031C]

269. Prag has *cellis* for *sertis*, corruptly.

270. Chamillard rightly refutes Iso, who interpreted the green *baccae* as pearls, since they are rather emeralds. Consult Pliny and Isidore, Book XVI, with Grialius’s notes.

272. Rot. has *rubet coma* (“the hair is red”). Heinsius, Book I of the *Adversaria*, chapter 17, says that perhaps *nexa* (“interwoven”) is preferable to *texta*, and collects many similar examples; no fewer examples could be collected in favor of *texta*.

273. In Egm. and Pal. I cannot see what lies beneath the word printed as *edita* for *taedet*. Besides Pignorius, Guasco, in his work *On Female Adorners*, 1775, collects much learned material and discusses cosmetics, or female adorners, eruditely, transcribing several of their funerary inscriptions; for such eulogies were once commonly placed for slaves and maidservants, either by relatives or by their masters.

275. Vat. A, Alex., Urb., Mar., in the second hand, the manuscripts of Heinsius with Widm. above, and Palat. have *pigmentis*. This is better than *figmentis* in Prag., Aldus, and Giselinus in the text, and in Weitz. Our poet uses *pigmenta* for ointments more than once, as does Dracontius in the *Hexaemeron*.

276. Giselinus in the margin has *quod fuit ex falso* (“which arose from a false reading”).

277. Widm. above has *imo* for *arcto*. Everyone agrees unanimously that the female sex is weaker. Beware, however, of those who place women in a species somehow different from human beings. See Alcimus in *To His Sister*: “Lest anyone henceforth dare despise the female sex, it seemed worthwhile to show this in a few words,” etc.

278. An imitation of Virgil, whose phrases are: “he fluctuates in the heat of anger”; “he fluctuates in the heat of cares”; “he fluctuates vainly in a varied heat.”

[Col. 1032C] 280. Vat. A, in the first hand, has *carne recisam* (“cut from the flesh”).

281. The apostle Peter, First Epistle, chapter III, verse 7: “Husbands, likewise, live with them according to knowledge, showing honor to the woman as to a weaker vessel.” Besides Tiraquellus, at the passage cited, see P. Faber, *Semestria*, Book I, chapter 16. Nothing in these verses of Prudentius is more vigorous for rebuking women’s immoderate and effeminate luxury in men. If you wish, add Chrysostom’s unlabored eloquence in *Homily 50*, or 49, on Matthew: “What disgrace do you think it is for you, when you carefully weave in silken threads which an honorable man would never even insert into garments? How much laughter do we think this deserves? … You say that they walk through the streets with their feet raised, generally consumed by excessive anxiety lest their shoes be stained by mud in winter or dust in summer. What are you doing, man? … But if you wish to keep your footwear clean from such defilement, fasten it to your neck or head.”

286. Giselinus with Pulmann’s manuscripts and Daventr., Rat. in the first hand, Prag., Mar. in the second hand, Weitz., Egm., Bong., and Widm. in the first hand have *leves*. Alex., with its gloss *flabiles* (“flexible”), and Oxon. from Heinsius’s manuscripts, Urb. and Iso, have *lues*, which Aldus and others followed.

287. Pliny, on the region of the Seres and the manufacture of clothing, Book VI, chapter 16: “It is obtained through such intricate workmanship and from so distant a world that a matron shines through in public.” Among the Seres, silk garments were made from the down of leaves. Pliny discusses garments of *bombyx* silk likewise in Book XI, chapter 23.

289. Heinsius, with Festus, writes *scutilis*. Our manuscripts have *scutulis*, together with Ald., Sich., Giselinus’s second edition, and others. *Scutulatae vestes* are garments marked with circular designs.]

[Col. 1031A] or to encircle her pure neck with glowing garlands,

[270] or to hang green gems from her heavy ears.

A shining pearl from shells is also woven

into her hair, and her braided locks bristle with golden chains.

I am weary of recounting the sacrilegious cares of mothers,

who, endowed by God with gifts, stain the forms he fashioned with cosmetics

[275] 521 so that, covered with pigments, the skin loses

what it had been, no longer recognizable beneath its false color.

This is what the weak sex does, whose fragile mind

in a constricted breast fluctuates easily in the heat of vices.

What of the fact that the very head of the female body, and the king

[280] [Col. 1032A] who rules the weak part cut from his own flesh,

who governs the tender vessel by his authority,

himself is dissolved into luxury? You may see old heroes

softening themselves through adornment—men whose rough limbs

the Craftsman had formed, and whose hardened joints he had strengthened with bones.

[285] But they are ashamed to be men: they seek every kind of vanity

with which to shine; to loosen their natural strength,

522 they rejoice in taking flowing garments—not woven

from the fleece of sheep, but from the eastern world’s acquired

spoils of trees—and in covering their sturdy bodies with patterned fabric.

[290] Art is added, so that threads saturated with repeatedly boiled herbs

may imitate various patterns with variegated thread.

[Col. 1033B] 291. *Illudant*: color.

292. *Fere*: nearly, almost.

293. *Pectitur*: is adorned.

294. *Venantem*: buying. *Versicolorum*: of various colors.

295. *Plumea*: soft. *Pluma* is said of a needle; hence in the *Bibliotheca* one reads *opere plumario* (“in feather-work”), Vat. A.

296. *Peregrino*: foreign, exotic.

298. *Luxus*: luxury, extravagance, vanity. *Vegetamina*: powers, strength or manliness, impulses.

300. *Auribus atque oculis*: hearing, sight, smell, and taste.

301. *Quaeritur*: is sought from those senses, or by us. *Infectus*: corrupted.

303. *Palpamen*: covering. *Fotibus*: nourishment. *Ambit*: seeks, desires.

[Col. 1034B] 304. *Ingenuas*: noble, natural.

305. *Dotes*: gifts of God.

306. *Perversum*: perversely. *Viget*: prevails.

307. *Vertunt*: human beings.

308. *Rogo*: I ask, I inquire. *Pupula*: pupil; *pupilla* and *pupula* mean the same thing.

309. *Semivirorum*: effeminate eunuchs.

310. *Vertigine*: circling, rotation.

311. *Incestans*: polluting. *Foedo oblectamine*: vile pleasure.

314. *Illecebras*: enticements, filth, sordid things. *Conciliata*: joined, glued together.

315. *Jacit*: throws, casts.

316. *Lyricae*: of a lyre-player, or musical.

317. *Calentis*: burning, hot.

319. *Cavernosos*: winding, hollow. *Meatus*: passages.]

[Note: [Col. 1033C]

291. Sich. has, incorrectly, *famine telas*.

292. Aldus, the manuscripts of Heinsius, and those Marietto saw have *ferae*; Heinsius suspects that one should read *Ut cuique est lanugo ferae* (“as the wild creature’s fleece is for each”). Alex., Urb., Weitz, and Gis. have *fere*, which is preferable.

293. The “wanton tunics” are either made of silk or variegated with obscene figures, as Chamillard suspects. For the lusts of the ancients, expressed even on cups and loaves, were intolerable. See Pignorius, *On Slaves*, p. 67 and following.

294. Widm. has, incorrectly, *ventantem*. Heinsius notes that his manuscripts also have *avium quoque versicolorum* (“of multicolored birds”), and certainly our manuscripts have this. In Giselinus’s first and second editions there is *versiculorum*, but I think this is an error, not a variant reading.

295. In the gloss of Vat. A, understand *Bibliotheca* to mean the sacred Bible, which the ancients often called by that name. The passage occurs in Exodus I, verse 1: “You shall make ten curtains of twisted fine linen, and blue, purple, and scarlet, varied in feather-work.” On garments woven from various feathers, see Seneca, letter 91. In antiquity a *plumarius* was one who made such garments, or also one who embroidered on clothing with a needle bosses, patterns, and things resembling bird feathers. See Turnebus, *Adversaria*, Book XI, chapter 25, no. 349, on the words of Vopiscus in *Carinus*: “very noble through the difficulty of feather-work.” He thinks Prudentius is referring to garments in which bird feathers are represented by needle-painting without added material.

296. Weitz has *et peregrino*. Aldus has *ex*. Giselinus’s first and second editions have *et*, together with most of the oldest copies—Mar., Rat., Prag., Vat. A, and others.

297. In Weitz, M. Berg. reads *aures* (“ears”) for *auras* (“breezes”).

[Col. 1034C] 299. A most beautiful description of the five senses and the corruption by which human beings pervert them.

300. Prag has, incorrectly, *tam* for *tum*.

301. Oxon., Prag., and Mar. in the second hand have *artubus*. Read *artibus*.

302. Alcimus Avitus, Book I, verse 85: “The touch alone, judge throughout the whole body, which perceives…” Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, Book II: “Touch, however, is spread evenly throughout the whole body,” etc. Cicero says more about the senses there.

303. Mar. has *et*; above, *e*. Prag. and Widm. have *et*. Aldus and Giselinus in Weitz have *ex*, but he intended to say something else, since Giselinus’s second edition has *e*; or Weitz may mean Giselinus’s first edition.

307. An imitation of Virgil, Book II: “turning their pursuits in opposite directions.”

308. It should be noted that Chamillard acknowledged his error at verse 874, where he interpreted *pupulam*, which is the pupil of the eye, as “girl” here.

310. The obscenity of the ancient theater is indicated here, and it is sufficiently well known; although I have no doubt that the modern theater too contains many things that pollute the eyes of wretched people with vile pleasure.

312. Rat. has *atque ideo* (“and therefore”), less well.

313. Aldus, Prag., and Widm. omit the passage.

315. Vat. A has *Quis pigmentato meretrix jacet improba crine* (“What shameless prostitute lies with painted hair?”). The others’ *quas jacit* (“which she casts”) is better.

316. Pignorius observes, *On Slaves*, pp. 78–79, that female lyre-players once served in domestic employment. He cites the epitaph of Auxesis, a lyre-player, and notes that Prudentius elegantly touched on this occupation. In the same work one may see several kinds of lyres drawn.

317. Aldus has *et convivae recalentis*, which could be retained; but the parchment manuscripts prefer *et convivale calentis carmen nequitiae* (“and the banqueting song of hot depravity”).]

[Col. 1033A] They tease out various designs with a distinct warp.

Whatever fleece is softest to the touch,

it is combed. You may see one man eagerly hunting down

wanton tunics, and weaving the garments of multicolored birds

[295] into new fabrics of feathers;

another, sprinkling feminine fragrances with sweet-smelling pigments and exotic

523 powder [*tupiter*, uncertain].

Luxury possesses every resource of our life,

setting them among the five senses that the Creator established.

[300] Through ears and eyes, then through nostrils and palate,

a corrupted use is sought by vicious arts.

Even touch, which is powerful throughout the whole body,

seeks the tender caress supplied by pleasing sources.

[Col. 1033B] Alas that nature’s noble laws should perish,

[305] and her gifts be dragged captive while lust reigns!

[Col. 1034A] Every perverse right prevails, while whatever the Almighty

had given for use, human pursuits turn in the opposite direction.

Is that why, I ask, the observant pupil is placed

beneath the soft eyelid, so that it may watch the shameful limbs

[310] of effeminate men being whirled about in theatrical motion,

thereby polluting wretched eyes with vile pleasure?

524 Or do the conjoined nostrils breathe, extending twin passages from the central citadel of the brain,

so that ill-allied pleasure may drink in the enticements

which the shameless prostitute casts from her dyed hair?

[315] Is it for the empty melodies of a lyre-playing girl,

the sounds of strings, and the banqueting song of hot

[Col. 1034B] depravity, that God gave ears open wide

and ordered the path of the voice to pass through cavernous passages?

[320] [Col. 1035A] Is the journey of the voice, then, or the flavor infused into the moist mouth,

alive for this reason: that seasoned dishes may feed

the sluggish gullet and the forbidden appetite of the glutton?

So that the glutton may prolong meals, furnished with varied flavors, into the night

525 and wear out the heavy belly with his own drunkenness?

[325] Did God wish us to know by touch, with the sense of contact as interpreter,

what is hard, what soft, what smooth, what rough,

what hot or cold?

But we spread out the luxuries of feathers and woven linen,

and polish the skin while the support beneath us softens it.

[330] [Col. 1035B] Happy is the one who has been able to use the gifts granted

with moderation and preserve a frugal measure in enjoyment!

The wealthy spectacle of the world, its pleasant beauty,

and its abundant riches, deceiving through their splendor,

do not captivate him like a child, nor devote him to foolish love;

[335] [Col. 1036A] he detects, beneath the shaded sweetness,

the bitter poison of false goodness lying hidden beneath its covering.

But once this was holy and good for us,

when Christ was creating the world at the beginning of all things:

“For God saw that it was good”—as Moses himself,

[340] the historian of the world’s birth, bears witness.

He says: “God saw that whatever he had created was good.”

This I shall follow; this, fixed firmly in my mind, I shall hold,

as the holy prophet, inspired by God,

recalled and proclaimed the beginnings of the ancient light:

[345] [Col. 1036B] whatever God and Wisdom made was good.

The Father, therefore, the Creator, is the author of goodness, and Christ with the Father.

For God is God, and the Father is God, and the Son is one:

[Note: [Col. 1037B]

354. *Nor a turbid stream*: our origin is pure and blameless, I.

357. *Praelambit*: flows before, swims before, I.

358. *Olivum*: oil, in the wrestling-schools, I, Vat. A.

361. *Circi*: of that spectacle, I.

362. *Levitatis*: swiftness. *Fragoris*: disorderly sound, I.

363. *Inops*: helpless, inert, I.

364. *Infami*: shameful. *Donum*: the horse, I.

365. *Lacedaemonias*: Lacedaemonian; Lacedaemon itself is Sparta, a city of Greece, where this practice was first devised. *Palaestras*: wrestling-schools; PALO, that is, “I flee” or “I wrestle”; hence *palaestrae*, I.

366. *Succum*: oil, Mar.

368. *Proscenia*: vestibules or forecourts before the stage. *Palaestrita*: wrestler; the rope calls the very steps *proscenia*; *proscenia* and *pulpita* are the steps of the stage; concerning *schoenobatae*, that is, rope-walkers, I.

369. *Feras*: horses. *Volucri*: swift, I.

370. *Discrimina*: dangers, I.

371. *Edit*: brings forth, displays, I.

372. *Publicum*: for sale. Iso.]

[Note: [Col. 1037C]

348. Vat. A has *fecit*, against the metre.

350. Rat. has *nec tamen*.

351. Prag. has *nulla sine est*. Clericus dared to maintain that the Nicene Fathers defined nothing else against Arius than that divinity is divided not into three natures of different species, but into three essences of the same form and equal rank; and that the term *homousion* signifies only equality of substance and a certain likeness or affinity of nature, not identity. He repeats the same impudent opinion in his *Life of Prudentius*, vol. XII of the *Bibliotheca universalis*. He says, indeed, that in this verse Prudentius denies that there are three makers of things, diverse in species or kind, since there is no difference of kind. What could be imagined more alien to Prudentius’ mind? Does Prudentius not very often use *genus* for nature? Is not the whole purpose of this book to prove that the three persons have the same nature, and that two gods distinct in nature cannot subsist? See above, verse 47: “And he may dare to divide the powers of one nature.” That others too use *genus* for nature I noted on verse 33. Compare what John Lamius argues against Clericus’ *Art of Criticism* in his dissertation *On the Right Faith of the Nicene Fathers*, where he admirably defends our poet.

353. Prag. has *peperit quoniam omnia*. Mar., second hand, Egm., Fab., Gis. in the margin, and Urb. have *peperitque*. Giselinus has in the text *peperit bona nam omnia*. Other old witnesses have *peperit bona omnia*, without elision of *a* in *bona*, which many think is not unusual in Prudentius.

357. Prag.; Vat. A, second hand; and Mar., first hand, have *sordent*. Others have *sordet*, which suits the sense. The poet has elsewhere used *praelambo*. He frequently attributes *lambere*, “to lick,” *mordere*, “to bite,” *stringere*, “to graze,” and *radere*, “to scrape,” to rivers.

361. Aldus wrongly has *nece cum* for *nec equum*. Isidore, *Etymologies* XVIII.59: “A Christian ought to have nothing to do with the madness of the circus.”

362. Two very old Heinsian manuscripts, Rot., and Alex. have *rabidi*, which Gallandius disliked in Chamillardus. Mar. has both *rabidi* and *rapidi*. Most others have *rapidi*. Statius, *Silvae* III, to Claudia: “nor do the contests of the swift circus delight you.”

365. Weit. has *Lacedaemonicas*. Propertius and others discuss these. Servius, book II of the *Georgics*, explains the etymology touched upon by the gloss.

367. Terence calls these men *funambuli*; others call them *funirepi*, others *schoenobatae*. Manilius, book V, describes their art.

369. Giselinus reports that he heard that among Italians a game of this sort is highly esteemed, in which they provoke bulls to frenzy with sharpened and burning reeds. But whatever glory belongs to it is peculiar to the Spaniards. See a charming description of that game in Vanier’s *Country Estate*. Compare Claudian, poem 17, verses 294 ff., on the procession in the amphitheatre, and Cassiodorus, book V, letter 42 of King Theodoric, where there is more on a similar game in Titus’ Roman amphitheatre, including this on the leap: “Then, when the body is raised into the air in a leap, the upturned limbs are cast about like the lightest garments; and while a certain bodily arch, balanced above the beast, delays its departure, the beast’s swiftness passes away beneath it.”

372. Put., Rot., and Mar., first hand, have *consensus*, which more recent editors preferred to follow. With Alex., Vat. A, Prag., Urb., and most others, both printed editions and manuscripts, I retain *consessus*. Virgil, *Aeneid* V: “There was a circus, whither the hero betook himself amid the central assembly with many thousands and sat down on the constructed seat . . . Here the whole assembly of the vast auditorium fills . . . with cries.” I omit Cicero and others. Prudentius himself, *Against Symmachus* II, verse 1090: “Then to the assembly of the auditorium.” Arnobius, book II: “They kill others without any cause of offence, but for the pleasing pleasure of the assembled spectators.” In the gloss read *Venale, publicum*.

374. Put. and Ald. have *hilaram*, with Alex. and Vat. A; Egm.’s *philaram* points to the same reading. Others have *hilarem*, as do Mar., Rat., Prag., and Urb.]

[Col. 1037A] Indeed, nature makes one, since the two are joined

in one will, law, power, and love.

[350] Yet for that reason there are not two divine powers, nor two

makers of created things, since there is no difference of kind.

527 Therefore there is no difference in the work, none

in creative intelligence: one Creator brought forth all things good.

No muddy stream flows from the source,

[355] nor does a turbid current arise or violate the vein at its first origin;

but while the incorrupt liquid laps the bluish sands,

it grows foul amid putrefying contagions.

Did horse, iron, bull, lion, rope, or olive-oil

possess within themselves the power of crime when they were formed?

[360] [Col. 1037B] That a man is slaughtered, the iron is not the cause of the fury,

[Col. 1038A] but the hand is; nor does the fiery madness of the circus

regard the horse as the author of its fickleness or rushing din.

The crowd, devoid of reason, does not rage at the horses’ running;

through infamous enthusiasm the useful gift perishes.

[365] Thus we know that the Lacedaemonian wrestling-schools were drenched with oil,

and that the soothing fluid served crimes.

528 From there, hanging upon a rope through the air,

reckless courage climbs the lofty platforms with secure feet.

From there reckless bodies leap over wild beasts in swift jumps

[370] and play amid the perils of death;

the public assembly displays spectacles of human blood,

and the laws order a punishment to be prepared for sale,

so that human limbs, torn apart by bloody

[Col. 1038B] bites, may entertain the cheerful crowd with a death.

[Note: [Col. 1039B]

375. *Stolidi*: foolish, stupid. *Bacchantia*: raging, acting madly.

376. *Percensere*: to enumerate, Iso.

378. *Altum*: heaven, I.

379. *Excitat*: raises, lifts up, I.

381. *Aera*: toward heavenly things. *Librat*: places, advances, I.

382. *Contentam*: sufficient. *Stertere*: to rest, sleep; that is, the mind is said to “snore” (*runcare*) when it is bowed down beneath earthly cares and in no way wishes to raise itself in thought toward things above. *Runcare*: Vat. T.

383. *Domino*: the devil. *Perituraque*: the things of this world, I.

384. *Curvo*: crooked, perverse, turned aside, I.

386. *Lubrica*: unstable. *Commendat*: grants, permits. *Perniciosa*: dangerous, I.

387. *Velut*: that is, he thinks it beautiful. *Excitus*: stirred, swift, in motion, I.

388. *Exemplo*: by likeness, similarly. *Transvolat*: passes over, flies past, I.

389. *Pestibus*: kinds, disturbances. *Urget*: agitates, I.

390. *Praedo*: the devil, I.

391. *Bibunt*: they inwardly conceive, within their inmost hearts. *Medullitus*: in the inner parts of the soul, around the heart, I.

392. *Ministros*: diseases or vices, I.

[Col. 1040B] 393. *Illic*: in the marrow or limbs. *Numerosa*: numerous, manifold. *Cohors*: a cohort of devils or vices. *Principe*: the devil, I.

394. *Circumsidet*: that cohort surrounds, I.

395. *Superstitio*: empty religion, paganism. *Moeror*: sadness. *Luxus*: lust, or gluttony of the belly, I.

396. *Sitis*: desire; murder. *Vini sitis*: drunkenness. *Sitis auri*: greed, covetous desire, I.

397. *Livor*: envy. *Adulterium*: violation of marriage. *Obtrectatio*: detraction, I.

398. *Horrent*: appear horribly. *Facies*: the images or forms mentioned above, I.

399. *Ambitio*: covetous desire; vain or empty pride, I.

400. *Personat eloquium*: the speech resounds, he speaks loudly, I.

401. *Canina*: named from dogs, I.

402. *Vilis*: worldly. *Clavam*: Hercules’ club, with which he conquered everyone; hence he calls the dialecticians’ syllogisms “the club,” by which they think they defeat everyone—the club of Hercules, I.

403. *Vicatim*: through the individual streets. *Gymnosophistas*: philosophers who debated naked; naked sages. The gymnosophists are said to philosophize naked in the wilderness by day, Iso.]

[Note: [Col. 1039C]

378. The saying “No one raises his mind …” is excellent, after he had reviewed the empty occupations and destructive pursuits of human beings.

382. Aldus, Prag., and some Vulgate manuscripts with Pal. read *contentam sternere*. The best witnesses read *contentam stertere*. Bong. has *contentus* for *contentam*, and *contentus* occurs in some Vulgate manuscripts, but not in Aldus, as Weitzius thought—unless Aldus had two editions, which I do not believe.

384. From Persius, satire 2: “O souls bent toward the earth and empty of heavenly things.”

385. Widm. has *perit*; above, *parit et capit*. Bong. has *capit*. The others have *parit*, which is correct.

[Col. 1039D] 390. Ecclesiastical writers often call the devil a robber and thief. In the preface to the second book of the *Apotheoses*, verse 45, and in the *Apotheoses*, verse 408, he is likewise called a thief.

394. Mar., first hand, has *horrendas*, incorrectly. Ald. has *circumsedit*; Weitz., Vat. A, *circumsedet*. With the others, one should read *circumsidet*.

395. The Epistle of Blessed Paul to the Galatians 5:19: “Now the works of the flesh are manifest: fornication, uncleanness, immodesty, lust, service of idols, sorceries, enmities, strife, rivalries, angers, quarrels, dissensions, sects, envies, murders, drunkennesses, revelries, and things like these.” Vat. A and Pal. have *luctus*—mourning—which is not correct in place of *luxus*.

398. Ald. and Mar. have *habitu*, against the meter of the poem, instead of *habitu*; Vat. A likewise has *abitu*. *Habitus* means form, appearance, condition, or bodily dress. Virgil, *Aeneid* 1: “Bearing the face and appearance of a maiden.”

399. 1 Corinthians 8:1: “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up.”

400. Ald. incorrectly has *addita* for *abdita*.

401. The canine eloquence of the lawyers has passed into a proverb.

402. Fabricius assigns Hercules’ club to wisdom, because Hercules was worshiped by learned men, who ought to be industrious and beneficent; thus Hercules shared a temple with the Muses in the Circus Flaminius. Giselinus thinks, more plausibly, that this passage refers to the Cynics, whose equipment consisted of a staff and a wallet. That the club was counted among the insignia of philosophers is clear from Apollinaris Sidonius, poem 15: “He commends cloaks with the mark of the knotted club.” Sirmondus, in his note on Sidonius, p. 45, supplies much concerning the beard, cloak, and club of philosophers, and interprets these very verses of Prudentius’ philosophical club. Chrysostom, *On the Statues* 7: “Where are now those who wrap themselves in cloaks, display their grown-out beards, and carry clubs in their right hands—the foreign philosophers?” Saint Augustine, *City of God* 14.17: “We still see philosophers who not only wrap themselves in a cloak but also carry a club.”

403. In the Parma edition the printers’ error *Ostenta* should be corrected. In the gloss of Isidore one should read *Indiae* rather than *in die*, from Isidore, book 8, chapter 6.]

[375] [Col. 1039A] I am weary of recounting a thousand other mad pleasures

of the foolish world, which, forgetful of the true Thunderer,

roll human life onward through wretched errors.

No one raises to heaven a mind mindful of the supreme Father,

no one sends sighs toward heaven;

[380] 529 nor, recalling the summit of his native throne,

does he look back to the Creator himself, nor balance hope beyond the air;

but, content with cares that weigh it down, he lets his mind snore,

submits it, prone, to an unworthy master,

and loves what is destined to perish, seeking earthly things

with a crooked understanding.

[385] He praises what the earth produces as beautiful,

what unstable glory bestows,

what destructive pleasure commends—

what, like a wind stirred up by scattered dust,

[Col. 1039B] passes away, what flies swiftly past like a thin shadow.

[Col. 1040A] The powerful robber presses these sick souls

[390] with the plagues of diseases: he, diffused through them

with silent powers, is inwardly drunk in by human hearts.

He sows all wickedness deep in their marrow

and scatters his attendants through their limbs.

For there a numerous cohort serves beneath such a leader

and surrounds souls with dreadful weapons:

[395] 530 anger, superstition, grief, discord, luxury,

the black thirst for blood, the thirst for wine, and the thirst for gold,

envy, adultery, deceit, slander, theft;

misshapen faces glare horribly, threatening in their appearance;

windy ambition swells; learning grows proud;

[400] speech resounds; hidden fraud weaves its knots.

From there canine eloquence barks throughout the forum.

[Col. 1040B] Here worthless wisdom carries Hercules’ club

and displays its gymnosophists through the individual streets.

[Note: [Col. 1041B]

404. *Idololatrix*: worshiping idols, serving idols, I.

405. *Advolvitur*: bends down, I.

406. *Premit*: constricts, presses, I.

407. *Armigeris*: with armor-bearers, that is, with vices and ambushes. *Ferrata*: hard, iron-clad. *Satellite*: with a soldier, I.

408. *Triumphat*: conquers, I.

409. *Chananeus*: a people; it is interpreted as “their movement.” *Cham* is interpreted as “hot” or “agitated.” Here he recalls the seven nations that rose against the children of Israel, but in place of seven he has set vices, or signifies spiritual wickednesses that rise against human beings, I.

410. *Casside*: helmet. *Setarum*: of the beard; on the beard, I.

411. *Cuspide*: spear, I.

412. *Furens*: angry. *Ardet*: burns, crackles, I.

413. *Amorrhaei*: sadness; *Amorrhaeus* means “bitter” or “speaking.” *Gergeseorum*: *Gergeseus*, “driving out a settler,” or “a neighboring stranger,” I.

[Col. 1042B] 414. *Volitantia*: because of the speed of the horses, Iso.

415. *Eminus*: from afar, opposite. *Confligunt*: they fight. *Cominus*: close by, I.

416. *Jebusaicae*: *Jebuseus*, that is, “trampled,” or “their manger,” I.

417. *Aurea tela*: greed. *Tincta*: poisoned, I.

420. *Cethaee*: *Cethaeus*, cut off from Christianity. *Juvat*: delights. *Phereza*: *Pherezeus*, separated, or without a wall, I.

422. *Rex*: the devil. *Hevaeorum*: *Hevaeus*, savage or fierce, I.

423. *Thoraca*: a breastplate, the chest, or a helmet, because it covers the chest, I.

424. *Subnixa*: subjected, supported, raised. *Viris*: vices, I.

428. *Mammoneamque*: diabolical, money-loving, or worldly and greedy, I.]

[Note: [Col. 1041C]

404. Aldus printed *idololatrix*; the corrector changed it to *incera(t) lapides fumosos idolatres*, incorrectly reading both *incerat* and *idolatres*. The later corrector in Rat. was no better, substituting *vana deorum* for *idololatrix*, or *idololatris*. Gronovius, *Ecclesiastical Observations* chapter 5, preferred *idololatris*, and Heinsius and other recent editors were not displeased by it; changing *s* to *x* because of the similarity of sound would indeed be easy. But the manuscripts require *idololatrix*, and this was Prudentius’ own usage, as well as that of his age, which formed certain Greek-Latin words such as *primoplastus*. In the Parma edition the meter is corrupted by *incerat fumosos lapides*.

406. The corrector in Rat., after erasing the earlier words, ineptly substituted: “Alas, how many mortal kind the wicked enemy presses with soldiers.” Gis., Fabr., and Cell. printed *premit genus*. Ald. and our witnesses have *genus premit*. Heinsius retained this.

408. The active form *triumpho* occurs in the Vulgate; Livy, Tacitus, and Pliny used the verb in that way, namely with a passive sense, “to be triumphed over.”

409. Aldus first printed *Chananaeus, atque agmina denset*, and later corrected it to *Chananaeus, et agmina denset*. Giselinus adopted the latter. Latinius in Torn. read *Chananaeus, atque agmina denset*, but observed that either *Chananeus* must be trisyllabic, or, if *Chananaeus* is quadrisyllabic, that one should read *Chananaeus, et agmina*. In Latinius’ Bible I believe *surgite* is a mistake for *surgit*. The manuscripts have *Chananaeus, atque agmina denset*, with the diphthong *-eus*. See *Apotheoses* verse 982, *Mattheus*. Prag. has *densat* instead of *denset*, as does Giselinus in Weitzius; in his second edition, however, he has *denset*. See Lauretus, *Forest of Allegories*, for the allegorical interpretation of these nations, with references to similar passages in the Fathers.

410. Ald. has *terribili*; the others, *terribilis*. Fabricius printed *ponderamento* for *pondera mento*, an error that was not typographical, since in the Index he noted that Prudentius used the noun *ponderamentum*; in the Commentary he confirmed this, explaining that it means “weight.” Many such errors entered Prudentius’ text through the joining of words. In fact, Aldus reads *ponderamento*.

411. Prag. has *vibrans*; above, *quassans*.

413. Vat. A mistakenly has *greges eorum* for *Gergeseorum*. All these were peoples of the land of Canaan; see Joshua and its interpreters.

416. Put., Egm., and Vat. A have *Zebusiacae*. Mar., Prag., and Gis., *Jebusaicae*. Weitz. and Urb., *Jebusiacae*. Aldus and Alex., *Gebusaicae*.

418. Ald., Mar. first hand, Widm., and Bong. have *micant, radiantque, micantque*. In Prag. it seems originally to have been *micant, radiantque, nutantque*, which conflicts with the meter. Oxon. has *micant, radiantque nitentque*. Fabr. and Gis. have *nitent, radiantque, micantque*. Most older witnesses have *micant, radiantque, necantque*. The typographical error in the Parma edition must be corrected to *radiantque, necatque*.

420. Put. has *Cittee*; Egm., *Chitee*. Others have *Cethaee*; Giselinus, second edition, *Gethee*. Put. has *gens Phereza*, which I follow, since *Pherezaea* conflicts with the meter. Chamillardus would prefer *Bettaee*, if the meter allowed it. Another error occurs in the Parma edition: *sed gens Pherezae sagittis*. Teolius perhaps intended *Pherezaea*.

422. Put., Rot., Ald., Pal., and Egm. have *Euveorum*. Vat. A and Bong., *aeveorum*. Mar., Prag., and Weitz., *Eveorum*. Others have *Bevaeorum*, and others forms slightly different. Some Vulgate witnesses have *praemovet* for *promovet*.

424. The power of crimes, as in Scripture, “the power of darkness.”

426. *Indociles* is used in the sense in which we said in hymn 3 of the *Cathemerinon*, verse 111, that *indocile* can mean *docile*, just as *infractus* can mean *fractus*.

427. This imitates Virgil, *Aeneid* 2: “Unwitting, believing them allied forces,” and what follows. See also verses 551 and following of the *Psychomachia*.]

[Col. 1041A] 531 Idolatrous religion smears smoky stones

[405] and bends pale over deaf altars.

Alas, with how many armour-bearers the wicked enemy oppresses mortal kind!

With what iron-clad retinue the leader wages wars,

with what dominion he triumphs over the conquered!

The Canaanite rises to help and thickens his ranks,

[410] dreadful in his helmet, shaking the weight of his beard

and brandishing his right hand with a heavy spear.

But on the other side a raging army burns,

that of the Amorite king; then thousands of Gergesites

pour out a battle-line flying over the whole field:

[415] these strike from afar, those fight at close quarters.

[Col. 1042A] Behold, the Jebusite companies boil for battle;

their golden weapons, stained with the dragon’s blood,

shine with deadly brilliance, radiate—and kill.

You too, Cethaean, delight to arm terrifying troops with spears;

[420] but the Pherezite people assail with arrows

of equal strength, though with different weapons.

Finally the king advances the wedge of the Hivites,

wearing a scaly breastplate made from a serpent’s skin.

With these men the perverse power of crimes supported

[425] subdues weak minds, which, untrained in simplicity

and inexperienced in war, under a false treaty

first believe the gloomy allied forces of friendship

and follow Mammon’s faith beneath the appearance of peace.

[Note: [Col. 1043B]

430. *Addictis*: subjected, subjugated, assigned. *Nebulosum*: dark, black, I.

432. *Ille*: someone, a certain person. *Supervacuis*: overflowing through plunder. *Fundis*: estates, properties, inheritances, buildings, lands or farms; a *fundus* is called a field because it “founds” or produces fruit for us, I.

436. *Barbaricis*: diabolical. *Habenis*: bonds, I.

437. *Hic*: a certain person, someone, I. *Ventosae*: empty, Vat. A.

438. *Cavo*: empty, I.

439. *Ambitionis*: greed, I.

440. *Successu*: prosperity. *Trementes*: fearing, I.

441. *Exanimare*: to kill, mortify. *Fasces*: powers, dignities, I.

442. *Exercere*: to increase. *Secures*: the lictors’ axes, I.

[Col. 1044B] 444. *Limat*: purifies, I.

445. *Hostica*: hostile, I.

446. *Cohibent*: restrain, constrict. *Ergastula*: from Greek *ergon*, “work”; hence *ergastulum*, a place where some work is carried out, I.

449. *Assur*: interpreted as “directing,” I.

450. *Quam*: the nation, I.

451. *Orbatam*: widowed. *Ululavit*: lamented. *Urbem*: Jerusalem, I.

452. *Num*: whether, surely, I.

453. *Persica*: diabolical, I.

456. *Barbara*: pagan, I.

458. *Profanato*: filthy, I.

459. *Abolent*: forget; at the urging of those wicked beings. Alienation is detestable ruin, I.]

[Note: [Col. 1043C]

430. Egm., Weitz., Iso, Giselinus in the margin, and Gifan. in the *Index to Lucretius* have *nebulosum*, from an old book, as though it meant “of mists.” Rat. likewise has it, with the gloss “deceitful, dark.” Most, including Alex., Urb., Mar., Vat. A, Prag., and the Heinsian manuscripts, have *nebulonum*. There is no doubt that *nebulo*, like *nebulosus*, is appropriately said of the devil.

431. Egm. and Ald. have *aptant*; the others, *optant*. In Mar., *ferocibus* has correctly been made from *feracibus*.

433. Vat. A and Egm. have *contento limite*, as though from *extento*, or with the boundary itself “contained,” while people covet the neighboring little fields. The others’ *contempto* is better. Horace, *Satires* 2.6: “Oh, if only that neighboring corner might be added, which now disfigures the little field.” Teolius cites all the Vatican manuscripts for *contempto*, or, as he himself writes it, *contemto*. An *n* could easily have been mistaken for *m*, or the reverse.

435. It was customary to lead captives before a triumphal chariot.

440. Prag. incorrectly has *successum*. Among the herald’s duties was to publish judgments and sentences.

441. Egm., Wid., Mar. second hand, Prag., [Col. 1043D] Vat. A, and Ald. have *examinare*. It is surprising that this error should occupy so many codices. The meter requires *exanimare*, which is found in other witnesses. Rat. has *exanimare* in a recent hand; otherwise it had *examinare*. Alex. has *exanimare*, but its gloss is “to investigate,” as though the glossator had read *examinare*. Ald., Alex., Urb., and Gis. have *in corpora*, as in hymn of Saint Cassian, verse 47, *in ora frangere tabellas*. Heinsius noted nothing to the contrary from his witnesses. Mar. has *corpore*, in a recent hand *in corpore*. Prag., Rat., and Weitz. have *in corpore*.

446. Add to the gloss, from Isidore, book 15, chapter 6, that *ergastula* are also places where criminals are assigned to some work.

447. Chamillardus understands *virtus non intellecta* as vices that deceive under the appearance of virtue. Cellarius interprets it as true virtue, which avenges ignorance of itself and contempt by the service of punishments. Perhaps it is better to say that *virtus non intellecta* means a certain hidden power, not understood by those themselves who are subjected to punishments. Thus above, verse 436: “Nor does he feel himself subjected to barbarian reins.”

448. Widm. has *nostra* above, less well. He continues his denunciation of the vices that deceive under the appearance of virtue and reduce captive people to slavery. Juvenal treats such vices in satire 14.

450. Jeremiah, Lamentations 1:1: “How does the city sit solitary, that was full of people? She has become like a widow, the mistress of nations.”

452. Because of a different spelling, Prag. and Rat. have *aud*; Egm. and Vat. A have *haud* for *aut*.

453. Prag. has *quos*, and in the following verse *captivos*, less suitably than *quas* and *captivas*, namely souls.

455. Vat. A writes *disuescunt*.

456. Rat. has *ex patriis*, Prag. *exuti*, as above *quos captivos*. All these matters can be seen in the Lamentations of Jeremiah.

458. The Israelite captives, including those who had fled to Egypt, had turned to the worship of idols; Jeremiah rebuked them.

459. Palat., Widm., and Egm. have, as a variant reading, *petulantia pectora*; Weitz. and Vat. A, *petulanti e pectore*, with Ald. and others; Mar., first hand, Rat., and Prag., *petulanti pectore*. In Mariet. another hand has *a vel e pectore*. Saint Paulinus, *Psalm* 136: “When we carried Zion in our remembering breast.” There too the first vowel is lengthened, as Fortunatus also lengthened it. See other examples in Fabricius’ Index to Christian poets. Others shorten it; I noted in the Prolegomena that this can occur in such nouns. Among the Jews held captive in Babylonia were some who remembered Zion and abhorred the worship of idols, as is clear from the cited psalm: “By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down and wept, when we remembered Zion.” Prudentius rebukes them with Jeremiah, because they had followed the customs and rites of the nations.]

[Col. 1043A] Soon they are ready to be dragged to chains; willingly

[430] they submit their necks to harsh yokes and desire to serve

the savage commands of shadowy spirits.

That man, increasing his patrimony with unnecessary estates

and coveting neighboring little fields beyond a despised boundary,

is led bound by handcuffs and a thousand chains,

[435] his hands tied behind his back before triumphal chariots,

yet he does not feel himself subjected to barbarian reins.

This man, who climbs the heights of empty fame

and is puffed up by the hollow honor of popular acclaim,

who thinks the increase of ambition through success

to be the highest and solid good,

[440] delights in striking down trembling defendants at the heralds’ cry,

534 in breaking the fasces upon the bodies of the wretched,

[Col. 1043B] and in wielding the dreadful axes of the laws—

he has already given his neck to the noose,

is already bound in a hard shackle, and files the servile bonds upon his feet.

[445] [Col. 1044A] Believe this, mortal captives, whom hostile prisons,

already condemning you, restrain,

whom a virtue not understood constrains to the servitude of punishments:

this is that Babylon, this is the transmigration of our race,

and the dreadful victory of the prince of Assur,

[450] the city whom Jeremiah lamented in mournful song,

wailing for her bereavement of her own citizens.

Is it hidden, or is there any doubt, that souls sprung from Jacob

suffer exile among the nations—whom Persian kingdoms

535 hold captive and compel into their covenants?

[455] There they cease to live according to their ancestral custom;

stripped of their native ways, they degenerate into barbarian laws,

and follow a new language and a new dress;

[Col. 1044B] from a profaned worship they learn to grow filthy,

and from a wanton heart they banish and forget their nurse, Zion.

[Note: [Col. 1045B]

461. *Organa*: praises of God. *Anathemata*: destructions, alienations, I. *Alienationes*: Vat. T.

462. *Memphitidis*: Egyptian, I.

463. *Tolerasse*: to endure. *Sinistris*: adverse, contrary, I.

464. *Pharaonis*: Pharaoh, who was called Cenclis or Chenclis, I.

465. *Sub pedibus*: under domination, under power, I.

466. *Immodicae*: great, abundant. *Spurco*: with filthy belching. *Crudos*: gorged, full, undigested, I.

467. *Quo*: why there, I.

468. *Rebellem*: unfaithful, rebellious, I.

469. *Ope*: by help, I.

470. *Virga*: because the rod was changed into a serpent. *Serpente*: being present, I.

472. *Calcasse*: to walk, I.

473. *Prodita*: exposed, revealed, I.

477. *Perdidit*: read as *perdit*. *Botryonis*: the land of promise. *Opimam*: fertile, I.

478. *Versare*: to plow, overturn, cultivate the earth, I.

480. *Jerichon*: the city of the devil, overcome by holy prophecy, I.

484. *Sudoribus*: labors. *Urbem*: Jerusalem, I.

485. *Culmina*: virtues, desires, I.

486. *Lapis*: Christ; he is both wall and stone, an unquenchable stone and an unfailing defense, I.

488. *Vis*: force applied with strength, I.]

[Note: [Col. 1045C]

460. Weitz., Widm., and others have *nam* for *jam*. Weitzius does not explain whether it means the ancestral homeland, the mystical homeland, or both; for *jam* is repeated twice. Chamillardus reports Pineda’s opinion, book 7 of *On Solomon*, chapter 10, that the Jews hung their harps from willows which stood before the temple of Bel-Jupiter in Babylon itself, based on his interpretation of Psalm 136: “Upon the willows in the midst of it we hung our instruments.” He asserts that Prudentius held the same opinion. To me this is not clear: Prudentius rebukes those Jews who had broken their instruments, not those who had hung them up. Nor does Lorinus approve Pineda’s opinion; he discusses the matter at length and learnedly in his commentary on that psalm.

[Col. 1045D] 461. Vat. A lacks *et* after *organa*. Here *anathemata* are sacrifices, profane customs and rites. *Anathema*, meaning an accursed person, is an ecclesiastical word, as are *anathematizare* in Saint Jerome and others. Teolius notes that *anathemata*, when the penultimate syllable is lengthened as here, means gifts dedicated to a deity. Perhaps he meant to write “with the third syllable lengthened.” One might conjecture *anademata*. Lucretius, book 4: “the headbands of a mitre.”

462. It would take far too long to set out everything the poet indicates or relates from Holy Scripture. The matters touched upon here may be seen in Exodus 1:5 and following.

466. The poet says that the Israelites refreshed themselves in Egypt with excessive meat, because they themselves said in Exodus 16:3: “Would that we had died by the hand of the Lord in the land of Egypt, when we sat by the pots of meat and ate bread to satiety.”

467. Horace, *Epistles* 1.5: “What good are riches to me, if I am not allowed to use them?”

472. Cauchius preferred *purpurea* in his manuscript, because the subject is the Red Sea. But *pulverea* is more elegant with the other manuscripts, as though the Israelites had crossed the sea not only on dry foot, but also by a dusty road through the middle of the sea. Thus immediately afterward the mud dried up. Paulinus likewise, *Natales* 9, said *arente profundo* and “dusty footprints” of the crossing of the Jordan.

474. Weitz. and Gis. have *sub gurgite*. The Heinsian manuscripts, Pal., and our codices have *in gurgite*.

475. Vat. A and Egm. have *sic victor*, incorrectly.

477. Martial, book 11, epigram 38: “Nor does he think you worthy of a whole *botryon*.” Some understand here a cluster of preserved grapes, others cuttlefish eggs or a sauce made from fish eggs. Palladius certainly used *botryon* for a cluster of grapes. Prudentius is speaking of the clusters or bunches of grapes of the land of promise. Consult Numbers 13 and Joshua 6 and following.

480. Aldus writes *Hierico*; others, *Hiericon*, *Jericon*, or *Jerichon*.

482. Ald. has *rivis*; others, *ripis*. Vat. A has *refluis* for *reflui*.

486. Ald. has *illest* for *ille est*. It is clear that this is Christ, the stone of which Paul speaks in Ephesians 2:20 and following. See also the thirty-first tetrastich of the *Dittochaeum*, “The Temple’s Pinnacle.”

487. Sich. and Bong., first hand, have *terris* for *turris*. Vat. A incorrectly has *inexpugnabilis*.

488. The oldest witnesses, Put. and Thuan. in Heinsius, and Alex., first hand, read this way. The additions made by others are superfluous and smell of tautology: *hostibus obsistens, hosticus, arietis vis quatit, arietat, insiliens*. Giselinus: “A defense which neither the hostile crash, nor the ram’s force, nor the violence driven against it shakes; which no bronze siege-engine leaps upon with its beak”; and in the margin, “not a bronze engine.” Aldus: “A defense which neither the hostile crash of the ram nor the force applied shakes, nor does a bronze engine assault it with its beak.” Weitzius: “A defense which neither the hostile crash nor the force of the ram strikes, nor does a bronze machine assault it with its bronze beak.” Gis., first edition, in the margin: “A defense which neither the hostile crash nor the ram’s force shakes, nor does a bronze engine assault it.” Sichardus: “A defense which neither the hostile crash shakes with the ram’s force applied, nor does a bronze engine assault it with its beak.” Thus in the margin; for in the text it agrees with Giselinus’ first edition. The manuscripts likewise disagree among themselves. Rat., Prag., Mar., recent hand, and Egm. agree with Weitzius, except that the latter mistakenly has *arietus* for *arietis*. Teolius cites three Vatican codices for the same reading. I have judged otherwise. Mariettus, first hand: “The hostile crash of the ram or the force applied shakes, not a bronze engine.” Mariettus had cited Sichardus incorrectly; in his first edition, which I have seen, Sichardus printed it as I have just said. Alex., in the margin, Urb., and Oxon. have: “A defense which neither the hostile crash, nor the force applied by the ram shakes, nor a bronze engine with its beak,” against the meter. Rot. and three Torr. have: “The force applied shakes him whom the bronze engine strikes with its beak.”]

[460] [Col. 1045A] Now they are weary of remembering their homeland; now they break

the mystic instruments and praise the *anathemata*—the accursed offerings—of a foreign kingdom.

Was it not better for our fathers to have endured

536 the savage rule of the court of Memphis

and to have sat wholly beside hostile hearths?

To have been placed beneath the feet of unjust Pharaoh,

[465] ready to serve amid mud and straw,

and to be filled with excessive meat through filthy belching?

Why did the Lord pour out so much aid through miraculous signs,

while saving a rebellious people by undeserved help,

while loosening the necks subjected to chains

[470] and restraining Egypt with the serpent-bearing rod?

What good was it to tread the sea’s deep,

as the waters withdrew, by a dusty road,

when the rocks, conscious of the sea,

were exposed beneath an unknown sky,

[Col. 1045B] and the thirsty mud dried up in the midst of the whirlpool?

[475] If, victorious through God’s power, once cleaving the midst

of darkness with a pillar of light, the army

lost the rich valley of the discovered grape-cluster;

537 if he does not know how to plow the soil for whom the flowing earth,

rich in perpetual honey, mingles its milky clods

with snowy streams;

[480] if he allows conquered Jericho, at the sound of trumpets

and the brazen music, to rise again into its ancient walls;

if he is driven from the banks of the retreating Jordan

and now abandons the allotted territory measured into acres;

finally, if he cannot defend the city built with such labors,

[485] and the heights that rise above the cloud-born storms;

if he does not know what that stone is,

[Col. 1046B] standing against enemies as an impregnable tower

and defense—which no machine with its bronze beak [Note: [Col. 1047B]

491. *Seriem*: order, I.

494. *Eminus*: from afar, in opposition. *Arce*: high, lofty. *Fide*: by faith, I.

495. *Fretus*: trusting, Iso.

496. *Regina Tyri*: greed, I.

497. *Parthus*: a heretic. *Rapiet*: namely, will seize the captive. *Indus*: uncleanness, I.

499. *Gigantas*: followers of the devil, I.

501. **Tutus**: safe, protected, I.

[Col. 1048B] 502. **Charon**: the navigator of the underworld, the devil. — **Numen**: God; the evil god, I.

505. **Fluxo**: unstable, flowing away, failing, I.

506. **Fallo**: I deceive, I lie, I mislead, I.

507. **Orsus**: he had said, I.

508. **Perjuro**: deceitful. — **Latroni**: the devil, I.

490. Concerning Christ, the cornerstone who contains both the walls and the foundation, see Chrysostom, *Homily 6*, chapter II, on Ephesians.

494. Weit. and Gis.: *praecingit* (“girds”). Rat.: *praecingit* or *praecinget* (“will gird”).

496. Some ineptly referred this to the queen of Sheba, others to Dido. Prudentius understands the Tyrians allegorically as either avarice or pride, which is signified by Tyre. See Ezekiel XXVIII, Rupert of Deutz, chapter IX on Hosea, and Lauretus, *Silva Allegoriarum*.

498. Carolus Paschalius, *De Coronis*, p. 200, infers from these verses that the Indians—and among them the Bactrians—were skilled at archery and accustomed to crown their heads with arrows.

499. The Heinsian and Alexandrian manuscripts have *gigantas*; others have *gigantes*. By the names of these peoples are understood the vices that in some manner dominated them, or the demons who inspire those vices. See the glosses.

500. I discussed in the *Prolegomena* why the *y* in *Allophylus* is short. *Allophylus* in Greek means “foreigner.” Christian writers commonly use it for “Philistine”; and the translators of the Septuagint render “Philistines” by *allophylos*. Saint Orientius, *Commonitorium*, book I, in the new collection of Edmond Martène, p. 11: “Beauty delivered Samson, famous for wondrous strength, to ten savage Allophyles.” Saint Paulinus, *Natalis* 8: “Believe that the peoples of the Allophyles are not to be feared for weapons or strength.” And in the poem to Cytherius concerning the shipwreck of Martinianus: “The Allophyle woman is a carnal law to me.” Other examples may be found in Sulpicius Severus and in Atto’s account of the siege of Paris.

503. Prag. has *varias* (“various”) instead of *vanas* (“empty”).

504. Vat. A: *Jam vanum* (“Already empty”). Prag.: *Nam vanum est* (“For it is empty”).

505. Pal. has *cuncta volubilibus* (“all things with revolving [elements]”), less satisfactorily.]

[Col. 1048D] 506. In some Vulgate manuscripts, incorrectly, *creaturum* (“the one who will create”) instead of *creaturam* (“creation”). Romans VIII, 20: “For creation was subjected to vanity, not willingly,” etc.; “for we know that the whole creation groans . . . and we ourselves groan inwardly, awaiting the adoption of the children of God, the redemption of our body.”

509. Prudentius takes this not from the Epistle to the Romans but from another epistle, Ephesians VI, 12; we defended his interpretation in the *Prolegomena*, chapter 9.

518. Gis. and Fabr. have *ac vacuo* (“and in the void”).

520. Egm. has *Bellia*. The Vulgate has *Belial*. The older witnesses have *Belia*. Prudentius customarily pronounces such proper names—*Helia*, *Belia*, *Iuda*—in this form, although they otherwise end in *-as*. As for the fact that others shorten the first two syllables in *Belia* or *Belial*, that is of no consequence.]

[Col. 1047A] “Does it butt as it leaps, and do iron blows not shake it?”

[490] 538 This is the corner of the gate, at its summit; it holds together the entire

series of stones and strengthens the constructed thresholds.

Whoever knows how properly to insert it into his walls as a defense,

and girds himself and his battlements with a triple rampart,

standing far off upon a lofty citadel,

[495] trusting in love of the rock and ever-watchful with chaste weapons—

him neither the queen of Tyre, nor the Parthian inhabitant of the great

Euphrates, nor the dark-skinned Indian will carry away,

his black temples crowned with winged arrows.

Indeed, even if the Allophyle tyrant, gathering lightning-swift giants

[500] for battle, should wish to destroy your camp,

you will be safe. Charon himself, the world’s Charon, Marcion’s divinity, will not move you

from your firm station—he who rules vain shadows beneath the airy sun.”

[Col. 1047B] 539 “For whatever the sun beholds is empty: all things consist

[505] of dissolvable elements and a flowing substance.”

[Col. 1048A] “I am mistaken unless the Apostle-teacher, having declared that all creation is subjected

to vain labors against its will,

groaned in pity that it serves the perjured robber.

‘He is mistaken,’ he says, ‘who thinks that our struggle is with blood,

[510] flesh, veins hot with passion, and vicious bile,

or that the soul sins through the warm marrow.

It is not the mind’s own limbs that oppress it, nor does earthly strength

attack its lucid senses or challenge them to war.

Rather, day and night we contend with dark spirits,

[515] whose dominions this moist and dense air,

heavy with sluggish mists, obeys.

This intervening region, between heaven and the lowest earth,

[Col. 1048B] which lies open and hangs the clouds in empty space,

supports the reins of various powers and, beneath

[520] the ruler Belia, shudders under wicked governors.

With these plunderers we struggle, as the holy pronouncement of the witness, the apostolic mouth,

sets forth.”]

525. Mar. has *nimiosque* (“and excessive”), but above it a later hand has written *minimosque* (“and very small”).

530. Alex., together with some Heinsian witnesses, has *resistet* (“will resist”). Ald. and other printed editions, together with Urb. and other manuscripts, have *resistit* (“resists”), and I do not know why Heinsius condemns it, since the sense is the same. The commonly printed editions incorrectly punctuated the passage as *dedere regnanti domino* (“to surrender to the reigning lord”).

533. Prag. has *transcendit* (“surpasses”) instead of *transcurrit* (“passes across”). Gifanius notes that Lucretius elegantly speaks of the course of a javelin or weapon, and cites this example from Prudentius.

535. Ald., Weitz., and Mar. have *volucris* (“winged,” singular); others more correctly have *volucres* (“winged,” plural). In ancient manuscripts such cases often end in *-is*, from which this variation may have arisen.

537. Fabr., Bong., Mar., and Sich. have *rumpit* (“breaks”), not implausibly.

538. Egm., in a second hand; Bong. and Sich. in the margin; Put., Oxon., and Thuan. have *penetrans* (“penetrating”). Egm., in the first hand, Alex., Urb., and others of our witnesses, together with the common editions, have *rapiens* (“snatching”).

543. Egm. has *segni* (“sluggish”), not correctly, instead of *segnis* (“sluggish”). Ald. has *ut* (“as”); others have *aut* (“or”).

546. Rat., in the first hand, Mar., Prag., Weitz., and Gis. read *nobile* (“noble”). But all of Heins., Ald., Vat. A, Alex., and Rat. in the second hand have *mobile* (“mobile”). The latter is better, as is *vegetabile* in Thuan., first hand, Alex., and the very old Boherian manuscript. *Agitabile*, found in other witnesses, means the same as *mobile*. Nevertheless, the reading *nobile, agitabile* found in Urb. and others should not be dismissed. Teolius saw *nobile* in only one Vatican manuscript.

547. The best Heinsian witnesses, Mar., Rat., Alex., Sich., and Weitz., have *casta* (“chaste”). Vat. A, Ald., Gis., and Urb. have *facta* (“made”).

549. Rat. originally had *falsificantis*, but the *n* was inserted. *Falsificus* is a Plautine word. Facciolatus relegated *falsificare* to the barbarisms, although he admitted several other words into Latin solely on Prudentius’s authority. In the second edition of Giselinus, and in a copy of Weitz’s edition, the margin has *vel* (“or”) instead of *aut*.

551. Mar. and Weitz. have *ne* (“lest”); others *nec* (“and not”). Rat. has *non* (“not”). Some printed editions incorrectly punctuate *nec sub fasce jacens alieno, et dedita regno* (“and not lying beneath another’s burden, and surrendered to the kingdom”). In Heinsius there is the error *nec sub face*.

552. Aldus has *ne* instead of *non*.

553. Weitz. has *mundi hominumque* (“of the world and of human beings”); the others, more correctly, *mundique, hominumque* (“of the world and of human beings”). After Prudentius has demonstrated that God is not the author of sin, but that the devil is the one who has drawn human beings into sins, he turns to demonstrating freedom of choice, lest he appear to move toward the opposite position and so as to overthrow another Marcionite error.

556. Others have *de corde parenti* (“from the generating heart”). The sentence is taken from Matthew XV, 19: “For from the heart come evil thoughts, murders,” etc.]

[Col. 1049A] “The testimony of the apostolic mouth reveals what we speak.

540 Let no one blame nature’s condition or the body’s provocations

when he sins: it is easy to restrain rebellious

[525] passions of the flesh, and to curb the excessive impulses

of fragile matter, and to tame conquered entrails.

For the mind is far superior, since it has been sent down from the highest

ether; if it wishes to oppress its limbs beneath it

with heavy authority and subject them to stern commands,

[530] no bodily strength will resist the ruling lord.

There is a greater power within a human being, which injects

air-borne poison and wounds the delicate mind with subtle air.

The Parthian arrow does not traverse the winds in like manner,
nor can any eye encompass its course:

[535] for it is swift, while flying on its wings through the breezes;

[Col. 1049B] it comes unexpectedly, and no whistling announces its arrival

before it breaks open the hidden recesses of the breast,

snatching away secure life with a poisoned wound.

But swifter still, and more poisonous, is the arrow

[540] 541 that the slippery dominion of the shadowy world launches,

evading the eyes when shot, and fixing itself in the heart’s inward parts

[Col. 1050A] with the swift flight of its flying shaft.

Nor is the soul’s nature sluggish or slow to guard against a wound:

for God has placed in it a fiery intellect,

[545] pure, wise, subtle, serene,

mobile, watchful, swift, life-giving, and keen.

If only it venerates its chaste Creator,

serves him, and tramples the conquered world beneath sober feet,

without taking delight, in foolish pleasure, from pestilential riches

[550] or the falsified spoils of the earth,

so that, lying beneath another’s burden and surrendered to a foreign kingdom,

it cannot avoid the enemy’s cunning arrows.

But why do I turn every evil of the world and of wicked humanity

to cast blame upon the hostile enemy, when our evils,

[555] [Col. 1050B] formed from our own souls, possess their origin, source, and power?

542 What they are and what they can do, let them derive from the generating heart.

He indeed is the fuel and cause of our evils.

But he can disturb or deceive only as much as ...”

559. The devil is compared to a roaring lion in 1 Peter V, 8.

560. In Mar. there was *futtule* instead of *futile*, corruptly.

561. Saint Augustine—or rather Caesarius of Arles, sermon 37 in the appendix to Saint Augustine, elsewhere numbered 197 *De Tempore*—compares the devil to a chained dog and says: “He can bark; he can harass; he cannot bite at all unless the person is willing.”

569. Weitz cites Ald., Fabr., and Bongar. for *duros* (“hard”). But Aldus, as I see it, has *diros* (“dreadful”). In Fabricius I likewise read *diros*. Gis., in the margin, has *duros*, which he retained in the first edition. The others’ *diros* is better. The subject is sins that come forth from the generating heart.

[Col. 1051D] 572. Vat. A has *depopulatur* (“it lays waste”); correctly, a recent hand changed it to *depopulantur* (“they lay waste”).

574. Cauchius conjectures *vero* instead of *verum*. I do not see what basis this conjecture could have against the manuscripts.

576. Here *tristes* (“sad”) is understood as “evil” or “wicked”; note the gloss. It also signifies angry, difficult, savage, harsh, or unfortunate.

577. Alex., Put., Thuan., Rot., Egm., Palat. in the first hand, and Cauchianus have *sereret sua crimina* (“would sow his crimes”); Vat. A is not far from this. But Mar., Urb., Ald., Weitz., and Gis., with others, have *misceret crimina* (“would mingle crimes”). Either reading may be retained.

578. Vat. A has *turbasset* (“had troubled”); the reading above, *turbaret* (“would trouble”), is more correct, since the preceding verse has *sereret*.

581. Ald. incorrectly has *ex ethnicis* instead of *ex ethicis*. This error entered some old codices, such as Mar. and Prag., in which a correction was made by a recent hand. Rat. has *et ethicis* instead of *ex ethicis*. Neither Chamillardus, Teolius, nor Cellarius noticed in their indices that the *e* in *ethicis*, which is long, is shortened by Prudentius.

582. Giselinus correctly observes that the poet adds “as they say”; for the story was in fact adopted by Pliny and other ancient writers. I would remark in passing that pious writers should not be accused of sin or defective judgment because they transfer such little stories—whether false or insufficiently verified—into examples for forming morals. They rightly use them either as true events, if they happened, or as fables, if they were invented. I do not understand Teolius, who says that Prudentius would have spoken differently had he been brought into our own age, since it is established that all animals of every kind are born from an egg in which they have been formed. Does Prudentius deny that the viper is born from the egg in which it was formed? He later says plainly, “after the mature seed,” etc. Pliny, book X, chapter 62: “Again, among terrestrial animals, serpents lay eggs . . . The male viper inserts its head into the mouth, which the female bites off in the sweetness of pleasure. Of terrestrial creatures, she alone produces within herself eggs of a single color, and soft, like those of fish.” The question concerns insects: whether, as they say, they are born from putrefaction.

584. Vat. A has *sexus* instead of *sexu*.

587. Aldus printed *trilinguae* and corrected it to *trilingue*; I think he intended to say *trilingue*. Alex., Urb., Fabr., Bong., and Gis. have this in the text. Put., Thuan., Weitz., and others have *trilinguae*, from *trilinguus*, which Heinsius reports Salmasius approved; Heinsius had not seen Aldus’s correction when he asserted that Aldus had printed no other form.]

[Col. 1051A] “We will it: we give the decrepit lion

[560] weapons supplied to him; the savage creature grows cold, gnashing uselessly,

unless it grows through the support of humankind.

We generate every evil of ours from our own body:

as David, otherwise the best of fathers, fathered

one crime, Abessalon: that father begot a grim one, but only one;

[565] among innocent offspring he fathered a parricide,

who dared to draw the sword against the author of his race.

Ah, piety! He drove standards contrary to his father’s standards

and joined the weapons of one blood in civil war.

Likewise, our breasts, burning with a dreadful offspring,

[570] give birth to children who immediately, turned against us,

[Col. 1051B] learn to live upon the sufferings of their progenitors.

For they lay waste the excessively fertile entrails of their parents,

[Col. 1052A] and are nourished by the destruction of their generative stock.

But that supreme king and prophet of God,

[575] the father also of the virgin who was to give birth,

had varied his offspring between the sorrowful and the pious,

so that Abessalon, brother of Solomon, might sow his crimes among righteous

children and trouble his sweet household with bitter ones.

We possess nothing worthy of Solomon; as degenerate beings,

[580] we are filled only by Abessalon, who tears pious entrails with the sword.

If it is permitted to infer anything from ethics, or if an example may be taken

from physics, then the viper, as they say,

dies from its teeth, through the offspring poured out within its entrails.

544 The mother is fertile by her own death, not through sex or

[585] [Col. 1052B] through intercourse with a swollen womb; but when inflamed

by the fire of female desire, she thirsts for her doomed husband

with open, obscene mouth; he inserts his three-tongued head [into it].”

593. Gisel., Palat. above, and Mar. have *ac* instead of *at*. Vat. A incorrectly has *ad*.

597. Gisel. has *pectore*; in the margin, *crimine*, which is found in all the others. M. Bergius, apud Weitz, observes that this is very expressively said: piety is what avenges the father’s death, whereas crime is what kills the mother.

600. Burmannus, volume I of the *Anthologia*, p. 463, reads *jam quia* from Egm. and supports it with many examples, showing that old scribes often changed *jam* into *nam*. This variant reading in the Egmond manuscript escaped Weitz and Heinsius.

603. This accords with an ancient belief, opposed by the experience of modern times. Pliny explains the matter thus, book X, chapter 62: “On the third day she hatches the young within her womb; thereafter she gives birth to them one by one on successive days, nearly twenty in number. Thus the others, impatient of delay, break through her sides, killing the mother.”

[Col. 1054C] 606. Vat. A has *prolis* instead of *proles*.

607. Ald., Gis., and other printed editions have *matri* (“to the mother”); the older Heins., Rat., Mar. in the first hand, Prag., Alex., and Urb., together with Weitz and others, have *matris* (“of the mother”).

610. Ald. and Fab. incorrectly have *Beliadae*, and Ald. likewise *hausto*. Giselinus says that in this patronymic name the second syllable of *Beliade* is shortened, although it was long in *Belia* at verse 520, because of the license permitted in proper names. In addition to this license, synaeresis may be admitted in the second and third syllables, making *Belia* a spondee. I would read, if the manuscripts permit it, *conjuge Belia* (“with Belia as spouse”), for there is no need to derive a patronymic: the poem later speaks of the seed of the accomplice serpent, who is Belia or Belial himself, that is, the devil.

614. *Complex* belongs to later Latin usage. Sidonius, Cassiodorus, and their contemporaries spoke in this way. Isidore, book X of the *Etymologies*, notes that *complex* is never used of a good person, which is what Iso is referring to.

618. Prag. has *proles*; the others *soboles*.

620. The Heinsian witnesses and ours, together with the Weitzian witnesses, have *pastos* (“fed”); Ald. and Gisel. in the text have *partos* (“born”).

622. John VIII, 44: “You are of your father the devil.”

624. Weitz, with Fabr. and Gis., against almost all the manuscripts, has *percurre* (“run through”). Bong., Widm. above, and Sich. have *perquire* (“investigate”). All the Heinsian witnesses, Egm., Alex., and Urb. have *percense* (“review”), together with Aldus and other witnesses of ours, except that Mar. in the margin has *percurre*. Heinsius had at one time considered *pertende* (“proceed through”), but later acknowledged that *percense* was correct, a word Prudentius likes to use. *Percenseo* generally belongs to the second conjugation, but is sometimes transferred to the third, as with *luceo*, *ferveo*, *frendeo*, and *extorqueo*. Heinsius noted that Alcimus Avitus made a dactyl from *contine* in book II.]

[Col. 1053A] “He enters hotly into the wife’s throat and mouth,

inserting the generative poison of intercourse into her mouth.

[590] The wife, wounded by the force of pleasure, bites through

the husband’s throat as she swallows it amid tender embraces,

and drinks the saliva poured into her, while the husband’s flesh perishes.

That father is consumed by these pleasures, but the enclosed offspring

kills the mother; for after the mature seed

[595] begins to creep throughout the body in its warm hiding places,

and the little bodies, shaken, strike the womb with their blows,

the mother burns with the inward crime of piety,

545 and, conscious of her condemned sex, laments her murderous offspring,

which breaks through the barriers enclosing its birth.

[600] For since no exit for birth lies open, the belly,

[Col. 1053B] tortured by the offspring striving toward the light,

is torn apart, and, lacerated through the entrails, opens a passage.

At last, with the death of the nourishing mother, that whole brood of sorrows

emerges, scarcely having escaped into life and carving out its birth

[605] through crime. The crawling young lick the mother’s natal corpse;

the offspring, while it is being born, is bereaved,

[Col. 1054A] having never experienced the light except as the posthumous offspring

of its wretched mother.

The conception of our mind is not unlike this. Thus it drinks in poison

poured from the viperish mouth of its spouse Beliade;

[610] thus it devours kisses in a draught,

burning inwardly with the bile of lust,

546 and is filled with vices, mingled with its doomed husband.

Then, pregnant, it bears a deadly progeny: works conceived

by a malign intellect, from the seed of its accomplice serpent.

[615] This accomplice serpent must first pay for its deeds in punishments,

for the violation of the corrupted soul and for the world destroyed.

Then cruel wounds tear the soul itself apart

through a thousand births, as it gives birth from itself

to offspring generated against nature—

[620] [Col. 1054B] namely, repeated sins—and to children fed upon their mother’s death.

Hence comes that just rebuke of the Lord Christ:

‘Is not the demon your father? I rebuke you, sinners: did

iniquitous seed, thirsting for intercourse of the flesh,

beget you? Reader, review the sacred volume:'

[625] [Col. 1055A] what I say, you will find that the Lord said to profane

mortals, confronting them with the truth. For, ‘if you had been begotten

547 from my Father,’ he says, ‘piety itself would prove it,

and the work of piety. Ah, blind desire! What is this?

When the good mind knows that it has been betrothed

[630] to a rightful marriage chamber, and is summoned to the bed

to marry the king—and to the king who is ever young,

who, having cast off old age, preserves divine beauty

eternally upon his face—

it prefers adultery, and sells itself cheaply

[635] for gold to the filthy embraces of the night-dwelling Indian,

despising the offspring of God poured through the limbs of the virgin

[Col. 1055B] and calling the children born in the brothel sweet.

I understand what opposing lawsuit deceit raises,

with what tooth thorny slander, standing firm, fights,

[Col. 1056A] and calls us to struggles when truth has been challenged.’

[640] 548 ‘If God does not want evil to exist, why does he not forbid it?’ you ask.

It makes no difference whether he was the author and supporter of evils,

or whether, although able to prohibit them, he allows the fairest works

to be turned toward vice and crime. If the Almighty wished all

to act innocently, and holy will did not

[645] degenerate or defile itself by any deed,

then the Lord created the evil that he watches from above,

and permits and approves it to be done, as though he himself had created it.

Indeed, he himself created what, although he can separate it,

he does not abolish but allows to grow through long usage.

[650] [Col. 1056B] Stop up my ears, merciful Father, and close the passages

of my dulling head, lest the open passage

652. The Gospel passage indicated by Iso occurs in Matthew XVIII, verses 8 and following. In Heinsius there is the error *concipias*.

655. In some printed editions *ab arce* (“from the citadel”) appears incorrectly instead of *ab aure* (“from the ear”). Giselinus’s first edition has *ab arce*; the second has *ab aure*, but the margin has *ab arce*.

659. It is clear that this passage concerns original sin, through which all human beings perished. Giselinus, however, thinks that the poet is speaking of Adam and Eve and of others transferred to immortality together with the resurrected Christ. But what, he asks, does this contribute to the confirmation of the matter under discussion? Chamillardus therefore thinks that the sole reference is to the restoration of human beings through Christ’s incarnation, not to those who rose with Christ. I believe that the poet joined these two things together: namely, that human beings were redeemed and raised from their tombs so that they might reign in heaven together with Christ. Both belong to the will to save human beings that Prudentius attributes to God; and that will is greater in proportion as God honors the human being with greater glory. Concerning the resurrection, Prudentius, *Apotheosis*, verse 780: “Restoring everything that is human; this from the tombs, that from the abyss.”

661. Prag. has *facit* (“he makes”); the others *jubet* (“he commands”).

664. Put., Thuan., Widm., and Bong. in the margin, Alex. in the first hand, Prag., and Rat. in an ancient hand have *ope restaurare secunda* (“to restore by a second work”), which pleased Heinsius. Other old witnesses have *opere instaurare secundo* (“to restore through a second work”), which appears in the ancient editions; more recent editions generally follow Heinsius. Burmannus, volume I of the *Anthologia*, p. 459, argues with Egm. that *opere instaurare secundo* should be read, since it is certainly more Latin and therefore should be retained. Prudentius elsewhere also uses the verb *instaurare*, and, speaking of the resurrection, calls it *instauratio* in *Apotheosis*, verse 1071.

667. Prag. and Bong., in the first hand, have *praestat* (“he provides”); the others *praestet* (“may provide”); Gis.’s first edition has *praestet*; the second has *praestat*.

669. The Marcionite says that no one can sin against God’s will. Prudentius answers that God granted the human being freedom so that he might act worthily of praise; consequently, the human being can use it for good or evil. See the *Prolegomena*, chapter 16.

674. Instead of *nescis*, Fabr. and Bong. have *nescisque* apud Weitz, who also cites Aldus for this reading. Aldus, as I see it, has *nescis ab origine*, which is more harmonious. Claudius Marius Victor, preface to his commentary on Genesis, treats the same argument; these verses deserve notice: “Furthermore—forgive me if I may say this, Father, without offending your Peace—it may perhaps be of greater worth before you not to have sinned through life’s slippery times than, for the wretched, to have sinned; but you will see how this stands, and the reasons for everything we entrust to the one in whom we believe.”

[Col. 1057A] 549 receive such sounds. Is it worth so much to destroy— [sentence continues]

The office of life extinguished in part of the brain,

may the soul preserve itself immune and free from accursed

[655] hearing, happy in being removed from the foolish ear.

Who could endure these insults hurled at God, who remembers that he has been ennobled by divine gifts beyond others? To say nothing of much else, this one fact alone proves God benevolent: that he raises from their tombs human beings who have been destroyed by love of what was forbidden, and commands them to share in his kingdom throughout the ages. If he were the author and preserver of evil, he would never wish, after the losses of salvation and the deaths of sinners, to bring healing again, nor to restore what had been lost by a second act of creation.

the other abolishes the work of the perishing person and cancels his merit.

nor approve beforehand what he afterward washes away.

Can anyone sin against the Thunderer against his will,

[670] when it would be easy for him to arrange in the human heart whatever feelings he pleased,

to animate all its fibers with chaste impulses,

You do not know, fool, that the power of your freedom was given by him,

your Creator? You do not know how much power was granted to you from the beginning,

[675] and authority over the world and over your own mind, released and unconstrained—
