688. Widmann above has “without any,” incorrectly. This is the effective argument that the holy Fathers, theologians, and philosophers use to establish freedom: there can be no future praise and no merit unless there is a clear distinction between living justly along the two paths; in the language of the schools, unless there is freedom of indifference. The theologians will produce the authorities of the holy Fathers in abundance.

690. Vatican A has “let it be” instead of “it becomes.” Prudentius explains freedom of indifference more and more fully, and perhaps more clearly than some would wish. See also note I on Symmachus, verse 335, which Petavius praises highly.

693. Saint Augustine repeatedly requires a will free from every necessity in order to act laudably, by arguments embraced by our poet. In *On Nature and Grace*, chapter 65, he strongly approves these words of Saint Jerome: “God made us with free choice, and we are not drawn toward virtue or toward vices by necessity; otherwise, where there is necessity, there is no crown.” To these words Augustine replies in agreement:

“Who would not recognize this? Who would not receive it with all his heart?” Why would Saint Augustine not recognize this indifference of free choice, when he admitted that it was praised by shepherds, poets, the uneducated, the educated, teachers, bishops, and the whole human race? Hear his words in chapter 11 of *On the Two Souls against the Manichaeans*:

“Were even these obscure books to be searched by me, so that I might learn that no one deserves blame or punishment who either wills what justice does not forbid him to will, or does not do what he cannot do? Do not shepherds sing this in the mountains, poets in the theaters, the uneducated in their gatherings, the educated in their libraries, teachers in the schools, bishops in sacred places, and the human race throughout the world? But if no one deserves blame or condemnation either for acting contrary to justice’s prohibition or for not doing what he cannot do, who could doubt that sin exists when the will is unjust and the refusal is free?” Therefore that definition is both true and extremely easy to understand, and I could have stated it not only now but also then: “Sin is the will to retain or obtain what justice forbids, and from which it is free to abstain.”

He explains this more fully in the following chapter:

“To hold anyone guilty of sin because he did not do what he could not do is the height of injustice and madness. Therefore, whatever those souls do, if they do it by nature and not by will—that is, if they lack a free movement of mind both to do and not to do—and if, finally, no power of abstaining from their action is granted them, we cannot hold them guilty of sin.”

Thus Saint Augustine, who professed that on the freedom necessary for doing good he thought the same as the educated, teachers, and bishops, indeed as shepherds, poets, and the uneducated, certainly did not hold the opinion that one would vainly seek among shepherds, poets, and the uneducated—not to mention teachers, doctors, and bishops who lived before or with him. Those who turn Augustine’s meaning in another direction readily concede these authorities to us. Why all this? Why? So that it may be clear that our poet’s view of freedom is Catholic: he taught only what Augustine, that great teacher of grace, embraced with open arms.

Some manuscripts indeed have this reading, but the three older Heinsian manuscripts, Alexandria, Urbino, together with Aldus and Fabricius, read “Go, he says.” Elmenhorst, in his commentary on Arnobius, book II, page 60, illustrates this passage and confirms Arnobius’s statement: “God imposes necessity on no one.”

698. In Put., “and” is absent after “man,” as in Aldus and Mariettus from the first hand. Put., Oxford, Aldus, Giselinus, Urbino, Boherius, and Egmond together with others have “insubjecte,” meaning “innate, inborn,” not badly; but since the subject is man’s dominion over created things, Isonius, Alexandria, Vatican A, Prag, Rat, Weitz, Mariettus, and others are better with “powerful over created things.” Egmond has “arbiter of the world,” and Heinsius suspects “of the world, and arbiter.” Vatican A has “arbiter of things,” incorrectly. The correct reading is “arbiter of things, the same arbiter.”

704. Heinsius, with Giselinus, reads “horrid night,” followed by the more recent editors, as though this passage concerned the saying, “Whoever does evil hates the light.” Gallandius maintains that “horrid night” is required by the antithesis “light and night.” Our manuscripts, those of Weitz together with Aldus, Sichardus, and others, rightly have “death,” because the subject is the reward of good work, which is called light, and the punishment of evil, which is death. “Choose the matter of life,” the poet continues. Weitz, who reads “death,” nevertheless inserts “night” in his commentary and spends much effort approving the familiar saying that the sinner loves darkness; Chamillard partly copies him. The poet refers to Ecclesiasticus 15:14 and following: “God from the beginning created man, and left him in the hand of his own counsel. Before man are life and death, good and evil; whichever he chooses will be given him.” And to Deuteronomy 30:19: “I call heaven and earth to witness today that I have set before you life and death, blessing and curse. Therefore choose life,” and so forth.

In “wandering,” the final syllable is lengthened by the caesura. Teolius cites some Vatican manuscripts for “vigorous”; I have seen it only in Mariettus.

on one side God calls him, on the other the tyrant,

Irenaeus, book IV, chapter 51, also handed down that Lot’s wife’s statue existed, that if anything were taken from it, it was restored and grew again; and so did Cyprian, or Tertullian, or another author in the poem *On Sodom*: “Indeed, if some stranger mutilates her form, immediately from itself it fills the wounds.” Josephus, book I of the *Antiquities*, chapter 19, reports that he saw the statue. Calmet, in his dictionary and commentary, supplies various interpretations and names authors who wrote special dissertations on the subject. I hold firmly to the meaning preferred by Scripture unless a certain argument persuades otherwise. Whether that statue of salt remained for so many centuries and still remains belongs to the credibility of human history.

761. Vatican A corruptly has “propalas.” Read “propolas,” as is clear from its gloss. Fabricius noted that a *propola* is one who buys something in order to sell it at a higher price; but here Prudentius uses the feminine form for places in which male sellers display their goods. Prudentius lengthens the first syllable, following the example of Lucilius and Terence in *Prologues*. See Scaliger on Virgil’s *Culex*. *Meritoria* are buildings where impure women or prostitutes stood available. Barthius, in *Adversaria*, book XLII, chapter 17, explaining this passage of Prudentius, says that the *meritoria* were raised by several stairways and divided by galleries, in which the women were placed and, separated into their own cells, stood available according to their prices.

762. In Giselinus and the Weitzian edition, mentioned often, *propinas* is written in the margin instead of *popinas*. Isonius’s gloss on *popina* and *propina* is also found in Isidore, who incorrectly says that *propinae* is the corrupt form.

763. An imitation of Juvenal, satire 1, verse 86: “Whatever human beings do,” and so forth. Most editors place the punctuation after “human beings”: “the fires of Sodom.”

[Col. 1065D] 767. Vatican A and Prag have *motabilis*. Others have the more Latin *mutabilis*.

769. Above he said that he had set before us a conspicuous historical sign of freedom in Lot and his wife: one, because he wished to do so, freely obeyed God; the other, because she wished, turned her eyes back toward Sodom against God’s command. He now concludes: “Behold, Marcion, a marked proof of freedom.”

770. The Palatine, Giselinus, Prag, Rat, and recent editions have “by which”; Mariettus, Vatican A, Aldus, and Weitz have “that.”

772. Vatican A has “commanded,” incorrectly.

773. Aldus, Fabricius, and Bongars have “snatches away.”

774. On the verb *renuto*, which Lucretius also uses, see Gifanius’s index to Lucretius.

776. Prag incorrectly has “this thing here.” The Virgilian phrase is: “Pleasure draws each person.”

777. Egmond, Widmann, Bongars above, Weitz, Rat, Mariettus from the first hand, Sichardus, and Isonius have “mute.” Aldus, Giselinus, Prag, and recent editions have “many.” Heinsius recorded nothing from his manuscripts.

778. Weitz has “of the race”; the others, “of the nation.” Put. has “Orphan”; Aldus, “Orpham.” Vatican A, Mariettus, and Prag have “Orphan”; Rat has “Ortan.” This history is related in the book of Ruth, and Paulinus also transfers it to an argument for freedom in *Natalia* 9. The history seems brief, but it signifies great mysteries of war. When Naomi urged these Moabite women to return to their homeland, Orpah kissed her mother-in-law Naomi and returned; Ruth clung to her mother-in-law, chapter I, verse 14. Philo, or someone else writing under Philo’s name, and several rabbis later report that Orpah was the mother of the giant Goliath. Prudentius seems to agree with them at verse 784, “to nourish the stock of Goliath.” Chamillard declares this opinion vain and absurd, because Goliath’s mother was a Philistine from Gath in Palestine, living in the time of Saul, whereas Orpah was Naomi’s Moabite daughter-in-law and Ruth’s contemporary. Teolius thinks that, by the license very common among poets, Goliath could have been used for any barbarous and savage man. But I do not see what sense could underlie the passage unless the true Goliath is designated by this name. Nicholas Serarius, in his commentary on Ruth, chapter 1, question 10, confirms that Prudentius adhered to the opinion of the rabbis. But Prudentius’s words signify not so much that Orpah was the mother of the giant as that he arose from her stock.

779. Put. and Egmond have “Noomin.” Others have “Noemi” or “Noemin.”

780. Vatican A has “and yet in the marriage chambers.” Rat has “or not in the marriage chambers,” though this is an error for “and yet.” Mariettus and Prag have “and in.” Heinsius records “and yet” from his manuscripts. The sense is clear: “and yet,” or, if preferred, “and-yet.” After Prudentius has explained that Orpah withdrew from her mother-in-law Naomi but Ruth did not, he adds: “and yet both were free; both had lost their husbands; both, now vacant from marriage beds and sacred rites, enjoyed their own right.”

782. Serarius, who illustrates his commentary on Ruth with these verses of Prudentius, says that the ancient ritual of the shrines had become obsolete, not that Orpah had ever withdrawn from the worship of idols. Some think that Orpah and Ruth renounced their ancestral errors when they married Hebrew brothers.]

[Col. 1065A] and the customs of the people, the archives, laws, forum,

baths, sellers’ stalls, brothels, temples, theaters,

and the circus with its crowd, and the dripping taverns.

558 The conflagrations envelop in righteous flames, and condemn with Christ as judge,

whatever the people of Sodom do.

[765] It is enough for our Lot to have fled these things once:

he does not look back again. But his fragile wife looks back,

and revisits what she had fled, her face changeably turned backward,

and remains fixed amid the ashes of her homeland.

Behold, Marcion, a marked proof of freedom,

[770] by which God wished us to know that whatever must be pursued

lies under our authority and is everywhere left open:

to tread either path. The two were commanded to withdraw

from Sodom; one rushes out, the other hesitates.

He hastens his step in flight; she resists.

[775] Their minds are both free, but their wills are unlike.

Their desires, seizing each person, divide them here and there.

The sacred books record such a silent image.

559 Look at Ruth of the Moabite nation, and at Orpah beside her.

She follows her mother-in-law Naomi with faithful love;

[780] but this woman leaves the marriage chambers, although both, freed

from the marriage law, vacant from Hebrew marriage beds and sacred rites,

enjoyed their own right; nevertheless, the ancient ritual of Orpah’s shrines

[Col. 1067A] persuaded her to prefer barbarous foreskins

and to nourish the stock of half-savage Goliath.

[785] Ruth, while she is scorched by the rustic heat among the stubble,

560 earned Boaz’s couch and, admitted to a chaste bed,

became fertile for a house destined to bear Christ,

produced the Davidic kingdoms, and mingled mortal births with God.

Often I myself remember twin brothers arrive together

[790] at a gaping fork in the road, with youth wavering,

and hesitate for a long time beneath the divided path, wondering which

was the better way: while on the right a thorny wood

confined the road with prickles, and a rocky path far ahead

led toward a lofty ridge along a steep slope;

[795] but on the left a shady grove adorned the gentle, pleasant greenery

with rich fruit and offered a broad plain as an easy road.

I remember seeing one of the two content to crawl

over steep rocks among the harsh thorns,

while the other indulged himself in the field on the left;

[800] the former raised his head to mingle with the neighboring stars,

561 while the latter suddenly fell into muddy marshes.

[Col. 1068A] One nature underlies them all, but one and the same outcome does not

come to pass for all, because the pattern of their choices differs.

It is just as if, once in clear weather, a milky cloud of doves,

having fallen, should descend into the tilled field

[805] of a fruitful countryside,

where a crafty birdcatcher has stretched snares,

smeared the twigs with slow-setting birdlime,

and scattered traps with deceptive pods or grain.

Some grains entice the birds by their deceit and fasten

[810] their greedy throats in restraints of twisted bristles,

while soft glue binds their entangled wings all around.

But others, whom no desire for eating allures,

walk with innocent steps across the barren grass,

and take care not to turn their eyes toward the suspicious bait.

[815] Soon, when they must fly back into the sky, one part seeks the starry air,

free, beating its wings above the atmosphere;

another lies captive, wounded with torn feathers,

struggling on the ground and looking up vainly at the winged breezes.

Thus souls of a single nature, from the springs of heaven—

826. *Infernalis* as a Latin word, introduced by Cellarius, has Prudentius alone as its author.

828. In some Vulgate copies, *pennis*, incorrectly, in place of *poenis*. On the worms of the damned, see Isaiah, chapter LXVI.

831. Mar., Prag., Weitz., and others read *infusam*; Mariettus thinks *formatam* is a gloss, and indeed it is Iso’s gloss. Yet all the Heinsian copies, Ald., Gis., Vat. 832. Aldus’s error is glaring: *virtus* for *vitiis*. Heinsius replaced *rursum* with *sursum*, as elsewhere. Thuan., Boher., and Alex. have *sursum*. Mariettus, however, seems to have read *rursum* in all his copies; this is found in Ald., Weitz., Gis., Urb., and others, and the reading is by no means contemptible. [Col. 1069D]

833. Widm., in a first hand, has *mersandum*.

835. Aldus’s correction here is remarkable. He had printed: “He gave it immortality, lest the punishment should perish with age.” He emended it to: “He gave it immortality, with age, lest the punishment should perish.” Why this alteration, which contradicts the very sense?

837. Mar., Gis., and others write *materiem*. Ald., with some others, has *materiam*. Heinsius, in Book I of the *Posthumous Adversaria*, chapter 6, thinks *ratam* should be corrected to *datam*. I shall not do so against the manuscripts. In Vat. A is found *ipsam*; it should be corrected to *ipsa*. On the eternal punishment by which souls are forever punished and do not perish, see Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 48; Minucius Felix; Augustine; and others. [Col. 1070C]

839. Prag. has the inferior reading *et diversa* for *at diversa*. In some Vulgate copies, *adversa* for *diversa*.

843. Gis. correctly has *rite*; but in the first edition, *recte*.

844. Weitz., Pragens., Rat., and Mar., in a second hand, have *miseri et properanda*. Others have *miseri properanda* by epexegesis. The dangers are said to be *properanda* because they must be avoided and fled swiftly and hastily, as Iso and Mariettus explain. In some Vulgate copies is found *properando*; Gis. has this in both editions, with no absurd sense: “they fled by hastening,” or “while hastening.” It may also be explained as “the dangers that threaten, hasten or are hastened.” Horace, Book XII of the *Epodes*: “For whom the Tyrian fleeces, doubled with purple shells, were being prepared!”

846. Vat. A has *vivificaverat*, correctly emended above to *vegetaverat*. Aulus Gellius, Book XVII, chapter 2, and others use this verb actively.

847. Prag. has *terrae*; the others have *vitae*.

[Col. 1070D] 850. Chamillardus asserts that the poet is speaking according to the opinion of pagan philosophers, since he calls the soul a burning spark. I think this false. Prudentius calls not only the soul but also God “fire,” not because he thinks God or the soul consists of fire, but because of a certain resemblance that can be drawn from corporeal things in order, to some extent, to understand spiritual things.

852. Weit., with Egm., writes *postlimineo*.

853. “Hoary faith” is Virgil’s expression.

855. Rat. has *dolores*; others, *labores*.

[820] [Col. 1069A] Nature pours it into the earth; but there they are held fast by pleasing enticements, and only a few climb back to the ether; the viscous food ensnares many and does not allow them to travel through the upper air.

Then the Father, who foresaw all this, kindles the livid Tartarus with lead and digs out, with dark pitch, the bituminous pits of infernal water in Avernus; beneath the Phlegethontic whirlpool he decrees that greedy worms should grow old in perpetual punishments for their crimes.

For he knew that, from its own breath, a life-giving principle exists in our bodies, and that the soul, formed from the everlasting mouth, cannot die; yet, once polluted by vices, it cannot return upward to the vaulted heavens:

563 It must be plunged utterly into the pit of the burning abyss.

He gave it an immortal age amid worms, flames, and torments, lest the punishment perish through old age, while the soul itself did not perish. The tortures tear apart and sustain the material granted without end; death itself abandons eternal groans and compels them to live in tears.

[Col. 1070A] But elsewhere, far away, the sovereign who knows the future established rewards in the regions of paradise for pure spirits removed from every stain, and for those who did not look upon the ruins of Gomorrah. With eyes rightly turned away, they left behind them the darkness and the dangers of the world, wretched though those dangers were and swift to be fled.

[845] First they are borne back to the stars on an easy flight, whence the flowing soul had given life to fashioned Adam. For, since the downward weights of life do not restrain its subtle nature, nor an iron fetter delay it, returning in swift flight it cuts through the dense air,

564 and, a burning spark, rises above the pole it has retraced, hating the prisonlike places in which it had remained as an exile.

[Col. 1070B] Then, returning by the right of return, hoary faith receives it in her lofty bosom and delights the tender fosterling with ambrosial pleasures, while it recounts in complaining speech the many labors it suffered after the lodgings of the flesh.

[Note: [Col. 1071A]]

856. Mariettus interprets *latus exporrecta* as “lying comfortably outstretched,” as those who have made a long journey commonly do.

858. Put., Oxon., Rot., three Torr., Egm., Ald., Alex., Vat. A, and Mar. have *stramine* for *toro* or *stramento*. Urb., Gis., Weitz., Prag., and Rat. have *gramine*. “On rose-colored grass” is not absurd, since *gramen* means any green plant. Seneca gives a flower to grass in the *Medea*. See Burmann, page 490, volume I of the *Anthology*. After this verse, some manuscripts insert six other verses, absent from all the Heinsian copies, Egm., Pal., Ald., Alex., Urb., and rejected by Heinsius because they disturb the sense of the passage. Rat., Mar., Weitz., Gis., and several printed copies insert them. Giselinus gives the six verses as follows:

> But the others, whom dire plague and malignant error  
> immersed in darkness and besieged in vast Avernus,  
> confess, not without punishment, alas, that they themselves are absent from the assemblies  
> of the righteous and bear deserved punishments through the ages—  
> those whom the abyss of the ancient father, or of the suffering reverent one,  
> excludes, while the rich have attained the world’s goods with death, and for a long time…

In verse 3, Mar. has *piis semet deesse*, and above, *abesse*. Two Torrentian copies and Rat. have *semet deesse*. Gifanius likewise has *piis semet deesse*. In verse 4, Mar., the two Torrentian copies, Gifanius, and Rat. have *meritas poenas per saecula ferre*. In Mar., as a variant, *ferre et per saecula poenas*. In verse 5, Mar. has *Quis patris antiquo*, with *antiqui* above. Mar. and the younger Boher. have *Quis patris antiquo reverentius aegri abysso*. In Mar., in the margin, *aut aegri reverentis abysso*. In Prag. appears *Quis Patris antiqui, aut aeger reverentis abysso*, with the gloss *QUIS*, “for whom,” and *EXCLUSIS ABYSSO*, that is, “through the abyss,” namely, through the great chaos. Gifanius, in the index to Lucretius, under the word *CONCILIUM*, says: “Thus I think it should be read from the old book, for the common reading *abyssus*, frankly speaking, is not at all pleasing to me. I believe it entered because the more extended hyperbaton was not understood: for *IMPLORATA NEGAT* cannot properly be joined to *ABYSSO*, but to the majesty of God; therefore what was placed earlier must be brought here, namely, *MAJESTAS GNARA FUTURI*.” Heinsius says that Gifanius struggled more than enough in explaining these spurious verses. Yet Gifanius was attempting to explain the ancient reading, which everyone then accepted. Marietto was not fully satisfied with Gifanius. Accordingly, Mariettus undertakes to restore and clarify the passage by conjecture; he thinks it should read *aut aegri reverentia abysso*. This is his explanation, by which the verses omitted by us are joined to those cited and explained: “To those souls condemned, excluded from the abyss, or through the whole abyss; to those who possessed the world’s riches with death, or until death, and who were separated by a long interval, tormented and burning with such great thirst that they thought they could drink rivers and all the rains of heaven—the respect of the ancient father, that is, Abraham, or of the suffering man, that is, Lazarus, when begged, denies the insertion of a finger into the palate.” The poet refers to the parable—or, better, the history—of the avaricious rich man in Luke, chapter XVI. Iso too, who appended glosses to these verses, considered them Prudentian. Giselinus, who restored *abyssus* for *abysso* from manuscripts, recognizing the difficulty of the passage, says: “If in healing this wound I had been as cruel a physician as Manutius once was, nothing would have been easier; but it is one thing to restore a body to its former health, and another, when one can do better, to mutilate some part by applying the final remedy.” Weitzius falsely says that Aldus read *abyssus*, unless he had another edition at hand: for among the six verses Aldus omitted—Giselinus incorrectly counted seven—one was precisely the verse in which *abyssi* occurs.

859. In Oxon. appears *divitibus longo*. Heinsius conjectures *ditibus at longo*.

860. Aldus incorrectly has *tutos* for *totos*.

861. In some Vulgate copies, *palatu*, incorrectly. Cellarius explains *implorata* as referring to hoary faith from verse 853. I prefer to understand it of the blessed soul, which Prudentius places in paradise as in Abraham’s bosom.

866. He may perhaps allude to the opinion of theologians who place the seat of the damned in the earth’s depths. After this verse some add the heading: “On the integrity of the soul’s vision.”

868. Wid., Bong., in a second hand, and Ald. have *Aestimat involvi, vitreo quos lucida palla*. Others have *Aestimat, involuit vitreo quos lucida palla*. Cauchius conjectures *pala*. Heinsius does not approve. See the glosses. Some enumerate six membranes of the eye: conjunctiva, cornea, uvea, arachnoid, retina, and vitreous membrane. Giselinus, interpreter and physician, praises this description of the visual organ; he distinguishes seven membranes of the eye and notes that the eyes present the form of a mirror, whose principal parts are three condensed or coagulated humors. From this you will understand what *concreta coagula* means.

870. Gregory the Great calls the eyes “windows of the soul” in Book XXI of the *Moralia*. Gifanius observes in Book III that Lucretius most elegantly uses *postes*, “doorposts,” for the eyes themselves: “Once the eyes have been removed, the mind seems all the more able to see things, with the doorposts themselves taken away.”

871. Vat. A incorrectly has *oculi lenso*.

[Col. 1071A] There, stretched out on a purple couch, it breathes in fragrances from everlasting flowers and sips the dew of ambrosia from rose-colored straw.

565 To the rich, who smoke at a long distance, and who thirst for rivers and all the rains of heaven, it denies, when begged, the insertion of a finger into the palate and the extinguishing by touch of the tips of the flames.

Nor should you wonder that, in places far distant from one another, among the damned and the righteous souls, visions meet, conspicuous and deserving of recognition across the great intervals that the pole divides at the center of the world.

[Col. 1072A] He is mistaken who judges souls by the limits of our eyes, which a shining membrane envelops in a glassy covering, whose mirror dense coagulated humors cover and whose wandering windows they impede with an overlying moisture.

[870] Do rounded drops roll over the eyes of souls amid dense covering matter? Or do they bristle outside with eyelash-hairs, or are they covered by a shadowing eyelid?

[Note: [Col. 1073B]]

873. Vat. A incorrectly has *aliove umbrante*.

874. In Alexandr., Thuan., Rot., and three Torr. appears *et pupula*. Others have *nec pupula*, which seems consistent with the sense; Cellarius and Teolius followed this. Heinsius suspects *nec pupula parva* is corrupt. To me, the only true reading is *nec pupula parva*.

875. Vat. A has *nebulae et vasti penetrator*. The description of the eyes may also be seen in Cicero, Book II of *On the Nature of the Gods*.

876. In the Parma edition, the corrupt reading *solidumve mentibus* should be emended, and *solidumve tuentibus* restored.

878. Aldus, against the meter, has *patenti cedit*.

881. Some write *Tile*, others *Thyle*, others *Thule*, and in the genitive *Thulae* or *Thules*. On Thule, see Elmenhorst on Arnobius’s words in Book VI, “the farthest Thyle.” The ancients called this island the farthest because they had not advanced beyond it; it is Iceland. Seneca’s prophecy about the eventual discovery of a new world is well known—for that is what they call it. In the chorus of Act II of the *Medea* he sings:

> There will come, in late ages,  
> centuries when Ocean  
> shall loosen the bonds of things  
> and a vast land lie open,  
> and Tiphys shall reveal  
> new worlds; nor shall Thule  
> be the farthest land.

As I read this, I do not think Seneca was thinking of our New World, but only wished to praise what was being carried out by Claudius in the British expedition. Many assert, and it seems established, that he composed that tragedy about Medea and Jason on the occasion of the first voyage, to flatter Claudius and secure his recall from exile. Accordingly, he introduces a chorus predicting what he saw occurring in his own time, without concerning himself with future generations, while exaggerating Claudius’s maritime triumphs. On this subject, hear Pomponius Mela, Book III: “What Britain is like and what kind of people it produces will soon be told more certainly and with fuller knowledge. For behold, the greatest of princes is opening what had remained closed for so long—not merely victorious over the peoples already before him, but also over unknown nations; and, just as he sought confirmation of his own achievements in war, he will display it in triumph.”

882. The better manuscripts—Vat. A, Mar., the Heinsian copies, Weitz., and others—have *transadigit*. Gis., with Ald. and Bongars. in a first hand, has *transadiit*. In the margin of Gis. is *transcurrit*; others have *transuadit*. The Vulgate copies have *transabiit*. Egm. and Widm. have *transadigit*. Heinsius noted that *transadigere* is a Virgilian verb.

883. Vat. A, Egm., and Pal. have *oculis* for *omnes*. I do not approve it. The sense in which colors perish by night is stated in Hymn 2 of the *Cathemerinon*, verse 7.

885. Thuan., Mar., Prag., Rat., Gis., and Weitz. have *exutae*, that is, “the souls.” All the Heinsian copies except Thuan. have *exuti*, as do Alex., Urb., and others. In that case, “sights” are understood as stripped away. Prag. has *viscera*; Vat. A has *pendunt*. Both are false for *viscere* and *perdunt*.

887. Aldus has *animam*; others, *animas*. This passage long troubled Chamillardus. Read Iso’s gloss and understand that the subject is the final judgment and the lot, whether good or bad, that souls will possess. I do not know whether Teolius intended to accept *animam* or *animas*, for I think it a typographical error. One soul always has one face; but he rightly adduces for this passage Ecclesiastes XI, 3: “If a tree falls toward the south or toward the north, in whatever place it falls, there it will remain.”

892. Thus Put., Oxon., Cauch., Rot., three Torr., Alex., Urb., Rat. in a second hand, Eg., Ald., and Bonon. Others read *expertos visus*, with Mar., Rat. in a first hand, Prag., and Weitz.; Giselinus printed this reading. He later noted that in some copies appears *Experto dubitas animas percurrere visu*, which pleased him greatly and which he had adopted in the first edition. Before Giselinus, Sichardus had followed *expertos visus*. In Thuan. the first hand had *expertas*, the second *expertis*. The poet gives an example of what we experience in dreams. Most people punctuate this passage incorrectly. I conjecture *expertes*, that is, “separated souls.”

896. Prag. has *nec sese segregat*, inelegantly.

897. In some Vulgate copies, *artibus*, incorrectly.

[Col. 1073A] Do they bristle with hairs, or are they covered by a shadowing eyelid?

For them there is living vision, and no small pupil, but a fire that traverses the mist and penetrates the vast darkness.

Nothing rusty or solid obstructs those who look. Nocturnal mists yield; black clouds yield; the smooth round expanse of the sky yields to the swift one stretched before it.

567 The spirit not only passes through the airy openings by sight, but crosses by its light the mountains set against it, passes beyond Ocean’s bounds and Thule’s farthest shores, and sends its flying eyes into Tartarus.

For surely all colors perish beneath night for our eyes, and forms are erased by blind time.

[885] Will souls stripped of their limbs and their flesh also lose the recognition of things, or wander in their courses?

[Col. 1074A] One face always belongs to souls, and one color of air, according to the total measure of each person’s merits, whether on the left or on the right. Changeable time neither turns nor varies these alternations; whatever it is, it is long-lasting and perpetual: one course rolls out its ages.

Do you, having experienced it, doubt that souls traverse hidden places by sight, when the living mind, with its bodily eyes often lulled to sleep by the dew of rest, sees far-off and distant places, directing its gaze across fields, stars, and seas?

For the soul itself does not separate from the living limbs before death, nor flee as an exile from the blood and flesh; it strips itself from the innermost recesses and marrow,

[Note: [Col. 1075B]]

909. **Vellere**, dark cloud, I.

912. **Sequestra**, separated, I.

[Col. 1076B] 917. **Mugitus**, which will occur on the day of judgment. — **Gravium**, great, loud, I.

919. **Secedente**, wandering, I.

920. **Flatus**, soul, I.

921. **Involucris**, wrappings; we call *volucra* wrappings of clothing, but here he calls the wrapping of a dead body in a tomb *involucra*, I. *Volucra*, or *volucla*, means wrappings. Vat. T.

922. **Certa**, eternal; namely, “it is.” — **Subterna**, where perpetual night exists, Iso.

899. Aldus incorrectly has *abiit de pectore*.

900. Aldus incorrectly has *manens speculator*.

903. In dreams things are represented as though they were seen by bodily eyes.

904. In Vat. A, against the meter, *situm* is placed; above, *positum* is correct.

906. Vat. A lacks *vultus*. In some Vulgate copies, *vultu*, incorrectly.

907. Vat. A has *nihil*, a monosyllable.

908. Vat. A has *denseta*; Alex., Mar., and others have *densata*. Both forms are used, *denso* and *denseo*. Heinsius prefers *denseta* with Put. and Oxon.

910. The better Heinsian copies, Alex., Ald., Weitz., and others of our copies have *futuris*. Fabr., Sich., Prag., Bong., and Gis. have *figuris*.

911. Some have *Joannes*, others *Joannis*, and some both forms, as Alex.

912. I discussed whether Saint John saw the Apocalypse in sleep in Hymn 6 of the *Cathemerinon*, verse 74. Fabricius, in his commentary on the Christian poets under the heading *EVANGELISTAE*, says that Prudentius asserts that the evangelist John saw what he wrote with the mind, not the eyes, and not while dreaming but while awake, after the mists had been removed. Sedulius, however, seems to Fabricius to testify that John saw these things in dreams. It must nevertheless be understood that this Sedulius is none other than Prudentius himself, whose *Dittochaeon* Fabricius wished to attribute to Sedulius. Prudentius repeatedly mentions John’s sleep in recounting the Apocalypse.

913. Mar., Sich., and some Vulgate copies have in the margin *liberat intuitum*, less suitably.

914. Rat. has *venturus*, incorrectly.

916. In Put. and Thuan., in a second hand, *tristes* for *raucos*. On the final destruction of the world by fire and on the trumpet whose roar will precede it, see Hymn 11 of the *Cathemerinon*, toward the end. Most hold that the things revealed in the Apocalypse will not be fulfilled until the end of the world; others think they have already been fulfilled. [Col. 1076C]

918. That the body is a kind of prison for the soul was sufficiently stated in Hymn 10 of the *Cathemerinon*. Some think this was drawn from the teachings of the Egyptians and Socrates. There is no reason to resort to that, since the sacred books lie open. Others call the body a cave, others bonds, others a vessel, as we have already noted.

920. Prag. has *notabis*. Rat. has *notabat*. *Notabit* is better.

921. Aldus first printed *involuclis*, then corrected it to *involucris*. Thus all printed editions and most manuscripts read. But in some very ancient manuscripts I find *involuclis* in a second, though ancient, hand; and in the gloss, two or three times *involucla*, as if *involucula*, contracted to *involucla*.

922. The more authoritative Heinsian copies, with Egm., Ald., Alex., Vat. A, Urb., have *rapidos*. Many others—Mar., Prag., Rat., Weitz., Gis., Fabr., Widm., and Bongars.—have *rabidos*. “Swift paths” (*rapidos caminos*) is more elegant. Ald., Egm., the better Heinsian copies, Alex., Urb., Vat. A, and Mar. have *subterna*. [Col. 1076D] Weitz., Fabr., and Gis. have *sub tetra*. Prag. and Rat. have *aeterna*, which Iso seems to have read. Teolius, unless the typesetter erred, divided it as *sub terna*. *Subterna* is preferable; Prudentius also uses the word in Book I against Symmachus, verse 392. According to Fabricius’s explanation, *subternus* means subterranean, although Fabricius wonders whether in Book I against Symmachus one should read *sub terris*. It seems that *subternus* is derived from *subter*, just as *supernus* is from *super*.

924. Aldus has *remotis*; others have *remoti*, that is, “the poor man Lazarus.”

925. Heinsius notes that in the oldest manuscripts *setius*, not *secius*, is written, not only in Prudentius but also frequently in Virgil, Ovid, Silius, and others. You see an orthographical controversy in which I will by no means follow Weitzius, who printed *saecius* on the authority of the Bongarsian manuscript alone.

[Col. 1075A] It strips away, or drives from the breast, the life that has been removed:

[900] 569 Yet remaining in its bodily seat, it observes everything with keen eyes and, wherever it has directed the sharp gaze of its light nature, sees the world set before its eyes, without any obstruction,

while beneath the world’s mass there lies the foul element of the underworld.

[905] Meanwhile earth lies in the way, but does not obstruct the soul’s vision. Indeed, if it turns its face toward the star-bearing pole, nothing intervening prevents the fire of the ever-watchful soul from seeing, although thick clouds weigh upon the sky and darken it with an opposing fleece.

[910] Thus corporeal John, not yet released from the flesh, sees the mysteries covered by silent futures: by the gift of sleep, while his flesh is briefly set aside, he is free for contemplation and, with sense and eyes, traverses the years arranged in order for coming ages.

[Col. 1076A] 570 He sees the angelic army already preparing the world’s destruction by fire and hears with his ear the hoarse roar of the great trumpets at the world’s end.

He saw these things before death, enclosed in the prison of his limbs, with the soul withdrawing but not departing.

[920] Will not the bodiless spirit all the more perceive everything once the body’s wrappings have been laid away in the cold tomb?

A sure faith holds that beneath the lower night swift paths cook the polluted soul through long ages in everlasting fire, displayed to the eyes of poor Lazarus though far removed across a long void; and, no less, that the golden gifts

[Col. 1076B] of the righteous and their gleaming crowns are shown, with chaos dividing them, from afar to those sunk in the prison of punishments.

[Note: [Col. 1077B]]

930. After this verse Mar. and Rat. give the heading *Oratio*. Giselinus has *Precatio* in the margin. Some doubt whether it is Prudentius’s, but unjustly, since all manuscripts and Theodulf of Orléans claim it for Prudentius.

931. Gis. has *cunctipotens* in the margin; in the text, *cunctiparens*, which the others have and which is also read in Hymn 14 of the *Peristephanon*, verse 128.

939. Some connect *precanti* with *Dona*, that is, “grant better gifts.”

944. Weitz., with Widm. and Iso, has *condefleta*. Others have *conclamata*.

946. I agree with Teolius, who thinks that Hieronymus Vida imitated this passage to some extent:

> Grant, Father, that when the final hour of life arrives,  
> I may die in your presence, with no shadows terrifying me;  
> and pour out my rejoicing soul into your embracing arms.

I write *amplexus*, not *complexus*, since the latter is a metrical error in the Parma edition, where Hieronymus Vida is also incorrectly called *Hieron. Suida*, and the passage is cited as Book XXV of the *Christiad*, although the *Christiad* has only six books. The verses are found at the end of Hymn 1, *To God Most Good and Great*, volume I, page 214, Padua, 1731, printed by Joseph Cominus. [Col. 1078C] Another verse follows there, making the imitation of Prudentius clearer: “Add this alone to me, while others wish for more.”

947. Rat. has *rapidum*, less suitably, for *rabidum*.

954. Prag. incorrectly has *sint illinc castra*.

956. Prag. has *sic flore*. *Sit* is better.

957. This explains Matthew XIX, 12: “There are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven.” Some fools had wrongly understood this of the body, whereas it must be understood of the soul, which must be restrained from every carnal pleasure and enticement.

959. Mar., in a first hand, has *occurrit*; it was correctly emended to *occurrat*, since *devoret* follows. In the Parma edition I think *avida* is a mistake for *avidae*.

961. In Mar., *esto* has been correctly restored from *acto*. This verse could be punctuated *hic esto cavernoso*, with *esto* meaning “although.”

963. Aldus has *mirificos*; *mitificos* is more correct.

966. *Glorifico* is an ecclesiastical word, formed by analogy with similar words. In Vat. A, after *clementer adurat*, appears: “Here ends Book II of the *Hamartigenia*.” In the Marietti manuscript: “Here ends Book D of the *Hamartigenia*,” which Mariettus interprets as “the book so called.” In others: “Here ends the *Hamartigenia*.”

[Col. 1077A] Hence, after dreadful sufferings, the inhabitant of paradise is shown to the blessed man; the unhappy spirit, howling amid the pestilence of guilt, is shown in turn, and they behold the reciprocal recompense of their merits.

[930] O God, Father of all, O God, giver of the soul, O Christ God, from whose mouth the one Spirit of God exists: under your direction I am ruled; with you as my prince I lead my life; before you as judge I tremble, pale; before you as the same judge I take hope that whatever I do may be pardonable in your sight, however unworthy of pardon my deeds and words may be.

I confess—gladly forgive and spare the one who confesses!—that I have deserved every evil. But you, good judge, take away what I have deserved; favoring the one who prays, grant better gifts.

[940] Grant my soul, at some time, when it has left the lodging of this body, constructed from sinews, skin, blood, bile, and bones, which its corrupt inhabitant, alas, has embraced and cherished too much in luxury; when the mournful hour has closed these eyes and the material, lamented by all, lies dead,

[Col. 1078A] while the mind, stripped bare, enjoys its own eyes, let it not see some savage member of the race of robbers, cruel, rabid, threatening in face and voice, a terrifying being who, like a bandit, may drag me, stained with the spray of my vices, headlong into the depths and plunge me, falling, into black caverns, exacting to the last smallest farthing everything owed for my ruinous life.

[950] There are many dwellings in the Father’s treasuries, Christ, distinguished in different regions. I do not ask for a blessed home in that land. Let there be there pure bands of men who, scorning earthly wealth, sought your riches; let virginity, white with everlasting bloom, flourish there, with its chastened and severed soul.

[Col. 1078B] For me it is enough if no face of the Tartarean minister should meet me, and if the hungry flame of Gehenna should not devour this soul, plunged into the lowest furnaces.

[960] Yet let sorrowful fire swallow me in cavernous Avernus, since this is necessary because of bodily sin:

573 At least let the slow fires breathe forth gentle vapors, and let their heat grow mild in languid warmth.

[965] Let immense light glorify others, and let their temples be bound with crowns; let a gentle punishment burn me mercifully.

**ORDER OF THE MATTERS CONTAINED IN THIS VOLUME**

**SAINT GELASIUS, POPE I**
### Pope St. Gelasius I

**Prolegomenon.** 9

**Letters and Decrees.** 13

**First Letter.** — Gelasius writes to Euphemius that no one can be admitted to communion with the Apostolic See who has not condemned the name of Acacius. He therefore urges him to anathematize Acacius just as he has anathematized Eutyches and the other heretics. Same place.

**Letter II.** — Having been elevated to the pontificate according to the custom of the Roman Church, he prescribes a formula of faith to Laurentius, bishop of Lignido. 19

**Reply of the bishops of Dardania to Gelasius**, in which they give thanks because he warned them whom they should avoid. 21

**Letter III.** — Gelasius announces to the bishops of Dardania that he has been elected pope; he sends them a statement of the Catholic faith, urges them not to communicate with the Eutychianists, and to keep watch over their pastoral office. 22

**Letter III bis.** — To Natalis, abbot. 24

**Letter IV.** — Gelasius’s admonition to Faustus, serving as legate at Constantinople. 26

**Letter V.** — Gelasius warns Honorius, bishop of Dalmatia, not to allow the Pelagian heresy, detested by so many pontiffs, to revive. 30

**Letter VI.** — He writes to the same man that he ought not to have been surprised that Gelasius had warned him that vigilance was necessary lest the Pelagian heresy should again sprout. 32

**Letter VII** (to all the bishops throughout Picenum). — He refutes the three principal tenets of the Pelagian heresy: first, that infants are born without original sin; second, that they are not condemned on account of original sin alone; third, that grace is not necessary for salvation and is bestowed according to human merits. 34

**Letter VIII** (to the emperor Anastasius). — After first explaining why he had not written to the emperor, he urges him to obey the Apostolic See and, once the name of Acacius has been condemned, to take care that peace be restored to the Churches. 41

**Letter IX** (to the bishops of Lucania). — Several ecclesiastical institutions are set forth. 47

**Letter X** (to the bishops of Sicily). — The property of the Church ought to be distributed by bishops among clergy and the poor; dioceses and Church property possessed by bishops for thirty years are not to be taken from them. 57

**Letter XI.** — Writing to the bishops of Dardania and Illyricum, he commends their religious devotion; he indicates that the bishop of Thessalonica, who refused to condemn the names of the heretics, has been deprived of communion with the Apostolic See, and that Acacius, having died under excommunication, cannot be absolved. Same place.

**Letter XII.** — He warns Aeonius, bishop of Arles, that mutual charity must be maintained together with the Catholic faith. 60

**Letter XIII** (to the bishops of Dardania). — He demonstrates that Acacius was justly condemned by the judgment of the Apostolic See alone. 61

**Letter XIV.** — A treatise of Pope Gelasius in which he presents examples from the letters of Pope Simplicius and Pope Felix, showing that they formerly recognized—or appeared to have recognized—the impiety of Timothy the Cat and Peter of Alexandria. He then continues in his own words, explaining what ought to be answered to the Greeks. 85

**Letter XV** (to the Eastern bishops). — That no new synod was needed for the condemnation of Acacius and the others, and that Acacius could not absolve Peter of Alexandria without the authority of the Apostolic See. Then, concerning Catholic bishops expelled from their sees without investigation. 90

**Ten fragments of Gelasius’s letters.** 99

**Gelasius’s volume on the bond of anathema.** 102

**Against Andromachus the senator and the other Romans who had decreed that the Lupercalia should be celebrated according to the ancient custom.** 110

**Against the Pelagian heresy.** 116

**Decree.** — What has been peacefully possessed for thirty years cannot be reclaimed. 137

**Another decree.** — One ought not to abstain after their death from the alms of those with whom one did not cease to communicate during life. 137

**Constitutions of Pope Gelasius**, which bishops receive at their ordination. Same place.

**Letter XV bis.** — He relates what assistance he received from Rusticus, bishop of Lyons, and how great a persecution he is suffering from Acacius. 138

**Second Appendix, or Canons Attributed to Gelasius.** 141

## Three Books On the Contemplative Life

415

### Book I

Same place.

**Prologue.** Same place.

**Chapter I.** — That this is the distinctive character of the contemplative life: God is seen by the pure in heart. 418

**Chapter II.** — On the nature of the future life. 419

**Chapter III.** — That, by the judgment of God, the saints are to be separated from the wicked just as the blessed angels were previously separated from the unclean spirits. 420

**Chapter IV.** — On the resurrection, or the life of the saints. 421

**Chapter V.** — That even here the blessedness of the contemplative life delights those who despise present things. 423

**Chapter VI.** — That the perfection of the contemplative life attainable here cannot be compared with future perfection. Same place.

**Chapter VII.** — That the saints cannot see God perfectly until they have attained the blessedness of the future life. 424

**Chapter VIII.** — What and how great is the perfection of the contemplative life in this flesh, and how those who despise the world cleave to it in order to enjoy it. 425

**Chapter IX.** — That the difference between the perfection of this life and that of the future is as great as the difference between those who do not wish to sin and those who are no longer able to sin. 426

**Chapter X.** — That here the saints saw God in the assumed creature. 427

**Chapter XI.** — On the nature of the glorified bodies that will exist in the future resurrection. Same place.

**Chapter XII.** — How great the difference is between the contemplative and active life. Same place.

**Chapter XIII.** — That holy priests can become participants in the contemplative life. 429

**Chapter XIV.** — Where the speaker excuses himself for not daring to teach the teachers of the Church. 430

**Chapter XV.** — On the negligence of the priest who, acting contrary to his teaching, cannot fulfill the role of teacher. Same place.

**Chapter XVI.** — What danger awaits those who either wish to abandon the Church entrusted to them or disdain to govern it vigorously. 431

**Chapter XVII.** — Where he encourages one anxious because he can neither abandon nor govern the Church, by suggesting that he govern it better by his example. 432

**Chapter XVIII.** — That showing by example what ought to be done is of little value unless the priest also teaches by instruction what must be believed. Same place.

**Chapter XIX.** — On the virtue of faith: that it consists not only in believing or understanding, but also in doing good. 433

**Chapter XX.** — That it benefits a priest nothing, even if he lives well, if by remaining silent he does not correct one who lives badly. 434

**Chapter XXI.** — A mournful description of a priest living according to the flesh. 435

**Chapter XXII.** — That, according to the prophet’s saying, those perish through their own fault who despise the rebukes or admonitions of priests. 437

**Chapter XXIII.** — That priests, even when they are capable of more, ought to teach so simply that everyone understands them as teachers. 438

**Chapter XXIV.** — What difference there is between teachers who build up the Church by teaching simply and those who display their eloquence in brilliant declamations. 439

**Chapter XXV.** — What priests must be like if they wish to become participants in the contemplative life. Same place.

### Book II

441

**Preface.** Same place.

**Chapter I.** — That, according to the diversity of sinners, some are to be borne with and others corrected. 443

**Chapter II.** — On the praise of holy priests. 444

**Chapter III.** — On apostolic testimonies and their exposition. 445

**Chapter IV.** — Objection: Why do holy priests, whose duty is to rebuke those living ruinously, tolerate hypocrites in religion with equanimity? 447

**Chapter V.** — Answer: The reasons requiring that the weakness of certain persons be treated gently are demonstrated. 449

**Chapter VI.** — That those accuse the sins of others impatiently who do not consider their own. 450

**Chapter VII.** — How much remedy confession of sins provides, [Col. 1082] and what punishment deceitful concealment deserves. 451
